### Glossary

- **beyond**: Further away than something; on the far side of it.
- **warren**: A crowded home where lots of animals live close together, like rabbits in their tunnels.
- **huddle**: To crowd close together, often to keep warm.
- **patient**: Able to wait calmly, without getting cross or giving up.
- **stitched**: Sewn on with a needle and thread.
- **symmetry**: When one half of a shape is a mirror image of the other half.
- **simile**: A way of describing something by saying it is like something else.
- **wades**: Walks through water.
- **reunion**: When people or animals who were apart meet again.
- **opinions**: What someone thinks or believes about things.

## S9. The Gate That Sticks

- `s9-step1`: Take the old trowel to Hazel. · _She’s on the cottage step. Give it to her from your bag._
- `s9-step2`: Go down to the gate at dusk tomorrow. · _Corvin comes at sundown. Stand by the gate. You don’t need to open it._
- `s9-step3`: Be at the gate at first light, before the others come. · _Chapter 12 begins at dawn. Go to the gate before anything else._

#### `s9-dusk`

_Dusk, on Hazel’s second evening home. The gate rattles._  
_Not the clean clack of someone who knows the trick. A long, unsure rattle. Then another._  
**Gran Hazel**: That’ll be him.  
_Hazel doesn’t get up from the step. She doesn’t look round. Her eyes are shut._  
**Gran Hazel**: Go on. I jammed it so I’d hear him. I’ve heard him. That’s my part done.  
_Corvin Vale is at the gate, with no hat, in a coat he has slept in. No runners behind him. No rows._  
_His hands are on the top bar, red and sore, like hands brought in out of the snow._  
**Corvin Vale**: I can feel my hands. I’d forgotten it hurts, warming up. Nobody mentions that it hurts.  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): why cold hands sting as they warm up  
> _When very cold hands warm up again, they often sting and ache for a while._  
> _That’s blood rushing back in, and the nerves waking up. It hurts, and then it passes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that very cold hands can sting as they warm up, and why._

_His hand goes to his breast pocket, finds it flat, and comes away. He does it twice while you watch._  
_He lifts the latch and pushes, as anyone would. The gate shifts in its frame, and sticks._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): friction, and why lifting a dragging gate helps  
> _The gate is stuck. Its bottom edge drags on the ground, and the rubbing holds it still. That rubbing force is called friction._  
> _Why does lifting the gate before you push help?_  
> - ✅ Lifting takes its weight off the spot where it rubs. → Yes. Less weight pressing down means less friction. Then a push is enough to move it.
> - Lifting makes the gate lighter. → The gate weighs the same. But lifting takes its weight off the ground, so it rubs less. Less friction, easier push.
> - It’s magic. → It does feel like magic! But it’s friction: lift the weight off the rubbing spot, and a push can move it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned about friction, and why lifting a dragging gate makes it easier to push._

**Corvin Vale**: It used to open for me. I’d wait, and it would just swing. I thought that meant something.  
**Corvin Vale**: It was the cold from the stone in my pocket. It shrank the wood. I took it for a welcome.  
_He passes something through the bars, handle first: a trowel, its blade worn thin._  
**Corvin Vale**: Hers. I dug with it, under the long grass, twenty-two years ago. I’ve kept it oiled. Don’t say it’s from me.  

**Choices**

- **Why now?**
    - **Corvin Vale**: Because I can feel my hands. I didn’t have a reason before. I had a stone.
    - He goes down the lane. He looks back once, at the cottage, where Hazel sits with her eyes shut.
- **Do you want to come in?**
    - **Corvin Vale**: Want to? Yes.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Not tonight. I haven’t asked. If I ever come in, it’ll be because I asked.
    - He goes down the lane, and doesn’t look back. You think it costs him something not to.
- **Say nothing. Take the trowel.**
    - You take it. The handle is warm from his coat.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Thank you.
    - He goes down the lane. He looks back once, at the cottage, where Hazel sits with her eyes shut.

#### `s9-trowel`

_Hazel turns the trowel over in her hands, and runs her thumb along the worn edge._  
**Gran Hazel**: I wondered where that went. I bought another. It was never as good.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a lever turns on a pivot  
> **Gran Hazel**: Good trowel, this. When you dig, you push the handle down, and the blade lifts the soil up.  
> **Gran Hazel**: That makes it a lever: a bar that turns on a pivot. Here, the pivot is the edge of the hole.  
> **Gran Hazel**: A lever helps a small push lift something heavy. Corvin dug up a stone with this one.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a lever and a pivot are, using a garden trowel._

**Gran Hazel**: You’ll want the story. You’ve been very good about not asking. It’s been unbearable to watch.  
**Gran Hazel**: He came to me at twenty-two. Clever. Quick. In a hurry, which I took for keen.  
**Gran Hazel**: He found the old clay tablets in this cottage. Older than me. Older than the wall. They told him where the fourth shard lay.  
**Gran Hazel**: One winter he tried their method on my Nubbins, in my Grove. Quiet as stones, by morning.  
**Gran Hazel**: I stopped him. I said things. He said things. I was right, which is very tiring for everyone.  
**Gran Hazel**: That night he opened the gate, let the buyers in, and went with them. Nubbins, and the stone.  
**Gran Hazel**: In the morning I wedged the gate.  
**You**: So he couldn’t get back in.  
**Gran Hazel**: No, love. So I’d hear him if he ever came back.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): work out a character’s motive  
> _Hazel wedged the gate so it would stick._  
> _Why did she do it?_  
> - ✅ So she’d hear Corvin if he ever came back. → Yes. A stuck gate rattles. She wanted to know if he came home. That’s her motive: her reason.
> - To keep Corvin out for ever. → That’s what you’d guess! But Hazel says no. She wanted to hear him if he came back. That’s her motive.
> - Because she couldn’t fix it. → Hazel can fix most things. She did it on purpose: so she’d hear him if he ever came back.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character’s motive (her reason for doing something) from what she says._


**Choices**

- **How can you not hate him?**
    - **Gran Hazel**: I did, for a good while. Hating someone is heavy. I had Nubbins to look for, so I put it down.
    - **Gran Hazel**: I didn’t forgive him. I just needed both hands.
- **Did you find them? The ones he took?**
    - **Gran Hazel**: Most of them. It’s in the register. The rest I stopped looking for, one winter. I’ve never forgiven myself for stopping.
- **Sit down next to her. Say nothing.**
    - You sit. She leans, just a little, so your shoulders touch.
    - **Gran Hazel**: There. Better than anything you could have said. Don’t go getting big-headed about it.

_She sets the trowel on the step beside her, blade down, as if it might get away._  
**Gran Hazel**: He’ll be back tomorrow at dusk. Same time. He was always a creature of habit. That was half the trouble.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): understand a saying (“creature of habit”)  
> _“A creature of habit” is a saying. It means someone who does the same things at the same times._  
> _It doesn’t mean Corvin is an animal. Though Hazel might enjoy you thinking so._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the meaning of a common saying, “a creature of habit”._

**Gran Hazel**: I’m not going down there. I’ve done my part. I listened for twenty-two years.

> _For grown-ups: Learned that patient listening helps people say difficult things._


#### `s9-ask`

_Sundown. He is there before you, as if he never left. Perhaps he didn’t._  
**Corvin Vale**: I’ve been practising this. In the lane. Out loud. A sheep heard most of it.  
_He puts both hands on the top bar. He doesn’t try the latch._  
**Corvin Vale**: Twenty-two years ago I stood here and opened this gate for men with carts. I didn’t ask anyone.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): asking permission is a rule of respect  
> _Here is a basic rule of respect: you ask before you go into someone else’s home._

**Corvin Vale**: So.  
_…_

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.4, ask): why a writer repeats a line  
> _Corvin says the same words twice: “I would like to come in.”_  
> _Why do you think he says it a second time?_  
> - ✅ The first time, he was too scared to look at you. → That’s how it reads. First he says it to the gate. The second time, he’s brave enough to say it to you.
> - He forgot he’d said it. → He’s been practising all day, so he hasn’t forgotten! The first time he said it to the gate. The second time, to you.
> - The sheep didn’t hear. → Ha. The sheep has heard plenty. He says it again because the first time was to the gate, and the second is to you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a writer repeats a line, and what the repetition shows._

**Corvin Vale**: I’ll wait here till first light. If it’s still shut then, I’ll understand. Better than anyone.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): fair decisions listen to every side

#### `s9-gate`

_First light. The pond is grey and still. Hazel sits beside it with a cup, her back to the gate._  
_Corvin is at the gate. He has been there all night._  
_There’s frost on his shoulders: the ordinary kind, the kind that melts._  
**Corvin Vale**: Hazel’s grandchild.  
_His hands rest on the top bar. They aren’t blue any more. They shake a little, the way warm hands do in the cold._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): hinges, and why handles go far from them  
> _A gate swings on its hinges: the metal joints that hold it to the post._  
> _Push near the hinges and it barely moves. Push far from them, out by the latch, and it swings easily._  
> _That’s why latches and handles always go on the far side._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a push far from a hinge turns a gate more easily, which is why handles sit far from hinges._

_At the edge of the long grass, a grey ear turns towards his voice, and goes flat._  
**Corvin Vale**: I know who’s sitting by that pond. I know what I took from her. I’m asking anyway.  
_Behind you, Hazel drinks her tea and does not turn round. She is listening to every word._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): forgiveness and trust (think question)  
> _Corvin is sorry. He gave back the trowel. He asked, instead of taking._  
> _But the grey ear in the long grass still goes flat when he speaks._  
> _Can you forgive someone, but not trust them yet?_  
> - Yes. Forgiving and trusting are different. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Forgiving is letting go of the anger. Trust gets built slowly, one visit at a time.
> - No. If you forgive, you should trust them again. → That’s a fair answer, and a generous one. Some people feel that way. Others think trust takes longer than sorry.
> - It depends on what they did. → That’s a wise answer. Small things are easy to forgive and trust again. Big things, like taking Ash, can take years.
> - I’m not sure yet. → That’s an honest answer, and it’s allowed. Hazel took twenty-two years. You can take your time too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between forgiving someone and trusting them (a think question with no wrong answer)._


**Choices**

- **Open it for him. Don’t show him how.**
    - You lift and push, and the gate opens. He watches your hands. You turn them so he can’t quite see.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Thank you.
    - **Corvin Vale**: I’ll have to knock, every time. That’s right. That’s more than right.
    - By the pond, Hazel lifts one hand a little and lets it fall. It might be a wave.
- **Leave it shut.**
    - You don’t move. He looks at you, then at the latch, and nods, as if you’ve told him the time.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Yes. All right. Yes.
    - **Corvin Vale**: It ought to cost something. I’d think less of this place if it didn’t.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Thank you for taking the trowel. I mean that.
    - He takes his hands off the gate one at a time. He goes down the lane, and is gone before Sparks arrives.
    - By the pond, Hazel finishes her tea. She sits a while longer than she needs to.

_Sparks arrives first, at a run, as always. Then Fern. Then everyone: a whole valley coming up the lane._  
_Sparks, Fern, Marina, Clover, Pixel, Luna, Ember, Byte, Dusty and Nova._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiply equal groups  
> _Every Keeper does two moves: lift, then push. Ten Keepers come through._  
> _How many moves is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 20 → Yes. Ten groups of two: 10 × 2 = 20. Lift, push, twenty times.
> - 12 → That’s 10 + 2. But each of the ten Keepers does two moves: 10 × 2 = 20.
> - 10 → That’s one move each. But it’s lift AND push: two moves each, so 10 × 2 = 20.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication for equal groups (10 Keepers × 2 moves = 20)._

**Gran Hazel**: Good gate, that. I never did unwedge it.  
_She doesn’t say anything else about it, then or ever._  
_You understand that this is how she says it’s finished._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): an object in a story can be a symbol  
> _In stories, an object can stand for a big idea. That’s called a symbol._  
> _Here, the gate that sticks stands for home: a place that hears who comes back, and lets in the ones who ask._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an object in a story can be a symbol for a bigger idea._


### Glossary

- **friction**: A force that slows or stops things when they rub together.
- **trowel**: A small garden spade you hold in one hand.
- **lever**: A bar that turns on a point, to help you lift or move things.
- **motive**: The reason someone does something.
- **creature of habit**: Someone who likes to do the same things in the same way, every day.
- **sundown**: Sunset: the time when the sun goes down.
- **point of view**: The way one person sees and thinks about something.
- **hinge**: A metal joint that lets a gate or door swing open and shut.
- **forgive**: To stop being angry with someone for something they did.
- **symbol**: A thing that stands for an idea, like a heart standing for love.

- `s10-step1`: Wish one: write your Nubbins into Hazel’s hatch register. · _The register is on the cottage bookshelf. Add a row for every Nubbin you’ve hatched: number, name, first sound, weather._
- `s10-step2`: Wish two: enter any race while Hazel watches from the back row. · _Open Races from the top bar. Any course, any level. Winning doesn’t matter._
- `s10-step3`: Wish three: walk Hazel to the other three lanterns: the stream, the old wall and the long grass. · _Keep to her pace. She stops at each post. Stop with her._
- `s10-step4`: Tell Hazel what the Grove will be. Then walk with her to the foot of the hill. · _After the final choice in chapter 12, follow Hazel across the Grove to the hill path._

#### `s10-step`

_Dusk, on her first evening home. Hazel sits on the cottage step with her boots off and her feet in a bowl of warm water._  
_She is very pleased about the water. She has a blanket round her shoulders, though the evening is mild._  
**Gran Hazel**: Sit. Not there. There. I like to see the pond.  
_Gran Hazel is very poorly. The doctors can’t make her better. She knows, and now she’s going to tell you._

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): months in a year, and finding a difference  
> _The doctor said a year. A year is twelve months. Gran has had fourteen._  
> _How many extra months has she had?_  
> - ✅ 2 → Two. Two whole bonus months, love. I spent them well.
> - 26 → That’s 14 + 12, adding. We want the difference: 14 − 12 = 2 extra months.
> - 12 → Twelve is what the doctor said. She’s had 14, so 14 − 12 = 2 extra months.
> _For grown-ups: Learned there are 12 months in a year and found a difference (14 − 12 = 2)._

_She says it the way she’d talk about the weather. Then she watches to see how you take it._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): sad feelings are allowed, and sharing them helps  
> _Gran doesn’t want you to pretend to be fine. Sad, scared and cross are all allowed._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that it’s all right to show sad feelings, and that sharing them helps._

**Gran Hazel**: I want them to come round and argue about races and the weather. I don’t want a week of goodbyes.  
**Gran Hazel**: So. Will you keep it? It’s a big thing to ask. I’m asking anyway.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): compare what a character says with what she does  
> _Hazel says she never minded about winning. Sparks says she once threw a hat at a finish line._  
> _What does the hat tell you about Hazel?_  
> - ✅ She cared about winning more than she says. → Yes! What a character does can tell you more than what she says. Hazel minded. A lot. Small hat or not.
> - She didn’t like the hat. → Ha, maybe! But you throw a hat at a finish line when you really, really want to win. Hazel minded more than she says.
> - She never minded at all. → That’s what Hazel says. But actions are clues. Throwing a hat shows she minded, at least back then.
> _For grown-ups: Compared what a character says with what she does, to understand her better._

#### `s10-cheer`

_The usual roar from the stands. Under it, from the back row, one voice carries over all the others._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step money problem with Shells  
> _Hazel paid for her two pies with a 10-Shell coin._  
> _How many Shells did she get back?_  
> - ✅ 2 → Yes. Two pies at 4 Shells is 8 Shells. 10 − 8 = 2 Shells change.
> - 6 → That would be one pie: 10 − 4 = 6. But she had two: 4 + 4 = 8, and 10 − 8 = 2.
> - 8 → 8 Shells is what the pies cost. Her change is 10 − 8 = 2 Shells.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step money problem with Shells (2 × 4 = 8, then 10 − 8 = 2)._

**Gran Hazel**: That one runs for you. Don’t ever spend that.

> _Look at the frozen pond. Ice floats on water, so a pond freezes from the top down._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that ice floats, so ponds freeze from the top and fish survive in the water below._

**Gran Hazel**: Rule three. I thought I’d made it up. I’d been on the end of it for a whole winter.

_At the stream lantern, she laughs at nothing at all. Then she explains that Briar would have._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: how stories carry the past  
> _Each post has a story. Gran learned them from people who learned them from people older still._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that oral history keeps the past alive through stories told aloud._

_Then the long grass. The fourth post is lit. It has burned steady since the Long Night, all on its own._  
_Hazel stops. She looks at it for a long time._  
**Gran Hazel**: Twenty-two years I came out every night and looked at this post. Flicker, flicker.  
**Gran Hazel**: I stopped hoping, after a while. I never stopped looking. They’re different things. Remember that.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): hope and patience (think question)

> _Can you keep looking for something even after you’ve stopped hoping?_

> - No. If you’re still looking, you must still hope a bit. → Maybe you’re right. Maybe a tiny bit of hope stayed, hiding under the looking. That’s a fair answer, and Gran likes it.
> - I don’t know. → Neither did I, for twenty-two years. That’s allowed. That’s an honest answer.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between hoping and keeping on (a think question with no wrong answer)._

_…_  
**Gran Hazel**: Can I ask you something? I’ve never asked anyone. There’s never been anyone to ask.

    - **Gran Hazel**: I’d have dragged him home by the ear. He’d have hated me properly, and the valley might never have gone grey.

    - **Gran Hazel**: That was the one I wanted. Thank you, love.

#### `s10-letter`

_Morning. Your Nubbins are up before you. The gate is stuck. You lift and push._  
_Her lantern is back on the hook by the cottage door. Somebody carried it down at first light._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): grief: what it is and what helps  
> _The big, heavy sadness you feel when someone you love dies is called grief._  
> _Grief can come in waves: all right one minute, very sad the next. That’s normal._  
> _What helps is people, and remembering. Gran made sure you’d have both._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word grief, that it comes in waves, and that people and remembering help._

_On the signpost, under the stone, where the first one was: a letter in your grandmother’s writing._  
**Gran Hazel**: “If you’re reading this, I’ve gone up the hill, and this time I’m staying. Don’t be dramatic about it.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Be a little dramatic. I’ve earned a little.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “You kept my three rules, more or less, which is more than I did. Here’s a fourth, because I can’t help myself.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Show up. Every morning, same stuck gate, same stubborn chin. That’s all a Grove ever was. The rest is fruit.”

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): how a letter is set out  
> _Gran’s letter talks straight to you, and ends with a sign-off: “Love, Gran.”_  
> _“P.S.” is short for postscript, which means “written after”. It’s for one last thing you think of after you sign._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a letter is set out, including the sign-off and the P.S. (postscript)._

_Behind you, someone lifts and pushes the gate: Fern, with a basket. Then Sparks. Then everyone, one by one._  
_They have come to see why you are standing so still. You hold the letter out. You don’t have to say anything._  

### Glossary

- **poorly**: Ill; not well.
- **exhausting**: Making you feel very, very tired.
- **register**: A book or list where things are written down, to keep a record.
- **column**: A line of boxes going down a table, all for the same kind of fact.
- **nuisance**: Someone or something that annoys people.
- **hoarse**: Having a rough, croaky voice from shouting or a sore throat.
- **metaphor**: Describing something by talking about it as if it were something else.
- **flashback**: A part of a story that jumps back to the past.
- **thaw**: When ice and snow melt because the weather is warming up.
- **gloomy**: Sad, and without much hope.
- **oral history**: The past as people remember it and tell it out loud.
- **ordinary**: Normal and everyday; nothing special.
- **handkerchief**: A square of cloth for wiping your nose or eyes.
- **grief**: The deep sadness you feel when someone you love dies.
- **P.S.**: Short for postscript: a note added at the end of a letter, after the name.

## S11. The Blight

- `s11-step1`: Go next door and look at the sick plum trees in Fern’s orchard. · _Go through the gap in the hedge, past Fern’s water butt. The sick trees are at the bottom of the slope._
- `s11-step2`: Check every tree in the orchard with Byte’s hand lens, and give it a label. · _Look at a leaf, the bark and the fruit of each tree. Then pick a label. Notice which way the wind blows._
- `s11-step3`: Catch one of the things riding the wind into the bottom row. · _Keep the sun in front of you (never look straight at it), so your shadow falls behind you. The bugs drop the moment your shadow touches them._
- `s11-step4`: Help Clover let her ladybirds go in the hedge where the beetles breed. · _Open Clover’s jar by the dead wild plum, or where it stood. Then step back and keep still._

#### `s11-fern`

_Fern is at your gate before breakfast. She holds a plum out on her flat hand, as if it might bite._  
**Fern**: Don’t touch it. Just look at it. Then tell me I’m imagining it.  
_The skin is freckled with black. When she tilts her hand, the plum caves in and pours out a soft grey dust._  
**Fern**: Three trees at the bottom of my orchard. Fine yesterday. Today they’re… that.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): some plant diseases are caused by a fungus, which spreads by spores  
> **Fern**: It’s the dust that frightens me. I think it’s spores. I think this is a fungus.  
> **Fern**: Mushrooms and mould are fungi too. Some fungi are friendly. Some make plants ill.  
> **Fern**: A fungus lets go of spores into the air, the way a dandelion lets go of seeds. Only far, far smaller.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some plant diseases are caused by a fungus, and that fungi spread by tiny spores._

**Fern**: I know what you’re thinking. “Keeping the trees alive, badly.” Yes. I said it first. I’ve said it for years.  
_Through the hedge, wasps buzz over the windfalls, the plums that dropped in the grass. The whole slope smells of hot jam._  
**Fern**: Hazel grafted half those trees for me, the year I moved in. She whitewashed every trunk herself, every spring.  
**Fern**: I haven’t told anyone. If I tell someone, it’s real.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): sharing a worry with someone you trust  
> _Fern has kept a big worry all to herself. What would help her most?_  
> - ✅ Telling someone she trusts. → Yes. Telling someone doesn’t make the problem real. It was already real. Telling someone makes it shared. Then other people can help carry it.
> - Keeping it secret, so nobody gets upset. → That’s a kind thought. But secrets can make a worry feel heavier and heavier. When we tell someone we trust, they can help. That’s why Fern came to your gate.
> - Pretending it isn’t happening. → Lots of people try that. But the trees stay sick whether we look or not. Telling someone she trusts is braver, and it means help can come sooner.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why sharing a worry with a trusted person helps._


**Choices**

- **Go and look now.**
    - You go through the hedge. Fern follows two steps behind, as if the trees might hear her coming.
- **Put an arm round her first.**
    - **Fern**: Oh, don’t. I’ll go soggy. I’ve got a whole orchard to be soggy about.
    - She leans on you for exactly one second. Then she marches off through the hedge.
- **Say you’ll fetch Byte.**
    - **Fern**: Byte. Yes. Byte will put it in a chart. Then it’s a problem instead of a tragedy.

#### `s11-ember`

_Three trees at the bottom of the slope. Their leaves have curled up like little black fists._  
_Grey dust lies under them like spilt flour._  
_Someone else has seen. Ember stands at the orchard wall, arms folded so tight her knuckles are white._  
**Ember**: Burn it. All of it. Tonight, before the blight spreads.  
**Fern**: All of it? Ember, there are forty trees.  
**Ember**: There’ll be none if you wait. I know how waiting goes. You’re polite, you wait, and then it’s too late.  
_Clover has come up behind you with a basket of bandages. That’s what Clover brings to everything._  
**Clover**: You can’t burn forty trees for three. You don’t even know what it is yet.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction within 100  
> _Clover is thinking about the numbers. Forty trees. Three are sick._  
> _How many healthy trees would Ember burn?_  
> - ✅ 37 → Yes. 40 take away 3 is 37. Thirty-seven healthy trees, burned for three sick ones.
> - 43 → Careful: that’s 40 add 3. We want the trees that are left when we take the sick ones away. 40 − 3 = 37.
> - 3 → Three is how many are sick. The healthy ones are all the rest: 40 − 3 = 37.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted within 100 (40 − 3) to see what a rash plan would cost._

**Ember**: I didn’t know what he was either, till he had Ash. Ask me how that went.  
_Fern sits down on an upturned crate between them, and says nothing at all._  
**Clover**: That’s cinder-love, that is. Holding on so tight you’d burn the lot. Don’t tell her I said so.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): working out a character’s motive from her past  
> _Why does Ember want to burn everything, so fast?_  
> - ✅ She lost Ash by waiting, and she’s scared it will happen again. → Yes. Ember’s past explains her now. She waited once, and lost Ash. So when something goes wrong, her fear shouts: don’t wait!
> - She likes fires. → Nothing in the story says that. Listen to what she says: “I know how waiting goes.” She lost Ash by waiting. She’s frightened of waiting again.
> - She’s cross with Fern. → She sounds cross. But she isn’t cross with Fern. She mentions Ash. Her anger is covering up a fear: that waiting will cost her everything again.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s past to explain why she acts the way she does._


#### `s11-lens`

_Byte arrives at a jog. He has a hand lens on a string, a roll of luggage labels, and a pencil behind each ear._  
**Byte**: Nobody burns anything until it’s been looked at. That isn’t a rule. That’s just being a person.  

> **Lesson** (science, do): how a hand lens magnifies  
> **Byte**: This is a hand lens. See how the glass is curved, thicker in the middle than at the edges?  
> **Byte**: That curve bends the light coming through it, so things look bigger. We say it magnifies them.  
> **Byte**: Try it. Hold the lens near a leaf, then move it slowly until the tiny spots look big and sharp.  
> Check: `edu:focus:lens:leaf`
> _For grown-ups: Used a hand lens and learned that its curved glass bends light to make small things look bigger._

**Ember**: You’ve got till dusk. Then I’m doing it, with or without your little labels.  
**Byte**: They’re standard labels. They’re not little. They’re regular.  
_He ties the first label to the first sick tree. In capitals: NOT FINE._  
_The next gets PROBABLY FINE. The next gets FINE (ACCORDING TO FERN). The water butt gets DO NOT DRINK._  
**Byte**: Forty trees, one lens. You look, I write. Clover, stop bandaging that branch. It isn’t hurt. It’s a branch.  
**Clover**: It looked lonely.  
**Byte**: Leaves for spots. Bark for holes. Fruit for dust. And don’t lick anything. I have to say that. I’ve met people.  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): staying safe around mould  
> **Byte**: While you’re looking: say you find a mouldy plum on the grass. What’s the safe thing to do?  
> - ✅ Leave it, and wash my hands if I touched it. → Correct. Mouldy food can make you ill. Leave it, and wash your hands. You may keep your tongue.
> - Taste a tiny bit, to check. → No! That’s the licking! I knew it! Never taste mouldy food or plants you don’t know. Leave it, and wash your hands if you touched it.
> - Sniff it really closely. → Close sniffing can put spores right up your nose. Not nice. Look with the lens instead. Leave it, and wash your hands if you touched it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned not to eat or sniff mouldy food, and to wash hands after touching it._

_On his way past the wall, he labels Ember, very small and very fast: VOLATILE. She doesn’t notice. Yet._  

#### `s11-map`

_By mid-afternoon the orchard flutters with paper labels, like a washing line. You spread the map on Fern’s crate._  
_Three trees are NOT FINE, in a crooked row at the bottom. Six are INCONCLUSIVE, SMELLS. The rest are fine._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step subtraction  
> **Byte**: Forty trees on the map. Three NOT FINE. Six INCONCLUSIVE. How many are FINE?  
> - ✅ 31 → Yes. 40 − 3 = 37. Then 37 − 6 = 31. Two steps. Thirty-one fine trees.
> - 37 → Nearly. That takes away the three NOT FINE. Now take away the six INCONCLUSIVE too. 37 − 6 = 31.
> - 9 → Nine is the trees we’re worried about: 3 + 6. The fine ones are the rest. 40 − 9 = 31.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step subtraction problem (40 − 3 − 6) from a map._

**Byte**: Inconclusive means I can’t tell yet. Those six have wasp bites. Wasps aren’t a disease. They’re just rude.  
**Byte**: Now look. It isn’t random. Every sick tree is in a line with the wind that comes up off the falls.  
**Byte**: An illness you catch by touching goes from each tree to the next one. This one skipped trees. It came through the air.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): using a map pattern to see how a disease spreads downwind  
> _On the map, the sick trees make a line along the wind, with healthy trees in between._  
> _What does that pattern tell Byte?_  
> - ✅ Something is being carried on the wind. → Exactly. The wind carries things the way it blows. They land downwind. So we follow the line back the way the wind comes from, and find where it starts.
> - Trees pass it to the tree next door. → If they did, the sick trees would be in a clump, all touching. These have healthy trees between them. A line along the wind means the wind is carrying something. It lands downwind.
> - The bottom trees are just old. → Some are old. But old trees all over the orchard are fine. The sick ones line up with the wind. Something is riding it, and landing downwind.
> _For grown-ups: Read a pattern on a map to work out that a disease was spreading on the wind._

**You**: So what’s in the air?  
**Byte**: Good question. I have a jar.  

#### `s11-jar`

_Byte hands you a jam jar with a muslin lid. Clover hands you a second one, in case the first gets lonely._  
**Byte**: Something is landing on the sick side. If we catch one, we can stop guessing.  
_You crouch in the long grass. The sun is hot on your neck. Dust lifts off the black plums like smoke._  
_Something small and grey lands on a leaf. The moment your shadow touches the leaf, it folds its legs and drops._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): how small animals use their senses to escape danger  
> **Clover**: To a tiny bug, a sudden shadow can mean a bird swooping down to eat it.  
> **Clover**: So lots of small creatures drop or hide the moment the light changes. Their senses keep them alive.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many small animals sense a sudden shadow as danger and hide._

**Clover**: Keep the sun in front of you (never look straight at it), so your shadow’s behind you. Shy things hide from shadows. I would.  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows fall on the side away from the light  
> _The sun is low in the west. If you turn to face it, where will your shadow fall?_  
> - ✅ Behind me. → Yes. Light travels in straight lines. Your body blocks it, so your shadow lands on the far side. Sun in front, shadow behind. Now the bugs won’t see you coming.
> - In front of me. → That’s what happened before, when the sun was on your neck, behind you. A shadow always falls on the side away from the light. Face the sun, and it falls behind you.
> - Nowhere. Shadows go away in the sun. → Bright sun makes the sharpest shadows of all! Your body blocks the light, so the shadow falls on the side away from the sun. Face it, and it’s behind you.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a shadow falls on the side of an object away from the light._

**Ember**: Or we could burn the lot and not crawl about in the grass.  
_She says it, but she doesn’t leave. She stands at the wall and watches every catch you miss._  

#### `s11-beetle`

_In the jar: a beetle no bigger than a lentil. It’s grey as pencil dust, with wings folded like a paper fan._  
**Byte**: Under the lens it’s covered in spores. Black ones. It isn’t the disease. It’s the postman.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): the difference between a disease and the carrier that spreads it  
> _Byte calls the beetle “the postman”. What does he mean?_  
> - ✅ It carries the spores from tree to tree. → Yes. A postman doesn’t write the letters. He carries them. The fungus is the disease. The beetle is the carrier: the spores ride on it to the next tree.
> - The beetle is the disease. → Close, but no. The disease is the fungus. Its spores are stuck all over the beetle. The beetle just carries them, like a postman carries letters. It’s the carrier.
> - It bites the trees and makes them sick. → It might nibble. But look at the black spores on its back. They’re the problem. The beetle carries the spores to new trees, like a postman with letters. It’s the carrier.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a disease and the creature that carries it are not the same thing._

_Byte follows the sick trees back the way the wind comes. They lead to a dead wild plum in the hedge by the stream._  
_The dead tree is crawling with beetles. Each puff of wind lifts a few and carries them down the row._  
**Byte**: They can’t fly against the wind. Only the trees downwind of that stump get them. The rest are safe.  
**Byte**: We can contain it. Keep it in one place, so it can’t spread.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): where the word “quarantine” comes from  
> **Byte**: Keeping the sick ones apart, so an illness can’t spread, has a name. Quarantine.  
> **Byte**: It comes from an old Italian word for forty. Long ago in Venice, ships had to wait forty days before anyone came ashore.  
> **Byte**: That way, if a sailor was ill, it showed before it spread. Forty. Like the trees. I find that oddly comforting.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what quarantine means and that the word comes from the forty days ships waited long ago._

**Clover**: Ladybirds eat beetle eggs, you know. I keep a jar of them at home. They have no manners at all.  
**Clover**: That one’s clean. Right in the middle of the sick row. Look.  
**Fern**: Grudge. Hazel’s old damson. Sourest fruit in the valley. I’ve been meaning to cut it down for years.  
_Byte ties a new label to the jar. It says: GUILTY._  

#### `s11-dusk`

_The sun goes down behind the western hill. Bats come out over the stream. Then a light comes through the hedge, low and orange._  
_It’s Ember, with a burning torch. In the firelight her face isn’t angry. It’s very, very frightened._  
**Ember**: I’m sorry, Fern. I’m not waiting. I waited once.  
**Fern**: Ember…  
**Ember**: When Ash went, I kept thinking: tomorrow. I’ll go and get her back tomorrow. Then tomorrow was years.  
**Ember**: Fast is the only thing I’ve got. Don’t take it off me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): thinking about acting fast when you are scared  
> _Ember is scared. Her fear is telling her: act now, and act big._  
> _What do you think? Is it a good idea to act fast when you’re scared?_  
> - Yes. Sometimes waiting makes things worse. → That’s a fair answer. Ember learned it the hard way, with Ash. Sometimes fast really is right, like pulling your hand away from something hot.
> - No. Fear can make you do too much. → That’s fair too. Clover would say fear makes everything look bigger than it is. Ember’s fear saw forty trees. The real problem was three.
> - Stop, breathe, look at the facts. Then act fast. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Byte would like it: fast and right. A slow breath only takes a moment. Sometimes it’s the moment that saves thirty-seven trees.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how fear pushes us to act fast, and when pausing first helps._

_Byte holds the map. Clover holds Fern’s hand. Everybody looks at you._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): comparing solutions to a problem  
> _Three plans for the orchard. Which one stops the blight and saves the most trees?_  
> - ✅ Take out the three sick trees and the dead plum. Keep watching the rest. → Yes. It stops the beetles where they start, and it saves thirty-seven trees. Taking out only the sick ones and keeping them apart from the healthy ones is a quarantine.
> - Burn all forty trees. → That would stop the blight. But it destroys thirty-seven healthy trees too. A better plan removes only the three sick trees and the dead plum, where the beetles start.
> - Do nothing, and hope. → That saves trees today. But the beetles would keep blowing down the row, and more trees would fall ill. A better plan removes the three sick trees and the dead plum, where the beetles start.
> _For grown-ups: Compared three solutions to a problem and chose the one with the best result and least harm._


**Choices**

- **Stand between her and the trees.**
    - You step in front of the first healthy tree. The torch is close enough to warm your face.
    - **Ember**: Move.
    - **You**: No.
    - For a long moment nobody breathes. Then the torch drops, slowly, until it points at the grass.
    - **Ember**: You’d better be right. You’d better be right, or I’ll never forgive you.
    - She doesn’t leave. In the dark, without a word, she helps Fern chop down the three sick trees and the dead stump.
- **Hand her the map. Let the evidence speak.**
    - You hold out Byte’s map. She doesn’t want to take it. She takes it.
    - She reads it by her own torchlight: the line of the wind, the dead plum, the jar marked GUILTY.
    - **Ember**: Three. Not forty.
    - **Ember**: Three.
    - She pushes the torch into the water butt. It goes out with a long hiss, like a held breath.
    - **Ember**: Show me the stump. I’ll do the stump.
- **Take the torch with her. Burn only the three sick trees, together.**
    - You put your hand on the torch, next to hers. She looks at you. Then she lets you hold it too.
    - You burn the three sick trees and the dead wild plum, and nothing else. It takes a long time. Neither of you lets go.
    - **Clover**: Goodbye, trees. You were very good plums.
    - **Ember**: That’s how it should have gone, with Ash. Not on my own. Not in a rush.
    - Fern brings out tea. Ember drinks hers standing up, watching the fire, until it’s only warm.

#### `s11-ladybirds`

_Clover unscrews her jar. Out pour ladybirds, hundreds of them, red as rosehips. They settle along the hedge._  
**Clover**: Off you go, then. Every beetle egg you can find. Manners not required.  
**Fern**: No fire. No poison. Just hungry little helpers. Hazel would have liked that.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-4, notice): using a predator to protect plants when a habitat changes  
> **Clover**: A ladybird is a predator. It hunts and eats other small creatures, which we call its prey.  
> **Clover**: Ladybirds eat greenfly and the eggs of other insects. Gardeners love them.  
> **Clover**: Using a predator to protect plants is a way to solve a problem without harming the rest of the garden.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that ladybirds are predators, and that gardeners can use them instead of poison to protect plants._

_One lands on your thumb and won’t get off. Then three more._  
_Each one is bright red, with seven neat black spots._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Four ladybirds on your thumb. Seven spots each. How many spots altogether?_  
> - ✅ 28 → Yes. Four groups of seven: 4 × 7 = 28. These are seven-spot ladybirds. Some people say the spots tell a ladybird’s age. They don’t. That’s a myth.
> - 11 → That’s 4 + 7. But each ladybird has seven spots, so it’s four groups of seven. 7, 14, 21, 28. 4 × 7 = 28.
> - 24 → Close! Let’s count in sevens, one ladybird at a time: 7, 14, 21, 28. 4 × 7 = 28.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 × 7 by thinking of equal groups._

_After a while they are, more or less, yours._  
**Byte**: I tried to label them. It isn’t possible. They’re all called LADYBIRD now.  

#### `s11-complete`

_A week later the orchard is quiet. Three stumps at the bottom of the slope. Thirty-seven green trees above them._  
_In the middle of the bare row stands one tree, untouched: Grudge, the old damson, heavy with sour purple fruit._  
**Fern**: Byte says the beetles hate Grudge’s bark. Too bitter. Hazel used to say Grudge was too stubborn to die.  
**Fern**: She always told me to graft off it. I never did. Who wants sour plums? Here. She left this at mine.  
_A short curved knife with a plum-wood handle, wound in green twine. The edge is still sharp._  
**Fern**: Bind a cutting of Grudge onto a young tree, and the young tree grows up stubborn too. Her trick. Yours now.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): grafting, and how a helpful trait helps a plant survive  
> **Fern**: Grafting is real, you know. Lots of fruit trees are grown this way.  
> **Fern**: You join a twig from one tree onto a young tree. The two grow together, and the new branch keeps the old tree’s ways.  
> **Fern**: Grudge has bitter bark. In a beetle year, that’s what helped it survive when the others didn’t.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about grafting, and that a trait like bitter bark can help a plant survive a pest._

**Fern**: You saved my orchard. That makes you its warden, whether you like it or not.  
_Ember comes past the wall. She has found Byte’s label in her pocket. She reads VOLATILE, and looks at him._  
_Byte takes it, crosses it out, and writes something else: FRIGHTENED. Then, underneath: (FAIR)._  
**Ember**: …Fair.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): understanding why a character changes their mind  
> _Why did Byte change VOLATILE to FRIGHTENED?_  
> - ✅ He understood that Ember’s anger was really fear. → Yes. At dusk, Byte saw Ember’s face in the firelight. She wasn’t wild. She was scared. The new label is fairer, and Ember knows it.
> - He wanted to tease her. → The first label was a bit of a tease. But look what he writes underneath: (FAIR). He changed it because he understood her: her anger was really fear.
> - He made a spelling mistake. → Byte never makes spelling mistakes. Just ask him. He changed it because he understood Ember better: her anger was really fear.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a character changed his opinion of someone else._


### Glossary

- **orchard**: A field or garden of fruit trees.
- **fungus**: A living thing, like a mushroom or mould, that is not a plant and feeds on living or dead things. More than one are fungi.
- **blight**: A disease that makes plants wither, rot and die.
- **magnify**: To make something look bigger than it really is.
- **volatile**: Likely to flare up or explode suddenly, like a quick temper.
- **inconclusive**: Not clear enough to decide yet.
- **downwind**: In the direction the wind is blowing towards.
- **muslin**: Thin cotton cloth with tiny gaps that let air through.
- **carrier**: Something that carries a disease to others without being the disease itself.
- **quarantine**: Keeping sick living things apart from healthy ones so an illness can’t spread.
- **evidence**: Facts and things you have found that show what is true.
- **predator**: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
- **prey**: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
- **graft**: To join a cutting from one plant onto another so they grow together.
- **warden**: Someone whose job is to look after and protect a place.

## S15. Lucky Eggs

- `s15-step1`: Help Byte keep a tally of what comes out of thirty Mystery Eggs. · _Stand by the wagon. Each time a child opens an egg, make a mark under PLAIN or SPARKLY. Bundle your marks in fives._
- `s15-step2`: Get Jackpot on his own and ask him some questions. · _Dashwood naps after lunch. Creep along the stream side of the wagon, where a bell has fallen off. Don’t touch the wheels._
- `s15-step3`: Shine a lantern through the Legendary egg and see what’s really inside. · _This is called candling. It works best somewhere dim. Try under the bridge._
- `s15-step4`: Set up an honest egg stall with Byte, and chalk up the real odds. · _Byte has a slate and chalk. Put the stall by the bridge or at your gate, and write the true numbers on the board._

#### `s15-wagon`

_A wagon comes down the lane, striped red and cream. A hundred little bells on its roof ring at every pothole._  
_On the driver’s seat sits a man in a mustard waistcoat. On his shoulder sits a brass parrot that ticks._  
**Dashwood Prance**: Children of the valley! Gather round! Dashwood Prance has come, and Dashwood Prance has brought you luck!  
**Dashwood Prance**: Mystery Eggs! Ten Shells each! Every egg a winner! Some eggs more winner than others!  
**Jackpot**: MOST EGGS ARE PLAIN.  
**Dashwood Prance**: Thank you, Jackpot.  
_A poster unrolls down the side of the wagon in gold letters: 1 IN 3 SPARKLY! Underneath, much smaller: (approx.)_  
_In the window, on a velvet cushion, an egg glitters like frost on a web. Its card says LEGENDARY. NOT FOR SALE (YET)._  
**The children**: Sparkly! Sparkly! Sparkly!  
**Pip**: I’ve got forty Shells. I’ve saved since my birthday. That’s four eggs. That’s one and a third sparkly!  
_Byte appears at your elbow with a clipboard. He has the face of someone who has just heard maths done wrong._  
**Byte**: One in three. Says who? I want to see it happen. Thirty eggs. We count every single one.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.B.3, do): keeping a tally in bundles of five  
> **Byte**: We’ll keep a tally. One stroke for every egg, under PLAIN or SPARKLY.  
> **Byte**: Four strokes standing up. The fifth goes across them, like a gate. That’s a bundle of five.  
> **Byte**: Bundles are quick to count: five, ten, fifteen… Try it. Mark the first five plain eggs as one gate.  
> Check: `edu:tally:eggs:gate-of-five`
> _For grown-ups: Learned to keep a tally, bundling marks in fives so they are quick to count._

**Byte**: And while we count, read that poster again. Properly.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): spotting the small print in an advert  
> **Byte**: Which part of that poster should make you most careful?  
> - ✅ The tiny word (approx.). → Yes. “Approx.” is short for approximately: roughly, more or less. Tiny writing under a big promise is a clue. It means: check before you believe it.
> - The shiny gold letters. → Gold letters are there to grab your eye. They’re not a lie, just a lot of shine. The real clue is the tiny word: (approx.). It means “roughly”. Tiny writing under a big promise means: check.
> - Nothing. Posters always tell the truth. → Some do. But posters are made to make you buy. Some stretch the truth. See the tiny word, (approx.)? It means “roughly”. Tiny writing under a big promise means: check.
> _For grown-ups: Looked closely at an advert and noticed how small print can soften a big promise._


**Choices**

- **Buy an egg yourself. For science.**
    - **Dashwood Prance**: A Keeper! A person of taste! Choose with your heart!
    - You choose with your heart. It’s plain. Jackpot looks at it and says nothing, very loudly.
    - **Byte**: That’s one. Twenty-nine to go. Don’t look like that. It’s data.
- **Ask Pip to wait before she spends it all.**
    - **Pip**: Wait? The sparkly ones might run out!
    - **Dashwood Prance**: They might! They very well might! That’s the magic of a limited time!
    - **Jackpot**: THEY WILL NOT RUN OUT.
- **Ask Dashwood where his odds come from.**
    - **Dashwood Prance**: From the heart, friend! From the very bottom of the heart, where the best numbers live!
    - **Byte**: That is not where numbers live.

#### `s15-tally`

_By noon Byte’s card is full. Thirty eggs. Thirty faces, mostly falling._  
_The tally says it all. PLAIN: five gates and two extra strokes. SPARKLY: three strokes._  
**Byte**: Twenty-seven plain. Three sparkly. That isn’t one in three. Not even close.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): chance as a fraction: 3 in 30 is 1 in 10  
> **Byte**: Three sparkly in thirty eggs. Split the thirty into three equal groups of ten. One sparkly in each.  
> **Byte**: So what’s the real chance of a sparkly egg?  
> - ✅ 1 in 10 → Yes. 3 in 30 is the same as 1 in 10. As a fraction, one tenth: 1/10. The poster said 1 in 3. That would be ten sparkly in thirty. We saw three.
> - 1 in 3 → That’s what the poster says. If it were true, we’d have seen ten sparkly in thirty. We saw three. Three groups of ten, one sparkly in each: 1 in 10.
> - 3 in 10 → That would be nine sparkly in thirty. We only saw three. Three groups of ten, one sparkly in each: 1 in 10. One tenth.
> _For grown-ups: Read a tally chart and saw that 3 in 30 is the same chance as 1 in 10 (one tenth)._

**Byte**: The poster is out by three point three three three… and the threes go on forever.  
**Byte**: That’s called recurring. I’ve underlined it. Twice.  
_Pip sits on the bridge with four plain eggs in her lap. She isn’t crying. She is being extremely brave at the water._  
**Pip**: The plain ones are nice too. They’re warm.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): helping a friend with disappointment  
> _Pip is disappointed, and trying very hard to be brave. What might help her?_  
> - ✅ Sit with her, and tell her it’s all right to feel disappointed. → Yes. You sit on the bridge beside her. Feelings are allowed, even the droopy ones. …They are quite warm, though.
> - Tell her to cheer up. → People often say that. But it can make someone feel they’re not allowed to be sad. Sitting with her, and saying it’s all right to feel disappointed, helps more.
> - Buy her another egg. → That’s a kind thought. But remember the tally: another egg would very likely be plain too. Sitting with her, and saying it’s all right to feel disappointed, might help most.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to comfort a friend who is disappointed._


#### `s15-sneak`

**Byte**: We need a witness. Someone who’s seen the books.  
**Byte**: That parrot. Every time Dashwood says something untrue, it corrects him. I don’t think it can help it.  
_After lunch the wagon goes quiet. The mustard waistcoat hangs over the step. Inside, a snore like a slow saw._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile tells you  
> _Dashwood’s snore is “like a slow saw”. What does that tell you about it?_  
> - ✅ It’s a long, rough, rasping sound. → Yes. A saw going slowly through wood goes rrrrasp… rrrrasp. So does Dashwood. Comparing two things with “like” or “as” is called a simile.
> - He’s sawing wood in his sleep. → Ha! No. The snore only sounds like a saw. It’s a comparison. A slow saw goes rrrrasp, so the snore is long and rough. Comparing with “like” is a simile.
> - It’s a very quiet snore. → A saw isn’t quiet. Think of the sound: rrrrasp… rrrrasp. So the snore is long and rough. Comparing with “like” is a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a simile (“a snore like a slow saw”) tells the reader._

_Jackpot sits on a perch at the open window, ticking. His eyes are brass buttons. One is sewn back on with red thread._  
**Byte**: Careful of the bells. Touch the wagon and they’ll all ring. Come round the stream side. There’s a gap where one fell off.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): sound is made by vibration  
> **Byte**: A bell rings because it vibrates. It shivers, very fast, when something knocks it.  
> **Byte**: The shivers shake the air, and the air carries the sound to your ears.  
> **Byte**: Bump the wagon, and a hundred bells shiver at once. Hence: tiptoe.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a bell makes sound by vibrating, and the air carries the sound._

_Stepping stones lead along the stream. One wobbles. One is a frog._  

#### `s15-jackpot`

**Jackpot**: GOOD AFTERNOON. I CANNOT LIE. IT IS A FAULT IN MY SPRINGS.  
**You**: How many eggs are sparkly, Jackpot?  
**Jackpot**: ONE IN TEN. HE KNOWS. HE WROTE IT IN THE LEDGER IN VERY SMALL WRITING.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying by 10 in a money problem  
> **Byte**: This morning the children bought thirty eggs, at ten Shells each. How many Shells did Dashwood take?  
> - ✅ 300 Shells → Yes. 30 × 10 = 300. Three hundred Shells, for three sparkly eggs.
> - 40 Shells → That’s 30 + 10. But every one of the thirty eggs cost ten Shells. Thirty lots of ten: 30 × 10 = 300.
> - 30 Shells → That would be one Shell an egg. They were ten each. 30 × 10 = 300 Shells.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 30 × 10 to work out money taken in a story problem._

**Byte**: And the poster?  
**Jackpot**: HE SAYS THE POSTER IS A POEM. I CANNOT LIE. A POEM IS NOT A NUMBER.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): telling a fact you can check from a claim you can’t  
> **Jackpot**: I CANNOT LIE. WHICH OF THESE CAN BE CHECKED?  
> - ✅ “One egg in ten is sparkly.” → CORRECT. YOU COUNTED IT. A FACT CAN BE CHECKED. “Every egg a winner” is a feeling dressed up as a fact. You can’t measure it.
> - “Every egg a winner!” → HOW WOULD YOU CHECK IT? WHAT IS A WINNER? HE NEVER SAYS. That’s a feeling dressed up as a fact. “One in ten” is a fact: we counted it.
> - “Dashwood has brought you luck!” → LUCK CANNOT BE WEIGHED. I HAVE TRIED. That’s a claim you can’t check. “One in ten” is a fact: we counted it.
> _For grown-ups: Sorted a checkable fact from claims that can’t be checked._

**You**: What happens to the eggs nobody buys?  
**Jackpot**: THEY GO UP THE VALLEY. TO A MAN WHO BUYS IN BULK. HE NEVER HAGGLES. HE NEVER SMILES.  
_Among the stickers on the tailboard, you notice one small, neat silver square: the Circuit’s mark._  
**Jackpot**: ALSO THE LEGENDARY EGG IS NOT LEGENDARY. I HAVE TRIED NOT TO SAY THAT. IT IS VERY UNCOMFORTABLE.  
_The snoring stops. You both freeze. It starts again._  

#### `s15-legendary`

_Dashwood wakes up exactly as charming as he went to sleep. He polishes the Legendary egg on his sleeve._  
**Dashwood Prance**: Admiring her? Course you are. Hold her if you like. One Shell a minute. Feel the luck soak in.  
**Byte**: Here’s three Shells. We’ll need exactly three minutes.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: a quarter of an hour  
> **Byte**: One Shell a minute. How many Shells would it cost to hold her for a quarter of an hour?  
> - ✅ 15 Shells → Yes. An hour is 60 minutes, so a quarter of an hour is 15. Fifteen Shells. I am not paying that.
> - 4 Shells → Four is how many quarters make an hour. But one quarter of 60 minutes is 15 minutes. So, 15 Shells.
> - 25 Shells → Close-ish. An hour is 60 minutes. Split it into four equal parts: 15 each. So, 15 Shells.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a quarter of an hour is 15 minutes._

_Under the bridge it is dim and green, and smells of watercress. Byte lights the stub of a lantern._  
**Byte**: Candling. Hazel showed everybody. Shine a light behind the egg, and you can see what’s growing.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): candling: light passes through a thin eggshell  
> **Byte**: Farmers really do this with hens’ eggs. An eggshell is translucent: it lets some light through, but not a clear picture.  
> **Byte**: Shine a bright light behind it, and anything inside shows up as a shadow.  
> **Byte**: That’s why we’re under the bridge. In the dark, the glow is much easier to see.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how candling works: a thin eggshell lets light through, showing shadows inside._

**Byte**: A sparkly egg glows all through, like a pearl. A plain one shows a little curled shadow. This one… we’ll see.  

#### `s15-painted`

_The light comes through the shell. The glitter on it throws stars all over the underside of the bridge._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understanding a metaphor  
> _The glitter “throws stars” all over the bridge. Are there real stars under the bridge?_  
> - ✅ No. It means little sparkles of light that look like stars. → Yes. Describing one thing as if it really were another is called a metaphor.
> - Yes, real stars. → That would be a very crowded bridge! The sparkles only look like stars. Describing one thing as if it really were another is called a metaphor.
> - Someone threw the glitter at the bridge. → Nobody threw anything. The light bounces off the glitter and makes little star-like sparkles. Describing one thing as if it really were another is called a metaphor.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a metaphor (“throws stars”) means._

_Under the glitter, the egg glows plain pink. Inside is a small curled shadow, and it’s moving._  
**Byte**: Plain. It’s a plain egg, painted. There’s a thumbprint in the varnish. A big one.  
**Byte**: A healthy plain egg, mind. It’ll hatch in about a week. It just won’t be legendary. It’ll be a Nubbin.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): what grows inside an egg  
> **Byte**: That curled shadow is the baby growing inside. In a bird’s egg it’s called an embryo.  
> **Byte**: It feeds on the yolk while it grows. When it’s big enough, it hatches, and a new life cycle begins.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an embryo grows inside an egg, fed by the yolk, as part of a life cycle._

**Byte**: So the LEGENDARY card was a lie. And it’s still a perfectly good egg. Both of those are true.  
_Glitter comes off on your fingers. It doesn’t come off for days._  

#### `s15-verdict`

_You come back up the bank with glitter on your hands. Dashwood sees it, and his smile stays exactly where it is._  
_He steers you round the back of the wagon, where the children can’t see, and sits down on the step._  
**Dashwood Prance**: When I was eight, a man came through my village with a wagon. Not as nice as mine.  
**Dashwood Prance**: He sold me a golden egg for every Shell I had. I carried it home in my hat. I slept curled round it like a cat.  
**Dashwood Prance**: It hatched brown. Brown as a boot. It had been painted.  
**Dashwood Prance**: And I loved that brown thing more than anything since. The best week of my life was the week before it hatched.  
**Dashwood Prance**: That’s what I sell, friend. Not eggs. The week before.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): understanding a character’s motive from his past  
> _What does Dashwood mean when he says he sells “the week before”?_  
> - ✅ The exciting feeling of waiting and hoping. → Yes. That happy, fizzy, waiting feeling has a name: anticipation. Dashwood had it once, as a boy. He’s been trying to sell it ever since.
> - Eggs that are a week old. → Not quite. Think about his story. The best week was the one before his egg hatched. He means the fizzy feeling of hoping. That feeling is called anticipation.
> - Nothing. He’s making it up. → Jackpot says he believes it, and Jackpot can’t lie. He means the fizzy feeling of waiting and hoping. That feeling is called anticipation.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s childhood story to understand why he does what he does._

**Jackpot**: HE BELIEVES THIS. I CANNOT LIE. HE DOES.  
_Round the front of the wagon, the children are waiting. Pip holds her four plain eggs. Byte holds the tally._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about honesty and fairness in selling  
> _Dashwood sells hope, and he really believes in it. But his poster wasn’t true._  
> _What do you think? Is it fair to sell hope with a poster that isn’t true?_  
> - No. People should know the real odds, and then choose. → That’s a fair answer. Byte would agree: Pip spent her birthday Shells on a promise that wasn’t true. Knowing the truth lets people make their own choice.
> - Maybe. People enjoyed the hoping. → That’s a fair answer too. Dashwood’s best week ever was a week of hoping. Byte would ask: would Pip still have bought four eggs, if she’d known it was 1 in 10?
> - He could sell the hope, and tell the truth. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Maybe the week before is just as lovely when you know the odds. An honest stall might be the way to find out.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether hope can be sold fairly when the advertising isn’t true._


**Choices**

- **Show everyone the tally and the painted egg.**
    - You climb on the wagon step and hold up the painted egg. Byte reads the tally aloud, slowly, including the recurring.
    - **The children**: ONE IN TEN?
    - The roof bells ring as children kick the wheels. Dashwood’s smile finally goes, and something small looks out from behind it.
    - **Dashwood Prance**: It was a poem. It was only ever a poem.
    - He drives off before dark. He leaves his spare trestle, a crate of eggs, and the parrot, who refuses to get on.
    - **Jackpot**: I CANNOT LIE. I DID NOT WANT TO GO.
- **Make him post the true odds and give the children their Shells back.**
    - **Dashwood Prance**: Refunds? Refunds! Do you know what that does to a man’s margins?
    - **Jackpot**: HIS MARGINS ARE ENORMOUS.
    - Dashwood counts Shells back into small hands, one by one. He does it with a flourish. He can’t help that either.
    - He paints out the 3 on his poster and paints in a 10. Then, after a long look, he adds: STILL WORTH IT.
    - **Pip**: I’m keeping one egg. I want to see what comes out. I don’t mind if it’s plain.
    - He leaves the valley the next morning with a lighter crate. The parrot stays, by very honest agreement.
- **Buy his wagon, and run an honest stall yourself.**
    - **Dashwood Prance**: Buy her? Buy Marigold? You don’t buy a wagon, friend. You marry it.
    - **Dashwood Prance**: …How much were you thinking?
    - It takes most of an afternoon and most of your Shells. Byte does the haggling. Byte enjoys it far too much.
    - **Dashwood Prance**: Paint the stripes once a year. She likes a polish. And never, ever let her near a goat.
    - He walks off down the lane with his hands in his pockets, whistling, lighter than he came.

#### `s15-odds-board`

_Byte nails up a slate. He chalks it in big, honest numbers: PLAIN 9 IN 10. SPARKLY 1 IN 10. LEGENDARY: NO._  
_Underneath, smaller: ALL OF THEM ARE WARM._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): tenths that make a whole  
> **Byte**: 9 in 10 plain. 1 in 10 sparkly. Nine tenths and one tenth. What do they make together?  
> - ✅ Ten tenths: one whole. Every egg. → Yes. 9/10 + 1/10 = 10/10, which is one whole. Every egg is either plain or sparkly.
> - Ten twentieths. → Careful. When the bottom numbers match, you only add the top numbers. Tenths stay tenths. 9/10 + 1/10 = 10/10: one whole. Every egg.
> - Half the eggs. → Half would be five tenths. Nine and one make ten tenths: the whole crate. Every egg is plain or sparkly.
> _For grown-ups: Added tenths (9/10 + 1/10) to see that they make one whole._

**Pip**: Those are worse odds. Why do I like it better?  
**Byte**: Because you know where you are. Knowing where you are is the second-best feeling there is. After winning.  
_The children queue anyway. Some buy. Some just come to read the board._  
**Pip**: I’ve got ten Shells left. An egg, or a bag of honey drops for the walk home? I need to think.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, notice): scarcity: having only so much means choosing  
> **Byte**: Ten Shells can be an egg, or honey drops. Not both. When you only have so much, you have to choose.  
> **Byte**: That’s why true numbers matter. You can’t choose well if the board is telling you a poem.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that having limited money means choosing, and that honest information helps people choose._


#### `s15-complete`

_The last egg in the crate is wrapped in a red spotted handkerchief. It glows all through, like a pearl in a lamp._  
**Jackpot**: THAT ONE IS REAL. I CANNOT LIE. I CHECKED. I CHECKED TWICE.  
_Tucked in the knot is a card in loopy gold writing: “For the Keeper. Every egg a winner. This one actually. —D.P.”_  
**Byte**: Statistically, that’s the only certain thing he ever sold.  

> **Lesson** (maths, ask): the language of chance: certain, unlikely, impossible  
> **Byte**: Chance words. Picking a sparkly egg from Dashwood’s full crate, with your eyes shut. Was it…  
> **Byte**: certain, unlikely or impossible?  
> - ✅ Unlikely. → Yes. 1 in 10 is unlikely, but not impossible. Three children did get one. This egg, checked twice? Certain. That’s the difference.
> - Certain. → Certain means it must happen. Twenty-seven of the thirty eggs were plain, so it wasn’t certain. 1 in 10 is unlikely.
> - Impossible. → Impossible means it can never happen. But three children did get sparkly ones. 1 in 10 is unlikely, not impossible.
> _For grown-ups: Used the words certain, unlikely and impossible to describe chance._

_Jackpot hops onto your shoulder. He ticks. He weighs about as much as a teapot._  
**Jackpot**: I WOULD LIKE TO LIVE WITH YOU. I CANNOT LIE. I HAVE WANTED TO SAY THAT FOR A WHILE.  
_On his way out, Dashwood pushed the painted egg into Pip’s hands. She hasn’t let go of it since._  
_Pip carries the painted egg home in her hat. A week later it hatches, brown as a boot._  
_She loves it beyond all reason._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): finding the theme of a story  
> _Pip loves her plain brown Nubbin beyond all reason. What do you think this story is saying?_  
> - ✅ Plain things can be precious, and the truth is worth knowing. → Yes. That big idea is the story’s theme. Pip knew the truth, chose anyway, and loves what she got.
> - Sparkly things are always best. → Dashwood might say so! But look at Pip. Her plain brown Nubbin is the thing she loves most. The story’s big idea, its theme, is that plain things can be precious, and the truth is worth knowing.
> - Never buy an egg. → The children still buy eggs at the honest stall. They just know the odds now. The story’s big idea, its theme, is that plain things can be precious, and the truth is worth knowing.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the theme, the big idea, of a story._


### Glossary

- **approximately**: Roughly; close to a number, but not exactly. Often shortened to “approx.”
- **legendary**: So special or famous that people tell stories about it.
- **tally**: A quick way of counting by making a mark for each thing, in bundles of five.
- **recurring**: Happening again and again. A recurring number repeats forever, like 3.333…
- **witness**: Someone who saw or knows what really happened.
- **ledger**: A book where someone writes down money and things bought and sold.
- **bulk**: A very large amount, bought all at once.
- **candling**: Shining a light through an egg to see what is growing inside.
- **translucent**: Letting some light through, but not clearly enough to see through.
- **varnish**: A clear, shiny coat painted on to protect something or make it gleam.
- **embryo**: A baby animal in its very first stage, before it is born or hatched.
- **anticipation**: The excited feeling of waiting for something you are looking forward to.
- **margin**: The money a seller keeps after paying for what they sell.
- **odds**: How likely something is to happen, like 1 in 10.
- **statistically**: Going by the numbers you have counted.
- **certain**: Sure to happen.

## S16. The Workyard

- `s16-step1`: Go upriver with Sparks and Clover and see the Workyard. · _Follow the river path north, past the stepping stones. You’ll hear the saws long before you see the sheds._
- `s16-step2`: Watch the Workyard’s Nubbins for a day. Write down what each one does when nobody is asking. · _Stay hidden behind the log piles and sheds. If a Nubbin sees you, it starts working to be polite, and that note doesn’t count._
- `s16-step3`: Build a Fair Roster with Brisk: jobs the Nubbins like, rests, fruit breaks, a bell, and no more treadwheel. · _Put each Nubbin’s card under the job it chose when nobody was asking. Then hold Sparks’s ladder while she moves the lights to the waterwheel._
- `s16-step4`: Go back to the Workyard in a week, and see how the Fair Roster is working. · _Any day from a week on. Follow the river path north. Brisk will have the kettle on._

#### `s16-sparks`

_Sparks turns up with a coil of wire over each shoulder, like a very small, very loud pirate electrician._  
**Sparks**: Job upriver! A big one! A sawmill wants lights in every shed. I need someone to hold the ladder and say “wow”.  
**Sparks**: The owner’s called Brisk Hollins. Nice man. Very nice. Suspiciously cheerful. I’ve brought Clover. She’s good with ladders.  
**Clover**: I’m not good with ladders. I’m good at not falling off them. It’s different.  
_The river path is soft after the rain. Somewhere ahead the saws are going: a bright, busy whine, like wasps in a jar._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): sound bends round things; light travels in straight lines  
> **Clover**: Funny. We can hear the saws, but we can’t see them.  
> **Sparks**: Sound spreads out and bends round trees and corners. Light goes in straight lines, so the trees block the view.  
> **Sparks**: That’s why you hear a sawmill long before you see it. Same with thunder. And me.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound can travel round obstacles, while light travels in straight lines._

**Sparks**: He says his Nubbins love it there. Love it! He wrote it in his letter twice, and underlined it both times.  
**Clover**: Twice is a lot of underlining.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading between the lines  
> _Why does Clover think twice is a lot of underlining?_  
> - ✅ When someone insists very hard, something might not be quite right. → Yes. Clover is reading between the lines: noticing what the words don’t say. If the Nubbins really loved it, would Brisk need to underline it twice?
> - She thinks underlining is untidy. → Ha. Maybe! But Clover is noticing something else. When someone insists very hard, it can be a clue that something isn’t quite right. That’s reading between the lines.
> - She doesn’t like Brisk. → She hasn’t met him yet! She’s noticing a clue in his letter. When someone insists very hard, it can mean something isn’t quite right. That’s reading between the lines.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a clue in how something was written, not just what it said._


#### `s16-yard`

_The Workyard opens out at a bend in the river. Sheds, log piles, a waterwheel that isn’t turning, and Nubbins. Dozens._  
_Each one wears a tiny hard hat made from half a walnut shell, painted yellow. They chop, they stack, they haul._  
_Over the gate, a banner says WORK IS PLAY! In the middle of the yard, three Nubbins run inside a big wooden treadwheel._  
_Wires run from the treadwheel to every shed. Every bulb in the yard flickers in time with their feet._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): a device that changes energy from one form to another  
> _Why do the bulbs flicker in time with the Nubbins’ feet?_  
> - ✅ Their running turns the wheel, and the wheel makes the electricity. → Yes! The energy changes form: running feet, turning wheel, electricity, light. Every step is a push. Between pushes the wheel slows a bit, so the lights flicker.
> - The bulbs are dancing. → I wish! No. The running feet turn the wheel, and the wheel makes the electricity. Energy changes form: moving feet, turning wheel, electricity, light. Each push makes a flicker.
> - The wind is blowing the wires. → Good guess, but the flicker matches their feet exactly. The running turns the wheel, and the wheel makes the electricity. Energy changes form: moving feet, turning wheel, electricity, light.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a treadwheel changes movement energy into electricity and then light._

**Brisk Hollins**: Welcome! Brisk Hollins. Pleased as punch. Output’s up this month. More logs than ever!  
**Brisk Hollins**: I’m no Circuit man, mind. Mine get Sundays off.  
_A big Power Nubbin trundles past with a log three times his size on his back, humming. His hat says LUG in pencil._  
**Brisk Hollins**: That’s Lug. Best worker I’ve got. Can’t stop him. Tried once. He sulked for a week.  
_Behind the log pile sit five Nubbins. Their colours have worn grey at the edges, like a flag left out all summer._  
**Clover**: Those ones are tired. Not lazy. Tired.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): reading how someone feels from their body  
> **Clover**: Look at how they sit. Slumped. Eyes half shut. Colours faded. Bodies tell you a lot, if you look.  
> **Clover**: Lazy means not wanting to. Tired means your body can’t any more. They need different things.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned to notice how someone feels by looking at their body, and that tired is not the same as lazy._


#### `s16-shadow`

**Brisk Hollins**: Tired? Nonsense! Look at the chart!  
_He unrolls a chart. A red line climbs so steeply it runs off the paper and carries on, in pencil, across the table._  
**Clover**: That chart is about logs. I’m asking about them.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.B.3, ask): a graph only shows what it measures  
> _Look at the labels on Brisk’s chart. What does it actually measure?_  
> - ✅ How many logs get made. → Yes. A chart can only tell you about the thing it counts. This one counts logs. It can’t tell you how a single Nubbin feels.
> - How happy the Nubbins are. → That’s what Brisk thinks it shows. But read the labels: LOGS, and WEEKS. A chart can only tell you about the thing it counts. This one counts logs, not feelings.
> - How long the table is. → Ha. The line does run all the way across it. But read the labels: LOGS, and WEEKS. A chart only tells you about the thing it counts. This one counts logs.
> _For grown-ups: Read a graph’s labels to see what it does and doesn’t measure._

**Brisk Hollins**: Same thing! Happy Nubbins, happy logs. The logs are very happy.  
**Sparks**: Brisk. When nobody’s telling them what to do, what do they do?  
_Brisk opens his mouth to answer. He shuts it again. He has clearly never once wondered._  
**Brisk Hollins**: …Well. Good question. Splendid question. Find out! Have a clipboard. I’ve got forty.  
**Clover**: Observe them from where they can’t see you. If they know they’re watched, they’ll work to be polite. Nubbins are like that.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): observing animals without changing what they do  
> **Clover**: Scientists who study wild animals often watch from a hide: a little hut or screen the animals can’t see into.  
> **Clover**: That way the animals behave as they really would. And the notes are true.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that scientists observe animals from hiding so the animals behave naturally._


**Choices**

- **Start with Lug.**
    - Lug puts down a log, sees you, and at once picks up a bigger one, to show you. You’ll need to be sneakier.
- **Start with the tired ones behind the log pile.**
    - **Clover**: Good. Start with the ones nobody’s counting.
- **Start with the treadwheel.**
    - **Sparks**: The wheel. Yeah. That thing’s bothered me since we walked in. It’s wired backwards, for a start.

#### `s16-notes`

_By sundown your clipboard is full of small handwriting and one large sawdust thumbprint._  
_You watched eight Nubbins. Here is what each one chose, when nobody was asking._  
_The two choppers chop on their breaks too. They like the thunk. One chops the same stump all day, very happily, for no reason._  
_The stacker stacks. The two wheel runners step out the moment Brisk turns his back, and sit under the bench with their eyes shut._  
_The two tired ones you watched never once choose work. They lie in a patch of sun and watch the river go by._  
_And Lug, on his breaks, carries offcuts. Not to the stack. Out to the bank, behind the reeds, one at a time._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.B.3, do): turning notes into a bar chart and reading it  
> _Turn your clipboard into a bar chart. One bar for each choice: CHOP 2, STACK 1, REST 4, CARRY 1._  
> _Which bar is tallest? REST: four of the eight Nubbins. Four out of eight is one half._  
> _Half the Nubbins you watched chose rest, when nobody was asking._  
> Check: `edu:chart:bar:nubbin-choices`
> _For grown-ups: Made a bar chart from observation notes, found the tallest bar, and saw that 4 out of 8 is one half._

_You follow him. In the reeds stands a little lean-to of planks and bark, roofed with moss. All five tired ones are asleep inside._  
**Clover**: He built them a house.  
**Sparks**: Nobody asked him to. He just… did.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using evidence to explain a character’s actions  
> _Why do you think Lug built the lean-to?_  
> - ✅ He saw the tired ones needed somewhere to rest, and he cared. → Yes. The evidence: he carried the wood on his own breaks, one piece at a time, and nobody asked. Lug never speaks. His actions say it for him.
> - Brisk told him to. → Look at the evidence: Sparks says nobody asked Lug. Brisk didn’t even know it was there. Lug saw the tired ones needed somewhere to rest, and he cared.
> - He wanted to show off. → Show-offs like an audience. Lug hid the lean-to behind the reeds. He saw the tired ones needed somewhere to rest, and he cared. His actions say it for him.
> _For grown-ups: Used evidence from the story to explain why a character did something._


#### `s16-roster`
