_You show Brisk the clipboard, and then the lean-to in the reeds. He stands in the wet grass a long time._  
**Brisk Hollins**: I thought they loved it. They looked like they loved it. They were always so busy.  
**Brisk Hollins**: …Busy isn’t the same thing, is it.  
_He takes down WORK IS PLAY! and puts up a new banner: WORK IS… OFTEN PLAY!_  
**Sparks**: That’s worse.  
**Brisk Hollins**: I know. I’m working on it.  
**Sparks**: Right. That treadwheel’s coming off the wires. Your lights go on the waterwheel. Like a normal person’s.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, notice): the waterwheel: a wheel and axle that turns moving water into electricity  
> **Sparks**: A waterwheel is a simple machine: a wheel and axle. The axle is the rod in the middle. It turns with the wheel.  
> **Sparks**: The river pushes the paddles round. Hook the axle to a generator, and the moving water’s energy becomes electricity.  
> **Sparks**: And a river never gets tired. It just keeps coming.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a waterwheel is a wheel and axle, and that it can change moving water’s energy into electricity._

**Clover**: And every Nubbin gets a card on a roster, under the job it picked. And breaks. With fruit.  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): why bodies need rest, food and water  
> **Clover**: Why do you think workers need breaks, with fruit?  
> - ✅ Working tires your muscles. Rest, food and water help your body recover. → Yes. Muscles get tired when they work hard. Rest lets them recover, and food and water refuel you.
> - Breaks are just for being lazy. → Lots of people think that. But a tired body works badly, and can get hurt. Rest lets tired muscles recover, and food and water refuel you.
> - Only weak workers need breaks. → Even the strongest runners rest between races. Even Lug. Every body’s muscles get tired. Rest lets them recover, and food and water refuel you.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rest, food and water help a tired body recover._

**Brisk Hollins**: And the ones who don’t want a job at all? What then? What’s a yard for?  
_Nobody answers. Brisk puts up another banner: REST IS A KIND OF WORK?? It has two question marks._  

#### `s16-bell`

_By evening the Fair Roster hangs by the gate: a board of little painted cards, one for every Nubbin, under the job it chose._  
_Beside it hangs a small brass bell, low enough for the smallest Nubbin to reach. Clover has painted on it: NO THANK YOU._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fair rules work for everyone  
> _Why did Clover hang the bell so low?_  
> - ✅ So everyone, even the smallest Nubbin, can use it. → Yes. A rule is only fair if everyone can use it. A bell the small ones can’t reach would be no use to them.
> - So nobody steals it. → A low bell is actually easier to take! Clover had a better reason. She wanted everyone, even the smallest Nubbin, to reach it. A fair rule works for everybody.
> - Because Clover is short. → I heard that. She hung it low so everyone, even the smallest Nubbin, could reach it. A fair rule works for everybody.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why fair rules must work for everyone, including the smallest._

_The big treadwheel stands still. Sparks has hung a sign on it: RETIRED. A Nubbin is already asleep inside it._  
_A wheel runner waddles to the bell. It looks round at everyone. Then it rings it. Once. Very softly._  
_Then it goes and sits in the sun. Nobody stops it. It looks astonished._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): saying no, and having it respected  
> **Clover**: The wheel runner looks surprised because nobody ever listened to its “no” before.  
> **Clover**: Saying no is allowed. When you ask first, and listen to the answer, that’s called consent.  
> **Clover**: It goes for people too. Your body, your answer. And a good friend listens.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that saying no is allowed, and that asking first and listening is called consent._

**Brisk Hollins**: Well, I’ll be. I’ll be. Output’s going to be awful.  

#### `s16-question`

_Brisk walks you to the river path, hands in his pockets. He has a new slogan in his head. You can tell._  
**Brisk Hollins**: Can I ask you something, Keeper? Honestly? Your lot at the Grove. They fetch you things, don’t they?  
**Brisk Hollins**: Apples. Sticks. Do you ask them? Or do they just do it, because you’re the one who feeds them?  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, notice): what animals need to be well  
> _Real working animals, like sheepdogs and horses, need more than food._  
> _They need water, shelter, rest, a chance to play, and someone who notices how they are feeling._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that working animals need water, shelter, rest and play, not just food._

_You think of your Nubbins dragging fallen apples to your door. How pleased they look. How pleased you look back._  
**You**: I don’t know.  
**Brisk Hollins**: No. Me neither. That’s the trouble with being liked. You never find out what they’d do if they didn’t like you.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about fairness and consent for animals  
> _Brisk has asked a hard question. When an animal does a job because you feed it, is it really choosing?_  
> _What do you think?_  
> - Yes. If it looks happy, it’s choosing. → That’s a fair answer. Lug really does love carrying logs. Clover would add: the NO THANK YOU bell is how you find out for sure.
> - Not always. It might just want the food. → That’s a fair point. Brisk’s Nubbins looked busy, and some of them were worn out. Asking, and listening for a no, is how you find out.
> - You can’t know unless it’s allowed to say no. → That’s a thoughtful answer. It’s exactly what the bell is for. A yes only really counts if no was allowed too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether an animal that works for food is really choosing, and why a “no” must be allowed._

**Brisk Hollins**: Now. The five in the reeds. They don’t want to work. Not a bit. What do I do with them?  

**Choices**

- **Send them to the Grove. They can rest with you.**
    - **Brisk Hollins**: …Yes. Yes, that’s kind. Lug will want to visit. Lug will want to carry them there.
    - Lug, who has been listening, is already lifting the whole lean-to off the ground, with them inside it.
- **Keep them on, as “morale officers”.**
    - **Brisk Hollins**: Morale officers! Officially in charge of sitting in the sun and being lovely. Yes!
    - **Clover**: They’ll be the best in the yard at it. Leave them where Lug can see them.
    - **Sparks**: Are we sure that isn’t just a job with a nicer hat?
- **Let them go wild, up the river.**
    - **Brisk Hollins**: Wild? Out there? Who’ll feed them? Who’ll—
    - **Clover**: They will, maybe. Some Nubbins are happiest belonging to nobody.
    - Brisk looks up the river a long while. He doesn’t like it. He doesn’t say no.

#### `s16-week`

_A week later the Workyard is louder, and slower. The saws stop for fruit at eleven o’clock and at three. Somebody has hung a hammock._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals in hours  
> _Fruit at eleven o’clock, and again at three in the afternoon. How long between the two fruit breaks?_  
> - ✅ 4 hours → Yes. Eleven to twelve is one hour. Twelve to three is three more. 1 + 3 = 4 hours.
> - 8 hours → That’s 11 − 3. But clocks go round: after twelve comes one again. Count on: eleven to twelve is one hour, twelve to three is three more. 4 hours.
> - 3 hours → Nearly! Twelve to three is three hours. But don’t forget eleven to twelve. 1 + 3 = 4 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval across noon by counting on in hours._

_Brisk’s banner has been through several drafts. You can read them all, crossed out, one under the other:_  
_WORK IS PLAY! · WORK IS… OFTEN PLAY! · REST IS A KIND OF WORK?? · ASK FIRST._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): drafting and redrafting  
> _Brisk wrote four drafts. Which one says best what he learned?_  
> - ✅ ASK FIRST. → Yes. Two words that hold the whole story. Writers often need several drafts. Each try gets a little closer to what they really mean.
> - WORK IS PLAY! → That was his first draft, before he watched the Nubbins. It turned out not to be true for all of them. Writers often need several drafts to find what they mean. His last one, ASK FIRST, says what he learned.
> - REST IS A KIND OF WORK?? → He was getting closer! But two question marks means he wasn’t sure yet. Writers often need several drafts to find what they mean. ASK FIRST says what he learned.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that writers redraft to get closer to what they mean, and chose the clearest draft._

**Brisk Hollins**: Output’s down eleven per cent. Lights stay on, mind. The waterwheel’s steadier than three tired Nubbins. Who knew?  
**Sparks**: I knew. I said. I said it loudly.  
_Lug trundles past with a log on his back, humming. Nobody asked him. He just likes it._  

#### `s16-complete`

**Brisk Hollins**: Here. Can’t have a Keeper on my yard without a hat. Regulations. My regulations. New ones.  
_A yellow hard hat in your size, painted to match the walnut-shell ones. On the brim, in Lug’s pencil: KEEPER._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): how a hard hat protects your head  
> _A real hard hat has a tough shell, and straps inside that hold it a little way off your head._  
> _If something drops on it, the shell and the gap take the knock, not your head. That’s why builders wear them._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a hard hat protects the head, and why builders wear them._

**Brisk Hollins**: And take a copy of the roster. Try it at the Grove. Let them pick their jobs, and see what they pick.  
**Clover**: And see what they don’t. That’s just as worth knowing.  
_Back home you nail the Fair Roster by the cottage door. By morning, three Nubbins have pushed their cards under jobs._  
_One has chosen watering. One has chosen fetching apples. One has pushed its card under “sitting with Moss”, and won’t be moved._  
**Sparks**: That last one isn’t a job.  
**Clover**: It is to Moss.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): your point of view and a character’s  
> _Sparks says sitting with Moss isn’t a job. Clover says it is, to Moss. What’s your point of view?_  
> - Sparks is right. A job is making or fixing something. → That’s a fair point of view. Sparks likes jobs you can see: lights on, wires fixed. Clover sees it from Moss’s side. Same Nubbin, two ways of looking.
> - Clover is right. Keeping someone company helps them. → That’s a fair point of view too. Moss is old and fading, and company matters to him. Sparks sees it differently. Same Nubbin, two ways of looking.
> - Both. It depends whose eyes you look through. → That’s a thoughtful answer. To Sparks it’s sitting. To Moss it’s everything. Seeing a thing from more than one side is a big part of being fair.
> _For grown-ups: Compared their own point of view with two characters’ different views._


### Glossary

- **electrician**: Someone whose job is to fit and fix electric wires and lights.
- **suspiciously**: In a way that makes you think something might be wrong.
- **treadwheel**: A big wheel that turns when people or animals walk or run inside it.
- **output**: How much of something is made, like logs from a sawmill.
- **observe**: To watch something carefully, to learn about it.
- **hide**: Here: a small hut or screen where you can watch animals without them seeing you.
- **offcuts**: Small leftover pieces cut off a bigger piece of wood.
- **lean-to**: A simple shelter with a sloping roof, often propped against something.
- **roster**: A list that shows who does which job, and when.
- **axle**: The rod through the middle of a wheel, which turns with it or lets it turn.
- **consent**: Saying yes because you really want to, when saying no is allowed too.
- **astonished**: Very, very surprised.
- **slogan**: A short, catchy phrase that is easy to remember.
- **morale**: How cheerful and confident a group of people feels.
- **draft**: One try at writing something, before it is finished.
- **per cent**: Out of every hundred. Eleven per cent means eleven in every hundred.
- **regulations**: Official rules.

## S12. The Hum

- `s12-step1`: Carry Solo home to the Thrums in the old wall. · _Hush’s old wall is the tumbled stone one on the north side of the Grove. Keep the teacup level: Solo gets seasick._
- `s12-step2`: Put your ear to the old wall at dusk and listen for the Queen-Mother. · _She lives at the heart of the wall, low down by Hush’s lantern post. Go when the hum is quietest, and keep still._
- `s12-step3`: Sit with Solo in Luna’s garden until the first warm, still morning. · _Sit on the bench by the moonflowers after dark, and don’t get up. Solo doesn’t need answers. It needs company._
- `s12-step4`: Follow the swarm by sound with Pixel’s tuning fork. · _Strike the fork and turn slowly. It buzzes hardest when you face the swarm. If you lose them, stand still and strike it again._

#### `s12-solo`

_Dusk in Luna’s night garden. The moonflowers open one by one, with a sound like someone unwrapping a sweet._  
**Luna**: Keeper. Over here. Quietly. I’ve got something in a teacup, and I don’t know what to do with it.  
_In the teacup is a beetle the size of your thumb. It is round and bronze, with a fuzzy back like a peach._  
_It is, just about, a Nubbin. Its wings buzz whenever anyone speaks._  
**Luna**: It’s a Thrum. Hundreds of them live in Hush’s old wall, in a colony. They hum. They never come out alone.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): insects that live together in a colony  
> **Luna**: Thrums live a bit like honeybees. A honeybee colony can be tens of thousands of bees, all sharing one home.  
> **Luna**: Each bee has a job: cleaning, building wax, feeding babies, guarding the door, fetching nectar.  
> **Luna**: Together they survive things no single bee could. Alone, one bee doesn’t last long at all.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that honeybees live in colonies where each bee has a job, and the group helps them all survive._

_The beetle looks up at you. It clears its throat, which for a beetle is mostly wings._  
**Solo**: We are— no.  
**Solo**: I. I am. Good evening. I am sorry. I am not sure who is sorry. I think it is me.  
**Luna**: It’s been doing that for an hour. It finds it very upsetting.  
**Luna**: It needs a name, I think. Things that say “I” usually do.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the meaning of the word “solo”  
> **Luna**: In music, when one person sings on their own, it’s called a solo.  
> **Luna**: So what might “Solo” mean, as a name for a beetle?  
> - ✅ One on its own. → Exactly. A solo is one voice on its own. That’s what this beetle is, for the first time ever.
> - Very loud. → A solo can be loud, but that isn’t what the word means. It means one on its own. A solo singer sings alone.
> - A kind of beetle. → Good guess, but no. “Solo” means one on its own, like a singer singing alone.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of “solo” from its use in music._


**Choices**

- **Call it Solo.**
    - **Solo**: Solo. Solo is… one of something. Yes. That is what I am. For now.
    - **Luna**: For now. Good. Always leave yourself a way back.
- **Give it a name of your own.**
    - You say a name. The beetle repeats it three times under its breath, like testing a step.
    - **Solo**: Nobody has ever said a thing just to me before. It is very loud.
- **Ask what it would like to be called.**
    - **Solo**: Like? I have never liked anything on my own. We like things. Together. When we all agree.
    - **Solo**: …I would like you to choose. Is that allowed? That is my first like.
    - You call it Solo. It seems to fit, the way a borrowed coat fits.

#### `s12-wall`

_The old wall hums. You feel it before you hear it. Lay a palm on the stone and it buzzes like a purring cat._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): sound is made by vibration, and vibration can be felt  
> _The wall buzzes under your hand. Stone can’t hum by itself. So what are you feeling?_  
> - ✅ Hundreds of tiny wings shaking, and the shaking passing into the stone. → Yes. Fast shaking is called vibration. The Thrums’ wings vibrate, and that makes the hum. The vibration travels into the stone, so your hand can feel the sound as well as hear it.
> - The wind blowing through the cracks. → Wind can whistle, but tonight the air is still. It’s the Thrums’ wings. They shake very fast. That shaking is called vibration, and it makes the hum.
> - The stone is warm. → Warmth doesn’t buzz. A buzz is a shake. The Thrums’ wings shake very fast. That’s vibration, and vibration makes sound you can feel.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound is made by vibration, and that vibrations can be felt through solid things._

_The cracks smell faintly of honey. Every crack has a tiny round door, and every door has a face in it._  
**The Thrums**: Good evening, Keeper.  
**The Thrums**: We would like to say: thank you for returning the one.  
**The Thrums**: We would also like to say: the one is welcome. One moment. We are checking we all agree about “welcome”.  
_There is a long pause, full of buzzing._  
**The Thrums**: We do. Welcome. We are sorry about the delay. We are very many.  
_Solo does not get out of the teacup. Solo climbs up your sleeve instead, and stays there, humming quietly, alone._  
**Solo**: In a minute. I will go in in a minute.  
_It does not go in._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): noticing when someone isn’t ready  
> _Solo says “in a minute”, but doesn’t move. Sometimes that means: I’m not ready, and I don’t know how to say so._  
> _You don’t have to push. You can let someone stay close until they are ready._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that a character wasn’t ready, and that giving someone time is a kind response._


#### `s12-flat`

_Next morning Pixel is at the old wall with a tuning fork, a notebook and a very serious face._  
**Pixel**: Hi. Don’t move. Sorry. You can move. Just don’t buzz.  
**Pixel**: I tune my lantern timer to this wall. Have done for years. It hums a perfect B-flat. Nearly. Always has.  
_She taps the fork on her knee and holds it to the stone. The fork sings. The wall sings back, a tiny bit lower._  
**Pixel**: It’s gone flat. Walls don’t go flat. Walls don’t do anything. That’s their whole thing.  

> **Lesson** (music, 1-PS4-1, ask): pitch: what “flat” means in music  
> **Pixel**: A tuning fork always plays the same note. That’s what makes it useful.  
> **Pixel**: The wall’s note is now a little lower than the fork’s. So what does “flat” mean in music?  
> - ✅ A note that’s a bit lower than it should be. → Exactly. Flat means a little too low. A bit too high is called sharp. Slower vibrations make lower notes. Something in that wall has slowed down.
> - A note that’s too loud. → Loud and soft is a different thing. That’s volume. Flat is about pitch: a note that’s a little too low. Slower vibrations make lower notes.
> - A wall with no bumps. → Ha! That’s the other meaning. Same word, two jobs. In music, flat means a note a little too low. Slower vibrations make lower notes.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that “flat” means a note slightly too low, and that slower vibrations make lower notes._

**The Thrums**: Good morning. We are sorry about the flat.  
**The Thrums**: It is our Queen-Mother. She is the middle of the hum. She is getting quieter.  
**The Thrums**: When the middle goes quiet, the hum splits. Half of us leave with a new queen. Half of us stay.  
**The Thrums**: We have done it before. We do not remember it. The ones who remember always leave.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): how a honeybee colony swarms and splits  
> **Pixel**: Real honeybees do this too. It’s called swarming. When a hive gets crowded, the colony splits in two.  
> **Pixel**: In bees it’s the old queen who leaves, with about half the workers. A new queen grows up in the old hive.  
> **Pixel**: Thrums aren’t bees, so they do it their own way. But a split is how one colony becomes two.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a honeybee colony splits by swarming: the old queen leaves with about half the bees._

**Pixel**: That is the saddest thing a wall has ever said to me.  
_In your sleeve, Solo has gone completely still._  

#### `s12-queen`

_At dusk you lie in the grass with your ear against the bottom stone, where the moss is warmest._  
_Deep in the wall, under all the others, there is one slow note, like a big bee in a shut room._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, do): sound travels well through solids  
> _Press your ear right against the stone. Now lift it away, just a little. Now press it back._  
> _The deep note is clearer with your ear on the stone. Sound travels through solids, and often better than through air._  
> _It’s why you can hear a tap on a table so clearly with your ear pressed to the wood._  
> Check: `edu:listen:old-wall:ear-to-stone`
> _For grown-ups: Compared listening through stone and through air, to learn that sound travels through solid things._

**The Queen-Mother**: Ah. The Keeper. And the one in your sleeve. Yes, I can hear it. I can hear all of them.  
**The Queen-Mother**: I am going to tell you something, and you are not to tell the we.  
**The Queen-Mother**: I have said “I” for a very long time. Somebody has to, in the middle of a we. Somebody has to decide when.  
**The Queen-Mother**: It is quite lonely. Nobody tells you that about the middle.  
_Solo makes a small sound in your sleeve, like a question with no words in it._  
**The Queen-Mother**: On the first warm, still morning, half will go. The young one must choose. Go, stay, or something else.  
**The Queen-Mother**: Don’t choose for it. That would be the we all over again, only taller.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): letting others make their own choices  
> _Why does the Queen-Mother tell you not to choose for Solo?_  
> - ✅ Because Solo has only just learned to say “I”, and should get to choose. → Yes. If you chose, you’d be the we all over again: deciding for Solo. You can help someone think. The choice is still theirs.
> - Because she wants to choose herself. → She could, but she doesn’t. She says the young one must choose. Solo has just started saying “I”. Choosing for itself is part of that.
> - Because it doesn’t matter what Solo does. → It matters a lot to Solo. That’s exactly why the choice should be Solo’s. You can help someone think. The choice is still theirs.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people should get to make their own choices, with help rather than orders._


#### `s12-dark`

_Solo won’t go into the wall and won’t come out of your sleeve. So that evening you take it to Luna’s garden._  
_Luna has raked the gravel into slow spirals. In the dark they shine a little, like the inside of a shell._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): similes: comparing with “like”  
> _“Like the inside of a shell” is a simile. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”._  
> _It helps you picture the gravel: pale, smooth, with a soft shine._  
> _For grown-ups: Spotted a simile and talked about the picture it puts in the reader’s mind._

**Solo**: In the hum I am warm on every side. Nothing is my fault. Nothing is mine. It is very restful.  
**Solo**: Out here everything is mine. The dark is mine. The cold is mine. This leaf is mine, and I did not ask for it.  
**Solo**: If I go back, I stop. Not die. Stop being the one who is frightened. I would quite like to stop.  
**Solo**: But I would also like to see what happens next. To me. Is that greedy?  
**Luna**: I garden at night because nobody else does. I liked being on my own before I liked anything else.  
**Luna**: No. That’s not true. It took years. Some nights I still don’t like it. I come out anyway.  
**Luna**: That isn’t an answer. I haven’t got one. I’ve just got a garden.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): thinking about belonging and being yourself  
> _Solo is torn. In the hum it belongs, and it’s safe. Out here it’s itself, and it’s scared._  
> _What do you think matters more: belonging to a group, or being yourself?_  
> - Belonging. Being part of something keeps you warm and safe. → That’s a fair answer. Groups look after us, and nobody does well completely alone. The Queen-Mother might add: a good group still lets you be you inside it.
> - Being yourself. You should get to think your own thoughts. → That’s a fair answer. Your own thoughts, likes and choices matter. Luna might add: being yourself can be lonely sometimes, and that’s all right too.
> - Both. You can be yourself and still belong. → That’s a fair answer, and a hard one to manage. Most people spend their whole lives working on it. Friends who like you as you are are a way of having both.
> - I don’t know yet. → That’s an honest answer. Luna doesn’t know either, and she’s had years to think about it. Some questions are worth carrying around for a while.
> _For grown-ups: Think question (no right answer): weighed belonging to a group against being yourself._


#### `s12-swarm-goes`

_You wake on the bench with dew in your hair. The air is warm and doesn’t move. It is the morning she meant._  
_Across the Grove, the old wall roars._  
_Bronze pours out of every crack at once and turns in the air, glittering, like a handful of pennies thrown at the sun._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): when and how swarms leave  
> **Pixel**: Honeybees swarm on warm, calm days too. Thousands pour out at once and swirl in a big cloud.  
> **Pixel**: Swarms are usually gentle. They have no home and no honey to guard yet, so they’re busy, not cross.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that honeybee swarms leave on warm days and are usually gentle because they have no home to guard._

**The Thrums**: Goodbye. Goodbye. We are leaving. Some of us are leaving. We are deciding which.  
**The Thrums**: It is going very slowly. We are sorry. We are trying to be quick and also polite.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): finding half of a number  
> **Pixel**: Say there were 400 Thrums in the wall, and exactly half leave. How many are leaving?  
> - ✅ 200 → Yes. Half means two equal parts. 200 go and 200 stay. 200 and 200 make 400.
> - 100 → 100 is a quarter of 400: that’s four equal parts. Half means two equal parts. 400 split in two is 200 and 200.
> - 40 → Not quite. 40 is much smaller than half. Half of 4 is 2, so half of 400 is 200. 200 go and 200 stay.
> _For grown-ups: Found half of 400 by splitting it into two equal parts._

**Solo**: I want to see where they go. Not to go. To see. Is there a difference?  
**Pixel**: There’s a difference. I’ve got a tuning fork. Come on.  

#### `s12-follow`

_Pixel presses the fork into your hand. It is warm from her pocket and has PROPERTY OF PIXEL scratched on the handle._  
**Pixel**: Strike it on your knee. Hold it up. Turn slowly.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): a tuning fork vibrates to make its note  
> _Strike the fork and look closely. The two prongs blur. They are shaking back and forth very fast._  
> _That shaking pushes the air, and the pushes reach your ear as sound. Dip a ringing fork in water and it splashes._  
> _As the shaking dies away, the sound fades. That’s why you have to strike it again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a tuning fork makes sound by vibrating, and the sound fades as the vibration dies away._

**Pixel**: When the fork and the swarm match, it buzzes in your fingers. That means you’re facing them.  
**Pixel**: Walk that way. Strike it again when it goes quiet.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, do): using sound to find where something is  
> _Strike the fork. Turn slowly, a little at a time. Stop when it buzzes hardest in your fingers._  
> _Your ears do this all day, too. Turn your head, and a sound gets louder when you face it._  
> Check: `edu:turn:tuning-fork:loudest`
> _For grown-ups: Turned to find the direction a sound was strongest, to locate something by hearing._

**Pixel**: Don’t walk into the stream. People do.  
**Pixel**: Not me. Other people. Specific other people.  

#### `s12-settled`

_The fork leads you over the stream to Hazel’s crooked tree._  
_The swarm hangs from a branch in a great buzzing lump, the shape of a pear._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): how a swarm finds a new home  
> _A real bee swarm does this too. It hangs in a cluster on a branch, with the queen tucked safely inside._  
> _Scout bees fly off to look for a new home, like a hollow tree._  
> _Back at the cluster, a scout does a special dance that shows the others which way to go._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a bee swarm waits in a cluster while scout bees find a new home and dance to share it._

_Pixel holds her fork to it, then towards the wall, then to it again. Then she sits down hard on the bank._  
**Pixel**: It was never one note.  
**Pixel**: It’s hundreds. All a tiny bit apart. They lean towards each other till it sounds like one. That’s all a hum is.  
**Pixel**: I’ve been tuning a clock to a crowd. For years.  

> **Lesson** (music, notice): many voices on nearly the same note sound like one  
> **Pixel**: A choir works the same way. Lots of voices, each a tiny bit different, blend into one big, rich sound.  
> **Pixel**: One voice is a solo. Lots together is a chorus. Both are music.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how many voices singing nearly the same note blend into one sound, as in a choir._

**The Thrums**: We are here. We are a new we. We are not yet sure what we are like.  
**The Thrums**: One. Solo. Will you come into a we? This one or the old one. Either is warm.  
**Solo**: Keeper. I don’t know. Sit with me. No. Tell me. No. Both. Is that allowed?  
_You don’t choose for it. You sit down on the bank beside the teacup, and wait for Solo to decide._  

**Choices**

- **Solo chooses the hum. You nod.**
    - You carry the teacup back to the old wall. Solo looks at you for a long moment, then climbs out.
    - **Solo**: I will forget being frightened. I think I will forget this, too. Will you remember it for me?
    - It walks in through a round door in the stone. The hum goes on, a tiny bit fuller than before.
    - **Pixel**: Listen to that. B-flat. Nearly. It’s back in tune.
- **Solo chooses a home of its own. You nod.**
    - You find it a knot-hole in the gatepost, out of the wind, with a view of the pond. It inspects it for a long time.
    - **Solo**: Mine. The knot-hole is mine. I chose it. Nobody agreed.
    - **Solo**: It is very quiet in here. I will get used to it. Or I will get used to not being used to it.
    - Every dusk after that, a tiny hum comes from the gatepost. One note. Slightly flat. All its own.
- **Solo asks the hum to leave a little room. You nod.**
    - **Solo**: Lean. But leave a gap. For one. Is that allowed?
    - **The Thrums**: We will discuss it.
    - They discuss it. It takes until lunch. Pixel eats a sandwich. Then a second sandwich. Then yours.
    - **The Thrums**: We have agreed. We will be a hum with gaps in it. Ones may go out, and come in, and go out.
    - **The Thrums**: We have also agreed this was the longest meeting in the history of the wall. We are very proud.
    - **Solo**: In for supper. Out for the stars. I can do that. I can be both, slowly.

### Glossary

- **colony**: A big group of animals of one kind that live together and help each other.
- **vibration**: A very fast shaking, back and forth. Vibrations make sound.
- **flat**: In music, a note that is a little lower than it should be.
- **swarm**: A big group of insects flying together, like bees leaving to find a new home.
- **simile**: A way of describing something by comparing it to another thing, using “like” or “as”.
- **scout**: Someone sent ahead to look around and find out what is there.
- **chorus**: A group of voices speaking or singing together.
- **hexagon**: A flat shape with six straight sides.

## S17. Nightjar

- `s17-step1`: Search the nursery and the fence for clues. · _Look closely at the straw, the nursery roof and the top rail of the fence. Show Luna anything you find._
- `s17-step2`: Creep through Luna’s garden to the hide by the nursery without being heard. · _Move when the wind rustles the leaves. Keep to moss and thyme, off the gravel, in the shadows of the big flowers._
- `s17-step3`: Climb slowly to Nightjar’s nest on the cliff. · _Use the cracks with ferns growing in them: those are the solid ones. Keep still whenever she turns her head._
- `s17-step4`: Carry the Grove’s eggs back to the nursery, one at a time, while Nightjar watches. · _Carry each egg in both hands, and walk, don’t run. If you hurry, she follows you down and you start that egg again._
- `s17-step5`: Visit Nightjar’s nest on the night the wild egg hatches. · _Take the cliff path after dark. Sit below the ledge and wait. She shuffles aside when she’s ready._

#### `s17-missing`

_Autumn. The first conkers are down, and the nursery straw is damp with dew._  
_In the straw there is a round, warm dent where an egg was last night. It is the fourth dent this fortnight._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues to back up an idea  
> _Luna says, “Whatever it is, it’s careful.” Which clue tells her that?_  
> - ✅ There’s never a crack or a crumb of shell. → Yes. A clumsy thief would break things. Not one crumb means something handled the eggs very gently.
> - It takes one egg a night. → That clue tells us how often it comes, not how it behaves. The careful clue is the shells: never a crack, never a crumb.
> - The straw is damp with dew. → The dew tells us it was a cool, damp night. It doesn’t tell us about the thief. The careful clue is the shells: never a crack, never a crumb.
> _For grown-ups: Picked the clue in the text that supports a character’s idea._

**Nova**: Morning. I’m not stopping. I was passing, and I heard there was a mystery, and I’m not stopping.  
**Nova**: Badger.  
**Luna**: It’s not a badger.  
**Nova**: A tall badger.  
**Luna**: Look at the straw before you trample it, both of you. Then we can talk about tall badgers.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-LS1-2, notice): eggs need steady warmth to grow  
> **Luna**: Notice it always takes the warmest egg. A bird’s egg needs steady warmth, or the chick inside can’t grow.  
> **Luna**: That’s why parent birds spend most of the day and night sitting on their eggs.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a bird’s egg needs steady warmth from a parent for the chick inside to grow._


#### `s17-clues`

_On the top rail of the fence: a grey feather as long as your forearm, soft as smoke. Its edge is torn, as if on rock._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): choosing the right unit of length  
> _You want to write down how long the feather is. Which unit would you use?_  
> - ✅ Centimetres → Yes. Centimetres suit things you can hold in your hands. This feather is about 30 centimetres long.
> - Kilometres → A kilometre is a thousand metres: about a quarter of an hour’s walk. Far too big for a feather! Centimetres suit things you can hold. This feather is about 30 centimetres long.
> - Metres → A metre is about one big stride. The feather is much shorter than that. Centimetres fit better. This feather is about 30 centimetres long.
> _For grown-ups: Chose centimetres as the sensible unit for measuring a feather, comparing it with metres and kilometres._

_On the roof, faint scratches. Something landed very gently here, and left very gently._  
_And the dent in the straw is still warm, hours later. Something kept that egg warm until the last second._  
**Luna**: That’s an owl’s. A big owl. Bigger than an owl has any business being.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how owls fly silently  
> **Luna**: Run your finger along the front edge. Feel that soft fringe, like the teeth of a comb?  
> **Luna**: Most birds’ feathers are stiff and smooth there. An owl’s break up the rushing air, so its wings hardly make a sound.  
> **Luna**: That’s how an owl flies silently. Mice don’t hear it coming. And nor did we.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the soft, comb-like edges of owl feathers let owls fly almost silently._

**Nova**: Two badgers in a coat, holding an owl feather to throw us off.

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, do): sorting materials by a property: quiet or noisy underfoot

**Choices**

#### `s17-reveal`

_Midnight. The wind drops. Something crosses the moon without a sound, and the garden goes still beneath it._  
_An owl lands on the nursery roof. She is enormous, grey as ash, and one long feather on her left wing is torn._  
_She lifts an egg out of the straw in her feet, slowly, the way you would carry a held breath._  
_Then she turns her head right round and looks at your hiding place. For a long moment she only looks._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): why owls turn their heads  
> _You can look sideways just by moving your eyes. Why does an owl turn its whole head instead?_  
> - ✅ Its eyes can’t move in their sockets. → Yes. An owl’s eyes are shaped like short tubes, fixed in place. So it turns its head instead. Its neck bends so well that it can turn its head about three-quarters of the way round.
> - Because it’s showing off. → It does look like showing off! But an owl has to do it. Its eyes are fixed in place and can’t roll like ours. So it turns its head, nearly three-quarters of the way round.
> - To hear better. → Turning helps owls hear too. But the main reason is its eyes: they can’t move in their sockets. So it turns its whole head, about three-quarters of the way round.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that owls’ eyes are fixed in their sockets, so owls turn their heads to look around._

**Nightjar**: Hoo-oo.  
_Then she’s gone towards the cliffs, low over the hedges, carrying the egg as if it were the only thing in the world._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): how owls see at night  
> **Luna**: How did she find the nursery at midnight? Her eyes. An owl’s eyes are huge for the size of its head.  
> **Luna**: Big eyes let in lots of light, so owls can see well when it’s nearly dark. Animals active at night are called nocturnal.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that owls’ very large eyes gather lots of light, helping them see at night._

**Nova**: …I’m crossing off the badgers.  
**Luna**: Nightjar. That’s what Hazel called her. I thought she was a story. The biggest owl in the valley, Hazel said.  
**Luna**: And the saddest.  

#### `s17-cliffs`

_Next night you follow the way she flew, past the ridge to the high cliffs. The wind smells of salt and cold stone._  
_Halfway up, wedged in a crack, is a ledge. On it is a nest the size of a cartwheel._  
**Nova**: I’ve slept up here. Years back. An owl called all night, the same two notes. I thought it was the wind.  
**Luna**: She hunts at the turn of the tide. That’s soon. We could climb up while she’s out.  
**Luna**: Or we could wait for her, and let her see us coming. Owls remember faces.  
**Luna**: Either way, slowly. It’s her home, not ours.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): being fair to animals: not frightening them  
> _Luna says it’s Nightjar’s home. How would you feel if someone climbed into your home while you were out?_  
> - ✅ Scared or cross, coming back to find a stranger there. → Most of us would. Animals feel fear too. Letting her see you coming gives her the choice. That’s fairer, even if it’s slower.
> - I wouldn’t mind. → Maybe you’re very easy-going! But a wild mother on her nest would probably be frightened. Letting her see you coming gives her the choice. That’s fairer.
> - It depends who it was. → That’s true. A friend is different from a stranger. To Nightjar, you’re still a stranger. Letting her see you coming is how you start to stop being one.
> _For grown-ups: Put themselves in an animal’s place and thought about fair, gentle ways to approach wildlife._


**Choices**

- **Climb while she’s out hunting.**
    - You climb fast, hand over hand. You are nearly at the ledge when a shadow drops past you, silent, and settles.
    - She is home. She sits on the nest and looks at you, and does not move.
    - **Nova**: Well. She was always going to be home, wasn’t she.
- **Wait for her, where she can see you.**
    - You sit on a rock below the ledge, in plain view. She comes home at the turn of the tide and looks at you a long time.
    - Then she shuffles over, just a little, as if making room.
    - **Luna**: That’s an invitation. Or a warning. With owls it’s mostly both.

> **Luna**: Real birds do this. Sitting on eggs to keep them warm is called incubating.

> **Luna**: And they turn their eggs often. It helps the chick inside grow properly and stops it sticking to the shell.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that birds incubate eggs with their body heat and turn them often to help the chicks grow._

> _Grief can last a long time. It isn’t wrong. It shows how much she loved them._

_…_

#### `s17-return`

_She won’t let you take them all at once. You lift two, and she clacks her beak once, like a door shutting._  
**Luna**: One at a time, then. Down and back. Let her watch each one go, and see you come back for the next.  
**Nova**: That’s four climbs. In the dark.  
**Luna**: That’s four climbs. In the dark.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Nova says four climbs. But each egg needs one trip down and one trip back up._  
> _Four eggs. How many trips is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes. 4 eggs, 2 trips each: 4 × 2 = 8. Down, up, down, up, down, up, down, up. Nova will be thrilled.
> - 4 → That’s just the trips down. You have to come back up each time too. 4 eggs, 2 trips each: 4 × 2 = 8 trips.
> - 6 → Close! Let’s count in pairs: down-up for each egg. 2, 4, 6, 8. 4 eggs, 2 trips each: 4 × 2 = 8 trips.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a trips problem as 4 equal groups of 2 (4 × 2 = 8)._

_Nightjar watches you lift the first egg._  
_Her eyes follow it all the way down, and all the way back up to you._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): building trust slowly  
> **Luna**: This is why we go one at a time. Each trip shows her the egg is safe and you come back.  
> **Luna**: Trust gets built like that: small promises, kept, again and again.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that trust is built through small promises kept over and over._


#### `s17-wild`

_Dawn. Four eggs are back in the nursery straw. You climb up one last time for the lantern you left behind._  
_There is still one egg under her. Small, speckled like lichen, and it doesn’t glow. It isn’t the Grove’s._  
**Nova**: That’s nobody’s. Wild. Its mother never came back, I’d guess. It happens.  
_Nightjar looks at the egg, then at you. She does not hide it. She does not move off it, either._  
**Luna**: Leave it with her. Let somebody keep something warm and have it work.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about right and wrong when someone is hurting  
> _Nightjar took eggs that weren’t hers. But she kept every one safe and warm, because she was grieving._  
> _Was what she did wrong?_  
> - Yes. They weren’t hers to take. → That’s a fair answer. Taking what isn’t yours causes worry, even if you mean well. Luna might add: you can say something was wrong and still feel sorry for the one who did it.
> - No. She was sad, and she kept them safe. → That’s a fair answer. She never harmed a single egg. Nova might add: the nursery still worried all fortnight. Kind reasons don’t stop other people being upset.
> - A bit of both. → That’s a fair answer. Lots of things are like that: a wrong thing, done for a sad, loving reason. Understanding why helps you choose what to do next.
> _For grown-ups: Think question (no right answer): considered whether an action can be wrong even when the reason is love and grief._

_You leave it. On the way down, Luna stops on the path._  
**Luna**: Next spring she’ll come back to the nursery. Grief keeps a better calendar than I do. What do we do?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphors: saying one thing is another  
> _Luna says grief “keeps a better calendar” than she does. What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ Sad feelings remember the time of year a sad thing happened, and come back then. → Yes. Nightjar’s chicks died in a cold spring. So every spring, the sadness comes round again, right on time. Grief can’t really keep a calendar. Talking about a feeling as if it were a person with a diary is a metaphor.
> - Owls can’t read calendars. → True, and funny! But Luna means something bigger. Grief remembers the time of year a sad thing happened, and comes back then. Saying it “keeps a calendar” is a metaphor.
> - Grief is over quickly. → It’s nearly the opposite. Grief remembers, sometimes better than we do. Her chicks died in spring, so spring brings the sadness back. That’s why she’ll come back next spring.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the meaning of a metaphor about grief._


**Choices**

- **Leave the nursery open, with a lantern lit for her.**
    - **Nova**: A night nurse. With a beak. That’s either brilliant or a disaster.
    - **Luna**: If she wants eggs to sit on, she can sit on ours, where we can see. Hazel would have done that.
    - **Luna**: Then worried all night. Then done it again.
- **Move the nursery in by the stove, with a latch.**
    - **Luna**: That’s fair. The eggs come first. Feed them before you feed yourself, nearly.
    - **Nova**: She won’t take it personally. She’ll just sit on the roof and look at the chimney. Sadly. For ever.
    - **Luna**: Then I’ll leave her a mouse on the step now and then. Grief gets hungry.

> **Luna**: A big owl sits on her eggs for about four or five weeks before they hatch.  
> **Luna**: All that time she keeps them warm and turns them. She hardly leaves the nest at all.

**Luna**: Go after dark. Take nothing. Just go.

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): converting weeks to days  
> _Say it takes 4 weeks. A week has 7 days. How many days are there in 4 weeks?_  
> - ✅ 28 → Yes. 4 × 7 = 28. That’s 28 nights of sitting still on a cold cliff. Owls are very patient.
> - 11 → That’s 4 + 7. But we need 4 lots of 7. 7, 14, 21, 28. Four weeks is 28 days.
> - 24 → Close. Let’s count in sevens: 7, 14, 21, 28. Four weeks is 28 days.
> _For grown-ups: Converted 4 weeks into 28 days by counting in sevens._

> **Luna**: See the tiny hard point on its beak? That’s an egg tooth. Chicks use it to chip their way out. It drops off soon after.

**Nightjar**: Hoo-oo. Hoo-oo.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how a character’s feelings change the meaning  
> _Nightjar calls the same two notes she always calls. Why don’t they sound the same?_  
> - ✅ Because now she’s happy, not grieving. → Yes. The notes are the same. The feeling behind them has changed, and you can hear it.
> - Because she has a cold. → Ha! No. Look at her mood: happy. Same notes, new feeling. For the first time in twenty-two years, her call isn’t sad.
> - Because it’s a different owl. → It’s Nightjar, all right. The torn feather’s still there. Same owl, same notes, new feeling. Now she’s happy.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a character’s change of feeling changes how the same words or sounds come across._

#### `s17-complete`

_At the end of autumn Nightjar moults, and the wind brings her old grey feathers down into the Grove._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): why birds moult  
> _Feathers wear out, like old socks. So birds moult: old feathers drop out, and new ones grow in their place._  
> _Most birds don’t lose them all at once. They swap a few at a time, so they can still fly and keep warm._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that birds moult, replacing worn feathers a few at a time._

**Luna**: I’ve sewn them into a cloak. Don’t ask how long it took. I’ll tell you, and then you’ll feel bad.  
_It is as light as breath and as warm as a bird._  
_That night, on the cliff top in the cloak, you hear a hush of wings behind you. Two careful feet take hold of your collar._  
_The valley turns under you, silver and black. The Grove comes up to meet you, as gently as an egg set down in straw._  
**Nova**: Show-off. I walked for years to see this valley properly, and you did it in a minute.  
**Nova**: …Take me next time.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): asking for what you want  
> _Nova never asks for things. “Take me next time” was hard for her to say. That’s why it came out so quietly._  
> _Asking for what you’d like can feel brave. Good friends are glad you asked._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that asking for what you want can take courage, and that friends welcome it._


### Glossary

- **fortnight**: Two weeks, or fourteen days.
- **trample**: To tread heavily on something and squash it.
- **nocturnal**: Awake and active at night, and asleep in the day.
- **incubate**: To keep eggs warm so the babies inside can grow.
- **grief**: The deep sadness you feel when someone you love has died.
- **metaphor**: Words that describe something as if it were something else, to make you see it in a new way.
- **owlet**: A baby owl.
- **moult**: When a bird’s old feathers drop out and new ones grow in their place.

## S18. The Grove Museum

- `s18-step1`: Dig three fossils from the cliff layers with Dusty, and sort them from oldest to youngest. · _Lower layers were laid down first, so they are older. Note how deep each find was, then sort them._
- `s18-step2`: Run the moth trap in Luna’s garden and wait quietly for three night finds. · _Sit still near the sheet: every time you move, the finds come more slowly. At dawn, look under the ash tree._
- `s18-step3`: Find three shore creatures in Marina’s rock pools before the tide turns. · _Look under the weed and the flat stones, and put each stone back the way you found it. When the water reaches the barnacles, the tide is turning._
- `s18-step4`: On a clear night on the hill, find the Pole Star with Nova, then wait up for the Moon. · _Find the seven stars of the Plough. The two at the end of the pan point to the Pole Star. The Moon rises late, in the east._
- `s18-step5`: Fill the centre case, then talk to Professor Delve at the barn door. · _Place the centre-case exhibit in the middle of the barn, then speak to the professor by the door._

#### `s18-barn`

_Hazel’s old barn smells of hay, apples and long-ago rain. Swallows’ nests line the rafters like little clay cups._  
_In the middle of the floor stands a mole in a tweed waistcoat, beside a wheelbarrow full of empty glass cases._  
**Professor Delve**: Ah. The grandchild. Professor Delve, archivist. I wrote to your grandmother about a museum. She said yes.  
**Professor Delve**: In principle. Eleven years ago. Moles are patient. I have come to collect the principle.  
**Professor Delve**: Four wings. Three exhibits each. Fossils, night creatures, shore life, the heavens. Twelve. A tidy number.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> **Professor Delve**: Check my sums, please. Four wings, three exhibits in each. How many exhibits altogether?  
> - ✅ 12 → Correct. 4 groups of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. Or 4 × 3 = 12. A tidy number, as I said.
> - 7 → That is 4 + 3. But we have four groups, with three in each. 3, 6, 9, 12. Four lots of three is 12.
> - 16 → That would be four in each wing. We have three. 3, 6, 9, 12. Four lots of three is 12.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 4 groups of 3 as 4 × 3 = 12._

**Professor Delve**: Every exhibit gets a plaque, and every plaque must be true. Not nearly true. Not true-ish. True.  
_A small brown moth drifts down from the rafters and lands on the end of his nose._  
**Professor Delve**: Oh. Oh dear. Oh, no, not one of—  
_Professor Delve faints, quite neatly, into the wheelbarrow._  
**Professor Delve**: I’m perfectly all right. I’m simply horizontal.  
_A muddy figure stands in the doorway: Dusty, two days after the rain on the hill, holding a trowel with nothing to dig._  
**Dusty**: I heard “fossils”. From the lane. My hands want something to do. Can they do this?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): how keeping busy can help with grief  
> _Dusty’s Nubbin, Fossil, died on the hill two days ago. Dusty is still very sad._  
> _Sometimes, when you’re grieving, it helps to give your hands a job, especially alongside a friend._  
> _It doesn’t make the sadness go away. It gives it somewhere to sit for a while._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a gentle, shared task can help someone who is grieving._


#### `s18-fossils`

_The cliff is striped like a cake: sand, then red rock, then grey shale, then a dark band just above the beach._  
**Dusty**: Deeper’s older. Rock goes down in layers, like blankets on a bed. Nobody puts the bottom blanket on last.  
_A coiled shell near the top. A fern pressed flat in the red rock. And deep in the dark band, a little armoured bug._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS1-1, do): rock layers: deeper layers are older  
> **Dusty**: Put the three finds in order, oldest first. Remember the blankets: the deepest layer went down first.  
> _Oldest: the armoured bug from the dark band. Then the fern from the red rock. Youngest: the coiled shell near the top._  
> Check: `edu:order:fossils:oldest-first`
> _For grown-ups: Put fossils in order of age using the rule that deeper rock layers are older._

**Dusty**: Fossil used to sit right there while I dug. Supervising. She was terrible at it. She slept.  
**Dusty**: …It’s quiet without the snoring.  
_Back at the barn, Professor Delve reads each plaque aloud before he’ll let it go on the wall._  
**Professor Delve**: “Trilobites were sea animals with jointed shells, relatives of insects and crabs. They lived for over 250 million years.”  
**Professor Delve**: “Ferns have no flowers and no seeds. They spread by spores, which usually form under their leaves.”  
**Professor Delve**: “Ammonites were sea animals related to squid and octopus. They died out about 66 million years ago.”  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-1, ask): what fossils tell us about the past  
> **Dusty**: Trilobites and ammonites lived in the sea. But we dug them out of a cliff, on dry land.  
> **Dusty**: What does that tell us?  
> - ✅ Long ago, this land was under the sea. → Yes. When they died, mud and sand on the sea floor buried them. Over millions of years the mud pressed into rock, and the shells turned into fossils. Later the land rose.
> - They crawled up the cliff. → Good thought, but they were sea animals. They couldn’t live out of water. They’re in the cliff because this land was once sea floor. Mud buried them, and over millions of years it became rock.
> - Someone put them there. → Nobody could. They’re inside solid rock, deep in the layers. This land was once sea floor. Mud buried them, and over millions of years it became rock.
> _For grown-ups: Used sea fossils found on land to work out that the area was once under the sea._

**Professor Delve**: True, true and true. Wing one. Somebody check my nose for moths.  

#### `s18-night`

_Luna hangs a white sheet between two apple trees and sets a lantern under it. The sheet glows like a sail at sea._  
**Luna**: A moth trap. Nothing gets hurt. They land on the sheet, we look, we draw, and at dawn they go home.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): moths and butterflies: how to tell them apart  
> **Luna**: Most moths fly at night, and lots of them are drawn to lights. That’s why the lantern works.  
> **Luna**: To tell a moth from a butterfly, look at the antennae, the feelers on its head.  
> **Luna**: A butterfly’s end in little knobs. Most moths’ are thin, or feathery like tiny ferns.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that most moths fly at night and can be told from butterflies by their antennae._

**Luna**: The museum gets the drawings. Living things aren’t exhibits. They’re neighbours.  
**Professor Delve**: I shall supervise from a safe distance. Of about a mile.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): exaggeration for a joke  
> _Luna’s garden is not a mile long. So why does Professor Delve say “about a mile”?_  
> - ✅ He’s exaggerating, to show how scared of moths he is. → Yes. To exaggerate is to make something sound much bigger than it is. Here it’s a joke, and it tells us how he feels.
> - He measured it. → A mile is a long walk: about 20 minutes. He’d be in the next valley! He’s exaggerating: making it sound bigger than it is, to show how scared he is.
> - He can’t count. → He counts very well. He’s a professor! He’s exaggerating: making it sound bigger than it is, to show how scared he is.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised exaggeration used for humour and to show a character’s feelings._

_He sits under a blanket at the far end of the garden, holding a tin of smelling salts like a cup of tea._  
**Luna**: Now the hard part. We wait, and we don’t talk.  
**Luna**: …That was me talking. Starting now.  

#### `s18-night-finds`

_Near midnight a moth lands on the sheet, green and black like lichen on old bark. You lose it twice while looking at it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, ask): camouflage helps animals survive  
> _You lost the moth twice, and it was right in front of you. Why is it so hard to see on bark?_  
> - ✅ Its colours match the lichen, so it blends in. → Yes. That’s called camouflage. Birds hunting by day fly right past it. Moths that blend in best are the ones most likely to survive.
> - It’s invisible. → It just seems that way! It’s there, but its green and black match the lichen. Blending in like that is called camouflage. It keeps the moth safe from hungry birds.
> - It’s too small to see. → It’s small, but you could see it easily on the white sheet. On bark, its colours match the lichen. That’s camouflage, and it hides the moth from birds.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that camouflage helps animals hide from predators and survive._

**Luna**: Merveille du Jour. It means “marvel of the day”, and it flies by night. Somebody had a sense of humour.  
_From the far end of the garden comes a soft thump. Professor Delve has fainted from a mile away, on principle._  
_By dawn you have a drawing of the moth, a spider’s web lifted whole onto black card, and an owl pellet from under the ash._  
**Professor Delve**: “The Merveille du Jour is a moth that flies in autumn. Its green and black wings hide it on lichen-covered bark.”  
**Professor Delve**: “Owls swallow small prey whole. The fur and bones they can’t digest are pressed into a pellet and coughed up.”  
**Professor Delve**: “Garden spiders spin webs from silk made in their own bodies. They often eat the old web before spinning a new one.”  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, do): spiders are not insects  
> _Count the legs in your drawings. Tap each one. The moth has 6 legs. The spider who made the web has 8._  
> _Insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts. Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts. So a spider isn’t an insect at all._  
> Check: `edu:sort:legs:insect-spider`
> _For grown-ups: Counted legs to sort an insect (6) from a spider (8), and learned spiders are not insects._

**Professor Delve**: Recycling. Admirable. Somebody turn the moth drawing to face the wall whenever I walk past.  

#### `s18-shore`

_Low tide past the ridge. Marina’s rock pools are full of sky, and the seaweed smells of salt and pennies._  
**Marina**: Rules. Turn a stone, turn it back the same way up. That’s somebody’s roof.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-3, do): looking after living things in their habitat  
> _Lift a flat stone gently. Underneath: tiny shrimps, a curled worm, a periwinkle. It’s damp and dark down there._  
> _Now turn it back the same way up. The creatures underneath need the shade and wet to stay alive._  
> Check: `edu:turn:stone:same-way-up`
> _For grown-ups: Turned a rock-pool stone back carefully, learning to protect the creatures that live under it._

**Marina**: Living things go back before the tide turns. The museum gets drawings, and whatever they’ve finished with.  
**Marina**: And the tide comes back whether you’re ready or not. It’s very rude like that.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: working out when the tide comes in  
> **Marina**: On most coasts the sea comes in and goes out about twice a day.  
> **Marina**: From low tide to high tide takes about 6 hours. Low tide today is 11 o’clock in the morning. When is high tide?  
> - ✅ About 5 o’clock in the afternoon. → Spot on. 11 o’clock, plus 1 hour is 12, then 5 more hours is 5 o’clock. Plenty of time, if we don’t dawdle.
> - About 6 o’clock. → Count on from 11: 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. That’s 6 hours, and we land on 5 o’clock.
> - About 17 o’clock. → Ha! On a 24-hour clock, that’s right: 17:00 is 5 o’clock in the afternoon. On a normal clock face we’d just say 5 o’clock.
> _For grown-ups: Added 6 hours to 11 o’clock to find a later time._

**Professor Delve**: I have brought a bucket, a net and a deep respect for things with pincers.  
_A small crab sidles past the professor’s boot. He doesn’t faint. He looks extremely pleased about it._  
**Professor Delve**: Not a moth. A good day.  

#### `s18-shore-finds`

_A sea star the colour of a ripe apricot, one arm short and growing back. A limpet, clamped in its own worn hollow._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): a sea star is not a fish  
> **Marina**: Some people call it a starfish. Is a sea star really a fish?  
> - ✅ No. It has no backbone, no fins and no gills like a fish. → Right. That’s why “sea star” is the better name. It moves on hundreds of tiny tube feet under its arms. Fish don’t have those.
> - Yes. It lives in the sea. → Lots of things live in the sea that aren’t fish: crabs, limpets, seaweed. A sea star has no backbone and no fins. That’s why “sea star” is the better name.
> - Yes. It’s got “fish” in its name. → Names can trick you! A sea star has no backbone and no fins, so it isn’t a fish. That’s why “sea star” is the better name.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a sea star is not a fish, because it has no backbone or fins._

_And a hermit crab halfway between houses, hurrying out of a cramped winkle shell into a roomy whelk._  
**Professor Delve**: Drafts for the plaques. “A sea star can regrow an arm it has lost. Many have a simple eye at the tip of each arm.”  
**Professor Delve**: “A limpet grazes on the rock when the tide is in. When the tide goes out, it returns to its own spot, its home scar.”  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how a limpet survives low tide  
> **Marina**: Try to lift a limpet once it’s clamped down. You can’t. Don’t try too hard, mind.  
> **Marina**: Its strong foot grips the rock and holds a little seawater in. That stops it drying out till the tide comes back.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a limpet’s shell and strong foot help it survive when the tide goes out._

**Professor Delve**: “A hermit crab keeps its soft body inside an empty snail shell. When it outgrows one, it moves to a bigger one.”  
**Marina**: Look. It’s left the old shell behind. Perfect, that. Somebody else will want it. A smaller crab.  
**Professor Delve**: Or a museum. A museum would want it very much. I am only saying.  

**Choices**

- **Take the empty shell for the museum.**
    - **Marina**: Fair. There are plenty of shells. There’s only one museum.
    - **Professor Delve**: It shall have a velvet cushion. A small one. The crab would want it small.
- **Leave the shell for the next crab.**
    - **Marina**: Good. That’s how pools work. Somebody’s old house is somebody’s new one.
    - **Professor Delve**: Then we shall have a drawing. Drawings never need a bigger house.

#### `s18-stars`

_Nova is on the western hill at nightfall, flat on her back in the cold grass beside the memorial flowers._  
**Nova**: Clear night. No moon till late. Best sky in the valley. I’ve slept under most of them, so I’d know.  
**Nova**: I brought you something for the museum. I don’t give people things. It’s a rock. Don’t make it a moment.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): working out a character’s hidden feelings  
> _Nova carried that rock for years. So why does she say, “Don’t make it a moment”?_  
> - ✅ It matters a lot to her, and she feels shy showing it. → Yes. Some people go gruff when they care most. Carrying it for years gives her away.
> - She doesn’t care about the rock. → Nobody carries a rock for years and walks two days for it unless they care. She feels shy about showing how much it matters, so she keeps it short.
> - She’s in a hurry. → She’s lying in the grass all evening. Not much of a hurry! She cares a lot, and feels shy showing it, so she keeps it short.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s actions to understand feelings she doesn’t say out loud._

_She drops a stone the size of a walnut into your palm: black, heavy for its size, with a crust like burnt toast._  
**Nova**: I watched it come down over the moor, years back. Walked two days to find it. Carried it ever since.  
**Professor Delve**: A meteorite! Oh, that is wonderful. And it isn’t a moth. A very good day.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what a meteorite is  
> **Professor Delve**: A meteorite is a rock from space that falls all the way to the ground.  
> **Professor Delve**: That black crust formed as its outside melted, rushing down through Earth’s air.  
> **Professor Delve**: Many meteorites have iron metal inside. That’s why it feels so heavy for its size.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a meteorite is, why it has a burnt crust, and why many feel heavy._

**Nova**: Now. Find me north. Then you can have the other two exhibits as well.  

#### `s18-star-finds`

_The Pole Star isn’t the brightest. It’s just the one that stays put while the whole sky wheels slowly round it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, do): finding the Pole Star from the Plough  
> **Nova**: Find the Plough first: seven bright stars in the shape of a saucepan with a bent handle.  
> **Nova**: Tap the two stars at the end of the pan. Draw a line through them, about five times the gap between them.  
> **Nova**: That’s the Pole Star. Face it, and you’re facing north. Turn round, and that’s south.  
> Check: `edu:draw:pointer-line:pole-star`
> _For grown-ups: Used the two pointer stars of the Plough to find the Pole Star and north._

**Nova**: That one got me home more times than I’ve told anyone. Which is none.  
_Near midnight the Moon comes up over the ridge, low and orange, and turns white as it climbs._  
**Nova**: Same face. Always the same face. Hazel looked at that face. So did whoever was here before her.  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): why the stars and Moon seem to move  
> _The sky isn’t really wheeling. The Earth is spinning, once every day, and we spin with it._  
> _That’s why the Moon rises in the east and sets in the west, like the Sun._  
> _The Pole Star sits almost right above the North Pole, the middle of the spin, so it barely seems to move._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Earth’s daily spin makes the stars and Moon seem to move across the sky._

**Professor Delve**: “Polaris, the Pole Star, sits almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it hardly moves across the night sky.”  
**Professor Delve**: “The Moon always shows Earth the same face. Its pull, together with the Sun’s, raises the tides.”  
**Professor Delve**: “A shooting star isn’t a star. It is space rock or dust burning up in Earth’s air. A piece that lands is a meteorite.”  
**Nova**: You read plaques to the sky, Professor.  
**Professor Delve**: The sky has never once corrected me. I find that very restful.  

#### `s18-heart`

_Twelve cases full, and one more. The big one in the middle of the barn, under the empty swallows’ nests, is bare._  
**Professor Delve**: The centre case. Every museum has one. It holds the thing the rest of the museum is for.  
_Dusty comes in out of the cold, turning something over in their hands: a card, bent at one corner._  
**Dusty**: Fossil’s card. From the hill. The rain got at it, so I made a new one for the flower and kept this.  
**Dusty**: I don’t want it in a drawer. I don’t want it rained on. I want it somewhere people come.  
**Professor Delve**: That is exactly what a museum is for. A museum is a place where a valley remembers.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): what museums are for  
> _Professor Delve says a museum is where a valley remembers. What do you think a museum is for?_  
> - Remembering people and the past. → That’s a fair answer, and it’s the professor’s too. Things in a museum help us picture lives long ago, and people we’ve lost.
> - Learning true things. → That’s a fair answer. Every plaque here has to be true. People come to find out about the world. Dusty might add: you can learn about a person, too, not just about rocks.
> - Keeping precious things safe. → That’s a fair answer. Glass cases keep things safe from rain, dust and drawers. And safe means they’ll still be there for people a hundred years from now.
> - Sharing special things with everyone. → That’s a fair answer. A thing in a drawer belongs to one person. A thing in a museum belongs to everyone who visits. That’s what Dusty wants: somewhere people come.
> _For grown-ups: Think question (no right answer): considered what museums are for, from remembering the past to sharing knowledge._

**Professor Delve**: Though I wonder. Your grandmother kept a hatch register. Every egg in forty years, and its first sound.  
**Professor Delve**: That is not one Nubbin remembered. That is all of them. It could go in the middle. On loan, naturally.  
**Dusty**: …That’s fair. That’s a good thing. It just isn’t Fossil.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): remembering helps with grief  
> _Dusty agrees the register is a good idea. But a good idea can still feel wrong when you miss someone._  
> _Moss says we are made of being remembered. Dusty wants people to remember Fossil, and that’s a kind of love._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how remembering someone who has died is part of grieving, and a kind of love._


**Choices**

- **Put Fossil’s card in the centre case.**
    - **Dusty**: Thank you. She’d hate the glass. She’d sit on top of it.
    - **Professor Delve**: And the register stays in the cottage, where it is still being written. Quite right. It isn’t finished.
- **Put Hazel’s hatch register in the centre case.**
    - **Dusty**: Can her card go in it? Tucked in the front. Like a bookmark.
    - **Professor Delve**: A bookmark is permitted. A bookmark is, in fact, encouraged.
    - **Professor Delve**: It is only on loan, mind. The moment the family wants it back, I shall carry it home myself.
- **Leave the case empty, for whoever comes next.**
    - You prop a card in the empty case: “For whoever this valley remembers next.”
    - **Professor Delve**: An empty case. Most unusual. People will stand in front of it for a very long time.
    - **Dusty**: Good. Let them. Fossil’s card can go on the ledge beside it, where people put their hands.

#### `s18-door`

_The barn is swept. Twelve plaques shine._  
_The swallows are long gone south, and have left their little clay cups behind._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): birds that migrate  
> _Swallows migrate. In autumn they fly south, thousands of kilometres, to Africa, where it’s warm and there are insects to eat._  
> _In spring they fly all the way back. Many return to the very same barn, and even the same nest._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that swallows migrate south in autumn and return in spring, often to the same nest._

**Professor Delve**: One last matter. The door. Glass needs polishing. Plaques come loose. Archivists need… worms.  
**Professor Delve**: Two Shells a visit would pay for the upkeep and keep the place standing.  
**Professor Delve**: Or it could be free, and we would manage. Somehow. Probably.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying to find a total cost  
> **Professor Delve**: Suppose 9 visitors come on a Saturday, and each pays 2 Shells. How many Shells is that?  
> - ✅ 18 → Correct. 9 × 2 = 18. Enough for polish, glue, and a modest quantity of worms.
> - 11 → That is 9 + 2. But each of the nine pays two. 9 lots of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. 18 Shells.
> - 16 → Close. That would be 8 visitors. Let us count all nine in twos. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. 18 Shells.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 9 visitors × 2 Shells = 18 Shells._

_Dusty raises an eyebrow at the word “worms”. The professor pretends not to see._  

**Choices**

- **Charge two Shells, for upkeep.**
    - **Professor Delve**: Sensible. A place that costs nothing is a place nobody remembers to mend.
    - **Professor Delve**: Anyone shorter than the door handle goes free. I insist. I have measured.
- **Keep it free.**
    - **Professor Delve**: Free. Hm. A place where a valley remembers ought to belong to the valley. I agree.
    - **Professor Delve**: I shall put out a jar. Nobody need put anything in it. The jar is merely hopeful.

#### `s18-complete`

_On opening day half the valley comes. Most of them stand at the centre case longer than they meant to._  
_Children press their noses to the trilobite. Sparks reads every plaque aloud, loudly, to people already reading them._  
**Professor Delve**: You did this, Curator. I only had the principle.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): working out a new word from context  
> _The professor calls you “Curator”. You found the exhibits, checked the plaques and filled the cases. So what is a curator?_  
> - ✅ Someone who looks after a museum’s collection. → Yes. A curator chooses, cares for and explains the things in a museum. That’s been you, all along.
> - A kind of doctor. → It does sound a bit like “cure”! But a curator looks after a museum’s collection. They choose things, care for them and explain them. Just what you did.
> - Someone who faints at moths. → That’s just the professor! A curator looks after a museum’s collection. They choose things, care for them and explain them. Just what you did.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of “curator” from clues in the story._

_He gives you a brass magnifying glass on a ribbon, worn smooth where a great many thumbs have held it._  
**Professor Delve**: It was mine. I can’t see much through it any more. I’d like it to keep looking at things.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how a magnifying glass works  
> _A magnifying glass has a lens: glass that bulges out in the middle._  
> _The curved glass bends the light coming through it, so things look bigger than they really are._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a magnifying lens bends light to make things look bigger._

_Then a moth comes in through the open door, and the Curator’s first official act is to catch the professor._  

### Glossary

- **archivist**: Someone whose job is to look after old records and important things from the past.
- **horizontal**: Lying flat, side to side, like the horizon.
- **shale**: A soft grey rock made from mud pressed hard over a very long time. It splits into thin layers.
- **antennae**: The two long feelers on an insect’s head, used to touch and smell.
- **exaggerate**: To make something sound bigger or more than it really is.
- **camouflage**: Colours or patterns that help an animal blend in with what is around it.
- **sidles**: Moves sideways, slowly or shyly.
- **tide**: The rise and fall of the sea, which happens about twice a day.
- **backbone**: The row of bones down the middle of the back of animals such as fish, birds and people.
- **meteorite**: A rock from space that has fallen all the way to the ground.
- **on loan**: Lent for a while, and given back later.
- **migrate**: To travel a long way to a different place at a certain time of year, and back again.
- **upkeep**: The work and money needed to keep something in good condition.
- **curator**: A person who looks after the things in a museum and explains them to visitors.

## S13. The Mill Cellar

- `s13-step1`: Get past the rats in the grain store, and find the hatch to level two. · _Feed the rats, or creep past them along the wall. The hatch is under the sacks. The old hoist will lift them._
- `s13-step2`: Drain the flooded sluice room. Open its three gates in the right order. · _Water flows downhill. Open the lowest gate first, then the middle, then the top, or the room fills again._
- `s13-step3`: Find what is jamming the great wheel, and get past it to the bottom stair. · _Watch which gear shudders when the river pushes. Never stand between the spokes._
- `s13-step4`: Unlock the iron door and go down to the bottom of the cellar with Tobin. · _Use Tobin’s key on the iron door past the wheel pit. Take a lantern: there’s no light down there._
- `s13-step5`: Do what you decided with Aldous’s letter. · _Keep it safe at home, burn it in the mill’s old stove, or take it to the grave under the alders by the race._

#### `s13-tobin`

_Autumn. Below the falls the river runs brown and loud. The old mill leans over it like a man trying to hear something in the water._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): spot a simile and say what it helps you picture  
> _The mill “leans over the river like a man trying to hear something”. A comparison that uses “like” or “as” is called a simile._  
> _What does this simile help you picture?_  
> - ✅ The mill is tipped forward, bent over the water. → Yes. Picture someone bending close to listen. The old mill is bent the same way, over the river.
> - The mill can really hear things. → It’s a fun thought, but a simile only compares. The mill isn’t listening. It leans the way a listening man leans.
> - The mill is very noisy. → The river is noisy! But this simile is about shape. The mill is bent over the water, like someone leaning in to hear.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised a simile and described the picture it creates._

_Its great wheel hasn’t turned in twenty years. Moss sits on the old millstone by the door. It’s the only thing here he approves of._  
_A very old man in a lamplighter’s coat is unlocking the door with a key the size of a ladle._  
**Old Tobin**: Hazel’s grandchild. Thought so. You’ve got her chin, and her habit of standing exactly where I’m about to swing a door.  
**Old Tobin**: Tobin. I lit the lamps in this valley for fifty-one years. Every lane, every bridge, every dusk.  
**Old Tobin**: Then they put in new lamps that light themselves, and I was free to tell stories full time. Nobody’s thanked them for that.  
**Old Tobin**: This was Aldous Vale’s mill. Corvin Vale’s father. Yes, that Corvin. Him with the cold garden.  
**Old Tobin**: There’s a cellar under it. Four levels, going down. I’ve kept it shut for twenty years.  
**Old Tobin**: But the river’s getting in. By spring it’ll have the lot. Somebody ought to see what’s down there first.  
**Old Tobin**: There was one winter, the year of the Three Hats, when the wheel ran so hard the floor smoked, and—  
_He stops. He looks at the door. He looks at you._  
**Old Tobin**: Where was I? Cellar. Yes. Dark.  
**Moss**: He has been telling that one since before you were born. He has never once reached the end.  
**Old Tobin**: I heard that, Moss. I reach the end all the time. I just don’t bring anyone with me.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, notice): how a watermill turns moving water into work  
> **Moss**: Before you go down, learn what’s above you. A mill turns moving water into work.  
> **Moss**: The river pushes the paddles on the wheel, and the wheel turns. The wheel turns an axle, and gears pass the turning along.  
> **Moss**: At the end, a heavy millstone spins on top of a still one. Grain caught between them is crushed into flour.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a watermill changes the energy of moving water into turning that grinds grain into flour._
