- `q14-s1`: Carry the comfy chair over from the Workshop. · _It is the big red armchair by the Workshop door. Pick it up and carry it to the nest._
- `q14-s2`: Put your most tired Nubbin in the comfy chair. · _Tiredness shows on a Nubbin’s status card. Pick up the sleepiest one and put it on the chair._

#### `q14-intro`

_You are quietly brushing a Nubbin by the nest when the gate bangs open._  
_Three Keepers in long red robes sweep in. One trips on the step. They sweep in again, more carefully._  
**Brother Pouffe**: Surprise! It is the Nap Patrol!  
_There is a long silence. Your Nubbin, halfway through being brushed, stares at them._  
**You**: We… did not see that coming.  
**Brother Pouffe**: Exactly! We rely on surprise. Surprise, and cushions. Two things: surprise and cush—  
**Brother Bolster**: And blankets.  
**Brother Pouffe**: Three things! Hang on. Everybody out. We shall do the door again.  
_They go out. The gate bangs. They sweep in, nobody trips, and Brother Bolster raises two plump cushions, menacingly._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): working out a word from context  
> _Brother Bolster raises the cushions “menacingly”._  
> _What do you think “menacingly” means?_  
> - ✅ In a threatening, scary way. → Yes: as if he’s about to do something terrible. With a cushion. That’s the joke: cushions are not scary.
> - Very gently. → Good guess, cushions ARE gentle! But “menacingly” means in a threatening way. A threatening cushion is very silly.
> - Very slowly. → He might be slow too! But “menacingly” means in a threatening way. That’s what makes it funny.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the scene to work out that “menacingly” means in a threatening way._

_Sister Tuft holds up three folded blankets, just as menacingly._  
**Brother Bolster**: Soft. Very soft. You have been warned.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): adding three numbers  
> _Bolster has 2 cushions. Tuft has 3 blankets. Soon there will be 1 big chair too._  
> _How many soft things will the Nap Patrol have?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes: 2 + 3 = 5, and 1 more chair makes 6. Six soft things. Very well armed.
> - 5 → That’s the cushions and blankets: 2 + 3 = 5. Don’t forget the chair! 5 + 1 = 6.
> - 3 → Three is how many robed Keepers there are! Soft things: 2 cushions + 3 blankets + 1 chair = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Added 2 cushions, 3 blankets and 1 chair to make 6 soft things._

**Brother Pouffe**: Your Nubbins look tired. Overworked. Under-napped. We shall see to that. Sister Tuft!  
**Brother Pouffe**: Bring forth… the big red chair!  
**Sister Tuft**: We left it at your Workshop. You said you’d carry it.  
**Brother Pouffe**: …Keeper. Would you be so good as to carry it over for us?  

**Choices**

- **Fine. I’ll fetch it.**
    - **Brother Pouffe**: Splendid. We shall wait here, being terrifying.
- **Can I hold a cushion?**
    - **Brother Bolster**: …Just for a minute.
    - It is extremely soft. You can see why he is so proud of it.

#### `q14-chair`

_You carry the chair back to the nest. It is deep, red and squashy, with a fringe round the bottom._  
_It is heavier than it looks. Most comfortable things are._  
**Sister Tuft**: Behold. The comfy chair.  
_Brother Pouffe cracks his knuckles. Brother Bolster raises the cushions._  
_Sister Tuft fluffs the chair twice, then a third time, to be safe._  
**Brother Bolster**: Feel that cushion. Go on. Feathers inside. Full of air.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, do): sorting materials by how they feel  
> _Sort what’s in the nest into soft and hard: cushion, blanket, gate post, pebble, feather, flowerpot._  
> **Brother Bolster**: Feathers and wool trap lots of tiny pockets of air. That’s why they squash. Wood and stone keep their shape.  
> Check: `edu:sort:materials:soft-hard`
> _For grown-ups: Sorted things into soft and hard and learned that soft things trap air._


#### `q14-sentence`

**Brother Pouffe**: Now. Bring us your most tired Nubbin.  
**Brother Pouffe**: It shall sit in the comfy chair until lunchtime. With a cushion behind it. And another cushion. Beside.  
**Brother Bolster**: And a blanket over its knees. A woolly one.  
**Sister Tuft**: And no getting up. Not even for a snack.  
**Brother Pouffe**: Unless it is a very small snack.  
_The Workshop clock says half past ten. Lunch in the Grove is at half past twelve._  
_They exchange grim nods. They have done this many times, and it always goes exactly to plan._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _It is half past ten. The nap lasts until lunch at half past twelve._  
> _How long will the nap be?_  
> - ✅ 2 hours → Yes. Half past ten to half past eleven is 1 hour. To half past twelve is 2 hours.
> - 30 minutes → Half an hour is a short nap! Count the hours: 10:30 to 11:30, then to 12:30. That’s 2 hours.
> - 12 hours → That’s a whole night’s sleep! From 10:30 to 12:30 is just 2 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that half past ten to half past twelve is 2 hours._


**Choices**

- **Bring the sleepiest Nubbin.**
    - Your sleepiest Nubbin yawns so wide it nearly falls into itself.
- **Offer to sit in the chair yourself.**
    - **Brother Pouffe**: Ha! Keepers are safe from cushions today. Bring us a Nubbin.

#### `q14-asleep`

_The Nubbin sinks into the chair. Brother Bolster tucks in a cushion._  
_Sister Tuft lays a woolly blanket over its knees._  
_It is asleep before the blanket lands._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): why sleep matters  
> **Sister Tuft**: Sleep is not doing nothing. While you sleep, your body grows and mends itself.  
> **Sister Tuft**: Your brain tidies up the day, too. Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sleep helps the body grow and repair, and that children need about 9 to 12 hours a night._

_It snores very softly, like a kettle thinking about boiling._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile tells us  
> _The Nubbin snores “like a kettle thinking about boiling”._  
> _What does that tell you about the snore?_  
> - ✅ It’s a soft, quiet, rising sort of sound. → Yes. A kettle about to boil makes a gentle, growing hum. The simile lets you hear the snore in your head.
> - It’s very loud and whistly. → A boiling kettle whistles! But this one is only THINKING about boiling, so it’s soft and quiet.
> - It’s hot. → Kettles are hot, but the simile is about the sound: soft and quietly rising, like a kettle not quite boiling.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a simile (“like a kettle thinking about boiling”) tells the reader about a sound._

**Brother Pouffe**: Shh. The Patrol is working.  
_All three tiptoe to the edge of the nest and stand guard. Nobody has ever guarded a nap so fiercely._  

#### `q14-complete`

_Two hours later, at half past twelve, the Nubbin wakes. It stretches. It glows._  
_It looks as if it has slept for a week._  
**Brother Pouffe**: Ha! Look at it. Utterly refreshed. Our work here is done.  
**Brother Bolster**: Best nap we have ever given. Possibly the best nap anyone has ever had.  
**Sister Tuft**: We should go. We have three more Groves to burst into before tea.  
_They sweep out. One trips on the step. Then they sweep back in, because they forgot the chair._  
**Brother Pouffe**: Keep it. We have another. We have a whole room of them.  
**Brother Pouffe**: One last question, Keeper. When did YOU last sit down?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): thinking about rest and looking after yourself  
> _Brother Pouffe has a point. Keepers look after everyone else. Who looks after the Keeper?_  
> _Is resting a waste of time, or part of the job?_  
> - Part of the job. You can’t help others if you’re worn out. → That’s a wise answer. The Nap Patrol would give you a cushion for it.
> - A waste of time. There’s too much to do! → That’s honest, and lots of grown-ups feel the same! The Patrol would say a rested Keeper gets more done, not less.
> - It depends how tired you are. → Thoughtful. Noticing how tired you feel is the first step. Then you can choose.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether resting is a waste of time or part of looking after others; any reasoned answer was welcomed._

_From now on, a tired Nubbin on the comfy chair naps back to full twice as fast._  

**Choices**

- **Sit in the chair, just for a minute.**
    - You sit. Sister Tuft tucks a blanket over your knees.
    - You wake an hour later with a cushion on your face and no idea what day it is.
    - **Brother Pouffe**: Ha! Another one rested. Our work is never done.
- **No time. There’s too much to do.**
    - **Sister Tuft**: That is what they all say.
    - **Brother Pouffe**: Keep the chair, then. It will wait for you. Chairs are excellent at waiting.

### Glossary

- **menacingly**: In a threatening way, as if about to do something nasty.
- **fringe**: A border of hanging threads along the edge of something.
- **grim**: Very serious and stern.
- **fiercely**: In a strong, determined way.
- **refreshed**: Full of energy again after a rest.

## Q15. The Fruitless Fruit Stall

- `q15-s1`: Ask Mr Dibble for six different fruits. · _Pick a fruit from the order list at the stall. Each fruit counts once._
- `q15-s2`: Keep asking until you have tried all twelve fruits. · _Keep choosing from the order list, and keep a tally. Something changes at twelve._

#### `q15-intro`

_A smart green stall has opened by the bridge. The sign says: DIBBLE’S. EVERY FRUIT IN THE VALLEY, AND THEN SOME._  
_Behind it stands Mr Pomeroy Dibble, in a striped apron and a straw boater, beaming._  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Good morning! Whatever fruit you fancy, we have it. Every fruit in the valley. Possibly more.  
_Behind him are twelve crates, each under a cloth. Neat, clean, suspiciously flat cloths._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): making an inference from a clue  
> _Look closely at those cloths: “suspiciously flat”._  
> _What might the flat cloths be telling you?_  
> - ✅ There might be nothing under them. → Good detective work. A cloth over fruit would be lumpy. Writers leave clues like this on purpose.
> - The fruit is very small. → Possible! But even small fruit makes bumps. Flat cloths are a clue the crates might be empty.
> - The cloths are brand new. → They might be! But “suspiciously” is the clue word. The writer wants you to wonder what’s under them. Maybe nothing.
> _For grown-ups: Used a clue word (“suspiciously flat”) to guess that the crates might be empty._

**You**: A run fruit, please.  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Ah. Run fruit. Just out, I’m afraid. There was a rush on them. They ran.  
**You**: A swim fruit, then.  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Swim fruit! Normally, yes. Today the delivery Nubbin went for a swim, and so did the fruit.  

**Choices**

- **Keep asking politely.**
    - **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Please do! Asking is half the fun. For me.
- **Lift a cloth.**
    - You lift a corner. Mr Dibble lowers it again, gently, with one finger.
    - **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Let’s not spoil the surprise.

#### `q15-six`

**You**: Fly fruit?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Flew.  
**You**: Power fruit?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Lifted. By a very strong Nubbin. Carried off over its head.  
**You**: Stamina fruit?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Eaten by a tired one. Fair enough, really.  
**You**: Sun fruit?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Set. They do that, in the evening.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words with more than one meaning  
> _Mr Dibble’s excuses are word jokes. “The sun fruit set.”_  
> _What does “set” mean when we talk about the sun?_  
> - ✅ It goes down in the evening. → Yes. The sun sets in the evening. So the sun fruit “set” too, and vanished. Very convenient.
> - A group of things, like a set of pens. → That IS a meaning of “set”! Words can have several. For the sun, “set” means going down in the evening.
> - Ready to go, like “ready, steady, set”. → Another real meaning! But with the sun, “set” means going down below the hills in the evening.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the joke in “the sun fruit set”: “set” can mean the sun going down._


> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction within 20  
> _The order list has twelve fruits. You have asked for six. Every one was “just out”._  
> _How many fruits are left to ask about?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes: 12 − 6 = 6. Halfway. Mr Dibble needs six more excuses.
> - 18 → That’s 12 add 6. You’ve used some up, so take them away: 12 − 6 = 6.
> - 0 → Not yet! You’ve asked for 6 of the 12. 12 − 6 = 6 still to go.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 12 − 6 = 6 fruits left to ask about._


#### `q15-twelve`

_You keep going. Mr Dibble keeps smiling. It is a smile that has had a great deal of practice._  
_Somewhere behind the stall, a Nubbin is plucking a tiny mandolin. Slowly. The same three notes._  
**You**: Moon fruit?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Only at night. And at night I’m closed.  
**You**: Heart fruit?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: A Nubbin looked at it with such love that I hadn’t the heart to sell it. I gave it away.  
**You**: A coconut. Just one coconut.  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: There is one palm in the whole valley, and frankly it has had a difficult week.  
**You**: Could the music stop?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Stop? It’s the atmosphere.  
_The Nubbin plays the three notes again, more slowly, out of spite._  

> **Lesson** (music, ask): tempo: how fast or slow music goes  
> _The Nubbin played the same three notes, but slower. The speed of music is called its tempo._  
> _What happened to the tempo?_  
> - ✅ It got slower. → Yes. Same notes, slower tempo. Slow music can feel sleepy or sad. Or, in this case, very annoying.
> - It got louder. → Louder is about volume, not tempo. Tempo is speed, and the Nubbin played slower.
> - It got higher. → Higher or lower is about pitch. Tempo is speed. The notes stayed the same; they just got slower.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tempo means the speed of music, and told it apart from volume and pitch._


#### `q15-confess`

_By the twelfth fruit, Mr Dibble has stopped smiling. He takes off his boater and holds it in both hands._  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: I have a confession. There has never been any fruit. Not a single pip.  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: I just liked the stall.  

> **Lesson** (maths, do): keeping a tally  
> _Make a tally of the fruits you asked for: one mark each, and every fifth mark crosses the other four._  
> _Twelve fruits: two bundles of five, and two more. Fruits sold: zero marks at all._  
> Check: `edu:tally:fruits-asked:12`
> _For grown-ups: Kept a tally of 12 fruits asked for (two bundles of five and two more) against 0 sold._

**You**: So the stall that sells every fruit sells… no fruit.  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: When you put it like that, it sounds bad.  
**You**: How would you put it?  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: …Exactly like that, really.  
_Mr Dibble looks at his twelve empty crates as if seeing them for the first time._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about honest signs and fairness to customers  
> _Mr Dibble’s sign promised EVERY FRUIT. He had none._  
> _Is it fair for a sign to promise something that isn’t true, even if the stall is friendly?_  
> - No. People trust signs. → That’s a fair answer. A sign is a kind of promise. Breaking it, even kindly, wastes people’s time.
> - It’s fine. It’s only a joke. → Some people would agree, and it IS funny! But someone who really needed fruit might not laugh.
> - It depends who it affects. → Thoughtful. Asking “who does this affect?” is a great way to judge whether something is fair.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a sign that promises something untrue is fair, even when it is friendly._


**Choices**

- **Let’s stock it. With real fruit.**
    - **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Real fruit? But then people would buy it. And then it would be gone.
    - **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: …I’ll put out one run fruit. On a cushion. Facing the wall, so it doesn’t get ideas.
- **Don’t change a thing.**
    - **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Really? You don’t mind?
    - **You**: It’s the friendliest stall in the valley. It just isn’t a shop.
    - **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: That is the nicest thing anyone has ever said to me over an empty crate.

#### `q15-complete`

**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: You’re right. Quite right. But I’ll tell you what I do have. Knowledge.  
_From under the counter he brings out a thick, beautifully drawn page: every fruit in the valley, with notes on each._  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Where it grows. What it does. Which Nubbins like it best.  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: I know everything about fruit except where to get any.  
_He slips it into your Collection book. It fits perfectly, as if there was always a gap for it._  
**Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: And the boater. Take it. It belongs on someone with fruit.  

> **Lesson** (maths, do): writing an inventory with subtraction  
> _A shop keeps an inventory: a list of everything it has. Help Mr Dibble write his._  
> _Crates: 12. Cloths: 12. Mandolins: 1. Boaters: 1, take away the one he gave you, makes 0. Fruit: still 0._  
> Check: `edu:list:inventory:dibble-stall`
> _For grown-ups: Wrote a shop inventory and used subtraction (1 − 1 = 0) to update it._

_As you leave, you hear him greet the next customer with great cheer: “Just out, I’m afraid!”_  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): scarcity means choosing  
> **Mr Pomeroy Dibble**: Suppose I DID put out one run fruit, and two customers both wanted it. What then?  
> - ✅ Only one could have it, so they’d have to choose, or share it. → Exactly. When there isn’t enough of something to go round, people have to make choices. That’s called scarcity. It’s why I never stock anything. Far less worrying.
> - They could both have it. → Both? It’s one fruit! Unless they cut it in half and share it. When there isn’t enough to go round, that’s scarcity.
> - Just make more fruit appear. → If only. Fruit takes time to grow. When there isn’t enough to go round, people must choose. That’s scarcity.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that when there is not enough of something, people must choose; this is called scarcity._


### Glossary

- **suspiciously**: In a way that makes you think something is not quite right.
- **stamina**: The energy to keep going for a long time.
- **tempo**: The speed of a piece of music.
- **mandolin**: A small stringed instrument with a rounded back, a bit like a little guitar.
- **confession**: Telling someone the truth about something you have done.
- **tally**: A way of counting with marks, where every fifth mark crosses the four before it.
- **inventory**: A list of everything a shop or person has.
- **scarcity**: When there is not enough of something for everyone who wants it.

## Q16. The Argument Booth

- `q16-s1`: Pay Byte 5 Shells for an argument. · _Tap Byte’s booth and choose Pay. You need 5 Shells._
- `q16-s2`: Win the argument before the sand runs out. · _Saying the opposite back only feeds him. Point out that he isn’t giving any reasons._

#### `q16-intro`

_Byte has set up a booth outside the Workshop. The sign says: ARGUMENTS. 5 SHELLS. ONE MINUTE EXACTLY._  
_There is a sand timer on the counter. Byte is looking at it the way other people look at cake._  
_Next to it stands a smaller booth marked COMPLAINTS: 2 SHELLS. It is also Byte, in a different hat._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): adding prices  
> _An argument costs 5 Shells. A complaint costs 2 Shells._  
> _How much for one of each?_  
> - ✅ 7 Shells → Yes: 5 + 2 = 7. Byte has priced this very carefully.
> - 3 Shells → That’s the difference between them: 5 − 2 = 3. For one of each, add them: 5 + 2 = 7.
> - 10 Shells → That would be two arguments! One argument and one complaint is 5 + 2 = 7.
> _For grown-ups: Added two prices (5 + 2 = 7 Shells) for an argument and a complaint._

**Byte**: Good afternoon. Would you like an argument?  
**You**: What sort of argument?  
**Byte**: The best sort. You give reasons. I give reasons. The sand keeps it fair.  
**Byte**: It is five Shells. Please pay first. I find arguments about payment unpleasant.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): negotiating calmly with a reason  
> _You could try to haggle: offer a lower price._  
> _Which way of asking is most likely to work?_  
> - ✅ Offer four Shells, calmly, and give a good reason. → Yes. In a negotiation, a reason helps the other person see what’s in it for them. Even then, they might still say no. That’s fair too.
> - Just say “four Shells” and stare. → Sometimes that works at a market! But with no reason, Byte has no reason to agree. Give one.
> - Shout “Five is too much!” → Shouting makes people dig their heels in. A calm offer with a good reason works much better.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a calm offer with a good reason is the best way to negotiate, and that the other side may still say no._


**Choices**

- **Pay the five Shells.**
    - **Byte**: Thank you. Your minute begins when you sit down.
- **Four Shells?**
    - **Byte**: No. And you gave no reason. That one was free. Please do not do it again.

#### `q16-flip`

_You sit down on the stool. Your Nubbin climbs onto the stool beside you._  
_Byte turns the sand timer over with great ceremony._  
_The sand begins to trickle through the narrow middle, in a thin, steady stream._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how a sand timer uses gravity  
> **Byte**: Gravity pulls the sand down. The middle is narrow, so only a little gets through at a time.  
> **Byte**: Make the neck the right size, and all the sand takes exactly one minute. That is how sand tells time.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls the sand down, and a narrow neck makes it fall slowly enough to measure time._

**Byte**: Your minute has begun. Sixty seconds. Please begin.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): seconds in a minute  
> _One minute is 60 seconds._  
> _When half the sand has fallen, how many seconds will be left?_  
> - ✅ 30 seconds → Yes. Half of 60 is 30. Watch for the halfway point.
> - 50 seconds → Half of 60 is 30, not 50. When half the sand is gone, 30 seconds are left.
> - 6 seconds → That would be a very quick argument! Half of 60 seconds is 30 seconds.
> _For grown-ups: Used 1 minute = 60 seconds to work out that half a minute is 30 seconds._

**Byte**: I will not count them aloud. I will count them inside, very loudly.  
_Your Nubbin stares at the falling sand as if it might do a trick._  

#### `q16-minute`

**You**: Your booth is very nice.  
**Byte**: Disagree.  
**You**: It’s a lovely day for it.  
**Byte**: False. It is a medium day.  
**You**: It’s sunny AND drizzling. There’s a rainbow.  
**Byte**: That is a smudge.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): what makes a rainbow  
> _Rainbow or smudge? Think about what makes a rainbow._  
> _What do you need to see a rainbow?_  
> - ✅ Sunshine and raindrops at the same time. → Yes. Sunlight shines into raindrops and splits into colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Sunny and drizzling is perfect rainbow weather. It’s a rainbow.
> - Just rain. → Rain is half of it. You need sunshine too. Sun plus raindrops makes a rainbow, and today has both.
> - A smudge on the window. → Ha! That’s Byte’s answer, and he gave no reason. You need sun and raindrops, and today has both.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a rainbow needs sunshine and raindrops at the same time, and named its colours in order._

_Your Nubbin, on the stool beside you, looks from Byte to the window, then back to Byte._  
**You**: You’re just contradicting everything I say.  
**Byte**: Incorrect.  
_The sand is half gone. Thirty seconds left._  

**Choices**

- **Agree with Byte, to see what happens.**
    - **You**: You’re right. It’s a smudge.
    - **Byte**: It is clearly a rainbow.
    - Byte hears himself. He frowns. That was not supposed to happen.
- **Take a breath.**
    - You take a breath. Byte takes one too, in case that was a point.

#### `q16-win`

**You**: Hold on. You’re not giving me any reasons.  
**Byte**: I am.  
**You**: Saying “no” every time isn’t a reason. It’s just the opposite of what I said.  
**You**: A real argument goes: I think this, because of that.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): a good argument: a claim plus a reason  
> _A good argument has a claim (what you think) and a reason (why you think it)._  
> _Which of these is a real argument?_  
> - ✅ “It’s a rainbow, because it’s sunny and raining and the colours are in order.” → Yes. Claim: it’s a rainbow. Reason: sun, rain, colours in order. That beats “smudge” every time.
> - “Is.” “Isn’t.” “Is.” “Isn’t.” → That’s just saying the opposite, back and forth. Nobody learns anything. Add a reason: “because it’s sunny and raining”.
> - “It’s a rainbow, and you’re silly.” → Calling someone silly isn’t a reason, and it makes them less likely to listen. Give a reason instead.
> _For grown-ups: Told a real argument (a claim with a reason) apart from simple contradiction and name-calling._

_Byte opens his mouth to disagree. Then he stops, and looks at the sand timer for help._  
_The sand timer, being sand, offers none._  
**Byte**: …That is a fair point.  

**Choices**

- **Take it up with Complaints.**
    - You step next door. Byte swaps hats and steps next door too.
    - **Byte**: Complaints. Go on.
    - **You**: The argument man just said the opposite of everything.
    - **Byte**: Did he. I shall have a word with him.
    - He swaps hats, turns to face the empty stool, and has a long, stern word with himself.
- **Shake hands. Good game.**
    - **Byte**: It was not a game. It was a— yes. Fine. Good game.

#### `q16-complete`

_The last grain of sand drops. Byte stares at it for a long moment._  
**Byte**: Nobody has ever won before. Most people just get cross until the sand runs out.  
**Byte**: Disagreeing is easy. I have been doing it for years and calling it thinking.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): disagreeing vs thinking  
> _Byte says he has been disagreeing for years and calling it thinking._  
> _What’s the difference between disagreeing and really thinking?_  
> - Thinking means you might change your mind. → That’s a deep answer. Real thinkers listen, and sometimes the other person is right. Byte just found that out.
> - Thinking means having reasons. → A strong answer. Disagreeing with no reasons is just noise. With reasons, it’s thinking.
> - There isn’t one. Disagreeing is fine! → Fair: disagreeing is fine, and often useful. Byte might say the trouble starts when you disagree with everything.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between disagreeing and really thinking, such as having reasons and being open to changing your mind._

**Byte**: You may keep the timer. I will make another. I have a great deal of sand.  
**Byte**: And I am putting you on the board. Debate Club. Founding member. There are no other members.  
**You**: Is there a club?  
**Byte**: There is now. Do not argue.  

### Glossary

- **haggle**: To argue politely about a price, to try to make it lower.
- **negotiation**: Talking together to reach an agreement both sides can accept.
- **ceremony**: A special, serious way of doing something.
- **gravity**: The force that pulls things down towards the ground.
- **drizzling**: Raining lightly, in tiny drops.
- **contradict**: To say the opposite of what someone else has said.
- **claim**: Something you say is true.
- **debate**: A discussion where people give reasons for different sides.

## Q17. The Dock Dance

- `q17-s1`: Learn the steps of the dock dance. · _Open Karate on the dock. Tap in time with the beat markers: step, bow, tap._
- `q17-s2`: Dance the full performance on the dock. · _It is a timing bout on the karate screen. Hit every beat. The last beat is not yours to win._

#### `q17-intro`

_On the end of the dock, two Keepers in crisp white shirts and sun hats stand very straight._  
_Each holds a small, shiny rubber fish. They hold them the way other people hold violins._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): how fish breathe, and being fair to animals  
> _Why do you think the dancers use rubber fish, not real ones?_  
> - ✅ Real fish need to stay in water to breathe. → Quite right. Real fish breathe through gills, which take oxygen out of water. Out of the water, they can’t breathe. We would never.
> - Rubber fish are shinier. → They are rather shiny. But real fish breathe through gills, in water. We would never take one out.
> - Real fish are too heavy. → Some are! But the real reason is that real fish need water to breathe, through their gills. Rubber ones don’t mind.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real fish breathe through gills and need water, which is why the dancers use rubber fish._

**Mr Pilchard**: Good morning. Pilchard. This is Grampus. We are a dance society.  
**Mr Grampus**: Of two.  
**Mr Pilchard**: We perform the old dance of the dock. It is very formal. We have an opening for a third.  
**Mr Grampus**: The last third went in.  
_Mr Pilchard shows you: a small step, a bow, and a gentle tap on Mr Grampus’s cheek with the fish. Squeak._  
_Mr Grampus does it back. They both bow. Neither smiles. It is beautiful, in a confusing way._  
**Mr Grampus**: Will you dance?  

**Choices**

- **I’d be honoured.**
    - **Mr Pilchard**: Splendid. You will need a fish.
- **Do the fish mind?**
    - **Mr Grampus**: These ones are rubber. The real fish stay in the pond, where they are happy.
    - **Mr Pilchard**: The rubber ones were consulted. They squeaked yes.

#### `q17-learned`

_Step, bow, tap. Step, bow, tap. Your fish is a sprat: small, rubber and very squeaky._  
_It does its best._  
**Mr Pilchard**: Good. Very good. The wrist is a little eager.  
**Mr Grampus**: Eager wrists end up in the water.  
**Mr Pilchard**: Again. Feel the beat. Step on one, bow on two, tap on three.  

> **Lesson** (music, do): keeping a steady beat in threes  
> _Clap along: ONE, two, three. ONE, two, three. Keep it steady._  
> **Mr Pilchard**: A beat in threes, with the first one strongest, is the same pulse as a waltz. Very formal. Very us.  
> Check: `edu:clap:beat:step-bow-tap`
> _For grown-ups: Clapped a steady beat in groups of three, with the first beat strongest, like a waltz._

_Step, bow, tap. Squeak. Step, bow, tap. Squeak._  

#### `q17-performance`

**Mr Pilchard**: Now. The full performance. In front of the whole pond.  
_A small audience of Nubbins has gathered on the bank. One has brought a snack._  
**Mr Grampus**: Keep the timing. Whatever happens, keep the timing.  
_Mr Grampus reaches behind a crate and brings out a second rubber fish._  
_It is much, much bigger: a herring as long as a draught excluder._  
**You**: That’s not the same fish.  
**Mr Grampus**: It is the finale fish.  
**Mr Pilchard**: Your sprat is 10 centimetres long. The finale herring is 80.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): comparing lengths with division  
> _How many sprats, laid nose to tail, would make one finale herring?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes: 80 ÷ 10 = 8. Eight sprats long. That is a lot of finale.
> - 70 → 70 is how much LONGER it is. To find how many sprats fit, divide: 80 ÷ 10 = 8.
> - 90 → That’s 80 add 10. To find how many 10s fit into 80, count in tens: 10, 20, 30… 80. That’s 8 sprats.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that an 80 cm herring is 8 times as long as a 10 cm sprat (80 ÷ 10 = 8)._


> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): fish that live in shoals  
> **Mr Pilchard**: Real sprats and herring are cousins. They swim together in enormous groups called shoals.  
> **Mr Grampus**: In a crowd, it is much harder for a hungry bird to pick out just one. Safety in numbers.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real sprats and herring swim in big groups called shoals, which helps keep them safe._


**Choices**

- **Keep the timing.**
    - You set your feet. Your sprat trembles. Squeak.
- **Ask what the finale involves.**
    - **Mr Pilchard**: Water, mostly.
    - **Mr Grampus**: Gently, though. We are a very polite society.

#### `q17-splash`

_Step, bow, tap. Step, bow, tap. Perfect timing, every beat._  
_Then Mr Grampus swings the finale fish, very slowly and very gently._  
_Boing. It nudges your shoulder. You wobble. You wobble some more._  
_You topple off the dock into the pond with a soft splash._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced and unbalanced forces  
> _You were standing still, perfectly balanced. Then the herring pushed you._  
> _Why did you fall in?_  
> - ✅ The push was a force, and nothing balanced it. → Yes. When the forces on something are balanced, it stays still. The herring’s push made them unbalanced, so you moved. Splash.
> - The dock was slippery. → It might be! But here it was the push. A push with nothing to balance it makes things move.
> - The herring was magic. → Ha. Not magic, just a push. When a push isn’t balanced by anything, things move.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a push with nothing to balance it makes things move._

_The water is warm. A duck paddles over and looks at you. Its feathers are perfectly dry._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how ducks stay dry  
> _Ducks have a little gland near their tail that makes oil. They spread it over their feathers with their beaks._  
> _The oil keeps water out, so the duck stays dry. You, sadly, have no such gland._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that ducks spread oil on their feathers to keep water out._

_The Nubbins on the bank cheer as if this was the plan. It was._  

#### `q17-complete`

_You climb out. Mr Pilchard hands you a towel. Mr Grampus hands you the finale fish._  
**Mr Grampus**: Traditional. The one who goes in keeps the herring.  
**Mr Pilchard**: It is excellent for knocking fruit out of trees from a distance. Give it to your strongest Nubbin.  
**Mr Pilchard**: And you may keep the bow. It suits you.  
**Mr Grampus**: We dance it every morning. Usually for nobody.  
**Mr Grampus**: It is nice to be watched. But we would do it anyway.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): doing things for the joy of them  
> _Pilchard and Grampus dance every morning, even when nobody watches._  
> _Is there something you would do even if nobody ever saw it?_  
> - Yes, something I just love doing. → That’s a lovely answer. Doing things for the joy of it is one of the best feelings there is.
> - Not really. I like an audience. → That’s honest! Lots of people love sharing what they do. Even Grampus admits he likes being watched.
> - I’m not sure yet. → That’s fine. Noticing what you’d do with nobody watching is a good way to find out what you love.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what they would do even if nobody was watching, and why._

_Your Power Nubbins can now knock fruit down from afar with the herring. You also have a new karate victory pose._  

### Glossary

- **formal**: Done in a proper, serious way, following set rules.
- **society**: A club of people who share an interest.
- **eager**: Very keen; wanting to do something a lot.
- **finale**: The last, biggest part of a show.
- **draught excluder**: A long, stuffed cloth tube laid by a door to stop cold air getting in.
- **topple**: To wobble and fall over.
- **traditional**: Done the same way for a very long time.

## Q18. Fruit Defence Class

- `q18-s1`: Disarm the Nubbin with the banana. · _When the Nubbin swings the banana, tap Peel at the top of the swing._
- `q18-s2`: Catch every raspberry in the bowl. · _Slide the bowl left and right under the falling raspberries: five waves of eight. Missing three restarts the drill._
- `q18-s3`: Toss the pineapple to your Nubbin from across the clearing. · _Hold the pineapple, aim at your Nubbin and tap Throw. Your Nubbin will run to meet it._

#### `q18-intro`

_In the clearing, a Keeper with a moustache like a yard brush is pacing in front of a row of logs._  
_Three Nubbins sit on the logs. They look as if they were here first and have been told off for it._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: YOU! Late! Sit! On a log!  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Sergeant Grimble. Tonight’s class: what to do when somebody waves fresh fruit at you, with menace.  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Dried fruit is next week. Dried fruit is a whole different animal.  
_A Nubbin on the end log raises a paw._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: NO. Not sticks. Every class wants sticks. Tonight is FRUIT.  
_The Nubbin lowers its paw very slowly. It was going to ask about sticks._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: First. The banana. Somebody waves a banana at you, very meaningfully. What do you do?  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): why bananas are curved  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: Know your enemy. Bananas grow in big bunches, hanging from the plant.  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: As each one grows, it bends up towards the light. THAT is where the curve comes from. Sneaky.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bananas curve because they bend upwards towards the light as they grow._


**Choices**

- **Duck.**
    - **Sergeant Grimble**: DUCK? A banana CURVES, Keeper. It will find you.
- **Talk them down.**
    - **Sergeant Grimble**: With a BANANA in their hand? They are beyond reason!
- **Peel it.**
    - **Sergeant Grimble**: …Correct. Who told you? Nobody ever knows that.

#### `q18-banana`

_A Nubbin lunges at you with a banana._  
_You peel it in one smooth move: zip, zip, zip._  
_The Nubbin stares at the bare banana, deeply embarrassed._  
_It sits back down on its log and looks at its feet._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: TEXTBOOK! A peeled banana is a defeated banana!  
_The Nubbin’s ears droop a little lower._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): helping someone who feels embarrassed  
> _The Nubbin feels embarrassed. Its ears are drooping._  
> _What could you do to help it feel better?_  
> - ✅ Say “Good swing!” and offer it half the banana. → That’s kind. A friendly word and a share can turn embarrassed back into fine.
> - Laugh at it. → It IS a funny sight! But laughing at someone who already feels embarrassed makes it worse. A kind word helps more.
> - Ignore it. → Sometimes people want space. But a quick kind word, like “Good swing!”, usually helps.
> _For grown-ups: Chose a kind way to help someone who felt embarrassed._


#### `q18-raspberry`

**Sergeant Grimble**: Next. The raspberry. Small. Fast. Underestimated. The raspberry is a professional.  
**Sergeant Grimble**: It does not come alone. Where there is one raspberry, there are forty.  
_A Nubbin rises from its log holding a bowl of raspberries, eyes narrowed._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: They will come in five waves. Eight raspberries a wave.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Five waves. Eight raspberries in each wave._  
> _How many raspberries is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 40 → FORTY! Five eights are forty. As I said. I am never wrong about raspberries.
> - 13 → That’s 5 add 8. But there are five waves OF eight: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. That’s 40.
> - 35 → Close! That’s five sevens. Five eights: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 5 waves × 8 raspberries = 40._

**Sergeant Grimble**: Your defence is a bowl. Hold out a bowl. Catch them all. Leave none on the floor.  
**You**: Why can’t any land on the floor?  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Because they STAIN, Keeper. Do you want your floor to remember this?  

#### `q18-raspberry-done`

_Wave one. Wave two. Wave three. You slide the bowl left and right._  
_Wave four. Wave five. Forty raspberries. Forty catches._  
_Your bowl is full and the floor is spotless._  
_The Nubbin with the empty bowl looks at its paws, then at yours, then quietly eats one of yours._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Acceptable. Move on.  
_You look into the bowl. Each raspberry is a little cluster of tiny round bumps._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what a raspberry is made of  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: Each tiny bump is called a drupelet. Every drupelet has its own little seed inside.  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: So one raspberry is not one fruit. It is a whole squad. I respect that.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a raspberry is made of many tiny parts called drupelets, each with its own seed._


#### `q18-pineapple`

**Sergeant Grimble**: And now. The big one.  
_He lifts the cloth off a crate. In it sits a whole pineapple, prickly and enormous, wearing a small pair of sunglasses._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): protecting your eyes from the sun  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: Sensible sunglasses, mind. Bright sun can harm your eyes.  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: And never look straight at the Sun. Not even with sunglasses. Not even if a pineapple dares you.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bright sunlight can harm eyes and that we should never look straight at the Sun._

**Sergeant Grimble**: The pineapple. Spiky. Heavy. Thinks it’s better than you. It may be right.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): how pineapples grow  
> **Sergeant Grimble**: Know your enemy. Where do pineapples grow?  
> - ✅ In the middle of a low, spiky plant on the ground. → CORRECT. One pineapple grows in the middle of a low, spiky plant. Not on a tree. And it is really lots of little fruits, all joined together into one.
> - On tall trees, like coconuts. → Most people think so! But pineapples grow in the middle of a low, spiky plant, near the ground.
> - Underground, like potatoes. → Good guess, but no. They grow above the ground, in the middle of a low, spiky plant.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a pineapple grows in the middle of a low, spiky plant, not on a tree._

**Sergeant Grimble**: Nobody defends against the pineapple. You can only teach it to be on your side.  
**You**: How?  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Throw it. Gently. To your Nubbin. Let your Nubbin catch it, and you have an ally.  

**Choices**

- **Just toss it.**
    - **Sergeant Grimble**: No ceremony. I like it.
- **Take its sunglasses off first.**
    - **Sergeant Grimble**: Bold. Very bold. It respects that.

#### `q18-catch`

_You toss the pineapple, gently, in a high, slow curve._  
_Your Nubbin runs, jumps, and catches it in both arms with a soft “oof”._  
_It holds the pineapple up like a trophy._  
_The pineapple seems content with the arrangement._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): personification  
> _The pineapple “seems content”. Can a pineapple really feel content?_  
> - ✅ No. The writer gives it a human feeling, to be funny. → Yes. Giving human feelings to things that aren’t human is called personification. It turns the pineapple into a character.
> - Yes, pineapples have feelings. → In this story it seems to! But real pineapples can’t feel. The writer is using personification, for fun.
> - Only when it wears sunglasses. → Ha! The sunglasses help. But it’s the writer giving it human feelings. That’s called personification.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised personification: a writer giving human feelings to something that is not human._

**Sergeant Grimble**: Did you see that? Soft hands. Both arms. Textbook.  
_The three class Nubbins on the logs clap their paws. One claps a raspberry by mistake._  

#### `q18-complete`

**Sergeant Grimble**: CLASS DISMISSED!  
**Sergeant Grimble**: You are now qualified to face fresh fruit without fear. And, more importantly, to throw it.  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Between you and me, Keeper? Forty years, and not once has anybody attacked me with fruit.  
**Sergeant Grimble**: I have been ready the entire time. It has been exhausting.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): managing worries about things that may never happen  
> _Sergeant Grimble spent forty years ready for something that never happened._  
> _What could help someone who worries about things that probably won’t happen?_  
> - Talking to a friend about the worry. → That’s a wise answer. Saying a worry out loud often makes it smaller.
> - Checking how likely it really is. → Good thinking. Forty years, zero fruit attacks: the evidence says he can relax!
> - Doing something fun to take their mind off it. → That works for lots of people. Perhaps Grimble should join the dance on the dock.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ways to handle worries about unlikely things, such as talking, checking the evidence or doing something fun._

_He presses a battered brass whistle into your hand. It has clearly been blown a great deal._  
**Sergeant Grimble**: Blow that, and your Nubbins will look up. Throw, and they will catch. Any fruit. Any distance.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): sound is made by vibration  
> _When you blow the whistle, the air inside it shakes very fast. These shakes are called vibrations._  
> _The vibrations travel through the air to your Nubbins’ ears, and they hear a sound._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a whistle makes sound by making the air vibrate._

**Sergeant Grimble**: Except dried fruit. Next week. Bring a hat.  
_From now on, your Nubbins can catch fruit you toss to them from a distance._  

### Glossary

- **armed**: Holding a weapon. Or, tonight, a fruit.
- **embarrassed**: Feeling silly and uncomfortable because others saw something go wrong.
- **textbook**: Done exactly right, as if copied from a book of instructions.
- **underestimated**: Thought to be weaker or less important than it really is.
- **drupelet**: One of the tiny round bumps that make up a raspberry, each with a seed.
- **ally**: A friend who is on your side.
- **content**: Happy and satisfied.
- **personification**: Giving human feelings or actions to something that is not human.
- **qualified**: Trained and allowed to do something.
- **vibrations**: Very fast shaking movements, like the ones that make sound.

## Q19. The Grand Toffs’ Cup

- `q19-s1`: Enter the Grand Toffs’ Cup in the meadow. · _Sign the entry book on Mrs Thackery’s table._
- `q19-s2`: Win the Grand Toffs’ Cup. · _Run the course. Jump the matchboxes and step round the sleeping Keeper. Don’t wake them; it takes ages._

#### `q19-intro`

_A banner over the meadow reads: THE GRAND TOFFS’ CUP. ENTRANTS WELCOME. NO EXPERIENCE NEEDED, OR WANTED._  
**Mrs Thackery**: Roll up! The obstacle race! Three gentlemen entrants so far. We could do with a fourth.  
_The three gentlemen are standing on the start line. One of them is facing the wrong way._  
**The Hon. Bunty Fairweather-Flute**: I say. Is this the start or the end? It looks awfully like the start.  
**Piers Tumbledown-Hoop**: It’s the middle, Bunty. Everything is the middle, if you think about it.  
**Lord Algernon Spoon**: I have entered every year for nine years. I have never once found the start line. Tremendously exciting.  
_The finish flag is to the north. Bunty is looking south, at a cow._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions  
> _The finish flag is to the north. Bunty is facing south._  
> _Which way should Bunty turn to face the finish?_  
> - ✅ Turn right round, to face north. → Yes. North and south are opposites. A half turn takes Bunty from facing south to facing north.
> - Turn to face east. → East is only a quarter turn, towards the side of the course! North is opposite south: a half turn.
> - Stay facing south. → Then Bunty would run away from the finish, towards the cow. Turn halfway round to face north.
> _For grown-ups: Used north and south as opposites to turn a racer the right way._


**Choices**

- **Sign up.**
    - **Mrs Thackery**: Splendid! Pop your name in the book. Spell it however you like.
- **Turn Bunty round first.**
    - You turn Bunty round to face north. Bunty thanks you warmly, then turns back round, to be polite.

#### `q19-ready`

**Mrs Thackery**: Four entrants! Record turnout!  
**Mrs Thackery**: The course: one row of matchboxes, one low wall, one sleeping Keeper. Mind the Keeper.  
_There are six matchboxes in the row, laid end to end. Each one is 5 centimetres long._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying to find a length  
> _Six matchboxes, end to end. Each is 5 centimetres long._  
> _How long is the whole row?_  
> - ✅ 30 centimetres → Yes: 6 × 5 = 30. Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.
> - 11 centimetres → That’s 6 add 5. But there are six boxes OF 5 cm each: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. That’s 30 cm.
> - 65 centimetres → Hmm, that’s a 6 and a 5 side by side! Six lots of 5 cm is 6 × 5 = 30 cm.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that six 5 cm matchboxes laid end to end make 30 cm._

_At the far end of the course, a Keeper is snoring in a deckchair._  
_Nobody knows who put them there. Nobody likes to ask._  
**Lord Algernon Spoon**: Is that the start line? It’s very snory.  

#### `q19-race`

**Mrs Thackery**: On your marks! Get set!  
_A whistle blows. You run. Behind you, nobody else moves._  
**Mrs Thackery**: And the Keeper is away! Bunty is checking which way is forward. Piers is tying his shoelace. To Algernon’s shoelace.  
_At the matchboxes, Piers finally arrives and leaps each one with enormous effort, about 30 centimetres too high._  
**Lord Algernon Spoon**: I’ve found the start line! Hello, start line!  
_Bunty reaches the sleeping Keeper, stops, and taps them gently on the shoulder._  
**The Hon. Bunty Fairweather-Flute**: Frightfully sorry. Would you like to come? It’s ever so jolly.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): describing a character from their actions  
> _Bunty is in a race, but stops to invite the sleeping Keeper along._  
> _Which word best describes Bunty?_  
> - ✅ Kind → Yes. Bunty puts someone else ahead of winning. What a character DOES tells us who they are.
> - Fast → Bunty is not fast! Look at what Bunty does: stopping to include someone. That shows kindness.
> - Sneaky → Nothing sneaky here! Bunty stops to include someone who might feel left out. That’s kind.
> _For grown-ups: Used what a character does to choose a word that describes them (kind)._


**Choices**

- **Keep a straight face and run.**
    - You keep a perfectly straight face. It is the hardest thing you have ever done.
- **Laugh all the way to the finish.**
    - You laugh so hard you have to walk the last stretch. You are still miles ahead.

#### `q19-win`

**Mrs Thackery**: The Keeper wins! By a margin of… well. By everybody.  
_Piers comes second, trailing a very long shoelace._  
_Far behind, Algernon is waving goodbye to the start line as if seeing off a ship._  
_Bunty finishes last of all, having walked the whole course arm in arm with the sleeping Keeper._  
_The sleeping Keeper is still asleep._  
**Mrs Thackery**: Results! First, the Keeper. Second, Piers. Third, Bunty. Algernon: still saying goodbye.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about fair prizes: speed or kindness  
> _Bunty came last, but stopped to help someone along the way._  
> _Should there be a prize for helping, even in a race?_  
> - Yes. Kindness matters more than speed. → That’s a warm answer. You might be able to persuade Mrs Thackery.
> - No. A race prize is for the fastest. → That’s fair too. A race measures speed, and rules are rules. Maybe kindness needs a prize of its own.
> - Yes, but a different prize. → Clever. One prize for speed and another for kindness. Then both get noticed.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed whether helping someone should earn a prize in a race, thinking about rules and kindness._


**Choices**

- **Bunty should get a prize for stopping to help.**
    - **Mrs Thackery**: There isn’t a prize for that.
    - **You**: There should be.
    - **Mrs Thackery**: …There is now. It’s a slightly smaller hat.
    - Bunty accepts it with tears in both eyes, and puts it on the sleeping Keeper.
- **Accept graciously.**
    - You bow. Piers bows back. Algernon bows to the start line, which he has grown very fond of.

#### `q19-complete`

_The three gentlemen gather to congratulate you. Two of them congratulate a fence post first._  
**Piers Tumbledown-Hoop**: Jolly well run. Frightfully fast. We had no idea people could go in that direction.  
**The Hon. Bunty Fairweather-Flute**: Here. The prize. It’s a top hat. And the monocle’s from me. I’ve two more. I can’t find either.  
_The hat is tall and glossy. The monocle stays in only if you raise one eyebrow, permanently._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how a lens helps us see  
> _A monocle is a single lens, for one eye. A lens is a piece of curved glass that bends light._  
> _Bending the light the right way makes blurry things look sharp. Glasses are just two lenses joined together._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a lens is curved glass that bends light so blurry things look sharp._

**Lord Algernon Spoon**: Same time next year? That will be my tenth go. I shall start looking for the start line tonight.  
_The sleeping Keeper wakes, sees you in the top hat, and goes straight back to sleep._  

### Glossary

- **entrant**: Someone who has entered a race or competition.
- **obstacle**: Something in the way that you have to get over or round.
- **turnout**: The number of people who come to an event.
- **frightfully**: Very. A posh, old-fashioned way of saying it.
- **margin**: The amount by which someone wins.
- **graciously**: In a polite, kind way, especially when you have won.
- **monocle**: A single round lens worn in front of one eye.
- **congratulate**: To tell someone you are pleased about their success.

## Q20. The Larch Lesson

- `q20-s1`: Find and tap one of every kind of tree in the Grove. · _Your Grove has one tree for each fruit, plus the palm on the coast. Keep a tally: your journal ticks each one off._
- `q20-s2`: Photograph Mr Arbour’s board from the meadow. · _Open Photo mode, zoom in on the far ridge, and take the picture with the board in frame._

#### `q20-intro`

_At the orchard’s edge, a Keeper in a grey suit stands beside a signboard showing a tree._  
**Mr Arbour**: Good afternoon. Today we shall learn to recognise the different trees of the Grove.  
**Mr Arbour**: From quite near, mostly. My eyesight is not what it was.  
**Mr Arbour**: Tree number one.  
**Mr Arbour**: Behold. A larch.  
_He points at the picture. It is a tall, thin, pointy tree, quite unlike anything in your Grove._  
**You**: There aren’t any of those here.  
**Mr Arbour**: Correct. Tree number two.  
_He turns the board over. It is the same tree._  
**Mr Arbour**: Behold, once more. A larch.  
**You**: That’s the same tree.  
**Mr Arbour**: It is a larch. It is very important to recognise it. Particularly when it is absent.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how to recognise a larch  
> **Mr Arbour**: Since you ask, which you did not: the larch is a conifer. It grows cones, and needles instead of flat leaves.  
> **Mr Arbour**: Its needles grow in little tufts. And, unlike most conifers, in autumn they turn gold and fall off.  
> **Mr Arbour**: So in winter a larch can look quite bare. It is only waiting for spring.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a larch is a conifer with needles in tufts, and that unlike most conifers it drops its needles in autumn._

**Mr Arbour**: Your task: find one of every tree you DO have, and tap it. Recognise it. Up close.  

**Choices**

- **Is number three a larch?**
    - **Mr Arbour**: …Let us not get ahead of ourselves.
- **Off I go, then.**
    - **Mr Arbour**: I shall wait here, by my larch.

#### `q20-trees`

_Run, swim, fly, power, stamina, sun, moon, heart. Eight fruit trees._  
_Then the palm, on the coast, looking tired._  

> **Lesson** (maths, do): tallying and adding  
> _Make a tally mark for each kind of tree as you tap it._  
> _Eight fruit trees and one palm: 8 + 1 = 9 kinds. Larches: 0._  
> Check: `edu:tally:trees:9`
> _For grown-ups: Tallied each kind of tree as it was found: 8 fruit trees + 1 palm = 9 kinds._

_Each tree, once tapped, rustles slightly, as if pleased to be recognised._  
_You look closely at each one: the shape of its leaves, the feel of its bark, the fruit it bears._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): clues for identifying trees up close  
> _Up close, which clues help you tell one kind of tree from another?_  
> - ✅ Leaves, bark, fruit and shape: all of them. → Yes. Tree experts use every clue: leaf shape, bark, fruit or seeds, and the shape of the whole tree.
> - Only the colour. → Colour helps, but lots of trees are green! Leaves, bark, fruit and shape are better clues.
> - Only how tall it is. → Height changes as a tree grows. Leaves, bark, fruit and shape tell you much more.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that leaves, bark, fruit or seeds, and shape are all clues for identifying a tree._

_There is no larch. You check twice._  
_You feel, absurdly, that you have let Mr Arbour down._  

#### `q20-far`

**Mr Arbour**: Very good. Now the advanced class. Recognising a tree from quite a long way away.  
_He picks up his signboard and walks off with it. He keeps walking. He goes over the hill._  
_After a while, a tiny figure appears on the far ridge, holding up a tiny board._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): distance makes things look smaller  
> _Mr Arbour is exactly the same size as before. He only looks tiny because he is far away._  
> _The further away something is, the smaller it looks. Hold up your thumb: it can hide him completely._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that things look smaller the further away they are, even though their real size stays the same._

**Mr Arbour**: Can you see it?  
_You can just make out the board. It shows a tall, thin, pointy tree. Of course it does._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): identifying trees from far away by their outline  
> _From far away you can’t see needles or bark. What helps you recognise a tree from a distance?_  
> - ✅ Its outline: the shape of the whole tree. → Yes. From far away, the outline is the best clue, and a larch’s is tall and pointed. It’s called a silhouette.
> - Its leaves. → Too small to see from here! From far away, the outline of the whole tree is what you can see.
> - Its smell. → Not from the meadow! From far away, the best clue is the outline: the shape of the whole tree.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that from a distance a tree’s outline, or silhouette, is the best clue to what it is._

**Mr Arbour**: Take a photograph! I shall stand here until you do, which is fine! I have brought a sandwich!  

#### `q20-photo`

_You open Photo mode and zoom in, and in, and in._  
_Click._  
_The picture is mostly sky, a bit of hill, and one small, clear, unmistakable larch._  

> **Lesson** (art, ask): contrast in a picture  
> _The larch is tiny in your photo, but easy to spot. Why?_  
> - ✅ It stands out against the plain sky. → Yes. A dark shape against a plain, light background really stands out. Artists call that contrast.
> - Because it’s in the middle. → Being in the middle can help! But the big reason is contrast: dark board, light sky.
> - Because it’s the biggest thing. → It’s actually tiny! It stands out because of contrast: a dark shape against light sky.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a dark shape against a plain, light background stands out; artists call this contrast._

_Far away, a tiny Mr Arbour lowers the board._  
_He takes a dignified bite of his sandwich._  
_Even from here, you can tell it is cheese and pickle. You don’t know how._  

#### `q20-complete`

_Mr Arbour returns, slightly out of breath, and studies your photograph for a long time._  
**Mr Arbour**: Yes. That is a larch.  
**Mr Arbour**: Most people walk past every tree they own and never once look up. You tapped all of yours.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): noticing the everyday world around you  
> _Mr Arbour says most people never look up at their own trees._  
> _What’s something near you every day that you’ve never really looked at?_  
> - Something outside, like a tree or the sky. → Lovely. Next time you pass it, give it a proper look. Mr Arbour would be proud.
> - Something at home, like a picture on the wall. → Good one. Things we see every day can become almost invisible. Looking again can surprise you.
> - I’m not sure. That’s why I’ve never looked! → Ha! A very honest answer. Maybe today is the day to find out.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about something they pass every day but have never really looked at._

**Mr Arbour**: The larch was only there to get you looking. You are the first student ever to recognise it twice. Here. Plant your own.  
_He presses a small, winged seed into your palm. A larch seed: a new tree for your Grove._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, do): the life cycle of a tree  
> _Put the larch’s life in order: seed, seedling, young tree, grown tree with cones, new seeds._  
> **Mr Arbour**: Larch seeds grow inside the cones. They have little wings, so the wind can carry them off to grow somewhere new.  
> Check: `edu:order:larch-life-cycle`
> _For grown-ups: Put the stages of a larch’s life cycle in order, from seed to cones and new seeds._

**Mr Arbour**: And a little button for your camera. Press it, and the picture turns into something else entirely.  
_Photo mode has a new button that swaps to a random filter._  
_Mr Arbour walks back to the orchard edge to stand beside nothing._  
_A very large foot comes down out of the sky, considers the orchard, and goes back up again. Nobody mentions it._  

### Glossary

- **recognise**: To know what something is because you have seen it before.
- **conifer**: A tree that grows cones, usually with needles instead of flat leaves.
- **bark**: The tough outer skin of a tree’s trunk and branches.
- **absurdly**: In a silly, unreasonable way.
- **silhouette**: The dark outline of something, seen against a light background.
- **ridge**: A long, narrow hilltop.
- **contrast**: A big difference between two things, like dark against light.
- **dignified**: Calm, serious and proud.
- **seedling**: A very young plant that has just grown from a seed.

## Q21. Bear Comes Too

- `q21-s1`: Mr. Tweed has lost his bear. Follow his pointing down to the pond and look for a clue. · _Search the reeds on the near side of the pond. Clues sparkle faintly when you are close._
- `q21-s2`: Follow the little wild Nubbin up the western hill and find where it took the bear. · _Wild Nubbins nest in the long grass near the top. Walk slowly: if you run, it will hide._
- `q21-s3`: Carry Bear back down to Mr. Tweed. · _He is still sulking on his rock by the pond. Hand him the bear with Give._

#### `q21-intro`

_A man in a tweed jacket is standing at his gate, patting every pocket he owns. Some of them twice._  
_He looks inside his hat. He looks under a stone._  
_He lifts a sleeping duck, peers underneath, and puts it back with a sorry little pat._  
_This is Mr. Tweed. He lives at the end of the lane, and nobody has ever heard him finish a sentence._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hnn.  
_He holds his hands apart, about as far as a school ruler is long. Then he hugs the empty air, very tenderly._  
_He points at the empty space in his arms, then at you, then at the empty space again._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): reading body language  
> _Mr. Tweed hasn’t said a single proper word. But his body is saying a lot._  
> _What is he telling you?_  
> - ✅ He has lost something he loves. → Yes. The patting, the searching, the hug with nothing in it: he’s showing you the shape of what’s missing.
> - He wants a hug. → Close! But the hug is for something that isn’t there. He’s showing you the shape of something he has lost.
> - He’s doing a silly dance. → It does look a bit like one! But look again: pockets, hat, under a stone. He’s searching for something he loves.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what someone was feeling and asking for from their actions alone, with no words._

**You**: Something’s missing?  
**Mr. Tweed**: Bear.  
_He makes two little ears on top of his head with his fingers, in case you were unsure about the bear._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): choosing sensible units of length  
> _His hands were about a school ruler apart. A school ruler is 30 centimetres long._  
> _So about how long is the bear?_  
> - ✅ About 30 centimetres. → Yes: about as long as your ruler. Small enough to hug, big enough to miss.
> - About 30 metres. → 30 metres is longer than a swimming pool! That bear wouldn’t fit in any pocket. Metres are for big things like rooms. Centimetres are for small things, like bears. About 30 centimetres.
> - About 30 millimetres. → 30 millimetres is only 3 centimetres: about as long as a grape. Far too small to hug! The bear is about 30 centimetres.
> _For grown-ups: Chose centimetres, not metres or millimetres, as the sensible unit for a small object._

_Then he points down the lane towards the pond, very firmly, and nods as if that settles everything._  

**Choices**

- **I’ll help you look.**
    - **Mr. Tweed**: Mm!
    - He shakes your hand with both of his, for slightly too long.
- **What does the bear look like?**
    - He mimes it: small, brown, one chewed ear, and a look of enormous dignity.
    - You are not sure how he mimed the dignity. But he did.
- **Ask your Nubbin to sniff it out.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs Mr. Tweed’s sleeve, sneezes, and trots off towards the pond.
    - **Mr. Tweed**: Ah!

#### `q21-scarf`

_In the reeds at the edge of the pond, something catches your eye._  
_It’s a tiny knitted scarf. It is exactly bear-sized, and slightly damp._  
_Mr. Tweed arrives at a jog, sees the scarf, and clutches it to his chest._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Ohh.  
_He looks at the pond. He looks under a lily pad. He looks at the sky, in case bears can fly._  
_There is no bear._  
_He sulks so hard that his whole face folds in, like a letter going back into its envelope._  
**You**: The scarf is here, but the bear isn’t. So where did it go?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): using clues to make an inference  
> _Be a detective. The scarf is here. The bear is not. What do the clues tell you?_  
> - ✅ Something carried the bear away, and the scarf fell off. → Good detective work. A bear can’t walk off by itself, so something must have carried it. The scarf slipped off on the way.
> - The bear fell in the pond. → It’s a fair worry! But Mr. Tweed checked the pond. And a bear that fell in would probably float. More likely, something carried it away and the scarf slipped off.
> - The bear went for a walk. → Ha! In a story, maybe. But this bear can’t walk. Something must have carried it, and the scarf fell off on the way.
> _For grown-ups: Used two clues in the story to work out something the story doesn’t say straight out._


#### `q21-sulk`

_Mr. Tweed sits on a rock and sulks. It is a big, proper sulk, with the bottom lip and everything._  
_Every so often he glances up the western hill. Then away. Then up again._  
**You**: Is the bear up there?  
_He shrugs. It is a very small shrug, about the size of a bear._  
_Then he points. A wild Nubbin is waddling uphill with something brown in its arms._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-2, notice): animals line their nests with soft things  
> _Lots of animals carry soft things home to line their nests._  
> _Birds use moss, grass and feathers, and even tufts of sheep’s wool. A soft nest keeps eggs and babies warm._  
> _To a wild Nubbin, a small brown bear would make a very fine nest indeed._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals collect soft materials to build and line their nests, changing the place around them._

**Mr. Tweed**: Hm!  
_He stands, marches three steps after it, remembers he is sulking, and sits back down._  
_He folds his arms. The sulk resumes, a bit louder, for anyone who might be watching._  
_He waves you on. This is your job now. He has a sulk to finish._  

#### `q21-nest`

_Near the top of the western hill, the long grass has been pressed into a round, cosy nest._  
_In the middle, a wild Nubbin is fast asleep. It is cuddling a small brown bear._  
_The bear has one chewed ear and, somehow, a look of great dignity._  
_The Nubbin’s tummy goes up and down. It gives a tiny snore._  
_It doesn’t know the bear belongs to anyone. It just found something soft to love._  
_You need the bear back. But the little Nubbin looks so happy._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): being gentle and fair with animals  
> _How could you get the bear back without upsetting the little Nubbin?_  
> - ✅ Slowly and gently, and leave it something else to cuddle. → That’s kind and fair. Mr. Tweed gets his bear, and the little one still has something to hold.
> - Grab it fast, before it wakes up. → That might work. But waking up to a grab is a horrible shock, and wild creatures can learn to be scared of people. Slow and gentle is better, and it’s fair to leave it something else.
> - Shout “Give it back!” → It’s fair to want the bear back! But a shout would frighten it, and it didn’t mean any harm. Slow and gentle works better, and you could leave it something to cuddle instead.
> _For grown-ups: Chose a way to solve a problem that was fair to a small animal as well as to the owner._


**Choices**

- **Ease the bear out gently.**
    - The Nubbin stirs, sighs, and lets go. You leave it a piece of fruit to cuddle instead.
    - It hugs the fruit and goes straight back to sleep.
- **Offer the little scarf in trade.**
    - The Nubbin sniffs the scarf and wraps it round its own neck. It looks very smart. Fair trade.
    - Mr. Tweed may have opinions about the scarf.

#### `q21-carry`

_The bear is lighter than it looks, and it looks very light._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): choosing units of mass: grams and kilograms  
> _If you wanted to weigh this light little bear, which unit would you use?_  
> - ✅ Grams → Yes. Grams are for light things, like apples, letters and small bears.
> - Kilograms → A kilogram is 1,000 grams. That’s as heavy as a big bag of sugar: far too heavy for this little bear. Grams are better for light things.
> - Metres → Metres tell you how long something is, not how heavy. For a light bear, use grams.
> _For grown-ups: Chose grams as the right unit for weighing a light object, and heard that 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams._

_Your Nubbin wants to carry it. It holds the bear the way Mr. Tweed did: very seriously, with both arms._  
_Down by the pond, a tweed shape is still sulking on its rock._  
_He hasn’t seen you yet. He is trying very hard not to look up the hill._  
_Your Nubbin hides the bear behind its back. The bear is wider than its back._  
_A chewed ear sticks out on one side. A paw sticks out on the other._  
**You**: Ready? Let’s surprise him.  

#### `q21-complete`

_Mr. Tweed sees the bear. His face unfolds all at once, like a deckchair snapping open._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understanding a simile  
> _“His face unfolds like a deckchair snapping open.” Comparing two things using “like” or “as” is called a simile._  
> _What is this simile telling you?_  
> - ✅ His sad, folded-up face opened into a big happy one, all at once. → Exactly. A deckchair goes from flat and folded to wide open in one snap. So did his face.
> - He looks like a piece of furniture. → Ha! Not quite. A simile borrows one picture to describe another. A deckchair snaps from folded to wide open in one go. His face went from sad to happy just as fast.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile (a comparison using “like”) tells us about a character’s face._

**Mr. Tweed**: Bear!  
_He hugs the bear. He checks its chewed ear, then its good ear, then the chewed one again._  
_He tucks it into his top pocket, so only its head pokes out._  
_Then he notices your Nubbin, gazing at the bear with enormous longing._  
_Mr. Tweed holds up one finger. He rummages in his jacket, then his trousers, then, briefly, his sock._  
_Out comes a second bear, no bigger than your thumb. He places it on your shoulder, very solemnly._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Bear.  
_It stays there. It seems to like the view._  
_That evening you pass his window. He is laying the table: two plates, one of them very small._  
_He pulls out the small chair first._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): thinking about loneliness and company  
> _Mr. Tweed lives on his own. Tonight he has set a place at the table for his bear._  
> _Why do you think he does that?_  
> - Bear is his friend, and friends eat together. → That’s a lovely answer. To Mr. Tweed, Bear isn’t just a toy. Bear is company.
> - He might be lonely. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Living alone can feel lonely, and a bear across the table helps a little. Maybe a neighbour could help a little more.
> - It’s just a funny joke. → It is funny! And lots of funny things have a little bit of sad tucked inside them. Both can be true at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone who lives alone might set a place at the table for a toy._


### Glossary

- **tenderly**: In a gentle, loving way.
- **dignity**: A calm, proud, serious way of being that makes others respect you.
- **clutches**: Holds something tightly, as if afraid to lose it.
- **sulk**: To be quiet and grumpy because you feel upset or let down.
- **resumes**: Starts again after a pause.
- **grams**: Small units for measuring how heavy something is. 1,000 grams make 1 kilogram.
- **simile**: A way of describing something by comparing it to something else, using “like” or “as”.
- **solemnly**: In a very serious way, as if something is important.

## Q22. The Armchair Drive

- `q22-s1`: Help Mr. Tweed tie the armchair on top of his hand cart. · _Use rope from your bag on the cart, then tap each corner of the chair to tie it down. Four corners, four knots._
- `q22-s2`: Clear the path to Mr. Tweed’s house before the cart gets there, so nothing falls off. · _Lift the branch, carry the sleeping Nubbin to the grass at the side, and unhook the washing line. The cart won’t stop for you._

#### `q22-shop`

_At the market, Mr. Tweed has bought an armchair. It is green, deep and enormous._  
_His hand cart stands beside it. The whole cart is about as big as the chair’s cushion._  
_He lifts one end of the chair and looks at the cart. Then he lifts the other end, in case that end is smaller._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hnn.  
_He tries the chair upside down. He tries it on its side._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): finding a difference in length (will it fit?)  
> _Will it fit? Let’s measure. The armchair is 95 centimetres wide. The cart is 60 centimetres wide._  
> _How much wider is the chair than the cart?_  
> - ✅ 35 centimetres → Yes: 95 take away 60 is 35. The chair is 35 centimetres too wide to go in the cart. And turning it upside down doesn’t make it one bit smaller!
> - 45 centimetres → Nearly! Let’s check by counting on: 60 add 35 makes 95. So the chair is 35 centimetres wider.
> - 155 centimetres → That’s the two added together. To find how much wider, take away instead: 95 take away 60 is 35.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted two measurements in centimetres to find how much too big something is._

_He sits in it and tries to push the cart with his feet. The cart is too far away._  
_Then a light comes on behind his eyes. He points at the chair, then at the top of the cart, then mimes a knot._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Rope!  
_He looks at you the way people look at someone who definitely has rope._  

**Choices**

- **Hand over some rope.**
    - He takes it with a little bow and starts a knot that goes under, over, and somehow through himself.
- **Is this a good idea?**
    - **Mr. Tweed**: Mm.
    - He nods firmly, which answers a different question. You fetch some rope.
- **We could just carry it.**
    - He looks at you, at the chair, and at the long road home. Then he gives a tiny, pitying shake of the head.

#### `q22-tied`

_The chair sits on top of the cart, tied down at all four corners._  
_It is also tied, by accident, to a lamp post._  
_You untie the lamp post. Mr. Tweed says sorry to it with a small bow._  
_He climbs up into the armchair and settles in, very pleased with himself._  
_The cart creaks. Up there, the chair and Mr. Tweed are a long way off the ground._  
_He wobbles left. He wobbles right. He grips the armrests and stays very, very still._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): top-heavy loads tip easily  
> _When a load has lots of weight high up, we call it top-heavy. Top-heavy things tip over easily._  
> _Where should the heavy part of a load go, to keep a cart steady?_  
> - ✅ Low down and in the middle → Yes. The lower and more central the weight, the harder it is to tip. That’s why lorries carry their heaviest loads near the floor, not stacked on the roof.
> - High up on top → That’s exactly where Mr. Tweed is sitting! Weight up high makes a cart wobbly and tippy. Low down and in the middle is steadiest.
> - Hanging off one side → Then the cart would lean that way and might tip over. Low down and in the middle is steadiest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a load is steadiest when its weight is low down and in the middle._

_Then he takes a long stick, pokes the ground behind him, and the cart begins to roll._  

#### `q22-road`

_The cart wobbles off down the lane. Mr. Tweed steers by leaning, and now and then by stick._  
_Up in the armchair, he can’t see the ground. He can see the sky, the trees and the birds. He waves at them._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Ooh.  
_Ahead you spot three obstacles: a fallen branch, a Nubbin asleep in the path, and a rather low washing line._  
_You’ll have to run ahead and clear the way. Anything that hits the cart falls off the cart._  
_Including, probably, Mr. Tweed._  
_Then the lane tips downhill. The cart notices at once and speeds up._  
_Mr. Tweed notices much later. He grips the armrests and lifts both feet off the ground, as if that will help._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity speeds things up on a slope  
> _Mr. Tweed has stopped pushing with his stick. So why is the cart going faster?_  
> - ✅ The slope: gravity is pulling it downhill. → Exactly. Gravity always pulls things down. On a slope, that pull rolls the cart forward, faster and faster. Lifting his feet doesn’t help at all. But it does look very brave.
> - Because he lifted his feet. → He’d like to think so! But his feet weren’t touching anything. The real pull is gravity, dragging the cart down the slope.
> - The wind is pushing it. → Wind can push things, but there isn’t much today. The cart sped up when the lane tipped downhill. That’s gravity.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a cart speeds up downhill because gravity pulls it, an unbalanced force._


**Choices**

- **Sprint ahead.**
    - You sprint. Behind you, Mr. Tweed hums a little driving tune that he has just made up.
- **Send your Nubbin to wake the sleeper.**
    - Your Nubbin trots ahead and pokes the sleeping one. It rolls over, which is not the same as moving.

#### `q22-arrive`

_The cart rolls up to Mr. Tweed’s gate and stops against it with a gentle bonk._  
_His hat flies off. He catches it with one foot and flicks it back onto his head._  
_He looks round to see if anyone saw. You saw. You give him a thumbs up._  
_Nothing has fallen off, technically._  
_Mr. Tweed checks anyway: himself, the chair and the stick, in that order._  
_The chair has slid sideways. One rope is holding on by a single, very tired knot._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): working out a word from context  
> _“Nothing has fallen off, technically.” What does “technically” mean here?_  
> - ✅ It’s true by the exact rules, but only just. → Yes. Nothing fell all the way off, so it’s true. But one tired knot is all that saved the chair!
> - Using lots of machines. → Good thinking: “technical” can be about machines and gadgets. But here “technically” means “by the exact rules”. It’s true, but only just.
> - Very carefully. → Mr. Tweed was not very careful! Here “technically” means “by the exact rules”. Nothing fell off, but only just.
> _For grown-ups: Used the story around a word to work out what “technically” means._

**Mr. Tweed**: Ha!  

#### `q22-complete`

_Mr. Tweed climbs down. He looks at the chair. He looks at his small front door. He goes very quiet._
