**King Rumbold**: You passed. All three. Do you know why I set them?  
**Pemba**: To see if we were brave?  
**King Rumbold**: No. To see if you’d have fun. Most people forget how to play. I wanted to see if you remembered.  
**Tuk**: That’s… surprisingly wise.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think question: why play matters  
> **King Rumbold**: Most people forget how to play as they grow up. Why do you think playing matters, even for kings?  
> - It makes you happy, and happy people are kinder. → Ha! Yes. A happy king makes fewer silly laws. Mostly.
> - You learn things when you play. → Exactly! You learned about slopes today, and you never even noticed.
> - It helps you make friends. → It does! I have never once made a friend while doing paperwork.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why play matters for people of every age._

**King Rumbold**: I know! Now take a bit of my mail chute. And my laugh. I have plenty.  
**King Rumbold**: Biscuit also says thank you. He is saying it by eating your hat.

### Glossary

- **throne**: A special chair for a king or queen.
- **bray**: The loud, harsh noise a donkey makes.
- **impressed**: Feeling that someone has done something surprising or very good.
- **bleats**: Makes the shaky cry of a goat or a sheep.
- **thoughtfully**: In a way that shows you are thinking hard.
- **wails**: Cries out loudly and sadly.
- **opponent**: The person or team you play against.
- **hulking**: Very big and heavy-looking.
- **chute**: A sloping slide or tube that things slide down.
- **steeply**: Going up or down at a sharp angle.

## Q64. Kaito’s Big Speech

- `q64-s1`: Help Kaito rehearse his speech three times. · _Pick the advice you think helps. Each try, he gets a little less awful._
- `q64-s2`: Stand by Kaito while he asks to join the group. · _Stay close to the campfire. Kaito does better with someone friendly beside him._

#### `q64-rehearse`

_Behind a broken pillar, you find Kaito pacing in circles, muttering to a rock._  
**Kaito**: Oh! Keeper. I wasn’t… I’m not talking to a rock. Why would I be talking to a rock.  
**Kaito**: Fine. I was talking to the rock. I’m practising. I want to ask Pemba if I can join his group.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): practice makes hard things easier  
> _Practising out loud is a real trick. Actors, singers and sports players all rehearse before the big moment._  
> _Each try helps your brain and your mouth learn the way. It gets a little easier every time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rehearsing out loud makes a hard moment easier._

**Kaito**: The problem is, I keep getting it wrong. Last time I said “I have changed” and then stood there for a whole minute.  
_Your Nubbin climbs onto the rock and sits on it, as if it were the audience._  
**Kaito**: Can you listen? Tell me if it’s bad. It’s going to be bad. Okay. Here goes.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): kind self-talk  
> _Kaito just told himself, “It’s going to be bad.” What could he say to himself instead?_  
> - ✅ “I can do this. If I muddle it, I can try again.” → …That sounds better than what’s usually in my head.
> - “I’m hopeless.” → That’s what Kaito usually tells himself, and it makes him more nervous. Kinder words, like “I can try again”, help much more.
> - “Everyone will laugh at me.” → Worries like that make it harder. Telling yourself “I can try again” is kinder, and it really helps.
> _For grown-ups: Practised swapping a worried thought for kind, encouraging self-talk._

**Kaito**: Pemba. Greetings. I am… a person. Who used to be… the bad kind of person. But now I’m the good kind. Probably. Thanks.  

**Choices**

- **Tell him it’s a bit stiff**
    - **Kaito**: Stiff. Right. I can do less stiff. I think.
- **Tell him it’s a good start**
    - **Kaito**: Really? You’re not just saying that?
    - You are just saying that, a little.
- **Suggest he smiles**
    - Kaito smiles. It looks like it hurts. Your Nubbin hides behind the rock.
    - **Kaito**: Too much?

#### `q64-rehearse-done`

**Kaito**: Attempt two. “Pemba. I have brought you a gift. The gift is me.”  
_Your Nubbin falls off the rock._  
**Kaito**: No. Awful. Attempt three. “I’m sorry. I want to help.”  
_It is the shortest one. It is also, by far, the best._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): saying something clearly  
> _Why is attempt three the best one?_  
> - ✅ It says clearly what he feels and what he wants. → Yes. “I’m sorry” says how he feels. “I want to help” says what he wants. Nothing extra gets in the way.
> - It has the most words. → It has the fewest! Short can be strong: “I’m sorry. I want to help” says exactly what he means.
> - It rhymes. → It doesn’t rhyme, actually. It’s best because it says clearly what he feels and what he wants.
> _For grown-ups: Compared three versions of a speech and explained why the short, clear one works best._

**Kaito**: Okay. Okay. I think that’s it. Short and friendly. Short and friendly.  
**Kaito**: What if I just wave? Waving is friendly. Isn’t it?  

#### `q64-ask`

_Pemba, Nalu, Tuk and Bao sit round a campfire in the ruins. Kaito steps out of the shadows. Everyone jumps._  
**Tuk**: Oh good. A surprise prince. Exactly what this evening needed.  
**Bao**: Relax. His heart’s going like a rabbit’s. He’s more scared than you are.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, notice): what fear does to your body, and how to calm it  
> **Bao**: When you’re scared, your heart beats faster and you breathe faster. That’s your body getting ready for trouble.  
> _Slow, deep breaths can help your body calm down again. Try it: in through your nose, and slowly out through your mouth._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fear speeds up the heartbeat and breathing, and that slow breaths help calm the body._

_Kaito raises one hand in a stiff little wave. Then he forgets to put it down._  
**Kaito**: Um. Hi. Hello. It’s me. Hi.  
**Kaito**: …That was not the speech. That was not any of the speeches.  
**Nalu**: What do you want, Kaito?  
_Kaito looks at you. Your Nubbin looks at you. Everyone, suddenly, is looking at you._  

**Choices**

- **Tell them he’s been practising for hours**
    - **Pemba**: Practising? For us? Kaito, that’s the nicest thing anyone’s ever done badly.
- **Nudge him to try again**
    - **Kaito**: I’m sorry. I want to help. I was wrong about a lot of things. I want to be on your side, if you’ll let me.
- **Wave back**
    - You wave back. Pemba waves too. Bao waves in entirely the wrong direction, on purpose.

#### `q64-ask-done`

**Pemba**: Okay. You can join. Welcome to the team!  
**Kaito**: Really? Just like that?  
**Tuk**: No. Not just like that. There will be a trial period. With paperwork.  
**Nalu**: I haven’t forgotten what you did, Kaito.  
**Kaito**: Good. You shouldn’t. I don’t want you to forget it. I want the chance to be more than it.  
**Nalu**: …One chance.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): think question: second chances  
> _Nalu is still hurt by what Kaito did before. But she gives him one chance._  
> _When someone has hurt you and says sorry, should you give them another chance?_  
> - Yes, if they really mean it. → That’s what I’m trying. I’ll be watching to see if he means it.
> - Only after they show they’ve changed. → Exactly. Hence the paperwork.
> - You can forgive them and still be careful. → Yes. That’s exactly how I feel. Both at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about forgiveness and how trust can be rebuilt after someone says sorry._


#### `q64-complete`

_Later, Kaito finds you by the pillar. His hand is still slightly raised, as if it got stuck._  
**Kaito**: Thank you. For listening. And for the rock.  
**Kaito**: I’m still not good at this. Talking. People. Waving.  
**Kaito**: But I think I got a bit better today. Three tries, and the last one was nearly normal.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how a character changes  
> _Think back to Kaito muttering to a rock. How has he changed since then?_  
> - ✅ He’s braver about saying what he really feels. → Yes. He started with stiff, silly speeches. He ended by saying sorry, simply and honestly.
> - He hasn’t changed at all. → He’s still awkward! But he went from talking to a rock to saying sorry to real people. That’s a big change.
> - He’s become a great speech-maker. → Not quite yet! But he’s braver about saying what he feels, and that matters more.
> _For grown-ups: Described how a character changed from the start of the story to the end._

_He waves at you. It is stiff, awkward and slightly too long._  
_Your Nubbin copies it perfectly. Kaito pretends not to be pleased. He is extremely pleased._  

### Glossary

- **pacing**: Walking up and down, often because you feel nervous.
- **rehearse**: To practise something before you do it for real.
- **attempt**: A try at doing something.
- **awkward**: Clumsy or uncomfortable, especially around other people.

## Q65. The White Lotus

- `q65-s1`: Learn the tile game: finish Uncle Tenzo’s practice round. · _Grow flowers in the middle and block with rocks at the edge. Uncle Tenzo will point out mistakes, kindly._
- `q65-s2`: Win a game of tiles against Uncle Tenzo. · _Save your lotus tile for last. It can’t be blocked, and it changes the whole board._

#### `q65-tiles`

_Rain patters on the leaves. Under the big tree, Uncle Tenzo has laid out a round wooden board and a box of painted tiles._  
**Uncle Tenzo**: Ah, Keeper. Will you keep an old man company? This game is no fun alone. I always win, and then I feel bad.  
_The tiles show flowers, rocks and wind. One tile, set apart from the rest, shows a single white lotus._  
**Uncle Tenzo**: The rules are simple. Flowers grow. Rocks block. Wind moves things. The lotus does nothing at all.  
**Uncle Tenzo**: Which is, of course, why it is the most important tile.  
**Kaito**: Uncle, every time you explain this game, it gets more confusing.  
**Uncle Tenzo**: That is how you know it is a good game, nephew. The rules are easy. The game is not.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): work out what a character means  
> _Uncle Tenzo says, “The rules are easy. The game is not.” What does he mean?_  
> - ✅ Learning the rules is quick, but playing well takes practice. → Just so. You can learn the rules over one cup of tea. Playing well takes many pots.
> - The rules are secretly very hard. → No, no. The rules really are easy! It is using them well that takes time and practice.
> - The game is impossible to win. → Not impossible. I have lost twice. Learning the rules is quick; playing well takes practice.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the meaning behind a character’s saying: easy rules, but skill takes practice._

_Your Nubbin picks up a flower tile and sniffs it hopefully. It is wood. It is disappointed._  

**Choices**

- **Ask him to teach you properly**
    - **Uncle Tenzo**: With pleasure. First lesson: a tile placed in a hurry is a tile you will stare at all game.
- **Ask what the lotus tile does**
    - **Uncle Tenzo**: Patience. In this game, and perhaps outside it, the quiet ones matter most.
- **Ask if there are snacks**
    - **Uncle Tenzo**: There are always snacks. A board game without snacks is a punishment.

#### `q65-tiles-done`

_You play slowly. Uncle Tenzo points out mistakes kindly, and only once each._  
_Your flowers spread in a growing pattern. Turn one: 1 flower. Turn two: 3. Turn three: 5. Turn four: 7._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): find the rule in a number pattern  
> **Uncle Tenzo**: 1, 3, 5, 7… Can you see the rule? How many flowers will there be on turn five?  
> - ✅ 9 → Yes! The rule is “add 2” each turn: 7 add 2 is 9. A pattern tells you the future better than any fortune teller.
> - 8 → Close. But each turn adds 2, not 1: 1, 3, 5, 7… so next comes 9.
> - 14 → That would be doubling 7. But the rule is “add 2”: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
> _For grown-ups: Found the rule “add 2” in the pattern 1, 3, 5, 7 and used it to predict the next number._

**Uncle Tenzo**: Good. You don’t rush. You look at the whole board, not just your own tile. That is rare.  
**Kaito**: He says that to everyone.  
**Uncle Tenzo**: I have never said it to you, nephew.  
**Kaito**: …  

#### `q65-game`

**Uncle Tenzo**: Now, a real game. I will not go easy on you. I will go medium.  
_The rain grows heavier. The tea grows cold. Kaito falls asleep against the tree trunk, snoring gently._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from hot things to cooler things  
> **Uncle Tenzo**: My tea has gone cold again. It always does when the game is good.  
> _Heat always moves from hot things to cooler things. The hot tea warms the air around it, and loses its own heat._  
> _It keeps cooling until the tea and the air are the same temperature._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat moves from a hot drink into the cooler air until they are the same temperature._

**Uncle Tenzo**: Do you know why I love this game? Because every tile matters, but no tile wins alone.  
**Uncle Tenzo**: A general learns that slowly. A gardener learns it quickly. Be a gardener, Keeper.  
**Uncle Tenzo**: And if you lose, do not sulk. A lost game is a lesson the board gives you for free.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a metaphor  
> _Uncle Tenzo says a lost game is “a lesson the board gives you for free”. What does he mean?_  
> - ✅ Losing teaches you something, so it isn’t wasted. → Exactly. Every loss shows you a move you will never make again.
> - The board can talk. → Ha! I wish. No: it means a loss teaches you something, like a lesson you didn’t have to pay for.
> - You have to pay if you lose. → The opposite! It costs nothing, and it teaches you something. That is a good deal.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor comparing a lost game to a free lesson._

_Your Nubbins sit in a row by the board, watching each move like it is the most exciting thing in the world._  
**Uncle Tenzo**: Hmm. That was a clever move. Did you mean it, or was it luck?  

**Choices**

- **Say you meant it**
    - **Uncle Tenzo**: Then I am in trouble.
- **Admit it was luck**
    - **Uncle Tenzo**: Honest! Luck is kinder to honest players than you would think.
- **Point at your Nubbin**
    - **Uncle Tenzo**: Ah! A Nubbin with a strategic mind! I should have known.

#### `q65-game-done`

_You place your last tile, the white lotus. Nothing can block it._  
_Flowers bloom across the board. The pattern is symmetrical: the left side is a mirror of the right._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry in a square  
> **Uncle Tenzo**: Each tile is a square. How many lines of symmetry does a square have?  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes! Top to bottom, side to side, and corner to corner both ways. Four ways to fold it so the halves match.
> - 2 → Two is a good start: top to bottom and side to side. You can also fold it corner to corner, both ways. Four!
> - 1 → There are more! Top to bottom, side to side, and both diagonals. A square has four lines of symmetry.
> _For grown-ups: Found the four lines of symmetry of a square._

**Uncle Tenzo**: Beaten! Fair and square! What a happy afternoon!  
_Uncle Tenzo sits back and smiles, very wide. He looks happier than if he had won._  
**Uncle Tenzo**: Shake my hand, Keeper. A good winner is as rare as a good loser. I think you are both.  
**Kaito**: (sleepily) Did someone win? Was it me?  

#### `q65-complete`

**Uncle Tenzo**: Keep this. The white lotus tile. It belongs with someone who has learned patience.  
_He presses the little tile into your palm. It is old, smooth, and warmer than wood should be._  
**Uncle Tenzo**: And now a secret. In any town, any market, if you see this tile on a stall or a door, you are among friends.  
**Uncle Tenzo**: There are more of us than you would think. Old people who play slow games and keep an eye on things.  
**Kaito**: …Uncle. Are you in a secret society?  
**Uncle Tenzo**: I am in a tea society. Mostly. Go back to sleep, nephew.  
_Your Nubbin carries the board home on its head. The lotus tile hangs from your belt, quietly mattering._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think question: quiet people who matter  
> **Uncle Tenzo**: The lotus does nothing, yet it matters most. Some people are like that too: quiet, but very important.  
> _What kind of quiet person matters most to you?_  
> - Someone who listens when I’m sad. → Ah. A listener. They are worth more than a hundred talkers.
> - Someone who helps without being asked. → Yes. The kind of help you only notice when it stops. Remember to thank them.
> - Someone who notices when people are left out. → A rare and precious kind of person. Perhaps you are one yourself.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on the quiet people in their life who matter, and why._


### Glossary

- **patters**: Makes quick, light tapping sounds.
- **nephew**: The son of your brother or sister.
- **rare**: Not found or seen very often.
- **general**: An army leader in charge of many soldiers.
- **sulk**: To be quiet and grumpy because you are upset.
- **symmetrical**: When one half is a mirror image of the other half.
- **society**: A group of people who meet because they share an interest.

## LH1. Shalom, Ori!

- `lh1-step1`: Greet Ori at the gate. · _Tap Ori at the gate. When he says שָׁלוֹם (shalom), say it back: sha-LOME._
- `lh1-step2`: Teach three Nubbins to wave at שָׁלוֹם (shalom). · _Say shalom and wave next to a Nubbin. When it waves back, say תּוֹדָה (toda): toe-DAH._
- `lh1-step3`: Say לַיְלָה טוֹב (laila tov, “good night”) to Fern, Clover and Nova. · _Find each of them before they go indoors and tap to say it: LIE-la TOVE._

#### `lh1-s1`

_The gate rattles. Someone on the other side is lifting and pushing, and losing._  
**Nova**: Lift AND push, Ori. Both at once. It’s a Grove thing.  
_The gate gives. In tumbles a boy in a football shirt, hugging a biscuit tin like a trophy._  
**Ori**: שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “hello”)! Sorry. I had a fight with your gate. Your gate won.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, SL.K.1, do): greet someone in Hebrew and reply  
> _Say it back to Ori: sha-LOME. The strong part comes at the end: sha-LOME._  
> **Ori**: Shalom! Perfect. You sound like you’ve been saying it for years.  
> Check: `edu:say:he:shalom`
> _For grown-ups: Greeted Ori in Hebrew by saying “shalom” back, with the stress on the last syllable._

**Nova**: This is Ori. He’s staying with me for three weeks. He’s ten, and he lives in Israel.  
**Nova**: He has already told me forty star names.  
**Ori**: Forty-two. You stopped listening at forty.  
**Ori**: In Hebrew, shalom means hello. It also means goodbye. And peace. It’s a very hard-working word.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): why one word can have several meanings (think question)  
> _Shalom means hello, goodbye and peace, all at once._  
> _Why might one word mean all three?_  
> - When you meet or leave someone, you wish them peace. → That’s a lovely answer. Every hello and goodbye can carry a wish for the other person.
> - It saves having lots of words. → That’s a fair answer. Languages often let one word do more than one job.
> - I’m not sure. Maybe it just grew that way. → That’s an honest answer. Words grow and change over a long time, and people don’t always know why.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a single word, shalom, can mean hello, goodbye and peace._

**Ori**: אֲנִי (ani) means “I”. קוֹרְאִים לִי… (korim li…) means “my name is…”. Korim li Ori!

**Ori**: To ask “How are you?”, I say מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? (ma shlomkha?) to a boy.

- **Ask me “ma shlomekh?”**
    - **Ori**: Ma shlomekh?
    - **You**: בְּסֵדֶר (beseder, “fine”). I think?
    - **Ori**: Beseder! That means “OK, fine”. Short and strong, like a header into the top corner.
- **Either one. Just say shalom!**

    - **You**: Beseder.
    - **Ori**: Perfect. You sound like my uncle. That’s a compliment. Mostly.

### Glossary

- **שָׁלוֹם (shalom)**: Hello, goodbye and peace, all in one word (say it: sha-LOME).
- **אֲנִי (ani)**: The Hebrew word for “I” (say it: ah-NEE).
- **קוֹרְאִים לִי… (korim li…)**: How you say “my name is…”; it means “they call me” (say it: kor-EEM lee).
- **מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? (ma shlomkha?)**: “How are you?” when you ask a boy or man (say it: mah shlom-KHA).
- **מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ? (ma shlomekh?)**: “How are you?” when you ask a girl or woman (say it: mah shlo-MEKH).
- **בְּסֵדֶר (beseder)**: OK, fine (say it: beh-SEH-der).
- **תּוֹדָה (toda)**: Thank you (say it: toe-DAH).
- **בְּבַקָּשָׁה (bevakasha)**: Please, and also “you’re welcome” (say it: beh-vah-kah-SHAH).
- **טוֹב (tov)**: Good (say it: TOVE).
- **כֵּן (ken)**: Yes (say it: KEN).
- **לֹא (lo)**: No (say it: LOW).
- **בֹּקֶר טוֹב (boker tov)**: Good morning (say it: BO-ker TOVE).
- **עֶרֶב טוֹב (erev tov)**: Good evening (say it: EH-rev TOVE).
- **לַיְלָה טוֹב (laila tov)**: Good night (say it: LIE-la TOVE).
- **לְהִתְרָאוֹת (lehitra’ot)**: See you, for when you’ll meet again later (say it: leh-heet-rah-OTE).
- **תּוֹדָה רַבָּה (toda raba)**: Thank you very much: the big thank-you (say it: toe-DAH rah-BAH).

- `lh2-step1`: Find the four letters of שָׁלוֹם (shalom) hidden round the garden. · _Look by the pond, the gate, the orchard and Ori’s tent. Line the pebbles up from the right: ש ל ו ם._

#### `lh2-s1`

**Ori**: Today: the alef-bet. That’s our alphabet. It’s named after its first two letters, alef and bet.  
**Ori**: Rule one: Hebrew goes right to left. You start on the right side of the page and travel left.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): Hebrew is read and written right to left  
> _Ori says Hebrew goes right to left. Where does the first letter of a Hebrew word go?_  
> - ✅ On the right → Ken! The right side. Then you travel left.
> - On the left → That’s where English starts. Hebrew starts on the right and travels left.
> - In the middle → Not quite. Hebrew starts on the right side and travels left.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Hebrew starts on the right and is read right to left._

_The Wobbler hears “right to left”, thinks very hard about it, and starts walking backwards._  
**Ori**: I hid the letters of שָׁלוֹם round the garden, painted on pebbles. Four letters.  
**Ori**: ש is shin. It says “sh”. Three arms reaching up, like a goalie celebrating.  
**Ori**: ל is lamed. It says “l”. It’s the tallest letter: it sticks up above all the others.  
**Ori**: ו is vav. A stick with a little hook. Here it makes an “o” sound.  
**Ori**: Vav can say v, o or u. Very flexible. A real midfielder.  
**Ori**: Mem says “m”. At the end of a word it changes shape and closes up like a box: ם.  
**Ori**: Five letters do that. They have a special shape just for the end of a word.  
**Ori**: Find shin, lamed, vav and final mem. Then line them up from the RIGHT.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): finding and ordering letters right to left

**Ori**: Now look at the word with its dots and lines: שָׁלוֹם.  
**Ori**: The little dots and lines are the vowels. They’re called niqqud.  
**Ori**: Children’s books use them. Grown-ups mostly leave them out and just know.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): why vowel points are often left out (think question)  
> _Grown-ups mostly leave the vowel dots out. Why might they do that?_  
> - It’s quicker to write without them. → That’s a fair answer. Fewer marks means faster writing.
> - They know the words, so they don’t need the help. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Once you know a word well, you can read it from its letters alone.
> - I think they should keep them! → That’s a fair point too. The dots help learners, which is why children’s books keep them.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why Hebrew vowel points (niqqud) are used in children’s books but often left out by adults._

> **Ori**: Twenty-two letters. You know eleven. What fraction of the alef-bet is that?  
> - ✅ One half → Half! Eleven is half of twenty-two. It’s half-time!
> - One quarter → A quarter of 22 would be only about 5. Eleven is exactly half: 11 + 11 = 22.
> - One third → A third of 22 would be about 7. Eleven and eleven make twenty-two, so eleven is one half.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that 11 letters out of 22 is one half._

### Glossary

- **ש (shin)**: The letter that says “sh”, with three arms reaching up.
- **ל (lamed)**: The letter that says “l”; the tallest letter of all.
- **ו (vav)**: A stick with a hook that says “v”, and can also stand for “o” or “u”.
- **ם (final mem)**: The shape mem takes at the end of a word, closed like a box; mem says “m”.
- **א (alef)**: The first letter: it is silent and holds a vowel.
- **ב (bet)**: Says “b” with a dot inside, or “v” without it (then it is called vet).
- **ג (gimel)**: The letter that says “g”.
- **ד (dalet)**: The letter that says “d”.
- **ה (hey)**: The letter that says “h”.
- **ר (resh)**: The letter that says “r”, shaped like a bent elbow.
- **י (yod)**: The smallest letter; it says “y”, or can stand for “i”.
- **אוֹר (or)**: Light (say it: ORE).
- **אוֹרִי (Ori)**: Ori’s name, which means “my light”; spelled alef, vav, resh, yod.

## LH3. Counting Plums

- `lh3-step1`: Help Fern count plums in Hebrew, from אַחַת (achat, 1) to עֶשֶׂר (eser, 10). · _Tap each plum as it goes in the basket and say its number. Ori helps with six to ten._
- `lh3-step2`: Play “How Many?”: count Ori’s goals in Hebrew. · _After each goal, tap the right Hebrew number. A wrong tap just gets a “lo” and another try._
- `lh3-step3`: Count ten stars with Ori on the western hill. · _Go up the hill after dark. Tap a star and say its number in Hebrew._

#### `lh3-s1`

_In Fern’s orchard the plum trees are heavy. Fern sits under one with two baskets, looking lost._  
**Fern**: Ten plums for each basket, for the market. I’ve counted four times and got four different numbers.  
**Ori**: Let me. I count in Hebrew. It’s faster. It isn’t faster. It sounds faster.  
**Ori**: אַחַת (achat, 1). שְׁתַּיִם (shtayim, 2). שָׁלוֹשׁ (shalosh, 3).  
**Ori**: אַרְבַּע (arba, 4). חָמֵשׁ (chamesh, 5).  
**Ori**: Chamesh has a throaty “ch”, like the end of “loch”.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): the throaty “ch” sound in Hebrew  
> **Ori**: Try it: say “loch” the Scottish way, and hold the end. Chhh.  
> _In Hebrew, “ch” and “kh” stand for this throaty sound, like the end of the Scottish word “loch”._  
> _For grown-ups: Practised the throaty Hebrew “ch” sound, as in Scottish “loch”._

**Fern**: Achat… shtayim… I keep wanting to sneeze it.  
**Ori**: Sneezy is close! SHTAI-yim. Say it like you mean it.  
**Ori**: Six to ten, I’ll call them and you copy. Tomorrow you do them alone.  
_The Wobbler sits under the tree, catching every plum that falls. Mostly with its face._  

> **Lesson** (maths, K.CC.B.5, do): counting to ten in Hebrew  
> _Count the plums into Fern’s basket: achat, shtayim, shalosh, arba, chamesh…_  
> _…then copy Ori: שֵׁשׁ (shesh), שֶׁבַע (sheva), שְׁמוֹנֶה (shmone), תֵּשַׁע (tesha), עֶשֶׂר (eser)!_  
> Check: `edu:count:he:plums:10`
> _For grown-ups: Counted ten plums in Hebrew, one number for each plum._


**Choices**

- **I’ll count. You check.**
    - **Ori**: Deal. If you’re wrong, I say lo. If you’re right, I say ken. I expect to say ken a lot.
- **Let Fern count. We’ll cheer.**
    - **Fern**: No pressure, then.
    - **Ori**: Huge pressure. Stadium pressure. Achat!

**Ori**: Twenty. But twenty is a different lesson. Don’t get greedy.  
_The Wobbler has a plum balanced on its head. Nobody mentions it._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): asking for help

_Ori sets up four jumpers, a goal at each end, and bounces his football on his knee._

**Ori**: The game is called “How Many?” I shoot. You count the goals in Hebrew. Right answer, you get the ball.  
**Ori**: You need the big numbers now. שֵׁשׁ (shesh, 6). שֶׁבַע (sheva, 7). שְׁמוֹנֶה (shmone, 8).  
**Ori**: תֵּשַׁע (tesha, 9). And עֶשֶׂר (eser, 10). Ten is my shirt number. Ten is the best number.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): Hebrew numbers six to ten  
> **Ori**: Shirts before kick-off. I’m ten, obviously. You can be שְׁמוֹנֶה (shmone). Which number goes on your back?  
> - ✅ 8 → Shmone, eight! Ken!
> - 6 → Six is shesh. Shmone is eight.
> - 10 → Ten is eser, Ori’s shirt number. Shmone is eight.
> _For grown-ups: Matched the Hebrew number shmone to 8._

_The Wobbler is in goal. It has decided that being in goal means waving at the ball._  
**Ori**: Warning. I am a very good footballer and a very bad loser.  
**Ori**: Ask my savta. She hid all our board games.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): handling losing (think question)  
> _Ori says he’s a very bad loser. What could help someone who hates losing?_  
> - Remembering it’s just a game. → That’s a good answer. Games are for fun, and fun works best when everyone enjoys it.
> - Taking a deep breath before saying anything. → That’s a wise answer. A slow breath gives the cross feeling time to settle.
> - Saying “well played” even when it’s hard. → That’s a brave answer. Being a good sport is a skill, and it gets easier with practice.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ways to cope with losing a game._

**Ori**: Ready? Achat, shtayim, shalosh, GO!

- **Bring it on.**

#### `lh3-s2-done`

_Final score: Ori ten, the Wobbler one._  
_The Wobbler waved, and the ball bounced off its tummy. It rolled the whole length of the grass and into Ori’s goal._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): finding “how many more” by taking away  
> _Ori scored eser (10), and the Wobbler scored achat (1)._  
> _How many more goals did Ori score?_  
> - ✅ 9 → Nine more. Which is fine. Totally fine. I’m fine.
> - 11 → Eleven is how many goals altogether. To find how many MORE, take away: 10 − 1 = 9.
> - 10 → Close! Ori scored 10, but the Wobbler scored 1, so Ori scored 10 − 1 = 9 more.
> _For grown-ups: Found the difference between two scores by subtracting: 10 − 1 = 9._

**Ori**: That’s… that’s one. Achat! It scored ACHAT.  
**Ori**: Best of three. Best of shesh. Best of sheva. Best of eser!  
**Nova**: Ori.  
**Ori**: …Beseder. Toda for the game. Well played, Wobbler.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): being a good sport  
> _Ori was cross. Then he took a moment and said “well played”._  
> _Losing can feel big. Noticing the feeling, then choosing kind words anyway, is what being a good sport means._  
> _For grown-ups: Saw how a character calms down after losing and chooses kind words._

_He means it about halfway. That’s a start._

**Ori**: Best sky I’ve ever seen. No city lights. At home I have to squint.

**Ori**: Each kochav is a sun, just really, really far away.

**Ori**: It makes no light of its own. The sun lights it up.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): stars make light; the moon reflects sunlight  
> _Stars make their own light, like our sun does. The moon doesn’t._  
> _We see the moon because sunlight bounces off it, the way a torch lights up a wall._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stars are distant suns and that we see the moon because it reflects sunlight._

_Something on a branch says “hoo”. Two round eyes blink at you._  
**Ori**: יַנְשׁוּף (yanshuf)! An owl! Shalom, yanshuf! Sorry. I’m excited. Owls are night people, like me.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): how owls find food at night  
> _The yanshuf hunts at night. What helps an owl find food in the dark?_  
> - ✅ Big eyes for dim light, and very sharp hearing → Ken! Owls have huge eyes for dim light, and ears sharp enough to hear a mouse moving in the grass.
> - It glows, like a lantern → Owls don’t glow! They use big eyes and sharp hearing instead.
> - It waits for the sun to come up → Owls that hunt at night don’t wait for morning. Their big eyes and sharp hearing work in the dark.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that owls use large eyes and sharp hearing to hunt at night._

**Ori**: Count ten stars before the clouds come in. Out loud. In Hebrew.  
_The Wobbler lies on its back next to you and waves at the sky._

## LH4. Colours of the Orchard

- `lh4-step1`: Sort Nova’s market fruit by colour, using Hebrew colour words. · _Three baskets: אָדֹם (adom, red), יָרֹק (yarok, green), צָהֹב (tsahov, yellow)._
- `lh4-step2`: Fetch “something אָדֹם (adom)” for Clover’s fussy Nubbin. · _Look in Nova’s crate for something red. Sagol (purple) things won’t do._
- `lh4-step3`: Paint Fern’s fence in the three colours Ori calls out. · _Listen for the Hebrew word, then dip your brush in that tin._

#### `lh4-s1`

_Nova drops a crate on the cottage table. It’s full of fruit from the valley market, all jumbled up._  
**Nova**: I bought one of everything. I was hungry, and the stallholder was very persuasive.  
**Ori**: Sorting game! By colour. In Hebrew.  
**Ori**: אָדֹם (adom) is red. יָרֹק (yarok) is green. צָהֹב (tsahov) is yellow.  
**Ori**: Now fruit. תַּפּוּחַ (tapuach) is an apple. בָּנָנָה (banana) is… banana. You’re welcome.  
**Ori**: And לִימוֹן (limon) is a lemon. Hebrew is being nice to you today. Don’t get used to it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words that are shared between languages  
> _One of these Hebrew words sounds the same as in English. Which?_  
> - ✅ בָּנָנָה (banana) → Banana! Same word. And limon is pretty close to lemon too.
> - תַּפּוּחַ (tapuach) → Tapuach means apple, but it doesn’t sound like “apple”. Banana sounds the same in both.
> - יָרֹק (yarok) → Yarok means green. The one that sounds the same is banana.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that some words, like banana, are shared by Hebrew and English._

**Ori**: A limon goes in tsahov. A banana goes in tsahov. A tapuach goes in adom, or yarok.  
**Ori**: It depends on the tapuach.  
_The Wobbler sits in the middle of the table, hugging a banana. It does not look ready to share._  

> **Lesson** (maths, K.MD.B.3, do): sorting into groups and counting each  
> _Sort the fruit into three baskets: adom, yarok and tsahov. Then count each basket._  
> _Which basket has the most? Which has the fewest?_  
> Check: `edu:sort:he:fruit:colour`
> _For grown-ups: Sorted fruit by colour using Hebrew colour words, then counted and compared the groups._


**Choices**

- **Put the green apple in yarok.**
    - **Ori**: Yarok! Ken. An apple doesn’t have to be adom. Apples can be whatever they like.
- **Put the red apple in adom.**
    - **Ori**: Adom! Ken. The classic. Like in a picture book.

#### `lh4-s1-done`

_Three neat piles: adom, yarok, tsahov._  
_There’s also a small fourth pile under the table, guarded by the Wobbler._  
**Ori**: The Wobbler has invented a new colour. It’s called “mine”.  
**Nova**: It’s a very popular colour. I see it a lot at markets.  
**Ori**: Banana, limon… some Hebrew words sound a lot like English ones.  
**Ori**: Some words travel. They move from language to language, like Nova.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): what changes when a word moves between languages (think question)  
> _Banana is the same in Hebrew and English. Limon is close to lemon._  
> _When a word moves into another language, what does it keep, and what might change?_  
> - It keeps its meaning, but the sound changes a little. → That’s a sharp answer. Limon and lemon mean the same fruit but sound a bit different.
> - It might lose where it came from. → That’s a thoughtful answer. People often forget which language a word started in.
> - It keeps everything. A banana is a banana. → That’s a fair answer! Some words, like banana, hardly change at all.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what a word keeps and loses when it moves into another language._

_Clover is by the pond with a little Nubbin who hasn’t eaten all day._  
**Clover**: This one will only eat red things. Don’t ask me why. We all have our ways.  
**Ori**: Something adom! On it. I’m fast. I play on the wing.  
**Ori**: רִמּוֹן (rimon) is a pomegranate. Red outside, and full of red seeds inside. My favourite.  
**Ori**: עֲנָבִים (anavim) are grapes. These ones are סָגֹל (sagol), purple. Not adom. Close, but lo.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): colour words change their ending for feminine words  
> **Ori**: Adom is the form we use to name the colour red.  
> **Ori**: Hebrew sorts words into masculine and feminine. When a colour describes a feminine word, its ending changes, for example adumah.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Hebrew colour words change their ending to describe feminine words (adom, adumah)._

**Ori**: תְּאֵנָה (te’ena) is a fig. Also a bit sagol.  
**Ori**: And תָּמָר (tamar) is a date. Brown and sticky.  
_A צִפּוֹר (tsipor), a small bird, lands on the crate and pecks at the te’ena._  
**Ori**: Tsipor! Lo! That’s not yours! …Fine. One bite. Bevakasha.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): recognising a colour word

> **Lesson** (art, ask): mixing paint colours  
> **Fern**: Oh no. Wait. The katom tin is empty. Can we mix some?  
> _Which two colours mix to make orange?_  
> - ✅ Adom and tsahov (red and yellow) → Red and yellow… it’s working! Katom!
> - Kachol and lavan (blue and white) → Blue and white make a light blue. For orange, mix red and yellow: adom and tsahov.
> - Shachor and yarok (black and green) → That makes a very dark green. For orange, mix red and yellow: adom and tsahov.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that red and yellow paint mix to make orange._

> - כָּחֹל (kachol) → Kachol is blue. Pink is varod.
> - שָׁחֹר (shachor) → Shachor is black. Pink is varod.
> _For grown-ups: Matched the Hebrew word varod to pink._

    - **Ori**: Varod, yarok, katom. Don’t argue. Art doesn’t argue.

### Glossary

- **אָדֹם (adom)**: Red; the ending changes to describe a feminine word, for example adumah (say it: ah-DOME).
- **יָרֹק (yarok)**: Green (say it: yah-ROKE).
- **צָהֹב (tsahov)**: Yellow (say it: tsa-HOVE).
- **תַּפּוּחַ (tapuach)**: Apple (say it: tah-POO-akh).
- **בָּנָנָה (banana)**: Banana, the same word as in English (say it: bah-NAH-nah).

- `lh5-step1`: Read one of the letters in Savta’s tin with Ori. · _Sit with Ori at the cottage table and tap the letter. Tap any Hebrew word to hear it._
- `lh5-step2`: Draw a family tree with Hebrew words. · _Label each branch: ima, aba, ach, achot, chaver or chavera._
- `lh5-step3`: Tell Ori how a Nubbin is feeling, in Hebrew. · _Look at the shy Nubbin by the gate. Ori uses the girl forms for her._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): how letters carry the past  
> **Nova**: When Hazel and Savta started writing, there were no video calls. A letter could take a week or more to arrive.  
> _Letters keep the past safe. Years later, you can still read exactly what someone wrote._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how people kept in touch by letter before video calls, and how letters keep the past._

_“Is the כֶּלֶב (kelev, ‘dog’) still stealing socks? Does the חָתוּל (chatul, ‘cat’) still sit on your letters?”_

> _Hazel used to write one letter every month._

> - 14 → Count the months: 12 in one year, 12 in the next. 12 + 12 = 24.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that one letter a month for two years is 24 letters._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps someone who is sad or alone  
> _The shy Nubbin is alone, looking at the hill. What might help her?_

> - Shout “shalom!” to cheer her up. → Ori would love that, but a quiet Nubbin might jump. Sitting near her quietly is gentler.
> - Leave her completely alone. → Some quiet time can help. But being nearby, without fussing, lets her know she isn’t alone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to comfort someone who seems sad or lonely._

### Glossary

- **סַבְתָּא (savta)**: Grandma (say it: SAHV-tah).
- **מִשְׁפָּחָה (mishpacha)**: Family (say it: meesh-pah-KHAH).
- **סַבָּא (saba)**: Grandpa (say it: SAH-bah).
- **כֶּלֶב (kelev)**: Dog (say it: KEH-lev).
- **חָתוּל (chatul)**: Cat (say it: kha-TOOL).
- **אִמָּא (ima)**: Mum (say it: EE-mah).
- **אַבָּא (aba)**: Dad (say it: AH-bah).
- **אָחוֹת (achot)**: Sister (say it: ah-KHOTE).
- **אָח (ach)**: Brother (say it: AKH).
- **חָבֵר (chaver)**: A friend who is a boy (say it: khah-VER).
- **חֲבֵרָה (chavera)**: A friend who is a girl (say it: khah-veh-RAH).
- **שָׂמֵחַ (sameach)**: Happy, when a boy is feeling it (say it: sah-MEH-akh).
- **שְׂמֵחָה (smecha)**: Happy, when a girl is feeling it (say it: smeh-KHAH).
- **עָצוּב (atsuv)**: Sad, when a boy is feeling it (say it: ah-TSOOV).
- **עֲצוּבָה (atsuva)**: Sad, when a girl is feeling it (say it: ah-tsoo-VAH).
- **עָיֵף (ayef)**: Tired, when a boy is feeling it (say it: ah-YEF).
- **עֲיֵפָה (ayefa)**: Tired, when a girl is feeling it (say it: ah-yeh-FAH).

- `lh6-step3`: The review party: greet, count, colours, family and feelings, all in Hebrew. · _Answer Ori’s rounds by the lanterns. The Nubbins act out every answer._

**Ori**: ט״ו בִּשְׁבָט (Tu BiShvat). “The New Year of the Trees.” Trees get a birthday!  
**Ori**: It’s on the fifteenth of a Hebrew month called Shevat. Usually in January or February.  
**Ori**: People plant trees. And they eat fruit, especially dates, figs, pomegranates, olives and grapes.

> _Tu BiShvat is on the 15th of the Hebrew month of Shevat, usually in January or February._  
> _People plant trees and eat fruit, especially dates, figs, pomegranates, olives and grapes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about Tu BiShvat, the New Year of the Trees: when it falls and how people mark it._

**Ori**: A tree is an עֵץ (ets). Short word, big thing.  
**Ori**: In Israel, the שָׁקֵד (shaked) trees often blossom around then. Almond trees.  
**Ori**: Lavan and pale pink, in the middle of winter.

> - Planting trees helps the future. → That’s a wise answer. A tree planted today gives fruit and shade for years.
> - Birthdays are fun, and trees deserve one! → That’s a fair answer! Ori agrees completely.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people celebrate and plant trees._

> - Promise to write, like Savta and Hazel did. → That’s a great answer. Letters kept Savta and Hazel friends for forty years.
> - Just say shalom. It means goodbye and peace. → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes one good word is enough.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about kind ways to say goodbye to a friend._

## LJ1. Konnichiwa, Hana!

- `lj1-step1`: Say hello to Hana at the gate in Japanese. · _Tap Hana and choose Greet. Say “konnichiwa” (こんにちは). A little bow is a nice touch._
- `lj1-step2`: Teach three Nubbins to bow when you say “konnichiwa”. · _Tap a Nubbin and say こんにちは a few times. Nubbins learn by copying you._
- `lj1-step3`: Say “oyasumi” (good night) to everyone before bed. · _At dusk, tap each Nubbin, Nova and Hana, and say おやすみ._

#### `lj1-s1`

_The gate sticks, like always. Someone on the other side lifts and pushes, hard. It bangs open._  
_A girl in running shoes skids through first, a sketchbook under her arm. Nova follows, carrying both bags._  
**Nova**: This is Hana. She’s staying with me for the summer. She raced me from the bridge.  
**Hana**: I won by eleven seconds. Nova says nine. Nova is wrong.  
**Hana**: こんにちは (konnichiwa, “hello”)!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a word with two meanings: こんにちは  
> _Hana said こんにちは (konnichiwa) as she came through the gate. What do you think it means?_  
> - ✅ Hello → はい! Hello. It can also mean “good afternoon”. One word, two jobs.
> - Goodbye → いいえ, goodbye is a different word. I only just got here! こんにちは means “hello”, or “good afternoon”.
> - Thank you → Not that one. Thank you is tomorrow’s word. こんにちは means “hello”, or “good afternoon”.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that こんにちは (konnichiwa) means “hello” and also “good afternoon”._

_She bows: a small, quick dip from the waist, then straight back up._  
**Hana**: That’s おじぎ (ojigi), bowing. At home we bow to say hello, thank you and sorry.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, notice): bowing (おじぎ) as a greeting in Japan  
> **Hana**: A small bow is friendly. A deeper bow shows more respect.  
> **Hana**: So you bow a little to a friend, and lower to say a big thank you, or a big sorry.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that in Japan people bow (おじぎ, ojigi) to greet, thank and apologise, and that a deeper bow shows more respect._

**Hana**: はじめまして (hajimemashite) means “nice to meet you”. You only say it the first time you meet someone.  
**Hana**: わたしは はな です (watashi wa Hana desu) means “I am Hana”. Your own name goes in the middle, like a sandwich.  
**Hana**: Then finish with よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu): “please treat me kindly”, or “pleased to meet you”.  
**Nova**: I practised that all the way here. On the ticket man, a cow and a postbox.  
**Hana**: Ready? Say はい (hai, “yes”) or いいえ (iie, “no”). Actually, just say はい.  

**Choices**

- **Bow and say “konnichiwa”.**
    - You bow. Hana bows back, a little deeper. She seems to think that means she won.
    - **Hana**: はい! Perfect. You meant that one.
- **Wave and say “konnichiwa”.**
    - **Hana**: A wave works too. Friends wave all the time. Next time, add a tiny bow. Like this. Easy.
- **Try the lot: “Hajimemashite. Watashi wa… desu. Yoroshiku onegaishimasu.”**
    - **Hana**: You did the whole sandwich! It took Nova three days to get that right.
    - **Nova**: Two days.
    - **Hana**: いいえ. Three.

#### `lj1-s1-done`

_Hana is already drawing you. She drew Nova, the gate and a passing bee while you said hello._  
**Hana**: Done! Your nose is very good. Your ears are a bit much. That’s my fault, not yours.  
_Behind the water butt, three Nubbins have watched everything._  
_One of them tries a bow. It tips forward and rolls into the herbs._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, do): greeting someone new kindly  
> **Hana**: Show the Nubbins how. Say こんにちは and do a little bow. Nubbins learn by copying.  
> Check: `edu:bow:konnichiwa`
> _For grown-ups: Greeted a shy Nubbin with こんにちは and a bow, practising a kind, calm hello._

**Hana**: They want to learn! Tomorrow we teach them. Properly.  
**Hana**: Also, is that a frog? I’m not scared of frogs. I’m just saying. In case it comes up.  

#### `lj1-s2`

_Morning. Dew on everything. Hana was up before you, and she mentions it twice._  
**Hana**: おはよう (ohayō, “good morning”)! That’s for friends and family.  
_Fern climbs over the fence with a bucket of plums and a sleepy face._  
**Hana**: おはようございます (ohayō gozaimasu), Fern! That’s the polite one, for grown-ups and teachers.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): friendly and polite forms of a greeting  
> **Hana**: Japanese has friendly words for family and friends, and polite words for grown-ups and people you don’t know well.  
> **Hana**: おはよう is friendly. おはようございます is polite. The polite one is longer. It usually is.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the friendly おはよう (ohayō) and the polite おはようございます (ohayō gozaimasu), and when to use each._

**Fern**: Good morning to you too. I’ve been up since five, keeping the trees alive, badly.  
**Hana**: ありがとうございます (arigatō gozaimasu)! That’s a polite thank you. With friends, it’s just ありがとう (arigatō).  
**Hana**: Right. When I say こんにちは, the Nubbins bow. Three Nubbins, three bows. That’s the plan.  
_She sprints at the herb bed and bumps a small round Nubbin right off its feet._  
**Hana**: ごめんなさい (gomen nasai, “I’m sorry”)! Sorry, sorry!  
_She bows low to the Nubbin, because she means it. It copies her, and lands on its face._  
**Fern**: That one’s Dumpling. He eats things. Bows aren’t food, Dumpling.  
**Hana**: But that was a good おじぎ. Very sincere.  
**Hana**: すみません (sumimasen, “excuse me”), everybody! Come a bit closer? That’s how you ask nicely.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): why languages have polite forms (think question)  
> _Hana uses short words with friends and longer, polite words with grown-ups._  
> _Why do you think some languages have different polite forms?_  
> - To show respect. → That’s a good answer. A polite form is a way of showing respect with words, a bit like a deeper bow.
> - So people know how well you know each other. → That’s a thoughtful answer. The words you choose can show whether someone is a close friend or someone new.
> - English does it too, a bit. → Sharp thinking! English has “hi” and “good morning”, “thanks” and “thank you very much”. Many languages do this in their own way.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why languages have polite and friendly ways of saying the same thing._

**Hana**: Who shall we start with?  

**Choices**

- **The shy one under the bench.**
    - You crouch and say こんにちは, very softly. The shy one peeks out and dips its head, just a tiny bit.
    - **Hana**: That counts. Small bows count.
- **The bouncy one on the wall.**
    - You say こんにちは. The bouncy one bows so hard it bounces off the wall and has to start again.
    - **Hana**: Enthusiastic. I respect it.
- **The sleepy one in the sun.**
    - You say こんにちは. The sleepy one bows very slowly, and doesn’t come back up for a while.
    - **Hana**: Is it still bowing? Or asleep?
    - **Fern**: Bit of both.

#### `lj1-s2-done`

_Three Nubbins in a row. You say こんにちは. Three small bows, nearly together._  
**Hana**: That was beautiful! I’m drawing it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): saying thank you  
> _The three Nubbins worked hard. Hana wants to thank them. Which word should she use?_  
> - ✅ ありがとう (arigatō) → はい! ありがとう, everyone! Thanking people for trying is the best bit.
> - ごめんなさい (gomen nasai) → That one is for saying sorry. To say thank you, it’s ありがとう.
> - おはよう (ohayō) → That’s “good morning”. For thank you, it’s ありがとう.
> _For grown-ups: Chose ありがとう (arigatō) to thank the Nubbins for trying, and practised saying thank you for effort._

_Then a fourth bow, from the end of the row: Dumpling, late, copying the others._  
_He is facing the wrong way._  
**Hana**: Other way, Dumpling.  
_He turns round, bows again, bumps into the water butt, and looks extremely pleased with himself._  

#### `lj1-s3`

_Evening. The light goes gold, then orange, then the colour of weak tea._  
_Luna comes up the path with a trowel and a jar of moths, on her way to the night garden._  
**Hana**: こんばんは (konbanwa, “good evening”), Luna!  
**Luna**: Konbanwa. Did I say it right? Nova taught me last summer. I’ve been saving it.  
**Hana**: Perfect!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): when は is read “wa”  
> **Hana**: Look at the last letter of こんばんは and こんにちは. It’s は. On its own, は says “ha”.  
> **Hana**: But at the end of these two greetings, it says “wa”. Japanese likes to keep you on your toes.  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that the last letter of こんにちは and こんばんは is は, read “wa” here, not “ha”._

**Fern**: I’m off to bed. Goodbye, all.  
**Hana**: Not さようなら (sayōnara)! That’s goodbye for a while. You’ll see us in the morning.  
**Hana**: Say またね (mata ne, “see you”). Or at bedtime, おやすみ (oyasumi, “good night”).  
**Fern**: Mata ne, then. Oyasumi.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, SL.K.1, ask): choosing the right goodbye  
> _Fern will be back over the fence tomorrow morning. Which goodbye fits best tonight?_  
> - さようなら (sayōnara) → That one’s for a goodbye that lasts a while. Fern will be back tomorrow, so おやすみ or またね is better.
> - ✅ おやすみ (oyasumi) → はい! She’s going to bed, so おやすみ. And またね works too: see you.
> - こんにちは (konnichiwa) → That’s hello! Fern’s leaving. At bedtime, say おやすみ.
> _For grown-ups: Chose between さようなら (goodbye for a while), またね (see you) and おやすみ (good night) for the situation._

**Hana**: For grown-ups you want to be extra nice to, it’s おやすみなさい (oyasuminasai). The polite one.  
**Hana**: Now you. Everyone gets an oyasumi before bed. Nubbins, Nova, Dumpling, me. That’s the rule.  
_Dumpling is already asleep, standing up, in the herb bed._  

**Choices**

- **Start with the Nubbins.**
    - You go along the row. Oyasumi, oyasumi, oyasumi. Three sleepy bows and one snore.
    - **Hana**: The snore was Dumpling. It still counts.
- **Start with Nova.**
    - You say おやすみなさい to Nova, with a little bow.
    - **Nova**: The polite one! I feel very grand.
- **Start with Hana.**
    - **Hana**: Me first? Oyasumi! I’m first to bed. I win.
    - **Nova**: It’s not a race.
    - **Hana**: Everything is a race.

#### `lj1-s3-done`

_You say oyasumi to everyone. Even the herb bed, just in case._  
**Nova**: おやすみなさい. You’re better at this than I was after a whole week.  
_Dumpling bows to the moon. The moon does not bow back, but it seems to appreciate it._  
_The sky over the hill turns dark blue, then darker._  
_Hana is asleep on the bench. Her pencil is still moving, drawing a line off the edge of the page._  
**Nova**: Right now it’s morning at Hana’s home in Japan. Her family is just waking up.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): why it is night here and day somewhere else  
> **Nova**: The Earth spins all the way round every day. When our side turns away from the Sun, it gets dark here.  
> **Nova**: At the same time, the other side of the world is turning towards the Sun, and it’s morning there.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the spinning Earth makes day and night, so it can be night in one country and morning in another._

**Nova**: It’s a welcome sign, for everyone who comes through, whatever language they speak.  
**Hana**: I made up a song on the train. An おじぎ song. Bow at the end of every line.  
**Hana**: おはよう (ohayō), up comes the sun! こんにちは (konnichiwa), hello, everyone!

> **Lesson** (music, RL.2.4, do): a rhyming chant with a repeated action  
> **Hana**: Your turn! Sing it with me and bow on the last word of each line. Listen for the rhymes: sun, everyone, fun, done.

_Three Nubbins bow at the end of every line. Dumpling bows one line late every time, and has to lie down afterwards._  
**Hana**: はい. You can bow now. Properly. I’m giving you that.  
**Fern**: Is there a polite version of the song?  
**Hana**: いいえ. It’s already perfect.  

### Glossary

- **こんにちは (konnichiwa)**: Hello, or good afternoon.
- **おじぎ (ojigi)**: Bowing. People in Japan bow to greet, thank and say sorry; a deeper bow shows more respect.
- **はじめまして (hajimemashite)**: Nice to meet you. Only said the first time you meet someone.
- **わたしは ___ です (watashi wa ___ desu)**: I am ___. Put your name in the gap.
- **よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu)**: Please treat me kindly, or pleased to meet you. A polite thing to say after your name.
- **はい (hai)**: Yes.
- **いいえ (iie)**: No.
- **おはよう (ohayō)**: Good morning, to family and friends.
- **おはようございます (ohayō gozaimasu)**: Good morning, the polite way.
- **ありがとう (arigatō)**: Thank you.
- **ありがとうございます (arigatō gozaimasu)**: Thank you, the polite way.
- **ごめんなさい (gomen nasai)**: I’m sorry.
- **すみません (sumimasen)**: Excuse me, or sorry.
- **polite**: Showing good manners and respect to someone, often with special words.
- **こんばんは (konbanwa)**: Good evening.
- **さようなら (sayōnara)**: Goodbye, when you won’t see someone for a while.
- **またね (mata ne)**: See you.
- **おやすみ (oyasumi)**: Good night, the friendly way.
- **おやすみなさい (oyasuminasai)**: Good night, the polite way.

## LJ2. The Hiragana Pond

- `lj2-step1`: Find あ い う え お on the stepping stones, in order. · _Start with あ, nearest the bank. Some stones are sideways, so look carefully._
- `lj2-step2`: Trace か き く け こ in the sand. · _Follow the numbered strokes, in order. Top to bottom, left to right, mostly._
- `lj2-step3`: Write はな, Hana’s name, on her sketchbook. · _は first, then な. You can write across or down._

#### `lj2-s1`

_Hana has been up since dawn, painting the flat stones in the pond. Marina watches, the way she watches anyone touching water._  
**Marina**: She asked you first. Mostly.  
**Hana**: These are hiragana. It’s one of the ways we write Japanese. There are forty-six basic ones.  
**Hana**: Today we need five: あ い う え お. You say them a, i, u, e, o. Like “ah, ee, oo, eh, oh”.  
**Hana**: They come first in the hiragana chart. Nearly every other hiragana ends in one of those five sounds.  
_She has hidden the five painted stones among plain ones. Some face up. Some are sideways._  
**Hana**: Find them in order, あ first. Step on the wrong one and you have to say “sorry, stone”.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): recognising the five vowel kana あ い う え お  
> **Hana**: Find あ, い, う, え and お on the stones, in that order. Say each sound as you step on it.  
> Check: `edu:find:ja:vowels`
> _For grown-ups: Found and read the five Japanese vowel letters あ い う え お (a, i, u, e, o), in order._

**Hana**: Then we spell words. うえ (ue) means “up”. いえ (ie) means “house”. あお (ao) means “blue”.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): reading a two-letter word: うえ  
> **Hana**: Which two stones spell うえ, “up”?  
> - ✅ う, then え → はい! う, え. Ue. Up!
> - え, then う → Close! That spells え, う, which isn’t a word. Read it in order, left to right: う first, then え.
> - あ, then お → That spells あお: blue! Nice reading. But for うえ, step on う, then え.
> _For grown-ups: Read the word うえ (ue, “up”) letter by letter, in order._

**Marina**: And if somebody falls in?  
**Hana**: Nobody falls in. I’m very fast.  
_On the お stone sits a frog. It is fat, wet and not interested in hiragana at all._  
**Hana**: That’s fine. That is a normal frog and I am being normal about it.  

#### `lj2-s1-done`

_あ, い, う, え, お. You hop across in order. On the お stone, the frog moves exactly one centimetre._  
**Hana**: Now spell うえ. Up!  
_You jump onto う, then え, then up onto the bank. Hana claps._  
**Hana**: いえ next. Then あお.  
**Hana**: And nobody mention the frog.  
**Marina**: Nobody mentioned the frog.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): reading how someone really feels  
> _Hana keeps saying she’s “normal” about the frog. She also won’t go near it. How do you think she really feels?_  
> - ✅ A little scared, but she doesn’t want to show it. → That’s what it looks like. What people say and what they do can tell different stories. Being kind about it helps.
> - She loves frogs. → Hmm. She’s keeping very far away from it. Her actions say she’s a little scared, even if her words don’t.
> - She doesn’t care at all. → Look where she’s standing, though. People sometimes hide being scared. Her actions give it away.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that what a character does can show a feeling her words hide._


#### `lj2-s2`

_Dusty has raked a patch of sand flat by the pond. They lean on the rake like it’s an old friend._  
**Dusty**: Smooth as I can get it. There was a spoon under here. And another spoon. I don’t know whose spoons these are.  
**Hana**: Now put a “k” in front of the five sounds. You get か き く け こ. Ka, ki, ku, ke, ko.  
**Hana**: Every hiragana has its strokes in the same order, every time.  

> **Lesson** (art, notice): stroke order in handwriting  
> **Hana**: Stroke order means which line you draw first, and which way it goes.  
> **Hana**: The rule of thumb is top to bottom, left to right. Doing it the same way every time makes your writing neat and steady.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that each hiragana is written with its strokes in a set order, usually top to bottom and left to right._

_She traces く with one finger: a single stroke, like a bird’s beak. Then こ: two short lines, one above the other._  
**Hana**: く is one stroke. こ is two. か has a little dash off to one side, like it’s waving.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): tracing か き く け こ  
> **Hana**: Trace か き く け こ in the sand. Follow the numbers, one stroke at a time. Say each sound as you finish it.  
> Check: `edu:trace:ja:ka-row`
> _For grown-ups: Traced the five kana か き く け こ (ka, ki, ku, ke, ko) in stroke order._

**Hana**: Words! いけ (ike) is “pond”, like this one. かお (kao) is “face”. あか (aka) is “red”.  
**Dusty**: So I’ve been raking next to an いけ all morning and didn’t know it.  
_The frog from the お stone has followed you. It sits in the sand, right where く should go._  
**Hana**: It’s not in the way. I’ll write round it. Frogs are fine. It’s fine.  

**Choices**

- **Gently move the frog back to the pond.**
    - You scoop it up in both hands and set it down at the water’s edge. Hana breathes out, quietly.
    - **Hana**: I was fine. But ありがとう.
- **Write round the frog.**
    - You draw く in a curve round the frog. It looks like the frog is getting a hug.
    - **Hana**: That’s actually a really good drawing.
- **Ask Hana if she’s scared.**
    - **Hana**: Me? いいえ. No. Not at all.
    - She is standing on one leg, as far from the frog as a person can be while still holding a stick.

#### `lj2-s2-done`

_か き く け こ, in a neat row in the sand._  
_Dusty steps back to admire it and treads right on the け._  
**Dusty**: Sorry. ごめんなさい. I’ll rake it.  
**Hana**: Now write かお, and I’ll put a face in it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): reading two-letter words in kana  
> _Hana wants to draw a face in the sand. Which word should you write for her?_  
> - ✅ かお (kao) → はい! か, お. Kao, face. Now watch me draw on it.
> - いけ (ike) → That’s “pond”: い, け. Face is かお: か, お.
> - あか (aka) → That’s “red”: あ, か. Face is かお: か, お.
> _For grown-ups: Read three kana words, いけ (pond), かお (face) and あか (red), and picked the one meaning “face”._

_She draws two eyes in the お and a smile under the か. It looks a lot like Dusty._  
**Dusty**: That’s me, isn’t it.  
**Hana**: はい.  

#### `lj2-s3`

_Hana lays her sketchbook open on the grass. The first page is blank. For Hana, that is very rare._  
**Hana**: The last two for today: は (ha) and な (na). Put them together: はな. That’s me. Hana.  
**Hana**: はな also means “flower”. I like to think the flowers were named after me.  
**Hana**: There’s another way to write it: 花. That’s kanji. Kanji came from Chinese, and each one carries a meaning.  
**Hana**: So Japanese has three scripts: hiragana, kanji, and katakana, which is mostly for words borrowed from other languages.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): the three Japanese scripts  
> **Hana**: Hiragana is for Japanese words, like はな. Katakana is mostly for borrowed words, like ピンク.  
> **Hana**: And kanji carry meaning, like 花. Lots of Japanese sentences use all three at once.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Japanese uses three scripts: hiragana, katakana (mostly for borrowed words) and kanji (characters that carry meaning)._

**Hana**: Like ピンク (pinku). Say it.  
_You say it. It sounds a lot like “pink”._  
**Hana**: Exactly. Japanese borrowed it, and it came out a bit different.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, L.3.4, ask): how words travel between languages (think question)  
> _Japanese borrowed “pink” and made it ピンク (pinku). English borrowed “koi” from Japanese._  
> _When a word moves into another language, what do you think changes, and what stays?_  
> - The sound changes a bit, but the meaning stays. → That’s a good answer. The word gets a new accent to fit its new home, and usually keeps its meaning. In Japanese, こい is any carp. In English, koi are the colourful pond kind.
> - It gets new letters to fit the new language. → That’s a fair answer. Pink got katakana letters. Koi got English letters. Same idea, new clothes.
> - Both languages end up sharing a little piece. → That’s a lovely answer. Borrowed words are like presents that languages give each other.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what happens to a word, like pink or koi, when it is borrowed into another language._

**Hana**: And は is sneaky. Mostly it says “ha”. But in わたしは, it says “wa”, because it points at who the sentence is about.  
**Hana**: Write はな on my sketchbook. Big. You can go across in a row, or down in a column. Japanese can do both.  

**Choices**

- **Write it across, left to right.**
    - You write は, then な, side by side across the page.
    - **Hana**: Like a name on a door. Good.
- **Write it down, top to bottom.**
    - You write は at the top and な underneath, in a column.
    - **Hana**: Very fancy. When a page is in columns, you read the columns from right to left.

**Hana**: I’m keeping this page forever. I won’t even draw on it. Much.  
_The frog hops onto the sketchbook and sits on the は._  
_Hana makes a very small noise. It is definitely not a scream._

_Marina has helped Hana paint the rest of the stones. Twelve kana cross the pond now. A Nubbin waits on the bank._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: rows of five  
> _The stones are two rows of five, あ い う え お and か き く け こ, plus は and な._  
> **Marina**: How many painted stones is that altogether?  
> - 10 → That’s the two rows: 2 lots of 5 is 10. Then add は and な. 10 + 2 = 12.
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. 2 rows of 5 is 10, and 2 more makes 12.
> - 7 → That’s 5 + 2. But there are two rows of five: 5 + 5 = 10. Add は and な: 12.
> _For grown-ups: Counted 2 equal rows of 5 kana stones plus 2 more: 12 in all._

**Hana**: Quick-fire! I call a word, the Nubbin hops on the letters. Go! うえ!  
_う, え. The Nubbin hops twice and points up._  
**Hana**: いえ! いけ!  
_A house, a pond. The Nubbin points at your cottage, then at the pond, very pleased._  
**Hana**: かお! あか! あお!  
_Face, red, blue. The Nubbin pulls a face, goes pink in the cheeks, then sits down, worn out._  
**Hana**: Last one: はな.  
**Marina**: I’d keep the stones. They’re better than plain ones.  
**Hana**: Hiragana stepping stones! Now anyone who crosses this pond is reading Japanese, whether they like it or not.  

### Glossary

- **hiragana**: One of the three ways of writing Japanese, used for Japanese words and grammar. It has 46 basic characters.
- **うえ (ue)**: Up, or above.
- **いえ (ie)**: House.
- **あお (ao)**: Blue.
- **stroke order**: The order and direction you draw the lines of a letter.
- **いけ (ike)**: Pond.
- **かお (kao)**: Face.
- **あか (aka)**: Red.
- **はな (hana)**: Flower. Also Hana’s name. In kanji: 花.
- **katakana**: A Japanese script used mostly for words borrowed from other languages, like ピンク (pinku, pink).
- **kanji**: Characters that came from Chinese and carry meaning, like 花 (flower).

## LJ3. Counting Koi

- `lj3-step1`: Count the new koi into the pond in Japanese, from いち to じゅう. · _Tap each fish as it swims in and say its number. After ご, copy Hana._
- `lj3-step2`: Race Hana round the pond, counting the laps in Japanese. · _Say each lap number as you pass the lap counter. Use よん, なな and きゅう._
- `lj3-step3`: Count ten stars in Japanese, then find the moon. · _Go up the hill after dark. Planes don’t count. The moon is low, behind the plum trees._

#### `lj3-s1`

_Marina is at the pond with two big buckets. Something inside flashes orange and white._  
**Marina**: New fish. A friend upriver had too many. Like people with courgettes.  
**Hana**: こい (koi)! They’re koi! I’ve drawn about a thousand of them.  
**Hana**: You say koi in English too. Same word. Japanese lent it to English.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): words English has borrowed  
> **Marina**: Lots of English words came from other languages. Koi is one from Japanese.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that English has borrowed words from Japanese, such as koi._

**Marina**: We count them in, so we know nobody’s missing later. Hana says we’re counting in Japanese.  
**Hana**: Hold up your fingers. いち (ichi), one. に (ni), two. さん (san), three.  
**Hana**: よん (yon), four. ご (go), five. One whole hand.  
_A koi slides out of the bucket into the pond. Then another. They don’t wait for anyone to be ready._  
**Hana**: Quick! いち! に!  

> **Lesson** (maths, K.CC.B.5, do): counting to five in Japanese  
> **Hana**: Count the first five koi as they swim in: いち, に, さん, よん, ご. One finger for each fish.  
> Check: `edu:count:ja:koi:5`
> _For grown-ups: Counted five fish in Japanese: いち, に, さん, よん, ご (ichi, ni, san, yon, go)._

**Marina**: There are ten. Five in this bucket, five in that one.  
**Hana**: After ご, I’ll call the next numbers and you copy me. Don’t blink.

**Hana**: After ご came ろく (roku), six. なな (nana), seven. はち (hachi), eight.  
**Hana**: Then きゅう (kyū), nine. And じゅう (jū), ten!  
**Hana**: Ten koi! Ten fingers! Nobody fell in!  
**Marina**: A little dramatic. But correct.  
_Ten koi drift round in a slow orange circle._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how fish breathe with gills  
> **Marina**: See the little flaps just behind their heads? Those cover the gills.  
> **Marina**: Fish take water in through the mouth. As it flows out past the gills, the gills take the oxygen from it. That’s how they breathe.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fish breathe with gills, which take oxygen from the water flowing past them._

_Dumpling sits on the bank, counting them with his head._

**Sparks**: I HEAR SOMEONE HERE THINKS SHE’S FAST.  
**Hana**: I don’t think I’m fast. I know I’m fast.  
**Pixel**: Lap counter. It flips a tile for every lap round the pond. Hana painted the numbers.  
_The first three tiles say 一, 二 and 三. One line, two lines, three lines._  
**Hana**: Kanji for one, two and three. The easiest kanji in the world. You just count the lines.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): kanji for one, two and three  
> **Hana**: 一 is one line. 二 is two lines. 三 is three lines.  
> **Hana**: Not all kanji are this easy. Enjoy it while it lasts.  
> _For grown-ups: Read the kanji 一, 二 and 三 (one, two, three) by counting their lines._

**Byte**: I’ll keep the official time. And the laps. And a record of who says “it was just a practice”.  
**Hana**: Count the laps out loud, in Japanese. Loser feeds the さかな (sakana, “fish”).  
**Marina**: Sakana means any fish. Koi are one kind of sakana.  
**Hana**: Some numbers have two names. Four is よん or し (shi). Seven is なな or しち (shichi). Nine is きゅう or く (ku).  
**Hana**: For counting games, use yon, nana and kyū. Ready?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplying equal laps  
> **Byte**: One lap of the pond is 40 strides. The race is 3 laps. How many strides is the whole race?  
> - 43 → That adds 40 and 3. But it’s 3 lots of 40: 40 + 40 + 40 = 120.
> - ✅ 120 → Correct. 3 × 40 = 120. Officially.
> - 80 → That’s 2 laps. One more lap: 80 + 40 = 120.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 3 laps of 40 strides as 3 × 40 = 120._


**Choices**

- **A fair start.**
    - **Byte**: Fair start. Nobody moves until I say. Nobody. Hana.
    - **Hana**: I wasn’t moving. I was leaning.
- **Give Hana a head start.**
    - **Hana**: I don’t need a head start!
    - **Hana**: …But I’ll take it. Strategically.
- **Let Sparks race too.**
    - **Sparks**: THREE-WAY RACE. Yes. YES.
    - **Hana**: Fine. I’ll beat you both. Count my laps louder than hers.

_The lap counter clacks. The last tile flips. Everyone flops on the grass, puffing._  
**Byte**: Official laps: counted, in Japanese. Official excuse from Hana: pending.  
**Hana**: That was a practice one. Whoever won.  
**Byte**: There it is.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): how it feels to lose, and what helps (think question)  
> _Hana calls every race she loses “a practice one”. What helps you most when you lose a game?_  
> - Asking for a rematch, like Hana. → That’s a fair answer. Wanting another go shows you care, and you might get better each time.
> - Saying “well done” to the winner. → That’s a kind answer. It’s hard to do when you feel cross, which is why it means a lot.
> - Taking a breath before I say anything. → That’s a wise answer. Big feelings settle a bit if you give them a moment.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the feelings that come with losing a game and ways to handle them._

**Hana**: Rematch tomorrow. Now let’s feed the さかな. All of us.  
**Hana**: Because I’m kind. Not because of anything else.

### Glossary

- **こい (koi)**: A kind of carp, a pond fish. English borrowed the word from Japanese.
- **いち, に, さん, よん, ご (ichi, ni, san, yon, go)**: One, two, three, four, five.
- **ろく, なな, はち, きゅう, じゅう (roku, nana, hachi, kyū, jū)**: Six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
- **一 二 三**: The kanji for one, two and three: one, two and three lines.
- **さかな (sakana)**: Fish. Any fish; koi are one kind.
- **し, しち, く (shi, shichi, ku)**: Other ways to say four, seven and nine. Counting games use よん, なな and きゅう.
- **ほし (hoshi)**: Star.
- **つき (tsuki)**: Moon.

- `lj4-step3`: Draw three fruits for Hana’s sketchbook. · _Pick any three: いちご, もも, りんご, みかん or Fern’s plums._

> **Lesson** (art, do): naming colours while arranging a picture

> _Before eating, Hana says いただきます. After, ごちそうさま. Why do you think people have special words for the start and end of a meal?_

> - So everyone starts together. → That’s a good answer. Saying something together turns a meal into something you share.

> **Hana**: Look closely at your いちご. Where are a strawberry’s seeds?

## LJ5. Obāchan’s Letters

- `lj5-step1`: Read one of Obāchan’s letters with Hana. · _Tap the letter on the kitchen table. Tap any Japanese word to hear it._
- `lj5-step2`: Draw a family picture and label it in Japanese. · _Draw anyone who is family to you. Use おかあさん, おとうさん, おばあちゃん, おじいちゃん, ともだち, or a name._
- `lj5-step3`: Tell Hana how each Nubbin feels, in Japanese. · _Look at each face. Choose うれしい, かなしい, たのしい, こわい or ねむい._

#### `lj5-s1`

_Rain on the cottage roof. Hana opens a tin on the kitchen table. Inside is a bundle of letters tied with string._  
**Hana**: Hazel used to write to my grandma, for years and years. Grandma kept a copy of every letter she sent back.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): letters as a way to keep in touch, then and now  
> **Hana**: Before email and video calls, friends far apart wrote letters. A letter could take days or weeks to arrive.  
> **Hana**: Some people kept writing to the same friend for their whole lives.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how people kept in touch by letter in the past, compared with today._

**Hana**: In my family, I call my grandma おばあちゃん (obāchan). My grandpa is おじいちゃん (ojīchan).  
**Hana**: She gave me these to bring here. They’re in English, but she put Japanese words in for Hazel to learn.  
_The paper is thin and soft from folding. The writing is very neat and very small. Hana reads it aloud._  
**Hana**: Dear Hazel. ありがとう for the seeds. They came up!  
**Hana**: Our ねこ (neko, “cat”) sleeps on my letters. The いぬ (inu, “dog”) next door barks at her. The とり (tori, “birds”) ignore them both.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): reading animal words in hiragana  
> **Hana**: Which word in the letter means “cat”?  
> - ✅ ねこ (neko) → はい! ねこ, cat. Obāchan’s cat thought she owned the house.
> - いぬ (inu) → いぬ is the dog next door. Cat is ねこ.
> - とり (tori) → とり means birds. Cat is ねこ.
> _For grown-ups: Read the animal words ねこ (cat), いぬ (dog) and とり (bird) in a letter._

**Hana**: Ojīchan says hello and asks how your Nubbins are. From your ともだち (tomodachi, “friend”).  
_Hana sits back and reads the last line again, to herself._  
**Hana**: “Your ともだち.” Not just “from”. “Your friend.”  
**Hana**: Your turn. Read the next bit. Watch out for the ねこ. Obāchan drew her in the margin.  

#### `lj5-s1-done`

_You read the rest together, a line each. Hana does the voices. Obāchan’s ねこ gets a very grand voice._  
**Hana**: Obāchan says a letter is a little visit. You open it, and the person is there for a bit.  
**Hana**: I said さようなら to her at the station, because a whole summer is a long time.  
**Hana**: I miss her. She’s fine. She’s at home. I just miss her.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): missing someone, and what helps  
> _It’s normal to miss someone who is far away, even when you’re having fun._  
> _Writing to them, drawing for them or talking about them can help, like Hana’s little visits._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about missing someone far away and the things that help, like writing or drawing for them._

_Hana pins the letter above her bed, next to a drawing of a ねこ asleep on an envelope._  
_Then she starts a new page: a drawing for obāchan._

_The rain stops. Hana spreads big paper across the floor and tips out every pencil she owns._  
**Hana**: Let’s draw our かぞく (kazoku), our families. With labels. In Japanese.  
**Hana**: My おかあさん (okāsan), my mum. My おとうさん (otōsan), my dad. Obāchan, glasses on her head, looking for her glasses.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): how a long vowel changes a word  
> **Hana**: Careful! おばあちゃん (obāchan) is grandma. おばちゃん (obachan) is auntie.  
> **Hana**: The only difference is the long “aa”. Hold it, or you’ll turn your grandma into your auntie.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a long vowel changes meaning: おばあちゃん (obāchan, grandma) and おばちゃん (obachan, auntie)._

**Hana**: And ojīchan. He died when I was six. I still put him in every family picture. He’s still in my family.  
_She draws him in the corner, in a hat, holding a fishing rod. She doesn’t rush it._  
**Hana**: And our うさぎ (usagi), our rabbit. She’s called Biscuit. She bites.  
**Hana**: There’s an owl in the tree by obāchan’s house. ふくろう (fukurō). Not family exactly, but it was always there.  
**Hana**: Now yours. Anybody who’s family to you. People, pets, people who feel like family. They all count.  

> **Lesson** (art, do): drawing and labelling a family picture  
> **Hana**: Draw the people and animals who are family to you, then label them. Use the Japanese words you know, or their names.  
> Check: `edu:draw:ja:kazoku`
