> _Count along, and you will find Monkey ninth. Remember this list, because the pilgrims will meet more of its animals._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned the order of the twelve zodiac animals and where Monkey sits in it._

**Monkey**: Cousin! You came back down. Tomorrow I’m going to do something enormous. I haven’t decided what.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): big plans and care (a think question)  
> _“Something enormous” could mean a lovely thing or a terrible thing. How would you plan it?_  
> - Ask a friend what they think first → That is a fair answer. Monkey could use a friend like that.
> - Try it and see → That is a fair answer. Trying teaches a lot, though, as we will see, it also gets Monkey into trouble.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about how to plan something ambitious._

_He gives your Nubbin a peach that is mostly bite marks. Your Nubbin holds it like treasure._  
_Nova has drawn a tiny peach in the margin. Now a tiny ink monkey sits beside it, eating it._  
_Far above, someone important is still wondering what, exactly, he has just seen._  
_The page rustles softly, as if it too would like to know what happens next._  

### Glossary

- **weathering**: The slow wearing away of rock by wind, rain and ice.
- **herald**: A messenger who brings important news.

## A2-2. The Water-Curtain Cave

- `a02-02-s1`: Follow the stream up to its waterfall. · _Walk up beside the stream with the monkeys._
- `a02-02-s2`: Leap through the waterfall and look behind it. · _Dive after Monkey. Water is not a wall._
- `a02-02-s3`: Sit at the feast in the cave. · _Find a seat near Monkey in the cave._

#### `a02-02-stream`

_A hot afternoon. The monkeys splash in the stream until somebody asks where all the water comes from._  
_Nobody knows, so everybody goes to look. You and your Nubbin go too, because everybody means everybody._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): the water cycle feeds streams  
> _The monkeys ask where the stream’s water comes from. What is the best answer?_  
> - ✅ Rain falls on the mountain, runs downhill, and later rises again as clouds → Yes. Rain feeds streams, streams reach the sea, the sun lifts water into clouds, and the cycle goes round.
> - A spring that never stops, with no rain at all → Springs are real, but they too are fed by rain that soaked into the ground. The whole cycle is rain, runoff, sea, vapour and cloud.
> _For grown-ups: Your child described where stream water comes from and how it cycles._

_The stream ends at a waterfall that hangs down the cliff like a white curtain. Behind it, nobody can see anything._  
**An old gibbon**: Whoever goes through that curtain and comes back with all their fur on, we make them king.  
_Every monkey looks at its own feet. A few look at their neighbours’ feet, which is a sort of suggestion._  
**Monkey**: I’ll go! I was born from a rock. Rocks don’t mind water.  
_Your Nubbin steps up beside him, quite serious about it. It has always liked a waterfall._  

**Choices**

- **Tell them both to be careful.**
    - **Monkey**: Careful is for monkeys who aren’t going to be king.
- **Offer to count them in.**
    - **Monkey**: Yes! Count. Kings should start on a number.
    - You count to three. Monkey goes on two.

#### `a02-02-stream-done`

_He crouches, shuts his eyes tight, and leaps._  
_Just before he goes, the curtain of water swings in the wind._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: curtain  
> _A curtain usually hangs at a window. What does “curtain” mean for a waterfall?_  
> - ✅ Water hanging down in a sheet that hides what is behind → Yes. The word is borrowed because the water looks like fabric.
> - A piece of cloth sewn onto the cliff → It is not real cloth; it is a comparison. The water hangs down like a curtain.
> _For grown-ups: Your child worked out a second meaning of "curtain" from context._


#### `a02-02-leap`

_Your Nubbin dives after him, and you follow your Nubbin. The water thunders on your head, and then it stops._  
_Behind the curtain it is dry. An iron bridge crosses to a cave with stone beds, stone pots and stone bowls._  
_Over the doorway someone has carved the cave a name, long ago, in tidy characters._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, notice): Chinese writing uses characters  
> _Chinese is written in characters. Each one stands for a word or a part of a word, and a name can be carved in just a few of them._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that Chinese is written with characters._

**Monkey**: Nobody lives here! It’s got beds. It’s got pots. It’s got a front door made of waterfall!  
_Suppose there are four rows of stone beds, with six beds in each row. Your Nubbin tries them all in turn._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiply: 4 rows of 6  
> _Four rows of stone beds, six in each row. How many beds does your Nubbin have to try?_  
> - ✅ 24 → Yes. Four groups of six: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24.
> - 10 → That adds 4 + 6. We need four equal groups of six. 4 × 6 = 24.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used equal groups to multiply (4 × 6)._

_It finds every one of them exactly right._  
**Monkey**: Wait here. If I come back alone they’ll say I made it up.  

#### `a02-02-leap-done`

_He shoots back out through the curtain, shouting. A moment later, a lot of wet monkeys shoot in._  
_The roar of the waterfall shakes the cave walls so that you can feel it in your teeth._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: shoot  
> _Monkey “shoots” out, and the wet monkeys “shoot” in. What does shoot mean here?_  
> - ✅ To move very fast → Yes. Here shoot means to move very fast, like a shooting star.
> - A new green stem on a plant → That is another meaning: a plant’s new shoot. Here the monkeys are moving very fast, so shoot means to rush.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used context to choose the right meaning of "shoot"._


#### `a02-02-king`

_They make him king, as promised. He takes the name Handsome Monkey King, and nobody dares laugh._  
_The page turns a few years, as easily as a page. The feasts go on and on, and then, one night, the king cries._  
**Monkey**: One day I’ll be old. One day I’ll stop. All this, and one day it won’t be mine.  
_The cave goes very quiet. Your Nubbin climbs into his lap, which is all it knows to do._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): every living thing has a life cycle  
> _Every living thing has a life cycle: it begins, grows, may have young, grows old, and ends._  
> _Trees, monkeys and people all do. It is a hard thing to feel, and it is allowed to make you sad._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that all living things have life cycles, and that sadness about it is allowed._

**An old gibbon**: There are some who never grow old, they say. Buddhas, immortals and sages. They live far off, among people.  
**Monkey**: Then I’ll go and find them. I’ll learn it. I’ll learn not to stop.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): fear of growing old (a think question)  
> _Monkey is afraid of growing old and stopping. Is that fear helpful, or does it just hurt?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - It can push us to live well → That is a fair answer. Many people feel that a short time makes each day matter.
> - It mostly just hurts → That is a fair answer. Fear can crowd out the present, and a friend in your lap helps.
> - Both, depending on the day → That is a fair answer. A feeling can be useful and heavy at the same time.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on a hard feeling about time and ageing._


**Choices**

- **Tell him growing old isn’t the worst thing.**
    - **Monkey**: You say that because you aren’t a king.
    - He keeps your Nubbin on his lap, though.
- **Tell him to go and find out.**
    - **Monkey**: Yes. That’s the right answer. Cousin’s keeper gives the right answers.

#### `a02-02-complete`

_In the morning the monkeys build him a raft and pile it with fruit. They wave until he is a dot._  
_You and your Nubbin are on the raft too. It seems rude to wave from the shore._  
**Monkey**: I’ll be back. When I come back, I won’t ever have to stop.  
_Suppose the monkeys loaded five baskets with twelve fruits in each. Your Nubbin counts them twice, to be sure._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 5 baskets of 12  
> _Five baskets with twelve fruits in each. How many pieces of fruit are on the raft?_  
> - ✅ 60 → Yes. 5 × 12 = 60. Five tens and five twos: 50 + 10.
> - 17 → That adds 5 + 12. Five equal baskets means we multiply. 5 × 12 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Your child multiplied 5 × 12._

_Years go by on the water, as fast as you can turn a page. He learns to wear clothes and to walk like a person._  
_Behind them, the waterfall swings shut like a curtain, and the cave goes back to being quiet._  

### Glossary

- **immortal**: Someone who never dies or never grows old, in stories.

## A2-3. Lessons in Shape-Changing

- `a02-03-s1`: Visit Monkey’s teacher in his cave. · _Climb the quiet mountain with Monkey._
- `a02-03-s2`: Wait on the back step through the night. · _Sit outside the back door and keep still._
- `a02-03-s3`: Watch Monkey show off under the pines. · _Stand in the yard and watch._

#### `a02-03-lesson`

_High on a quiet mountain there is a cave, and in the cave a teacher with a great many students._  
**Master Subhuti**: A monkey. Then you shall have a name: Sun Wukong, Awake to Emptiness. It suits you. You are mostly noise.  
_The page turns seven years of sweeping floors. Then the teacher offers Monkey a choice of lessons._  
**Master Subhuti**: I could teach you to see fortunes. To sit still. To make medicines. To read the old books.  
**Monkey**: Will any of them make me live for ever?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): choosing a goal (a think question)  
> _Monkey turns down every lesson except the one that might make him live for ever. Was that a wise way to choose?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes, he knew what he wanted → That is a fair answer. A clear goal can stop you wasting years.
> - No, the other lessons had value → That is a fair answer. Patience and medicine might have helped him more than he knew.
> - Both are true → That is a fair answer. A single goal gives focus, and it can also make you miss other good things.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about choosing a goal and what it might cost._

**Master Subhuti**: No.  
**Monkey**: Then no, thank you.  
_The teacher climbs down from his seat, taps Monkey three times on the head with his ruler, and walks out with his hands behind his back._  
_The other students are furious. Monkey is grinning from ear to ear._  

**Choices**

- **Ask Monkey why he’s grinning.**
    - **Monkey**: Three taps: come at the third watch of the night. Hands behind his back: use the back door.
    - **Monkey**: He’s going to teach me in secret. Don’t tell the others. Don’t tell Cousin, it can’t keep a secret.
- **Work it out for yourself.**
    - Three taps, hands behind the back. You catch Monkey’s eye, and he winks.

#### `a02-03-night`

_At the third watch the back door is open a crack, and Monkey slips through it. You sit outside on the step._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: the five watches of the night  
> _In old China the night, from about 7 in the evening to 5 in the morning, was split into five equal watches. How long is one watch?_  
> - ✅ 2 hours → Yes. Ten hours shared into five equal parts is two hours each. The third watch is the middle of the night.
> - 5 hours → Five is the number of watches. Share the ten hours into five equal parts instead. 10 ÷ 5 = 2 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Your child divided a time span into equal parts (10 hours ÷ 5)._

_Your Nubbin falls asleep against the door almost at once. It snores in a small, polite way._  
_Inside, the teacher talks for a long time in a low voice. You don’t hear the words, and you aren’t meant to._  
_The page turns three more years of nights. Then one evening Monkey comes out walking a foot above the ground._  
**Monkey**: Seventy-two changes! I can be anything. And look, look at this.  
_He does a somersault on a cloud, and is gone. A moment later he is back, a little out of breath._  
**Monkey**: A hundred and eight thousand li in one go! Cousin, did you see?  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4.MD.A.1, notice): the li and a big journey  
> _A li is an old Chinese unit of distance. Today it is taken as half a kilometre (in the old days it varied)._  
> _So 108,000 li is 54,000 kilometres, and the Earth is only about 40,000 kilometres round._  
> _Monkey claims one somersault goes further than all the way round the world._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child converted an old unit of distance and compared it with the size of the Earth._


#### `a02-03-pine`

_The other students have heard rumours. They gather round Monkey under the pines, all asking at once._  
**Monkey**: A pine tree? Easy.  
_There is a pop, and in Monkey’s place stands a pine tree, very proud of itself. The students cheer._  
_Your Nubbin stands beside it with both arms up, very still. It is being a small pine tree._  

> **Lesson** (art, notice): shadow puppets: light, a screen, and shadows  
> _Monkey turning into a pine is a favourite scene in Chinese shadow-puppet plays._  
> _Flat figures are held between a lamp and a white screen, and the audience sees only their shadows._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard how shadow-puppet theatre works._


> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadow size depends on distance from the lamp  
> _A puppeteer wants a bigger shadow on the screen. What should she do with the puppet?_  
> - ✅ Move it closer to the lamp, away from the screen → Yes. The closer a puppet is to the light, the more of the light it blocks, so the bigger its shadow.
> - Move it closer to the screen → That makes the shadow sharper and smaller. To make it bigger, move it towards the lamp.
> _For grown-ups: Your child predicted how moving a puppet changes the size of its shadow._

**Master Subhuti**: Who is shouting in my yard?  
_The pine tree turns back into a monkey, quite quickly._  
**Master Subhuti**: You show off. A gift you show off makes other people want it, and then they come for it. And for you.  
**Master Subhuti**: Go home. And never tell anyone who taught you. Not one word.  

**Choices**

- **Tell the teacher Monkey meant no harm.**
    - **Master Subhuti**: I know. That is the trouble with him. He never means any.
- **Stay out of it.**
    - You stay out of it. Your Nubbin, still being a pine tree, stays out of it too.

#### `a02-03-complete`

_Monkey bows to his teacher, properly, all the way to the floor. For once he doesn’t say anything clever._  
**Monkey**: Hold on to my tail, Cousin’s keeper. I know a quick way home.  
_One somersault, and the world rolls under you like a rug being shaken. Then there are peaches again._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes and metaphors  
> _“The world rolls under you like a rug being shaken.” Is that a simile or a metaphor?_  
> - ✅ A simile, because it uses “like” → Yes. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”.
> - A metaphor → A metaphor says one thing is another. This one says it is like another. So it is a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Your child told a simile from a metaphor._

_Your Nubbin tumbles off the cloud and lies on the grass, beaming. It would like to do that again, please._  
_Far behind you, a teacher in a cave sighs, smiles, and goes back to his books._  
_He says nothing to the others, and nobody asks._  

### Glossary

- **watch**: In old China, one of the five parts into which the night was divided.

## A2-4. Havoc in Heaven

- `a02-04-s1`: Visit the heavenly stables. · _Go up to Heaven with Monkey._
- `a02-04-s2`: Look at the peach trees in the garden. · _Walk slowly. Your Nubbin is watching the peaches._
- `a02-04-s3`: Watch what happens at the banquet. · _Follow Monkey to the Jade Pool._

#### `a02-04-stables`

_Since the teacher, Monkey has been busy. He has an iron staff from the sea-dragons, and he has rubbed his name out of the Book of Life and Death._  
_Heaven decides it would be simpler to give him a job. So up you all go._  
**Monkey**: Keeper of the Heavenly Horses! A grand title. They must think a lot of me.  
_He is very good with the horses. They grow fat and shiny, and your Nubbin rides one round the paddock._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): a horse’s eyes and senses  
> _A horse’s eyes sit on the sides of its head, so it can see almost all the way round without turning._  
> _That is a useful sense for an animal that is hunted._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned how a horse’s eyes help it survive._

**Monkey**: Wait. What rank is Keeper of the Horses, exactly?  
_A stable hand tells him: it is the lowest job in Heaven. Monkey throws down his hat and goes straight home._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): does a title matter? (a think question)  
> _Monkey storms off because the job’s rank is low, even though he was good at it. Does a title matter more than the work?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - The work matters more → That is a fair answer. The horses were happy, and he was doing it well.
> - Respect matters too → That is a fair answer. Feeling valued helps people do their best.
> - A bit of both → That is a fair answer. A good job and fair respect both count.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed rank against the value of doing good work._

_Heaven sighs, and tries again: Great Sage Equal to Heaven. A big title with no work at all._  

#### `a02-04-stables-done`

**The Jade Emperor**: Give him the Peach Garden to look after. It will keep him busy and out of trouble.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why does the Jade Emperor choose the Peach Garden for Monkey?_  
> - ✅ He hopes a job will keep Monkey busy and out of trouble → Yes. That is his motive. The ministers, who know about peaches and monkeys, are not so sure.
> - He wants Monkey to eat the peaches → No. He means it as a safe task. He does not see the problem yet. The ministers do.
> _For grown-ups: Your child read a character’s motive from what he says._

_Several ministers look at each other and say nothing, which says a great deal._  

#### `a02-04-garden`

**The garden spirit**: Three thousand six hundred trees, Great Sage. These ripen every three thousand years. These, every six thousand.  
**The garden spirit**: And these at the back, every nine thousand. Eat one, and you live as long as heaven and earth.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide: 3,600 trees in three equal groups  
> _The trees are in three groups of equal size, each ripening on a different cycle. If there are 3,600 trees in all, how many are in each group?_  
> - ✅ 1,200 → Yes. 3,600 ÷ 3 = 1,200. Think 36 hundreds shared by three: 12 hundreds.
> - 1,800 → That is half of 3,600. We need a third. 36 ÷ 3 = 12, so 3,600 ÷ 3 = 1,200.
> _For grown-ups: Your child divided 3,600 by 3._

_Your Nubbin has gone very still. It is looking at the peaches the way it looks at you at teatime._  
**Monkey**: Thank you. You may go. I shall inspect the trees alone. Very carefully.  
_The spirit goes. Monkey shrinks to the size of your thumb, climbs the oldest tree, and eats the best peach on it._  
_Then the next best. Then he falls asleep in a fork of the branches, round as a plum._  
_A ripe peach drops into the grass at your Nubbin’s feet. It glows faintly, like a lamp turned low._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, notice): fruit helps seeds travel  
> _A peach has one large stone, with a seed inside._  
> _Fruit is tasty so animals will carry the stone away and drop it somewhere new. That is one way plants spread._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that tasty fruit helps animals spread seeds._


**Choices**

- **Hang the peach back on its branch.**
    - You can’t, of course; it won’t stay. You put it gently at the foot of the tree instead.
    - Your Nubbin watches you do it, sighs from its toes, and lets it go.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff it, and no more.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs it for a long, long time. It glows a tiny bit just from the smell, and leaves it be.

#### `a02-04-banquet`

_Seven fairy maidens come to pick peaches for the Queen Mother’s banquet. They find very few left._  
_They tell him who is invited: everyone. Everyone except the Great Sage Equal to Heaven._  
**Monkey**: Everyone?  
_He freezes the maidens where they stand with one word, and is off to the Jade Pool before you can blink._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): being left out, and what you do next (a think question)  
> _Monkey was not invited, and that hurt. Does being hurt excuse what he did next?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - No, it hurts but it is no excuse → That is a fair answer. A feeling explains an action, and it does not make it fair.
> - Partly, the invitation was unfair → That is a fair answer. Leaving someone out was unkind, and what he did in reply was still too much.
> _For grown-ups: Your child separated the reason for an action from whether it was fair._

_He puts the servants to sleep and eats the whole banquet. Then he wanders into Lord Lao’s palace._  
_On the table are five gourds of golden elixir pills. He eats them like roasted beans._  
**Monkey**: Oh. Oh, no. That might have been a mistake.  
**Monkey**: Cousin! Keeper! Home! Now!  

#### `a02-04-complete`

_Heaven sends its armies after him. They fight for days, and it is all dust and thunder and bonks on helmets._  
_Nothing can hurt him now. He has eaten the peaches, the banquet and the elixir._  
**Monkey**: Ha! Equal to Heaven? I’m better than equal. Tell them, Cousin.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): your point of view and a character’s  
> _Monkey thinks “better than equal” is a triumph. How might the fairy maidens see it?_  
> - ✅ As a disaster: their trees are bare → Yes. They were frozen and the garden was emptied. Two people can see the same event very differently.
> - As a triumph for Monkey, too → Only Monkey sees it that way. For the maidens it is a loss. Point of view means who is looking, and from where.
> _For grown-ups: Your child compared a character’s point of view with another’s._

_Your Nubbin, behind a rock, would rather not tell anybody anything._  
_The fairy maidens unfreeze at last, look at the empty trees, and go to tell the Queen Mother._  
_Far below, the garden is very quiet, and one small peach stone lies in the grass._  

### Glossary

- **banquet**: A large, grand meal for many guests.
- **elixir**: A magic liquid or pill, said to heal or make people live longer.

## A2-5. Under the Mountain

- `a02-05-s1`: Wait by the furnace door. · _Sit by the furnace. Your Nubbin will not move._
- `a02-05-s2`: Talk with the Buddha by his open palm. · _Stand near the Buddha’s wrist._
- `a02-05-s3`: Sit with Monkey under the mountain. · _Climb down and sit by his free hand._

#### `a02-05-furnace`

_In the end a great warrior and his dog catch Monkey, and nothing in Heaven can harm him. So Lord Lao puts him in his furnace._  
_Forty-nine days the fire burns. Your Nubbin sits by the furnace door the whole time, worried, and won’t be moved._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide: 49 days in weeks  
> _The fire burned for forty-nine days, and a week has seven days. How many weeks was Monkey in the furnace?_  
> - ✅ 7 weeks → Yes. 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Seven weeks of seven days.
> - 6 weeks → Six weeks would be 42 days. Count seven more: 42 + 7 = 49. So it is 7 weeks.
> _For grown-ups: Your child converted 49 days to 7 weeks._


> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): waiting with a friend  
> _Your Nubbin sat at the furnace door for seven weeks. You can’t fix everything for a friend, but you can stay._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that staying beside a friend is a way to help._

_Monkey hides in the one corner where there is only wind. The smoke makes his eyes red, and then gold._  
_On the forty-ninth day the lid comes off with a bang. Out jumps Monkey, with eyes like two little suns._  
**Monkey**: Cousin! You waited. Stand back. I’m going to be very rude to everyone.  
_He kicks the furnace over and runs the length of Heaven, scattering generals like skittles._  

#### `a02-05-furnace-done`

**The Jade Emperor**: Fetch the Buddha. Ask him, please, to come.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why the Emperor calls on the Buddha  
> _Why does the Jade Emperor send for the Buddha, and not another general?_  
> - ✅ No army can stop Monkey, so he needs a different kind of strength → Yes. Force has failed. He turns to wisdom.
> - The Buddha is the strongest fighter → The story does not say the Buddha fights. He is calm and wise. The Emperor needs a different sort of help.
> _For grown-ups: Your child inferred a character’s reason for asking for help._

_It is the first time anyone in Heaven has said “please” about Monkey._  

#### `a02-05-palm`

_The Buddha comes in quietly. Everything else goes quiet with him, even Monkey, for a breath._  
**The Buddha**: What is it you want?  
**Monkey**: The Jade Emperor’s throne. He’s had it long enough. It’s my turn.  
**The Buddha**: Then here is a wager. Jump out of my right hand, and the throne is yours. If you cannot, go back down and learn.  
**Monkey**: Your hand? It isn’t a foot across. I go a hundred and eight thousand li in one somersault!  
_He jumps onto the open palm, and is gone in a streak of cloud._  
_You can see Monkey fly to five pink pillars at the edge of the world, and write his title on the middle one._  
_You can see that the pillars are fingers._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): point of view (a think question)  
> _Monkey thinks he reached the end of the world, but the Buddha knows he never left the hand. Who is right?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - The Buddha, because he sees the whole → That is a fair answer. From above, you can see how little ground Monkey really covered.
> - Both, from where they stand → That is a fair answer: Monkey reports what he saw, and the Buddha knows what it was.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about how point of view changes what seems true._


**Choices**

- **When he lands, tell him gently: it was the hand all along.**
    - **Monkey**: Rubbish. I went to the end of the world. I wrote my name on it.
- **Say nothing. Let the Buddha show him.**
    - You say nothing. The Buddha glances at you, briefly, and something in his face says thank you.

#### `a02-05-palm-done`

_The Buddha lifts his hand. On the base of one finger, in very small and very familiar writing, is Monkey’s title._  
**Monkey**: That’s… that can’t… I went…  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): evidence tests a claim  
> _Monkey claims he flew to the end of the world, but the writing on the finger is evidence. What does evidence do?_  
> - ✅ It shows whether a claim is true → Yes. Careful thinkers check a claim against the evidence, even when the claim is their own.
> - It proves the loudest person is right → Shouting does not change the writing on the finger. Evidence shows what really happened, whoever is loudest.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that evidence is used to test a claim._


#### `a02-05-mountain`

_The Buddha turns his hand over. It comes down gently and becomes a mountain with five peaks._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the five elements in Chinese thought  
> _In traditional Chinese thought, the world moves through five elements, or phases: wood, fire, earth, metal and water._  
> _Five peaks for five elements: the mountain’s name is chosen with care._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard about the five elements in Chinese tradition._

_Monkey is underneath, with only his head and one hand sticking out. He is not hurt, only, for the first time, stopped._  
**The Buddha**: Feed him when he is hungry. Give him water when he is thirsty. When he has learned enough, someone will come.  
**Monkey**: How long?  
**The Buddha**: As long as it takes. Not one day more.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, notice): Earth changes quickly and slowly  
> _Some changes to the Earth are fast, like a rockfall. Others are very slow, like a river carving out a valley._  
> _Monkey’s mountain will sit there for five hundred years, slowly gathering grass and moss._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that Earth changes both quickly and slowly._

_Your Nubbin climbs down and sits by Monkey’s free hand. Monkey holds on to one of its feet and says nothing at all._  

#### `a02-05-complete`

_Heaven holds a feast to thank the Buddha. The Queen Mother of the West brings him a dish of her peaches._  
_She looks at your Nubbin, who is trying very hard not to look at the peaches._  
**The Queen Mother of the West**: You stood by my trees and took nothing. Here. This one is given, not taken. That makes it a different fruit.  
_Your Nubbin eats it slowly, with its eyes shut, and glows all over like a paper lantern._  
**The Queen Mother of the West**: Keep the stone. Plant it somewhere you will be glad to see it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): peaches really come from China  
> _Peaches really do come from China, where people have grown them for thousands of years. That is why they are so much a part of its stories._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that peaches originated in China._

_Then the page turns, and turns, and turns. Five hundred years go by, and you sit through all of them with Monkey._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide time: 500 years in centuries  
> _A century is 100 years. How many centuries is five hundred years?_  
> - ✅ 5 centuries → Yes. 500 ÷ 100 = 5. Five hundred years is five centuries.
> - 50 centuries → That would be 5,000 years. One century is 100 years, so 500 is five of them.
> _For grown-ups: Your child converted 500 years into 5 centuries._

_Grass grows in his ears, and moss on his hand. Your Nubbin keeps one foot in that hand the whole time._  

### Glossary

- **wager**: A bet: an agreement about who wins, and what they get.

## A2-6. The Monk

- `a02-06-s1`: Carry the monk’s luggage along the road. · _Take the luggage when he asks._
- `a02-06-s2`: Climb the mountain and peel off the gold paper. · _Hold the monk’s staff and push when he slips._
- `a02-06-s3`: Wait at the roadside while tempers cool. · _Sit down by the road and wait._

#### `a02-06-road`

_A monk comes along the road on a pale horse. He has a begging bowl, a staff, a robe, and far too much luggage._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Good morning. Forgive me. Is this still the road west? Everyone who was walking with me has gone home.  
**Tang Sanzang**: I am Tang Sanzang. The emperor sent me to India, to bring back the true scriptures. It is a long way.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the real monk Xuanzang  
> _The monk in the novel is based on a real man, Xuanzang, who lived in the 600s._  
> _He left China in 629 and came home in 645, bringing back hundreds of Buddhist texts. He was away for sixteen years, many of them spent studying in India._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard about the real traveller behind the story’s monk._

_He says “a long way” the way people say it about the bottom of the garden. He has no idea._  
**Tang Sanzang**: You are carrying nothing, and I am carrying everything. Would you think it rude if I asked?  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows and the morning sun  
> _The monk walks west in the morning, and the sun rises in the east. Which way do his shadows fall?_  
> - ✅ Ahead of him, to the west → Yes. The sun is behind him, so his shadow stretches out in front, away from the sun.
> - Behind him, to the east → The sun is behind him, in the east. A shadow always points away from the light. So it falls ahead of him, to the west.
> _For grown-ups: Your child worked out which way a morning shadow falls._

_You take the luggage. It weighs about as much as your Nubbin, which climbs on top of it to make it heavier._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Thank you. Then you are my first disciple. No, my second. I keep forgetting the horse.  

#### `a02-06-road-done`

_From the mountain ahead, a voice you know shouts loud enough to shake the leaves._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues to infer  
> _The narrator says it is “a voice you know”. Whose voice do you think it is?_  
> - ✅ Monkey’s, from under the mountain → Yes. Who else shouts that loudly? The clue is “a voice you know”.
> - The monk’s → The monk is right beside you, on the road. A voice from the mountain you know already: it must be Monkey.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used a clue in the text to work out who was speaking._

_It sounds like someone who has been shouting at nobody for five hundred years._  

#### `a02-06-seal`

**Monkey**: Master! Master! You’ve come! A lady told me to wait for a monk, and I waited, and you’re a monk!  
_Monkey’s head sticks out of the mountainside, with grass in his ears. He sees your Nubbin and nearly cries._  
**Monkey**: Cousin. Cousin, you’re still here.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Oh dear. Are you a demon?  
**Monkey**: I’m your disciple. I’ve been your disciple for five hundred years. Go up and peel the paper off the top. Please.  
_The monk climbs. You hold his staff and push when he slips, which is often._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): pushes and pulls: gravity  
> _When the monk slips, you push him up the slope. Which invisible force is pulling him down?_  
> - ✅ Gravity → Yes. Gravity pulls everything towards the ground. Your push has to be bigger than the pull to help him up.
> - Wind → Wind might push a little, but the steady pull down the slope is gravity. Your push works against gravity.
> _For grown-ups: Your child named gravity as a force that pulls things down a slope._

_At the top there is a strip of gold paper. He peels it away, very carefully, as if it might mind._  

#### `a02-06-seal-done`

_The mountain splits like bread. Monkey bounds out, bows four times to the monk, and hugs your Nubbin off its feet._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a feeling after a long wait  
> _Monkey has waited five hundred years, and now he is free. Which pair of words best fits how he feels?_  
> - ✅ Relieved and thankful → Yes. Relief is the feeling when a long worry ends, and he shows thanks with his four bows.
> - Bored and sleepy → He is bouncing, hugging and bowing. That is energy and gladness. Relieved and thankful fits best.
> _For grown-ups: Your child named a feeling from a character’s actions._

**Monkey**: Right! Where are we going? India? Easy. I’ll have us there by lunch.  

#### `a02-06-band`

_Six robbers jump out of the trees. Monkey chases them over three hills with his staff, roaring, until there are no robbers anywhere._  
**Tang Sanzang**: You frightened them half to death! A monk must not frighten people half to death.  
**Monkey**: Five hundred years under a mountain, and this is the thanks?  
_He somersaults off in a huff, and the road is suddenly very empty._  
_An old woman comes along. She gives the monk a cap with a thin gold band, and teaches him a few quiet words._  
_As she goes, she looks back at you. Her eyes are very kind and very old, and you are almost sure she isn’t an old woman._  
_When Monkey comes back, a little sheepish, he sees the cap and puts it straight on._  
**Monkey**: Very fine. Does it suit me?  
_The monk murmurs the quiet words. The band tightens, and Monkey goes hopping round the road, holding his head._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): is the band fair? (a think question)  
> _The band lets the monk control Monkey from a distance. Is that fair, kind or useful?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Not fair: nobody should be forced → That is a fair answer. Monkey never agreed to it, and the monk says he never knew it was so strong.
> - Useful: it keeps others safe → That is a fair answer. Monkey’s strength is huge, and some limit may protect people, though it matters who decides.
> - Only fair if Monkey agrees and it is used rarely → That is a fair answer, and it is just what the monk promises: to use it only when he must.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up fairness, safety and consent._


**Choices**

- **Ask the monk to stop.**
    - **Tang Sanzang**: Oh! Yes. Of course. I had no idea it would be so strong.
    - **Tang Sanzang**: I will only use it when I must. I promise you both.
- **Wait. He’s stopping already.**
    - The monk stops almost at once, looking as shaken as Monkey. He clearly had no idea it would be so strong.

#### `a02-06-complete`

_Monkey tugs at the band. It won’t come off, and as far as anyone knows, it never will._  
**Monkey**: Fine. I’ll behave. Mostly. Some of the time.  
**Tang Sanzang**: That is all anyone can promise.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: learning to live with others  
> _What is this quest mostly about? Choose the best statement of its theme._  
> - ✅ Even strong, clever people have to learn to live with others → Yes, that is the theme: Monkey’s strength is not the problem, and living well with friends is the lesson.
> - You should always wear a cap → The cap matters in the plot, but it is not the big idea. The theme is about learning to live with others.
> _For grown-ups: Your child identified the theme of a story section._

_You pick up the luggage, and your Nubbin climbs onto it. The four of you, and the horse, set off west._  
_The road ahead is long and dusty, and for the first time it has company on it._  
_Somewhere in the distance, the old woman’s kind eyes are watching, and she is almost smiling._  

### Glossary

- **disciple**: A student or follower of a teacher.
- **sheepish**: A little embarrassed, because you know you did something silly.

## A2-7. The White Dragon Horse

- `a02-07-s1`: Walk to Eagle Grief Stream. · _Follow the sound of rushing water._
- `a02-07-s2`: Talk with the lady of the willow branch. · _Stand at the water’s edge._
- `a02-07-s3`: Watch the dragon change. · _Stay close to the bank._

#### `a02-07-stream`

_Eagle Grief Stream runs fast and green between steep rocks. The horse doesn’t like it, and neither does your Nubbin._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, ask): erosion by fast water  
> _The rocks beside the stream are steep and smooth, because fast water carries sand that scrapes them. What is this slow wearing-away called?_  
> - ✅ Erosion → Yes. Erosion is when water, wind or ice carries away bits of rock and soil, little by little.
> - Evaporation → Evaporation is water turning into vapour. Wearing away of rock is erosion.
> _For grown-ups: Your child named erosion as the wearing away of rock by moving water._

_Out of the water comes a white dragon, all teeth and spray. It swoops the horse up, saddle and all, and is gone._  
**Tang Sanzang**: My horse! How will I ever cross the world now?  
**Monkey**: I’ll get it back. Wait there.  
_Monkey fights the dragon up and down the stream. Every time he gets close, it dives where he can’t follow._  
**Monkey**: It won’t come out. Water is cheating.  
_Your Nubbin, who likes water a great deal, peers down into the stream and sees a long white shape, sulking._  

#### `a02-07-stream-done`

**Monkey**: The local spirits say a lady put that dragon here. I know which lady. I’m fetching her.  
_He is gone in a streak of cloud, muttering about people who give out headbands._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues to infer  
> _Monkey mutters about “people who give out headbands”. Which character does he mean?_  
> - ✅ The old woman on the road, who gave the cap → Yes. She gave the monk the cap with the band. Clues in the text let us work it out.
> - The Buddha → The Buddha put him under the mountain, but the old woman gave the band. That points to the old woman with the cap.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used clues to work out who a character meant._


#### `a02-07-guanyin`

_A light comes over the water like morning, though it is already afternoon. In it stands a lady with a vase and a willow branch._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Guanyin in Chinese Buddhism  
> _Guanyin is the bodhisattva of compassion in Chinese Buddhism._  
> _She is often shown with a willow branch and a vase of pure water. Many people pray to her for kindness and help._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned who Guanyin is in Chinese Buddhism._

_You know her eyes. She was the old woman on the road._  
**Monkey**: You gave him the band! You told him the words!  
**Guanyin**: I did. Without it, you would not listen to him. Without him, you would never get there.  
**Guanyin**: You are cleverer than all of them, Monkey. That is exactly why you need someone to walk beside.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): do clever people need others? (a think question)  
> _Guanyin says Monkey needs someone to walk beside because he is clever. Do very clever people need others?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes, nobody sees everything → That is a fair answer. A friend sees what a clever mind misses.
> - Not always, but it helps → That is a fair answer. Cleverness can do a lot, and company makes it wiser.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on why even clever people need companions._

_Monkey has no answer. Your Nubbin offers Guanyin a pebble, which is its highest honour, and she takes it._  

#### `a02-07-dragon`

**Guanyin**: Prince Yulong. Come up. The monk you were told to wait for is standing on your bank.  
_The white dragon rises from the stream, dripping and ashamed of itself._  
**Prince Yulong**: I didn’t know who he was. I was hungry, and cross, and sorry for myself.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a feeling word: ashamed  
> _The dragon rises “dripping and ashamed of itself”. What does ashamed mean here?_  
> - ✅ Feeling bad about something wrong you did → Yes. He knows taking the horse was wrong, and he feels it. Guanyin gives him a way to put it right.
> - Proud of a clever trick → Proud is nearly the opposite. He hangs his head because he knows he did wrong.
> _For grown-ups: Your child worked out the meaning of a feeling word from context._

**Guanyin**: Then be something better. Carry him all the way, and you will be forgiven all the way.  
_She touches his head with the willow branch. He shrinks and changes, and a white horse stands on the bank._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): ordinal numbers: Dragon is fifth, Horse is seventh  
> _In the zodiac, Dragon is fifth and Horse is seventh. How many animals come between them?_  
> - ✅ One: the Snake, sixth → Yes. Fifth, sixth, seventh: only the Snake sits in between.
> - Two → Count the places between: sixth only. 7 − 5 − 1 = 1.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used ordinal numbers and subtraction with the zodiac animals._

_The horse shakes the water out of his mane, straight over your Nubbin._  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin give the horse its peach stone to sniff.**
    - The horse sniffs the stone and blows softly. Your Nubbin takes this as the start of a long friendship.
- **Stroke his nose.**
    - He lets you. His nose is cool, like the inside of a river.

#### `a02-07-complete`

_Guanyin gives Monkey three hairs from the willow branch, for the day he truly needs them. Then the light goes off the water._  
**Tang Sanzang**: A dragon. I am riding a dragon. Nobody at home will believe me.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a repeating pattern: 12-year zodiac cycle  
> _The zodiac repeats every twelve years. If this year is a Dragon year, how many years until the next Dragon year?_  
> - ✅ 12 years → Yes. The pattern repeats every twelve years, so the next Dragon year is 12 years later.
> - 5 years → Dragon is fifth in the list, but the cycle has twelve animals. It takes the full twelve years to come back to Dragon.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used a repeating pattern of 12 to predict a future year._

**Monkey**: They won’t believe the rest of it either. Get used to it.  
_The white horse doesn’t speak again. He carries the monk with great care, all the way._  
_The stream behind you goes back to being only a stream, green and quick between its rocks._  
_The monk pats the white horse’s neck, and the horse flicks one ear, which is as good as a reply._  

### Glossary

- **erosion**: The slow carrying away of rock and soil by water, wind or ice.
- **bodhisattva**: In Buddhism, a wise and kind being who helps others find peace.

## A2-8. The Stolen Robe

- `a02-08-s1`: Visit the monastery’s guest hall. · _Go inside with the monk._
- `a02-08-s2`: Look into the smoke in the guest hall. · _Follow your Nubbin to the door._
- `a02-08-s3`: Find the robe on Black Wind Mountain. · _Carry the little round pill up on a dish._

#### `a02-08-hall`

_The monastery is rich and the abbot is very old. He has collected fine robes for two hundred years and shows you every one._  
**The old abbot**: Seven hundred robes! Has anyone, anywhere, ever seen more?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide: 700 robes on 7 shelves  
> _Suppose the abbot keeps his 700 robes on seven shelves, the same number on each. How many robes are on a shelf?_  
> - ✅ 100 → Yes. 700 ÷ 7 = 100. Seven hundreds shared by seven is one hundred each.
> - 70 → Seventy times seven is only 490. Try 100 × 7 = 700.
> _For grown-ups: Your child divided 700 by 7._

**Monkey**: My master has one better than all of them. Show him, master.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Please, no. One should never show off to a collector.  
_Monkey shows it anyway. It is the robe the Buddha himself sent with the monk, and the whole hall fills with light._  
**The old abbot**: Oh. Oh my. May I borrow it, just for tonight? Only to look at. An old man’s eyes are slow.  
_The monk sighs, and says yes. The abbot looks at the robe the way your Nubbin looks at peaches, only worse._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when does wanting turn into taking? (a think question)  
> _The abbot already has seven hundred robes and still wants one more. When does wanting something turn into a problem?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - When we stop caring about the other person → That is a fair answer. The monk’s robe is not the abbot’s to take.
> - When having more never feels like enough → That is a fair answer. Wanting that never ends can hide what we already have.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about greed and what it costs._


#### `a02-08-fire`

_In the night your Nubbin wakes you by sitting on your face. There is smoke under the door._  
_The abbot’s monks have piled firewood round the guest hall. They mean to keep the robe and blame the fire._  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): what to do if there is smoke  
> _There is smoke under the door. What is the safest thing to do?_  
> - ✅ Stay low, get out, and warn others → Yes. Smoke rises, so the air is clearest near the floor. Leave, and tell everyone.
> - Hide in a cupboard → Hiding can trap you. Smoke and flames find hiding places. Stay low, get out and warn others.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned to stay low, leave and warn others if there is smoke._

_Monkey is already awake. He has borrowed a fireproof cover from Heaven and spread it over the monk, who is still asleep._  
**Monkey**: And now a little wind. Let’s see whose hall burns.  
_He blows, and the fire turns round and goes the other way, away from the guest hall._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): what a fire needs  
> _Fire needs three things to keep burning. Which set is right?_  
> - ✅ Heat, fuel and air → Yes: take away any one and the fire goes out. Monkey’s wind pushes the fire towards new fuel instead.
> - Water, wood and wind → Water puts fires out. Wood is a fuel, and wind gives air. A fire needs heat, fuel and air.
> _For grown-ups: Your child named the three things a fire needs._

_Your Nubbin is already at the door, pulling your sleeve towards the dormitory where the young monks sleep._  

**Choices**

- **Run and shout until every monk is out.**
    - You run through the cloisters shouting. Monks tumble out of doorways in their nightclothes, coughing, all safe.
    - **Monkey**: You’re rescuing them? They lit it!
    - Monkey grumbles. Then he blows the fire away from the dormitory, just slightly.
- **Wake the monk. He would want to know.**
    - **Tang Sanzang**: Fire? Then everyone out. Everyone, Wukong. I don’t care who started it.
    - Monkey groans, and blows the fire away from the dormitory.

#### `a02-08-fire-done`

_On the hill above, something large and black has come down to “help” with the fire. It finds the robe instead._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): quotation marks that hint at doubt  
> _The narrator puts “help” in quotation marks. What does that hint?_  
> - ✅ The black shape is not really helping → Yes. The marks tell us the word is doubtful. The black shape has come for the robe.
> - Someone said it out loud → Quotation marks do show speech, but nobody spoke here. Here they hint that the “help” is not honest.
> _For grown-ups: Your child read meaning into quotation marks used as a hint._

_By morning the robe is gone, and so is the black shape, and the abbot is nowhere to be seen._  

#### `a02-08-bear`

_On Black Wind Mountain, the Black Bear is planning a party called the Feast of the Buddha’s Robe. He is very pleased with the name._  
_Guanyin has come. She takes the shape of the Bear’s friend, a guest on his way to the feast._  
_Monkey turns himself into a pill, a little round red one. You carry it up the mountain on a dish._  
**The Black Bear**: A gift from my old friend! How kind. I’ll take it straight away.  
_He swallows it. There is a short silence, and then a great deal of somersaulting inside the Bear._  
**The Black Bear**: Ow. Ow! All right! The robe! Take the robe!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): is trickery fair? (a think question)  
> _The Bear stole the robe, and Monkey tricked him to get it back. Is it fair to use a trick against someone who stole?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes, he started it → That is a fair answer. Many people feel a thief has little right to complain.
> - No, two wrongs don’t make a right → That is a fair answer. Guanyin was there to see the end of it fairly.
> - It depends how much harm the trick does → That is a fair answer. A harmless trick is easier to defend than a harmful one.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed whether a trick is fair against someone who stole._


**Choices**

- **Tell the Bear you’re sorry about his tummy.**
    - **The Black Bear**: So am I. You’re the only one who has said so.
- **Hold out your arms for the robe.**
    - The robe comes back into your arms, warm and faintly smoky. Your Nubbin smooths it flat, very seriously.

#### `a02-08-complete`

_Monkey pops out of the Bear’s mouth, very pleased with himself. The Bear sits down hard._  
**Guanyin**: You have a strong arm and a greedy heart. Come and guard my mountain. It will use the one and quiet the other.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what words refer back to  
> _Guanyin says guarding her mountain will “use the one and quiet the other”. What are “the one” and “the other”?_  
> - ✅ His strong arm and his greedy heart → Yes. Guarding uses his strength and gives his greed less room, so a job may help him change.
> - The robe and the feast → Read back to what she has just said: a strong arm and a greedy heart. His strength gets used, and his greed gets quieter.
> _For grown-ups: Your child read back in the text to find what two phrases refer to._

**The Black Bear**: Yes. All right. Thank you. I think.  
_Back at the monastery the monks sweep up very quietly. The monk gives them the last of his rice, which surprises them most of all._  
_Black Wind Mountain is quiet at last, and a little smoky, and smells faintly of pine._  
_Your Nubbin folds the robe into a square so neat that even the monk is impressed._  

### Glossary

- **abbot**: The head of a monastery.
- **dormitory**: A big room where many people sleep.

## A2-9. Pigsy

- `a02-09-s1`: Talk with Old Gao at the farm. · _Listen to his story._
- `a02-09-s2`: Wait quietly in the back house at night. · _Hide behind the screen with your Nubbin._
- `a02-09-s3`: Talk with Pigsy outside his cave. · _Bring the flowers your Nubbin kept._

#### `a02-09-gao`

**Old Gao**: He came three years ago. A fine strong young man. He ploughed without an ox, and dug without a spade.  
**Old Gao**: Then his face started to change. Now he has big ears and a long snout, and eats a whole barn a week.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): how a snout helps a pig  
> _Pigs have long snouts. How does a snout help a pig survive?_  
> - ✅ It roots in the soil for food and has a strong sense of smell → Yes. A pig’s snout is strong and sensitive, perfect for digging up roots and finding food.
> - It helps the pig fly → Pigs cannot fly, but their snouts are very useful on the ground. Digging up food and sniffing it out is what it is for.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned how a pig’s snout helps it find food._

**Old Gao**: And he’s shut my daughter in the back house and won’t let anyone see her. Can you send him away?  
**Monkey**: A monster with big ears who eats a lot? I’ll sort it. I’ll need a dress.  
**Tang Sanzang**: A what?  
**Monkey**: A dress. Trust me.  

#### `a02-09-backhouse`

_Miss Gao goes safely home to her father. In her bed, in her nightcap, lies Monkey, looking deeply unconvincing._  
_You and your Nubbin hide behind a screen. Your Nubbin has its paws over its mouth, just in case._  
_A wind blows the door open. In comes a big, round, black-bristled fellow with a snout, carrying flowers._  
**Pigsy**: I brought you some flowers. I picked them myself, mostly. Why are you so hairy tonight, my dear?  
**Monkey**: I’m not well. My father says he’ll fetch a holy man to chase you off.  
**Pigsy**: Ha! Let him. Nobody can catch me. Unless it’s that stone monkey who caused all that havoc in Heaven.  
**Monkey**: Funny you should say that.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): dramatic irony: you know more than the character  
> _You know it is Monkey in the bed, but Pigsy doesn’t. How does that make the scene funnier?_  
> - ✅ We know more than Pigsy, so we wait for him to find out → Yes. When the reader knows something a character does not, we watch and wait. That is called dramatic irony.
> - It makes the scene sadder → This one is comic. Waiting for him to find out is part of the fun. We know more than Pigsy does.
> _For grown-ups: Your child explained how knowing more than a character adds humour._

_Monkey sits up and pulls off the nightcap. The son-in-law gives a squeal and is out of the window in a gust of wind._  

#### `a02-09-backhouse-done`

_Your Nubbin picks up the dropped flowers and keeps them. Somebody ought to._  
_It sniffs them, and a fat bee, which has followed them all the way from the garden, sniffs them too._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, notice): flowers and pollinators  
> _Bees visit flowers for nectar, and pollen sticks to their bodies on the way._  
> _They carry it to the next flower. That is pollination, and it helps plants make seeds and fruit._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned how bees pollinate flowers._


#### `a02-09-cave`

_Monkey and the son-in-law fight all night outside his cave, staff against nine-toothed rake._  
**Pigsy**: Who are you, anyway? What are you doing here?  
**Monkey**: Escorting a monk from the East to fetch the scriptures. Tang Sanzang. You won’t have heard of him.  
_The rake drops. The pig-faced fellow goes pink all over._  
**Pigsy**: Tang Sanzang? The lady told me to wait for him! I’ve been waiting! I just got hungry while I waited.  
**Pigsy**: I used to be a marshal in Heaven, you know. I got a bit too merry at a party. Long story.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): lazy, greedy and lovable (a think question)  
> _Pigsy is lazy and greedy, and he is also warm and funny. Can one person be all of those at once?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes, people are mixed → That is a fair answer. Most people are a bit of everything, and that is what makes friendship interesting.
> - Only if the good outweighs the bad → That is a fair answer. We often weigh a friend’s faults against how kind they are.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on how a person can have both faults and virtues._


**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin give him back his flowers.**
    - **Pigsy**: You kept them! Oh, you’re a good little thing. I’m going to like you.
- **Tell him there’s room on the road.**
    - **Pigsy**: Is there room for lunch on the road? That’s the main thing.

#### `a02-09-complete`

_He burns his cave down to show he means it, and walks back to Gao Village with his rake over his shoulder._  
**Tang Sanzang**: You shall be called Bajie. It means Eight Rules. They are mostly about not eating.  
**Pigsy**: Pigsy for short. Everyone does.  
**Pigsy**: Father-in-law, keep my room for me, will you? Just in case the scriptures don’t work out.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): the zodiac order: the Pig comes last  
> _Pigsy is a pig, the twelfth and last animal in the zodiac. Which animal comes just before the Pig?_  
> - ✅ The Dog → Yes. Rooster, Dog, Pig: the Dog is eleventh, just before the Pig.
> - The Monkey → Monkey is ninth. After him come the Rooster and the Dog. So the Dog comes just before the Pig.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used the order of the zodiac animals._

_Old Gao says nothing, very politely. Pigsy takes the luggage pole for a whole mile before giving it back to you._  
_The road west lies ahead, and Pigsy has already found a reason to stop for a snack._  

### Glossary

- **snout**: The long front part of an animal’s face, with its nose and mouth.
- **marshal**: A high-ranking officer.

## A2-10. Sandy

- `a02-10-s1`: Walk to the River of Flowing Sands. · _Follow the monk to the bank._
- `a02-10-s2`: Swim down and meet the river spirit. · _Follow your Nubbin into the river._
- `a02-10-s3`: Wait on the bank for Moksa. · _Sit by the water and wait._

#### `a02-10-river`

_The River of Flowing Sands is eight hundred li wide and the colour of weak tea. A stone on the bank says that not even a feather floats on it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): convert li to kilometres  
> _A li is about half a kilometre. How wide is a river that is 800 li across?_  
> - ✅ 400 kilometres → Yes. Half of 800 is 400, so the river is about 400 kilometres wide, wider than any real river.
> - 1,600 kilometres → That doubles it. A li is half a kilometre, so halve it. 800 ÷ 2 = 400.
> _For grown-ups: Your child converted 800 li to about 400 kilometres._

_Your Nubbin drops a feather in, to check. It sinks._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): what makes things sink or float  
> _A feather would float on any ordinary river, yet a small stone sinks. What does it depend on?_  
> - ✅ How heavy it is for its size → Yes: things that are heavy for their size sink, and things light for their size float. This magic river sinks even a feather.
> - Only the colour → Colour does not matter. It depends on how heavy something is for its size.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that sinking and floating depend on weight for size._

**Pigsy**: Well, that’s that. Back to Gao Village, everyone.  
_Out of the water, with a roar, comes a big blue-faced river spirit with a monk’s spade. He reaches for the monk._  
_Monkey knocks him back, and Pigsy dives in after him. They splash and bellow and come up spitting sand._  
**Monkey**: I can’t fight in water. Pigsy can, but Pigsy keeps stopping for a rest.  

#### `a02-10-under`

_Your Nubbin slips into the river without a splash. You hold your breath and follow it._  
_Down in the brown water, the river spirit is sitting on a rock by himself, with his chin on his spade._  
_He is not frightening down here. He looks like someone who has been waiting a very long time for a ferry._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile  
> _“He looks like someone who has been waiting a very long time for a ferry.” What does this comparison tell us?_  
> - ✅ He seems patient, sad and used to being alone → Yes. A simile uses a picture we know to show a feeling.
> - He is about to catch a ferry → The ferry is only a picture to compare. It is not a plan. It shows he has been waiting, and lonely.
> _For grown-ups: Your child read the feeling in a simile._

**Sandy**: Another one. Every traveller who comes to this river wants to fight me, or run away.  
**Sandy**: I used to lift the curtains in Heaven. I broke a crystal cup. One cup. They sent me here.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): is the punishment fair? (a think question)  
> _Sandy lost his home in Heaven for breaking a single cup. Is that fair?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - No, the punishment is too big → That is a fair answer. A mistake should be matched by a fitting response.
> - We don’t know the whole story → That is a fair answer. We hear only his side so far.
> - Maybe, if the cup was very precious → That is a fair answer. How much harm was done matters, and so does what happens afterwards.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up fairness in a punishment._

_Your Nubbin pats his knee. He looks at it with great surprise, and then, slowly, pats it back._  

#### `a02-10-under-done`

_You come up gasping. Monkey has already somersaulted off to fetch help from the South Sea._  
_You take a long breath. Your lungs feel very glad to be lungs._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification  
> _“Your lungs feel very glad to be lungs.” Can lungs really feel glad?_  
> - ✅ No: it is a playful way to say how good the air feels → Yes. Giving human feelings to things that are not people is called personification.
> - Yes, lungs have feelings → Lungs help us breathe, but they do not feel glad. The writer gives them a feeling to show how good that breath is.
> _For grown-ups: Your child recognised personification._


#### `a02-10-moksa`

_Monkey comes back with Moksa, Guanyin’s disciple, who carries a small red gourd._  
**Moksa**: Sha Wujing! The monk you were told to wait for is on the bank. Come up.  
_The river spirit comes up out of the water at once, spade over his shoulder, and kneels on the sand._  
**Sandy**: I didn’t know. Nobody told me he’d look so ordinary.  
**Tang Sanzang**: I am very ordinary. That is rather the point.  
_Moksa sets the red gourd on the water. It grows into a raft, steady as a floor._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balance: why heavy things go low  
> _Why is it wise to load the heaviest things at the bottom of a raft?_  
> - ✅ It keeps the raft steady and hard to tip → Yes. Low weight keeps the raft’s centre of gravity low, so the forces stay balanced.
> - It makes the raft look tidy → Tidy is nice, but there is a better reason. Heavy things at the bottom keep it from tipping.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned why heavy loads go low on a raft._


**Choices**

- **Offer Sandy the other end of the luggage pole.**
    - **Sandy**: Thank you. I’ll carry it. I like carrying things. You know where you are with a weight.
- **Help Sandy load the raft.**
    - He loads it neatly, heaviest at the bottom. Pigsy sits on the lightest bit and calls it helping.

#### `a02-10-complete`

_The raft crosses eight hundred li in what feels like an afternoon. On the far bank it shrinks back into a gourd._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Wujing. Sha Wujing. We shall call you Sandy.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide: speed of the raft  
> _Suppose the raft crosses its 800 li in four hours. How many li does it cover each hour?_  
> - ✅ 200 li → Yes. 800 ÷ 4 = 200. Eight hundreds shared by four is two hundred.
> - 400 li → That would take two hours, not four. 800 ÷ 4 = 200.
> _For grown-ups: Your child divided distance by time to find a speed._

**Tang Sanzang**: Wukong, Bajie, Wujing, the horse, and you. My fifth disciple. I think I have the count right at last.  
_Now there are six of you, and the horse. Sandy takes the back end of the luggage pole, and you take the front._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): pack animals on the real Silk Road  
> _On the real Silk Road, traders crossed deserts with two-humped camels that could carry heavy loads for days._  
> _Sharing the load was a skill every traveller knew._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard how traders on the Silk Road used camels to carry loads._

_It is much easier like that. Your Nubbin rides in the middle and does the steering._  
_Behind you the river of sand flows on, as brown as weak tea, and as wide as ever._  

### Glossary

- **personification**: Describing a thing as if it were a person, with feelings or actions.

## A2-11. The Ginseng Fruit

- `a02-11-s1`: Visit the quiet temple. · _Walk in with the monk._
- `a02-11-s2`: Look at the tree in the garden. · _Go through to the garden._
- `a02-11-s3`: Carry water to the fallen tree. · _Fetch jade cups of water and pour gently._

#### `a02-11-temple`

_The temple is quiet and lovely. Its master is away, and two young acolytes, Bright Moon and Pure Wind, look after it._  
**Bright Moon**: Our master said a monk would come, and we were to give him two of the fruits from the tree.  
**Pure Wind**: They ripen once in nine thousand years. Smell one, and you live three hundred and sixty years.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): ginseng is a real plant  
> _Ginseng is a real plant. Its root has been used in Chinese medicine for a very long time._  
> _The tree in this story is made up, but the name is borrowed from the root._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that ginseng is a real plant whose root is used in medicine._

_They bring two fruits on a dish. Each is shaped like a tiny sleeping baby._  
**Tang Sanzang**: No! No, no. Take them away. I couldn’t possibly.  
**Bright Moon**: They’re fruit. They grow on a tree.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Take them away, please.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): refusing because of what something resembles (a think question)  
> _The monk won’t eat fruit shaped like babies, even though it is only fruit. Is he being wise, or just fussy?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Wise: he follows his conscience → That is a fair answer. Sometimes a feeling is a good guide, even when it cannot be explained.
> - Fussy: it is only fruit → That is a fair answer. Reason and a bit of curiosity can quieten a worry.
> - Both can be true → That is a fair answer. We often keep a principle and still learn it was stricter than needed.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed instinct against reason in a small decision._

_So the acolytes eat them themselves, in the kitchen. Pigsy, listening at the wall, makes a small hungry sound._  

#### `a02-11-tree`

**Pigsy**: Brother. Elder brother. Wise and handsome brother. Just three. One each. Nobody would notice.  
_Monkey knocks a fruit down with a golden rod. It hits the ground and sinks straight into it, like water._  
_He knocks down three more and catches them in his robe. Monkey, Pigsy and Sandy eat one each, very fast._  
**Pigsy**: I didn’t taste it. I swallowed it whole. Get me another so I can taste it.  
_The acolytes count their fruit and come back shouting thief. They shout it a great many times._  
**Monkey**: Thief? Thief? Fine. Then nobody gets any.  
_Monkey goes back to the garden in a temper and pushes the whole tree over. Its roots come up out of the ground._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): roots anchor a plant and take in water  
> _Roots hold a plant in the soil and soak up water and minerals. A tree knocked out of the ground can’t drink, so its leaves curl._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that roots anchor a plant and take in water._


**Choices**

- **Tell the acolytes the truth: you saw it all.**
    - **Bright Moon**: Thank you. At least someone in this party is honest.
    - Monkey glares at you. Then, after a moment, he stops glaring.
- **Go and kneel by the fallen tree.**
    - Its leaves are already curling. Your Nubbin lies down beside the roots, the way it lies by anything that’s hurt.

#### `a02-11-tree-done`

_Master Zhenyuan comes home that night. With one sweep of his sleeve he scoops up all six of you and the horse, like crumbs._  
**Master Zhenyuan**: Mend my tree, and I will let you go. I don’t much mind how.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): putting right a mistake  
> _When we break something that matters to someone, what is a good way to make up for it?_  
> - ✅ Put it right as well as we can, and say sorry → Yes. Repair and an apology go together. That is what the pilgrims now have to do.
> - Hope they forget → Forgetting does not fix a tree. Mending what we broke is the honest way forward.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about repairing a mistake._


#### `a02-11-mend`

_Monkey searches the three islands of the immortals for a cure, and nobody has one. At last he goes to the South Sea._  
_Guanyin comes with her vase. She draws a sign on Monkey’s palm and has him lay his hand on the roots._  
**Guanyin**: Bring water. Jade cups only. Pour gently.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): why a wilting plant needs water  
> _The tree is drooping and curling. What does a wilting plant need?_  
> - ✅ Water, soaked up through its roots → Yes. Plant stems stand up because they are full of water, so a drink is the first thing to try.
> - A bigger pot → A pot is not the problem here. Wilting means a plant is short of water, so water through the roots is what it needs.
> _For grown-ups: Your child said that a wilting plant needs water._

_You carry cup after cup. Your Nubbin carries a very small cup, and pours very slowly, and gets most of it in._  
_Suppose each jade cup holds 250 millilitres and Nubbin’s little cup holds 50._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): divide: millilitres in cups  
> _One jade cup holds 250 millilitres, and your Nubbin’s cup holds 50. How many of its little cups would fill one jade cup?_  
> - ✅ 5 → Yes. 250 ÷ 50 = 5. Five small cups make one jade cup.
> - 50 → 50 is the size of the little cup, not how many. 250 ÷ 50 = 5.
> _For grown-ups: Your child divided to compare two volumes in millilitres._

_Guanyin dips her willow branch in the vase and sprinkles the dew over all of it._  
_The tree stands up, and its leaves uncurl, green and glossy. There are fruit on it, exactly the right number._  

#### `a02-11-complete`

**Master Zhenyuan**: Well. That is the most trouble anyone has caused me in a thousand years. Come and eat with me.  
_There is a feast of the ginseng fruit. This time the monk eats one, now he knows it is only fruit._  
**Tang Sanzang**: It tastes like the first morning of spring.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile for taste  
> _“It tastes like the first morning of spring.” What feeling does this simile give the fruit?_  
> - ✅ Fresh, new and hopeful → Yes. Spring mornings mean a new start, so the taste feels fresh and bright.
> - Sour and cold → Spring can be chilly, but the simile is about a hopeful start. Fresh, new and hopeful.
> _For grown-ups: Your child read the feeling behind a simile about taste._

_Master Zhenyuan and Monkey swear to be brothers. Monkey looks almost embarrassed, which is new._  
_In the garden, the tree stands tall again, and a single new fruit is just beginning to swell._  
_Your Nubbin lies at the foot of it, sleepy and content, with a jade cup still in its paws._  

### Glossary

- **acolyte**: A helper or junior member of a temple.
- **ginseng**: A plant whose root is used in traditional medicine.

## A2-12. The White Bone Demon

- `a02-12-s1`: Watch the girl on White Tiger Ridge. · _Stay by the monk._
- `a02-12-s2`: Watch the old woman on the ridge. · _Stay by the monk, and keep your Nubbin close._
- `a02-12-s3`: Choose whom to believe. · _Think about what you saw and what you were told. Then say why._
- `a02-12-s4`: Walk to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. · _Go with Pigsy. It is easier with two._

#### `a02-12-girl`

_White Tiger Ridge is all bare rock and thin wind. The monk is hungry, and Monkey has gone to find fruit._  
_A girl comes down the path with a basket of rice and noodles. She smiles at everyone and doesn’t blink._  
**A stranger on the ridge**: Kind travellers! Please, eat. I brought this up for my father, but you need it more.  
_Your Nubbin hides behind your legs. It has never once hidden from somebody with food._  
_Monkey comes back, takes one look, and swings his staff. The girl crumples like an empty coat, and a cold puff of air goes up._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Wukong! She was only a girl with a basket!  
**Monkey**: She was a demon in disguise. Look in the basket.  
_In the basket there are no noodles, only worms and frogs, wriggling. The monk looks, and looks away._  
**Pigsy**: He’s turned the noodles into worms so you won’t be cross with him. He can do that, you know.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): deciding between conflicting accounts (a think question)  
> _The monk sees a girl, Monkey sees a demon in disguise, and Pigsy says Monkey is making it up. How can we decide who is right?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Look for more evidence before we decide → That is a fair answer. Careful people collect more clues before they judge.
> - Trust the one who knows them best → That is a fair answer: a friend’s record counts. It is also worth asking how they know.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up conflicting accounts of the same event._


#### `a02-12-girl-done`

_The monk says the quiet words. Monkey holds his head and says nothing back._  
_He could have shouted. He chooses, this time, to be silent._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how a character responds to an event  
> _Monkey is hurt and angry, but he chooses silence. What does that choice show about him?_  
> - ✅ He is learning to calm down before he speaks → Yes. A pause keeps him from saying something he would regret, and that is new for Monkey.
> - He has nothing to say → Monkey always has something to say. This time he holds it back, which shows he is learning to calm down.
> _For grown-ups: Your child explained what a character’s response shows about him._


#### `a02-12-old-woman`

_An old woman comes up the path, leaning on a stick, weeping. She is looking for her daughter._  
**A stranger on the ridge**: Have you seen my girl? She went this way with a basket.  
_She doesn’t blink either. Your Nubbin is pressed so hard against your ankles you can feel it shaking._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-2, ask): what fear does to the body  
> _Your Nubbin is trembling and pressed against you. What happens in our bodies when we are scared?_  
> - ✅ Our hearts beat faster and our muscles get ready to run or freeze → Yes. Fear is a built-in alarm that prepares the body, and it is a normal reaction.
> - Nothing, fear is only in the mind → The body reacts too, with a faster heart, quick breathing and shaky legs. It is normal, and it passes.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that fear is a normal bodily alarm._

_Monkey swings again. The old woman folds away like paper, and a puff of cold air goes up and over the ridge._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Twice! Twice in one morning!  
**Monkey**: The same demon twice. She keeps getting away, and she keeps coming back.  

#### `a02-12-bones`

_An old man comes last, fingering prayer beads, looking for his wife and daughter. He does not blink._  
_This time Monkey calls the mountain spirits to stand guard, so she can’t slip away. Then he swings._  
_The old man folds up like an empty coat. Where he stood lies a small heap of white bones, chalky as old shells._  
**Monkey**: There. Bones. There’s your demon. Now do you believe me?  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): the skeleton  
> _Bones are real parts of a living body. About how many bones does an adult human skeleton have?_  
> - ✅ 206 → Yes. An adult has 206. Babies have more, because many of their bones join together as they grow.
> - 50 → Many more than that: 206 in an adult. Your hands alone have 54.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned how many bones an adult human skeleton has._

**Pigsy**: He’s made them look like bones. It’s a trick, so you’ll stop saying the words.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Three people, Wukong. A girl, her mother, her father. I can’t walk beside someone who does that.  
_The monk writes a letter of dismissal and holds it out. Then everybody, even Monkey, looks at you._  
**Tang Sanzang**: You carry our things. You have seen all we have seen. What do you think?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): who do you believe? (the big think question)  
> _Do you trust what you saw, in the way your Nubbin hid, or what you were told, that you can’t strike on a hunch?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Give your reason, then choose._  
> - What I saw: my Nubbin hid, and that matters → That is a fair answer. A gut feeling can be a signal, though the monk may still ask for proof.
> - The rule: don’t act on a hunch → That is a fair answer. Rules guard people from our mistakes, though Monkey may feel unheard.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed first-hand evidence against a rule of caution._


**Choices**

- **Believe Monkey. You saw your Nubbin hide.**
    - **You**: I believe him. My Nubbin hid from her three times. It never hides from anyone.
    - **Tang Sanzang**: A Nubbin’s feelings are not proof. I am sorry. I can’t risk it.
    - **Monkey**: Cousin’s keeper. Thank you. Remember you said it.
- **Believe the monk. You can’t strike people on a hunch.**
    - **You**: Even if you’re right, you can’t just hit people because you’re sure.
    - **Monkey**: I wasn’t sure. I knew.
    - **Monkey**: Fine. Remember you said it, Cousin’s keeper.

#### `a02-12-bones-done`

_Monkey can’t leave without bowing to his master, and the monk won’t look at him. So he pulls three hairs and blows on them._  
_Three more Monkeys appear, and the monk is surrounded. Four bows, on every side, all the way to the ground._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiply: four Monkeys, four bows each  
> _Suppose each of the four Monkeys bows four times. How many bows is that in all?_  
> - ✅ 16 → Yes. Four groups of four make 16.
> - 8 → That adds 4 + 4. There are four groups of four. 4 × 4 = 16.
> _For grown-ups: Your child multiplied 4 × 4._

_Then Monkey is gone, and your Nubbin sits in the road looking at the place where he was._  

#### `a02-12-return`

_Without Monkey, it goes badly. A demon in a yellow robe catches the monk and turns him into a tiger, of all things._  
**Pigsy**: I’ll have to fetch him. I’ll have to say sorry. I hate saying sorry. You come too, it’s easier with two.  
_Back at the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, Monkey is king again, with his feet up. Your Nubbin runs at him and he catches it._  
**Pigsy**: The demon says he isn’t frightened of you. Says you’re just a jumped-up monkey.  
**Monkey**: He said that? He said that? Right.
