> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why does Pigsy tell Monkey that the demon called him a “jumped-up monkey”?_  
> - ✅ To make him angry enough to come and fight → Yes. Pigsy knows Monkey’s pride, and he uses it to bring him back.
> - Because he is repeating gossip → Look at the wink. It is a plan, not gossip. Pigsy wants Monkey angry enough to come.
> _For grown-ups: Your child worked out a character’s hidden motive._

_Pigsy winks at you. It is the cleverest thing you have ever seen him do._  

#### `a02-12-return-done`

_Monkey beats the demon, and the monk is a monk again, shaking and ashamed._  
**Tang Sanzang**: I was wrong to send you away, Wukong. I am sorry.  
**Monkey**: You were wrong about her. You weren’t wrong to be scared of what I can do. I’m scared of it too, sometimes.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): saying you are scared of your own strength  
> _Monkey admits he is sometimes scared of what he can do. Does that make him weak?_  
> - ✅ No: it shows he understands his own power → Yes. Knowing the size of your strength, and respecting it, is wise.
> - Yes: strong people never feel fear → Everyone feels fear, including the strongest. Admitting it can be a strength.
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that admitting fear can show wisdom._


#### `a02-12-complete`

_The monk takes Monkey’s hand in both of his. It is the first time either of them has done that._  
_Sandy picks up the back of the luggage pole. You pick up the front._  
**Monkey**: Cousin’s keeper. I haven’t forgotten what you said.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Xuanzang wrote a travel book  
> _The real Xuanzang wrote down what he saw on his travels._  
> _His book describes cities, deserts and customs along the way, and historians still read it today to learn about those places._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that the real monk wrote a travel record that historians use._

_He doesn’t say whether that is good or bad. Your Nubbin rides on his shoulder for the rest of the day._  
_The ridge behind you is only rock and thin wind again, and nothing whispers._  
_Somewhere ahead, the road is waiting, and so, for once, is a calmer pilgrim._  

### Glossary

- **disguise**: Clothes or a shape you use to hide who you really are.
- **evidence**: Facts or clues that help show whether something is true.

## A2-13. The Magic Gourd

- `a02-13-s1`: Talk with Monkey in the pine wood. · _Listen to the rule of the gourd._
- `a02-13-s2`: Wait at the cave and do not answer. · _Keep your mouth shut. So does your Nubbin._
- `a02-13-s3`: Watch the gourd get swapped. · _Stay still and quiet._

#### `a02-13-rule`

_On Level Top Mountain live two demon brothers, Gold Horn and Silver Horn. They have caught the monk and Pigsy already._  
**Monkey**: They have a gourd. Purple and gold. They call your name, and if you answer, whoosh, you’re inside it.  
**Sandy**: So don’t answer.  
**Monkey**: I answered. I gave them a made-up name, and answered to that, and it still got me. It doesn’t care if the name is real.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what the rule really is  
> _Monkey answered to a made-up name, and the gourd still caught him. What does that tell us about how the gourd works?_  
> - ✅ It is the answering that counts, not the name → Yes. The trick works on the reply, which is why silence is the only safe answer.
> - It only works on real names → Monkey’s made-up name worked too. It is the answering that counts.
> _For grown-ups: Your child worked out the hidden rule from an example._

**Monkey**: It only cares that you answered. I got out by pretending I’d melted. Don’t ask.  
_Your Nubbin looks very hard at its own mouth, as if to check it is shut._  

#### `a02-13-gourd`

_Silver Horn stands at the cave mouth with the gourd held upside down, and calls into the trees._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): gourds are real fruits  
> _Gourds are real. They are the fruit of plants in the same family as pumpkins and squashes._  
> _People have dried hard gourds and used them as bottles and bowls for thousands of years._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that gourds are real fruits that people have used as containers._

**Silver Horn**: Little round one! You, with the big eyes! Little Nubbin!  
_Your Nubbin looks at him, and blinks, and says nothing. It has never said anything in its life._  
**Silver Horn**: Answer me! It’s rude not to answer!  
_It blinks again. Silver Horn shakes the gourd, as if it might be broken._  
**Silver Horn**: All right. You, then. The one carrying the luggage. Answer me!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): is silence ever right? (a think question)  
> _Silver Horn says it is rude not to answer. When someone demands a reply, is it ever right to say nothing?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes, when answering would put me in danger → That is a fair answer. We do not owe everyone a reply, especially someone who means harm.
> - Usually no: manners matter, so I would say “no, thank you” → That is a fair answer. A short, polite refusal can protect us without being rude.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on when silence is the right response._


**Choices**

- **Keep your mouth shut, like your Nubbin.**
    - You say nothing. Your Nubbin looks up at you with enormous approval.
- **Start to say, “Who wants to know?”**
    - You get as far as “Who” before the gourd begins to pull. Monkey yanks you behind a rock by the collar.
    - **Monkey**: What did I just say? What did I literally just say?

#### `a02-13-swap`

_While Silver Horn shouts at your Nubbin, a little fly lands on his sleeve. A moment later his gourd has been swapped for a fake._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): insects have six legs  
> _The little fly is really Monkey in disguise. How many legs does a real insect such as a fly have?_  
> - ✅ Six → Yes. Insects have six legs and three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.
> - Eight → Eight legs belong to spiders, which are not insects. Insects have six.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that insects have six legs._

_Monkey stands on a rock with the real one, upside down._  
**Monkey**: Silver Horn!  
**Silver Horn**: What?  
_Whoosh. Monkey puts the stopper in, and shakes the gourd next to his ear._  
**Monkey**: Never answer to your own name, little brother. Didn’t anyone tell you?  

#### `a02-13-swap-done`

## A2-14. Red Boy

- `a02-14-s1`: Look at the boy tied to the pine tree. · _Look at your Nubbin, then at the boy._
- `a02-14-s2`: Carry water to Monkey at Fire Cloud Cave. · _Run with the bucket._
- `a02-14-s3`: Talk with Guanyin at the cave. · _Stand by the lotus seat._

#### `a02-14-pine`

_A child is tied to the top of a pine tree, crying for help. He is about seven, with a red jacket and a hopeful face._  
**Red Boy**: Robbers left me here! Please, kind master, take me home!  
**Tang Sanzang**: Wukong, untie him at once and carry him.  
_Monkey looks at the boy. Then he looks at you, the way he looked at you on White Tiger Ridge._  
**Monkey**: Master, a child doesn’t tie himself to the top of a pine tree. Robbers aren’t that tidy.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Wukong. A child is crying. Untie him.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): kindness or caution? (a think question)  
> _The monk wants to help a crying child at once, but Monkey wants to be careful. Which matters more here?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Kindness: a child in trouble comes first → That is a fair answer. A kind heart is the monk’s whole strength.
> - Caution: ask questions first → That is a fair answer. Monkey has seen this trick before.
> - Both: help, but carefully → That is a fair answer, and it is what Monkey tries: carry him, but keep a close watch.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up kindness against caution._


**Choices**

- **Look at your Nubbin first.**
    - Your Nubbin isn’t hiding. It is staring at the boy with its head on one side, puzzled, as if he smells of bonfires.
    - **Monkey**: Puzzled. Not scared. Good. I’ll carry him. Carefully.
- **Help untie him.**
    - The knots are very easy to undo, too easy. Monkey takes the boy on his back without a word.

#### `a02-14-pine-done`

_The boy makes himself as heavy as a mountain on Monkey’s back. Then, with a gust of wind, he and the monk are gone._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile that uses “as”  
> _“As heavy as a mountain.” Which pair of words makes this a simile?_  
> - ✅ “as … as” → Yes. “As … as” compares two things, which is the mark of a simile.
> - “heavy” and “mountain” → Those are the things being compared. The “as … as” frame is what makes it a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Your child spotted the "as … as" pattern in a simile._

**Monkey**: Of course. Of course he was.

**Red Boy**: I am Red Boy! The Bull Demon King is my father. You’re supposed to be my uncle, but I don’t care.  
_Monkey calls the dragon kings, and they rain on the fire. It only burns hotter: this fire doesn’t mind water at all._  
_Monkey comes out singed and smoking, and dives into a cold stream to cool off. The cold knocks him flat._  
**Sandy**: Water. More water, cold. Not too fast.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, do): friction makes heat  
> _(Rub your hands together hard for ten seconds, and feel them get warm. That is friction turning movement into heat.)_  
> Check: `edu:rub:hands:warm`
> _For grown-ups: Your child felt friction make heat by rubbing their hands._

_Suppose your bucket holds five litres, and you make six trips._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 6 trips of 5 litres  
> _Your bucket holds five litres, and you make six trips. How many litres of water do you bring?_  
> - ✅ 30 litres → Yes. 6 × 5 = 30 litres.
> - 11 litres → That adds 6 + 5. Six equal trips means we multiply. 6 × 5 = 30.
> _For grown-ups: Your child multiplied 6 × 5 in a word problem._

_Your Nubbin lies on Monkey’s chest, because that is where it would want someone to lie._

**Monkey**: Ugh. I’m all right. I’m all right. Get off, Cousin. No, stay there a minute.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): what we say and what we mean  
> _Monkey says “get off” and then “stay a minute”. People often say one thing and need another, and a good friend listens to both._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that words and wishes can differ._

**Monkey**: Fire I can’t beat, demon I can’t catch. There’s only one person for this.  

#### `a02-14-lotus`

_Guanyin comes from the South Sea. She sets a lotus seat on the ground outside the cave, and steps away from it._  
**Guanyin**: Bring him out, Monkey. Then let him see this seat.  
_Red Boy chases Monkey out, sees the lovely lotus seat with nobody on it, and sits straight down on it, laughing._  
_The seat closes gently round him like a flower at evening. He can’t get up, and the fire goes out of him._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): lotus flowers open and close with the day  
> _Real lotus flowers open in the morning and close again in the evening. Lotus seeds are tough: some have sprouted after sleeping for hundreds of years._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that lotus flowers close at night and their seeds can survive for centuries._

**Red Boy**: Let me go! Let me go! I want my mother!

#### `a02-14-complete`

_The monk is untied, smelling of smoke. Red Boy goes with Guanyin, walking a step behind her, quite quiet._  
**Tang Sanzang**: He was only a boy, really.  
**Monkey**: He was a boy who set fire to me. But yes.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): kindness to someone who hurt you (a think question)  
> _Monkey says Red Boy was a boy who set fire to him, “but yes”. Can you feel kind towards someone who hurt you?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes, understanding is not the same as forgiving → That is a fair answer. You can understand why someone acted that way without saying it was fine.
> - Only if they say sorry → That is a fair answer. An apology can open the door, and some people find kindness comes first.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on whether kindness can coexist with being hurt._

_Your Nubbin finds a little red ribbon from his jacket by the cave. It keeps it, for his mother, in case._

## A2-15. The Two Monkeys

- `a02-15-s1`: Carry the luggage along the road. · _Hold on to the pack._
- `a02-15-s2`: Watch the two Monkeys at the South Sea. · _Stand beside Guanyin._
- `a02-15-s3`: Choose which Monkey is the real one. · _It is allowed to say you cannot tell._
- `a02-15-s4`: Talk with the Buddha at the monastery. · _Follow the two Monkeys into the hall._

#### `a02-15-snatch`

_It happens again: bandits on the road, Monkey too rough with them, the monk too angry. Monkey is sent away._  
_This time nobody cries; everyone is too tired. Pigsy goes to find water, and Sandy goes after Pigsy._  
_Then Monkey comes back, alone, with a cup of water held out in both hands._  
**Monkey**: Master. I’m sorry. Here. Drink.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Go away, Wukong. I meant it.  
_Monkey’s face changes. He knocks the monk flat, and grabs for the luggage you are carrying._  
_Your Nubbin hisses at him. It has never hissed at Monkey in its life._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): noticing clues that something is wrong  
> _Which clue best tells us this Monkey is not the real one?_  
> - ✅ He turned from gentle to violent in a moment, and your Nubbin hissed → Yes. Sudden changes in behaviour, and a trusted friend’s reaction, are strong clues.
> - He is carrying a cup of water → A cup of water on its own is not suspicious. The sudden switch, and the hiss, are the clues.
> _For grown-ups: Your child used behaviour as evidence._


#### `a02-15-snatch-done`

_He tears the pack off the pole and is gone in a streak of cloud. The monk sits up, dizzy but unhurt._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): what a cloud is made of  
> _Monkey escapes on a streak of cloud. What is a real cloud made of?_  
> - ✅ Tiny drops of water, or ice crystals, floating in the air → Yes. Clouds form when water vapour cools and turns into droplets.
> - Cotton and smoke → They look like cotton, but they are water. Droplets of water or ice.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned what clouds are made of._

**Sandy**: That wasn’t like him. Even at his worst, that wasn’t like him.  

#### `a02-15-twins`

_Sandy goes to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He comes back with news: Monkey is there with a monk, a Pigsy, a Sandy and your luggage._  
_At Guanyin’s island Sandy finds the real Monkey, who has been sulking there all along. Then the false one turns up, and there are two of him._  
**Monkey**: Who are you? Why have you got my face?  
**Monkey**: Who are you? Why have you got my face?  
_Guanyin says the quiet words of the band. Both Monkeys clutch their heads and roll on the ground together._  
**Guanyin**: I cannot tell them apart.  
_They fight all the way up to Heaven. The Jade Emperor’s mirror shows two Monkeys, exactly the same, down to the last hair._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry  
> _The mirror shows two identical Monkeys, as if one were folded onto the other._  
> _A line of symmetry is a fold that makes both halves match. How many lines of symmetry does a square have?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. Two through the middles of the sides and two through opposite corners.
> - 2 → Two is a good start: fold it top to bottom and left to right. Then try corner to corner. That makes four in all.
> _For grown-ups: Your child counted the lines of symmetry in a square._

_Your Nubbin, who can always find Monkey in a crowd, looks from one to the other and starts to cry._  

#### `a02-15-which`

_The two Monkeys tumble down out of the sky and land in the road in front of the monk, still fighting._  
_The monk stands up. He doesn’t look at either of them; he looks at you._  
**Tang Sanzang**: On White Tiger Ridge, you believed him when I would not. You trusted what you saw.  
**Tang Sanzang**: So look now. Which one is my disciple?  
_Two Monkeys, two staffs, two golden bands. Both faces are looking at you, hopeful and furious, exactly alike._  
_Your Nubbin is holding both their tails, one in each paw, and won’t let go of either._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): is “I can’t tell” an answer? (a think question)  
> _You cannot tell which Monkey is real. Is it better to guess, or to say plainly that you cannot tell?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Say it plainly: a guess might hurt someone → That is a fair answer. Honest uncertainty is better than a confident mistake. Scientists say “we do not know yet” all the time. It is where careful testing starts.
> - Guess: someone needs an answer now → That is a fair answer. Sometimes we have to act, though we should say it is a guess.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed honesty about uncertainty against the pressure to answer._


**Choices**

- **Point at the one on the left.**
    - **Monkey**: Ha! You see? The little luggage-carrier knows me.
    - **Monkey**: Ha! You see? The little luggage-carrier knows me.
    - They say it at the same moment, in the same voice, with the same grin. Your pointing finger feels very foolish.
    - **Tang Sanzang**: That settles nothing. I am sorry I asked you to carry it.
- **Point at the one on the right.**
    - **Monkey**: There! Somebody with eyes in their head at last.
    - **Monkey**: There! Somebody with eyes in their head at last.
    - Both of them bow to you. Both bows are exactly as deep, and exactly as rude.
    - **Tang Sanzang**: That settles nothing. I am sorry I asked you to carry it.
- **Say it plainly: “I can’t tell. I won’t pretend I can.”**
    - Both Monkeys open their mouths, and then neither of them says anything at all.
    - **Tang Sanzang**: Thank you. That is the first true thing anyone has said since this began.
    - **Sandy**: Then we stop asking people who can’t know, and go to the one who does.

#### `a02-15-named`

_The two Monkeys fight all the way to the Buddha’s hall. The Buddha is talking with his disciples, and he stops, and smiles._  
**The Buddha**: There are four kinds of monkey that the world does not list. This is the one with six ears. He hears everything, from everywhere.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): why some animals have big or many ears  
> _The six-eared monkey “hears everything”. Why do animals with large ears often hear well?_  
> - ✅ Bigger ears can collect more sound → Yes. Large ears gather sound waves, like a satellite dish, which is why bats, foxes and elephants have such good hearing.
> - Large ears keep their eyes warm → Some big ears, like an elephant’s, help cool the body, but for hearing it is about collecting sound.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned how large ears help animals hear._

**The Buddha**: He heard your story, Wukong, and wanted to be you. That is all.  
_The false Monkey tries to run. The Buddha’s golden bowl comes down over him like a lid on a pot._  
_When it lifts, there is only a small monkey with six ears, shaking. Monkey raises his staff._  
_Then he looks at the monk, and at your Nubbin, and lowers it._  
**Monkey**: Go on. Go. Be yourself somewhere. It’s harder, but it’s yours.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being yourself  
> _Monkey tells the copycat to be himself, even though it is harder. Why is it worth it?_  
> - ✅ Copying someone leaves you without a self of your own → Yes. Being yourself is harder, but it is the only way to have a life that is truly yours.
> - Copying is easier, so it is better → Easier, yes. Better, not usually. Being yourself is harder and more yours.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about why being yourself is worthwhile._


#### `a02-15-complete`

_The six-eared monkey runs off into the trees and doesn’t look back. The luggage comes home, a bit dusty._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Wukong. Will you come back? Please?  
**Monkey**: Only if you say it twice.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character wants  
> _Why does Monkey ask the monk to say “please” twice?_  
> - ✅ He is hurt and wants to be sure he is truly wanted → Yes. The repeat shows that he needs to hear it again, to believe it.
> - He is just being annoying → It sounds like teasing, but look at his mood: soft. He needs to be sure he is wanted.
> _For grown-ups: Your child inferred a character’s feelings from a small request._

**Tang Sanzang**: Please.  
_Your Nubbin lets go of the tail it has been holding. It has been holding the right one, as it happens, all along._  
_By evening the four of you, and the horse, are walking west again, and nobody mentions the cloud._  

### Glossary

- **symmetry**: When one half of a shape matches the other half, like a mirror image.

## A2-16. The Flaming Mountains

- `a02-16-s1`: Talk with Princess Iron Fan. · _Hold out the red ribbon._
- `a02-16-s2`: Watch Monkey try the fan. · _Stand well back from the flames._
- `a02-16-s3`: Carry the real fan across the mountains. · _Hold it up with Sandy._

#### `a02-16-ask`

_Ahead the whole land is on fire: the Flaming Mountains, eight hundred li of them. The only way over is a magic palm-leaf fan._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): the real Flaming Mountains  
> _The Flaming Mountains are real: a range of red sandstone hills in the Turpan area of north-west China, on the old Silk Road._  
> _Summer days there can pass 40 °C (104 °F). The real Xuanzang travelled through that region._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard about a real place in China on the Silk Road._

_It belongs to Princess Iron Fan. She is Red Boy’s mother._  
**Princess Iron Fan**: You! You gave my son to that lady! He lives on her island and sweeps her floors now!  
**Monkey**: He’s happy! He’s learning things! He’s not setting fire to people any more!  
_She takes out the fan and waves it once. Monkey goes flying fifty thousand li, end over end, and out of sight._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): compare distances: 50,000 li and the Earth  
> _Fifty thousand li is about 25,000 kilometres, and the Earth is about 40,000 kilometres round. Has Monkey flown more or less than halfway round the world?_  
> - ✅ More: half of 40,000 is 20,000, and 25,000 is bigger → Yes. Monkey has flown more than halfway round the world in a single wave of the fan.
> - Less than halfway → Halfway round would be 20,000 kilometres. 25,000 is more than 20,000.
> _For grown-ups: Your child compared a distance with half the Earth’s circumference._

_Your Nubbin steps forward and holds out the red ribbon from Red Boy’s jacket._  

**Choices**

- **Tell her where your Nubbin found it.**
    - **Princess Iron Fan**: His. That’s his. He was always losing it.
    - She holds it for a long time. She doesn’t give you the fan, but she doesn’t blow you away, either.
- **Let her take it without a word.**
    - She takes it and turns away, and you hear her breathe out, slowly. The door stays open.

#### `a02-16-ask-done`

_Monkey comes back with a wind-fixing pill in his cheek, turns into a tiny fly, and gets into her tea._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: fly  
> _Monkey turns into a “fly”, and earlier he went “flying” fifty thousand li. What are the two meanings of fly?_  
> - ✅ A small insect, and to move through the air → Yes. The same word spelled the same way can have more than one meaning, and context tells us which.
> - Only the insect → The fan makes Monkey fly through the air, too. Two meanings: insect, and moving through the air.
> _For grown-ups: Your child found two meanings of "fly" from context._

_After some time, and some kicking from inside, the princess hands over a fan. Monkey comes out very pleased._  

#### `a02-16-fake`

_Monkey stands at the edge of the flames and waves the fan with a flourish._  
_The fire leaps up twice as high. He waves again, and it leaps higher still, and his tail starts to smoke._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): why fanning makes a fire bigger  
> _Monkey waves the fan, and the fire leaps up higher. Why does fanning a fire make it bigger?_  
> - ✅ It brings more air, and fire needs air to burn → Yes: fanning pushes in fresh air with oxygen, and that feeds the flames. The fan really was a fake.
> - It cools the fire so it grows → Fanning does cool things sometimes, but a hot fire needs the air more. More air makes it burn harder.
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that moving air feeds a fire._

**Monkey**: It’s a fake! She gave me a fake!  
**Pigsy**: Run!  
_Everybody runs. Pigsy runs fastest, which nobody has ever seen before._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Wukong, your tail. Your tail is on fire.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): was it fair to trick him? (a think question)  
> _Princess Iron Fan gave Monkey a fake fan, just after he crept into her tea. Who is more in the wrong, and does one trick ever cancel out another?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Monkey: he tricked her first → That is a fair answer. Monkey crept into her tea, and she was entitled to be angry.
> - The princess: a fake that burns someone is cruel → That is a fair answer. She knew what the fake would do.
> - Both: and neither fixed anything → That is a fair answer. Two tricks leave two people angry.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up two tricks and who was more at fault._


**Choices**

- **Pat out Monkey’s tail.**
    - **Monkey**: Thank you. That’s my good tail. I only have the one.
- **Try very hard not to laugh.**
    - You fail. Your Nubbin fails too, rolling about in the dust.
    - **Monkey**: Yes. All right. It was quite funny.

#### `a02-16-real`

_There is a long and complicated business with the Bull Demon King, Monkey in disguise, and Pigsy in a temper._  
_In the end, Princess Iron Fan comes out herself with the real fan, and gives it to the monk, not to Monkey._  
**Princess Iron Fan**: Wave it forty-nine times. Then the fire goes out for ever, and it rains, and things grow.  
**Princess Iron Fan**: My boy would have wanted the fire. I think I want the rain.  
_The fan is enormous. It takes you and Sandy together to hold it up, and Monkey to swing it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide: 49 waves  
> _Suppose Monkey swings the fan seven times a minute. How many minutes will forty-nine waves take?_  
> - ✅ 7 minutes → Yes. 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Seven groups of seven waves.
> - 9 minutes → Nine minutes at seven a minute would be 63 waves. 49 ÷ 7 = 7.
> _For grown-ups: Your child divided 49 by 7._

_Your Nubbin sits on top of your head and counts on its paws. It runs out of paws at four, and starts again._  

#### `a02-16-real-done`

_Forty-nine, and the flames go out. The first rain in a thousand years comes down, cool and grey, and steam rises everywhere._  
_The steam climbs, cools, and gathers into a small, grey cloud._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): the water cycle in a few steps  
> _Rain on hot ground turns partly to steam. Steam is water as a gas._  
> _High up it cools into droplets and makes clouds, and clouds make more rain. That is the water cycle._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard how steam, clouds and rain make a cycle._

_You walk over the Flaming Mountains in the rain. The ground is warm under your feet, and already a bit green._  
_Monkey gives the fan back to Princess Iron Fan, which surprises everyone, including Monkey._  
**Princess Iron Fan**: Tell my son I kept his ribbon.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): why a small kindness can change things  
> _Why does Princess Iron Fan, who started out angry, end up kind?_  
> - ✅ The ribbon showed her that someone cared about her son → Yes. A small kind act told her that she and her son mattered, and it changed how she felt about the pilgrims.
> - She was tired of fighting → That might be part of it, but the ribbon came first. Kindness changed her heart.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about how a small kindness can shift someone’s mood._

**Tang Sanzang**: We shall tell him.  
_Behind you, the Flaming Mountains steam and hiss, green where there was red._  
_Your Nubbin puts one paw on the damp ground, and a tiny shoot has already pushed through._

- `a02-17-s1`: Visit the pretty cottage at the edge of the trees. · _Follow the monk quietly._
- `a02-17-s2`: Find where the web is tied. · _Follow one thread with your Nubbin._
- `a02-17-s3`: Help the monk out of the cave. · _Walk him to the cave mouth._

#### `a02-17-cottage`

**Tang Sanzang**: All this way, and you have fetched every meal. Let me fetch one. I am a monk. Begging is my job.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): monks and alms  
> _Buddhist monks have traditionally lived on alms: food that kind people choose to give them._  
> _“Begging” in the story means collecting alms, a respected part of a monk’s life._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned what alms means for Buddhist monks._

**Monkey**: Master, I really think…  
**Tang Sanzang**: Let me.  
_So he goes alone to a pretty cottage at the edge of the trees. Monkey sends you and your Nubbin after him, quietly._  
_Seven women sit in the garden, spinning, very politely. Their eyes are a little too many, and a little too shiny._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 7 spiders with 8 legs  
> _The seven women turn out to be spiders, and a spider has eight legs. How many legs is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 56 → Yes. 7 × 8 = 56. Eight legs is how you tell a spider from an insect, which has six.
> - 15 → That adds 7 + 8. Seven spiders with eight legs each means we multiply. 7 × 8 = 56.
> _For grown-ups: Your child distinguished spiders from insects._

**A spinning woman**: A monk? How lovely. Come in. Do sit down. Do stay.  
_Your Nubbin tugs your sleeve. There are threads across the path behind the monk, fine as hair, catching the light._  

#### `a02-17-cottage-done`

_When he tries to leave, the threads are everywhere. The monk is wrapped up and hung in the doorway like a parcel._  
_Each thread is as fine as a hair, and none of them breaks._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): spider silk is thin and strong  
> _Spiders make silk inside their own bodies. Thread for thread, spider silk is among the strongest natural materials: thin as a hair, yet hard to snap._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that spider silk is thin but very strong._


#### `a02-17-web`

_The cottage is really a cave, and the cave is all web. Silk hangs everywhere in great white sheets._  
**Monkey**: I can cut it, but there’s more every time. It’s like trying to sweep up fog.  
_Suppose each of the seven spiders has spun nine metres of thread._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 7 spiders, 9 metres each  
> _Seven spiders have each spun nine metres of thread. How many metres of silk is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 63 metres → Yes. 7 × 9 = 63 metres. No wonder it is like fog.
> - 16 metres → That adds 7 + 9. Seven equal lengths means we multiply. 7 × 9 = 63.
> _For grown-ups: Your child multiplied 7 × 9._

_Your Nubbin puts one paw on a thread and follows it with its eyes. Then it starts walking along it._  
_It goes round three rocks and under a root, very slowly, to a peg of stone at the back. Every thread comes back here._  
**Sandy**: Of course. Everything that holds on has to hold on to something.  
**Monkey**: Cousin. If I’d been a bit smaller and a lot more patient, I’d have found that.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): patience or strength? (a think question)  
> _Monkey could not solve the web by force, but your Nubbin solved it by being patient. When is patience stronger than strength?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - When the problem is tangled and force makes it worse → That is a fair answer. Cutting the web only added more web.
> - Never: strength gets things done faster → That is a fair answer. Strength is useful, though here it was the patient search that won.
> - Both are needed at different times → That is a fair answer. Patience found the peg, and a single stroke of force finished the job.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up patience against force._


**Choices**

- **Untie the anchor thread from the peg.**
    - You untie it. All through the cave, the white sheets go slack, and drift down, and lie on the floor like snow.
- **Call Monkey to cut it.**
    - **Monkey**: There? That little one? Cousin, you’re a genius.
    - One stroke. The whole web sighs down to the floor.

#### `a02-17-out`

_Sandy unwraps the monk, who is grey with dust, and furious with himself, and fine._  
**Tang Sanzang**: I wanted to do one thing for you all. One thing.  
**Monkey**: You did. You showed us where the spiders lived.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: everyone contributes  
> _The monk wanted to do “one thing”. What is the best way to state the idea in this scene?_  
> - ✅ Even a mistake can help, and everyone has something to give → Yes. Monkey turns the monk’s mistake into a contribution, which is a kind way to look at it.
> - Monks should never beg → The scene does not say that. The idea is that everyone can help, even through a mistake.
> _For grown-ups: Your child stated the theme of a short scene._

_The seven spinners have become seven spiders, scuttling for the cracks. Pigsy lifts his rake._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Leave them. Let them spin somewhere else.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): spiders help keep insects in balance  
> _Spiders eat large numbers of insects, including pests, so without them there would be far more flies and mosquitoes._  
> _Letting them go is a small gift to the gardens nearby._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned that spiders help keep insect numbers in balance._

_Pigsy lowers it. Your Nubbin watches the last spider go, and waves._  

#### `a02-17-complete`

_That night the monk eats the supper Monkey fetches, and says thank you twice._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Perhaps it is all right to be the one who is carried, now and then.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): it is okay to receive help  
> _The monk always carried others’ burdens, and he finds it hard to be carried. Receiving help gracefully is a skill, too._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that accepting help is part of being kind and strong._

**Pigsy**: I’ve always said so. Nobody listens.  
_Your Nubbin has a thread of silk caught round one ear. It keeps it there for days, like a ribbon._  
_Outside the cave mouth the stars come out, and Sandy says that it is a good night for walking._  
_Pigsy has found a log to lean on, and the monk has found someone to talk to._  

### Glossary

- **alms**: Food or gifts given freely to monks or those in need.
- **anchor**: A fixed point that holds something in place.

## A2-18. Vulture Peak

- `a02-18-s1`: Walk the green road to Vulture Peak. · _Follow Monkey. He knows the way now._
- `a02-18-s2`: Cross the river in the bottomless boat. · _Take one step. Your Nubbin will help._
- `a02-18-s3`: Talk with the Buddha and take the scrolls. · _Load the horse and the pole gently._

#### `a02-18-road`

_The page says you have been walking for fourteen years. It feels like a long afternoon, and also like a life._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): the Silk Road and the real journey  
> _The Silk Road was a web of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, India and beyond._  
> _The real Xuanzang followed parts of it. Silk, paper, spices and ideas all travelled the same roads._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard what the Silk Road was._


> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): time: how long was the real journey?  
> _The real Xuanzang left in 629 and came home in 645. How many years was he away?_  
> - ✅ 16 years → Yes. 645 − 629 = 16. The novel says fourteen, so story and history differ a little.
> - 26 years → Be careful with the tens: 645 − 629. 45 − 29 = 16.
> _For grown-ups: Your child subtracted years to find a time interval._

_The land ahead is quiet and green. People look up from their fields and smile, as if they knew the pilgrims were coming._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Is this it? Wukong, is this it?  
**Monkey**: That’s it, master. That mountain there. You can stop worrying now.  
_The monk sits down in the road, and cries, and laughs, and cannot stop doing either._  
_Your Nubbin climbs into his lap. Pigsy sits down too, mainly because everyone else is sitting._  

#### `a02-18-boat`

_Between you and the mountain runs a wide river. The only bridge is a single slippery log._  
_A ferryman poles over in a boat with no bottom. You can see the water rushing straight through it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): why real boats float  
> _Real boats float because their hulls push aside water, and the water pushes back up._  
> _A boat with no bottom could not do that, so this one has to be magic._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned why real boats float._

**Tang Sanzang**: I can’t. It has no bottom. I really can’t.  
**Monkey**: You’ve walked fourteen years on trust, master. Try one more step.  
_Monkey gives him a gentle shove. The monk steps in, and the bottomless boat holds him up as if it were stone._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): trust: when is it wise? (a think question)  
> _Monkey asks the monk to trust him and step into a boat with no bottom._  
> _When is it wise to trust a friend, and when is it wise to check first?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Trust when they have earned it over time → That is a fair answer. Fourteen years of walking together is a good record.
> - Check first when the risk is big → That is a fair answer. A bottomless boat deserves a second look, even from a friend.
> - Both: trust, and keep your eyes open → That is a fair answer. Many wise travellers do just that.
> _For grown-ups: Your child weighed up trust against checking first._

_The ferryman smiles at you, and holds out a hand._  

**Choices**

- **Step in after him.**
    - Your foot goes onto nothing, and the nothing holds. Your Nubbin hops in after you, looking very pleased with itself.
- **Let your Nubbin go first.**
    - Your Nubbin hops in without a second thought; it has never once doubted a boat. You follow it.

#### `a02-18-boat-done`

_On the far side, everyone feels lighter, as if they have put down a pack they forgot they were carrying._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a metaphor for worry  
> _“As if they have put down a pack they forgot they were carrying.” What is the pack really standing for?_  
> - ✅ Worries and tension → Yes. A comparison with a heavy pack helps us feel what carrying worry is like, and how it feels to set it down.
> - The luggage → The luggage is still on the pole. The pack stands for worry and tension.
> _For grown-ups: Your child read a figure of speech about worry._

_Nobody had noticed how tired they were until the tiredness went._  

#### `a02-18-scriptures`

_The Buddha’s hall is full of light and very calm. The monk kneels, and Monkey kneels too, without being asked._  
**The Buddha**: You have come a long way. Rest a little, and then take what you came for.  
_Disciples bring out scrolls, bundle after bundle. You load them onto the horse and the pole with Sandy, carefully._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): translating and copying texts  
> _The real Xuanzang spent the rest of his life translating the Buddhist texts he brought home into Chinese._  
> _Before printing was common, texts were copied by hand, one careful scroll at a time._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard how the real monk’s texts were translated and copied._

_Halfway down the mountain a wind tears open a bundle. The pages inside are blank, every one._  
**Tang Sanzang**: Blank? After all this? Did we do something wrong?  
_You go back up. The Buddha is not cross, and not surprised._  
**The Buddha**: The blank ones are the truest. But in the East, people need words. So: words.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): words and silence (a think question)  
> _The Buddha says the blank scrolls are truest, but that people need words. What can words give that silence cannot, and what can silence give that words cannot?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Words let ideas travel across distance and time → That is a fair answer. A written page can reach someone far away, long after it was written.
> - Silence lets us notice what words cannot say → That is a fair answer. Some things are felt before they can be named.
> - We need both → That is a fair answer. The Buddha seems to say just that.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on what words and silence each offer._

_As thanks, the monk gives the golden bowl the emperor gave him, which is all he has. The new scrolls are full of writing._  

#### `a02-18-complete`

_Five thousand and forty-eight rolls of scripture, tied up in neat bundles. You and Sandy take the pole between you._  
**Tang Sanzang**: We have them. We actually have them.  
**Monkey**: Told you. India by lunch.  
**Pigsy**: It was fourteen years.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): compare: rolls and days  
> _Fourteen years is about 5,110 days, and the pilgrims brought back 5,048 rolls. Are there more rolls than days, or fewer?_  
> - ✅ Fewer: 5,048 is less than 5,110 → Yes. That is nearly one roll for every day of the trip.
> - More: 5,048 is bigger → Compare digit by digit: 5,0 is below 5,1. 5,048 is less than 5,110.
> _For grown-ups: Your child compared two four-digit numbers._

**Monkey**: A very long lunch.  
_The mountain behind you glows in the late sun, and the scrolls hang from the pole like a great, patient bird._  

### Glossary

- **pilgrim**: A person who makes a long journey for a holy reason.
- **scripture**: A holy text.

## A2-19. The Eighty-First Hardship

- `a02-19-s1`: Swim with the old white turtle. · _Dive in. Your Nubbin is already there._
- `a02-19-s2`: Lay the scrolls on the rock to dry. · _Set them out in the sun, one by one._
- `a02-19-s3`: Bring the scrolls home to Chang’an. · _Walk to the city gate with the monk._

#### `a02-19-turtle`

_Far away, Guanyin is reading a list of every hardship the pilgrims met. There were eighty, and there ought to be eighty-one._  
**Guanyin**: One more, then. A gentle one.  
_At the River of Heaven, the old white turtle who carried you all across on the way out is waiting, smiling._  
_The page skipped that crossing years ago, between one chapter and the next. The turtle has not skipped anything._  
**The old white turtle**: Welcome back. Did you ask the Buddha my question? When I shall stop being a turtle, and become a person?  
**Tang Sanzang**: Oh. Oh, no. I forgot. I am so sorry. I forgot.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what to do when you forget something that matters  
> _The monk forgot the turtle’s question. What is the best thing to do when you forget something that matters to someone?_  
> - ✅ Say sorry, and then do what you can to put it right → Yes. An honest sorry, followed by an action, is a strong mix.
> - Hope they won’t mind → The turtle did mind, quietly. An honest apology and a plan work better.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about how to apologise for forgetting._

_The turtle doesn’t say anything. He just sinks, very slowly and quite sadly, into the river._  
_Everyone goes into the water: monk, Monkey, Pigsy, Sandy, horse, scrolls, you. Your Nubbin is delighted._  

#### `a02-19-turtle-done`

_Your Nubbin swims round and round the turtle, then sits on his shell and pats it, as if to say it was a fair point._  
**The old white turtle**: No harm done. I only wanted to be remembered.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: stories keep people remembered  
> _Before most people could read, families kept the past alive by telling it, from grandparent to grandchild._  
> _Monkey’s adventures were told aloud in teahouses and acted on stages for centuries, before and after the novel was written down._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard how telling stories aloud keeps people and the past remembered._


#### `a02-19-rock`

_You all haul the scrolls out of the river and lay them on a big flat rock to dry in the sun._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, notice): drying in sun and wind  
> _Wet paper dries when the water in it turns to vapour and drifts away._  
> _Sun warms it, and wind carries the vapour off, which is why a sunny, breezy rock is a good drying place._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child learned why sun and wind dry wet things._

_When you lift them, a few of the last pages stick fast to the stone. They tear, and the ends stay behind._  
**Tang Sanzang**: No. No! We came all this way. We crossed the whole world. And now they’re not whole.  
_Monkey looks at the torn edges for a long time. He doesn’t make a joke._  
**Monkey**: Heaven and earth aren’t whole either, master. Nothing is. These are just honest about it.  
**Monkey**: Maybe they’re meant to be not quite finished. So there’s room for whoever reads them next.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): is something less valuable if it is unfinished? (a think question)  
> _Monkey says the scrolls may be meant to be not quite finished. Is something less valuable if it is incomplete?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - No: gaps leave room for others → That is a fair answer. An unfinished thing can invite the next person in.
> - Yes: complete is better → That is a fair answer. Whole things are easier to use, though the monk learns to live with this one.
> - It depends what is missing → That is a fair answer. A missing last page and a missing foundation are not the same.
> _For grown-ups: Your child reflected on the value of unfinished things._


**Choices**

- **Try to peel the last pages free.**
    - You try, very carefully, but they stay where they are. In the end you leave them, and the rock keeps a few words for itself.
- **Leave them on the rock.**
    - You leave them. Your Nubbin pats the torn edges, as if they were a pet that had done its best.

#### `a02-19-rock-done`

**Tang Sanzang**: Not quite complete. Yes. All right. That will do.  
_The words left on the rock face the sun, ending in the middle of a sentence._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, do): write the missing words  
> _(Write one sentence that could finish the torn page. What would a traveller like to read next?)_  
> Check: `edu:write:sentence:missing-words`

#### `a02-19-home`

_The city of Chang’an turns out to meet you. The pines by the monastery gate, people say, all turned to point east the morning he came home._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): Chang’an is Xi’an  
> _Chang’an was a real capital city, the eastern end of the Silk Road. Today it is called Xi’an._  
> _A tall pagoda built there to keep the scrolls, the Great Wild Goose Pagoda, still stands._  
> _For grown-ups: Your child heard that Chang’an is today’s Xi’an and where the scrolls were kept._


> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows at sunrise  
> _The pines point east, towards the rising sun. At sunrise, which way do the pines’ shadows point?_  
> - ✅ West, away from the sun → Yes. A shadow points away from its light, so sunrise shadows are long and fall to the west.
> - East, towards the sun → A shadow always falls on the side away from the light. The sun is in the east, so shadows fall west.
> _For grown-ups: Your child worked out the direction of a sunrise shadow._

_The emperor himself walks out to meet the monk, and the scrolls are carried in with music._  
_Then, before anyone has finished cheering, the pilgrims are lifted back to Vulture Peak on a soft wind._  
_The Buddha gives each of them a new name. The monk becomes a buddha, and so does Monkey._  
**Monkey**: A buddha! Me! Then take this band off, master. A buddha in a headband looks silly.  
**Tang Sanzang**: Touch your head, Wukong.  
_Monkey touches his head, and the band is gone. Nobody saw it go._

**Monkey**: Gone. It went when I stopped needing it. Of course it did.  
_He turns to you. His eyes are still little suns, but kinder now, the way the sun is kinder in the evening._  
**Monkey**: You believed me once, when nobody else did. On the ridge. I never forgot.  
**Tang Sanzang**: And you were right. I was afraid, and I called it being careful. I am glad he came back.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): admitting you were afraid  
> _The monk says, “I was afraid, and I called it being careful.” Why is that a brave thing to say?_  
> - ✅ It means looking honestly at your own feelings → Yes. Naming a fear for what it is takes courage, and often helps mend things.
> - It is not brave, it is just an excuse → An excuse hides the truth. The monk is doing the opposite. Naming the fear honestly is brave.
> _For grown-ups: Your child thought about why admitting fear is brave._

_He plucks a hair and blows on it. It becomes a thin gold band, just Nubbin-sized._
