## A5-1. The Hunters’ Prophecy

- `a05-01-s1`: Step into the red-earth page and find the young griot. · _Touch the page, then follow the sound of a balafon to the town gate._
- `a05-01-s2`: Stand at the back of the king’s court and listen to the hunter. · _Stay beside Balla under the silk-cotton tree, and listen closely._

#### `a05-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page the colour of red earth, patterned black and white like cloth dyed with mud._  
_In the corner, in Nova’s hand: “Griots have told this for eight hundred years, and no two tell it alike.”_  
_Under that: “Listen to more than one.”_  
_The earth warms under your palm. Then it is dust, and round thatched houses, and the smell of millet smoke._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): Manding and the Mali Empire on the map: West Africa, and how old this story is  
> _This page is set in Manding, in West Africa, south of the Sahara desert. Today its lands lie in Mali and Guinea._  
> _The story tells how the Mali Empire began, about 800 years ago. Today’s Mali is named after it, and griots across the region still tell it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the story is set in Manding, in West Africa, where the Mali Empire began about 800 years ago, and that griots still tell it._

**Balla Fasséké**: You came out of a picture. My father said someone would, one day. He says a lot of things.  
**Balla Fasséké**: I’m Balla Fasséké, son of Doua, who is griot to the king. One day I’ll be a griot too. Today I carry his things.  
**Balla Fasséké**: You could carry some. A griot needs an apprentice, and I haven’t got one yet.  
_Your Nubbin is already sitting on his balafon, a row of wooden keys with gourds hung underneath._  

**Choices**

- **Ask what a griot does.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: We remember. Who married whom, who fought where, who was brave and who only said so.
    - **Balla Fasséké**: A king without a griot is a king nobody will remember. It makes kings polite to us.
- **Offer to carry the balafon.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Gently. It’s older than my father, and it knows it.

#### `a05-01-page-done`

**Balla Fasséké**: Come. The king sits under the silk-cotton tree in the mornings. Something is going to happen there today.  
_You don’t know how he knows. By the look of him, he doesn’t either._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a think question: what do you predict, and why?  
> _Balla says something will happen today, and can’t explain how he knows. What do you think is going on?_  
> - He has a griot’s feeling for stories → A good guess. A griot learns to sense when a story is about to start.
> - He has heard a rumour → Could be. News travels fast in a king’s town.
> - He is just guessing → That’s a fair answer. To be honest, I’m not sure myself.
> _For grown-ups: Made a prediction from a clue in the text and gave a reason for it (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-01-court`

_King Naré Maghan sits in the shade of a great silk-cotton tree, with his court around him._  
_Beside him stands Doua, who seems to be listening to everything at once._  
_A stranger comes in off the road: a hunter, with a bow on his back and a bag of cowrie shells at his belt._  
**The Hunter of Sangaran**: I’m a hunter of Sangaran, king. I’ve come because the shells told me to.  
**King Naré Maghan**: Then sit, hunter. A king should hear what the shells say, even when he doesn’t like it.  
_The hunter throws the cowries on a goatskin and looks at them for a long time._  
**The Hunter of Sangaran**: Two hunters will come to your gate with a woman. She is strong. Marry her.  
**The Hunter of Sangaran**: She will give you a son, and that son will make the name of Manding last as long as the sun does.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: stories carried by memory and the word “prophecy”  
> _A prophecy is a statement about what will happen in the future._  
> _Stories like this one were passed down aloud for centuries._  
> _That is called oral history: the past kept alive by spoken words instead of books. Griots train for years to remember it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a prophecy is a statement about the future, and what oral history is._


**Choices**

- **Watch the king’s face.**
    - The king says nothing. He turns a kola nut over in his fingers, slowly, like a man deciding to remember.
- **Watch Balla.**
    - Balla’s lips are moving. He is saying the hunter’s words over to himself, so that he will have them.

#### `a05-01-court-done`

**Doua**: Hunter, the king thanks you. Eat before you go, and eat well.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Did you get all that? Say it back to me tonight. Then we’ll both have it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, CASEL: Self-management, ask): ways to remember something heard once  
> _You have to remember the hunter’s words by tonight. Which helps most?_  
> - ✅ Say it aloud in order, again and again → Yes. Repeating in order is how griots keep a long telling safe.
> - Hope you remember it → Hope is nice, but practice works better. Say it aloud, in order.
> - Think about something else → Your mind will wander off. Say it aloud, again and again.
> _For grown-ups: Chose repetition aloud, in order, as a way to remember something._


#### `a05-01-complete`

_That night, by the fire, you say the hunter’s words back to Balla. You get most of them, and he fills in the rest._  
**Balla Fasséké**: That’s the first thing a griot learns. Hear it once, keep it always.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Some tellers leave the hunter out, and start with the two brothers and the buffalo. My father starts here.  
**Balla Fasséké**: He says a story should begin with a promise. Then everybody listens to find out if it’s kept.  
_Balla taps one key of the balafon with his thumb. It makes a low, round sound, like water moving in a gourd._  
_Your Nubbin taps a shorter key. The sound comes out higher and flatter, and much more pleased with itself._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): vibration and pitch: longer bars make lower notes  
> _Balla’s key sounds low and round, and your Nubbin’s sounds higher. Which key is longer?_  
> - ✅ Balla’s key, the lower one → Yes. Longer bars vibrate more slowly, and slower vibrations make lower notes.
> - Your Nubbin’s key → It’s the other way round: longer keys shake slowly, giving low notes. Short keys give high ones.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that vibrations make sound, and that longer balafon keys make lower notes._

**Balla Fasséké**: We’ll work on it.  

### Glossary

- **griot**: A West African storyteller, singer and keeper of history, who remembers things for a whole people.
- **prophecy**: A statement about something that will happen in the future.
- **oral history**: The past kept alive by spoken words and memory instead of written books.

## A5-2. Sogolon

- `a05-02-s1`: Sit by the fire and hear Balla tell the tale of the buffalo of Do. · _Find Balla at the fire behind Doua’s house and sit down._
- `a05-02-s2`: Walk with Sogolon from the gate to the king’s court. · _Meet the two hunters at the gate and walk beside the woman with them._

#### `a05-02-fire`

**Balla Fasséké**: Before the strangers reach the gate, you should know where they’ve been. Sit. This is a fire story.  
**Balla Fasséké**: In the land of Do there was a buffalo nobody could hunt. It trampled the fields, and the best hunters came home with nothing.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Two brothers went after it. On the road they met an old woman, hungry and alone, and they shared their food with her.  
**Balla Fasséké**: She told them the truth: she was the buffalo. Because they’d been kind, she told them how to win.  
**Balla Fasséké**: She asked one thing. The king of Do would offer them any girl they liked. They were to choose the plainest. Her name was Sogolon.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): kindness is repaid  
> _What made the old woman help the two brothers?_  
> - ✅ They shared their food with her → Yes. They were kind when they didn’t need to be.
> - They begged her for help → They didn’t beg. They shared their food, and she chose to help.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that the brothers’ kindness is why the old woman helped them._

_Your Nubbin has crept so close to the fire that its feet are warm. It doesn’t move them._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Some tellers say the old woman was Sogolon’s aunt. Some say she was Sogolon’s own spirit, walking about without her.  
**Balla Fasséké**: My father says it doesn’t matter which. What matters is that she was strong, and that it came to the girl.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): a think question: why do tellings differ?  
> _Balla tells two versions of who the old woman was, and won’t say which is true. Why might a griot do that?_  
> - Each version teaches something → A fair answer. Each version shows a different thing about Sogolon.
> - Nobody knows for sure → That could be it. Stories passed by mouth change a little in every telling.
> - So listeners can choose → A good thought. A griot trusts the listener to think too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a storyteller might share more than one version (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Ask which one Balla believes.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: I believe whichever one I’m telling. That’s the job.
- **Say the brothers won by being kind.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Yes. Write that one down in your head. It comes back.

#### `a05-02-fire-done`

_Out on the road a dog barks, and then another. Balla is on his feet before the third._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): animals’ senses: dogs hear more than people  
> _Dogs can hear much softer and higher sounds than people can._  
> _That’s why the village dogs notice travellers long before anyone else. Their ears are an early warning._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dogs hear better than people, which is why they bark at faraway visitors._

**Balla Fasséké**: That’s them. Come on.  

#### `a05-02-gate`

_Two dusty hunters come through the gate. Between them walks a young woman, stooped, with a hump on her back and very bright eyes._  
**The Elder Hunter**: We bring her to the king of Manding. We were told he would know why.  
_People come out of their doorways to look. Someone whispers, and someone else doesn’t bother to whisper._  
**Sogolon**: I’ve been looked at before. It doesn’t wear me out the way they hope.  
**The Elder Hunter**: She walked from Do on her own feet. We offered her a donkey. She said the donkey looked tired.  
**Sogolon**: It did look tired.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps someone who is being stared at  
> _People stare at Sogolon as she walks. What would help her most?_  
> - ✅ Walk beside her → A stranger from a picture, and a small round thing. Good company.
> - Stare to see what she looks like → Staring is exactly what hurts. Walking beside her says “you are not alone”.
> - Whisper to a neighbour → Whispering is another way of staring. Walking beside her is kinder.
> _For grown-ups: Chose to walk beside someone who is being stared at, rather than join in staring._


**Choices**

- **Walk beside her.**
    - You fall in beside her. She glances at you, and something in her shoulders lets go a little.
    - **Sogolon**: A stranger from a picture, and a small round thing. Good. I like the company of odd things.
- **Offer to carry her bundle.**
    - **Sogolon**: No. It’s mine, and it’s light. But thank you for asking instead of taking it.
    - Your Nubbin takes hold of one corner anyway, and walks the rest of the way like that, helping.

#### `a05-02-gate-done`

_Under the silk-cotton tree, the court laughs out loud when it sees her. The king doesn’t._  
**King Naré Maghan**: Doua. The hunter of Sangaran. Do you remember what he said?  
**Doua**: Every word, my king.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s silence tells us  
> _The court laughs, but the king doesn’t. What does that tell you about him?_  
> - ✅ He takes the prophecy seriously → Yes. He’s thinking about the hunter’s words, not about how she looks.
> - He is bored → A bored king wouldn’t be asking Doua to recall the prophecy.
> - He is angry at Sogolon → He asks about the prophecy, not about her. He’s listening, not judging.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s motive from his actions: the king takes the prophecy seriously._


#### `a05-02-complete`

**King Naré Maghan**: Then I know why you brought her to me. Sogolon of Do, will you be my wife?  
_The laughing stops all at once, like a pot taken off the fire._  
**Sogolon**: I will. And I’ll thank your court to stop staring. I haven’t grown a second head.  
_Doua is the first to laugh, warmly this time. Then the king laughs too, and the rest of the court has to._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): how a character handles being laughed at  
> _Sogolon turns laughing-at into laughing-with. What gave her that dignity?_  
> - ✅ She spoke up, honestly and with humour → Yes. Dignity means keeping your self-respect, even when others don’t.
> - She ignored everybody → She didn’t ignore them. She answered, calmly and with a joke.
> - She got angry and shouted → Her words were sharp, but she stayed calm. That calm is dignity.
> _For grown-ups: Described how Sogolon kept her dignity: speaking up honestly, calmly and with humour._

**Balla Fasséké**: Remember that. She made them laugh with her, not at her, in one breath. My father has been trying to do that for twenty years.  

### Glossary

- **dignity**: Keeping your self-respect and calm, even when others are unkind.

## A5-3. The Boy Who Couldn’t Walk

- `a05-03-s1`: Visit Sogolon’s house and keep her son company. · _Sogolon’s house is the small one at the back of the royal yard._
- `a05-03-s2`: Go with Sogolon to ask Queen Sassouma for baobab leaves. · _Walk with Sogolon across the yard to the queen mother’s house._

#### `a05-03-house`

_The atlas page turns a little, the way a griot skips ahead. A wedding, a birth and seven rainy seasons pass in a breath._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): wet and dry seasons in West Africa  
> _In much of West Africa the year is split into a rainy season and a dry season, rather than summer and winter._  
> _Seven rainy seasons means seven years. The rains grow the crops, which are harvested as the dry season begins._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that much of West Africa has rainy and dry seasons, and that seven rainy seasons means seven years._

_Sogolon’s son is seven years old. He sits in the dust outside her door, broad and solemn, and he crawls wherever he goes._  
**Balla Fasséké**: His name is Mari Djata. He doesn’t talk much. He eats like three boys and he watches everything.  
_Your Nubbin toddles over and sits down in front of him. The boy looks at it for a long time._  
_Then he puts out one hand, very slowly, and pats it on the head._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading a character’s trust from what he does  
> _Sundiata doesn’t pat many people. How can you tell he trusts your Nubbin?_  
> - ✅ He chose to touch it, slowly and gently → Yes. Actions can show feelings that words don’t.
> - He said so out loud → He didn’t say a thing. What he did tells us.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s feeling from his actions rather than his words._

**Sogolon**: He doesn’t do that for many people. Your little round friend is honoured.  
**Balla Fasséké**: The old king died in the dry season, with my father beside him. Dankaran Touman is king now, and his mother rules.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Some people say the hunter was wrong. They say it where Sogolon can hear.  

**Choices**

- **Sit down in the dust with the boy.**
    - You sit, and nobody says anything. The boy goes on watching the yard, and you watch it with him.
    - After a while you notice he isn’t waiting for anything. He’s just looking, very hard, at all of it.
- **Ask Sogolon if he’ll walk one day.**
    - **Sogolon**: He will walk when he walks. I don’t pull up seedlings to make them grow faster.
    - **Sogolon**: And until then, he is my son, and that is already a great deal.

#### `a05-03-house-done`

**Balla Fasséké**: Mark this, apprentice. He isn’t waiting to become someone. He already is someone. He’s just not finished.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): a think question: is slow the same as behind?  
> _Balla says Sundiata is already someone, only not finished. Is going slowly the same as being behind?_  
> - No. Everyone grows at their own pace → A thoughtful answer. A seed isn’t behind a tree. It’s a seed.
> - Sometimes, but it can still be fine → That’s honest. Being slower can feel like being behind, even when it isn’t.
> - I’m not sure → That’s fair. It’s the kind of question griots chew on for years.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether going slowly means being behind (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-03-leaves`

**Sogolon**: I need a few baobab leaves for the sauce. Ours are gone. Sassouma has plenty.  
_Queen Sassouma sits in her own yard with her women, under a baobab heavy with leaves. She sees Sogolon coming a long way off._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): baobabs drop their leaves in the dry season to save water  
> _A baobab is deciduous: it loses all its leaves in the dry season, and grows them again when the rains come._  
> _Dropping leaves saves water. In many parts of West Africa, fresh baobab leaves are cooked in sauces, which is why a tree full of them is worth asking for._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that baobabs lose their leaves in the dry season to save water, and that the leaves are eaten._

**Sogolon**: Sister. A handful of leaves, for my son’s supper.  
**Sassouma Bérété**: Take them, of course. My son picked them for me himself, this morning. He climbed up to fetch them. On his own two legs.  
**Sassouma Bérété**: Your son, I hear, still fetches things the way a lizard does.  
_The women laugh. Sogolon takes the leaves, and her hand doesn’t shake, quite._  

**Choices**

- **Say nothing, and walk out beside Sogolon.**
    - You walk out beside her. She keeps her back straight all the way to her own door, which is a long way, for her.
- **Look Sassouma in the eye.**
    - You look at Sassouma. She looks back, cool and pleasant, as if you were a cloud that might rain.
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Good. She’ll remember your face. Mind you, that may not be good.

#### `a05-03-leaves-done`

_At her own door, Sogolon sits down on the step and cries, quietly, with her face in the leaves._  
_Her son crawls over to her. Your Nubbin sits on her other side and leans._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): how to comfort someone who is crying  
> _Sogolon is crying. Which is the best way to comfort her?_  
> - ✅ Sit close and stay → Yes. Being there is the comfort; you don’t have to fix anything.
> - Tell her to stop crying → Crying is a way of letting sadness out. Sit close and let her.
> - Change the subject → Changing the subject can make a sad person feel unheard. Stay close instead.
> _For grown-ups: Chose to sit close and stay with someone who is crying._


#### `a05-03-complete`

**Sundiata**: Mother. Why are you crying?  
_Sogolon looks up. So does Balla, and so, it seems, does the whole yard._  
**Sogolon**: Because of leaves. Because of a woman with a sharp tongue. Because of you, my son.  
**Sundiata**: Then dry your eyes, Mother. Today I stand up.  
**Sundiata**: Send to the forges. Ask the smiths for a rod of iron, so heavy it takes all of them to carry it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to change years into months  
> _Sundiata crawled for seven years, and there are 12 months in a year. How many months is that?_  
> - ✅ 84 months → Yes: 7 × 12 = 84. Eighty-four months of crawling, and he never stopped trying.
> - 19 months → That’s 7 + 12. We need 7 groups of 12: 7 × 12 = 84.
> - 70 months → Close, but 7 × 10 is 70. A year has 12 months: 7 × 12 = 84.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 7 × 12 to find the number of months in seven years._

_Balla’s mouth is open. He shuts it, and you see him say the words over to himself, quickly, so he will have them._  

### Glossary

- **deciduous**: Describes a plant that loses all its leaves for part of the year.

## A5-4. The Iron Rod

- `a05-04-s1`: Run to the smiths with Sogolon’s message. · _The forges are down by the river, where the smoke is blackest._
- `a05-04-s2`: Watch the boy stand. · _Stand with Balla at the edge of the crowd outside Sogolon’s door._
- `a05-04-s3`: Gather the baobab’s leaves for Sogolon. · _Pick up the leaves around the baobab now standing at Sogolon’s door._

#### `a05-04-forge`

_The smiths’ quarter smells of charcoal and hot water. Hammers ring on every side, each on its own beat._  
_The master smith is a big, quiet man with burn marks up both forearms. He listens to the whole message without stopping work._  
**The Master Smith**: The heaviest rod we’ve ever made. For the crawling boy.  
**The Master Smith**: My father forged a rod years ago, for a day like this. He said someone would come asking. He kept it under the bellows.  
_It takes six of his apprentices to drag it out. It is as long as two of you and dark as a wet night._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, notice): heating makes iron soft; cooling makes it hard again  
> **The Master Smith**: A forge is a hearth, hot enough to make iron glow. Bellows pump air in to make the charcoal burn even hotter.  
> **The Master Smith**: Hot iron goes soft, so I can bend and hammer it. When it cools, it goes hard again. That change can be done again and again.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heating softens iron and cooling hardens it, and that bellows feed the fire with air._

**The Master Smith**: Smiths keep secrets, apprentice. That’s half of what we are. The other half is patience.  

**Choices**

- **Take hold of the rod with the apprentices.**
    - You take hold, and it is so heavy your arms forget they are yours. Your Nubbin pushes from behind, which helps exactly nothing.
- **Ask if a boy can really lift that.**
    - **The Master Smith**: No. A boy can’t. That’s the point of asking for it.

#### `a05-04-forge-done`

_The whole quarter downs hammers and follows the rod up the hill. So do half the children in Niani._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to find a total  
> _Six apprentices drag the rod, and say each one could drag 15 kilograms alone. How much can they drag together?_  
> - ✅ 90 kilograms → Yes: 6 × 15 = 90. And still it took all six to move it.
> - 21 kilograms → That’s 6 + 15. Six groups of 15 is 6 × 15 = 90.
> - 60 kilograms → Try again: 6 × 10 = 60, and 6 × 5 = 30. Together, 90.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 6 × 15 to find the combined pull of six apprentices (an in-story sum)._

**Balla Fasséké**: Everyone wants to see it. Half of them want to laugh. Stay close to me and keep your ears open.  

#### `a05-04-stand`

_The smiths lay the rod down in front of Sogolon’s door. The crowd goes quiet in a ring around it._  
_The boy crawls to it. He takes it in both hands, and sets one end in the dust._  
_He pulls, and his arms shake. Sweat runs down his face, and still he pulls, slowly, hand over hand, up the rod._  
_He is on his knees, then on one foot. Then he is on both feet, with the iron rod bent in his hands like a hunter’s bow._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced and unbalanced forces  
> _Gravity pulls Sundiata down towards the ground. For him to pull himself up the rod, what must be true?_  
> - ✅ His pull must be bigger than gravity’s pull on him → Yes. When forces are unbalanced, things move, and his muscles finally won.
> - Gravity must switch off → Gravity never switches off. His pull has to be stronger than the pull down.
> - The rod must pull him up → The rod is just a handle. It’s Sundiata’s pull that wins over gravity.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an object moves when one force is bigger than the other (unbalanced forces)._

**Balla Fasséké**: He’s standing.  
_Then Balla is singing. It is a praise song, his own, made on the spot, and the whole hill takes it up._  
**Sogolon**: My son is standing.  

**Choices**

- **Cheer.**
    - You cheer. Your Nubbin cheers, too, which is a high round squeak, and runs three times round his feet.
- **Look at Sogolon.**
    - Sogolon isn’t cheering; she has her hands over her mouth. She has waited seven years, and she is still waiting, one breath more.

#### `a05-04-stand-done`

**Balla Fasséké**: Some tellers say the first rods snapped in his hands, and he leaned on his mother’s stick in the end. Some say it was a baobab branch.  
**Balla Fasséké**: I was there. It was iron. It bent. But I’ll tell you the stick version, too, because that one’s also true.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): a think question: can two tellings both be true?  
> _Balla says the stick version is also true. How can two different tellings both be true?_  
> - Each one holds a true part of the story → A fair answer. The truth can have more than one side.
> - They can’t both be true → That’s a fair answer too. Historians also ask which telling is most likely.
> - It depends what “true” means → A sharp thought. Is “true” about facts, or about what the story means?
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how differing tellings can both hold truth, and compared a teller’s view with their own (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-04-baobab`

**Sundiata**: Mother. You wanted baobab leaves.  
_He walks, a little stiffly, to the edge of the town where a young baobab grows. He puts his arms around it._  
_In Niane’s telling, and plenty of others, he pulls it up by the roots and carries it home._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): baobabs: huge trunks that store water, live for centuries  
> _A real baobab has a trunk so wide it can store thousands of litres of water. That helps it survive long dry seasons._  
> _Baobabs grow slowly and can live for hundreds of years, some for over a thousand. Pulling one up is the kind of thing only a legend could do._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that baobabs store water in their trunks, grow slowly and can live for centuries._

_He sets it down at his mother’s door. The leaves shake all over the yard._  
**Sundiata**: From now on, the women of Niani will come to you for leaves.  
**Sogolon**: That’s enough for one day, my son. Sit down, before you fall down.  

#### `a05-04-baobab-done`

_You and your Nubbin gather the leaves into baskets. There are a great many._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide into equal groups  
> _You gather 24 leaves and share them equally between 4 baskets. How many go in each basket?_  
> - ✅ 6 leaves → Yes. 24 ÷ 4 = 6, because 4 × 6 = 24.
> - 20 leaves → That’s 24 − 4. Dividing means equal groups: 24 ÷ 4 = 6.
> - 8 leaves → Check it: 4 × 8 = 32, too many. 4 × 6 = 24, so it’s 6.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 24 leaves into 4 equal baskets: 24 ÷ 4 = 6._

_Across the yard, Queen Sassouma’s door is shut. Nobody saw it close._  

#### `a05-04-complete`

**Balla Fasséké**: From today they’ll call him Sogolon’s Djata. Say it quickly, and you get Sundiata.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Djata means lion. So that’s his mother and the lion, both, in one name. Some tellers make it from other words. They’re not wrong either.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphors: calling a person a lion  
> _Calling Sundiata a lion is a metaphor, which says one thing is another. What does it tell us about him?_  
> - ✅ He is brave and strong → Yes. A metaphor lends the lion’s qualities to the person.
> - He has a mane → A metaphor isn’t about looks here. It’s about the lion’s courage and strength.
> - He lives on the grassland → He doesn’t literally. The metaphor borrows what a lion is like: brave and strong.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what the metaphor “lion” says about Sundiata’s character._

_Sogolon gives you a baobab seed, round and hard as a pebble, and folds your fingers over it._  
**Sogolon**: For your own yard. They grow very slowly. Don’t let that worry you.  
_Your Nubbin tries to eat it, and you take it back. Sogolon laughs out loud._  

### Glossary

- **forge**: A very hot fire where a smith heats metal to shape it.
- **bellows**: A pump that blows air onto a fire to make it hotter.
- **metaphor**: A comparison that says one thing is another, such as “he is a lion”.

## A5-5. The Griot

- `a05-05-s1`: Stand witness when Balla is given to Sundiata as his griot. · _Meet Doua and Balla at the hunters’ clearing outside the town._
- `a05-05-s2`: Let Balla teach your Nubbin a tune on the balafon. · _Sit your Nubbin at the balafon by Balla’s house and choose the tune it learns._

#### `a05-05-given`

_Sundiata is ten now, and hunts with the older boys. Every hunter in Manding has already started telling stories about him._  
_In the hunters’ clearing, Doua puts his hand on his son’s shoulder and walks him forward._  
**Doua**: The old king asked for this before he died. Every king has a griot. My son will be yours.  
**Sundiata**: I don’t need someone to sing at me.  
**Doua**: No. You need someone to remember you. You’ll do things you’ll forget. He won’t.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive: why a king needs a griot  
> _Sundiata says he doesn’t need someone to sing at him. Why does Doua say he does need a griot?_  
> - ✅ To remember him, and tell him the truth → Yes. A good griot is memory and conscience together.
> - To keep him entertained → Songs are part of it, but Doua says it’s about being remembered.
> - To carry his things → That’s a small job. Doua is talking about something much bigger.
> _For grown-ups: Identified why a king needs a griot: to remember him and tell him the truth._

**Balla Fasséké**: And I’ll tell you when you’re being a fool. That’s in it too. Nobody mentions that part.  
**Sundiata**: Then you’d better stay close. I’ll need telling.  
**Balla Fasséké**: In my father’s telling, the old king gave me to Sundiata while he was still crawling. I tell it now, because now is when I knew.  

#### `a05-05-given-done`

_Sundiata and Balla shake hands, very formally, like two old men. Then Sundiata trips Balla into the grass._  
**Balla Fasséké**: He’s going to be a great king. Write that down.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): time intervals: subtract ages  
> _Sundiata stood up at age 7, and now he is 10. How many years have passed since he stood?_  
> - ✅ 3 years → Yes: 10 − 7 = 3. Three years of walking, hunting and growing.
> - 17 years → That’s 10 + 7. To find how long has passed, subtract: 10 − 7 = 3.
> - 7 years → Seven is how old he was. The gap to 10 is 10 − 7 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted ages to find a time interval: 10 − 7 = 3 years._


#### `a05-05-lesson`

**Balla Fasséké**: Now. If you’re my apprentice, your round friend is too. It’s been staring at this balafon for ten years.  
_He puts a pair of beaters into your Nubbin’s paws. They are nearly as long as it is._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Wood on wood. The gourds underneath sing back. You don’t hit the key. You ask it.  
_Your Nubbin asks it, and the key answers, round and low. Your Nubbin looks up at you with enormous pride._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): resonators: the gourds make the sound louder  
> **Balla Fasséké**: A struck key only shakes a little. The gourd underneath is a resonator: air inside it shakes along and makes the note louder.  
> **Balla Fasséké**: That’s why a balafon’s gourds are different sizes. Each one is matched to the key above it.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gourd resonators amplify balafon notes by vibrating air._

**Balla Fasséké**: Good. One tune, to start. A griot has a thousand, but everyone has a first.  
**Balla Fasséké**: There’s the hunters’ tune, quick and stamping, the one they play for Sundiata when he comes home with meat.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Or there’s the one Sogolon hums at night, when she’s grinding millet. She doesn’t know anybody hears it. Everybody does.  

> **Lesson** (music, ask): tempo: fast and slow  
> _Balla describes two tunes. Which one has the faster tempo? (Tempo means the speed of the music.)_  
> - ✅ The hunters’ tune → Yes. Quick and stamping. Fast tempo.
> - Sogolon’s lullaby → The lullaby is slow and rocking, like a grinding stone. That’s a slow tempo.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the faster tune and learned that tempo means the speed of music._

**Balla Fasséké**: Which one?  

**Choices**

- **The hunters’ tune.**
    - Balla plays it once through: quick, stamping, a tune for a lot of feet coming home at dusk.
    - Your Nubbin plays it back, in roughly the right order. Its feet stamp, too, which isn’t part of the tune, but helps.
    - **Balla Fasséké**: That’s a tune for a crowd. You’ll never be lonely with that one in your hands.
- **Sogolon’s lullaby.**
    - Balla plays it once through: slow, rocking, the sound of a grinding stone going round and round in the dark.
    - Your Nubbin plays it back, very carefully, as if it might wake somebody.
    - **Balla Fasséké**: That’s a tune for one person. Whoever hears it will think it’s for them.

#### `a05-05-lesson-done`

_Your Nubbin plays its tune all evening. By night it can play it all the way through without stopping._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): number patterns that follow a rule  
> _Practising, your Nubbin plays 2 notes, then 4, then 6, then 8. If the pattern continues, how many notes next?_  
> - ✅ 10 notes → Yes. The rule is “add 2 each time”: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
> - 9 notes → Look at the gaps: 2, 4, 6, 8. Each time we add 2, so next is 10.
> - 16 notes → That would be doubling the last. The pattern adds 2 each time: next is 10.
> _For grown-ups: Found the rule (+2) in a number pattern and continued it._

_Across the yard, Sogolon’s door is open, and she is sitting just inside it, listening._  

#### `a05-05-complete`

**Balla Fasséké**: Keep that tune. Don’t trade it, don’t lose it. A tune you know by heart is a door you can always find in the dark.  
**Balla Fasséké**: I can’t tell you which door yet. I’ll tell you when we get there.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a think question: what does Balla’s metaphor mean?  
> _Balla says a tune you know by heart is a door you can always find in the dark. What do you think he means?_  
> - Music can lead you home when you’re lost or scared → A fair answer. A tune can be a place to go.
> - Something learned by heart is always with you → Yes, that’s one way. It can’t be taken away, even in the dark.
> - It will open something later in the story → That’s a good hunch. I did say I’d tell you which door.
> _For grown-ups: Interpreted a metaphor in their own words (no single right answer)._

_Your Nubbin plays the first three notes again, just to check they’re still there. They are._  

### Glossary

- **resonator**: A hollow space, like a gourd, that makes a sound louder when air inside it vibrates.
- **tempo**: The speed of a piece of music.

## A5-6. Exile

- `a05-06-s1`: Keep watch in Sogolon’s vegetable garden at night. · _Hide behind the gourd vines with Sundiata and wait for the visitors._
- `a05-06-s2`: Say goodbye to Balla before he is sent away. · _Find Balla at the palace gate, where the king’s envoys are setting out._
- `a05-06-s3`: Leave Niani with Sogolon’s family before dawn. · _Meet Sogolon and her children at the west gate in the dark._

#### `a05-06-garden`

**Balla Fasséké**: Sassouma has paid nine old women to come into Sogolon’s garden tonight. Everyone in Niani knows, except Sassouma, who thinks it’s a secret.  
**Balla Fasséké**: They have powers, these nine. Some say they were sent to harm him. Some say only to steal, and make him angry enough to harm them.  
_The garden is silver with moonlight. Nine bent shapes come through the gap in the fence and begin to fill their baskets with gourds and greens._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): the Moon shines because it reflects sunlight  
> _The Moon has no light of its own. It looks silver because it reflects light from the Sun._  
> _On a clear night with a bright Moon, you can see a whole garden in silver and shadow, even with no fire at all._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Moon reflects sunlight rather than making its own light._

_Sundiata stands up out of the vines. The nine freeze._  
**Sundiata**: Grandmothers. You don’t need to creep. Take what you want.  
**Sundiata**: If you’d asked in daylight, I’d have given you more. Here, these ones are better. Those ones are still green.  
_He fills their baskets for them. Your Nubbin, catching on, brings them a gourd each, with difficulty._  

#### `a05-06-garden-done`

**The Eldest of the Nine**: We were paid to make you angry, son of Sogolon. You’ve made us ashamed instead.  
**The Eldest of the Nine**: From tonight, we watch over you. Go carefully. The one who sent us won’t stop at nine old women.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a think question: why did kindness work better than anger?  
> _The nine women came to make Sundiata angry, but he was kind, and they changed sides. Why do you think that worked?_  
> - They had expected a fight and had no answer to kindness → A sharp answer. Kindness can leave an unkind plan with nothing to push against.
> - They realised what they were doing was wrong → A fair answer. Sometimes people need to see themselves clearly before they change.
> - It may not always work → That’s honest. It worked here. Kindness isn’t magic, but it often opens a door.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why kindness can change someone’s behaviour better than anger (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-06-sent`

_In the morning there are horses at the palace gate, loaded with gifts. Balla stands beside them with his balafon on his back._  
**Dankaran Touman**: The king of Sosso grows strong. I send him gifts, and I send him a griot, to sing him our friendship. Balla Fasséké will go.  
**Sundiata**: You can’t take a man’s griot. He’s mine. My father gave him to me.  
**Dankaran Touman**: Your father’s dead, brother. I am king.  
_Balla puts a hand on Sundiata’s arm. Sundiata shakes with anger, and doesn’t move._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive: why Balla goes quietly  
> _Balla doesn’t refuse to go. Why does he let himself be sent away?_  
> - ✅ A fight now would hurt Sundiata and he’d lose → Yes. Knowing when not to fight is a kind of strength.
> - He is afraid of the king → Look at what he says: it’s about protecting Sundiata, not himself.
> - He wants to go to Sosso → He doesn’t. He goes because refusing would put Sundiata in danger.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out Balla’s motive: going quietly protects Sundiata from a fight he would lose._

**Balla Fasséké**: Apprentice. Listen. I can’t go with him now, so you’ll have to.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Wherever he goes, remember it for me. All of it. The good and the foolish. Then one day you’ll tell it back, and I’ll have it.  

**Choices**

- **Promise him.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Good. Then I’m not leaving him. I’m only going ahead.
- **Ask why he won’t refuse.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Because if I refuse, Sundiata will fight his brother for me, here, in the gate, and lose. He isn’t ready yet.
    - **Balla Fasséké**: A griot has to know when to be carried off quietly. Remember that, too.

#### `a05-06-sent-done`

_The horses go out of the gate. Your Nubbin plays the first three notes of its tune after them, as loud as it can._  
_Far down the road, faintly, the balafon on Balla’s back answers with the next three._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): sound gets quieter as it travels  
> _Sound is energy that travels in waves. As the waves spread out and travel further, they get weaker._  
> _That’s why Balla’s answer is faint: it has come a long way. Close up it would sound loud._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound energy spreads out and weakens with distance._


#### `a05-06-leave`

**Sogolon**: We go tonight. While my son is angry, he isn’t safe here, and while we stay, nor is anyone who loves him.  
_There are five of them at the west gate: Sogolon, Sundiata, his sisters Kolonkan and little Djamarou, and his half-brother Manding Bory._  
**Manding Bory**: My mother says I should stay. I said I’m going where Djata goes. She cried, and then she packed me food.  
**Kolonkan**: Walk quietly. The road out of Niani has ears.  
_Sundiata looks back once at the town, at the dark shape of the baobab at his mother’s door._  
**Sundiata**: I’ll come back. Remember I said so.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: facing west, what is behind you?  
> _At the west gate, the family walks out facing west, away from the town. In which direction is the town behind them?_  
> - ✅ East → Yes. East is the opposite of west, so the town is behind them to the east.
> - North → North is to their right as they face west. Behind them, the opposite of west, is east.
> - West → West is where they’re heading. The town is opposite: east.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions: the opposite of west is east._


**Choices**

- **Pick up a handful of Niani’s red earth.**
    - You tie it in a corner of your cloth. It is very light, and it feels heavier as the night goes on.
- **Take Djamarou’s hand.**
    - Djamarou takes your hand without looking up, and holds on, and doesn’t let go until the sun is up.

#### `a05-06-complete`

_By sunrise Niani is a smudge behind you. Nobody talks, and even your Nubbin walks without bouncing._  
_You find you are counting things to remember: the shape of the hills, the colour of the sky, who carried what._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, CASEL: Self-management, notice): memory tricks: group things in threes  
> _You noticed the hills, the sky and who carried what. Three things._  
> _Griots, like many people, remember best by grouping things in small sets, and saying them in the same order every time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that grouping information into small sets helps memory._

**Sundiata**: You’re doing what Balla does. Your lips move.  
**You**: I promised him.  
**Sundiata**: Then remember this. My mother walked out of her husband’s town with her head up. Tell him that first.  

## A5-7. Kingdom to Kingdom

- `a05-07-s1`: Watch Sundiata play the king of Djedeba at wori. · _Sit by the game board in the king’s yard, and watch Kolonkan._
- `a05-07-s2`: Sit in on the council of the king of Wagadou. · _Go into Wagadou’s council house with Sundiata and keep quiet at the back._
- `a05-07-s3`: Walk the long road with the family. · _Keep pace with Sogolon at the back of the line._

#### `a05-07-djedeba`

_The first court on the road is Djedeba. Its king is friendly, too friendly, and very fond of games._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): wori belongs to a family of seed games played across Africa and beyond  
> _Wori is one of a large family of “sowing” games, played with seeds or stones in rows of pits, across Africa and parts of Asia for many centuries._  
> _Players take turns, scooping seeds and dropping one in each pit round the board. It rewards counting and planning ahead._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that wori is one of an old family of seed-sowing board games played across Africa and Asia._

**The King of Djedeba**: Sit, son of Sogolon. Play me at wori. Seeds into pits, round and round. If you win, you have my hospitality.  
**The King of Djedeba**: If you lose, well. We’ll talk about that if it happens.  
_The board is carved wood with two rows of hollows. The king’s seeds click into them very fast._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.C.3, ask): odd and even  
> _A pit on the wori board holds 7 seeds. Is 7 odd or even?_  
> - ✅ Odd → Yes: seven seeds make three pairs, with one left over. Odd numbers always have one left over.
> - Even → Pair them up: 2, 4, 6 seeds make three pairs, and one is left over. So 7 is odd.
> _For grown-ups: Decided that 7 is odd by pairing objects._

**Kolonkan**: He plays with a ring on his finger, brother. Watch the ring, not the seeds.  
_Kolonkan says it so softly that only you, Sundiata and your Nubbin hear. Your Nubbin immediately stares at the ring._  
_Sundiata watches the ring. Then he starts to win._  

**Choices**

- **Count the seeds for Sundiata.**
    - You count under your breath, and Sundiata nods once without looking at you. He was already counting, but he likes the company.
- **Let your Nubbin keep staring at the ring.**
    - The king notices, and becomes very uncomfortable. He moves the ring to the other hand, then into his sleeve.

#### `a05-07-djedeba-done`

**The King of Djedeba**: You play like an old man, son of Sogolon. You don’t hurry and you don’t forgive a mistake.  
**The King of Djedeba**: Stay the night. Then go on. I don’t want a boy like you near my throne.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): vocabulary in context: hospitality  
> _The king promised “hospitality” to Sundiata if he won. What does hospitality mean?_  
> - ✅ Welcoming guests kindly, with food and a bed → Yes. Hospitality is looking after visitors, even strangers.
> - A game played with seeds → That’s wori. Hospitality is what the king offers: food, a bed and a welcome.
> - A fee to enter a town → Not a fee. Hospitality is a welcome given freely to guests.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of “hospitality” from context._


#### `a05-07-wagadou`

_Wagadou is old: older than Manding, older than anything you have seen on this page. Its king is kind, and tired, and careful._  
**The King of Wagadou**: Sogolon’s family is welcome. Your father was my friend. Sit at my council, young man, and learn how a king listens.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Wagadou, the early kingdom often called ancient Ghana  
> _Wagadou is the name the Soninke people gave to a great kingdom of the western Sahel. Outsiders called it Ghana, though it was not where today’s Ghana is._  
> _It grew rich on the trade in gold and salt, and it was already ancient when Mali began._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Wagadou (often called ancient Ghana) was an early West African kingdom built on the gold and salt trade._

_All day, people come to the king: a farmer with a quarrel about a field, a widow, two traders with one goat between them._  
_The king hears every one of them right to the end, even the goat men, who take a long time._  
**Sundiata**: Why do you let them talk so long, king? You knew the answer straight away.  
**The King of Wagadou**: So did they, most of them. They came to be heard. A king who answers too quickly only rules people. He doesn’t keep them.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): a think question: what does the king mean?  
> _The king says a king who answers too quickly only rules people, but doesn’t keep them. What do you think he means?_  
> - People stay loyal when they feel listened to → A fair answer. Being heard builds trust.
> - Quick answers can be wrong answers → That’s true as well. Listening first gives better decisions.
> - He’s just tired and likes to talk → Ha. That’s a fair guess. But I think there is more in it.
> _For grown-ups: Interpreted a king’s advice about listening in their own words (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-07-wagadou-done`

_That night Sundiata sits up late, turning the king’s words over like seeds in a pit._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes and metaphors  
> _“Turning the king’s words over like seeds in a pit.” Is that a simile or a metaphor?_  
> - ✅ A simile, because it uses “like” → Yes: a simile compares two things using “like” or “as”. A metaphor says one thing is another.
> - A metaphor, because it compares → Both compare, but a simile uses “like” or “as”, as this one does.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a simile by the word “like”._

**Sundiata**: Did you get that? Put it in the list for Balla. Put it near the top.  

#### `a05-07-road`

_Months of road. Thorn trees, dry river beds, a sky so big it makes your Nubbin hold on to your ankle._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): the Sahel: dry land with thorny trees and seasonal rivers  
> _The road crosses the Sahel, a belt of dry grassland south of the Sahara. Trees there are thorny and spaced apart, and many rivers only run in the rainy season._  
> _Plants and animals that live there are adapted to long dry spells._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sahel is a dry habitat with thorn trees and seasonal rivers._

_Sogolon walks more slowly every week. Nobody mentions it._  
**Manding Bory**: Djata, we could get there by the new moon if we pushed on.  
**Sundiata**: We go at my mother’s pace. That’s the fastest pace there is, because it’s the one where we all arrive.  
_Sundiata drops back and walks beside his mother, and so the whole family walks at the back._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _At Sogolon’s pace the family walks 3 kilometres in an hour. How far do they go in 6 hours?_  
> - ✅ 18 kilometres → Yes: 3 × 6 = 18. Slow and steady adds up, and everyone arrives.
> - 9 kilometres → That’s 3 + 6. Each hour adds 3 km, six times: 3 × 6 = 18.
> - 36 kilometres → Check it: 6 × 6 is 36. They walk 3 km each hour, so 3 × 6 = 18.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied speed by time (3 km/h × 6 h) to find a distance._

**Kolonkan**: He used to be the slowest of us. Now he’s the one who waits. I think that’s the same lesson, turned round.  

**Choices**

- **Offer to carry Sogolon’s water gourd.**
    - **Sogolon**: Thank you. My hands are glad. My pride isn’t, but my pride can walk on its own.
- **Ask your Nubbin to play its tune as you walk.**
    - Your Nubbin plays the tune on its own knees, tapping. The family walks to it without meaning to, all at the same pace.

#### `a05-07-complete`

_Seven years on the road go by in a turn of the page. Sundiata is a man now, broad as a door._  
**Kolonkan**: Tellers argue about this road. Some send us to Tabon first. Some leave Djedeba out. Some add three more kings.  
**Kolonkan**: I was on it, and I couldn’t tell you the order either. Roads are like that.  
**Sundiata**: What I learned was in the order it came. Patience, then listening, then my mother’s pace. Remember it that way.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: what the road teaches  
> _Patience, listening, and walking at a mother’s pace. What is the theme of the road?_  
> - ✅ Going slowly and together can be a strength → Yes. That’s what I carry out of it.
> - Faster travel is always better → The story says the opposite: the slowest pace was the one where everyone arrived.
> - Kings never listen → Kings in this chapter listen carefully. The theme is about patience and care.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of the chapter: slowness and togetherness as strength._


### Glossary

- **hospitality**: Welcoming guests kindly, with food, a bed and good company.

## A5-8. Mema

- `a05-08-s1`: Watch Sundiata ride out with the army of Mema. · _Climb the watch-mound by Mema’s wall and watch the horsemen._
- `a05-08-s2`: Sit with Sogolon. · _She is resting on the mat in the shade behind the house. Just sit._

#### `a05-08-army`

_Mema is a city on a river, with a king who loves horses and has a great many of them._  
**King Moussa Tounkara**: Sogolon’s son. I’m told you can ride, and hunt, and that you don’t lose your temper. Can you lead?  
**Sundiata**: I don’t know yet, king. Give me twenty horsemen and I’ll find out.  
_From the mound you watch them go out, a line of dust across the plain, Sundiata at the front._  
_They come back at dusk with banners they didn’t leave with, and nobody missing. The city goes out to meet them._  
**King Moussa Tounkara**: Twenty horsemen, and none lost. Tomorrow, take two hundred.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply by 10  
> _The king gives Sundiata 20 horsemen first, and then 200. How many times as many is 200 as 20?_  
> - ✅ 10 times as many → Yes: 20 × 10 = 200. Ten times the riders, and he lost nobody the first time.
> - 2 times as many → Doubling 20 gives 40. To reach 200 we need 20 × 10.
> - 180 times as many → 180 is the difference, not the multiple. 20 × 10 = 200.
> _For grown-ups: Found that 200 is 10 times 20._


**Choices**

- **Add it to the list for Balla.**
    - You add it: Mema, the dust, the banners, and that nobody was missing. You think Balla will like that best.
- **Wave your Nubbin’s paw at the riders.**
    - Sundiata sees it, all the way from the gate, and lifts his spear in answer.

#### `a05-08-army-done`

_Year by year Moussa Tounkara gives him more. In time Sundiata is second only to the king._  
**King Moussa Tounkara**: I have no son, and I am getting old. I don’t say anything by that. I just say it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading between the lines  
> _The king says he has no son and is getting old, “and doesn’t say anything by that”. What is he hinting?_  
> - ✅ That Sundiata could become his heir → You read me well.
> - That he is bored of ruling → Look at what he says: no son, getting old. He’s thinking about who comes next.
> - That he wants a horse → He’s hinting about something bigger than a horse: who will rule after him.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a hint: the king is suggesting that Sundiata could be his heir._


#### `a05-08-mat`

_Sogolon rests a great deal now. She lies on a mat in the shade, and the shade moves round her as the day goes._  
**Sogolon**: Sit, apprentice. You and your round one. I like a quiet visitor. My son visits like a herd of cattle.  
_You sit, and your Nubbin lies down against her side. She puts her hand on it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): why shade moves during the day  
> _Sogolon’s shade moves round her as the day goes. Why does it move?_  
> - ✅ The Earth turns, so the Sun seems to cross the sky → Yes. As the Sun’s place in the sky changes, shadows swing round and change length.
> - The tree is slowly walking → Trees stay put. The light moves instead, because the Earth turns.
> - The wind blows the shade → Wind moves the leaves, not the shade. Shade moves because the Sun seems to cross the sky.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shadows move during the day because the Earth turns and the Sun appears to cross the sky._

**Sogolon**: I won’t see Niani again. Don’t argue. I’m old and I can count.  
**Sogolon**: I’ve done my part. I carried him, and I waited for him, and I walked him to the edge of the world. He can do the rest.  
**Sogolon**: Tell Balla that I wasn’t sad about it. Tell him I was very proud, and very tired, and both are fine.  

**Choices**

- **Stay, and say nothing.**
    - You stay. She closes her eyes, and the shade moves.
    - After a while she is humming, very low, the tune from the grinding stone.
- **Promise to tell Balla.**
    - **Sogolon**: Good. Say it in my voice. Make him laugh at the cattle bit.

#### `a05-08-mat-done`

_That night, Sogolon dies. Her body stops working, and it will not start again._  
_In the morning her children sit around her mat, and you sit with them. Nobody says anything for a long time, and that is right._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): grief: sadness is allowed, and being together helps  
> _When someone you love dies, you can feel sad, numb, cross, or all of them. None of those feelings is wrong._  
> _Sitting together, crying, remembering and telling stories all help. Grief comes from love, and it softens with company._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard plainly that Sogolon died, that all feelings in grief are allowed, and that company and remembering help._


#### `a05-08-complete`

**Kolonkan**: She waited for him seven years in the dust. She’d want us to stop crying before seven days. She was strict like that.  
**Sundiata**: She was the strongest person I’ve ever met. Stronger than the iron rod. I only bent it. She carried it, all those years.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): figurative language: stronger than the iron rod  
> _Sundiata says his mother was “stronger than the iron rod”. What is he comparing?_  
> - ✅ Her patience and love against the rod’s hardness → Yes. She carried what couldn’t be lifted with hands.
> - How heavy she was → He doesn’t mean her weight. He means her strength of spirit.
> - Their colour → It isn’t about colour. It’s about inner strength.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the comparison in a metaphor about Sogolon’s strength._

_Your Nubbin goes and sits on the empty mat in the shade, where it is still warm. Nobody moves it._  
_After a while, Kolonkan sits down beside it, and puts her hand on its head the way her mother did._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): a think question: what is remembering for?  
> _Kolonkan says her mother would want them to stop crying. Does remembering someone mean being sad, or something else?_  
> - It means keeping their stories and habits alive → A lovely answer. She’d like that: her way of laughing, living on.
> - It can mean both sadness and gladness → That’s honest. Remembering often holds them together.
> - I’m not sure → That’s fine. Nobody is sure at first.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what remembering someone means: sadness, gladness, or keeping their ways alive (no single right answer)._


### Glossary

- **heir**: The person who will take over a title or land after its owner.

## A5-9. The Sorcerer King

- `a05-09-s1`: Follow the atlas back to Sosso, and find Balla. · _The atlas has turned its own pages. Look for Balla inside Sosso’s tower._
- `a05-09-s2`: Stand by Balla in Soumaoro’s secret chamber. · _Stay behind Balla at the great balafon. Don’t touch the owls._
- `a05-09-s3`: Watch from the tower as Sosso’s army marches on Manding. · _Stand at the tower window with Balla._

#### `a05-09-sosso`

_The atlas pages riffle, as if a wind has come in at the window. When they settle, the red earth is grey with smoke._  
_You are in Sosso, years ago, on the day Balla arrived with Dankaran Touman’s gifts. The atlas goes where the story is._  
_Sosso is a city of forges. Its walls ring with hammers, and above them stands a tall tower with seven floors._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to count steps  
> _The tower has 7 floors, with 12 steps between floors. How many steps in all, if you climb every floor?_  
> - ✅ 84 steps → Yes: 7 × 12 = 84. Your Nubbin counted every one of them, slowly.
> - 19 steps → That’s 7 + 12. Seven floors of 12 steps each: 7 × 12 = 84.
> - 72 steps → Check it: 6 × 12 is 72, one floor short. For 7 floors, 7 × 12 = 84.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 7 × 12 to count the steps of a seven-floor tower._

**Balla Fasséké**: Apprentice? You’re not supposed to be here. You’re supposed to be with him.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Oh. It’s the page, isn’t it. A griot can stand in two places: where it happened, and where it’s told.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, notice): a storyteller can stand where it happened and where it’s told  
> _A griot tells a story as it happened, and as tellers before him told it._  
> _Those are two points of view, and a good griot holds both._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that a storyteller can show events as they happened and as they are told, two different points of view._

**Balla Fasséké**: Soumaoro is out. And at the top of his tower is a door that nobody is allowed through. So, naturally.  

**Choices**

- **Tell him it’s a bad idea.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: It’s a very bad idea. I’m going anyway. You’ll want to be there, so you can say I was warned.
- **Follow him up the stairs.**
    - You follow him up seven floors of stairs. Your Nubbin follows you, one step at a time, with great determination.

#### `a05-09-sosso-done`

_The door at the top isn’t locked, because nobody in Sosso would dare. Balla pushes it open._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): careful decisions: planning for the unexpected  
> _Balla is about to open a door that is forbidden. What would a careful person do first?_  
> - ✅ Keep a lookout, and know the way out → Yes. If you’re going to take a risk, plan your escape.
> - Shout, so everyone knows → Shouting would bring the guards. A careful person stays quiet and watches.
> - Run away at once → Running away is safe, but Balla chooses to look. If you do, plan your way out.
> _For grown-ups: Chose to keep a lookout and plan a way out before taking a risk._


#### `a05-09-chamber`

_The chamber is dim and close. Owls sit on perches in the dark and turn their heads to watch you._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): owls: nocturnal hunters with special senses  
> _Owls are nocturnal: they sleep by day and hunt at night. Their huge eyes gather scraps of light, and their soft feathers let them fly almost silently._  
> _An owl can turn its head about 270 degrees, because its eyes are fixed in place and cannot move._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that owls are nocturnal and have large eyes, silent feathers and a very flexible neck._

_There are jars and bundles on shelves, and on one wall, a row of old crowns from kings Soumaoro has beaten._  
_In the middle stands a balafon bigger than any you have seen. Its keys are dark with age, and its gourds hang like moons._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Oh. Oh, look at that.  
**Balla Fasséké**: A griot can’t see a balafon like that and not play it. It would be rude. To the balafon.  
_He sits. He looks at you, and at your Nubbin, and you see him decide something._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Your tune. The one your round friend learned. Let’s see what it sounds like on a king’s instrument.  

#### `a05-09-chamber-done`

_Balla plays the hunters’ tune. On this balafon it is enormous: quick, stamping, a sound like a hundred hunters coming home._  
_Your Nubbin stamps along, and the owls shift on their perches. Somewhere below, a door bangs, and heavy feet climb the stairs fast._  

> **Lesson** (music, 1-PS4-1, ask): bigger instruments make lower sounds  
> _Soumaoro’s balafon is much bigger than Balla’s little one, with bigger keys and gourds. Will its lowest note be lower or higher than Balla’s?_  
> - ✅ Lower → Yes. Bigger bars and bigger resonators mean slower vibrations and deeper notes.
> - Higher → It’s the other way round. Longer keys and bigger gourds make deeper, lower notes.
> _For grown-ups: Predicted that a larger balafon makes lower notes._

_Soumaoro Kanté fills the doorway, tall, in a cloak the colour of iron, his face like thunder. Then he hears the tune._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: That is a hunters’ tune. My father’s hunters played that, coming home, when I was small.  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Nobody touches that balafon.  
_Balla doesn’t stop. He plays the tune to its end, then moves into a praise song for Soumaoro._  
_It names the forges, his fathers and the walls of Sosso, and gets every one right._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Hm.  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Dankaran Touman sent you as a gift, griot. I think he gave me more than he knew. You stay here, and you play for me.  
_Balla bows. When he straightens, he looks at you once, and you understand: he isn’t free, but he isn’t finished._  

#### `a05-09-march`

_The page turns forward again. From the tower window, you watch Soumaoro’s army go out of Sosso like smoke out of a forge._  
**Balla Fasséké**: He’s taking Manding. Dankaran Touman sent him gifts, and a griot, and it wasn’t enough. It never is, with a man like that.  
_Far off, the page shows Niani, small, with its gates open, and Dankaran Touman riding hard the other way._  
**Dankaran Touman**: Don’t tell anyone I ran. No. Tell them. It doesn’t matter now.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Manding has no king now. It has Soumaoro.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a think question: can gifts keep the peace?  
> _Dankaran sent gifts and a griot, hoping to keep the peace. Why might gifts not be enough?_  
> - A powerful person may just want more → A sharp answer. Gifts can show that you are weak and invite more asking.
> - Peace needs trust, which gifts cannot buy → That’s a thoughtful one. Trust has to be earned, not paid.
> - Gifts might work sometimes → That’s fair. Sometimes they do. Here, they didn’t.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about why gifts alone might not keep the peace (no single right answer)._

**Balla Fasséké**: Go back to him, apprentice. Remember for me still. I’ll keep the tune going here, so he has something to come home to.  

#### `a05-09-complete`

**Balla Fasséké**: In Sosso they tell this differently. To them Soumaoro was a great smith and a great king, who stood up to bigger kings.  
**Balla Fasséké**: In some of their tellings he was fighting for his own people, and Manding was the one in the wrong. Remember that too.  
**Balla Fasséké**: I’m his griot now, so I have to sing him well. I find that I can. He loves music more than anyone I’ve met.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view: why would Sosso tell the story differently?  
> _Point of view means how someone sees events. Why might griots in Sosso tell Soumaoro’s story differently?_  
> - ✅ They are on Sosso’s side and know different things → Yes. Who tells a story, and who it is for, shapes what is told.
> - They are telling lies on purpose → Not necessarily. People remember from where they stand, and two views can both be honest.
> - They have forgotten the story → They remember it carefully. They just see it from Sosso’s side.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a storyteller’s side and knowledge shape how the story is told._

_The pages riffle again. Grey smoke goes back to red earth, and you are in Mema, in the morning, with your Nubbin asleep on your feet._  

### Glossary

- **nocturnal**: Awake and active at night, and asleep in the day.

## A5-10. The Call Home

- `a05-10-s1`: Help Kolonkan at her market stall. · _Kolonkan sells greens from home in Mema’s market. Mind the stall with her._
- `a05-10-s2`: Pack Sundiata’s basket for the king of Mema. · _Find the three things Sundiata asks for around the old house, and put them in the basket._

#### `a05-10-market`

_Mema’s market is all noise and colour. Kolonkan keeps a little stall at the end, selling baobab leaves and the roots they cook at home._  
_This morning, the morning after, she has opened it anyway. Her mother would have._  
**Kolonkan**: Nobody here buys them. I keep the stall so the smell is somewhere. Is that foolish?  
_Four tired men in travelling clothes stop dead in front of the stall. One of them picks up a bunch of leaves and smells it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): smell and memory  
> _Smell is closely linked to memory. The part of the brain that handles smell sits next to the parts that store memories and feelings._  
> _That’s why a single sniff of leaves can bring a man all the way home._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that smell is closely tied to memory, which is why a familiar scent can bring a place to mind._

**Messenger from Manding**: These are Manding leaves. Who sells Manding leaves in Mema?  
**Kolonkan**: Sogolon’s daughter does.  
**Messenger from Manding**: Sogolon’s daughter. Then her son is here. We’ve searched every market from the river to the sand for him.  
**Messenger from Manding**: Soumaoro has Manding. The king ran. The people send us to find the lion. Is he here?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to find a cost  
> _The four men each buy a bunch of leaves for 8 Shells. How many Shells do they spend in all?_  
> - ✅ 32 Shells → Yes: 4 × 8 = 32. Kolonkan has her first sale in days.
> - 12 Shells → That’s 4 + 8. Four men, 8 Shells each: 4 × 8 = 32.
> - 24 Shells → That’s 3 × 8. There are four men: 4 × 8 = 32.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 × 8 to find the total cost._


**Choices**

- **Run for Sundiata.**
    - You run. Your Nubbin runs too, a little behind, and arrives just as Sundiata does, out of breath and very proud of itself.
- **Stay with Kolonkan.**
    - **Kolonkan**: Stay. My hands are shaking. Hold the stall while I find my brother.

#### `a05-10-market-done`

**Sundiata**: I said I’d come back. My mother heard me say it.  
**Sundiata**: Now I have to go and do it, and she isn’t here to see.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): missing someone and keeping a promise  
> _Missing someone doesn’t go away when you get on with things. It can sit beside you while you do them._  
> _Sundiata keeps his promise even though the person he made it to cannot see it. Some promises are for the people we have lost._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that missing someone sits alongside action, and that keeping a promise can honour someone who has died._


#### `a05-10-basket`

_There is one more thing. Sogolon must be buried, and Moussa Tounkara is not pleased that his best general is leaving._  
**King Moussa Tounkara**: A stranger’s grave needs ground, and ground has a price. And I had hoped you would stay and be my heir.  
**Sundiata**: He’s grieving too, in his way. He’ll get his price. Apprentice, bring me a basket.  
**Sundiata**: Put in some broken pots from the rubbish heap. Some old straw from a fallen roof. And a few feathers, from the yard.  
_You gather them into a very odd basket. Your Nubbin adds a feather of its own choosing, a large one._  
**Sundiata**: Now take it to the king’s house. Set it down in front of his council, and say nothing at all.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): a think question: when is a message without words clearer than words?  
> _Sundiata sends a message with no words, only objects. When might that be clearer, or less clear, than speaking?_  
> - Objects can say hard things without anyone being insulted → A fair answer. A basket can be a blunt message with a polite shape.
> - Words are clearer, because objects can be misread → That’s true too. It works here only because the old counsellor can read it.
> - It depends who is reading it → Yes. A symbol only works if people share the same understanding of it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the clarity of a symbolic message compared with spoken words (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Ask what it means.**
    - **Sundiata**: He has old counsellors. Let one of them tell him. It sounds better in an old voice.
- **Work it out yourself.**
    - Broken pots, a fallen roof, feathers scattered in a yard. It looks like a town after a war has been through it.
    - **Sundiata**: You’ve been listening to Balla. Don’t say it. Let them say it.

#### `a05-10-basket-done`

**The Old Counsellor**: King. This is a ruined town, in a basket. He says: give my mother her ground, or one day this is Mema.  
**King Moussa Tounkara**: I know what it says.  
**King Moussa Tounkara**: Give her the best ground we have. And give him horsemen. Half of mine. I’d rather be his friend than his basket.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what a decision shows about a character  
> _The king gives the best ground and half his horsemen. What does that tell you about him?_  
> - ✅ He values friendship over keeping his army → Yes. Choosing a friend over a fight shows wisdom, and some generosity.
> - He is afraid of the basket → He says he knows what it says, so he isn’t afraid of a basket. He’s choosing wisely.
> - He doesn’t care about his horsemen → He cares, but he values the friendship more. That’s a choice, not carelessness.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s values from the choice he makes._

_Sogolon is buried in Mema, under a tree, with all honour. Moussa Tounkara stands at the graveside with his head bowed._  
**Kolonkan**: Balla will tell you the messengers came first, and that she lived just long enough to hear them. Plenty of griots tell it that way.  
**Kolonkan**: I like that telling. I won’t say it’s wrong. I just wasn’t there for it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): how historians use oral history alongside other sources  
> _Different griots tell the same events in slightly different orders. Historians don’t throw the tellings away._  
> _They compare many tellings and, where they can, written records and the places themselves, to see what most agree on._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that historians compare many tellings and other sources when using oral history._

_Then the horses are saddled, and the road west is open, and Sundiata is going home._

## A5-11. Tabon

- `a05-11-s1`: Greet the kings who come to join Sundiata. · _Stand with Manding Bory at the camp gate and welcome each king in._
- `a05-11-s2`: Watch the battle from the ridge. · _Climb the ridge above the pass and stay there with the drummers._
- `a05-11-s3`: Sit in on Sundiata’s council fire. · _The council sits at the big fire in the middle of the camp._

#### `a05-11-allies`

_Word goes ahead of him on the road. At the iron hills of Tabon, kings are waiting with their people._  
**Fran Kamara**: Fran Kamara, king of Tabon. I played with you when we were boys, Sogolon’s son. You used to cheat at wrestling.  
**Sundiata**: I crawled. It was the only way to win.  
**Fran Kamara**: Tabon is with you. So are the hunters of Sibi, and more are coming.  
**Manding Bory**: Every king who’s been afraid of Soumaoro is walking up this road, Djata. They’ve just been waiting for someone to go first.  
_All day they come in, with drums and banners. Your Nubbin greets every single one at the camp gate, very seriously._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): add within 20: totals of arrivals  
> _Two kings arrive in the morning, five at noon, and four at dusk. How many kings is that in all?_  
> - ✅ 11 kings → Yes: 2 + 5 + 4 = 11. Your Nubbin greeted every one.
> - 9 kings → That’s 5 + 4. Add the morning kings too: 2 + 5 + 4 = 11.
> - 13 kings → Count again: 2 + 5 = 7, and 7 + 4 = 11.
> _For grown-ups: Added three numbers within 20 to find a total._


**Choices**

- **Add every king’s name to the list for Balla.**
    - By sunset the list for Balla is the longest thing you have ever written in your head. You keep it all.
- **Let your Nubbin play its tune for the newcomers.**
    - A drummer from Sibi picks up your Nubbin’s tune and plays it back bigger. Soon half the camp has it.

#### `a05-11-battle`

_From the ridge the battle is dust, horns and banners, moving like weather across the plain._  
_Sundiata’s horsemen go through Sosso’s lines like water through a broken dam. Sosso’s banners fall back._  
_Then a figure in an iron-coloured cloak rides out alone on a black horse. The arrows fly at him and fall short, or slide off, or turn._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Son of the buffalo. You’ve grown. It won’t help you.  
_Sundiata rides at him, and Soumaoro is simply not there any more. He is on the hill opposite, watching._  
_Your Nubbin hides its face in your coat. Then, slowly, it looks out again._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): how to help someone who is frightened  
> _Your Nubbin is frightened. Which helps a scared friend most?_  
> - ✅ Hold them close and breathe slowly together → Yes. A calm body helps a scared one calm down.
> - Tell them there is nothing to be scared of → Fear is real, even if danger is far. Holding close and breathing together helps more.
> - Make them watch → Watching can make fear worse. Holding close and breathing slowly is kinder.
> _For grown-ups: Chose to hold a frightened friend close and breathe slowly together._


**Choices**

- **Hold your Nubbin close.**
    - You hold it. Its heart is going very fast, and so is yours.
- **Keep watching Soumaoro.**
    - He doesn’t look angry. He looks interested, like a smith testing a new blade, and that is worse.

#### `a05-11-battle-done`

_By evening the pass is Sundiata’s, and Sosso’s army has gone back over the hills. Soumaoro went first, untouched._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4-ESS2-2, notice): what a mountain pass is, and why armies fight over them  
> _A pass is a gap between hills or mountains that people can travel through. Tabon’s pass is a narrow route between high ground._  
> _Whoever holds a pass can control who travels, trades or marches through the land beyond it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a mountain pass is and why controlling one matters._


#### `a05-11-council`

**Sundiata**: We’ve won the pass. We’ll win the next battle, and the one after. And we still won’t have touched him.  
**Fran Kamara**: Iron doesn’t cut him. Arrows don’t find him. He goes from one hill to the next like a bird.  
**Sundiata**: Then he has a secret. Every great sorcerer has one thing that undoes him.  
**Manding Bory**: And nobody alive knows what it is. Except Soumaoro.  
**Sundiata**: And whoever he trusts.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): a think question: is trust a risk?  
> _Sundiata says whoever Soumaoro trusts may know the secret. Is trusting someone always a risk, and why?_  
> - Yes, because they could pass your secret on → A fair answer. Trust is a bet, and bets can be lost.
> - Yes, but it’s worth it for good friends → A thoughtful one. Without some trust, nobody could be close.
> - It depends who you trust → True. Trust is easier to give to people who’ve earned it.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether trusting someone is a risk (no single right answer)._

_Sundiata looks into the fire for a long time. You know that look: his mother had it, waiting._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, notice): defining a problem is the first step to solving it  
> _Sundiata names the problem exactly: “We can’t hurt him, so what protects him?” Engineers and scientists start the same way._  
> _Once a problem is clearly stated, you can compare ideas for solving it, and test which works best._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stating a problem clearly is the first step in comparing solutions._

**Sundiata**: Apprentice. My griot is in Sosso, in Soumaoro’s house. If anyone in the world can learn his secret, it’s Balla.  
**Sundiata**: So we wait. And we win battles while we wait, because that keeps people alive. But mostly we wait.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: how waiting connects the story  
> _Sogolon waited for years, and now Sundiata waits for Balla. How are the two waits alike?_  
> - ✅ Both use patience as a kind of strength → Yes. In this story, patience isn’t doing nothing; it’s doing the right thing at the right pace.
> - Both are just wasting time → Neither wastes time. The waiting leads to standing up, and to the secret.
> - Both are about to give up → Nobody gives up. Your Nubbin plays its notes again, anyway.
> _For grown-ups: Linked two moments of waiting to the story’s theme of patience as strength._

_Your Nubbin plays the first three notes of its tune, softly, towards Sosso. Nobody answers, and it plays them again anyway._  

### Glossary

- **pass**: A gap between hills or mountains that people can travel through.
