#### `a05-12-watch`

_It is your turn to keep the night watch. The camp sleeps behind you, and your Nubbin sleeps on your feet._  
_Very late, two figures come out of the dark, on foot, slowly, holding each other up._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): we see only when light reaches our eyes: firelight at night  
> _At night, you can’t see the two figures until they come into the light. We see things when light bounces off them and enters our eyes._  
> _The watch fire sends out light, and the figures reflect a little of it back to you._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we see objects when light bounces off them into our eyes._

_One is a young woman in a torn cloak. The other has a balafon on his back._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Apprentice. You kept the fire lit. Of course you did.  
_Your Nubbin is awake. It is across the ground and up Balla’s front before he can put the balafon down._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Yes. Hello. Yes. I missed you too. I played your tune every night, did you know? Soumaoro got very tired of it.  

#### `a05-12-watch-done`

_Sundiata comes out of his tent, sees who it is, and doesn’t say anything at all. He just holds on to Balla for a long time._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): words for feelings: relief  
> _Sundiata says nothing and holds on to Balla. Which word names what he feels?_  
> - ✅ Relief and joy → Yes. Relief is the feeling when a long worry finally lifts.
> - Boredom → A long hug from a silent man is rarely boredom. It’s relief and joy.
> - Anger → He holds Balla close. That is relief, mixed with joy.
> _For grown-ups: Named a character’s feelings (relief and joy) from his actions._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, do): oral history: griots retell events in order  
> _(Put the journey in order: the west gate, the wori game, the king of Wagadou, then Mema.)_  
> _Retelling in order is how a griot makes sure nothing is lost._

> _For grown-ups: Put the events of the journey in the order they happened._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): an opening line holds up the rest of a story  
> **Balla Fasséké**: The first line of a telling is like the centre pole of a tent. Everything else hangs from it.

- **Start with Sundiata walking at his mother’s pace.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Good. That’s the whole king, right there. The rest is only battles.
- **Start with “nobody missing”.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: A griot’s start. Most people want the glory first. You picked the counting. Keep doing that.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral and written traditions both keep the past  
> _Many cultures keep the past in memory, through griots, songs and sayings; others write it down. Mali would later keep it both ways._  
> _Neither is better. A story kept by memory depends on people like you, passing it from one generation to the next._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that memory and writing are both ways to keep the past, and that oral traditions depend on people._

_In Sundiata’s tent, the young woman lets her hood fall. She is Nana Triban, his half-sister: Sassouma’s daughter._  
**Nana Triban**: My brother the king married me to Soumaoro, to keep him friendly. It didn’t work. Nothing does, with him.  
**Nana Triban**: So I made him trust me. I praised him, and listened, and laughed in the right places, for a long time.  
**Nana Triban**: One night he told me what he fears. Not iron, not arrows. A white rooster’s spur, on the point of an arrow.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): a rooster’s spur is a hard spike used for defence  
> _A spur is a hard, pointed spike on the back of a rooster’s leg. Roosters use their spurs to defend themselves and their flock._  
> _Like claws, beaks and horns, spurs are body parts that help animals survive._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a rooster’s spur is a body part that helps it defend itself._

**Sundiata**: You’re Sassouma’s daughter. Your mother drove mine out of Niani. Why would you bring me this?  
**Nana Triban**: Because I’m my own daughter too, brother. And because Sogolon once gave me baobab leaves, when my mother wasn’t looking.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a think question: why do people choose differently from their family?  
> _Nana Triban chooses differently from her mother. What makes a person choose a different path from their family?_  
> - A single kindness can change how you see someone → A fair answer. Sogolon’s kindness stayed with me.
> - Seeing the harm others do → A thoughtful one. Sometimes you see what the family can’t.
> - Thinking for yourself → Yes. We all belong to our families and to ourselves.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on why someone might make different choices from their family (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-12-complete`

_In the morning a farmer of the camp brings a white rooster’s spur: from an old bird who died of nothing but years._  
_A smith fixes it to the point of an arrow, and you hold the shaft still while he works. Your Nubbin holds your elbow still._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide to compare lengths  
> _The spur is about 3 centimetres long, and the arrow is 60 centimetres. How many spurs laid end to end would match the arrow?_  
> - ✅ 20 spurs → Yes. 60 ÷ 3 = 20, because 3 × 20 = 60.
> - 57 spurs → That’s 60 − 3. We want how many 3s fit in 60: 60 ÷ 3 = 20.
> - 180 spurs → That’s 60 × 3. Dividing gives how many 3s fit in 60: 20.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 60 by 3 to compare two lengths._

**Balla Fasséké**: Some tellers say Balla stole the secret. Some say it was Nana Triban alone. Some say they found it together.

### Glossary

- **spur**: A hard, pointed spike on the back of a rooster’s leg.

- `a05-13-s1`: Welcome Fakoli and his smiths into the camp. · _Meet Fakoli at the camp gate with Balla._
- `a05-13-s2`: Watch the arrow at Kirina. · _Stand with Balla on the rise behind Sundiata’s lines._

#### `a05-13-fakoli`

_A big man comes up the road with a company of smiths behind him, their hammers on their shoulders._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): in Mande society, crafts such as smithing and griotry were handed down in families  
> _In the Mande world, certain crafts, such as working iron and being a griot, were traditionally passed down in particular families, from parent to child._  
> _Smiths were honoured for their skill, and they kept it in the family, just as the Kouyaté kept the telling of this story._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that smithing and griotry were traditionally family crafts handed from parent to child._

**Fakoli**: I am Fakoli, son of Soumaoro’s sister. I’ve made his iron all my life. I’ve come to make yours.  
**Sundiata**: Why would Soumaoro’s nephew change sides on the eve of a battle?  
**Fakoli**: Because he took my wife Keleya out of my house and into his. Because nothing is ever enough for him.  
**Fakoli**: A man who will take that from his own family will take everything from everyone. So I’ve come.  
**Balla Fasséké**: In Sosso they’ll call Fakoli a traitor. In Manding they’ll call him a hero. He’s a man who had enough.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view: traitor or hero?  
> _A traitor is someone who betrays their own side. Why is Fakoli called a traitor in Sosso, but a hero in Manding?_  
> - ✅ Each side judges him by who it thinks he should be loyal to → Yes. Loyalty and betrayal look different from different places.
> - Because Sosso and Manding are wrong → Neither side is simply wrong. They see the same act from different points of view.
> - Because he changed his name → His name didn’t change. What changed was which side he stood on.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that “traitor” and “hero” depend on the point of view of whoever is judging._


**Choices**

- **Bring him water.**
    - **Fakoli**: Thank you. That’s the first thing anyone has given me in a long time without wanting something back.
- **Show the smiths where to set up their forge.**
    - By nightfall the camp has a forge, glowing at the edge. Your Nubbin sits as close as it’s allowed, warming its feet.

#### `a05-13-kirina`

_The plain of Kirina at dawn: two armies in long lines, with banners, horns and drums, and dust already rising._  
_Soumaoro rides out alone again, in his iron-coloured cloak, as he did at Tabon. He doesn’t need anyone else._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Lion cub. I’ve beaten kings who could walk before you could talk. Go home.  
_Sundiata draws his bow. The arrow is plain, except for its point, where a small white spur is bound with thread._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, notice): a bent bow stores energy and changes it to motion  
> _When Sundiata draws a bow, the bent wood stores energy, like a stretched spring._  
> _When he lets go, that stored energy turns into the motion of the arrow. A bow is a device that changes one form of energy into another._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a drawn bow stores energy that changes into the arrow’s motion._

_He looses it. It doesn’t strike hard; it only grazes Soumaoro’s shoulder._  
_Soumaoro looks at his shoulder. Then he looks up at the sky, as if something has just flown out of him._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Who told you?  

#### `a05-13-kirina-done`

_Soumaoro turns his horse and rides. His army breaks behind him and runs, and Sundiata’s horsemen go after it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how characters respond to events  
> _Soumaoro rides away after the arrow. How does his army respond?_  
> - ✅ It breaks and runs behind him → Yes. Without its leader, the army loses its courage.
> - It charges even harder → The text says it breaks and runs. The army follows its leader’s example.
> - It stands still → It doesn’t stand still. It breaks and runs behind its leader.
> _For grown-ups: Described how a group responds to what happens to its leader._

**Balla Fasséké**: Not him. Leave him to Sundiata. Come on, apprentice. A griot follows the end of a story, not the middle.  

#### `a05-13-cave`

_High in the hills of Koulikoro, Sundiata has stopped his horse at the mouth of a cave._  
_Soumaoro’s black horse stands outside it, riderless, cropping the grass._  
**Sundiata**: He went in. Nobody has come out.  
_The cave is dark all the way back. No sound comes out of it at all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): echoes: sound waves bounce off hard surfaces  
> _When sound waves hit a hard, smooth surface such as a cave wall, they bounce back. That bounce is an echo._  
> _Caves are good at echoes because their walls are rock and the space is closed in._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that echoes are sound waves bouncing off hard surfaces such as cave walls._

**Balla Fasséké**: Some say he’s still in there. Some say he became stone, part of the hill. In Sosso they say he simply went where he chose.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Everyone agrees on one thing: he was never seen again.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): a think question: why not pick one ending?  
> _Griots tell three versions of where Soumaoro went. Why not pick one, and which would you tell?_  
> - Keeping all three is more honest → A fair answer. When no one knows, honesty means saying so.
> - I would pick the one that seems most likely → That’s a good approach too. A historian would think that way.
> - I would tell the one I like best → A storyteller’s answer. Just be honest that it’s your choice.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about how to tell a story with several endings (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Wait at the cave mouth a little while.**
    - You wait, and Sundiata waits with you. Nothing comes out but a little cool air, and then the sun moves.
- **Let your Nubbin play its tune into the cave.**
    - Your Nubbin plays its tune into the dark, softly. It comes back off the walls, the same and not quite the same.
    - **Balla Fasséké**: He loved music. Whatever else he was, he loved it. That should be remembered too.

#### `a05-13-complete`

**Sundiata**: He was the greatest enemy I’ll ever have. I don’t want him sung badly, griot.  
**Balla Fasséké**: He won’t be. Not by me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): fairness to someone who was an enemy  
> _Sundiata wants his greatest enemy sung truthfully, not badly. What does that show about him?_  
> - ✅ He is fair, even to an enemy → Yes. Telling the truth about an enemy takes courage and fairness.
> - He still hates him → If he hated him, he’d want him sung badly. He wants the truth told.
> - He has forgotten what happened → He remembers everything. That’s why he wants it sung truthfully.
> _For grown-ups: Understood that wanting an enemy remembered truthfully shows fairness._

_Sundiata takes the black horse’s bridle and leads it down the hill. He doesn’t ride it; he walks beside it, all the way back._  

### Glossary

- **traitor**: Someone who betrays the side they once belonged to.

## A5-14. The Assembly

- `a05-14-s1`: Go to the great assembly at Kurukan Fuga. · _Walk with Balla to the wide clearing where the kings are gathering._
- `a05-14-s2`: Choose what you ask Balla to remember. · _Find Balla at the edge of the ring, where the griots sit._

#### `a05-14-assembly`

_At Kurukan Fuga, on a wide plain near Kangaba, the kings and peoples of Manding gather in a great ring._  
_There are more people than you can count, and more drums than you can hear separately. Your Nubbin tries to count anyway._  
_One by one the kings come forward and lay down their spears before Sundiata, and say what their people will do._  
**Fran Kamara**: Tabon gives its iron. Its people keep their own ways and their own names.  
**Fakoli**: The smiths give their skill. Their craft stays theirs, father to son, and nobody may take it from them.  
_Then the whole ring is quiet, and Sundiata stands up._  
**Sundiata**: Manding is one now. Every clan keeps its name and its work. A stranger is a guest. Nobody harms a messenger.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): fairness and rules: guests and messengers  
> _Sundiata names rules: a stranger is a guest, and nobody harms a messenger. Why would these be good rules for a large kingdom?_  
> - ✅ They let people travel and talk safely, so peace can last → Yes. Rules that protect strangers help many peoples live together.
> - They make the king richer → The rules are about safety, not riches. A messenger who is safe can carry words instead of weapons.
> - They only matter in battle → They matter most in peacetime: travel, trade and talk all depend on them.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why rules protecting guests and messengers help peoples live together._

**Sundiata**: And every person’s life is worth something. Even the least of them. Even the ones who crawl.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): the Manden Charter and Kurukan Fuga  
> _A charter is a set of rules for how people live together._  
> _The Manden Charter is remembered as proclaimed at Kurukan Fuga, and it is still spoken today._  
> _UNESCO, a United Nations organisation, lists it as part of humanity’s intangible cultural heritage: a living tradition, kept in people rather than in stone._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what the Manden Charter is, and that UNESCO lists it as intangible cultural heritage._


#### `a05-14-assembly-done`

**Balla Fasséké**: Tellers argue to this day about the exact words said here. That’s how you know they mattered.  
**Balla Fasséké**: The rules agreed here are still remembered. People call them the Manden Charter.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of time: centuries  
> _Balla says this will be told for 800 years, and a century is 100 years. How many centuries is that?_  
> - ✅ 8 centuries → Yes: 800 ÷ 100 = 8. Eight centuries of telling and arguing.
> - 80 centuries → That’s 80 × 10. A century is 100 years, so 800 ÷ 100 = 8.
> - 100 centuries → That would be 10,000 years. 800 years is 8 centuries.
> _For grown-ups: Converted 800 years into 8 centuries._

_The ring roars, and they name him Mansa, king of kings. Kolonkan is crying and pretending she isn’t._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a think question: are fair rules easy to keep?  
> _The assembly agrees that every life is worth something, even the least. Is a rule like that easy to keep, and why?_  
> - No, because people are tempted to put themselves first → A fair answer. Good rules matter most when they are hard.
> - Yes, if everyone agrees and reminds each other → A hopeful answer. That is why the charter is spoken aloud, again and again.
> - It depends who is watching → A sharp thought. The best rules are kept even when nobody watches.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether fair rules are easy to keep (no single right answer)._


#### `a05-14-ask`

_At the edge of the ring, where the griots sit, Balla is tuning his balafon. He looks happier than you’ve ever seen him._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Sundiata has made my family his griots for ever. My children, and theirs. The Kouyaté. We’ll keep this story as long as we last.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): jeli: a living tradition of storytellers  
> _In the Mande languages, a griot is called a jeli (plural jeliw). Jeli families, such as the Kouyaté, have kept their people’s history for centuries._  
> _They are still telling Sundiata’s story today, in Mali, Guinea and nearby countries, so it is a living tradition, not an old story that has ended._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that jeliw are hereditary keepers of history, and that the tradition is alive today._

_Your Nubbin climbs onto the balafon’s frame and sits there, as it did on the very first day._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Which means I’ll tell it ten thousand times, and every time a little differently. That’s allowed. That’s the life in it.  
**Balla Fasséké**: But some things a griot never leaves out, however he tells the rest. One thing in every telling.  
_Around you the other griots are tuning too. Each of them, you realise, will tell this day their own way._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Apprentice, you were there for most of it. What should I never leave out?  

**Choices**

- **That it took him seven years to stand, and that was all right.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Yes. Everyone remembers the rod. I’ll make them remember the dust before it, and the years nobody hurried him.
- **That his mother was the strongest person in it.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Sogolon. Yes. She goes in the first line, every time. I’ll make it a law in my family.
- **That Nana Triban chose to bring the secret.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: Sassouma’s daughter, choosing for herself. Yes. People forget her. I won’t let them.
- **That the enemy loved music.**
    - **Balla Fasséké**: That’s the hardest one to sing, and the truest. Yes. I’ll keep Soumaoro whole.

_The ring falls quiet. Balla stands before the kings to tell, for the first time, the story of Sundiata._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Before I begin, my apprentice’s round friend will play us in. It learned the tune I’d have chosen myself.  
_Your Nubbin plays the hunters’ tune on Balla’s balafon. A hundred hunters stamp along, and the whole ring stamps with them._  
**Sundiata**: My hunting tune. The one they played when I came home.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Eight hundred years from now, my children’s children will still be telling this. And they’ll argue about it.  
**Balla Fasséké**: That’s how you know a story is alive. Nobody argues about a dead one.  
_He puts the little balafon into your arms, and the beaters into your Nubbin’s hands._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Go home, apprentice. Remember us properly.  
_The red earth goes soft under your feet, then smooth, then paper._  
_You are back in the Grove with Nova’s atlas on your knee. From under the cover a tune keeps going, and your Nubbin taps it out, very nearly in time._  

> **Lesson** (music, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the balafon today: the Sosso-Bala is still kept in Niagassola  
> _A very old balafon called the Sosso-Bala is still kept in Niagassola, in Guinea, by Kouyaté families._  
> _Tradition says it is Soumaoro’s own great balafon, the one Balla played in the tower._  
> _UNESCO lists its tradition as heritage worth protecting._  
> _Balafons are still played at weddings, celebrations and ceremonies across West Africa, and the keys are still tuned by ear._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the balafon tradition is alive today, and that the Sosso-Bala is kept in Niagassola, Guinea._

_You think about what you chose to keep, and what a griot would keep for you._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): later Mali: Mansa Musa and the libraries of Timbuktu  
> _Less than a hundred years after Sundiata, Mali’s most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made a celebrated journey to Mecca._  
> _He carried so much gold that people talked about it for generations._  
> _Under later Malian and Songhai rulers, Timbuktu became a centre of learning._  
> _Its libraries still hold hundreds of thousands of handwritten manuscripts: science, law, poetry and history._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Mansa Musa ruled Mali less than a century later, and that Timbuktu’s libraries hold ancient manuscripts._


### Glossary

- **charter**: A set of rules for how people live together.
- **intangible cultural heritage**: Traditions that live in people, such as stories, music and skills, rather than in buildings or objects.
- **jeli**: The Mande word for a griot. The plural is jeliw.
- **manuscript**: A book or document written by hand.

## A6-1. Two Sinbads

- `a06-01-s1`: Help your friend the porter carry his load of paper across Baghdad. · _Pick up the basket by the porter and follow him through the lanes._
- `a06-01-s2`: Rest on the bench by the great house on the way home. · _Sit down beside the porter in the shade by the gate._
- `a06-01-s3`: Go in and meet the master of the house. · _Follow the steward through the courtyard to the long room._

#### `a06-01-street`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page the colour of hot stone: a round city on a river, drawn from above._  
_You touch the river. The heat comes up off the paper, and you are standing in a lane with a basket on your back._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Steady. Steady! That basket is worth more than both of us, and it isn’t even heavy.  
_The man beside you carries three baskets to your one. He is a porter called Sinbad, and he has been your friend, it seems, for years._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Paper, from the paper-makers’ market, for the scholars at the House of Wisdom. They write on it faster than I can fetch it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Baghdad was planned as a round city; paper travelled from China  
> **Sinbad the Porter**: This whole city was built in a perfect circle: four gates, the palace in the middle. People called it the City of Peace.  
> **Sinbad the Porter**: And paper? Somebody in China worked out how to make it. The skill walked west along the trade roads until it reached us.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Baghdad was planned as a round city and that paper-making spread from China along trade routes._

**Sinbad the Porter**: Every book in Baghdad has been on my back at some point. I can’t read a single one of them.  
_Your Nubbin rides on top of your basket, among the rolls, like a cat on a warm wall._  
_The lane smells of bread, cumin and river mud. A man is selling cold sherbet, and everybody wants some._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> **Sinbad the Porter**: Three baskets on my back, one on yours. Every basket holds six rolls of paper. How many rolls are we carrying?  
> - ✅ 24 → Yes! Four baskets, six rolls in each: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24, or 4 × 6.
> - 18 → That’s my three baskets alone: 3 × 6 = 18. Add yours, another 6, and we get 24.
> - 10 → That’s 4 + 6. But each of the four baskets holds six, so it’s 4 groups of 6: 24.
> _For grown-ups: Solved an equal-groups problem (4 baskets of 6 rolls = 24)._


**Choices**

- **Take one of his baskets as well.**
    - **Sinbad the Porter**: You’re a good friend and a terrible porter. Lift from the knees.
    - Your Nubbin shifts to balance the load, and very nearly manages it.
- **Ask what the scholars do with all this paper.**
    - **Sinbad the Porter**: They put books into Arabic, from Greek and Persian and the languages of India. Stars, medicine, numbers.
    - **Sinbad the Porter**: And they argue. Mostly they argue. Paper’s cheaper than it was, so they argue at length.

#### `a06-01-street-done`

_At the House of Wisdom a young scholar with ink to the elbow counts the rolls twice, and pays exactly._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Exactly. He always pays exactly. Never one copper over.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): what a scholar is; what a translation does  
> **Sinbad the Porter**: A scholar is somebody who studies one subject for years and years. These ones also translate.  
> **Sinbad the Porter**: To translate is to carry a book from one language into another, so people who couldn’t read it before can. It’s porter’s work, really. Only with words.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the words scholar and translate, and that translating carries a book into another language._

_Behind him, a long room of desks is full of people copying, translating and arguing in four languages at once._  

#### `a06-01-bench`

_On the way home the porter stops in the shade of a great house, and sets his empty baskets on a stone bench._  
_Cool air comes from the gate with a smell of roast lamb and rosewater. Somewhere inside, a lute is playing._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Listen to that. Somebody in there has never carried anything heavier than a spoon.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: I carry from first light to the last call to prayer, and I go home to lentils. He sits still, and gets lamb.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Same God made us both. I’m not complaining. I’m saying it out loud, which is different.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): think: is it fair?  
> _The porter works from dawn and eats lentils. The man inside sits still and eats lamb. Is that fair? There’s no right answer. What do you think?_  
> - No, work this hard should earn more. → A fair answer. Lots of people have felt that, in every century. Hard work and good pay don’t always travel together.
> - It depends how each of them got what they have. → That’s a careful answer. Maybe we should find out before deciding. I suspect somebody’s about to tell us.
> - Fair or not, grumbling aloud won’t change it. → That’s a fair point too. Though I notice the window opened. Speaking up can change things after all.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether the porter’s situation is fair, giving their own reasons._

_He says it quite loudly. A window above the gate is open._  
_Your Nubbin looks up at the window, then at you, the way it does in the Grove when someone is about to be caught._  

**Choices**

- **Tell him to keep his voice down.**
    - **Sinbad the Porter**: Why? It’s just as true in a whisper.
- **Say it isn’t fair.**
    - **Sinbad the Porter**: Thank you.
    - **Sinbad the Porter**: It isn’t, is it? I feel much better. No, I feel worse.

#### `a06-01-bench-done`

_The gate opens. A steward in a spotless turban looks at the porter, then at you, then at your Nubbin._  
**The Steward**: My master asks for the man who was talking. And his friend. And… that.  
_The porter’s face does something between a wince and a grin._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): feelings can be mixed: the porter is worried and curious at once  
> _The porter’s face is doing two things at once. He’s worried he’ll be told off, and curious who’s asking._  
> _Feeling two things together is normal. A mixed-up feeling isn’t wrong: it just has more than one part._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that people can feel two different things at once._


#### `a06-01-hall`

_Inside there is a courtyard with a fountain, then a long room of cushions, and more food than you have ever seen at once._  
_At the head of the room sits an old man with a white beard, and a face burnt brown by a great deal of weather._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Sit, sit. Eat first. A man shouldn’t have to argue with God on an empty stomach.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: You heard that.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: The whole street heard. What’s your name?  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Sinbad. Sinbad the porter.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: So is mine. Sinbad the sailor. Well, Sinbad, anyway. The sailor part I had to earn.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: You think I sat here and the lamb walked in. Let me tell you what this house cost.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character motive  
> _The old man heard the porter’s complaint, and instead of being cross he invited him in. Why do you think he did that?_  
> - ✅ He wanted to show the porter that things aren’t always as they look. → Quite right. That’s exactly it. A fair guess from somebody who’s been watching closely.
> - He wanted to make the porter feel small. → Hm, possible, but look: he feeds the porter first and shares his name. People who want to make you feel small don’t usually offer lamb.
> - He was lonely and wanted company. → That could be part of it, too. A house this big can be very quiet. Motives are often mixed.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s motive from what he does._


#### `a06-01-hall-done`

_The porter sits on the very edge of a cushion, as if it might send him a bill._  
_A kitchen boy puts a plate of dates beside him, and he takes exactly one._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): helping a guest feel welcome  
> _The porter perches on the edge of the cushion and takes exactly one date. He feels out of place. What could help him feel welcome?_  
> - ✅ The host saying “eat first” and sharing his own name. → Yes. The old man has already done both. Small, warm acts tell a nervous guest they belong.
> - Leaving him alone until he relaxes. → Some people like a little space, but on his own he might never relax. A friendly word helps him settle.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how a host helps a nervous guest feel welcome._

**Sinbad the Sailor**: Seven times I went to sea. Seven times I swore I never would again.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Seven voyages won’t fit in one supper. I’ll tell them one at a time, and you’ll take food home for whoever is waiting.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: My daughter. She’ll want to know why I’m late.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Then you’ll have a story to tell her. That’s the price of supper: you listen properly.  
_The old man looks at you and your Nubbin, as if he always knew the porter would bring you._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: You too. Sit closer. When I tell a thing, it has a way of happening again.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, do): time: seven nights make a week  
> **Sinbad the Sailor**: One voyage a night, seven voyages. How many days is that? A whole week. Count the evenings on your fingers.
