> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree native to Sri Lanka  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: cinnamon comes from the inner bark of a tree that grows wild in Sri Lanka. The bark is peeled, dried, and curls into the sticks you know.  
> **Nova**: The tree needs warmth and plenty of rain. Sri Lanka has both, which is why it was famous for cinnamon for a very long time.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cinnamon comes from the inner bark of a tree native to Sri Lanka._

_Your Nubbin rubs every tree it passes, and arrives at the palace smelling like a pudding._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions  
> **A Farmer of Serendib**: A stream is shared equally between four terraces. What fraction of the water does each terrace get?  
> - ✅ One quarter (1/4). → Yes! Four equal parts, so each terrace gets 1 of the 4: one quarter.
> - One half (1/2). → Half would be for two terraces. With four sharing, each gets one quarter, 1/4.
> - One fourth of four (4/4). → 4/4 would be all of it. One terrace gets just one part of the four: 1/4.
> _For grown-ups: Found a unit fraction (1/4) for four equal shares._


**Choices**

- **Ask the farmer about the trees.**
    - **A Farmer of Serendib**: Cinnamon. Your merchants buy it from us, and sell it in Baghdad for ten times the price.
- **Ask about the water in the terraces.**
    - **A Farmer of Serendib**: It comes down from the hills, field to field. Each farmer passes it on to the next. That’s the rule.

#### `a06-12-bank-done`

_The palace is cool and open, full of birds. The king is already waiting, curious as a boy._  
_Nobody has told him to be solemn. He is leaning forward, with his chin on his fist._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): a simile for a character  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: “Curious as a boy.” A simile that shows the king’s character in a few words: eager, open, not hiding his interest.  
> **Nova**: A few well-chosen words can show who a person is, and a whole room can be seen through them.  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how a simile quickly shows a character’s nature._


#### `a06-12-court`

**The King of Serendib**: Welcome. Sit. They tell me you came by our river, through the mountain?  
**Young Sinbad**: I did, majesty. Not on purpose.  
**The King of Serendib**: Then you came by a road nobody has used. Tell me about your Caliph. Is he a just man?  
**Young Sinbad**: I’ve never met him. They say he walks the city at night in plain clothes, to see how his people live.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why a leader should see for themselves  
> _The king likes that the Caliph walks the city to see for himself. Why might that make someone a better leader?_  
> - ✅ They learn what people’s lives are really like. → Yes. You can’t understand someone’s life from a palace window. Seeing for yourself builds empathy.
> - It shows off. → Maybe, but the king is impressed that he does it quietly, in plain clothes. That suggests he really wants to learn.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about why leaders learn by seeing people’s lives for themselves._

**The King of Serendib**: A king who goes to look for himself. Good. Then I will write to him.  
**The King of Serendib**: When a ship sails for Basra, you will carry my letter, and my gifts. You will be my messenger.  

**Choices**

- **Nudge Sinbad to accept.**
    - **Young Sinbad**: It would be an honour, majesty.
    - He says it beautifully. Then he whispers to you, “What have I done?”
- **Let your Nubbin bow to the king.**
    - It bows so low it rolls over. The king laughs out loud, and the whole court is allowed to laugh too.

#### `a06-12-peak`

_Before the ship sails, Sinbad climbs the island’s great mountain with the pilgrims, all night, to see the sun rise._  
_At the top there is a footprint in the rock, far bigger than any foot._  
**A Farmer of Serendib**: Some say it’s Adam’s, the first man. Some say the Buddha’s. Some say Shiva’s, and some say Saint Thomas’s.  
**A Farmer of Serendib**: We all climb the same steps. It’s a good mountain for that.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): different beliefs can share a place with respect  
> _People of different faiths climb the same steps to the same summit, each honouring it in their own way. What makes that possible?_  
> - ✅ Respect: each person lets the others honour it their way. → Yes. Sharing a place doesn’t need everyone to agree. It needs everyone to be respectful.
> - They all believe the same thing. → They don’t! The farmer lists four different beliefs. What they share is respect for each other.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people of different beliefs can share a special place through mutual respect._

_The sun comes up red over the sea. Everyone on the summit goes quiet at once, whoever they came for._  
_Your Nubbin sits on your foot, very still, the way it does for the first frost in the Grove._  

#### `a06-12-complete`

_The king gives Sinbad a letter, and gifts for the Caliph, and a ship home._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: A king who writes to another king, because a sailor washed up in his river.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think: should a king trust a stranger?  
> _A sailor washed up in the king’s river, and the king trusted him with a letter. Is it wise to trust a stranger? There’s no single right answer._  
> - Yes, if they’ve shown good character. → A fair answer. Sinbad showed honesty and courage, and a good king notices that.
> - Not at first: trust should be earned slowly. → A fair answer. The king tested Sinbad with questions before he trusted him with the letter.
> - It depends how much is at stake. → A thoughtful answer. A small favour needs little trust, and a royal letter needs a lot.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on trusting a stranger, with no right answer._

**Sinbad the Sailor**: That’s how most friendships between countries start, I think. Somebody washes up.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): trade and letters connected countries  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: kingdoms around the Indian Ocean traded gems, spices, cloth and ideas, and wrote letters and sent envoys to each other.  
> **Nova**: Friendships between countries often started this way: with one traveller, one letter, and a reason to keep writing.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that trade and letters connected kingdoms around the Indian Ocean._

**Sinbad the Porter**: Did you swear again?  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: I did. That one very nearly took.  

### Glossary

- **terrace**: A flat strip of land cut into a hillside like a step, used for farming.
- **pilgrim**: A person who makes a special journey for religious reasons.
- **summit**: The very top of a mountain.
- **messenger**: A person who carries a message or letter from one place to another.

## A6-13. The Caliph’s Gift

- `a06-13-s1`: Go with Sinbad to the Caliph’s court with the King of Serendib’s letter. · _Enter the palace of the Green Dome and wait to be called._
- `a06-13-s2`: Sail with the monsoon and deliver the Caliph’s letter to Serendib. · _Board at Basra when the wind turns, and carry the letter to the king._

#### `a06-13-palace`

_Sinbad comes home through the Basra Gate of the round city, and goes straight to the palace of the Green Dome._  
_The court is crowded with petitioners, scholars and inky clerks. One man selling figs has got in by mistake._  
**Harun al-Rashid**: Peace be upon you. You are the man who came out of a mountain?  
**Young Sinbad**: And upon you, peace, Commander of the Faithful. Through a mountain, rather.  
**Harun al-Rashid**: And the King of Serendib has written to me. Read it to us, please.  
**The Translator**: He writes that he has heard of your justice. He sends a cup cut from a single ruby, and asks to be your friend.  
**The Translator**: It is written in Arabic, majesty, and very good Arabic. Somebody in Serendib has been reading our books.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): translation carries ideas between languages  
> **The Translator**: Scholars here read Greek, Persian, Syriac and Sanskrit, and write it all out again in Arabic. Whole sciences have crossed that way.  
> **The Translator**: The numbers you use for counting came to us from India, and from Arabic they went on to Europe. Ideas travel by translation.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that translators carried books and ideas, including numbers, between languages and cultures._

**Harun al-Rashid**: Then he shall have more of them, and an answer. Sinbad, you will carry it.  
**Young Sinbad**: Majesty, I have sworn never to go to sea again.  
**Harun al-Rashid**: Then swear again afterwards. You seem to be good at it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): kind teasing and unkind teasing  
> _“Then swear again afterwards. You seem to be good at it.” The Caliph is teasing Sinbad. Is it kind teasing or unkind teasing?_  
> - ✅ Kind: Sinbad can laugh too, and nobody is made small. → Yes. Kind teasing is a shared joke that the other person enjoys. If they stop laughing, it’s time to stop.
> - Unkind: he is making fun of Sinbad. → It can feel close. But he is smiling and trusting Sinbad with a gift. Teasing is kind when both people enjoy it.
> _For grown-ups: Told kind teasing from unkind teasing, and when to stop._


**Choices**

- **Ask the translator which languages they read at the House of Wisdom.**
    - **The Translator**: Greek, Persian, Syriac, Sanskrit. A little Chinese, badly.
    - **The Translator**: If a book exists anywhere, somebody in this city is putting it into Arabic. Or wants to.
- **Let your Nubbin look into the ruby cup.**
    - It sees its own face in the cup, small and red, and is delighted.
    - **Harun al-Rashid**: I see the gift has found its true admirer.

#### `a06-13-palace-done`

_The Caliph sends books with the letter, and fine cloth, and a saddle worked in silver._  
_Sinbad looks at the saddle for a long moment, and says nothing at all._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): inference from a silent reaction  
> _Sinbad stares at the silver saddle and says nothing. What might he be remembering?_  
> - ✅ The saddles he made for the kingdom where his wife lived. → Yes. That’s the link: in the fourth voyage he made saddles for the horses, and loved a wife there. A silent look can hold a lot of memory.
> - He is wondering how much it costs. → Possible, but a merchant would say so. His silence suggests something deeper: a memory of the saddles from the fourth voyage.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s memory from a silent reaction._


#### `a06-13-monsoon`

_Basra, in the season of the winds. Dhows crowd the quay, every one of them waiting for the same thing._  
**The Captain**: Half the year the wind blows from the south-west, and half the year from the north-east.  
**The Captain**: We go out on one, and come home on the other. Miss it, and you wait a year. So nobody misses it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): monsoon winds reverse with the seasons because land and sea heat differently  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: in summer, land heats up faster than sea.  
> **Nova**: Warm air rises over land, and cooler air rushes in from the sea to replace it: a wet wind from the south-west.  
> **Nova**: In winter the land cools faster than the sea, so the wind reverses and blows from the north-east. This yearly flip is called the monsoon.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that monsoon winds reverse with the seasons because land and sea heat and cool at different rates._

**Young Sinbad**: Six voyages, and I never once asked why we left when we did.  
**The Captain**: That’s because you’re a merchant. You only ask what things cost.  
_The wind turns in the night. In the morning every sail in Basra fills at once, like a flock lifting._  
_Weeks of blue. Then green hills, and terraces of rice, and a king waiting on the shore._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, do): distance, speed and time  
> **The Captain**: From Basra to Serendib is about five thousand kilometres by sea. On a good day, a dhow sails a hundred kilometres. How many days is that?  
> Check: `edu:calculate:voyage:days`
> _For grown-ups: Divided 5,000 km by 100 km/day to get 50 days._

**The King of Serendib**: Books! He sent books!  

#### `a06-13-monsoon-done`

**The King of Serendib**: Go home safely, messenger. Tell your Caliph I am reading.  
_The king stands on the quay with an armful of books until the ship is a speck._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading between the lines of a short message  
> _“Tell your Caliph I am reading.” It’s only five words. What else is the king saying to the Caliph?_  
> - ✅ Thank you for the books, and I want to stay friends. → Yes. A short message can carry a lot: thanks, pleasure, and an invitation to keep writing.
> - Please stop sending me books. → He is hugging an armful of them on the quay! “I am reading” is a thank-you, and a wish to keep the friendship going.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred the fuller meaning of a short message._


#### `a06-13-complete`

_On the way home, pirates take the ship and sell everyone aboard in the market of a far town. Sinbad is bought by a merchant who deals in ivory._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): slavery was real, and it was unjust  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: to be bought and sold means being treated as property, forced to work and not allowed to leave. That is called slavery.  
> **Nova**: It happened in many places and times in history. It was cruel and wrong, and it is against the law in every country today.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned plainly that slavery was real in history, was unjust, and is illegal today._

**Sinbad the Porter**: After all that? After the letter?  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: After all that. The sea never once asked me whether I deserved it.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: The last part I want you both to see. There is a choice in it, and it isn’t mine.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think: do people get what they deserve?  
> _The old man says the sea never asked whether he deserved it. Do good and bad things happen to people because of what they deserve?_  
> _There’s no single right answer._  
> - No: luck and other people’s choices play a big part. → A fair answer. Many wise people have said the same. Which is why we try to help one another when bad luck falls.
> - Partly: our choices matter, but not for everything. → A fair answer. Choices can steer a voyage, but they can’t stop every storm, or every pirate.
> - Yes: in the end, people get what they deserve. → A fair answer, and a hopeful one. It’s a belief many hold, though the tale suggests the sea doesn’t always agree.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about whether people get what they deserve, with no right answer._


### Glossary

- **petitioners**: People who come to a ruler or court to ask for something.
- **monsoon**: A wind that blows from one direction for part of the year and the opposite for the rest, often bringing heavy rain.
- **translator**: A person who turns writing or speech from one language into another.
- **slavery**: A system where one person is owned by another and forced to work without freedom.

## A6-14. The Elephant Hunter

- `a06-14-s1`: Sit in the tree by the elephants’ path with Sinbad. · _Climb up beside Sinbad before dawn, and watch the path._
- `a06-14-s2`: Go where the herd takes you. · _Hold on to Sinbad, and let the elephants lead._
- `a06-14-s3`: The master is at his gate. Decide what to tell him. · _Talk to the master at the gate._

#### `a06-14-tree`

**The Ivory Merchant**: You’re the one who talks to kings? Good. Can you shoot?  
**Young Sinbad**: Badly.  
**The Ivory Merchant**: It doesn’t matter. Sit in the tree by the elephants’ path. When they pass, shoot. I need ivory.  
_Every morning Sinbad sits in the tree with the bow. You sit beside him, and your Nubbin sits on the branch above._  
_Every morning the herd comes past in the half-light, slow and huge, led by an old cow with one tusk broken short._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): elephant herds are families led by the oldest female  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: an elephant herd is a family of mothers, aunts, sisters and calves, led by the oldest female, the matriarch.  
> **Nova**: She remembers where the water is, and the way home.  
> **Nova**: Staying together helps them survive: more eyes to spot danger, and many adults to protect each calf.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an elephant herd is a family led by the oldest female, and that group living helps survival._

_Every morning Sinbad’s arrows land in the mud, a long way from any elephant._  
**Young Sinbad**: I’m the worst archer in the world. On purpose. Don’t tell him.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step word problem  
> _Sinbad “misses” with three arrows every morning. How many arrows is that in a week of seven mornings, and then in six weeks?_  
> - ✅ 21 a week; 126 in six weeks. → Yes! 3 × 7 = 21 a week, and 21 × 6 = 126. No wonder the master keeps buying more.
> - 21 a week; 27 in six weeks. → Right for a week: 21. But six weeks is 21 × 6, not 21 + 6: that’s 126.
> - 10 a week; 60 in six weeks. → That adds 3 + 7. Three arrows each morning for seven mornings is 3 × 7 = 21, and six weeks is 21 × 6 = 126.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step multiplication problem (3 × 7 = 21; 21 × 6 = 126)._


**Choices**

- **Promise not to tell.**
    - **Young Sinbad**: Thank you. He isn’t a bad man. He’s just a man with a warehouse.
- **Count the calves in the herd.**
    - Four calves, walking under their mothers like boats in a harbour. One stops to look up at you, and is hurried on.

#### `a06-14-tree-done`

_Weeks of mud and missed arrows. The master grumbles, and buys more arrows._  
_Sinbad starts to look forward to the dawn: he has begun to know the herd by sight._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): doing the right thing quietly  
> _Sinbad is secretly missing on purpose, and not telling his master. Is it right to secretly disobey an order you believe is wrong?_  
> - It’s hard: but protecting a living thing can matter more than the order. → A fair answer. Many people have faced that choice. Honesty and kindness can pull in different directions.
> - No: he should tell the master the truth. → That’s a fair view too. Honesty matters, and Sinbad could have spoken openly. Notice that he is choosing not to harm, which is a good aim.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed obedience against protecting a living thing, honouring the child’s reasoning._


#### `a06-14-herd`

_One morning the herd doesn’t pass. It stops, and gathers round the tree, and is very quiet._  
_The old cow wraps her trunk round the tree and pulls it over slowly, the way you would pull a weed you were fond of._  
_Sinbad falls. She catches him in her trunk, sets him on her back, and the herd turns off the path._  
**Young Sinbad**: Don’t let go of me! Come with me!  
_She lets you climb up behind him. She doesn’t seem to mind your Nubbin at all._  
_They walk all day, up into the hills, to a valley whose floor is white._  
_It is a valley of old bones and old tusks. This is where the elephants come when they are very old, to lie down._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): real elephants investigate the bones of their dead, and remember  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: real elephants have no secret graveyard, but they do stop at the bones of elephants that have died, touching them gently.  
> **Nova**: Elephants have large brains and long memories. The old female may remember a waterhole, or a path, from many years ago.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real elephants investigate the bones of dead elephants, and that they have long memories._

_The cow sets you down, unhurt. The herd stands round you in a ring, looking, and then they turn and go._  
**Young Sinbad**: They brought me here. They’re saying: here, take these, and leave us alone.  

#### `a06-14-herd-done`

**Young Sinbad**: Go on ahead to the town. I’ve twisted my ankle, and I’ll be slow. He’ll ask you first.  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): looking after a sprained ankle  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: a twisted ankle is usually a sprain, a stretched band inside the joint. It swells and aches, but it heals.  
> **Nova**: Rest it, keep your weight off it, and hold something cool on it. If it’s very bad, a grown-up should get it checked.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned simple first aid for a sprained ankle: rest, keep weight off it, cool it, and get it checked._

**Young Sinbad**: You decide what he’s told. I’ve done all the deciding for elephants I ever want to do.  

#### `a06-14-gate`

_The master meets you at his gate, and he is worried, and not only about his ivory._  
**The Ivory Merchant**: The tree’s down. The path’s churned up. I thought the beasts had trampled him.  
**The Ivory Merchant**: Where is he? Where did Sinbad go?  
_Behind you, far off on the hill road, the herd is walking home in a long grey line._  
_The master follows your eyes to the hills, and back again._  
_Your Nubbin looks at the herd, then at the master, then at you. It waits._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think: a promise, or a secret?  
> _You could tell the master, if he promises to take only old tusks and never hunt. Or you could keep the herd’s secret._  
> _Which is wiser: trusting a promise, or protecting a secret? There’s no single right answer._  
> - Trust his promise: he is worried, and might keep his word. → A fair answer. Giving someone a chance to be trusted can bring out their best, though it’s a risk.
> - Keep the secret: the elephants can’t speak for themselves. → A fair answer. Protecting someone who has no voice is a serious reason. Notice it costs Sinbad a season.
> - Hard to know: both could go wrong. → An honest answer. Sometimes there’s no perfectly safe option, only a best guess made with care.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed trusting a promise against keeping a secret, with no right answer._


**Choices**

- **Tell him, once he swears to take only the old tusks and never hunt again.**
    - **You**: There’s a valley. They took him there. Before I show you, swear something.
    - **The Ivory Merchant**: Swear what?
    - **You**: Only what’s already lying there. And no more hunting. Not ever.
    - **The Ivory Merchant**: …I swear it. On my children.
- **Keep the elephants’ secret.**
    - **You**: I don’t know where he went.
    - **The Ivory Merchant**: You don’t know? Or you won’t say?
    - You say nothing. Beside you, your Nubbin says nothing very loudly.
    - **The Ivory Merchant**: …He’ll come back. Where else would he go?

#### `a06-14-gate-done`

_That evening Sinbad limps in through the gate. He looks at you and at the master, and understands everything without a word._  
_He puts a hand on your shoulder, once, and goes in to supper._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, notice): body language shows feeling  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: Sinbad says nothing, but a hand on the shoulder tells you he is grateful. Writers use gestures, not only words, to show feelings.  
> **Nova**: Next time you read, look for what a character does with their hands, face and feet. It often says more than their words.  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that gestures can show feelings without words._


#### `a06-14-complete`

_The master takes his carts to the valley, and loads them with the tusks the herd let fall when they died old._  
_On the road back, the herd passes the carts. They don’t stop, and the master bows his head to them until they’re gone._  
**The Ivory Merchant**: You’ve made me rich, Sinbad. You’re free. Go home, and take your share.  
**Young Sinbad**: The elephants paid for my freedom. I want to remember that I didn’t.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-4, notice): conservation: how people protect elephants  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: real elephants are in danger from ivory hunters and shrinking habitats. Selling ivory across borders has been banned since 1989.  
> **Nova**: Elephants are also protected by rangers, reserves, and by people leaving them wild land. Keeping them safe takes many people and many years.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that elephants are protected by bans on ivory trade, reserves and rangers._

**The Ivory Merchant**: Nobody in this town will hunt them again. There’s no need now, and I’ve sworn.  

### Glossary

- **ivory**: The hard, creamy-white material of an elephant’s tusks.
- **matriarch**: The oldest and most senior female, who leads a family group.
- **herd**: A large group of animals that live and travel together.
- **tusk**: A very long pointed tooth that sticks out beside an animal’s mouth.

## A6-15. Home

- `a06-15-s1`: Come home to Baghdad with Sinbad. · _Walk with Sinbad from the quay to the round city._
- `a06-15-s2`: Walk the porter home to his street. · _Leave the great house with the porter and his daughter._

#### `a06-15-quay`

_The ship comes into Basra early, on the first of the winds, sitting low in the water._  
**Young Sinbad**: Home. Rich, early, and in one piece. That has never once happened before.  
_He hires a boat up the river, and walks in through the Basra Gate with porters behind him, and you beside him._  
_At the palace he tells the Caliph that the King of Serendib is reading. The Caliph laughs, and is pleased._  
**Young Sinbad**: Seven times. Seven! And I swear it now, in front of you two: there is no eighth.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think: what makes a homecoming good?  
> _Sinbad is rich and early. In the other version of the story he is poor and late. What makes coming home good? There’s no single right answer._  
> - Being safe, and having someone waiting. → A fair answer. The porter and the old man have each other. That’s a good homecoming at any price.
> - Bringing something back to share. → A fair answer. Sharing what you’ve brought is a way of making home better for everybody.
> - Feeling you’ve learned something. → A fair answer. A voyage that changes you is a voyage you can bring home, whatever’s in your pockets.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what makes coming home good, with no right answer._

_For once, he keeps it. You can tell, because the old man in the long room is sitting so very still._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): a ship sits lower when it is loaded: floating and weight  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: a heavy cargo pushes a ship lower in the water until the upward push of the water equals the weight.  
> **Nova**: A mark on the hull, a load-line, shows the safe depth.  
> **Nova**: A ship “sitting low” is a quick, true clue that the hold is full, even before you’ve seen inside.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a loaded ship sits lower until the water’s upward push balances its weight._


**Choices**

- **Say you believe him this time.**
    - **Young Sinbad**: So do I. That’s new.
- **Ask how long it will last.**
    - **Young Sinbad**: Ha! Fair.
    - **Young Sinbad**: This time, I think, for good. I’ve run out of things to be bored of.

#### `a06-15-street`

_The carpet turns back into a carpet. The old man is smiling down at his own hands._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: I came home heavy that time, heavier than ever. I’ve always wondered what to do with it.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Porter. Your street. Does it have a fountain?  
**Sinbad the Porter**: There’s a well at the far end. The women walk there and back all morning.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Then it has a fountain now. Or it will by the spring.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): public water fountains were a gift to a whole community  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: in many cities of the old Islamic world, the rich paid for public fountains, called sabils, so anyone could drink for free.  
> **Nova**: Fresh water close to home saves hours of walking, especially for children and the people who carried it.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that public drinking fountains were built as a gift to the whole community._

_Next morning, when you walk the porter home, there are workmen on his street with a cart of stone, marking out a fountain._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication and time  
> **The Porter’s Daughter**: The women walk to the well and back every morning. If each trip takes 20 minutes and a woman makes 3 trips, how many minutes does she walk?  
> **The Porter’s Daughter**: And how many hours is that?  
> - ✅ 60 minutes: one hour. → Yes! 3 × 20 = 60 minutes, which is exactly 1 hour. A fountain on the street gives that hour back!
> - 23 minutes. → That adds 3 + 20. Three trips of 20 minutes is 3 × 20 = 60 minutes, which is one hour.
> - 120 minutes. → That doubles. Three trips of 20: 3 × 20 = 60 minutes, which is one hour.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 3 × 20 = 60 minutes and converted it to 1 hour._

**The Porter’s Daughter**: Baba! They’re building water! Right here!  

**Choices**

- **Ask the old man why.**
    - **Sinbad the Sailor**: Because a man complained on my bench, and he was right.
- **Promise the daughter you’ll come back for the first drink.**
    - **The Porter’s Daughter**: You have to! I’ll save you the first cup. And one for the little one.

_Later, back in the long room, the old man opens a chest._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Before you go, I have something for you and your little one.  
_It is a sail, folded small: old canvas, salt-stained, with a patch on it you have seen before._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: From my first ship. The one that left me on the whale, and came back with my bales.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): wind as a force on a sail  
> _Hung from a pole, the sail swings round to show the wind’s direction. If the wind is pushing the sail towards the east, which way is the wind blowing from?_  
> - ✅ From the west. → Yes! A wind blowing from the west pushes things towards the east. Wind is named for where it comes from.
> - From the east. → A wind from the east would push the sail towards the west. A push towards the east means the wind comes from the west.
> - From above. → Wind moves sideways across the ground. A push to the east means a wind from the west.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned that a wind that pushes a sail eastwards blows from the west._

**Sinbad the Sailor**: Hang it somewhere you can see the wind. It’s no use to me now. I don’t go anywhere.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Then give me one more evening. Next time, you’ll hear mine.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Yours?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): a character decides to become a teller  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: the porter has spent seven nights as a listener, and now says he has “got one”: a story of his own.  
> **Nova**: Characters in good stories change, and this is his change.  
> **Nova**: Notice that he doesn’t say he is clever or brave. He says he has been listening. Listening, the story suggests, is where telling begins.  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how a character changes from listener to teller._

**Sinbad the Porter**: I’ve been listening for seven nights. I think I’ve got one.  

### Glossary

- **load-line**: A mark painted on a ship’s side that shows how low it can safely sit in the water.
- **fountain**: A built structure that supplies drinking water, or sends water into the air.
- **canvas**: Strong, heavy cloth used for sails and tents.
- **sabil**: A public drinking fountain, paid for as a gift to everyone who passes.

#### `a06-16-telling`

_The last evening. The long room is full: the steward, the cook, the porter’s daughter, and the old man, for once a listener._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: I’ve never told a story. I’ve carried a few. Bear with me.  
_He takes something from his sash and sets it on the low table. The lamplight finds it: a small clear stone, no bigger than a lentil._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: This is the first line of my story. A friend brought it out of a valley that nobody comes back from.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: I’ve carried other people’s jewels all my life. This is the only one anybody ever brought for me. So I’ll never sell it.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: My story is short. I’m a porter in Baghdad. I carry paper to the House of Wisdom, and I can’t read, so I listen.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral storytelling: stories can be carried without writing  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: for most of history, stories were told aloud, not written. A teller learned a tale by listening, then told it in their own way.  
> **Nova**: Tales like Sinbad’s were told aloud long before anyone wrote them down. A porter who can’t read is just the sort of person who carried them.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stories were passed on aloud for centuries before being written, and that a person who cannot read can still carry a story._

**Sinbad the Porter**: I listened to a rich man for seven nights, and I found out he was paid for, the same as me. Only in different coins.  

#### `a06-16-telling-done`

**Sinbad the Porter**: And at the end, a herd walked home through the hills, and nobody shot at them, and nobody ever will.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: The elephants were paid for in bones.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphor in the porter’s last line  
> _“The elephants were paid for in bones.” The porter is using “paid for” in a surprising way. What is he saying?_  
> - ✅ That Sinbad’s freedom came from the old tusks the elephants left, not from killing any. → Yes. “Paid for” turns bones into a kind of coin. It says freedom cost the elephants nothing they hadn’t already left behind.
> - That the master paid the elephants money. → Not literally. “Paid for in bones” is a figure of speech: the price was what the herd had already left behind.
> _For grown-ups: Interpreted a figurative use of “paid for”._

_Nobody says anything. Then the old man claps, slowly, and the steward joins in, and then everybody does._

_It is fat and round and faded, embroidered with a small ship under a big sail._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: He’s done telling. Now he wants to listen. Fifty years late, he says, and he’s starting with me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): listening is a gift  
> _The old man says he is done telling, and now wants to listen. Why might being listened to be a gift for the person who is speaking?_  
> - ✅ It shows they matter and that their words are valued. → Yes. Being heard makes people feel they matter. It costs nothing but attention, and it is rare.
> - It doesn’t matter either way. → It matters a lot! The porter has listened for seven nights, and today he gets to be heard. That’s a gift.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that being listened to shows we matter._

**The Porter’s Daughter**: And me. I’m telling him the giant one tomorrow. With the pepper.

_You sit on the cushion. All the small faces turn up to you._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think: being nervous before you share  
> _You have never told a story before, and you feel nervous. What could help a person who is nervous about sharing something of their own?_  
> - Take a breath, and begin small. → Yes. A breath and a small first line is how the old man started, and how the porter did too.
> - Wait until it is perfect. → Perfect might never come! Stories improve by being told. A small start is better than a perfect wait.
> - Ask a friend to sit nearby. → Very good. Your Nubbin does exactly that. A friend at your side makes beginning easier.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what helps when you feel nervous about sharing._

_Then you begin._

    - **You**: Once there was an island that was fast asleep…
    - Your Nubbin rolls on to its back, being the whale.
- **Begin with the porter on the bench.**
    - **You**: Once there was a man who carried every book in Baghdad, and couldn’t read a single one…
- **Begin with the elephants.**
    - **You**: Once there was a herd of elephants who only wanted to be left alone…

**Nova**: That page always tells it a bit differently. I’ve never heard the porter get the last word before.  
**Nova**: Who told it first? Nobody knows. In the book, it’s a woman in Persia, telling a king one story a night.  
**Nova**: She kept a cruel king listening for a thousand and one nights, until he learned to be kind.  
**Nova**: Persian and Arabic, then French, then English, and now you, on a cushion. Stories travel like sailors. They come home changed.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): stories travel across languages and cultures  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: the Thousand and One Nights was written down in Arabic. Its frame story came from an older Persian book.  
> **Nova**: Sinbad’s tales joined it, and it was later translated into French, English and many other languages.  
> **Nova**: Translators carried the tales across the world. Each new version is a bridge between people who didn’t share a language.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sinbad tales spread across many languages through translators._

_Your Nubbins don’t leave the ring for a long time, even after the stars are out._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think: whose story is it?  
> _A story told in Persian, then Arabic, then French, then English, and changed by every teller. Whose story is it now? There’s no single right answer._  
> - Everyone’s who has told or heard it. → A fair answer. A story keeps growing as it’s shared, and each teller adds to it.
> - The first teller’s, though others have changed it. → A fair answer. The first teller started it, and that matters, even if nobody knows who they were.
> - Mine, once I have told it in my own way. → A fair answer. Telling a story makes it yours for the moment, and it’s still the world’s.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how stories change as they travel and whose they are, with no right answer._


### Glossary

- **embroidered**: Decorated with a design sewn on cloth in thread.
- **lentil**: A small, flat, round seed eaten as food.
- **metaphor**: A way of describing something by saying it is something else.
- **symmetry**: When two halves of a shape or pattern match each other exactly.

#### `a7-01-plaza`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page of orange flowers and little paper flags, cut into birds and skulls and stars._  
_A warm wind blows, with a smell of baking in it. You and your Nubbin are standing in a town square in Mexico._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): where Mexico is, its capital and its languages  
> _Santa Cecilia is a made-up town, but Mexico is a real country. It lies south of the United States and north of Guatemala and Belize._  
> _Its capital is Mexico City. Most people speak Spanish, and many also speak one of more than sixty Indigenous languages._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned where Mexico is, that Mexico City is its capital, and that Spanish and many Indigenous languages are spoken there._

_Strings of papel picado flutter overhead. Everybody carries armfuls of marigolds, as orange as tiny lamps._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a simile (as orange as tiny lamps)  
> _“As orange as tiny lamps.” What is being compared to what?_  
> - ✅ The marigolds are compared to lamps → Yes. A simile uses “as” or “like” to compare. Marigolds glow with colour, the way lamps glow with light.
> - The lamps are compared to the town → Not quite. The marigolds are the thing described, and lamps are what they are compared to.
> - The flags are compared to birds → The flags are cut into birds, but this simile is about the flowers. They are compared to lamps.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the two things compared in a simile._

_Under a statue of a man with a guitar, a boy is polishing a shoe and talking much faster than he is polishing._  
**Miguel**: …and he started with nothing, just a kid from Santa Cecilia like me, and he became the greatest musician in the world!  
_The customer leaves. The boy notices you, and then your Nubbin, and his eyes go very wide._  
**Miguel**: Whoa. Are you here for Día de Muertos? Everyone comes home for Día de Muertos.  

**Choices**

- **“We’re visitors. From very far away.”**
    - **Miguel**: Then you have to see our ofrenda. My abuelita’s is the best in town. Don’t tell anyone I said that, they’ll all want to fight her.
- **Ask who the man on the statue is.**
    - **Miguel**: Who is… that’s Ernesto de la Cruz! The most famous musician who ever lived. He was born right here.
    - **Miguel**: Come on. If you don’t know that, you don’t know anything. I’ll show you around.
- **Let your Nubbin say hello.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs onto the shoe-shine box and sits in it. Miguel laughs so hard he has to sit down too.

> _Miguel says “mucho gusto”. When would you say it?_  
> - ✅ When you meet someone new → Exactly. Mucho gusto: pleased to meet you.
> - When you say goodbye → Close, but no. Goodbye is “adiós”. Mucho gusto is for meeting someone.
> - When you say thank you → Thank you is “gracias”. Mucho gusto is for meeting someone.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mucho gusto is a polite Spanish phrase for meeting someone._

> **You**: Why are marigolds so bright?

_The basket is empty. Your arms smell of marigolds, and so does your Nubbin._

_She brings out a loaf of pan de muerto, a sweet round bread with strips of dough on top shaped like bones._  
**Abuelita**: Eight pieces. Three of you. Everybody takes two.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step word problem  
> _There are eight pieces. You, Miguel and Nubbin each take two. How many pieces are left?_  
> - ✅ Two → Yes. Three people take 3 × 2 = 6 pieces, and 8 − 6 = 2 are left.
> - Six → Six is how many were taken: 3 × 2 = 6. Now take that from 8, and 2 are left.
> - Five → Try it in two steps. Three people take 3 × 2 = 6. Then 8 − 6 = 2 left.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem with multiplication and subtraction._


#### `a7-01-photo`

_The ofrenda rises in steps against the wall: candles, marigolds, sugar skulls with names iced on, bread, water, and a little dish of salt._  
_And photographs. Dozens of them, some so old the faces are the colour of tea._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): an ofrenda is a family altar, and a living tradition  
> _An ofrenda is a family altar for remembering people who have died. Some have two levels, some three, some seven._  
> _Families add photos, marigolds, candles, water, salt and favourite foods. It is a living tradition, kept by millions of families today._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what an ofrenda holds and why Mexican families make one._

**Miguel**: That’s Papá Julio. Tía Rosita. Tío Óscar and Tío Felipe, the twins. And that’s Mamá Imelda. She started the shoemaking.  
_In the oldest photo, a stern woman stands beside a little girl. Beside them is a man holding a guitar._  
_The man’s face has been torn away. Someone has folded the edge under, so you can hardly see that anything is missing._  
**Miguel**: Her husband was a musician. He left to play for the world, and he never came back.  
**Miguel**: So Mamá Imelda threw music out of the house. We make shoes instead.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): think about a character’s motive  
> _Why might Mamá Imelda have thrown music out of the house? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Music reminded her of being left → That is a thoughtful answer. When something hurts, we sometimes push away whatever reminds us of it.
> - She wanted to keep her family safe → That is a fair answer. Rules are sometimes made out of fear, even when they hurt other people.
> - She just didn’t like noise → That is possible. But the story says she loved music once, so there may be a deeper reason.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a character made a rule, using clues from the story._

_In a wheelchair beside the ofrenda sits a woman so old and so small she looks like a folded letter._  
**Miguel**: This is Mamá Coco. My great-grandmother. The little girl in the photo is her.  
**Mamá Coco**: Who are you? Are you new?

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): being patient and kind when someone asks the same question again  
> _Mamá Coco asks about her papá again. What is the kindest way to answer?_  
> - ✅ Answer gently, and stay close → Yes. Gentle answers and a steady presence tell her she is safe and loved.
> - Tell her she already asked → That might make her feel worse. A gentle answer works better, even the hundredth time.
> - Change the subject quickly → Sometimes that helps, but she asked a real question. A gentle, honest answer shows respect.

> _Supper starts at 6:40 and lasts 50 minutes. What time does it end?_  
> - ✅ 7:30 → Yes. 6:40 plus 20 minutes is 7:00, and 30 more minutes makes 7:30.
> - 7:00 → That is only 20 minutes after 6:40. Add 30 more minutes to reach 7:30.
> - 7:40 → That would be 60 minutes. Supper lasts 50, so it ends at 7:30.

### Glossary

- **papel picado**: Paper with patterns cut into it, hung in strings for celebrations in Mexico.
- **cempasúchil**: The orange marigold flowers used at Día de Muertos. The word comes from Nahuatl.
- **pan de muerto**: A sweet round bread, with strips on top shaped like bones, baked for Día de Muertos.
- **ofrenda**: A family altar for remembering people who have died, with photos, flowers, candles and food.

- `a7-02-s1`: Follow Miguel up to his secret hideout. · _Climb the ladder at the back of the workshop and squeeze in behind the loose boards._
- `a7-02-s2`: Walk with Miguel through the square to the talent-show sign. · _Keep close to Miguel and keep an eye out for Abuelita._
- `a7-02-s3`: Go after Miguel when he runs out of the house. · _Follow him out of the gate. When you find him, sit down with him._

#### `a7-02-hideout`

_Up a ladder, behind a loose board, there is a little room in the roof that smells of dust and candle wax._  
_It is a shrine to Ernesto de la Cruz: posters, records, old film reels, and candles all round his picture._  
_Miguel lifts a guitar out from under a blanket. It is homemade, the body a wooden box, the frets marked in pen._  
**Miguel**: I learned off his old films. I play along with the tape, and I stop it, and I go back and play it again.  
_He plucks a string, and a note hangs in the air. Your Nubbin sways from side to side._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): plucked strings vibrate and make sound; shorter strings sound higher  
> _When a string is plucked, it vibrates, which means it shakes back and forth very fast. The shaking passes through the air as sound._  
> _A shorter or tighter string shakes faster and sounds higher. That is why a guitarist presses a string down to change the note._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that vibrating strings make sound, and that shorter strings sound higher._

**Miguel**: There’s a talent show tonight. In the square. If I win, my family has to see I’m a musician.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about whether to tell a family a hard truth  
> _Miguel hasn’t told his family about his music. What might happen if he tells them, and what if he doesn’t?_  
> - They might be angry, but at least it is honest → A fair answer. Honesty can be uncomfortable, but it lets people know the real you.
> - Hiding it will keep the peace for now → A fair answer too. But secrets can grow heavy, and he may have to face it later.
> - He could tell one person he trusts first → That is a thoughtful middle path. Practising with someone safe can make a hard talk easier.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the costs of telling or hiding something important from family._


**Choices**

- **“You should tell them.”**
    - **Miguel**: Tell them? Abuelita would… you don’t understand. You’ve never seen her with a shoe in her hand.
- **“Play it again.”**
    - He does, grinning, a little faster. Your Nubbin tries to clap along and claps exactly between the beats.
- **Ask why music is banned, really.**
    - **Miguel**: Because of him. The man in the photo. That’s all anyone says. Nobody ever says the rest.

**Miguel**: Come on. I need to see where they’re putting up the stage. Don’t say anything. Act like a tourist.  
_You already are one, so this is easy._  
_Miguel says he will “play” tonight. You wonder how many things that one word can mean._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: play  
> _Which of these uses “play” in a different way from “play a guitar”?_  
> - ✅ We went to see a play at the theatre → Yes. Here “play” is a noun, a story acted on a stage. “Play a guitar” is a verb.
> - Play the song again → That is the same meaning as “play a guitar”: to make music with it.
> - Play it on the record player → That also means to make music, so it matches “play a guitar”.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that one word, play, can be a verb or a noun with different meanings._


#### `a7-02-square`

_In the square, a man is pinning up a sign: a talent show, tonight, in honour of Ernesto de la Cruz._  
**Miguel**: I just need a guitar. A real one. I can’t walk out there with a box.  
_A mariachi with a kind face lets Miguel try his guitar on a bench._  
**Abuelita**: MIGUEL!  
_Abuelita crosses the square like weather. The mariachi suddenly remembers he has somewhere to be._  
**Abuelita**: Music? In the square? On Día de Muertos, with your whole family watching from the ofrenda?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): managing big feelings before speaking  
> _Abuelita is furious. What could help her handle that feeling before she speaks?_  
> - ✅ Pause and breathe, then speak → Yes. A pause lets the big feeling settle, so the words come out how we mean them.
> - Say whatever comes first → That is natural, but words said in a rush can hurt more than we intend.
> - Walk away without a word → That can help for a moment. But going back to talk once calm is what solves it.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about pausing and breathing to manage a big feeling before speaking._

_The guitar in the old photo has a skull carved on its head, with a gold tooth set in the skull. You saw the same one on the statue._

> **Lesson** (maths, ask): counting generations: great-great means four steps back  
> _Count back from Miguel: parent (1), grandparent (2), great-grandparent (3). How many steps back is a great-great-grandfather?_  
> - ✅ Four steps → Yes. Each “great” adds one step: parent, grandparent, great-grandparent, great-great-grandparent.
> - Two steps → Two steps back is a grandparent. Each “great” adds a step, so great-great is four.
> - Three steps → Three steps is a great-grandparent. Add one more “great” for four.
> _For grown-ups: Counted generations back to a great-great-grandfather._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): think about a character’s motive and regret  
> _Abuelita looks as if she hurt her own hand. Why might she do something she seems to regret? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Big feelings can come faster than thoughts → A thoughtful answer. Anger and fear can make us act before we think.
> - They believe they are protecting someone → A fair answer. Sometimes we hurt people while trying to keep them safe.
> - They don’t know another way to help → That is wise. Learning other ways to cope takes practice, for children and grown-ups alike.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on why people act in ways they later regret._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what helps a friend who is very upset  
> _Miguel is very upset. Which of these helps most, right now?_

> - Tell him it’s not a big deal → That might make him feel unheard. Sitting with him respects how big it feels.
> - Give him advice straight away → Advice can come later. First he needs company and a little quiet.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about sitting with an upset friend instead of rushing to fix things._

#### `a7-03-cemetery`

_The cemetery at dusk is the busiest place in town. Every grave has a family round it._  
_People are scrubbing headstones, laying marigold petals, setting out candles and unpacking suppers._  
_An old man tells a story to a grave, and laughs at his own jokes. Two children are asleep on a blanket._  
**Miguel**: Everybody stays all night. It’s called a vigil. You bring their favourite food, and you talk to them, and you remember.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): some families keep a night vigil at the cemetery on Día de Muertos  
> _Many families in Mexico really do spend Día de Muertos at the cemetery. They clean the graves, share food and tell stories._  
> _The festival is a time to celebrate people’s lives, not only to mourn. Customs differ from town to town._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Día de Muertos is a celebration of lives, and that customs differ between places._

**You**: It isn’t sad.  
**Miguel**: It’s sad a bit. Mostly it’s a party. They’re visiting, so you have to make it nice.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): an occasion can be sad and happy at once  
> _Miguel says it’s “sad a bit” and “mostly a party”. Can one evening feel both?_  
> - ✅ Yes, feelings can mix → Yes. Missing someone and being glad to remember them can sit side by side.
> - No, it has to be one or the other → Many people find the feelings do mix. Remembering can make us smile and ache at once.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on feeling sad and happy at the same time._

_At the top of the hill there is a tomb as big as a chapel, with ERNESTO DE LA CRUZ over the door in stone._  
_It is locked. There is a window, high up, and it is open a crack._  

#### `a7-03-cemetery-done`

**Miguel**: Give me a boost. And hold the window. Don’t let it bang.  
_You make a step with your hands. Your Nubbin holds Dante, or Dante holds your Nubbin; it’s hard to say which._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced and unbalanced forces  
> _Miguel stands on your hands. Gravity pulls him down. What must your push do to lift him?_  
> - ✅ Be bigger than gravity’s pull → Yes. An unbalanced force changes motion: your push up must beat the pull down.
> - Be the same as gravity’s pull → Equal forces are balanced, and he would stay where he is. To lift him, your push must be bigger.
> - Be smaller than gravity’s pull → Then gravity would win and he would stay down. To lift him, push harder.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that lifting needs an upward force bigger than gravity’s pull._

_You lean in after him, holding the frame. Moonlight comes in with you._  
_Inside the mausoleum, high on the wall in a glass case, is a white guitar with a skull on its head._  
**Miguel**: Señor de la Cruz. Please don’t be mad. I’m Miguel. Your great-great-grandson. I think.  
**Miguel**: I need to borrow this. Just for tonight. I’ll bring it straight back. I promise.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): borrowing and permission  
> _Miguel promises to give the guitar straight back. Is it fair to borrow something without asking, if you promise? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. You should ask the owner first → A fair view. Asking shows respect, and the owner might say yes.
> - Maybe, if nobody could ask → That is a real puzzle. When you can’t ask, you have to think hard about what the owner would want.
> - Yes, a promise is enough → A promise matters. But the owner never agreed, and that is worth thinking about.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a promise is enough when you cannot ask permission._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): echoes: sound bounces off hard surfaces  
> _Why did the chord echo? Sound travels in waves. When the waves hit hard, smooth stone, they bounce back, and you hear the sound twice._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that echoes happen when sound waves bounce off hard surfaces._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): Spanish family words: tía and tío  
> _The ofrenda photos show Tía Rosita and Tío Óscar. In Spanish, who are they?_  
> - ✅ An aunt and an uncle → Yes. Tía is aunt and tío is uncle. The plural, tíos, can mean uncles, or aunts and uncles together.
> - A grandmother and a cousin → Not quite. Grandmother is abuela, and cousin is prima or primo. Tía is aunt and tío is uncle.
> - A mother and a father → Those are mamá and papá. Tía is aunt and tío is uncle.
> _For grown-ups: Matched the Spanish words tía and tío with aunt and uncle._

_It is 11:15 at night. Sunrise is at 6:45 in the morning._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals across midnight  
> _It is 11:15 at night and sunrise is at 6:45 in the morning. How long is it until sunrise?_  
> - ✅ 7 hours 30 minutes → Yes. 11:15 to midnight is 45 minutes, and midnight to 6:45 is 6 hours 45 minutes. Together that makes 7 hours 30 minutes.
> - 6 hours 30 minutes → Check the first part: 11:15 to midnight is 45 minutes, then 6 h 45 min more. That makes 7 h 30 min.
> - 8 hours 30 minutes → Try it in two parts: 45 minutes to midnight, then 6 h 45 min. That makes 7 h 30 min.
> _For grown-ups: Found a time interval across midnight in two parts._

- `a7-04-s2`: Go through the departures gate on the far side of the bridge. · _Join the queue by the gate and wait your turn with the family._

#### `a7-04-bridge`

_Beyond the cemetery wall, where the field should be, there is a bridge made of marigold petals, all the way across._  
_It arches out into a blue dark. On the far side there is a city of lights, stacked up like a cake with too many tiers._  
**Tía Rosita**: Where we stay. Tonight we visit. Tomorrow we go home. Come on, it holds. It’s only flowers, but it holds.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): marigold petal paths are a real Día de Muertos custom  
> _In Mexico, families really do scatter marigold petals in a path from the street to the ofrenda._  
> _The bright colour and strong scent are meant to guide their loved ones home. On this page, the idea becomes a bridge._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that families scatter marigold petals as a path for loved ones._

_With every step, the petals under your feet flare gold and orange, and then settle, like embers being kind._  
_Halfway over, your Nubbin stops. Its body is changing colour, slowly, like paint soaking into paper._  
_A row of dots runs down its tail: yellow, yellow, pink, yellow, yellow, pink, and on and on._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): number patterns that follow a rule  
> _The pattern is yellow, yellow, pink, repeating. In the first 12 dots, how many are pink?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. Each group is 3 dots with 1 pink, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 groups, so 4 pink dots.
> - 3 → Check the rule: every third dot is pink. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 4 are pink.
> - 6 → That would be every second dot. The rule is every third dot, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 pink.
> _For grown-ups: Used a repeating pattern rule to count how many dots are pink._


**Choices**

- **Let it look at itself in a puddle of light.**

> **Lesson** (art, notice): alebrijes: real painted creatures from Mexico, and the page’s story idea  
> _Alebrijes are real. Pedro Linares, an artist in Mexico City, began making them in the 1930s, and carvers in Oaxaca now carve them from copal wood._  
> _Each one is painted by hand in bright patterns. Spirit guides are this story’s idea, not an alebrije belief._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that alebrijes are real painted creatures from Mexico, and that spirit guides are this story’s idea._

_At the far desks, a queue of skeletons in their best clothes waits to cross into the living world for the night._  
**Departures Officer**: Next. Look into the camera, please. Is your photo up on an ofrenda tonight?  
_Each skeleton steps up to a screen. Their photo appears on it, on some family’s altar, and the officer waves them through._  
_Then a woman steps up who is all straight back and folded arms. You know her from the photo at once._  
**Departures Officer**: I’m sorry, señora. No photo. No ofrenda. You can’t cross tonight.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): think about fair rules  
> _The officer follows a rule: no photo, no crossing. Is that rule fair? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. It punishes people for what others forgot → A strong point. Imelda didn’t choose to be left off. A fair rule shouldn’t blame her for that.
> - Yes. Rules apply to everyone equally → Equal rules matter. But a fair rule should also make sense for the people it affects.
> - It depends on why the rule exists → A wise answer. Good rules have a purpose, and we can ask whether a rule still serves it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a rule that applies to everyone can still be unfair._

**Mamá Imelda**: That’s impossible. My photo is up every year. Every year.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): read how someone feels from how little they say  
> _Mamá Imelda says only one word: “Miguel?” What does that tell us about how she feels?_  
> - ✅ She is too shocked to say more → Yes. One short word and a question can show how stunned a character is.
> - She is bored → Not likely. Her eyes went straight to Miguel, so she is surprised, not bored.
> - She is delighted and chatty → Chatty people say more. One word suggests shock rather than delight.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s few words to understand how she feels._

**Miguel**: Hola, Mamá Imelda…

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): word parts: re- and union  
> _A “reunion” is when people come together again. What does the prefix “re-” mean?_  
> - ✅ Again → Yes. Re- means again: re-read, redo, reunion. A reunion is a union, or joining, again.
> - Before → That is “pre-”. Re- means again, so reunion is coming together again.
> - Not → That is “un-”. Re- means again, so a reunion is a joining again.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that the prefix re- means again, as in reunion._

- **alebrije**: A brightly painted fantasy creature, a Mexican folk art.
- **reunion**: When people who have been apart come together again.

#### `a7-05-queue`

_The Department of Family Reunions is a long room of desks, rubber stamps and filing cabinets. It is bureaucracy at its finest: lots of forms and lots of rules._  
_You take a ticket that says 2,409. The board says 2,377._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtract within 100 to find the gap  
> _Your ticket is 2,409 and the board says 2,377. How many numbers until yours?_  
> - ✅ 32 → Yes. 2,409 − 2,377 = 32. The thousands and hundreds match, so you only need 409 − 377.
> - 42 → Check the tens: 409 − 377 = 32, not 42. Take away 300, then 70, then 7.
> - 132 → The hundreds are the same in both numbers, so they cancel out. The difference is 32.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted to find how many numbers are left in a queue._

**Tío Óscar and Tío Felipe**: It’s quick tonight. Last year we waited four years.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): numbered tickets make queues fair  
> _Why do offices use numbered tickets? So everyone is served in the order they arrived._  
> _A queue is a simple kind of fairness: first come, first served, and nobody gets to jump ahead._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that numbered tickets and queues are a way to share turns fairly._

> _The painter said, “someone I need to see before she forgets me.” What do you think he means? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Someone he loves is growing forgetful → A thoughtful guess. Her forgetting him seems to matter more to him than the rules.
> - He is playing a trick on the clerk → He might be. But his voice went sad, so it sounds like more than a trick.

**Mamá Imelda**: That’s the blessing. That’s the only blessing. I will not lose another one to a guitar.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): think about a blessing with a rule attached  
> _A blessing is a kind wish. Is a blessing with a rule attached still a blessing? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. A real blessing has no conditions → A strong view. Many people feel a gift with strings attached is more like a trade.
> - Yes, if the rule comes from love → A fair view. Love can ask for things. The question is whether the rule helps or hurts.
> - It depends on whose rule it is → A thoughtful answer. A rule you chose differs from one handed to you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a blessing with conditions is still a blessing._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): noticing an automatic habit and pausing  
> _Miguel reached for the guitar without thinking. How can we notice an automatic habit?_  
> - ✅ Pause and ask what I am about to do → Yes. A tiny pause gives us a chance to choose instead of just reacting.
> - Hurry up so there is no time to think → Hurrying makes habits stronger. A pause gives us room to choose.
> - Ignore it and hope it stops → Habits need noticing before they can change. A pause helps us notice.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about pausing to notice an automatic habit._

**Miguel**: Ernesto de la Cruz. He’s my great-great-grandfather. And he’ll give me his blessing without any rules!  
**Mamá Imelda**: That man is not…  
_But Miguel is already running, down the stairs and out into the streets of the Land of the Dead._  
_Dante bounds after him, delighted, as if this is the best game anyone has ever invented._  
_Mamá Imelda looks at you. Her face is fierce, and frightened under the fierce._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): explain a character’s motive from the clues  
> _Mamá Imelda’s face is “fierce, and frightened under the fierce”. What might the fear be about?_  
> - ✅ Losing Miguel, as she lost her husband → Yes. Her fear of losing another family member sits under her anger.
> - Missing the talent show → Not likely. Her fear is about Miguel’s safety, not the show.
> - Being late for supper → That doesn’t fit the clues. Her fear seems to be about someone she loves.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues to explain that a character’s anger covers a deeper fear._


**Choices**

- **“I’ll stay with him. I’ll keep him safe.”**
    - **Mamá Imelda**: Keep him safe, then. And bring him back to me.
- **“Why do you hate music so much?”**
    - **Mamá Imelda**: I don’t hate it. I loved it. That’s the trouble.
    - **Mamá Imelda**: Go on. Go after him. Quickly.

#### `a7-05-run-done`

_You catch up with Miguel in a back street, out of breath, his see-through fingers stuffed in his pockets._  
**Miguel**: I just need to find Ernesto. That’s all. How hard can it be?  
_Above you, on every wall, his smiling face is on a poster. All of them say SOLD OUT._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication word problem: equal rows  
> _One wall has 4 rows of posters, with 7 in each row. How many posters is that?_  
> - ✅ 28 → Yes. 4 rows of 7 is 4 × 7 = 28 smiling Ernestos.
> - 11 → That is 4 + 7. Equal rows mean multiplying: 4 × 7 = 28.
> - 21 → That is 3 rows of 7. With 4 rows, 4 × 7 = 28.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 × 7 to count posters in equal rows._

_Behind you, in the Department, Mamá Imelda is filling out a form for a missing boy. She presses so hard the pen goes through._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a metaphor about feelings  
> _Imelda is angry and frightened at once. Sometimes anger is fear wearing a coat._  
> _What does “anger is fear wearing a coat” mean?_  
> - ✅ Anger can hide a feeling underneath, like fear → Yes. It is a metaphor: the coat is the anger we show, and the fear is what it covers.
> - Angry people wear coats → Not really. It is a metaphor, not about clothes. The anger covers a hidden fear.
> - Fear keeps you warm → A funny picture! But the coat stands for anger, covering the fear underneath.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor, and that anger can cover other feelings, such as fear._

_Somewhere in the city, a tall thin skeleton picks the last bit of eyebrow off his face and looks thoughtfully at the poster too._  

### Glossary

- **bureaucracy**: A system with a lot of forms, rules and desks, where it is hard to get things done.
- **blessing**: A kind wish, or a gift of permission or good luck, given to someone.

## A7-6. Héctor

- `a7-06-s1`: Hear out the tall skeleton who follows you down the alley. · _He’s waving from behind the bins. Go and talk to him._
- `a7-06-s2`: Go with Héctor to Shantytown to borrow a guitar from his friend. · _Follow Héctor down the stairs to the edge of the city, to the hut by the water._
- `a7-06-s3`: Héctor asks you to remember his name. Decide how. · _Sit with Héctor on the step outside the hut and answer him._

#### `a7-06-alley`

**Héctor**: Psst. Psst. Living boy. Over here. And the… friend. And the… very colourful thing.  
_It is the painter from the Department, without the dress. His suit is shabby and his hat has a hole in it._  
**Héctor**: Héctor. A pleasure. I couldn’t help hearing you need Ernesto de la Cruz. And I need a favour.  
**Héctor**: I get you to him. And you, when you go home, put my photo on your ofrenda. Just one year. So I can cross.  
**Miguel**: Why do you need to cross so badly?  
**Héctor**: Somebody up there I want to see. Before she forgets me. Before it’s too late.  
_He holds out a bony hand. Miguel looks at you._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about trust  
> _Héctor admits he can’t be trusted completely, and Miguel shakes his hand anyway. Why might Miguel do that? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Because honesty about faults is a kind of trust → A thoughtful answer. Someone who admits his flaws is easier to judge than someone who hides them.
> - Because Miguel has no other choice → A fair point. Sometimes we have to take a chance because there is no better road.
> - Because Miguel liked him → A good point. We often trust our feelings about a person, for better or for worse.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a person might trust someone who is honest about being unreliable._


**Choices**

- **Nod to Miguel: shake on it.**
    - **Miguel**: Deal.
    - **Héctor**: Deal! Ha! You won’t regret this. Probably.
- **“Can we trust you?”**
    - **Héctor**: Absolutely not. But I’m all you’ve got, amigo.
    - Miguel shakes his hand anyway. You think it’s the honesty that does it.

#### `a7-06-alley-done`

_He tucks a small, creased photo of himself into Miguel’s pocket, beside the old family one._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): use context clues to find a meaning  
> _The photo is “small” and “creased”. What does creased mean?_  
> - ✅ Folded or wrinkled → Yes. A creased photo has lines where it has been folded. It has been kept close for years.
> - Brand new and shiny → Not quite. “Creased” suggests an old photo that has been handled a lot.
> - Torn in half → A crease is a fold or wrinkle. A tear would split the paper.
> _For grown-ups: Used context to work out the meaning of creased._

#### `a7-06-shantytown`

_At the bottom of the city, under all the lights, there is a place of tin roofs and string, where the forgotten live._  
_In a hammock in a hut lies an old skeleton with a bad temper and a guitar on his chest._  
**Chicharrón**: Héctor. Last time I lent you something, I never saw it again.  
**Chicharrón**: Fine. Take it. Only play me something first. One of mine. Something I used to like.  
_Héctor plays an old, rude, silly song about a man and his fine moustache. Chicharrón laughs with his eyes shut._  
_As the last note goes, a soft gold light lifts off Chicharrón, like dust in a sunbeam._  
**Chicharrón**: Ah. That’s nice. That’s… nice.  
_And then the hammock is empty, and still gently swinging. Chicharrón has faded, which in this story means he is gone for good._  
**Héctor**: Nobody up there remembers him any more. When the last one forgets you, you go. That’s all.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: people are carried by being remembered and talked about  
> _Before most people wrote things down, stories were passed by speaking. This is called oral history._  
> _Names, songs and family stories can carry a person across hundreds of years, one retelling at a time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that oral history keeps people and stories alive by telling them aloud._

_It is this story’s idea, and a gentle one. He wasn’t hurt, and he went laughing._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps when someone we know has died  
> _Héctor is sad that Chicharrón has died. What helps people when someone they know has died?_  
> - ✅ Talking, hugging and remembering them → Yes. Sharing the feeling and keeping their memory alive both help.
> - Never talking about them → Many people find that makes the sadness heavier. Talking and remembering often helps.
> - Pretending nothing happened → It is natural to want to, but feelings need room. Hugs and stories help.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what helps people cope when someone has died._


#### `a7-06-shantytown-done`

_Héctor puts the guitar in Miguel’s hands. His own hand is shaking, and it shines, very faintly, gold at the edges._  
**Miguel**: Héctor. Your hand.  
**Héctor**: It’s nothing. It comes and goes. Mostly comes, lately.  
_Miguel tunes the guitar. Six strings, thick to thin, low notes to high._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): thicker strings make lower notes  
> _A guitar usually has six strings. The thickest string sounds lowest and the thinnest sounds highest._  
> _Thick strings shake more slowly, and slow shaking makes a low note. Thin strings shake fast and make a high one._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that thicker strings vibrate more slowly and sound lower._


#### `a7-06-name`

_Miguel walks a little way off with the guitar, trying chords. You sit on the step with Héctor, and Dante sits on Héctor._  
**Héctor**: There’s one person up there who still remembers me. Only one. And she’s very old.  
**Héctor**: When she forgets, I go the way Chicharrón went. So I’m asking everyone I meet. Even strangers. Even you.  
**Héctor**: Will you remember my name? Héctor. That’s all. Just Héctor.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): the accent mark in Héctor shows which part to stress  
> _In Spanish, an accent mark like the one on the É shows which syllable to say loudest: HÉC-tor._  
> _The little mark is part of how the name is spelled. Writing it correctly is a way of respecting the person._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Spanish accent marks show which syllable to stress._

_He looks at your Nubbin’s orange ribbon. He pulls a loose thread from the cuff of his old jacket._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): compare a stitched name with a promise  
> _Which keeps a name safer: stitched in cloth, or promised aloud? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Stitched: it stays even if I forget → A fair point. Things we make can hold a memory when our own memory slips.
> - Promised: I carry it with me everywhere → A fair point. A promise lives in a person and goes wherever they go.
> - Both, and best of all together → A wise answer. Written things and spoken promises protect one another.
> _For grown-ups: Compared stitching a name with promising to remember it._

**Héctor**: Or, if it’s not too much, you could put it somewhere it couldn’t fall out of your head.  

**Choices**

    - Héctor threads his jacket thread onto a fishbone needle. You stitch, slowly, with your Nubbin very still: H, É, C, T, O, R.
    - The letters are crooked, and the accent is a bit big. Héctor holds the ribbon up to the light for a long time.
    - **Héctor**: Nobody’s written my name down in a hundred years. It looks good. It looks like somebody.
- **Promise him. Just your word.**
    - **You**: Héctor. I won’t forget. I promise.
    - He looks at you hard, the way people look at a coin to see if it’s real.
    - **Héctor**: A promise. All right. I’ve made a lot of those. Let’s see if one of us can keep one.

#### `a7-07-paint`

**Héctor**: Hold still. A living boy at a talent show for the dead. They’ll have you out of there by your ear.  
_Héctor paints Miguel’s face white with a brush, then black round his eyes, then a row of skull teeth across his lips._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): calaveras: painted skulls are a cheerful part of Día de Muertos art  
> _Calavera is Spanish for skull. In Mexico, people paint calavera faces and make sugar skulls with names iced on them._  
> _The skulls are bright and smiling, a happy way of showing that death is part of life. Painting a face this way is a respectful art, not a costume party._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that calaveras are bright, friendly skulls used in Día de Muertos art._

**Miguel**: Do I look dead?  
**Héctor**: You look like a boy who fell in some paint. But it’s dark in there.  
_Your Nubbin, all pink and green and yellow, holds up a little mirror. Miguel grins, and the painted teeth grin too._  
**Héctor**: Now. Stage fright. You have stage fright?

    - **Héctor**: Look at that! A natural. You’ve been dead for years.
- **Let your Nubbin dab a dot on Miguel’s nose.**
    - **Miguel**: Hey!
    - **Héctor**: No, leave it. It’s good. It’s… artistic.

#### `a7-07-paint-done`

_Overhead, the papel picado flags across the square are cut into dancing skeletons. They wave in the warm wind._  

> **Lesson** (art, notice): papel picado is hand-cut paper, a Mexican folk art  
> _Papel picado means “punched paper”. Makers stack sheets of tissue paper and cut patterns with tiny chisels, or fold and snip with scissors._  
> _It decorates streets, altars and ofrendas, and is a folk art in Mexico, passed from maker to maker._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how papel picado is made and used._

_Each flag was folded, then cut, so the left side matches the right._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry  
> _Papel picado is made by folding paper and cutting. When you unfold it, the design is symmetrical. What does that mean?_  
> - ✅ One half is a mirror image of the other → Yes. A line of symmetry splits a shape into two matching halves.
> - The paper is very big → Size has nothing to do with it. Symmetry means the two sides match.
> - The paper has lots of colours → Colours can vary. Symmetry is about matching halves.
> _For grown-ups: Explained symmetry as matching halves, using folded cut paper._

**Compère**: Next! The… boy with the paint. And the tall one. And the little bright thing.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): stage fright: butterflies are normal, and a friend or a breath helps  
> _Stage fright feels like butterflies in the tummy and a dry mouth. Nearly everyone gets it, even famous performers._  
> _A slow breath, a friendly face and starting small can help the butterflies settle._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nerves before performing are normal and that breathing and a friendly face help._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): read the mixed feelings in someone’s shout  
> _Mamá Imelda shouts Miguel’s name with her shoe in her hand. Which feelings might be mixed in her shout?_  
> - ✅ Anger and worry → Yes. She has been looking all night, so relief and fear can be mixed in with the anger.
> - Pure joy → She may feel some joy, but the shout and the shoe suggest worry and anger too.
> - Boredom → Boredom doesn’t shout across a crowd. She feels strongly, and worry and anger are likely.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred that a character’s shout can carry several feelings at once._
