> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): your point of view versus a character’s  
> _Miguel says Héctor is “just using” him. From where you stand, is that fair? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. Héctor cares about Miguel too → A fair view. You saw Héctor’s face during the song, so you know more than Miguel does.
> - Partly. Héctor did ask for a favour → A fair view. Asking for something in return isn’t using someone, but it can feel that way when you are hurt.
> - Yes. He only talks about his photo → That is how it looks to Miguel. You may know something he doesn’t, which is a good thing to notice.
> _For grown-ups: Compared a character’s view with what the reader knows._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): repairing a quarrel  
> _Miguel and Héctor both said hurtful things. What helps repair a quarrel?_  
> - ✅ Cool down, say sorry, and really listen → Yes. Calm, an honest sorry and listening are the three steps of repair.
> - Wait for the other person to apologise first → Waiting can leave the hurt in place. Either person can start by saying sorry.
> - Pretend it never happened → The hurt usually stays hidden. A sorry and a talk help it heal.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how to repair a quarrel: calm, sorry, listening._

#### `a7-08-gate`

_The tower at the top of the city is Ernesto’s house. At the gate, a doorman is checking a list._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): mariachi music comes from western Mexico  
> _Mariachi is a kind of music that grew up in western Mexico, in the state of Jalisco and nearby._  
> _A mariachi band usually has violins, trumpets and several kinds of guitar, including a big bass one called the guitarrón._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mariachi music comes from western Mexico and which instruments it uses._

**Miguel**: I’m with the band. We’re all with the band.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): how different instruments make sound  
> _A trumpet player buzzes their lips into the mouthpiece. What is vibrating to make the sound?_  
> - ✅ The player’s lips and the air in the tube → Yes. Lips buzz, the column of air inside shakes, and that is the sound. Strings do the same job in a guitar.
> - The shiny metal on the outside → The outside is not what makes the note. It is the buzzing lips and the air inside.
> - Nothing vibrates → Every sound comes from a vibration. In a trumpet, it is the lips and air.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that all instruments make sound by vibration._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think about charm and kindness  
> _Everyone laughs before Ernesto’s jokes are finished. Is being charming the same as being kind? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. A charming person can still be unkind → A good point. Charm is how someone makes us feel. Kindness is how they treat us.
> - Often, but not always → A fair answer. The two can go together, but watching what someone does tells you more.
> - Yes. If someone is charming, they’re kind → That would be nice. But it is worth watching how people act when no one is cheering.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between being charming and being kind._


#### `a7-08-pool`

> **Lesson** (science, notice): why wood floats: it is less dense than water  
> _Wood floats because it is less dense than water. Dense means a lot of material packed into a small space._  
> _A solid block of wood has less mass than the same volume of water, so the water pushes it up to the surface._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that things float when they are less dense than the liquid._

_Your Nubbin dives straight in after both. It swims like a little painted fish, round and round Miguel._  
_Then a big white sleeve comes down into the water, and a big hand hauls Miguel up onto the side._  
**Ernesto de la Cruz**: Easy, easy! Are you all right, my boy? Saved, just like in the movies!  
_Ernesto laughs, and everyone laughs with him. Then he sees the paint run off Miguel’s face, and stops._  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): getting warm after getting wet  
> _Miguel is shivering after the pool. What helps him warm up fastest?_  
> - ✅ Dry off and put on warm, dry things → Yes. Wet clothes pull heat from the body, so drying off and wrapping up keeps warmth in.
> - Stay in his wet clothes → Wet clothes make you colder, because water carries heat away from your skin.
> - Run around until he is dry → Moving can warm you a bit, but dry, warm things work faster and better.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that drying off and wrapping up helps the body keep heat._

**Ernesto de la Cruz**: Wait. You’re… you’re alive. A living boy. Here?

_The crowd cheers, and Ernesto lifts Miguel onto his shoulders. Miguel looks as if every birthday has come at once._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about praise that feels too good  
> _Everyone is cheering, yet your Nubbin isn’t clapping. Can attention that feels wonderful still be worth being careful about? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Yes. Watch what people do, not just what they say → A wise answer. Actions over time tell us more than a warm welcome.
> - No. If it feels good, it is good → Feelings are real, but they are not the whole picture. It is still worth looking a little further.
> - Sometimes, if something feels off → Good thinking. A quiet feeling that something is off can be a clue to look closer.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about being careful with praise and trusting a quiet feeling of doubt._


#### `a7-08-complete`

**Ernesto de la Cruz**: Stay! Stay the night! It’s the best party in the Land of the Dead. It’s my party, so it would be.  
_Fireworks go up from the roof, and Miguel is laughing. Ernesto has his arm round him, and the cameras are flashing._  
_Your Nubbin, dripping, sits by your feet and watches Ernesto, and doesn’t clap._  
_You find you aren’t clapping either. You couldn’t say why._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): notice foreshadowing: a small clue about what comes next  
> _Everyone claps for Ernesto except you and your Nubbin. Writers sometimes plant a small clue like this._  
> _What might the clue be hinting? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Ernesto is not what he seems → A sharp guess. Keep watching him, and see if the story proves you right.
> - Your Nubbin is just tired and wet → Possible! But a writer rarely mentions it twice for nothing. Keep an eye out.
> - Something is about to go wrong → A fair guess. A quiet moment in a loud party often warns of trouble ahead.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a clue a writer plants about what comes next (foreshadowing)._


## A7-9. The Truth

- `a7-09-s1`: Watch Ernesto’s old films with Miguel, and see who walks in. · _Sit with Miguel in the film room off the party._
- `a7-09-s2`: Hear Héctor remember the night he died. · _Stand by Miguel and listen. Keep your Nubbin close._

#### `a7-09-films`

_In a room of velvet chairs, Ernesto shows Miguel his old films. Miguel knows every line, and Ernesto is delighted._  
_Then the door opens. It is Héctor, soaking, with a torn jacket, and very out of breath._  
**Héctor**: Ernesto. Old friend.  
**Ernesto de la Cruz**: Héctor? What are you doing here? Who let him in?  
**Héctor**: The boy. He has to put my photo up. You promised me, years ago. You said you’d take my songs and my name with you.  
**Héctor**: You took the songs. You left the name.  
**Miguel**: Your songs? What does he mean, your songs?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty: giving credit for who made something  
> _Héctor says Ernesto took his songs and called them his own. What is the honest thing to do with someone else’s work?_  
> - ✅ Say clearly who made it → Yes. Giving credit is honest, and it is fair to the person who did the work.
> - Say it was yours if no one knows → Even if no one finds out, it isn’t true. Honesty means telling the truth when nobody is checking.
> - Say nothing and hope people assume → Letting a false idea stand is still a kind of dishonesty. Naming the maker is the honest choice.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about giving honest credit for someone else’s work._

_On the screen, one of Ernesto’s old films is playing: a scene of two friends and a farewell toast with two glasses._  

#### `a7-09-films-done`

_Héctor stops. He stares at the screen, and watches the glasses chink._  
**Héctor**: I know this. I know this. This is how it went. Only that’s not quite how it went.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view: why two tellings of one event differ  
> _Héctor says the film shows the toast, but not “quite how it went”. Why might two tellings of one event differ? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - The teller leaves out the parts that look bad → A sharp answer. Whoever tells a story chooses what to put in and what to leave out.
> - People remember things differently → A fair answer. Memory and viewpoint both shape how an event is told.
> - A film is made to be exciting → A good point. Films shape events for the audience, so they may not match what happened.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why different tellings of the same event can differ._


#### `a7-09-toast`

**Héctor**: I was going home. I’d had enough. I missed my little girl. I packed my guitar and my songs, and I told you I was going.  
**Héctor**: You poured us a drink. One for the road, you said. And I never got home.  
_Ernesto doesn’t say anything. His face says it for him._  
**Miguel**: You… you did something to him. You stopped him going home.  
_Héctor died that night, long ago. That is why he never came back to his family._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): hearing something terrible: big feelings are allowed, and telling someone helps  
> _When you hear something terrible, it is normal to feel shocked, angry or sad, sometimes all at once._  
> _Telling a trusted person how you feel helps. Héctor has Miguel now, and the story is still on his side._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about big feelings when hearing something terrible, and telling someone you trust._

**Héctor**: You took my guitar. You took my songs. You took my whole life and sang it, and you let them forget me.  
**Ernesto de la Cruz**: I did what I had to do. Anyone would have. And look. Look what I made of them.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): understand a character’s traits from how he speaks  
> _Ernesto says it “like a man explaining the weather”. What does his calm tell us about him? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - He doesn’t feel sorry → A strong reading. Saying something terrible calmly suggests he doesn’t feel the weight of it.
> - He has said it to himself many times → A thoughtful reading. People can talk themselves into believing their own excuses.
> - He is used to getting away with it → A fair reading. His calm suggests he has never been made to answer for it.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s traits from the way he speaks._

_He says it like a man explaining the weather. It is the most unsettling thing you have seen all night._  
**Ernesto de la Cruz**: Guards. Take them away. The boy too. He’s seen too much.  

**Choices**

- **Stand in front of Miguel.**
    - You step in front of Miguel. It doesn’t stop anything, but it means he isn’t alone when the guards come.
- **Grab for Héctor’s photo.**
    - Ernesto is quicker. He steps back out of reach, pats his jacket, and smiles.

#### `a7-09-toast-done`

_The guards march you all out, through a back door and down a long stair, to a deep round hole in the ground._  
_Dante, out in the gardens, sees you go, and starts to bark and bark and bark._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): raise the alarm and get help when a friend is in trouble  
> _Dante sees his friends taken away, and barks for help. What could you do if you saw a friend in trouble?_  
> - ✅ Tell a grown-up you trust, straight away → Yes. Getting help fast is brave and sensible. Dante is doing his own version.
> - Keep quiet so nobody notices you → That can feel safer, but your friend needs help. Telling a trusted grown-up is the brave choice.
> - Try to fix it alone, whatever happens → Brave, but risky. Getting a grown-up to help is usually the safest way to help.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about getting help from a trusted grown-up when a friend is in trouble._


#### `a7-09-complete`

_The guards drop Miguel and Héctor into the hole. You jump after them, because you are not letting Miguel go alone._  
_Your Nubbin jumps after you, glowing all the way down like a dropped lantern._  
_You land in cold water. Far above, the circle of sky closes, and your Nubbin’s glow lights the wet rock in pink and green._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): we see things when light reaches our eyes  
> _The cave is dark, yet you can see the rock. How is that possible?_  
> - ✅ Your Nubbin’s light bounces off the rock into your eyes → Yes. We see an object when light from a source bounces off it and reaches our eyes.
> - The rock makes its own light → Not this rock. It is lit by your Nubbin, and the light bounces back to you.
> - Eyes shine light out to see → Eyes don’t send light out. They catch light that bounces off things.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that we see because light bounces off objects into our eyes._


## A7-10. The Cenote

- `a7-10-s1`: Find a way round the dark cenote, and find Héctor. · _Your Nubbin’s glow lights the way. Follow the rock ledge round the water._
- `a7-10-s2`: Sit with Héctor and Miguel by the water. · _Sit down on the ledge with them. There’s no rush now._
- `a7-10-s3`: Watch for help from above. · _Look up at the rim of the cenote. Something is coming._

#### `a7-10-dark`

_The cenote is a deep round well of limestone, with a pool of black water at the bottom. The walls go straight up._  
_The only light is your Nubbin. Its painted stripes glow pink and green on the wet rock._  
**Miguel**: Héctor? Héctor!  
_You find him sitting on a ledge at the edge of the water, his hat in his hands._  
**Héctor**: All this time. I thought I was just unlucky. I thought I’d slipped on the road home or something stupid.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): the stories we tell ourselves when we do not know the truth  
> _Héctor thought he was “just unlucky”. When we don’t know the real reason for something, what stories do we tell ourselves?_  
> _(There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Stories where it is our own fault → A common one. Our minds sometimes fill gaps with blame, even when we did nothing wrong.
> - Stories that call it bad luck → Also common. Luck can feel easier than imagining someone chose to hurt us.
> - We keep asking until we find out → A strong answer. Asking questions is how Héctor, and you, find out the truth.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how people explain events to themselves when the truth is hidden._

**Héctor**: He took the songs. Fine. Songs are songs. But I never got home to my girl.  
**Miguel**: Your girl?  
**Héctor**: My daughter. She was this high. She had a laugh like a hiccup. I wrote her songs. One every night, almost.  
**Héctor**: Coco. Her name’s Coco.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): how cenotes form: rain dissolves limestone, and the roof collapses  
> _Cenotes are real, and many are in the Yucatán Peninsula, in south-east Mexico. They form where rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, leaving caves._  
> _When a cave roof collapses, it makes a deep, round hole open to the sky. The ancient Maya treated many cenotes as sacred places._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cenotes form when rain wears away limestone and a cave roof collapses._


**Choices**

- **Look at Miguel.**
    - Miguel’s face has gone white under the last of the paint. He is holding his breath.
- **Ask Héctor about her.**
    - **Héctor**: She’d be old now. Very old. Nearly as old as me, which is a joke, because I’m dead.

#### `a7-10-dark-done`

_Miguel goes absolutely still. He takes the old family photo out of his pocket: Imelda, the little girl, and a man with no face._  
**Miguel**: Mamá Coco. That’s Mamá Coco. You’re the man in the photo. You’re my great-great-grandfather.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): family history: counting generations  
> _Mamá Coco is Miguel’s great-grandmother. So Coco’s papá, Héctor, is Miguel’s…?_  
> - ✅ Great-great-grandfather → Yes. Coco is three steps back, so her papá is four steps back: great-great-grandfather.
> - Great-grandfather → Not quite. Coco is the great-grandmother, so her father is one step further back.
> - Grandfather → A grandfather is two steps back. Héctor is four.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a great-great-grandfather by counting generations._

**Héctor**: I’m your what?  

#### `a7-10-water`

_For a while, nobody says anything. Héctor and Miguel just look at each other, as if they are learning a song by heart._  
**Héctor**: You play like me. I knew it. Tonight on the stage. I knew it, and I didn’t know what it was.  
**Miguel**: She remembers you. Mamá Coco. She still asks for you. She asks if her papá is coming home.  
**Héctor**: She still asks?  
_His hand shines gold at the edges, brighter than ever. He holds it up and looks through it at the water._  
**Héctor**: Not for long, though. She’s fading up there. So I’m fading down here. It’s the same thing.  
_Your Nubbin climbs onto Héctor’s knee. Its orange ribbon, with his name stitched crooked on it, catches the glow._  
**Héctor**: Look at that. Still there. Still mine. Somebody wrote me down.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: how remembering keeps people close  
> _Héctor says Coco fading and himself fading are “the same thing”. What do you think the story is saying about remembering? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - People live on in those who remember them → A thoughtful theme. Many stories say that we continue in the memories we leave.
> - Remembering takes effort, from everyone → A fair theme. A name stitched in cloth or spoken aloud is something you do, not just something you feel.
> - Being forgotten is a real loss → A fair theme. The story takes that loss seriously, and shows what we can do about it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the theme of remembering in the story._

_He touches the letters, one at a time, as if checking the spelling._

**Héctor**: If I go before you get home. Tell her. Tell her her papá was coming home. He was on his way.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): understand why someone needs to be understood  
> _Héctor asks Miguel to tell Coco he “was coming home”. Why does that matter so much to him?_  
> - ✅ He wants her to know he never left her on purpose → Yes. Being thought of as someone who abandoned her would hurt far more than being gone.
> - He wants to look brave → Not likely. His voice is sad, and he cares most about Coco’s feelings.
> - He wants the guitar back → The guitar isn’t on his mind. His message is about Coco.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a character wants a particular message passed on._

**Miguel**: You tell her. You’re coming too.

**Miguel**: Dante! Dante’s a real alebrije! You were a spirit guide the whole time?  
_Your Nubbin answers the light. Its colours flare up all at once, every stripe and spot alight, its little wings glowing._  
_Then a huge shape drops over the rim: a winged jaguar as big as a horse, painted every colour there is, with Mamá Imelda on her back._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): jaguars: the largest cat in the Americas  
> _Jaguars are real. They are the biggest wild cats in the Americas, and they live in forests, wetlands and grasslands from Mexico down to South America._  
> _Jaguars are excellent swimmers, which suits a painted jaguar who has just appeared over a well of water._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that jaguars are the largest wild cat in the Americas and live in several habitats._

**Mamá Imelda**: Pepita. Down. Gently.  
_The great alebrije lands on the ledge. Mamá Imelda looks at Miguel, and then at Héctor, for a long, long time._  
**Mamá Imelda**: You.  
**Héctor**: Hola, Imelda.  

#### `a7-10-glow-done`

**Miguel**: He didn’t leave you, Mamá Imelda. He was coming home. Ernesto stopped him.  
_Mamá Imelda says nothing. But she holds out her hand, and pulls Héctor up onto Pepita’s back behind her._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): helping and forgiving are not the same thing  
> _Imelda pulls Héctor up, but says they will “talk”. Is helping someone the same as forgiving them? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. You can help before you forgive → A wise answer. Forgiveness can take time, and kindness can begin before it is finished.
> - Yes. If you help, you have forgiven → That can be true for some people. For others, forgiving comes later, after talking.
> - It depends on the person → A fair answer. Everyone forgives in their own way and at their own speed.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether helping someone is the same as forgiving them._

**Mamá Imelda**: We are going to get that photo back. And then we will talk, you and I.  

#### `a7-10-complete`

_Pepita rises out of the cenote in great slow wingbeats, with all of you clinging on._  
_Each downbeat of her wings pushes air down, and the air pushes back up on her._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): forces: lift from pushing air down  
> _Pepita’s wings push air down. What does the air do back to her?_  
> - ✅ Pushes her up → Yes. Every push has an equal push back. Air pushed down pushes the wings, and the animal, up.
> - Pulls her down → That is gravity’s job. The air pushed down by the wings pushes her up.
> - Nothing at all → Pushes always have a push back. Pushing the air down pushes the wings up.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that wings push air down and the air pushes back up._

_Your Nubbin rides on Dante’s back, both of them blazing with colour, both of them very pleased with themselves._  
_Below, the city glitters. Ahead, the sky over the Land of the Dead is starting, very faintly, to go grey._  

### Glossary

- **limestone**: A pale rock that rainwater can slowly dissolve.

## A7-11. The Blessing

- `a7-11-s1`: Sneak backstage at the Sunrise Spectacular with the Rivera family. · _Keep close to the family, behind the stage flats, while Mamá Imelda goes on._
- `a7-11-s2`: Watch Ernesto in front of the cameras. · _Stay behind the scenery and watch the big screens._
- `a7-11-s3`: Before sunrise, Miguel needs a blessing. Speak up for him. · _Go to Mamá Imelda on the ledge and choose what you plead for._

#### `a7-11-backstage`

_Ernesto’s great dawn concert, the Sunrise Spectacular, fills a stadium. Thousands of the dead are waiting for him._  
_The whole Rivera family slips in through the back, in borrowed costumes: the twins are both ends of a pantomime horse._  
**Papá Julio**: Find the photo. Find Ernesto. Get the photo. Get out. Simple.  
**Tío Óscar and Tío Felipe**: We are the back end. We don’t know where we’re going.  
_A stage manager grabs Mamá Imelda by the arm, thinking she is the next act, and pushes her out into the lights._  
**Mamá Imelda**: I… I don’t…  
_She stands in front of thousands of people. She hasn’t sung in a hundred years._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why might someone stop doing what they love  
> _Mamá Imelda hasn’t sung in a hundred years. Why might a person stop doing something they love? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - It reminds them of something painful → A thoughtful answer. Joy and grief can be tied together, so one brings back the other.
> - They think they must give it up for others → A fair answer. People sometimes give up a love in order to keep a promise or protect someone.
> - Life gets busy and they stop → That is common too. But Imelda’s reason runs deeper, as the story shows.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a character might stop doing something she loves._

_Then Héctor, in the wings, starts to play an old tune they both know. Mamá Imelda closes her eyes, and sings._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): how a voice works: vocal folds vibrate  
> _When you sing, two small folds of tissue in your throat, the vocal folds, vibrate as air from your lungs passes over them._  
> _Tighter folds vibrate faster and make a higher note. That is the same rule as a guitar string._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the voice is made by vibrating vocal folds, like a string._

_It is an old song, slow and fierce. The whole stadium goes quiet to hear it._  

#### `a7-11-backstage-done`

_When the song ends, Mamá Imelda looks into the wings at Héctor. Something in her face has come undone, just a little._  
**Mamá Imelda**: Don’t. Don’t say anything. Not yet.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): feeling several feelings at once  
> _Mamá Imelda feels something “come undone”. Can a person feel anger, love and sadness all at once?_  
> - ✅ Yes. Feelings often come in mixtures → Yes. Naming each strand helps us understand our feelings, instead of being swept away.
> - No. You feel one thing at a time → Many people feel several at once. It can be confusing, and that is normal.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people can feel several feelings at once, and that naming them helps._

**Ernesto de la Cruz**: I did it to him. I’ll do it to you. Nobody will ever know.  
_Every screen in the stadium is showing his face, and thousands of the dead have heard every word. He has confessed in front of everyone._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: being caught is not the same as being sorry  
> _Ernesto was caught on camera. Is being found out the same as being sorry? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - No. Sorry is about how you feel and what you change → A strong answer. Being sorry means understanding the hurt and wanting to put it right.
> - Sometimes being caught makes people sorry → A fair point. Being found out can wake someone up, though real sorry has to go deeper.
> - Yes. If you are caught you are sorry → Many people are sorry they got caught. It is worth asking whether they are sorry for the harm.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between being caught and being truly sorry._

_The crowd starts to boo. Then they start to throw things: shoes, fruit, a whole tray of pan de muerto._  
_Somewhere above, a great bell knocked loose in the scuffle swings once, and comes down. Ernesto is under it, stuck, and very cross._  
_Nobody is hurt. In the scramble, Héctor’s photo slips out of Ernesto’s jacket and flutters down into the water by the stage._  
**Miguel**: No. No! The photo!  

#### `a7-11-screens-done`

_Héctor stumbles. The gold light is all over him now, and you can see the stage through his arm._  
**Héctor**: It’s all right, chamaco. It’s all right. It’s my fault for being forgettable.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being kind to yourself: not everything is your fault  
> _Héctor says it’s his fault for being forgettable. Is it his fault?_  
> - ✅ No. Being forgotten is not his fault → Right. Others failed to remember him. He didn’t fail anyone.
> - Yes. He should have been more memorable → Nobody earns being forgotten. Blaming himself doesn’t change what happened to him.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about not taking the blame for things outside your control._


> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): transparent and opaque materials  
> _You can see the stage through Héctor’s arm, as if he were made of glass. Which of these materials lets light pass right through?_  
> - ✅ A clear glass window → Yes. Glass is transparent: light passes through, so we see clearly through it.
> - A wooden door → Wood is opaque: it blocks light, so we can’t see through it.
> - A brick wall → Brick is opaque too. Light can’t pass through it.
> _For grown-ups: Sorted materials by whether light passes through them._

_On a ledge above the city, at the edge of the dawn, the family gather round Miguel. His hands are almost all bone now._  
_Héctor is barely there. He is a shape of gold light in a shabby jacket._  
**Miguel**: If I go back and Mamá Coco forgets him, he’s gone. I have to go back. I have to make her remember.  
**Mamá Imelda**: Miguel.  
_Mamá Imelda takes a marigold petal from her shawl. She looks at it, and at Miguel, and then at you._  
**Mamá Imelda**: You came all this way with him. You watched him. Tell me. What blessing should I give?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): weighing choices by what they value  
> _You can plead for a blessing with no conditions, for one that includes Héctor, or sit with Miguel and let him ask._  
> _Which values matter most to you? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Freedom, with no strings → A fair value. A gift with no conditions treats a person as trusted.
> - Forgiveness, with everyone included → A fair value. Bringing everyone back in is brave and generous.
> - Patience, letting him speak for himself → A fair value. Sometimes the most helpful thing is to stand beside someone as they speak.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on which values guide a hard choice._


**Choices**

    - **Mamá Imelda**: No conditions. Yes. That’s what a blessing is. I forgot.
    - **Mamá Imelda**: Miguel, I give you my blessing. No conditions. Go home.

    - **Mamá Imelda**: Héctor. You. I never forgave you.
    - **Mamá Imelda**: Miguel, I give you my blessing. No conditions. Go home, and bring your papá Héctor home with you, in every way you can.
    - Héctor laughs, softly, a sound like someone very surprised to be given a present.
- **Say nothing. Sit beside Miguel, and let him ask.**
    - You sit down next to Miguel on the ledge, and wait, and your Nubbin sits too. Mamá Imelda watches you both.

_The petal glows in Miguel’s hand. The whole family gives him their blessing then, all together, one after another._  
**Héctor**: Go. Go on, chamaco. Go home.  
_The sun comes up over the edge of the world. Gold petals swirl round Miguel, and round you, and round your bright Nubbin._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): the Sun rises in the east, and shadows point west at sunrise  
> _The Sun always rises in the east. At sunrise your shadow is long and stretches out to the west, away from the Sun._  
> _This is because the Earth turns, which makes the Sun appear to move across the sky._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sun rises in the east and sunrise shadows point west._


#### `a7-11-complete`

_The atlas in your pocket goes warm. The Land of the Dead turns to petals, and the petals turn to morning._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a metaphor  
> _“The Land of the Dead turns to petals, and the petals turn to morning.” Is that a simile or a metaphor?_  
> - ✅ A metaphor: it says one thing becomes another → Yes. There is no “like” or “as”. The writer says the scene becomes petals, then morning, to show how gently it changes.
> - A simile: it uses “like” or “as” → A simile does use “like” or “as”, but this line doesn’t. It states that one thing becomes another, which makes it a metaphor.
> _For grown-ups: Told a metaphor from a simile._

_You are on your knees on the cold floor of Ernesto’s tomb. Miguel is beside you, with the white guitar in his arms._  
_Your Nubbin is beside you too, blue again, mostly. There is still a little pink at the tips of its ears._  
**Miguel**: Mamá Coco. Come on. Come on, quick!  

### Glossary

- **confessed**: Admitted that you did something wrong.

## A7-12. Remember

- `a7-12-s1`: Run home with Miguel through the waking town. · _Follow Miguel down from the cemetery to the Riveras’ gate._
- `a7-12-s2`: Sit with Mamá Coco by the ofrenda. · _Go to Mamá Coco’s chair and sit down beside her._
- `a7-12-s3`: Listen while Miguel sings to Mamá Coco. · _Stay by Mamá Coco and listen. Everyone else will come to the door._

#### `a7-12-home`

_The cemetery is full of families waking up on their blankets, candles burnt down, marigold petals everywhere._  
_Miguel runs through the square, past the statue, which has a pigeon on its head. Nobody stops to look at it now._  
_At the Riveras’ gate, the whole family is out in the street: his father, his mother, Abuelita, cousins, aunts._  
**Papá**: Miguel!  
_His father holds him so tight that Miguel’s feet come off the ground. Abuelita holds them both._  
**Abuelita**: Where were you? Where were you? We looked all night.  
**Miguel**: I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I have to see Mamá Coco. Right now. Please.  
_Abuelita sees the guitar, and her face goes hard. Then she sees Miguel’s face, and her own face stops being hard._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why a character’s feelings change  
> _Abuelita’s face goes hard, and then stops being hard. What changed her feelings?_  
> - ✅ She saw how much it mattered to Miguel → Yes. Seeing his face made her put her worry about the guitar aside.
> - She forgot about the guitar → Not forgot. Her feeling for Miguel was simply bigger than her feeling about the rule.
> - She got tired → Tiredness doesn’t explain it. The change comes when she sees Miguel’s face.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a character’s feelings change in a scene._


**Choices**

- **Nod at the door: let him go in.**
    - Abuelita follows your look to the door, and to the little room beyond it where Mamá Coco sits.
- **Offer Abuelita your arm.**
    - **Abuelita**: Hm. Visitors. Always carrying something.
    - She takes your arm anyway, and holds on tighter than she means to.

#### `a7-12-home-done`

**Abuelita**: Go. Go to her. Quickly.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): Spanish word endings: abuela and abuelita  
> _Abuela is Spanish for grandmother. Adding -ita turns it into abuelita, which means “dear little grandmother”._  
> _The ending -ita can show smallness or love: casa and casita, the house and the little house._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Spanish ending -ita can show love or smallness, as in abuelita._

_Dante gets through the door first, as usual. Nobody tells him off._  

#### `a7-12-coco`

_Mamá Coco is in her chair in her room, with the curtains half drawn. She is looking at nothing at all._  
**Miguel**: Mamá Coco? Mamá Coco, it’s me. It’s Miguel.  
_She doesn’t answer, and her eyes don’t move. Miguel’s face crumples._  
**Miguel**: Please. You have to remember your papá. If you forget him, he’ll be gone. Gone for good.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): some very old people forget; patience, touch and music can help  
> _Some people find remembering harder as they grow very old. It isn’t their fault, and they are still the same person inside._  
> _Patience, gentle touch and familiar songs can help. Families often find that music reaches memories words cannot._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that forgetting in old age is not anyone’s fault, and that patience, touch and music can help._

_Your Nubbin climbs into Mamá Coco’s lap and settles there. Her hand comes down, very slowly, on its back._  
_Her fingers find the orange ribbon round its neck. They find the crooked letters stitched there, and stop._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): animals’ and people’s senses: touch  
> _Mamá Coco finds the letters with her thumb, in the dark. Which sense is she using?_  
> - ✅ Touch → Yes. Your fingertips are packed with nerve endings, so they can read shapes, like Braille.
> - Hearing → She is using her thumb, so it is touch. Hearing would use her ears.
> - Smell → Smell uses the nose. She is reading with her thumb, which is touch.
> _For grown-ups: Identified touch as the sense used to read stitched letters._

**Mamá Coco**: H… Hé…  
_She runs her thumb over the letters again and again, like a person reading in the dark._  

#### `a7-12-coco-done`

_Miguel looks at Mamá Coco’s moving lips, and then at you, and he picks up the guitar._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): use clues to understand how a character is changing  
> _What clue tells us Mamá Coco is starting to remember?_  
> - ✅ Her lips are moving, as if shaping a word → Yes. Small, quiet signs like moving lips are how stories show a change.
> - She stands up from her chair → She doesn’t stand. The clue is her lips moving.
> - She sings a whole song → That comes later. For now, it is her moving lips.
> _For grown-ups: Used small details to track a character’s change._

**Miguel**: Mamá Coco. Your papá wrote you a song. I’m going to sing it for you.  

#### `a7-12-song`

_Miguel sings the lullaby Héctor wrote for his little girl, with the guitar soft underneath. It is slow and simple, a song for a bedside._  
_One by one, the family come to the doorway. Abuelita opens her mouth to say no, and then she doesn’t._  

> **Lesson** (music, notice): lullabies: slow, soft songs found in every culture  
> _A lullaby is a gentle song for helping a child fall asleep. Families have sung them in every culture and every language._  
> _Lullabies are usually slow and soft, with a rocking rhythm, a bit like a heartbeat or a swing._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that lullabies are slow, gentle songs found in every culture._

_Mamá Coco’s eyes move, and find Miguel. They fill with light, the way a window does when someone comes home._  
**Mamá Coco**: Papá…  
_And then, in a thin, cracked, perfectly true voice, she begins to sing along._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why might music reach a memory that words do not?  
> _Coco couldn’t answer Miguel’s words, yet she joined the song. Why might music reach a memory when words don’t? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - Songs are learned over and over, so they stay deep → A good answer. Repetition and rhythm help songs stick in memory for a lifetime.
> - Songs are tied to strong feelings → A good answer. Feelings help memory, and songs are full of them.
> - She heard her papá’s voice in it → A lovely answer. For her it was the voice of someone she loved.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why music can reach memories that words cannot._

_Abuelita has her hand over her mouth. Miguel’s father is crying without trying to hide it._  
_When the song ends, Mamá Coco opens the drawer of her bedside table, and takes out a folded scrap of paper._  
_It is a corner of an old photograph: a smiling man with a moustache, and a guitar. It fits the torn photo exactly._  
**Mamá Coco**: I kept him. I kept him all this time. Papá used to sing to me.  

#### `a7-12-song-done`

_Miguel fits the corner back into the old photo. It is mended: a family of three, all their faces showing._  
_Imagine folding the photo in half, and in half again. Coco’s corner would fill exactly one of the equal parts._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions  
> _Folded in half twice, a photo has 4 equal parts. Coco kept 1 of them. What fraction is that?_  
> - ✅ 1/4 → Yes. One part out of four equal parts is one quarter, written 1/4.
> - 1/2 → A half would be 1 out of 2 equal parts. This is 1 out of 4, so 1/4.
> - 4/1 → The top number is the parts you have, and the bottom is how many equal parts: 1/4.
> _For grown-ups: Named a unit fraction: one of four equal parts is 1/4._

_You untie the orange ribbon from your Nubbin’s neck, with HÉCTOR stitched on it, and tie it round the mended photo._  
**Mamá Coco**: There. Now he won’t get lost.  

#### `a7-12-complete`

_The atlas turns its own page, gently. It is a year later, and Día de Muertos again._  
_The Riveras’ ofrenda is bigger than ever. Héctor’s photo is on it now, in the middle, the ribbon still tied round the frame._  
_Mamá Coco’s photo is on it too, beside her papá’s. She died in the spring, in her chair, with her family round her._  
_Tonight she is crossing the marigold bridge, holding her papá’s hand and her mamá’s, coming home to visit._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): when someone dies it is very sad, and remembering together helps  
> _When someone dies, their body stops working and cannot start again. It is very sad, and feeling sad is okay._  
> _Families also find comfort in remembering together: a photo, a story, a favourite song._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked plainly about death, that sadness is okay, and that remembering together helps._

_The whole house is full of music, with Miguel playing in the courtyard. Abuelita is dancing, badly, and doesn’t care who sees._  
_Mamá Imelda listens from the ofrenda, and lets him play as long as he likes. Nobody puts down any rule tonight._  
_You think about the ofrenda, and how it is built from small things: a photo, a flower, a name, a song._  
_The page settles under your hand. You are back in the Grove, with a marigold petal still glowing in your pocket._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme of the whole page  
> _What is the biggest idea this page of the atlas is trying to share?_  
> - ✅ People live on while we remember them and tell their stories → Yes. That is the heart of it, and it is also the heart of Día de Muertos.
> - Music is dangerous → The page shows the opposite. Music helped Coco remember.
> - Never talk to strangers → The page is about family and remembering, not strangers.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme: people live on while we remember them._


### Glossary

- **lullaby**: A slow, soft song to help a child fall asleep.

## A8-1. Caesar’s Challenge

- `a08-01-s1`: Step into the small green dot on the map of Gaul. · _Everything else is Roman red. Look by the sea, top left._
- `a08-01-s2`: Go to the village and hear what the Romans want. · _Follow Obelix and the boars. Everyone is in the village square._

#### `a08-01-map`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a map of Gaul, around 50 BC. It is painted Roman red from the mountains to the sea._  
_Not quite all of it. Up by the sea, one small green dot sits untouched, with the red curving carefully round it._  
_Four tiny Roman camps ring the dot like cats round a hedgehog, unsure where to start._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): where Gaul was, and when Caesar’s wars happened  
> _Gaul was the Roman name for a big region, roughly where France is today, plus parts of Belgium and nearby lands._  
> _Julius Caesar’s army fought the peoples of Gaul in the Gallic Wars, from about 58 to 50 BC. “BC” counts years backwards to the year 1._  
> _So on this map, nearly all of Gaul is Roman red. The map’s green dot is the story’s joke._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Gaul was roughly modern France, that Caesar’s Gallic Wars ran about 58 to 50 BC, and read a map key by colour._

_You touch the green dot, and it is warm and smells faintly of roast boar. Then you are standing in a beech wood._  
_Something small and white shoots out of the bracken, stops nose to nose with your Nubbin, and wags so hard it nearly falls over._  
_It is a very small dog with a black-tipped ear. He and your Nubbin look at each other, very serious, for a long moment._  

**Choices**

- **Let them work it out.**
    - They work it out in two seconds: some circling, one sneeze, and then they are best friends.
- **Crouch down and hold out a hand.**
    - The dog licks your hand once, politely, then goes straight back to your Nubbin. You know your place.

#### `a08-01-map-done`

_Two men come crashing through the trees after the dog: one small, with a winged helmet, and one enormous, with a boar under each arm._  
**Obelix**: Dogmatix! Oh. He has found a friend. Look, Asterix, a little round friend.  
_For someone big enough to carry two boars at once, Obelix crouches very slowly, so as not to frighten your Nubbin._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): being gentle with someone smaller  
> _Obelix is huge and strong, but he crouches slowly beside your Nubbin. Why might a big person move gently near someone small?_  
> - ✅ So the small one feels safe → Yes. Being big means taking care. Moving slowly tells a small creature, “I will not hurt you.”
> - Because he is afraid of it → He is careful, not afraid. He does it so he will not frighten the Nubbin, which is kind.
> - It makes no difference → It does to the Nubbin. A sudden, big movement can be scary, even from a friend.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how a bigger, stronger person can help a smaller one feel safe._


#### `a08-01-square`

_The village is round, fenced and loud. A chief stands on a shield held up by two men who are clearly tired of holding it._  
**Caius Pupus**: Salve! That is Latin for hello, and I am Caius Pupus. I bring the words of Julius Caesar.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): Latin: salve, and where English gets its words  
> **Caius Pupus**: The Romans spoke Latin. “Salve” means hello, and there is “vale” for goodbye. You will hear both on this journey.  
> **Caius Pupus**: English is full of Latin words. “Vocabulary” and “audience” both come from Latin.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the Latin greeting “salve” and that English borrows many words from Latin._

**Caius Pupus**: Caesar hears that you Gauls are gods. He does not believe it. He proposes twelve tasks, like the labours of Hercules.  
**Caius Pupus**: Pass them all, and you are gods. Fail one, and you will kindly become Roman, like everybody else.  
**Vitalstatistix**: Twelve tasks! Ha! We will do thirteen, fourteen if there is lunch.  
**Asterix**: Who decides if we pass? Not a Roman. You would fail us for breathing.  
**Caius Pupus**: And not a Gaul. You would pass yourselves for sneezing.  
_Every head slowly turns to the one person who is neither: you, at the back, with a Nubbin and a dog._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness: who should referee, and why  
> _The village wants a referee who is neither Roman nor Gaul. Why does that matter? Is a stranger always fair?_  
> - A referee must not favour either side → That is a good reason. Being on neither side makes it easier to be fair. Whether it is enough is a good thing to keep thinking about.
> - A stranger might still have a bias → A fair answer. Even a stranger can have hidden favourites. The best referees notice their own bias, and say so.
> - Rules matter more than the referee → A fair answer. Clear rules help any referee. But somebody still has to apply them fairly, and that is your job.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what makes a referee fair, and whether being outside the sides is enough._


**Choices**

- **“All right. I’ll referee.”**
    - **Vitalstatistix**: Splendid! A referee from the land of books. Nobody can say fairer than that.
- **“Me? I only came in through a map.”**
    - **Asterix**: Exactly. You do not owe anybody anything. That is what makes you fair.
    - You find you cannot argue with that.

#### `a08-01-square-done`

**Caius Pupus**: Here is your wax tablet. A tablet is a flat board with wax on it, and you scratch letters in the wax with a stick.  
_Down its side, in neat Roman numerals, it counts from I to XII. Every line is blank._  
_The Romans wrote numbers with letters: I is one, V is five and X is ten. You make other numbers by adding them up._  

> **Lesson** (maths, notice): Roman numerals: I, V, X and adding them  
> **Caius Pupus**: Look: II is one and one, so two. III is three. VI is five and one, so six. XII is ten and one and one, so twelve.  
> **Caius Pupus**: You will tick them off one at a time. I to XII, one for every task.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Roman numerals use letters I, V and X, and that the numbers are made by adding them._


#### `a08-01-complete`

_Getafix the druid, white-bearded and unhurried, stirs a cauldron by his hut. He ladles a flask full for Asterix._  
**Getafix**: The potion, for the tasks. Strength for a while, and not one drop for Obelix.  
**Obelix**: I only want a little bit. A taste.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): saying no kindly, with a reason  
> _Getafix says no to Obelix. How could he say no in a way that still shows he cares?_  
> - ✅ Explain why, and say it gently → Yes. A reason, a kind voice and a little humour help a no feel like care.
> - Say no and walk away → That is quick, but it can leave a friend feeling shut out. A short reason helps.
> - Give in, to avoid a fuss → It is tempting, but if a no matters for someone’s sake, kindness means keeping it, gently.
> _For grown-ups: Practised saying no kindly with a reason._

**Getafix**: You fell in when you were a baby. It is permanent. You are the reason I keep a lid on it.  
_Obelix sulks for exactly as long as it takes to remember the boars. Dogmatix and your Nubbin are asleep in a heap by the fire._  
**Caius Pupus**: We leave at dawn for task one. I should warn you, I have a very good eye for cheating.  

### Glossary

- **tablet**: A flat board covered in wax, which people scratched writing into.
- **numeral**: A symbol that stands for a number.

## A8-2. Asbestos

- `a08-02-s1`: Pace out the course and meet the runner. · _Walk from the start stone to the finish post, then talk to Asbestos._
- `a08-02-s2`: Start the race and see who reaches the post. · _Drop your hand to start. Then watch the road, not Asterix._

#### `a08-02-track`

_Task one is a race along a straight dirt road, from a stone to a post far off. You pace it out, and stop counting._  
_At the start, a young man in a short white tunic is stretching. He stretches parts of himself you did not know stretched._  
**Asbestos**: Asbestos, of Greece. I have won at Olympia, where the Games began. Gods and people came to watch us run.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the Olympic Games began in Greece  
> **Asbestos**: The ancient Games were held at Olympia, in Greece. Tradition says the first was in 776 BC. After that they came every four years.  
> **Asbestos**: Athletes ran, wrestled and threw. Today’s Olympic Games were started again in Athens in 1896, and they still come every four years.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Olympic Games began in ancient Greece, at Olympia, every four years, and were revived in 1896._

**Asbestos**: You will not see me after the start. That is not boasting. It is a description.  
**Caius Pupus**: The referee will start the race. Please be impartial. I mean, please be quick.  
_Your Nubbin and Dogmatix crouch at the start stone with their bottoms in the air, very serious._  

**Choices**

- **Let them race too.**
    - **Caius Pupus**: Animals are not in the rules.
    - You point out that animals are not out of the rules either. Pupus writes that down, crossly.
- **Scoop them up out of the way.**
    - You lift your Nubbin. Dogmatix sits down on your foot, as if that settles it.

#### `a08-02-track-done`

_You lift your hand. Asbestos goes still as a statue, and Asterix yawns._  
_The road is one stade long: the length of a Greek running track, nearly two football pitches end to end._  
_The Greeks called the track a “stadion”, and the Romans said “stadium”. That is where our word comes from._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, notice): units of length: the stade and the metre  
> _The stade at Olympia was about 192 metres. Five stades would be 960 metres, nearly a kilometre._  
> _Old units like the stade changed from place to place. Today’s races use metres, so any two tracks can be compared._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a stade was about 192 metres, and compared it with metres and kilometres._


#### `a08-02-race`

_Your hand drops. Asbestos is a white blur, then a cloud of dust, then a dot._  
_Asterix ambles off the line with his hands behind his back, like a man going to look at the weather._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _“Like a man going to look at the weather” compares Asterix’s walk to something. What is it called when you compare with “like” or “as”?_  
> - ✅ A simile → Yes. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”. It paints a picture quickly.
> - A metaphor → Close. A metaphor says one thing is another. A simile says it is like another thing, using “like” or “as”.
> - A rhyme → Rhymes repeat sounds. Here the words compare two things with “like”, which is a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a simile (a comparison using “like” or “as”)._

**Caius Pupus**: Is he trying?  
_Halfway along the road he has one sip from his flask. Then the road is empty where he was._  
_Down at the far end two dots become one, and that dot is Asterix, sitting on the finish post, waving, with an apple._  
_Asbestos reaches the post at a speed nobody has ever reached anything, sees Asterix, and keeps going out of pure surprise._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying to find a distance  
> _Say Asbestos runs 8 metres every second. How far has he run after 5 seconds?_  
> - ✅ 40 metres → Yes. 8 metres a second for 5 seconds is 5 times 8, which is 40 metres.
> - 13 metres → That adds 8 and 5. Each second he runs 8 metres, so it is 5 groups of 8: 5 times 8 is 40 metres.
> - 85 metres → Not quite. Five groups of eight is five times eight, which is 40 metres.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication to find distance: 5 seconds at 8 metres a second._


#### `a08-02-race-done`

_Far away, over the hills, a small white figure is still running. Obelix shades his eyes and watches him go, a little enviously._  
**Obelix**: Is he all right? He looked a bit surprised.  
**Asterix**: He will be fine. He just needs somebody to tell him he ran well, because he did.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): losing well and being kind to someone who lost  
> _Asbestos is the fastest runner in the world, and he has just lost. What could help him feel better?_  
> - Telling him honestly that he ran well → A fair answer. Honest, specific praise helps, and it is true. He did run well.
> - Pretending he won → A kind wish. But he would know it was not true, and honest praise lasts longer.
> - Leaving him alone → A fair answer. Some people want space after losing. A kind word can still help later.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be kind and honest to someone who lost._


#### `a08-02-complete`

_You scratch a mark beside I on the wax tablet. Pupus looks at it, sighs, and initials it._  
**Obelix**: I could have done that, if there had been a boar at the end.  

> **Lesson** (maths, notice): I is one, and the numerals read left to right  
> **Caius Pupus**: I is a single stroke, like one finger held up. It is the smallest Roman numeral.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Notice that the Romans had no symbol for zero. Counting began at I.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Roman numeral I is one, and that Roman numerals had no zero._

**Asterix**: He was very fast. He just was not first.  
**Caius Pupus**: One task. Eleven to go. I have brought a great many spare tablets.  

### Glossary

- **impartial**: Fair to everyone, and not taking anyone’s side.
- **stade**: An ancient Greek measure of length, the length of a running track.

## A8-3. Verses

- `a08-03-s1`: Carry the javelins out to the throwing field. · _There are three javelins on the cart. Carry them one at a time._
- `a08-03-s2`: Watch both throws and measure them. · _Stand by the far marker. Count your steps from the line to where each javelin lands._

#### `a08-03-field`

_Task two is a wide field of short grass with a white line at one end. A tall man in an embroidered coat waits beside it._  
**Verses**: Verses, of Persia, at your service. Forgive me if I do not shake hands. These hands are working today.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): ancient Persia, and throwing as an ancient sport  
> **Verses**: Persia was a great empire, in the lands that today include Iran. It was famous for its long roads, fast messengers and fine gardens.  
> **Verses**: Javelins began as hunting spears. Throwing them for distance became a sport in the ancient Olympics.  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that Persia was a great empire in the region of modern Iran, and that javelin throwing began as hunting and became a sport._

_He has three javelins on a cart, each wrapped in silk. He unwraps them like a man introducing his children._  
**Verses**: This one is Swift. This one is Patient. And this one I have never thrown. I am saving her for an occasion.  
**Asterix**: Is this an occasion?  
**Verses**: It is beginning to feel like one.  

**Choices**

- **Carry them very carefully, like Verses would.**
    - **Verses**: You carry them like friends. Thank you.
- **Ask Obelix to help.**
    - Obelix carries all three in one hand and the cart in the other, and asks where you would like the cart.

#### `a08-03-field-done`

_You lay the javelins on the grass by the line. Your Nubbin sits beside the one called Patient, which seems right._  
_You decide to measure the throws. You could count your paces, but your Nubbin’s paces are very small._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): why we use standard units  
> _Your paces are longer than your Nubbin’s. Why is a measuring rope, marked in metres, better than counting paces?_  
> - ✅ Metres are the same for everyone → Yes. A standard unit means everyone gets the same answer, however long their legs are.
> - Paces are always shorter → Not always. The point is that paces change from person to person, and a metre never does.
> - It makes no difference → It does. If you measure in paces and your Nubbin measures in paces, you will get different numbers for the same throw.
> _For grown-ups: Understood why standard units of length matter: paces vary, metres do not._


#### `a08-03-throws`

_Verses takes Swift, steps up, and throws. It goes up like a bird and comes down at the end of the field, quivering._  
**Caius Pupus**: A record, surely. Referee, measure it.  
_You measure it. It takes a long time, and you start again twice, because Dogmatix keeps bringing you sticks._  
_Asterix takes a sip from his flask and borrows a plain javelin. He throws it underarm, almost lazily._  
_It goes over Verses’ javelin, over the trees and over the hill. The whistle of it fades away._  
**Verses**: Where is it going?  
**Asterix**: I could not tell you. I just threw it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness when a result cannot be measured  
> _Verses says you cannot measure a throw that has not finished. Is it fair to give Asterix the win without a number? What would you do?_  
> - Give him the win, because it clearly went further → A fair answer. When the evidence is clear, a number may not be needed. Pupus might want it in writing, though.
> - Wait until it lands, then measure → A fair answer. Fairness sometimes means being patient and waiting for the facts, even when it takes a week.
> - Say neither wins, and try again → A fair answer. Starting again with equal rules is one way to be sure. It might also be a long afternoon.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness when a result cannot be measured._


**Choices**

- **Start walking after it with your tablet.**
    - **Caius Pupus**: Come back. Come back! We will be here for a week.
    - You come back. You give it the win on what you are calling “visible evidence of leaving”.
- **Call it: the javelin is still going.**
    - **Verses**: A fair ruling. One cannot measure a throw that has not finished.

#### `a08-03-complete`

_You scratch two strokes on the wax tablet and Pupus initials them. Verses wraps Swift in silk again and bows to Asterix._  
**Verses**: A good throw is a good throw, whoever makes it. I am going to find out where yours lands.  

> **Lesson** (maths, notice): II is two, and what the numerals add up to  
> **Caius Pupus**: Two strokes: I and I. The Romans wrote II for two, and III for three. Up to three, you just keep adding strokes.  
> **Caius Pupus**: After that it gets tidier. Four is IV, as you will see.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Roman II and III are made by repeating the stroke I, and that four is written differently._

_He sets off over the hill with the cart, and the javelin he was saving still in its silk._  
**Obelix**: He is nice. Are all the champions going to be nice?  
**Caius Pupus**: No.  

### Glossary

- **javelin**: A light spear that is thrown, often as a sport.
- **embroidered**: Decorated with patterns sewn in thread.

## A8-4. Cilindric

- `a08-04-s1`: Read Cilindric’s rulebook before the bout. · _You are the referee: the rules are your job. Open the book on the bench._
- `a08-04-s2`: Referee the bout. · _Stand by the rope. Asterix has an idea; let it play out._

#### `a08-04-rules`

_Task three is a ring of rope in a meadow. Inside it a short, square man in a white wrap is folding a towel into perfect quarters._  
**Cilindric**: Cilindric. Good morning. Before we begin, the referee will please read the rules.  
_He hands you a book as thick as a loaf, every page ruled into neat columns._  
**Cilindric**: My art is about using your opponent’s strength. But also about doing it correctly. In the right order. With the right bow.  
_Rules one to forty are about bowing. Rule forty-one says what to do if the bow is returned too low._  
**Asterix**: Is there a rule for what happens if the other man does not want to wrestle?  
**Cilindric**: Rule three hundred and twelve. It is very firm.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): what makes a rule a good rule  
> _Cilindric has hundreds of rules, mostly about bowing. Which of these is the best kind of rule?_  
> - ✅ A short rule that keeps people safe and is the same for everyone → Yes. Good rules are clear, fair and have a reason. Rules about safety are the first you want.
> - A rule nobody can remember, but which is very detailed → A rule nobody can remember cannot help anyone. Good rules are simple enough to follow.
> - A rule that only helps the person who wrote it → That is not fair. A good rule should be fair to everyone it covers, not just its author.
> _For grown-ups: Compared good and bad rules: clear, fair and for a reason._


**Choices**

- **Read every rule, properly.**
    - **Cilindric**: Ah. A referee who reads. You have my respect.
    - It takes until lunch. Pupus brings sandwiches, and seems to understand completely.
- **Skim it and nod wisely.**
    - **Cilindric**: Hm. You have skipped the section on nodding.

#### `a08-04-rules-done`

_You close the book. Cilindric bows to it, then to you, then to Asterix, then, after a moment’s thought, to the meadow._  
**Caius Pupus**: Vale, book. That is Latin for goodbye. It comes from a word meaning “be well”.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): everyday Latin: salve, vale, gratias  
> **Caius Pupus**: Three words to keep: salve for hello, vale for goodbye and gratias for thank you.  
> **Caius Pupus**: “Vale” began as “be well”, like our “farewell”. Many words begin as a wish for someone.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the Latin words salve, vale and gratias, and that “vale” meant “be well”._

_Pupus looks pleased with himself. He has been waiting all day for someone to ask about Latin._  

#### `a08-04-bout`

_They face each other and bow. Cilindric moves like water, and suddenly Asterix is upside down and then the right way up._  
**Asterix**: Wonderful. Could you show me that again, slowly? I want to be sure I have the rules right.  
**Cilindric**: Of course. Rule eighty. First the hand, here. Then the foot, here. Then the turn, so.  
**Cilindric**: Rule eighty-one follows rule eighty, with the elbow under, so, and then the knee comes through, so…  
_Cilindric, demonstrating on nobody but himself, turns, tucks, turns again, and ties himself into a tidy, polite knot._  
**Cilindric**: I appear to have won, against myself. Which, under rule three hundred and twelve, means I have lost.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when rules get in your own way  
> _Cilindric was undone by his own rules. Is that his fault? Can there be too many rules?_  
> - Yes. Too many rules can trip you up → A fair answer. Rules should help us, and a rulebook as thick as a loaf is hard to follow even for the person who wrote it.
> - No. He just made a mistake → A fair answer. Even with good rules, people slip. What matters is how kindly he and everyone else handle it.
> - The rules are fine; the knot was bad luck → A fair answer. Sometimes things go wrong without anyone to blame. A kind reaction still helps.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether having too many rules can trip people up._


**Choices**

- **Help untie him.**
    - It takes you, Obelix and both animals. Cilindric thanks each of you by name, including the dog.
- **Look up rule three hundred and twelve to be sure.**
    - **Cilindric**: Correct. A referee who checks. I would wrestle under you again any time.

#### `a08-04-complete`

_You scratch a third stroke on the wax tablet. Cilindric folds his towel again, perfectly._  
**Cilindric**: A clean result. Unusual, but clean. Please keep the book. I have three more at home.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, do): III is three; counting the tablet  
> _(Count the strokes on your tablet: I, II and now III.)_  
> **Caius Pupus**: Three strokes for three tasks. Count what is left: nine more.  
> Check: `edu:count:tablet-marks:3`
> _For grown-ups: Counted three Roman strokes on the tablet and worked out nine remain._

**Obelix**: He was nice too.  
**Caius Pupus**: They are all nice. That is the trouble. Nobody nice ever wins anything for Rome.  

### Glossary

- **demonstrating**: Showing how something is done.

## A8-5. The Isle of Pleasure

- `a08-05-s1`: Row across to the island. · _Take the oars. Do not let Obelix row alone, or you will go in circles._
- `a08-05-s2`: Get everybody back to the boat. · _Find your Nubbin and Dogmatix first. Obelix will take care of Asterix._

#### `a08-05-boat`

_Task four is an island in a blue lake, with soft music coming over the water and a smell of honey cakes._  
**Caius Pupus**: The task is simple. Cross the island and leave it. Nobody ever has. They all stay.  
**Asterix**: Why?  
**Caius Pupus**: Because it is lovely. That is the whole difficulty.  
_Obelix rows with one oar and you row with the other. The boat goes forward, mostly, and sideways the rest of the time._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): why boats float: balanced forces  
> _The boat floats because water pushes up on it. Gravity pulls down, and the water’s push balances it._  
> _A boat is shaped to push aside a lot of water, which gives a big upward push._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a floating boat is held up by water’s upward push, balanced against gravity._

_Dogmatix stands at the front like a figurehead. Your Nubbin leans beside him into a wind it is not really getting._  

#### `a08-05-boat-done`

_The boat bumps onto white sand. There are cushions on the beach, left there on purpose._  
_A ripple laps at the boat. “Aqua” is the Latin for water, Pupus says, and it is why you have an aquarium._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): English words from the Latin “aqua”  
> _“Aqua” is Latin for water. Which of these English words has “aqua” in it?_  
> - ✅ Aquarium → Yes. An aquarium is a place for water animals. “Aquatic” also comes from “aqua”.
> - Aeroplane → “Aero” means air, not water. “Aquarium” is the one that starts with “aqua”.
> - Acorn → An acorn is a nut from an oak tree. “Aquarium” is the word with “aqua”, water.
> _For grown-ups: Identified an English word built from the Latin “aqua”._


#### `a08-05-isle`

_Kind women in pale robes come down to the shore with plates of cakes and jugs of cool fruit juice._  
**The Island’s Hostess**: Welcome, travellers. You look so tired. Sit down. Rest. There is a bath, and a sofa, and nobody will ever ask you to do anything again.  
_Asterix sits down on a cushion. He looks surprised, as if his legs did it without asking him._  
**Asterix**: Only for a moment.  
**The Island’s Hostess**: Of course. Only for ever.  
_Your Nubbin and Dogmatix have found a garden of butterflies and are rolling in the clover with their eyes half shut._  
**Obelix**: Excuse me. Is there any boar?  
**The Island’s Hostess**: We have honey, and figs, and peaches, and little cakes with…  
**Obelix**: So no boar.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): safe and comfortable is not the same as well  
> _Everything on the island is soft and kind. Is a life with nothing to do, and no effort, good for us? Why is it so hard to leave?_  
> - Rest is good, but we also need purpose → A fair answer. Rest is important. Many people feel better when they have something to do and people to do it with.
> - It would be wonderful, so staying is fine → A fair answer. Rest and comfort are lovely, and nothing is wrong with enjoying them. The question is whether you would miss the things you left.
> - It is only hard to leave because we are tired → A fair answer. Tiredness is part of it. So is the feeling that nothing will ever be asked of us again, which is both pleasant and a little sad.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a comfortable life with nothing to do is the same as a good life._


**Choices**

- **Go and fetch the Nubbin and the dog.**
    - You lift them out of the clover, one under each arm. They are warm and floppy and very sleepy, and they let you.
- **Have just one cake first.**
    - It is the best cake you have ever eaten. You notice that you have sat down, and get up again, quickly.

#### `a08-05-isle-done`

_Obelix picks Asterix up off the cushion, tucks him under one arm, and walks back to the boat without stopping._  
**Obelix**: Sorry. Thank you. Lovely island. No boar.  
_It is not that Obelix is not tempted. It is that, for him, nothing on earth compares to a good boar._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character traits and motives  
> _Obelix walked away from the island because he wanted boar. What trait does that show, and is it a strength here?_  
> - ✅ Determination: knowing what you want → Yes. Knowing what he wants keeps him from drifting. It is a strength here, even if it is also a little funny.
> - Greed: he only wants food → Food is what he wants, but the trait here is that he keeps his focus. That saved everyone.
> - Shyness: he was scared of the women → Nothing in the story says he is shy. He is focused on boar, and that is what saves them.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a character’s trait (determination) and its effect in the story._


#### `a08-05-complete`

_Halfway home across the lake, Asterix sits up and shakes his head, like someone coming out of a warm bath._  
**Asterix**: I was going to stay. I really was going to stay.  
**Obelix**: You were not. There was no boar.  
_You scratch a fourth mark on the tablet: IV. Pupus nods._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, notice): IV is four: subtracting by writing a smaller numeral first  
> **Caius Pupus**: Here is the Roman trick. When a smaller numeral comes before a bigger one, you take it away. I before V is five minus one: four.  
> **Caius Pupus**: When it comes after, you add: VI is five plus one, six. Romans sometimes wrote IIII too, but IV is the usual way today.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Roman IV means five minus one, while VI means five plus one, so order matters._

**Caius Pupus**: In all the records, nobody has ever rowed away from that island. And nobody has ever left it in a sulk.  

### Glossary

- **aqua**: The Latin word for water.
- **figurehead**: A carved figure at the front of a ship; here, a dog standing in its place.

## A8-6. Iris

- `a08-06-s1`: Find the hypnotist’s tent. · _Follow the painted eyes on the trees to a tent with a moon on it._
- `a08-06-s2`: Referee the staring contest. · _Sit between them, and look at the sand timer, not at either of them._

#### `a08-06-tent`

_Task five waits at the end of a path lined with painted eyes. They seem to follow you, which is probably the point._  
_The tent is dark inside and smells of incense. A man in a tall headdress sits very still on a cushion._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): how your eyes handle dim light  
> _Inside the dark tent, the black circle in the middle of your eye, the pupil, grows bigger. That lets in more light._  
> _In bright sunshine, the pupil shrinks again. Your eyes adjust all the time, without you thinking about it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the pupil widens in dim light and shrinks in bright light._

**Iris**: I am Iris, from Egypt, where we have been looking at things for a very long time. Look into my eyes.  
_His eyes are enormous and dark, with a faint glow in them, like coals. You find you have already looked._  
**Iris**: Your task is to hold my gaze. Whoever looks away first, loses. And whoever loses will believe whatever I say they are.  
**Caius Pupus**: He is very good. Last week he convinced a centurion he was a teapot.  

**Choices**

- **Try a practice stare yourself.**
    - You last about two seconds. When you come round, you are holding your Nubbin and humming like a beehive.
- **Look at the floor, sensibly.**
    - **Iris**: A wise referee. The floor is safe. Mostly.

#### `a08-06-stare`

_Asterix sits down opposite Iris. You turn the sand timer over, and keep your eyes firmly on the sand._  
**Iris**: You are growing sleepy. You are a small, soft creature. You are… a dormouse.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time with a sand timer  
> _The sand timer takes 3 minutes to run through. If you turn it over twice, how many minutes have gone by?_  
> - ✅ 6 minutes → Yes. 3 minutes twice is 3 times 2, which is 6 minutes.
> - 5 minutes → That adds 3 and 2. Each turn is 3 minutes, and there are 2 turns, so 3 times 2 is 6.
> - 32 minutes → That writes the numbers side by side. It is 2 lots of 3 minutes, which is 6 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Found a time interval by multiplying: two 3-minute turns make 6 minutes._

**Asterix**: No, I am not.  
_Iris leans closer, and the glow in his eyes brightens. The glow in Asterix’s, after a sip from his flask, brightens further._  
**Asterix**: Actually, I think you are the one who is sleepy.  
_Something in Iris’s face goes uncertain. His nose twitches, his shoulders go round, and he snuffles at the cushion._  
_He is quite sure, now, that he is a wild boar, and trots out of the tent on all fours, grunting happily._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty, tricks and who gets to say who you are  
> _Iris tries to convince people they are something they are not. Is that a harmless trick, or something that could hurt? When is it okay?_  
> - It is harmless if everybody agrees to play → A fair answer. Agreement matters. A trick everyone has chosen to play is different from one played on someone who did not choose.
> - It is not okay to make people believe false things → A fair answer. Being tricked can feel awful, because it takes away our choice about what to believe.
> - It depends how much it matters to them → A fair answer. A teapot joke is not the same as a trick that makes someone give up something they care about.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when a trick is harmless and when it takes away someone’s choice._

**Asterix**: Obelix, no. He is a person. He will be a person again by supper.  

#### `a08-06-stare-done`

_The last grain of sand falls. Dogmatix is barking at the tent door, and your Nubbin has hidden behind your boots._  
_When Iris’s eyes were at their brightest, they glowed like embers in a banked-up fire. Now they are just a man’s eyes, soft and a little puzzled._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes and metaphors  
> _Iris’s eyes “glowed like embers”. That uses “like”, so it is a simile. Which of these is a metaphor instead?_  
> - ✅ “His eyes were two coals” → Yes. A metaphor says one thing is another, without “like” or “as”.
> - “His eyes glowed like coals” → That uses “like”, so it is a simile. A metaphor says his eyes were coals.
> - “His eyes were big” → That is a plain description, not a comparison. A metaphor compares two different things.
> _For grown-ups: Told a metaphor from a simile._


#### `a08-06-complete`

_You scratch a fifth mark on the tablet: a V. Pupus looks at it, sighs, and initials it._  
_Outside, Iris is rooting cheerfully among the acorns. Pupus watches him with deep sympathy._  

> **Lesson** (maths, notice): V is five  
> **Caius Pupus**: V is the symbol for five. Some people think it looks like an open hand, with the thumb on one side and four fingers on the other.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Whether or not that is true, the V is the main milestone. Everything up to ten is built from I, V and X.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that V stands for five, and that Roman numerals up to ten use I, V and X._

**Caius Pupus**: It wears off. Usually. I will make sure somebody brings him a cushion.  
**Obelix**: He looks happy.  
**Asterix**: He does, a bit. Come on. Seven to go.  

### Glossary

- **headdress**: A decorated covering or hat worn on the head.
- **incense**: A material burned for its sweet smell.

## A8-7. Mannekenpix

- `a08-07-s1`: Help carry the dishes from the kitchen. · _Take them from the hatch to the long table. The big ones need two hands._
- `a08-07-s2`: Keep the plates coming and watch Obelix finish. · _Stand by the table with your tablet. Count the courses._

#### `a08-07-kitchen`

_Task six is a meal. On a long table in a hall with low beams, a single plate is set, and a single, very large chair._  
_In the kitchen behind it, a round, red-faced man in an apron is stirring four pots and tasting a fifth._  
**Mannekenpix**: Mannekenpix, chef, from the north. The Belgae, if you like. Nobody leaves my table hungry.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the Belgae, and where Belgium gets its name  
> **Mannekenpix**: The Belgae were the peoples of the north of Gaul. Caesar himself wrote that they were the bravest of all the Gauls.  
> **Mannekenpix**: The country of Belgium takes its name from them. Names can stay on a map for two thousand years.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Belgae lived in northern Gaul and gave their name to modern Belgium._

**Mannekenpix**: The task is to finish. Everything. To the last crumb. Whoever has tried has had to be carried home on a door.  
**Obelix**: Me? Oh, all right then. If I must.  

**Choices**

- **Ask what’s in the soup.**
    - **Mannekenpix**: Everything I had, and a bit of love. The love is the secret. The everything helps.
- **Just carry, and carry quickly.**
    - **Mannekenpix**: Good! Hot food goes out hot. You have the makings of a waiter.

#### `a08-07-kitchen-done`

_Soup, then fish, then three kinds of pie. Then a dish of crisp fried potatoes that Mannekenpix places down as if it were a crown._  
**Mannekenpix**: Each pie is cut into four equal slices. Count them as they go.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions  
> _A pie is cut into 4 equal slices, and Obelix eats one. What fraction of the pie has he eaten?_  
> - ✅ One quarter, written 1/4 → Yes. One slice out of four equal slices is one quarter, 1/4.
> - One half, written 1/2 → One half would be two slices out of four. One slice out of four is one quarter.
> - One third, written 1/3 → A third needs three equal slices. This pie has four, so one slice is one quarter, 1/4.
> _For grown-ups: Named one slice of four equal slices as the unit fraction 1/4._

_The first pie loses one slice at once._  

#### `a08-07-feast`

_Obelix eats steadily, happily, and without hurry. Each dish goes in and the plate comes back so clean it shines._  
_You count courses on your tablet. You run out of room at twenty and start a second tablet._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): food gives energy; listen to your body  
> _Food is fuel. Our bodies turn it into energy for moving, thinking and growing, and a mix of foods gives us what we need._  
> _Your body tells you when you are hungry and when you are full. Listening to those signals is a good habit. Obelix is… a special case._
