> _For grown-ups: Learned that food gives energy, and that listening to hunger and fullness is a healthy habit._

**Mannekenpix**: He has eaten the pies. He has eaten the stew. He has eaten the second stew, which was for me.  
_At last the hatch is empty. Mannekenpix leans in the doorway, floury and astonished, with nothing left to bring._  
**Obelix**: That was a lovely starter. When is the main course?  
**Mannekenpix**: Thirty years I have been waiting for someone to ask me that.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): generosity, and when too much is not kind  
> _A big feast is a generous gift. But is it kind to challenge a guest to eat everything on the table? Where is the line between generous and too much?_  
> - Generous means offering, not forcing → A fair answer. A host who offers and lets the guest decide is generous. A challenge that nobody can win can be a trap.
> - It is fine, because Obelix chose it → A fair answer. Choosing matters a lot. Obelix is happy, and nobody is being made to do anything.
> - The chef is just proud of his cooking → A fair answer. Pride in cooking is a lovely thing, and it can be shown with a smaller table too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between generosity and pressure._


**Choices**

- **Save the scraps for the Nubbin and Dogmatix.**
    - There are no scraps. Obelix gives them each a crust from his own pocket, which seems to be where he keeps them.
- **Applaud the chef.**
    - You clap, and Pupus claps, and Obelix claps with his mouth full. Mannekenpix takes a deep, floury bow.

#### `a08-07-complete`

**Mannekenpix**: Here. For the road. You will be hungry again by the river.  
_He gives Obelix a wrapped parcel of fried potatoes. Obelix holds it like a newborn._  
_You scratch a sixth mark: VI. Pupus initials it, and looks as though he would like to sit down._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, notice): VI is six, and halfway through twelve  
> **Caius Pupus**: V and then I: five and one, so VI is six. Six out of twelve is exactly half.  
> **Caius Pupus**: You can write that as 6/12, which is the same as 1/2. Half the tasks are done.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that VI is five plus one, and that six out of twelve is one half._

**Caius Pupus**: Halfway. Six tasks. Caesar is going to be very quiet when I tell him.  

### Glossary

- **course**: One dish served at a meal, such as soup or pie.
- **astonished**: Very, very surprised.

## A8-8. The Cave of the Beast

- `a08-08-s1`: Go into the cave with a lantern. · _Light the lantern at the entrance. Keep the wall on your left._
- `a08-08-s2`: Find out what lives in the cave. · _Do not lift the lantern too high. Sit down, and let it come to you._

#### `a08-08-mouth`

_Task seven is a black hole in a hillside, with old bones round the entrance. Pupus stands well back from the bones._  
**Caius Pupus**: The task is to go in, and come out. Something lives in there. Nobody who has gone in has said what.  
_From inside, very deep down, comes a long, rumbling sound, like a cart going over a wooden bridge._  
_Dogmatix’s ears go flat, and your Nubbin presses against your leg. You light the lantern._  
_The first ten steps are only a cave: drips, cold air, and your own breath. Water falls from the roof, drop by drop._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, notice): how caves grow stalactites over a very long time  
> _Each drip that falls from the roof carries a tiny trace of mineral. Over thousands of years, those traces build into hanging stone spikes called stalactites._  
> _Many stalactites grow only about a centimetre in a hundred years. Nature can change a place, but sometimes very slowly._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dripping mineral water slowly builds stalactites, and that some natural change is very slow._


**Choices**

- **Go first, with the lantern.**
    - **Asterix**: Brave referee. We are right behind you.
    - **Obelix**: A little behind.
- **Ask everyone to go in side by side.**
    - It is a tight fit, and Obelix goes sideways. It is much better, side by side.

#### `a08-08-mouth-done`

_The passage opens into a chamber so big the lantern light does not reach the roof. The rumble is very near now._  
_Your heart is going fast, and your hands feel cold. Your Nubbin is holding on to your sleeve._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): noticing fear in your body, and what helps  
> _You are scared, and your heart is pounding. What could help you feel steadier?_  
> - ✅ Slow breaths, and staying close to friends → Yes. Slow breaths calm a pounding heart, and friends close by make a scary place feel smaller.
> - Running back out alone → That is a natural wish. But running alone often makes fear grow, and you would leave your friends behind.
> - Pretending you feel nothing → Pretending does not make fear go away. Saying “I am scared” and breathing slowly works better.
> _For grown-ups: Named the signs of fear in the body and chose calming strategies._


#### `a08-08-beast`

_At the edge of the light there is a shape, as big as a haystack, curled tight. The rumble is coming from it._  
_It is not growling but shaking. Whatever it is, it is very large, and very frightened of the light._  
**Asterix**: It is scared of us.  
**Obelix**: Everybody is scared of me. I do not know why.  
_You turn the lantern down low, and sit on the cold floor, and say nothing._  
_Dogmatix sits beside you, then your Nubbin. Then, very carefully, so the floor will not shake, Obelix._  
_After a long time, something huge and soft, with very small eyes, puts its nose out and sniffs your Nubbin._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): animals in the dark use other senses  
> _An animal that lives in a dark cave cannot rely on its eyes. Its nose and its ears do much more of the work._  
> _That is why the Beast sniffs first. A smell tells it who you are, long before it could see you._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals in dark places often rely more on smell and hearing._

_Your Nubbin sniffs back. The rumble stops._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why gentleness works, and why the visitors keep it secret  
> _The Beast calmed down when you sat quietly. Why does gentleness work on a scared animal? And why would nobody tell the secret?_  
> - Scared creatures need to feel safe first → A fair answer. Safety has to come before trust. Sitting still and small showed you meant no harm.
> - They kept the secret to protect the Beast → A fair answer. If everyone knew, people might come to stare or to hurt it. Some kindness is quiet.
> - It is just more fun to leave it a mystery → A fair answer. A shared secret can feel like a gift. And in this story, it is also a way of protecting something.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why gentleness helps a frightened creature, and about keeping a kind secret._


**Choices**

- **Leave the lantern, turned down low.**
    - You set it on a rock, at its gentlest. The great shape settles beside it like a cat by a stove.
- **Back out quietly, in the dark.**
    - You go out the way you came, slowly. Behind you, the rumble starts again, but slower now, like snoring.

#### `a08-08-complete`

_Outside, the daylight is very loud. Pupus is still standing well back from the bones._  
**Caius Pupus**: Well? What was it?  
**Asterix**: Nothing you need to worry about.  
_You scratch a seventh mark: VII. It is V with two strokes after it, five and two more._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, notice): VII is seven; reading numerals as a sum  
> **Caius Pupus**: Read VII left to right: V is five, then I and I add two. Five and two make seven.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Seven is more than half of twelve. Five tasks to go.  
> _For grown-ups: Read the Roman numeral VII as 5 + 1 + 1 = 7, and found that 5 tasks remain._

**Caius Pupus**: You are all the same, you lot. You go in, and you come out kind.  

### Glossary

- **entrance**: The way in to a place.
- **chamber**: A large room, such as one inside a cave.

## A8-9. The Place That Sends You Mad

- `a08-09-s1`: Go into the Place That Sends You Mad and ask for Permit A38. · _Start with the porter at the front door. Be polite._
- `a08-09-s2`: Try to get the permit the proper way. · _Go from counter to counter. Keep track of where each one sends you._
- `a08-09-s3`: Design your own impossible form for the clerks. · _Write it on a fresh page of your tablet. The sillier it is, the better._
- `a08-09-s4`: Hand in your form while Asterix asks for Permit A39. · _Give the form to the clerk at counter one, then stand back._

#### `a08-09-door`

_Task eight is a building: tall, white and humming, with more windows than there are days in the year. It is a famous bureaucracy._  
**Caius Pupus**: Inside, you must obtain Permit A38. That is all. Many great warriors have gone in for it.  
**Asterix**: And?  
**Caius Pupus**: Some of them still work there.  
_The hall is full of counters, and stairs, and people holding papers and looking at the ceiling with a terrible calm._  
**The Porter**: Good morning. Do you have an appointment? You need counter one, which will send you to counter two.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): what a bureaucracy is  
> **Caius Pupus**: This is a bureaucracy: an organisation run by officials, with lots of rules, forms and offices. The word comes from “bureau”, meaning a writing desk.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Rome needed officials and records to collect taxes and count its people. Rules and forms can be useful. Trouble starts when they stop helping people.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a bureaucracy is an organisation of officials and forms, useful when it serves people._


#### `a08-09-door-done`

_Dogmatix lies down by the porter’s desk with your Nubbin, as if they have both decided to wait this one out._  
_You have been waiting for a long time, and you are beginning to feel cross._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): handling frustration while waiting  
> _You have waited ages and you are getting cross. What would help you stay calm?_  
> - ✅ Breathe, count, or do a quiet activity → Yes. Slow breathing and a small, quiet activity give your body time to settle.
> - Shout at the porter → It might feel good for a moment, but the porter did not make the rules, and shouting rarely gets help.
> - Give up and go home → Sometimes walking away is wise. Here, you have friends and a plan, so a few calm breaths first is better.
> _For grown-ups: Chose a calming way to handle frustration while waiting._


#### `a08-09-counters`

**A Clerk**: Counter one. Permit A38? Not here. You need the blue form, from counter two.  
_Counter two is on the third floor. The clerk is eating lunch, though it is ten in the morning._  
**A Clerk**: The blue form? You need the pink form first, to prove you are allowed to ask for the blue form. Counter three.  
_Counter three sends you back to counter one. You write it all down: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3._  
_A man in a dusty toga drifts past, holding a scroll. He has a long white beard and looks about your age._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a repeating pattern, using its rule  
> _The counters go 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 without end. If you start at counter 1 and take 10 steps, which counter are you at?_  
> - ✅ Counter 2 → Yes. Every 3 steps you return to counter 1, so 9 steps ends at counter 1, and the tenth step goes to counter 2.
> - Counter 1 → Nine steps ends at counter 1, because 9 is a multiple of 3. Step ten goes on to counter 2.
> - Counter 3 → Count the cycle: after 9 steps you are at counter 1, so the tenth step reaches counter 2.
> _For grown-ups: Used the rule of a repeating pattern, a cycle of 3, to find the tenth step._

_You look at your tablet. The arrows on it make a perfect circle._  

**Choices**

- **Join the longest queue, just to see.**
    - You get to the front just as the clerk puts up a sign: “Closed for reorganisation. Please queue at the back.”
- **Draw a map of the counters.**
    - **Asterix**: Show me that.
    - Asterix looks at your circle of arrows for a long while. Then he smiles, slowly.

#### `a08-09-counters-done`

**Asterix**: They have built a machine for saying no.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphor  
> _Asterix calls the building “a machine for saying no”. It is not really a machine. What does the metaphor mean?_  
> - ✅ It says no again and again, without thinking → Yes. A machine repeats the same action without caring. The metaphor shows that the clerks never think about what you need.
> - It is made of metal and wheels → It is not literally made of metal. A metaphor says one thing is another to make a point about it.
> - It is very noisy → The building hums, but this metaphor is about how it answers: always the same, always no.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor (the building as a machine for saying no)._

**Asterix**: So let us ask it for something it cannot say no to, because it does not exist.  

#### `a08-09-form`

**Asterix**: Here is the plan. I ask for Permit A39, which nobody has ever heard of.  
**Asterix**: And while they look, the referee hands in a new form, so strange they have to pass it round.  
_You find a fresh page of your tablet. Obelix leans over your shoulder, breathing heavily and helpfully._  
**Obelix**: Make it a good one. Make it the silliest one ever.  
**Caius Pupus**: The silliest form only wins if it looks completely serious.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): rules that help people, and rules that only help themselves  
> _This building has rules that seem only to protect themselves. How do you tell a rule that helps from one that does not? Which would you keep?_  
> - Keep rules that protect people and are clear → A fair answer. A rule that keeps people safe and treats them equally has a good reason behind it.
> - Keep rules only if they can be explained → A fair answer. If nobody can say why a rule exists, that is a sign to look at it again.
> - Keep few rules, and check them often → A fair answer. Every rule costs people a little time and effort. It helps to look at them often, and ask whether they still serve a purpose.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to tell helpful rules from rules that only serve themselves._


**Choices**

- **Form 0: Application to Find Out Whether You Need This Form.**
    - It has one box, which says, in small letters: “Please attach a completed copy of this form.”
    - **Caius Pupus**: That is… that is beautiful. That could go round this building until the sun burns out.
- **The Pink-and-Blue Form: Proof That You Are Not a Boar, to be signed by a boar.**
    - Obelix signs it on the boar’s behalf, with a hoof print he makes with his knuckle. It looks extremely official.
    - **Obelix**: Somebody will have to find a boar who can write.
- **A short form: your name, what you need, and a signature.**
    - It fits on one page, and it is clear. A child could fill it in in a minute.
    - **Caius Pupus**: They will never accept this. Nobody in here has ever seen anything so sensible.

#### `a08-09-form-done`

_Pupus, sighing, finds a sheet of papyrus in his toga. You copy the form out fair, and Asterix straightens his helmet._  
_“Fair copy” means a neat, final copy, with no mistakes. It has nothing to do with being fair, or with a fair full of rides._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words with more than one meaning: fair  
> _“Fair” can mean just and equal, neat and clean, or a funfair. In “fair copy”, which meaning is it?_  
> - ✅ Neat and clean → Yes. A fair copy is a neat, final version, written out carefully.
> - Just and equal → That is one meaning of fair, but here it means neat. The context, “copy out”, is the clue.
> - A funfair → That is another meaning, but a funfair does not copy anything out. “Fair copy” is a neat copy.
> _For grown-ups: Used context to pick the right meaning of a multiple-meaning word._


#### `a08-09-a39`

**Asterix**: Good morning. I would like Permit A39, please. As set out in the new circular.  
**A Clerk**: A39? There is no A39. There is A38.  
**Asterix**: Not since the new circular. Have you not had it? Everybody else has.  
_The clerk goes pale and turns to the clerk behind him, who turns to the clerk behind her. A whisper runs up the stairs._  
_You slide your form across the counter. The clerk stamps it out of habit, and passes it on._  
_Within a minute, every clerk in the building is running, and papers are flying._  
_A bell rings at the top of the building. A door opens on the highest landing, and a man in a purple-edged toga looks down._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): honesty, and tricking an unfair system  
> _Asterix invents Permit A39 to get past a building that seems unfair. Is it okay to trick a system that is not fair? Where would you draw the line?_  
> - Yes, if nobody is hurt and the system is unfair → A fair answer. Many people feel that a harmless trick on an unfair system is different from lying to a friend. You still might think about who else it affects.
> - No, honesty matters whatever the system is → A fair answer. Some people keep to honesty always, because trust is hard to repair once it is broken.
> - It depends on the cost, and who pays it → A fair answer. If the clerks only lose an afternoon, that is different from if someone loses their home. The cost matters.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about honesty and fairness when a system seems unfair._


#### `a08-09-a39-done`

**The Prefect**: Who is responsible for this? What do you want? Whatever it is, take it, and go, and let us have our building back.  
**Asterix**: Permit A38, please.  
_Asterix says “please”, even to a furious prefect on a stair._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): staying polite when someone else is angry  
> _The prefect is angry, and Asterix stays polite. Why might that be a good idea?_  
> - ✅ Politeness keeps things calm, so people listen → Yes. A calm, polite voice makes it easier for everyone to think. It does not mean giving in.
> - It means he is afraid → Not at all. Staying polite when someone else is angry usually takes strength.
> - It is just a trick → It might work as one. But the real reason to be polite is that it helps everyone stay calm and be heard.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why staying polite helps when someone else is angry._


#### `a08-09-complete`

_The prefect stamps a small grey square of papyrus without reading it, and lets it flutter down the stairwell to you._  
_It says PERMIT A38 in very large letters. In Roman numerals, it would be XXXVIII: thirty and eight._  
**Caius Pupus**: In the whole history of the building, nobody has ever got one. I did not think it was real.  
_You scratch an eighth mark on the tablet: VIII, which is V and III, five and three._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, notice): VIII is eight; building bigger numerals like XXXVIII  
> **Caius Pupus**: VIII is V and III: five and three make eight. The usual rule is never more than three of a symbol in a row, so next comes IX.  
> **Caius Pupus**: For XXXVIII, add up the parts: X and X and X is thirty, then VIII is eight. Thirty and eight make thirty-eight.  
> _For grown-ups: Read VIII as 5 + 3 = 8 and XXXVIII as 30 + 8 = 38, and learned the three-in-a-row rule._

**Obelix**: That was the best one. Can we do that one again?  
**Asterix**: Never, Obelix. Never, ever again.  

### Glossary

- **bureaucracy**: A system run by officials, with many rules, forms and offices.
- **circular**: An official notice sent round to many people.

## A8-10. The Crocodile Ravine

- `a08-10-s1`: Walk to the edge of the ravine and look for the rope. · _Stand at the post on this side. Look carefully across to the other post._
- `a08-10-s2`: Find another way across. · _Dogmatix will not let Obelix pull up a living tree. Look along the edge for one that has already fallen._

#### `a08-10-edge`

_Task nine is a deep, narrow ravine with a river at the bottom. In the river there are a number of crocodiles, all looking up._  
_There is a post on this side, and a post on the far side. Between them, there is nothing at all._  
**Caius Pupus**: The task is to cross on the magic rope. It is invisible. Only the worthy can see it.  
**Asterix**: Can you see it?  
**Caius Pupus**: I am an observer. I am not required to see anything.  
_You throw a pebble out from the post. It falls straight down, past where a rope would be, and a crocodile catches it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity pulls things down  
> _The pebble fell straight down, and no rope held it up. What force pulled it down?_  
> - ✅ Gravity → Yes. Gravity pulls everything toward the ground. Without a rope, or anything else holding it up, the pebble falls.
> - The wind → Wind can push light things sideways, but the pebble fell straight down. That is gravity.
> - Magic → It is a good story, but the real reason is gravity, which pulls all objects toward the Earth.
> _For grown-ups: Identified gravity as the force pulling the pebble down._


**Choices**

- **“There’s no rope.”**
    - **Caius Pupus**: There is a rope. It is simply very, very good at being invisible.
    - **Asterix**: So is a hole.
- **“Mr Pupus, would you show us how, first?”**
    - **Caius Pupus**: I… The observer must not interfere.
    - Pupus takes three firm steps away from the edge, to observe better.

#### `a08-10-log`

**Obelix**: I will make a bridge. I will pull up a tree.  
_He puts his arms round the nearest oak. Dogmatix gives a howl of real grief, and Obelix lets go at once._  
**Obelix**: Sorry, Dogmatix. I forgot. Not that one.  
_Your Nubbin sits beside Dogmatix, leaning on him, until his ears come back up._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): doing what is easy versus what a friend cares about  
> _Obelix forgot Dogmatix cares about trees. When something is easy for you but upsets a friend, how do you decide what to do?_  
> - Stop and ask what matters to the friend → A fair answer. Asking first shows respect, and Obelix does stop at once, which was a good start.
> - Do the easy thing, then say sorry → A fair answer. Sorry matters. But asking first might spare the hurt, and the sorry.
> - Look for a way that works for both → A fair answer. That is what you did, with the fallen pine. Sometimes there is a solution that nobody has to give up anything for.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about balancing what is easy with what a friend cares about._

_You walk along the edge, looking. A little way off, a huge old pine lies dead on its side, long since fallen._  
**You**: This one. It fell on its own.  
_Obelix gives it one punch at the root end. It slides, swings, and drops with a crash across the ravine: a perfect bridge._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): comparing solutions to a problem  
> _Three ways to cross: an invisible rope, pulling up a living tree, or using a fallen tree. Which is best, and why?_  
> - ✅ The fallen tree: it is real, strong and harms nothing → Yes. A good solution works, is safe, and does not cost something else. The fallen tree wins on all three.
> - The invisible rope, because it is free → It is free, but it does not exist, so nobody can cross on it. A solution has to actually work.
> - Pulling up a living tree, because it is fastest → It is quick, but it harms a living tree, and it upsets Dogmatix. A good solution looks at the cost too.
> _For grown-ups: Compared three solutions and chose the one that works and does least harm._

_The crocodiles, below, look at each other with what seems to be disappointment._  

**Choices**

- **Cross first, carrying the Nubbin.**
    - The trunk is wide as a road. Dogmatix trots across beside you with his tail up, the tree business forgiven.
- **Offer Pupus your hand.**
    - **Caius Pupus**: I do not need… thank you.
    - He takes it, all the way across, and does not let go until his sandals are on grass.

#### `a08-10-complete`

**Caius Pupus**: That is not the magic rope. Technically, you have not crossed on the magic rope.  
**Asterix**: Technically, there is not one.  
_Pupus opens his mouth, closes it, and looks at the empty air between the posts for a long moment._  
**Caius Pupus**: Fine. Fine. Write it down.  
_You scratch a ninth mark: IX, which is X, ten, with an I in front. One less than ten is nine._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, notice): IX is nine: one before ten  
> **Caius Pupus**: Here is the subtraction trick again. I before X means ten minus one, so nine. It is the same idea as IV, which is five minus one.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Only I, X and C are ever put before a bigger numeral to subtract. So you will never see VX for five. It is just V.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that IX is 10 − 1 = 9, and that only some numerals can be subtracted._


### Glossary

- **ravine**: A deep, narrow valley with steep sides.
- **observer**: Someone who watches without joining in.

## A8-11. The Old Man of the Mountain

- `a08-11-s1`: Climb to the top of the mountain. · _Take the goat path. It is longer, but the goats know what they are doing._
- `a08-11-s2`: Answer the Old Man’s riddle. · _Listen to every clue. Then look around the cave._

#### `a08-11-climb`

_Task ten is a mountain with its top in the clouds. A narrow path winds up it in loops, and so do some goats._  
**Caius Pupus**: At the top lives the Old Man of the Mountain, who is very wise. He will ask you a riddle. You must answer it.  
**Obelix**: What if we do not know?  
**Caius Pupus**: Then you stay up there until you do. Some people have been up there since they were young.  
_The path is steep. Obelix carries Dogmatix, and Pupus, and after a while, the goats._  
_Near the top, the air is thin and cold, and there is a smell of something faintly perfumed, like a fancy bathhouse._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4.MD.A.2, notice): why it is colder high up a mountain, and why paths zigzag  
> _Air gets thinner and cooler the higher you go. As a rough guide, it is about 6 degrees Celsius colder for every 1,000 metres you climb._  
> _So if the valley is 20 °C (68 °F), a spot 1,000 metres higher is about 14 °C (57 °F). A zigzag path makes a steep slope gentler._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that it gets colder with height (about 6 °C per 1,000 m), and that zigzag paths make steep slopes gentler._


**Choices**

- **Stop and look at the view.**
    - All Gaul is spread out under the clouds, green and brown and silver with rivers. Somewhere down there is the village.
- **Keep going: no stopping on mountains.**
    - **Asterix**: Good thinking. If I stop, I will never start again.

#### `a08-11-climb-done`

_At the summit, by a cave, an ancient man with a beard down to his knees sits cross-legged on a rock, eyes closed._  
_Your legs are wobbly after the climb, and your Nubbin is panting. Obelix offers it a ride on his shoulder._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): knowing when to ask for help  
> _You are very tired, and you still have to answer the riddle. What is a good thing to do?_  
> - ✅ Rest a moment, and ask a friend to help carry things → Yes. Resting and asking for help are signs of good judgement, not weakness.
> - Pretend you are fine, so nobody worries → That is a common feeling. But being honest about being tired lets friends help, and lets you think more clearly.
> - Give up and go back down → You have come most of the way. A rest and a bit of help will get you there.
> _For grown-ups: Chose to rest and ask for help when tired._


#### `a08-11-riddle`

**The Old Man of the Mountain**: Travellers. You have climbed far. Hear now the great riddle, and answer, or remain.  
**The Old Man of the Mountain**: What is white as the snows, yet melts in your hands? What is soft as a lamb, and smells of the meadows?  
**The Old Man of the Mountain**: What leaves you cleaner than the river, and costs only two copper coins, or three for five?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): comparing prices to find the better deal  
> _One soap costs 2 coins, or 3 cost 5 coins. How many coins do you save by buying 3 for 5?_  
> - ✅ 1 coin → Yes. Three single soaps cost 3 times 2, which is 6 coins. Three for five costs 5, so you save 1 coin.
> - 2 coins → Three single soaps cost 6 coins, and the deal costs 5. The difference is 6 minus 5, which is 1 coin.
> - No coins → Check the sums. Three at 2 coins each is 6 coins. The deal is 5 coins, so you do save one.
> _For grown-ups: Compared unit price and bundle price: 3 × 2 = 6, against 5, saves 1._

_Behind the Old Man, in his cave, are stacks of small white cakes, wrapped in leaves, each stamped with his face._  
**Asterix**: Is it… soap?  
**The Old Man of the Mountain**: It is the Old Man of the Mountain’s Own Mountain Soap! Made with goat’s milk! Gentle on the beard!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): adverts and persuasion  
> _The “riddle” turned out to be an advert. Is an advert that pretends to be a riddle honest? How could you tell what an advert wants?_  
> - It is clever, but not fully honest → A fair answer. Hiding what something is for can feel like a trick. Good adverts say plainly what they are.
> - It is fine, as long as the soap is good → A fair answer. If the soap is real and the price is fair, nobody is cheated. It is still worth noticing when someone is selling to you.
> - Check who gains if you believe it → A fair answer. Asking who benefits is one of the best questions to ask about any advert.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how adverts persuade, and how to spot what they want._


**Choices**

- **Buy three for five.**
    - **The Old Man of the Mountain**: A wise traveller! I shall throw in a fourth, because you have honest eyes.
- **“That wasn’t a riddle. That was an advert.”**
    - **The Old Man of the Mountain**: All the best riddles are, in the end. Have a free sample.

#### `a08-11-complete`

_The way down is quicker. You smell of goat’s milk and meadow flowers, and so, to his great dismay, does Obelix._  
**Obelix**: I smell like a lamb. Asterix, I smell like a lamb.  
**Asterix**: You smell lovely.  
_You scratch a tenth mark: a single X, two strokes crossed, the Roman ten._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, notice): X is ten, and where the symbol may come from  
> **Caius Pupus**: X is ten. Nobody is sure where it came from. One idea is tally sticks, where every tenth notch was marked with a cross.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Another idea is two Vs joined point to point. V is five, and five and five make ten. A neat sum, if it is true.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that X is ten, and two ideas about its origin, one of them two Vs (5 + 5)._

**Caius Pupus**: Two more. Only two. I have stopped knowing whether I want you to win.  

### Glossary

- **summit**: The very top of a mountain.
- **copper**: A reddish metal, used long ago for cheap coins.

## A8-12. The Haunted Plain

- `a08-12-s1`: Wait on the plain for midnight. · _Set up camp by the standing stone. Stay awake until the moon is overhead._
- `a08-12-s2`: Complain to the ghosts until they leave. · _Talk to the centurion at the front. Be specific. Ghosts hate specifics._

#### `a08-12-camp`

_Task eleven is a wide, flat plain under a big moon, with one standing stone and a lot of mist._  
**Caius Pupus**: Spend one night on the Haunted Plain. At midnight the ghosts come. Nobody has ever stayed till morning.  
_You make a small fire by the stone. Obelix unwraps the last of Mannekenpix’s fried potatoes and shares them, which is love._  
_Dogmatix and your Nubbin curl up in the crook of Obelix’s arm. Asterix sharpens a stick for no reason._  
_The moon climbs and the mist thickens. Very far off, something clanks, like armour being carried by someone who is not there._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what mist is, and why it forms at night  
> _Mist is tiny drops of water floating in the air. When damp air cools at night, its invisible vapour turns into tiny drops._  
> _That change is called condensation. It is the same reason a cold glass of water gets wet on the outside on a warm day._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mist is tiny water drops formed when damp air cools (condensation)._


**Choices**

- **Tell a story to pass the time.**
    - You tell them about the Grove, and the hill, and the pond. Obelix asks if there are boar, and you say no, gently.
- **Keep watch in silence.**
    - You watch the mist. Pupus watches it too, sitting very close to you, as if by accident.

#### `a08-12-camp-done`

_The mist parts. Out of it, glowing faintly green, march two lines of ghostly legionaries, chains clanking, moaning on the beat._  
**Caius Pupus**: A whole legion, with a centurion at the front. Or what is left of them.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): how a Roman legion was organised  
> **Caius Pupus**: Roman armies were very well organised. A legion had thousands of soldiers, split into smaller groups called centuries.  
> **Caius Pupus**: Despite the name, a century was only about eighty men, and its leader was a centurion. “Century” and “centurion” both come from the Latin for a hundred.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a Roman legion was divided into centuries led by centurions, and that those words come from the Latin for “hundred”._

**Caius Pupus**: Quite a lot of ghosts, really. I would count them, but I would rather not.  

#### `a08-12-ghosts`

**A Ghostly Centurion**: Woooo. We are the lost legion. We march for ever. Fear us. Woooo.  
**Obelix**: Excuse me. Some of us are trying to sleep.  
**A Ghostly Centurion**: We… we are ghosts. We are meant to be frightening.  
**Asterix**: You are very loud. And your chains need oiling. And you are standing in our potatoes.  
**A Ghostly Centurion**: We are not standing in anything. We are ghosts.  
**Obelix**: Your sheets are grubby, too. When did you last wash those?  
_The centurion looks down at his robe. It is, it must be said, a bit grey round the hem._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): specific, polite complaints work better  
> _Asterix and Obelix name exactly what is wrong: the noise, the chains, the potatoes. Why does being specific work better than just saying “go away”?_  
> - ✅ It shows exactly what to fix → Yes. A specific complaint tells the other person what to change, and it feels fairer than a general insult.
> - It makes the ghosts feel bad → It can sting a little. But a clear, polite complaint is kinder than a rude one, and more likely to work.
> - It takes longer, so it is annoying → It takes a bit longer, but it gets results. “Go away” gives the ghosts nothing to act on.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that clear, specific, polite complaints work better than vague, rude ones._


**Choices**

- **“And the moaning is out of tune.”**
    - **A Ghostly Centurion**: It is NOT out of tune. Marcus. Marcus, are we out of tune?
    - Marcus, at the back, does not answer, which is an answer.
- **“Have you got a permit for this?”**
    - **A Ghostly Centurion**: A permit? For haunting? I do not think we ever applied.
    - A ripple of worry goes down the ghostly lines.

#### `a08-12-ghosts-done`

**A Ghostly Centurion**: Well. If we are not wanted. We know when we are not wanted. Come on, lads. We will go and haunt somewhere grateful.  
_They shuffle off into the mist, sulking, chains dragging. One of them, at the back, looks round at your tablet as if it were a summons._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): complaining without taking away someone’s dignity  
> _The ghosts left feeling unwanted. Could you have complained and still let them keep their dignity? How?_  
> - Ask them to haunt somewhere else, kindly → A fair answer. Saying what you need, without insulting them, lets them leave with their heads high.
> - It was their job to be scary, so they should leave → A fair answer. They did want to frighten people. It might still have been kind to thank them for trying.
> - Offer them a potato and a seat → A fair answer. Making friends of a problem is sometimes the surest way to solve it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about complaining kindly, so that others keep their dignity._

> **Caius Pupus**: X is ten, and I after it adds one. Ten and one make eleven. Eleven out of twelve marks are done.  
> **Caius Pupus**: The twelfth will be XII, which is X, I and I. Ten plus one plus one.  
> _For grown-ups: Read XI as 10 + 1 = 11, and looked ahead to XII as 10 + 1 + 1._

### Glossary

- **legion**: A big group of Roman soldiers, about five thousand strong.
- **centurion**: A Roman officer who led a group of about eighty soldiers.

## A8-13. The Circus Maximus

- `a08-13-s1`: Go with the village to Rome. · _The whole village is coming. Help the chief onto his shield; mind his feet._
- `a08-13-s2`: Referee the last task from the arena’s edge. · _Stand at the gate with your tablet. Watch the lions, and then watch the crowd._

#### `a08-13-rome`

_For the last task the whole village comes to Rome. Caesar has ordered it: the Gauls, all of them, in the Circus Maximus._  
_Rome is enormous, white and gold and full of steps. The village walks through it in a long, loud, curious line._  
_The chief is carried on his shield. Getafix walks with his hands behind his back, looking at the aqueducts with interest._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): how aqueducts move water  
> **Getafix**: Look at those tall arches. They are aqueducts, bridges that carry water into the city from far away.  
> **Getafix**: They work with gravity. The channel slopes very slightly downhill, a little at a time, so the water flows all the way.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Roman aqueducts used a gentle downhill slope and gravity to carry water._

**Cacofonix**: Shall I sing something, for the journey? Something to make Rome weep?  
**Vitalstatistix**: No.  
_Under the huge arena, the village is shown into a stone room with a gate at one end. Through the gate, you hear the crowd._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): history and story: what the real Circus Maximus was  
> _A note from Nova’s atlas: the real Circus Maximus in Rome was a huge racing track, mostly for chariot races, long and narrow, with seats for a great crowd._  
> _Wild-animal shows were held there sometimes too. Later the Colosseum, built over a hundred years after Caesar, became the famous place for them._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the real Circus Maximus was mainly a chariot-racing track that sometimes held animal shows, and that the Colosseum came later._


**Choices**

- **Look through the gate.**
    - Sand, and sun, and tier on tier of faces. On a balcony at the top, a man in purple and a laurel crown.
- **Ask Pupus if he is all right.**
    - **Caius Pupus**: I do not know any more. I have watched you for eleven tasks. I think I would like you to win.

#### `a08-13-arena`

_The gate goes up, the village walks out onto the sand, and the crowd roars. Another gate goes up, and the lions come out._  
_The first lion bounds at Asterix, and Asterix catches it under the front legs and dances with it, in a slow, stately circle._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): Latin numbers and the English words from them  
> **Caius Pupus**: Count the lions in Latin: unus, duo, tres, quattuor, quinque. Which English word comes from “tres”, three?  
> - ✅ Triple → Yes. “Tri-” and “tres” both mean three: triple, triangle, tricycle.
> - Duet → A duet has two players, and “duo” means two. “Triple” comes from “tres”, three.
> - Unit → “Unit” comes from “unus”, one. The word from “tres”, three, is “triple”.
> _For grown-ups: Counted in Latin to five and linked “tres” to English words like triple._

_Obelix rubs the second lion behind the ears until it rolls on its back. Gladiators run out; the chief invites them to dinner._  
_Someone lights a fire in the middle of the sand, and someone else has brought the boar. Somehow, there is a feast._  
_High in the stands, a white figure is cheering: Asbestos. Beside him are Verses, Cilindric, a floury Mannekenpix, and Iris, a person again._  
_The crowd is not booing the Gauls any more. It is coming down the steps to join the party._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): how a shared meal can turn rivals into friends  
> _The crowd that came to see a fight ends up at a party. Why does sharing food and laughter change how people feel about each other?_  
> - It makes people feel safe and welcome → A fair answer. When people feel safe, they stop defending themselves and start noticing each other.
> - It gives people something to enjoy together → A fair answer. A shared good time creates memories, and it is hard to stay angry at someone you have laughed with.
> - It only works in stories → A fair answer. Real life is harder. But many peace talks and families do begin with sharing a meal.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how sharing a meal and laughter can build friendship._


#### `a08-13-arena-done`

_Up on the balcony, Caesar stands, and the arena goes quiet. He looks down at the feast in his circus for a long moment._  
**Julius Caesar**: Well. That is the twelfth. I suppose I had better be a good loser. It will be a new experience.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s words reveal  
> _Caesar says being a good loser “will be a new experience”. What does that line tell you about him?_  
> - ✅ He hardly ever loses, and he knows it → Yes. It is a joke at his own expense. Caesar is proud, but he can laugh at himself, and that makes him a good sport.
> - He has lost many times → If he had lost often, it would not be new. The joke is that he almost never loses.
> - He is furious → He may be cross inside, but his words are dry and polite. He is choosing to lose well.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character’s traits from a line of dialogue, and saw how he chooses to lose well._

**Julius Caesar**: Gauls, you have done the twelve tasks of Hercules, and a few of your own. Rome declares you gods. Rome hopes you will be quiet ones.  
**Vitalstatistix**: Thank you, Caesar! Come to dinner. Bring a boar.  
**Julius Caesar**: I think not. But I shall look at your little dot on the map with… respect.  
_Pupus climbs up beside you, takes the wax tablet, and initials the last mark with a flourish: XII, which is X, I and I._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): reading and adding a Roman numeral  
> _The last mark is XII. Adding its parts, which number does it stand for?_  
> - ✅ Twelve: 10 + 1 + 1 → Yes. X is ten, then two I strokes add two. Ten, one and one make twelve.
> - Eleven: 10 + 1 → That is XI. XII has two strokes after the X, so ten plus one plus one is twelve.
> - Eight: 10 − 2 → Strokes after a bigger numeral are added, not taken away. Ten plus two is twelve.
> _For grown-ups: Read XII as 10 + 1 + 1 = 12._

**Caius Pupus**: Referee. Your scoring was impartial, generous, and occasionally very strange. I would observe you again.  

### Glossary

- **aqueduct**: A bridge-like structure that carries water, often over a long distance.
- **arena**: A big open space with seats all round it, for shows and contests.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): Latin roots: amicus  
> _“Amicus” is Latin for friend. Which English word do you think comes from it?_  
> - ✅ Amicable, meaning friendly → Yes. “Amicable” means friendly and peaceful, as in an amicable chat.
> - Amazing → “Amazing” has a different history. “Amicable”, meaning friendly, comes from “amicus”.
> - Ambulance → “Ambulance” comes from a Latin word for walking. “Amicable” comes from “amicus”, friend.
> _For grown-ups: Linked the Latin “amicus” (friend) to the English word “amicable”._

_The lyre goes on being tuned. Each string, when plucked, wobbles back and forth, and the wobble makes the note._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): sound, vibration and pitch: strings  
> _A plucked string vibrates, moving to and fro very fast. That vibration shakes the air, and our ears hear it as sound._  
> _A shorter, tighter or thinner string vibrates faster and makes a higher note. A long, loose, thick string makes a low one._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plucked strings vibrate to make sound, and that shorter or tighter strings give higher notes._

**Asterix**: Referee. You have not still got that form from the Place That Sends You Mad, have you?  

#### `a08-14-tie`

_You take the form out of your satchel, where it has been since the porter handed it back. It is covered in stamps._  
**Asterix**: That might do nicely.  
**Cacofonix**: What? What are you doing? I have not even started the overture!  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): multiplying and converting minutes  
> _The bard’s song has forty-two verses. If each verse takes two minutes, how long is the whole song?_  
> - ✅ 84 minutes, which is 1 hour 24 minutes → Yes. 42 times 2 is 84 minutes. 60 of those make an hour, which leaves 24 minutes: 1 hour 24 minutes.
> - 44 minutes → That adds instead of multiplying. Forty-two lots of two minutes is 42 times 2, which is 84 minutes.
> - 80 minutes → Close. 40 times 2 is 80, and the other 2 verses add 4 more minutes: 84 minutes, or 1 hour 24 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 42 × 2 = 84 minutes and converted it to 1 hour 24 minutes._

**Getafix**: Hold still, Cacofonix. If it is long enough, it is an honour. You will be bound in official papers.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): teasing, kindness and being heard  
> _The village ties up the bard, gently, so he cannot sing. Is that teasing, or unkind? How would you want friends to handle an annoying habit of yours?_  
> - It is gentle teasing, because everyone loves him → A fair answer. Teasing can be a way of showing affection, as long as the person is in on it, and is not hurt.
> - It is unkind, because nobody listens to him → A fair answer. Feeling unheard hurts. A kinder way might be to listen to one verse, or tell him honestly how long it is.
> - Telling him honestly would be best → A fair answer. Honest and kind is hard, and it usually works better than tying anybody up.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the line between gentle teasing and unkindness, and about honest kindness._

_Getafix reads the form’s heading by the light of the fire, and his eyebrows go up._  

#### `a08-14-tie-done`

_The whole village gathers round to see what you wrote, back in the building of endless counters._  
**Cacofonix**: Bound in official papers? I am a bard, not a book!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words with more than one meaning: bound  
> _Getafix said the bard would be “bound in official papers”. Which meaning of “bound” is the joke using?_  
> - ✅ Both: tied up, and made into a book → Yes. A book’s pages are “bound” inside its cover, and the bard is about to be bound up in a form. Two meanings, one joke.
> - Only tied up → That is one meaning. But books are “bound” too, which is why the bard says he is not a book.
> - Bound, as in a big jump → A bound can be a big leap, like a lion’s. Here, though, it means tied up, and bound like a book.
> _For grown-ups: Used context to see a joke that uses two meanings of the word “bound”._

## A9-1. Strange Signs

- `a09-01-s1`: Step into the valley on the atlas page and meet whoever lives in the tall blue house. · _Touch the blue house on the page, then follow the path to the garden gate._
- `a09-01-s2`: Follow Sniff’s secret path down to the shore and see what is wrong with the sea. · _Take the narrow path behind the woodshed. It goes through the bushes, not round them._
- `a09-01-s3`: Ask the Muskrat in the hammock what the grey dust means. · _He is in the hammock between the two birch trees, and he will not be getting out of it._

#### `a09-01-valley`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a green valley by the sea, with a tall blue house in it like a stove that grew._  
_You touch the chimney. The page smells of wet grass, and then so does the air._  
_It is morning, but a grey one. Everything looks dusted with ash and forgotten._  
_A round white someone is standing in the garden, holding a cup and frowning at the sky._  
**Moomintroll**: Oh! Hello. Are you a visitor? Mamma will be pleased. She likes visitors best on grey days.  
_A smaller, sharper someone pops out from behind the water butt and looks straight at your Nubbin._  
**Sniff**: What’s that? Is it valuable? It looks valuable. It looks like it would fit in a pocket.  
**Moomintroll**: That’s Sniff. He means hello.  
**Sniff**: I mean hello AND is it valuable.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s words tell us about him  
> _Sniff’s first question is whether your Nubbin is valuable. What does that tell us about Sniff?_  
> - ✅ He likes to collect and keep things safe. → Yes. He asks about value and pockets, so he is a collector who worries about losing things.
> - He wants to be rude. → He is blunt, but he says hello too. His question is really about what he cares about: keeping things close.
> - He does not like Nubbins. → Not at all. He wants to put it in his pocket, which is his way of liking something.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character trait (a collector who wants things safe) from his first lines._


**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin try Sniff’s pocket.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs into Sniff’s coat pocket, turns round twice and settles, as if it has been waiting all its life for this pocket.
    - **Sniff**: It fits! It fits exactly. I’ll be very careful with it. Probably.
- **Keep your Nubbin in your arms for now.**
    - **Sniff**: Suit yourself. I only offered. It’s a very good pocket.
    - Your Nubbin looks at the pocket for a long moment. Then it wriggles down and climbs in anyway.

> _Finland has two national languages: Finnish, which most people speak, and Swedish, which some Finns speak as their first language._  
> _Tove Jansson, who created the Moomins, grew up speaking Swedish in Finland. She wrote the books in it._  
> _Hello is “hei” in Finnish and “hej” in Swedish. They look nearly the same, but the languages are very different._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Finland has two national languages, Finnish and Swedish, and that the Moomin books were written in Swedish by a Finn._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): waves wear stones round, slowly (weathering and erosion)  
> _Why are beach stones round? Waves roll them against each other, over and over, for hundreds or thousands of years._  
> _Each knock wears away a few grains, and the sharp corners go first. Wearing away like this is called erosion._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that moving water slowly rounds off stones, which is a kind of erosion._

_Along the shore, under a lip of rock, there is a cave. The mouth is low; inside it is dry, and the floor is soft sand._  
**Sniff**: That’s our cave. Mine, mostly. You can come in, but don’t touch anything.  
_There is nothing in it to touch. Sniff looks round it proudly anyway._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): figurative language: “being kept”  
> _Moomintroll says the cave “feels like being kept”. What does he mean?_  
> - ✅ It feels safe, like somebody is looking after you. → Yes. “Kept” is how you talk about something precious that someone looks after. He feels cherished and safe.
> - He wants to take the cave home. → A fair guess, but he does not mean owning it. He means how the cave makes him feel: held safe.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor (“feels like being kept”) as feeling safe and looked after._

_Back in the garden, a Muskrat lies in a hammock with his paws folded on his stomach, thinking very hard about nothing._  
**Moomintroll**: Muskrat, the sea’s gone grey. Do you know why?  
**The Muskrat**: Of course I know why. Something is coming. Something always is.  
**The Muskrat**: A comet, very probably. A star with a tail, falling where it likes.  
**Sniff**: Falling where? Not here. Somewhere else. Somewhere a long way off with nothing valuable in it.  
**The Muskrat**: Where it falls is no concern of a philosopher. Everything ends. It is rather restful, if you think about it.  
_Sniff does think about it. You can tell, because he goes the colour of the sea._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): the same thought can feel different to different people  
> _The Muskrat finds “everything ends” restful. Sniff goes pale. Why might one thought feel so different to two people?_  
> - They care about different things. → That’s a fair answer. The Muskrat loves quiet, and Sniff loves his pockets and his friends, so there is more for Sniff to lose.
> - One of them is more frightened than the other. → That’s a fair answer. Fear is part of it, and what we are afraid of depends on what matters to us.
> - The Muskrat has not really thought about it. → That’s a fair answer. Perhaps he says it so often that it has stopped feeling real. Sniff is feeling it for the first time.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why one idea can comfort one person and frighten another._

**Moominpappa**: There’s an Observatory in the Lonely Mountains, full of professors with telescopes. They’ll know.

#### `a09-01-hammock-done`

_That night you all stand on the veranda, and Moominmamma points._  
_Low over the mountains there is a new star. It has a tail, faint and red, like a match just blown out._  
_Over the next days, the tail will grow, and it will always point one way: away from where the Sun is._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a comet’s tail points away from the Sun, and grows as it nears it  
> _A comet is a lump of ice and dust, a bit like a dirty snowball, often only a few kilometres across._  
> _Far from the Sun it is frozen and dark. As it gets closer, the ice turns to gas and loosens dust. Both stream away and glow._  
> _Sunlight and a stream of particles from the Sun push that gas and dust away._  
> _So the tail always points away from the Sun, even when the comet is heading out again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a comet is, and why its tail grows near the Sun and always points away from it._
