### Glossary

- **valuable**: Worth a lot to somebody, in money or because they love it.
- **veranda**: A roofed porch along the outside of a house.
- **philosopher**: A person who thinks long and hard about big questions.

## A9-2. The Raft

- `a09-02-s1`: Help Moominpappa build a raft on the riverbank. · _Carry planks from the woodshed to the bank. Moominpappa will tell you where they go._
- `a09-02-s2`: Load the raft and push off into the river. · _The basket goes in the middle. Sniff’s things go wherever Sniff can be talked into putting them._
- `a09-02-s3`: Steer the raft downriver until it is time to make camp. · _Keep to the middle of the river and watch the banks._

#### `a09-02-build`

_Moominpappa has laid out planks on the riverbank in the shape of a raft: two metres wide, three metres long._  
**Moominpappa**: Now. A raft must be sound, and it must have a mast, and it must have a name.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: “sound”  
> _Moominpappa says a raft must be “sound”. “Sound” can also be what your ears hear. Which meaning does he intend?_  
> - ✅ Strong and in good condition. → Yes. A sound raft has no weak planks or loose knots. The same word means what we hear, but the sentence tells us which.
> - Noisy. → That would be a funny raft! Check the rest of the sentence: it is about a raft that must not fall apart. That is “sound” meaning strong.
> _For grown-ups: Chose the right meaning of the multiple-meaning word “sound” from context._

**Moomintroll**: Does it need a name?  
**Moominpappa**: Everything that goes anywhere needs a name. Otherwise how will it know it’s gone?  
_You carry planks and Moomintroll ties knots. Sniff supervises from a stump and offers advice nobody takes._  
**Sniff**: That plank’s crooked. That one’s too short. That one is fine, I suppose, if you like that sort of plank.  
_By noon there is a raft, and it floats. Moominpappa looks as if he has built a ship of the line._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.D.8, ask): perimeter of a rectangle  
> _Moomintroll wants to tie a rope all the way round the edge of the raft: 2 m wide, 3 m long. How much rope goes round the edge?_  
> - ✅ 10 metres → Yes: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10. The distance round the edge is called the perimeter.
> - 6 metres → That is the area in square metres: 2 × 3. The rope goes round the edges: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10 metres.
> - 5 metres → That is only one width and one length. The rope goes right round: two widths and two lengths, which is 10 metres.
> _For grown-ups: Found the perimeter of a 2 m by 3 m rectangle by adding all four sides._

**Moominpappa**: What shall we call her?  

**Choices**

- **Suggest calling it after Moominmamma.**
    - **Moominpappa**: Ah. Yes. Then she’ll be sure to bring you home.
    - He paints the name on the stern in careful blue letters.
- **Suggest “The Valuable”.**
    - **Sniff**: Oh. Oh, that’s a very good name. That’s the best name.
    - Moominpappa paints it on, and Sniff stands next to it for a long time with his paws behind his back.

#### `a09-02-build-done`

_Moominmamma comes down the bank with a basket so full the lid will not close._  
**Moominmamma**: Sandwiches on top. Pullovers underneath. Don’t eat the pullovers.  
_A nail drops out of Moominpappa’s pocket and sinks to the bottom of the river at once, while a plank bobs beside it._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): why things float: density  
> _The nail sinks and the plank floats. Why does a whole wooden raft float, even loaded with a basket and three passengers?_  
> - ✅ Wood is lighter than the same amount of water, so the water holds it up. → Yes. Wood is less dense than water, so it floats. Iron is denser, so a lone nail sinks.
> - The river is calm. → A calm river helps us steer, but it is not why it floats. Wood weighs less than the same volume of water.
> - Because the raft is big. → Size alone does not decide it. A big stone still sinks. A raft floats because wood is less dense than water.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that things float when they are less dense than water._


#### `a09-02-launch`

_Sniff arrives with a sack of his things: a tin box, a broken compass, a piece of red glass and a great many buttons._  
**Moomintroll**: Sniff, there isn’t room for all that.  
**Sniff**: There’s room for the Nubbin. The Nubbin’s valuable. These are valuable. It’s the same thing.  
_Your Nubbin, in his pocket, looks at the sack. Then it looks at you._  
**Moominmamma**: Sniff, dear. Things are lovely, but they don’t row.  
**Sniff**: These ones might. You don’t know. Nobody’s ever asked them.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): what makes something valuable  
> _Sniff says his buttons are “valuable”. Is a thing valuable because of what it costs, or because of what it means to someone? Think about it._  
> - Because of what it costs. → That’s a fair answer. Money is one way people measure value. Sniff’s buttons would not sell for much, though, so he must mean something else too.
> - Because of what it means to someone. → That’s a fair answer. A single button can be priceless to the person who found it. Value can be a feeling as well as a price.
> - Both, depending on who you ask. → That’s a fair answer. A jeweller and Sniff may both call something valuable, for different reasons.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether value comes from price or from what a thing means to a person._


**Choices**

- **Help Sniff choose the one thing he’d miss most.**
    - It takes Sniff a very long time. In the end he picks the red glass, because the sun comes through it.
    - **Sniff**: The rest can stay with Moominmamma. She’s nearly as careful as me.
- **Find room for all of it.**
    - You find room. The raft sits a little lower in the water and turns, very slowly, in a circle.
    - Halfway round, Sniff quietly takes the buttons back up the bank to Moominmamma.

#### `a09-02-launch-done`

_Moominpappa pushes the raft off with his foot. Moominmamma waves her apron until the bend._  
_Then there is only the river, the grey sky and the red tail low over the hills._  
_Sniff takes out his broken compass. The needle swings, wobbles and sticks, pointing at nothing in particular._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a compass needle is a magnet that points north  
> _A compass needle is a small magnet. The Earth is a giant magnet too, so the needle swings round until it points to the magnetic north pole._  
> _That is why a working compass points the same way wherever you stand. Sailors have used one for hundreds of years._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a compass needle is a magnet that lines up with the Earth’s magnetic field, pointing north._


#### `a09-02-river`

_The river carries you through woods and meadows. Everything you pass seems to be leaving._  
_Birds fly low and quiet, all one way. A line of ants crosses a log with their eggs held over their heads._  
**Moomintroll**: Where are they all going?  
**Sniff**: Away. Which is what sensible people do. We’re going TOWARDS it.  
**Moomintroll**: We’re going towards finding out. That’s different.  
**Sniff**: It doesn’t feel different. It feels exactly the same.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): the same action can feel different from inside  
> _Moomintroll and Sniff are walking the same way. Moomintroll feels he is going to find out._  
> _Sniff feels he is going to meet the thing he fears. Doing a brave thing can feel scary and brave at once._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that two people can do the same thing and feel differently about it, and that bravery can sit alongside fear._

_The river forks round a rock. One way is quick and white; the other is slow and dark under the trees._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-1, ask): animals move where their needs are met  
> _Animals often leave a place when it stops giving them what they need. Which of these is a real reason birds and ants might move away?_  
> - ✅ Food, water or shelter is running out, or the weather is changing. → Yes. Animals move to places where their needs are met. Many sense changes in weather before we do.
> - They have finished their holiday. → A funny thought, but animals move for survival. They go where food, water and shelter are.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals move to places where their needs for food, water and shelter are met._


**Choices**

- **Take the quick channel.**
    - The raft bucks and spins and shoots out into a pool, and everybody laughs, even Sniff, once it is over.
    - **Sniff**: I wasn’t frightened. My pocket was frightened.
- **Take the slow channel.**
    - You drift under the trees in green half-dark. A heron watches you go by and does not bother to move.
    - **Moomintroll**: This is nice. You could almost forget.

#### `a09-02-river-done`

_You pushed off at one o’clock. At dusk, at seven in the evening, you pull in to a sandy bank._  
_Moomintroll unpacks the sandwiches._  
_Upstream, a thin line of smoke rises from somebody else’s fire._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _You set off at 1:00 in the afternoon and landed at 7:00 in the evening. How long were you on the river?_  
> - ✅ 6 hours → Yes. From 1 to 7 is 6 hours: 1 to 2, 2 to 3, and so on.
> - 8 hours → Count the hours from 1 to 7: that is 6. If it helps, count on your fingers one hour at a time.
> - 7 hours → 7:00 is the end time, not the length. Count from 1 up to 7 and you get 6 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval of 6 hours from 1:00 to 7:00._


#### `a09-02-complete`

_Sniff eats his sandwich very slowly, to make it last._  
**Sniff**: When I was small, I thought the sky was a lid. Like on a tin. And nothing could get through it.  
**Moomintroll**: And now?  
**Sniff**: Now I think it’s just sky. Anything can get through sky.  
_Your Nubbin climbs out of his pocket and sits on his knee, which is as near as it can get to a lid._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why does Sniff tell Moomintroll about the lid, just now, at the end of a long day?_  
> - ✅ He is saying out loud what really frightens him. → Yes. A lid would keep the comet out. “Anything can get through sky” is his fear, spoken at last.
> - He is bored and wants to chat. → Not quite. Look at how he says it: softly, and sadly. It is a worry he has been keeping inside.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out why Sniff shares a childhood memory: to say his fear aloud._


### Glossary

- **sound**: Strong and in good condition. (It can also mean something you hear.)
- **perimeter**: The distance all the way round the outside edge of a shape.
- **compass**: A tool with a magnetic needle that points north, so you can find your way.

## A9-3. Snufkin

- `a09-03-s1`: Find whoever is camping upstream. · _Follow the smoke along the bank; listen for music._
- `a09-03-s2`: Sit by Snufkin’s fire and hear how he travels. · _Sit on the log nearest the fire._
- `a09-03-s3`: Look at the comet with Snufkin before you all sleep. · _Walk down to the water’s edge, where the trees open up._

#### `a09-03-camp`

_You follow the smoke along the bank. Before you see the fire, you hear a tune._  
_It is a harmonica, playing something that goes up like a question and comes down without needing an answer._  

> **Lesson** (music, ask): pitch: high and low notes  
> _Snufkin’s tune “goes up like a question and comes down without needing an answer”. When a tune goes up, are the notes getting higher or lower in pitch?_  
> - ✅ Higher → Yes. Going up in a tune means the pitch is rising. Try humming a question, such as “Really?”. Your voice goes up at the end.
> - Lower → Lower is going down. A question tends to lift at the end, like the start of Snufkin’s tune. Try saying “Really?” and listen to your voice rise.
> _For grown-ups: Identified rising pitch as the notes going higher._

_A small green tent stands by the water. In front of it, someone in an old green hat sits on a stone, fishing._  
_The tune stops. He does not turn round._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): a harmonica makes sound with vibrating reeds  
> _Inside a harmonica are tiny metal strips called reeds. Breathe across one and it vibrates, wobbling to and fro very fast._  
> _That vibration shakes the air, and the shaking air is the sound you hear. Short, stiff reeds vibrate faster and make higher notes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that vibrating reeds make the sound of a harmonica, and that faster vibration gives a higher note._

**Snufkin**: Come and sit down, if you’re coming. The fish have heard you anyway.  
**Moomintroll**: We didn’t mean to scare them.  
**Snufkin**: They don’t mind. They’re only pretending to be scared, so they don’t have to be caught.  

#### `a09-03-camp-done`

**Snufkin**: I’m Snufkin. There’s coffee, if you don’t mind it out of the one cup.  
_He passes the cup round, and it goes round twice. Nobody minds._  
_There are four of you: Snufkin, Moomintroll, Sniff and you. Everybody takes one sip each time round._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups: 4 people × 2 rounds  
> _The cup goes round twice, with one sip each time for each of the four of you. How many sips is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes. Two rounds of four sips: 4 × 2 = 8. Or 4 + 4.
> - 6 → Close. Each round has four sips, not three. Two rounds is 4 + 4, which is 8.
> - 4 → That is only one trip round. It goes round twice: 4 + 4 = 8 sips.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 4 × 2 = 8 using equal groups._


#### `a09-03-fire`

_Sniff is looking around the camp with growing alarm._  
**Sniff**: Where’s all your stuff?  
**Snufkin**: This is all my stuff. A tent, a pipe, a cup, a harmonica. A hat.  
**Sniff**: That’s not stuff. That’s hardly anything. What do you do when you want something?  
**Snufkin**: I look at it. Then I leave it where it is, and it’s still beautiful, and I don’t have to carry it.  
_Sniff holds his pocket as if Snufkin might suggest leaving your Nubbin where it is._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, notice): needs and wants  
> _A need is something you cannot do without, like food, water, warmth and shelter._  
> _A want is something you would like, like a collection of buttons. People often disagree about which is which._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the difference between needs and wants._

**Snufkin**: Not that. You don’t own a friend; you just walk next to them.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): does owning more make us feel safer?  
> _Snufkin owns almost nothing and seems content. Sniff owns a lot and is always worried. Does owning more make people feel safer? Think about it._  
> - Yes, more things means more protection. → That’s a fair answer. Having enough food and a roof really does help us feel safe. Snufkin has what he needs, too.
> - No, feeling safe comes from somewhere else. → That’s a fair answer. Many people find that friends, and trusting that they can cope, matter more than things.
> - It depends how much they already have. → That’s a fair answer. After our needs are met, extra things may add less and less, while worry about losing them can grow.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether having more possessions makes people feel safer._


**Choices**

- **Ask where he’s going.**
    - **Snufkin**: South, in the end. I always go south in the end. But I’ve no hurry.
    - **Snufkin**: Except there’s that.
    - He tips his hat back and looks at the tail over the hills.
- **Ask if he ever gets lonely.**
    - **Snufkin**: Sometimes. Then I go and find someone. Then I go away again. Both are good.
    - **Moomintroll**: You could come with us.
    - **Snufkin**: I could.

#### `a09-03-fire-done`

_He plays again, softer. The tune goes round the fire and out over the water, and comes back sounding older._  
_Your Nubbin climbs out of Sniff’s pocket and sits by Snufkin’s boot to listen._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): echoes: sound bounces off surfaces  
> _Sound travels in waves, and when a wave meets a hard surface, such as a cliff or still water, some of it bounces back. That bounce is an echo._  
> _On a quiet night by the water, the echo arrives a moment after the tune, a little fainter, which is why it “comes back older”._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound waves bounce off hard surfaces, making echoes._


#### `a09-03-sky`

_By the water the trees open up. The comet is brighter than last night, and its tail is longer._  
**Snufkin**: It looks lonely, doesn’t it. Coming all that way on its own, and nobody pleased to see it.  
**Moomintroll**: Are you frightened of it?  
**Snufkin**: A bit. Being frightened’s all right. It just means you’ve noticed something.  
**Sniff**: I’ve noticed EVERYTHING.  
**Snufkin**: Then you’re very well informed, Sniff.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): naming a worry and talking about it  
> _Snufkin names his fear out loud (“a bit frightened”) and talks about it calmly. What does naming a worry do?_  
> - ✅ It makes the worry smaller and easier to share. → Yes. A named worry is easier to look at, and a friend can help carry it.
> - It makes the worry bigger. → It can feel that way at first. But a worry kept silent usually grows. Saying it, as Snufkin does, tends to shrink it.
> - It makes the worry go away for ever. → Not quite. The worry may still be there, but it feels lighter once someone else knows. That is still a big help.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that naming a worry out loud can make it feel smaller and easier to share._

_Sniff thinks about this, and decides it is a compliment, and stands slightly taller._  
**Snufkin**: I’ll come with you to the mountains. I like a mountain, and I’d like to know about this one.  

#### `a09-03-sky-done`

_Snufkin rummages in his tent and comes out with a second harmonica, dented, with one cover loose._  
**Snufkin**: I’ve got two. I don’t like having two of anything. It makes me feel heavy.  
_He holds it out to you. Now he will have one harmonica left of his two: one half of what he started with._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: one half  
> _Snufkin had two harmonicas and gave one away. What fraction of his harmonicas did he give away?_  
> - ✅ One half → Yes. One out of two equal parts is one half, written 1/2.
> - One third → One third would mean one out of three. He had two, so one of them is one half.
> - Two halves → Two halves would be both of them. He gave away one, so it is one half.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised one out of two as the unit fraction 1/2._


#### `a09-03-complete`

_You try a note. It comes out like a duck in a cupboard._  
**Snufkin**: That’s the right note. You just played it in the wrong place.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _“It comes out like a duck in a cupboard.” This compares the note to a duck, using “like”. What is that kind of comparison called?_  
> - ✅ A simile → Yes. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”. It paints a funny picture of a squawky note.
> - A metaphor → Close. A metaphor says one thing is another. A simile says one thing is like another, as here.
> - A rhyme → Not here. A rhyme is words with matching sounds. This compares a note to a duck: it is a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a simile (“like a duck in a cupboard”)._

_Your Nubbin claps. Sniff claps, a beat later, because the Nubbin did._  
**Snufkin**: Play it when you’re home. Then the tune will know where it lives.  

### Glossary

- **pitch**: How high or low a musical note sounds.
- **reed**: A thin strip of metal or cane that vibrates to make a sound in a musical instrument.
- **echo**: A sound that bounces off something and comes back.

## A9-4. The Observatory

- `a09-04-s1`: Climb the Lonely Mountains to the Observatory. · _Follow the cairns up the path. Snufkin knows where the rope is needed._
- `a09-04-s2`: Ask the professors when the comet will come. · _They are by the great telescope. You may have to ask twice._
- `a09-04-s3`: Sit with Sniff on the Observatory step before you go back down. · _He is on the outside step, holding his pocket._

#### `a09-04-climb`

_The Lonely Mountains are grey stone and grey sky, with nothing growing on them that has not had to argue for it._  
_A cairn, a neat pile of stones, marks the path every ten metres. By the slab you have passed six of them._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: equal jumps  
> _There is a cairn every ten metres, and you have passed six. How far have you climbed along the path?_  
> - ✅ 60 metres → Yes. Six lots of ten: 6 × 10 = 60 metres.
> - 16 metres → That adds 6 and 10. Each cairn is ten metres apart, so six cairns is 6 × 10 = 60.
> - 10 metres → That is just the first gap. With six of them, it is 6 × 10 = 60 metres.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 6 × 10 to find the distance of 60 metres._

_Snufkin goes first, then Moomintroll, then you, then Sniff, complaining._  
**Sniff**: My legs are shorter than everybody’s. That means this mountain is taller for me. It isn’t fair.  
**Snufkin**: Then you’ll have climbed more of it than anybody, when we’re at the top.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): looking at a difficulty a different way  
> _Snufkin turns Sniff’s complaint into a compliment. What did he do?_  
> - ✅ He found a different way to look at the same fact. → Yes. Sniff’s legs are still short, but now it means he is climbing further. Looking at a problem another way can change how it feels.
> - He pretended the mountain was small. → He did not change the facts. Short legs still mean more steps. He changed how Sniff sees it.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how re-framing a difficulty can change how we feel about it._

**Sniff**: …I hadn’t thought of that.  
_Halfway up there is a steep slab. Snufkin ties a rope round a rock and throws you the end._  
_Above you, against the clouds, sits a round white building with a slot in its roof, like a money box for stars._  

**Choices**

- **Give Sniff a hand up the slab.**
    - Sniff takes your hand and pretends he does not need it, and holds on hard all the way.
    - **Sniff**: I could have done it. I just didn’t want to.
- **Wait at the top and let Sniff do it himself.**
    - It takes him a while. When he gets to the top, he is so proud of himself he forgets to complain.
    - **Sniff**: Did you see? Did everybody see?

#### `a09-04-climb-done`

_The Observatory door is open. Inside, somebody is counting in a whisper._  
_The slot in the roof is open too, and a telescope as long as a boat points through it at the sky._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how a telescope works  
> _A telescope gathers far more light than your eye can, using a big lens or a curved mirror, and brings it to a point._  
> _That makes dim, faraway things such as stars and comets look brighter and bigger._  
> _The slot in the roof lets the telescope see the sky while the building keeps off the wind._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a telescope gathers extra light with a lens or mirror, so distant things look bigger and brighter._


#### `a09-04-telescope`

_Two professors stand under a telescope as long as a boat, both writing in notebooks and not looking up._  
**Moomintroll**: Excuse me. We’ve come from the valley by the sea. We want to know about the comet.  
**The Professor**: So do we. Everybody does. It is a most remarkable comet.  
**The Other Professor**: Most remarkable. Its tail alone is a thousand…  
**The Professor**: Two thousand.  
**The Other Professor**: …a great many miles long.  
**Moomintroll**: But when will it come? And where?  
**The Professor**: It will arrive on the seventh of October, at eight forty-two in the evening. To the minute.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): telling time to the minute  
> _The comet is due at 8:42 in the evening. On a clock, how many minutes is that before 9:00?_  
> - ✅ 18 minutes → Yes. From 42 to 60 is 18 minutes. Count up: 42 to 50 is 8, and 50 to 60 is 10; 8 + 10 = 18.
> - 42 minutes → That is how many minutes past 8 it is. To find how many until 9, count from 42 up to 60: that is 18.
> - 12 minutes → Count carefully from 42 up to 60. The distance is 18 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Read 8:42 and worked out there are 18 minutes until 9:00._

**The Other Professor**: Possibly eight forty-three. We are arguing about the forty-three.  
**Moomintroll**: And where will it land?  
**The Professor**: Oh, somewhere about here, we think. It will be extremely interesting to observe.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a comet’s tail can be millions of kilometres long  
> _The professors argue about the length of the tail._  
> _A real comet’s tail can stretch millions of kilometres, many times the distance from the Earth to the Moon._  
> _It is thinner than the finest mist._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that comet tails can be millions of kilometres long yet very thin._


#### `a09-04-telescope-done`

_Nobody says anything. One of the professors writes down that nobody says anything._  
**Moomintroll**: Mamma doesn’t know. She doesn’t know the date.  
**Snufkin**: Then we’d better take it to her.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): humour and character  
> _Why is it funny that a professor writes down that nobody says anything?_  
> - ✅ He records facts about everything, but misses what people are feeling. → Yes. The professors observe carefully, but they have missed that the news has frightened Moomintroll. That mismatch is the joke.
> - He wants to remember the silence. → Perhaps, and that may be part of it. But the main joke is that he is writing instead of noticing how everybody else feels.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the humour of a professor who notes facts but misses feelings._


#### `a09-04-step`

_Outside, the light is going. Moomintroll is already at the top of the path, hopping from foot to foot to be gone._  
_Sniff sits on the step with both paws round his pocket. Your Nubbin is asleep in it._  
_You sit down next to him. The comet hangs over the far peaks, closer than yesterday._  
**Sniff**: The seventh is in four days. I counted.  
**Sniff**: Will it hit? You can tell me. I’m very brave about things, once I know them.  
_He looks at you. He is not very brave, and you both know it, and he is asking anyway._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty and comfort with a frightened friend  
> _Sniff asks a question nobody can answer for certain. What is the kindest thing to say to a frightened friend when you do not know? Think about it._  
> - Tell him the truth: you don’t know. → That’s a fair answer. An honest “I don’t know”, said gently, can be more trustworthy than a promise you cannot keep.
> - Tell him it will be fine, to make him feel better. → That’s a fair answer. Comfort matters. The risk is that he may not believe it, or may be more upset if it turns out wrong.
> - Say what you do know, and stay with him. → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes the best help is facts you are sure of, plus company.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be honest and kind to a frightened friend._


**Choices**

- **“I don’t know.”**
    - **You**: I don’t know, Sniff.
    - He nods slowly, as if that is a heavier thing to carry than a yes, and also a truer one.
    - **Sniff**: No. Nobody does. Not even them, with their telescope.
- **“We’ll be home by then.”**
    - **You**: We’ll be home by then.
    - Sniff looks at you for a long moment. Then he tucks the words away somewhere, like a button.
    - **Sniff**: Home by then. All right.

#### `a09-04-step-done`

_Sniff gets up, and then, after a moment, holds out his paw to help you up._  
_It is the first thing he has ever given anybody._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how a character changes  
> _“It is the first thing he has ever given anybody.” What does this small moment show about Sniff?_  
> - ✅ He is starting to trust and care about you. → Yes. Sniff has always held on to things. Giving help is a big step for him, and it shows he trusts you.
> - He is tired of sitting. → Possibly, but the narrator makes a bigger point of it: the first thing he has ever given. It marks a change in him.
> _For grown-ups: Saw a small action as evidence of how a character is changing._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): time: hours in days  
> _Four days remain. A day has 24 hours. How many hours is that? (Hint: 4 × 24 is the same as 4 × 20 plus 4 × 4.)_  
> - ✅ 96 hours → Yes. 4 × 20 = 80 and 4 × 4 = 16, and 80 + 16 = 96 hours.
> - 88 hours → Check the second part: 4 × 4 is 16, not 8. So 80 + 16 = 96.
> - 100 hours → That is close, but not exact. 4 × 24 = 96.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that 4 days is 4 × 24 = 96 hours._

**Sniff**: I always stop to look at things.

### Glossary

- **cairn**: A pile of stones that marks a path or a place.
- **observatory**: A building with telescopes for studying the sky.
- **remarkable**: Unusual and worth noticing.

## A9-5. The Snork Maiden

- `a09-05-s1`: Look into the glinting crack in the rocks on the way down. · _It is beside the path where it turns, just below the rope._
- `a09-05-s2`: Run to whoever is calling for help in the valley below. · _Follow the voice down into the trees. Stay behind Moomintroll._
- `a09-05-s3`: See the gold ring find its owner. · _Sit with everyone in the clearing while she gets her breath back._

#### `a09-05-crevice`

_In the morning, on the way down, something glints in a crack in the rock._  
_Moomintroll lies on his stomach and reaches in up to the shoulder. He comes out with a small gold ring._  
**Moomintroll**: It’s too big for a paw and too small for a crown. What’s it for?  
**Sniff**: It’s for me. I saw it first. I saw the glint before the glint even glinted.  
**Moomintroll**: You were looking at your feet.  
**Sniff**: I saw it with my feet.  
_Sniff goes off to sulk behind a boulder, and comes back with a tiny red stone, smooth and polished by the weather._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): weathering makes stones smooth  
> _“Polished by the weather” is real. Rain, wind, frost and ice slowly wear a stone’s surface, grain by grain. This slow wearing is called weathering._  
> _Garnets are real gems. They form deep in rock, often as dark red crystals, and they are hard, so they stay shiny for a very long time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that weather slowly wears stone smooth, and heard that garnets are hard, red gems._

**Sniff**: Fine. I found my own. It’s a garnet, probably. It’s better than a ring, probably.  
**Sniff**: You hold it. Not keep it. Hold it. I’ve got too many pockets full.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): trust and generosity: holding, not keeping  
> _Sniff gives you the garnet “to hold, not keep”. Why might that be hard for a collector like Sniff, and a big step?_  
> - ✅ He is trusting you with something he loves. → Yes. Letting someone hold something precious is a way of saying you trust them.
> - He has too many pockets full. → That is what he says, and it is funny, but the real reason is underneath: he is choosing to trust you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how lending something precious shows trust._


#### `a09-05-crevice-done`

_The garnet is warm from his paw. Snufkin raises an eyebrow at Sniff, and says nothing, kindly._  
_Sniff pretends not to see. His ears have gone slightly pink._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading what is not said  
> _Snufkin “says nothing, kindly”. Why is saying nothing the kind thing to do here?_  
> - ✅ Sniff is being generous, and teasing him would spoil it. → Yes. A comment might embarrass Sniff. Snufkin’s silence lets him have the moment.
> - Snufkin has nothing to say. → He has plenty on his mind, as the eyebrow shows. He chooses silence out of kindness.
> _For grown-ups: Understood why a character’s silence can be kind._


#### `a09-05-bush`

_Below the mountain there is a valley of strange, thick plants. Somebody in it is shouting for help._  
_In a clearing a bush with long dark branches has wound itself round a small someone with a golden fringe._  
_The branches move slowly, like fingers that have all the time in the world._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how plants defend themselves  
> _A plant cannot run away, so many have other defences: stinging hairs, thorns, bitter or poisonous leaves._  
> _Real nettles, for example, have tiny hairs that inject a stinging liquid. Those features help the plant survive, even if this bush in the story is much bolder._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plants have structures such as stinging hairs and poisons that help them survive._

**The Snork Maiden**: Don’t touch it! It stings! Its leaves are poison!  
_Moomintroll does not even stop. He pulls out his penknife and goes at the branches._  
**Moomintroll**: Hold still! Hold quite still!  
_Snufkin pulls branches back with his walking stick. You find a long dead branch and pin the nearest one down._  
_Your Nubbin hides in Sniff’s pocket, and Sniff hides behind you. Everyone is, in their way, helping._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): helping safely  
> _Moomintroll charges in with a penknife. Snufkin uses a long stick, and you use a dead branch. Whose way of helping keeps the helpers safest?_  
> - ✅ Using a stick or branch, to stay out of reach of the stings. → Yes. Tools keep your skin away from the danger, so you can help without becoming a second person who needs rescuing.
> - Rushing in with bare paws. → Brave, but risky. A helper who gets stung cannot help. A tool, and a plan, is safer.
> _For grown-ups: Compared ways of helping someone and chose the one that keeps the helper safe._


#### `a09-05-bush-done`

_The last branch gives. Moomintroll catches her before she falls, and they both sit down hard in the grass._  
**The Snork Maiden**: You came straight at it. You didn’t even think.  
**Moomintroll**: There wasn’t time to think. I’ll think later.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): bravery  
> _Moomintroll acted before he thought. Is that the same as being brave? What do you think?_  
> - Yes, being brave means acting even when you are afraid. → That’s a fair answer. Some bravery is just doing the right thing quickly, when someone is in trouble.
> - No, bravery means thinking first, then acting. → That’s a fair answer. Careful bravery can keep everybody safer. Snufkin’s stick shows a thoughtful kind.
> - Both can be brave, in different moments. → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes there is time to plan, and sometimes only to act. Good judgment helps tell them apart.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether acting without thinking is bravery._


#### `a09-05-ring`

_She is shaking a little, and pretending not to. She smooths her fringe and checks it twice._  
**The Snork Maiden**: I was looking for something. I lost a gold ring in the mountains, a little one I wear round my ankle.  
_Moomintroll goes very pink and holds out his paw._  
**Moomintroll**: Is it this?  
**The Snork Maiden**: My ankle ring! Where did you find it?  
**Moomintroll**: In a crack. I reached in up to here.  
**Sniff**: I saw it first.  
**The Snork Maiden**: Then thank you both. Thank you very much.  
_Sniff, who was ready for an argument, has nowhere to put it and goes rather quiet._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): lost property belongs to its owner  
> _Sniff says he saw the ring first. Moomintroll found it. But whose ring is it, and what is the right thing to do?_  
> - ✅ It is the Snork Maiden’s, so it should go back to her. → Yes. Finding something does not make it yours if someone else lost it. Returning it is the honest and kind thing.
> - It belongs to whoever saw it first. → Seeing first can matter for a race, but not for ownership. The ring had an owner already: the one who lost it.
> - It belongs to whoever needs it most. → A kind thought, but the ring already has an owner who wants it back, and she should have it.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a found item should be returned to its owner, whoever saw it first._


**Choices**

- **Tell her about the comet.**
    - **You**: There’s a comet coming. The seventh, at eight forty-two in the evening.
    - **The Snork Maiden**: I know. I’ve seen the tail. I thought if I kept busy it wouldn’t notice me.
- **Ask if she’s all right.**
    - **The Snork Maiden**: I am now. I wasn’t. It’s a strange thing, being all right after not being.
    - She slips the gold ring round her ankle and looks at it, to be sure it is still there.

**The Snork Maiden**: I’m the Snork Maiden. My brother is somewhere about, probably making a list.  
**The Snork Maiden**: Can we come with you? I don’t want to be anywhere on my own just now.  
**Moomintroll**: Of course. Mamma always makes enough for everybody.  
_Moominmamma’s basket still holds twelve buns. With the Snork Maiden, there are five friends and a Nubbin: six in all._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: sharing equally  
> _Twelve buns are shared equally among five friends and a Nubbin, six in all. How many does each get?_  
> - ✅ 2 → Yes. 12 ÷ 6 = 2, because 6 × 2 = 12.
> - 3 → Check it: 6 × 3 = 18, which is too many. 6 × 2 = 12, so each gets 2.
> - 6 → That is the number of sharers. Divide 12 by 6 to find each share: 2.
> _For grown-ups: Shared 12 equally among 6 and found 12 ÷ 6 = 2._

_The garnet is still in your hand. Sniff has not asked for it back._  

### Glossary

- **weathering**: The slow wearing away of rock by rain, wind, frost and ice.
- **garnet**: A hard, usually deep red gemstone.

## A9-6. The Snork

- `a09-06-s1`: Find the Snork Maiden’s brother. · _Look for a neat camp with a sign on it._
- `a09-06-s2`: Sit through the Snork’s meeting and help it reach a decision. · _Sit in the circle. When a vote comes, put your paw up._

#### `a09-06-snork`

_Her brother has made camp under a pine, very neatly. There is a sign on the tent that says OFFICE._  
**The Snork**: Sister. You are late. I had you down for back at four.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character traits  
> _The Snork has a sign saying OFFICE on a tent, and a list for everything. Which trait describes him best?_  
> - ✅ Orderly: he loves rules and lists. → Yes. His neat camp, sign, list and meetings all show a love of order.
> - Lazy. → He is the opposite. He keeps busy, checking and recording everything.
> - Careless. → He is very careful, even about a bush trying to eat his sister, which he still writes on his list.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a character trait (orderly) from his actions and belongings._

**The Snork Maiden**: A bush tried to eat me.  
**The Snork**: That is not on the list.  
_He writes it on the list, then crosses it off, because it is over._  
**The Snork**: And who are all these people? Have they been introduced? Has anyone taken their names?  
**Moomintroll**: We’re going home before the comet. We’ve come to fetch you both.  
**The Snork**: Going home? Without a meeting? Nothing should be decided without a meeting.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when is a meeting the best way to decide?  
> _The Snork says nothing should be decided without a meeting. Is a meeting always the best way to decide? Think about it._  
> - Yes, so everybody has a say. → That’s a fair answer. Meetings can make decisions fair, because every voice gets heard.
> - No, sometimes you must act at once. → That’s a fair answer. If someone is in danger, a long meeting could cost too much time.
> - It depends how big and how urgent the decision is. → That’s a fair answer. Small, slow decisions suit meetings. Emergencies need quick action, and a meeting afterwards.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when group meetings are the best way to decide._


#### `a09-06-snork-done`

**The Snork**: Everybody sit in a circle. I shall be the chairman, and also the secretary, as nobody else has a pencil.  
**Snufkin**: I have a pencil.  
**The Snork**: Then you may be the audience.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, notice): how a meeting works  
> _In a real meeting the chairman leads, so that one person talks at a time. The secretary writes the minutes, a record of what was decided._  
> _A list of topics is called an agenda. The Snork’s “items” are an agenda, which is how groups stay on track._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the roles in a meeting (chairman, secretary) and the words agenda and minutes._


#### `a09-06-meeting`

**The Snork**: Item one. The comet. Is it coming? Show of paws.  
_Everybody puts a paw up. There are six of you, one paw each, and your Nubbin puts up both of its own, from Sniff’s pocket._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): adding to count a vote  
> _Six of you put one paw up each, and your Nubbin puts up two paws. How many paws are in the air?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes. Six paws plus two paws: 6 + 2 = 8.
> - 7 → The Nubbin puts up both paws, so that is two, not one. 6 + 2 = 8.
> - 12 → That would be everyone with two paws up. Only the Nubbin used both: 6 + 2 = 8.
> _For grown-ups: Added 6 and 2 to count the paws raised in a vote._

**The Snork**: Carried. Item two. Should we be concerned? Show of paws.  
**Sniff**: Both my paws. And my ears, if they count.  
**The Snork**: Carried. Item three: what to do about it. I shall now accept suggestions.  
_There is a pause, in which nobody suggests anything and the comet moves a little further across the sky._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): voting is a fair way to decide  
> _A show of paws is a vote. Each person gets the same say, and the choice with the most votes wins._  
> _Counting votes carefully, as the Snork does, is part of what makes a vote fair._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that voting gives each person an equal say and the most votes wins._


**Choices**

- **Propose going home at once.**
    - **You**: I propose we go home. Now.
    - **The Snork**: That is a motion. Does anyone second it?
    - **The Snork Maiden**: Me! And Moomintroll. And everyone. You’re outvoted before you’ve counted.
- **Propose a subcommittee to decide on the way.**
    - **The Snork**: A subcommittee! Now that is a sensible person.
    - **Snufkin**: The subcommittee will meet while walking. Very fast. Towards the valley.
    - **The Snork**: …Agreed.

#### `a09-06-meeting-done`

_The Snork writes the minutes and reads them back. Under “Any other business” he has written: Sniff is worried._  
**Sniff**: Well, I am.  
**The Snork**: It is in the minutes. It is official. Everybody is to bear it in mind.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): naming a worry so that others can help  
> _The Snork writes “Sniff is worried” in the minutes. What does it do for Sniff?_  
> - ✅ It makes his worry known and taken seriously by the group. → Yes. A written worry is a worry nobody can ignore. The group has promised to bear it in mind, which is a way of caring.
> - It embarrasses him. → It might have, but look at Sniff’s answer: “Well, I am.” He accepts it, because it is said kindly and nobody laughs.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how naming a worry in front of caring friends helps._


#### `a09-06-complete`

_The Snork folds his tent into a parcel so small and square that Sniff looks at it with something like love._  
_The parcel is six centimetres on each side._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a square  
> _A square with sides of 6 cm covers how many square centimetres? (Area = side × side.)_  
> - ✅ 36 → Yes. 6 × 6 = 36 square centimetres. Imagine six rows of six little squares.
> - 24 → That is the perimeter (6 + 6 + 6 + 6). Area is the space inside: 6 × 6 = 36.
> - 12 → That is 6 + 6. For area we multiply: 6 × 6 = 36.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a 6 cm square as 6 × 6 = 36 square centimetres._

**The Snork**: Meeting closed. We march.  
_You march. The Snork walks at the front, and Snufkin walks at the front of him, and the Snork does not notice._  

### Glossary

- **chairman**: The person who leads a meeting.
- **minutes**: The written record of what was said and decided in a meeting.
- **agenda**: The list of things a meeting will talk about.

## A9-7. The Hemulen

- `a09-07-s1`: Find out who is crashing about in the meadow with a net. · _Follow the sound of somebody falling over things._
- `a09-07-s2`: Help the Hemulen find his rare butterfly. · _Look on the tall flowers at the edge of the meadow, where the sun still reaches._

#### `a09-07-meadow`

_In a meadow full of late flowers, a large person in a long dress is running in circles with a butterfly net._  
_He swings, misses, falls into a bush, gets up and swings again, without once looking anywhere but up._  
**The Hemulen**: Hold still, you! You! I know what you are! You’re the very last one I need!  
**Sniff**: Who’s that?  
**Snufkin**: A Hemulen. You can tell, because he’s busy.  
**Moomintroll**: Excuse me! Have you seen the comet?  
**The Hemulen**: The what? No. Is it a butterfly?  
**Moomintroll**: It’s a star with a tail. It’s coming on the seventh. It might land here.  
**The Hemulen**: Then it had better land quietly. There is a Mourning Blue in this meadow and I will not have it disturbed.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): the life cycle of a butterfly  
> _A butterfly goes through four stages._  
> _It begins as an egg, hatches into a caterpillar that eats and grows, then forms a chrysalis, and finally comes out as an adult butterfly._  
> _This change of body shape is called metamorphosis. The Hemulen only ever hunts the last stage, the one with wings._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the four stages of a butterfly’s life cycle: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult._


#### `a09-07-meadow-done`

**The Snork Maiden**: He’s not listening. Hemulens never listen when they’re collecting.  
**Snufkin**: Then we’ll have to help him finish collecting.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): getting a busy person’s attention kindly  
> _Snufkin’s idea is to help the Hemulen finish collecting first. Why might that work better than interrupting him over and over?_  
> - ✅ He will have time and attention for us once his task is done. → Yes. Joining in with what matters to someone can win their attention kindly.
> - It will annoy him less than shouting. → True, and that is part of it. But helping also changes the situation, so he can listen.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that helping a busy person finish a task can be a kind way to get their attention._


#### `a09-07-butterfly`

_Everyone spreads out across the meadow, walking softly. Even the Snork, who makes it a motion._  
**The Hemulen**: Softly. Softly. It is the colour of the hour after sunset, and it hates a fuss.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): butterflies are cold-blooded and rest when it cools  
> _Butterflies are cold-blooded, which means they rely on the air and sunshine to keep warm. They need warmth to fly._  
> _At dusk, when the air cools, a butterfly settles to rest and keeps still, so it is easier to approach._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that butterflies depend on outside warmth, so they rest when it cools at dusk._

**Sniff**: So do I. Nobody ever asks.  
_Your Nubbin climbs out of Sniff’s pocket and stands very still on a stone._  
_A butterfly the colour of dusk comes down out of nowhere and lands on your Nubbin’s head._  
_Your Nubbin does not breathe, and nor do you. Somewhere behind you, the Hemulen draws in a huge breath._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, do): slow breathing to stay calm and still  
> _Be as still as your Nubbin. Breathe in slowly for a count of four, out slowly for four. Do it five times._  
> Check: `edu:breathe:still:5`
> _For grown-ups: Practised slow breathing to stay calm and still._


**Choices**

- **Call the Hemulen over, softly.**
    - The Hemulen tiptoes over, which for a Hemulen is like a cupboard tiptoeing.
    - He does not swing the net. He just looks, for a long time, with his mouth a little open.
    - **The Hemulen**: There. There it is. Oh, I’ll put it in the book, and it will be complete.
- **Keep quiet and let it fly.**
    - The butterfly opens its wings once and goes up into the evening. Nobody says a word.
    - The Hemulen comes over with his net hanging down. He saw it go.
    - **The Hemulen**: It sat on your little one. It chose. I suppose I can write that down instead.

#### `a09-07-butterfly-done`

_The Hemulen writes in a fat notebook with his tongue between his teeth._  
**The Hemulen**: Complete, as far as this meadow goes. Now. What was it you were saying about a star?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): watching and owning  
> _The Hemulen records the butterfly instead of catching it. Is watching something as good as owning it? Think about it._  
> - Yes, it can be better, because the butterfly stays alive and free. → That’s a fair answer. Watching leaves the living thing unharmed, and many people find the memory lasts.
> - No, owning means you can keep it for ever. → That’s a fair answer. Keeping something can feel good. But some things, like a living butterfly, are only themselves while they are free.
> - It depends on the thing. → That’s a fair answer. A book can be owned and read again; a butterfly is better watched.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether watching a living thing can be better than owning it._

_He wrote down what he saw. He never needed to catch it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): writing a field note: where, when, what you saw  
> _Write a three-line field note for the Hemulen’s book: where you were, when it was, and what you saw. Include one colour and one number._  
> Check: `edu:write:field-note:butterfly`
> _For grown-ups: Wrote a short field note with place, time and observations._

**Moomintroll**: It’s coming on the seventh. We’re going to my valley. Mamma will look after everyone.  
**The Hemulen**: Will there be butterflies?  
**Moomintroll**: After. There are always butterflies after.  
**The Hemulen**: Then I shall come. I can be very useful, when I have finished something.
