_Butterflies have a pattern on the left wings that matches the right. Fold a picture of one down the middle and the halves would meet._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry  
> _A butterfly’s pattern matches on both sides of its body. How many lines of symmetry does a typical butterfly have?_  
> - ✅ One, down the middle. → Yes. One line down the middle of the body turns the left half into the right half. That is a line of symmetry.
> - Two. → A rectangle has two. A butterfly has only the line down its body.
> - None. → It does have one. Imagine folding it in half down the body: the sides would match.
> _For grown-ups: Identified one line of symmetry on a butterfly._


### Glossary

- **metamorphosis**: A big change of body shape as an animal grows, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.
- **chrysalis**: The resting stage, inside a hard skin, when a caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

## A9-8. The Dry Sea

- `a09-08-s1`: Come down to the shore and see what has happened to the sea. · _The path ends at the cliff top. Look out._
- `a09-08-s2`: Help Snufkin make stilts for everyone. · _Gather long straight poles from the driftwood above the tideline._
- `a09-08-s3`: Walk out across the seabed on stilts. · _Stay in the line and step where Snufkin steps._

#### `a09-08-shore`

_You come over the last hill and stop. Everyone stops, all along the line._  
_The sea has gone. Where it was there is a great grey hollow of mud and weed and rock, going down and down._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): tides and the Moon  
> _On real coasts the sea rises and falls every day. These tides are caused mainly by the Moon’s pull on the water, with a smaller pull from the Sun._  
> _At low tide the sea draws back and shows the sand and rocks beneath. The sea in the story has gone out far, far further than any real tide would._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tides are caused mostly by the Moon’s pull, and that low tide uncovers the shore._

**Moomintroll**: It was here. There was a whole sea here.  
**Snufkin**: It’s hiding. Everything hides from something that big.  
**The Snork**: The valley is on the other side. Around the bay is three days. Across is one.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction: days saved  
> _Around the bay takes three days and straight across takes one. How many days does the shorter way save?_  
> - ✅ 2 days → Yes. 3 − 1 = 2 days saved.
> - 4 days → That adds them. To find how much is saved, subtract: 3 − 1 = 2.
> - 1 day → Across takes one day, but the saving is the difference: 3 − 1 = 2 days.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 1 from 3 to find 2 days saved._

**Sniff**: Across WHAT? It’s all squelch!  
_Far out on the seabed, a stranded fish flaps once in a puddle that is, for now, just enough._  

#### `a09-08-shore-done`

_Three days is more than you have. Nobody needs to say it._  
_Nobody does. The silence is long, and it is not an empty one._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): saying the hard thing out loud  
> _Everyone knows three days is too long, and nobody says it. Is it better to say a frightening thing out loud, or to leave it unsaid? Think about it._  
> - Say it, so everyone can face it together. → That’s a fair answer. A worry shared can be planned around, and nobody has to carry it alone.
> - Leave it, so nobody panics. → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes people need a moment, and too much talk can add to fear.
> - Say it gently, and straight away follow it with a plan. → That’s a fair answer. Snufkin does exactly this next: he moves on to what can be done.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to say a frightening thing aloud._


#### `a09-08-stilts`

**Snufkin**: Stilts. We walk over the mud on stilts.  
_You gather driftwood along the old tideline. Snufkin binds footrests on with string from his pockets._  
_The Hemulen’s stilts are the tallest, ninety centimetres, and the Snork’s are measured exactly. Sniff’s are thirty centimetres._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): comparing lengths  
> _The Hemulen’s stilts are 90 cm and Sniff’s are 30 cm. How much taller are the Hemulen’s?_  
> - ✅ 60 cm → Yes. 90 − 30 = 60 centimetres.
> - 120 cm → That adds them. To compare, subtract: 90 − 30 = 60.
> - 30 cm → That is Sniff’s height. The difference is 90 − 30 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 30 from 90 to find a 60 cm difference._

**Sniff**: Mine are short.  
**Snufkin**: Short stilts fall over less far.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balance: lower is steadier  
> _Snufkin says short stilts fall over less far. Why are short stilts easier to balance on?_  
> - ✅ Your body is nearer the ground, so there is less of a topple and less far to fall. → Yes. The lower your weight is, the steadier you are, and the smaller the fall if you do tip.
> - Short stilts are lighter. → They are lighter, but the main reason is height. A lower body is steadier, and a smaller drop hurts less.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a lower centre of weight makes balance easier and falls smaller._

_Everybody practises on the sand, and everybody falls over: Moomintroll often, the Snork Maiden gracefully._  
_Sniff falls over on purpose, to get it done._  
_Your Nubbin rides in Sniff’s pocket, a little higher off the ground than it is used to, and looks impressed._  

**Choices**

- **Ask for tall stilts.**
    - You can see the whole bay from up here, and the long red stripe of the comet beyond it.
    - You fall over once, magnificently, and the Hemulen picks you up by the collar.
- **Ask for short stilts, like Sniff’s.**
    - **Sniff**: Oh, good. Now we’re the short-stilts club. We’ll have meetings.
    - **The Snork**: All meetings must be registered with me.

#### `a09-08-stilts-done`

_Snufkin looks at the line of you all, wobbling. He puts his harmonica away, which means it is time._  
_He does not say it. He does not need to._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): inference: what actions tell us  
> _Snufkin puts his harmonica away “which means it is time”. What can we infer?_  
> - ✅ He plays when he is relaxed, so putting it away means it is time to get serious. → Yes. The harmonica is how he relaxes. Packing it away shows the real crossing is about to begin.
> - The harmonica broke. → Nothing says that. We infer from his habits: music is for easy times, silence for serious ones.
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference from a character’s habit (putting the harmonica away)._


#### `a09-08-seabed`

_You walk out on to the seabed. It sucks at the stilts with a sound like somebody finishing soup._  
_There are things down here nobody was meant to see: a sunk rowing boat, a broken anchor, a wardrobe._  
**The Snork Maiden**: Why is there a wardrobe?  
**The Snork**: I shall note it.  
_In a puddle beside your stilt lies a pink shell with a curl in it, still wet._  
_You lean down, very carefully, and pick it up. When you hold it to your ear, there is no sea in it at all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): a shell protects the animal that grows it  
> _The shell once belonged to a soft-bodied sea animal. How does a shell help the animal that grows it survive?_  
> - ✅ It is a hard shield against predators and knocks. → Yes. A shell protects the soft body inside, so the animal can hide and rest safely.
> - It helps the animal fly. → Shells are heavy! They protect, rather than lift. The hard outer layer shields the soft body.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a shell is a protective body part for a soft-bodied animal._

**Sniff**: Is it broken?  
**Moomintroll**: It’s waiting. It’s listening for the sea, the same as us.  

#### `a09-08-seabed-done`

_You put the shell in your pocket. It is very light, and it seems to want carrying._  
_You tell yourself a shell cannot want anything. Still, your hand goes back to your pocket twice._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification  
> _“It seems to want carrying.” A shell cannot want anything. What is the writer doing?_  
> - ✅ Describing an object as if it had feelings, like a person. → Yes. This is called personification. It makes the shell feel alive, and makes you feel gently responsible for it.
> - Telling a fact about shells. → Not a fact. Shells cannot want things, so the writer is using imagination to give the shell feelings.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised personification: giving a non-living thing human feelings._


#### `a09-08-complete`

_The sun goes down behind you. Out on the seabed, the light comes from the sky now, red and steady._  
**Snufkin**: We’ll go on in the dark. The comet will light the way. That’s one thing to be said for it.  
_Sniff counts his stilts, his pocket, his Nubbin, and you, and seems relieved that the number comes out the same._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a comet shines because of the Sun  
> _A comet has no fire inside. Sunlight bounces off its dust, and its gas glows when sunlight hits it._  
> _Even after the Sun has set where you stand, the comet, far out in space, is still in the Sun’s light._  
> _That is why you can see it in a night sky._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a comet shines because of sunlight: its dust reflects it and its gas glows in it._


### Glossary

- **tide**: The regular rising and falling of the sea, mainly caused by the Moon.
- **personification**: Writing about a thing, like a shell, as if it had feelings or acted like a person.

## A9-9. The Octopus

- `a09-09-s1`: Cross the deep part of the seabed by the comet’s light. · _Keep to the ridge of rock. Don’t go near the dark pool._
- `a09-09-s2`: Keep everyone together while the Snork Maiden acts. · _Hold the line on the ridge. Hold a light up if you have one._

#### `a09-09-deep`

_The seabed dips into its deepest part. The mud gives way to black rock and pools that go down further than light._  
_Everything is red under the comet. The puddles shine like spilt jam._  
**The Snork**: We keep to the ridge. Single file. That is a rule.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): why we keep safety rules even when they cost time  
> _The Snork’s rule is “keep to the ridge, single file”. It is slower than cutting corners. Why is it still a good rule here?_  
> - ✅ The ridge is the safe path, and the pools are unknown. → Yes. A rule can save you from dangers you cannot see. Cutting the corner saved seconds and risked much more.
> - The Snork likes being in charge. → He does, and that is true. But a rule can be bossy and sensible at once, and this one is sensible.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about why a safety rule is worth following even when it is slower._

_Moomintroll is in front, looking ahead to where the valley must be. He is going too fast._  
**Moomintroll**: Not far now. I can almost smell the house. I can almost smell the jam.  
_He steps off the ridge to cut a corner. His stilt sinks into the edge of the biggest, darkest pool._  
_The water in the pool moves, though there is no wind._  

#### `a09-09-deep-done`

**Snufkin**: Moomintroll. Come back on the ridge. Slowly.  
_Snufkin does not shout. His voice is low and even, as if there is all the time in the world._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): a calm voice helps in a frightening moment  
> _Why does Snufkin speak calmly and slowly instead of shouting?_  
> - ✅ A calm voice helps the other person stay steady and listen. → Yes. Shouting can make fear grow, and calm helps people think. Calm is catching.
> - He doesn’t realise it is dangerous. → He knows exactly how dangerous it is. That is why he stays calm: it is the best way to help Moomintroll get out safely.
> _For grown-ups: Understood that a calm voice helps a frightened person stay steady._


#### `a09-09-octopus`

_A long arm comes out of the pool, and then another, grey and slow and curious._  
_An octopus as big as a cart lifts its head out of the water and looks at Moomintroll with one large, sad eye._  
_An arm curls round his stilt, and another round his middle. He cannot get back on the ridge._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how an octopus’s body works  
> _A real octopus has eight arms, three hearts and no bones, so it can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak._  
> _Its soft body would be easy prey, but it makes up for it with clever eyes and brain, and by changing colour to hide._  
> _Octopuses are curious animals, not hunters of people._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned facts about octopuses: eight arms, three hearts, no bones, camouflage and curiosity._


> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction: arms holding and arms free  
> _Two of the octopus’s eight arms are holding Moomintroll. How many arms are not holding anything?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes. 8 − 2 = 6 arms free, curling in the water.
> - 10 → That adds them. Take the two holding arms away: 8 − 2 = 6.
> - 2 → Two are holding him. The rest are free: 8 − 2 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 2 from 8 to find the octopus’s free arms._

**Moomintroll**: Help! It’s got hold! I can’t pull free!  
_Sniff squeaks and dives behind the Hemulen. The Hemulen holds his net up, which is no use at all, but brave._  
_The Snork Maiden is already moving. She takes the lantern off the Snork’s pack, lights it and runs at the pool._  
**The Snork Maiden**: Let him GO!  
_She swings the lantern up into the octopus’s eye. The light flares on the wet rock, gold in all that red._  

**Choices**

- **Hold your own light up behind her.**
    - You hold up the pink shell from the seabed. It catches the lantern and throws the light back, twice as bright.
    - The octopus blinks, both eyes, very slowly, and its arms open.
- **Grab Moomintroll’s paw and pull.**
    - You lean out from the ridge and catch his paw. The Hemulen catches your collar, and the Snork catches the Hemulen.
    - The octopus blinks at the lantern, and its arms open, and you all fall backwards in a heap.

#### `a09-09-octopus-done`

_The octopus slides back into its pool without a splash, as if embarrassed. The water closes, and it is gone._  
_Moomintroll is sitting on the ridge in the mud with his stilts crossed, staring at the Snork Maiden._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): fairness to animals  
> _The octopus was curious, not cruel, and it was frightened by the lantern. Is it fair to frighten an animal to protect a friend? Think about it._  
> - Yes, protecting a friend comes first, as long as the animal is not hurt. → That’s a fair answer. The Snork Maiden used light, not force, and the octopus went home unharmed.
> - No, we should have found a way that did not scare it. → That’s a fair answer. Animals can be frightened too, and a gentler way is worth looking for when there is time.
> - It depends on whether anyone was in danger. → That’s a fair answer. When a friend is held, there is little time. Afterwards we can still think about how to be kinder next time.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to balance protecting a friend with fairness to an animal._


#### `a09-09-complete`

**Moomintroll**: You saved me.  
**The Snork Maiden**: You saved me first. Now we’re even. It’s much better being even.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: “even”  
> _The Snork Maiden says, “Now we’re even.” “Even” can also describe numbers like 2, 4 and 6. Which meaning is it here?_  
> - ✅ Equal: each of them has helped the other. → Yes. “Even” here means level, with nothing owed either way. Friends often like keeping things even.
> - A number that divides by two. → That is another meaning of “even”, but here nobody is talking about numbers. They are talking about favours: each has rescued the other.
> _For grown-ups: Chose the right meaning of “even” from context._

**Moomintroll**: I didn’t know you could do that.  
**The Snork Maiden**: Neither did I. I was too busy doing it to find out.  
_Sniff comes out from behind the Hemulen, and your Nubbin out of his pocket. Both look surprised to be alive and fine._  
**The Snork**: I am noting that the Snork Maiden was brave. I am underlining it. Twice.  

### Glossary

- **camouflage**: Colours or patterns that help an animal hide by matching its surroundings.

## A9-10. The Race Home

- `a09-10-s1`: Get off the seabed and on to the road home under the red sky. · _Climb the shingle bank on the far side, then keep walking._
- `a09-10-s2`: Hold on together when the tornado comes. · _Get everyone into the lee of the stone wall and hold on to the nearest paw._
- `a09-10-s3`: Run the last stretch to the valley. · _Down through the birch wood. You know the way from here._

#### `a09-10-road`

_You climb off the seabed in the morning and leave the stilts in a heap on the shingle._  
_The sky is red now in the daytime too. The air is hot and still, and the leaves on the trees hang down, tired._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): tornadoes and warning signs  
> _In real life, hot, heavy, still air can come before a big storm. A tornado forms under a huge thundercloud, when warm damp air rises quickly and starts to spin._  
> _Tornadoes are rare, and weather forecasters watch for them. People are told to shelter in a strong building, away from windows._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how tornadoes form and what people do to stay safe._

**The Snork Maiden**: What day is it?  
**The Snork**: The seventh. I have it written down. I wish I didn’t.  
**Sniff**: It’s today. It’s actually today.  
**Moomintroll**: We can still do it. It doesn’t come till the evening. We can be home long before that.  
_Sniff looks at you, quickly, and then away, and walks a little faster._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): reading how others feel  
> _Sniff glances at you quickly, then looks away and walks faster. What might he be feeling?_  
> - ✅ Hopeful and worried at the same time. → Yes. He is hoping your words come true, and worried that they might not. Feelings often come in pairs.
> - Bored. → Boredom does not make people walk faster. His quick glance and hurry show hope and worry together.
> _For grown-ups: Read two mixed feelings from a character’s quick glance and faster walking._


#### `a09-10-road-done`

_At a crossroads there is a milestone: Valley, eighteen kilometres._  
_On the stone, a second Hemulen in a large flowered dress is fanning himself with a hymn sheet._  
**The Other Hemulen**: Cousin! What are you doing out on a day like this?  
**The Hemulen**: Walking very fast, cousin. You should too. We walk at six kilometres an hour.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _The valley is 18 km away and the group walks 6 km every hour. How many hours will it take?_  
> - ✅ 3 hours → Yes. 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so 3 hours.
> - 12 hours → That subtracts. Divide the distance by the speed: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 hours.
> - 6 hours → That is the speed per hour. 18 km at 6 km an hour is 18 ÷ 6 = 3 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 18 km by 6 km per hour to find 3 hours._


#### `a09-10-tornado`

_The wind comes all at once, out of a still sky. Dust goes up in a spinning column that walks across the fields._  
**Snufkin**: Tornado! Down behind the wall, everybody!  
_It does not care about walls. It picks up a haystack, a gate, two hens, and then it picks up the other Hemulen._  
_His flowered dress fills like a sail. He goes up, and grabs the first thing he can, which is Moomintroll._  
_Moomintroll grabs the Snork Maiden, the Snork Maiden grabs Sniff, and Sniff grabs you._  
_Then nobody is on the ground at all._  
**The Other Hemulen**: This is very irregular!  
**Snufkin**: Hold your skirts out wide! Like wings! Wide as you can!  
_The other Hemulen spreads his dress, and the spinning stops, and you are gliding. All of you, in a chain, under a flowered sky._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): air resistance  
> _When the Hemulen spreads his dress, you glide down slowly instead of falling fast. Which force is pushing up against the wide dress?_  
> - ✅ Air resistance: the air pushing back as the cloth moves through it. → Yes. A wide surface catches lots of air, so the air pushes back harder. That is how parachutes work.
> - Magnetism. → Magnetism pulls on magnets and some metals, not on cloth. It is air resistance that slows a wide dress.
> - Gravity. → Gravity pulls you down. The force pushing up against it is air resistance.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that air resistance pushes up against a wide surface and slows a fall, as in a parachute._


**Choices**

- **Hold on tight to Sniff.**
    - Sniff has his eyes shut. He has both paws on you and one foot on his pocket.
    - **Sniff**: Tell me when it’s over. Tell me exactly when.
- **Open your eyes and look down.**
    - Below you the whole country is laid out like a map in red light: the mountains, the dry sea, the river.
    - And at the end of the river, a green valley, and a tall blue house in it like a stove.

#### `a09-10-tornado-done`

_The wind drops you all, gently in the end, in a long meadow, one after the other like washing off a line._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _“One after the other like washing off a line.” What does this simile help you picture?_  
> - ✅ Everyone landing softly in a row, one at a time. → Yes. Washing floats down one piece at a time, which makes the landing look gentle and funny.
> - Everyone crashing down together. → Washing off a line drops softly, not with a crash. The simile shows a gentle, one-by-one landing.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile makes the reader picture._

**The Other Hemulen**: My best dress. My very best dress. It has never been so useful.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): useful or beautiful?  
> _The Hemulen calls it his “best dress” and says it has “never been so useful”._  
> _Is something worth more when it is beautiful, or when it is useful? Think about it._  
> - Beautiful things are worth more, because they bring joy. → That’s a fair answer. Beauty feeds the heart, and a good life needs it.
> - Useful things are worth more, because they help us survive. → That’s a fair answer. A thing that saves lives has a value you can measure.
> - Some things, like this dress, can be both. → That’s a fair answer. The dress was lovely first, and now it has earned a second kind of value.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether beauty or usefulness gives something more worth._


#### `a09-10-run`

_Everyone sits up in the meadow and counts themselves. The Snork counts everyone else, and writes it down._  
**The Snork**: Seven, and a Nubbin, and a cousin. Nobody missing. Nobody even bent.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): adding to count a group  
> _The Snork counts seven friends, plus a Nubbin, plus a cousin. How many is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 9 → Yes. 7 + 1 + 1 = 9.
> - 8 → You have counted one of the extras. There are two extras: the Nubbin and the cousin. 7 + 2 = 9.
> - 10 → Check it: 7, then 8 for the Nubbin, then 9 for the cousin. That is nine.
> _For grown-ups: Added 7 + 1 + 1 to count a group of 9._

_The comet fills a third of the sky now. The light is the colour of the inside of an ember._  
**The Snork Maiden**: How far is it to the valley?  
**Moomintroll**: Over the hill and down through the birch wood. Not far. Not far at all.  
_Snufkin is patting his head. His hat has gone._  
_You look round. It is caught on a thistle three steps away, rocking in the last of the wind._  

**Choices**

- **Run and catch it.**
    - You grab it just as it lifts. It is old and soft and smells of woodsmoke and rain.
    - **Snufkin**: Hold on to it for me. I’ve got my hands full of Sniff.
- **Let your Nubbin fetch it.**
    - Your Nubbin jumps out of Sniff’s pocket, runs, and arrives under the hat, which settles over it completely.
    - The hat walks back to you. Snufkin laughs out loud, for the first time on the whole road.

#### `a09-10-run-done`

_Then you run, all of you, down through the birch wood, the hat in your arms, the comet filling half the sky._  
**Moomintroll**: There! There’s the house! There’s the smoke from the chimney!  
_The comet looks bigger and bigger as you run, the way a cart does as it comes up the lane._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): things look bigger as they come closer  
> _Why does something coming towards you look bigger and bigger?_  
> - ✅ The nearer it is, the more of your view it fills. → Yes. Distance changes how big an object looks. Real comets stay millions of kilometres away, so none ever fills the sky like this one.
> - It really is growing. → It looks that way, but the object does not change size. It only fills more of your view because it is closer.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nearer objects look bigger because they fill more of our view._


#### `a09-10-complete`

_The garden is empty and the house is shut. A note is pinned to the door in Moominmamma’s round writing._  
**Moomintroll**: “Gone to the cave. Come quickly. Have brought the cake.”  
**Sniff**: The cave. Our cave. My cave!  
_The other Hemulen is still holding his dress out, in case. Nobody tells him he can stop._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading a note for character  
> _Moominmamma’s note says where she has gone and mentions the cake. What does it tell us about her?_  
> - ✅ She planned ahead, stayed calm, and is looking after her family. → Yes. She picked a safe place, left a clear message, and even remembered the cake. Her calm is a kind of care.
> - She forgot the family. → She did the opposite. She left a note so they could find her.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s calm and care from the note she left._


### Glossary

- **shingle**: Small, rounded stones on a beach.
- **tornado**: A fast, spinning column of air that reaches from a thundercloud to the ground.

## A9-11. The Cave

- `a09-11-s1`: Get everyone down to the cave on the shore. · _Take Sniff’s secret path. It is the quickest, and it is still a secret, mostly._
- `a09-11-s2`: Choose the one thing you bring into the cave. · _Moominmamma is at the cave mouth. Show her what you are carrying._
- `a09-11-s3`: Sit with Sniff in the dark while the comet comes. · _He is at the very back of the cave. Sit down beside him._

#### `a09-11-arrive`

_Sniff leads the way down his secret path, very fast, with everyone behind him. He does not mention it is a secret._  
_The cave mouth glows. Inside, Moominmamma has made it a room._  
_There are blankets on the sand, and lamps, and the rocking chair, and the clock from the kitchen, ticking._  
**Moominmamma**: There you are. There you all are. And more of you than went.  
_Moomintroll runs into her apron and stays there for a while._  
**Moominmamma**: Come in, all of you. There’s cake. There’s always cake, at the end of the world. That’s what cake is for.  
**Moominpappa**: I brought my memoirs. In case they were needed.  
**The Muskrat**: I brought my hammock. Nobody else thought of the hammock.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what goes in an emergency kit  
> _Moominmamma brought blankets, lamps, a clock and food. Which of these is most useful in a real family emergency kit?_  
> - ✅ Water, food, a torch, a blanket and a first-aid kit. → Yes. Water, food, light, warmth and first aid are the basics for staying safe until help comes. A radio and a list of phone numbers are good additions.
> - A hammock and a book of memoirs. → Lovely for comfort, but the basics are water, food, light, warmth and first aid. Mamma packed some of those, too.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what to put in an emergency kit: water, food, light, warmth and first aid._


#### `a09-11-arrive-done`

_The kitchen clock says half past seven. It ticks very loudly, as clocks do when everybody is listening._  
_The comet is due at 8:42._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _It is 7:30 now, and the comet is due at 8:42. How long is that?_  
> - ✅ 1 hour 12 minutes → Yes. 7:30 to 8:30 is 1 hour, and 8:30 to 8:42 is 12 more minutes.
> - 1 hour 42 minutes → That would be 7:30 to 9:12. Count 7:30 to 8:30 (1 hour) and then 8:30 to 8:42 (12 minutes).
> - 42 minutes → 42 is the minutes on the comet’s time, not the wait. 7:30 to 8:42 is 1 hour and 12 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Found the interval from 7:30 to 8:42 as 1 hour 12 minutes._


#### `a09-11-door`

_Moominmamma stands at the cave mouth with a blanket over her arm, looking at what everybody has carried._  
**Moominmamma**: It’s a small cave, dear, and there are a lot of you now. One thing each, and only what you love fits.  
**Moominmamma**: The rest can wait out here on the rock. It’ll be there in the morning.  
_The Snork puts down his minutes, and the Hemulen his net. Snufkin, who has nothing, keeps it._  
_You empty your pockets on to the rock. The harmonica can wait, and Snufkin’s hat isn’t yours to choose._  
_That leaves three: the shell from the seabed, the garnet Sniff gave you to hold, and your Nubbin._  
_Your arms are only so big._  

> **Lesson** (sel, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): what we choose to carry  
> _“Only what you love fits.” If you can carry only one thing, is it the one worth the most, or the one you would miss most? Think about it._  
> - The one worth the most. → That’s a fair answer. Worth matters, and sensible people think about what could be replaced.
> - The one I would miss the most. → That’s a fair answer. What we love is not always what costs the most.
> - Whatever is alive and needs me. → That’s a fair answer. Something that depends on you, like a Nubbin, can matter more than anything you own.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how we choose what to keep when we cannot keep everything._


**Choices**

- **The shell with no sea in it.**
    - You bring the shell. Your Nubbin, who was never going to be left outside, comes in as Sniff’s one thing.
    - **Moominmamma**: That one’s waiting for something. Yes. Bring it in.
- **The garnet Sniff gave you to hold.**
    - You bring the garnet. Sniff sees, and pretends very hard not to have seen.
    - **Moominmamma**: Somebody’s been generous. That’s worth a lot of room.
- **Nothing but your Nubbin, held in both arms.**
    - You lift your Nubbin out of Sniff’s pocket and hold it in both arms. Everything else you leave on the rock.
    - **Moominmamma**: Yes. That’s the right size for arms.

#### `a09-11-dark`

_The lamps go out one by one, to save oil. The kitchen clock says twenty to nine._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): minutes to the hour  
> _“Twenty to nine” means 20 minutes before nine o’clock. What time is that written as? And how long is it until 8:42?_  
> - ✅ 8:40, so 2 minutes until 8:42. → Yes. Twenty to nine is 8:40, and 8:42 is two minutes later.
> - 9:20, so 22 minutes to go. → “To” means before the hour, so twenty to nine is earlier than nine: 8:40. 8:42 is two minutes after that.
> - 8:20, so 22 minutes to go. → “Twenty to nine” means 20 minutes before 9:00, which is 8:40. “Twenty past eight” would be 8:20.
> _For grown-ups: Read “twenty to nine” as 8:40 and found 2 minutes until 8:42._

_Outside, the sky is so red it comes in at the cave mouth and lies on the sand like a carpet._  
_A sound begins, very far off. It is like the whole sky taking in a breath._  
_Sniff is at the very back of the cave, as far back as there is. You go and sit down beside him._  
_He doesn’t ask you anything this time. You said you didn’t know, and he remembers._  
_In the dark his paw finds your hand and holds on._  
_Neither of you says a word. You sit there together and wait, and that is the whole of what you can do._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): being with someone can matter more than words  
> _Sniff does not need an answer this time. Sometimes the most helpful thing is to sit beside someone and stay._  
> _You cannot take the fear away, but you can be there while they feel it._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that staying with a frightened friend can help even without words._


#### `a09-11-dark-done`

_The kitchen clock says eight forty-two._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): suspense: why a single short line?  
> _This scene is just one short sentence. Why might the writer give the time on a line of its own?_  
> - ✅ To build suspense, so you feel the moment arrive. → Yes. A short line on its own slows time down and makes you hold your breath.
> - The writer ran out of ideas. → Quite the opposite. Ending on a single line is a deliberate choice that creates suspense.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a very short sentence can create suspense._


#### `a09-11-complete`

_Then everything is light and noise. The ground shakes, gently, like a cupboard when a train goes by._  
_Moominmamma’s voice comes through it, quite calm, saying what she always says at bedtime._  
**Moominmamma**: Hush now. Hush. Everyone is here.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): comforting words and staying calm  
> _“Hush now. Everyone is here.” When something frightening happens, calm, familiar words can help us feel safe._  
> _They do not stop the noise, but they remind us we are not alone._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how calm, familiar words comfort us in frightening moments._


### Glossary

- **memoirs**: A book in which someone writes about their own life.
- **suspense**: The tense, waiting feeling you get when you are keen to know what happens next.

## A9-12. The Night It Missed

- `a09-12-s1`: Wait out the night in the cave. · _Stay where you are. It is nearly over._
- `a09-12-s2`: Go out of the cave in the morning and see what the comet left. · _Walk out of the cave mouth and down to the water._
- `a09-12-s3`: Say goodbye to the valley and give Snufkin back his hat. · _Snufkin is at the gate with his pack on. Bring the hat._

#### `a09-12-night`

_The roar goes over. It goes on a long time, and then it is less, and then it is going away._  
_You can feel it going, the way you feel a cart go past in the street with your eyes shut._  
**The Muskrat**: Hm. It seems to have missed. How very unphilosophical of it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): irony and humour  
> _The Muskrat said the end of everything was restful, but now complains the comet “missed”. What makes his remark funny?_  
> - ✅ He sounds disappointed, which shows he did not mean what he said. → Yes. The joke is that his own gloomy view turned out to be less comforting than he claimed. That kind of contrast is called irony.
> - He was never worried. → Perhaps, but the joke is the contrast between his gloomy talk and his disappointed tone. That is irony.
> _For grown-ups: Understood the irony in a character’s remark._

_Somebody laughs in the dark: the Snork Maiden. Then Moomintroll, and then everybody._  
**Sniff**: Has it gone? Is it over? Tell me exactly.  
**Moominpappa**: It brushed us with its tail and went on its way. It had somewhere else to be, I expect.  
_The lamps come back on and Moominmamma cuts the cake. Nobody remembers afterwards if it was good, only that it was there._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): real comets orbit the Sun and almost always pass by  
> _Real comets travel round the Sun on long, stretched-out paths called orbits. Some come back again and again._  
> _The most famous, Halley’s Comet, returns about every 76 years. A real comet almost never comes close to hitting the Earth; it passes at a safe, great distance._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that comets orbit the Sun, that Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years, and that they almost always pass safely._


#### `a09-12-night-done`

_One by one, everybody falls asleep where they are sitting, in a heap, like puppies._  
_It has been a very long day, and a very long night._  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): sleep for growing children  
> _After a big day, everybody falls asleep. How much sleep do children aged 6 to 12 need each night, according to doctors?_  
> - ✅ About 9 to 12 hours → Yes. Children this age need roughly 9 to 12 hours. Sleep helps your body grow and your mind sort out the day.
> - About 4 to 5 hours → That is far too little. Growing children need about 9 to 12 hours.
> - About 15 hours → That is closer to a baby’s needs. Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep._


#### `a09-12-dawn`

_In the morning you wake up with sand in your ear and your Nubbin asleep on your chest._  
_The light at the cave mouth is not red. It is ordinary, yellow, wonderful morning._  
_You go out, and the grey has gone off everything. The grass is green, and wet, and has never looked so like grass._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): sensory words  
> _“Green, and wet, and has never looked so like grass.” Which word here tells you about how grass feels or looks?_  
> - ✅ Wet → Yes. “Wet” is a sense word. It helps you feel the morning, and the green helps you see it.
> - Never → “Never” tells us about time, not the senses. “Wet” and “green” tell us how the grass feels and looks.
> _For grown-ups: Picked out words that describe what the senses notice._

_And the sea is coming back. It comes in over the seabed in long, slow, shining sheets, filling every hollow._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): tides: the sea moves in and out each day  
> _On a real coast, the sea comes back after low tide, twice a day._  
> _The Moon’s pull makes the water rise and fall in a steady rhythm, so the sea always returns._  
> _For grown-ups: Reviewed the idea that tides rise and fall twice a day, driven by the Moon._

**Moomintroll**: It came back. Everything came back.  
**Snufkin**: Things mostly do. Not always. But mostly.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): your view and a character’s: honest comfort  
> _Snufkin says things “mostly” come back, “not always”. Would you rather hear “it will be fine” or “things mostly turn out all right”? Think about it._  
> - “It will be fine” is better, because it comforts. → That’s a fair answer. Comfort has real value, especially when you are small and scared.
> - “Mostly” is better, because it is honest. → That’s a fair answer, and it is Snufkin’s view. Honesty lets us trust the person who comforts us.
> - Both, with the honest one for when we are ready. → That’s a fair answer. Comfort first, truth gently after, is a way to be kind and honest.
> _For grown-ups: Compared their own view with Snufkin’s on comfort and honesty._

_The Hemulen is already in the long grass with his notebook, because there are butterflies._  

#### `a09-12-dawn-done`

_Your Nubbin scrambles down to the water’s edge, sits in the first wave and lets the sea come home round it._  
**Sniff**: It’s all right, then. It’s all right. I can tell, because it’s doing that.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): naming relief  
> _Sniff’s worry has gone. Which word best names how he feels?_  
> - ✅ Relieved → Yes. Relief is the loosening you feel when a worry lifts.
> - Furious → Not furious. Sniff is glad and loose, as the worry lets go. That is relief.
> - Bored → Not bored! He is happy and light, which is relief.
> _For grown-ups: Named relief as the feeling when a worry lifts._


#### `a09-12-gate`

_Snufkin is at the garden gate with his tent on his back. He is going south, in the end._  
_You hold out his hat. He looks at it for a while._  
**Snufkin**: Keep it. I’ll find another. Hats come to me; it’s the strangest thing.  
**Snufkin**: And if I had it back I’d have two again, sooner or later. You know how I feel about two.  
_He puts it on your head, and it comes down over your eyes. Your Nubbin laughs, which is a sort of hiccup._  
**Moominmamma**: Before you go, dear. Something to remember the house by.  
_She gives you a little blue stove, the same blue as the house, small enough to carry and warm in your hands._  
**Moominmamma**: For your own house. Wherever you light it, that’s where people come home to.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: what makes a home  
> _Moominmamma says, “Wherever you light it, that’s where people come home to.” What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ A home is made by the people who gather there, not by the building. → Yes. A warm stove stands for welcome, and welcome can be made anywhere. This is a theme of the whole story.
> - The stove must be lit in a house of the same blue. → She is not talking about colour. She means that a home is wherever people are welcomed and warm.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme that home is made by the people who gather there._


#### `a09-12-gate-done`

_Snufkin is already at the bend in the road. He plays a few notes without looking back, and you play a few back._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-1, notice): migrating birds travel south for winter  
> _Snufkin goes south for the winter. Many birds of the north migrate that way too._  
> _Swallows that nest in Finland spend the winter in southern Africa, many thousands of kilometres away._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that birds from Finland, such as swallows, migrate thousands of kilometres south for winter._

_They come out like a duck in a cupboard. He waves his hand over his head, which means: right note, wrong place._  

> **Lesson** (music, do): call and response  
> _Snufkin plays a call and you answer. Try it: hum three notes (a call) and ask someone to echo them back (the response). Then swap._  
> Check: `edu:play:call-and-response`
> _For grown-ups: Practised call and response by echoing a short tune._

_The page starts to curl at its edges, the way a page does when its story has got where it was going._  
**Moomintroll**: Will you come back? You can, you know. There’ll always be a bed. Mamma keeps a spare one for exactly this.  
**Sniff**: Bring the Nubbin. My pocket will be empty otherwise. It’s a very good pocket.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, notice): thank you in Finnish and Swedish  
> _You were a guest in a Finnish story. In Finnish, “thank you” is “kiitos”. In Swedish, the other national language of Finland, it is “tack”._  
> _Try both aloud. People in Finland often know more than one language, which is a good way to make friends._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned “thank you” in Finnish (kiitos) and Swedish (tack), the two national languages of Finland._

_The blue house, the green valley, the sea coming home: they go flat and still, and they are paper._
