> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme of the whole story  
> _Think about the whole story, from the grey sea to the blue stove. What is it mostly about?_  
> - ✅ Facing something frightening together, and coming home. → Yes. Worry is named, shared and carried by friends, and the story ends with everyone safe and together.
> - How to build a raft. → The raft is one part. The story’s heart is bigger: friends facing a fear together.
> - How to collect butterflies. → That is one funny strand. The main theme is facing a scary thing together, with friends.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of the whole story: facing fear together and coming home._


### Glossary

- **orbit**: The curved path an object takes round another in space.
- **irony**: When what is said or happens is the opposite of what you expect, often for humour.
- **migrate**: To travel a long way each year to find food or a warmer place.

## A10-1. The Chosen One

- `a10-01-s1`: Step onto the island and find the voice telling a story. · _Touch the page, then follow the children’s laughter to the open house._
- `a10-01-s2`: Hear the rest of the story, the frightening bit included. · _Stay in the shade with the children until the story is done._
- `a10-01-s3`: Watch over the baby turtle on the beach. · _Go down to the waterline where the toddler has escaped to._

#### `a10-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page washed in sea-blue. There is an island in the middle of it, very green, ringed with white._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 2-ESS2-2, notice): the Pacific is the largest ocean; maps show land and water  
> _Nova’s page is a map of the Pacific Ocean. The Pacific is the largest ocean on Earth, bigger than all the world’s land put together._  
> _Thousands of islands are scattered across it. Motunui is one tiny green dot among them._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Pacific is the largest ocean and holds thousands of islands._

_The paint goes warm under your hand, then wet. Then it is sand, and you and your Nubbin are standing in it._  
_Behind the palms there is a house with no walls, only a roof on posts. A crowd of small children sits inside it._  
_An old woman is telling them a story with her hands. A painted cloth hangs behind her: an island shaped like a sleeping woman._  
**Gramma Tala**: Before the palms, before the fish, there was the sea and nothing else. Then the mother island came up out of it.  
**Gramma Tala**: Her heart could make things grow. She gave that away to every island she could reach. Green, and more green, and more.  
_She spots you at the edge of the shade, and doesn’t miss a beat. She just shuffles up to make room._  
**Gramma Tala**: Sit, sit. Somebody from past the reef. We don’t get many. Your little one can sit on the end.  
_Your Nubbin sits on the end, beside a toddler with a great deal of hair. The toddler pats it, firmly, like a drum._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile compares  
> _Your Nubbin is patted “firmly, like a drum”. What does that simile tell us about the way the toddler pats?_  
> - ✅ Firmly, with a steady beat, as if she were drumming → Yes. A drum is struck firmly and in rhythm, so the simile gives us the sound and the feel of her pats.
> - Very gently, like stroking a cat → A drum is hit, not stroked. The simile means firm, steady pats.
> - She is not patting it at all → She is patting it, and the simile compares her pats to drumming.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a simile tells us about how a character acts._


#### `a10-01-page-done`

**Gramma Tala**: Now. Where was I? The heart. Everyone wanted it. And one of them came to take it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about why people take what is not theirs  
> **Gramma Tala**: Everyone wanted the heart. And one of them came to take it.  
> _Why might someone take something that was never theirs to take? Think it over._  
> - They were greedy → Greed is one reason. Keep that in mind: later, the story gives a different one.
> - They wanted to be loved or admired → That is a deep answer. People sometimes do wrong things to feel they matter.
> - They did not think anyone would mind → That happens too. Not asking is easier than finding out what others think.
> _For grown-ups: Gave a reason someone might take what is not theirs._


#### `a10-01-story`

**Gramma Tala**: A trickster. A shapeshifter, with a great fish hook the gods gave him. Maui.  
**Gramma Tala**: He took the heart, and the mother island began to crumble. As he fled, a demon of earth and fire rose up after him.  
_Most of the children squeal and hide behind each other. The toddler leans forward, delighted._  
**Gramma Tala**: Maui was struck from the sky, and the heart and his hook fell into the sea. Nobody has found them since.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: knowledge kept by telling  
> _Gramma Tala tells this story by heart. For centuries, Pacific peoples kept stories, family histories and star paths by learning them and telling them aloud._  
> _Each generation had to listen carefully, because the knowledge lived only in people’s memories._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Pacific peoples kept their history by telling it aloud, generation to generation._

**Gramma Tala**: And the darkness is still spreading, island by island. One day it will reach us.  
_A tall man ducks in under the roof, with the face of a father who has heard this story before._  
**Chief Tui**: Mother. That’s enough. They won’t sleep for a week.  
**Chief Tui**: There is no darkness, and nobody here needs to cross the reef. We have fish, we have coconuts, we have each other. That’s plenty.  
_The children scatter. The toddler is carried off under his arm, upside down, still waving at your Nubbin._  
**Gramma Tala**: He’s my son, and he’s a good chief. He’s also wrong. Both at once. You’ll find that’s quite common.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): being good and wrong at once  
> _Gramma Tala says her son is a good chief and also wrong, both at once. Can that be true of a person?_  
> - Yes. Good people can be wrong sometimes → That is a kind way to see it. A mistake does not cancel a person’s goodness.
> - No. A good person is never wrong → That is a strong view. Think of a time a good person you know made a mistake.
> - It depends what they are wrong about → A fair point. Some mistakes are small, and some cost a great deal.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a good person can be wrong._


#### `a10-01-story-done`

_Gramma Tala picks up a stick and walks off towards the shore, humming. She doesn’t look back to see if you follow, and you do._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what actions show about a character  
> _Gramma Tala walks off without checking that you are following. What does that tell us about her?_  
> - ✅ She trusts you and expects you to come along → Yes. She does not look back because she is sure you will follow, and actions can show trust.
> - She has forgotten you are there → She noticed you at once, earlier. Not looking back is a sign of trust, not forgetting.
> - She wants to be left alone → Then she would not have taken you in. She expects you to follow.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s action to work out what she trusts._


#### `a10-01-turtle`

_The toddler has got loose again. She is down on the wet sand, frowning at something small and flat._  
_It is a baby turtle, trying to reach the water. Seabirds circle above it, with ideas._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): a sea turtle’s life cycle  
> _Sea turtles lay eggs in nests dug in warm sand. When the babies hatch, they crawl to the sea by themselves, usually at night._  
> _Only a few survive to be adults. Birds and crabs eat many on the way, which is why the toddler’s leaf-roof matters._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how sea turtles begin life: eggs in sand, then a dangerous crawl to the sea._

_The toddler pulls a big leaf off a bush and holds it over the turtle like a roof. She walks beside it, step by step._  

**Choices**

- **Send your Nubbin to walk on the other side.**
    - Your Nubbin waddles along the other side of the turtle, holding up its arms. Together they make a very small, very slow parade.
- **Wave the birds away.**
    - You flap your arms at the birds, and your Nubbin flaps its tiny wings. The birds decide, on balance, to go and bother someone else.

#### `a10-01-turtle-done`

_The turtle reaches the foam and is gone. The toddler claps, and so does your Nubbin, mostly missing._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): caring for wildlife responsibly  
> _In the story the toddler helps. In real life, hatchlings need to crawl to the sea on their own, and people should not pick them up._  
> _What does help is keeping beach lights off at night, because bright lights can lead hatchlings away from the water._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how people really help baby sea turtles: leave them be and keep lights off._


#### `a10-01-complete`

_Then the sea pulls back from the toddler’s feet, and keeps pulling, and stands up in a wall of clear water._  
_Fish hang in it like flecks in glass. The wall leans down to look at her, the way a dog leans down to a puppy._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile tells us  
> _The water “leans down to look at her, the way a dog leans down to a puppy.” What does this tell you about the ocean?_  
> - ✅ It is huge and gentle, and curious about her → Yes. A big dog leaning to a puppy is careful and interested, so the ocean seems the same.
> - It is about to attack her → A dog leaning down to a puppy is friendly. The simile shows the ocean is gentle.
> - The ocean is really a dog → A simile compares two different things. The sea is like a big, kind dog, but it is still the sea.
> _For grown-ups: Used a simile to understand a character: the ocean._

_It sets a shell in her hands, then another. Then a small green stone with a spiral cut into it._  
**Chief Tui**: Moana! Moana, where are you?  
_The water falls back to being just the sea. The toddler runs to her father’s voice, and the green stone drops in the sand._  
_Gramma Tala bends, slowly, and picks it up. She tucks it into the shell at her neck._  
**Gramma Tala**: The sea picks who it picks, and never explains itself. Grandchildren are the same.  
_The page ripples. When it settles, the palms are taller, and some years have gone by._  

### Glossary

- **trickster**: A character in stories who plays tricks and breaks rules, sometimes to cause trouble and sometimes to help.
- **shapeshifter**: Someone in a story who can change into a different creature or shape.

## A10-2. The Reef

- `a10-02-s1`: Walk the village with the chief’s daughter, and see the coconut trees. · _Meet Moana by the chief’s house and go up to the grove._
- `a10-02-s2`: Go down to the lagoon, where the nets have come in empty. · _Find the fishermen at the boat shelter._
- `a10-02-s3`: Go out to the breakers with Moana, and bring her back in. · _Wade out to the reef edge and be ready to pull._

#### `a10-02-coconuts`

_Moana is sixteen now, and is being taught to be chief, which mostly means people bringing her problems._  
**Moana**: You’re Gramma’s guest! She said you’d come back. She says that about everyone, but she was right this time.  
**Moana**: Come on. The coconut farmers want me. They always want me before breakfast.  
**Coconut farmer**: Look at this. Cracked one open this morning.  
_He holds out a coconut split in half. Inside, where it should be white, it is black and soft and smells of nothing good._  
**Coconut farmer**: Whole trees of them. Not just old trees. Young ones too.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-4, notice): plant disease spreads, and coconuts travel by sea  
> _Plant diseases can spread from tree to tree, which is why farmers clear sick trees and plant new ones on clean ground._  
> _Coconuts float, and sea currents carried them between islands. That is one way coconut palms reached so many shores._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plant diseases spread, and that floating coconuts can cross the sea._

**Moana**: Then we clear those trees and plant a new grove over there. It’s good ground. We just haven’t used it.  
_The farmer nods slowly, which on Motunui means yes, and also means we’ll see._  

**Choices**

- **Offer to dig the first hole for the new grove.**
    - **Coconut farmer**: A guest who digs. Now I’ve seen everything.
    - You dig. Your Nubbin helps by sitting in the hole, to check it is the right size.
- **Ask how long the trees have been sick.**
    - **Coconut farmer**: Since the rains. It started on the far side and walked this way, a tree at a time.
    - Moana looks towards the far side of the island, and then past it, at the sea. She doesn’t say anything.

#### `a10-02-coconuts-done`

**Moana**: That’s one. Next it’ll be the roofs, or the fishing. It’s always the fishing.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): noticing how someone else feels  
> _Moana is learning to be chief, and every problem lands on her. How might she be feeling, do you think?_  
> - Overwhelmed → A good guess. Trouble after trouble before breakfast is a lot to carry.
> - Proud to be trusted → That could be true too. People can feel proud and tired together.
> - Lonely, because nobody else can fix it → That is thoughtful. Being the one people turn to can feel lonely.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how a young leader might feel under pressure._


#### `a10-02-lagoon`

_The fishing canoes are drawn up on the sand, their nets draped over them, dry. Nothing in them but weed._  
**Old fisherman**: Every day, fewer. Today, none. The lagoon’s been fished out, or the fish have gone somewhere.  
**Moana**: Different nets? The far side of the island?  
**Old fisherman**: Tried both. Nothing.  
_Moana looks past the lagoon, to where the waves break white on the reef. Past that, the sea is a darker blue._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): what a reef and a lagoon are  
> _A reef is a ridge of rock or coral just under the sea’s surface. Waves break on it, so the water behind it, the lagoon, stays calm._  
> _That calm water is a safe nursery for young fish, and a good place to fish from a canoe._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a reef shelters a calm lagoon._

**Moana**: Then we go out past the reef. The fish must be out there somewhere.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): scarcity means choosing  
> _When there are fewer fish, the village has to make choices. Which of these is a choice caused by scarcity?_  
> - ✅ Sharing the few fish fairly, or looking for new fishing grounds → Yes. When something runs short, people must decide how to share it or where to find more.
> - Choosing what colour to paint a canoe → A paint colour is a choice, but the fish running short does not cause it.
> - Pretending there is no problem → Ignoring it is not a plan. Scarcity means people must choose how to cope.
> _For grown-ups: Linked fewer fish to the choices a village must make._

_The fishermen go very quiet. One of them looks over your shoulder, where the chief has just walked up._  
**Chief Tui**: We don’t cross the reef.  
**Chief Tui**: We have one rule, and it keeps us safe. You know it. You’ll be chief. You’ll keep it too.  
_Moana opens her mouth, and closes it again. Your Nubbin, sensing a mood, sits on her foot._  

#### `a10-02-lagoon-done`

_The chief walks off. Moana watches the reef for a long time, chewing the inside of her cheek._  
**Moana**: He didn’t say why. He never says why.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a rule that halves each time  
> _Say the lagoon’s catch fell over four days like this: 48 fish, 24, 12, 6. What is the rule, and what comes next?_  
> - ✅ Halve it each day, so 3 fish next → Yes. 48 ÷ 2 = 24, 24 ÷ 2 = 12, 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
> - Take away 6 each day, so 0 fish next → Check it: 48 − 6 is 42, not 24. The amount lost shrinks each day, so the rule is halving.
> - Take away 12 each day → 48 − 12 is 36, not 24. Halving matches every step: the next number is 3.
> _For grown-ups: Found a halving rule in a number pattern and extended it._


#### `a10-02-breakers`

_An hour later, Moana is pushing a small canoe off the sand, with a spotted pig sitting in the front of it._  
**Moana**: That’s Pua. He’s coming for luck. Don’t tell anyone. I’m only going to look.  
_She paddles well in the lagoon. At the reef, the waves come in bigger and closer, one after another, like a crowd at a door._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): coral reefs are built by tiny animals  
> _Coral looks like rock or a plant, but a reef is built by animals. Each coral polyp is tiny, with a soft body and tentacles._  
> _A polyp makes a hard limestone skeleton around itself. Over thousands of years, billions of polyps build a reef big enough to stop ocean waves._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps._

_The third wave lifts the canoe, turns it over, and throws it back towards the beach like a leaf._  
**You**: Moana!  
_You wade in up to your chest. Your Nubbin paddles past you, much faster, its tiny wings going like a fan._  
_Between you, you get hold of her arm, and then Pua, who is very much not enjoying this._  

#### `a10-02-breakers-done`

_Moana sits on the sand with a cut on her foot and the canoe in two pieces beside her. Pua stands well up the beach, sulking._  
**Moana**: Fine. Fine. Point taken.  
_Your Nubbin comes out of the shallows last. In its mouth is a small white shell with a spiral on it, like a tiny staircase._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile compares  
> _The shell has a spiral “like a tiny staircase.” What do a spiral shell and a staircase have in common?_  
> - ✅ Both wind round and round, step by step, to a centre → Yes. A spiral turns round a middle point, as a spiral staircase does.
> - Both are made of wood → Not wood. The simile is about the shape: winding round and round.
> - Both are cold → Temperature is not the point. They share a winding shape.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a shell and a staircase have in common in a simile._


#### `a10-02-complete`

**Moana**: He’s right. I nearly drowned the pig. Maybe I’m meant to stay, and be a good chief, and keep the rule.  
_She looks at the cut on her foot, and not at the reef. It takes some effort._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what helps after a failure  
> _Moana failed, and now she wonders whether she should give up. What helps most after a failure?_  
> - ✅ Rest, work out what went wrong, and try again with help → Yes. Failing teaches, and trying again with a plan and a helper is how people get better.
> - Never try again → Giving up keeps you safe, but it also stops you learning.
> - Blame someone else → Blaming feels easier, but it does not show you what to change.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about learning from a failure and trying again._

_Your Nubbin drops the spiral shell in your hand, very pleased with itself. You put it somewhere safe._  
_Down the beach, out of sight round the point, somebody is laughing on her own, and splashing._  
**Moana**: That’ll be Gramma. She dances with the sea. Everybody thinks she’s odd. She says that’s their business.  

### Glossary

- **grove**: A small group of trees growing together.
- **lagoon**: A calm stretch of shallow sea water, often sheltered by a reef or a ring of coral.
- **reef**: A ridge of rock or coral near the surface of the sea, where waves break.
- **polyp**: A tiny coral animal with a soft body and tentacles that builds a hard skeleton around itself.

## A10-3. Gramma Tala

- `a10-03-s1`: Find Gramma Tala dancing at the water’s edge. · _Walk round the point, to where the waves come in long and low._
- `a10-03-s2`: Let Gramma Tala teach your Nubbin one step. · _Stand in the shallows with your Nubbin and choose a step._
- `a10-03-s3`: Sit on the sand with Gramma and Moana while the tide turns. · _Sit down beside Gramma Tala on the dry sand._

#### `a10-03-point`

_Round the point, the waves come in long and slow. Gramma Tala is dancing in the edge of them, in a skirt that is soaked to the knee._  
_She moves the way the water moves. Forward when it comes in, back when it goes, as if the two of them had rehearsed._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): waves move energy, not water  
> _Wind pushing on the sea makes waves. A wave carries energy across the water, but the water itself mostly just moves up and down in small circles._  
> _That is why a floating coconut bobs on a wave and does not rush ashore with it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that waves carry energy while the water mostly bobs in place._

_On her back, from shoulder to shoulder, is a tattoo of a manta ray. It is old, and the lines have softened, and it is beautiful._  
**Gramma Tala**: Don’t stand there like a post. The sea doesn’t bite. Not today.  
**Moana**: Gramma, you shouldn’t be out here on your own.  
**Gramma Tala**: I’m not on my own. I’ve got the sea, and a guest, and a round little thing with wings. That’s a crowd.  
**Gramma Tala**: Mantas are my favourites. When I’m finished here, that’s what I’ll be. I’ve told everyone. They don’t have to go to meetings.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what humour shows about a character  
> _Gramma says that when she is a manta, she will not have to go to meetings. What does this show about her?_  
> - ✅ She is playful and not afraid of growing old → Yes. She can joke about the future, which shows she is at peace with it.
> - She is cross with everyone → Her tone is warm and teasing, not cross.
> - She wants to leave the island → She is joking about what she will be, not about leaving.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s joke to understand her outlook._

**Moana**: Gramma!  

#### `a10-03-point-done`

_Your Nubbin has crept down into the foam and is trying to copy her. It mostly falls over, very sincerely._  
**Gramma Tala**: Oh, now. That one has the makings.  

> **Lesson** (art, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): dance carries stories  
> _Across the Pacific, dance is more than fun. It is a way of telling stories, remembering people and showing respect for the land and sea._  
> _Gramma’s dance with the waves is part of that long tradition, in the story’s own invented way._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that dance can tell stories and keep memories alive across Pacific cultures._


#### `a10-03-step`

**Gramma Tala**: Come here, small one. Feet in the water. Feel it pull? That’s the sea saying hello.  
_Your Nubbin stands in the foam, rocking a little each time it goes out._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, do): balance: forces and leaning  
> _(Stand with your feet apart. Lean slowly to one side until you feel you might wobble, then come back to centre.)_  
> _You stay up while your weight is over your feet. Lean too far, and the forces are unbalanced, so you fall._  
> Check: `edu:balance:lean:hold`
> _For grown-ups: Felt the balance point when leaning, and learned why leaning too far makes you fall._

**Gramma Tala**: I’ve got two steps for a beginner. One for the manta, one for the wave. You only get one today. I’m old, my knees are older.  
**Gramma Tala**: Which shall it be?  

**Choices**

- **The stingray glide.**
    - **Gramma Tala**: Arms out wide, and soft. Lean, and let the sea carry you sideways. Don’t flap. Mantas never flap. They fly in the water.
    - Your Nubbin spreads its arms, leans, and slides along the foam on one foot, perfectly level, for very nearly a second.
- **The wave step.**
    - **Gramma Tala**: Up on your toes when it comes in. Down and back when it goes. Roll your arms like the water rolls over itself.
    - Your Nubbin rises, sinks, rises, rolling its little arms, a beat behind the sea and then, suddenly, right on it.

#### `a10-03-step-done`

**Gramma Tala**: There. That’s yours now. A step’s like a name. Once somebody’s taught it to you, it doesn’t come off.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile means  
> _Gramma says, “A step’s like a name. Once somebody’s taught it to you, it doesn’t come off.” What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ What you are given with love belongs to you for good → Yes. A name, or a step, is yours once someone gives it to you.
> - Names are written in ink → She does not mean ink. “Doesn’t come off” means it cannot be taken away.
> - You must never learn another step → She is describing how teaching lasts, not forbidding new things.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of a simile about learning._


#### `a10-03-sand`

_Gramma sits down on the dry sand with a noise like a sack of shells. Moana sits beside her, and you on the other side._  
**Moana**: I tried to go past the reef this morning. I nearly drowned Pua.  
**Gramma Tala**: I know. I saw. You went out on the wrong side, in the wrong boat, at the wrong tide. Otherwise, very good.  
**Moana**: Dad says the reef keeps us safe.  
**Gramma Tala**: It does. Safe is a good thing. It isn’t the only thing.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): is safe the same as well?  
> _Gramma says safe is a good thing, but not the only thing. Is being safe the same as being well?_  
> - Safe is what matters most → Staying safe is very important. Think about what you would miss if you stayed safe all the time.
> - Safe can mean missing things that make life good → That is what Gramma seems to mean: a very small life is safe, but may not be a full one.
> - Both matter, and it depends on the risk → A wise answer. Good decisions weigh the danger against what is gained.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being safe is the same as being well._

**Gramma Tala**: Your father once had a reason for his rule. You should ask him for it, one day. Gently.  
_She looks at Moana for a long moment, as if she is weighing something in her hand._  
**Gramma Tala**: You’ve got a question in you the size of a canoe. You always have. Ask it.  

#### `a10-03-sand-done`

**Moana**: Who we are. Where we came from. Why we never leave.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): genealogies: knowing who we come from  
> _Moana asks who they are and where they came from. Pacific peoples answered with genealogy: a spoken record of ancestors, back to the first._  
> _Reciting a genealogy told you where you belonged, and who had come before you._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Pacific peoples used spoken genealogies to say who they are and where they come from._

**Gramma Tala**: Good. Get your guest. Bring a torch. It’s a walk.  

#### `a10-03-complete`

_Gramma gets up, which takes three tries and a hand from you. She does not mention the hand._  
_Your Nubbin walks behind her up the beach, still doing its step, a little crooked, every few paces._  
**Gramma Tala**: It’ll come. Everything worth having comes slow. Mantas, grandchildren, steps.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to find a total  
> _Gramma says everything worth having comes slowly. If your Nubbin practises its step for 5 minutes a day for 12 days, how many minutes is that?_  
> - ✅ 60 minutes, which is one hour → Yes: 12 × 5 = 60, and 60 minutes make one hour. Slow practice adds up.
> - 17 minutes → 17 is 12 + 5. Each of the 12 days has 5 minutes, so multiply: 12 × 5 = 60.
> - 50 minutes → Close: 10 days would be 50. With 12 days it is 12 × 5 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal daily amounts of practice time and converted to hours._


### Glossary

- **genealogy**: A record of a family’s ancestors, naming each generation back through time.

## A10-4. The Cave of Canoes

- `a10-04-s1`: Follow Gramma Tala behind the waterfall. · _Carry the torch up the stream to where the water falls over the rocks._
- `a10-04-s2`: Find what is hidden at the bottom of the cave. · _Go down the passage and look at the shapes in the dark._
- `a10-04-s3`: Watch what the drum remembers. · _Stand back while Moana beats the drum._

#### `a10-04-falls`

_Gramma leads you up a stream to a rock face with a waterfall coming down it, thin and noisy._  
**Gramma Tala**: There. Behind it. I’ve been waiting a long time to show somebody. You first, Moana. Guest second. Round one third.  
_Moana looks at the waterfall, then at Gramma, and steps through. You hear her gasp on the other side._  
_You follow, and the water hits your head like a cold hand. Your Nubbin goes through at a run with its eyes shut._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): moving water wears away rock  
> _Falling water is strong. Over thousands of years it wears away the rock below it, a process called erosion._  
> _That is how some waterfalls cut hollows behind them, big enough to hide a passage._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that falling water slowly erodes rock and can carve hollows._

_Behind the falls there is a passage in the rock, sloping down, and the sound of the sea somewhere at the bottom of it._  
**Gramma Tala**: Go on, then. Light the way. I’ll be along. My knees take the long way round.  

#### `a10-04-falls-done`

_The torch makes the wet rock shine. Your Nubbin’s emote ball glows a little too, which is no help but is company._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a narrator’s joke means  
> _Your Nubbin’s emote ball glows, “which is no help but is company.” What does the narrator mean?_  
> - ✅ It does not light the way, but it is nice not to be alone → Yes. Light helps you see and company helps you feel brave, but the glow gives only the second.
> - The ball is broken → The glow is working. It just does not give enough light to see by.
> - Nubbins are afraid of caves → The line is about comfort, not about fear of caves.
> _For grown-ups: Understood a narrator’s dry joke about comfort._


#### `a10-04-canoes`

_The passage opens into a cavern as big as the meeting house. A dim blue light comes in from the sea at the far end._  
_Moana lifts the torch, and the shapes in the dark turn into boats._  
_Not fishing canoes. Great voyaging canoes, twin-hulled, with their sails furled and their steering oars laid along the decks._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): real voyaging canoes  
> _Real Pacific voyaging canoes were often double-hulled, two hulls joined by a deck. In Hawaiian this is a waʻa kaulua._  
> _Builders lashed them together with cord made from plant fibre, and the canoes carried families, plants and animals across open ocean._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Pacific peoples built double-hulled voyaging canoes lashed with plant-fibre cord._

_There are dozens of them, under dust and cobweb, and every one is finer than anything on the beach._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to find a total  
> _There are dozens of canoes. Say there are 4 rows with a dozen in each row: how many canoes are there?_  
> - ✅ 48 → Yes. A dozen is 12, and 4 × 12 = 48.
> - 16 → 16 is 4 × 4. A dozen is 12, so each row has 12: 4 × 12 = 48.
> - 412 → That glues the numbers together. Multiply: 4 × 12 = 48.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied rows by a dozen to find 48._

**Moana**: Whose are these? Who built them? We don’t build these. Nobody builds these.  
_Your Nubbin climbs up onto the nearest hull and sits there, very small, under a mast as tall as a tree._  
_At the front of the cave is a great drum. The skin is old, but tight._  

**Choices**

- **Brush the dust off the nearest prow.**
    - Under the dust the wood is carved: waves, stars, and a long line of small figures, each with a hand on the next one’s shoulder.
- **Hold the torch high so Moana can see.**
    - You hold the torch up. Moana walks the length of the cave touching each hull as she passes, the way you’d count heads.

#### `a10-04-canoes-done`

**Gramma Tala**: Bang the drum, Moana. Go on. It’s been waiting for you.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): sound and vibration  
> _When Moana hits the drum, its skin vibrates, and the shaking passes to the air as sound._  
> _A big drum vibrates slowly, so it makes a deep sound. A small drum vibrates faster and sounds higher._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that vibrations make sound, and that bigger drums sound deeper._


#### `a10-04-drum`

_Moana beats the drum once. The sound goes all round the cave and comes back bigger._  
_She beats it again, and again, and the torchlight seems to move on the sails, as if a wind were filling them._  
_Then you are not in a cave. You are on the open sea, on the deck of one of those canoes, in full sail under the stars._  
_All round you are more canoes, and on them people steering, singing, reading the sky, laughing at the tops of their voices._  
_A woman at a steering oar looks straight at you and grins, the way you’d grin at someone who has nearly worked out a joke._  
_They find an island, and land, and plant, and build. Then they load the canoes again and sail on to find the next one._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Pacific settlement and canoe plants  
> _Over more than two thousand years, voyagers settled islands from Tonga and Samoa out to Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa New Zealand._  
> _They carried “canoe plants” like coconut, taro and breadfruit, and animals like pigs and chickens, to start new homes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how Pacific voyagers settled distant islands and carried plants and animals with them._

_Your Nubbin, on the deck beside you, is doing its step without seeming to know it._  

#### `a10-04-drum-done`

_The drum stops ringing. You are in the cave again, with dust on your feet and the sound of the sea at the far end._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply rate by time  
> _A steady drum beats twice every second. How many beats are there in 30 seconds?_  
> - ✅ 60 → Yes. 2 beats × 30 seconds = 60 beats.
> - 32 → 32 is 30 + 2. Each second has 2 beats, so multiply: 2 × 30 = 60.
> - 15 → 15 is 30 ÷ 2, which would be one beat every two seconds. This drum beats twice a second, so 60.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied beats per second by seconds to find a total._


#### `a10-04-complete`

**Moana**: They didn’t stay. They went. Every island, they found it and they left it and went on. We did that.  
**Gramma Tala**: We did. Until the darkness came, and the boats stopped coming home, and the chiefs said: no more. Stay inside the reef.  
**Gramma Tala**: And we hid the boats. And we forgot. All but a few of us, being stubborn.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): good decisions that cost something later  
> _The chiefs hid the boats to keep everyone safe, and in time people forgot who they were. Was that a good choice?_  
> - Yes, it kept people alive → Safety matters. But notice the cost: the people lost a part of their story.
> - No, forgetting cost too much → That is a strong view. Think about whether there was another way to be safe and remember.
> - It was good then and poor later → A subtle answer. Choices can fit one time and not the next.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about a decision that protected people now but cost them later._

_Gramma opens the shell at her neck and takes out the green stone with the spiral on it._  
**Gramma Tala**: The ocean gave you this when you were small. I kept it for you. It’s the heart of Te Fiti, the mother island.  
**Gramma Tala**: The darkness is here, Moana. The coconuts, the fish. Someone has to find Maui and make him put it back.  
**Moana**: I have to tell Dad. Now. Right now.  
_She is out of the cave before Gramma has finished smiling. Your Nubbin runs after her, and then back for you._  

### Glossary

- **voyaging**: Making long journeys, especially across the sea.
- **hull**: The main body of a boat, which floats on the water.

## A10-5. Setting Sail

- `a10-05-s1`: Stand by Moana while she tells the chief what she found. · _Go to the meeting house, where the elders are gathered._
- `a10-05-s2`: Sit with Gramma Tala in her house. · _Go to Gramma’s house and sit by her mat._
- `a10-05-s3`: Carry food and water down to the hidden canoe in the dark. · _Take the bundles from Sina and carry them to the cave’s sea mouth._

#### `a10-05-council`

_Moana bursts into the meeting house with cobweb in her hair. The elders look up from a very long talk about roof thatch._  
**Moana**: Our people sailed. There are boats in a cave, real boats, and we can find more fish, and Maui, and fix everything.  
**Chief Tui**: The cave. She showed you the cave.  
**Moana**: You knew? You knew, and you never…  
**Chief Tui**: We are not going past the reef. I’ll burn those boats before I see one leave this beach.  
_The meeting house goes very still. Somebody puts down a roof bundle without a sound._  
**Chief Tui**: When I was your age, I went past the reef. My best friend came with me. The sea was rough, and I came home, and he died out there.  
**Chief Tui**: I won’t lose you to it. I won’t.  
_For a moment he isn’t a chief at all, only a man who has been afraid for a very long time._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): is fear a good reason for a rule?  
> _Tui would burn the boats to keep Moana safe. Is fear a good reason to make a rule?_  
> - Yes. Fear can protect people → Fear can warn us of real danger. Ask whether the rule still fits the danger today.
> - No. Fear makes rules that are too big → Often it does. A rule made from grief can keep out safety and joy together.
> - It is a starting point, and the rule should be checked → A wise answer. Fear tells us something matters, then we have to look at it clearly.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether fear is a good basis for a rule._


#### `a10-05-council-done`

_Then a boy runs in from outside, breathless, with news: Gramma Tala has fallen, down by the shore._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how a plot event changes a scene  
> _Just as Moana and Tui reach their worst moment, a boy runs in with news. What does this do to the story?_  
> - ✅ It interrupts the argument and shifts what matters most → Yes. The news breaks the argument off and turns everyone’s attention to Gramma Tala.
> - It makes the argument longer → The boy’s news stops the argument. Something more urgent has come up.
> - It solves the problem → Nothing is solved. It simply changes what everyone must do next.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how a sudden event shifts the direction of a scene._


#### `a10-05-bedside`

_Gramma lies on her mat with a healer beside her. She is very small all of a sudden, and her hands are cool._  
_Moana kneels by her head, and you sit at the foot. Your Nubbin sits on the mat, carefully, as if it knows._  
**Gramma Tala**: Don’t fuss. I’m old. Old people do this. It’s allowed.  
**Gramma Tala**: You have to go. Tonight. While your father is busy being frightened of the right thing for the wrong reason.  
**Moana**: I can’t leave you. Not now.  
**Gramma Tala**: I’ll be the bit of you that keeps going when you want to stop. That’s not poetry. That’s just how grandmothers work.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): grief can come before a death  
> _When someone we love is very old or ill, we can feel sad before anything has happened. That is normal._  
> _Spending time with them and saying what is in your heart can help, as Moana is doing._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sadness about a loved one’s illness is normal and that spending time together helps._

_She presses the shell with the heart in it into Moana’s hand and folds her fingers over it._  
**Gramma Tala**: Find Maui. Take him across the sea. Make him give it back. And mind your guest. Guests are a responsibility.  
_Then she turns her head to your Nubbin, and smiles, and moves one hand on the mat, in the step she taught it._  

#### `a10-05-bedside-done`

**Gramma Tala**: Go on, my girl. I’m so proud of you.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): writing or saying a short message to someone you love  
> _(Think of someone you love. Say to them, or write down, one thing you most want them to know.)_  
> _Gramma Tala made sure Moana knew she was proud of her. Words like that stay with people._  
> Check: `edu:write:kind-words`

#### `a10-05-pack`

_In Moana’s house, someone is already packing. It’s her mother, Sina, folding food into bundles by the light of one lamp._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how drying keeps food  
> _Sina packs dried fish. Drying takes the water out of food, and without water, the bacteria and moulds that spoil food cannot grow._  
> _That is why dried and salted food can last for weeks on a long voyage._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that drying food stops it spoiling, so it keeps on long voyages._

**Sina**: Dried fish. Coconuts, the good ones. Water. More water. You always forget water.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to find a total  
> _Sina says you always forget water. If Moana needs 3 gourds a day for 7 days, how many gourds must she load?_  
> - ✅ 21 → Yes. 7 days of 3 gourds each: 7 × 3 = 21.
> - 10 → 10 is 3 + 7. Each day needs its own 3 gourds, so multiply: 7 × 3 = 21.
> - 4 → 4 is the difference. Count equal groups instead: seven groups of 3 is 21.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied gourds per day by days to plan supplies._

**Moana**: Mum. I…  
**Sina**: I know. I heard. I’m not going to stop you. I’m going to make sure you’ve got enough to eat.  
_She holds Moana for a long time. Then she holds you, briefly, as if you were hers too, and hands you a bundle._  
_You carry the bundles down the dark path to the cave’s sea mouth, where Moana has dragged out the smallest of the canoes._  
_It still looks enormous. Moana loads it with her jaw set and her hands shaking._  

**Choices**

- **Hold the canoe steady while she loads.**
    - You hold the hull still against the swell. By the third bundle her hands are steadier, or she has stopped letting you see.
- **Tell her what Sina said about water.**
    - **Moana**: I do always forget water.
    - She counts the water gourds out loud, all of them, and then once more, for her mother.

#### `a10-05-pack-done`

_When you turn round, your Nubbin is gone. So is the village rooster, Heihei, who is not known for going anywhere on purpose._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): predict from clues in the story  
> _Your Nubbin and Heihei have gone missing, and Heihei is “not known for going anywhere on purpose.” What can you predict?_  
> - ✅ Heihei followed your Nubbin, perhaps onto the canoe → A good guess. The clue is that Heihei never goes anywhere on purpose, so he probably tagged along.
> - Heihei flew to another island → Chickens cannot fly that far, and he does nothing on purpose. A nearby hiding place is likelier.
> - Nobody can possibly guess → The story gives clues. Heihei follows and wanders, so the canoe is a good bet.
> _For grown-ups: Predicted what happens next using clues about a character._


#### `a10-05-complete`

_Moana pushes the canoe off into the dark lagoon. The sail goes up crooked, and she doesn’t know how to fix it yet._  
_From under the deck at the bow comes a small, determined cluck, and then a small, determined squeak._  
**You**: Wait! Moana! My Nubbin’s in your boat!  
_You wade in after it, up to your waist, up to your chest. Then the sea lifts you, quite gently, and puts you on the deck._  
**Moana**: Did the ocean just give me a passenger?  
_Behind you, on the shore, the lamps are lit in Gramma Tala’s house. As you watch, the brightest of them goes out._  
_Gramma Tala has died, quietly, with her family round her. Moana sees the light go, and knows._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): grief and what helps  
> _When someone dies, their body stops working and cannot start again. Grief can feel like sadness, anger, tiredness, or even a sudden laugh._  
> _All of that is normal. It helps to tell someone, remember the person together, and do something in their honour._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what dying means, that grief has many feelings, and what helps._

_Then, under the canoe, something glows. A great manta ray, lit from inside, glides past beneath you and out through the reef._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how a manta ray feeds  
> _A real manta ray can have a wingspan of up to about seven metres. It eats tiny drifting animals called plankton, which it strains from the water as it swims._  
> _Two flaps on either side of its mouth, called cephalic fins, help funnel the water in._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a manta ray’s body helps it feed on plankton._

_Moana wipes her eyes, and turns the canoe after it._  

### Glossary

- **elders**: The oldest and most respected people in a community.

## A10-6. Maui

- `a10-06-s1`: Ride out the storm in the canoe. · _Bail water and hold on to the mast._
- `a10-06-s2`: Meet the demigod on his rock. · _Walk up the beach towards the giant shadow._
- `a10-06-s3`: Get out of the cave Maui shut you in. · _Climb up inside the great carved figure to the hole at the top._

#### `a10-06-storm`

_The first day is blue and easy. Your Nubbin and Heihei come out of the hull and sit on the deck, both looking surprised to be at sea._  
**Moana**: Gramma said to sail by the hook-shaped stars. Those. There. I think. Maybe.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 5-ESS1-2, notice): Maui’s fishhook in the stars  
> _In Hawaiʻi and across Polynesia, the curved tail of the constellation Scorpius is told as Maui’s great fishhook._  
> _Navigators used it, with other stars, to keep their direction on the open sea._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Polynesian stories see Maui’s fishhook in the constellation Scorpius._

_On the second night a storm comes up out of nowhere, black and loud, and the sea stands up in hills._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): how tropical storms form  
> _Tropical storms grow over warm ocean water, about 26.5 °C (80 °F) or more, where warm, moist air rises and spins._  
> _Pacific sailors learned the signs of a coming storm: swell patterns, wind shifts and clouds._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tropical storms form over warm seas, and that sailors read the signs._

**Moana**: Bail! Bail, and hold on to something!  
_You bail with a coconut shell. Your Nubbin bails with its hands, very fast, mostly onto you._  
_A wave the size of the meeting house rolls the canoe over, and everything goes dark and cold and loud._  

#### `a10-06-storm-done`

_You wake on a beach with sand in your mouth. The canoe lies tipped on its side nearby, and Moana is shaking water out of her ears._  
_Your Nubbin is asleep on top of Heihei, who hasn’t noticed._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what makes a line funny  
> _“Your Nubbin is asleep on top of Heihei, who hasn’t noticed.” What makes this line funny?_  
> - ✅ Heihei is too oblivious to notice, right after a terrifying storm → Yes. The calm, silly detail contrasts with the danger just before it.
> - Heihei is badly hurt → Nobody is hurt. The humour comes from Heihei being clueless.
> - Nubbins always sleep on chickens → The joke is about this moment, and about Heihei missing everything.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a calm, silly detail after a scary scene creates humour._


#### `a10-06-maui`

_A shadow falls across the beach. It belongs to a man the size of a small hill, with hair like a storm cloud and a broad grin._  
_Every part of his skin that you can see is covered in tattoos. Each one is a picture of a great deed._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): tattoo as a record, with respect  
> _In many Pacific cultures, tattoo (tatau in Samoa, tā moko in Aotearoa, kākau in Hawaiʻi) records a person’s family, rank and deeds._  
> _Trained experts make them, and they are sacred and personal: not decoration to copy for fun._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that traditional Pacific tattoos record family and deeds and deserve respect._

**Maui**: Visitors! At last. A thousand years on a rock, and finally, an audience. You’ll want to know who I am.  
**Maui**: Maui. I pulled islands up out of the sea on a fishing line. I slowed the sun so your days would be long enough.  
**Maui**: I brought fire down to people so they could cook. Most people like to say thank you. Some of them cry. Either is fine.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): pride and boasting  
> _Maui lists his great deeds and says some people cry with thanks. Is there a difference between being proud of what you have done and boasting?_  
> - Pride is quiet and boasting is loud → That is one way to tell. Boasting often wants others to react.
> - Boasting is pride that needs an audience → A sharp answer. Maui does call his visitors an audience.
> - They are the same thing → Some people feel that way. Ask what each one wants from other people.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between being proud and boasting._

_He leans down to your Nubbin, which leans back._  
**Maui**: And what is this? A coconut with opinions?  
**Moana**: My island is dying because of what you took. I’m Moana, and you’re coming with me to put it back.  
**Maui**: Am I.  

**Choices**

- **Thank him for the long days.**
    - **Maui**: See? Somebody was brought up properly.
    - Moana gives you a long look. You are supposed to be on her side.
- **Keep your Nubbin behind your legs.**
    - Your Nubbin peers round your knee at him, and Maui peers back. Your Nubbin doesn’t blink first, which bothers him more than it should.

#### `a10-06-maui-done`

**Maui**: Thanks for the boat, by the way. I’ve been waiting a very long time for a boat.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a quick line shows about a character  
> _Maui thanks you for the boat, “by the way.” What does that tell us about him?_  
> - ✅ He has already decided to take it, and the thanks is a polite excuse → Yes. After a thousand years on a rock, a boat is exactly what he wants.
> - He is giving the boat back → He is thanking you, not returning it.
> - He does not care about boats → He has waited a long time for one, so he cares a great deal.
> _For grown-ups: Read a throwaway line to understand a character’s plan._


#### `a10-06-statue`

_Somehow, in the space of three boasts, he has herded you all into a cave and rolled a boulder over the mouth._  
**Moana**: He’s taking the boat. He is taking my boat!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): using anger well  
> _Moana is furious that Maui is taking her boat. What helps people use anger well, instead of just exploding?_  
> - ✅ Breathe, then turn it into a plan, as Moana does by climbing out → Yes. Anger can give you energy, and a plan points it somewhere useful.
> - Shout until it goes away → Shouting lets off steam, but it rarely solves the problem.
> - Pretend you are not angry → Hiding it does not help. Naming it and steering it does.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about turning anger into a plan._

_Inside the cave there is a huge stone figure of Maui, carved by somebody who admired him very much. It is hollow._  
_Moana starts climbing up inside it. You go after her, with your Nubbin riding on your shoulder._  
_At the top is a hole, and through the hole is the sky, and far below is the sea and a canoe sailing away from the island._  
**Moana**: Right.  
_She jumps, and you shut your eyes and jump after her. Your Nubbin shuts its eyes too, which is unnecessary, as it is already falling._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide to find how long  
> _Say the hollow statue is 30 metres tall and Moana climbs 5 metres each minute. How many minutes does she take to reach the top?_  
> - ✅ 6 minutes → Yes. 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
> - 25 minutes → 25 is 30 − 5. Ask how many 5s fit into 30: 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
> - 150 minutes → 150 is 30 × 5. Division fits here: six 5-metre climbs make 30.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a height by a climbing rate to find the time._


#### `a10-06-statue-done`

_The sea catches you all like a hand. It sets you on the canoe’s deck in a neat row, damp and blinking._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): personification  
> _In this story the ocean acts like a character that makes choices. Which detail shows this best?_  
> - ✅ It sets you on the deck in a neat row, as though it cares → Yes. Catching you like a hand and setting you down gently is how a person would act.
> - It is blue and wet → Those are facts about water. We want a detail that shows choice.
> - It is very deep → Depth is a fact too. Look for something the sea does on purpose.
> _For grown-ups: Found a detail that shows the sea acting like a character._

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add to find a total  
> _The sea puts Moana back twice, your Nubbin once, and Heihei once. How many times does the sea put someone back on board?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.
> - 3 → Count again: Moana twice, Nubbin once, Heihei once. 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.
> - 5 → That is one too many. Moana 2, Nubbin 1, Heihei 1 makes 4.
> _For grown-ups: Added small numbers to count how often the sea returned the passengers._


### Glossary

- **tattoo**: A design marked into the skin for life. In many Pacific cultures, tattoos record a person’s family and deeds, and are made by trained experts.
- **deed**: Something a person does, especially something brave or important.

## A10-7. The Kakamora

- `a10-07-s1`: Watch the strange boat come out of the fog. · _Stand at the stern and look into the fog bank._
- `a10-07-s2`: Get Heihei back from the pirates. · _Follow Moana across to the big raft. Your Nubbin will be welcome there._
- `a10-07-s3`: Get the canoe clear of the pirate raft. · _Take the sheet line and hold the sail tight while Maui steers._

#### `a10-07-fog`

_Maui has agreed to nothing, but he is steering, which Moana is counting as a start._  
_A fog bank lies across the sea ahead. Out of it comes a sound of drums, and then a boat made of driftwood and lashed-together logs._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): how sea fog forms  
> _Fog forms when warm, moist air drifts over cooler water. The air cools, and its water vapour turns into tiny droplets that hang in the air._  
> _Fog is really a cloud sitting on the sea, which is why it is so hard to see far._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fog is a cloud at the surface, formed when warm moist air cools._

_Then another boat, and another, all joined into one great floating raft, crewed by little round people in coconut armour._  
_Each one has a face painted on the front of its coconut. Some faces are fierce; some are just very proud of their paint._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiply to find a total  
> _Say the raft is made of 5 boats, and each boat has 8 Kakamora. How many Kakamora in all?_  
> - ✅ 40 → Yes. Five groups of 8: 5 × 8 = 40.
> - 13 → 13 is 5 + 8. There are 5 groups of 8, so multiply: 5 × 8 = 40.
> - 58 → That joins the digits. Multiply instead: 5 × 8 = 40.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups to count a crowd._

**Maui**: Kakamora. Pirates. Everything they see, they take. Including small things. Including you.  
_Your Nubbin looks at the Kakamora, and the Kakamora look at your Nubbin. A long, round silence passes between them._  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin wave at them.**
    - Your Nubbin waves. Forty coconuts wave back, slowly, all at once, which is somehow worse than drums.
- **Scoop your Nubbin up and hold it close.**
    - You pick your Nubbin up. Across the water, several painted faces look hurt, and one of them looks at you.

#### `a10-07-fog-done`

**Moana**: Why are they looking at it like that?  
**Maui**: They think it’s one of theirs. A little one. That has lost its coconut.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): a character’s point of view  
> _Maui says the Kakamora think your Nubbin is “one of theirs.” From their side, what is happening, and do they believe they are being bad?_  
> - They think they are welcoming a lost friend → That fits what they do next. Someone can act kindly and still be a pirate.
> - They know they are pirates and do not mind → Possible. People do not always see themselves as the villain, though.
> - They do not think much at all, they just love shiny small things → A fair guess. Their fondness for your Nubbin is simple and warm.
> _For grown-ups: Considered how the Kakamora see a situation differently from the heroes._


#### `a10-07-chase`

_Darts thunk into the deck as coconut-armoured pirates swarm aboard. One of them grabs Heihei and scampers off with him._  
**Moana**: Heihei’s swallowed the heart! I saw him! He thought it was a pebble!  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): why chickens swallow stones  
> _Heihei thought the heart was a pebble, and real chickens do swallow small stones on purpose._  
> _The stones sit in a muscular part of the body called the gizzard and help grind up hard seeds, since chickens have no teeth._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that chickens swallow small stones to grind food in their gizzards._

**Maui**: Then I’d say goodbye to the heart. And the chicken. Lovely chicken.  
_Moana jumps across to the pirate raft. Your Nubbin, after a moment’s thought, jumps after her._  
_The Kakamora part to let it through, and some of them pat it. One of them paints a fierce face on its tummy._  
_Your Nubbin walks straight through their ranks to Heihei, picks him up under one arm, and walks back out again._  
_Nobody stops it. They are too busy cheering what they think is the smallest pirate they have ever seen._  

#### `a10-07-chase-done`

_Moana swings back across on a rope with your Nubbin clinging to her back, and Heihei clinging to your Nubbin._  
_Heihei is calmly eating a dart._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple meanings of a word  
> _Heihei is “calmly eating a dart”, a small pointed missile. What else can the word “dart” mean?_  
> - ✅ To move suddenly and quickly → Yes. A fish can dart away, and Moana darts across the raft.
> - To sleep for a long time → Not that. To dart is to dash quickly.
> - A kind of drum → A drum is a drum. “Dart” as a verb means to move fast.
> _For grown-ups: Learned a second meaning of “dart”._


#### `a10-07-escape`

**Maui**: Hold that line! Tighter! No, the other line!  
_You hold a rope that hums like a bowstring. The canoe leans over and leaps away._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): sails and forces  
> _Wind pushes on a sail. Pulling the rope, called the sheet, changes the angle of the sail to the wind, so the push can drive the canoe forward or sideways._  
> _Sailors balance that push against the water’s grip on the hulls, trimming the sheet as the wind changes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the angle of a sail changes how the wind pushes a canoe._

_The raft comes after you, drums going, faster than anything that big should be._  
_Moana scrambles to the bow, finds the gap between two raft-boats, and points._  
**Moana**: There! Go between them!  
_Maui swings the steering oar and the canoe shoots through the gap. Behind you, the two halves of the raft bump, and come unlashed._  

#### `a10-07-escape-done`

_The pirates drift away in the fog, drumming crossly, in two directions at once._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple meanings of a word: cross  
> _The pirates drift off “drumming crossly.” The word cross has more than one meaning. Which one fits here?_  
> - ✅ Grumpy and annoyed → Yes. Crossly means in a grumpy way. They are cross about losing Heihei.
> - Going from one side to the other → That is another meaning: you cross the sea. Here crossly means grumpily.
> - Shaped like an X → A cross can be an X shape, but crossly describes their mood: grumpy.
> _For grown-ups: Chose the right meaning of a word with several meanings (cross)._


#### `a10-07-complete`

_Heihei coughs up the green stone onto the deck with no fuss at all. Moana washes it, twice._  
**Moana**: Now. You’ll help me. You owe me. I saved your boat.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness and claims  
> _Moana says, “You owe me. I saved your boat.” Maui answers, “My boat.” Does saving something give you a claim on it?_  
> - Saving it earns thanks, not ownership → A clear view. Gratitude and ownership are different things.
> - Yes, Maui owes her something for it → Perhaps a favour, even if not the boat. Debts of kindness are real.
> - It depends who owned the boat first → Fair. Who built or found it matters in deciding whose it is.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether doing someone a favour gives a claim on what you saved._

**Maui**: My boat.  
**Maui**: Listen. Te Fiti’s heart has a demon of fire guarding it. Te Kā. I can’t get past Te Kā without my hook.  
**Maui**: And my hook is at the bottom of the world, in the Realm of Monsters. And you can’t even sail.  
**Moana**: Then teach me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): asking for help when you are cross  
> _Moana asks Maui to teach her, even though she is cross with him. Why is asking hard, and why is it brave?_  
> - ✅ It means putting pride aside to get something that matters → Yes. Asking means admitting you need something, and that takes courage.
> - It is easy, so it is not brave → It can feel easy, but when you are cross with someone it is very hard to ask them for help.
> - Nobody should ever ask for help → Everyone needs help sometimes. Asking is how we learn.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about why asking for help can be brave._

_Your Nubbin still has a fierce face painted on its tummy. It looks down at it, often, with pride._

## A10-8. Wayfinding

- `a10-08-s1`: Learn to read the stars with your hand. · _Sit at the stern after dark and hold your hand out to the horizon._
- `a10-08-s2`: Feel the swell through the hull. · _Lie down on the deck and put one hand flat on the wood._
- `a10-08-s3`: Watch for the bird that is going home. · _At dusk, keep watch from the bow for a single bird._

#### `a10-08-stars`

_Night falls clear. The sky is so full of stars that it looks crowded._  
**Maui**: Right. You want to sail, you start with the stars. Hold your hand out. Flat. Little finger on the line of the sea.  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): the star compass: stars rise and set at fixed points  
> _This skill is called wayfinding. A navigator pictures the horizon as a ring of “houses”, and the Hawaiian star compass has 32 of them._  
> _Each star rises in its own house and sets in another, in the same places every night. Learn the houses and you can tell direction._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stars rise and set at fixed points on the horizon, which wayfinders use as a compass._

_Moana holds out her hand, and you hold out yours. Your Nubbin holds out something, roughly hand-shaped._  
**Maui**: Stars rise in the same places on the sea’s edge, every night. Learn where each one comes up, and where it goes down.  
**Maui**: Then you know which way you’re pointing. Your hand tells you how high it climbs at its highest, and that tells you how far north you are.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiply to estimate an angle  
> _A closed fist held at arm’s length covers about 10 degrees of sky. If a star sits three fists above the horizon, about how high is it?_  
> - ✅ About 30 degrees → Yes. Three fists of 10 degrees each: 3 × 10 = 30.
> - About 13 degrees → 13 is 3 + 10. Each fist is 10 degrees, so three fists are 3 × 10 = 30.
> - About 3 degrees → 3 is the number of fists. Each one covers 10 degrees, so the height is 30.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication to estimate how high a star is with fists._

**Moana**: That’s it? That’s the secret?  
**Maui**: That’s the first night of it. It takes years. Most of a life.  

#### `a10-08-stars-done`

_Moana checks her hand against the same star every few minutes, as if it might move without asking._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what actions show about a character  
> _Moana checks her hand against the same star again and again. What does this tell us about the way she learns?_  
> - ✅ She is eager and careful, and tests what she has just learned → Yes. Checking and re-checking is how skills become reliable.
> - She does not trust Maui at all → She trusts the lesson enough to practise it. She is testing herself, not him.
> - She is bored → Boredom would make her stop. She keeps checking because she cares.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s repeated action to understand how she learns._


#### `a10-08-swell`

**Maui**: Clouds come and cover the stars. Then what?  
**Moana**: Then… you’re lost?  
**Maui**: Lie down. Put your hand on the hull. Shut your eyes. And for once in your life, be quiet.  
_You lie on the warm wood. Underneath you, the canoe is lifting and falling, lifting and falling, slow as breathing._  
**Maui**: That’s the big swell. It comes from far away, from the same quarter, for days. Keep it at the same angle, you keep your course.  
**Maui**: And when it bounces off an island, it crosses itself. You can feel the island before you can see it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): swells travel far and bend round islands  
> _Ocean swells can travel thousands of kilometres from a distant storm, keeping a steady direction for days._  
> _When a swell meets an island, it bends round it and crosses itself. Marshall Islanders even made “stick charts” of swell patterns to remember them._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that swells keep direction over long distances and bend around islands, which navigators feel._

_Moana lies very still. Her face changes, the way a face does when it hears its own name in a crowd._  
**Moana**: There. Two. Two swells. One from there, one from there.  

**Choices**

- **Feel for the second swell yourself.**
    - You press your palm flat and wait. It takes a long time, and then there it is: a smaller lift, crossing the big one, like a second heartbeat.
- **Let your Nubbin try.**
    - Your Nubbin lies down with its whole face on the wood. Whatever it feels, it feels it very deeply, and falls asleep.

#### `a10-08-swell-done`

**Maui**: Huh. Not bad. Not good. Not bad.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): honest feedback  
> _Maui says, “Not bad. Not good. Not bad.” How can honest, plain feedback like this help someone learn more than “perfect!” or “terrible!”?_  
> - It shows how far there is to go without discouraging → Yes, it says what is true and keeps the door open.
> - It can still feel a bit cold → It can. Honest feedback works best when the learner knows you are on their side.
> - It depends on the person → True. Some people like it blunt, others need warmth.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how honest feedback helps someone learn._


#### `a10-08-birds`

_At dusk, Maui sits at the bow beside your Nubbin. The two of them watch the sky with the same squint._  
**Maui**: In the morning, fishing birds fly out from land. In the evening, they fly home to it. Watch which way they go.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): how land birds and clouds point to land  
> _Seabirds such as terns and noddies sleep on land but fish at sea. They fly out at dawn and return at dusk, so an evening bird shows the way home._  
> _Wayfinders also watch for a greenish glow on the underside of a cloud, which comes from light reflecting off a shallow lagoon beneath it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how seabirds at dusk and the green glow under a cloud can point to land._

_A single white bird crosses the red sky, low and steady, in a hurry to be somewhere._  
_Your Nubbin points at it with its whole arm. Then its whole body._  
**Maui**: Good. That way’s land. And see that cloud? Green on its belly. That’s a lagoon under it, shining up.  
**Moana**: Stars. Swells. Birds. Clouds.  
**Maui**: The rest is memory. Every turn you’ve made since your own beach, kept in your head in order. Lose that, and the sky can’t help you.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance from speed and time (dead reckoning)  
> _Maui keeps every stretch of the voyage in his head. If Moana sails east for 3 hours at 6 kilometres an hour, how far east has she come?_  
> - ✅ 18 kilometres → Yes. 3 × 6 = 18. Keeping count of direction, speed and time like this is called dead reckoning.
> - 9 kilometres → 9 is 3 + 6. Each of the 3 hours covers 6 kilometres, so 3 × 6 = 18.
> - 2 kilometres → 2 is 6 ÷ 3. She goes 6 kilometres in every hour, so 3 hours make 18.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied speed by time to find a distance, the sum behind dead reckoning._


#### `a10-08-birds-done`

_Moana takes the steering oar for the first time. Maui lets her, which is the nicest thing he has done so far._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Hōkūleʻa and Mau Piailug  
> _In 1976 the double-hulled canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti with no compass and no map._  
> _Its navigator, Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia, shared his knowledge with Hawaiian sailors, who have carried it on ever since._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about the 1976 Hōkūleʻa voyage and the navigator Mau Piailug._


#### `a10-08-complete`

_That night Moana sits up late, weaving with strips of pandanus leaf left over from patching the sail._  
_In the morning there is a tiny woven sail tied to your Nubbin’s back, between its wings. It fits perfectly._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): pattern and division  
> _Moana weaves in a pattern: over two strips, under one, over two, under one. In a row of 12 strips, how many does she pass under?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. Each “over 2, under 1” group has 3 strips, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 groups and 4 unders.
> - 6 → 6 would be half of 12. Each group of 3 has only one “under”, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
> - 8 → 8 is the number of overs. The pattern has 2 overs for each under, so unders are 4.
> _For grown-ups: Used a repeating pattern and division to count weaving strips._

**Moana**: Every voyager needs a sail. Even a small one. Especially a small one.  
_Your Nubbin turns round and round, trying to see it. Heihei turns round too, in solidarity, or by accident._  

### Glossary

- **wayfinding**: Finding your way across land or sea, without maps or instruments, using clues from nature.
- **horizon**: The line in the distance where the sea or land seems to meet the sky.
- **swell**: A long, smooth wave that rolls across the open sea, often from a storm far away.
- **pandanus**: A tropical plant with long, tough leaves that people weave into mats, baskets and sails.

## A10-9. Lalotai

- `a10-09-s1`: Climb the tall rock at the edge of the world. · _Climb the stone pillar after Moana, ledge by ledge._
- `a10-09-s2`: Find your way through the Realm of Monsters. · _Follow the glowing plants and keep your Nubbin close._
- `a10-09-s3`: Get the hook back from the crab who has it. · _Keep Tamatoa talking while Moana works round behind him._

#### `a10-09-pillar`

_A stone pillar stands alone in the sea, so tall the top of it is in cloud._  
**Maui**: The way down to Lalotai is at the top. Yes, the way down is up. Don’t look at me like that. I didn’t build it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): a word’s parts: lalo and tai  
> _In Samoan, lalo means “below” and tai means “sea”, so Lalotai means “beneath the sea”. In some Pacific stories it is a realm under the ocean._  
> _Knowing the parts of a word can help you work out what it means, in any language._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that breaking a word into parts, here lalo and tai, can reveal its meaning._

_Maui climbs it the easy way, which is by being enormous. Moana climbs it the hard way, with her fingers and her toes._  
_You climb behind her. Your Nubbin climbs behind you, holding your heel, which you would rather it didn’t._  
_At the top there is a flat place, and a great carved stone, and the wind tugging at everything._  
_Maui puts his hands on the stone and says some old words, low and quiet. The page doesn’t write them down._  
_The rock opens like a mouth. Below it there is nothing at all, and a long way down, a glow._  

#### `a10-09-pillar-done`

**Maui**: Wait here. This is a monster realm. No place for a… Moana? Moana!  
_She has already jumped, and so has your Nubbin. You sigh, and jump after them._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): courage and caution  
> _Moana jumps into the unknown, and her courage is real. What would make her jump wiser?_  
> - ✅ Taking a moment to look and think about what could go wrong, then deciding → Yes. Courage with a moment of thought is the strongest kind.
> - Waiting until it is completely safe → Nothing new is ever completely safe. A pause and a plan is the aim.
> - Never jumping → That would keep her safe, but she would never find the hook.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about combining courage with a moment of careful thought._


#### `a10-09-depths`

_You land on something soft that turns out to be a giant flower, which closes up a little, interested._  
_Lalotai is upside down. The sea is the sky here, a far-off ripple overhead, and everything below glows: purple, green, gold._  
_Plants swing round to watch you pass. Something with too many eyes blinks at you from a crack, and decides not to bother._  
**Moana**: Maui’s hook. He said it would be with something that collects things. Something that likes shiny things.  
_Your Nubbin’s emote ball floats above its head, glowing softly, as it always does._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): bioluminescence in real deep-sea animals  
> _The glowing plants are made up, but real deep-sea animals, like some jellyfish and anglerfish, do make light inside their bodies. It is called bioluminescence._  
> _They glow to find food, to scare enemies, or to find a mate in water where sunlight never reaches._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some real deep-sea animals make their own light._

_A lot of eyes in the dark turn towards it at once._  

#### `a10-09-depths-done`

_A trail of shining things leads down into a cave: shells, bones, a lost earring, a whole fishing canoe painted gold._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to count piles  
> _Say the shiny trail has 7 piles of shells, with 8 shells in each pile. How many shells in all?_  
> - ✅ 56 → Yes. 7 × 8 = 56.
> - 15 → 15 is 7 + 8. Seven piles of 8 means 7 × 8 = 56.
> - 48 → 48 is 6 × 8. With seven piles, it is 7 × 8 = 56.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied piles by shells to find a total._


#### `a10-09-lair`

_At the bottom of the cave is a crab the size of a house. His shell is crusted all over with treasure, and he is admiring it._  
_On the very top of his shell, among the gold, is a huge fish hook carved from bone._  
**Tamatoa**: Visitors. How rare. Most things that come down here are lunch, and lunch doesn’t usually knock.  
**Tamatoa**: Oh. Oh, what is that? On the little round one. The floating thing. It glows.  
_He leans right down to your Nubbin’s emote ball, his eyes on stalks, very close._  
**Tamatoa**: I must have it. It would go just here, by my left eye. Everyone would look at it, and then at me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): why people want things  
> _Tamatoa wants the glowing ball so everyone will look at it, and then at him. Why do people want things, and is wanting to be admired wrong?_  
> - To feel valued → That is often true. The trouble comes when things are the only way we feel it.
> - Because beautiful things bring joy → A fair reason. Collecting what you love is different from needing it to impress people.
> - It is a way of showing off, and that is fine in small amounts → An honest view. Wanting to be seen is human; what matters is how far it goes.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people want things and whether wanting admiration is wrong._

_Your Nubbin, worried, turns its ball into a question mark. Tamatoa gasps with delight._  
**Tamatoa**: It does tricks!  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin show off its ball.**
    - Your Nubbin makes a heart, a spiral, a plain ball, an exclamation mark. Tamatoa claps his claws, completely lost.
- **Ask Tamatoa about his shell.**
    - **Tamatoa**: Since you ask. Every piece is a story, and every story is about me. Let me start at the bottom left…

#### `a10-09-lair-done`

_Behind him, Moana has climbed up his shell with her hands full of glowing weed, and is quietly lifting off the hook._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): crabs and the real coconut crab  
> _Crabs have a hard outer skeleton and shed it as they grow. The real coconut crab of the Pacific, the largest land crab, climbs palms and cracks coconuts._  
> _Tamatoa is a story, but some crabs, called decorator crabs, really do stick seaweed and sponges on their shells as camouflage._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about crab bodies, the coconut crab, and how crabs decorate their shells._


#### `a10-09-complete`

**Tamatoa**: Wait. That’s mine. Everything here is mine.  
_Moana throws the hook to Maui, and Maui catches it. Tamatoa turns, and turns, and topples onto his back with his legs waving._  
**Tamatoa**: Somebody turn me over! This is very undignified! I am never undignified!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): the prefix un- in undignified  
> _Tamatoa says he is never undignified. Dignified means calm and grand, and the prefix un- means not._  
> _So undignified means not grand at all: stuck on your back with your legs waving, for example._  
> _For grown-ups: Used the prefix un- to work out the meaning of undignified._

_A geyser of warm water bursts up from the floor and carries all of you, very fast, back up into the real sky._  
_You land in the sea beside the canoe. Your Nubbin lands in it too, and the paint on its tummy finally washes off._  
_Down below, faintly, you can still hear Tamatoa asking for help, and also for compliments._  

### Glossary

- **realm**: A kingdom, or a place with its own rules and creatures.
- **undignified**: Looking silly or embarrassed, instead of calm and grand.
- **bioluminescence**: Light made by a living thing, like the glow of some deep-sea animals.

## A10-10. The Hook

- `a10-10-s1`: Watch Maui try to change shape. · _Keep well back on the deck while Maui practises._
- `a10-10-s2`: Sit with Maui while he tells you about his tattoos. · _Sit down near Maui at the stern. Don’t push._
- `a10-10-s3`: Help Maui find his hawk. · _Hold the canoe steady and steer into the wind while Maui tries again._

#### `a10-10-practice`

**Maui**: Right. Now we’re back in business. Hawk.  
_There is a flash of light. Where Maui was, there is a fish, flapping on the deck._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how fish, pigs and hawks breathe  
> _Maui turns into a fish, a pig, and a hawk. A fish takes oxygen from water through gills, while pigs and hawks breathe air into their lungs._  
> _Each body is shaped for its habitat: fins to swim, legs to run, and wings to fly._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gills, lungs and body shape suit each animal’s habitat._

**Maui**: Hawk!  
_A flash, and a pig. Your Nubbin and Pua would have got on._  
**Maui**: A thousand years without it. It’s like a muscle. It’s like… stop laughing. Hawk!  
_A flash. Something with a hawk’s wings and a shark’s head flops off the side of the canoe into the sea._  
_Your Nubbin, to be supportive, flaps its own wings. It doesn’t take off either._  

#### `a10-10-practice-done`

_Maui climbs back aboard as himself, dripping, and sits down hard at the stern with his back to everyone._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): frustration and starting again  
> _Maui is frustrated about losing a skill that used to be easy. What helps when we feel like that?_  
> - ✅ Say how you feel, rest, then try again with kind people nearby → Yes. Naming the feeling and having encouragement make it easier to start again.
> - Never try again → Giving up ends the frustration, but also the chance to improve.
