> - Blame everyone around you → Blame is easy, but it makes the problem harder to fix.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about handling frustration when a skill feels harder than it used to._


#### `a10-10-story`

_Nobody says anything for a long time. Moana sits near Maui, you sit near Moana, and your Nubbin sits nearest of all._  
**Moana**: Your tattoos. Are they all things you did?  
**Maui**: Every one. I earned every one. The sun. The fire. The islands. The coconut. The wind.  
**Moana**: There’s a space. On your back. With nothing in it.  
_Maui is quiet for so long that you think he won’t answer._  
**Maui**: I wasn’t born a demigod. I was born a baby. To people. And they didn’t want me. They let the sea take me.  
**Maui**: The gods found me. Made me what I am. And I went back to the people and gave them everything. Islands. Fire. Long days.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why did Maui give people islands, fire and long days?_  
> - ✅ He hoped they would love him and keep him → Yes, he tells us so himself. His gifts were generous, but they came from a hurt.
> - He wanted to show off → He does like an audience, but he says his real reason was to be wanted.
> - The gods ordered him to → The gods made him what he is, but he says the giving was his own choice.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character’s hidden reason for his actions._

**Maui**: So they’d want me. So they’d love me. That’s what the gifts were for. All of them.  
_Moana doesn’t say anything for a moment. Then she says the true thing, plainly._  
**Moana**: The gifts were kind. But nobody should have to earn being kept. Babies don’t. You didn’t.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): do we have to earn being kept?  
> _Moana says nobody should have to earn being kept. Thinking about why Maui gave so many gifts, do you agree?_  
> - Yes. Everyone deserves love just for being themselves → That is what Moana says. Gifts can be kind without being the price of belonging.
> - Mostly, but people also show love by giving → Giving is lovely. The trouble is when you give because you are afraid of being sent away.
> - I am not sure → That is honest. It is a big question, and the story is still working on it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether love must be earned._


**Choices**

- **Pass him the water gourd.**
    - You hand him the water. He takes it without looking, and holds it, and doesn’t drink, and doesn’t give it back.
- **Say nothing. Sit a little closer.**
    - You shift along the deck, not much. Your Nubbin, who has never understood not much, climbs into Maui’s lap and stays there.

#### `a10-10-story-done`

_Maui doesn’t answer. But he doesn’t turn his back again either._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how actions show feelings  
> _Maui does not answer, but he does not turn his back again either. What does this show?_  
> - ✅ He is listening and feels a little less alone → Yes. Staying turned toward someone can say what words cannot.
> - He is angry → Angry people turn away. He is staying.
> - He is falling asleep → The line is about him opening up, not about tiredness.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s body language to understand a feeling._


#### `a10-10-hawk`

**Moana**: Try again. Not because you have to. Because you can.  
**Maui**: …Hawk.  
_A flash, and the flash is softer this time._  
_A great hawk lifts off the stern, beats once, twice, and climbs into the sky in a long, wide spiral._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how hawks use wind and wide wings  
> _A hawk has wide wings that catch rising air, so it can soar in great circles without flapping much. Birds usually take off facing the wind, for more lift._  
> _That is why Moana has you hold the canoe into the wind._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that hawks soar on rising air and take off into the wind._

**Moana**: Ha! Look at him go!  
_You hold the canoe into the wind. Your Nubbin stands on the bow with its arms up, as if it’s doing the flying._  

#### `a10-10-hawk-done`

_The hawk dives, pulls up just over the waves, and lands on the mast. It is very obviously grinning._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): a fraction of attempts  
> _Maui tried four times: fish, pig and a hawk-shark came first, and the real hawk came fourth. What fraction of his tries made a proper hawk?_  
> - ✅ 1/4 → Yes. One try out of four equal tries is one quarter.
> - 1/3 → There were four tries in all, not three. One out of four is 1/4.
> - 3/4 → 3/4 is the failed tries. The real hawk was 1 of the 4, so 1/4.
> _For grown-ups: Wrote a unit fraction for one success in four tries._


#### `a10-10-complete`

**Maui**: Did you see that? The roll at the end? I did a roll.  
**Moana**: We saw. Everyone saw. The fish saw.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): practice and encouragement  
> _Maui relearned the hawk by trying, failing and trying again, with Moana saying “because you can”._  
> _Practice works best when it comes with encouragement rather than pressure, and a mistake is part of learning, not the end of it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that practice with encouragement helps you improve and that mistakes are part of learning._

_He teaches her the rest that afternoon, properly: tacking, steering, reading the shapes of waves. He’s a good teacher, when he forgets to show off._  
_That evening, Moana steers alone while Maui sleeps. Your Nubbin keeps watch beside her, until it doesn’t._  

### Glossary

- **demigod**: In old stories, someone who is part god and part human.

## A10-11. Te Kā

- `a10-11-s1`: Sail up to the barrier islands at night. · _Keep watch from the bow as the canoe closes on the dark islands._
- `a10-11-s2`: Get the canoe out from under the fire. · _Bail and hold the sail as Moana turns for the gap._
- `a10-11-s3`: Stand by while Maui and Moana argue. · _Stay on the deck. This isn’t your argument._

#### `a10-11-barrier`

_A ring of black islands lies across the sea, smoking. Behind them, faint and far, is the shape of a great green island, asleep._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, notice): how volcanic islands form  
> _Many Pacific islands, including Hawaiʻi, began as volcanoes on the sea floor. Each eruption added lava that cooled to rock until the peak broke the surface._  
> _Over millions of years, the sea, wind and rain wear a volcanic island down, and corals build reefs around it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how volcanic islands rise from the sea floor and slowly change._

**Maui**: Te Fiti’s behind the ring. And between us and her is Te Kā. Keep away from the shore. Let me go first.  
**Moana**: I can get through. I know the swell now. There’s a gap.  
**Maui**: Moana. Let me go first.  
_The ash on the black island moves, and stands up. It is a giant made of rock and fire, taller than the pillar at the edge of the world._  
_Your Nubbin hides under the deck with Heihei, which is the first sensible thing either of them has done all trip._  

#### `a10-11-barrier-done`

_Te Kā roars. It isn’t a word: it’s the sound of a mountain having a very bad day._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification  
> _Te Kā’s roar is “the sound of a mountain having a very bad day.” What does this phrase tell us about the roar?_  
> - ✅ It is huge and angry, like a rumbling mountain → Yes. Treating the mountain like a cross person gives the roar size and temper.
> - It is quiet and gentle → A mountain in a bad mood is rumbling and angry, not gentle.
> - The mountain is really speaking words → The narrator says it is not a word. The phrase is a comparison.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a funny comparison shows the size and anger of a roar._


#### `a10-11-gap`

_Moana turns for the gap. Maui flies as the hawk, at Te Kā’s face, to draw it off._  
_Te Kā swats at him with a hand like a hillside. He swerves, and dives, and comes back again._  
**Moana**: Nearly. Nearly there!  
_Te Kā turns from the hawk to the canoe. Its hand comes down._  
_Maui drops out of the sky in his own shape and blocks it with his hook. There is a crack like lightning._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): light travels faster than sound  
> _Maui’s hook meets Te Kā’s hand with “a crack like lightning.” In real storms, why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?_  
> - ✅ Light travels much faster than sound → Yes. Light arrives almost at once, but sound is slow enough that you can count the gap.
> - Thunder happens first but hides → Both happen together. Light just reaches you far sooner.
> - Sound is faster but louder things are slow → Sound is much slower than light, whatever its loudness.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that light travels faster than sound._

_The wave throws the canoe backwards, out past the ring, far out into the dark sea. You hold on to anything you can._  

**Choices**

- **Grab the sail line.**
    - You get the line and keep it, though it burns your palms. The sail tears, but it stays on the canoe, because of you.
- **Grab Heihei, who has wandered out again.**
    - You catch Heihei by the tail feathers as he strolls towards the edge. He looks at you as if you are the strange one.

#### `a10-11-gap-done`

_When the sea is quiet again, the canoe is a long way off, with a torn sail. Te Kā’s glow sinks back down into the ash._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Say the wave carried the canoe 3 kilometres from the barrier, and the canoe sails back at 1 kilometre every 20 minutes. How long does it take to return?_  
> - ✅ 60 minutes, or 1 hour → Yes. 3 km at 20 minutes per km is 3 × 20 = 60 minutes.
> - 23 minutes → 23 is 3 + 20. Each kilometre takes 20 minutes, so multiply: 3 × 20 = 60.
> - 20 minutes → 20 minutes is one kilometre. There are three, so 3 × 20 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Used distance and speed to work out a journey time._


#### `a10-11-crack`

_Maui is holding his hook in both hands. There is a crack running right through it, from the point nearly to the grip._  
**Maui**: I told you to turn back. I told you. Look at it.  
**Moana**: We can fix it. We’ll try again. We’ll go round the other way.  
**Maui**: One more hit and it’s gone. That hook is the only thing anyone ever wanted from me. Break it, and there’s nothing left to want.  
**Moana**: That’s not true. You know that’s not true.  
**Maui**: The sea should have asked somebody who listens.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): when someone leaves because they feel useless  
> _Maui decides to leave because his hook is cracked and he thinks nobody will want him. Was he right to go?_  
> - Yes, it was honest of him to say he was sorry and step back → He did apologise. But he left Moana alone with the problem.
> - No. He gave up on her and on himself → A tough view. Notice that he comes back later.
> - He was scared, and fear makes people leave → A kind reading. Fear can look like leaving, even when someone cares.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone might leave when they feel useless._

_That lands, and stays. Moana doesn’t answer._  
**Maui**: I’m sorry. I am. Good luck.  
_There is a flash. A hawk lifts off the stern, and flies away to the north, and doesn’t look back._  

#### `a10-11-crack-done`

_Moana watches until he is a speck, and then until he isn’t._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): figurative meaning of a word  
> _Moana watches “until he is a speck.” What does speck mean?_  
> - ✅ A tiny spot, because he is far away → Yes. A speck is a very small dot, and a hawk far away looks like one.
> - A kind of bird → Not a bird. A speck is a tiny spot.
> - A big shadow → The opposite: a speck is tiny.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of “speck” from context._


#### `a10-11-complete`

_Moana sits at the bow with the green stone in her hand. She doesn’t cry, which is worse._  
**Moana**: I can’t do this. I’m not enough for it.  
**Moana**: Find somebody who is. Please. Take it back.  
_She leans over the side and holds out the stone. The sea rises up, gently, and takes it from her hand, and sinks back down._  
_You don’t say anything; you sit down beside her. Your Nubbin comes out from under the deck and sits beside you._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): company helps more than advice  
> _You say nothing. You just sit beside Moana, and so does your Nubbin._  
> _When someone is very discouraged, advice often does not help but company does. Sitting beside them says, “You are not alone.”_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sitting beside a discouraged friend can help more than advice._

_The three of you sit like that, with Heihei, for a long time, while the canoe drifts._  

### Glossary

- **speck**: A tiny spot.

## A10-12. The Manta Ray

- `a10-12-s1`: Watch the light that comes up through the water. · _Look over the side of the canoe._
- `a10-12-s2`: Watch the manta, and let your Nubbin answer it. · _Bring your Nubbin to the side and let it see the manta move._
- `a10-12-s3`: Listen to Gramma’s song. · _Sit with Moana and Gramma under the stars._

#### `a10-12-light`

_Late in the night, a soft blue light comes up through the sea under the canoe._  
_It is a manta ray, glowing from inside, circling slowly round the hulls._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): manta rays  
> _Giant manta rays are the largest rays in the sea, up to about seven metres wide. They are gentle and harmless to people._  
> _They “fly” through the water with slow beats of their wing-like fins, gliding between beats, and they eat plankton._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that manta rays are huge, gentle plankton-eaters that “fly” through water._

_Moana looks up. Sitting at the stern, as if she has always been there, is Gramma Tala._  
**Gramma Tala**: Well. You’re a long way past the reef.  
**Moana**: Gramma?  
**Gramma Tala**: I told you. I said I’d come back as one of those. Nobody listens to their grandmother.  
_Moana goes to her and holds on, and Gramma holds on back. She is a bit see-through round the edges, but her arms are real enough._  

**Choices**

- **Go to the bow and give them room.**
    - You take your Nubbin to the bow and look at the stars for a while. Over Moana’s shoulder, Gramma catches your eye and nods.
- **Bring your Nubbin to say hello.**
    - Your Nubbin pats Gramma’s knee, very gently, as if checking that she is there. She is, just about.
    - **Gramma Tala**: Hello, small one. Still a bit crooked? Good. Crooked is how you know it’s yours.

#### `a10-12-light-done`

**Gramma Tala**: I’m not here to tell you what to do. I never did that. I’m here because you’re sad, and I’m nosy.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): missing someone is a kind of love  
> _Moana misses Gramma. Missing someone is one of the ways we go on loving them._  
> _People keep their loved ones close by telling stories about them, keeping their words, and passing their skills on._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that missing someone is a form of love and that remembering keeps them close._


#### `a10-12-manta`

_The manta turns in the water and rises, and moves along the side of the canoe with its great wings out wide and level._  
_It isn’t swimming. It is gliding: leaning, letting the sea carry it sideways, never once flapping._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): how gliding differs from flapping  
> _The manta “isn’t swimming, it is gliding.” Which of these is gliding?_  
> - ✅ Moving smoothly without flapping, carried by the water → Yes. Gliding is moving without effort, using the flow around you.
> - Flapping hard to go faster → Flapping is the opposite. Gliding is smooth and steady.
> - Standing still → A glider keeps moving. It just does not push hard.
> _For grown-ups: Defined gliding as smooth movement without flapping._

_Your Nubbin stands up very slowly on the deck._  
_Then it spreads its arms, and leans, and slides along the planks on one foot, level and soft, the way Gramma taught it._  
_The manta glides, and your Nubbin glides. They go up the side of the canoe together, the big one in the sea and the small one on deck._  
**Gramma Tala**: There. You didn’t forget. I told you it doesn’t come off.  
_Moana laughs, wet-faced. It is the first time she has laughed since the barrier._  

#### `a10-12-manta-done`

**Gramma Tala**: Things you’re taught with love, you keep. You don’t have to try. They stay put.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _Gramma says, “Things you’re taught with love, you keep.” What big idea (theme) is she giving Moana?_  
> - ✅ What we learn from people who love us stays with us → Yes. The step, the swells and the stories are all still Moana’s.
> - Dancing is better than sailing → The theme is bigger than one skill. It is about what love leaves behind.
> - Nothing can be learned → The opposite: Gramma says what we learn with love lasts.
> _For grown-ups: Named the theme of a character’s words._


#### `a10-12-song`

**Gramma Tala**: Tell me about yourself. Not the chief’s daughter bit. The rest.  
**Moana**: I don’t know. I thought I did. I got it all wrong.  
_Gramma doesn’t answer. She starts to sing instead, very low, an old voyaging song you have never heard._  
_It has no words you can catch. It has the names of islands in it, and the names of people, one after another, going back and back._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): songs that carry knowledge  
> _Pacific navigators sometimes memorised star paths and island names in songs and chants, so the knowledge could be passed on without writing._  
> _Gramma’s song has names in it, going back and back. The story does not write the song down, so it stays hers._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that songs and chants helped Pacific navigators remember and pass on knowledge._

_Overhead, the stars move. They become sails: the great canoes from the cave, crossing the sky, full of people looking down._  
_Your Nubbin looks up at them with its mouth open. One of the steerers waves._  
_Moana stands. She is crying and she is standing up straight, both at once._  
**Moana**: Everything I was taught, I’ve still got. Gramma’s stories. Dad’s care for people. Maui’s swells. None of it came off.  
**Moana**: It doesn’t matter who picked me. I’m picking me. I’ll take it back myself.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): who we are: given and chosen  
> _Moana says it does not matter who picked her: she is picking herself. Can we choose who we are, or is some of it given to us?_  
> - We are given family and place, but we choose what we do with them → A strong answer. Moana keeps everything she was taught and chooses her course.
> - We choose almost everything → Some people feel that way. Consider the things you did not pick, like where you were born.
> - We are mostly given our lives → There is truth in that. Moana’s moment is about taking one thing back: the choice.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what in a person is given and what is chosen._


#### `a10-12-song-done`

_She dives over the side, down and down into the dark, and comes up a long minute later with the green stone in her fist._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.4, ask): repetition for effect  
> _The line says she dives “down and down into the dark.” Why does the writer repeat the word “down”?_  
> - ✅ Repeating it makes the dive feel long and deep → Yes. Repetition stretches time, so we feel every metre of the dive.
> - The writer forgot → It is deliberate. Repeating a word can set a rhythm and a mood.
> - It means she went up → It means the opposite. “Down and down” is a deep dive.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how repeating a word changes the feel of a line._


#### `a10-12-complete`

_When she climbs back aboard, the stern is empty. Out on the water, the manta turns once, and glides off towards Te Fiti._  
_Moana mends the sail by starlight while you hold the edges. Your Nubbin holds Heihei, who is trying to eat the thread._  
**Moana**: She’s not gone, is she? Not really.  
**You**: I don’t think anybody you love is ever all the way gone.  
**Moana**: No. I don’t either.  
_At dawn she turns the canoe back towards the ring of black islands, and doesn’t hesitate._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): why the Sun rises: the Earth spins  
> _Moana turns the canoe at dawn. Why does the Sun seem to rise every morning?_  
> - ✅ The Earth spins, turning our side towards the Sun → Yes. The Earth keeps spinning, and as our side turns towards the Sun, it looks as if the Sun climbs up.
> - The Sun travels round the Earth each day → People once thought so. In fact the Earth spins, and that makes the Sun seem to move.
> - The clouds move out of the way → Clouds can hide the Sun, but dawn comes because the Earth turns us towards it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sunrise happens because the Earth spins._


## A10-13. Te Fiti

- `a10-13-s1`: Run the barrier again. · _Hold the sail while Moana weaves the canoe through the ring._
- `a10-13-s2`: Look across at the island where Te Fiti should be. · _Climb the mast to see over the black rocks._
- `a10-13-s3`: Walk the path behind Moana, in your own way. · _Follow Moana down the path through the sea. Choose how you go._

#### `a10-13-run`

_This time Moana doesn’t go straight. She reads the swell bouncing off the black islands and sails the cross of it, left, right, left._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): finding a term in a repeating pattern  
> _Moana zig-zags through the ring: left, right, left, right, and so on. What is her 9th turn?_  
> - ✅ Left, because odd turns are left → Yes. Turns 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 are left, and the even turns are right.
> - Right, because 9 is a big number → Size does not decide it. Odd-numbered turns are left, and 9 is odd.
> - It could be either → The pattern fixes it. Turn 9 is odd, so it is left.
> _For grown-ups: Found the 9th item in a repeating pattern._

_Te Kā rises out of the ash, roaring. Its fire falls where the canoe was a moment ago, and never where it is._  
**Moana**: Hold it! Hold it, now let go! Now!  
_You let go of the sail line. The canoe spins round a rock as if it were dancing._  
_Then Te Kā’s hand comes down ahead of you, and there is nowhere left to go._  
_And a hawk drops out of the sky, and turns into a man with a cracked hook, and stands in front of the canoe._  
**Maui**: Told you to let me go first.  
**Moana**: You came back!  
**Maui**: I’ve got a lot of other tattoos. I could do with one I didn’t do for applause.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character has understood  
> _Maui says he could do with “one I didn’t do for applause.” What has he understood?_  
> - ✅ A brave deed done because it is right is worth more than one done for praise → Yes. He is finally acting from his own heart, not for a crowd.
> - He wants more tattoos → The tattoo is a way of saying something deeper: he wants to do good for its own sake.
> - He is joking about nothing → There is humour, but the line shows real change in him.
> _For grown-ups: Understood how a character’s attitude has changed._


#### `a10-13-run-done`

**Maui**: Go! I’ll hold her! Go!  
_He meets Te Kā’s fist with the hook, and the crack spreads, and the hook breaks in his hands. He stands there anyway._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): courage while afraid  
> _Maui comes back, and stands in front of the danger he left behind. He is not unafraid._  
> _Courage does not mean having no fear. It means doing what matters while you are afraid._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that courage means acting while afraid, not having no fear._


#### `a10-13-spiral`

_Moana scrambles up the mast. You go up behind her, to see what she sees._  
_Past the ring of black islands, where the great green island should be sleeping, there is nothing. Only a hollow in the sea._  
**Moana**: She’s gone. Te Fiti isn’t there.  
_Moana looks back at Te Kā. On its chest, among the cracks and the glowing rock, there is a mark: a spiral._  
_It is the same spiral that is on the stone in her hand. The same spiral on the shell in your pocket._  

> **Lesson** (art, notice): spirals in nature and Pacific art  
> _Spirals appear in nature: fern fronds unfurl in one, and many shells grow in one. In Aotearoa, the koru, an unfurling fern, is a spiral symbol of new life._  
> _Here the spiral on the stone, the shell and Te Kā’s chest is the story’s own sign that they belong together._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed spirals in nature and learned about the koru as a symbol of new life._

**Moana**: Oh.  
**Moana**: She’s not guarding the heart. She is the heart’s home. She’s Te Fiti, without it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): making an inference  
> _Moana says, “She’s not guarding the heart. She is the heart’s home.” What has she worked out about Te Kā?_  
> - ✅ Te Kā is Te Fiti, who lost her heart and became furious → Yes, the spiral is the clue. The scary one is the island, missing the thing that made her herself.
> - Te Kā is a guard hired by Maui → The spiral on her chest matches the stone, so she is more than a guard.
> - Te Kā is a volcano with no feelings → She is a volcano, but the story shows she has been hurting.
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference from a clue about who a character really is._


#### `a10-13-spiral-done`

_Moana climbs down. She faces the open water between the canoe and Te Kā, and she holds up her hand._  
_The sea parts. A path opens, wet sand and shells, straight from the canoe to the burning giant._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): tides can uncover paths of sand  
> _Real seas do not part on command. But at low tide, some sandbars are uncovered, and people can walk across to small islands._  
> _Tides rise and fall about twice a day, mostly because of the pull of the Moon, so the path is covered again later._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that low tide can uncover sandy paths, and that the Moon mostly causes the tides._


#### `a10-13-walk`

_Moana walks down the path through the sea. Te Kā sees her, and turns, and comes roaring down to meet her._  
_She doesn’t run, or raise a hand. She keeps walking._  
_You step down onto the wet sand behind her, with your Nubbin at your side. Your heart is going like Moana’s drum._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): three ways to approach someone upset  
> _Te Kā frightens you, but she is hurting. When is a gift, a word, or quiet walking with open hands the best way to reach someone like that?_  
> - A gift, when something was lost that you can return → A fair match. A thoughtful gift can show you understand.
> - A word, when they need to know they are remembered → Yes. Words can reach someone who feels forgotten.
> - Just walking, when nothing needs fixing but they need company → Quiet presence is often the kindest of all.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about gift, word and quiet company as ways to approach someone who is hurting._


**Choices**

- **Carry the spiral shell, held out in your open hand.**
    - You take out the little spiral shell your Nubbin found on Motunui’s reef, and walk with it held out on your palm.
    - Te Kā’s glowing eyes drop to it: the same spiral. For a moment the roar goes quieter.
- **Say, out loud, that you remember her.**
    - **You**: We remember you. All the green. The islands. We remember who gave them.
    - Your voice is very small against the fire. It carries anyway, the way voices do over water.
- **Just keep walking, slowly, hands open.**
    - You don’t say anything, and you don’t hold anything. You walk, slowly, with your hands open, the way Moana is walking.
    - Your Nubbin walks beside you, step for step, which is a lot of steps for it.

#### `a10-13-walk-done`

_Te Kā reaches Moana and stoops, enormous, fire running off it like water. Moana stands still and lifts her face._  
**Moana**: I see the spiral. I know you. You’ve been waiting a long time for somebody to bring it home.  
_She touches her forehead to Te Kā’s, gently. The giant goes very still._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): greetings that share breath  
> _Moana touches her forehead to Te Kā’s. In many Pacific cultures people greet by touching noses or foreheads: the hongi in Aotearoa, the honi in Hawaiʻi._  
> _It is a sign of respect, and of sharing breath and life._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that touching noses or foreheads is a respectful greeting in some Pacific cultures._


#### `a10-13-complete`

_Moana sets the green stone into the spiral on Te Kā’s chest. It fits like a key._  
_The fire goes out of the rock, and the cracks fill with moss, then ferns, then flowers. The giant’s shape softens into a green woman, lying down._  
_She becomes an island again: green and more green and more, as far as you can see._  
_Te Fiti opens her eyes, just once, and looks at Moana, and then at you, and then, for rather a long time, at your Nubbin._  
_She reaches into the earth of herself and takes out Maui’s hook, mended and new, and holds it out to him._  
**Maui**: I’m sorry. For what I took. I’m sorry.  
_Te Fiti smiles. Then she lies back down, and is an island, and the sea round her goes clear and full of fish._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-4, notice): protecting reefs  
> _When water is clean and cool, reef fish and corals do well. When seawater gets too warm, corals can turn white (bleaching), and may recover if it cools._  
> _People help reefs by fishing carefully, keeping the sea clean and slowing the warming of the oceans. Te Fiti’s return does the same here._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that clean, cool water helps reefs, and how coral bleaching happens and can recover._


### Glossary

- **spiral**: A shape that winds round and round a centre point.

## A10-14. Voyagers Again

- `a10-14-s1`: Say goodbye to Maui. · _Stand with Moana on the deck while Maui gets ready to fly._
- `a10-14-s2`: Bring the canoe home to Motunui. · _Sail in through the gap in the reef._
- `a10-14-s3`: Sail out with Motunui’s first voyage, and watch from the bow. · _Help carry the canoes out from the cave, then take your place at the bow._

#### `a10-14-farewell`

_The canoe rides easy on a clear sea. Maui sits on the stern for the last time, turning his new hook over in his hands._  
**Maui**: You could come with me, you know. Lots of islands. You’d be good at it.  
**Moana**: I know. I’ve got an island. And a lot of people to teach.  
**Maui**: Teach them well. The stars, the swells. The birds. Don’t leave out the birds.  
_He looks down at his arm. Among the old marks of his deeds, there is a new one: a girl at a steering oar._  
**Maui**: I didn’t do that one. It just turned up. Best one I’ve got.  
_He gives your Nubbin a tap on the head with one finger, very carefully._  
**Maui**: Goodbye, coconut. You were the least use of anybody, and I’ll miss you most.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what teasing can mean  
> _Maui says, “You were the least use of anybody, and I’ll miss you most.” What is going on?_  
> - ✅ He is joking, to say something warm without being soppy → Yes. Teasing is one way people show they care without saying it outright.
> - He means every word as an insult → The second half, “I’ll miss you most,” shows affection.
> - He is making fun of Moana → He is talking to your Nubbin, and the teasing is kind.
> _For grown-ups: Read a teasing goodbye as a sign of affection._


**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin say goodbye its own way.**
    - Your Nubbin turns its emote ball into a heart and holds it up as high as it can reach. Maui looks at it a moment longer than he means to.
- **Tell him you’ll watch for hawks.**
    - **You**: We’ll watch for hawks. Any hawk. Just in case.
    - **Maui**: Do. If it does a roll at the top, it’s me.

#### `a10-14-farewell-done`

_A flash, and a hawk climbs into the sky in a long spiral, does a roll at the top, and is gone._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4-ESS2-2, notice): the Polynesian Triangle on the map  
> _Polynesian voyagers settled nearly every habitable island in a huge triangle, with corners at Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa New Zealand and Rapa Nui (Easter Island)._  
> _Each side is thousands of kilometres long, and most of it is open water._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Polynesian voyagers settled islands across the huge triangle bounded by Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa and Rapa Nui._


#### `a10-14-home`

_Motunui comes up over the edge of the sea, green and greener. The coconut trees are heavy with fruit._  
_There are fish in the lagoon. You can see them from the canoe, flicking silver over the sand._  
_Moana steers in through the reef herself, through the same breakers that threw her out, without a wobble._  
_Her mother is running down the beach. Her father is running behind, which a chief does not usually do._  
**Chief Tui**: Moana!  
_He holds her so tightly she squeaks. Then he holds her at arm’s length and looks at her, the way you look at a map._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): mixed feelings  
> _Tui holds Moana at arm’s length, looking at her “the way you look at a map.” Which feelings might he have all at once?_  
> - ✅ Relief, pride and a little leftover fear → Yes. Feelings are often mixed, and naming them all helps.
> - Only anger → He is angry no longer. Look at how tightly he held her.
> - Only boredom → He ran down the beach. He is anything but bored.
> _For grown-ups: Named several feelings a parent could have at once._

**Chief Tui**: You went past the reef.  
**Moana**: I went past the reef. And I came home. Both.  
**Sina**: Of course she did. I packed her lunch.  

#### `a10-14-home-done`

_Moana climbs the cairn of chiefs’ stones on the hill, and sets a shell on top, where her stone should go._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): a new word: cairn  
> _A cairn is a pile of stones built as a marker or memorial. Here each chief has added a stone, so it holds a whole line of leaders._  
> _Moana’s shell on top says: this leader belongs in the line that came before._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word cairn, and how each chief’s stone adds to a line of leaders._


#### `a10-14-bow`

_The whole village goes up the stream and through the waterfall. One by one, the great canoes come out of the cave into the light._  
_You carry the end of a steering oar and your Nubbin carries Heihei. Pua carries nothing, and supervises._  
_The sails go up, all of them. Moana stands at the steering oar of the first canoe, holding her hand out flat to the horizon._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): what the name Hōkūleʻa means  
> _The canoe Hōkūleʻa is named for the star Arcturus, called “star of gladness” in Hawaiian. Arcturus passes straight overhead in Hawaiʻi._  
> _Its 1976 voyage to Tahiti showed the world that Pacific peoples could navigate by nature alone._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what Hōkūleʻa’s name means and why its 1976 voyage mattered._

_Out past the reef, a blue light comes up under the hulls. The manta, gliding beside you, wings out wide._  
_Your Nubbin climbs to the very tip of the bow. Then it spreads its arms, and leans, and does Gramma’s glide, out over the water._  
_The manta glides with it. The people on the canoes see, and point, and some of them begin to laugh, and some to cry._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Hawaiʻi to Tahiti is about 4,000 kilometres. If a canoe could sail 100 kilometres every day, how many days would it take?_  
> - ✅ 40 days → Yes, 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40. Hōkūleʻa took about 34 days in 1976, so it sailed a little faster.
> - 4 days → 4 days would need 1,000 km a day. 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40.
> - 400 days → 400 would be 10 km a day. At 100 km a day, 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a voyage distance by a daily distance to find the days taken._

**Chief Tui**: That’s my mother’s step. She did it on the beach every evening. I thought it was just her.  
**Moana**: It’s never just one person. That’s the whole point of it.  

#### `a10-14-bow-done`

_The canoes sail on together, towards the next island, which nobody has seen yet._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): the steady star  
> _In Hawaiʻi, the North Star sits low in the northern sky. Hawaiians call it Hōkūpaʻa, the “steady star”, because it hardly moves while the others wheel past._  
> _Voyagers used it to check how far north or south they were._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the North Star hardly moves and that Hawaiians call it Hōkūpaʻa._


#### `a10-14-complete`

_Moana finds you at the bow at sunset, and sits beside you a while._  
**Moana**: You never told me where you came from. Somewhere past the reef, Gramma said.  
**You**: A garden. With a pond in it. I’m a long way from it.  
**Moana**: Then you know the way home. You always know where you started.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): knowing where you started  
> _Moana says, “You always know where you started.” What does she mean, and can knowing where you started help you work out where to go?_  
> - It means remembering who you are and where you come from → Yes. A voyager who forgets the start cannot find the way home.
> - It means knowing the way back if you are lost → That is the navigator’s view. Dead reckoning needs a starting point.
> - It is mostly about feeling at home inside yourself → A lovely reading. Home can be a place and a feeling.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what “knowing where you started” means for a voyager and for a person._

_Out in the sea behind you, where the path through the water was, Te Fiti’s shore is green. Your spiral shell is on it somewhere, with her._  
_The page gives a long, slow sigh, like a sail letting go of the wind._  
_You are back in the Grove with Nova’s atlas on your knee. The ground will not hold still; it sways like a deck, and your Nubbin smells of salt._  
_By the pond there is a small voyaging canoe, twin-hulled, with a woven sail no bigger than a tablecloth._  
_Up on the hill, a ring of flat stones has appeared in the grass, each one marked with a house of the rising stars._  
_A small white spiral shell is painted on the canoe’s prow, where the real one would have gone. Your Nubbin checks on it twice, then sits in the boat._  

### Glossary

- **cairn**: A pile of stones put up as a marker or a memorial.

## A11-1. A Bear on the Stairs

- `a11-01-s1`: Step into the pencil Forest and meet the boy at its edge. · _Touch the page, then walk up the path to the boy with the bear._
- `a11-01-s2`: Hold the balloon string while Pooh floats up to the bees. · _Stand under the tall oak and keep both hands on the string._
- `a11-01-s3`: Help get Pooh down again, without laughing. · _Keep the string steady while Christopher Robin aims his popgun._

#### `a11-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page drawn in soft pencil: a stream, a bridge, and a hill with a ring of trees on top._  
_Across the top there is writing, in slow, careful print._  
_It is the start of a story about a bear who comes downstairs in a very bumpy way._  
_The pencil goes soft under your fingers, then softer. Then it is pine needles, and you and your Nubbin are standing in them._  
_A boy is coming up the path with a bear under his arm, upside down. Neither of them seems to mind._  
**Christopher Robin**: Hallo. You’re not from the Forest. I know everybody in the Forest.  
**Christopher Robin**: This is Pooh. He came down the stairs on his head, so he may be a bit muddled. He usually is anyway.  
**Pooh**: How do you do. Is that a Heffalump?  
**Christopher Robin**: No, Pooh.  
**Pooh**: A very small one, I expect. They start small. Everything does.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): saying “I don’t know” instead of guessing  
> _Pooh is sure your Nubbin is a very small Heffalump, though nobody knows what a Heffalump is. Is it better to say “I don’t know”, or to guess?_  
> - Say “I don’t know” → That’s honest, and it leaves room to find out. Pooh’s sort of guess is more fun, but yours is safer.
> - Make a good guess → A guess can be a fine start, if you say it is a guess. Pooh says his like a fact, and that is where it gets tricky.
> - It depends on the question → That is a thoughtful answer. Some questions need care, and some are only a game.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when it is better to say “I don’t know” than to guess._

_Your Nubbin looks behind itself, in case there is a Heffalump there._  

**Choices**

- **Tell Pooh it’s a Nubbin.**
    - **Pooh**: A Nubbin. Yes. That’s just what a very small Heffalump would say.
- **Let your Nubbin decide.**
    - Your Nubbin sits on Pooh’s foot. Pooh decides that is a friendly thing for a Heffalump to do, and lets it.
- **Ask what a Heffalump is.**
    - **Christopher Robin**: Nobody knows exactly. That’s the best sort of animal.

#### `a11-01-page-done`

**Pooh**: I was just going to see about some honey. You can come, if you like.  
**Pooh**: Honey always goes better with somebody watching.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): a character’s motive is the reason they act  
> **Christopher Robin**: A motive is the reason a character does something. Pooh’s motive for going out today is honey.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Knowing a character’s motive helps you guess what they will do next. Try it on the bees.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a motive is the reason a character does something._


#### `a11-01-balloon`

_High in an oak there is a buzzing. Pooh stops so suddenly that your Nubbin walks into the back of him._  
**Pooh**: That is a honey sort of buzz. I’d know it anywhere.  
**Pooh**: The trouble with honey is that it’s always at the top of things. Christopher Robin, have you got such a thing as a balloon?  
**Christopher Robin**: I’ve got two. A green one and a blue one. What do you want a balloon for?  
**Pooh**: Honey.  
**Pooh**: The blue one, please. Bees won’t mind a bit of blue sky. And I shall roll in the mud, so I look like a small black cloud.  
_He does, very thoroughly. Your Nubbin rolls in the mud too, in case it’s a rule._  
**Christopher Robin**: You hold the string. Don’t let go unless he says. And don’t laugh. It hurts his feelings.  
_Up goes Pooh, past the branches, round and black and very hopeful. He stops at exactly the height of the nest._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced forces: a balloon pulling up, gravity pulling down  
> _Pooh hangs in the air, neither rising nor falling. The balloon pulls him up and gravity pulls him down. What do we call it when the pulls are equal?_  
> - ✅ Balanced forces → Yes. Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out, so Pooh stays put.
> - Unbalanced forces → Not quite. With unbalanced forces he would be rising or falling. He is still, so the pulls are equal.
> - No forces at all → Forces are still there. Gravity never switches off. They are just equal, so he does not move.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that equal forces pulling in opposite directions are balanced and cause no movement._


#### `a11-01-balloon-done`

_The string tugs in your hands like a kite that has been told about honey._  
**Pooh**: Christopher Robin? These bees are looking at me in a very suspicious sort of way.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): using context to work out a new word: suspicious  
> **Christopher Robin**: Suspicious means not trusting someone, and thinking they may be up to something. The bees are quite right to be.  
> **Christopher Robin**: You can often work out a new word from what is around it. A muddy “cloud” has come for their honey: no wonder they look at it oddly.  
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the word suspicious from context._


#### `a11-01-bees`

**Pooh**: Would you walk up and down with your umbrella, Christopher Robin, and say it looks like rain? Then they’ll believe I’m a cloud.  
_Christopher Robin walks up and down under his umbrella, saying it looks like rain. It doesn’t, and the bees know._  
**Pooh**: I think these are the wrong sort of bees. They would make the wrong sort of honey. I shall come down now.  
**Christopher Robin**: How?  
_Pooh hadn’t thought about that. He holds on, with the face of a bear doing a hard sum._  
**Pooh**: If you were to shoot the balloon with your popgun, I should come down. Gently. I hope.  
**Christopher Robin**: I might miss.  
**Pooh**: You might. Try not to.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what to do when a laugh hurts someone  
> _Christopher Robin says laughing hurts Pooh’s feelings, then admits he laughed too. What is the best thing to do if you laugh and someone is hurt?_  
> - ✅ Say sorry, and mean it → Yes. Funny things can still sting. A real sorry mends it faster than anything.
> - Pretend you did not laugh → That tends to make it worse. The hurt is still there, and now it is a secret too.
> - Say it was only a joke → “Only a joke” does not take the sting away. Saying sorry does.
> _For grown-ups: Chose a real apology after a laugh hurt someone’s feelings._


**Choices**

- **Bite your lip and hold steady.**
    - You bite your lip, and the string stays steady. Pooh looks down at you gratefully.
- **Laugh, a little, into your sleeve.**
    - **Pooh**: I heard that.
    - **Christopher Robin**: It’s all right. I laughed the first time too. He forgave me by lunch.

#### `a11-01-bees-done`

_Pop goes the popgun. “Ow!” says Pooh._  
**Christopher Robin**: Did I miss?  
**Pooh**: You hit something. It wasn’t the balloon.  
_The second cork gets the balloon. Pooh floats down into your arms like a large, muddy leaf._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): a simile compares two things using like or as  
> _“Pooh floats down into your arms like a large, muddy leaf.” That is a simile: it compares two things using “like” or “as”._  
> _Try one of your own: “Pooh was as round as…” What would you pick?_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a simile compares two things using like or as._


#### `a11-01-complete`

_Pooh’s arms have held the string so long that they stay up in the air, like a bear about to be surprised._  
**Christopher Robin**: They’ll come down in a week or so. If a fly lands on his nose, he has to blow it off. Like that. Pooh!  
_Pooh blows a fly off his nose. He looks pleased to be good at something._  
**Christopher Robin**: You can come back, you know. There’s always something on in the Forest. Or nothing, which is better.  
_He ties a blue ribbon round your Nubbin’s middle, in a careful double bow._  
**Christopher Robin**: So everyone knows it’s a Friend. Otherwise Piglet will think it’s a Woozle, and then there’s no talking to him.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying days: 2 weeks of 7 days  
> _Christopher Robin says Pooh’s arms will come down in about a week. A week has 7 days. How many days is 2 weeks?_  
> - ✅ 14 days → Yes. Two groups of seven is 2 × 7 = 14.
> - 9 days → Check again: 2 weeks is 7 + 7, which is 14. That is 2 × 7.
> - 12 days → Close. Two weeks is 7 + 7 = 14 days.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication to work out the days in two weeks._


### Glossary

- **gravity**: The pull that drags everything towards the ground.
- **motive**: The reason a character does something.
- **suspicious**: Not trusting someone, and thinking they may be up to something.
- **simile**: A comparison that uses “like” or “as”, such as “as round as a ball”.

## A11-2. A Tight Place

- `a11-02-s1`: Go visiting with Pooh, to Rabbit’s. · _Follow Pooh along the sandbank to the hole in it._
- `a11-02-s2`: Fetch Christopher Robin to look at the stuck bear. · _Run up the path to Christopher Robin’s house, then walk him back._
- `a11-02-s3`: Read to Pooh while he gets thinner. · _Sit by Pooh’s head and pick something to read; the week passes as the story goes on._

#### `a11-02-visit`

_Pooh is humming along the sandbank, which is what he does when he isn’t doing anything else._  
**Pooh**: A hole. A hole means Rabbit, and Rabbit means company, and company means a little something.  
**Pooh**: Hallo? Anybody in?  
**Rabbit**: Nobody’s in. Go away.  
**Pooh**: Then who said that?  
**Rabbit**: Nobody. I said it for him.  
_Rabbit puts his head out, sighs, and looks at your Nubbin._  
**Rabbit**: And what is that?  
**Pooh**: A very small Heffalump.  
**Rabbit**: It is not. It’s wearing a bow. Heffalumps don’t wear bows. Come in, then, both of you. Wipe your feet.  
_Rabbit gets out the honey. Pooh has a little, and then a little more, and then the rest, so it won’t feel left out._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, notice): bees carry pollen from flower to flower while making honey  
> **Christopher Robin**: To make honey, bees drink a sweet juice called nectar from flowers. A single worker makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon in her whole life.  
> **Christopher Robin**: As she goes from flower to flower, pollen sticks to her. That is how bees help plants make seeds. We say they pollinate.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bees make honey from nectar and pollinate flowers as they feed._

_Your Nubbin has one crumb. Rabbit watches it eat the crumb as if it might be the start of something._  

#### `a11-02-visit-done`

**Rabbit**: Well. Must you be going? Already? What a shame.  
_Pooh starts out of the front door, and his front half gets out. The rest of him has had too much honey to follow._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtracting to find the gap: 45 − 30  
> _Rabbit’s door is 30 cm wide. Pooh, after all that honey, is 45 cm across. By how many centimetres is Pooh too wide?_  
> - ✅ 15 cm → Yes. 45 − 30 = 15. That is a lot of honey.
> - 75 cm → That is 45 + 30. To find the gap, take the smaller from the bigger: 45 − 30 = 15.
> - 5 cm → Try again: 45 − 30. Take away 3 tens to get 15.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted two measurements to find how much wider Pooh was than the door._

**Pooh**: Oh, dear. I seem to have stopped.  

#### `a11-02-stuck`

_Pooh is stuck. His head and arms are out in the morning, and the rest of him is in Rabbit’s hall._  
**Pooh**: I can’t go forwards and I can’t go back. It’s all on account of the door being too narrow.  
**Rabbit**: It’s all on account of somebody eating too much honey. I’m only saying.  
**Rabbit**: You. Keeper. Go and get Christopher Robin. Run.  
_You run. Christopher Robin comes back at a sensible walk, because he has seen this sort of thing before._  
**Christopher Robin**: There’s only one thing for it. He’ll have to stay there until he’s thin again.  
**Pooh**: How long does getting thin take?  
**Christopher Robin**: About a week, I should think.  
**Pooh**: A week! What about meals?  
**Christopher Robin**: No meals. That’s rather the point.  
_A tear rolls down Pooh’s nose and drips on the sand. Your Nubbin sits in front of him, nose to nose._  
**Pooh**: Then would you read to me? Something comforting. A sustaining sort of book, for a Bear in a Tight Place.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): whether to say “I told you so” to someone in trouble  
> _Rabbit says it is all on account of somebody eating too much honey. He is right. But is it kind to say so to someone who is stuck?_  
> - Yes, it is only true → It is true. But true and helpful are not always the same thing. What does Pooh need most right now?
> - No, help first, talk later → Rabbit might agree, if he were not so cross. Help is the thing a stuck bear remembers.
> - It depends how you say it → A good point. A friendly “bit of a squeeze, isn’t it?” is very different from “I told you so”.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being right justifies saying “I told you so”._


#### `a11-02-stuck-done`

**Christopher Robin**: We’ll take turns. You read in the mornings, and I’ll read in the afternoons.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): sustaining means giving strength; context clues  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pooh asked for a sustaining sort of book. Sustaining means something that keeps you going, like a hearty soup.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Could you tell from the sentence? When a word is new, look at the words around it for clues.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word sustaining and practised using context clues._


#### `a11-02-week`

_So for a week you sit on the sandbank and read to the North end of Pooh. Christopher Robin takes the afternoons._  
_At the South end, inside, Rabbit has hung his washing on Pooh’s back legs._  
**Rabbit**: It’s a waste of a perfectly good pair of legs otherwise. Do you mind, Pooh?  
**Pooh**: I don’t mind. I should like to know what’s on them, though.  
**Rabbit**: Tea towels.  
**Pooh**: Ah.  
_Your Nubbin brings Pooh an acorn to look at, since he isn’t allowed to eat anything._  
**Pooh**: What are we reading today?  

> **Lesson** (maths, do): a tally of the days of a week  
> **Christopher Robin**: A week has seven days. Let us keep a tally: one stroke for each day, four strokes standing up and the fifth across them like a gate.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Make one gate and two more strokes. That is seven, and Pooh is free on the seventh day.  
> Check: `edu:tally:days-of-week:7`
> _For grown-ups: Made a tally of seven, bundling the first five marks into a gate._


**Choices**

- **A story about a bear who was exactly the right size.**
    - **Pooh**: I like him already. Does he get stuck?
    - **You**: Never.
    - **Pooh**: Lucky bear.
- **A book about the sea, where there aren’t any doors.**
    - **Pooh**: No doors at all? That sounds like a very comfortable place for a bear.
- **Just sit with him. Don’t read anything.**
    - You sit by his head and say nothing at all.
    - **Pooh**: That’s the most sustaining one so far.

#### `a11-02-week-done`

_On the seventh day Christopher Robin takes Pooh’s front paws. Rabbit takes Christopher Robin._  
_Rabbit’s friends-and-relations take Rabbit, all of them, in a long line. You take the end, and your Nubbin takes you._  
**Christopher Robin**: Pull!  
_For a long time nothing happens. Then, with a pop like a ginger-beer cork, out comes Pooh, and everyone sits down at once._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): unbalanced forces: friction holds, a bigger pull wins  
> **Christopher Robin**: All week the door gripped Pooh tightly. That grip, between surfaces rubbing together, is called friction.  
> **Christopher Robin**: By the seventh day Pooh was thinner, so the grip was weaker, and the long line of friends pulled harder than it held. Unbalanced forces: out he popped.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that friction can hold something until a bigger pull makes it move._


#### `a11-02-complete`

**Pooh**: Thank you. All of you. Especially the one at the end, who I couldn’t see but could feel.  
_Pooh nods to his friends and walks off into the Forest, humming, a little thinner and not at all wiser._  
**Rabbit**: He’ll be back. He knows where the honey is now. I shall have to get a wider door.  
_Rabbit looks at the hall where the legs were. He looks very nearly as if he misses them._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): feelings can be mixed: glad and a little lonely  
> _Rabbit wanted Pooh out of his door. Now Pooh is out, and Rabbit looks as if he misses him._  
> _Two feelings at once is normal. You can be relieved and a bit lonely in the same minute._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that people can feel two different things at once._


### Glossary

- **nectar**: The sweet juice inside flowers that bees collect.
- **pollinate**: To carry pollen from flower to flower so plants can make seeds.
- **sustaining**: Keeping you going and giving you strength, like a hearty meal.
- **friction**: The grip between two surfaces that rub against each other, which slows things down.

## A11-3. The Woozle

- `a11-03-s1`: Follow Pooh round the spinney after the mysterious tracks. · _Walk round the larch spinney in the snow behind Pooh and Piglet. Don’t spoil it._
- `a11-03-s2`: Watch from the oak with Christopher Robin until they work it out. · _Climb the big oak by the spinney and keep quiet._

#### `a11-03-tracks`

_It is a fine winter’s day. Piglet is brushing snow off his front step when Pooh goes past, round in a circle._  
**Piglet**: Pooh? Why are you going round and round?  
**Pooh**: Following something. I don’t know what yet. That’s the exciting part.  
**Pooh**: Look. Paw-marks. Something has been round here, and round, and I have been round after it.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): tracks tell us size, speed and direction  
> **Christopher Robin**: Animal trackers read prints like a story. The size shows how big the animal is, and the spacing shows how fast it moved.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A line of prints shows where it went. A circle of prints, though, shows somebody going round in circles.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tracks show an animal’s size, speed and direction._

**Piglet**: Could it be… a Woozle?  
**Pooh**: It might. Woozles are very hard to tell from the front.  
_Piglet looks at your Nubbin, hard. Your Nubbin looks back with great innocence._  
**Piglet**: That one’s got a bow on. Christopher Robin s-said it was a Friend. But a Woozle would say that.  
_Your Nubbin trots after Pooh round the spinney of larches, putting its small feet very carefully in the snow._  

**Choices**

- **Tell them the little prints are your Nubbin’s.**
    - **Pooh**: Yes, yes. And these others are something else. Do keep up.
    - Nobody is listening. It is very hard to spoil a thing when nobody is listening.
- **Say nothing. Let it play out.**
    - You say nothing. It feels like carrying a very full cup, very still.
- **Let your Nubbin go round once more.**
    - Your Nubbin goes round once more, very pleased with itself. Now there is one more set of tracks.

#### `a11-03-tracks-done`

_Round they go. Every time they come back to the same place, there are more tracks than before._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a pattern that follows a rule: adding 2 each lap  
> _Each lap round the larches, Pooh and Piglet each add one set of prints._  
> _After lap 1 there are 2 sets. After lap 2 there are 4. How many after lap 5?_  
> - ✅ 10 sets → Yes. The rule is add 2 each lap: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
> - 8 sets → That is lap 4. Keep going one more: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
> - 5 sets → That would be adding 1. The rule here is add 2 each lap, so lap 5 gives 10.
> _For grown-ups: Continued a number pattern by applying the rule add 2._


#### `a11-03-count`

**Pooh**: Look! Two of them now. And one very small. And a third, and something else besides.  
**Piglet**: Three Woozles and a Wizzle, perhaps. Pooh, I’ve just remembered something I meant to do yesterday. I’d better go and do it.  
_Up in a big oak, Christopher Robin is sitting very still. He beckons you up, and your Nubbin rides in your hood._  
**Christopher Robin**: Don’t say anything. He gets there in the end. He always does, and it’s better when he gets there himself.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): letting someone find out for themselves  
> _Christopher Robin says it is better when Pooh gets there himself. Would you have told Pooh the answer early? Why, or why not?_  
> - Yes, tell him early → That is kind, and it would save Pooh a lot of walking. But Christopher Robin thinks finding it himself is worth something.
> - No, let him find out → That is Christopher Robin’s view too. When you work it out yourself, you remember it.
> - Tell him if he asks → A fair middle path. Being ready to help without taking the discovery away from someone is a skill.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about helping someone without taking away their chance to discover._

_Pooh stops and looks at the tracks. He puts his own foot into one of them, and it fits._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a hypothesis is an idea you can test  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pooh has an idea: these prints belong to a Woozle. An idea you can test is called a hypothesis.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pooh tests his by fitting his own foot in the print. It fits, so the hypothesis is in trouble.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a hypothesis is an idea that can be tested._

**Pooh**: Oh.  
_He puts his foot into another. It fits too._  
_Piglet, a little way off, looks at the tiny prints, then at your Nubbin’s feet, and goes pink._  

#### `a11-03-count-done`

_Christopher Robin climbs down from the tree._  
**Christopher Robin**: Oh, Pooh. Whose footprints do you think those are?  
**Pooh**: I have been going round and round after my own feet. I am a Bear with no Brain worth mentioning.  
**Christopher Robin**: There isn’t a better bear anywhere. I’d know.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): kind words when someone feels silly  
> _Pooh feels silly: he followed his own feet. Christopher Robin does not laugh. He says something warm._  
> _When someone feels foolish, a kind sentence can turn the whole day around._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard how a kind reply helps someone who feels silly._


#### `a11-03-complete`

**Pooh**: Being silly is very hungry work. Is it lunch?  
_Pooh and Christopher Robin go home together. Piglet walks a long way round your Nubbin, then, after a while, a shorter way._  
**Piglet**: I knew it wasn’t a Woozle. Mostly.  
_Your Nubbin holds out a paw. Piglet shakes it quickly, and then a second time, slower._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): actions show a character’s feelings  
> _Piglet walks a long way round your Nubbin, then a shorter way, then shakes its paw twice. Nobody says he is less afraid._  
> _His actions tell you instead. Watching what characters do, not only what they say, is how readers find out how they feel._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that a character’s actions can show a change of feeling._


### Glossary

- **hypothesis**: An idea about how something works that you can test.

## A11-4. Eeyore’s Tail

- `a11-04-s1`: Find out what is wrong with Eeyore. · _Eeyore stands in the thistly corner of the Forest._
- `a11-04-s2`: Go with Pooh to ask Owl. · _Owl lives at The Chestnuts, high in a tree, behind the grandest door in the Forest._
- `a11-04-s3`: Hold the tail straight while Christopher Robin nails it back on. · _Carry the tail back to the thistles and hold it where Christopher Robin points._

#### `a11-04-gloomy`

_Eeyore, the old grey donkey, stands by himself in a thistly corner of the Forest, with his head on one side._  
_Sometimes he thinks sadly about things. Sometimes he just thinks._  
**Pooh**: Good morning, Eeyore.  
**Eeyore**: Good morning, Pooh. If it is a good morning. Which I doubt.  
**Pooh**: Why, what’s the matter?  
**Eeyore**: Nothing. Nobody minds. Nobody ever does.  
_Pooh walks all the way round Eeyore. Then he walks round again, to be sure._  
**Pooh**: Eeyore. What has happened to your tail?  
_Eeyore turns slowly to look, and turns, and turns, and comes back to where he started._  
**Eeyore**: You’re right. It’s gone. That explains a great deal.  
**Eeyore**: Somebody must have taken it. How like them.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): gloomy does not always mean “leave me alone”  
> _Eeyore says “Nobody minds. Nobody ever does.” Does that mean he wants to be left alone, or something else?_  
> - He wants to be left alone → Sometimes people do. But Pooh asked, and then stayed, and Eeyore did not send him away.
> - He wants somebody to notice → That fits the story. “Nobody minds” is often a quiet way of hoping somebody does.
> - You can only find out by asking → A wise answer. Asking, and then staying close, is how Pooh does it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what a gloomy friend might really need._


**Choices**

- **Promise you’ll help find it.**
    - **Eeyore**: Kind of you. Don’t trouble. I expect somebody is using it for something important.
- **Sit with him for a moment first.**
    - You sit in the thistles beside him, which are very prickly. Eeyore notices, and doesn’t say so, which is a sort of thank you.
- **Look behind the thistles.**
    - Your Nubbin looks behind the thistles, under a stone and inside its own bow. No tail.

#### `a11-04-gloomy-done`

**Pooh**: I shall find your tail for you, Eeyore. Me. Pooh.  
**Eeyore**: Thank you, Pooh. You’re a real friend. Better than most.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): thistle prickles protect the plant; donkeys cope  
> **Christopher Robin**: A thistle is covered in sharp spines. The spines are a structure that helps the plant survive, because most animals do not want a mouthful.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Donkeys really do eat thistles. Their lips and mouths are tough enough for the prickles.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that thistle spines protect the plant and that donkeys can eat thistles._


#### `a11-04-owl`

_Owl lives at The Chestnuts, high in a tree, behind a very grand door with a knocker and a bell-pull._  
_There are two notices by the door, in Owl’s spelling: one says to ring, and the other to knock if the ringing doesn’t work._  
_Pooh knocks and rings. Your Nubbin, who can reach neither, stands on Pooh._  
**Owl**: Ah, Pooh. And company. How do you do. What can I do for you?  
**Pooh**: Eeyore has lost his tail, and he’s very sad about it. Could you tell me how to find it?  
**Owl**: Well. In cases of this sort there is a Proper Procedure. First, one Issues a Notice.  
**Pooh**: I’m only a small bear, Owl, and big words make my head go fuzzy.  
**Owl**: It means the Thing to Do. Then one offers a Reward. Then one considers the Matter in all its Aspects.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words with more than one meaning: notice  
> _You can notice a tail is missing: that means to see. Owl says to “Issue a Notice”. What does notice mean there?_  
> - ✅ A sign with information on it → Yes. As a noun, a notice is a sign. A word can change its meaning with its job.
> - To see something → That is the verb. Owl is using the noun: a notice is a sign you pin up for everyone.
> - To forget something → Not quite. A notice is a sign that tells people something, like a lost tail poster.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that notice can mean to see or a sign, depending on how it is used._

_Owl talks for some time, in longer and longer words. Pooh nods at the places where nodding seems to be wanted._  
_Your Nubbin isn’t listening. It is looking at the bell-pull, which is grey, and hairy, and has a tuft at the end._  

#### `a11-04-owl-done`

**Pooh**: Owl. That bell-pull. Where did you get it?  
**Owl**: Came across it in the Forest, hanging on a bush. I gave it a pull to see who was in. Nobody was. It came away in my wing.  
**Pooh**: It belongs to Eeyore. He’s been missing it all morning, and the back of him hasn’t known what to do.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): returning what you find  
> **Christopher Robin**: Owl found the tail on a bush and made it his bell-pull. He did not know whose it was, but he never asked around either.  
> **Christopher Robin**: When you find something that might be lost, the fair thing is to ask whose it is, or hand it in. Someone may be missing it.  
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the fair thing to do with something you find._


#### `a11-04-nail`

_You carry the tail back through the Forest, very carefully, as if it might wake up._  
_Christopher Robin meets you at the thistles with a little hammer and one very short nail._  
**Christopher Robin**: Hold it straight. Not that straight. There. Eeyore, this won’t hurt. It’s a very small nail.  
**Eeyore**: Don’t mind me. Nobody does.  
_Tap, tap: Eeyore doesn’t flinch. Your Nubbin flinches for him, both times._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): sound is vibration  
> **Christopher Robin**: Each tap of the hammer makes the nail and the wood vibrate, shaking very fast and very slightly. The shaking pushes the air, and you hear it as a tap.  
> **Christopher Robin**: All sounds are vibrations. That is why you can feel a drum with your hand.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound is caused by vibrations travelling through the air._

_Then Eeyore swishes his tail, carefully, like somebody trying a new door._  
**Eeyore**: Hm. It works. Not that anybody asked.  
_He swishes it again, and frisks about among the thistles. He is happy, though he would rather you didn’t mention it._  

#### `a11-04-nail-done`

**Eeyore**: Thank you, Pooh. And the one with the bow. Thank you.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): gratitude names the people who helped  
> _Eeyore thanks Pooh, and then the one with the bow. He names who helped._  
> _Thanks land best when they are specific. “Thank you for holding it straight” beats just “thanks”._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that naming what someone did makes thanks feel more real._


#### `a11-04-complete`

_Pooh walks home feeling that he has done a Good Deed, which he has._  
_He feels so pleased that he is ready for a little something by eleven o’clock. So he has one._  
**Pooh**: Owl knows ever such a lot. Long words and everything. But it was your Nubbin who looked at the bell-pull.  
_Your Nubbin looks proud. Then, to be safe, it looks for every other bell-pull in the Forest, and there aren’t any._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: 10:20 to 11:00  
> _Pooh leaves Eeyore at 10:20, and his little something is at eleven o’clock. How many minutes does he have to wait?_  
> - ✅ 40 minutes → Yes. From 10:20 to 11:00 is 40 minutes: 10:20 to 10:30 is 10, then 30 more.
> - 30 minutes → Count again: 10:20 to 10:30 is 10 minutes, and 10:30 to 11:00 is another 30. That is 40.
> - 20 minutes → That is the minutes already on the clock. The wait to 11:00 is 40 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval from 10:20 to 11:00._


### Glossary

- **procedure**: The steps for doing something in a set order.
- **notice**: A sign that gives people information. It can also mean to see something.

## A11-5. The Heffalump Trap

- `a11-05-s1`: Help Pooh and Piglet dig a Very Deep Pit by the Six Pine Trees. · _Dig where Pooh points; Piglet supervises the supervising._
- `a11-05-s2`: Keep the lantern steady while Pooh checks on the honey in the night. · _Walk with Pooh to the Six Pine Trees and hold the lantern still._
- `a11-05-s3`: Let Piglet meet the Heffalump. Don’t explain. · _Stay by the pit with the lantern and let the morning happen._

#### `a11-05-dig`

**Christopher Robin**: I saw a Heffalump today. I think.  
_Christopher Robin says it carelessly, the way you might mention rain, and then goes home to his lunch._  
**Piglet**: A Heffalump. Here. Pooh, what does one do with a Heffalump?  
**Pooh**: Catch it. In a Very Deep Pit. A cunning one, near where Heffalumps walk. The Six Pine Trees, I should think.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a rectangle  
> _Pooh wants the pit floor to be 3 metres long and 2 metres wide. What is its area?_  
> - ✅ 6 square metres → Yes. Area of a rectangle is length × width: 3 × 2 = 6.
> - 5 square metres → That is 3 + 2. For area, multiply: 3 × 2 = 6.
> - 10 square metres → That is the distance round the edge (perimeter). Area is 3 × 2 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a rectangle by multiplying length by width._

_Piglet digs and Pooh supervises. You do most of it, and your Nubbin moves one pebble a long way, very proudly._  
**Piglet**: Won’t the Heffalump see the pit?  
**Pooh**: We cover it with sticks and leaves. And at the bottom we put something it likes, so it comes.  
**Piglet**: What do Heffalumps like?  
**Pooh**: Honey.  
**Piglet**: Are you sure?  
**Pooh**: Everybody likes honey.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): whether it is fair to trap an animal you have never met  
> _Pooh and Piglet set a trap for a creature they have never met, because they are curious and a little afraid. Is that fair to the creature?_  
> - No, it did nothing wrong → That is a strong point. Being afraid of something is not a reason to harm it.
> - Yes, if it is dangerous → They do not know if it is dangerous. That is the problem: they have only guessed.
> - Find out about it first → Many people would agree. Looking and learning before acting is fairer to animals and safer for us.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness to an animal you know nothing about._


**Choices**

- **Ask what they’ll do once it’s caught.**
    - **Pooh**: Be very polite to it, I expect. It’ll be cross otherwise.
    - **Piglet**: Oh, d-dear.
- **Dig a little step in one side, in case.**
    - **Piglet**: A step? For the Heffalump?
    - **You**: For anyone who falls in by mistake.
    - **Pooh**: Very sensible. Nobody will.
- **Check it’s deep enough.**
    - You climb in to look, and it comes up to your chin. Your Nubbin, at the top, looks down at you as if you are the Heffalump.

#### `a11-05-dig-done`

_Pooh fetches his very last jar of honey and lowers it into the pit. He looks at it for some time after._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): an inference is a conclusion from clues  
> _Pooh looks at the honey for some time after. The story does not say he is sorry to leave it there, but you can tell._  
> _Working something out from clues, when the text does not say it, is called an inference. Good readers do it all the time._  
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference about a character’s feelings from a clue._


#### `a11-05-night`

_That night Pooh can’t sleep. He tries counting sheep, but they keep turning into Heffalumps, and all of them are eating his honey._  
**Pooh**: Who’s there? Oh, it’s you. Good. I am going to see if the honey is still there. Only to see. Will you hold the lantern?  
_You walk to the Six Pine Trees with the lantern. Your Nubbin walks inside the circle of light and won’t step out of it._  
_The honey is still there. Pooh climbs down into the pit and looks at it closely, the way you’d look at an old friend._  
**Pooh**: I’ll just check it’s honey all the way down. It might be cheese at the bottom. You never know with jars.  
_He puts his head in to look, and licks, to be sure. Then he licks further in._  
**Pooh**: Mmff. Mmff mff.  
_Pooh stands up in the bottom of the pit with the jar on his head._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound is muffled by a jar  
> _Pooh talks with a jar on his head and it sounds like “Mmff”. Why is his voice muffled?_  
> - ✅ The jar traps and muffles the sound vibrations → Yes. His voice makes vibrations, but the jar round his head keeps most of them in. Only a muffled sound gets out.
> - The jar makes his voice louder → A jar sometimes echoes, but with it on his head, most of the sound stays inside. So it is quieter.
> - He is tired → He may well be! But this one is the jar, not sleepiness.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a jar over the head muffles a voice._


**Choices**

- **Hold the lantern steady and wait.**
    - You hold it steady. It trembles only once, because you are laughing, and you stop, because you mustn’t.
- **Try to pull the jar off.**
    - It won’t come, because Pooh’s ears are on the inside. This will have to be a morning job.

#### `a11-05-night-done`

_Pooh climbs out somehow and wanders off into the grey morning, booming inside the jar._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): writers show how someone sounds, not only what they say  
> _“Mmm mmff.” Writers spell out muffled sounds so you can hear them in your head._  
> _Dialogue can show how someone sounds, not just what they say. Try writing Piglet saying “help” very quietly._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that spelling can show how a voice sounds._


#### `a11-05-morning`

_At first light Piglet comes to see if there is a Heffalump in the pit. He comes very quietly, and very slowly._  
_There is a Heffalump. It is walking round the pit with a huge round head, and it is roaring._  
**Piglet**: Help! Help! It’s a Heffalump! And it’s got Pooh’s honey!  
_Piglet runs all the way to Christopher Robin’s door without touching the ground more than four times._  
_He comes back with Christopher Robin. You are still there with your lantern, not explaining, because some things are better found out._  
_The Heffalump bangs its head on a tree root. The jar breaks, and there is Pooh, sticky and very pleased to see everyone._  
_Christopher Robin begins to laugh, and laughs, and can’t stop._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows and dim light can fool us  
> _At dawn Piglet sees a huge round-headed shape and shouts “Heffalump!” Why did Pooh with a jar look so strange?_  
> - ✅ In dim light we see only an outline → Yes. With little light, we cannot see colours or details, only a dark shape, and our brain guesses.
> - Pooh really grew bigger → He did not! Low morning light makes long shadows and big outlines, which can make small things look huge.
> - The jar was magic → It was only a jar. Light and shadow did the rest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that in dim light we see only outlines, which can be misread._

**Piglet**: …Oh. It was Pooh.  

#### `a11-05-morning-done`

_Piglet goes home to bed with a headache. Pooh goes home to breakfast._  
_Your Nubbin keeps one piece of the broken jar: the piece with a little honey left on it._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): calming down after a fright  
> _Piglet’s heart is still thumping from his fright, and he has a headache._  
> _A few slow breaths, a drink of water, and telling somebody what happened all help the body settle._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned ways to calm down after a fright._


#### `a11-05-complete`

**Pooh**: I did think, for a moment, that I might be a Heffalump. It was very dark and echoey in there.  
**Christopher Robin**: You’re not. You were a bear in a jar. That’s much better.  
**Pooh**: Then who is the Heffalump?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, notice): authors let readers know more than characters  
> _You knew it was Pooh in the jar before Piglet did. Your point of view is bigger than his._  
> _When an author lets you know more than a character, it can be funny, or tense. Here it is funny._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that a reader can know more than a character._

_Everyone looks at your Nubbin. Your Nubbin looks behind itself again._  
**Pooh**: A very small one. I’m nearly sure.  

### Glossary

- **inference**: A conclusion you work out from clues.

## A11-6. Eeyore’s Birthday

- `a11-06-s1`: Find out why Eeyore is gloomier than usual. · _Eeyore is down by the stream, looking at himself in the water._
- `a11-06-s2`: Go with Pooh and Piglet to fetch presents. · _Carry the honey pot for Pooh as far as he lets you._
- `a11-06-s3`: Choose what your Nubbin gives Eeyore. · _There is no wrong present. Nothing at all is one of the choices._

#### `a11-06-stream`

_Eeyore is standing by the stream, looking at himself in the water._  
**Eeyore**: Look at him down there. Even the reflection’s glum, and it doesn’t have to be.  
**Pooh**: Good morning, Eeyore.  
**Eeyore**: Is it? It would be just like it.  
_Pooh hums at him, to be cheerful. Eeyore waits for the hum to finish, politely, as if it were rain._  
**Eeyore**: It’s my birthday, as it happens. Not that it matters.  
**Pooh**: Your birthday?  
**Eeyore**: Of course it is. You can tell by all the presents. All none of them.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what “it doesn’t matter” can really mean  
> _Eeyore says “It’s my birthday. Not that it matters.” Do you think he means it?_  
> - Yes, he really does not mind → Maybe. But he mentions it, and he is standing alone looking at the water. Hmm.
> - No, he hopes someone will notice → That fits the clues. People often say “it doesn’t matter” when it matters a lot.
> - I can’t tell from just that → A careful answer. That is why Pooh does not argue: he just goes to fetch presents.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what people mean when they say something does not matter._

_Pooh looks to the right and to the left, very carefully, in case there are presents he has missed. There aren’t._
