**Pooh**: Wait here, Eeyore.  
_Pooh hurries off home. Your Nubbin stays behind for one moment, looking at Eeyore, and then follows._  

#### `a11-06-presents`

_At home, Pooh finds he has a pot of honey, which is the right sort of present for anybody._  
_Piglet has a balloon, a big green one he was saving for something special. This is special._  
_Somewhere on the way, your Nubbin has picked a thistle. It carries it in both paws, prickles and all, and won’t say why._  
_Halfway there, Pooh begins to feel a little eleven o’clock-ish. He sits down and takes the lid off the honey, only to see._  
_He licks the top, and round the edges, and the bottom. Then there is nothing left in the pot._  
**Pooh**: Bother. I had a present, and I’ve eaten it.  
**Pooh**: But a pot is a Very Useful Thing. You can put things in it. I shall give him a Useful Pot, for keeping things in.  
_Meanwhile Piglet, running to be first, trips in a rabbit-hole and lands flat on his balloon. Bang._  
**Piglet**: Oh, d-dear. Oh, dear, oh, dear. It was a balloon, and now it’s a bit of damp rag.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): why a balloon bursts when squashed  
> _Piglet falls on his balloon and it goes bang. What happens to the air inside when he lands on it?_  
> - ✅ It is squeezed until the rubber cannot stretch more → Yes. Air presses outwards on the rubber in every direction. Squash it, and the pressure rises until the rubber tears.
> - The air disappears → Air does not vanish. It rushed out through the tear in a hurry: that is the bang.
> - The air gets colder → Not really. It is the pressure that matters: Piglet squeezed it harder than the rubber could take.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that squeezing a balloon raises the air pressure until the rubber tears._

_He picks up the bit of damp rag, very sadly, and carries it on to Eeyore’s anyway._  

#### `a11-06-presents-done`

_Your Nubbin looks at the empty pot, and at the rag, and down at its own blue bow, and at the thistle._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): a gift that fits the person  
> _Your Nubbin chose a thistle without being told. Eeyore eats thistles, so it is a gift that fits him._  
> _A good gift is one that shows you thought about the person: what they like, what they need._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that a good gift shows you thought about the person._


#### `a11-06-gift`

**Piglet**: Many happy returns of the day, Eeyore. I’ve brought you a balloon.  
**Eeyore**: A balloon? For me?  
**Piglet**: It was a balloon. It got burst. I’m very sorry.  
**Pooh**: And I’ve brought you a Useful Pot. To put things in. There’s nothing in it. That’s what makes it so useful.  
_Eeyore looks at the pot, and at the rag. Then he picks up the rag in his teeth and drops it in the pot._  
_He takes it out, and puts it back in. He takes it out again._  
**Eeyore**: It goes in and out. You wouldn’t think it, but it does.  
_Everyone watches Eeyore being happy, which nobody has seen before. Nobody says anything, in case it stops._  
_Your Nubbin steps forward. It has something to give too, or nothing, which is also a thing._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, notice): choosing means giving something up  
> _Your Nubbin has three things it could give: the ribbon, the thistle, or its time. It cannot give all three at once._  
> _Whenever you pick one thing, you give up the others. People call that a choice, and it is how every shop, family and garden works._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that choosing one thing means giving up others._


**Choices**

- **Your Nubbin gives Eeyore its blue ribbon.**
    - Your Nubbin tugs at its double bow until it comes undone, and lays the blue ribbon at Eeyore’s feet.
    - **Eeyore**: That’s your Friend ribbon. Christopher Robin tied it. I know what it says.
    - **Eeyore**: Well. I shan’t wear it. I’ll keep it. Somewhere safe. In the pot.
- **Your Nubbin gives him the thistle it carried.**
    - Your Nubbin holds out the thistle. It has been prickling its paws every step of the way.
    - **Eeyore**: The good sort. Purple on top. Somebody carried that a long way, by the look of their paws.
    - **Eeyore**: I shan’t eat it. Not today. I’ll keep it for a bit.
- **Nothing. You both just sit with him.**
    - You sit down on the bank beside Eeyore, and your Nubbin sits down beside you. Nobody says anything.
    - Pooh and Piglet go home after a while. You stay, and the afternoon goes by slowly, the way they do when nobody hurries them.
    - **Eeyore**: Hm. Nobody’s done that before. Sat, I mean. Without wanting anything.

#### `a11-06-gift-done`

_By evening Eeyore is still putting the balloon in the pot and taking it out again. He looks, for Eeyore, almost cheerful._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): repetition makes a funny image  
> _In, out, in, out, in, out. Authors repeat a small action to make a moment funny, or touching._  
> _Here it does both: it is silly, and it shows that a small thing can make Eeyore happy._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how repetition can make a moment funny and touching._


#### `a11-06-complete`

_Christopher Robin arrives late with a cake, and everyone has a slice, and Eeyore has the piece with the most icing, under protest._  
**Eeyore**: A Useful Pot, a balloon, and cake. People will say I’m spoiled.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: one slice of eight  
> _Christopher Robin cuts the cake into 8 equal slices and gives Eeyore the one with the most icing. What fraction of the cake is that slice?_  
> - ✅ 1/8 → Yes. One of eight equal parts is one eighth, written 1/8.
> - 1/2 → One half would be 4 of the 8 slices. One slice on its own is 1/8.
> - 8/1 → Careful: the fraction goes one part over the total number of parts: 1/8.
> _For grown-ups: Named a unit fraction: one equal slice out of eight._

**Pooh**: Will they?  
**Eeyore**: No. But they could.  
_Pooh turns out to have another empty pot at home, which is lucky, as he is very good at making them. He gives it to you._  
_Eeyore tears off a corner of balloon to go in it._  
**Eeyore**: Every pot wants something to go in and out. Otherwise what’s the point.  

## A11-7. Kanga and Baby Roo

- `a11-07-s1`: Listen to Rabbit’s plan about the newcomers. · _Rabbit is holding a meeting by his front door. He has a list._
- `a11-07-s2`: Make sure Roo has a nice time in Rabbit’s pocket. · _Run alongside Rabbit to his burrow and keep Roo company._
- `a11-07-s3`: Go back and see how Piglet is getting on. · _Kanga’s house is by the Sandy Pit._

#### `a11-07-plan`

_Nobody knows where they came from, but there they are in the Forest: Kanga, and Baby Roo in her pocket._  
**Rabbit**: One morning, nobody. Next morning, a Kanga. Who said she could? And she keeps her child in her pocket!  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-LS1-2, notice): baby kangaroos grow in the pouch  
> **Christopher Robin**: Real kangaroos are marsupials. A baby, called a joey, is born tiny and finishes growing in its mother’s pouch.  
> **Christopher Robin**: The pouch keeps it warm and safe, and she can feed it there. Nobody in the Forest has seen that before.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that kangaroo joeys grow in their mother’s pouch._

**Pooh**: Where should she keep it?  
**Rabbit**: That’s not the point. Here is the plan. We wait until Kanga isn’t looking. We take Baby Roo, and hide him.  
**Rabbit**: Then she says, “Where is Baby Roo?” And we say, “We know where he is.” And she says, “Oh, I see,” and goes away.  
**Rabbit**: And Piglet jumps into her pocket instead, so she doesn’t notice. Piglet is very small.  
**Piglet**: V-very small. Yes. Small enough to be b-brave about it.  
_Your Nubbin looks at you, and you look at Rabbit. Rabbit is looking at his list._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): how to treat newcomers  
> _Rabbit wants Kanga and Roo to leave, just because they are new and do things differently. Pooh asks “Where should she keep it?” Whose side is the better one?_  
> - Rabbit’s: newcomers should fit in → Fitting in matters to Rabbit. But what is the harm in a pocket? That is Pooh’s question.
> - Pooh’s: there is no harm → Pooh asks it lightly, but it is a good test. If no one is hurt, why would they need to leave?
> - Neither, give them time → Many of the best neighbours start as strangers. Time and a little curiosity often do the work.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness towards people who are new and different._


**Choices**

- **Say it’s a bad plan.**
    - **Rabbit**: It is a very good plan. It has Steps.
    - There is no stopping a plan once it has Steps.
- **Ask what happens to Roo.**
    - **Rabbit**: He comes to stay at mine. Briefly. He’ll be quite safe.
    - You decide you will be there when he does.
- **Say nothing, and go along.**
    - You go along. Somebody should be there who isn’t part of the plan.

#### `a11-07-plan-done`

**Rabbit**: You look after Roo on the way, Keeper. Keep him happy. Happy Roos don’t squeak.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): a grown-up must always know where a child is  
> _In the Forest, Kanga knows all along and it is a game. In real life, a child should never be taken away from their grown-up, even as a game._  
> _If it happens, say no loudly, stay close to other people, and tell a trusted adult straight away._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a grown-up should always know where a child is, and who to tell if not._


#### `a11-07-swap`

_By the Sandy Pit, Kanga is teaching Roo to jump. Pooh distracts her with a very long poem about nothing in particular._  
_While she looks the other way, Rabbit lifts Roo out, and Piglet jumps in, with his eyes shut._  
_Rabbit runs off with Roo in a pillowcase he has made into a pocket for the purpose. You run alongside._  
**Roo**: Is this a game? I like games. Am I in a pocket? It’s a different pocket. It smells of carrots.  
**Rabbit**: Hush. You’re being Hidden. Hidden things are quiet.  
**Roo**: Can your Nubbin come in the pocket too?  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): tendons store energy for a kangaroo’s hop  
> **Christopher Robin**: A kangaroo’s back legs have long, stretchy tendons. Each landing stretches them like springs, and they spring back to help with the next hop.  
> **Christopher Robin**: That saves the kangaroo energy, so a big red kangaroo can keep hopping for a long way.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that kangaroo tendons store energy like springs._


**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin ride with Roo.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs into the pillowcase. Roo laughs so much the pocket wriggles all the way to Rabbit’s.
- **Count the trees with Roo as they go by.**
    - **Roo**: One, two, lots, lots, lots, lots, lots, home!
- **Tell Roo a story.**
    - **Roo**: Is there a Roo in it?
    - **You**: There is now.
    - **Roo**: Good. Make him jump a lot.

#### `a11-07-swap-done`

_At Rabbit’s, Roo practises jumping off the front step. Rabbit pretends not to count the jumps, and counts them anyway._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: 6 hops a minute for 5 minutes  
> _Roo hops off Rabbit’s step 6 times every minute. How many hops in 5 minutes?_  
> - ✅ 30 hops → Yes. Five groups of six: 5 × 6 = 30.
> - 11 hops → That is 6 + 5. Each minute has 6 hops, so multiply: 5 × 6 = 30.
> - 36 hops → Close, but that would be 6 minutes. Five minutes is 5 × 6 = 30.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication to count hops over five minutes._


#### `a11-07-bath`

_At Kanga’s house, Kanga has noticed. Kangas always notice._  
**Kanga**: Bath-time, Roo dear.  
_She says it to Piglet, looking straight at Piglet, and runs the bath anyway._  
**Piglet**: I’m not Roo! I’m Piglet!  
**Kanga**: Of course you are, dear. And the water’s lovely and cold.  
_Kanga scrubs Piglet very thoroughly, and gives him a big spoonful of medicine, to make him strong._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): medicine is only safe from a trusted adult  
> _Medicine can help a body get well, but the dose matters. Too much can make you ill instead._  
> _So only a trusted grown-up should give you medicine. Never take it by yourself, even if it tastes like a sweet._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that only a trusted adult should give medicine._

**Piglet**: Ugh. I’m Piglet. Ask anyone. Ask the Keeper.  
_You open your mouth. Kanga catches your eye over Piglet’s head, and you close it again: she knows, and she is enjoying herself._  
_Piglet escapes the towel at last, rolls in the road to get his own colour back, and runs home._  

#### `a11-07-bath-done`

_Kanga collects Roo from Rabbit’s with a smile that says she has known all along. Rabbit says he was only borrowing._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): borrowing means asking first  
> _Rabbit says he was only borrowing. Which of these is really borrowing?_  
> - ✅ Asking, then giving it back → Yes. Borrowing needs permission and a return. Without them, it is just taking.
> - Taking it quietly and returning it later → The “returning” part is good. But without asking first, the owner has no say.
> - Keeping it until someone notices → That is a long way from borrowing. Borrowing has an end, and the owner agrees to it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that borrowing means asking first and giving it back._


#### `a11-07-complete`

**Rabbit**: Well. She can stay. I suppose. Roo jumps very well, for a Roo.  
_Kanga is friendly to everybody from then on, and Rabbit is friendly back, a bit stiffly, like a new shoe._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): a simile for stiff friendliness  
> _“Rabbit is friendly back, a bit stiffly, like a new shoe.” Another simile._  
> _A new shoe is stiff because it has not been worn in. The simile tells us Rabbit’s friendliness is real but unpractised._  
> _For grown-ups: Understood how a simile can describe a feeling._

**Roo**: Can I go in the pillowcase again? Can your Nubbin come?  
**Kanga**: Thank you for keeping an eye on him, dear. I knew somebody was.  

### Glossary

- **marsupial**: An animal that carries its baby in a pouch, like a kangaroo.
- **joey**: A baby kangaroo.
- **tendon**: A strong, stretchy cord that joins muscle to bone.

## A11-8. The Expotition

- `a11-08-s1`: Join Christopher Robin’s Expotition to the North Pole. · _Christopher Robin is outside his house, in his Big Boots._
- `a11-08-s2`: Help get Roo out of the stream. · _Take the other end of Pooh’s pole and hold it across the water._
- `a11-08-s3`: Help Christopher Robin mark the spot. · _Push the pole into the bank where Christopher Robin points._

#### `a11-08-setoff`

_Christopher Robin is putting on his Big Boots, which means an Adventure._  
**Christopher Robin**: We’re going on an Expotition. All of us. To discover the North Pole.  
**Pooh**: Oh. What is the North Pole?  
**Christopher Robin**: It’s… a thing. At the North. You’ll know it when you find it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 2-ESS2-2, ask): north on a map  
> _Pooh asks what the North Pole is. On most maps, north is at the top. If you face north, which way is east?_  
> - ✅ To your right → Yes. Facing north, east is on your right and west on your left.
> - To your left → That is west. Facing north, east is on your right.
> - Behind you → Behind you is south. East is on your right when you face north.
> _For grown-ups: Used the compass directions: east is to the right when facing north._

_Everyone comes: Rabbit and all his friends-and-relations, Kanga and Roo, Owl, Piglet, and Eeyore last, being last._  
**Eeyore**: Nobody told me. Well, somebody did. But not properly.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): being told “not properly”  
> _Eeyore says: “Nobody told me. Well, somebody did. But not properly.” Is that being left out, or just Eeyore being gloomy?_  
> - He was left out → That is how it sounds. Being told in passing is not the same as being asked.
> - He is just being gloomy → Maybe. But gloomy people are often the ones who feel left out most.
> - Perhaps both → That is very possible. Feelings and facts can both be true.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between being informed and being included._

**Rabbit**: Single file! And look out for Ambushes!  
**Pooh**: Is an Ambush a sort of gorse-bush?  
**Piglet**: I th-think it’s worse.  
_Your Nubbin marches between Pooh and Piglet in single file, which it takes very seriously._  

**Choices**

- **Walk at the back with Eeyore.**
    - **Eeyore**: Somebody has to bring up the rear. It might as well be the ones nobody notices.
- **Walk at the front with Christopher Robin.**
    - **Christopher Robin**: Good. You can look out for the Pole.
- **Look out for Ambushes.**
    - You look out for Ambushes. You find two gorse-bushes, a fallen log and Owl.

#### `a11-08-roo`

_By a pool in the stream everyone stops for lunch. Roo washes his face and paws, to show Kanga he can._  
_Then Roo falls in, with a small splash, and the water carries him off._  
**Roo**: Kanga, look! I’m swimming! Am I swimming? I am!  
**Kanga**: Are you all right, Roo dear?  
_Eeyore turns round and dangles his tail in for Roo to hold. Owl explains how important it is not to panic._  
_Your Nubbin, who doesn’t mind getting wet, is in at once, paddling beside Roo like a small furry float._  
_Pooh has found a long pole. He holds it across the stream lower down, and you take the other end._  
_Roo bumps into the pole, and holds on, and the two of you lift him out, dripping and delighted._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): water safety: reach, throw, do not go  
> **Christopher Robin**: Nubbins do not mind water, but people should. If someone falls in, the safe rule is reach or throw, do not go.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Hold out a pole or a branch from the bank, or throw something that floats, and shout for a grown-up.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the water-safety rule: reach or throw, do not go in._


#### `a11-08-roo-done`

**Roo**: Did you see me swimming? Did you?  
**Kanga**: We did, dear. Now come and be dried.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): streams run downhill and carry things along  
> **Christopher Robin**: Water always runs downhill, pulled by gravity. A stream can carry leaves, sticks and even a small Roo along with it.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Remember that: it matters for a game on the bridge later.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that streams flow downhill and carry things along._


#### `a11-08-pole`

**Christopher Robin**: Pooh. Do you know what you’re holding?  
**Pooh**: A pole. A wet one.  
**Christopher Robin**: It’s the North Pole. We’ve discovered it. Well, you have.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a word with two meanings: pole  
> _Pooh holds a wet pole. Christopher Robin says it is the North Pole. Are those the same kind of pole?_  
> - ✅ No: one is a stick, one is a place → Yes. “Pole” can mean a long stick or either end of the Earth. Context tells you which.
> - Yes: the same thing → Not quite. The real North Pole is a place at the top of the world. This one is a stick, which is the joke.
> - Neither is real → Both are real! One is a stick, and the other is a place on Earth.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that pole can mean a stick or a place at the end of the Earth._

**Pooh**: Oh!  
_Pooh looks at the pole as if he ought to have recognised it._  
_Christopher Robin pushes the pole into the bank, and writes a notice on it saying who found it, spelled about as well as you’d expect._  
**Eeyore**: I’ve had my tail in a pool for ten minutes. Nobody noticed. It’s gone numb. But don’t mind me.  
**Christopher Robin**: Oh, Eeyore. Here, let me dry it.  

#### `a11-08-pole-done`

_Everyone walks home in a long happy line, with Roo asleep on Kanga, and Pooh walking very upright, the way discoverers do._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): the real North Pole is a spot on a frozen ocean  
> **Christopher Robin**: The real North Pole is a point at the very top of the Earth. It is not land but floating sea ice on the Arctic Ocean.  
> **Christopher Robin**: An expedition is a journey made for a purpose, like exploring. Pooh’s was a very short one.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the real North Pole is on floating sea ice, and what an expedition is._


#### `a11-08-complete`

**Christopher Robin**: There were two poles, really. This is the spare. Every Expotition needs somewhere to hang its hat afterwards.  
_He gives you a shorter pole with a forked top, which has been, all along, a perfectly good hat-stand._  
**Pooh**: Did I really discover it?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry  
> _The hat-stand pole forks into a neat Y shape, with two equal arms. How many lines of symmetry does a Y have?_  
> - ✅ One → Yes. Fold it down the middle, from top to bottom, and both halves match.
> - None → Look again: there is one line, straight down the middle, that makes the halves match.
> - Two → A second fold, across the middle, would not match top and bottom. Just one line works.
> _For grown-ups: Found the one line of symmetry in a Y shape._

**Christopher Robin**: You did.  
**Pooh**: I thought it would be bigger. But it’s very nice.  

### Glossary

- **expedition**: A journey made for a purpose, such as exploring.

## A11-9. Entirely Surrounded by Water

- `a11-09-s1`: Find out where Piglet is, in all this rain. · _Watch the flood from the high bank across from Piglet’s beech tree._
- `a11-09-s2`: Help Pooh get the message to Christopher Robin. · _Paddle the wash-tub alongside the Floating Bear to the hill where Christopher Robin lives._
- `a11-09-s3`: Sail The Brain of Pooh to Piglet’s tree. · _Keep your wash-tub beside the umbrella, and look out for Piglet’s window._

#### `a11-09-rain`

_The rain comes down all day, and all night, and all the next day. Then it keeps going._  
_The stream climbs over its banks and the Forest fills up, until the low places are ponds and the ponds are lakes._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): the water cycle and floods  
> **Christopher Robin**: Rain starts as water vapour rising from seas and lakes. It cools into drops, which fall as rain. Rivers carry it back to the sea.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A flood happens when rain falls faster than the ground and streams can carry it away.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rain is part of the water cycle and that floods happen when too much falls too fast._

_Piglet’s house is in the middle of a beech tree, and the beech tree is in the middle of the water._  
**Piglet**: Everyone else will be all right. Pooh can float. Owl can fly. Kanga can jump. And I’m just… small. And wet.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether being small means being weak  
> _Piglet says everyone else can float, fly or jump, and he is “just small and wet”. Then he sends a message in a bottle. Is small the same as weak?_  
> - Yes, he cannot do much → He did one clever thing, though: he asked for help in writing. That is not weak.
> - No, he has other strengths → That fits. A clear message and the sense to send it are real strengths.
> - Everyone feels small sometimes → They do. It is worth remembering when you see a friend who looks small.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being small means being weak._

_He finds a bottle, a pencil and a scrap of paper. He writes HELP, then his name, then that it is him, in case anyone wonders._  
_He corks the bottle and throws it as far as he can, which is not very far, and watches it float away._  
_You and your Nubbin, up on the high bank, see the bottle go by._  

#### `a11-09-rain-done`

_You follow it along the bank. It bobs all the way to where Pooh is sitting on a branch above his own front door, with his honey._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): a corked bottle floats because it is mostly air  
> **Christopher Robin**: A corked bottle is mostly air, so it is light for its size. We say it is buoyant, and it floats.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A stone is heavy for its size, so it sinks. Weight alone does not decide it: size and shape matter too.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that something light for its size, like a corked bottle, floats._


#### `a11-09-bear`

**Pooh**: A bottle with a letter in. I can’t read it, except the P. P is for Pooh, so it must be for me.  
**Pooh**: Christopher Robin can read. I must get to him. But he’s on the high ground, and I’m on a branch.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): one clue may not be enough  
> _Pooh can read only the letter P, and decides the letter is for him. Is that good reasoning?_  
> - ✅ Not quite: Piglet starts with P too → Yes. A single clue can fit more than one answer. Good readers look for another clue before deciding.
> - Yes, P is for Pooh → It might be! But P also fits Piglet, and the message is from him. One clue is not always enough.
> - He should not read it at all → Reading as much as you can is good. Just keep an open mind about what the rest might say.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that one clue can fit more than one answer._

_Pooh thinks. Then he takes his largest empty jar, lays it on the water, and climbs aboard._  
_It turns over at once. Pooh tries again, the other way up, and sits on top, and it floats._  
**Pooh**: This is my boat. It’s called the Floating Bear. Mostly it floats. Sometimes it’s mostly Bear.  
_You find Christopher Robin’s old wash-tub caught in a bush, and climb in, and paddle with your hands._  
_Your Nubbin rides on your head, well out of the wet. It would be happy to swim, but today you’d rather it didn’t._  

**Choices**

- **Paddle close enough to grab him.**
    - Twice the Floating Bear turns over, and twice you push it back up. Pooh carries on as if nothing has happened.
- **Tow him with a bit of string.**
    - **Pooh**: A tow! Like a proper ship. I shall sit very still and be steered.

#### `a11-09-bear-done`

_You bump into the hill where Christopher Robin lives. It is an island now, with a boy on it._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 2-ESS2-2, notice): floods make temporary islands; high ground is safe  
> **Christopher Robin**: The hill is an island now: land with water all around it. On a map, an island is land surrounded by blue.  
> **Christopher Robin**: In a real flood, high ground is the safest place. Water fills the lowest places first.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what an island is and that high ground is safest in a flood._


#### `a11-09-umbrella`

**Christopher Robin**: It says help. It’s from Piglet. He’s stuck in his tree, and the water’s still coming up. We need a boat.  
**Christopher Robin**: The Floating Bear isn’t big enough for two. And I’m much too big for a jar.  
**Pooh**: Your umbrella is a sort of bowl, if you turn it over. And a bowl is a sort of boat.  
_Christopher Robin looks at Pooh for a long moment. Then he opens his umbrella and sets it upside down on the water._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, notice): comparing two designs for a boat  
> **Christopher Robin**: There are two boats now: an empty jar for one, and an upturned umbrella for two. Both float because their shape holds air and pushes water aside.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Comparing designs is how engineers choose. The umbrella is wider, so it carries more. The jar is easier to steer.  
> _For grown-ups: Compared two boat designs and learned why bowl shapes float._

_It floats, and wobbles, and holds. Christopher Robin climbs in, and then Pooh, and it holds them both._  
**Christopher Robin**: I name this ship The Brain of Pooh. Because it was your idea.  
**Pooh**: The Brain of Pooh. Oh.  
_Off they go, slowly, turning round and round, with you paddling alongside and your Nubbin as lookout._  

#### `a11-09-umbrella-done`

_Piglet is at his window, very small and very wet. When he sees The Brain of Pooh, he jumps up and down._  
**Piglet**: Pooh! Christopher Robin! And the Keeper! You came!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): asking for help is a strength  
> _Piglet was scared, but he wrote HELP and his name and sent it. It reached the right person._  
> _Asking for help is a skill, not a failure. The people who love you would far rather know._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that asking for help is a skill._


#### `a11-09-complete`

_Piglet climbs down into the umbrella, and it holds three, just. The ship turns round twice and heads for home._  
**Piglet**: I knew somebody would come. I didn’t know it would be a bear on a jar and a boy in an umbrella.  
**Christopher Robin**: It was Pooh’s idea. All of it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step problem with a remainder  
> _The umbrella boat carries 3 friends at a time. How many trips would it need to carry 10 friends?_  
> - ✅ 4 trips → Yes. Three trips carry 9 friends, and a fourth trip takes the last one.
> - 3 trips → Three trips carry only 9. The tenth friend needs a fourth trip.
> - 7 trips → That would be too many. 10 ÷ 3 is 3 with 1 left over, so 3 + 1 = 4 trips.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a division problem and handled the remainder._

**Pooh**: Was it? It was a very good idea. I must have more of them.  
_Your Nubbin, on your head, sneezes once. It is the driest thing for miles._  

### Glossary

- **flood**: Too much water flowing over land that is usually dry.
- **buoyant**: Able to float.

## A11-10. The Pooh Party

- `a11-10-s1`: Help Owl tell everyone about the party. · _Go round the Forest with Owl, and tell everyone again in words they can follow._
- `a11-10-s2`: Set the long table, and save Eeyore a seat at the end. · _Lay the plates down the long table, then put a cushion on the last chair._

#### `a11-10-invites`

**Christopher Robin**: Owl, fly round to everybody and tell them there’s a party. For Pooh. Because of what he did, saving Piglet.  
**Owl**: A party. Very good. I shall Announce it.  
_Owl flies off to tell everyone, and you go too, to tell everyone again in shorter words._  
_At the Gloomy Place, Owl tells Eeyore. Eeyore nods slowly, and stops listening halfway._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): choosing words for the audience  
> _Owl “Announces” the party in grand words. You tell it in shorter ones. Which message would reach a sleepy Eeyore best?_  
> - ✅ “Party for Pooh, today, come along!” → Yes. Short, clear words fit the listener. Grand words are fine at a ceremony, less so on a doorstep.
> - “A convivial gathering is to be convened.” → That is very grand, and Eeyore would understand about half of it. Pick words your audience will catch.
> - “Something’s on.” → Short, but he would not know what or why. Clear needs enough detail too.
> _For grown-ups: Chose words to suit the listener._

**Eeyore**: A party. For me. Well. Fancy that. Better late than never, I suppose.  
**Owl**: No, it is for…  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): assuming something is about you  
> _Eeyore hears about a party and assumes it is for him, in his gloomy way. Is it kind to correct him straight away?_  
> - Yes, honesty comes first → Honesty matters. But so does choosing a gentle way and a good moment to say it.
> - No, let him enjoy it → That is kind, but the party is for Pooh, and the misunderstanding may sting later.
> - Tell him kindly, and give him a seat → That is what you do. You tell the truth and make sure he has a place.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about telling someone the truth kindly._

_But Eeyore has turned away to think about it, and Owl has a great many more trees to visit._  

**Choices**

- **Tell Eeyore it’s for Pooh.**
    - **Eeyore**: Is it. Well. Somebody’s party. I’ll come anyway, if I’m wanted. Which I doubt.
- **Tell him there’ll be a seat for him.**
    - **Eeyore**: A seat. At the end, I expect.
    - **You**: Wherever you like.
    - **Eeyore**: …The end. I like the end. You can see who’s leaving.

#### `a11-10-table`

_Christopher Robin has made a long table out of some long pieces of wood, out in the open, and everyone helps lay it._  
_You lay the plates. Your Nubbin puts one leaf on each plate, very exactly, as a napkin._  
**Rabbit**: Not there! Owl at the top, because he’s Owl. Then Kanga, then me, then my friends-and-relations, all of them…  
_Rabbit organises the seats until there aren’t any left. There is one chair at the very end, where Rabbit hasn’t looked._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): equal groups: 12 seats in 3 rows  
> _Rabbit seats 12 friends-and-relations in 3 equal rows. How many are in each row?_  
> - ✅ 4 in each row → Yes. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, since 3 × 4 = 12.
> - 9 in each row → That is 12 − 3. Share 12 equally into 3 rows: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
> - 3 in each row → Three rows of 3 would be only 9. Three rows of 4 make 12.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 12 into 3 equal groups._

_You put a cushion on it, and a card that says EEYORE in your best letters._  
**Eeyore**: A place. At the end. With my name on. I didn’t ask.  
**Eeyore**: …The cushion’s a nice touch.  
_Everyone sits. There is a great deal of eating, and Roo talks with his mouth full, and nobody minds._  

#### `a11-10-table-done`

**Christopher Robin**: Everybody! This party is because of what somebody did, and we all know who.  
_Eeyore half stands up to make a speech. Then Christopher Robin hands Pooh a present, and Eeyore sits down again._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): showing character through action  
> _Eeyore “half stands up to make a speech”, then sits down again. The author never says he is shy or doubtful._  
> _We work it out from what he does. That is called showing, not telling, and it is how stories get under your skin._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that actions can show a character’s feelings without saying them._


#### `a11-10-complete`

_Pooh’s present is a Special Pencil Case. Inside are pencils with letters on them, B and HB and BB, and Pooh is sure every letter is about him._  
**Pooh**: Oh!  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): pencil grades: B, HB and H  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pencil “lead” is really graphite mixed with clay. More clay makes it harder and lighter. More graphite makes it softer and blacker.  
> **Christopher Robin**: B means black and soft. H means hard. HB is in the middle, the pencil most of us use at school.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pencil grades describe how soft or hard the graphite is._

_Pooh can’t write, but he looks at every pencil, one at a time, and is very happy._  
**Eeyore**: Pencils. Hm. When I was young we had sticks. You could do a great deal with a stick.  
_Walking home, Pooh and Piglet don’t say anything for a long time. It is the friendly kind of quiet._  

### Glossary

- **graphite**: The soft, dark mineral in pencils that leaves marks on paper.

## A11-11. A House at Pooh Corner

- `a11-11-s1`: Help Pooh and Piglet build Eeyore a house. · _Carry sticks from the heap on the other side of the wood to Pooh Corner._
- `a11-11-s2`: Go with Christopher Robin and Eeyore to look for Eeyore’s missing house. · _Walk Eeyore through the snow to Pooh Corner._
- `a11-11-s3`: Let Eeyore work it out his own way. · _Stand back and let Eeyore look at the house._

#### `a11-11-snow`

_It is snowing, and the Forest is white and soft. Pooh is humming a hum about snow, which gets longer as it goes, like snow does._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): snow is frozen water; freezing point  
> **Christopher Robin**: Snow is water that has frozen into tiny crystals. Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F).  
> **Christopher Robin**: When the air warms above that, snow melts back into water. In spring, it feeds the streams.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that snow is frozen water, and that water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F)._

_He goes round to Piglet’s, humming. Piglet is sitting by his fire, warming his toes._  
**Pooh**: I’ve been thinking about Eeyore. He hasn’t got a house. Everybody has a house except him.  
**Piglet**: We could build him one. Here, at Pooh Corner. Out of sticks.  
_There is a heap of sticks on the other side of the wood, in a sheltered spot. Nobody seems to be using it._  
_You carry sticks. Your Nubbin carries one stick at a time, the long way round, for reasons of its own._  
**Piglet**: It’s a very good house. Eeyore will be pleased.  
**Pooh**: Nobody’s ever built him one before.  

**Choices**

- **Make the doorway wide enough for a donkey.**
    - You make it wider. Pooh, remembering Rabbit’s, approves of wide doors in general.
- **Put a roof on, in case.**
    - **Piglet**: In case of snow? It already is snow.
    - **You**: In case of more.
    - **Piglet**: Oh. Yes. There might be.
- **Let your Nubbin choose the last stick.**
    - It chooses a crooked one. It looks right, somehow.

#### `a11-11-snow-done`

_The house stands at Pooh Corner, a little lopsided, in the snow._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.D.8, ask): perimeter: the wall of sticks  
> _Eeyore’s house is a rectangle, 3 metres long and 2 metres wide. How many metres of sticks does it take to go all the way round?_  
> - ✅ 10 metres → Yes. Perimeter is the distance round: 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10.
> - 6 metres → That is 3 × 2, the area of the floor. Perimeter adds all four sides: 10.
> - 5 metres → That is only two of the sides. Add all four: 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10.
> _For grown-ups: Found a perimeter by adding all four sides._


#### `a11-11-missing`

_Meanwhile, at Christopher Robin’s door, Eeyore is standing in the snow, with snow on his back._  
**Eeyore**: I don’t want to complain. But it’s snowing, and I built a house, and now it isn’t there.  
**Christopher Robin**: Your house? Where was it?  
**Eeyore**: Down by the wood. A house of sticks. I built it myself, in a sheltered spot. I came back and it had gone.  
_You think of a heap of sticks in a sheltered spot. Something goes cold in your middle, and it isn’t the snow._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): a cold feeling in your middle can be guilt  
> _Something goes cold in your middle, and it is not the snow. That feeling is often guilt, or worry that you have caused a problem._  
> _It is not a bad feeling. It is a signal. It tells you something may need putting right._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that guilt is a signal that something may need putting right._

**Christopher Robin**: Let’s go and look. Come on, Keeper.  
_You walk with them through the snow. Your Nubbin walks very close to your boots and doesn’t look anyone in the eye._  

#### `a11-11-missing-done`

_At Pooh Corner there is a house of sticks, standing up in the snow. Pooh and Piglet are admiring it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, notice): dramatic irony: knowing more than the characters  
> _Pooh and Piglet are admiring the house. You know something they do not: whose sticks those were._  
> _When the reader knows more than the characters, it is called dramatic irony. It makes a scene funny and a little uncomfortable at once._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the term dramatic irony._


#### `a11-11-wind`

**Eeyore**: There. That’s my house. It’s here. And I built it there.  
**Eeyore**: The wind must have done it. Picked it up, all in one piece, over the wood, and set it down here.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): wind is moving air  
> **Christopher Robin**: Wind is air on the move. When the sun warms the ground, the air above rises, and cooler air rushes in to take its place.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A gentle wind rustles leaves. It would take an enormous one to carry off a whole house, so Eeyore’s idea needs some help.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wind is moving air caused by warm air rising and cool air rushing in._

_Pooh and Piglet look at each other, and then at you. You say nothing, which, all things considered, is the kind thing._  
**Eeyore**: And it’s better here. Not so draughty. The wind did a better job than I did.  
**Eeyore**: Funny thing, wind. You never know.  
**Christopher Robin**: It’s a lovely house, Eeyore.  
**Eeyore**: It is, isn’t it. Better than before. Somebody somewhere must like me. I’d never have thought it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): kind silence versus honesty  
> _Eeyore believes the wind moved his house, and he is happy. Pooh, Piglet and you say nothing. Is staying quiet kind, or should someone tell him the truth?_  
> - Stay quiet: it is kind → It does feel kind. But it also means Eeyore cannot understand what really happened, or thank anyone.
> - Tell him: honesty matters → Honesty does matter. A good way might be to tell him gently, and to offer to fix things.
> - It depends on what he needs → A thoughtful answer. Sometimes the kindest thing is to wait, and sometimes to speak. Think who it helps.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when kind silence is right and when honesty matters more._


#### `a11-11-door`

_Eeyore goes in, turns round, and comes out again to look at his door._  
_On the latch, tied in a careful double bow, is a blue ribbon. It was in the Useful Pot, and now it is here._  
**Eeyore**: Keeps the door from banging. Useful. Like a Friend.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): theme: small kindnesses come back  
> _The ribbon from the Useful Pot is now on the door. A small gift from earlier comes back later, doing a job._  
> _A theme is the big idea under a story. One theme here: small kindnesses are never wasted._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that a small gift returning later can show a story’s theme._


#### `a11-11-complete`

_Pooh and Piglet walk home in the snow. For a long time neither of them says anything about the sticks._  
**Piglet**: Pooh. Did we… take Eeyore’s house?  
**Pooh**: We did. And then we gave it back, in a better place. I think that counts.  
**Piglet**: I think it counts too.  
_Your Nubbin walks behind them in Pooh’s footprints all the way home, which takes a great deal of jumping._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): distance: 14 hops of 30 cm  
> _Your Nubbin hops from footprint to footprint, each 30 cm apart. It makes 14 hops. How far is that in metres?_  
> - ✅ 4 metres 20 centimetres → Yes. 14 × 30 = 420 cm, which is 4 m and 20 cm.
> - 42 metres → That is ten times too big. 420 cm is 4.2 m.
> - 4 metres → Nearly: 14 × 30 = 420 cm. That is 4 m and a further 20 cm.
> _For grown-ups: Converted centimetres to metres after multiplying._


### Glossary

- **perimeter**: The distance all the way round the edge of a shape.
- **dramatic irony**: When the reader knows something the characters do not.
- **theme**: The big idea underneath a story.

## A11-12. Tigger Comes to the Forest

- `a11-12-s1`: Find out what is making that noise at Pooh’s door. · _You are staying the night at Pooh’s. Open the door._
- `a11-12-s2`: Help Tigger try honey, haycorns and thistles. · _Go from Pooh’s to Piglet’s to Eeyore’s with Tigger._
- `a11-12-s3`: Take Tigger to Kanga’s for one last try. · _Kanga’s house is by the Sandy Pit. Roo is having his medicine._

#### `a11-12-night`

_In the middle of the night, at Pooh’s house, there is a noise. You and your Nubbin, on the sofa, hear it first._  
_It is a growly, wobbly sort of noise: the noise of something very pleased about something._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): a growl is a low pitch: slow vibrations  
> **Christopher Robin**: A growl is a low-pitched sound: the throat vibrates slowly. A squeak is high-pitched, with very fast vibrations.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Volume is how loud. They are different things.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pitch depends on how fast something vibrates._

**Pooh**: What is it? Is it you?  
_It isn’t you. Pooh opens the door._  
**Tigger**: Hallo! I’m Tigger. I’ve just come. Is this where everybody is?  
_Tigger sees the tablecloth, and has a fight with it, and wins, and is very proud._  
_Then he sees your Nubbin, and bounces it over, gently, to say hello. Your Nubbin bounces back._  
**Tigger**: A small Tigger! Is it a Tigger?  
**Pooh**: It’s a very small Heffalump.  
**Tigger**: Is it? It bounces like a Tigger.  

**Choices**

- **Offer to help find Tigger some breakfast.**
    - **Tigger**: Breakfast! Tiggers like everything for breakfast. Probably.
- **Put the tablecloth back.**
    - You put it back. Tigger watches it, in case it starts something again.
- **Ask Tigger where he came from.**
    - **Tigger**: From the Forest. From over there. From just now. Is there breakfast?

#### `a11-12-night-done`

_In the morning Pooh sets out a pot of honey for Tigger. The very best kind._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): volume in millilitres  
> _Pooh puts out a jar with 500 millilitres of honey. If Tigger tries 50 millilitres at a time, how many tries would empty the jar?_  
> - ✅ 10 tries → Yes. 500 ÷ 50 = 10.
> - 5 tries → Five tries would be only 250 millilitres. You need 10.
> - 50 tries → That is far too many. Each try is a tenth of the jar, so 10 tries.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a volume of 500 millilitres into 50 millilitre portions._


#### `a11-12-breakfast`

_Tigger takes a large mouthful of honey. Then he looks up at the ceiling, with his head on one side._  
**Tigger**: Ugh. Honey is far too sticky for a Tigger.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): taste and touch: two senses at work  
> **Christopher Robin**: Tigger uses touch and taste at once. His tongue feels that honey is sticky and tastes that it is sweet, and nerves send both messages to his brain.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Our senses are our body’s way of gathering information. A thistle is a good lesson in touch.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that senses send information to the brain._

_Pooh tries to sound sorry. He is secretly relieved, and has the rest himself._  
_So you all go to Piglet’s, where there are haycorns. Tigger takes a large mouthful, and his face goes slowly round._  
**Tigger**: Ee-ugh. They’re all corners. Tiggers don’t do corners.  
_So you go on to Eeyore’s, where there are thistles. Eeyore offers one, the way you offer a thing you hope will be refused._  
_Tigger takes a large mouthful, and sits down, and puts a paw in his mouth, and takes it out again._  
**Tigger**: Ow! Prickly! That’s not a breakfast. That’s a punishment.  
**Eeyore**: I see. Some of us eat them every day and don’t complain. Much.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): trying new food, and saying you dislike it  
> _Tigger tries three foods and likes none of them. Is it worth trying new foods when you might not like them?_  
> - Yes, you might find a favourite → Tigger did, in the end. Trying costs a moment and can win you a lifelong favourite.
> - No, stick to what you know → It is safe. But Tigger would have gone hungry. Safe is not always the same as well.
> - Try a little, and it is fine to say no → Many people agree. A small taste, and honesty about it, seems fair to everyone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the balance between trying new food and saying you dislike it._


#### `a11-12-breakfast-done`

**Pooh**: There’s nobody left but Kanga. She might have something. Kangas usually do.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): money-style addition with Shells  
> _At the market, honey costs 3 Shells, haycorns 2 Shells and thistles 1 Shell. How many Shells to buy all three for Tigger to try?_  
> - ✅ 6 Shells → Yes. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
> - 5 Shells → Check again: 3 + 2 is 5, plus 1 more makes 6.
> - 7 Shells → Close. 3 + 2 + 1 comes to 6.
> _For grown-ups: Added three prices in Shells._


#### `a11-12-malt`

_At Kanga’s house, Roo is having his medicine. He does not want it; he wants anything else._  
**Roo**: Do I have to? It’s Extract of Malt. It’s brown, and it sticks to the spoon, and it goes on and on.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how malt extract is made  
> **Christopher Robin**: Extract of malt is made from barley. The grains are soaked until they sprout, then dried: that is malt.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Soak the malt in hot water, boil the sweet liquid down, and you get a thick, sticky syrup: the extract. No wonder it sticks to the spoon.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that malt extract is made from sprouted, dried barley._

**Kanga**: Just one spoonful, dear. It makes you big and strong.  
_Tigger leans over Roo’s shoulder, sniffs, and takes the whole spoonful._  
_Kanga stares, and Roo stares. Your Nubbin, who has been staring at everything since the thistles, stares harder._  
**Tigger**: That’s it! That’s the one! That’s a Tigger breakfast!  
**Roo**: He can have mine! All of it! Always!  
**Kanga**: Well. I suppose he’d better stay, then. I’ll fetch another spoon.  

#### `a11-12-malt-done`

_So Tigger lives at Kanga’s from then on, and has Extract of Malt for breakfast, dinner and tea._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): finding where you fit  
> _Tigger found a home because Kanga made room, and Roo shared. Nobody asked him to be like the others first._  
> _A good group has room for different tastes. Belonging does not have to mean being the same._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that belonging does not require being the same as everyone else._


#### `a11-12-complete`

**Pooh**: So Tiggers like the one thing nobody else does. That’s very handy, really.  
**Tigger**: And Tiggers like Keepers! And small bouncy whatever-they-ares! Bounce!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): theme: being different can be handy  
> **Pooh**: Tiggers like the one thing nobody else does. That is very handy, really.  
> _A theme is the big idea under a story. Here, it might be: being different is not a problem, it is just a different shape of fit._  
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme about being different._

_Tigger bounces your Nubbin, gently, right over. It lands on its feet and looks, for the first time, as if it might bounce back on purpose._  

### Glossary

- **extract**: The strong part of something, squeezed or boiled out of it.

## A11-13. The Search for Small

- `a11-13-s1`: Get your orders from Captain Rabbit. · _Rabbit has a list, a pencil and a Captain’s face._
- `a11-13-s2`: Search by the Six Pine Trees, where the old pit is. · _Walk with Pooh to the Six Pine Trees. Mind the pit._
- `a11-13-s3`: Help everyone out of the pit, and look carefully at Pooh. · _Take one of Pooh’s paws while Christopher Robin takes the other._

#### `a11-13-orders`

_Rabbit is very busy, and likes it. He has a list, and a pencil, and a Captain’s face._  
**Rabbit**: Small is missing. One of my friends-and-relations. A very small beetle. Nobody has seen him since yesterday.  
**Pooh**: What does Small look like?  
**Rabbit**: Small.  
**Pooh**: Ah. That helps.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units: millimetres in a centimetre  
> _Small is a beetle about 5 millimetres long. There are 10 millimetres in a centimetre. How many Smalls, end to end, make 1 centimetre?_  
> - ✅ 2 → Yes. 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Two Smalls make one centimetre.
> - 5 → Five Smalls would be 25 millimetres. 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
> - 10 → That would be 50 millimetres. Divide: 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
> _For grown-ups: Converted millimetres to centimetres to compare lengths._

**Rabbit**: Pooh, you search by the Six Pine Trees. Keeper, go with Pooh. Your Nubbin is low to the ground. That’s useful.  
**Rabbit**: Everybody is to be Thorough. That means looking under things.  
_Your Nubbin looks under a leaf at once, to show it understands._  

**Choices**

- **Salute.**
    - **Rabbit**: Good. Good. Somebody here understands organisation.
- **Ask how small, exactly.**
    - **Rabbit**: Smaller than that. Smaller than you think. No. Smaller.
- **Start looking straight away.**
    - Your Nubbin is already under a stone.

#### `a11-13-pit`

_Pooh walks along thinking about Small, and about honey, but mostly about honey, and doesn’t look where he is going._  
_You remember the pit by the Six Pine Trees. You remember it a moment too late._  
_Pooh disappears with a whump. From down below comes a small, squeaky voice._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity pulls everything down  
> _Pooh walks into the pit and falls onto Piglet. What pulls him down?_  
> - ✅ Gravity → Yes. Gravity pulls everything towards the ground, whether it is a bear or a beetle.
> - The wind → The wind can push, but this is gravity: a pull towards the Earth.
> - Piglet → Piglet wishes! The pull comes from the whole Earth. We call it gravity.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls everything towards the ground._

**Piglet**: Help! Help! Something’s fallen on me! It’s… it’s the Heffalump!  
**Pooh**: It isn’t, Piglet. It’s me. I think. I hope.  
_You look over the edge. There is Pooh, and under Pooh there is Piglet, and both of them are looking up at you._  
**Piglet**: Pooh, what are you doing in the Heffalump trap?  
**Pooh**: Falling in it, mostly. What are you doing?  
**Piglet**: I was searching. Very Thoroughly. Under things.  

#### `a11-13-pit-done`

_Christopher Robin arrives at the top of the pit. He takes one look, and sits down on the edge to laugh._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): what makes laughter kind  
> _Christopher Robin laughs, and Pooh and Piglet do too. Laughter is kind when everybody is in on it._  
> _A good test: would the person laugh if they could see it from outside? With friends, they usually do._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard how to tell kind laughter from unkind laughter._


#### `a11-13-small`

**Christopher Robin**: Out you come. Pooh, take my hand. Keeper, take his other paw.  
_You heave. Up comes Pooh, and up comes Piglet after him, holding on to Pooh’s leg._  
_Your Nubbin climbs up Pooh to help, stops in the middle of his back, and stares._  
_There, sitting quietly in Pooh’s fur, is a very small beetle, as if it has been waiting all morning for somebody to notice._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): beetles go through four stages of life  
> **Christopher Robin**: A beetle starts as an egg, hatches into a larva, becomes a pupa, and finally an adult. That change is called metamorphosis.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Small has finished all four stages. He is as grown as a beetle gets.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that beetles change through egg, larva, pupa and adult stages._

**Christopher Robin**: Pooh! You’ve found Small!  
**Pooh**: Have I? Where was he?  
**Christopher Robin**: On you.  
**Pooh**: Ah. I thought something was looking at me.  

#### `a11-13-complete`

**Rabbit**: Found! Found by my search, which I organised. Well done, everybody. Especially me.  
_Small says nothing, being a beetle, and goes back to his own business, which is very small._  
**Pooh**: I found him without looking. That’s the easiest way.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): who deserves credit  
> _Rabbit says he found Small by organising a search. Pooh says he found him without looking. Who deserves the credit?_  
> - Rabbit, he organised it → Organising made the search happen. Without it, nobody would have been looking. That is real work.
> - Pooh, he had Small on him → It was luck, but he was also the one willing to be rescued from a pit. Credit can be funny.
> - Everyone who helped → That is the most generous answer, and probably the most accurate.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about who deserves credit for a team effort._

_Your Nubbin looks under every leaf on the way home anyway, in case there are other beetles who’d like to be found._  

### Glossary

- **metamorphosis**: A big change in an animal’s body as it grows, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

## A11-14. Tiggers Don’t Climb Trees

- `a11-14-s1`: Follow Tigger and Roo into the Forest. · _They went towards the tall pines with a bag of sandwiches._
- `a11-14-s2`: Hold one corner of the tunic while Tigger jumps. · _Pull your corner tight and don’t let go, however long Tigger thinks about it._

#### `a11-14-climb`

_Tigger is taking Roo for a walk, with Kanga’s permission and a bag of malt sandwiches._  
**Roo**: Can Tiggers climb trees?  
**Tigger**: Climb trees? Tiggers are the best tree-climbers there are. Better than Poohs.  
_Up the tall pine goes Tigger, with Roo on his back, very fast. Your Nubbin sits at the bottom with its head right back._  
_Then Tigger looks down. He looks down for a long time._  
**Tigger**: Tiggers can climb up. That part’s easy. It’s the coming down. It’s not their best thing.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): cats climb up easily; claws curve one way  
> **Christopher Robin**: Real cats do the same as Tigger: up a tree in a flash, then stuck. Their claws curve backwards, which is ideal for climbing up.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Going down head-first, the claws point the wrong way. Cats have to learn to back down, or be rescued.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why cats find climbing down harder than climbing up._

**Roo**: We’re stuck! Isn’t it lovely? We’re up a tree!  

**Choices**

- **Call up that help is coming.**
    - **Tigger**: Good! Good. Tiggers aren’t worried. But do hurry.
- **Send your Nubbin up to sit with them.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs to the lowest branch, then the next, and sits there, halfway, for company. It can’t do more, and that’s all right.
- **Run for Christopher Robin.**
    - You run. Pooh and Piglet are already coming, with Christopher Robin and Eeyore behind.

#### `a11-14-climb-done`

_Soon everyone is standing at the bottom of the pine, looking up._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): is it brave to say you are scared  
> _Tigger said “Tiggers aren’t worried” while stuck up a tree. Is it braver to say you are scared, or to pretend you are not?_  
> - Say you are scared → Many people think so. It tells your friends what you need, and it takes courage to say.
> - Pretend you are not → Pretending can feel strong, but it can leave you without help when you need it most.
> - Say it and carry on anyway → That is a very good answer. Brave does not mean you are never scared.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether admitting fear is brave._


#### `a11-14-tunic`

_Christopher Robin takes off his tunic and holds it out under the tree like a sheet. Everyone takes an edge._  
**Christopher Robin**: You take that corner, Keeper. Pull it tight. Pooh, yours is sagging.  
**Pooh**: It isn’t sagging. It’s having a little sit-down.  
**Christopher Robin**: Roo first!  
_Roo jumps, squeaking with joy, lands in the middle, and bounces right out and in again._  
**Roo**: Again! Can I do it again?  
**Christopher Robin**: No. Now you, Tigger!  
**Tigger**: In a moment. Tiggers like to think about jumping first. For quite a long time.  
_Tigger thinks, and you hold your corner. Your arms begin to ache, and you don’t let go._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): sharing a load between four holders  
> **Christopher Robin**: Four people share the weight of Tigger’s landing, so each pulls less than one would alone. The tunic must be tight, so it does not sag to the ground.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Spreading the force over more people and more cloth is how safety nets and trampolines work.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sharing a load makes each person’s job smaller._

_Then Tigger jumps, all at once, the way he does everything._  

#### `a11-14-tunic-done`

_There is a great crash. Everyone falls over in a heap, and somebody at the bottom of the heap says something gloomy._  
**Eeyore**: Thank you. I was quite comfortable down here. Nobody need hurry.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): a character acts true to character  
> _At the bottom of a heap of friends, Eeyore says something gloomy. It is exactly what Eeyore would say._  
> _Writers keep characters consistent so readers feel they know them. That is why the joke works._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that characters behave consistently, which makes humour work._


#### `a11-14-complete`

**Tigger**: Did you see me? Tiggers can jump out of trees. It’s a thing they do. Easily.  
**Christopher Robin**: Let’s say it’s a thing they do with help.  
_Christopher Robin puts his tunic back on. It has a Tigger-shaped stretch in the middle now, and he says he likes it better._  
_Your Nubbin finds it can’t get down the last bit of its branch either, and has to be lifted._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a square  
> _Christopher Robin’s tunic is a square, 2 metres on each side. What is its area?_  
> - ✅ 4 square metres → Yes. A square’s area is side × side: 2 × 2 = 4.
> - 8 square metres → That is the perimeter, going round the edge. Area is 2 × 2 = 4.
> - 2 square metres → Multiply the sides, not just count one: 2 × 2 = 4.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a square by multiplying the side by itself._


## A11-15. Rabbit’s Busy Day

- `a11-15-s1`: Go with Rabbit to Christopher Robin’s house. · _Rabbit is off to tell Christopher Robin what to do today._
- `a11-15-s2`: Ask Owl what the note means. · _Take the note to The Chestnuts._
- `a11-15-s3`: Ask Eeyore, who has been learning something with sticks. · _Eeyore is standing over three sticks in the Gloomy Place._

#### `a11-15-note`

_Rabbit wakes up feeling important, as if everything depends on him. It is a very Captain-ish sort of morning._  
**Rabbit**: I shall go and see Christopher Robin. He’ll want to know what to do today, and I shall tell him.  
_But Christopher Robin isn’t at home. There is a note pinned to his door._  
_It says he has gone out, and will be back soon, and is busy. It is in Christopher Robin’s spelling, which is generous with its letters._  
**Rabbit**: “Backson.” What is a Backson? Gone out with a Backson? Is it some sort of animal?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): sounding out an invented spelling  
> _Rabbit reads “Backson” on the note and panics. Say it slowly: back… son. What might Christopher Robin have meant?_  
> - ✅ Back soon → Yes. He wrote it the way it sounds. Sounding out is how everyone starts spelling.
> - A big animal called a Backson → Say it slowly again: back-son. Does it sound like another phrase that fits a note on a door?
> - A very bad spelling of “bus” → Interesting guess! Try sounding it in two parts: back… son.
> _For grown-ups: Sounded out an invented spelling and found it said back soon._

**Rabbit**: I must ask Owl. Owl can read. Owl can spell.  

**Choices**

- **Read the note again, slowly.**
    - You read it again, and it doesn’t get any clearer. Some notes are like that.
- **Ask Rabbit if he’s ever seen a Backson.**
    - **Rabbit**: Certainly not. But that’s just what a Backson would want me to say.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff the note.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs it. It smells of breakfast and pencil.

#### `a11-15-owl`

**Owl**: Ah. Yes. Let me see.  
_Owl reads the note upside down, then the right way up, then holds it very far away._  
**Owl**: A perfectly ordinary message. He has gone out. With a Backson. A busy one, by the look of it.  
**Rabbit**: What does a Backson look like?  
**Owl**: Like any Backson. Large, I should think. With a… with a sort of look about it.  
**Rabbit**: Owl may not know what a Backson is. But anyone who can spell the days of the week deserves a little respect.  
**Owl**: Tuesday. T, U… There is an S in it. There’s certainly a Y somewhere.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): weekday names come from old gods  
> **Christopher Robin**: Tuesday is named after Tiw, a god of war the early English believed in. Wednesday comes from Woden, and Thursday from Thor.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Many of our weekday names are old, and spelling them has been wobbly for a very long time. Owl is in good company.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that weekday names come from old gods._

_Your Nubbin, who can’t spell anything, looks at Owl with great respect too._  

#### `a11-15-owl-done`

**Rabbit**: Eeyore. Eeyore might have seen it. He sees most things, and complains about them.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time: finding the end time  
> _Rabbit leaves home at 10:15, walks for 20 minutes to Owl’s, and stays 15 minutes. What time is it when he leaves Owl’s?_  
> - ✅ 10:50 → Yes. 10:15 + 20 = 10:35, and 10:35 + 15 = 10:50.
> - 10:35 → That is when he arrives. He stays another 15 minutes, so 10:50.
> - 11:00 → Close. Add carefully: 10:15 + 20 = 10:35, then + 15 = 10:50.
> _For grown-ups: Added two time intervals to find an end time._


#### `a11-15-a`

_Eeyore is standing over three sticks laid on the ground: two lean together at the top, and one goes across the middle._  
**Eeyore**: Do you know what that is? It’s an A. I made it. Nobody else in the Forest knows that.  
**Rabbit**: It’s an A. Of course it is. Everybody knows that.  
_Rabbit says it airily, and Eeyore’s ears go down._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what to say instead of “everybody knows”  
> _Rabbit says “Everybody knows that,” and Eeyore’s ears go down. What could Rabbit have said instead?_  
> - “Well done, that’s an A.” → That would make Eeyore feel proud. Praise for the effort is a strong thing to give.
> - “Show me how you made it.” → That is generous too. Curiosity tells someone their work matters.
> - Nothing: he was right → He was right. But being right can feel small if it makes someone else feel small.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to respond kindly to someone proud of something new._

**Eeyore**: Everybody. Oh. I thought it was something. Learning.  
_You crouch down by the sticks with your Nubbin, and look at the A properly, the way it deserves._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, notice): the letter A has one line of symmetry  
> **Christopher Robin**: Look at Eeyore’s A. Fold it down the middle, from the point at the top to the ground, and the two halves match.  
> **Christopher Robin**: That fold is a line of symmetry. The letter A has exactly one.  
> _For grown-ups: Saw that the letter A has one line of symmetry._

**Eeyore**: Christopher Robin taught me it. He goes out in the mornings now. To learn things. Then he comes and tells me one.  
**Rabbit**: Learn? Then the Backson is… Christopher Robin is… Oh.  
_Rabbit stands very still. It is the first time today he hasn’t been busy._  

#### `a11-15-a-done`

**Eeyore**: Somebody has to look after the A. In case he forgets it, wherever he goes to learn the others.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): theme: learning takes courage at any age  
> _Eeyore is grown-up, and he is learning his letters from a boy. He minds a little, and he does it anyway._  
> _A theme here: it is never too late to learn something, and learning takes courage._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a theme about learning at any age._


#### `a11-15-complete`

_Christopher Robin comes home at lunchtime with ink on his fingers and a great many new words, some of them spelled right._  
**Christopher Robin**: Hallo! Did you see my note? I said I’d be back soon. And I am.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): spelling was not always fixed  
> **Christopher Robin**: “Back soon” turned into “Backson”: a spelling by ear. English spelling was not fixed until around the 1700s.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Before that, even famous writers spelled the same word several ways. Shakespeare’s own signatures vary. Wobbles are old news.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that English spelling was not fixed until about the 1700s._

_He is. But Rabbit walks home slowly, thinking about mornings, and doesn’t organise anything for the rest of the day._  
_Your Nubbin stands guard over Eeyore’s A until Eeyore says it can go._  

## A11-16. Poohsticks

- `a11-16-s1`: Watch Pooh invent a game on the bridge. · _Pooh is on the little wooden bridge with a fir-cone._
- `a11-16-s2`: Play Poohsticks with everyone on the bridge. · _Drop your stick on “now”, then run to the other side to see whose comes out first._
- `a11-16-s3`: Help Pooh wash Eeyore to the bank. · _Help lift the big stone to the rail and drop it beside Eeyore, not on him._

#### `a11-16-cone`

_Pooh is crossing the bridge with a fir-cone, thinking of a hum. He trips over nothing, and the fir-cone drops into the river._  
**Pooh**: Bother.  
_He goes to the other side to watch it float away. It comes out from under the bridge, which surprises him._  
**Pooh**: That’s interesting. I dropped it on that side and it came out on this one. I wonder if it would do it again.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): upstream and downstream  
> _Pooh drops the cone on one side of the bridge and sees it come out the other. Which side did he drop it on: upstream or downstream?_  
> - ✅ Upstream, where the water comes from → Yes. Upstream is where the water comes from. Downstream is where it flows to. Pooh drops it upstream.
> - Downstream, where it goes to → Downstream is where the water goes. He dropped the cone on the other side, upstream.
> - Either, it is a still pond → A still pond would not carry it. This is a stream, and it flows one way.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the words upstream and downstream._

_He drops two fir-cones at once, a big one and a small one, and runs across. The big one comes out first._  
**Pooh**: The big one won! I wanted the big one to win.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, notice): a fair test changes one thing and repeats  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pooh drops a big and a small cone together. The big one wins. Is that proof? A fair test changes one thing only and repeats it.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Pooh should try it again, and again, and drop them at the very same spot. One go is only a hint.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fair test changes one thing and is repeated._

_Fir-cones are hard to tell apart, so he goes on with sticks. That is how the game of Poohsticks begins._  

#### `a11-16-game`

_Soon everyone is playing: Pooh and Piglet, Rabbit and Roo, you and your Nubbin._  
**Christopher Robin**: Everybody drop on “now”. Then everybody run to the other side. And no pushing, Roo.  
_Your Nubbin drops its stick. Then, before anyone can stop it, it drops itself in after it._  
_It swims along beside its stick under the bridge, nudging it with its nose, in no hurry, enjoying the wet._  
**Roo**: That’s not fair! Is it fair? Can I do that?  
**Christopher Robin**: No, Roo.  
**Pooh**: I think it’s fair. Nothing in the game says you can’t go with your stick. I should have thought of it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): does a new player make the game unfair  
> _Your Nubbin went into the water with its stick. Pooh says “nothing in the game says you can’t”. Who decides if something is fair?_  
> - The people who play, together → That is how Pooh sees it: it is his game, and the players agree the rules.
> - The inventor, Pooh → Pooh invented it, and he agrees. Though rules usually work best when everyone has a say.
> - The rules written down → Rules help. But nobody wrote any here, so the players had to decide as they went.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about who decides whether a game is fair._

_Your Nubbin’s stick comes out first, and so does your Nubbin, very pleased and very wet. It shakes itself all over Piglet._  

> **Lesson** (science, do): the middle of a stream flows fastest  
> **Christopher Robin**: A stream flows fastest in the middle, away from the banks, which rub against the water and slow it.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Try it: drop one stick near the bank and one in the middle. The middle one wins. That is why the fast side wins.  
> Check: `edu:drop:stick:fast-water`
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a stream flows fastest in the middle, so a stick dropped there wins._

**Piglet**: Oh! Oh, d-dear. Woozles shake like that. I’m nearly sure.  

**Choices**

- **Let it count.**
    - **Pooh**: It counts. It’s my game, so I say.
- **Say it shouldn’t count.**
    - **Pooh**: Then it won the next best thing, which is getting wet on purpose.
- **Drop your own stick and run.**
    - Your stick comes out last. Some sticks just like the view.

#### `a11-16-eeyore`

_Then something big and grey comes out from under the bridge. It is Eeyore, floating on his back, upside down, looking calm._  
**Eeyore**: Don’t mind me. I’m just being upside down in a river. It’s very restful. Nobody should bother.  
**Christopher Robin**: Eeyore, what are you doing there?  
**Eeyore**: Floating. In a river. On my back. Not by choice, if anybody wondered. Nobody did.  
**Pooh**: If I drop a big stone in beside him, it will make a wave, and the wave will wash him to the bank.  
**Piglet**: What if you hit him?  
**Pooh**: I won’t. Probably.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: three lifters of 2 kg  
> _The stone weighs 6 kilograms. Pooh can lift 2 kilograms, and so can you and your Nubbin. Can the three of you lift it together?_  
> - ✅ Yes: 3 × 2 = 6 → Yes. Three lifters of 2 kg each make 6 kg, just enough.
> - No: 2 + 2 is only 4 → There are three lifters, not two: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
> - Only if Eeyore helps → He is busy floating! Three lifters at 2 kg each is already 6 kg.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups to check three lifters can lift 6 kg._

_The stone is too big for Pooh. You help him lift it, and your Nubbin pushes from underneath, and you hold it over the rail._  
**Pooh**: Now!  
_Splash: a great wave. Eeyore disappears, comes up, rolls over, and walks out on to the bank._  

#### `a11-16-bounced`

**Eeyore**: I was bounced. Into the river. Tigger bounced me.  
_Tigger, arriving, says he only coughed. Everyone looks at Tigger, and Tigger looks at the sky._  
**Tigger**: Just a cough. A big Tigger cough. Eeyore happened to be in front of it.  
**Eeyore**: Hm. Some coughs are bouncier than others. That’s all I’m saying.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what a good apology contains  
> _Tigger says “Just a cough. A big Tigger cough.” Which of these is a real apology?_  
> - ✅ “Sorry I bounced you, Eeyore. I’ll be more careful.” → Yes. A real apology says what you did, owns it, and offers to do better.
> - “It was only a cough.” → That explains, but it does not apologise. Eeyore is still soaked.
> - “You should have moved.” → That puts the blame on Eeyore. A real apology keeps the blame where it belongs.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the parts of a real apology._


#### `a11-16-complete`

_Afterwards everyone plays Poohsticks again, Eeyore too, dripping. He wins twice and says it doesn’t count._  
**Pooh**: The best thing about Poohsticks is that you can play it for ever, and it never gets any different.  
_Your Nubbin sits on the rail watching the water go under: the same water, and new water, both at once._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): the same river, always new water  
> _“Same water, new water.” A river looks the same each day, but its water is always new. It arrives from upstream and leaves downstream._  
> _All that water is on a long loop: sea, cloud, rain, river, and back to the sea. That loop is the water cycle._  
> _For grown-ups: Understood that a river is always carrying new water as part of the water cycle._

**Christopher Robin**: You could have a bridge like this at home, you know. Any stream will do. And any sticks.  

### Glossary

- **upstream**: In the direction a river comes from. The other way is downstream.
- **fair test**: An experiment where you change only one thing and repeat it.

## A11-17. Tigger Is Unbounced

- `a11-17-s1`: Hear Rabbit’s plan, and choose whom to walk with. · _Your choice decides where you are when the mist comes down._
- `a11-17-s2`: Get through the mist. · _Stay close to whoever you are with, and listen._

#### `a11-17-plan`

**Rabbit**: Tigger is getting very Bouncy. Too bouncy. Bouncing on Eeyore. Bouncing on everyone.  
**Rabbit**: Here is my plan. We take Tigger for a long walk, somewhere he’s never been, and lose him there. Then we go home.  
**Pooh**: Why?  
**Rabbit**: So that next morning he’s a smaller Tigger. A sorry sort of Tigger. A Tigger who says thank you.  
**Piglet**: That’s not very kind.  
**Rabbit**: It’s very kind. It’s for his own good. That’s the kindest sort.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): can something unkind be “for his own good”  
> _Rabbit says losing Tigger in the mist is “for his own good”. Piglet says it is not very kind. Can something unkind be for someone’s good?_  
> - Yes, if it teaches a lesson → Sometimes. But a lesson that comes from frightening a friend is rarely the one you meant to teach.
> - No, kindness is part of good → Many would agree. “For your own good” has been used to excuse many unkind things.
> - Only if the person agrees → That is a strong test. If Tigger agreed, it might be a game. If he did not, it is something else.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether something unkind can be for someone’s own good._

_A mist is coming up from the river, white and thick, and the Forest is going soft round the edges._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): mist is a cloud near the ground  
> **Christopher Robin**: Mist is made of tiny drops of water floating in the air. It forms when moist air cools, which is how clouds form too.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Mist is basically a low cloud. Fog is the same, only thicker. In thick fog you can barely see your own hand.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mist is tiny water drops that form as moist air cools._

**Tigger**: A walk! Where are we going? Tiggers love walks. Tiggers walk best of anyone.  

**Choices**

- **Go with Rabbit.**
    - **Rabbit**: Good. I knew somebody sensible would. Keep up, and keep quiet.
- **Stay with Tigger.**
    - **Tigger**: Hooray! Tiggers like company. Especially company that doesn’t run off.

#### `a11-17-plan-done`

_Into the mist they all go: Rabbit leading, everybody following, and Tigger bouncing round the outside of everybody._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, notice): foreshadowing  
> _The mist is coming up from the river. Authors use weather to hint at what is coming. That is called foreshadowing._  
> _Here, the soft white mist hints that someone is about to lose someone, and that it will not go as planned._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that foreshadowing hints at what will happen next._


#### `a11-17-mist`

_At the top of the Forest, in a hollow, Rabbit whispers “Now!”, and he and Pooh and Piglet duck behind a bank._  
_Tigger bounces on ahead without noticing. You go with him, because you said you would._  
**Tigger**: Where’s everybody gone? Hallo? Rabbit? Pooh?  
**Tigger**: They must have got lost. Poor things. Mist is very difficult if you aren’t a Tigger.  
_Tigger isn’t worried at all. He bounces along a short way home that his feet seem to know._  
_At Kanga’s, Pooh and Piglet arrive soon after, damp, following the smell of honey. Rabbit isn’t with them._  
**Tigger**: Rabbit? Lost? In the mist? Don’t worry. Tiggers never get lost. I’ll fetch him.  
_He bounces off into the white. You go after him, holding your Nubbin close, so the mist can’t have it._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what to do if you are lost  
> _Rabbit is lost somewhere in the mist. If you were lost in thick mist, what is the safest thing to do?_  
> - ✅ Stay where you are and call out → Yes. Stay put, call out, and wait. People find you faster when you are not moving.
> - Walk until you find something → It feels natural, but in thick mist you can walk in circles and get further from help.
> - Run, to get out of it faster → Running makes it easier to fall and harder to be found. Stay put and call.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the rule: if lost, stay put and call out._


#### `a11-17-found`

_You hear him before you see him: a small voice in a hollow, saying “Hallo?” to the mist, very bravely._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): we can tell which direction a sound comes from  
> **Christopher Robin**: In mist you hear before you see. Your two ears are a little apart, so a sound reaches one ear a split second before the other.
