> **Christopher Robin**: Your brain uses that tiny difference to tell which way the sound came from. You can follow a voice you cannot see.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that two ears let the brain work out the direction of a sound._

**Tigger**: Rabbit! There you are! I’ve come to find you. Tiggers are good at finding.  
_Rabbit comes out of the hollow and looks at Tigger. For once, he hasn’t got a plan._  
**Rabbit**: Tigger. Oh, Tigger. I am glad to see you.  

#### `a11-17-complete`

_Tigger takes everyone home, bouncing, by a way that is short and obvious once you’ve been shown it._  
**Rabbit**: He’s still very bouncy. Too bouncy.  
_Rabbit says it quietly, the way people say a thing they don’t quite mean any more._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): how a character changes  
> _Rabbit still says Tigger is too bouncy, but quietly, the way people say something they do not quite mean any more._  
> _Rabbit wanted a smaller, sorrier Tigger. By the end, the one who has changed is Rabbit. Stories often turn round like that._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how a character changes over a story._

**Tigger**: Tiggers don’t get lost. Tiggers find. That’s what Tiggers are for.  

### Glossary

- **foreshadowing**: Hints in a story about what will happen later.

## A11-18. Piglet Does a Very Grand Thing

- `a11-18-s1`: Visit Owl with Pooh and Piglet on a very windy day. · _Hold on to something on the way to The Chestnuts._
- `a11-18-s2`: Hold the string while Piglet climbs out through the letter-box. · _Take your place on the string behind Pooh and pull slowly._
- `a11-18-s3`: Help Eeyore find a new house for Owl. · _Follow Eeyore through the Forest. He is very pleased with what he has found._

#### `a11-18-wind`

_It is a very windy day. Piglet’s ears stream out behind him like flags, and he has to hold on to Pooh._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, notice): wind words: breeze, blustery, gale  
> **Christopher Robin**: Weather people have names for wind. A breeze is gentle. A blustery day has strong, gusty winds that come and go.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A gale blows at roughly 60 to 75 kilometres an hour (about 40 to 45 miles an hour). It can bring down branches, and sometimes chimneys.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the weather words breeze, blustery and gale._

**Piglet**: What if a tree fell, Pooh? While we were under it?  
**Pooh**: Then we’d be under it. But it mightn’t. Most trees stay up. That’s what they’re best at.  
_You all reach The Chestnuts and go in. Owl tells a long story about a great-uncle who once flew backwards through a wind like this._  
_Then there is a great crash, and the room tips over, slowly, and everything slides into one corner, including you._  
_When it stops, the floor is a wall, the wall is the floor, and the door is in the ceiling._  
**Piglet**: Pooh? Is it… is it still the same day?  
**Owl**: My house. My house is on its side. This has never happened to me before.  

**Choices**

- **Check everyone’s all right.**
    - Everyone is all right: Owl is ruffled, and Pooh is sitting on the tablecloth. Your Nubbin is under a chair, pleased to be found.
- **Look for a way out.**
    - The windows are full of branches. There is only the letter-box, high up in what used to be the door.
- **Hold Piglet’s hand.**
    - **Piglet**: Th-thank you. I’m not frightened. My hand is.

#### `a11-18-wind-done`

**Pooh**: The letter-box. It’s very high up and very small. Only somebody very small could get through it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction with measurements  
> _The letter-box is 25 centimetres wide. Piglet is 18 centimetres across. Will he fit, and by how many centimetres?_  
> - ✅ Yes, by 7 centimetres → Yes. 25 − 18 = 7. It is a tight squeeze, but he can do it.
> - No, he is too wide → Check: 18 is smaller than 25, so he fits, with 7 centimetres to spare.
> - Yes, by 43 centimetres → That is adding. To find the gap, subtract: 25 − 18 = 7.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted two measurements to see whether something fits._


#### `a11-18-letterbox`

_Everyone looks at Piglet. Piglet looks at the letter-box, and gets smaller._  
**Piglet**: M-me? Through there? And then what?  
**Pooh**: Then you fetch Christopher Robin, and he gets us out.  
**Owl**: I shall tie a string round you. My knots are well known.  
_Owl ties the string, and Pooh holds the end. You hold the end of Pooh, and your Nubbin holds the end of you._  
_Slowly, carefully, you all pull, and up goes Piglet to the letter-box in the ceiling._  
**Piglet**: I’m here. It’s very small. It’s very, very small.  
_He squeezes, and wriggles, and goes through with a squeak. You hear him scramble down the tree outside._  
**Piglet**: I’m going for Christopher Robin! I’m n-not frightened! Only a bit!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): being brave while scared  
> _Piglet shouts “I’m not frightened! Only a bit!” Is he brave? What does brave mean?_  
> - Yes: brave means going on while scared → Many people think so. Brave is not the lack of fear. It is what you do with it.
> - No: real brave means not scared → That is a common idea. But if you are not scared, there is nothing to be brave about.
> - He is both scared and brave → Exactly. Piglet is the best example in the Forest of both at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what brave means._


#### `a11-18-letterbox-done`

_Not long after, Christopher Robin arrives with a ladder, and Piglet arrives with Christopher Robin, very proud and trying not to be._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): climax and resolution  
> _A story’s climax is the moment of most tension. Piglet squeezing through the letter-box is this story’s._  
> _The resolution is how things settle after: here, the ladder arrives and Piglet arrives proud. Can you find both in your favourite book?_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the terms climax and resolution._


#### `a11-18-house`

_Afterwards Pooh makes up a long hum about Piglet’s Very Grand Thing. You hear all seven verses of it, as humming._  
_Piglet listens to every one, going pink at the bits about himself, and at the end he asks to hear it again._  
**Owl**: I shall need a new house. A suitable residence. With a knocker.  
**Eeyore**: Leave it to me. I know the Forest. I go everywhere, mostly alone.  
_Eeyore goes off, and comes back the next day, and leads you all to a beech tree, very pleased with himself._  
**Eeyore**: There. A house. Nobody using it, I should think. It’s got a name on and everything. And a step.  
_It is Piglet’s house. Everybody knows it is Piglet’s house, except Eeyore._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): owls nest in tree holes  
> **Christopher Robin**: Many owls are cavity nesters. They use holes in old trees, and sometimes barns, instead of building a nest.  
> **Christopher Robin**: So Owl in a hole of a beech tree is true to life. Different animals use different habitats: squirrels in dreys, badgers in setts, owls in holes.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many owls nest in holes in trees._

_Piglet looks at his house for a long time. Then he looks at Eeyore, who is happier than anybody has ever seen him._  

#### `a11-18-house-done`

**Piglet**: Yes. It’s just the house for Owl. I hope he’ll be very happy in it.  
_Piglet says it bravely, because he is brave, and then he has to look at the ground for a while._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): feelings can mix  
> _Piglet says yes bravely, then looks at the ground. He is proud of helping, and sad about the house. Both are true._  
> _When feelings mix, there is nothing wrong. You can name both: “I feel proud, and a little sad.”_  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that people can feel proud and sad at the same time._


#### `a11-18-complete`

**Pooh**: Piglet. You could come and live with me. Will you?  
**Piglet**: Oh, Pooh. Yes. Thank you, Pooh.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): a community looks after its own  
> _Piglet gave up a house. Pooh offered a home. One generous act led to another, and nobody in the Forest was left without a roof._  
> _That is what a community does: it notices who is in need, and the people who can help, do._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard how generosity spreads and communities look after each other._

_So Owl moves into Piglet’s old house, and gives it a grand new name, and spells it wrong._  
_Your Nubbin carries Piglet’s smallest chair to Pooh’s house, the long way round, as carefully as if it were made of eggs._  

### Glossary

- **blustery**: Windy, with strong gusts that come and go.
- **gale**: A very strong wind.
- **climax**: The most exciting or tense moment in a story.

## A11-19. The Rissolution

- `a11-19-s1`: Go to the meeting Rabbit has called, and sign the Rissolution. · _Everyone is gathered at Pooh Corner. Sign at the bottom, any way you like._
- `a11-19-s2`: Take the Rissolution to Christopher Robin. · _Walk with everyone to Christopher Robin’s door._

#### `a11-19-meeting`

_Christopher Robin is going away. Nobody knows how they know it, and nobody says it, but everybody knows._  
_Even Small knows, though he isn’t saying much. He never does._  
**Rabbit**: A Meeting has been called. By me. To pass a Resolution. Eeyore has written a poem for it.  
**Eeyore**: A Rissolution. That’s what it is. A poem. Don’t expect much.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): resolution has more than one meaning  
> **Christopher Robin**: Eeyore calls his poem a Rissolution. The real word is resolution, which has several meanings.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A resolution can be a firm decision, the end of a story, or how sharp a picture is. Context tells you which. Here it is a decision to remember.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that resolution has several meanings and that spelling wobbles are fine._

_Eeyore reads it out. It is long, and it rhymes in places, and it says, more or less, that they will all miss him._  
_Nobody laughs. Even Tigger stands still until the end._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): saying a hard thing aloud, or in a poem  
> _Everyone knows Christopher Robin is going somewhere, and nobody says it aloud. Instead, Eeyore writes a poem._  
> _Is it better to say hard things aloud, or to put them in a poem?_  
> - Say it aloud → Saying it plainly can be a relief. But it is hard, and not everyone is ready at once.
> - Put it in a poem → A poem can hold feelings too big for ordinary words. And you can give it away, like a present.
> - Whichever feels possible → That is wise. People find their own way to say goodbye. What matters is that it gets said.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about different ways of expressing hard feelings._

**Piglet**: It’s a very good poem, Eeyore.  
**Eeyore**: Is it? I hadn’t noticed. Bit long.  
**Rabbit**: Now everybody signs. Write your names at the bottom. Or something like your names.  

**Choices**

- **Sign your name.**
    - You sign it, in your best letters, under Piglet’s.
- **Let your Nubbin sign with a paw.**
    - Your Nubbin dips a paw in Owl’s ink and presses it carefully at the bottom: slightly crooked, and entirely its own.
- **Help Pooh with his letters.**
    - **Pooh**: P, O, O, H. Is that right? It looks right. It looks like me.

#### `a11-19-signed`

_Tigger signs next to you, with a T that bounces right off the edge of the paper._  
**Tigger**: Is he coming back? He’s coming back. Isn’t he?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): what characters do not say  
> _Tigger asks if Christopher Robin is coming back, and nobody answers. Sometimes what characters do not say tells you the most._  
> _If someone asks you a question like Tigger’s, an honest comfort is possible: “I don’t know, but he cares about you very much.”_  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed what a silence shows, and how to give honest comfort._

_Nobody answers. Tigger bounces once, very small, to show he doesn’t mind._  

#### `a11-19-scroll`

_Rabbit rolls up the scroll. Then he stops, because something is already round it: a blue ribbon, tied in a careful double bow._  
**Eeyore**: I had it in my pot. Seemed right. It’s a Friend ribbon. He’ll know what it says.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): scrolls and signatures  
> **Christopher Robin**: Before there were bound books, long texts were written on scrolls: rolls of papyrus or parchment. People have signed documents for thousands of years.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A signature says: I was here, and I agree. Every name on the Rissolution says that, in its own handwriting.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that long documents were once written on scrolls and signed._

_Everyone walks to Christopher Robin’s house together. At the door, nobody wants to go first._  
_In the end Eeyore goes first, because it is his poem, and everybody else crowds in behind him._  
**Christopher Robin**: What’s this?  
**Eeyore**: It’s a Rissolution. From all of us. You read it. We’ll just… we’ll go.  
_Christopher Robin reads it right to the end, and all the names, and he doesn’t say anything for a moment._  
**Christopher Robin**: Thank you. All of you. Thank you.  

#### `a11-19-scroll-done`

_Then everyone goes away, quietly, one by one, until only Pooh is left._  
_You go and wait by the gate with your Nubbin. Nobody asked you to, but it seems the right place to be._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, notice): how pace and quiet set a mood  
> _Everyone goes “quietly, one by one”. The story slows right down, and the sentences go quiet too._  
> _Writers set a mood with pace as well as words. Here the slow, quiet ending tells you this is a sad goodbye, and a gentle one._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how a writer uses pace to set a mood._


#### `a11-19-complete`

_After a while Christopher Robin comes out. Pooh is with him._  
**Christopher Robin**: We’re going for a walk. To the top of the Forest. Will you come? Some of the way?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): halves of a distance  
> _The path to the top of the Forest is 2 kilometres. Christopher Robin asks you to come “some of the way”. If you walk half, how far is that?_  
> - ✅ 1 kilometre → Yes. Half of 2 is 1. Some of the way, at its simplest.
> - 2 kilometres → That would be all of the way. Half of 2 is 1.
> - 4 kilometres → That is double. Half means divide by 2: 2 ÷ 2 = 1.
> _For grown-ups: Found half of a distance._

_Your Nubbin is already on its feet._  

### Glossary

- **resolution**: A firm decision. It can also mean the way a story’s problem is settled.

## A11-20. An Enchanted Place

- `a11-20-s1`: Walk with Christopher Robin and Pooh to the top of the Forest. · _Walk a little way behind them, up through the Forest to Galleons Lap._
- `a11-20-s2`: Wait at the edge of the circle while Christopher Robin and Pooh talk. · _Stay at the edge. This bit is theirs._

#### `a11-20-climb`

_Christopher Robin and Pooh walk up through the Forest, and you walk a little way behind, with your Nubbin._  
_Nobody is in a hurry. Christopher Robin points things out, the way you do when you want to remember the way._  
**Christopher Robin**: Pooh. Of all the things there are to do, what do you like best?  
**Pooh**: Coming round to yours. And you saying there’s honey. And there being honey. And Piglet. Mostly that.  
**Christopher Robin**: I like that too. But what I like best of all is doing Nothing.  
**Pooh**: Nothing? What does Nothing look like, when you’re doing it?  
**Christopher Robin**: It’s when you go out for no reason, and come back for no reason, and the whole day in between is yours.  
**Pooh**: Oh. I do that a lot.  
**Christopher Robin**: I know. You’re very good at it.  
_They come out at the top of the Forest. There is a ring of trees there, sixty-something of them, standing round as if they’ve been waiting._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, do): counting a circle in groups  
> **Christopher Robin**: Counting in a circle is tricky, because there is no first tree. Tie a ribbon on one, and count round until you come back to the ribbon.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Try groups to check: nine groups of seven trees is 9 × 7 = 63. Or ten groups of six and a few more. Try several ways and compare.  
> Check: `edu:count:trees:groups-of-7`
> _For grown-ups: Learned to count a circle by marking a start and checking in groups._

_Nobody has ever been able to count them: sixty-three, or sixty-four. It changes a little every time you try._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): is doing Nothing really nothing  
> _Christopher Robin says what he likes best is doing Nothing. Is doing Nothing really nothing? What happens when you do it?_  
> - It is resting your mind → Many people find that. Free time, without a plan, lets thoughts settle, and ideas arrive.
> - It is the best sort of something → Christopher Robin might say so. It is noticing and wandering, and that is not nothing at all.
> - It is boring → For some, at first. Sometimes the boredom is the doorway to something good.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the value of unplanned free time._


**Choices**

- **Count the trees.**
    - You count sixty-three, then again, and get sixty-four. Your Nubbin, counting on its paws, gives up at four and is content.
- **Don’t count them. Just look.**
    - You don’t count them. It seems like the kind of place that would rather not be counted.

#### `a11-20-knight`

_At the edge of the circle you stop. Your Nubbin stops too, and sits down without being told._  
_Christopher Robin and Pooh go into the middle, where the grass is soft, and sit, and talk about everything._  
_Kings and queens, and a thing called Factors, and a place called Brazil. Pooh listens, and doesn’t mind not knowing._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): factors of a number  
> _Christopher Robin and Pooh talk about a thing called Factors. Factors are numbers that multiply to make another._  
> _2 and 6 are factors of 12, because 2 × 6 = 12. Which of these is a factor of 12?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. 4 × 3 = 12, so 4 and 3 are factors of 12.
> - 5 → 5 does not divide 12 exactly: 5 × 2 = 10 and 5 × 3 = 15. Try 4.
> - 7 → 7 × 1 = 7 and 7 × 2 = 14, so 7 misses 12. Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a factor is and found one of 12._

**Christopher Robin**: Pooh. Stand up.  
_Christopher Robin takes a stick and touches Pooh on each shoulder with it, very gravely._  
**Christopher Robin**: Arise, Sir Pooh. Knight of the Forest, and my truest friend.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): knighthood and the accolade  
> **Christopher Robin**: In the Middle Ages, a knight was a trained warrior who served a lord.  
> **Christopher Robin**: To make someone a knight, the lord tapped each shoulder with a sword. That tap is called the accolade.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Christopher Robin uses a stick, which is the right size for a Bear. The honour is the same.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a knight was and how knighting worked._

_Pooh rises, and thinks about being a knight, and decides he likes it, though he isn’t sure what it involves._  
_Then Christopher Robin is quiet for a long time, looking at the trees._  
**Christopher Robin**: Pooh. Will you remember me, always? Even when I am grown up and enormous?  
**Pooh**: Will I be enormous too?  
**Christopher Robin**: No. You’ll be just the right size.  
**Pooh**: Then I promise.  
**Christopher Robin**: And if I’m not here so much, you’ll know it isn’t because of you. Won’t you?  
**Pooh**: I shall know. Even if I don’t know why.

> **Lesson** (maths, ask): why a marker helps when counting a circle  
> _Your Nubbin ties its ribbon round one tree. Why does a marker help when counting trees in a circle?_  
> - ✅ It shows where you started → Yes. In a circle you can go round again and again, so the ribbon tells you when you are back.
> - It makes the tree easier to climb → It might! But the real reason is that a marker tells you when the count is finished.
> - It does not help at all → Try counting without one and you may find yourself counting some trees twice.
> _For grown-ups: Understood that a marker shows where counting started._

### Glossary

- **factor**: A number that divides exactly into another number, such as 3 and 4 for 12.
- **accolade**: The ceremony of making someone a knight by touching their shoulders with a sword.

## A12-1. The Troll’s Mirror

- `a12-01-s1`: Step into the cut-paper town and take the room under the eaves. · _Touch the page, then climb the attic stairs to Grandmother._
- `a12-01-s2`: Hold the candle for Grandmother’s shadow-show. · _Stand by the attic wall and keep the candle still._
- `a12-01-s3`: Watch the troll’s mirror break. · _Keep the candle steady to the end of the show._

#### `a12-01-arrive`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page of cut paper: rooftops, chimneys, and two attic windows with a gutter between them._  
_The paper is so fine it stirs when you breathe. Then it’s a steep wooden stair, and you’re on it, with a bag and your Nubbin._  
**Grandmother**: There you are. The lodger. You’ll want the room under the eaves, and the bed by the chimney.  
**Grandmother**: Mind your head on the beam. Everybody hits it, the first week.  
_Grandmother is small and quick, with her spectacles pushed up into white hair._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): where Denmark is  
> _This town is in Denmark, a small country in northern Europe. It is one long peninsula and hundreds of islands._  
> _Denmark’s peninsula is joined by land to only one other country. Which one?_  
> - ✅ Germany, to the south → That’s right. Walk south out of Denmark and you’re in Germany. Every other way, there’s sea.
> - Australia → Australia is on the other side of the world! Denmark’s only land neighbour is Germany, to the south.
> - No country at all → Most of Denmark is islands, so that’s a good guess. But the peninsula touches Germany, to the south.
> _For grown-ups: Found Denmark on the map of Europe and learned it borders Germany._

_In the window across the gutter, two faces appear: a boy and a girl, both trying to see you at once._  
**Kay**: Is that the new lodger? Has it got a dog?  
**Gerda**: That’s not a dog, Kay. Look at its ears.  
**Grandmother**: And what’s this? It isn’t a cat. I’ve had cats.  

**Choices**

- **Tell her it’s a Nubbin.**
    - **Grandmother**: A Nubbin. Well, it can have the end of the bed and the heel of the loaf, same as a cat.
- **Say it’s your friend, and it goes where you go.**
    - **Grandmother**: Good. Things that go where you go are worth a bed.
- **Let your Nubbin bow.**
    - Your Nubbin bows, nearly falls down the stairs, and is caught by Grandmother without her looking.
    - **Grandmother**: Manners. It can stay.

#### `a12-01-arrive-done`

**Grandmother**: That’s Kay and Gerda. They live across the gutter, one each side, and they’re in here more than they’re out.  
**Grandmother**: Evenings, there’s a story. You can hold the candle. Lodgers always hold the candle.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): welcoming someone new  
> _Grandmother gives you a job on your first day. Why might that help a newcomer feel at home?_  
> - A job means you belong → That’s a fair answer. When you’re needed, you’re one of us.
> - It stops you feeling shy → It often does. It’s easier to talk when your hands are busy.
> - It doesn’t help at all → Maybe not for everyone. Then a friendly word and a warm bed do the rest.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the ways people make a newcomer feel welcome._


#### `a12-01-show`

_It’s late summer, and the light goes about nine. Kay and Gerda come across by the gutter boxes, the way they always do in summer._  
_Grandmother sits with a sheet of black paper and a long pair of scissors, snipping without looking._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): who Hans Christian Andersen was  
> _This story was written by Hans Christian Andersen, born in 1805 in Odense, a town in Denmark. It came out in 1844._  
> _Andersen often cut pictures out of paper while he told his stories, just as Grandmother does._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish storyteller who made paper cut-outs._

**Grandmother**: Candle a bit higher. There. Now the wall’s a stage, and you’re the sun. Don’t wobble; suns don’t.  
**Kay**: Do the troll one. The troll one’s best.  
**Gerda**: It’s frightening.  
**Kay**: That’s why.  
**Grandmother**: Right. Steady, all of you. This one starts badly and ends well, and those are the best sort.  
_A paper troll steps onto the wall, all knees and grin. He holds a mirror cut so thin the candle shows through it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): shadow size and distance from the light  
> **Grandmother**: If I hold the troll closer to the candle, what happens to his shadow on the wall?  
> - ✅ It gets bigger → Yes. Closer to the light, he blocks more of it, so the shadow grows. Watch him loom.
> - It gets smaller → Try it and see: closer to the candle, he blocks more light, and the shadow gets bigger.
> - It disappears → He’d still block the light, so the shadow stays. It grows bigger as he gets closer.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a shadow grows bigger when the object moves closer to the light._

**Grandmother**: He had made a mirror that was wrong in a particular way. Anything good shrank in it to nearly nothing.  
**Grandmother**: Anything mean or ugly got bigger and worse. A green meadow looked like boiled spinach.  
**Kay**: I’d like to look in it.  
**Gerda**: I wouldn’t.  

#### `a12-01-show-done`

_Grandmother does the troll’s voice. It’s lower than you would expect, and very pleased with itself._  
**The Troll**: Ha! Look how small goodness goes! Look how big the rest of it gets! Isn’t it wonderful?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character motive  
> _Why might a troll enjoy a mirror that makes good things look small?_  
> - ✅ He likes making people feel bad → Yes. He enjoys spoiling things. That’s what makes him the villain.
> - He wants to help people → Listen to his laugh again. He’s pleased when goodness shrinks, so he isn’t helping.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character’s motive from what he says and how he says it._


#### `a12-01-shards`

**Grandmother**: The troll kept a school, if you can believe it, and his pupils carried the mirror all round the world.  
**Grandmother**: Then they thought they’d fly up to the sky with it, and make fun of the angels too.  
_The paper mirror climbs the wall in little jerks. The higher it goes, the wider its painted grin spreads._  
**Grandmother**: And it grinned so hard it shook, and shook, until it slipped right out of their hands.  
_Grandmother opens her fingers. A handful of paper snips falls through the candlelight like snow._  
**Grandmother**: It broke into more pieces than there are people. Some were no bigger than a grain of sand.  
**Grandmother**: Get one in your eye and everything looks wrong. Get one in your heart and it goes hard and cold, like a stone in a frosty field.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _“Cold, like a stone in a frosty field” is a simile: it compares two things using “like” or “as”. What does this one tell you?_  
> - ✅ The heart stops feeling anything → Yes. A stone in frost can’t feel the sun. That’s what a cold heart is like.
> - The heart turns into a real stone → Not really. A simile says it’s like a stone: hard and unfeeling, but still a heart.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile means in a story._

**Kay**: And then what?  
**Grandmother**: Then you need somebody to come and fetch you.  

**Choices**

- **Brush the paper snips off Gerda’s sleeve.**
    - You brush them off. Gerda checks her other sleeve herself, twice, and then Kay’s.
- **Catch a snip as it falls.**
    - You catch one on your palm, and it’s only paper. You look at it anyway, a little longer than you meant to.
- **Ask who comes to fetch you.**
    - **Grandmother**: Whoever loves you most and is too stubborn to stop. That’s usually how it goes.

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): mirrors and glass reflect light  
> _The candle is out, so where did the glint come from? A little moonlight from the window, bouncing off glass._

_Later, in the room under the eaves, you lie in the bed by the chimney. The other bed creaks, as promised._  
_From your window you can see the gutter, the two boxes across it, and two small rose trees still flowering in the dark._  
_Your Nubbin curls up on your feet. Across the town a clock strikes ten, slow and sure._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals in hours  
> _The clock struck ten. If you sleep until seven in the morning, how many hours of sleep is that?_  
> - ✅ 9 hours → Yes. Two hours to midnight, then seven more: nine hours. A good long sleep.
> - 3 hours → Ten to seven isn’t three, because midnight comes in between. Two hours to midnight, plus seven: nine.
> - 17 hours → Ten plus seven is seventeen, but clocks start again at midnight. Two hours, then seven more: nine.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out an overnight time interval in hours._

_You fall asleep to the sound of rain beginning, very softly, on the roof._  

### Glossary

- **lodger**: Someone who pays to live in a room in another person’s house.
- **peninsula**: A piece of land with water on almost every side.
- **simile**: A way of describing something by saying it is like something else.

## A12-2. Two Windows

- `a12-02-s1`: Water the roses in the gutter boxes. · _Climb out to the gutter with the watering can and do the top of the arch._
- `a12-02-s2`: Warm a coin on the stove and melt a peephole in the frozen window. · _Hold a copper coin on the stove, then press it to the glass._
- `a12-02-s3`: Look out of your window that night. · _Wait at your peephole after the house has gone to bed._

#### `a12-02-roses`

_In the morning you see it all properly: two attics with roofs that nearly touch, and a lead gutter running between them._  
_Long ago the two families each put a box across the gutter. Now peas hang over the edges, and in each box grows a rose tree._  
_The roses have climbed into an arch. Under it are two little stools, and two children who think it’s the best room in town._  
**Gerda**: You’re tallest. You can do the top of the arch. Don’t drown the peas; they sulk.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): what plants need  
> **Gerda**: Why do roses up on a roof grow so well, do you think?  
> - ✅ Lots of sunlight, and we water them → Exactly. Plants need light and water. Up here there’s sun all day, and we bring the water.
> - Because it’s high up → Being high doesn’t feed them. It’s the sunlight up here, and the water we bring.
> - Roses don’t need anything → Everything living needs something! Roses need light, water and good soil.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plants need light and water to grow._

**Kay**: Peas don’t sulk.  
**Gerda**: These ones do.  
**Kay**: Gran says the roses are older than both of us put together. She says they’ll still be here when we’re old.  
_Your Nubbin tries to help by sitting in the watering can._  

**Choices**

- **Water the top of the arch, carefully.**
    - You water the high roses. A few drops roll off onto Kay’s head, and he pretends not to notice, very badly.
- **Give the peas a bit extra, in case.**
    - **Gerda**: See? They’re cheering up already.
    - **Kay**: They look exactly the same.
- **Lift your Nubbin out of the can first.**
    - Your Nubbin comes out of the can dripping and offended. Gerda dries it on her apron, and it forgives everybody.

#### `a12-02-roses-done`

**Gerda**: In winter we can’t climb across. We have to go down all our stairs and up all the others.  
**Kay**: It takes years.  
**Gerda**: It takes two minutes.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): minutes and seconds  
> _There are 60 seconds in a minute. How many seconds is Gerda’s two-minute trip?_  
> - ✅ 120 seconds → Yes. Sixty and sixty make a hundred and twenty. Not years at all.
> - 62 seconds → That’s one minute and two seconds. Two whole minutes is sixty plus sixty: one hundred and twenty.
> - 200 seconds → A bit too many. Sixty plus sixty is one hundred and twenty.
> _For grown-ups: Changed minutes into seconds._


#### `a12-02-frost`

_Winter comes, and the windows freeze over with ferns of ice. You can’t see across the gutter at all._  
_Kay and Gerda warm copper coins on the stove and press them to the glass. Copper passes heat on quickly, so the coin melts the ice fast._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): how frost forms  
> _Warm air indoors holds water you can’t see, called water vapour. When it touches glass colder than 0 °C (32 °F), it freezes._  
> _It turns straight into tiny ice crystals, which grow into those feathery ferns._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that frost forms when water vapour freezes on a very cold surface._

_Each coin melts a round peephole, as neat as a button. A bright eye looks through each one, across the snow._  
**Grandmother**: Look at the white bees swarming.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphors  
> _Grandmother calls the snowflakes “white bees”. Why is that a good metaphor?_  
> - ✅ They swarm and buzz about in the air → Just so. Snow in the wind whirls about like a swarm of bees, and every swarm has a queen.
> - Snowflakes can sting you → They don’t sting! It’s the swarming that’s alike: thousands of little white things, whirling.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor that compares snowflakes to bees._

**Kay**: Have they got a queen? Like real bees?  
**Grandmother**: They have. She flies where the swarm is thickest, and she never stays on the ground for long.  
**Grandmother**: Some nights she flies through the streets and looks in at the windows. That’s when the frost comes up in flowers.  
**Kay**: Let her try. I’d put her on the hot stove, and she’d melt.  

**Choices**

- **Tell Kay that’s no way to treat a guest.**
    - **Kay**: She isn’t a guest. She’s weather.
- **Ask Grandmother if she’s ever seen her.**
    - **Grandmother**: Once or twice. Through the glass. Not close, and that’s how I like it.
- **Look out of your own peephole.**
    - The flakes go past your peephole in their thousands. One of them seems, for a moment, to look back.

#### `a12-02-frost-done`

_Grandmother smooths Kay’s hair and starts a story about a goose instead._  
_She doesn’t mention the queen again._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): reading other people’s feelings  
> _Why do you think Grandmother changes the subject so quickly?_  
> - Kay’s boasting worried her → That’s a thoughtful answer. Grown-ups sometimes change the subject when something worries them.
> - She just likes geese → Maybe! But notice she smooths his hair first, which looks like care, or worry.
> - She was tired of the story → Could be. Watch her face next time Kay talks about the queen, and see what you think.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what a character’s actions show about her feelings._


#### `a12-02-night`

_That night you can’t sleep. Your Nubbin can’t either; it sits on the sill with its nose to your peephole._  
_Across the gutter Kay is up too, standing on a chair at his window._  
_A few flakes drift down. One, bigger than the rest, settles on the edge of a flower box, and stays._  
_It grows into a woman, tall and fine, dressed in white gauze made of a million starry flakes._  
_She is lovely, and she is ice, all of her, dazzling and glittering. And she is alive._  
_Her eyes are like two bright stars, but there is no rest in them at all._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): describing a character  
> _Which words tell you most clearly that the woman is not a warm, ordinary person?_  
> - ✅ “She is ice, all of her” → Yes. She looks like a woman, but she’s made of ice. That’s the clue that matters.
> - “Tall and fine” → Lots of people are tall and fine. The clue is “she is ice, all of her”.
> _For grown-ups: Used the words of a description to understand a character._

_She looks in at Kay’s window. She nods to him, and lifts one hand, and beckons._  

**Choices**

- **Knock on your window.**
    - You knock hard on the glass. Kay jumps down off his chair, and the woman turns her head towards you, slowly.
    - Then she isn’t there. Something large and white goes past the window, like a bird.
- **Call Kay’s name.**
    - You call his name across the gutter. Kay startles and jumps down from his chair.
    - When you look again there’s nobody on the box. Something white goes past, like a big bird in the dark.
- **Pull your Nubbin back from the glass.**
    - You lift your Nubbin away from the window. It’s cold right through, and it burrows into your shirt.
    - Kay jumps down off his chair. When you look again a big white bird is passing, and the box is empty.

_You sit up until morning._  
_The frost on your window has grown into flowers you have never seen in any garden._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): ice crystals grow  
> _Frost keeps growing all night. More water vapour freezes onto the crystals already there, so the patterns spread across the glass._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that frost patterns grow as more water vapour freezes onto them._

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-1, ask): the seasons in order  
> _The story began in late summer. Which season comes next, after this spring?_  
> - ✅ Summer → Yes. Summer, autumn, winter, spring, and round to summer again.
> - Autumn → Autumn comes after summer. After spring comes summer again.
> - Winter → Winter came before spring. Next it’s summer: the year goes round like a wheel.
> _For grown-ups: Put the four seasons in order._


### Glossary

- **gutter**: A channel along the edge of a roof that carries rainwater away.
- **water vapour**: Water that has turned into an invisible gas in the air.
- **beckons**: Signals to someone with a hand to come closer.

## A12-3. The Splinter

- `a12-03-s1`: Sit under the rose arch with Kay and Gerda. · _Climb out to the gutter and take the spare stool._
- `a12-03-s2`: Put the rose box straight after Kay kicks it. · _Lift the box back onto the gutter and press the earth round the roots._
- `a12-03-s3`: Go out in the snow when Kay calls you to see his glass. · _Follow Gerda down to the street and look where Kay shows you._

#### `a12-03-arch`

_It’s summer, and the roses have never been so good. Gerda has learned a hymn with roses in it, and hums it all day._  
_She hums it to Kay under the arch, and he hums it back. Your Nubbin hums the tune a beat behind them both._  
_They’re looking at a picture book of animals and birds. Kay is doing the noises, and the noises are terrible._  
**Kay**: That’s an elk. It goes like this.  
**Gerda**: It does not.  
_Across the town, the church clock begins to strike five._  
**Kay**: Ow! Something stung me. In my heart. And my eye, something’s gone in my eye.  
_In the low sun you see it: a glint, smaller than a grain of sand, there and gone._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how eyes protect themselves  
> _Eyes have their own defences. Blinking sweeps dust away, and tears wash out what blinking can’t._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how blinking and tears protect our eyes._


**Choices**

- **Look in Kay’s eye.**
    - You hold his eyelid gently and look, and there’s nothing there. You are almost sure there’s nothing there.
- **Hold Kay’s hand till it stops.**
    - You hold his hand, and it’s warm. After a moment it isn’t quite as warm, and you tell yourself it is.
- **Call Grandmother.**
    - Grandmother comes up, peers into his eye with her spectacles on, and finds nothing at all.
    - **Grandmother**: Blink. Again. There. Gone.

#### `a12-03-arch-done`

**Kay**: It’s gone. I think it’s gone.  
_It hasn’t gone._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view  
> _Kay thinks it’s gone, but the narrator says it hasn’t. Who knows more right now?_  
> - ✅ The narrator, and so do you → Yes. The storyteller lets you know something Kay doesn’t. That’s what makes you worry for him.
> - Kay → Kay can only feel the sting fading. The narrator sees the whole story, and says it’s still there.
> _For grown-ups: Compared what a character knows with what the reader knows._


#### `a12-03-kick`

**Gerda**: Kay? Are you all right?  
**Kay**: Why are you crying? It makes you look ugly.  
**Kay**: There’s nothing the matter with me. That rose has a worm in it. And that one’s all crooked.  
**Kay**: They’re ugly roses. They match the ugly boxes.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): whose fault unkindness is  
> _Is Kay choosing to be unkind, or is the splinter doing it? What do you think?_  
> - The splinter is doing it → That’s fair: something has got in front of the real Kay. It still hurts Gerda, though.
> - Kay is choosing it → That’s fair too. Even with a splinter, his words land on a real person.
> - A bit of both → A thoughtful answer. Hard days can make us unkind, and we still owe a sorry after.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people are sometimes unkind and how it affects others._

_He kicks the box. It skids along the gutter, and he snaps off two roses and drops them over the edge._  
_You reach for him, and then you understand what you saw._  
_You can’t take a splinter out of a heart. Not with your hands, and not with anything you own._  
_Kay goes in and slams his window. Gerda stands in the gutter with her picture book held against her chest._  
**Gerda**: He said it was a book for babies.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): actions that show feelings  
> _Look at Gerda: she holds her book tight against her chest. Writers often show a feeling through what a character does._  
> _She is hurt, and that’s allowed. When someone is unkind, it helps to be near a friend._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how a character’s actions show her feelings._


**Choices**

- **Fetch the two roses back for Gerda.**
    - You lean over the gutter’s edge and fish them back. Gerda puts them in a cup of water on her sill.
- **Knock on Kay’s window.**
    - You knock. Kay opens it, looks at you, and does a perfect, horrible impression of your face.
    - Then he shuts it again.
- **Say nothing. Straighten the box together.**
    - You and Gerda lift the box back into place without a word. Your Nubbin pats the earth flat round the roots.

#### `a12-03-kick-done`

_The rose tree has lost two flowers and a bit of bark._  
_Roses forgive that sort of thing, if they’re left alone. It still has ten flowers open, and more in bud._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction word problem  
> _Kay snapped two flowers off the rose tree, and ten are left. How many were there before?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Ten left, plus the two he snapped: twelve.
> - 8 → Eight would be ten take away two. But we want what was there before: ten plus two, twelve.
> - 10 → Ten is how many are left now. Add back the two he snapped: twelve.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a word problem by working backwards with addition._


#### `a12-03-glass`

_All that autumn Kay is clever and cruel. He puts on Grandmother’s spectacles and does her voice, and the whole street laughs._  
_He can do anybody. He does Gerda best of all, and he only does the bits that hurt._  
**Grandmother**: He’s a sharp lad. Too sharp, lately.  
_When the snow comes he runs out with a big burning-glass, and holds out the blue tail of his coat to catch the flakes._  
**Kay**: Look in the glass, Gerda. Look how perfect they are.  
_Under the glass each flake is a star, sharp and exact, every arm the same as every other._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, do): snowflakes have six arms  
> _Count the arms on the flake under the glass. Snow crystals almost always have six._  
> _When water freezes, its tiny particles lock together in a six-sided pattern, so the crystal grows six arms._  
> Check: `edu:count:snowflake-arms:6`
> _For grown-ups: Counted the six arms of a snowflake and learned why there are six._

**Kay**: Much better than real flowers. Not a single thing wrong with them. If only they didn’t melt.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry  
> _A line of symmetry cuts a shape into two matching halves. How many lines of symmetry can a perfect six-armed snowflake have?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Six. Through each pair of opposite arms, and between them too. Told you they were perfect.
> - 1 → Just one? Fold it any of six ways and it matches. Six lines.
> - 2 → More than that. There are three lines through the arms and three between them: six.
> _For grown-ups: Found the lines of symmetry in a six-armed snowflake._

**Gerda**: Real flowers smell of something.  
**Kay**: That’s what’s wrong with them.  

**Choices**

- **Look in the glass.**
    - You look. The flake is beautiful and perfect, and you feel nothing at all looking at it, which frightens you.
- **Throw a snowball at Kay.**
    - It gets him on the shoulder. For a second he almost laughs like he used to, then he brushes it off and looks bored.
- **Stand by Gerda.**
    - You stand next to Gerda, and neither of you says anything. Your Nubbin leans on her boot.

#### `a12-03-glass-done`

**Kay**: I’m allowed in the big square tomorrow, with the boys who go sledging. Gran said.  
**Gerda**: Gran said maybe.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty  
> _Grandmother said “maybe”, but Kay says she said yes. What is Kay doing?_  
> - ✅ Stretching the truth → Yes. “Maybe” isn’t “yes”. Turning one into the other is a kind of fib.
> - Telling it exactly → Not quite. She said maybe. Saying yes when it was maybe isn’t honest.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about the difference between telling the truth and stretching it._


#### `a12-03-complete`

_That evening Gerda sits on her stool in the gutter, in the cold, under the bare arch._  
**Gerda**: He’s still in there. I know he is. It’s just that something’s got in front of him.  
_She looks at you as if you might know what to do. You don’t, and you don’t pretend you do._  
_You sit down next to her instead, on Kay’s stool, and wait with her until Grandmother calls you both in._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): being with a friend who is sad  
> _You didn’t have an answer, so you sat with her. Being there is a real kind of help, even when you can’t fix anything._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that staying with a sad friend is a way of helping._


### Glossary

- **burning-glass**: An old word for a magnifying glass, a lens that makes small things look bigger.
- **symmetry**: When one half of a shape is a mirror image of the other half.

## A12-4. The Big Sledge

- `a12-04-s1`: Follow Kay to the great square. · _Go down to the square and keep Kay in sight._
- `a12-04-s2`: Run after the white sledge. · _Run! Keep after it through the town gate._
- `a12-04-s3`: Watch from the rise. · _Stay on the rise. You can’t reach them from here._

#### `a12-04-square`

_Kay comes past with big gloves on and his sledge on his back._  
**Kay**: I’m allowed in the big square. I’m going.  
**Gerda**: Go with him. Please. Just keep an eye on him. He won’t let me.  
_The square is full of noise. The boldest boys tie their sledges to farmers’ carts and get pulled a good way for nothing._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): friction on snow  
> _A cart can pull a loaded sledge across snow quite easily. Why does a sledge slide so well on snow?_  
> - ✅ Snow is slippery, so there’s little friction → Yes. Friction is the force that slows sliding things. Smooth snow and ice give very little.
> - Sledges are very light → Some are heavy! It’s the snow: it’s slippery, so there’s hardly any friction to slow them.
> - The cold pushes them along → Cold doesn’t push. The snow is slippery, so friction is low and the pull of the cart wins.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that friction is low on snow and ice, so things slide easily._

_Then a great sledge comes in, painted white. Somebody sits in it wrapped in a rough white fur, with a white cap on._  
_It drives round the square. Every boy watches it, and the white driver watches only Kay._  

**Choices**

- **Shout to Kay to stay put.**
    - **Kay**: Mind your own business, lodger!
    - He doesn’t even look round. He’s watching the white sledge.
- **Push through to get hold of his cord.**
    - You push through the crowd towards him. There are too many boys and too many sledges, and the square is suddenly very wide.
- **Pick up your Nubbin. It’s gone very still.**
    - You pick it up. It’s staring at the white sledge, and it’s cold to the touch, the way it was at the window.

#### `a12-04-square-done`

_Kay has his cord in his hands. He’s tying a careful knot, with his tongue between his teeth, the way he does sums._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): staying safe with strangers  
> _Kay is about to tie himself to a stranger’s sledge. What’s the safe thing to do when a stranger invites you to go with them?_  
> - ✅ Say no, and tell a grown-up you trust → Yes. Never go off with someone you don’t know, however friendly they look.
> - Go, if they look kind → Looking kind isn’t enough. Stay put, say no, and tell a grown-up you trust.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about saying no to strangers and telling a trusted adult._


#### `a12-04-chase`

_As the white sledge comes round again, Kay ties his little sledge to it, and off he goes._  
_Faster, into the next street, and faster. The driver turns and nods to Kay, kindly, as if they’ve known each other for years._  
_Every time Kay reaches to untie the cord, the driver nods again. Every time, Kay sits still._  
_You run. Your Nubbin runs ahead of you, and then you scoop it up and run faster._  
_The sledges go out through the town gate. The snow comes down so thick that you can’t see your own hand._  
**Kay**: Stop! Stop! I want to get off!  
_He tries to say his prayers, and all that comes is his times tables: six sevens are… six sevens are…_  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication facts  
> _Kay is stuck on his tables. What are six sevens?_  
> - ✅ 42 → Yes, forty-two: six groups of seven. Kay can’t find it, because his head is full of snow.
> - 13 → Thirteen is six plus seven. Six times seven, six groups of seven, is forty-two.
> - 36 → Thirty-six is six sixes. One more six makes six sevens: forty-two.
> _For grown-ups: Recalled a multiplication fact: 6 × 7 = 42._

_You lose them. Then the snow parts for a moment, and you see them from a rise: the sledge has stopped._  

#### `a12-04-chase-done`

_The driver stands up. The fur and the cap are all snow, and the driver is a lady, tall and slender and glittering white._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): word meaning from context  
> _“Tall and slender.” Which word means about the same as slender?_  
> - ✅ Thin and graceful → Yes. Slender means slim, in a graceful way.
> - Short and round → That’s nearly the opposite! Slender means thin and graceful.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of a describing word from the sentence._

_It’s the woman from the window. It’s the Snow Queen._  

#### `a12-04-kiss`

**The Snow Queen**: We’ve come a long way. But you’re shivering. Creep in under my bearskin.  
_She sits Kay beside her and wraps the fur round him. He looks as if he’s sinking into a snowdrift._  
**The Snow Queen**: Are you still cold?  
_She touches his forehead with a kiss colder than ice. It goes straight to his heart, which is nearly ice already._  
_After that he doesn’t feel the cold at all._  
**Kay**: My sledge! Don’t forget my sledge.  
_It’s tied to one of the white hens that fly behind her. She touches his forehead once more, and you watch him forget._  
_Gerda, Grandmother, the roses, the attic: you see them go out of his face like lamps going out down a street._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _“Like lamps going out down a street.” What does this simile show about Kay’s memories?_  
> - ✅ They go dark one by one → Yes. Not all at once: one, then the next, then the next, until the street is dark.
> - He is turning the lamps off → He isn’t doing it himself. His memories are fading, one by one, like lamps going out.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a simile about memories fading._

_Then the sledge rises over the forest. The wolves howl, and the moon comes out huge and white._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): feeling helpless  
> _Watching something bad and not being able to stop it is one of the hardest feelings. It isn’t your fault that you can’t reach him._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about the feeling of helplessness and that it is not anyone’s fault._


**Choices**

- **Call his name, as loud as you can.**
    - You shout his name. The wind takes it the other way, back towards the town, as if it means to deliver it to Gerda.
- **Stand and watch until they’re gone.**
    - You watch until the sledge is a speck, and then a star, and then nothing.

#### `a12-04-kiss-done`

_You walk back in the dark._  
_The town gate is still open, and nobody has noticed anything at all._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): telling a trusted grown-up  
> _You saw what happened, and nobody else did. What’s the most important thing to do now?_  
> - ✅ Tell someone who can help → Yes. When you see something worrying, tell a grown-up you trust, straight away.
> - Keep it a secret → Some secrets are too heavy to carry alone. Tell someone you trust.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about telling a trusted adult when something worrying happens._


#### `a12-04-complete`

_Gerda is waiting at the top of the stairs. You tell her everything: the white sledge, the lady, the cord._  
**Gerda**: Then he isn’t lost. He’s been taken. That’s different.  
_By the end of the week the town says Kay fell in the river by the school. People are very sure about it._  
**Gerda**: He didn’t. He hates getting wet. He’d never go near it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): rumour and evidence  
> _The town is “very sure”, but nobody saw Kay fall in the river, and you saw the sledge. Whose story would you trust?_  
> - The person who saw it → That’s a careful answer. Being sure isn’t the same as having seen it.
> - Whatever most people say → Lots of people saying it can feel convincing. Ask: did any of them see it?
> - Nobody, until there’s more to go on → A very careful answer. Sometimes waiting for more facts is the wise thing.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between rumour and what someone actually saw._

_Grandmother cries quietly for a long winter. Gerda doesn’t, which is worse._  

### Glossary

- **friction**: A force that slows things down when they rub or slide against each other.
- **slender**: Thin in a graceful way.

## A12-5. The Red Shoes

- `a12-05-s1`: Sit with Gerda through the long winter. · _Find Gerda on her stool by the gutter._
- `a12-05-s2`: Go down to the river with Gerda at dawn. · _Walk with Gerda out of the town to where the boats lie in the rushes._
- `a12-05-s3`: Jump into the boat after Gerda. · _Take a run along the bank and jump!_

#### `a12-05-winter`

_It’s a long, dark winter. Everybody in the town has stopped saying Kay’s name, except Gerda._  
**Gerda**: They say he’s dead. They say it to Gran in the shop, as if that’s helping.  
_Dead would mean his body had stopped working, for ever. But nobody saw that happen, and Gerda doesn’t believe it._  
_Then spring comes. The sun comes out over the roofs, warm on the gutter for the first time since the sledges._  
_The swallows come back from their winter far away, and sit on the gutter, chattering._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): birds that migrate  
> _Swallows migrate. Each autumn they fly thousands of kilometres south to Africa, where there are insects to eat, and come back in spring._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that swallows migrate south for the winter and return in spring._

**Gerda**: I don’t believe it. Kay isn’t dead. He’s somewhere.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): hope  
> _Everyone else has given up. Why do you think Gerda keeps hoping?_  
> - Because she loves him → That’s a lovely answer. Love can keep hope going when everyone else stops.
> - Because she saw no proof → That’s a sharp answer. Nobody actually saw anything happen to him.
> - Because she’s stubborn → Maybe! Grandmother said the one who fetches you is too stubborn to stop.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone might keep hoping when others give up._


**Choices**

- **“Nor do I.”**
    - **You**: Nor do I.
    - **Gerda**: Good. That’s three of us, and the swallows.
- **Remind her what you saw: the sledge went north.**
    - **Gerda**: North. Then I’ll go north. I’ll start by asking the river, in case.
- **Sit with her and say nothing.**
    - You sit together a long time. A swallow lands on the box between you and looks from one of you to the other.

#### `a12-05-winter-done`

**Gerda**: I’m going to give the river my red shoes. Kay never saw them. They’re the best thing I’ve got.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character motive  
> _Why does Gerda choose her red shoes, and not something else?_  
> - ✅ They are the most precious thing she owns → Yes. She offers her very best, to show how much she means it.
> - She doesn’t like them → She calls them the best thing she’s got. Giving them up is a real sacrifice.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a character gives up something precious._


#### `a12-05-river`

_Early in the morning Gerda puts on her new red shoes. She kisses Grandmother, who is still asleep, and goes out._  
_You go with her, out of the gate and down to the river, with your Nubbin under your arm._  
**Gerda**: River? Is it true you took my friend? I’ll give you my red shoes if you give him back.  
_The little waves nod at her, oddly, as if they understand._  
_She throws the shoes in. They don’t go far, and the waves carry them straight back to her feet._  
**Gerda**: I didn’t throw them far enough. The river can’t take them unless they go right out in the middle.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): how water moves near the bank  
> _Why do the shoes come straight back to the bank?_  
> - ✅ Little waves push floating things towards the shore → Yes. Near the edge, ripples wash floating things back in. Out in the middle, the current carries them away.
> - Shoes can’t float → These ones float. It’s the little waves at the edge that push them back to shore.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that waves near a bank push floating things ashore, while the current in the middle carries them off._

_There’s a boat among the rushes. Before you can say anything she climbs in and goes to the far end._  

**Choices**

- **Stay on the bank. It’s her offering.**
    - You stay on the bank. It’s hers to give, and she gives it.
- **Tell her to be careful.**
    - **Gerda**: I am being careful. I’m being careful and quick.

#### `a12-05-river-done`

_She throws the shoes from the end of the boat. The boat isn’t tied, and it slides out of the rushes, and keeps going._  
**Gerda**: Oh!  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): water safety  
> _In real life, what should you always have before getting into a boat?_  
> - ✅ A grown-up with you, and a life jacket on → Yes. Boats are fun with a grown-up and a life jacket. Never climb into one alone.
> - A snack → Snacks are nice! But the important things are a grown-up and a life jacket.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about staying safe near water and boats._


#### `a12-05-boat`

_The boat is a yard out already, and gliding. Gerda scrambles to the near end, but there’s only water between her and the bank._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, notice): units of length  
> _A yard is an old measure, a little less than a metre: about 91 centimetres. A big stride, or one jump._  
> _For grown-ups: Compared an old unit of length, the yard, with the metre._

_Your Nubbin jumps first. You don’t think about it at all; you jump after it._  
_You land in the bottom of the boat in a heap. Gerda grabs your coat with both hands, and doesn’t let go for a while._  
**Gerda**: You came. You didn’t have to come.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): showing up for a friend  
> _Nobody asked you to jump. Sometimes friendship means just being there when it matters._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what it means to show up for a friend._

_The sparrows fly along the bank beside you, as if to say they’d have come too, if they were bigger._  
_The red shoes float along behind the boat. They can’t catch up, and the boat can’t stop._  
**Gerda**: Maybe the river’s taking me to Kay. Maybe that’s its answer.  

**Choices**

- **Look for an oar.**
    - There’s no oar: only a bailing can, a bit of rope and a very old apple. Your Nubbin eats the apple.
- **Reach for the red shoes.**
    - You stretch over the side. Your fingers brush one shoe, and then the current takes it, as if the river has said yes.
- **Sit back and let it take you.**
    - You sit back. Gerda sits beside you in her stockings, and watches the banks go by.

#### `a12-05-boat-done`

_The banks are lovely: flowers, old trees, sheep and cows on the slopes. There isn’t a single person anywhere._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-2, ask): rivers flow downhill  
> _The boat drifts downstream all on its own. Which way does a river always flow?_  
> - ✅ Downhill, towards a lake or the sea → Yes. Water runs downhill, so every river flows down towards a lake or the sea.
> - Whichever way the wind blows → Wind makes ripples, but the river itself runs downhill, towards a lake or the sea.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rivers flow downhill towards lakes and seas._


#### `a12-05-complete`

_All day the boat goes downstream, about three kilometres every hour, for eight hours. Gerda sings a little, and your Nubbin hums along._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Three kilometres every hour, for eight hours. How far has the boat drifted?_  
> - ✅ 24 kilometres → Yes. Eight lots of three is twenty-four kilometres. A long way from home.
> - 11 kilometres → That’s three plus eight. It’s three kilometres for each of eight hours: three times eight, twenty-four.
> - 38 kilometres → A little too far. Three times eight is twenty-four kilometres.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a distance problem by multiplying speed by time._

_Then you come to a cherry orchard, and a little house with odd red and blue windows and a thatched roof._  
_Outside stand two wooden soldiers, presenting arms as the boat goes by._  
**Gerda**: Hello! Hello! Can you help us?  
_The soldiers don’t answer, being wooden. But somebody else does._  

### Glossary

- **migrate**: To travel a long way to another place when the seasons change.
- **current**: The steady flow of water in one direction, as in a river.

## A12-6. The Garden That Forgets

- `a12-06-s1`: Meet the old woman of the cherry house. · _Let her pull the boat in with her stick, then go inside._
- `a12-06-s2`: Spend the summer in the old woman’s garden. · _Explore the flower beds, and follow your Nubbin._
- `a12-06-s3`: Ask the flowers if they know where Kay is. · _Talk to the roses, then to the other flowers in turn._

#### `a12-06-cherries`

_A very old woman comes out of the house, leaning on a crooked stick. She wears a big sun hat painted with lovely flowers._  
**The Old Woman**: You poor little thing. However did you get out on this big wide river?  
_She hooks the boat with her stick and draws it in to the bank. She’s strong, for somebody so old._  
_She takes you both inside and gives you cherries, as many as you like. Gerda tells her everything._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): fruit holds seeds  
> _Every cherry has a hard stone in the middle. Inside the stone is a seed, which could grow into a whole new cherry tree._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fruit holds the seed of a new plant._

**The Old Woman**: Kay? Hm. He hasn’t come by. He will, I expect. Don’t be sad. Eat your cherries.  
_While Gerda eats, the old woman combs her hair with a golden comb. With every stroke Gerda looks a little less worried._  
_The old woman isn’t wicked. She knows a little magic, for her own amusement, and she has always wanted a little girl._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): kindness and letting go  
> _The old woman is kind, and lonely. Is it kind to keep someone with you if they need to be somewhere else?_  
> - No, kind means letting them go → That’s a thoughtful answer. Caring for someone means caring about what they need, too.
> - Yes, if you look after them well → Fair: she does look after Gerda well. But Gerda has somewhere she needs to be.
> - It depends → A wise answer. It depends on what the other person wants and needs.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether keeping someone close is always kind._

_You feel drowsy too, and the cherries are very good. It’s hard to remember what you were in such a hurry about._  

**Choices**

- **Have another cherry.**
    - You have another. It’s the best cherry you’ve ever eaten, and you can’t remember the second best.
- **Ask her the way north.**
    - **The Old Woman**: North? Nobody goes north from here. Have a cherry.
    - You have a cherry. You forget the question halfway through it.
- **Give a cherry to your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin takes the cherry and doesn’t eat it. It tucks it in your pocket, for later, and keeps one eye on the comb.

#### `a12-06-cherries-done`

_While you doze by the stove, the old woman goes out into the garden. She points her stick at every rose bush in turn._  
_One by one they sink into the black earth, and the earth closes over them as if they had never been._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): plants need light  
> _A real rose bush buried in the dark couldn’t last long. Green leaves need sunlight to make the plant’s food._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plants need sunlight on their leaves to make food._


#### `a12-06-garden`

_The garden has every flower you can think of, from every season, all in bloom at once. It never seems to change._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-1, ask): flowers bloom in their own seasons  
> _Snowdrops, daffodils and summer roses all in flower at once. Why is that a clue that this garden is magic?_  
> - ✅ In real life they flower in different seasons → Yes. Snowdrops come in late winter, daffodils in spring, roses in summer. Never all together.
> - Flowers never grow in gardens → They do! But each kind flowers in its own season, so all at once is the magic.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that different flowers bloom in different seasons._

_Gerda plays there all day, and sleeps in a bed with silk pillows stuffed with violets. She has stopped asking about Kay._  
_You can’t remember what day it is. You can’t remember if there have been days._  
_Your Nubbin keeps going back to one bare patch of earth by the wall, and digging, and looking at you._  
_One afternoon the old woman sits in the sun with her painted hat beside her on the bench._  
_Gerda looks at the hat. The best flower painted on it is a rose; the old woman forgot to wipe it off._  
**Gerda**: Roses. Where are the roses? There aren’t any roses here.  
_She runs from bed to bed, searching and searching. There isn’t one, anywhere._  

**Choices**

- **Show her where your Nubbin has been digging.**
    - You take her to the bare patch. Your Nubbin sits beside it, very upright, as if it has waited all summer to be asked.
- **Search with her.**
    - You search the whole garden with her, bed by bed. At the end, by the wall, your Nubbin is sitting on a bare patch.

#### `a12-06-garden-done`

_Gerda sits down by the bare patch and cries. Her warm tears fall on the earth, right where a rose bush sank._  
_The bush comes up all at once, in full flower, as fresh as the day it went down._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.K.3, ask): turning points in a story  
> _Until now Gerda had forgotten Kay. What brought her memory back?_  
> - ✅ Seeing the rose painted on the hat → Yes. One small reminder of home, and everything came back.
> - Eating cherries → The cherries made her forget! It was the painted rose that reminded her.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the event that changes the story’s direction._


#### `a12-06-flowers`

**Gerda**: Oh, I’ve been so long! I was going to find Kay! Do you know where he is? Is he dead?  
**The Roses**: He isn’t dead. We’ve been down in the earth all this time, and he wasn’t there.  
**Gerda**: Thank you. Oh, thank you!  
_Then Gerda goes to the other flowers, one after another, and asks each of them about Kay._  
_Every flower is dreaming its own story in the sun. Not one of them knows a thing about Kay._  
**The Bindweed**: There’s a castle with a balcony, and a girl leaning on it, waiting for someone. That is my story.  
**Gerda**: Is it Kay she’s waiting for?  
**The Bindweed**: It’s my story. It isn’t about anybody else.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): listening to others  
> _Gerda asks for help, and each flower only talks about its own story. What would a good listener do?_  
> - ✅ Listen to her question, then answer it → Yes. Good listeners hear what the other person needs before they talk about themselves.
> - Tell a longer story → That’s what the flowers do, and it doesn’t help Gerda. Listening comes first.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes someone a good listener._


**Choices**

- **Ask the snowdrop.**
    - **The Snowdrop**: Two girls on a swing between two trees, blowing soap bubbles. Every bubble is a whole world. Then it bursts.
    - **Gerda**: That’s a lovely story. It isn’t any help at all.
- **Ask the buttercup.**
    - **The Buttercup**: An old granny in a sunny yard, and her granddaughter comes home to see her. That’s all. It’s enough.
    - **Gerda**: Poor Gran. She’s at home without either of us.
- **Ask the narcissus.**
    - **The Narcissus**: I can see myself! I can see myself! Oh, how lovely I smell.
    - **Gerda**: That isn’t about Kay. That isn’t about anybody.

#### `a12-06-flowers-done`

**Gerda**: It’s no good. They only know their own stories.  
**Gerda**: I have to go. I’ve stayed far too long already.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): choosing what matters  
> _Gerda leaves a beautiful garden where she was happy. Was that hard, do you think, and why does she go?_  
> - Hard, but Kay matters more → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes we leave a nice thing for a more important one.
> - Easy, once she remembered → Maybe. Remembering what matters can make a hard choice feel simple.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about leaving something pleasant for something important._


#### `a12-06-complete`

_Gerda runs to the end of the garden. The gate is shut, the latch is rusty, and it won’t give._  
_You put your shoulder to it with her, and your Nubbin pushes too, and the gate creaks open._  
_Outside, it’s late autumn. The leaves are yellow and falling, and the mist is cold and wet._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-2, ask): why trees drop their leaves  
> _In autumn the days get shorter and colder. Why do many trees let their leaves fall?_  
> - ✅ To rest through winter, when there’s less light → Yes. With little sunlight and frozen water, leaves can’t do their job, so the tree rests till spring.
> - Because the wind pulls them all off → Wind helps them fall, but the tree lets go first, to rest through the dark winter.
> _For grown-ups: Learned why many trees drop their leaves in autumn._

**Gerda**: How long have I been? In there it was always summer.  
_Nobody comes after you. You look back once, and the garden is still in summer, as if nothing ever happens there._  
_Gerda’s feet are bare and sore. She keeps walking anyway, and you keep walking with her._  

### Glossary

- **drowsy**: Sleepy, as if you might drift off at any moment.
- **bloom**: When a plant has its flowers open.

## A12-7. The Raven

- `a12-07-s1`: Meet the raven in the snow. · _Rest by the hedge where the big black bird is hopping._
- `a12-07-s2`: Hear about the boy with the creaking boots. · _Sit by the hedge and let the raven tell it._
- `a12-07-s3`: Wait by the palace garden after dark. · _Wait in the avenue until the palace lights go out._

#### `a12-07-hedge`

_Winter comes on fast. You stop to rest by a hedge, and a big black raven hops across the snow towards you._  
**The Raven**: Caw! Good day. Good day! And where are you two going, out in the wide world all on your own?  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): ravens are clever birds  
> _Real ravens are among the cleverest birds. They solve puzzles, remember faces, and can copy sounds, even a few words._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned some real facts about how clever ravens are._

_Gerda tells him the whole story, and asks if he has seen Kay. The raven nods, very seriously._  
**The Raven**: It might be. It might be!  
**Gerda**: Really? Is he alive?  
**The Raven**: Gently, gently. I think it may be Kay. But I think he’s forgotten you, for the princess.  
**The Raven**: In this kingdom there lives a princess who is tremendously clever. She’s read every newspaper in the world.  
**The Raven**: And forgotten them all again. That’s how clever she is.  

**Choices**

- **Ask him, politely, to go on.**
    - **The Raven**: Politely! There’s a rare thing. I shall go on at once.
- **Ask how a raven knows all this.**
    - **The Raven**: I have a sweetheart at the palace. She’s tame. She tells me everything, and I tell everybody.
- **Let your Nubbin say hello.**
    - Your Nubbin bows to the raven. The raven bows back, lower, so as not to be outdone.

#### `a12-07-hedge-done`

**The Raven**: She wanted to marry. But she wanted a husband who could answer when he was spoken to.  
**The Raven**: Not one who just stood about looking grand.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): good conversation  
> _The princess wants someone who can really talk with her. What makes a good conversation?_  
> - ✅ Taking turns to listen and to speak → Exactly. Back and forth, like two birds on a branch.
> - One person talking the whole time → That’s a speech, not a conversation. You take turns.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about taking turns in a conversation._


#### `a12-07-boots`

**The Raven**: So they put it in the papers. Any good-looking young man could come and talk to her, and the best talker would marry her.  
**The Raven**: Such crowds! But they saw the guards in silver, and the footmen in gold on the stairs, and they went dumb.  
**The Raven**: On the third day along came a little fellow, no horse, no carriage, marching straight up to the palace.  
**The Raven**: His eyes shone like yours. He had lovely long hair, and very shabby clothes.  
**Gerda**: That was Kay! Oh, I’ve found him!  
**The Raven**: He had a little knapsack on his back.  
**Gerda**: No, that was his sledge. He had his sledge with him.  
**The Raven**: Very likely. But his boots creaked terribly, all over the hall, and he wasn’t the least bit afraid.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): vibrations make sound  
> _New leather boots creak because the stiff leather rubs and bends. That makes it vibrate, and vibrations are what we hear as sound._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sounds are made by vibrations._

**The Raven**: He said he’d only come to hear how clever she was. And he liked her, and she liked him.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): weighing evidence  
> _Gerda hears “knapsack” and turns it into “sledge”. Is the raven’s story enough to be sure it’s Kay?_  
> - Not yet; it could be any boy → That’s careful thinking. Shining eyes and creaky boots fit lots of boys.
> - Yes, it sounds just like him → Fair: it does sound like him. But notice how Gerda changes the bits that don’t fit.
> - She wants it to be Kay so much → A sharp answer. When we want something badly, we hear what we hope for.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how wanting something can change how we hear the evidence._


**Choices**

- **It must be Kay.**
    - **Gerda**: It must be. He was always clever. He could do sums in his head, even fractions.
- **Plenty of boys have long hair and creaky boots.**
    - **Gerda**: Not plenty. Not like Kay’s.
    - **The Raven**: She has a point. I’ve never met another pair that creaked like that.

#### `a12-07-boots-done`

**Gerda**: Please, can you get us in? I have to see him.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): asking for help  
> _Gerda can’t get in on her own, so she asks, clearly and politely. Asking for help is a strength, not a weakness._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about asking for help clearly and politely._

**The Raven**: I’ll speak to my sweetheart. Wait here.  

#### `a12-07-avenue`

_At dusk the raven comes back with a little bread roll from the palace kitchen, and gives it to Gerda._  
**The Raven**: My sweetheart sends her regards. You can’t go in by the front, of course. Guards in silver. Footmen in gold.  
**The Raven**: But don’t cry. My sweetheart knows a little back staircase up to the bedroom, and she knows where the key is kept.  
_You go into the palace garden, along the great avenue. The leaves are falling, one at a time._  
_In the palace the lights go out one by one. The raven leads you to a back door, standing just ajar._  
_Gerda’s heart is beating so hard you can hear it. Your own isn’t much quieter._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): what nerves do to your body  
> _When you’re nervous or excited, your heart beats faster and you breathe quicker: your body is getting ready. Slow breaths help it settle._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why the heart beats faster when we are nervous, and that slow breathing helps._


**Choices**

- **Go in first.**
    - You go in first, just in case. The back stairs smell of soap and toast.
- **Take Gerda’s hand.**
    - You take her hand. It’s shaking, and then it isn’t.

#### `a12-07-avenue-done`

_At the top of the stairs a little lamp burns on a cupboard. Beside it stands the tame raven, turning her head this way and that._  
**The Palace Raven**: My intended has told me so much about you, little miss.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): word meaning from context  
> _The palace raven calls the forest raven “my intended”. What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ The one she’s going to marry → Precisely. We are engaged. It is all very proper.
> - Someone she meant to bump into → Certainly not! My intended is the one I intend to marry.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out an old-fashioned word from its sentence._


#### `a12-07-complete`

**The Palace Raven**: Your story is very touching. Take the lamp, would you, and I’ll lead the way.  
_Things rush past you on the walls: shadows of horses with flying manes, of huntsmen, of ladies riding._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): moving light, moving shadows  
> _As you carry the lamp along, the shadows on the walls race past. Why do shadows move when the lamp moves?_  
> - ✅ The light hits things from a new angle → Yes. Move the light and every shadow swings round to the other side.
> - Shadows can walk by themselves → Only dream ones! Real shadows move because the light moves.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shadows move when the light source moves._

**The Palace Raven**: Only dreams. They come to fetch the gentlefolk’s thoughts out hunting. All the better: you can look at them asleep.  
_Your Nubbin ducks under a dream horse, just in case._  

### Glossary

- **shabby**: Old and worn, with signs of a lot of use.
- **ajar**: Open just a little.

## A12-8. Not Kay

- `a12-08-s1`: Climb the back stairs through the palace halls. · _Follow the tame raven, and keep the lamp low._
