- `a12-08-s2`: Wait while Gerda looks in the red bed. · _Keep the light steady while she bends back a red petal._
- `a12-08-s3`: See what the prince and princess give Gerda. · _In the morning, help Gerda ask for what she needs._

#### `a12-08-halls`

_You go from hall to hall, each grander than the last. The walls are rose-coloured satin, with silk flowers sewn on._  
_The dreams keep rushing past, so fast that you can’t make out whose they are._  
**The Palace Raven**: Wipe your feet. Not you, the little one. Well, all of you.  
_Then the bedroom. The ceiling is a great palm tree with leaves of glass, and from it hang two beds, each like a lily._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): materials and their properties  
> _Satin walls, glass leaves. Which word describes glass, but not satin?_  
> - ✅ Hard and see-through → Yes. Glass is hard and lets light through. Satin is soft, smooth cloth.
> - Soft and bendy → That’s satin! Glass is hard and see-through.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two materials by their properties._

_One bed is white, and the princess is asleep in it. The other bed is red._  
**Gerda**: Kay will be in the red one.  

**Choices**

- **Hold the lamp up for her.**
    - You hold the lamp up. It shakes a little in your hand, and you make it stop.
- **Stay back by the door with the raven.**
    - You stay by the door, because this bit is Gerda’s. The tame raven approves of your manners.

#### `a12-08-halls-done`

_Gerda tiptoes to the red bed._  
_Her hands are shaking, and she is smiling._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): mixed feelings  
> _Shaking and smiling at once: you can feel scared and hopeful at the same time. Mixed feelings are normal._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we can feel more than one feeling at the same time._


#### `a12-08-redbed`

_Gerda bends back one of the red petals. Underneath is a brown neck, and dark hair on the pillow._  
**Gerda**: Kay!  
_She says his name aloud and holds the lamp close. The dreams come galloping back into the room._  
_He wakes up. He turns his head._  
_It isn’t Kay. The prince has a neck like Kay’s, and that is all._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): words for feelings  
> _Gerda was so sure, and it isn’t him. Which word fits her feeling best?_  
> - ✅ Disappointed → Yes. Disappointed is when something you hoped for doesn’t happen. It can hurt a lot.
> - Bored → Not bored! She hoped so hard. The word is disappointed.
> _For grown-ups: Named the feeling of disappointment._

_He’s young and handsome and very surprised, and he isn’t Kay at all._  
_The princess peeps out of her white lily and asks what in the world is going on._  
_Gerda cries, and tells them the whole story, and everything the ravens have done for her._  

**Choices**

- **Say it’s all your fault, really.**
    - **The Princess**: Is it? It doesn’t sound like it. It sounds like the ravens’ fault, and quite a nice fault.
- **Put in a word for the ravens.**
    - You tell them the ravens only meant to help. The tame raven, in the doorway, fluffs up with pride.
- **Hold the lamp and let Gerda tell it.**
    - You hold the lamp and say nothing. Gerda tells it well, all of it, right from the troll’s mirror.

#### `a12-08-redbed-done`

**The Prince**: You poor child. You poor little thing.  
**The Princess**: Nobody’s angry. Though the ravens mustn’t make a habit of it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): responding to honest mistakes  
> _Strangers crept into their bedroom at night, and the prince and princess are kind about it. Why, do you think?_  
> - They can see it was an honest mistake → That’s a fair answer. Mistakes made out of love are easy to forgive.
> - They’re just kind people → Maybe so. Kindness is often a choice people make again and again.
> - They feel sorry for Gerda → Yes, they can see how far she’s come. That’s empathy.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people forgive honest mistakes._


#### `a12-08-gifts`

**The Princess**: Ravens, would you like to fly away free? Or have a post at court, with all the kitchen scraps you can eat?  
_Both ravens bow, and ask for the post. They are thinking of their old age._  
**The Raven**: A bird must think ahead.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): choices have costs  
> _Freedom, or a safe job with food for life: you can’t have both. Which would you pick, if you were a raven?_  
> - Freedom → A wild choice. Brave. Cold in winter, mind.
> - The safe job → A sensible choice, and mine. Scraps are scraps.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about choosing between two good things when you can’t have both._

_The prince lets Gerda sleep in his bed. She folds her hands and thinks how kind people and animals are._  
_In the morning she is dressed in silk and velvet from head to foot, and asked to stay at the palace and be happy._  
**Gerda**: Thank you. But please, could I have a little carriage and a horse, and some boots? I have to find Kay.  
**The Prince**: Boots. And a muff, for the cold. And not a little carriage. A proper one.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): why fur keeps you warm  
> _A fur muff traps lots of still air between its hairs. Still air holds heat in, so hands inside stay warm._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fur keeps things warm by trapping air._


**Choices**

- **Put your Nubbin in the muff.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs into the muff and turns round twice. Gerda puts her hands in after it.
    - **Gerda**: Oh, it’s warm! It’s like holding a little stove.
- **Check that the boots fit.**
    - You kneel and press the toes: room to grow, room for socks. While you’re busy, your Nubbin climbs into the muff.

#### `a12-08-gifts-done`

_The coach is pure gold. The prince’s and princess’s coat of arms shines on the door like a star._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): coats of arms  
> _Long ago, noble families had a coat of arms: a special picture on a shield, so everyone knew whose coach or castle it was._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a coat of arms was for in the past._


#### `a12-08-complete`

_The coach is lined with sugar plums, and there’s fruit and gingerbread on the seat. Footmen ride behind in golden crowns._  
_The raven rides along for the first few miles, sitting beside Gerda, because he can’t ride backwards._  
_Gerda counts twelve sugar plums, and shares them out fairly between herself, you and the raven._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): sharing equally (division)  
> _Twelve sugar plums, shared fairly between three. How many does each get?_  
> - ✅ 4 each → Four each. Three fours are twelve. Fair and square.
> - 3 each → Three each is only nine. There are three left over! Four each makes twelve.
> - 6 each → Six each would need eighteen. Twelve shared by three is four.
> _For grown-ups: Shared twelve things equally between three._

_His sweetheart stays in the palace doorway, flapping. She has had a headache since her promotion, from eating too much._  
**Gerda**: Goodbye! Goodbye!  
_The raven flies up into a tree, and flaps his black wings for as long as he can see the coach shining._  
_Gerda keeps her hands in the muff the whole way, and your Nubbin keeps them warm._  

### Glossary

- **satin**: A smooth, shiny cloth.
- **coat of arms**: A special picture on a shield that stands for a family.

## A12-9. The Robber Girl

- `a12-09-s1`: Ride the golden coach through the dark forest. · _Keep your head down when the coach stops._
- `a12-09-s2`: Go into the robbers’ castle. · _Follow the robber girl in, past the dogs._
- `a12-09-s3`: Answer the robber girl. She wants your Nubbin. · _Choose what to say. Either answer is honest._

#### `a12-09-forest`

_The road goes into a dark forest. The golden coach shines among the trees like a torch, and it shines too far._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): shiny things reflect light  
> _Gold is shiny because it reflects light so well. Even a little lantern light bounces off it, and can be seen a long way off._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shiny materials reflect light and can be seen from far away._

_Robbers come out of the dark, shouting “Gold! It’s gold!”, and grab the horses._  
_The coachman and the footmen jump down and run for the trees, crowns and all. Nobody stops them; nobody wants footmen._  
_An old robber woman peers in through the door. Then a girl shoves her out of the way._  
**The Robber Girl**: She’s mine. She can play with me. She can give me her muff and her pretty dress, and sleep in my bed.  
_The robber girl is Gerda’s size, broader in the shoulders, with black eyes that look almost sad._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): inferring feelings  
> _Her eyes “look almost sad”. What might that tell you about the robber girl?_  
> - She might be lonely → That’s a thoughtful guess. She grabs Gerda as a playmate, as if she hasn’t got one.
> - She’s just tired → Could be. Keep watching her and see if you change your mind.
> - Nothing at all → Maybe. But writers often hide clues in eyes, so keep an eye on hers.
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference about a character from a small detail._

**The Robber Girl**: Nobody touches her while I like her. Are you a princess?  
**Gerda**: No.  
_Gerda tells her everything, there in the dark coach. The robber girl pushes her hands into the muff to warm them._  
**The Robber Girl**: What’s this? It’s alive. It’s warm. Oh.  

**Choices**

- **Tell her it’s your Nubbin.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: A Nubbin. Never heard of one. I like it.
- **Let Gerda explain.**
    - **Gerda**: It’s the lodger’s. It’s kept my hands warm all the way from the palace.
    - **The Robber Girl**: Has it, now.

#### `a12-09-forest-done`

_The robber girl keeps one hand in the muff the whole way, and won’t take it out._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): warm-blooded animals  
> _Mammals and birds make their own body heat, so they stay warm even in a cold forest. That’s why a small animal feels warm in your hands._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mammals and birds make their own body heat._


#### `a12-09-castle`

_The coach stops in the yard of a robbers’ castle, cracked from top to bottom. Ravens and crows fly out of every hole._  
_Huge dogs leap up at you. They don’t bark; they aren’t allowed._  
_In the great hall a fire burns on the stone floor. Soup bubbles in a big pot, and the smoke goes where it likes._  
**The Robber Girl**: You’ll sleep with me and all my animals tonight.  
_In her corner there’s straw and old rugs. Above it, on rails and perches, sit about a hundred pigeons, asleep._  
**The Robber Girl**: All mine. Those two are wood pigeons; they’d fly off if they weren’t tied. And here’s my dear old Bae.  
_She tugs a reindeer forward by his antler. He has a bright copper ring round his neck, tied to the wall._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): reindeer antlers  
> _Reindeer are the only deer where females grow antlers as well as males. Antlers fall off and grow back every year._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that both male and female reindeer grow antlers, which regrow every year._

**The Robber Girl**: He’d run off too, if he could. Everybody would. That’s why you tie things.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): fairness to animals  
> _“That’s why you tie things,” she says. Is that fair to Bae, do you think?_  
> - No. Animals need freedom too → That’s a kind answer. Bae’s rubbed neck shows how long he’s been tied.
> - She’s scared of being left alone → A sharp answer. Maybe she ties things because nobody has ever stayed.
> - It’s her reindeer, so it’s fine → Hmm. Owning an animal means looking after what it needs, too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness to animals and why someone might hold on too tight._

_She pulls a long knife out of a crack in the wall and waves it about, mostly at the ceiling._  
**Gerda**: Do you sleep with the knife?  
**The Robber Girl**: Always. You never know what might happen.  

**Choices**

- **Ask her to put the knife away.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: No.
    - But she sticks it back in the wall, within reach, which for her is a kind of yes.
- **Stroke Bae’s nose.**
    - Bae lowers his head and lets you. His nose is soft and his eyes are tired.

#### `a12-09-castle-done`

**The Robber Girl**: Now tell me about Kay again. The lodger can listen. And the warm thing stays where I can see it.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): knives are for grown-ups  
> _In real life, knives are tools for grown-ups, never toys. If you find one, leave it and tell an adult._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about leaving knives alone and telling an adult._


#### `a12-09-keep`

_She holds out both hands, the way she held them out to the muff._  
**The Robber Girl**: I want that one. It’s warm. I’ll keep it with the pigeons and the reindeer. It’s mine now.  
**Gerda**: It isn’t yours. It isn’t mine either.  
**The Robber Girl**: I didn’t ask you.  
_Your Nubbin looks at you, not frightened. It looks as if it’s waiting to see what sort of person you are._  
_The robber girl’s hands are still out. They’re chapped, and there’s a scar across one knuckle._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): boundaries and trust  
> _Saying “no” kindly sets a boundary; saying “one night” gives trust, and neither is wrong. What matters most when you answer?_  
> - Being honest about what I want → That’s a strong answer. An honest no and an honest yes are both kind.
> - Thinking about my Nubbin → A caring answer. Your Nubbin isn’t a thing; it’s a friend, and it trusts you.
> - Thinking about the robber girl → A generous answer: she’s lonely. But your answer still has to be true for you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about saying no, and about trust, before making a choice._


**Choices**

- **“No.” Plainly, and kindly.**
    - **You**: No.
    - **The Robber Girl**: No?
    - **You**: No. It isn’t a thing you keep. It stays with me.
    - She stares at you a long time. Then she shrugs, as if she meant to lose.
    - **The Robber Girl**: Fine. Keep your warm thing.
- **“You can hold it for one night.”**
    - **You**: You can hold it tonight. In the morning it comes back to me.
    - **The Robber Girl**: One night?
    - She takes your Nubbin in both hands, very carefully, as if it might break or might bite.
    - **The Robber Girl**: One night. Fine.
    - Your Nubbin settles against her shoulder and goes straight to sleep. She looks at it as if nobody has ever done that before.

#### `a12-09-keep-done`

_The robber girl falls asleep with one arm round Gerda’s neck, and snores._  
_Gerda lies awake and stares at the pigeons. You lie awake and stare at Gerda._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, do): calming down with slow breaths  
> _When worry keeps you awake, try this with Gerda: breathe in slowly for four, and out slowly for four. Do it four times._  
> Check: `edu:breathe:slow:4`
> _For grown-ups: Practised slow breathing to calm worry._


#### `a12-09-complete`

_By the fire the robbers sing and drink. The old robber woman turns a somersault, badly._  
_Bae stands in the dark with his copper ring on, looking at the door._  
_The pigeons shuffle on their ten rails and murmur, about ten to a rail. One of them opens an eye._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Ten rails, about ten pigeons on each. About how many pigeons is that?_  
> - ✅ About 100 → Yes. Ten groups of ten is a hundred, the same hundred you saw asleep on the perches.
> - About 20 → Twenty is ten plus ten. Ten groups of ten is ten times ten: a hundred.
> - About 1,000 → Too many! Ten times ten is a hundred.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups to estimate a total._

_Nobody in the corner is asleep except the robber girl, and she sleeps like somebody who has won._  

### Glossary

- **antler**: A branching bone that grows on a deer’s head and falls off each year.
- **boundary**: A line you draw about what is and isn’t all right for you.

## A12-10. The Reindeer

- `a12-10-s1`: Listen to the wood pigeons in the night. · _Lie still in the straw and listen._
- `a12-10-s2`: In the morning, ask Bae the way north. · _Talk to Bae while the robber girl listens._
- `a12-10-s3`: Go with Gerda and Bae. · _Help tie Gerda onto Bae’s back, then climb on behind her._

#### `a12-10-pigeons`

**The Wood Pigeons**: Coo, coo. We have seen little Kay.  
**Gerda**: What? What did you say?  
**The Wood Pigeons**: A white hen was carrying his sledge. He was sitting in the Snow Queen’s carriage.  
**The Wood Pigeons**: It went low over the forest while we were in our nest. She breathed on us as she passed, and we were cold for a long time after.  
**Gerda**: Where was she going? Do you know?  
**The Wood Pigeons**: North, we think. To Lapland, where there’s always snow and ice. Ask the reindeer; he’s tied up just there.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-2, ask): compass directions on a map  
> _The carriage went north. On most maps, which way is north?_  
> - ✅ Towards the top → Yes. North is at the top of most maps, south at the bottom, east on the right, west on the left.
> - Towards the bottom → That’s south. North is at the top of most maps.
> _For grown-ups: Found north on a map._

**Bae**: Snow and ice! It’s glorious there. You can leap about free in great glittering valleys.  
**Bae**: The Snow Queen has her summer tent there. But her strong castle is far to the north, on the island they call Spitsbergen.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): the far north today  
> _Lapland is the far north of Norway, Sweden and Finland, much of it inside the Arctic. Spitsbergen is a real island, part of Svalbard, which belongs to Norway._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned where Lapland and Svalbard are._

**Gerda**: Oh, Kay. Little Kay.  

**Choices**

- **Whisper to Bae: does he know the way?**
    - **Bae**: Know it? I could find it with my eyes shut. I’d go tonight, if not for this ring.
- **Hold Gerda’s hand in the dark.**
    - You find her hand in the straw. She holds on so tight it hurts, and you don’t mind.
- **Hush them before the robber girl wakes.**
    - The robber girl stirs and mutters in her sleep. Everybody goes very quiet until she snores again.

#### `a12-10-pigeons-done`

_Nobody sleeps much after that, except the robber girl and, on the far perch, one very old pigeon._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how birds sleep  
> _Many birds sleep perched, gripping the branch with their toes and fluffing up their feathers to keep warm._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how many birds sleep on a perch._


#### `a12-10-morning`

_In the morning Gerda tells the robber girl everything the pigeons said. The robber girl looks serious, and nods._  
**The Robber Girl**: Lapland. Bae, do you know where Lapland is?  
**Bae**: Do I know? Ask a fish if it knows the river. I was born there. I ran on those snowfields as a calf.  
_His eyes shine as he says it. He has been standing in this corner a long time._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): words for feelings  
> _Bae’s eyes shine when he talks about where he was born. Which word fits how he feels?_  
> - ✅ Homesick → Yes. Homesick is missing your home so much it aches.
> - Grumpy → His eyes are shining, not scowling. He misses home: he’s homesick.
> _For grown-ups: Named the feeling of homesickness._

**The Robber Girl**: Listen. The men are all out. Only Mother’s here, and at noon she has a drink from the big bottle and a nap.  
**The Robber Girl**: Then I’ll do something for you.  

**Choices**

- **Thank her.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: Don’t thank me yet. I haven’t done it. I might change my mind.
- **Ask her why.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: Because I want to. That’s why I do everything.

#### `a12-10-morning-done`

_You have been waiting since nine o’clock in the morning._  
_At noon the old robber woman takes a long drink from the big bottle, sits down, and her chin goes onto her chest._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.MD.B.3, ask): time in hours  
> _Noon is twelve o’clock, and you started waiting at nine. How many hours did you wait?_  
> - ✅ 3 hours → Yes. Ten, eleven, twelve: three hours.
> - 21 hours → That’s nine plus twelve. Count on from nine instead: ten, eleven, twelve, so three hours.
> - 12 hours → Twelve is the time it is now. From nine to twelve is three hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out how many hours passed from nine o’clock to noon._


#### `a12-10-free`

_The robber girl goes to Bae. She doesn’t look at you, and she doesn’t look at your Nubbin._  
**The Robber Girl**: Don’t think this is because of you. I was going to anyway.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): actions and words  
> _She sounds cross, but she sets Bae free and gives Gerda boots and mittens. Is the robber girl kind?_  
> - Yes, her actions are kind → That’s a fair answer. What people do can say more than how they talk.
> - No, she’s rude → She is rude! Can someone be rude and kind at the same time, do you think?
> - She’s both → A thoughtful answer. People are often more than one thing at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how a character’s actions and words can tell different stories._

**The Robber Girl**: Bae, I’m untying you. Run home to Lapland and carry this girl to the Snow Queen’s, where her friend is.  
**The Robber Girl**: You heard her story. You were listening; she talks loud enough.  
_Bae leaps for joy. The robber girl lifts Gerda onto his back, ties her on, and gives her a little cushion to sit on._  
**The Robber Girl**: Here are your fur boots. It’ll be cold. I’m keeping the muff; it’s too pretty.  
**The Robber Girl**: But you’re not freezing on my account. Have Mother’s big mittens. They come right up to your elbows.  
**The Robber Girl**: Two loaves and a ham. And don’t cry. I hate it when people cry. Look happy.  
**Bae**: Climb on behind her, lodger. You weigh less than a sack of salt, and I’ve carried worse.  
_The robber girl coaxes the big dogs inside. Then she cuts Bae’s rope with her knife, and opens the door._  
**The Robber Girl**: Run! And look after her!  

**Choices**

- **Wave goodbye to the robber girl.**
    - You wave. She doesn’t wave back, but she watches until you’re out of sight, which is nearly the same.
- **Nod to her, as one equal to another.**
    - You nod. She nods back, once, hard, like somebody shutting a box.

#### `a12-10-free-done`

_Bae flies off over stumps and bushes, through the great forest, over marshes and plains, as fast as he can go._  
_Above you the sky flares up, green and white, in great sheets of light._  
**Bae**: Those are my old lights! Look at them flash!  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): the northern lights  
> _These are the northern lights, also called the aurora borealis. Tiny particles from the Sun hit the air far above the Earth and make it glow._  
> _Green is the most common colour. They’re seen best on dark winter nights in the far north._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what causes the northern lights._


#### `a12-10-complete`

_You ride north day and night. Gerda cuts each loaf into four equal pieces, but the bread runs out, and then the ham._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions  
> _A loaf cut into four equal pieces. What fraction of the loaf is one piece?_  
> - ✅ One quarter (1/4) → Yes. Four equal parts make a whole, so each one is a quarter.
> - One half (1/2) → A half would be two equal pieces. Four equal pieces are quarters: 1/4 each.
> _For grown-ups: Named a unit fraction: one quarter._

_Gerda’s hands are in the robber woman’s great mittens. Your Nubbin rides inside her coat, against her heart._  
**Gerda**: Is it much further?  
**Bae**: Yes. But we’re nearer than we were.  

### Glossary

- **Arctic**: The very cold region around the North Pole.
- **homesick**: Sad because you are missing your home.

## A12-11. The Sámi Woman

- `a12-11-s1`: Find the little house in the snow. · _Follow Bae towards the smoke and the lamplight._
- `a12-11-s2`: Get warm while Bae tells his story. · _Sit by the lamp and eat what you’re given._
- `a12-11-s3`: Carry the message on the dried fish. · _Take the fish from the Sámi woman and keep it safe._

#### `a12-11-hut`

_Bae stops at a little house. Its roof comes right down to the snow, and smoke rises from the middle of it._  
_The door is so low you have to go in on hands and knees. Your Nubbin goes in on its belly._  
_Inside, by the light of her lamp, a woman is frying fish. Nobody else is at home._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): the Sámi homeland, Sápmi  
> _This woman is Sámi. The Sámi are the Indigenous people of the far north, and have lived here for thousands of years._  
> _Their homeland, Sápmi, stretches across Norway, Sweden, Finland and part of Russia. How many countries is that?_  
> - ✅ Four → Yes, four. Sápmi is one homeland, though the map draws borders across it.
> - One → It’s one homeland, but it reaches across four countries: Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
> - Two → Count again: Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia. Four countries.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sámi homeland, Sápmi, spans four countries._

_A reindeer, a frozen girl and a lodger all crawl through her door at once. She doesn’t turn a hair._  
**The Sámi Woman**: Well. Come in, then. Shut the cold out behind you. Mind the pan.  
_Gerda is so cold she can’t speak. The woman sits her by the lamp straight away and rubs her hands._  

**Choices**

- **Help rub Gerda’s feet.**
    - You rub Gerda’s feet while the woman does her hands. Neither of you says much; there isn’t time for much.
- **Mind the pan.**
    - You mind the pan. The fish is nearly done, and you turn it, and the woman nods: right side, right moment.

#### `a12-11-hut-done`

**The Sámi Woman**: There. Fingers are coming back. Toes next. You’ve come a long way in those boots.  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): warming up cold hands safely  
> _Very cold fingers and toes should be warmed gently and slowly, with warm hands or warm, not hot, water._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how to warm up very cold hands and feet safely._


#### `a12-11-lamp`

_Bae tells his own story first, because it seems to him much the more important. Then he tells Gerda’s._  
**The Sámi Woman**: You’ve been tied up a long while, by the look of your neck. Hold still.  
_She looks over Bae’s legs and the rubbed place under his chin, quickly and gently, like somebody who has done it all her life._  
**The Sámi Woman**: My son has our herd out on the winter grazing. I know a tired reindeer when one comes to my door.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): reindeer herding as a living job  
> _Reindeer herding is a real Sámi job, in the past and today. Herding families move with their reindeer between summer and winter grazing lands._  
> _Today many herders use snowmobiles as well as skis. Most Sámi people do all sorts of other jobs too._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that reindeer herding is a living Sámi job today._

_She feeds you fish and broth, and fetches Bae a heap of lichen from her store. Nobody leaves her house hungry._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-1, ask): what reindeer eat in winter  
> _In winter the ground is deep in snow. How do reindeer find their lichen?_  
> - ✅ They dig through the snow with their hooves → That’s right. They can smell it under the snow, and dig down with their front hooves.
> - They eat snow instead → Snow isn’t food! They smell the lichen underneath and dig down to it with their hooves.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how reindeer find food under the snow._

**The Sámi Woman**: You’ve a long way still to go. Hundreds of miles, to where the Snow Queen is.  
**Gerda**: Do you know where she is? Have you seen her?  
**The Sámi Woman**: I know her weather. Everybody up here does. She lets off her lights every evening, further north.  

**Choices**

- **Ask about her herd.**
    - **The Sámi Woman**: Big enough. Too big to count in a hurry. My son knows each one by its face, and pretends he doesn’t.
- **Thank her for the food.**
    - **The Sámi Woman**: It’s only fish. You’d do the same, if I came to your door.
- **Help feed Bae his lichen.**
    - Bae eats from your hands, delicately, then all at once. The woman watches, and shows you how to hold it better.

#### `a12-11-lamp-done`

**The Sámi Woman**: I’ll tell you who’ll know more: my friend, further north. She knows that country better than I do.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the Sámi languages  
> _There are several Sámi languages, not just one. North Sámi is the one spoken most widely, and children can learn it at school today._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that there are several Sámi languages spoken today._


#### `a12-11-fish`

**The Sámi Woman**: I’ve no paper. I’ll write it on a fish. She’ll read it.  
_She takes a dried cod off the rack and writes a few lines on it, with care. Then she hands it to you._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): why dried food keeps  
> _Drying takes the water out of fish. The tiny living things that make food go bad need water, so dried fish keeps for months._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why drying food stops it going bad._

**The Sámi Woman**: Look after that. Don’t let the reindeer eat it, and don’t eat it yourself, however long the road.  
_She ties Gerda back onto Bae with her own knots, which are better. Then she gives you a reindeer skin, rolled up._  
**The Sámi Woman**: To sit on, wherever you end up sitting. Snow is colder from underneath.  
_She doesn’t say how she knows you’ll end up sitting. She knows the country._  

**Choices**

- **Put the fish inside your coat.**
    - You tuck it into your coat. It smells strongly of fish, and so will you, for the rest of the journey.
- **Ask why she thinks you’ll be sitting.**
    - **The Sámi Woman**: Everybody who goes north ends up waiting for somebody. That’s what the north is mostly for.

#### `a12-11-fish-done`

**The Sámi Woman**: Go well. And come back this way, after. I’ll want to know how it ends.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.K.3, ask): predicting  
> _She wants to know how it ends. How do you think Gerda’s journey will end?_  
> - She finds Kay and brings him home → A hopeful guess. Keep reading and see if you’re right.
> - Something surprising will happen → Stories do love a surprise. Watch for clues.
> - I can’t tell yet → That’s honest. Good readers wait for more clues before they decide.
> _For grown-ups: Made a prediction about how the story will end._


#### `a12-11-complete`

_Bae runs on into the night. Overhead the lights burn blue all night long, the most beautiful you have ever seen._  
**Gerda**: She didn’t ask for anything. Not even our names.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): hospitality and kindness to strangers  
> _She fed and warmed three strangers and asked for nothing back. Why do you think she did it?_  
> - In the cold north, people help each other → That’s a wise answer. Where the cold is dangerous, kindness to travellers matters.
> - She could see they needed help → Yes. Noticing what someone needs, and giving it, is real kindness.
> - She’d want the same if it were her → She said so herself: you’d do the same, if I came to your door.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people welcome and help strangers._

_The fish letter is warm inside your coat. Your Nubbin keeps sniffing at it, hopefully._  
**Bae**: Not far now. Further than you’d like, but not far.  

### Glossary

- **Indigenous**: Describes the first people to live in a place, whose families have lived there for a very long time.
- **lichen**: A crusty, plant-like growth on rocks and ground that reindeer eat.

## A12-12. The Finnish Woman

- `a12-12-s1`: Deliver the fish letter. · _There’s no door. Knock on the chimney._
- `a12-12-s2`: Listen while Bae asks the Finnish woman for help. · _Sit in the heat and listen._
- `a12-12-s3`: Ask the Finnish woman if you should go with Gerda. · _Ask her in the corner, before Bae sets off._

#### `a12-12-chimney`

_The Finnish woman’s house has no door at all. Bae knocks on the chimney with his antlers, and a voice inside says come down._  
_Inside, it’s so hot that the air shimmers. The Finnish woman is small, with her sleeves rolled up and very wise eyes._  
**The Finnish Woman**: Off. Boots off, mittens off, coat open, or you’ll cook. And you, put this on your head.  
_She puts a block of ice on Bae’s head. He looks very relieved._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): melting and freezing can be reversed  
> _The ice on Bae’s head is melting in the heat. If you took the water outside into the snow, what would happen?_  
> - ✅ It would freeze into ice again → Yes. Melting and freezing can go both ways. Heat melts ice; cold freezes water again.
> - It would stay water for ever → Out in the snow it’s far below 0 °C (32 °F). The water would freeze again.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that melting and freezing are changes that can be reversed._

_You give her the fish. She reads it once, twice, three times, until she has it by heart._  
_Then she puts it in the soup pot, because it’s good to eat and she never wastes anything._  

**Choices**

- **Watch the letter go in the soup.**
    - It goes in with a respectful plop. Your Nubbin watches the pot as if the message might still have something to add.
- **Ask for a block of ice for yourself.**
    - **The Finnish Woman**: Ha! Here. You’re cooking too. Everybody does, the first time.

#### `a12-12-chimney-done`

**The Finnish Woman**: Well. So you’re the ones.  
**The Finnish Woman**: Sit.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): remembering by rereading  
> _She read the letter three times before it went in the pot. Reading something again and again is a good way to remember it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rereading helps us remember._

_You sit. The soup bubbles, and the letter, it seems, has said its piece._  

#### `a12-12-power`

_Bae tells his own story first, and then Gerda’s. The Finnish woman blinks her wise eyes, and says nothing._  
**Bae**: You’re so clever. Can’t you give her something? A drink to give her the strength of twelve men, to beat the Snow Queen?  
**The Finnish Woman**: The strength of twelve men! Much good that would do her.  
_She takes Bae into a corner, puts fresh ice on his head, and speaks low. You’re near enough to hear._  
**The Finnish Woman**: Little Kay is with the Snow Queen. He thinks it’s the best place in the world.  
**The Finnish Woman**: That’s because there’s a splinter in his heart and a grain of glass in his eye. They must come out, or he’ll never be himself again.  
**Bae**: But can’t you give Gerda something? Something to make her stronger than all of it?  
**The Finnish Woman**: I can’t give her more than she’s got. People help her. Animals carry her. She’s come this far barefoot.  
**The Finnish Woman**: It doesn’t come from me. It comes from her heart: she loves somebody, and she means it all the way through.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _The Finnish woman won’t give Gerda magic, because Gerda already has what she needs. What is it?_  
> - ✅ Her love for Kay, and never giving up → Yes. That’s the big idea of this story: love that keeps going is a kind of strength.
> - A secret spell → No spell at all. It’s her love for Kay, and the way she never gives up.
> - The strength of twelve men → The Finnish woman laughs at that. Gerda’s strength is love, and not giving up.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of the story: love and persistence as strength._

**The Finnish Woman**: She mustn’t hear it from us. She has to reach him herself.  

#### `a12-12-power-done`

_Gerda, by the stove, hasn’t heard a word. She has fallen asleep in the heat, with her boots and mittens beside her._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): rest after hard effort  
> _After a long, cold journey, the body needs food, warmth and sleep to recover. Gerda’s is taking all three at once._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the body needs food, warmth and rest to recover._


#### `a12-12-ask`

_You go to the corner too, and ask it straight out: should you go with Gerda, all the way in?_  
**The Finnish Woman**: No.  
**The Finnish Woman**: Two miles on, the Snow Queen’s garden begins. There’s a big bush there with red berries, standing in the snow.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, notice): miles and kilometres  
> _A mile is a little more than one and a half kilometres. So two miles is about three kilometres: a long walk in the snow._  
> _For grown-ups: Compared miles with kilometres._

**The Finnish Woman**: You take her as far as the bush. Then you stop. Then you wait.  
**The Finnish Woman**: Some doors only open for one person. If you go through with her, it won’t open at all.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when only one person can do it  
> _You want to help Gerda all the way. Why might waiting be the most helpful thing?_  
> - Some things you have to do yourself → That’s a wise answer. Sometimes helping means stepping back.
> - It isn’t; I’d go anyway → That’s honest: it’s hard to stay behind. The Finnish woman says going in would close the door.
> - So someone is there when she comes back → Yes. Waiting is a job too. Someone has to be there.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when stepping back is the most helpful thing to do._

_She looks at your Nubbin, and then at you, as if checking that you’re the waiting sort._  

**Choices**

- **“How long?”**
    - **The Finnish Woman**: As long as it takes. That’s the only length waiting comes in.
- **“And if she doesn’t come out?”**
    - **The Finnish Woman**: Then you’ll still have waited, and that’s worth something. But she’ll come.
- **Nod. You understand.**
    - **The Finnish Woman**: Good. Most people argue. Most people have to be told twice.

#### `a12-12-ask-done`

**The Finnish Woman**: Now go. And don’t stand about talking at the bush. Put her down, and let the reindeer come straight back.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): following hard advice  
> _Following good advice is hard when you’d rather do something else. Taking a breath and trusting it is a skill._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about following good advice even when it is hard._


#### `a12-12-complete`

_The Finnish woman lifts the sleeping Gerda onto Bae. Bae is off like a shot, and you hang on behind._  
**Gerda**: Oh! My boots! My mittens! They’re by the stove!  
_Bae doesn’t dare stop. He runs and runs through the hard cold, towards a dark shape in the snow._  
_You look back once. The little hot house is a spark, and then nothing._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): imagery  
> _“A spark, and then nothing.” What does that picture tell you?_  
> - ✅ You are getting very far away, fast → Yes. The house shrinks to a tiny light, then vanishes behind you.
> - The house caught fire → No fire! It just looks tiny, like a spark, because you’re so far away.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a picture made of words shows._


### Glossary

- **shimmers**: Wobbles and shines, the way air does over something very hot.
- **theme**: The big idea a story is really about.

## A12-13. The Bush with Red Berries

- `a12-13-s1`: Reach the bush with red berries. · _Hold on to Bae until he stops at the bush._
- `a12-13-s2`: Wait by the bush, as long as it takes. · _Sit on the reindeer skin and wait. There’s nothing else to do, and that’s the job._

#### `a12-13-bush`

_The bush stands alone in the snow, dark green, covered in berries as red as Gerda’s shoes._  
_Bae sets Gerda down. He touches his nose to her cheek, and big bright tears run down his face._  
**Bae**: I can’t go further. She said. Go well, little one.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): sad goodbyes  
> _Bae cries, and runs off fast so he won’t change his mind. Why do you think he does it that way?_  
> - A quick goodbye hurts less → That’s a fair answer. Some people find a quick goodbye easier.
> - He’s scared of the palace → Maybe. The Finnish woman also told him to come straight back.
> - He’d stay if he waited → Yes, I think so too. He loves her, and leaving is hard.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why goodbyes are hard and how people manage them._

_Then he turns and runs back the way you came, as fast as he can, so that he won’t change his mind._  
_Gerda stands in the snow in her stockings, with no boots and no mittens, in the middle of the far north._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-2, notice): polar night  
> _You are far north of the Arctic Circle, where in midwinter the Sun doesn’t rise for weeks, or even months. That’s called polar night._  
> _It happens because the Earth is tilted, so in winter the far north leans away from the Sun._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about polar night and why it happens._

_In the distance something glitters, huge and cold: walls of drifted snow, and windows of wind._  

**Choices**

- **Offer Gerda your coat.**
    - **Gerda**: No. You have to wait, and waiting’s the coldest part. You keep it.
- **Offer her your Nubbin, to keep her hands warm.**
    - Gerda strokes your Nubbin once, and shakes her head.
    - **Gerda**: It would only get cold in there. Keep it warm for me, so it’s warm when we come back.
- **“Go on, then.”**
    - **You**: Go on, then.
    - **Gerda**: I’m going.

#### `a12-13-bush-done`

_Gerda runs off across the snow. She doesn’t look back, and you understand why._  
_Then you’re alone by the bush with your Nubbin, and the quiet comes down._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): being alone and calm  
> _Being alone can feel big and empty. Noticing small things around you, like berries and breath, helps you feel steady._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned a way to feel calm when alone._


#### `a12-13-wait`

_You unroll the Sámi woman’s reindeer skin and sit on it. She was right: snow is colder from underneath._  
_Your Nubbin climbs inside your coat and presses itself against you. You keep each other warm, the slow way._  
_There’s no wind here. Just the cold, and the quiet, and the bush, and the red berries._  
_The nearest branch has six bunches of berries, with five berries in each bunch. You count them._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Six bunches, five berries in each. How many berries on the branch?_  
> - ✅ 30 → Yes. Six groups of five: five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty.
> - 11 → That’s six plus five. Six groups of five is six times five: thirty.
> - 25 → That’s five fives. One more five makes six fives: thirty.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups to find a total._

_Then you count them again, get a different number, and decide not to mind._  
_Far off, the lights go up over the palace, green and white. Nobody is watching them but you._  
_You don’t know how long it will be. You know you’ll be here when it’s over._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): patience  
> _Waiting with no clock and no end in sight is hard. What helps you wait?_  
> - Counting, or humming → Good ideas. Keeping your mind gently busy makes time pass.
> - Having a friend with me → Yes. Your Nubbin is here. Waiting together is easier.
> - Knowing why I’m waiting → That’s a wise one. Waiting for someone you love has a point to it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about strategies that make waiting easier._


**Choices**

- **Count the berries again.**
    - Thirty again, or twenty-nine. Your Nubbin points at one you’ve missed.
- **Hum Gerda’s rose tune, under your breath.**
    - You hum it, not loud. Your Nubbin hums it back a beat behind, the way it did under the rose arch.
- **Just sit.**
    - You just sit, and it turns out you’re good at it. You didn’t use to be.

#### `a12-13-wait-done`

_Your feet go numb, and come back, and go numb again. You stay._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, notice): why cold feet go numb  
> _In the cold your body keeps its warm blood near your heart, so toes get less. Wiggling them gets the blood moving again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why feet go numb in the cold and how wiggling helps._


#### `a12-13-complete`

_Night comes, if it ever went. The stars come out so thick they look like frost on a window._  
_Straight above, one star never moves while the others wheel slowly round it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Pole Star  
> _The star that stays still while the others turn round it is the Pole Star. What has it helped travellers find for centuries?_  
> - ✅ Which way is north → Yes. The Pole Star sits almost exactly above the North Pole. In the far north it’s nearly overhead.
> - What time it is → Other stars can help with time, but the Pole Star’s job is showing north.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Pole Star shows the way north._

_Across the snow, very small, Gerda is still walking. Something is moving over the snow towards her._  
_You stand up on the skin to see better. You don’t step off it._  
_Your Nubbin sits up inside your coat and looks out. You hold it a little tighter, and you stay where you are._  

### Glossary

- **polar night**: A time in winter, near the Poles, when the Sun does not rise all day.
- **numb**: Unable to feel anything, often from cold.

## A12-14. The Snowflake Guards

- `a12-14-s1`: Watch Gerda from the bush. · _Stand on the reindeer skin and look out across the snow._
- `a12-14-s2`: Watch what Gerda does. · _Keep watching. Don’t look away._

#### `a12-14-guards`

_Gerda is a dark speck on the white. Towards her, along the ground, come the snowflakes._  
_They don’t fall from the sky; the sky is clear. They run along the snow, and the nearer they get, the bigger they grow._  
_You remember Kay’s burning-glass, and how big the flakes looked under it. These are bigger, and they are alive._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): measuring small things  
> _A real snowflake is tiny. About how wide is a real one, usually?_  
> - ✅ A few millimetres → Yes. Most are a few millimetres across, smaller than your fingernail. These guards are pure story.
> - A few metres → A metre-wide snowflake would be a monster! Real ones are a few millimetres.
> - A few kilometres → That would cover a town! Real snowflakes are a few millimetres across.
> _For grown-ups: Estimated a small length using millimetres._

_Some are like great prickly porcupines, and some like knots of snakes with their heads sticking out._  
_Some are like fat little bears with their fur on end. All of them are dazzling white._  
_They are the Snow Queen’s guards. They close round Gerda in a ring._  

**Choices**

- **Shout to her.**
    - You shout. The cold takes the sound out of your mouth and drops it in the snow a yard away.
- **Take one step off the skin.**
    - You take one step. Then you remember what the Finnish woman said, and you step back on.
- **Hold your Nubbin tight.**
    - You hold it, and it holds you. Neither of you takes your eyes off the speck in the ring.

#### `a12-14-guards-done`

_Gerda stops. She doesn’t run._  
_She stands quite still in the middle of the ring._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): staying calm when scared  
> _When something frightening happens, stopping to think, instead of running, can help you choose what to do._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about stopping to think when something is frightening._


#### `a12-14-prayer`

_Gerda folds her hands and says her prayer, the one Grandmother taught her. You can’t hear it from here, and you don’t need to._  
_It’s so cold that her breath comes out like smoke. The smoke grows thicker as she prays._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): why breath shows in cold air  
> _Your breath is warm and full of water vapour. In freezing air the vapour cools into tiny droplets of water, so you can see it like smoke._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why breath turns into a cloud on a cold day._

_Then it turns into small bright figures, with helmets on their heads and spears and shields in their hands._  
_They grow as they touch the ground, and there are more of them with every breath she takes._  
_By the time she has finished her prayer, a whole crowd of them stands round her, shining._  
_They break the snowflake guards into a hundred pieces, and clear the road ahead of her._  
_They stroke her hands and feet so that she feels the cold less, and she walks on, quickly and bravely._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): courage  
> _Gerda is surely frightened, and she walks on anyway. Is that brave, even though she’s scared?_  
> - Yes. Brave means scared, and doing it anyway → That’s a wise answer. Courage isn’t having no fear; it’s going on with it.
> - No. Brave people aren’t scared → Many people think so. But if you’re not scared, is it brave, or just easy?
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what courage means._


#### `a12-14-prayer-done`

_The bright figures go with her all the way to the palace gate. Then they’re gone, like breath on a window._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _“Gone, like breath on a window.” What does breath on a window do?_  
> - ✅ It fades away quickly → Yes. The misty patch shrinks and vanishes in a moment. So do the bright figures.
> - It stays for ever → Try it on a cold window: the mist fades away in seconds. So do the figures.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a simile using an everyday experience._


#### `a12-14-complete`

_The palace gate is made of cutting winds. Gerda says her evening prayer, and the winds drop as if they’ve gone to sleep._  
_She goes in. The gate closes behind her, and the winds get up again._  
_You sit back down on the reindeer skin. Your Nubbin puts its chin on your arm._  
_You sat down here at about four o’clock. Now it feels like about ten._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _From four o’clock to ten o’clock. How long have you been waiting by the bush?_  
> - ✅ 6 hours → Yes. Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten: six hours.
> - 14 hours → That’s four plus ten. Count on from four to ten: six hours.
> - 4 hours → Count on from four: five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Six hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval by counting on._

_Now there’s nothing to watch but the walls. You watch them anyway._  

### Glossary

- **porcupine**: An animal covered in long, sharp spines.
- **courage**: Being brave, even when you feel afraid.

## A12-15. The Ice Puzzle

- `a12-15-s1`: Watch the Snow Queen fly south. · _Look through the clear patch in the frost, then up at the sky._
- `a12-15-s2`: Watch Kay at his puzzle. · _Keep looking through the clear patch in the frost._

#### `a12-15-south`

_Your Nubbin breathes on the frozen crust by your feet. The frost clears like a window, and the atlas does what atlases do._  
_It shows you the next page while you’re still on this one: inside the palace, a little earlier, in cut paper and ice._  
_The halls are drifted snow, and the windows are cutting winds. There are more than a hundred of them, lit by the northern lights._  
_They are vast and empty and icy and glittering. Nobody has ever had any fun in them, not once._  
_The Snow Queen stands in the greatest hall, ready to go._  
**The Snow Queen**: I’m off to the warm lands. I want to look into the black pots, the ones that smoke. I’ll whiten them a little.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, notice): snow on volcanoes  
> _The “black pots that smoke” are volcanoes, like Etna and Vesuvius in Italy._  
> _The air gets colder the higher you go, so snow can lie on a tall volcano even in a warm country._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that high mountain tops are cold, so snow can settle on volcanoes in warm lands._

**The Snow Queen**: Work out the word while I’m gone. Make it, and nobody will ever tell you what to do again.  
**The Snow Queen**: I’ll give you the whole world for it. And a new pair of skates.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe is not the same as well  
> _The whole world, and never being told what to do, if Kay stays cold and feels nothing. Would that be a good deal?_  
> - No. Feelings matter more than prizes → That’s a thoughtful answer. A prize is no fun if you can’t feel glad about it.
> - Yes, the whole world is a lot → It is a lot! But who would Kay share it with, if he can’t feel anything?
> - Not sure → Honest: it’s a big question. Keep it in mind as you watch Kay.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being safe from feelings is the same as being well._


**Choices**

- **Look up as she passes.**
    - A moment later she goes over the bush, high up, a long white streak heading south. She doesn’t look down.
- **Keep your head down.**
    - You keep your head down. A long white shadow goes over the snow, and the berries rattle on the bush.

#### `a12-15-south-done`

_In the great hall Kay is alone. It’s miles long, and he is the only thing in it that moves, and only just._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): loneliness  
> _Feeling lonely is a signal, like feeling hungry: it tells us we need people. Kay is too cold to notice it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that loneliness is a feeling that tells us we need other people._


#### `a12-15-puzzle`

_In the middle of the hall is a frozen lake, cracked into a thousand pieces, every piece exactly like every other._  

> **Lesson** (maths, notice): shapes that fit together  
> _Some shapes, like squares, triangles and hexagons, fit together with no gaps. Bees build honeycomb that way, and the lake is cracked like floor tiles._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some shapes fit together with no gaps._

_The Snow Queen calls it the Mirror of Understanding. She says it’s the only one, and the best in the world._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): irony in a name  
> _It’s called the Mirror of Understanding. Does it help Kay understand anything?_  
> - ✅ No. It just keeps him busy and cold → Yes. The grand name is a kind of joke: it understands nothing, and neither does he while he’s on it.
> - Yes, it makes him wise → Look at him: stuck, stiff, frozen. The name promises understanding, but it doesn’t give any.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed when a name means the opposite of what something really does._

_Kay sits on it. He is blue with cold, nearly black, and he doesn’t notice; she took the shivering out of him._  
_He drags flat, sharp pieces of ice about, fits them together, pulls them apart, and fits them again._  
_To him the shapes are the most important things in the world. That’s the grain of glass in his eye._  
_He makes whole words out of ice. But there’s one word he can’t make, and it’s the only one she wants._  
**Kay**: Nearly. It’s nearly. It just needs one more piece.  
_It doesn’t. He sits and thinks until he creaks, so stiff and still that you’d think he had frozen._  

**Choices**

- **Say his name, out loud, to nobody.**
    - **You**: Kay.
    - Of course he can’t hear you. Somebody should say it, out here, so you did.
- **Look away for a moment.**
    - You look away, at the red berries, and it helps a bit. Then you look back, because somebody should.
- **Keep watching.**
    - You keep watching. Your Nubbin watches too, without blinking, the way it watches an egg that’s about to hatch.

#### `a12-15-puzzle-done`

_Then, at the far end of the hall, a small figure in stockings comes in through the gate of winds._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): dressing for the cold  
> _Gerda has no boots or mittens, but in real life you’d want warm feet, hands and head in the snow. Most body heat escapes where skin is bare._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned to cover up hands, feet and head in cold weather._


#### `a12-15-complete`

_Gerda walks into the empty hall. It is two kilometres long, and she walks about four kilometres an hour._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Four kilometres in an hour. How long will it take Gerda to walk two kilometres?_  
> - ✅ Half an hour (30 minutes) → Yes. Two is half of four, so it takes half an hour: thirty minutes.
> - Two hours → Two hours would get her eight kilometres. Two is half of four: half an hour.
> - Four hours → Much too long! Two kilometres is half of four, so it takes half an hour.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a speed, distance and time problem using halves._

_Kay doesn’t look up. He is still counting pieces._  
_Your Nubbin holds its breath. You find you’re holding yours._  
_Over the palace the northern lights go quiet, as if they want to see too._  

### Glossary

- **volcano**: A mountain that can let out hot melted rock, ash and smoke from inside the Earth.
- **irony**: When something turns out the opposite of what you would expect.

## A12-16. Gerda’s Tears

- `a12-16-s1`: Watch Gerda find Kay. · _Watch through the clear patch in the frost._
- `a12-16-s2`: Watch Kay come back. · _Keep watching. This is the part you waited for._
- `a12-16-s3`: Watch the ice spell the word. · _Watch the pieces of ice on the frozen lake._

#### `a12-16-found`

_Gerda sees him. She knows him at once, and she runs, and throws her arms round his neck and holds on._  
**Gerda**: Kay! Kay, it’s you! I’ve found you!  
_Kay sits quite still. He is stiff and cold, and he doesn’t know her._  
_Gerda cries. Not a little: she cries the way you cry at the end of a very long way._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): crying is allowed  
> _Crying is one way big feelings come out. It’s allowed, for anyone, and it often helps._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about crying as a healthy way to let big feelings out._

_Her tears fall on his chest. They’re hot, and they go through, all the way to his heart._  
_They thaw the ice round his heart. They melt the little splinter of glass inside it, as if it had never been._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): warmth melts ice  
> _Tears come out at about body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F). What happens when something that warm touches ice?_  
> - ✅ The ice melts → Yes. Warmth melts ice. In the story, Gerda’s warm tears melt the cold in Kay’s heart.
> - The tears freeze and nothing happens → In this story the warmth wins: warm things melt ice, and the ice turns to water.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that warm things melt ice._

_Kay looks at her._  

**Choices**

- **Stand up on the skin.**
    - You stand up; you can’t help it. Your Nubbin climbs onto your shoulder to see.
- **Stay perfectly still.**
    - You don’t move. You don’t want to break anything, even from two miles off.

#### `a12-16-found-done`

_Gerda hums the old tune with the roses in it, the one from the gutter boxes. You know it, and you hum it with her._  

> **Lesson** (music, do): humming a melody together  
> _Hum along, slow and soft. A tune you share with someone can bring back where you were together._  
> Check: `edu:hum:tune:slow`
> _For grown-ups: Hummed a slow melody along with the story._


#### `a12-16-tears`

_Kay bursts into tears. He cries so hard that the grain of glass washes out of his eye._  
_He blinks. He sees her._  
**Kay**: Gerda? Gerda, it’s you. Where did you go? Where did I go? How long have I been away?  
_He looks round the hall as if he’s seeing it for the first time._  
**Kay**: It’s so cold in here. It’s so big, and so empty.  
_He holds on to Gerda, and she laughs and cries at once. So, two miles away, do you._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): naming relief  
> _Gerda laughs and cries at the same time. What kind of tears are these?_  
> - ✅ Happy tears, from relief → Yes. Relief is the feeling when a big worry ends. It can make you laugh and cry at once.
> - Sad tears only → She’s laughing too! These are tears of relief: the long worry is over.
> _For grown-ups: Named the feeling of relief._


**Choices**

- **Cheer.**
    - You cheer out loud, alone, in the middle of the far north. Your Nubbin squeaks as loud as it can.
- **Sit down hard on the skin.**
    - Your legs go. You sit down on the reindeer skin and laugh, and can’t stop.

#### `a12-16-tears-done`

_Even the pieces of ice begin to move._  
_They shiver, and lift, as if they want to join in._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification  
> _The ice “wants to join in”: giving a thing human feelings is called personification. Why does the writer do it here?_  
> - ✅ To show the whole place is glad → Yes. When even the ice seems happy, you know how big this moment is.
> - Because ice really has feelings → Not real ice! It’s a way of showing that the gladness fills the whole hall.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a writer gives human feelings to an object._


#### `a12-16-word`

_It is such a glad moment that the pieces of ice dance. They spin round Kay and Gerda, glittering._  
_When they’re tired, they lie down. They lie down in the shape of a word, the very word Kay couldn’t make._  
_It says ETERNITY, in letters of ice, as clear as a sign._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Count the ice letters: E, T, E, R, N, I, T, Y. That makes eight._  
> _Each letter is made of six pieces of ice. How many pieces lie on the lake?_  
> - ✅ 48 → Yes. Eight groups of six: six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four, and on to forty-eight.
> - 14 → That’s eight plus six. Eight groups of six is eight times six: forty-eight.
> - 40 → That’s eight fives. Each letter has six pieces, so it’s eight sixes: forty-eight.
> _For grown-ups: Counted the letters in a word, then multiplied equal groups._

_Kay didn’t make it. It made itself, the moment he stopped trying to be clever and started being glad._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): word meaning  
> _“Eternity” is a long word. What does it mean?_  
> - ✅ For ever, with no end → Yes. Eternity means time that never ends.
> - A kind of ice → Not ice: eternity means for ever, time with no end.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the meaning of the word eternity._

_Gerda kisses his cheeks, and they go pink. She kisses his eyes, and they shine like hers._  
_She kisses his hands and feet, and he is well and strong again. The Snow Queen can come home whenever she likes._  

**Choices**

- **Read the word out loud.**
    - **You**: Eternity.
    - It’s a long word for something so simple. Your Nubbin seems to agree.
- **Look at Gerda instead of the word.**
    - You look at Gerda. The word is the Snow Queen’s business, and Gerda is yours.

#### `a12-16-word-done`

_Kay’s freedom is written there on the lake, in shining letters. Nobody can unwrite it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _Kay tried and tried to be clever enough to make the word, but it only came when he was glad. What do you think that means?_  
> - Love matters more than cleverness → That’s a big idea, and a fair one. Cleverness alone couldn’t fix Kay.
> - Some things can’t be forced → A wise answer. Some things only come when we stop pushing.
> - He just got lucky → Maybe! But notice when it happened: the moment he felt glad.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the theme of the story: love matters more than cleverness._


#### `a12-16-complete`

_Kay and Gerda take each other’s hands and walk out of the great palace._  
_They talk about Grandmother, and the roses up on the roof. Wherever they go, the winds drop and the sun comes out._  
_The clear patch in the frost fogs over. It doesn’t need to show you anything now; you can see them coming._  
**Gerda**: There! By the bush! That’s our lodger. They waited!  
**Kay**: Waited? Out here? For me?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): showing someone they matter  
> _Kay can hardly believe someone waited for him. Being remembered and waited for is one way we know we matter._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how waiting for someone shows that they matter._


### Glossary

- **relief**: The happy, loosening feeling when a worry or danger is over.
- **eternity**: Time that goes on for ever, with no end.

## A12-17. The Road Home

- `a12-17-s1`: Meet Bae back at the bush. · _Stay by the bush. Bae is coming back._
- `a12-17-s2`: Go south by the Finnish woman’s house and the Sámi woman’s. · _Stop at both houses on the way._
- `a12-17-s3`: Meet the rider in the forest. · _Walk on into the green forest._

#### `a12-17-doe`

_Bae is back at the bush when they reach it. He has brought a young doe with him, sleek and calm._  
_She gives the children her warm milk to drink, and touches her nose to their faces._  
**Bae**: I said I’d come straight back. I never said I’d stay away.  
**Kay**: Hello, lodger. Gerda says you saw the sledge. I’m sorry about the face I did at you.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): saying sorry  
> _Kay says sorry for something he did a long time ago. What makes an apology a good one?_  
> - ✅ Saying what you did, and meaning it → Yes. Kay names the face he pulled. A real sorry says what for, and means it.
> - Saying it fast so it’s over → A quick sorry can sound empty. Kay names exactly what he did, which shows he means it.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes a sincere apology._

_He means the impression at the window, a long time ago. He remembers it, and he’s ashamed of it, which is a good sign._  
**Gerda**: He’s back. He’s really back. He’s cross about his feet, which is how I know.  
_The sky is getting lighter every day now. Soon, up here, it won’t get dark at all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-2, notice): the midnight sun  
> _North of the Arctic Circle, in summer, the Sun doesn’t set at all for days, weeks or even months. That’s called the midnight sun._  
> _It’s the summer side of polar night: the Earth’s tilt now leans the far north towards the Sun._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about the midnight sun and why it happens._


**Choices**

- **Tell Kay it was a very good impression.**
    - **Kay**: It was, wasn’t it. I won’t do it again. Probably.
- **Hug them both.**
    - You hug them both at once. Your Nubbin gets squashed in the middle and doesn’t mind at all.
- **Wrap them in the reindeer skin.**
    - You wrap the skin round both of them. They look like a very small, very pleased bundle of reindeer.

#### `a12-17-doe-done`

_Bae and the doe carry them south. You walk alongside with a hand on Bae’s shoulder, and your feet don’t feel the snow._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-PS3-1, notice): sunlight melts snow in spring  
> _As the days get longer, the Sun has more time to warm the ground each day. That’s why snow melts in spring._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that longer days of sunlight warm the ground and melt the snow._


#### `a12-17-south`

_First you stop at the Finnish woman’s hot little house. The children get warm, and she gives Gerda back her boots and mittens._  
**The Finnish Woman**: I told you she’d come. You waited well. Most people fidget.  
_Then on to the Sámi woman. She has sewn new clothes for both children, and has her sledge ready._  
**The Sámi Woman**: Well. You’re back, and there’s two of them. So that’s how it ends.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Sámi National Day  
> _Every year on 6 February, Sámi people in all four countries celebrate Sámi National Day, with the Sámi flag, songs and gatherings._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Sámi National Day is celebrated on 6 February._

_She drives you south herself, with Bae and the doe running alongside, to the edge of her country._  
_There the first green is coming through the snow, and it’s time to say goodbye._  
**The Sámi Woman**: Go well, all of you. Even the one that wanted to eat my letter.  

**Choices**

- **Thank her for everything.**
    - **The Sámi Woman**: It was only fish and a skin. Keep the skin. You’ve made good use of it.
- **Say goodbye to Bae.**
    - **Bae**: Goodbye, lodger. You sit well. I’ve never seen anybody sit so well.
    - He touches his nose to your Nubbin, very gently, and turns for home.
