_Bae and the doe turn north and run, side by side, until they’re part of the snow._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-1, notice): animals move to where their needs are met  
> _In spring, many reindeer herds travel to their summer grazing lands, where fresh plants are growing. Animals go where they can find what they need._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals move to places that meet their needs._


#### `a12-17-rider`

_The first birds are singing, and the forest has green buds. Out of it comes a fine horse that Gerda knows: it pulled the golden coach._  
_On it rides a girl in a bright red cap. It’s the robber girl._  
**The Robber Girl**: I got bored at home. I’m off to see the world. North first, and somewhere else if north’s no good.  
_Two wood pigeons ride on her saddle, tied by the leg. They coo at Gerda as if they remember her._  
**The Robber Girl**: So this is him. Hm. I wonder if he was worth running to the end of the world for.  
**Kay**: I wonder that too.  
**Gerda**: How are the prince and princess? And the ravens?  
**The Robber Girl**: The prince and princess have gone abroad. The raven died. He was old.  
_He died: his body stopped working, and it won’t start again. He had a long life, and a good one._  
**The Robber Girl**: His sweetheart wears a black thread round her leg now, to remember him, and tells everybody about him.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): grief and remembering  
> _The raven’s sweetheart wears a black thread to remember him. What are some ways people remember someone who has died?_  
> - Telling stories about them → Yes. Like she does: telling everybody about him keeps him close.
> - Keeping something special → A lovely way. A thread, a photo, a flower on a hill.
> - Just missing them → Missing someone is a kind of remembering too. It shows how much they mattered.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the ways people remember someone who has died._


**Choices**

- **Say you’re sorry about the raven.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: Don’t be. He had a good post and all the scraps he wanted. Not many get that.
- **Admire her red cap.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: It’s a good cap. You can’t have it.

#### `a12-17-rider-done`

_As she rides off, she tosses something small and red over her shoulder. It lands on your Nubbin’s head: a little red cap._  
**The Robber Girl**: Robbers always have two of everything!  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _If robbers really have two of everything, how many caps do five robbers have?_  
> - ✅ 10 → Yes. Five groups of two: two, four, six, eight, ten.
> - 7 → That’s five plus two. Five groups of two is five times two: ten.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups of two._


#### `a12-17-complete`

_The robber girl rides off into the wide world without looking back. You suspect she never looks back._  
_Kay and Gerda walk on hand in hand. It’s spring, and there are flowers everywhere._  
_Your Nubbin wears its red cap at a slant, the way she does._  
_Somewhere ahead, church bells are ringing._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): how bells make sound  
> _How does a church bell make its sound?_  
> - ✅ The metal vibrates when it’s struck → Yes. The clapper hits the bell, the metal shakes very fast, and those vibrations travel to your ears.
> - Air blows through it like a whistle → That’s how a whistle works. A bell is struck, and its metal vibrates.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a bell makes sound by vibrating._


### Glossary

- **apology**: Saying sorry for something you did wrong, and meaning it.
- **grief**: The deep sadness we feel when someone we love dies.

## A12-18. Summer

- `a12-18-s1`: Walk home into the town. · _Follow the church bells to Grandmother’s door._
- `a12-18-s2`: Sit by the roses with Kay and Gerda. · _Climb out to the little stools under the rose arch._

#### `a12-18-bells`

_The church bells are ringing, and you know the high towers. It’s the town: yours for a while, and theirs for always._  
_You go through the streets to Grandmother’s door, up the stairs, and into the room._  
_Everything is where it was. The clock says tick, tick, and its hands go round._  
_But as Kay and Gerda come through the door, they notice something. They’ve grown up._  
**Kay**: Was the door always this low?  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): growing up  
> _The door hasn’t changed. Why does it seem lower to Kay?_  
> - ✅ He has grown taller → Yes. Children grow taller as they get older, and the door stayed the same.
> - The door shrank → Doors don’t shrink! Kay grew taller while he was away.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that children grow as part of the human life cycle._

**Gerda**: We’ve been gone a long time.  

**Choices**

- **Duck under the beam, out of habit.**
    - You duck. Kay, who never had to before, hits his head on it, and laughs.
- **Listen to the clock.**
    - Tick, tick: it kept going the whole time. Somebody kept winding it.

#### `a12-18-bells-done`

_The window is open. The roses in the gutter boxes are in full bloom, and they’re growing right in at the window._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-PS3-1, notice): summer warmth and growth  
> _Long summer days give the roses lots of warm sunlight. That’s why they flower so well in summer._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sunlight warms the ground and helps plants grow in summer._


#### `a12-18-roses`

_There are the two little stools under the arch. Kay and Gerda sit on them, holding hands, too big for them now._  
_The Snow Queen’s cold empty halls have gone out of their heads, like a heavy dream after breakfast._  
_Grandmother sits in the sun, reading aloud from her Bible. She reads slowly, and stops when she reaches a part she likes._  
_Kay and Gerda look at each other. All at once they understand the old hymn about the roses, the one they used to hum._  
_They’re grown up, and they’re children too, in the place where it counts._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _Grown up, and still children “where it counts”. What do you think it means to be a child at heart?_  
> - Still being able to play and wonder → That’s a lovely answer. Growing up doesn’t have to mean losing that.
> - Still loving the people you loved → Yes. Kay and Gerda kept that through everything.
> - Not growing up at all → They have grown up, though! It’s more about keeping something inside while you grow.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what it means to grow up but stay a child at heart._

_And it is summer: warm, glorious summer._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-1, notice): a year of seasons  
> _The story began in late summer, and it ends in summer. Gerda’s road went through autumn, winter and spring, all the way round the year._  
> _For grown-ups: Traced the seasons through the whole story._


**Choices**

- **Sit on the gutter’s edge beside them.**
    - You sit on the edge of the gutter with your feet over the boxes. Grandmother looks up, nods, and reads on.
- **Fetch the watering can.**
    - You water the top of the arch, carefully. A drop lands on Kay, and he pretends not to notice, very badly.

#### `a12-18-roses-done`

**Grandmother**: There you are, lodger. I kept your room.  
**Grandmother**: I thought you’d want it back, after.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): being remembered  
> _Grandmother kept your room ready the whole time. Being kept a place by someone is a way of being remembered._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how being remembered by others feels._


#### `a12-18-complete`

_Your Nubbin climbs out among the roses and sits there alone in the middle of them, in its red cap, quite content._  
_Nobody is holding it, and nobody needs to. It stays because it wants to._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): freedom and friendship  
> _You said no to the robber girl, and your Nubbin stayed with you. Why do you think it’s content to stay?_  
> - Because it chose to → That’s a fair answer. A friend who stays because they want to is the best kind.
> - Because it trusts you → Yes. You kept it with you, kindly, and it knows it.
> - Because the roses are nice → They are lovely! And it’s with you, which counts too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between holding on to someone and a friend choosing to stay._

_The page settles under your hand, like a paper cut-out laid flat on a table._  
_You’re back in the Grove, with Nova’s atlas on your knee. When you open it again, a rose petal slides out of the fold and lands on your boot._  
_On the cottage windowsill stands a window box with a rose tree in it that wasn’t there this morning._  
_Another stands on the lantern shed across the way, and between them somebody has laid a plank._  
_You think of everyone who helped Gerda on the way. She couldn’t have done it alone, and she never had to._  

### Glossary

- **content**: Quietly happy, with nothing more you need.

## A13-1. The Piece of Wood

- `a13-01-s1`: Step into the brown-ink page, and out of the rain. · _Touch the page. Then find the open door with sawdust on its step._
- `a13-01-s2`: Stay in Master Cherry’s shop while he planes the log. · _Stand by the bench. When the old men start, keep your Nubbin out from under their feet._

#### `a13-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page in brown ink: a hill town, a long white road, and along the bottom edge, the sea._  
_The words across the top begin the way stories for children do. Once upon a time there was… a king, you think._  
_No. Once upon a time there was a piece of wood._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Pinocchio’s author, Carlo Collodi, and the Tuscany he wrote about  
> _This page is a real place: Tuscany, in the middle of Italy, with hill towns, vineyards and a coast far to the west._  
> _The writer was Carlo Lorenzini. He called himself Collodi, after a Tuscan town, and his story first ran in a children’s newspaper in 1881._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Pinocchio comes from Tuscany in Italy, and that Collodi first published it in a children’s newspaper in 1881._

_The ink goes wet under your fingers, and then it is rain. You and your Nubbin are standing in a steep stone lane, getting wetter._  
_One door is open, with sawdust on the step and a warm smell of pine. You go in, because the rain has decided for you._  
**Master Cherry**: Come in, come in, shut the weather out. Mind the shavings. Mind the cat.  
**Master Cherry**: There isn’t a cat. Mind it anyway. It saves arguments.  
_The carpenter’s nose is so round and red and shiny that it looks like a ripe cherry. Everyone calls him Master Cherry._  
**Master Cherry**: I’m making a table leg. Out of this. A firewood log, a nothing log. Nothing special about it at all.  
_He spits on his hands and lifts the axe._  
**A Small Voice**: Don’t hit me too hard!  

#### `a13-01-page-done`

_Master Cherry looks under the bench, in the cupboard and up the chimney. There is nobody in the shop but you, and you are a stranger._  
**Master Cherry**: Did you say that? You didn’t say that. Your little friend didn’t say that. Nobody said that.  
**Master Cherry**: I imagined it. Wine and weather. That’s all it was.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): tree rings: one ring for each year of growth  
> _Master Cherry points at the end of the log. Inside it are rings, like a target. How might you tell how old the tree was?_  
> - ✅ Count the rings. Each one is a year. → Yes. Trees add one ring a year. A wide ring means a good year with plenty of rain and sun. A thin ring means a hard one.
> - Measure how tall the log is. → A log can be any length. The rings inside tell the age: one ring for every year the tree grew.
> - You cannot tell. → You can! Count the rings from the middle outwards. Each ring is one year.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a tree grows one ring each year and that rings can be counted to find its age._


#### `a13-01-plane`

_He gives the log a proper whack this time._  
**A Small Voice**: Ow! That hurt!  
_Master Cherry sits down on the floor, very suddenly. Then he gets up, very slowly, and picks up his plane instead._  
_He planes. The log giggles._  
**A Small Voice**: Stop it! You’re tickling!  
_Master Cherry falls flat like a sack of meal. His red nose goes quite blue with fright._  
_Somebody knocks, and in comes a little old man in a bright yellow wig._  
_The wig is exactly the colour of polenta, so the boys of the town call him Polendina. He hates it more than anything in the world._  
**Geppetto**: Good morning, Master Antonio. What are you doing down there?  
**Master Cherry**: Teaching the ants their letters. What brings you, Geppetto?  
**Geppetto**: An idea. A wooden puppet that dances and fences and turns somersaults. I’ll take him round the world and earn my crust.  
**A Small Voice**: Good idea, Polendina!  
_Geppetto turns the colour of a beetroot, and looks straight at Master Cherry._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): seeing a scene from two points of view  
> _You know the log spoke. Geppetto doesn’t. He thinks his friend called him a rude name._  
> _Is it fair to be angry with someone before you know the facts?_  
> - No. Find out first, then decide. → That’s a fair answer. Geppetto only has half the story, and so he is cross with the wrong person.
> - Yes. The name is rude whoever said it. → That’s fair too. Being called a name hurts. But the person who said it matters, and he has picked the wrong one.
> - You should tell him it was the log. → That’s fair. You do know the truth, and a true word can stop a quarrel. Whether he would believe it is another matter.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how knowing only half the story changes how we judge someone._


**Choices**

- **Tell Geppetto it was the log.**
    - **Geppetto**: The log. A log called me Polendina. And I suppose the bench calls me Grandad.
    - So that went well.
- **Keep out of it. It’s their argument.**
    - You keep out of it. That lasts about a second and a half.

#### `a13-01-plane-done`

_The two old men go at each other like cats on a roof._  
_When they come apart, Geppetto is wearing Master Cherry’s grey wig, and Master Cherry the yellow._  
_They swap back, shake hands, and swear to be friends for the rest of their lives._  
_Master Cherry gives him the log very gladly. It jumps out of his hands and cracks Geppetto on the shins, and they start all over again._  
_In the end, peace. Geppetto puts the log on his shoulder and limps off, and the rain has stopped._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what helps repair a friendship after a quarrel  
> _The old men argued, swapped wigs and made peace twice in one morning. What mends a quarrel best?_  
> - ✅ Listening, saying sorry, and shaking hands. → Yes. Listening shows you care what the other person felt, and sorry and a handshake close it.
> - Waiting for the other person to apologise first. → That feels fair, but it can leave the quarrel open for a very long time. Someone has to go first.
> - Pretending it never happened. → That sometimes works for tiny things. For bigger ones, the hurt stays unless somebody talks about it.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about listening, apologising and shaking hands as ways to mend a quarrel._


#### `a13-01-complete`

**Geppetto**: You. The traveller. You’ve no roof, have you? I can always tell. I’ve hardly a roof myself. Come on.  
_His room is under the stairs, lit by one small window. A chair, a poor sort of bed, and a table that has seen better tables._  
_In the back wall there is a fireplace with a fire in it and a pot on top, merrily steaming. It is painted._  
**Geppetto**: It’s a very good painting. It keeps me warm, if I don’t think about it.  
**Geppetto**: You sleep in the corner. I’d offer you supper, but that’s painted too.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): what a setting tells us about a character  
> _Geppetto has a painted fire and painted supper. What does that tell you about him?_  
> - ✅ He is very poor, but cheerful and inventive. → Yes. He can’t afford a real fire, so he paints one and makes a joke of it. The room tells us who he is.
> - He is a bad painter. → The painting is called “very good” in the story. It is meant to tell us about Geppetto, not about his brushwork.
> - He is rich and plays tricks. → There’s a poor bed and a tired table. Look at the details: the room says poor, not rich.
> _For grown-ups: Used details of a setting (a painted fire) to understand a character’s life and spirit._

_He hangs his felt cap on the nail by the door._  
_Your Nubbin climbs into it, turns round twice and settles, like a pip in a pod._  
**Geppetto**: Ha. It may stay. It’s the warmest thing in the house.  

### Glossary

- **plane**: a tool that shaves thin curls off a piece of wood to make it smooth
- **crust**: a living, the money you earn to eat; also the hard outside of bread

## A13-2. Geppetto Carves a Puppet

- `a13-02-s1`: Hold the lamp while Geppetto carves. · _Stand at his elbow with the lamp. Watch the nose._
- `a13-02-s2`: Help Geppetto teach the puppet to walk. · _Hold one wooden hand; Geppetto holds the other. Mind the door._

#### `a13-02-carve`

_Geppetto lays the log on his bench, rolls up his sleeves and looks at it for a long time, the way you look at a letter before you open it._  
**Geppetto**: What shall I call him? Pinocchio. I knew a whole family of Pinocchios once, and they all did splendidly.  
**Geppetto**: The richest of them begged for a living. You see? Lucky.  
_A pinocchio is a pine nut. It suits a thing made of pine, with a hard little head on it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): pinocchio means pine nut, and a name can carry a joke  
> _Pinocchio is a real Tuscan word for a pine nut, the small seed inside a pine cone. People in Italy put pine nuts in pesto._  
> _A pine nut is hard, small and tough. Collodi chose it to name a hard-headed little puppet carved from pine._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pinocchio is a Tuscan word for a pine nut and why the name suits the puppet._

_He carves the hair, then the forehead, then the eyes. The eyes move, and stare at him._  
**Geppetto**: Wooden eyes, why are you looking at me?  
_Nobody answers. He carves the nose, and the nose begins to grow._  
_He cuts it shorter, and it grows longer. He cuts it again, and it grows again, until he gives up and leaves it._  
_He carves the mouth. Before he has quite finished, it laughs at him and sticks its tongue out._  
**Geppetto**: Stop laughing!  
_The mouth stops laughing. It goes on sticking its tongue out._  

**Choices**

- **Point out that the nose is growing again.**
    - **Geppetto**: I know. I’ve decided not to notice. You should try it.
- **Keep the lamp steady and say nothing.**
    - You keep the lamp steady. Geppetto works faster, the way people do when their work is watching them back.

#### `a13-02-carve-done`

_Geppetto carves the hands. The moment they are finished, they snatch the yellow wig off his head and put it on their own._  
**Geppetto**: Pinocchio! Give that back this minute!  
_Pinocchio gives it back. His eyes are laughing._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): burattino is Italian for a hand puppet; the book’s puppet has no strings  
> _Collodi’s word for Pinocchio is burattino, an Italian puppet worked by a hand inside it, not by strings._  
> _That is why this page never mentions strings. Pinocchio moves on his own, which is the trouble._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the Italian word burattino and that Collodi’s puppet is not a string puppet._


#### `a13-02-legs`

**Geppetto**: You young rascal. You’re not even finished, and already you have no respect for your father.  
_He carves the legs and the feet. The first thing the feet do is kick him on the end of the nose._  
**Geppetto**: I deserved that. I ought to have thought of it before I made them.  
_He sets Pinocchio on the floor to teach him to walk. You take one wooden hand, and he takes the other._  
_The legs are stiff, then less stiff. Pinocchio takes one step, and another, and then he is running._  
**Pinocchio**: Ha! Legs! I’ve got LEGS!  
_He is out of the door before either of you can shut it, and away down the street, clack-clack-clack on the cobbles._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): walking works because the foot pushes back on the ground and friction grips  
> _To walk, your foot pushes backwards on the ground. Friction grips, and the ground pushes you forwards. That is an unbalanced force._  
> _Pinocchio’s first steps are wobbly because his balance and his grip are brand new. Babies learn it the same way._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that walking uses a push against the ground and the grip of friction, which are forces._

**Geppetto**: Catch him! Catch him!  
_People in the street watch him go by, and nobody catches him. They are laughing too hard to catch anything._  

#### `a13-02-street`

_At the bottom of the street a carabineer steps out and catches Pinocchio neatly by the nose. It is a very convenient nose for it._  
_Geppetto arrives out of breath and gives him a good shake. Pinocchio throws himself on the cobbles and refuses to walk another step._  
_A crowd gathers. The crowd decides, as crowds do, that the poor little puppet is frightened of the dreadful old man._  
**Carabineer**: Well. If that’s how he treats them, he can come along with me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): judging a situation from only part of what you saw  
> _The crowd saw a puppet on the floor and a shaking old man, and decided who was in the wrong._  
> _Have you ever judged a situation from only part of it?_  
> - Yes. I got it wrong, and I remember how it felt. → That’s a fair answer. Looking back is how we get better at pausing before we decide.
> - I try to ask what happened first. → That’s a fair answer. Asking questions first is how a crowd could have helped Geppetto.
> - I am not sure. It is hard to know what you missed. → That’s a fair answer, and it is the heart of the problem. If you cannot tell what you missed, it is wiser to wait and ask.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how seeing only part of an event can lead to the wrong judgement._


#### `a13-02-complete`

_So it is Geppetto who is marched off to prison, crying all the way._  
**Geppetto**: Wretched boy! I worked so hard to make him a good puppet. It serves me right. I should have thought.  
_Your Nubbin, still in the felt cap he snatched up as he ran, jumps out as he goes._  
_The carabineer walks him round the corner, and the street is empty._  
_Pinocchio picks himself up, brushes off his knees and runs home over the fields, as fast as a hare with somewhere to be._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): speed, distance and time  
> _A hare can run about 60 kilometres every hour, which is 1 kilometre every minute._  
> _If Pinocchio could keep up that pace for 5 minutes, how far would he get?_  
> - ✅ 5 kilometres → Yes. 1 kilometre a minute for 5 minutes is 5 kilometres. Pinocchio is not quite that quick, but the idea is the same.
> - 60 kilometres → That is how far in a whole hour. In 5 minutes it is only a small slice of the hour: 5 kilometres.
> - 15 kilometres → Try 1 kilometre a minute: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. After 5 minutes, 5 kilometres.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a speed, distance and time problem: 1 km a minute for 5 minutes is 5 km._

_You follow. The room under the stairs is very quiet without the old man in it._  

### Glossary

- **carabineer**: an Italian police officer; the word comes from the carbine, a short rifle
- **burattino**: the Italian word for a puppet worked by a hand inside it, not by strings

## A13-3. The Talking-cricket

- `a13-03-s1`: Find what is going cri-cri-cri in the dark. · _Listen along the wall by the hearth._
- `a13-03-s2`: Listen to the Talking-cricket. Then decide what to do about the hearth. · _Hear him out. When it goes quiet, you’ll know what you can do._

#### `a13-03-cri`

_Pinocchio bangs the door shut, sits on the floor and lets out a great sigh. A whole room, and nobody in it to tell him anything._  
**Pinocchio**: Mine. All of it. The chair, the table, the painted fire. You can stay too, if you don’t tell me anything.  
_Then, from somewhere in the room, a small sound: cri-cri-cri._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): crickets make sound by rubbing their wings, and chirp faster when it is warmer  
> _A real cricket sings by rubbing one wing against a rough ridge on the other._  
> _The rubbing makes the wing vibrate, and a vibration is a sound._  
> _It chirps faster on a warm night and slower on a cool one. Some people count the chirps to guess the temperature._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that crickets chirp by vibrating their wings and chirp faster when it is warm._

**Pinocchio**: Who’s that?  
_Cri-cri-cri, from the wall by the hearth. Your Nubbin’s ears go straight up._  
**Pinocchio**: It’s you, isn’t it? Doing a voice. Stop doing a voice.  

#### `a13-03-cri-done`

_There on the wall, climbing slowly upwards, is a big cricket. He has the air of somebody who has paid the rent._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): figurative language: “the air of somebody who has paid the rent”  
> _The narrator says the cricket has “the air of somebody who has paid the rent”. What does that tell you about how he behaves?_  
> - ✅ He acts as if he belongs there and has every right. → Yes. Someone who has paid the rent feels at home and expects respect. It is a joke about how grand a small cricket can look.
> - He is carrying coins. → The cricket doesn’t carry coins. It is an image, a picture in words, for how he stands and moves.
> - He is angry about money. → He isn’t cross about money. The phrase is about confidence: he is the oldest resident, and he knows it.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of a figure of speech and how it shows character._

**The Talking-cricket**: It is I. The Talking-cricket. I have lived in this room for more than a hundred years.  

#### `a13-03-cricket`

**Pinocchio**: Well, it’s my room now. Off you go. And don’t look back.  
**The Talking-cricket**: I shan’t go until I have told you one great truth.  
**The Talking-cricket**: Boys who turn their backs on their fathers, and run off from home to please themselves, come to no good. Sooner or later. Usually sooner.  
**Pinocchio**: Sing away, Cricket. I’m off at first light. If I stay, they’ll send me to school, and I’d rather chase butterflies.  
**The Talking-cricket**: Then you’ll grow up a perfect donkey, and everyone will laugh at you.  
**The Talking-cricket**: At least learn a trade. Something to earn an honest crust.  
**Pinocchio**: There’s only one trade I fancy. Eating, drinking, sleeping, having fun, and wandering about from morning till night.  
**The Talking-cricket**: Everyone who follows that trade ends up in hospital or in prison. I am sorry for you, Pinocchio.  
**Pinocchio**: Sorry? Why?  
**The Talking-cricket**: Because you are a puppet. And, worse, because you have a wooden head.  
_Pinocchio grabs the mallet off the bench and throws it, not really aiming. That is the trouble with not really aiming._  
_It catches the cricket and knocks him clean off the wall, down into the cold ash of the hearth. Then nothing._  
**Pinocchio**: I didn’t… He shouldn’t have said wooden head. He shouldn’t have.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): responsibility for something you did without meaning to  
> _Pinocchio says “not really aiming”. He didn’t mean to hit the cricket. Does that make it not his fault?_  
> - It still matters. He threw it, so he should put it right. → That’s a fair answer. Not meaning to hurt someone doesn’t take the hurt away, and putting it right is what makes it better.
> - Not at all his fault. It was an accident. → That’s a fair answer. Accidents happen. But a careless throw while you are angry is not quite the same as a true accident.
> - Partly. The cricket provoked him, but he still threw it. → That’s a fair answer, and probably the closest to the truth. Both things can be true at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about responsibility when you hurt someone without quite meaning to._


**Choices**

- **Search the hearth.**
    - You kneel at the hearth and sift the ash with your fingers. Your Nubbin finds him first, and squeaks.
    - He is on his back, grey with ash, one leg going round and round like a little wheel. He is very much alive, and very cross.
    - **The Talking-cricket**: I am not hurt. I am insulted. There is a difference, and I am a hundred years old, and I know it.
    - You carry him out in your cupped hands to the hedge by the door, and set him on a leaf.
    - He straightens his feelers with great dignity.
    - **The Talking-cricket**: Thank you. Tell him nothing. He wouldn’t listen. He never listens.
- **Leave it. It’s his mess to put right.**
    - You leave it. Pinocchio looks at the hearth for a long time, and then turns his back on it.
    - Later, when he isn’t looking, you look. There is a tiny track through the ash, all the way to the crack under the door.
    - Whatever made it was walking. Slowly, and in a temper, but walking.

#### `a13-03-cricket-done`

_The room is quiet._  
_Pinocchio sits at the table with his chin on his fists and says nothing for a long time, which for him is a minute._  
**Pinocchio**: Anyway. I’m hungry.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive when he changes the subject  
> _After a long silence Pinocchio says, “Anyway. I’m hungry.” Why might he change the subject like that?_  
> - ✅ He feels guilty and does not want to talk about it. → Yes. People often change the subject when something is too uncomfortable to face.
> - He has completely forgotten the cricket. → He sat in silence for a whole minute, which for him is a long time. He hasn’t forgotten.
> - He is just greedy. → He is hungry, but the long quiet before it hints at something else underneath.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s hidden feeling from how he behaves._

_Night comes on, and with it a hunger like a small dog barking inside him._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, notice): tummy rumbles come from the gut moving food and air about  
> _When your stomach rumbles, the muscles in your gut are squeezing air and liquid along._  
> _This happens all the time, and you hear it more when your stomach is empty._  
> _So a rumble does not mean something is wrong. It means your body is getting ready for the next meal._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a rumbling tummy is the gut’s muscles moving air and liquid, and is normal._

**Pinocchio**: Do you think the cricket was right? No. Don’t answer. I’m too hungry for answers.  
_You don’t answer, and your Nubbin curls up against your boot. Outside, the wind is getting up._  
**Pinocchio**: Is there any supper? There’s always supper. Somewhere.  

### Glossary

- **provoke**: to make someone angry or upset on purpose or by accident

- `a13-04-s1`: Help Pinocchio look for something to eat. · _Try the cupboard, the drawers, and the heap of sweepings in the corner._
- `a13-04-s2`: Watch Pinocchio cook his egg. · _Stand back from the pan. Something is about to happen to it._
- `a13-04-s3`: Go with Pinocchio into the storm, to the village. · _Keep your Nubbin under your coat. It’s a long way for very little._

#### `a13-04-hungry`

_Pinocchio runs to the fire to lift the lid off the pot. His nose goes straight through the canvas, where the pot is painted on it._  
**Pinocchio**: Painted. Even the soup’s painted. What kind of house is this?  
_He tries the drawers: a button, a cork, a bent nail. He tries the cupboard: dust, and a smell of dust._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, do): sorting materials by their properties: cork floats, a nail sinks  
> _Sort what is in Geppetto’s drawer by what it is made of: wood and cork on one side, iron on the other._  
> _Then guess which will float. Cork and wood are light for their size, so they float._  
> _A bent iron nail is heavy for its size, so it sinks._  
> Check: `edu:sort:drawer-things:float-or-sink`
> _For grown-ups: Sorted everyday objects by material and predicted which would float or sink._

_He would eat anything now: a cherry stone, a fish bone, the crust off a crust._  
**Pinocchio**: The cricket said this would happen. Not this exactly. He didn’t mention soup.  
_Your Nubbin goes to the heap of sweepings in the corner and begins to dig, as if it has an idea._  

**Choices**

- **Dig with your Nubbin.**
    - You dig too. It isn’t dignified, but it’s company.
- **Tell Pinocchio there’s sure to be something.**
    - **Pinocchio**: There’d better be. I’m wooden all the way through, and all of it is empty.

#### `a13-04-hungry-done`

_In the sweepings there is something round and white. An egg!_  
**Pinocchio**: An egg! A whole egg! I’ll fry it. No, I’ll poach it. No, I can’t wait to decide. I’ll fry it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): the life cycle of a chicken  
> _A hen sits on her eggs to keep them warm. About how long does it take for a chick to grow and hatch?_  
> - ✅ About 3 weeks (21 days). → Yes. A chick grows for about 21 days, fed by the yolk, kept warm by its mother. Then it pecks its way out.
> - About 3 hours. → Far too quick! A whole chick needs time to grow bones, feathers and a beak. It takes about three weeks.
> - About 3 months. → A bit too long. Chicks hatch after about three weeks of warmth.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a chick takes about 21 days to grow inside its egg._


#### `a13-04-egg`

_He sets a little pan on the brazier, with a drop of water in it for want of oil. The water begins to steam._  
_He cracks the egg over the pan. Out of it, instead of a yolk, comes a small, fluffy and extremely polite chick._  
**The Chick**: Many thanks, Master Pinocchio, for saving me the trouble of breaking the shell.  
**The Chick**: Good evening. Kind regards to all at home.  
_It flies out of the open window and away into the dark._  
_Pinocchio stands with the empty shell in his hands and his mouth wide open._  
**Pinocchio**: The cricket was right. The cricket was RIGHT. I wish I’d never run off. Babbo would have fed me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): regret: wishing something had been different, and what comes next  
> _Pinocchio says, “I wish I’d never run off.” Is wishing enough to put something right?_  
> - No. You have to do something about it as well. → That’s a fair answer. A wish can start the change, but a sorry, a repair or a new choice finishes it.
> - Yes. Once you truly feel sorry, it is fixed. → That’s a fair answer. Truly feeling sorry is the first step, and it matters. But the person you hurt may need to hear it or see it.
> - It depends what went wrong. → That’s a fair answer. Some things need only a thought, some need an apology, and some need real repair.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what regret is and whether wishing is enough to put things right._


#### `a13-04-egg-done`

_Outside, the wind has turned into a storm. Pinocchio puts his cap on._  
**Pinocchio**: There’s a village. Somebody in it will give me bread. I’ll ask nicely. I can ask nicely.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): why many Tuscan villages are built on hills  
> _Many old Tuscan villages sit on top of hills, with the farm fields below. Why might people have built them there long ago?_  
> - ✅ To see enemies coming, and to be easy to defend. → Yes. A hilltop gives a long view and is harder to attack. The fields and vines stayed down below in the good soil.
> - Because hills are warmer in winter. → Sometimes, but the main reason was safety: a hilltop is easier to watch and defend.
> - Because nobody wanted the valley. → The valleys are the best farmland! People built homes up on the hills to keep safe, and walked down to farm.
> _For grown-ups: Learned why many old Tuscan villages stand on hilltops: for the view and for defence._


#### `a13-04-storm`

_The night is black, with thunder rolling over the hills and lightning that turns the road white. The village is shut up tight._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): estimating distance from the gap between lightning and thunder  
> _Light arrives at once, but sound is slow: about 3 seconds for every kilometre. You count 6 seconds between a flash and its thunder._  
> _How far away is the lightning?_  
> - ✅ About 2 kilometres. → Yes. 6 seconds at 3 seconds a kilometre is 2 kilometres. A bigger gap means a farther storm.
> - About 6 kilometres. → Divide the 6 seconds by 3: it is 2 kilometres, not 6.
> - About 18 kilometres. → You multiplied. We divide: 6 seconds ÷ 3 seconds per kilometre = 2 kilometres.
> _For grown-ups: Estimated how far lightning is by dividing the seconds before thunder by 3._

_Every shutter is closed, and there isn’t even a dog in the street. It is like a village put away in a drawer for the night._  
_Pinocchio finds a doorbell and pulls it, and pulls it again, and goes on pulling it._  
**Old Man in a Nightcap**: What do you want at this hour?  
_An old man in a nightcap has put his head out of the window above._  
**Pinocchio**: Will you be kind enough to give me a bit of bread?  
**Old Man in a Nightcap**: Wait there. I’ll be straight down.  
_He isn’t straight down. He comes back to the window with a basin, and empties the whole of it over Pinocchio’s head._  

#### `a13-04-storm-done`

_You walk back together through the rain, Pinocchio dripping and you dripping. Your Nubbin, under your coat, is the only dry thing in the world._  
_At home he puts his wet feet up on the brazier to dry, and falls asleep in the chair. You sleep in the corner._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): burning is a change that cannot be reversed  
> _Pinocchio’s wooden feet are on the glowing brazier all night._  
> _Which change could be reversed afterwards: a puddle freezing and thawing, or wood burning to charcoal?_  
> - ✅ The puddle. Wood cannot be un-burnt. → Yes. Water freezes and melts back again, but burnt wood becomes charcoal and ash for good.
> - The wood, with some glue. → Glue can join pieces, but it cannot turn charcoal back into wood. Burning changes the material itself.
> - Neither can be reversed. → Freezing is reversible: thaw the ice and you have water again. Burning is not.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that melting and freezing can be reversed but burning cannot._

_In the morning there is a knock at the door. Pinocchio wakes up, yawning._  
**Geppetto**: Pinocchio! It’s me. Open the door.  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo!  
_He jumps up to run to the door, and falls flat on his face._  
_In the night his feet have burned away on the brazier, right down to two black stumps. He didn’t feel a thing; he’s wood._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-2, notice): pain is a warning signal that protects us  
> _Pinocchio felt nothing, and that is the problem. In people and animals, pain is an alarm: nerves tell the brain “move away, this is harming you”._  
> _Without it we would not pull our hands from a hot pan. Pain is unpleasant, but it is one of the senses that keeps us alive._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pain is a protective signal sent by the nerves, so feeling it helps keep us safe._

_Which is a mercy, and also the whole problem._  

### Glossary

- **brazier**: a metal pan or stand that holds a fire or hot coals to warm a room
- **sweepings**: the dust and scraps swept up from a floor

## A13-5. Three Pears

- `a13-05-s1`: Let Geppetto in. · _Pinocchio can’t reach the door now. The window is open; give Geppetto a hand over the sill._
- `a13-05-s2`: Help with breakfast: three pears, peeled. · _Pinocchio wants them peeled. Don’t throw the peel away. You’ll see._
- `a13-05-s3`: Wait at the window while Geppetto goes out into the snow. · _Keep the room warm for him. Watch the road._

#### `a13-05-window`

**Pinocchio**: Babbo, I can’t open the door! My feet have gone!  
**Geppetto**: Gone? Gone where? Open this door at once.  
**Pinocchio**: I can’t stand up! I’ll have to walk on my knees for the rest of my life!  
_Geppetto thinks this is another trick, so he climbs in through the window._  
_He tries to; he is not a young man, and it is not a large window._  
_You lean out and take his arm, and he comes over the sill like a sack of meal._  
**Geppetto**: Now, you young— Oh. Oh, my boy. Your feet.  
_He came in meaning to give Pinocchio the scolding of his life. He looks at the feet, and gathers him up instead, and kisses him._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): choosing comfort before a scolding when someone is hurt  
> _Geppetto came in to scold, and hugged instead. When should the scolding come, if at all?_  
> - After the person is safe and calm, if it is still needed. → That’s a fair answer. People hear a lesson much better once they feel safe.
> - Straight away, while it is fresh. → That’s a fair answer. A quick word can help. But if someone is frightened or hurt, they won’t take it in.
> - Never. A hug teaches more. → That’s a fair answer. Kindness teaches a lot, though sometimes a lesson needs to be said as well.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to comfort and when to correct someone who is hurt._


#### `a13-05-window-done`

**Pinocchio**: I’m so hungry, Babbo. I’ve had nothing but a chick, and the chick left.  
_Geppetto takes three pears out of his pocket: his breakfast. He holds them out and says nothing about it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): sharing equally: halves  
> _Imagine Geppetto cut the three pears in half and shared them equally with Pinocchio. How many halves would each of them get?_  
> - ✅ 3 halves each. → Yes. Three pears make 6 halves, and 6 shared by 2 is 3 halves each: one and a half pears.
> - 6 halves each. → There are 6 halves in total. Shared between 2 people, it is 3 each.
> - 2 halves each. → Count them: 3 pears × 2 halves = 6 halves. Split between two, each gets 3.
> _For grown-ups: Used halves to share three pears equally between two people._


#### `a13-05-pears`

**Pinocchio**: Peel them for me, please. I can’t eat skins. I’m very particular.  
**Geppetto**: Particular. At your age. With your feet in the fire. Well, well.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, ask): seeds spread by animals, and a seed inside a fruit  
> _Pinocchio throws away a pear core with the little seeds in it. How might an animal help a fruit’s seeds travel and grow?_  
> - ✅ It eats the fruit and drops the seeds somewhere new. → Yes. Birds and animals eat fruit and carry the seeds away. Many seeds even sprout better after being eaten and dropped.
> - It plants them with its paws. → A few animals bury seeds, like squirrels with nuts. But eating and dropping them is the most common way.
> - Animals do not help seeds at all. → They do a great deal! Birds, mice and foxes carry fruit and spread seeds far from the parent tree.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals spread seeds by eating fruit and dropping or burying the seeds._

_He peels them anyway, and lays the peel and the cores in a corner of the table._  
_Pinocchio eats the first pear in two bites and throws the core away. Then the second, then the third._  
**Pinocchio**: I’m still hungry.  
**Geppetto**: Well, I’ve nothing else. Except the peel and the cores.  
**Pinocchio**: I don’t eat peel. I don’t eat cores.  
_He looks at them for quite a long while._  

**Choices**

- **Ask Geppetto whether he has eaten.**
    - **Geppetto**: Me? Oh, yes. Ages ago. Hours.
    - His stomach rumbles, loudly. He talks over it.
- **Put the peel and cores on a plate, for later.**
    - You put them on a plate. Pinocchio says he won’t, and you say nothing, and the plate waits.

#### `a13-05-pears-done`

_A minute later the peel is gone, and the cores after it. Pinocchio pats his front._  
**Pinocchio**: I feel very well now.  
**Geppetto**: You see? It doesn’t pay to be too fussy, my boy. You never know what’s coming.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): scarcity: when there is not enough, we choose between needs and wants  
> _Geppetto has only enough for one breakfast. He gave it all away. In a hard time, how do we decide what to spend on first?_  
> - ✅ Needs first, like food and warmth, then wants. → Yes. A need is something you must have to be well. A want is nice but can wait. Choosing needs first is how families get through hard times.
> - Wants first, because they make us happy. → Wants do bring joy. But if the needs go unmet, the joy does not last long.
> - Whatever is cheapest. → Cheap helps, but it is not the test. Ask first: do I need this to be safe, fed and warm?
> _For grown-ups: Learned to sort needs from wants when there is not enough to go round._


#### `a13-05-snow`

_Pinocchio cries for new feet until Geppetto gives in. They take an hour, and they are the best feet he has ever made._  
_From the offcut, while the glue dries, he starts a little wooden Nubbin for you. He gets as far as the ears._  
**Geppetto**: I’ll finish it tomorrow. There’s always tomorrow for the small things.  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo, I’ll go to school! I’ll learn a trade, and I’ll look after you when you’re old.  
_Geppetto makes him a suit out of flowered paper, a pair of shoes out of bark, and a cap out of the soft middle of a loaf._  
_Pinocchio admires himself in a basin of water. He looks, he says, exactly like a gentleman._  
**Pinocchio**: But I haven’t got a spelling-book. You can’t go to school without a spelling-book.  
**Geppetto**: No. You can’t.  
_Geppetto has no money at all. He puts on his old coat, all patches and darns, and goes out, and it is snowing._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): a coat keeps you warm by trapping air and slowing heat loss  
> _Heat flows from warm things to cold ones, so your body is always losing a little to the winter air._  
> _A coat does not make heat. It traps a layer of still air and wool, which slows the escape._  
> _Geppetto’s patched old coat was doing that job._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a coat slows the loss of body heat by trapping a layer of air._


#### `a13-05-coat`

_He comes back an hour later with a spelling-book under his arm, in his shirt-sleeves. There is snow on his shoulders._  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo, where’s your coat?  
**Geppetto**: I sold it.  
**Pinocchio**: Why?  
**Geppetto**: It was too warm.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a kind not-quite-truth: is it ever right?  
> _Geppetto says his coat “was too warm”, in the snow. It is not true._  
> _Is it ever right to say something that isn’t quite true, to be kind?_  
> - Yes, when the truth would only add to someone’s worry. → That’s a fair answer. Geppetto does it out of love, so Pinocchio will not carry the cost. But he also hides something that Pinocchio might want to know.
> - No. A better kindness is to be honest. → That’s a fair answer. A kindness built on the truth is more lasting. But it is hard to see how Geppetto could have said it gently.
> - It depends how much the truth matters. → That’s a fair answer. A gift hidden to spare a child’s guilt is not the same as hiding a danger. Where do you draw the line?
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a loving, not-quite-true remark can be right._

_Pinocchio understands. He throws his arms round the old man’s neck and kisses him all over his face._

**Pinocchio**: Then I’ll earn lots of money, and buy Babbo a new coat. A gold one. With diamonds for buttons.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): predicting what will happen from what a character has already done  
> _Pinocchio promises school, work and a gold coat. He has made promises like this before. What do you predict will happen?_  
> - ✅ He will get distracted again. → Probably! His past behaviour, running off and chasing butterflies, is the clue. Good readers use clues like that.
> - He will keep every promise. → It is a nice hope. But he has said sweet things and then run off already, so the story gives us reason to doubt.
> - He will turn into a boy by lunchtime. → That would be quick! Nothing in the story so far suggests it. Look at what he has done instead.
> _For grown-ups: Made a prediction using clues from a character’s earlier actions._

- **particular**: fussy: hard to please about small details

## A13-6. The Puppet Show

- `a13-06-s1`: Walk Pinocchio to school. · _Keep to the road. Something down by the sea is making a lot of noise._
- `a13-06-s2`: Get into the puppet theatre. · _You have no ticket. Your Nubbin knows a gap under the canvas._

#### `a13-06-road`

_Halfway to school there is music: fifes, and a big drum going boom, boom, from down towards the sea._  
**Pinocchio**: Do you hear that? Fifes. And a drum.  

> **Lesson** (music, 1-PS4-1, ask): pitch: faster vibrations make higher sounds  
> _A fife is a tiny, shrill flute. The big drum goes “boom”. Which one makes the higher note, and why?_  
> - ✅ The fife: its air column is short and vibrates fast. → Yes. A fast vibration gives a high note and a slow one gives a low note. A small fife vibrates quickly; a big drum skin moves slowly.
> - The drum: it is louder. → Loud and high are different. Pitch is about how fast something vibrates. A big drum vibrates slowly, so its note is low.
> - They make the same note. → Listen again: the fife squeaks high, the drum thuds low. Fast vibration is high; slow vibration is low.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pitch depends on the speed of a vibration: fast is high, slow is low._

**Pinocchio**: School will be there tomorrow. School is always there. That’s the whole point of school.  
_He stands in the middle of the road, one foot pointing to school and one foot pointing to the music._  
**Pinocchio**: Today, the music. Tomorrow, school. School can’t run away.  
_At the bottom of the hill there is a great painted tent with flags on it. The poster says THE GREAT PUPPET THEATRE._  

**Choices**

- **Remind him what the spelling-book cost.**
    - **Pinocchio**: I know what it cost! I’ll go tomorrow. I’ll go twice tomorrow.
    - He doesn’t look at you while he says it.
- **Say nothing. It’s his road.**
    - You say nothing. He looks at you, as if he’d been hoping you would.

_A ticket costs four pennies, and Pinocchio hasn’t got four pennies. He has a spelling-book._  
_He sells it to a man who deals in old clothes, for four pennies exactly, before you can catch his arm._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): what something is worth: cost, value and trade-offs  
> _The book cost Geppetto his only coat. Pinocchio sold it for one evening’s ticket. Is something worth only what someone will pay for it?_  
> - No. It is worth what it cost the person who gave it. → That’s a fair answer. The four pennies were the price, but the coat was the cost, and it was paid in cold and love.
> - Yes. A thing is worth what it will sell for. → That’s a fair answer for the market. But some things are valued for who gave them, and the market misses that.
> - It depends who is asking. → That’s a fair answer. To a shopkeeper, four pennies; to Geppetto, a coat. Both are true at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between what a thing sells for and what it cost to the giver._


#### `a13-06-show`

_You crawl in under the canvas behind your Nubbin, and find a place at the back among the boots._  
_The curtain is up. On the stage Harlequin and Punchinello are quarrelling, as they always do, and about to hit each other with a stick._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Harlequin and Punchinello come from the old Italian masked theatre, commedia dell’arte  
> _Harlequin and Punchinello are stock characters from commedia dell’arte, Italian street theatre that began in the 1500s._  
> _Actors in masks acted out the same types again and again._  
> _Harlequin wears a patchwork of coloured diamonds and is quick and clever. Punchinello, from Naples, wears white and a black mask with a hooked nose._  
> _Punch of “Punch and Judy” is his English cousin._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Harlequin and Punchinello are traditional masked characters from Italian commedia dell’arte._

_The audience is laughing so much it hurts. Then Harlequin stops, and points out over everybody’s heads._  
**Harlequin**: Look! Look there! Is it? It IS!  
**Punchinello**: Our brother! It’s our brother Pinocchio!  
_Every puppet on the stage runs to the front. Pinocchio jumps from the cheap seats to the band, and from the band onto the stage._  
_Such hugging, such kissing, such friendly punches on the nose!_  
_The audience shouts for the show; they have paid. The puppets don’t care: they have a brother back._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): belonging: how a warm welcome feels  
> _The puppets stop their own show to hug someone they have never met. Why might a welcome like that matter so much to Pinocchio?_  
> - He has never belonged anywhere before. → That’s a fair answer. He is two days old and has run from everyone. Here, people like him are glad he exists.
> - He likes being the centre of attention. → That’s a fair answer too. Pinocchio does love a crowd. Being wanted and being watched can feel alike at first.
> - It doesn’t matter much; it’s only a show. → That’s a fair answer to think about. Notice, though, that the puppets choose their brother over the paying audience.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about belonging, and how it feels to be welcomed by people like you._


#### `a13-06-show-done`

_Then the showman comes out._  
_He is a giant of a man, with a black beard that reaches the floor, so that he treads on it when he walks._  
_His mouth is as wide as an oven, and his eyes are like two red lanterns. He cracks a long whip, and every puppet goes still._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes: comparing with like or as  
> _“His eyes are like two red lanterns.” Which of these is also a simile, a comparison using like or as?_  
> - ✅ His beard was as long as a river. → Yes. It compares the beard to a river using “as … as”. Similes make us picture something bigger than the plain words do.
> - His beard was a river of black. → That is a metaphor: it says one thing IS another. A simile uses “like” or “as” to compare.
> - He had a very long beard. → That is a plain description. A simile compares one thing to another, with “like” or “as”.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a simile and told it apart from a metaphor and a plain description._

**Fire-eater**: What is all this? Who is that?

_Pinocchio is hung by the back of his paper jacket on a nail in the wings, among the other puppets, kicking his bark heels._  
_The showman is called Fire-eater. You hope it is only a name._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): real fire-eating is a dangerous skill that only trained performers should do  
> _Real fire-eaters are trained performers who have practised for years, with safety crews close by, and even then they are sometimes burned._  
> _Fire is never a game. If you ever see a flame that is out of control, move away, and tell a grown-up straight away._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fire is dangerous, that only trained performers handle it, and to tell a grown-up about uncontrolled flame._


### Glossary

- **fife**: a small, high-pitched flute, often played with a drum
- **commedia dell’arte**: a kind of Italian theatre with masked stock characters, which began in the 1500s

## A13-7. Fire-eater Sneezes

- `a13-07-s1`: Follow the puppets to Fire-eater’s kitchen. · _Keep behind Harlequin. Fire-eater doesn’t look down much._
- `a13-07-s2`: Stay close while Pinocchio pleads for Harlequin. · _Stand near. This bit is his._

#### `a13-07-kitchen`

_After the show Fire-eater sits down to his supper. A whole sheep is turning on a spit before the fire, and the fire is getting low._  
**Fire-eater**: Wood. Not enough wood. Bring me that new puppet. He’s good dry pine; he’ll burn beautifully.  
_Harlequin and Punchinello look at each other. Then they go, because when Fire-eater says go, everybody goes._  
_They come back with Pinocchio between them, wriggling like an eel._  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo! Babbo, save me! I don’t want to burn!  
_Fire-eater looks terrible. But he isn’t so very wicked underneath, if you can find underneath._  
_He goes pale, his nose twitches and his eyes water. He holds it, and holds it, and then he sneezes._  
**Harlequin**: Good news, brother. When he sneezes, it means he’s sorry for you. You’re saved.  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, notice): a sneeze is a reflex that clears the nose; sneeze into your elbow to stop germs spreading  
> _A sneeze is a reflex: you cannot decide it. Something tickles the lining of your nose, and the body blasts the tickle out at high speed._  
> _Droplets from a sneeze travel metres, so a good habit is to sneeze into your elbow, then wash your hands._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a sneeze is a reflex that clears the nose, and that sneezing into an elbow stops germs spreading._


**Choices**

- **Step forward and speak up for Pinocchio.**
    - **Fire-eater**: And who are you? A traveller? Sit down, traveller. You’re in my light.
    - You sit. But he looks at you twice after that.
- **Hold your Nubbin tight and keep still.**
    - You keep still. Your Nubbin, held tight, watches the whip the way you’d watch a wasp.

#### `a13-07-kitchen-done`

**Fire-eater**: Very well. I won’t burn you. But my mutton must be cooked.  
**Fire-eater**: Bring me Harlequin. He’s good dry wood too.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character who is gruff outside and soft inside  
> _Fire-eater roars and threatens, yet he sneezes because he feels sorry. How would you describe his character?_  
> - ✅ Gruff on the outside, but tender-hearted underneath. → Yes. His sneeze gives him away: the body says what the mouth will not. Good writers show a feeling instead of just saying it.
> - Pure villain with no good in him. → A pure villain would not sneeze. The sneeze is the writer’s clue that something softer is hidden.
> - Completely kind and gentle. → He threatens to burn a puppet, so he is not simply gentle. He is both, which makes him interesting.
> _For grown-ups: Described a character who is rough on the outside but soft inside, using a clue from the text._


#### `a13-07-harlequin`

_Two wooden guards fetch Harlequin. He is so frightened that his legs have folded up under him like a camp stool._  
**Pinocchio**: Have pity, Mister Fire-eater!  
**Fire-eater**: There are no misters here.  
**Pinocchio**: Have pity, Sir!  
**Fire-eater**: No sirs, either.  
**Pinocchio**: Have pity, Your Excellency!  
_Fire-eater sits up a little straighter. He likes Your Excellency very much._  
**Fire-eater**: Well? What do you want?  
**Pinocchio**: If you have to burn somebody, burn me. It isn’t right that Harlequin should burn because of me.  
_He takes off his breadcrumb cap and holds it to his chest. He means it._  
_Fire-eater’s nose twitches. He sneezes, and sneezes again, and goes on sneezing until the pots rattle on the shelf._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): courage and self-sacrifice: standing up for a friend  
> _Pinocchio offers himself in Harlequin’s place. Is that brave, foolish, or both? Would you do it?_  
> - Brave. He is right to take the blame for his own trouble. → That’s a fair answer. It is his visit that caused this, and he faces it. Courage and fairness go together.
> - Foolish. He could have been hurt for nothing. → That’s a fair answer. Danger is real. A brave person still thinks about the risk, and it is wise to ask for help as well.
> - Both. Brave heart, risky choice. → That’s a fair answer. Many brave acts have a real risk inside them, and the heart behind them is what we remember.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about courage and risk when someone speaks up for a friend._


#### `a13-07-harlequin-done`

**Fire-eater**: Oh, very well! Nobody burns tonight. I shall eat my mutton half-raw.  
**Fire-eater**: But next time, woe betide! Atchoo!  
_The puppets dance till dawn, and so do you. Your Nubbin dances along Fire-eater’s beard, and he doesn’t even notice._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: how long from start to finish  
> _The puppets start dancing at 9:30 in the evening and stop at 6:00 in the morning. How long did they dance?_  
> - ✅ 8 hours and 30 minutes. → Yes. From 9:30 pm to midnight is 2 hours 30 minutes, then 6 more hours to 6:00 am: 8 hours 30 minutes.
> - 3 hours and 30 minutes. → That would be 9:30 to 1:00 am. Count on: to midnight is 2½ hours, and midnight to 6:00 is 6 hours more.
> - 9 hours and 30 minutes. → Close, but check: 9:30 to 10:00 is half an hour, then 10:00 to 6:00 is 8 hours. That is 8½ in all.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval across midnight: 9:30 pm to 6:00 am is 8 hours 30 minutes._


#### `a13-07-complete`

_In the morning Fire-eater calls Pinocchio over and asks him about his father._  
**Pinocchio**: He’s very poor. He sold his coat to buy me a spelling-book. And I sold the book.  
_Fire-eater sneezes again. He counts five gold pieces out of his purse into Pinocchio’s hand._  
**Fire-eater**: Take these to your father, with my respects. Tell him to buy a coat.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): people are more than first impressions  
> _Fire-eater looked frightening, yet he gave away five gold pieces. What does this teach about judging people?_  
> - ✅ First impressions can be wrong; look at what people do. → Yes. How someone looks or sounds is only a start. Their actions tell the better story.
> - Scary people are secretly always kind. → Not always. Some people who look scary really are. The lesson is to watch what they do, not to assume.
> - Never judge anyone at all. → We cannot help forming a first view. The skill is to hold it loosely, and let it change.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how first impressions can be wrong and why actions tell us more._

_Pinocchio thanks him a thousand times, hugs every puppet in the company twice, and sets off for home with the gold in his fist._  

### Glossary

- **reflex**: something your body does by itself, without you choosing, like a sneeze or a blink

## A13-8. The Fox and the Cat

- `a13-08-s1`: Walk home with Pinocchio and his five gold pieces. · _Keep to the road home. Watch who you meet on it._
- `a13-08-s2`: Stop for supper at the Inn of the Red Craw-fish. · _Pinocchio is paying. He doesn’t know that yet._

#### `a13-08-road`

_Half a mile along the road you meet a Fox who is lame in one leg, and a Cat who is blind in both eyes._  
_They lean on each other as they go._  
**The Fox**: Good day, Pinocchio.  
**Pinocchio**: How do you know my name?  
**The Fox**: I know your father well. I saw him yesterday at his door, in his shirt-sleeves, shivering.  
**Pinocchio**: Poor Babbo. But he won’t shiver any more. Look. Five gold pieces. I’m going to buy him a coat.  
_He holds them up. They catch the sun._  
_The Fox, without meaning to, stretches out the leg that is lame. The Cat opens two great green eyes, and shuts them again at once._  
_Nobody sees it but you._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): why we sometimes refuse to hear what we do not want to be true  
> _Even if you warn him, Pinocchio will not listen. Why do people so often ignore a warning that spoils a hope?_  
> - Because they want the hope to be true so much. → That’s a fair answer. Wanting something strongly can make a warning feel like an attack on the wish itself.
> - Because they do not trust the person warning them. → That’s a fair answer. A warning from someone we have only just met, or someone who nags us, can be easy to brush away.
> - Because they are afraid of being wrong. → That’s a fair answer. Admitting a mistake early feels worse than hoping, even when hoping is riskier.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people ignore warnings that clash with something they badly want._


**Choices**

- **Warn him. The Cat opened its eyes.**
    - **Pinocchio**: Shame on you. He’s blind. Poor animals get blamed for everything.
    - **The Cat**: We forgive you, traveller. We forgive everybody. It’s our only luxury.
- **Say nothing yet, and watch the Fox.**
    - You say nothing. The Fox catches you watching, and smiles at you very warmly, with all his teeth.

#### `a13-08-road-done`

**The Fox**: Five gold pieces. Is that all? Would you like to make them a thousand?  
**The Fox**: Just outside the town of Catchfools there is a field, the Field of Miracles.  
**The Fox**: Plant a gold coin there, and it grows a tree hung with gold.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): what a plant needs to start growing  
> _The Fox says a gold coin grows into a tree. What does a real tree grow from, and what does that need?_  
> - ✅ A seed, with soil, water, warmth and light. → Yes. A seed holds a tiny plant and a store of food. With water and warmth it sprouts, and leaves collect light to keep growing. A coin has none of that.
> - Any shiny thing buried in the dirt. → Shiny or not, a coin is only metal. Living things grow from living things: seeds.
> - Salt and a deep hole. → Salt does not help a seed; too much hurts it. A seed wants water, warmth, soil and, soon, light.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a plant grows from a seed that needs water, warmth, soil and light._

_On the hedge a white blackbird calls out to Pinocchio not to listen._  
_The Cat springs at it, and it gets away in a burst of feathers._  
**The Cat**: Only stretching. My legs. Being blind is very stiff work.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): gullible: easily fooled  
> _The Fox’s offer is too good to be true. A person who believes it at once could be called gullible. What does that word mean?_  
> - ✅ Easily fooled. → Yes. Gullible means ready to believe anything, even when it is unlikely. Checking a claim before you trust it is the cure.
> - Very greedy. → Greed and being gullible often go together, but gullible means easily fooled.
> - Very brave. → Not brave. It means someone who is easily tricked or too trusting.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word gullible and the habit of checking claims that sound too good to be true._


#### `a13-08-inn`

_By evening you reach the Inn of the Red Craw-fish and sit down to supper, because the Fox says no great venture was ever begun hungry._  
_The Cat orders thirty-five red mullet in tomato sauce and four helpings of tripe with cheese. He says he isn’t very hungry._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how a traditional Italian supper is served in courses  
> _In an Italian inn, supper comes in courses. What is the usual order, according to tradition?_  
> - ✅ A starter, then pasta or soup, then meat or fish, then a sweet. → Yes. Starter (antipasto), first course (primo), second course (secondo), and a dessert (dolce). The meal is slow and shared; the Cat and Fox are making it very long.
> - One big plate with everything at once. → Not at a traditional table. Italian meals come in courses, one after another, and people take their time.
> - Dessert first, to be safe. → A charming idea, but the tradition puts the sweet last.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the traditional order of an Italian meal: starter, first course, second course, dessert._

_The Fox would like something light: a hare in sauce, six chickens and a few young partridges. His doctor insists._  
_Pinocchio, too excited to eat, has a walnut and a heel of bread, and leaves half the bread._  
**Pinocchio**: Tonight a seed. Tomorrow a tree. Babbo will have a coat on every branch.  
_Then you all go up to bed. Pinocchio dreams out loud of gold coins clinking on branches, like little bells._  

**Choices**

- **Ask who is paying for all this.**
    - **The Fox**: Paying? Among friends? My dear fellow, what a question.
    - He changes the subject to the weather, which he says looks golden.
- **Wrap Pinocchio’s leftover bread for his pocket.**
    - You wrap the heel of bread in a cloth and tuck it in his pocket. He won’t thank you for it tonight.

#### `a13-08-inn-done`

_At midnight the innkeeper knocks: your friends have gone ahead. The Cat’s eldest kitten has chilblains, he says, and they had to hurry._  
**Innkeeper**: They said you’d settle the bill. One gold piece, and a bargain at that.  
_Pinocchio pays it without a word, and has four gold pieces left. He sets off alone into the dark, and you go after him._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a pattern that follows a rule: doubling  
> _Suppose the Fox’s promise were true and Pinocchio’s four coins doubled every day: 4, 8, 16, … What comes next, and how many coins would there be on day 5?_  
> - ✅ 32, then 64 on day 5. → Yes. Each term is the one before times 2: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. If a promise like that were real, everyone would be rich, and nobody would be selling it for a gold piece.
> - 20, then 24. → That adds 4 each time. The rule here is doubling: multiply by 2 each day.
> - 32, then 48. → 32 is right. Double it again for the next one: 32 × 2 = 64.
> _For grown-ups: Extended a doubling pattern and saw why a promise of endless doubling is too good to be true._


#### `a13-08-complete`

_The night is so dark you can’t see your own hand. Something rustles in the hedge beside the road._  
_Very faintly, from somewhere low in the leaves, comes a small sound: cri._  
**Pinocchio**: Not you. You’re… Not you. I’m not listening.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): conscience: the inner voice that tells us what is right  
> _Pinocchio says “I’m not listening”, but he can still hear it. What do we call the inner voice that tells us when we are doing wrong?_  
> - ✅ Our conscience. → Yes. A conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong. Everyone has one, and it grows stronger the more we listen to it.
> - Our imagination. → Imagination invents things. The conscience is the voice that judges whether what we are doing is right.
> - Our shadow. → A shadow is a shape made by light. The word you want is conscience.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word conscience and thought about listening to it._

_He walks faster. You look back once, and there is nothing in the hedge but dark._  

### Glossary

- **gullible**: easily fooled; ready to believe something without checking
- **conscience**: your inner sense of what is right and wrong

## A13-9. The Assassins

- `a13-09-s1`: Keep close to Pinocchio on the dark road. · _Stay on the road. Whatever is behind you is quicker than it looks._
- `a13-09-s2`: Run after Pinocchio across the fields. · _Follow the clack of his feet. Jump the ditch; don’t land in it._

#### `a13-09-sacks`

_Behind you, the leaves rustle. Two black shapes are following, wrapped in charcoal sacks, hopping along on tiptoe like ghosts._  
**Pinocchio**: Here they come. Robbers. Assassins!  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): charcoal: wood heated without much air changes for good  
> _The robbers hide in charcoal sacks. Charcoal is made by heating wood with very little air, so it cannot burn away._  
> _Can you turn charcoal back into wood?_  
> - ✅ No. Heating changed it into something new for good. → Yes. Some changes cannot be undone. Wood has become charcoal, which is mostly carbon, a new material that burns hot and clean.
> - Yes. Soak it in water. → Water won’t help. Charcoal is made of different material now, and it will not turn back.
> - Yes. Bury it in the ground. → Burying it will not bring wood back. Charcoal is a permanent change.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that making charcoal from wood is a change that cannot be reversed._

_He pops the four gold pieces into his mouth, under his tongue, quick as a squirrel._  
**The Taller Sack**: Your money or your life!  
_Pinocchio can’t say a word, because of the money. He makes a face instead, which isn’t an answer._  
**The Shorter Sack**: Your money, or you’ll be sorry. And your father too!  
_One of them sounds very like a Fox with a cold. The other sounds like a Cat trying hard to sound like nobody._  

**Choices**

- **Grab a stick and stand with him.**
    - You grab a stick. The taller sack takes it off you, quite politely, and puts you in the ditch.
    - The ditch is full of nettles. Your Nubbin comes in after you, to keep you company.
- **Pick up your Nubbin and shout for help.**
    - You shout until the hills shout back, and nobody comes. On this road, at this hour, nobody ever does.

#### `a13-09-sacks-done`

_The shorter sack takes Pinocchio by the jaw, to get his mouth open. Pinocchio bites down hard, and spits out what he bit._  
_It isn’t a hand. It’s a cat’s paw._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues to work out who a character is  
> _Nobody tells us the sacks are the Fox and the Cat. Which clues give them away?_  
> - ✅ A voice like a Fox with a cold, and a cat’s paw in the spit. → Yes. The narrator shows us instead of telling us. Good readers pick up clues like these and put them together.
> - The colour of the sacks. → Both sacks are black, so that tells us nothing. Look at the voices and the paw.
> - Nothing gives them away; it is a surprise. → The clues are quite plain: “a Fox with a cold”, and a cat’s paw. The writer wants you to guess.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the text to infer who the disguised characters are._

_While they are both staring at that, he is over the hedge and running._  

#### `a13-09-chase`

_He runs across the fields and you run after him, and the two sacks run after you both._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): comparing distances covered at different speeds  
> _Pinocchio runs at 6 metres every second and the sacks at 5. After 10 seconds, how much farther has Pinocchio run than the sacks?_  
> - ✅ 10 metres farther. → Yes. Pinocchio runs 60 metres and the sacks 50 in 10 seconds. A small difference in speed adds up, so he slowly pulls ahead.
> - 1 metre farther. → That is the difference every second. Over 10 seconds it adds up: 10 × 1 = 10 metres.
> - 60 metres farther. → 60 metres is how far Pinocchio ran. The sacks ran 50, so the gap is 10.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two speeds over 10 seconds and found a 10-metre gap._

_There is a ditch full of muddy water. Pinocchio jumps it, you jump it, and the sacks jump it too, and land in the middle._  
_They climb out dripping, and keep coming._  
_Far off among the trees there is a little house as white as snow. Pinocchio runs to its door and hammers on it._  
**Pinocchio**: Help! Open up! Please!  
_A window opens, and in it is a girl with blue hair and a face as white as wax._  
_Her eyes are shut, and her hands are folded._  
**The Fairy**: There is nobody in this house. Everybody has gone away.  
**Pinocchio**: Then you open the door!  
**The Fairy**: I am going away too. I am only waiting.  
_The window closes, without a sound._  

#### `a13-09-chase-done`

_The sacks catch him at the door. They shake him, and shake him, and the gold won’t come out._  
_So they tie him by the collar of his paper jacket to a branch of the Big Oak, and leave him swinging there._  
**The Taller Sack**: We’ll be back in the morning. Perhaps you’ll feel like opening your mouth by then.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what we hold on to too tightly  
> _Pinocchio keeps the coins in his mouth even while he is shaken and tied up. When is holding on tight to something a mistake?_  
> - When keeping it costs us more than it is worth. → That’s a fair answer. A coin is worth less than being safe. Knowing what to let go is a hard skill.
> - Never. If it is yours, hold on. → That’s a fair answer. Things that are ours matter. But some things matter less than our safety and our people.
> - When we are too afraid to think. → That’s a fair answer. Fear can lock our hands shut. Slow breathing and a moment to think can loosen them.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on when it is wiser to let something go than to hold on tight._

> _A north wind is a wind that blows FROM the north, not towards it. Winds are always named for where they start._

> _Sailors and farmers have long watched wind direction to guess the weather._
