## A13-10. The Big Oak

- `a13-10-s1`: Watch the Fairy’s falcon cut Pinocchio down. · _Stand under the oak. Be ready to catch._
- `a13-10-s2`: Wait by the bed while the doctors look at Pinocchio. · _Stand at the foot of the bed. Look at the third doctor._

#### `a13-10-falcon`

_The girl at the window is not just a girl._  
_She is a Fairy, who has lived at the edge of this wood for more than a thousand years._  
_She claps her hands three times. A great Falcon comes down out of the dark and lands on the sill._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): a falcon’s beak, claws and eyes are adaptations for hunting  
> _A falcon’s hooked beak tears food, its claws grip, and its eyes are sharper than ours: a peregrine can spot prey from over a kilometre away._  
> _Each of these is an adaptation, a body part that helps an animal survive where it lives._  
> _A falcon’s dive can top 300 kilometres an hour, the fastest of any animal._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a falcon’s beak, claws, eyes and speed help it hunt, as examples of adaptations._

**The Fairy**: Do you see that puppet on the Big Oak? Cut the knot with your beak, and let him down gently.  
_The Falcon goes, and the knot gives. You are under the branch, and you catch Pinocchio, and he is as light as a stick of kindling._  
**The Fairy**: Thank you. Bring him in. Medoro! The coach!  
_A poodle comes out of the house on his hind legs, in a coachman’s coat with gold buttons and a wig of white curls._  
_Behind him comes a little coach the colour of the air, lined with canary feathers and drawn by a hundred pairs of white mice._  
**Medoro**: Madam. Traveller. Patient. Mind the custard; it’s for the journey.  

**Choices**

- **Ask the Fairy who she is.**
    - **The Fairy**: Someone who lives here, and has been waiting for somebody to knock. Bring him in.
- **Lift Pinocchio into the coach yourself.**
    - You lay him on the canary feathers. Your Nubbin climbs in beside him and sits on his chest, to keep it warm.

#### `a13-10-falcon-done`

_The Fairy puts Pinocchio to bed, and sends for the three best doctors in the neighbourhood._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): sending for help is a strength, not a weakness  
> _The Fairy could have nursed Pinocchio alone, but she sent for three doctors. When is asking for help the strong thing to do?_  
> - ✅ When the problem is bigger than what one person knows. → Yes. Wise people know what they do not know. Asking others is how they get the right answer.
> - Only when you have already tried everything. → Trying first is good. But if it is serious, like an illness, it is wiser to ask straight away.
> - Never; strong people do it alone. → Strength includes knowing when to share a load. Even the Fairy asks for doctors.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about asking for help when a problem is bigger than one person can handle._


#### `a13-10-doctors`

_The doctors arrive one after another: a Crow, an Owl, and, last of all, a Talking-cricket._  
_You look twice. It is him, a little grey at the edges, a little stiff in one leg, in a very bad temper, and alive._  
**The Fairy**: Doctors, tell me. Is this poor puppet alive, or dead?  
**Doctor Crow**: In my opinion, the puppet is dead. But if by any chance he is not dead, then he is certainly alive.  
**Doctor Owl**: I am sorry to disagree with my learned friend. He is alive. But if by any chance he is not alive, then he is certainly dead.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): owls are built for night hunting: forward-facing eyes, sharp hearing, soft silent feathers  
> _An owl’s eyes face forward and gather lots of light. Its feathers have soft fringes that muffle the sound of flapping, so it flies almost silently._  
> _Some owls can locate a mouse under snow by sound alone. Good senses are how a night hunter survives._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how an owl’s eyes, ears and feathers help it hunt at night._

**The Fairy**: And you, sir? You say nothing?  
**The Talking-cricket**: A wise doctor, when he doesn’t know, keeps quiet. But I know this puppet. I have known him a little while.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): honestly saying “I do not know”  
> _The cricket says, “A wise doctor, when he doesn’t know, keeps quiet.” The Crow and the Owl guessed._  
> _Is it harder to say “I do not know”, or to guess? Why?_  
> - Harder to say “I do not know”. People fear looking foolish. → That’s a fair answer. Admitting we do not know feels risky, even though it is the honest thing, and it is how we learn.
> - Harder to guess; a wrong guess can do harm. → That’s a fair answer. A confident guess from a doctor could be dangerous. The honest doctor admits where his knowledge stops.
> - They are both hard in different ways. → That’s a fair answer. Guessing risks being wrong; admitting risks looking weak. A wise person weighs both.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on the honesty of saying “I do not know” instead of guessing._

_Pinocchio, who has been lying as stiff as a plank, gives a small shiver all over._  
**The Talking-cricket**: That puppet is a rascal, and a runaway, and a disobedient son. He will break his poor father’s heart.  
_From under the sheet comes a sound of crying._  
**Doctor Crow**: When the dead cry, it is a sign they are getting better.  
**Doctor Owl**: When the dead cry, it is a sign they are sorry to be dead.  

#### `a13-10-doctors-done`

_The doctors pick up their bags. The Talking-cricket goes last, very slowly, on one stiff leg._  
_Under the sheet, Pinocchio stops crying long enough to listen to that slow, uneven step go down the stairs._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: helping even those who hurt you  
> _The cricket came to help the puppet who threw a mallet at him. What larger idea does the writer seem to be showing us?_  
> - ✅ Kindness can be given even to someone who has wronged us. → Yes. That is a theme: an idea that runs through the whole story. The cricket’s limp is the price of his kindness.
> - Crickets are stubborn creatures. → Crickets can be! But a theme is a bigger idea about people and life, not about insects.
> - Doctors should always visit puppets. → That is a detail. The theme is about what the cricket’s choice says about forgiveness and duty.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: kindness to someone who has wronged you._


#### `a13-10-complete`

_When they have all gone, the Fairy sits on the edge of the bed and puts her hand on Pinocchio’s forehead. He is burning hot._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): reading a thermometer: temperature above normal  
> _A healthy body is about 37°C (98.6°F). Pinocchio’s temperature is 40°C (104°F). How many degrees Celsius above normal is that?_  
> - ✅ 3 degrees. → Yes. 40 − 37 = 3. A fever starts above about 38°C (100.4°F), so 40°C is a high fever, and a grown-up should call a doctor.
> - 37 degrees. → That is the normal temperature. The difference between 40 and 37 is 3.
> - 77 degrees. → That adds the two numbers. To find how far above, subtract: 40 − 37 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted to find how far a temperature is above normal and learned what a fever is._

**The Fairy**: Fever. Silly boy. Silly, silly boy.  
_She looks across at you, over the sheet._  
**The Fairy**: You came in with him. Stay, then. He will need somebody to be cross with when he wakes up.  

### Glossary

- **adaptation**: a body part or habit that helps an animal live where it does

## A13-11. The Nose

- `a13-11-s1`: Get Pinocchio to take his medicine. · _He’ll bargain. Let him. Sugar first, then the glass._
- `a13-11-s2`: Stay while the Fairy asks about the gold. · _You can’t stop him lying. You can stand where he can see you._

#### `a13-11-medicine`

**The Fairy**: Drink this, and you’ll be well in a day or two.  
**Pinocchio**: Is it sweet or bitter?  
**The Fairy**: Bitter. But it’s good for you.  
**Pinocchio**: If it’s bitter, I don’t want it. Give me a lump of sugar first. Then I’ll drink it. Probably.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): only take medicine from a trusted adult, and measure it carefully  
> _Medicine is only safe in the right amount, so a trusted grown-up should always give it, using the measuring spoon or cup that comes with it._  
> _Never take medicine by yourself, and never share yours with a friend. Even a sweet-tasting one can be dangerous in a big dose._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that medicine should only be given by a trusted adult, in the measured amount._

_The Fairy gives him a lump of sugar. He crunches it up, and pushes the glass away._  
**Pinocchio**: Another lump. Then I’ll drink it.  
_Another lump, more crunching, more pushing._  
**Pinocchio**: The pillow’s on my feet. I can’t drink with a pillow on my feet. Also, the door’s open.  
_The door opens wider. In come four rabbits, as black as ink, walking on their hind legs._  
**Black Rabbit**: We’ve come for you. We were told you weren’t taking your medicine.  
**Pinocchio**: Give me the glass! Quick, give it here!  
_He drinks the whole thing at one gulp._  
**Black Rabbit**: Well. That’s a wasted walk.  
_The four black rabbits go out again, grumbling between their teeth._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of volume: millilitres in a measuring spoon  
> _A dose is one 5-millilitre spoon, three times a day. How many millilitres is that in one day?_  
> - ✅ 15 millilitres. → Yes. 5 ml × 3 = 15 ml. That is why doses are always measured: a spoon from the kitchen drawer might hold a very different amount.
> - 8 millilitres. → That adds 5 and 3. Three doses of 5 is 5 × 3 = 15 ml.
> - 5 millilitres. → That is one dose. There are three each day, so 15 ml in all.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied a 5 ml dose by three to find the daily amount of medicine._


#### `a13-11-medicine-done`

_In a few minutes Pinocchio jumps out of bed, quite well. Puppets are lucky that way: ill quickly, and well quickly._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): bitter taste as a warning sense  
> _Medicines often taste bitter. Our tongue has taste buds for sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savoury._  
> _Why might it be useful to have a taste for bitter?_  
> - ✅ Many poisons taste bitter, so it warns us to be careful. → Yes. Bitterness is an early-warning sense. But some medicines are bitter and good for us, which is why a trusted adult must decide.
> - To help us find sugar. → Sweet taste helps us find sugar. Bitter is the opposite: a “careful!” signal.
> - It has no purpose. → Every sense has a purpose. Bitter taste evolved to warn animals about harmful plants.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the bitter taste can be a warning sense, which is why adults decide about medicine._


#### `a13-11-nose`

**The Fairy**: Now. Where are the four gold pieces?  
**Pinocchio**: I lost them.  
_He is lying; they are in his pocket. His nose, which is long already, grows two fingers longer._  
**The Fairy**: Where did you lose them?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): why lies show, and what it costs to tell them  
> _Pinocchio’s nose shows every lie. In real life lies do not show on our faces. Why might the Fairy still want people to be honest?_  
> - Trust: if we lie, nobody can believe us when it matters. → That’s a fair answer. Trust is easy to break and slow to mend. One lie makes the next truth harder to believe.
> - Lies get us tangled in more lies. → That’s a fair answer. Look at his nose: each lie needed another to hide it.
> - Because lies hurt the person we tell. → That’s a fair answer. A lie takes away a person’s chance to choose well, and that is a real hurt.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why honesty matters even when lies do not show._

**Pinocchio**: In the wood. Near here.  
_His nose grows again._  
**The Fairy**: Then we’ll go and look for them. Everything lost in this wood is always found.  
**Pinocchio**: Ah. No. Now I remember. I didn’t lose them. I swallowed them, with the medicine.  
_At that third lie his nose shoots out so far that he can’t turn round. It knocks the bed, and the window, and the wall._  
_He tries to get out of the door, and can’t, because his nose won’t fit through it._  
**The Fairy**: Lies are found out at once, my boy. Some lies have short legs, and some have long noses. Yours are the long-nosed kind.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): idioms and metaphor: “lies have short legs”  
> _The Fairy says, “Some lies have short legs.” What do you think she means?_  
> - ✅ They do not get far before they are found out. → Yes. A short-legged lie cannot run far: it is caught up with quickly. It is a metaphor, a picture in words.
> - Lies belong to short people. → It has nothing to do with height. It is a picture: a creature with short legs cannot run far.
> - Lies are slow to tell. → Lies are often quick to tell! The image is about how soon the truth catches up.
> _For grown-ups: Interpreted a metaphor: a lie with short legs is soon caught._


**Choices**

- **Laugh, kindly. You can’t help it.**
    - **Pinocchio**: It isn’t funny!
    - It is a bit funny. In a minute even he thinks so, though he would never say.
- **Tell him the coins are in his pocket. He knows.**
    - **Pinocchio**: …They’re in my pocket.
    - His nose doesn’t shrink. But it stops growing, which is a start.

#### `a13-11-nose-done`

_Pinocchio cries for half an hour, because he can’t get out of the room. The Fairy lets him; lessons take half an hour, she says._  
_Then she claps her hands._  
_A thousand woodpeckers fly in at the window and peck the nose back to its proper size in no time at all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): woodpeckers’ beaks, tongues and skulls are adaptations for pecking  
> _A real woodpecker hammers on a tree many times a second._  
> _Its chisel beak digs out insects, and its tongue is so long that it wraps around the back of its skull._  
> _Stiff tail feathers prop it up on the trunk, and a tough, cushioned skull keeps the knocks from hurting. Those body parts are all adaptations._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a woodpecker’s body is adapted for pecking wood._


#### `a13-11-complete`

**The Fairy**: There. I’ll be your sister, if you’ll be a good brother. And your father is on his way; I sent for him.  
**The Fairy**: He’ll be here by dark.  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo? Here? I’ll go and meet him on the road!  
_He is gone in a rattle of bark shoes._  
**The Fairy**: Go with him. He has never yet gone anywhere in a straight line.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): chosen family and belonging  
> _The Fairy offers to be Pinocchio’s sister, though they are not related. What might “family” mean beyond being born into one?_  
> - ✅ People who care for us and show up for us. → Yes. Families are often built from love and promises as well as birth. Many people have found family in friends, neighbours and carers.
> - Only people with the same last name. → Names help families belong together, but love and care are what make a family.
> - Only the people in our house. → Family can live apart and still be family. It is about care, not about the address.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about family as people who care for and show up for one another._


### Glossary

- **idiom**: a phrase whose meaning is not what the words say, like “lies have short legs”

## A13-12. The Field of Miracles

- `a13-12-s1`: Walk with Pinocchio to meet Geppetto on the road. · _The road goes past the Big Oak. Somebody is waiting there._
- `a13-12-s2`: Help Pinocchio plant his coins in the Field of Miracles. · _Dig, plant, water, salt. Then the Fox says to go away for twenty minutes._

#### `a13-12-oak`

_At the Big Oak, sitting in the shade as if nothing had ever happened, are the Fox and the Cat._  
**The Fox**: Our dear Pinocchio! What are you doing here?  
_The Cat keeps one paw tucked inside his coat, like a gentleman with a secret._  
**Pinocchio**: What happened to his paw?  
**The Fox**: Charity. We met a poor old wolf, starving on the road, and my friend gave him a hand. Well. A paw.  
_Pinocchio wipes away a tear. You remember whose teeth that paw last met, and say nothing._  
**Pinocchio**: Fox, I can’t come to the field. I’m going to meet my father. The Fairy said—  
**The Fox**: With four coins, when you could bring him two thousand? Think how proud he’ll be.  
_Pinocchio thinks of the Fairy, and of Babbo, and for a moment of the cricket. Then he thinks of two thousand._  
**Pinocchio**: Is it far?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): keeping a promise when something tempting comes along  
> _Pinocchio promised to meet his father, and now the Fox offers a shortcut to riches._  
> _What is a good test for an offer that sounds too good to be true?_  
> - ✅ Ask: why is a stranger giving me this for nothing? → Yes. If it sounds too good to be true, find out who gains. And talk to a trusted adult before you decide.
> - Take it quickly before it vanishes. → Pressure to hurry is a classic warning sign. A real good deal can wait while you ask someone you trust.
> - Ignore all offers ever. → Not all offers are tricks! The skill is to check before agreeing, not to refuse everything.
> _For grown-ups: Practised testing an offer that sounds too good to be true, and keeping a promise._


**Choices**

- **Remind him Geppetto is on this very road.**
    - **Pinocchio**: Then he’ll wait! He always waits. He’s good at it.
    - He says it as if it were a reason.
- **Go with him. Somebody should.**
    - You go with him. The Fox gives you the look of someone counting heads at a table.

#### `a13-12-oak-done`

_The town of Catchfools is full of coatless dogs yawning with hunger, shorn sheep shivering, and hens with no crests begging for a grain._  
_There are butterflies who have sold their wings, and peacocks ashamed of their tails._  
_Now and then a fine coach goes by, with a fox in it, or a magpie._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): needs, wants and selling what you cannot do without  
> _The animals of Catchfools sold their coats, wings and tails for money. Is it wise to sell something you need to buy something you want?_  
> _What does the town show us?_  
> - No. The things they sold were what kept them safe and warm. → That’s a fair answer. When you sell a need to pay for a want, you can be left worse off than before.
> - It depends how much they got and what they needed it for. → That’s a fair answer. A trade can be sensible if you truly do not need the thing, but here they were tricked.
> - Yes, if the money is a lot. → That’s a fair answer for something you can replace. A wing or a tail cannot be bought back, so it is a harder trade.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between selling things we want and things we need._


#### `a13-12-field`

_Just outside the town there is a lonely field that looks like every other field._  
**The Fox**: This is it. Dig a hole. Plant the coins. Cover them up. Water them from the ditch, and add a pinch of salt.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): what a seed needs to germinate  
> _A real seed in real soil can sprout. What does it need in order to germinate?_  
> - ✅ Water, warmth and air. → Yes. Once a seed is wet and warm, it swells and a tiny root pushes out, then a shoot. Light comes later, once the leaves are up.
> - Salt and a shiny coin. → Neither helps. A seed needs water, warmth and air, and it already carries its own food.
> - Bright light from the start. → Many seeds sprout in the dark, under the soil. Light matters once the shoot reaches the surface.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a seed needs water, warmth and air to germinate._

_Pinocchio digs with his hands, and you help._  
_He has nothing to carry water in, so he fills his shoe at the ditch and pours it on._  
**The Fox**: Now go away for twenty minutes. Trees are very shy when you watch them grow.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: twenty minutes later  
> _The Fox sends Pinocchio away at 10:15. If they come back exactly twenty minutes later, what time is it?_  
> - ✅ 10:35 → Yes. 10:15 plus 20 minutes is 10:35. Counting on in fives or tens makes it easy.
> - 10:20 → That is only five minutes later. Add the full 20: 10:15, 10:25, 10:35.
> - 11:15 → That is a whole hour. Twenty minutes is a third of an hour, so 10:35.
> _For grown-ups: Added 20 minutes to 10:15 to find the time 10:35._

**The Cat**: And we want nothing for it. Nothing at all. Our reward is your happiness.  
_They go off down the road together, very quickly for a lame Fox and a blind Cat._  

**Choices**

- **Offer to stay and watch the hole.**
    - **Pinocchio**: You heard him! Trees are shy! Come on. You’ll spoil everything.
    - He tugs you away by the sleeve.
- **Count the twenty minutes with him in town.**
    - He counts every minute aloud, and some of them twice.

#### `a13-12-field-done`

_Twenty minutes, and back to the field. There is no tree, only the hole, and it is empty._  
_In a tree nearby, a Parrot is preening his feathers and laughing so much that he nearly falls off his branch._  
**The Parrot**: I laugh at fools who believe every silly thing they’re told.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): parrots copy sounds, but copying is not the same as understanding  
> _Real parrots can copy human speech, because they have a flexible voice organ called a syrinx and a very good ear for sound._  
> _Many just copy, like a recording. A few well-trained parrots may link words to things._  
> _So a parrot saying clever things may or may not know what it means._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that parrots mimic sounds with a syrinx, and that copying is different from understanding._

**The Parrot**: While you were counting, your friends came back, dug up your gold and ran off like the wind. You’ll never catch them now.  

#### `a13-12-complete`

_Pinocchio digs and digs, until the hole is deep enough to stand a haystack in. There is nothing at the bottom but more field._  
**Pinocchio**: Then I’ll go to the judge. There’s a judge in this town. Judges are for exactly this.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being tricked is not the same as being foolish  
> _Pinocchio feels foolish and angry. The Parrot laughs. What is a wiser way to think about being tricked?_  
> - ✅ Tricksters are skilled; anyone can be fooled. Learn, and tell someone you trust. → Yes. Being tricked says more about the trickster than about you. The best answer is to learn the warning signs.
> - Never trust anyone again. → That would be very lonely, and it lets the tricksters win twice. Learning to check is better than refusing to trust.
> - Laugh at others who get tricked. → That adds more hurt. The Parrot’s laugh is exactly what makes tricked people hide and not ask for help.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that anyone can be tricked, and that learning from it is wiser than shame._

_The Parrot laughs again. Your Nubbin throws a small clod of earth at him, which is not like it at all._  
_The clod misses. The Parrot laughs at that too._  

### Glossary

- **germinate**: to start to grow: when a seed sprouts its first root and shoot

## A13-13. The Gorilla Judge

- `a13-13-s1`: Go with Pinocchio to the court in Catchfools. · _The courthouse has the biggest door in town. Wipe your feet._
- `a13-13-s2`: Wait outside the prison. · _His window is round the back. Your Nubbin fits between the bars._

#### `a13-13-court`

_The judge of Catchfools is a large old Gorilla, much respected for his age, his white beard and his gold spectacles._  
_The spectacles have no glass in them. He wears them, he says, for his weak eyes._  
_Pinocchio tells him everything: the names, the descriptions, the field, the hole, the Parrot. He asks for justice._  
**The Judge**: Dear me. Dear me. Poor boy.  
_The Judge listens with great kindness, nodding all the way through, and blows his nose. Then he rings a bell._  
_Two mastiffs come in, dressed as policemen._  
**The Judge**: This poor creature has been robbed of four gold pieces. Take him away, and put him in prison at once.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): what makes a judge fair: listening, evidence and equal rules  
> _The Judge listens kindly, then jails the victim. What should a fair judge do instead?_  
> - ✅ Look at the evidence and punish the one who did the wrong. → Yes. Justice means judging what was done, not who is easiest to punish. A fair judge treats everyone by the same rules.
> - Punish whoever is nearest, to keep order. → That is what the Gorilla does, and it is unjust. Order built on punishing the wrong person is not order at all.
> - Do nothing, in case it is awkward. → A judge who does nothing leaves the victim with no help. Fairness takes action.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fair judge weighs evidence and treats everyone by the same rules._


**Choices**

- **Object. He’s the one who was robbed!**
    - **The Judge**: Exactly so. And the robbers are not here, so who else am I to lock up?
    - In Catchfools, it seems, that counts as an answer.
- **Keep quiet. Nothing here makes sense anyway.**
    - You keep quiet. One of the mastiffs gives you a long, sorry look, as if he would have liked to object too.

#### `a13-13-court-done`

_Four months in prison, for the crime of being robbed. Pinocchio is led away with his mouth open, too surprised to cry._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of time: months, days and weeks  
> _Four months. If we count each month as 30 days, about how many days is that?_  
> - ✅ About 120 days. → Yes. 4 × 30 = 120 days, or a little over 17 weeks. That is a long time to wait for something you did not do.
> - About 34 days. → That adds 4 and 30. Four months of 30 days each is 4 × 30 = 120.
> - About 12 days. → A month is about 30 days, so four months is 4 × 30 = 120 days.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 months by 30 days to estimate about 120 days._


#### `a13-13-prison`

_The atlas turns its own pages, softly, and four months go by. You take a room over the baker’s, round the corner from his window._  
_Your Nubbin climbs in through the bars with crusts, and comes back out with messages, which are mostly “I’m bored”._  
_Then one morning, bells. The young Emperor of Catchfools has won a great victory over somebody, and there are flags everywhere._  
_All the prisons are to be opened. All the rogues are to go free._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): an amnesty is an official pardon; Collodi’s Italy had only just become one country  
> _An amnesty is when a ruler pardons many people at once, often to celebrate. Collodi’s readers would have known the idea well._  
> _Collodi himself fought in the wars that joined the Italian states into one country._  
> _Italy became one kingdom in 1861, only twenty years before Pinocchio first appeared in the newspaper._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word amnesty and that Italy became one kingdom in 1861, shortly before Collodi’s story._

_The jailer lets out the thieves, the cheats and the pickpockets. Then he shuts the door again in Pinocchio’s face._  
**Jailer**: Not you. You’re not one of them.  
**Pinocchio**: I beg your pardon. I’m a rogue as well.  
**Jailer**: Oh. Well, that’s quite different.  
_He takes off his cap, bows, and opens the door._  

#### `a13-13-prison-done`

_Pinocchio walks out into the sunshine. His nose, you notice, stays exactly where it is._  
_Make of that what you will._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): fairness: when a system rewards the wrong thing  
> _Pinocchio gets out only by calling himself a rogue, and his nose does not grow. Was it a lie?_  
> _And what does the scene tell us about a system that frees rogues but jails the robbed?_  
> - It is a joke at the system’s expense: the rules reward the wrong thing. → That’s a fair answer. Collodi is poking fun at an unfair rule, and the humour makes the unfairness easier to see.
> - It is a small lie, but a lie all the same. → That’s a fair answer. His nose does not grow, which suggests Collodi thinks the rule is the greater wrong.
> - It is the truth in a silly way: he did get tricked into trouble. → That’s a fair answer. “Rogue” is a stretch, but he has been foolish. The story keeps both ideas at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about an unfair rule and whether calling yourself a rogue to escape it is honest._


#### `a13-13-complete`

**Pinocchio**: Straight home now. Straight to the Fairy, then straight to Babbo. No stopping. Not for anything.  
_You set off at a great pace. After an hour he is walking more slowly, and after two he is looking at the vineyards._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): vineyards are a big part of Tuscan farming; grapes are picked in early autumn  
> _Tuscany is famous for its vineyards: rows of grapevines trained on wires over the hills. The grapes are harvested by hand in September and October._  
> _Some become wine, some are dried as raisins, and the Tuscan farmers have taken great care of them for centuries, which is why Pinocchio’s vineyard has a trap._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that vineyards are an important Tuscan crop, harvested in early autumn._

**Pinocchio**: Just one bunch of grapes. One. I’m so hungry I could eat my own cap. It is bread, after all.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): hunger is a reason to ask, not a licence to take  
> _Pinocchio is truly hungry, but the grapes belong to the farmer. What could he do instead of climbing the wall?_  
> - ✅ Ask the farmer, or offer to work for some grapes. → Yes. Hunger is real, and it is a good reason to ask for help. The farmer may well say yes.
> - Take just one; nobody will notice. → The farmer notices, as we are about to see. Taking without asking also takes away his choice to share.
> - Wait until it gets dark. → Hiding does not change whose grapes they are. Asking in daylight is simpler and kinder.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about asking or working for food instead of taking what is not yours._

_He is over the vineyard wall before you can say anything about whose grapes they are._  

### Glossary

- **amnesty**: an official pardon, when people who broke the law are set free
- **justice**: fair treatment: what is right, not just what is easy

## A13-14. The Guard Dog

- `a13-14-s1`: Go after Pinocchio into the vineyard. · _Watch where you put your feet. Something under the vines is set for thieves._
- `a13-14-s2`: Keep watch with Pinocchio by the hen-house. · _Sit in the dark. Don’t move when the visitors come._

#### `a13-14-trap`

_Pinocchio reaches for the first bunch. Snap: something under the vines closes on both his ankles, and holds._  
_It is a trap, set by the farmer for the martens that come after his hens._  
_His ankles are wood, so it doesn’t hurt; it just won’t let go._  
**Pinocchio**: Help! Get it off! Get it OFF!  
_You pull, and your Nubbin pulls on you. The trap does not care how many of you there are._  
_At dark a farmer comes along the rows with a lantern, and holds it up to Pinocchio’s face._  
**The Farmer**: So. You’re the one who’s been at my hens.  
**Pinocchio**: No! I only came for two bunches of grapes!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): assuming the worst about someone instead of asking  
> _The farmer decides a grape thief must be a hen thief. How could he have found out the truth instead of assuming?_  
> - Ask questions and look for evidence before deciding. → That’s a fair answer. Questions first, conclusions second, is a habit worth keeping.
> - Be stricter, so no thief ever gets away. → That’s a fair answer. But strictness without questions can punish the wrong person, as with the Gorilla Judge.
> - Trust that thieves are always hungry. → That’s a fair answer, and a kind one. Hunger does explain a lot. It does not answer who raided the hens.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how assuming the worst can lead to unfair judgements._

**The Farmer**: A grape thief is a hen thief, given time. My dog Melampo kept watch here for me. He died this morning.  
**The Farmer**: So you can be my watchdog tonight.  

**Choices**

- **Tell the farmer he’s only a hungry puppet.**
    - **The Farmer**: Then he’ll be a hungry watchdog. It’s one night. The kennel’s dry.
    - He isn’t unkind. He is a man with a great many hens and no dog.
- **Help Pinocchio settle into the kennel straw.**
    - You shake out the straw and pat it flat. Pinocchio climbs in and sits there in his paper suit, the saddest dog in Tuscany.

#### `a13-14-trap-done`

_The farmer buckles a brass collar round Pinocchio’s neck, on a long chain, and fastens the chain to the kennel._  
**The Farmer**: If thieves come, bark. Goodnight.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): dogs hear much higher sounds than humans can, which makes them good guards  
> _People hear sounds up to about 20,000 vibrations a second. Dogs can hear more than twice as high, up to around 45,000._  
> _So a dog hears faint, high scratchings that we miss, and can swivel its ears to find where a sound comes from._  
> _That is why dogs make good guards._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dogs hear much higher pitches than people and can locate sounds with their ears._

**Pinocchio**: The cricket said this would happen. Not the dog part. Everything else.  

#### `a13-14-martens`

_Around midnight four little shapes come slipping out of the dark. They have long bodies and short legs, and they smell of hens._  
_They are martens. They like eggs, and chickens, and most of all they like not being seen._  
**Marten**: Good evening, Melampo.  
**Pinocchio**: I’m not Melampo.  
**Marten**: Then where’s the old dog?  
**Pinocchio**: He died. This morning.  
**Marten**: Died? Poor beast. He was such a reasonable dog.  
**Marten**: You look reasonable too. Here’s what we had with him. You keep quiet, we take seven hens, and you get one, plucked.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step word problem with multiplication and subtraction  
> _Suppose each of the four martens took 7 hens. The farmer has 30 hens. How many would be left?_  
> - ✅ 2 hens. → Yes. First 4 × 7 = 28 hens taken, then 30 − 28 = 2 left. Pinocchio’s trick saved the other 28.
> - 11 hens. → That adds 4 and 7. Multiply first: 4 × 7 = 28, then subtract: 30 − 28 = 2.
> - 28 hens. → 28 is how many are taken. The question asks how many are left: 30 − 28 = 2.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem: 4 × 7 = 28, then 30 − 28 = 2._

**Pinocchio**: Oh, yes. Very reasonable. Go right in.  
_The martens go into the hen-house, one after another. Pinocchio waits until the last tail is through the door._  
_Then he pushes the door shut with his foot and rolls a stone against it. He barks like a proper dog: bow-wow, bow-wow, bow-wow!_  

#### `a13-14-martens-done`

_The farmer comes running in his nightshirt and nightcap, with his lantern, and catches all four martens in a sack._  
**The Farmer**: Well, I never! Well done, dog. Well done, boy. Whatever you are.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): nocturnal animals: how night hunters find their way  
> _Martens hunt at night. What helps a nocturnal animal find its way in the dark?_  
> - ✅ Sharp hearing and smell, big eyes and whiskers. → Yes. Nocturnal animals lean on senses that work without much light: ears, nose, whiskers and large eyes that gather every scrap of light.
> - A built-in torch. → A few animals make light, like glow-worms, but most night hunters rely on their senses.
> - They cannot see at all and bump around. → They see far better than we do in the dark, and use hearing and smell too.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nocturnal animals depend on sharp hearing, smell, whiskers and big eyes._


#### `a13-14-complete`

**The Farmer**: And Melampo, all those years. Did he take hens off them?  
_Pinocchio knows; you can see him knowing it. He looks at the empty kennel for a long moment._  
**Pinocchio**: Melampo has died. Let him keep his good name. It doesn’t cost anything.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: the choice to speak kindly of someone who is not there  
> _Pinocchio knows Melampo took hens, but chooses to let him “keep his good name”. What larger idea is the writer showing?_  
> - ✅ Kindness and fairness to someone who cannot answer back. → Yes. It costs nothing and does no harm, and it shows the grown-up Pinocchio is starting to appear.
> - That dogs should never be trusted. → The scene is about Pinocchio’s choice, not about dogs.
> - That lying always pays. → He is not lying. He is choosing not to say something unkind. That is a different thing.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: speaking kindly of someone who cannot answer back._

_The farmer takes off the collar and lets him go. He gives you both a handful of grapes for the road, which seems fair._

- **marten**: a small, quick, long-bodied hunter of the weasel family that hunts at night

## A13-15. The Stone and the Pigeon

- `a13-15-s1`: Go with Pinocchio to the Fairy’s white house. · _Through the wood, past the Big Oak. Read what you find there._
- `a13-15-s2`: Follow the Pigeon to the sea. · _The Pigeon takes Pinocchio. You take the coast road, and you’ll have to hurry._

#### `a13-15-stone`

_Pinocchio runs all the way to the Big Oak. Past it, where the little white house stood, there is no house._  
_There is grass, and a small white stone. On the stone there are words, cut carefully, in small letters._  
**Pinocchio**: What does it say? Read it. I can’t read. I was going to learn. I sold the book.  
_You kneel down by the stone. Your Nubbin brushes the leaves off it with both paws._  
**Pinocchio**: Read it. Please.  
_The wind goes through the grass. The Big Oak creaks behind you, the way it did that night._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): telling hard news: gently, but not dishonestly  
> _You can read the stone exactly as it is, or gently, in pieces. Which is the kinder way to give someone hard news?_  
> - Honestly but gently, so they are not left guessing. → That’s a fair answer. A careful voice and the full truth together are hard to beat.
> - Softly and in small pieces, so it does not hit all at once. → That’s a fair answer. Time to take it in matters. Pinocchio will ask for the rest, and you should give it.
> - Leave the sad part out. → That’s a fair answer, and it is tempting. But he will find out, and he may trust you less. Look at what the story shows.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about telling hard news honestly and gently._


**Choices**

- **Read it exactly as it is written.**
    - **You**: “Here the girl with blue hair waited for her little brother Pinocchio. He did not come, and she went away grieving.”
    - Pinocchio sits down on the grass very suddenly, as if his legs had come unglued.
- **Read it gently, and leave out the grieving.**
    - **You**: It says she waited for you. And then she had to go away.
    - **Pinocchio**: That isn’t all of it. Your mouth stopped. Read the rest.
    - **You**: “…and she went away grieving.”
    - Pinocchio sits down on the grass very suddenly, as if his legs had come unglued.

#### `a13-15-stone-done`

_He cries all night. The hills hear him and cry back, in echoes, until morning._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): an echo is sound bouncing back from a hard surface  
> _An echo is a sound that reflects, or bounces, off a hard, flat surface such as a hillside or a cliff, and comes back to your ears a moment later._  
> _Sound travels about 343 metres each second in the air._  
> _If you hear your echo after 2 seconds, the hill is roughly 343 metres away: it went there and back in that time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an echo is a reflected sound, and that the delay can show how far away the surface is._

**Pinocchio**: Little Fairy, come back. Where’s Babbo? Who’s going to give me bread now? Who’s going to tell me off?  

#### `a13-15-pigeon`

_In the morning a great Pigeon, as big as a turkey, comes circling down out of the sky._  
**The Pigeon**: Do you happen to know a puppet called Pinocchio?  
**Pinocchio**: Know him? It’s me!  
**The Pigeon**: Then you’ll know Geppetto. Three days ago I left him on the seashore, building himself a little boat.  
**The Pigeon**: He has walked the country for four months looking for you. Now he means to cross the sea and look for you on the other side.  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo! Is it far? Can you take me?  
**The Pigeon**: Climb on my back, and hold on. Traveller, it’s the coast road for you. I’m strong, but I’m not a cart.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4-ESS2-2, ask): compass directions: Tuscany’s sea is to the west  
> _Tuscany lies in the middle of Italy, and its coast is on the west._  
> _If you walk from the hills to the sea, which compass direction are you heading?_  
> - ✅ West. → Yes. The Tyrrhenian Sea lies to the west of Tuscany. Sunset points the way: the sun sets in the west.
> - East. → East is where the sun rises, and in Tuscany that is inland, towards the mountains. The sea is west.
> - North. → North heads towards the Alps. The sea is on Tuscany’s west side.
> _For grown-ups: Used a compass direction: Tuscany’s sea lies to the west._

_Off they go, over the trees. You and your Nubbin take the coast road, and walk all day and half the night._  

#### `a13-15-pigeon-done`

_At dawn you come out on the shore. There is a crowd on the beach, all pointing out to sea._  
_Far out there is a tiny boat, and an old man in it, rowing._  
_Pinocchio is on a rock at the water’s edge, waving his breadcrumb cap._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): homing pigeons navigate using the sun, Earth’s magnetism and landmarks  
> _Real homing pigeons can find their loft from hundreds of kilometres away._  
> _They seem to use the Sun’s position, the Earth’s magnetic field and landmarks they remember._  
> _For centuries, people tied small messages to pigeons’ legs. Pinocchio’s Pigeon is carrying a puppet instead, which is a heavier load._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that homing pigeons find their way using the Sun, magnetism and landmarks._


#### `a13-15-complete`

**Pinocchio**: Babbo! BABBO! It’s me!  
_Out on the water the little old man stops rowing, and waves back. He has seen._  
_Then a wave comes, bigger than all the others, and the boat is gone under it._  
_The crowd groans, but Pinocchio doesn’t make a sound. He climbs to the top of the rock, and jumps._  
**Pinocchio**: I’ll save him!  
_He swims like a fish, because he is wood, and wood floats._  
_He goes out and out through the waves, until you can’t see him at all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): floating: balanced forces  
> _A floating thing has its weight pulling down and the water pushing up._  
> _For a log of wood bobbing on the sea, what do you know about those two forces?_  
> - ✅ They are balanced: equal and opposite. → Yes. When the upward push of the water equals the downward pull of weight, the log neither sinks nor rises: it floats. Wood is light for its size, so a little water is enough to hold it up.
> - The water pushes harder than gravity. → If it did, the log would shoot up. At the surface the forces are equal and it sits steady.
> - There is no push from the water. → Water pushes up on anything in it. That upward push is called buoyancy, and it is what keeps boats afloat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that floating happens when the water’s upward push balances an object’s weight._


### Glossary

- **inscription**: words carved or cut into stone or metal

## A13-16. The Island of Busy Bees

- `a13-16-s1`: Cross to the island and find Pinocchio. · _A fishing boat will take you. Look for the puppet asking everybody for a penny._
- `a13-16-s2`: Help carry the water home. · _Pinocchio takes one can. Your Nubbin will try to take the other._
- `a13-16-s3`: Walk Pinocchio to the island school. · _He has promised. Walk beside him so he keeps it._

#### `a13-16-island`

_A fishing boat takes you over at first light._  
_On the island there is a town where everybody is busy, which is why it is called the Island of Busy Bees._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): honeybees live in a colony where every bee has a job  
> _A honeybee colony can hold tens of thousands of bees._  
> _Each has a job: one queen lays eggs, workers gather nectar, feed the young and guard the hive._  
> _Alone, a bee would not survive the winter. Together the colony keeps warm and fed._  
> _That is why Collodi named an island of hard workers after bees._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that honeybees survive as a colony in which each bee has a job._

_Pinocchio washed up here in the night, with no Babbo. A Dolphin told him the sea has a Terrible Dog-fish in it, and said no more._  
_Now he is going up and down the street, very hungry, asking everybody for a penny._  
**Coalman**: A penny? Help me pull this coal cart home, and I’ll give you forty.  
**Pinocchio**: Pull a cart? I’m not a donkey! I’ve never pulled a cart in my life!  
**Coalman**: Then eat your pride, lad, if you’re hungry. I’m told it’s very filling.  
_He asks a bricklayer next. Carry lime for an hour, says the bricklayer, and there’s a supper in it._  
**Pinocchio**: Lime is heavy. I’m not built for heavy. Look at my arms.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): whether work is something to avoid  
> _Pinocchio says work is for donkeys. Is work something to avoid, or part of a good life? Think about the coalman’s answer._  
> - Work can be tiring, but it also builds pride and independence. → That’s a fair answer. Many people find that effort brings its own kind of satisfaction, once they have finished.
> - Avoid it if you can. Life is for enjoying. → That’s a fair answer. Rest and joy matter greatly. The question is who provides the supper while you rest.
> - It depends whether the work is fair and chosen. → That’s a fair answer. Work that is fair, paid and chosen feels very different from work forced on someone.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether work is something to avoid or part of a good life._


**Choices**

- **Carry a hod of lime yourself, to show him.**
    - You carry it, and it is heavy. Your Nubbin carries one brick, very proudly, the whole way.
    - **Pinocchio**: You’re a Keeper. You’re made for that sort of thing.
    - You don’t think anybody is made for it. You just do it.
- **Tell him work isn’t the end of the world.**
    - **Pinocchio**: It’s the end of the morning, and that’s worse.
    - But he watches the coal cart go off up the hill, and for a moment he looks as if he might go after it.

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of mass and volume: a litre of water weighs a kilogram  
> _Each can holds 10 litres, and a litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram. How much weight is the little woman carrying in two full cans?_  
> - ✅ About 20 kilograms. → Yes. 10 kg × 2 cans = 20 kg. That is about the weight of a six-year-old child, which is why she asks for help.
> - About 12 kilograms. → That adds 10 and 2. Each can is 10 kg, and there are two cans: 10 × 2 = 20.
> - About 10 kilograms. → That is one can. She is carrying two, so 20 kilograms.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied to find that two 10-litre cans of water weigh about 20 kilograms._

> _Many Italian towns still have public fountains where people fetch water._  
> _Some are fed by springs, and some by channels first built by the Romans two thousand years ago._  
> _A fountain is where neighbours meet. That is why the Fairy, grown up, is found at one, carrying water like anyone else._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many Italian towns have public fountains, some fed by ancient Roman water systems._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): growth takes your own effort, and a helper cannot do it for you  
> _The Fairy says nobody can earn it for Pinocchio. What does a helper like the Fairy still do?_

> - Do the hard parts so you do not have to. → That would be a kindness for a day, but you would not grow from it. Growing is the part you do yourself.
> - Nothing. Helpers are no use. → Helpers matter very much. The Fairy is the reason Pinocchio is alive. They just cannot do the growing for him.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what a helper can and cannot do when someone is growing and learning._

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): the four seasons come from the tilt of the Earth as it circles the Sun  
> _A school year runs through spring, summer, autumn and winter. The seasons happen because the Earth’s axis is tilted about 23 degrees._  
> _When Tuscany leans towards the Sun, it gets longer, warmer days: summer. When it leans away, the days are short and cool: winter._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth as it travels around the Sun._

> _He always means it, “at the time”. What turns a good intention into something you really do?_  
> - ✅ Small habits repeated each day. → Yes. Habits carry us when feeling does not. Tiny actions, done often, turn a wish into who we are.
> - A very strong feeling in the moment. → Strong feelings fade. Habits hold when the feeling is gone.
> - Telling more people about the promise. → It can help, because others can remind us. But it is the daily doing that makes the difference.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how habits turn good intentions into real change._

- `a13-17-s1`: Go down to the beach with Pinocchio and the schoolboys. · _Keep up. They’re running, and they don’t want to be followed._
- `a13-17-s2`: Keep clear of the fight on the beach. · _You can’t stop it. Watch the books._

#### `a13-17-lure`

**Schoolboy**: Pinocchio! The Terrible Dog-fish has come to the beach! It’s as big as a mountain! Come and see!  
**Pinocchio**: The Dog-fish? Perhaps it’s the one that… Babbo’s boat…  
**Pinocchio**: After school. We’ll go after school.  
**Schoolboy**: After school he’ll be gone! Do you think he’ll wait for you? He’s a fish!  
_The schoolboys are already running. Pinocchio looks at the school door, and then at the road to the sea._  
_You know which one he’s going to choose. So does he._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): saying no to friends who push you to break a promise  
> _The boys push Pinocchio to skip school with “he won’t wait for you!” What could he say to keep his promise and keep his friends?_  
> - ✅ “I’ll come after school, and you can tell me all about it.” → Yes. A calm no plus a real offer keeps the friendship. A true friend can wait.
> - Run off with them and hope for the best. → That is what Pinocchio does. It is easy, but it breaks the promise he made.
> - Say nothing and stay put. → Staying put is brave. Saying why helps your friends understand and may stop them pressing.
> _For grown-ups: Practised a calm no to friends who pressure you, while keeping the friendship._


**Choices**

- **Tell him: school first, the beach after.**
    - **Pinocchio**: After! Everything’s after, with you. With everyone.
    - He runs. You follow, because somebody should.
- **Go with him. You want to see the Dog-fish too.**
    - You go. It is a bad idea, and you both know it, and the sun is out.

_At the beach the sea is flat and empty, as smooth as a plate. There is no Dog-fish, and there never was._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): pescecane is the Italian word for shark; it means “dog-fish”  
> _In the Italian book, the monster is a pescecane, literally a “fish-dog”. In modern Italian the word means shark._  
> _Real dogfish are small sharks, and shark skeletons are made of cartilage, the bendy stuff in your ears and nose, not bone._  
> _The translators called it a Dog-fish and Collodi’s readers thought shark._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pescecane (dog-fish) is Italian for shark, and that sharks have cartilage skeletons._


#### `a13-17-fight`

**Schoolboy**: Ha! You came! Now you’ll be in trouble like the rest of us. You make us look bad, being good all the time.  
_Pinocchio goes red under his paint. Somebody pushes somebody, and in a moment there is a fight._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why people resent someone for doing well  
> _The boys say Pinocchio “makes them look bad” by being good. Why might people feel cross at someone who is doing well?_  
> - They feel judged, or worry they are falling behind. → That’s a fair answer. Envy is often a hurt feeling in disguise, and it helps to notice it in ourselves.
> - They are just bullies. → That’s a fair answer. Teasing someone for trying is unkind. Still, asking why can show us how to answer it.
> - They feel left out and want company in bad behaviour. → That’s a fair answer. Groups sometimes pull their members down to feel the same, which is called peer pressure.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people sometimes resent a friend for doing well._

_They throw their school books at him. He ducks, and the books sail over his head into the sea._  
_The fish come up to taste them. They nibble a page, spit it out and swim off, as if they get enough of that at home._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): paper is made of wood fibres, and soaked paper falls apart  
> _Paper is made from wood: the trees are mashed to pulp, washed, pressed and dried into thin sheets of tangled fibres._  
> _In water, the fibres soak up water and the sheet loses its strength, so a soaked book turns to mush._  
> _That is why the fish nibble and spit._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that paper is made of wood fibres and weakens when it gets wet._

_Then somebody throws the big arithmetic book, the heaviest book in the school._  
_It misses Pinocchio. It hits a boy called Eugene on the head, and he goes down on the sand._  
_Everyone runs. Everyone except Pinocchio, who kneels by Eugene and wets his handkerchief in the sea for his forehead._  

#### `a13-17-fight-done`

**Eugene**: Ow. Who threw the sums?  
_Eugene sits up, with a bump on his head like half an egg. He is going to be all right, and Pinocchio goes weak with relief._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): first aid for a bump on the head: a cold pad, rest and a grown-up  
> _Eugene has a bump on his head. What is the right first aid, and what should always happen next?_  
> - ✅ A cold pad, a rest, and tell a grown-up straight away. → Yes. Cold reduces swelling. A knock on the head can be serious even when it looks small, so an adult must check for dizziness or sleepiness.
> - Rub it hard and carry on playing. → Rubbing and playing on is risky. Rest, a cold pad and a grown-up’s eyes are better.
> - Say nothing so nobody gets in trouble. → A head injury is too important to hide. Tell an adult; being honest is how you keep a friend safe.
> _For grown-ups: Learned first aid for a bump on the head: cold pad, rest, and tell a grown-up._

_Then two carabineers come down the beach. They see a wooden boy, a boy on the sand and a book, and decide what they’ve seen._  
_Pinocchio runs. They let their dog off the lead after him._  

#### `a13-17-alidoro`

_The dog is a great mastiff called Alidoro, and he runs like a train. Pinocchio throws himself into the sea, and Alidoro goes in after him._  
_Alidoro cannot swim. He goes under, comes up, and goes under again, paddling wildly and getting nowhere._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): vocabulary: words for swimming badly  
> _Alidoro is “paddling wildly and getting nowhere”. Which word best describes struggling clumsily in water?_  
> - ✅ Floundering. → Yes. To flounder is to struggle awkwardly, as in water or mud. It is also what people do when they cannot find the right words.
> - Gliding. → Gliding is smooth and easy. Alidoro is doing the opposite.
> - Diving. → Diving is a planned plunge. Alidoro is not planning anything.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word flounder and chose it to describe clumsy struggling._

**Alidoro**: Help! Pinocchio! Save me!  
_Pinocchio is already halfway to the horizon. He stops, and treads water, and looks back._  
**Pinocchio**: If I save you, will you promise not to chase me?  
**Alidoro**: I promise! I promise! Anything!  

#### `a13-17-alidoro-done`

_Pinocchio swims back and gets Alidoro by the tail. You wade in and take the other end, and the dog comes out like a wet carpet._  
**Alidoro**: You saved me. I don’t forget a thing like that.  
_He shakes himself all over you, by way of thanks, and trots off home._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): gratitude turns a good deed into a friendship  
> _Alidoro says he will never forget what Pinocchio did. Being thanked and remembered is a powerful reward, and it makes the next kind act more likely._  
> _Researchers who study kindness have found that grateful people tend to help others more. Thank-yous matter more than most of us think._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about gratitude and how thanks encourages more kindness._


#### `a13-17-fisher`

_Round the point there is a cave with smoke coming out of it. You go in carefully, and stop at the back in the dark._  
_A fisherman is frying fish._  
_He is green all over: green skin, green hair, and a beard of long green grass, like a lizard that has stood up._  
_He has a net full of fish, and he is sorting them, very pleased with himself. In the middle of the net is Pinocchio._  
**The Green Fisherman**: Mullet. Into the pan. Bream. Into the pan. Anchovies, into the pan. And what are you?  
**Pinocchio**: I’m a puppet!  
**The Green Fisherman**: A puppet-fish! I’ve never had a puppet-fish. A talking one, too. I’ll keep you for last, as a treat.  
_He rolls Pinocchio in flour from head to foot, until he looks like a plaster saint, and holds him over the pan by one leg._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: equal groups and batches  
> _The pan holds 4 fish at a time. The Green Fisherman has 12 mullet to fry. How many batches will he need?_  
> - ✅ 3 batches. → Yes. 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Division asks how many equal groups fit. Three batches of four.
> - 8 batches. → That subtracts: 12 − 4. Division asks how many groups of 4 fit in 12: 3.
> - 48 batches. → That multiplies. We want to know how many groups of 4 are in 12, so we divide: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 12 fish by a pan size of 4 to find 3 batches._

**Pinocchio**: I’m not a fish! Fish don’t wear shoes!  

#### `a13-17-fisher-done`

_Something big comes bounding past you into the cave: Alidoro, dry now, following his nose, which is a very good nose for flour._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): a dog’s sense of smell is hundreds of times more powerful than ours  
> _A dog has around 300 million smell receptors in its nose. A person has about 5 million._  
> _A big part of a dog’s brain is for reading smells._  
> _So Alidoro could pick Pinocchio’s scent out of a cave full of fish, smoke and flour, the way you might spot a friend in a crowd._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a dog’s nose has many more smell receptors than ours, which is why dogs track so well._

_He takes Pinocchio out of the fisherman’s hand, gently, in his teeth, and is gone before the green man can say “anchovy”._  
**Alidoro**: Now we’re even.  

#### `a13-17-complete`

_Pinocchio walks home to the Fairy that night, floured like a loaf, and knocks. The Snail who keeps the door looks out of the top window._  
_It takes her nine hours to come down. Pinocchio is asleep on the step when the door opens._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: when does the Snail arrive  
> _The Snail sets off from the top window at 4:30 in the morning and takes 9 hours to come down._  
> _What time does she open the door?_  
> - ✅ 1:30 in the afternoon. → Yes. 4:30 plus 9 hours is 13:30, which is 1:30 pm. Snails move on one muscular foot over a trail of slime, which is why they are not in a hurry.
> - 9:30 in the morning. → That adds only 5 hours. Count on 9 hours from 4:30: noon is 7½ hours, then 1½ more.
> - 4:30 in the afternoon. → That would be 12 hours. Nine hours from 4:30 am lands at 1:30 pm.
> _For grown-ups: Added 9 hours to 4:30 am to find 1:30 pm._

_The Fairy forgives him, again. He goes back to school, and works, and this time he is good for a whole year._  
**The Fairy**: Tomorrow you will stop being a puppet. Tomorrow, you will be a boy.  
**Pinocchio**: Tomorrow? Really tomorrow? I’ll invite everybody! I’ll go and invite them now!  

### Glossary

- **floundering**: struggling clumsily, as in water or mud, or when you cannot find your words
- **mastiff**: a very large, strong dog with a broad head

## A13-18. The Land of Toys

- `a13-18-s1`: Go with Pinocchio to invite his friends. · _The last one on his list is the hardest to find._
- `a13-18-s2`: Find Pinocchio in the Land of Toys. · _Look anywhere there’s noise. That narrows it down to everywhere._
- `a13-18-s3`: Stay near Pinocchio in the circus ring. · _He can’t talk any more. Watch the lady in the box above the ring._

#### `a13-18-candlewick`

_The last friend on Pinocchio’s list is the laziest boy in the school: tall and thin and pale, like the wick of a new candle._  
_Everyone calls him Candlewick._  
_You find him at midnight in a doorway on the road out of town, with a bundle._  
**Candlewick**: Me? A party? Can’t. I’m going away tonight. To the Land of Toys.  
**Candlewick**: No schools. No teachers. No books. The holidays start on the first of January and end on the last day of December.  
**Candlewick**: Every week has six Saturdays and a Sunday. Come with me. Why don’t you come?  
**Pinocchio**: I can’t. I promised the Fairy. Tomorrow I’m going to be a boy.  
_Down the road comes a coach, with no sound at all._  
_It is drawn by twelve pairs of donkeys, and the donkeys are all wearing white leather boots._  
_Driving it is a Little Man, wider than he is tall, soft and shiny like a pat of butter, with a little mouth that never stops smiling._  
**The Little Man**: Climb up, my dears. Plenty of room. There’s always room, for boys.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe is not the same as well: what a good life needs besides fun  
> _In the Land of Toys nothing is hard, nobody is cross, and there is no school._  
> _What might be missing from a place where it is always play and never effort?_  
> - Growing, learning and being useful to others. → That’s a fair answer. A place can feel wonderful and still leave you no room to grow. That is the trap the Little Man is selling.
> - Nothing is missing. It sounds perfect. → That’s a fair answer. It does sound perfect, and that is why the trick works. Ask what the donkey in boots knows that you don’t.
> - Rest and play are good; it is only too much that is the trouble. → That’s a fair answer. A good life has play, rest and work in the right amounts.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between a place that feels good and one that helps you grow._


**Choices**

- **Remind him of the coat Geppetto sold.**
    - **Pinocchio**: That was ages ago! I’ll be back before he… I’ll only stay a day.
    - He doesn’t look at you, and he climbs up anyway.
- **Take his hand and turn him towards home.**
    - He lets you, for three steps. Then he pulls his hand away and runs, and climbs up beside Candlewick.

#### `a13-18-candlewick-done`

_As he climbs up, the donkey nearest you turns its head and speaks, very low. Poor fool, it says, you’ll be sorry._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): a donkey’s long ears help it lose heat in the hot places its wild relatives come from  
> _The first donkeys were tamed in Africa more than five thousand years ago, from wild asses that lived in dry, hot country._  
> _Those long ears are an adaptation. Blood flows close under the thin skin, so the ears shed heat like radiators._  
> _Their loud voices carry far across open land._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that donkeys were first tamed in Africa and that long ears help them lose heat._

_Nobody else hears. The Little Man flicks his whip, and the coach goes without a sound, and you run after it all night._  

#### `a13-18-toys`

_The Land of Toys is boys and nothing else. Boys playing ball, boys on stilts, boys dressed as generals, boys shouting just to hear the noise._  
_On the walls, in chalk, it says LONG LIF TOYS and DOWN WITH SKOOL and NO MOR SUMS. The spelling is a matter of taste._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: one day out of seven  
> _Candlewick says every week has six Saturdays and one Sunday. That is still seven days. What fraction of those days is the Sunday?_  
> - ✅ One seventh (1/7). → Yes. One day out of seven equal days is 1/7. Silly names do not change how many days there are in a week.
> - One sixth (1/6). → There are 7 days in the week, so each day is one seventh, not one sixth.
> - One half (1/2). → A half would need 2 equal parts. A week has 7, so a single day is 1/7.
> _For grown-ups: Named one day of a seven-day week as the unit fraction 1/7._

_Pinocchio is in the middle of it all with Candlewick, laughing so hard that he has to hold on to a lamp-post._  
**Pinocchio**: Isn’t it wonderful? Admit it! Admit it’s wonderful!  
_At a stall your Nubbin finds a pair of paper donkey ears on a band, and wears them about._  
_They are only paper, and they come off._  
_The atlas turns its pages, one after another. Five months go by, and every one of them is a holiday._  

#### `a13-18-toys-done`

_Then one morning Pinocchio wakes up and puts his hand to his head. He has ears: long, hairy ears, like a donkey’s._  
_A little Marmot who lives upstairs looks at them, and shakes her head._  
**The Marmot**: Donkey fever. Boys who do nothing but play all catch it in the end.  
**The Marmot**: In an hour or two you won’t be a boy or a puppet. You’ll be a donkey.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): marmots survive winter by hibernating  
> _Real marmots live high in mountains, including the Italian Alps._  
> _In winter there is no food, so they hibernate: they curl up underground, and their hearts and breathing slow right down._  
> _A hibernating marmot lives off the fat it stored all summer. That is a way of surviving in a place where winter is harsh._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that marmots hibernate through the winter, living off stored fat._


#### `a13-18-circus`

_Candlewick has the ears too._  
_They laugh at each other until the laughing turns to braying, and then they are both donkeys, right down to the tail._  
_The Little Man comes to collect them, smiling his little smile, and sells them at the market. That was always his business._  
_Candlewick goes to a farmer._  
_Pinocchio goes to a circus, where the director teaches him to dance and jump through hoops, and is not gentle about it._  
_On the first night, in a box above the ring, there is a lady with a gold locket._  
_In the locket is a picture of a puppet._  
_Pinocchio sees her and tries to call out to her. What comes out is a bray, so loud that the audience laughs._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): animal sound words: which sound is a bray  
> _Pinocchio tries to call out and what comes out is a bray. Which animal sound is a bray?_  
> - ✅ The loud “hee-haw” of a donkey. → Yes. Bray is the harsh, loud call of a donkey. Words like bray, neigh, bleat and cluck sound a little like the animal.
> - The soft purr of a cat. → A cat purrs. The word bray is for a donkey’s call.
> - The quack of a duck. → Ducks quack. A donkey brays.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bray is the sound a donkey makes._

_He jumps for the hoop, catches his back leg on it and comes down hard. After that he is lame._  
_The director sells him for a few pennies to a drum-maker._  
_The man ties a rope to him and lowers him off a rock into the sea. You watch from the cliff, and can’t stop it._  

#### `a13-18-sea`

_After an hour the man hauls in his rope. Up out of the sea comes, not a donkey, but a wooden puppet, wriggling like an eel._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): sea water is salty and wood floats in it more easily than in fresh water  
> _Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in every litre._  
> _The salt makes the water denser, so it holds things up better than fresh water does._  
> _A wooden puppet floats in a fresh pond. In the sea, he floats even higher, which is how he bobs up out of a rope-and-rock job._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that salt makes sea water denser, so things float more easily in it._

**The Drum Man**: Where’s my donkey?  
**Pinocchio**: The sea washed him off. All the little fish had a nibble. It turns out the donkey was only a sort of coat.  
_He wriggles out of the rope, dives, and swims away laughing._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying by ten: salt in a bucket of sea water  
> _Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in each litre. How much salt is in a 10-litre bucket of it?_  
> - ✅ 350 grams. → Yes. 35 × 10 = 350 g. That is about a mugful of salt in one bucket of sea water.
> - 45 grams. → That adds 35 and 10. Ten litres means ten times as much: 35 × 10 = 350.
> - 3.5 grams. → That divides by 10. A bucket holds ten times as much as one litre, so multiply: 350.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 35 g by 10 litres to find 350 g of salt in a bucket of sea water._

_The drum man lends you his boat to go after his donkey, grumbling._  
_You row out, with your Nubbin in the bows, still in its paper ears._  
_Ahead, Pinocchio is swimming for a white rock where a little goat stands bleating at him. Her wool is blue._  
_Behind him, the sea rises up out of itself._  
_A head comes out of the water, as big as a house, with a mouth like a cave._  
_It is the Terrible Dog-fish. It breathes in, and in goes Pinocchio, and in goes the sea, and in go you, boat and all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): the whale shark, the biggest fish, gulps sea water and strains out tiny food  
> _Some real sharks feed a bit like this. The whale shark, the biggest fish in the sea, opens its huge mouth and gulps sea water._  
> _The water streams out through its gills, and sieve-like pads catch the plankton: tiny drifting animals and plants._  
> _The Dog-fish is imaginary, and much hungrier, but a shark that swallows the sea comes from nature._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the whale shark feeds by gulping sea water and straining out plankton._


### Glossary

- **hibernate**: to spend the winter in a deep, slow sleep to save energy
- **plankton**: tiny animals and plants that drift in the sea and are food for many sea creatures

## A13-19. The Terrible Dog-fish

- `a13-19-s1`: Find your way through the dark inside the Dog-fish. · _Follow the faint light, far off. Mind the puddles; they’re mostly sea._
- `a13-19-s2`: Go to the old man at the table. · _You know who it is. So does Pinocchio. Let him go first._
- `a13-19-s3`: Light the way to the Dog-fish’s mouth. · _Your Nubbin carries the candle. Walk softly; the Dog-fish is asleep._

#### `a13-19-belly`

_It is dark and wet, and it smells of fried fish, which is not reassuring when you are inside one._  
_Your boat lies on its side in a shallow pool._  
**Pinocchio**: Help! Help! Isn’t anyone here?  
**The Tunny**: Only us unfortunates.  
**Pinocchio**: Who’s that?  
**The Tunny**: A poor Tunny, swallowed at the same time as you. What sort of fish are you?  
**Pinocchio**: I’m not any sort of fish! I’m a puppet. And that’s a traveller, and that’s a Nubbin.  
**The Tunny**: Then why let yourselves be swallowed? Never mind. Now we wait to be digested, with dignity.  
**Pinocchio**: I don’t want to be digested!  
_Far away, down the long dark of the Dog-fish, there is a little light._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): we see only when light reaches our eyes  
> _It is completely dark inside the Dog-fish, yet you can spot one tiny candle from far away._  
> _Why does a small light show up so well in total darkness?_  
> - ✅ Because light travels straight to our eyes, and there is no other light to hide it. → Yes. Light moves in straight lines, and a dark place has nothing to drown it out. On a dark night, one candle flame can be seen from more than a kilometre away.
> - Because the candle makes a sound. → We see light, not sound. Light from the flame reaches your eyes, and that is how you see it.
> - Because eyes shine in the dark. → Eyes do not make light. They collect it. In a dark place, even a tiny flame is easy to spot.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we see when light reaches our eyes, and that a small light shows up in the dark._


**Choices**

- **Head for the light.**
    - You start towards it. Your Nubbin goes first, because it is smallest and has the best eyes.
- **Ask the Tunny how big the Dog-fish is.**
    - **The Tunny**: A mile long, not counting the tail. I have never counted the tail. Nobody comes back from counting the tail.
    - You decide to head for the light.

#### `a13-19-belly-done`

_The light is a candle, stuck in the neck of a green glass bottle on a little table._  
_At the table sits an old man, as white as snow, eating a very small fish._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): time units: two years in weeks  
> _Geppetto has been inside the Dog-fish for two years. A year has 52 weeks._  
> _If he lit one new candle every week, how many candles would he have burned?_  
> - ✅ 104 candles. → Yes. 52 × 2 = 104 weeks, so 104 candles. A ship’s whole store of candles could run out in two years.
> - 54 candles. → That adds 52 and 2. Two years means 52 weeks twice: 52 × 2 = 104.
> - 52 candles. → That is one year. Geppetto has been here for two: 104 candles.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 52 weeks by 2 years to find 104 weeks._


#### `a13-19-babbo`

_Pinocchio stops, and shakes all over. He tries to speak and can’t, and then he can._  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo! It’s you! It’s really you! I won’t leave you again. Not ever. Not ever, ever!  
**Geppetto**: Pinocchio? Is it you? My Pinocchio?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): how to tell when someone really means a promise  
> _Pinocchio promises “I won’t leave you again. Not ever.” He has made promises before. How can we tell whether someone really means a promise like that?_  
> - By what they do afterwards, not only what they say. → That’s a fair answer. A promise is proved over time. And the way he behaves in the next scenes is the real answer.
> - By how upset they are when they say it. → That’s a fair answer. Real feeling matters. But Pinocchio has been upset and sincere before, and still run off.
> - We cannot know. We choose to trust and watch. → That’s a fair answer. Trust is a choice, and it grows when promises are kept.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how promises are proved by actions over time._

_Pinocchio is in his arms before he has finished, kissing him, talking, crying, all at once._  
**Pinocchio**: I sold the book, and Fire-eater sneezed, and the Fox and the Cat, and the oak, and the nose, and I was a donkey, Babbo, a whole donkey—  
**Geppetto**: Hush. Hush. You’re here.  
**Geppetto**: Two years I’ve been in here. A ship was swallowed the same day, full of stores: biscuits, cheese, candles, matches. It lasted, till now.  
**Geppetto**: This is the last candle. When it goes out, we’ll be in the dark.  
**Pinocchio**: Then we have to get out. Now. Through the mouth.  
**Geppetto**: I can’t swim, my boy.  
**Pinocchio**: I can. I’m wood. I’ll carry you.  

#### `a13-19-babbo-done`

**Geppetto**: And you. The traveller who slept in my corner. You came all this way.  
_Your Nubbin climbs up onto his shoulder, the way it rode in his cap, and he laughs for the first time in two years._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): why dry food keeps and moist food goes mouldy  
> _Geppetto lived on biscuits and cheese for two years. Hard dry biscuits keep for a very long time, while a soft loaf goes mouldy in days._  
> _Why?_  
> - ✅ Mould is a fungus that needs moisture to grow. → Yes. Dry biscuits give mould little water, so it cannot spread. People have dried food for thousands of years, and ship’s biscuit was made to last for months.
> - Biscuits are too hard for mould to bite. → Mould does not bite. It grows on food from tiny spores, and it needs water to do it.
> - Mould only likes the colour of bread. → Mould does not care about colour. It cares about water, warmth and food.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mould needs moisture, so dry foods like ship’s biscuit keep for a long time._

_Your Nubbin carries the candle in its green bottle, held up in both paws, and leads the way up the long throat._  
_The Dog-fish is very old, and has asthma, and sleeps with its mouth open._  
_Past its teeth you can see a piece of sky full of stars._  
_You climb over the tongue, which is as wide as a road and as soft as a bad mattress._  
_Three rows of teeth stand up against the stars._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): different stars are seen in different seasons because the Earth moves around the Sun  
> _The stars you see on a summer night are not quite the same ones you see in winter._  
> _As the Earth circles the Sun, the night side faces a different part of the sky._  
> _Sailors have used that pattern for thousands of years to tell the seasons, and to steer by the stars when the coast was out of sight._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the stars visible at night change with the seasons as the Earth orbits the Sun._

**Pinocchio**: Babbo, climb onto my back, and put your arms round my neck. Hold on as tight as you can. Leave the rest to me.  
_Just as you all reach the teeth, the Dog-fish sneezes, and throws you back down its throat in a great rush of wind._  
_Up again, and over the tongue again. Quietly, this time, with nobody breathing._  
_Then Pinocchio jumps into the sea, with Geppetto on his back. You jump after him, and your Nubbin holds the bottle up high._

_Pinocchio swims and swims. The shore is far away, and Geppetto is heavy, and the water is cold._  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo. I can’t. I’m sorry. I’m going under.  
**The Tunny**: Who’s going under?  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): tuna are fast, powerful swimmers that must keep moving to breathe  
> _Real tunny, or tuna, are among the fastest fish in the sea. Some can sprint at more than 60 kilometres an hour._  
> _A tuna breathes by swimming with its mouth open, so water flows over its gills. Most kinds have to keep moving all their lives._  
> _This one keeps swimming, with two passengers._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tuna are fast swimmers that keep moving so water flows over their gills._

_On the sand Pinocchio helps his father up, gently, as if Geppetto were made of glass. Then he turns to the Tunny._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): grazie: thank you in Italian  
> _Pinocchio cannot find a word big enough, and in his own language it would have been grazie._  
> _What does it mean, and what is the best way to say thank you when words are too small?_  
> - ✅ Grazie means thank you; a kind action can say it when words fall short. → Yes. Pinocchio gives a kiss on the nose instead. A hug, a gift, or a favour back can say what words cannot.
> - Grazie means goodbye. → Goodbye is arrivederci or ciao. Grazie is thank you.
> - Grazie means please. → Please is per favore. Grazie is thank you.
> _For grown-ups: Learned grazie (thank you) and talked about saying thanks when words are not enough._

_The Tunny, who is not used to it, dives at once, so that nobody will see him cry._
