### Glossary

- **digested**: broken down in the stomach so the body can use it as food
- **unfortunates**: people in sad trouble; here, those unlucky enough to be swallowed

## A13-20. The Wheel and the Chair

- `a13-20-s1`: Walk with Pinocchio and Geppetto, and find shelter. · _Geppetto is weak, so go slowly. Somebody is begging by the road._
- `a13-20-s2`: Stand by Pinocchio while he speaks to the Talking-cricket. · _Let him say it himself. It has taken him the whole book._
- `a13-20-s3`: Help Pinocchio earn a glass of milk at the water-wheel. · _A hundred buckets for one glass. Count with him._
- `a13-20-s4`: Keep Pinocchio company through the winter. · _He works every day now. The pennies in the jar are for a new coat._

#### `a13-20-road`

_Geppetto can hardly stand. Pinocchio gives him his arm, you walk on his other side, and the three of you go up the road very slowly._  
_By the road sit two beggars: a Fox, thin and mangy, with no tail, and a Cat._  
_The Cat is blind. Really blind, now._  
**The Fox**: Oh, Pinocchio! Have pity on two poor sick old creatures!  
**The Cat**: Sick old creatures.  
**The Fox**: We’re so poor I had to sell my tail to a pedlar. He wanted it for a fly-whisk.  
**Pinocchio**: Goodbye, you cheats. You fooled me once. You won’t fool me twice.  
**Pinocchio**: Money you steal never lasts the week. And a tail you sell doesn’t grow back.  
_He walks on, holding his father up. Behind you, the Cat turns his face to the sound of your feet._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): kindness and fairness: should we help someone who wronged us  
> _The Fox and the Cat cheated Pinocchio, and now they are hungry. Does being unkind to others take away your right to kindness?_  
> _Think about what Pinocchio does, and what you might do._  
> - Everyone deserves basic kindness, even people who did wrong. → That’s a fair answer. Kindness to a hungry creature does not mean forgetting what they did. You can share a crust and still keep your coins safe.
> - They should face the results of what they did. → That’s a fair answer. Choices have consequences, and Pinocchio is right not to trust them again. Still, helping is a separate question from trusting.
> - It depends whether they are sorry. → That’s a fair answer. Sorrow changes things, though the Fox’s whining is not quite the same. Where do you draw the line?
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether to help someone who has treated you badly, and the difference between kindness and trust._


**Choices**

- **Give the Cat a crust from your pocket.**
    - You go back and put a crust into the Cat’s paw. You don’t say anything.
    - He can’t see who it was. He turns his face up the road, to where Pinocchio is walking, and calls after him.
    - **The Cat**: Thank you, Pinocchio. You were always the kind one.
    - Pinocchio stops, and his ears go red. He doesn’t say anything either, and neither do you, and that is how the Cat keeps it.
- **Walk on with Pinocchio.**
    - You walk on. Behind you, the Fox is explaining to the Cat that it was only the wind.

#### `a13-20-road-done`

_At the end of a lane there is a little hut of straw with a tiled roof._  
_A sign on the door says PULL THE CORD, so Pinocchio pulls it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): imperative verbs: words that give a command  
> _The sign says PULL THE CORD. Which word tells you what to do, and what kind of word is it?_  
> - ✅ “Pull”: a command word, called an imperative verb. → Yes. Commands like pull, push, stop and wait are imperative verbs. Signs use them because they have to be quick to read.
> - “Cord”: a describing word. → Cord is a noun, the thing you pull. The command word is “pull”.
> - “The”: the word that gives the order. → “The” just points to which cord. The order is in the verb: pull.
> _For grown-ups: Identified an imperative verb on a sign._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how a character changes across a story  
> _At the start Pinocchio threw a mallet at the cricket. Now he asks for pardon and begs the cricket to spare his father._  
> _How has he changed?_  
> - ✅ He has learned to care about others, and to own his mistakes. → Yes. A well-written character changes because of what happens to them. Pinocchio has been hurt, and he has helped, and it shows.
> - He is exactly the same. → Compare the mallet scene with this one. The same puppet now asks for forgiveness. That is a real change.
> - He is just afraid of the cricket. → Fear is possible, but he asks for pardon for his father, not for himself. He has learned something deeper.
> _For grown-ups: Compared a character at the start and end of a story to describe how he has changed._

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, notice): milk gives calcium, protein and fluid, which help bones and muscles recover  
> _Milk is a good drink for a weak, hungry person._

> _After two years of dry biscuit and cheese, Geppetto’s body needs gentle food and plenty of fluid. A glass of milk is a good start._

#### `a13-20-wheel`

_The gardener up the lane is called Giangio. He has milk, at a penny a glass, and Pinocchio hasn’t got a penny._  
**Giangio**: Then turn my water-wheel. Draw up a hundred buckets, and you’ll have your glass.  
_Pinocchio turns the wheel, and you count. Your Nubbin counts on its paws, and loses its place at four, every time._  
_He has never worked so hard in his life. At a hundred buckets he is wet through to the grain._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): time problems: how long for a hundred buckets  
> _Each bucket takes Pinocchio 12 seconds to draw up. How many minutes does it take to draw up all 100? (Hint: 60 seconds make a minute.)_  
> - ✅ 20 minutes. → Yes. 100 × 12 = 1,200 seconds, and 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20 minutes. A glass of milk was hard-earned.
> - 12 minutes. → That is 12 seconds written as minutes. Multiply by 100 first: 1,200 seconds. Then divide by 60.
> - 100 minutes. → That takes each bucket as a minute. They are 12 seconds each, so 20 minutes in all.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 100 by 12 seconds and converted 1,200 seconds to 20 minutes._

**Giangio**: Till now my donkey turned that wheel. He’s dying, poor beast.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, notice): a water-wheel is a wheel and axle: a simple machine that turns a pull into rotation  
> _Giangio’s water-wheel works like a windlass: a wheel and axle._  
> _A long turn of the big wheel winds a rope onto the small axle, so a small push lifts a heavy bucket._  
> _The machine does not make the work disappear. You turn a long way for a short lift._  
> _It just makes the work possible for a person who is not strong._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a wheel and axle is a simple machine that makes lifting easier by spreading the work over a longer turn._

_Pinocchio goes into the stable. On the straw lies a donkey, worn out with hunger and work, as thin as a ladder._

**Pinocchio**: Candlewick! Oh, Candlewick.  
_Candlewick lays his head in Pinocchio’s lap and closes his eyes._  
_After a little while he stops breathing, very quietly, like a candle at the end of an evening._  
_Candlewick has died. His body has stopped working, and it will not start again._

**Giangio**: Why cry over a donkey? He cost you nothing.  
**Pinocchio**: He was my friend. We sat at the same desk at school.  
_Your Nubbin sits down by the donkey’s head and doesn’t move, so you don’t either, for a while._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): grief: what it is and what helps  
> _Pinocchio is grieving for his friend. Grief is the feeling after someone dies. What helps a person who is grieving?_  
> - ✅ Letting the feeling be, talking, sitting together, remembering. → Yes. Grief comes in waves. It is not a problem to fix. Company, tears and good memories help, and so does time.
> - Pretending to be fine so no one worries. → Hiding it can make it heavier. People who care about you usually want to know.
> - Forgetting as quickly as possible. → Remembering is how we keep a friend near. The sadness does ease, but memories are worth keeping.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what grief is and what helps when someone is grieving._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: how long to save forty pennies  
> _Pinocchio saves 2 pennies a day. How many days does it take to save 40 pennies?_  
> - ✅ 20 days. → Yes. 40 ÷ 2 = 20. That is almost three weeks of weaving baskets, and he gives the lot away in a minute.
> - 42 days. → That adds. To find how many 2s are in 40, divide: 40 ÷ 2 = 20.
> - 80 days. → That multiplies. Division asks how many 2-penny days make 40: 20.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 40 pennies by 2 pennies a day to find 20 days._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: kindness passed on  
> _Geppetto gave up his coat for Pinocchio. Pinocchio gives up his coat money for the Fairy. What larger idea does this echo show?_  
> - ✅ Love gets passed on: what you receive, you learn to give. → Yes. That is the theme the whole book builds to. A kindness shown to us tends to be shown to others in turn.
> - Coats are very valuable. → The coat is a symbol. It stands for what someone gives up out of love.
> - Pinocchio has no use for money. → He chooses to give it away, which is different from not needing it.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: kindness is passed on from one person to the next._

> _Pinocchio becomes a real boy after he changes how he lives, not by magic alone. What does the story seem to say about becoming “real”?_

> - It happens by pure luck. → The story points to something else: he changes how he acts, and then he changes.

## A14-1. The Loom

- `a14-01-s1`: Step onto Ithaca and wait at the gate. · _Touch the page, then walk up to the courtyard gate._
- `a14-01-s2`: Sit with Telemachus and the old traveller, and listen. · _Take the seat by the far pillar, out of the suitors’ way._
- `a14-01-s3`: Watch from the stair as Penelope comes down. · _Stand at the foot of the stair, by the hall door._

#### `a14-01-gate`

_Nova’s atlas opens on a page of blue: the sea, a scatter of islands, and one rough island with goats on it._  
_The blue turns warm and salty under your fingers. Then you are standing at a courtyard gate with your Nubbin._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): find Greece and Ithaca on a map and say which way home lies from Troy  
> **Mentes**: This page shows Greece, in the south-east of Europe, with its ragged coast and hundreds of islands. Ithaca is one, out in the Ionian Sea.  
> **Mentes**: Troy stood far to the east, across the sea, in what is now Turkey. Odysseus is trying to sail home from there to Ithaca.  
> **Mentes**: Which way must he mostly sail?  
> - ✅ West → Yes. Troy is to the east of Ithaca, so home lies to the west. Greeks have sailed these seas for thousands of years.
> - East → Troy is already in the east. Going east would take him further from Ithaca. Home is back the way the sun sets: west.
> - North → Troy is a little north of Ithaca’s line, but mostly it lies far to the east. Home is mostly west.
> _For grown-ups: Located Greece, Ithaca and Troy and used compass directions: home from Troy lies to the west._

_Inside, young men lounge about playing counters. The air smells of roast meat and spilt wine._  
_Nobody comes to the gate. An old traveller with a bronze spear waits beside you._  
**Mentes**: A stranger should never be left standing at a gate. This was a good house once.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): xenia: the Greek word for guest-friendship  
> **Mentes**: The Greeks had a word for this: xenia (ZEN-ee-ah). It means guest-friendship.  
> **Mentes**: You feed a stranger and give them a seat before you ask a single question. Even your enemy’s guest was safe at your table.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the Greek word xenia, guest-friendship, and the custom of feeding strangers before asking their names._

_A young man sits among the noise as if he were somewhere else. He sees you, and goes red to the ears._  
**Telemachus**: Strangers at my gate, and nobody went out to you. Forgive us. Come in, both of you. Eat first, then tell me what you need.  

**Choices**

- **Wait to be asked in properly.**
    - **Telemachus**: Now you’re asked. Properly. I am Telemachus. It’s my house, for what that’s worth these days.
- **Step in. You’re hungry.**
    - You step in. The old traveller nods at you, as if that was the right answer too.
- **Let your Nubbin go first.**
    - Your Nubbin trots in ahead of you and waits by the hearth, as if it knows where guests go.
    - Telemachus laughs, for the first time in a while.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): read feelings from how someone acts  
> _Telemachus went red to the ears when he saw you waiting, and then looked at his father’s spears. What do you think he is feeling?_  
> - ✅ Embarrassed and sad. A host should have come out, and he misses his father. → Yes. His face, his hands and his eyes all tell you, even though he hasn’t said it. Noticing that is called empathy.
> - Angry with you for turning up. → He isn’t cross with you. He apologised straight away. Look at what he does: he blushes, then looks at the spears and goes quiet. That says embarrassed and sad.
> - Sleepy. → Sleepy people yawn and droop. Telemachus went red and stared at his father’s spears. That points to embarrassed and sad.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s feelings from his face and actions (embarrassed, missing his father)._

**Telemachus**: Over here, away from that lot. You won’t hear yourself think near them.

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add two parts to make twenty years  
> _Odysseus spent ten years fighting at Troy, then another ten years trying to get home. How long has he been away in all?_  
> - ✅ 20 years → Yes: 10 + 10 = 20. Telemachus was a baby when he left, so he is about twenty himself now.
> - 10 years → Ten years is only the war. Add the ten years of the voyage home: 10 + 10 = 20.
> - 2 years → That is far too short. Ten years at war plus ten more at sea makes 10 + 10 = 20 years.
> _For grown-ups: Added 10 + 10 to find that Odysseus has been away for twenty years._

**Telemachus**: Those men are suitors. They want my mother to marry one of them, so until she chooses, they eat here. Every day.

**Mentes**: He is not dead. He is held somewhere on the wide sea, and he is trying. He is a man who finds a way.

**Choices**

    - **Mentes**: Some things I know because I’ve seen them. Some, because I know him.
- **Tell Telemachus you’ll go with him.**
    - **Telemachus**: You would? You don’t even know us.
    - Mentes smiles into his cup. Here, it seems, a guest becomes part of the house for as long as they stay.
- **Eat, and listen.**
    - You eat, and listen. The bread is good: it’s the last of the good flour, and Telemachus gave it to the strangers.

_Mentes crosses the yard. A bird flies up through the smoke-hole in the roof, and there is no Mentes._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): warm air rises, which carries smoke upwards  
> _The bird went up through the hole in the roof, the same way the smoke goes. Why does smoke rise instead of staying in the room?_  
> - ✅ Hot air is lighter than the cooler air around it, so it floats up. → Yes. The fire heats the air, the hot air rises, and it carries the smoke with it. That is why old halls had a hole in the roof.
> - The smoke is trying to escape. → Smoke has no plans. It rises because the hot air carrying it is lighter than the cool air around it.
> - The roof pulls it up. → Nothing pulls it. Hot air is lighter than cold air, so it floats upwards, and the smoke goes along.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heated air is lighter than cool air and rises, carrying smoke up and out._

**Telemachus**: That was no traveller.

#### `a14-01-stair`

_In the hall the bard Phemius is singing for the suitors, about the Greeks coming home from Troy and the ones who never did._  

> **Lesson** (music, 1-PS4-1, ask): a thinner string makes a higher note  
> _Phemius plays a lyre. When he plucks a string it wobbles to and fro, and that wobble, called a vibration, is the sound you hear._  
> _His lyre’s strings are all about the same length, but some are thicker than others. Which string will sound the highest note?_  
> - ✅ The thinnest one → Yes. A thin string wobbles quickly, and quick wobbles make a high note. Thick strings wobble slowly and sound low.
> - The thickest one → That one wobbles slowly, and slow wobbles make a low note. For a high note you want a thin string.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound is vibration and that thin strings sound higher than thick ones._

_A woman comes down the stair with two maids, and stops in the doorway with a veil across her face._

**Telemachus**: That cloth has been on that loom as long as the suitors have been in this hall. Ask Antinous about it. He loves telling it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): use a small clue to work out what is odd  
> _A clue is a small detail that points to something bigger._  
> _Telemachus says the cloth has been on the loom for as long as the suitors have been eating his house. What is odd about that?_  
> - ✅ A cloth should be finished long before that. → Yes. Even a very big cloth gets finished in a few months. A cloth that is never done suggests somebody doesn’t want it done.
> - Nothing is odd. Cloth takes ages. → It does take time, but not years and years. A weaver who works every day should finish. Telemachus is giving you a clue.
> _For grown-ups: Used a small clue (a cloth that never gets finished) to notice that something is odd._

> _Telemachus’s house is being eaten bare, yet he gave two strangers his best bread. Why do you think he did?_  
> - Because a host looks after guests, however hard things are. → That’s a fair answer. In his world, welcoming a guest was close to a law, and he is proving he is not like the suitors.
> - Because sharing felt better than being as mean as the suitors. → That’s a fair answer too. He is choosing to be a different kind of person from the men who are taking from him.
> - Because he wanted something from you, such as help. → That’s a fair thought. People do ask for help from guests. But he fed you before he asked for anything, and that says something about him.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone might share when they have little (a think question with no single answer)._

### Glossary

- **xenia**: The Greek word for guest-friendship: the custom of welcoming and feeding strangers.
- **suitor**: A man who wants to marry someone and keeps coming to ask.

## A14-2. The Assembly

- `a14-02-s1`: Stand behind Telemachus at the assembly. · _Follow him to the meeting-place and stand behind his father’s seat._
- `a14-02-s2`: Listen to Antinous tell the story of the web. · _Stay by Telemachus while Antinous speaks._
- `a14-02-s3`: Hold the torch while Penelope works. · _Keep the torch high and steady by the loom._

#### `a14-02-assembly`

_At dawn the heralds call the men of Ithaca to the meeting-place. Nobody has called them together since Odysseus sailed._  
_Telemachus comes in with a spear in his hand and two hounds at his heels. The old men make room for him in his father’s seat._  
_You stand behind the seat with your Nubbin. The suitors sit in a row along the front, and grin._  
**Telemachus**: Nobody’s army is coming. I called you about my own trouble. My father is lost, and my house is being eaten.  
**Telemachus**: Go home, all of you, and eat your own dinners. Aren’t you ashamed?  
_He throws the speaker’s staff on the ground, and his eyes fill with tears. For a moment nobody says anything._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): a meeting needs a way to give people turns  
> _At Ithaca’s meetings, only the person holding the speaker’s staff could talk. Why might a meeting need something like that?_  
> - ✅ So everyone knows whose turn it is, and one person talks at a time. → Yes. Taking turns lets every voice be heard. Much later, in the city of Athens, citizens met in an assembly and used rules like this to make decisions together.
> - So the speaker looks taller. → Nice idea, but no. It was for turns: whoever held the staff had the right to speak, and the others waited and listened.
> - So nobody has to listen. → The opposite. While someone holds the staff, everyone else is meant to listen, and then it is their turn.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a speaker’s staff was a way of taking turns in an early assembly._

_Then someone in the front row laughs, and the rest of the row joins in._  

**Choices**

- **Pick up the staff and hand it back to him.**
    - You pick up the staff and give it back to him. He takes it without looking at you, and holds it like a rope.
- **Stare at the one who laughed first.**
    - You look straight at him. He stops laughing, remembers he’s a suitor, and starts again, a bit louder.
- **Stay where you are, right behind him.**
    - You don’t move. Telemachus feels it, and his back straightens a little against the noise.

#### `a14-02-assembly-done`

_A tall man in a bright cloak stands up from the front row: Antinous, the loudest of the suitors._  
**Antinous**: Blame us? Blame your mother. She is the cleverest woman in Greece, and she has led us on for years.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): who is to blame, and who made which choice  
> _Antinous says it is Penelope’s fault that the suitors are eating Telemachus’s house. Is he right?_  
> - No. Coming and staying was the suitors’ own choice. → That’s a fair answer. Penelope may have kept them waiting, but nobody made them come, and nobody made them eat the pigs.
> - Partly. She did keep them waiting. → That’s a fair answer too. Both can be true, but only one side was taking things that weren’t theirs.
> - It’s hard to say when everyone blames someone else. → That’s a wise thought. When people point fingers, it helps to ask who made which choice.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about blame: separating one person’s choices from another’s (a think question)._


#### `a14-02-antinous`

**Antinous**: Three years she promised, and three years we waited. Shall I tell you how she did it? Everyone else knows.  
**Antinous**: She put up a great wooden frame in her room, and began weaving the finest, biggest cloth you ever saw.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the word text comes from a Latin word for weaving  
> _Weaving gave us words. The Latin word texere means “to weave”, and it gave us textile, and also the word for the writing on this page._  
> _Which of these words comes from texere?_  
> - ✅ text → Yes. A text is something woven out of words, the way a textile is woven out of thread. That’s why we talk about weaving a tale.
> - tent → A tent comes from a Latin word meaning “stretch”, not “weave”. The word from texere is text: words woven together.
> - tell → Tell comes from Old English, where it meant both “count” and “relate”. It isn’t from texere. The one that is: text.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that “text” and “textile” both come from the Latin for weaving._

**Antinous**: She said it was a shroud, a funeral cloth, for old Laertes, Odysseus’s father. “Let me finish it first,” she said, “or the women will talk.”  
**Antinous**: Reasonable. We are reasonable men. We waited.  
_As he talks, the edges of the meeting-place go soft, as if the page itself were listening._  
_The stone turns to floorboards, and the daylight to torchlight. You are in an upstairs room, holding a torch you don’t remember picking up._

_In front of you stands the great loom. Penelope sits at it, alone, with a small knife._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply months in a year by three years  
> _Antinous says Penelope kept the suitors waiting for three years. There are 12 months in every year. How many months is three years?_  
> - ✅ 36 months → Yes. Three groups of twelve: 12 + 12 + 12 = 36, or 3 × 12 = 36.
> - 15 months → That is 3 + 12. We need three whole years of twelve months each: 3 × 12 = 36.
> - 24 months → That is two years (2 × 12). Three years is one more twelve: 24 + 12 = 36.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 3 × 12 to turn three years into 36 months._


#### `a14-02-loom`

**Antinous**: Every day we watched her weave. And every night, by torchlight, she took the stitches out again.  
_Penelope pulls a thread, and a day’s work comes undone in one long, soft sigh. She winds it back on the shuttle for tomorrow._  
**Penelope**: Hold the torch a little higher. There. Thank you.  
**Penelope**: Every row I weave is one more day for him to come home. Every row I take out gives that day back.  
**Penelope**: The long threads stand still and wait. The short one goes back and forth, back and forth. I know which one I am.  

> **Lesson** (art, L.3.4, ask): how a loom works: warp and weft  
> _On a loom, long threads are stretched tight and held still. They are called the warp._  
> _A shorter thread, the weft, is passed over one warp thread and under the next, back and forth._  
> _Penelope says the short one goes back and forth. Which thread is the weft?_  
> - ✅ The short thread that goes back and forth → Yes. Over, under, over, under: that pattern is how the weft locks the warp into cloth.
> - The long threads that stand still → Those are the warp, held tight on the frame. The weft is the short thread that travels across them.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the parts of a loom: still warp threads and a back-and-forth weft thread woven over and under._

_Your Nubbin holds the loose end of the thread so it doesn’t tangle. It is very serious about this._  
**Penelope**: They think I am slow. I am the fastest weaver on Ithaca. I have to be, to unpick it all by dawn.  
_Out in the dark passage, a floorboard creaks. Someone has been listening at the door._  

**Choices**

- **Go and look in the passage.**
    - You look, and a maid’s skirt whisks round the corner and is gone. You know where she’s going.
- **Tell Penelope someone heard.**
    - **Penelope**: I know. I’ve known for a week which one it would be. I thought I’d finish tonight’s row anyway.
- **Hold the torch steady. Keep going.**
    - You keep the torch steady, and she keeps going. Neither of you looks at the door.

#### `a14-02-loom-done`

_The torchlight goes thin, and it is daylight again. You are standing in the meeting-place with empty hands._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add and subtract to see why a total stays the same  
> _Say Penelope wove 12 rows on Monday and unpicked 12 that night. She did the same on Tuesday._  
> _How many rows does the cloth have on Wednesday morning?_  
> - ✅ 0 rows → Yes: 12 − 12 = 0 each night, so she is back where she started. That is why the cloth never got finished.
> - 24 rows → That is 12 + 12, the rows she wove. But she took out 12 each night as well: 24 − 24 = 0.
> - 12 rows → Close. Monday ends at 0 (12 − 12), and Tuesday ends at 0 again. So Wednesday begins with no rows at all.
> _For grown-ups: Used addition and subtraction to see that weaving 12 rows and unpicking 12 leaves 0._

**Antinous**: A maid told us. We caught her at it, so she had to finish the thing.  
**Antinous**: Send your mother back to her father’s house, boy, and let him marry her off. Until then, we eat.

**Mentor**: A ship, and twenty men to row it. I have found both. Fetch food for the voyage, and tell no one.  
_Eurycleia fills twelve jars of wine and twenty measures of barley-meal, crying the whole time._  
**Eurycleia**: Your father sailed over the sea and never came back. Now you. Who will I have left to scold?  
**Telemachus**: Don’t tell my mother. Not for eleven or twelve days, unless she asks.  
_At nightfall the ship slides out of the harbour. You sit in the stern with your Nubbin, and a wind comes up behind you from nowhere._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): a sail catches the push of the wind  
> _A sail is a big sheet that catches moving air. The wind pushes on it, and that push moves the whole ship._  
> _Which wind will carry your ship straight ahead?_  
> - ✅ A wind blowing from behind the ship → Yes. A wind from behind pushes the sail forwards, and the ship follows. Sailors call it a following wind.
> - A wind blowing straight at the front → That wind pushes against the ship and slows it. A ship wants the wind at its back.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wind pushes on a sail, and a wind from behind moves a ship forwards._

_Mentor sits by the steering oar and looks up at the sail. The wind is exactly as strong as it needs to be._  

### Glossary

- **shroud**: A cloth used to wrap someone who has died.
- **warp**: The long threads held tight on a loom while the cloth is woven across them.
- **weft**: The thread that goes back and forth over and under the warp to make cloth.

#### `a14-03-pylos`

_Sandy Pylos, at sunrise. The whole town is on the beach at a great feast to honour Poseidon, god of the sea._  
**Telemachus**: I can’t. I don’t know how to talk to an old king. What if I get it wrong?  
**Mentor**: Some of it you will think of yourself. The rest will be given you. Go on.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): find ways to feel braver before something nerve-racking  
> _Telemachus is frightened of talking to an old king and getting it wrong. What could help a person feel braver at a moment like that?_  
> - A slow breath, and remembering why he came. → That’s a fair answer. Slow breathing calms the body, and remembering your reason gives you something stronger than the fear.
> - A friend standing close by. → That’s a fair answer. You are that friend, right now. Feeling that someone is on your side can make a hard thing smaller.
> - Practising a first sentence in his head. → That’s a fair answer. A first sentence gets you started, and the rest often follows. Telemachus has one ready: his name and his father’s.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ways to manage nerves before a hard conversation (a think question)._

_Nestor’s son runs to meet the strangers before anyone asks who they are, and sits you all on soft fleeces on the sand._  
_Nestor is so old that he was old at Troy. He has outlived nearly everyone he went there with._  
**Nestor**: Eat first. Then names. Then, if you like, sorrows. There is always time for sorrows.  
**Telemachus**: I’m Odysseus’s son. I have come for news of my father. Any news, even bad.  
**Nestor**: His son! You talk just like him. I would never have thought a young man could sound so like him.  
**Nestor**: But I know nothing, child. We left Troy together, quarrelled, and parted at sea. He turned back. I came home.  

**Choices**

- **Ask who might know.**
    - **Nestor**: Menelaus. He was blown about longer than any of us, and came home last. Go to Sparta. My son will drive you.
- **Ask if there’s any hope.**
    - **Nestor**: With that one? There is always hope. I never once saw him stuck for long.
- **Let your Nubbin sit by the old king.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs onto the fleece beside Nestor. He rests an old hand on it, as if it were a grandchild, and goes on talking.

_When the feast is over, Mentor rises, and is a sea-eagle, and is gone over the water. Everyone on the beach falls silent._  
**Nestor**: That was Athena, daughter of Zeus. She stood by your father at Troy. If she walks beside you, you won’t go far wrong.  
_Nestor’s people honour her on the shore in the old way. You stand back with your Nubbin and keep quiet, as guests should._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): show respect at someone else’s ceremony  
> _Nestor’s people are honouring Athena in their own way. You and your Nubbin stand back and keep quiet. Why is that good manners for a guest?_  
> - ✅ It shows respect for what matters to other people. → Yes. You don’t have to share a belief to be respectful of it. For some people in Greece today, these old gods are still honoured, so a quiet guest is a kind guest.
> - It means nobody will notice you. → That might be a side effect, but it isn’t the reason. Standing quietly says: this matters to you, so it matters to me to be careful.
> - Guests aren’t allowed to see ceremonies. → Guests were often welcome to watch. The point is how you behave: quietly and politely, so you don’t spoil it for the people it belongs to.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that guests show respect at other people’s ceremonies by staying quiet and polite._


#### `a14-03-sparta`

_Two days in a chariot over the hills, with Nestor’s son Pisistratus at the reins. Your Nubbin rides up front and leans into the corners._  
_Sparta lies in a hollow among the hills. Menelaus’s house gleams with bronze and gold, amber, silver and ivory._  
**Telemachus**: Pisistratus, look at it. Is this what the house of Zeus is like?  
**Menelaus**: No mortal’s house is like Zeus’s, boy. And I would give two-thirds of all this to have back the friends who died at Troy.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): two-thirds means two of three equal parts  
> _Menelaus says he would give away two-thirds of his treasure. Picture it split into 3 equal piles, each one third._  
> _How many piles would he give away?_  
> - ✅ 2 of the 3 piles → Yes. Two-thirds is two of the three equal parts: 1/3 + 1/3. That leaves one pile for himself.
> - 1 of the 3 piles → One pile is one-third. Two-thirds is one more third on top: two of the three piles.
> - Half of it → Half is 1 of 2 equal parts. Two-thirds is 2 of 3 equal parts, which is a little more than half.
> _For grown-ups: Understood two-thirds as two of three equal parts (1/3 + 1/3)._

_He hasn’t asked your names. In Sparta, as in Pylos, a guest is fed first and asked after._  
_Then a woman comes down from a high room with her spindle, and stops, and stares at Telemachus._  
**Helen**: I have never seen anyone so like another. This must be Odysseus’s son. He has his father’s feet. His hands.  
**Menelaus**: Now that you say it… The hair, the look about the eyes. You are right, my dear.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS3-1, ask): children share traits with their parents  
> _Helen knew Telemachus was Odysseus’s son from his hair, eyes, hands and feet. Why do children so often look like their parents?_  
> - ✅ Traits such as hair and eye colour are passed from parents to children. → Yes. Many features are inherited, though every child is also a little different from both parents.
> - Children copy their parents’ faces as they grow. → Faces can’t be copied, but they can be inherited. Traits are passed down from parents before a child is even born.
> - It is only a coincidence. → It happens too often to be luck. Inherited traits are passed from parents to children, so families often look alike.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that inherited traits are passed from parents to children, so families look alike._

_Telemachus holds his cloak up in front of his face. Everyone weeps a little, even Pisistratus, who never met Odysseus at all._  

**Choices**

- **Tell them yes, it’s his son.**
    - You say it for him, because he can’t. Menelaus reaches across the table and grips Telemachus by the arm.
- **Let Telemachus answer.**
    - **Telemachus**: I am. I’ve come to ask whether my father is alive.

**Menelaus**: Sit. Eat. In the morning I’ll tell you something I’ve told nobody since I came home.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): waiting patiently for important news  
> _Telemachus must wait all night to hear Menelaus’s secret. What can help when you are waiting for something very important?_  
> - ✅ Eating, resting, and thinking about something calm. → Yes. Looking after your body and giving your mind a rest makes waiting easier. The news will still be there in the morning.
> - Asking again and again until he tells. → Asking can feel useful, but it often makes the wait feel longer, and it can wear out the person you’re asking.
> - Pretending you don’t care. → Pretending hides the feeling but doesn’t make it go away. It’s better to say you are impatient, and then find something calming to do.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about patience: calming ways to wait for important news._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): protean means able to change shape  
> _Proteus could turn into anything, so English borrowed his name. Protean describes something that keeps changing. Which of these is protean?_  
> - ✅ A cloud that keeps changing shape → Yes. A cloud can look like a lion, then a tree, then nothing. That is protean: always changing, like Proteus.
> - A stone wall that never moves → A wall stays the same, which is the opposite. Protean means changing shape again and again.
> - A clock that always strikes at noon → A clock keeps its pattern. Protean is for things that keep changing form, as Proteus did.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word “protean”, from Proteus, meaning able to keep changing shape._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): follow a route on a map using compass directions  
> _Telemachus came by sea to Pylos, then by chariot east to Sparta. To get back to his ship at Pylos, which way must the chariot go?_  
> - ✅ Roughly west → Yes. Sparta lies east of Pylos, so the way back is roughly west. Reverse a route and each direction flips to its opposite.
> - Roughly east → East is the way they came. To go back the way they came, flip it to its opposite: west.
> - Straight up to the sky → A chariot rides on the ground! On a map, reversing a journey flips each direction: east becomes west.
> _For grown-ups: Followed and reversed a route using compass directions (east on the way there, west on the way back)._

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add days of travel  
> _It took two days by chariot to get from Pylos to Sparta, and two days to ride back again._  
> _How many days of chariot riding is that in all?_  
> - ✅ 4 days → Yes: 2 + 2 = 4. A journey there and back is the same distance twice.
> - 2 days → That is only one way. The ride back takes two more days: 2 + 2 = 4.
> - 6 days → That is one day too many for each leg. Two days there and two back is 2 + 2 = 4.
> _For grown-ups: Added 2 + 2 to find the total days of a there-and-back journey._

#### `a14-04-ogygia`

_An island at the navel of the sea, far from anywhere. Alder, poplar and sweet cypress grow here, with owls and sea-crows nesting in them._  
_A vine heavy with grapes grows over the mouth of a cave. Four springs run out across meadows of violets and wild parsley._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, ask): animals live where their needs are met  
> _The island has trees, four springs and meadows, and owls and sea-crows are nesting in the branches. Why do you think the birds chose this place?_  
> - ✅ It has the water, food and nesting places they need. → Yes. Animals live where their needs are met: water to drink, food to eat, and safe places to raise their young.
> - Birds go wherever it is coldest. → Most birds prefer places that are comfortable and full of food. Here there are springs, trees and meadows, which is plenty.
> - They were lost at sea. → Some birds do get lost, but nesting birds stay because they have what they need: water, food and shelter.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals live where their needs for water, food and shelter are met._

_Someone lands on the beach beside you as lightly as a gull: a young man with golden sandals and a wand._

_In the cave a cedar fire is burning, and a woman is weaving at a loom with a golden shuttle, and singing._  
_She knows Hermes at once._  
**Calypso**: Hermes. You don’t often come. Tell me what you want, and then let me give you dinner.  
_She sets the food of the gods in front of him, ambrosia and red nectar. You are given bread and figs, which is food for people._  
**Hermes**: Zeus sends word. The man who is with you must go home. It is not his fate to die here, far from his own people.  
**Calypso**: You gods are hard. Whenever one of us loves a mortal, you begrudge it.  
**Calypso**: I found him clinging to a keel. I fed him. I told him I would make him never die and never grow old.  
**Calypso**: But nobody goes against the will of Zeus. Let him go, then, over the sea, if that is what he wants.  

**Choices**

- **Thank Calypso for the figs.**
    - **Calypso**: You’re welcome, little guest. You, at least, will go home glad.
- **Ask Hermes where Odysseus is.**
    - **Hermes**: On the shore. He is always on the shore.

> - Staying alone and not speaking. → Being alone with a big feeling for years is exactly what has made Odysseus so tired. Company helps, even quiet company.
> _For grown-ups: Named homesickness and thought about what helps: talking and company._

> - ✅ 84 months → Yes. 7 × 12 = (7 × 10) + (7 × 2) = 70 + 14 = 84 months.
> - 19 months → That is 7 + 12. Seven years of twelve months each means multiplying: 7 × 12 = 84.
> - 72 months → Close, but 72 is 6 × 12. Seven years is one more twelve: 72 + 12 = 84.

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): a thin edge pushes hard on a small spot, so an axe can cut wood  
> _An axe blade is thick at the back and very thin at the edge._  
> _When you swing it, all the push is squeezed onto that thin edge. Why does that help it cut wood?_  
> - ✅ The push is squeezed onto a tiny spot, so it presses very hard. → Yes. The same push spread over a wide, blunt edge wouldn’t cut at all. A thin edge focuses the force on a small spot.
> - A thin edge is lighter, so it floats through the wood. → Lighter isn’t the reason. The thin edge concentrates the push on a tiny spot, so it presses hard enough to split the wood.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a thin sharp edge focuses a push on a small area, which is why axes cut._

_He works four days: a deck, a mast and yard, a steering oar, a fence of willow against the waves. Calypso brings cloth for the sail._

**Calypso**: So you are going. If you knew all that is waiting out there, you would stay.  
**Calypso**: Stay, and you will never die. You will never grow old. Nothing will ever happen to you again.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about whether being safe is the same as being well  
> _Calypso offers Odysseus a life where nothing bad will ever happen to him, and nothing will ever happen at all. He chooses to go home anyway._  
> _Is being safe the same as being well?_  
> - No. A life with nothing in it can be safe but still empty. → That’s a fair answer. Odysseus seems to think so too: he would take his risky, real life over a safe, stuck one.
> - Yes. If nothing hurts, that is the best life. → That’s a fair answer. Nobody wants pain, and safety matters a great deal. Odysseus might ask whether you would still feel like yourself, though.
> - It depends what you would be missing. → That’s a thoughtful answer. For Odysseus it is home, his family and his own name. For someone else it might be different.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether safe is the same as well (a think question)._

**Calypso**: Is she lovelier than me? She can’t be. A mortal woman can’t compare with a goddess.

**Odysseus**: And I want to go home. I want it every day. If a god wrecks me on the way, I will bear it. I’ve borne worse.  
_Calypso doesn’t argue. Then he looks across the fire at you, as if he wants a witness._  
**Odysseus**: Tell me honestly, guest. Would you stay?  

**Choices**

- **“No. Home.”**
    - **Odysseus**: Home. Yes. The word does all the work, doesn’t it.
- **“I don’t know.”**
    - **Odysseus**: Good answer. It’s only easy once you’ve lost something.
- **“Not if nothing would ever happen again.”**
    - **Odysseus**: That’s it. That’s exactly it. She’d keep me safe for ever. Safe isn’t the same as alive.

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): stars show direction: north is on your left when you face east  
> _The Great Bear is a pattern of stars in the northern sky. Odysseus keeps it on his left._  
> _If north is on your left, which way are you facing?_  
> - ✅ East → Yes. Face east, and north is on your left and south on your right. Sailors have steered by the Great Bear for thousands of years.
> - West → Face west and north is on your right. With north on your left, you must be facing east.
> - South → Face south and north is behind you. For north to be on your left, you must face east.
> _For grown-ups: Used the northern stars to work out direction: north on your left means facing east._

_You sit on the deck with your back against the mast. Your Nubbin watches the island go small, and then go._  

#### `a14-04-complete`

_Calypso stands on the beach until he is out of sight. Then she goes back into her cave, to her loom._  
_She is weaving something. You don’t see what, and perhaps she doesn’t know yet either._  
_Seventeen days of wind in the sail._  
_On the eighteenth, the shadowy hills of a new land rise out of the sea like a shield laid on the water._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile compares two things using like or as  
> _The hills “rise out of the sea like a shield laid on the water”. That is a simile, a comparison that uses “like” or “as”._  
> _What is being compared?_  
> - ✅ The hills and a shield → Yes. Dark, rounded hills lying on the sea do look like a great shield laid flat. A simile lets you picture something new by comparing it to something you know.
> - The sea and a loom → The loom belongs to Calypso. The “like” in this sentence connects the hills to a shield laid on the water.
> - The wind and a sail → The wind and sail are just part of the voyage. The simile is “like a shield”, which describes the hills.
> _For grown-ups: Found the simile “like a shield laid on the water” and what it compares._

**Odysseus**: Land. Do you see? Whose, I don’t know. But land.  

### Glossary

- **ambrosia**: The food of the gods in Greek stories.
- **adze**: A tool like an axe, with the blade set across the handle, for shaping wood.

## A14-5. The Raft

- `a14-05-s1`: Hold on through the storm. · _Keep hold of your plank and keep your Nubbin on your head._
- `a14-05-s2`: Swim for the shore. · _Stay outside the surf and swim along the coast to the river mouth._
- `a14-05-s3`: Find somewhere dry to sleep. · _Climb the bank to the two olive bushes that grow from one root._

#### `a14-05-storm`

_Far off, coming home from the edge of the world, Poseidon, the god who shakes the earth, sees the little raft on his sea._  
_He knows the man on it. He has an old anger against him, for a reason you haven’t heard yet._  
_He gathers the clouds, and every wind comes at once. Night comes down out of the sky in the middle of the day._  
**Odysseus**: The ones who fell at Troy were the lucky ones. They had their friends round them. Out here there is nobody.  
_A wave as big as a house hits the raft. The mast snaps, and Odysseus goes under, and comes up, and climbs back on._  
_You are holding a plank with both arms. Your Nubbin sits on your head, holding on to your hair, and neither of you lets go._  
_Then a white sea-bird comes skimming through the spray, and lands on the raft, and is a woman._  
**Ino**: Poor man. Why is Poseidon so angry with you? He won’t drown you, though he would like to. Listen to me.  
**Ino**: Take off those heavy clothes. Leave the raft to the winds, and swim for the land of the Phaeacians.  
**Ino**: Here, tie my veil round your chest. While you wear it, you won’t drown.  
**Ino**: When you reach land, untie it and throw it back into the sea. And turn your face away as you throw.  
_She is a bird again, and gone into the dark water. Odysseus holds the veil and looks at it with deep suspicion._  
**Odysseus**: Another god’s trick? I’ll stay on the raft while it holds. Then I’ll swim.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): decide whether to trust help from someone you don’t know  
> _Odysseus isn’t sure whether to trust Ino’s gift. What would you want to find out before trusting help from someone you don’t know?_  
> - Why is she helping, and what does she get out of it? → That’s a fair answer. Asking about someone’s reasons is a good way to test whether an offer is honest.
> - Has she done anything to show she is kind? → That’s a fair answer. What people do usually tells you more than what they say.
> - What would a trusted grown-up say? → That’s a fair answer, and a very good rule for everyday life. When you’re unsure about an offer from a stranger, check with someone you trust.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to decide whether to trust a stranger’s help (a think question)._


**Choices**

- **“She meant it. Take it.”**
    - **Odysseus**: Perhaps. I’ve been tricked by kinder faces. I’ll take it, and still hold on to the raft.
- **Hold on, and say nothing.**
    - You hold on, and your Nubbin holds on. The raft holds on too, for now.
- **Help him tie the veil.**
    - Your fingers are numb, but you get the knot tied. He nods once, with water running off his beard.

#### `a14-05-storm-done`

_The biggest wave of all._  
_The raft goes to pieces like a heap of straw in a wind, and he climbs onto one beam as if it were a horse._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): wood floats because it is less dense than water  
> _The raft broke apart, but the wooden beam still holds Odysseus up. Why does wood float?_  
> - ✅ It is lighter than the same amount of water. → Yes. Scientists say wood is less dense than water. A few very heavy woods sink, but most float, which is why people have built boats from wood for thousands of years.
> - Because it is wet. → Getting wet doesn’t make a thing float. It floats because the same amount of wood weighs less than the same amount of water.
> - Because the sea is trying to help. → The sea has no plans, even in a story! The real reason is that wood is less dense than water, so water pushes it up.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wood floats because it is less dense than water._

_He strips off his cloak, ties the veil round his chest, and dives in. You let go of your plank and follow._  

#### `a14-05-swim`

_Two days and two nights in the swell. On the third morning the wind drops, a wave lifts you, and there is land, close._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): hours in two days and two nights  
> _Odysseus swims for two days and two nights. There are 24 hours in one day and night together. How many hours is that?_  
> - ✅ 48 hours → Yes. 24 + 24 = 48 hours, or 2 × 24. No wonder he can’t feel his arms.
> - 24 hours → That is only one day and night. He swam two, so double it: 24 × 2 = 48.
> - 12 hours → That is only half a day. Two whole days and nights is 2 × 24 = 48 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 2 × 24 to find that two days and two nights is 48 hours._

**Odysseus**: Land! I could cry. I have been crying. I could cry more.  
_But the shore is all cliff and reef, and the surf roars against it._  
_A wave throws him onto a rock, and he holds on, and loses skin to it._  
_He swims out again and along the coast, outside the surf, looking for a way in. Athena put that thought in his head, he says later._  
_There: the mouth of a river, clear of rocks and out of the wind._  
_He speaks to the river as a guest speaks at the door of a lord’s house. The current stills, and lets him in._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification: speaking to something as if it were a person  
> _Odysseus speaks to the river “as a guest speaks at the door of a lord’s house”, and the river lets him in._  
> _Treating a river as if it were a person is called personification. Which sentence is personification?_  
> - ✅ “The river welcomed him in.” → Yes. Rivers can’t welcome anybody, but the sentence gives it a person’s manners. Writers use personification to make nature feel alive.
> - “The river was wide and brown.” → That simply describes the river. Personification gives a non-human thing human actions or feelings.
> - “The river flows to the sea.” → That is a plain fact. For personification, the river would have to act like a person, for example by welcoming someone.
> _For grown-ups: Identified personification, where a river is described as if it were a person._

_He crawls up the bank into the reeds and kisses the ground. Your Nubbin lies down beside him, flat as a dropped mitten._  

#### `a14-05-swim-done`

_When his breath comes back he unties the veil and throws it into the river, and turns his face away._  
_The water carries it back to the sea._  
_You don’t look either. It seems the right thing._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): returning what you borrowed shows trust and thanks  
> _Odysseus gives the veil back exactly as he was told. What does it show when we return something we borrowed?_  
> - ✅ That we are trustworthy, and thankful for the help. → Yes. Giving things back, and saying thank you, keeps friendships strong and makes people glad to help us next time.
> - That we never needed the help. → He needed it very much. Returning what you borrowed isn’t about pretending you didn’t need it. It’s about being grateful and fair.
> - That it doesn’t matter either way. → It matters a lot to the person who lent it, and to whether they’ll lend again. Keeping a promise to return something builds trust.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why returning borrowed things matters: trust and gratitude._


#### `a14-05-olives`

**Odysseus**: If I sleep by the river, the cold will finish me. If I go up into the woods, the wild animals might. I’ll risk the woods.  
_Just above the bank, two olive bushes grow from one root, one wild and one tame, so close that no rain or wind or sun gets in._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, ask): plants survive hot, dry places with deep roots and small, tough leaves  
> _Olive trees grow where summers are hot and dry, and some live for hundreds of years. What helps a plant survive in hot, dry weather?_  
> - ✅ Deep roots, and small, tough leaves that lose little water. → Yes. Olive roots reach far down for water, and the narrow, leathery leaves keep it from escaping. That is why olives thrive around the Mediterranean.
> - Huge, thin leaves that catch every drop. → Big thin leaves lose water fast in the sun. Olives do the opposite: small, tough leaves hold water in.
> - Roots that stay right at the surface. → Surface roots dry out first. Olive roots go deep to find water that is still there when the surface is dry.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how olive trees survive hot dry summers: deep roots and small, tough leaves._

_Underneath, the dead leaves lie deep enough to cover two or three people in winter. Odysseus is glad to see them._  
_He lies down in the middle and heaps leaves over himself, the way a farmer far from neighbours buries an ember in the ashes to keep it alive._  
_There is room for you, and for your Nubbin, which burrows down until only its ears show._  
**Odysseus**: Two olives from one root. My wife would say that meant something. Goodnight, guest.  

**Choices**

- **Keep watch for a while.**
    - You keep watch. Nothing comes but an owl, which looks at your Nubbin’s ears and decides against it.
- **Pile more leaves over him.**
    - You heap them up to his chin, but he’s already asleep. In his sleep he says a name, and it isn’t Calypso’s.
- **Sleep.**
    - You sleep. It’s the first sleep anyone has had in three days.

_Athena pours sleep over his eyes, to rest him from all his labour._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): sleep lets the body and brain recover  
> _Odysseus has hardly slept for days. What does sleep do for a tired body and mind?_  
> - ✅ It lets the body repair itself, and the brain rest and sort out the day. → Yes. While you sleep your body mends and your brain tidies up what you learned. Children of school age need about 9 to 12 hours a night.
> - Nothing. It is just a way to pass the time. → Sleep is busy work for the body, even while you lie still. Muscles mend, the brain stores memories, and you wake up better able to think and feel.
> - It makes you older faster. → The reverse. Good sleep helps you grow and stay healthy. Not sleeping is what makes you feel old and grumpy.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sleep helps the body repair and the brain rest, and that school-age children need about 9 to 12 hours._

## A14-6. Nausicaa

- `a14-06-s1`: Help with the washing at the river. · _Carry the clothes from the cart to the washing-pools._
- `a14-06-s2`: Stand by Nausicaa as the stranger comes out. · _Don’t run. Stay by the princess._
- `a14-06-s3`: Follow the cart towards the town. · _Walk with the maids behind the cart, and stop at Athena’s grove._

#### `a14-06-river`

_Morning. Down the road comes a mule-cart piled with clothes, a girl on top holding the reins, and a crowd of maids walking beside it._  
**Nausicaa**: Last night I dreamt a friend came and scolded me. “You could be married any day, and all your clothes are dirty.” So.  
_She looks at you, a stranger standing by her river. She seems to decide that strangers are allowed at rivers._  
**Nausicaa**: You can help, if you like. We tread the clothes in the pools. It’s a race. The maids always win.  
_You tread the clothes with them. Your Nubbin treads too, in a smaller pool, and is very nearly washed._  
_The clothes are spread on the clean pebbles to dry. The girls eat their lunch on the bank, take off their veils, and play ball._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): the Sun’s heat dries wet things as water turns to vapour  
> _The wet clothes are spread on warm pebbles in the sun, and by afternoon they are dry. Where did the water go?_  
> - ✅ It turned into invisible water vapour and mixed with the air. → Yes. The Sun’s heat moves into the cloth and turns the water into a gas that floats away. That is called evaporation.
> - It soaked into the pebbles and stayed there. → The pebbles are only warmed. The water left the cloth as vapour, which is why a puddle on a sunny day shrinks too.
> - It vanished for ever. → Nothing vanishes. The water turned into vapour, an invisible gas, and it will fall as rain one day.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sun’s heat evaporates water from wet clothes into the air._

**Nausicaa**: Catch!  

**Choices**

- **Catch it.**
    - You catch it and throw it back, and she laughs. She is the tallest of them and the best at the game, and knows it.
- **Let your Nubbin catch it.**
    - Your Nubbin catches it with its whole body and falls over backwards. It counts.
- **Drop it, on purpose.**
    - You drop it, and everyone shrieks, delighted. Being bad at ball is very popular here.

_Nausicaa throws the ball to a maid, misses, and it lands in the deep water. Every girl screams at once._  
_Up in the olive bushes, the leaves stir, and something gets up._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): infer from a small detail what is happening  
> _The girls scream, and then “the leaves stir, and something gets up”. What is the writer hinting at?_  
> - ✅ Someone was lying hidden in the bushes, and the noise woke them. → Yes. “Gets up” suggests a person: a clue to something the page hasn’t said outright. Good readers fill gaps like this.
> - Just the wind in the leaves. → The wind could stir leaves, but wind doesn’t “get up”. That phrase points to someone who was lying down.
> - The ball falling out of a tree. → The ball landed in the water, not the bushes. The clue is that something got up, so someone was there.
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference from a clue (“something gets up”) to work out someone was hiding._

_A man comes out of the bushes, crusted with salt, holding a leafy branch in front of him because he has nothing else._  
_He looks like a mountain lion coming out of the rain. The maids scatter along the shore._  
_Nausicaa doesn’t run: Athena has put courage into her. She stands and waits, with the ball still in her hand._  
**Odysseus**: Lady, are you a goddess, or one of us? If a goddess, you’re Artemis, by your height. If mortal, your parents are lucky people.  
**Odysseus**: Once, at Delos, I saw a young palm tree growing by Apollo’s altar. I stood and looked at it a long time.  
**Odysseus**: You remind me of it.  
**Odysseus**: I’ve been twenty days on the sea.  
**Odysseus**: Show me the town, and give me a rag to wear, and may the gods give you all your heart’s wish.  
_He doesn’t come any closer. He stays exactly where he is, and asks from there._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about whether to run or stay when a stranger appears  
> _When the stranger appeared, the maids ran, but Nausicaa stayed because he kept his distance and asked politely. What would you have done?_  
> - Run like the maids. Being careful with strangers is sensible. → That’s a fair answer. Caution is wise. In real life, staying near other people and telling a trusted grown-up is a good plan.
> - Stay like Nausicaa, because he kept back and asked politely. → That’s a fair answer. How he behaved mattered: he stayed far away and spoke gently. It was still brave, and she had friends close by.
> - Stay back, but call the others to come and help. → That’s a fair answer. Having people near you, and getting help, is a clever middle way between running and facing a stranger alone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to respond when a stranger appears (a think question)._


**Choices**

- **Tell her he’s a good man.**
    - **Nausicaa**: You know him? Then he’s welcome. My father says every stranger at our door is sent by Zeus.
- **Pick up a clean cloak and hold it out.**
    - You hold out a cloak from the drying stones. He takes it and bows to you, as if you had given him a kingdom.
- **Stay back. It’s her choice.**
    - **Nausicaa**: You don’t look like a bad man. You look like a man who has had bad luck.

**Nausicaa**: Come back, all of you! Since when do we run from a man in trouble? Give him oil, and clothes, and something to eat.  
_He washes the salt off in the river, away from everyone._  
_When he comes back up the bank he looks taller and younger, and the maids stare._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): washing with clean water removes dirt and germs  
> _After days in the sea, Odysseus is crusted with salt and dirt._  
> _Why is washing with clean water, and soap when we have it, good for our bodies?_  
> - ✅ It washes away dirt and germs that could make us ill. → Yes. Washing hands and bodies removes germs and keeps cuts from getting infected. That is why a good wash makes Odysseus look like a new man.
> - It makes you taller. → He only looks taller because he stands up straight now that he is clean and fed! Washing keeps us healthy, not taller.
> - It isn’t important. → It is very important. Germs travel on dirty hands and skin, and washing is one of the best ways to stop illness spreading.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that washing removes dirt and germs and helps prevent illness._


#### `a14-06-road`

**Nausicaa**: Listen. Walk with the maids behind the cart as far as the town fields. Then wait in Athena’s grove, outside the walls.  
**Nausicaa**: If people see me come home with a man like you, they’ll talk all winter. Give me time to get home first.  
**Nausicaa**: Then ask anyone for the palace of Alcinous. Even a child could show you.  
**Nausicaa**: Go past my father. Go straight to my mother. She’ll be sitting by the fire, spinning purple wool. Kneel to her.  
**Nausicaa**: If she likes you, you’ll get home. Don’t ask me why it works like that. It just does.  
_Odysseus listens like a man taking notes. He has plainly been given directions before, and lost ships ignoring them._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): put directions in order: first, next, then  
> _Nausicaa gave Odysseus four steps: walk behind the cart; wait in Athena’s grove; ask for the palace; go straight to the queen._  
> _What does he do just before he asks anyone for the palace?_  
> - ✅ Wait in Athena’s grove → Yes. The order matters: cart, grove, ask for the palace, then the queen. Giving directions in order, with “first”, “next” and “then”, makes them easy to follow.
> - Kneel to the queen → That is the last step. Before asking for the palace he waits in the grove outside the walls, so that Nausicaa gets home first.
> - Walk behind the cart → That is the first step. He does that, then waits in the grove, and only then asks for the palace.
> _For grown-ups: Put four directions in order and answered which step comes just before another._

_You wait in the poplar grove with him until sunset._  
_He speaks quietly there to Athena, alone, and you walk off a little to give him room._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): give people privacy for things that matter to them  
> _Odysseus wants to speak to Athena alone, so you walk away a little. Why is giving someone room a kind thing to do?_  
> - ✅ It shows you respect that some things are private. → Yes. Letting someone have space when they need it tells them you trust them and respect what matters to them.
> - Because you’re bored of waiting. → Boredom isn’t the reason. Walking away is a way of saying: this is yours, and I won’t listen in.
> - Because he told you to go. → He didn’t have to say it. Noticing when someone wants privacy, without being told, is part of being a good friend.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about respecting privacy as a way of caring._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): spot repeated clues to work out who someone is  
> _This girl has grey eyes, walks very lightly, and vanishes. Earlier, Mentor also “walked too lightly for an old man”. Who do you think she is?_  
> - ✅ Athena, in disguise again → Yes. Two clues that repeat, light steps and a sudden vanishing, point to Athena. A good reader keeps a list of clues like this.
> - Just a girl from the town → She might be, but an ordinary girl doesn’t vanish from an empty lane. The repeated clues point somewhere else: Athena.
> - Nausicaa’s maid → A maid would head home, not disappear. And Odysseus says she has been with him since Troy. That points to Athena.
> _For grown-ups: Used repeated clues (light steps, vanishing) to infer that the girl is Athena._

## A14-7. The Phaeacian Hall

- `a14-07-s1`: Go into the king’s hall with him. · _Walk between the gold and silver dogs and in through the doors._
- `a14-07-s2`: Sit at the feast and hear the bard. · _Sit on the bench beside Odysseus when the bard is led in._
- `a14-07-s3`: Hear him say his name. · _Stay at the table while the hall waits._

#### `a14-07-hall`

_Walls of bronze with a blue band along the top, and doors of gold. On either side of the door sit dogs of gold and silver._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): bronze is a mixture of two metals, copper and tin  
> _The walls are bronze, the doors gold, the dogs gold and silver. Bronze isn’t a metal you dig up._  
> _It is made by melting two metals together. Which two?_  
> - ✅ Copper and tin → Yes. Mixing tin into copper makes bronze, which is harder than copper alone. A mixture of metals is called an alloy, and it can have better properties than its parts.
> - Gold and silver → Gold and silver are metals on their own here. Bronze is copper mixed with a little tin.
> - Iron and wood → Wood isn’t a metal. Bronze is copper melted together with tin.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bronze is an alloy made by melting copper and tin together._

_A god made those dogs, so that they would never grow old and never die. They watch you go in._  
_Behind the house is an orchard where the fruit never stops: pears and figs ripen while the next ones are still in flower._  
_Odysseus walks through the hall wrapped in a mist that hides him. Nobody sees him until he is on his knees before the queen._  
**Odysseus**: Arete, queen. I’ve come through great hardship to your knees, and your husband’s. Help me home. I’ve been so long away.  
_Then he sits down in the ashes by the hearth. The whole hall goes silent._  
_At last an old lord clears his throat and says what everyone is thinking: a stranger in the ashes is not right._  
**Alcinous**: He’s right. Up, friend. Here, take my son’s chair, beside me. Bring water for his hands. Bring him dinner.  

#### `a14-07-hall-done`

**Arete**: Stranger. Who are you? Where did you get those clothes? I know them. I made them.  
**Odysseus**: Your daughter gave them to me. Don’t blame her for not bringing me home herself. Coming alone was my idea.  
_It wasn’t his idea. You open your mouth, and close it again, and Arete sees you do it, and very nearly smiles._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about a kind not-quite-truth  
> _Odysseus says coming alone was his own idea, so that Nausicaa won’t be blamed. It wasn’t true. Is a kind not-quite-truth ever right?_  
> - No. A lie is a lie, even a kind one. He could have told the truth gently. → That’s a fair answer. Honesty builds trust, and the truth can usually be told kindly if you take a moment to find the words.
> - Sometimes, to protect someone from unfair blame. → That’s a fair answer. He wants to keep Nausicaa safe. Many people feel that is different from a lie told to get something for yourself.
> - It depends whether it hurts anyone, and whether you’d tell the truth later. → That’s a thoughtful answer. People who think about it like this often decide a kind truth is better, and a kind secret is sometimes necessary.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a kind not-quite-truth can ever be right (a think question)._


#### `a14-07-bard`

_Next day there are games, and dancing, and a feast. The herald leads in the bard Demodocus, who is blind, and whom the Muse loves._  
_They hang his lyre on a peg above his head, and guide his hand to it, so he can find it._  
_He sings of Troy: of a quarrel between two great captains, and the long war. The Phaeacians love it; they have never been to a war._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): stories were sung and remembered before they were written  
> _Homer’s great poems were first sung by bards like Demodocus, with no book at all. They were written down much later._  
> _How could a bard remember such long poems?_  
> - ✅ With a steady rhythm and phrases that come round again and again. → Yes. Beats, patterns and phrases that come round again act like handholds for the memory. People still use the same trick with songs and times tables.
> - He read it from a scroll with his fingers. → Bards in Homer’s day sang from memory. Writing wasn’t used for long poems then. They used rhythm and repeated phrases to remember.
> - Someone whispered every word to him. → Bards learned poems over years, from other bards. Patterns and rhythm helped them hold all those words in their heads.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Homer’s poems were sung and remembered before they were written, using rhythm and repeated phrases._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): crying is a normal way to let a feeling out  
> _Odysseus hid his face when the song made him cry. Is it all right to cry when a story reminds you of something sad?_  
> - ✅ Yes. Tears are a normal way of letting a big feeling out. → Yes. Crying is nothing to be ashamed of. Many people feel better afterwards, and a friend sitting nearby can help.
> - No. Grown-ups should never cry. → Grown-ups cry too, and Odysseus is a very brave man. Crying isn’t weakness. It is what a big feeling does when it needs somewhere to go.
> - Only when nobody is looking. → Some people like privacy when they cry, and that’s fine. But it’s also fine to cry with someone who cares about you.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the same story can use different names in different languages  
> _Many older English books call him Ulysses instead of Odysseus. Why do you think that is?_  
> - ✅ Roman writers used Latin forms of Greek names, and translators often kept them. → Yes. The Romans told the story in Latin, where Odysseus was Ulixes, and English made that Ulysses. Athena was matched with their own goddess, Minerva.
> - Ulysses was a different man. → Same man, same story. Latin has its own version of each Greek name, as languages often do: John is Juan in Spanish and Jean in French.
> - He changed his name on the way home. → He’s Odysseus on every page here. Ulysses is just the Latin form of his name, used by Roman writers and later translators.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Ulysses is the Latin form of Odysseus, and that names change between languages._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): a wick soaks up oil so a lamp can burn steadily  
> _The lamps in the hall burn olive oil. A twisted cloth called a wick dips into the oil. What does the wick do?_  
> - ✅ It soaks up oil and feeds it slowly to the flame. → Yes. Oil creeps up through the tiny gaps in the wick, and the flame burns it a little at a time. No wick, no steady light.
> - It makes the light by itself. → The wick doesn’t shine. The flame does, and it needs fuel. The wick carries oil up to it.
> - It keeps the oil cold. → A lamp wants the oil to burn. The wick draws it upwards so that the flame can use it.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what helps when you are very frightened or sad  
> _Your Nubbin’s heart is going like a bird’s, and it is very sad about the two men too. When we are frightened or sad, what helps?_  
> - ✅ A slow breath, and staying close to someone safe. → Yes. Slow breathing calms the body, and a safe friend beside you helps even more. It’s also all right to feel sad and scared together.
> - Pretending nothing is wrong. → Pretending can’t make a feeling go away. It’s better to say “I’m scared” or “I’m sad” out loud to someone you trust.
> - Running away blindly. → Running without a plan can make things worse, and here there is nowhere to run. Calm breathing and staying together is wiser.
> _For grown-ups: Learned ways to cope when frightened or sad: slow breathing, staying near someone safe, and saying how you feel._

> _Odysseus calls himself Nobody. Imagine the giant later shouts to his neighbours, “Nobody is hurting me!” What will the neighbours think?_  
> - ✅ That no one at all is hurting him, so he doesn’t need help. → Yes. “Nobody” can be a name or mean “no person”, and the neighbours hear the second meaning. A word with two uses can make a clever trick.
> - That a man called Nobody is hurting him. → That is what the giant means. But his neighbours have never heard of a man called Nobody, so they take the plain meaning: no one.
> - That he is making it up for fun. → They might suspect it, but the words tell them there’s no attacker. A word with two meanings is what makes the trick work.

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): heating can change a material for good  
> _The men hardened the tip of the wooden stake in a fire. The fire dried and charred the wood so that it was tougher._  
> _Could the charred wood turn back into soft, fresh wood?_  
> - ✅ No. Burning changes wood for good. → Yes. Some changes can be undone, like melting ice, but burning can’t. Once wood is charred it can never go back to fresh wood.
> - Yes, if you soak it in water. → Water can’t undo charring. Melting and freezing are changes that can reverse, but burning changes the material for good.
> - Yes, if you wait a year. → Waiting doesn’t help. Burning makes new materials, such as charcoal and ash, and they can’t turn back into wood.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heating can change a material permanently, as when fire chars wood._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups of three  
> _Each trio is three rams tied together, with one man hanging under the middle ram._  
> _If four men escape this way, how many rams are in the four trios altogether?_  
> - ✅ 12 rams → Yes. Four groups of three: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, or 4 × 3 = 12.
> - 7 rams → That is 4 + 3. Each of the four men has a trio of three rams, so it is four groups of three: 4 × 3 = 12.
> - 9 rams → That is three trios. With four men there are four trios: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups (4 groups of 3) to find 12._

#### `a14-09-aeolia`

_The island of Aeolus floats on the sea. A wall of bronze runs all the way round it, and sheer cliffs rise above the wall._  
_Aeolus, keeper of the winds, lives there with his wife and their twelve children. Every day they feast; every night they sleep on soft rugs._  
**Aeolus**: Troy! Tell me about Troy again. The horse part. And the ships. Tell me every part.  
_Odysseus tells it, for a whole month. He is a very good teller, and Aeolus a very good listener._  
_Your Nubbin sleeps through most of it, on a different rug every night._  
**Aeolus**: Now. You want to go home. Watch.  
_He takes the hide of a nine-year-old ox, and into it he ties all the howling winds. He binds the neck with a shining silver thread._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): wind is air on the move, started by warming air  
> _Aeolus ties the winds into a bag. In real life, wind is air on the move._  
> _When the Sun warms some air it rises, and cooler air rushes in to fill the space. What is wind?_  
> - ✅ Air that is moving → Yes. Warm air rises, cool air rushes in, and that moving air is wind. It is a push you can’t see but can feel on a sail.
> - Clouds being pushed along → Clouds are pushed by the wind, but wind itself is the moving air. You can’t see it, only what it moves.
> - The sea breathing out → A nice picture, but the sea isn’t breathing. Wind is air on the move, started by warm air rising and cool air rushing in.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wind is moving air, started when warm air rises and cooler air moves in._

_He stows it in the hold himself, so not a breath leaks out. Only the west wind he leaves free, to blow you home._  
**Aeolus**: Don’t open it. Not for anything. Do you understand me?

- **“We won’t.”**
    - **Aeolus**: Good guest. Off you go, then.
- **Ask what’s inside, exactly.**
    - **Aeolus**: Every wind there is, but one. Try not to let them out. They don’t go back in.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff the bag.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs the bag. Its ears blow straight back, and stay that way for an hour.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): winds are named for where they come from, so a west wind blows towards the east  
> _A west wind blows from the west, towards the east. Ithaca lies east of the floating island._  
> _Why is a west wind just right for sailing home?_  
> - ✅ It blows towards the east, the way they want to go. → Yes. Winds are named for where they come from, so a west wind pushes things east. Sailors have always used that to plan their routes.
> - It blows towards the west, the way they came. → A west wind comes from the west, so it blows towards the east. That is the direction of Ithaca.
> - It blows straight up. → Wind blows along the ground and sea. A west wind comes from the west and pushes towards the east, which is where home is.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that winds are named for where they come from: a west wind blows towards the east._

> - Theirs. The bag wasn’t theirs to open. → That’s a fair answer. Feeling left out is hard, but opening something that isn’t yours breaks trust.
> - Both. He should have told them, and they should have asked. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Usually trouble like this is shared: one side says too little, the other acts too soon.
