> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sailors measure wind strength on the Beaufort scale from 0 to 12  
> _Sailors measure wind on the Beaufort scale, from 0 for calm to 12 for a hurricane._  
> _With every wind at once, which number is the ship closest to?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Force 12 is a hurricane, with winds above 118 kilometres an hour. That would toss a small ship like a leaf.
> - 0 → Force 0 is a flat calm, with no wind at all. Every wind at once is the opposite end of the scale.
> - 6 → Force 6 is a strong breeze, which a ship can handle. Every wind in the world at once would be far worse.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the Beaufort scale from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane) and used it to judge wind strength._

_The winds blow you all the way back to the floating island. Odysseus walks up to the hall with one man, and you._  
_Aeolus is at dinner with his family. He sees who it is, and stands up._

**Odysseus**: My crew did it. My crew, and my own sleep. Help us. Just once more.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): own a mistake instead of blaming others  
> _Odysseus blames his crew and his own sleep. What is a good way to own a mistake?_  
> - ✅ Say what happened, say sorry, and ask how to put it right. → Yes. Owning a mistake means telling the truth about it, saying sorry, and offering to mend what you can. Odysseus’s own sleep is partly his to own.
> - Blame someone else so you feel better. → That might feel better for a minute, but it makes others trust you less. Owning your part is stronger.
> - Hide and hope nobody notices. → Hidden mistakes usually get found, and they grow. Telling the truth early is almost always easier.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how to own a mistake: tell the truth, say sorry, offer to put it right._

**Aeolus**: Go. Leave my island. When the gods are set against a man like this, I daren’t help him.  
_Nobody offers you dinner. It is the first door in this story that has been shut in your face._  

**Choices**

- **Go quietly.**
    - You go quietly. At the door Aeolus’s youngest daughter slips your Nubbin a fig, and says nothing.
- **Ask once more, for the crew.**
    - **Aeolus**: No. I’m sorry. No.

_After a harbour of giants that nobody will talk about, there is only one ship left of all the ships they had._  
**Odysseus**: I was so close I could see the smoke from their fires.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply days by 24 hours  
> _Odysseus steered for nine days and nights without a break. There are 24 hours in a day. How many hours is that?_  
> - ✅ 216 hours → Yes. 9 × 24 = (9 × 20) + (9 × 4) = 180 + 36 = 216 hours. No wonder he fell asleep.
> - 33 hours → That is 9 + 24. Nine days of 24 hours each means multiplying: 9 × 24 = 216.
> - 192 hours → That is 8 × 24, eight days. For nine days add another 24: 192 + 24 = 216.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 9 × 24 to find that nine days is 216 hours._

**Odysseus**: That’s the worst of it. Not that it was far. That it was close.

## A14-10. Circe

- `a14-10-s1`: Go up into the woods with Odysseus. · _Follow the smoke towards the house in the trees._
- `a14-10-s2`: Feed the pigs in the sty while he goes inside. · _Go round the side of the house to the sties._
- `a14-10-s3`: See the men turned back. · _Stay by the sty when the door opens._

#### `a14-10-woods`

_A low, wooded island, and smoke rising from a house deep in the trees. Odysseus sends half the men to look, under Eurylochus._  
_Eurylochus comes back alone, running, and can’t speak at first for crying._  
**Eurylochus**: Wolves and lions round the house, tame. They wagged their tails at us like dogs when their master comes home.  
**Eurylochus**: Inside, a woman was singing at a great loom. She called us in, and they all went. I stayed outside. I thought it was a trap.  
**Eurylochus**: They never came out. I waited and waited. Not one.  
**Odysseus**: Then I’ll go. Stay here if you like.  
_He slings his sword and bow on his shoulder and goes up into the woods. You go with him, because guests go with their hosts._  
_On the path a young man is standing with a gold wand, as if he’d been waiting. You have seen him before, on another beach._  
**Hermes**: Where are you going, alone, into these woods? Your men are in Circe’s sties. Will you free them? You’ll end up with them.  
**Hermes**: Here. Take this herb. It will keep her spell off you.  
_He draws it out of the ground: black at the root, with a flower as white as milk._  
_The gods call it moly, and it is hard for people to dig._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): what a plant’s roots do  
> _Moly has a black root and a flower white as milk. What is a plant’s root for?_  
> - ✅ To hold the plant in the ground and take in water. → Yes. Roots anchor a plant and drink water from the soil. Nobody knows which real flower moly was, but one guess is the snowdrop.
> - To make seeds. → Seeds are made in the flower. The root’s jobs are holding the plant steady and taking up water and minerals.
> - To catch sunlight. → Leaves catch sunlight. Roots stay underground, holding on and drinking.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the jobs of a plant’s roots: anchoring it and taking in water._

**Hermes**: When she strikes you with her wand, draw your sword. She will ask you to stay. Make her swear by the gods first.  
_Then he goes up through the trees to high Olympus, and the path is empty._  

**Choices**

- **Thank him as he goes.**
    - You thank him, and he inclines his head, gravely. Then the path is only a path, with a little hollow where a flower was.
- **Look at the flower.**
    - It’s a plain white flower that smells of nothing much. Odysseus holds it as if it were a lamp.

#### `a14-10-woods-done`

_The house is built of smooth stone._  
_The wolves and lions come up wagging their tails, and your Nubbin peers out at them from behind your legs._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): tell what a character feels from what they do  
> _Your Nubbin peers out at the wolves and lions from behind your legs. What does that tell you about how it feels?_  
> - ✅ Nervous, but curious → Yes. Hiding behind you shows it is nervous, and peeping out shows it wants to see. Actions tell us feelings, even when no one says them.
> - Bored → Bored animals don’t hide. Peeping from behind your legs shows it is both nervous and curious.
> - Sleepy → Sleepy animals curl up. This one is peering out, which means it is nervous but curious.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s feelings from what it does (peering out from behind legs)._


#### `a14-10-sty`

_Odysseus goes in. You don’t, because Hermes gave you no moly, so you go round the side of the house instead._  
_There are the sties, and in them the pigs: bristly, grunting, with pigs’ snouts and pigs’ voices._  
_But their minds are what they were, and you can see it in their eyes. They are crying._  
_Circe has thrown them acorns, beech-mast and cornel berries, the food that pigs eat. Some of it lies in the mud, untouched._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): a pig’s snout is made for finding food underground  
> _Real pigs poke about in the ground with strong, flat snouts, finding acorns, roots and berries. How does a snout like that help a pig survive?_  
> - ✅ It sniffs out and digs up food hidden in the ground. → Yes. A pig’s snout is a nose and a digging tool in one, which is why pigs are good at finding acorns in an oak wood.
> - It lets the pig fly short distances. → Pigs can’t fly! The snout is for smelling and digging up food from the ground.
> - It keeps the rain off. → Not at all. A pig’s snout is for finding and digging up food.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a pig’s snout is an adaptation for finding and digging up food._

_Your Nubbin stands at the rail and looks at the biggest pig for a long time. The pig looks back._  
_These are the men who opened the bag of winds, and you remember that. You feed them anyway._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): think about being kind to someone who has let you down  
> _These men opened the bag of winds, which cost everyone dearly, and you remember. You feed them anyway. Why?_  
> - Because everyone deserves kindness when they are suffering. → That’s a fair answer. Being kind doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened. It means seeing that someone is hurting.
> - Because anger won’t help them or you. → That’s a fair answer. Staying angry can feel heavy to carry. Feeding them is a way of putting some of it down.
> - Maybe I shouldn’t, until they say sorry. → That’s a fair answer too. Some people feel that trust has to be earned back. Kindness and fairness can pull in different directions.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about kindness towards someone who has made a mistake (a think question)._


**Choices**

- **Feed them, and talk to them as men.**
    - You feed them, and talk to them like the sailors they are, about the weather and the ship. One of them stops crying to listen.
- **Feed them, and scratch behind their ears.**
    - You feed them and scratch behind their ears, which isn’t dignified, and they lean into it anyway. Some things are true in any shape.
- **Let your Nubbin climb in with them.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs over the rail and lies down in the straw among them, and they settle round it, as if it had been their idea.

#### `a14-10-sty-done`

_From inside the house comes a shout, and a cry, and then a woman’s voice: not frightened, only very surprised._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): predict what has just happened from clues  
> _Odysseus went in carrying moly. You hear a shout, and then Circe’s voice, not frightened but surprised. What do you think just happened?_  
> - ✅ Circe’s spell didn’t work on him. → Yes. She is surprised, not scared, so something she expected to happen didn’t. Good readers use clues like this to predict.
> - Odysseus has been turned into a pig. → If so, you’d expect Circe to sound pleased, not surprised. The clue points to her spell failing.
> - Circe has dropped her cup. → That could make a shout, but the clue is that she sounds very surprised. That fits her spell failing on Odysseus.
> _For grown-ups: Predicted what happened offscreen from clues (a shout and a surprised voice)._


#### `a14-10-change`

_The door opens. Circe comes out with her wand, and Odysseus behind her, his sword still drawn._  
**Circe**: You are Odysseus. You must be. Hermes always said you would come one day, the clever one, on your way home from Troy.  
**Circe**: My cup did nothing to you. Nobody has ever drunk it and stayed himself. Put your sword away. Come in.  
**Odysseus**: Not yet. First swear by the gods you’ll do me no harm. And give me back my men.  
_She swears. Then she opens the sty and goes among the pigs with a salve, and touches each one._  
_The bristles fall away, and they are men again, younger than before, and taller. They hold Odysseus’s hands and weep._  
_The house rings with it. Even Circe is moved, and turns away to look at the trees._  
_The youngest of the men comes over and shakes your hand without a word. He remembers the acorns._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): show thanks in ways that need no words  
> _The youngest man says nothing, but shakes your hand because you fed him. How else can people show thanks without words?_  
> - ✅ A smile, a hug, or a kind turn later on. → Yes. A smile or a favour returned can say thank you as clearly as words. Showing thanks helps friendships stay strong.
> - There isn’t any other way. → There are lots. A nod, a smile, a hug, a gift, or helping later on can all say thank you.
> - Pretending it never happened. → Then the person who helped wouldn’t know it mattered. Even a small sign of thanks tells them it did.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ways to show gratitude without words._

**Circe**: Stay, all of you. Eat and drink until your strength comes back. You’ve been beaten so long you’ve forgotten how to be glad.  
_They stay. Days become months: feasts, and sleep, and more feasts._

**Odysseus**: A whole year. I didn’t count. You’d think I’d be the one counting.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): a year is 12 months; half a year is 6  
> _They stayed a whole year, which is 12 months, or about 52 weeks._  
> _If they had stayed only half a year, how many months would that be?_  
> - ✅ 6 months → Yes. Half of 12 is 6, because 6 + 6 = 12.
> - 3 months → That is a quarter of a year. Half of 12 is 6.
> - 24 months → That is two whole years. Half a year is half of 12, which is 6.
> _For grown-ups: Found half of a year in months (half of 12 is 6)._

## A14-11. The House of the Dead

- `a14-11-s1`: Sail with him to the edge of the world. · _Wait under the willows while he goes on alone._
- `a14-11-s2`: Stay near while the dead come. · _Keep still under the willows and watch._
- `a14-11-s3`: Sit with him afterwards. · _Stay under the willows when he comes back._

#### `a14-11-edge`

_This part of his story is about his mother, and about the dead._  
_It is sad and gentle, and you can stop and come back whenever you like._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): sad stories are allowed, and you can pause  
> _If a story makes you feel sad, that is not a mistake. It means you care._  
> _You can pause, take a slow breath, or talk to a grown-up about it. The page will wait for you._  
> _For grown-ups: Was told that feeling sad at a sad story is normal, and that pausing and talking to a grown-up can help._

_The wind carries the ship all day, to the edge of the world, where the river Ocean runs round everything._  
_A land of mist that the sun never reaches: tall poplars, and willows that drop their seeds before they ripen. Nobody lives here._  
**Odysseus**: Circe told me what to do. It’s mine to do, not yours. Stay back here by the trees, with the little one.  
_He goes on alone to the place she told him of, and makes the offering to the dead, the old way, out of your sight._  
_You sit under a willow with your Nubbin in your lap. The page is grey here, like paper left out in the rain._  

#### `a14-11-edge-done`

_Then they come: the dead, up out of the dark, more than you can count. They make a sound like birds a long way off._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile helps you hear or see something  
> _The dead make a sound “like birds a long way off”. What does that simile help you hear?_  
> - ✅ A faint, high, fluttering sound → Yes. Birds far away are quiet and thin, so the simile tells you the sound is faint and far off, and a little sad.
> - A very loud roar → A roar is loud and close. Birds a long way off are faint and high, which gives a soft, strange sound.
> - Complete silence → There is a sound, but it’s a quiet one. The simile helps you hear something faint, like distant birds.
> _For grown-ups: Used a simile (“like birds a long way off”) to picture a faint, distant sound._

_They don’t frighten you. They are only sad, and thin as breath, and looking for someone._  

#### `a14-11-shades`

_The prophet Tiresias comes first, old and blind, with a gold staff. He knows Odysseus at once._  
**Tiresias**: You want your homecoming to be sweet, Odysseus. A god will make it hard. Poseidon has not forgotten his son.  
**Tiresias**: Leave the Sun’s cattle alone, on the island where you find them. Harm them, and you’ll come home late, alone, on a stranger’s ship.  
**Tiresias**: And you’ll find trouble in your house: proud men eating your bread and courting your wife.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): ancient Greeks imagined the dead as shadows, and people’s beliefs differ  
> _In the old Greek stories the dead became pale shadows in a dim place beneath the earth. That is how those storytellers imagined it._  
> _People in different times and places have believed many different things about death, and every family’s beliefs deserve respect._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how ancient Greek storytellers imagined the dead, and that people hold many different beliefs about death._

_Then a woman comes up out of the dark, and Odysseus makes a sound you have never heard a grown man make._  
**Odysseus**: Mother?  
**Odysseus**: Mother. You were alive when I sailed. I didn’t know. Nobody told me.  
**Anticlea**: My child. How did you come here, living, through all that dark water? Have you still not got home?  
**Odysseus**: Not yet. Tell me how you died. Was it a long illness? Tell me about my father, my son. And my wife: does she wait still?  
**Anticlea**: She waits, and cries at night. Your son keeps the land. Your father lives out on the farm, sleeps on leaves in the vineyard, and grieves.  
**Anticlea**: And I wasn’t ill. It was missing you, and wondering where you were, and remembering how kind you were to me. It wore me out.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): missing someone is a big feeling and there are ways to cope  
> _In the story, Anticlea says missing her son wore her out._  
> _Missing someone is a very heavy feeling, but it is not what makes a body stop._  
> _Bodies stop for other reasons, such as being very old or very ill._  
> _What can help when you miss someone?_  
> - ✅ Talking about them, looking at pictures, or telling their stories. → Yes. Sharing memories keeps a person close in your heart, and talking to someone who listens makes the heavy feeling lighter.
> - Pretending you don’t miss them. → Pretending usually makes the feeling heavier. It’s all right to say “I miss them”, and it helps to say it to someone who cares.
> - Staying away from everyone. → Being alone with a big feeling is hard. Being near people who love you, even quietly, helps it get smaller.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that missing someone is a heavy but normal feeling, and ways to cope: talking, remembering, being with people._

_He reaches for her, and she goes through his arms like a shadow, or a dream. He reaches again, and a third time._  
**Odysseus**: Mother. Why won’t you stay, so we can hold each other, even here?  
**Anticlea**: It isn’t unkindness, child. It is what we are, once we’re dead. Go back to the light. Remember all of it, and tell your wife.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): think about what a character asks of someone and why  
> _Anticlea tells her son to go back to the light, remember it all, and tell his wife._  
> _What is she asking him to do for her, and why might that matter?_  
> - To keep her memory alive by telling it. → That’s a fair answer. A person who is remembered and talked about stays part of the people who loved them.
> - To go on living and not stay stuck in sorrow. → That’s a fair answer. She wants him to go home to the living, not linger with the dead. Loving someone can mean wanting them to be well.
> - To share the news so his wife isn’t left wondering. → That’s a fair answer. Telling the people who love you what happened is a kindness in itself.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what a mother asks of her son, and why remembering matters (a think question)._

_The dead go back down into the dark. Odysseus walks back to the willows, sits down beside you, and doesn’t say anything._  
_His hands are open on his knees, as if he were still holding something._  
_Far off, the ship is waiting. The men stand at the rail and don’t call him, because they know._  
**Odysseus**: She asked about my wife. My father. My son. Not once about herself.  
_Your Nubbin looks at him. Then it looks at you, the way it does when it wants to know what the rule is._  
_You remember what Hazel did, when she didn’t know what to do. You don’t have to remember very hard._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): sit beside someone who is sad; you don’t have to fix it  
> _Odysseus is very sad, and nothing you say can fix it. Hazel’s way was to sit beside someone and not hurry them._  
> _What helps a sad friend most?_  
> - ✅ Sitting beside them and listening. → Yes. Being there is often enough. You don’t need the right words. Staying close tells them they’re not alone.
> - Telling them to cheer up. → Cheer up can make a sad person feel they’re doing it wrong. They usually need company first, and cheerfulness later.
> - Changing the subject quickly. → Changing the subject can make someone feel unheard. Letting the sadness be there, with you beside them, is kinder.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sitting quietly beside a sad friend is a good way to help._


**Choices**

- **Sit with him. That’s all.**
    - You sit with him while the mist moves in the willows. After a long time he breathes out, all the way.
    - **Odysseus**: Thank you. I couldn’t have borne anyone talking.
- **“I’m sorry about your mother.”**
    - **Odysseus**: So am I. She waited too. Everyone in my house is waiting. Some of them couldn’t wait long enough.
- **Let your Nubbin climb into his hands.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs into his open hands and sits there. It is warm and solid, and it does not go through his fingers.
    - **Odysseus**: Oh.

_They sail back to Circe’s island in the morning, without a word between them all the way._  
_Odysseus stands at the stern and watches the edge of the world go grey behind him, and then go._  
**Odysseus**: My father sleeps on leaves in the vineyard. In winter he sleeps by the fire, in the ashes, with the farmhands. An old king.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): telling stories about people keeps them remembered  
> _Anticlea asked Odysseus to remember it all and tell it. How does telling stories about a person keep them remembered?_  
> - ✅ Each time a story is told, someone new learns who that person was. → Yes. Families and whole peoples have kept their past alive this way, long before books. Historians call it oral history.
> - It doesn’t. Only writing keeps people remembered. → Writing helps, but for most of human history stories were spoken. Homer’s poems were remembered for generations before anyone wrote them down.
> - Only the stories of kings are remembered. → Ordinary people are remembered too, in family stories, songs and sayings. Anyone can be remembered if someone keeps telling their story.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that telling and retelling stories (oral history) keeps people and the past remembered._

## A14-12. The Sirens

- `a14-12-s1`: Hear Circe’s advice for the voyage. · _Walk with them along the shore, away from the sleeping men._
- `a14-12-s2`: Let him seal your ears with wax. · _Sit on the bench and keep still while he does it._
- `a14-12-s3`: Watch him at the mast as the ship rows past. · _Stay on the bench by the mast. You won’t hear a thing._

#### `a14-12-advice`

_Back on Circe’s island the men sleep by the ship._  
_Circe takes Odysseus by the hand and leads him apart, and you walk on his other side._  
**Circe**: First you’ll come to the Sirens. They sing to every sailor who passes. Whoever stops to hear them never gets home.  
**Circe**: They sit in a green meadow by the sea, and the grass round them is full of the wrecks of sailors who stopped to listen.  
**Circe**: Warm some wax until it’s soft, and press it into every one of your men’s ears, so that not a note gets in. And row past.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): a soft plug blocks and soaks up the vibrations that carry sound  
> _Sound travels as vibrations in the air that shake the eardrum. Why does wax in your ears make the world quiet?_  
> - ✅ It plugs the ear, so most vibrations can’t reach the eardrum. → Yes. The wax seals the way in, and being soft, it soaks up much of what is left. Earplugs work the same way.
> - It makes the sound go backwards. → Sound doesn’t go backwards. The wax blocks the ear, so fewer vibrations reach the eardrum.
> - It tells the brain to stop listening. → The brain would still hear if the sound arrived. Wax works earlier, by blocking the vibrations before they reach the eardrum.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound is vibration and that a soft plug like wax blocks and soaks it up._

**Circe**: If you want to hear them yourself, let your men tie you to the mast, hand and foot.  
**Circe**: If you beg to be untied, they must tie you tighter.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): make a plan ahead of time so you can resist a temptation  
> _Odysseus knows he will beg to be untied, so he asks his crew to tie him up now and ignore his begging later._  
> _Why is deciding ahead of time a clever way to stay safe?_  
> - ✅ In the moment the pull may be too strong to think clearly. → Yes. When a strong feeling arrives, thinking gets harder. A plan made while calm can protect you from the version of you who isn’t.
> - Because rope is very strong. → Rope helps, but the clever part is the plan: he decided while calm, so his later self can’t undo it.
> - It isn’t clever. He should just be brave. → Bravery matters, but even brave people use plans. Deciding ahead is a way of being brave early, before the pull gets strong.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that making a plan while calm can help you resist a strong temptation later._

**Odysseus**: And after the Sirens?  
**Circe**: After them there are two ways, and both are bad. I’ll tell you of them when you need it. You will want to fight. Don’t.  

**Choices**

- **Ask if you should have wax too.**
    - **Circe**: Unless you want to stay in that meadow for ever. You too, little guest. And the small one.
- **Ask Odysseus why he wants to hear them.**
    - **Odysseus**: Because nobody has, and lived. Because I want to know. That’s always been my trouble.

#### `a14-12-advice-done`

_At dawn Circe walks off up the island and doesn’t look back. The ship slides out on a fair wind she sends after you._  

> **Lesson** (music, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): a steady beat helps a team move together  
> _When the wind drops, the crew will row. Rowers keep time with a steady beat so all the oars dip together._  
> _Why does a steady beat help?_  
> - ✅ Everyone moves at the same moment, so the boat goes smoothly. → Yes. A shared beat keeps a team together, whether they are rowing, marching or dancing.
> - It makes the oars quieter. → The beat doesn’t change the sound of the oars. It helps everyone pull at the same time, so the boat goes straight and fast.
> - It tells the wind to blow. → The wind doesn’t listen to the beat. The beat is for the rowers: it makes them pull together.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a steady beat keeps a team moving together, as when rowing._


#### `a14-12-wax`

_The wind drops, and the sea goes as flat as a plate. The men take down the sail and start to row._  
_Odysseus cuts a round cake of wax small with his sword, and kneads it in his strong hands until the sun has made it soft._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): warming softens wax and cooling hardens it again  
> _The sun warms the wax until it goes soft. After the wax sits in your ears and cools, what will happen to it?_  
> - ✅ It will go firm again, because cooling can reverse the change. → Yes. Warming and cooling wax is a change that can be reversed, like melting and freezing ice. That is why wax makes a good earplug: soft to shape, firm to stay.
> - It will stay soft for ever. → Wax goes firm as it cools. The change from hard to soft and back can be repeated, so it can be undone.
> - It will turn to water. → Wax doesn’t turn to water. Warming makes it soft, cooling makes it firm again.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that warming softens wax and cooling hardens it, a change that can be reversed._

**Odysseus**: Ears. Everyone. You first, Eurylochus, and stop making that face.  
_He goes down the benches one man at a time. Then he comes to you, and to your Nubbin, and does yours just as carefully._  
_The world goes muffled, then quiet, then silent. You can feel the oars knocking through the boards, but you can’t hear them._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words for sound have shades of meaning  
> _The world goes muffled, then quiet, then silent. Which order goes from loudest to quietest?_  
> - ✅ muffled, quiet, silent → Yes. Muffled is sound with a blanket over it, quiet is faint, and silent is none at all. Words with close meanings have shades, and good writers choose the right one.
> - silent, quiet, muffled → Silent is the very quietest, with no sound at all. It belongs at the end, not the start.
> - quiet, muffled, silent → Muffled is louder than quiet: it is sound with a layer over it. The order from loud to soft is muffled, quiet, silent.
> _For grown-ups: Put sound words in order (muffled, quiet, silent) and learned about shades of meaning._

_The men tie Odysseus to the mast, upright, hand and foot, and go back to their oars. He nods at you, and his lips say: watch._

_Your Nubbin keeps touching its ears with its paws, in case they have gone somewhere._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): protect your ears from very loud sounds  
> _Your Nubbin keeps checking its ears. Real ears are delicate, and very loud noise can damage hearing for good._  
> _What can you do around very loud sound?_  
> - ✅ Wear ear protection, or move away from the noise. → Yes. Ear defenders and earplugs protect hearing, and distance helps too. Hearing damage can’t be mended, so protecting it matters.
> - Turn it up and get used to it. → Getting used to loud noise doesn’t make it safe. It can damage hearing without your noticing, so it’s better to protect your ears.
> - Nothing can be done. → A lot can be done: earplugs, ear defenders, turning the volume down, and standing further away.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that very loud sounds can harm hearing and how to protect your ears._

_He strains at the ropes, and the cords stand out in his neck._  
_He nods and nods at the men to untie him, with his eyebrows, his whole face._  
_Eurylochus and Perimedes get up from their oars, tie him tighter, and go back to rowing, as they were told._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about whether curiosity is always good  
> _The Sirens promise to tell Odysseus everything, and he is tied up safely, yet he still wants to go to them._  
> _Is wanting to know everything always good?_  
> - Yes. Curiosity is how we learn. He just needs a safe way to do it. → That’s a fair answer. Curiosity is a wonderful thing, and Odysseus’s plan is a safe way to follow it: he hears, but he stays in the boat.
> - No. Some things are too dangerous to find out. → That’s a fair answer. Some kinds of knowing cost more than they give, and wise people can tell the difference.
> - It depends what it costs and who it puts at risk. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Odysseus risks only himself, and his crew are shielded. Who pays for your curiosity is worth asking.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether curiosity is always good, and what it might cost (a think question)._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): feel two opposite feelings at once  
> _Odysseus says he envies you, and doesn’t, both. Can a person feel two opposite feelings at once?_  
> - ✅ Yes. Feelings can be mixed. → Yes. You can be excited and nervous, or glad and sorry, in the very same moment. Naming both helps them feel less confusing.
> - No. You can feel only one thing at a time. → Feelings are often more crowded than that. Odysseus is a good example: he wanted to hear the song, and he is also glad he is safe.

- `a14-13-s1`: Watch the strait as he steers by the cliff. · _Stay low on the bench and keep rowing._
- `a14-13-s2`: Land on the island of the Sun. · _Go ashore with the crew, and keep away from the herds._
- `a14-13-s3`: Hold on to the fig tree over the whirlpool. · _Grab the fig tree and hang on until the timbers come back up._

#### `a14-13-strait`

_Two rocks: on one side, high up, a cave in a cliff too smooth to climb._  
_On the other, under a fig tree, the sea goes down a great hole._  
_That is Charybdis._  
_Three times a day she drinks the sea down, and three times she throws it up, and when she drinks you can see the sand._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-2, ask): whirlpools form where strong currents squeeze through a gap or meet  
> _Real whirlpools form where strong currents squeeze through a narrow gap or crash into each other._  
> _Many people think this story was inspired by the narrow Strait of Messina, between Italy and Sicily. Where is a whirlpool most likely?_  
> - ✅ A narrow strait with strong currents → Yes. Squeezed water speeds up and starts to spin. Sailors in Homer’s time had good reason to fear places like that.
> - A still pond on a calm day → A still pond has no strong currents, so there is nothing to make the water spin.
> - A puddle in the road → A puddle has no current at all. Whirlpools need moving water squeezed into a narrow space.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that whirlpools form where strong currents squeeze through narrow gaps._

_In the cave on the other side lives Scylla._  
_Circe told him of her: a thing with six long necks, and a small, high voice, like a puppy’s._  
**Odysseus**: Better to lose six than lose them all. Steer close under the cliff. And don’t tell the men about her. They’d stop rowing.  
_He puts on his armour, takes two spears and stands in the bow, against Circe’s advice. He can’t help it._  
_The men row, staring at Charybdis. Nobody is looking up._  
_Then the page goes dark for a moment, and comes back. Six of the crew are lost from the benches, and you didn’t see it happen._  
**Odysseus**: Row. Don’t look up. Row!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): sad things happen, and it helps to tell someone how it feels  
> _The six men have died._  
> _Losing friends is one of the hardest things there is, and Odysseus will carry that sadness for the rest of his life._  
> _If something sad happens in a story, or in real life, it helps to tell someone you trust how it feels._  
> _For grown-ups: Was gently told that losing friends is very hard, and that telling a trusted person how you feel helps._


#### `a14-13-strait-done`

_The strait opens out, and behind you the sea roars down Charybdis’s throat and comes back up. Ahead lies a green island, with cattle on it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): homophones: strait and straight sound alike  
> _A strait is a narrow stretch of water between two lands. It sounds just like straight, as in a straight line. Which sentence uses “strait” correctly?_  
> - ✅ The ship sailed through the narrow strait. → Yes. A strait is water, and this ship is sailing in it. Words that sound alike but mean different things are called homophones.
> - He drew a strait line. → A line that doesn’t bend is straight, spelled s-t-r-a-i-g-h-t. A strait is a narrow stretch of water.
> - The road ran strait ahead. → A road with no bends is straight. Strait is the narrow channel of water the ship has just passed through.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the homophones strait (narrow water) and straight (not bent)._


#### `a14-13-island`

_The island of the Sun. Fat cattle with broad brows and curling horns graze along the shore: seven herds, and seven flocks of sheep._  
**Odysseus**: Tiresias warned me. Circe warned me. We sail past.  
**Eurylochus**: You’re made of iron, you. We’re tired, and it’s getting dark. Let us land and sleep. One night.  
_The men all shout for Eurylochus. Odysseus makes them swear not to touch the cattle, and they swear, and you land._  
_In the night the wind changes and blows from the south for a month, and never stops. The food runs out._  
_The men fish, and snare birds, and go hungry. Odysseus goes inland alone to ask the gods for help, and falls asleep._  
_Eurylochus calls the men together. You can see what he’s going to say before he says it._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about a promise made when you are hungry and afraid  
> _The crew swore not to touch the Sun’s cattle. Weeks later they are hungry and frightened._  
> _Is a promise still a promise when keeping it is hard?_  
> - Yes. A promise that only holds when it’s easy isn’t worth much. → That’s a fair answer. Promises matter most exactly when they are hard to keep.
> - Partly. Staying alive matters, and a promise shouldn’t starve you. → That’s a fair answer. People do weigh promises against needs. The trouble here is that they didn’t try Odysseus’s plan, or wait for him.
> - It depends on who the promise was made to, and what else they could do. → That’s a thoughtful answer. A promise to the gods, made to the leader, with other food unfound, is a tangled one. Good decisions look for another way first.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about keeping a promise when it is hard (a think question)._


**Choices**

- **Go and find Odysseus.**
    - You run inland with your Nubbin, and find him asleep in a hollow out of the wind.
    - By the time you wake him, you can smell the fires.
- **Stay and argue with the crew.**
    - **Eurylochus**: Better to drown in one gulp than starve slowly on an island. We’ll make it up to the Sun. We’ll build him a temple.
    - Nobody listens to you. They’re too hungry to listen to anybody.
- **Stand with the cattle.**
    - You stand among the cattle, calm and huge and gold in the dusk. The men walk round you, quite politely, and take them anyway.

#### `a14-13-island-done`

_Odysseus comes down to the shore, smells the meat cooking, and cries out to the gods._  
_Far above, the Sun goes to the gods to complain, and Zeus listens. Nothing more is said aloud on the page._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): day and night happen because the Earth spins once in about 24 hours  
> _In the Greek story the Sun is a god who crosses the sky each day._  
> _Scientists later worked out that day and night happen because the Earth spins. How long does one full spin take?_  
> - ✅ About 24 hours → Yes. One spin is about a day. The side of the Earth facing the Sun has day, and the side turned away has night.
> - About one week → A week is seven days. The Earth makes seven full spins in a week, one each day.
> - About one hour → An hour is far too fast. The Earth takes about 24 hours to turn once, which is why we have 24 hours in a day.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that day and night come from the Earth spinning once about every 24 hours._

_Six days the men feast._  
_On the seventh the wind drops and you sail, and as soon as the island is out of sight a black cloud stands over the ship._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add days to find a total  
> _The south wind blew for a month, about 30 days. Then the men feasted for 6 days before sailing._  
> _About how many days did they spend on the island?_  
> - ✅ 36 days → Yes. 30 + 6 = 36 days. That’s a long time to be stuck on one small island.
> - 24 days → That is 30 − 6. We need to add the feasting days to the month: 30 + 6 = 36.
> - 6 days → That is only the feast. Add the month of wind: 30 + 6 = 36 days.
> _For grown-ups: Added 30 + 6 to find a total of 36 days._

_Zeus’s thunderbolt strikes the ship, and it fills with smoke. The men go into the sea, and the page doesn’t show you their faces._  
_All the crew are lost. They have died, and only Odysseus is left._  
_He lashes the mast to the keel with a leather strap, and rides them._  
_Odysseus is shaking. You and your Nubbin hold on to the mast, and to him._  
_All night the wind carries you back the way you came._  
**Odysseus**: No. Not back. Not back to her.  
_At dawn you are at Charybdis again. The sea goes down her throat, and the mast and keel go with it._  
_Odysseus leaps up and catches the fig tree above her, and hangs there like a bat._  
_You catch hold beside him, and your Nubbin holds on to you._  
_There is no foothold, and no climbing up. You can only hang, and wait for her to give the timbers back._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): muscles tire when they work hard, and rest helps them recover  
> _Your arms burn from hanging on. Muscles tire when they work hard for a long time. What helps tired muscles recover?_  
> - ✅ Rest, water and food → Yes. Rest gives muscles time to mend, water keeps them working, and food gives them fuel. After a hard effort, all three help.
> - Working them even harder straight away → Hard work after hard work can strain muscles. Rest, water and food help them recover.
> - Nothing. They never need to recover. → Every muscle needs recovery time. That is why athletes rest between hard sessions.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tired muscles recover with rest, water and food._


**Choices**

- **Hang on.**
    - You hang on, and your arms burn. Odysseus talks to you all the while, about nothing, about goats, so you don’t think about letting go.
- **Count, to make it go faster.**
    - You count, and get to a number you didn’t know you knew. Odysseus counts with you, under his breath.
- **Look at Odysseus.**
    - He is looking down into the whirlpool, quite calm: he has hung over worse. You decide, for now, to believe him.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): a frame story holds other stories inside it  
> _Odysseus tells his adventures to the Phaeacians, and we step inside them. A story told inside another story is called a frame story._  
> _What is the frame here?_  
> - ✅ The evening in the Phaeacian hall → Yes. The hall is the frame, and the Cyclops, the winds, Circe and the rest are stories inside it. Many famous books use this trick.
> - The Cyclops’s cave → The cave is one of the stories inside. The frame is the evening in the hall where Odysseus is telling them.
> - Penelope’s loom → The loom belongs to another part of the tale. The frame is the evening in the Phaeacian hall, where Odysseus tells his adventures.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a frame story holds other stories, and found the frame (the hall)._

#### `a14-14-ship`

_The Phaeacian ship has no steering oar. It doesn’t need one: it knows the way to every harbour in the world._  
_Odysseus lies down on a rug in the stern and is asleep at once, in a deep, deep sleep. He has earned it._  
_The ship runs faster than a falcon, and the water hisses along her sides._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): Ithaca is a real island off Greece’s west coast  
> _The dark shape ahead is Ithaca. It is a real island, still there today, on Greece’s west coast._  
> _If you stood on the Greek mainland and looked towards Ithaca, which way would you face?_  
> - ✅ West → Yes. Ithaca lies off the west coast, in the Ionian Sea. A few thousand people live there today.
> - East → East is inland, towards Troy and the sunrise. Ithaca lies the other way, out to sea in the west.
> - North → Ithaca is a little north of the middle of Greece’s west coast, but from the mainland you’d look mostly west, out to sea.
> _For grown-ups: Located Ithaca as a real island off Greece’s west coast, using compass directions._

- **Sleep too.**

#### `a14-14-ship-done`

_In the harbour an olive tree grows at the head of the bay, beside a cave of the nymphs, where bees keep honey in stone jars._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, ask): bees carry pollen from flower to flower as they gather nectar  
> _Bees visit flowers to collect nectar, which they turn into honey. What else do they do, without meaning to?_  
> - ✅ Carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds. → Yes. Pollen sticks to a bee’s fur and rubs off on the next flower. That is called pollination, and many fruits and nuts depend on it.
> - Pull weeds out of the ground. → Bees don’t weed. They move pollen between flowers, which is what lets many plants make seeds and fruit.
> - Wake the flowers up. → Flowers don’t need waking! A bee carries pollen as she feeds, and that’s how plants make seeds.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bees pollinate flowers by carrying pollen between them as they gather nectar._

_A young shepherd comes down the path: fine-boned, like a king’s son, with a good cloak and a spear in his hand._  
**A Young Shepherd**: You must be a long way from home, stranger, not to know this place. This is Ithaca. Even at Troy they’ve heard of Ithaca.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): nostalgia comes from the Greek nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain)  
> _The Greeks had a word for homecoming: nostos (NOS-toss). Another Greek word, algos, means pain._  
> _Put them together and you get an English word for the ache of missing home or the past._  
> _What is it?_  
> - ✅ nostalgia → Yes. Nostalgia is “homecoming-pain”. The Odyssey is the most famous homecoming story of all.
> - nostril → A nostril is part of your nose. The word from nostos and algos is nostalgia.
> - nautical → Nautical means to do with ships. The word that means the ache of missing home is nostalgia.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nostalgia comes from the Greek words nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain)._

_Odysseus’s heart leaps. Then, because he is who he is, he tells the shepherd a long, sad lie about being a runaway from Crete._  
_The shepherd smiles, and is a tall woman, grave and beautiful. You have met her before, more than once, in other faces._  
**Athena**: Even here, on your own island, you’d spin me a tale. That carefulness is why I have never been able to leave you.  
**Athena**: I am Athena, daughter of Zeus, who has stood by you in every trouble. Look. Your harbour. Your olive tree. Your mountain.  
_The mist lifts. He knows it all at once, and kneels, and puts his face to the ground._  
**Athena**: Your house is full of men who court your wife and eat your bread. Nobody must know you yet. Not one person.  
_She touches him with her wand. His skin wrinkles, his hair thins, and his fine clothes are rags that stink of smoke._  
_He is an old beggar with a staff and a torn bag on a cord. He looks down at himself, and laughs._  
**The Beggar**: Well. Nobody will know me now.  
**The Beggar**: You told me once to keep my name. I’m keeping it now.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about the difference between being careful and being honest  
> _Odysseus lies even to a friendly stranger on his own island, because being careful has kept him alive for twenty years._  
> _Is being careful the same as being honest?_  
> - No. You can be careful by staying quiet, without telling a lie. → That’s a fair answer. Keeping something private is different from saying something false, and many people feel that matters.
> - Sometimes a lie is needed to stay safe. → That’s a fair answer. Odysseus has good reasons. It’s still worth asking what each lie costs, and who gets hurt by it.
> - It depends who you are talking to. → That’s a thoughtful answer. We owe the people we trust more of the truth than we owe a stranger, and Athena has been testing him.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being careful is the same as being honest (a think question)._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, ask): caves form slowly as rainwater dissolves limestone  
> _Greece has many caves in limestone rock. Rainwater is very slightly acidic, and it slowly dissolves limestone and leaves hollows behind._  
> _Is that a fast change or a slow one?_  
> - ✅ Very slow, over thousands of years → Yes. Rain wears away rock a tiny amount at a time. Some changes to the Earth happen in a day, like a landslide, and others take longer than people have been alive.
> - Fast, in a single day → A big cave can’t form in a day. Water dissolves limestone so slowly that it takes thousands of years to carve out a hollow.
> - It can’t happen at all → It does happen. Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, and over a very long time it can carve out a cave.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some caves form very slowly as rainwater dissolves limestone._

**Athena**: Go to the swineherd. He has stayed true. I am going to Sparta, to bring your son home.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): name mixed feelings: joy and loneliness together  
> _Odysseus is home at last, but he cannot tell anyone. Which words fit how he might feel?_  
> - ✅ Joyful and lonely, both at once → Yes. Feelings can sit side by side. He is thrilled to be home and lonely because nobody can know it yet.
> - Only happy → He is certainly happy, but he also said he can’t tell anyone. That secret is a lonely thing to carry, so there is more than happiness here.
> - Only bored → Nothing here is boring to him. He is touching trees and remembering falls from rocks. Joy and loneliness are a better fit.
> _For grown-ups: Named mixed feelings (joy and loneliness) for a character who is home but must keep it secret._


### Glossary

- **nostos**: The Greek word for a homecoming, the root of the English word nostalgia.

#### `a14-15-hut`

_High on the hill, a yard walled with stones and topped with thorn: twelve sties, and four dogs as fierce as wolves._  
_The dogs see the beggar and rush at him, barking. He has the sense to sit down and let his staff fall._  
_A man runs out of the hut shouting, throwing stones at the dogs until they scatter. He has dropped the leather he was cutting for sandals._  
**Eumaeus**: Old man, they nearly had you. That would have been one more grief for me, and I’ve plenty.  
**Eumaeus**: Come in, both of you. Eat first. Then tell me where you’re from and what trouble you’re in.  
_He piles brushwood under a shaggy goatskin to make a seat._  
_He brings the best he has, and a drink in a wooden bowl, and serves you himself._  
**The Beggar**: May Zeus give you what you most want, friend, for taking me in like this.  
**Eumaeus**: Every stranger and beggar is in Zeus’s care. You don’t turn them away, even when you’ve only a little to give.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): a shared rule about welcoming strangers makes a community safer  
> _Eumaeus is poor, yet he gives a ragged stranger his best food and a seat. In his world everybody shared the rule of welcoming strangers._  
> _What does a community gain from a rule like that?_  
> - ✅ Travellers and people in need can count on being safe and fed. → Yes. When everyone follows the rule, anybody who falls on hard times, including you, can expect a welcome. A shared rule makes people safer.
> - Nothing. It only costs the host. → It costs a little, but the host gains too: someday he may be the stranger. A community where everyone helps looks after its own.
> - Everyone can ignore rules. → The reverse. A rule that everybody keeps is a promise between neighbours, and it works because people trust each other to follow it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a shared rule of welcoming strangers makes a community safer and more trusting._

**Eumaeus**: My master would have done better by you. He was good to me. But he’s dead somewhere far off, and nobody even knows where.  
_The beggar looks into his cup, and doesn’t say anything for a moment._  

**Choices**

- **“He might not be dead.”**

- **Ask Eumaeus about his master.**

- **Eat, and let the beggar talk.**

**The Beggar**: Mark my words: he will come, between the old moon and the new.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Moon takes about a month to go through its phases  
> _The beggar promised Odysseus would come “between the old moon and the new”, when the Moon is dark at the turn of the month._  
> _About how long is it from one new moon to the next?_  
> - ✅ About 29 or 30 days, roughly a month → Yes. The Moon goes through all its phases, from new to full and back to new, in about 29 and a half days. The word month comes from the word moon.
> - About one week → A week is only a quarter of the cycle. The Moon takes about a month to go from new, to full, and back again.
> - About one year → A year holds about twelve of those cycles. One new moon to the next takes about a month.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Moon takes about a month to go through its phases, from one new moon to the next._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply to find a total number of pigs  
> _There are twelve sties. If each sty held 5 pigs, how many pigs would Eumaeus look after?_  
> - ✅ 60 pigs → Yes. 12 × 5 = 60. You can do it as 10 × 5 = 50, plus 2 × 5 = 10, which makes 60.
> - 17 pigs → That is 12 + 5. Twelve sties with five pigs in each is a multiplication: 12 × 5 = 60.
> - 50 pigs → That is 10 × 5, only ten sties. Add the last two sties, 2 × 5 = 10, to get 60.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 12 × 5 to find the number of pigs in twelve sties._

_The night comes in cold and wet, with rain on a west wind. The beggar shivers in his rags by the fire._  
**The Beggar**: Let me tell you a story. Once at Troy we lay out all night in an ambush, and I’d forgotten my cloak…  
_It is a long story and a very obvious hint. Eumaeus laughs, and goes and finds him a cloak._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think about why someone gives up their own comfort for others  
> _Eumaeus gives the beggar a cloak, then goes out into the rain himself to sleep by the pigs. Why do you think he does that?_  
> - Because he cares about his animals and his guests more than his own comfort. → That’s a fair answer. For Eumaeus, looking after the pigs is looking after his master’s house, and looking after guests is part of the same job.
> - Because it is simply what he has done every night for years. → That’s a fair answer too. Some kindness is so much a habit that the person doesn’t think of it as special.
> - Because he wants the beggar to feel welcome, not guilty. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Giving up his bed without making a fuss lets his guest accept it without feeling like a burden.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone gives up comfort for others (a think question)._

- **Stay inside with the beggar.**
    - **The Beggar**: Look at him go. Out in that, for my pigs. And they say I’m a hard man to impress.
- **Offer Eumaeus your cloak.**
    - **Eumaeus**: Keep it, guest. I’ve done this every night for twenty years. I’d sleep worse indoors.

_In the hut, by the fire, the beggar lies awake a long time under the borrowed cloak, watching the door._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): clothing keeps you warm by trapping the heat your body makes  
> _The beggar was shivering until he got a thick cloak. Why does a thick cloak help you stay warm?_  
> - ✅ It traps the heat your body makes. → Yes. A cloak doesn’t make heat. It holds your own body’s warmth close, so less of it drifts away into the cold air.
> - It makes heat on its own. → A cloak has no fire in it. It keeps your own body’s heat from escaping, which is why a thick one works better than a thin one.
> - It keeps the rain from being cold. → Rain stays cold, but a thick cloak keeps the cold away from your skin and the warmth in. The heat you feel is your own.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that clothing keeps us warm by trapping body heat._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): happy tears are real: people can cry when they are glad  
> _Eumaeus is so glad that he drops the bowls and kisses Telemachus’s head. Before the day is over there will be tears._  
> _Can people cry when they are happy?_  
> - ✅ Yes. Happy tears are real. → Yes. Strong feelings of any kind can bring tears, including joy and relief. It’s the body’s way of letting a big feeling out.
> - No. Crying is only for sadness. → Crying can come with joy, relief and surprise too. Most people have shed a few happy tears at some point.
> - Only children cry when they’re happy. → Grown-ups do as well. Eumaeus is grown up, and he’s about to cry with joy.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people can cry when they are happy as well as when they are sad._

> - They are being noisy on purpose. → Nothing about it is on purpose. The simile shows feeling too big to hold in, like a bird calling for its young.

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtract to compare two groups  
> _Say there are about 100 suitors. On Odysseus’s side there are three: Odysseus, Telemachus and you. How many more suitors are there than friends?_  
> - ✅ 97 more → Yes. 100 − 3 = 97. The odds look impossible, which is why Odysseus is counting on a plan, not numbers.
> - 103 more → That is 100 + 3. To compare, take the smaller group away from the bigger: 100 − 3 = 97.
> - 3 more → Three is the number of friends. The suitors are the bigger group, so subtract: 100 − 3 = 97.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 100 − 3 to compare two groups and find the difference._

- `a14-16-s2`: Stop at the gate, by the heap. · _Stand at the courtyard gate with them._

#### `a14-16-road`

_Eumaeus and the beggar set off down the rough track to the town. The beggar leans on his staff, and you carry his bag._  
_At the spring outside the town, where people draw water, a goatherd driving goats to the suitors’ dinner sees you._  
_He jeers at the beggar and kicks out at him as he passes. The beggar takes it, and doesn’t fall, and doesn’t answer._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): stay calm and don’t hit back when someone is unkind  
> _The goatherd kicks the beggar, and the beggar doesn’t hit back, because he has a bigger plan._  
> _When someone is unkind to you, what are some good ways to respond?_  
> - ✅ Take a breath, walk away, and tell a trusted grown-up. → Yes. Staying calm keeps you in charge of what happens next, and telling a grown-up gets you help, especially if you were hurt.
> - Hit back harder. → Hitting back usually makes things worse and can get someone hurt. Walking away and telling someone is stronger.
> - Pretend it didn’t hurt. → It’s fine to feel hurt. Saying “that wasn’t okay” and telling someone you trust is better than keeping it in.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how to respond when someone is unkind: stay calm, walk away, tell a trusted grown-up._

**Eumaeus**: One day the master will come home and see to you, goatherd.  
_Your Nubbin stares at the goatherd all the way out of sight without blinking, which is all it can do, and it does it thoroughly._  
**The Beggar**: Leave it. I’ve had worse from the sea.

_The house comes in sight. You can hear a lyre from the yard and smell the meat: the suitors are at dinner._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): we use several senses at once to know what is near  
> _Before you can see inside the house, you hear a lyre and smell roasting meat. Which two senses told you the suitors were at dinner?_  
> - ✅ Hearing and smell → Yes. Ears pick up the sound of the lyre and the nose picks up the smell. Our senses work together to tell us what is nearby.
> - Touch and taste → You can’t touch or taste a house that is still far away. Sound and smell travel through the air, so hearing and smell reach you first.
> - Sight only → You can’t see inside yet. The clues are a sound and a smell, so it is hearing and smell.
> _For grown-ups: Identified hearing and smell as the senses that detect what is out of sight._

> _The beggar loves his dog, but if he kneels to him the whole town will know who he is._

> - Yes. His plan matters more than one moment. → That’s a fair answer. He is choosing the bigger good, though it costs him something precious.
> - No. Love is more important than any plan. → That’s a fair answer. Some people would say that a loved one waiting twenty years deserves a kind word, whatever the cost.
> - He can show love in small ways that nobody else notices. → That’s a thoughtful answer. A small, secret sign of love can be a way to keep faith with both his plan and his dog.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether hiding love to stay safe is right (a think question)._

_The beggar says one word under his breath, so that only the dog and you can hear it._  
**The Beggar**: Nobody.

> **Lesson** (health, K-LS1-1, ask): what an old dog needs to stay healthy  
> _Argos is old and thin and covered in ticks, because nobody is looking after him. What does an old dog need to stay healthy?_  
> - ✅ Good food, clean water, a soft bed, and visits to the vet. → Yes. Older dogs also like short walks and gentle brushing, and someone to check them for ticks. Looking after a pet well is a big and kind job.
> - Only a heap to lie on. → A dung heap isn’t kind or safe. Pets need food, water, shelter, and a person who cares for them.
> - Nothing. Dogs look after themselves. → Pet dogs depend on people for food, water, shelter and health checks. Argos shows what happens when nobody does it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what an old dog needs to stay healthy: food, water, a soft bed, vet visits and care._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): dogs have a keen sense of smell and remember people they love  
> _Argos knew his master through the rags._

> _Real dogs live ten to fifteen years, so twenty is the poem’s way of saying he waited a very long time._  
> _How did Argos know the beggar?_  
> - ✅ By his smell and his voice → Yes. A dog’s nose and ears are very sharp, and a loved scent stays in a dog’s memory. That is why pet dogs are so thrilled when you come home.
> - By his clothes → The beggar’s clothes are rags, which is no clue at all. A dog knows a person by scent and voice.
> - By his staff → Any old man might carry a staff, so it is no clue. A dog is far more likely to know him by the way he smells and sounds.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dogs recognise loved people by scent and voice, and that a dog’s sense of smell is far keener than ours._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what helps after a pet dies  
> _It is very sad when a loved animal dies. What can help us afterwards?_  
> - ✅ Remembering them, telling stories, and being with people who care. → Yes. Talking about the good times keeps them close, and the people who love you can share the sadness. Crying is part of it.
> - Pretending it never happened. → Pretending can make the sadness stay hidden and heavy. It helps to say “I miss him”, and to hear that others do too.
> - Getting a new pet straight away. → Some people do, in time. But a new pet can’t replace the one you lost. It’s kind to let yourself feel sad first.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that after a pet dies it helps to remember, talk and be with caring people._

- `a14-17-s2`: Hold the lamp while the old nurse washes his feet. · _Stand by the basin with the lamp._
- `a14-17-s3`: Hear Penelope’s dream. · _Stay by the fire while she talks._

#### `a14-17-hearth`

_Night, and the suitors have gone home to bed. The hall is a mess of cups and crusts and spilt wine._  
_Penelope comes down from her room and sits in her chair by the fire, the one inlaid with ivory and silver._  
**Penelope**: Stranger, first I’ll ask what everyone asks. Who are you? Where are you from? Who are your people?  
**The Beggar**: Ask me anything but that. If I start remembering I’ll cry, and your maids will think I’m foolish.  
**Penelope**: Since he went, I have no beauty and no strength left. These men wear me out.  
**Penelope**: I wove a shroud to keep them off, and they caught me.  
_Then the beggar tells her a long tale: that he is from Crete, and once had Odysseus as a guest in his house, on the way to Troy._  
**Penelope**: Then tell me what he wore. If you can, I’ll believe you.  
**The Beggar**: A purple cloak, double, with a gold brooch. On it a hound held a fawn in its paws as it struggled. Everyone stared at that brooch.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a small, specific detail is good evidence  
> _Penelope asks what Odysseus wore. Why is a detail like the hound on the brooch better proof than just saying “I knew him”?_  
> - ✅ Only someone who had really seen it would remember such a detail. → Yes. Specific details are hard to invent, so they work as evidence. Writers and detectives both look for them.
> - Because it is longer and sounds clever. → Length doesn’t prove anything. It’s the detail that matters, because a real memory contains small, odd things a liar wouldn’t think of.
> - Because it sounds beautiful. → Beautiful words don’t prove anything. A specific detail only someone who was there could know does.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that specific details work as evidence that someone really saw something._

_Penelope weeps, the way snow melts on the high mountains when the wind changes. She gave him that cloak herself._  
**The Beggar**: He’s near. He’s alive. He’ll be home within the year, between the old moon and the new.  

**Choices**

- **Look at the beggar’s eyes.**
    - His eyes are dry. He is holding them dry, like a man holding a door shut against the wind.
- **Pass Penelope a cloth for her eyes.**
    - **Penelope**: Thank you. You’re a kind guest. You keep strange company, but you’re kind.
- **Let your Nubbin sit at Penelope’s feet.**
    - Your Nubbin sits at her feet and leans on her ankle.
    - She puts her hand down to it without looking, the way you do with an old dog.

**Penelope**: You’re my guest now. Nurse! Come and wash this man’s feet. He’s the age your master would be.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): washing a guest’s feet was part of Greek hospitality  
> _In a hot, dusty land where people wore sandals, a host would have a guest’s feet washed. Why would that feel kind after a long walk?_  
> - ✅ It cools and cleans tired feet, and shows the host cares. → Yes. It soothes the guest and says, “You are welcome here.” Many cultures have a small kindness like this for guests.
> - It is just to make the floor clean. → The floor isn’t the point. The washing is a comfort and a welcome for the guest.
> - It shows the guest is a servant. → The opposite. A host washing a guest’s feet, or having them washed, honours the guest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that washing a guest’s feet was a welcoming custom in ancient Greek hospitality._

**The Beggar**: Not one of the young ones. They’ll laugh. If you have an old woman who has suffered as much as I have, let her do it.

_Old Eurycleia brings a shining basin and pours in cold water, and then hot._  
**Eurycleia**: Gladly, for her sake and for yours. Many strangers have come here, and none so like him. The feet, the voice.  
**The Beggar**: Everyone who saw us both says so.  
_He turns quickly away from the firelight, into the shadow. Too late: he has remembered the scar._  
_Long ago, as a boy, hunting on Mount Parnassus with his grandfather’s sons, a boar ran at him and tore his leg above the knee._  
_Eurycleia runs her hands down his leg, and finds it, and knows it. She lets go, and his foot drops into the basin._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, ask): a scar is new, thicker tissue that closes a healed wound  
> _Odysseus’s boar wound healed long ago, yet he still has a scar. Why does a deep cut leave a scar?_  
> - ✅ The body repairs it with new, thicker tissue that looks different from the skin around it. → Yes. Skin can mend a shallow scrape perfectly, but a deep wound is patched with scar tissue, which stays. It is the body’s repair work, still visible.
> - The cut never really heals. → It has healed. The scar is the repair: new tissue that closed the wound for good.
> - Scars only appear on old people. → Scars appear at any age. Anyone with a deep cut can get one, and many people have a scar with a story.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a scar is new tissue the body grows to repair a deep wound._

_The bronze rings and the basin tips. The water runs all over the floor._  
**Eurycleia**: You’re Odysseus. You are. My child. And I didn’t know you till I touched you.  
_She turns to tell Penelope. But Penelope is looking the other way: Athena has turned her thoughts elsewhere._  
_The beggar puts his hand over the old woman’s mouth and draws her close._  
**The Beggar**: Nurse. Do you want to ruin me? You nursed me yourself. Be quiet. Nobody must know. Nobody.  

**Choices**

- **Mop up the water, quickly.**
    - You mop it up with a cloth, fast, and fetch more hot water, so it looks like a spill. Penelope doesn’t turn round.
- **Watch Penelope.**
    - You watch Penelope, who is looking into the fire, very still. Whether she heard, you will never be sure.
- **Keep still and say nothing.**
    - You keep still. Eurycleia’s eyes go to you over his hand, and you nod, and she nods back.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about when keeping a secret is right, and when to tell  
> _You saw everything, and you are keeping the secret. When is it right to keep a secret, and when should you tell?_  
> - When keeping it protects someone, like a surprise or a safety plan. → That’s a fair answer. A secret that protects someone, or is a nice surprise, can be a kindness.
> - Never. Secrets cause trouble. → That’s a fair answer. Secrets do cause trouble, and many people prefer to be open. Still, a surprise party is a secret too.
> - If a secret makes you scared or worried, tell a trusted grown-up. → That’s a very wise answer, and a rule worth keeping. Secrets that make you feel unsafe are never yours to carry alone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to keep a secret and when to tell a trusted adult (a think question)._

**Penelope**: Stranger, one more thing, and then I’ll let you sleep. I had a dream. Tell me what it means.  
**Penelope**: I keep twenty geese in the yard. I love to watch them peck their grain. In my dream a great eagle came down from the mountain.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): share 20 into 4 equal groups  
> _Penelope keeps twenty geese. If she put them in four equal rows, how many geese would be in each row?_  
> - ✅ 5 geese → Yes. 20 ÷ 4 = 5, because 4 × 5 = 20.
> - 16 geese → That is 20 − 4. Dividing into four equal rows asks: what number times 4 makes 20? That is 5.
> - 80 geese → That is 20 × 4, which makes the groups bigger instead of sharing them. Share 20 into four rows: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 20 by 4 to share geese into four equal rows._

**Penelope**: When he flew off again, the geese were gone, every one. I wept, and the women came to comfort me.  
**Penelope**: Then the eagle came back and sat on the roof-beam, and spoke with a man’s voice. “I am your husband,” he said, “come home.”  
**The Beggar**: There’s only one way to read that, lady. The eagle told you himself.  
**Penelope**: Dreams are hard to read. They come to us through two gates: one made of horn, and one of ivory.  
**Penelope**: The dreams that come through the ivory gate deceive us. The ones through the gate of horn come true.  
**Penelope**: I don’t think mine came through the horn.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a symbol stands for a bigger idea  
> _Penelope’s two dream gates are a symbol: the ivory gate stands for false dreams, and the gate of horn for true ones. What is a symbol?_  
> - ✅ Something that stands for a bigger idea. → Yes. A gate, a dove, or a flag can each stand for something larger. Writers use symbols to say a lot in a few words.
> - A word that sounds like another word. → That’s a homophone, like strait and straight. A symbol is an object or image that stands for a bigger idea, like the two gates.
> - A very long description. → A symbol can be tiny, even one object. What makes it a symbol is that it stands for something bigger.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a symbol is something that stands for a bigger idea, like the two dream gates._

_Two gates. You think of yours, at home, and how it sticks, and how you always know who has come through it._

> - Staring at the worry as hard as you can. → Staring at a worry usually makes it bigger. A calm thought or a slow breath, or talking to someone, works better.
> - Telling yourself you must never worry. → Everyone worries sometimes. The trick is helping the worry quieten down, with breathing, calm thoughts or a chat with someone you trust.

#### `a14-18-axes`

_Morning: a feast day for Apollo the archer. The suitors come early, as they always do, and sit down to eat._  
_Penelope climbs to the high storeroom with a bronze key on an ivory handle. The doors groan open like a bull in a meadow._  
_Inside, on a peg, hangs the great bow in its case. A friend gave it to Odysseus long ago, as a guest-gift._  
_He never took it to Troy. He left it at home, to remember his friend by._  
_Penelope sits down with the bow across her knees and cries over it. Then she gets up and carries it down to the hall._  
**Penelope**: Listen to me, all of you. Here is my husband’s bow. Whoever strings it most easily and shoots through all twelve axes, I’ll go with him.  
_Telemachus digs a long trench in the floor, straight to a line, and sets the axes up one behind another._  
_You carry them in, two at a time._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide 12 by 2 to find the number of trips  
> _There are twelve axes, and you carry two at a time. How many trips do you make?_  
> - ✅ 6 trips → Yes. 12 ÷ 2 = 6, because 6 × 2 = 12. Counting in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 takes six steps.
> - 10 trips → That would carry just 1 axe on most trips. Count in twos to twelve: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. That is six trips.
> - 24 trips → That is 12 × 2, which is more than needed. Twelve axes, carried two at a time, is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 trips.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 12 axes into pairs to find 6 trips._

_Each axe-head has a ring at the top where the handle would go: twelve rings, in one straight line, for an arrow to pass through._  
**Telemachus**: I’ll try it first. If I can string it, my mother can stay here with me.  
_Three times he tries, and the fourth time he nearly has it. Then he sees the beggar give the smallest shake of the head, and stops._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): think about stopping when a trusted person signals you to wait  
> _Telemachus is very close to stringing the bow, then stops when his father shakes his head. Was that giving up, or being wise?_  
> - Wise. He trusted a bigger plan over his pride. → That’s a fair answer. Stopping when it was hard to stop took self-control. He chose the plan over looking strong.
> - Giving up. He was so close. → That’s a fair answer. It must have hurt to stop. The question is whether finishing would have helped or harmed the plan.
> - Both. It was hard, and it was the right thing. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Doing the wise thing is often also the hardest thing.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether stopping at a trusted signal is giving up or being wise (a think question)._


**Choices**

    - He says it well. He sits down near his father, and nobody notices that either.
- **Pass the bow along to the suitors.**
    - You carry it down the line. It is heavier than any bow you’ve ever held, and the string hums faintly when you touch it.
- **Watch the beggar.**
    - The beggar is looking at the bow the way you’d look at an old friend across a crowded room.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): a drawn bow stores energy that becomes the arrow’s movement  
> _When you pull back a bowstring, the bow bends and stores energy, like a stretched spring. What happens to that stored energy when you let go?_  
> - ✅ It turns into the movement of the arrow. → Yes. The bent bow springs straight and pushes the arrow forward. Stored energy becoming movement is how catapults and trampolines work too.
> - It disappears. → Energy never just disappears. Here it changes form: from stored energy in the bent bow to movement of the arrow.
> - It goes into the string and stays there. → Some warms the bow and string a little, but most becomes the arrow’s movement. That is what sends the arrow flying.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a drawn bow stores energy that changes into the movement of the arrow._

> _Leodes is the only suitor who ever disapproved of the others. What does that tell us about him?_

> - He is the strongest. → The scene says the opposite: his soft hands can’t bend the bow an inch. Disapproving shows his character, not his strength.
> - He is the tallest. → Nothing says anything about his height. What the writer tells us is that he disapproved of the others, which shows his sense of right and wrong.

**The Beggar**: My lords, let me try the old bow. I’d like to know if there’s any strength left in these old arms.  
**Antinous**: You? A beggar? You’re lucky we let you eat with us. Eat up and be quiet.

_She goes, wondering at her son, and upstairs Athena puts her into a deep sleep. She will hear nothing of what comes next._

_He plucks the string. It sings, clear and sweet, like a swallow._  

> **Lesson** (music, 1-PS4-1, ask): a tighter string makes a higher note  
> _The bowstring sings when it is plucked, just like a lyre string. If he tightened the string even more, what would happen to the note?_  
> - ✅ It would go higher. → Yes. A tighter string wobbles faster, and faster wobbles make a higher note. That is how musicians tune a lyre, a guitar or a violin.
> - It would go lower. → Lower notes come from slower wobbles, and a looser string. A tighter string wobbles faster and sounds higher.
> - It would stay exactly the same. → Tightening changes the note. The tighter the string, the faster it vibrates, and the higher the sound.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a tighter string vibrates faster and makes a higher note._

> - Holding your breath. → Holding your breath can make the heart feel louder. Slow, steady breaths calm it better.

#### `a14-19-threshold`

_He throws off his rags._  
_He leaps up onto the great stone threshold with the bow and the quiver, and pours the arrows out at his feet._  
_Telemachus stands on one side of him and Eumaeus on the other, with spears. You are just behind, with your Nubbin._  
_His first arrow knocks the gold cup out of Antinous’s hand as he lifts it to drink. The wine goes everywhere._  
_The suitors look round the walls for the shields and spears that always hang there. The walls are bare: Telemachus took them down last night._  
**Odysseus**: You thought I’d never come home from Troy. You ate my house. You courted my wife while I was alive. You didn’t fear the gods.  
_He doesn’t say his name, and he doesn’t need to. Every face in the hall has gone the colour of whey._  
**Eurymachus**: If you really are Odysseus, home again, then you’re right, all of it. We’ll pay it back. Every sheep, every cup, twenty times over.  
**Odysseus**: Not if you gave me everything your fathers ever had. This is my house.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): think about whether paying back is enough to make things fair  
> _Eurymachus offers to pay everything back twenty times over, and Odysseus says no._  
> _When someone has wronged others, is paying back enough to make things fair?_  
> - Yes. Repairing the damage is the heart of fairness. → That’s a fair answer. Putting right what was damaged matters a great deal, and many fair systems start there.
> - No. They must also be truly sorry and promise not to do it again. → That’s a fair answer. Paying for damage doesn’t show whether someone has changed. Trust usually needs both.
> - It depends on what was taken. Some things can’t be paid back. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Time, trust and safety can’t be handed back like a cup, and that is why wrongs of that kind are harder to put right.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness and whether paying back is enough to put things right (a think question)._


**Choices**

- **Stand with Telemachus.**
    - You stand by Telemachus. He’s trembling, and so are you, and neither of you moves.
- **Slip out and untie the rope on the yard gate.**
    - You slip out and untie the rope, and leave the yard gate standing open. Whatever happens in there, there should be a way out.
- **Put your Nubbin behind you.**
    - You put your Nubbin behind you. It puts its paws on the backs of your knees, to be sure you’re still there.
