> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): when we are frightened our heart and breathing speed up to get the body ready  
> _When you are scared, your heart beats faster and you breathe more quickly. Why does the body do this?_  
> - ✅ It gets the muscles ready to act, with extra blood and oxygen. → Yes. It is an old, useful alarm system. Slow, steady breathing tells the body the danger has passed.
> - Because the body is broken. → Not at all. It’s the body working exactly as it should, preparing you to run, fight, or stay very still.
> - Because the body wants to sleep. → The opposite. A fast heart and quick breathing wake the body up and get it ready for action.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a racing heart and quick breathing when scared are the body’s alarm system, and slow breathing calms it._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile compares a panicking crowd to cattle bothered by a gadfly

> - They walk away calmly. → Cattle bothered by a gadfly don’t walk calmly. They bolt. The simile shows the suitors panicking.
> - They stand still and watch. → A gadfly sends cattle running. The simile means the suitors scatter and run.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a simile (cattle and a gadfly) to show how the suitors panic._

> - It isn’t good. Winners should show off. → Showing off might feel good for a minute, but it hurts others and makes new quarrels. Being gracious is stronger.
> - It doesn’t matter either way. → It matters a lot to the people who lost. Kindness after winning can turn an enemy into a neighbour.

> - 82 cups → That is 41 + 41. Your Nubbin found just one extra cup, so it is 41 + 1 = 42.

#### `a14-20-hall`

**Eurycleia**: Wake up, child! He’s home. He’s here. The beggar in the hall was him all along. Telemachus knew!  
**Penelope**: Nurse, the gods have made you mad. Why wake me? I was sleeping so well. I haven’t slept like that since he went.  
_Penelope comes down the stair, and stops. She sits down across the hearth from him in the firelight, and looks at him, and doesn’t speak._  
_He sits by a pillar with his eyes down, waiting for her to say something. She doesn’t._  
**Telemachus**: Mother. Hard mother. Your heart’s harder than stone. Any other woman would have run to him after twenty years.  
**Penelope**: Child, I can’t. I can’t speak, or ask, or look him in the face. If it is him, we have signs between us. Secret ones.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think about being careful with a hope that seems too good to be true  
> _After twenty years of false stories, Penelope doesn’t run to him. She wants proof first. Is she being hard-hearted, or wise?_  
> - Wise. She has been tricked before, and needs to be sure. → That’s a fair answer. Careful hope protects a person from being hurt again.
> - Hard-hearted. After twenty years she should believe him. → That’s a fair answer. Telemachus feels exactly that. It’s hard to see someone you love hold back.
> - Neither. She is afraid of hoping too much. → That’s a thoughtful answer. When something matters this much, hope and fear can feel like the same thing.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being careful with a long-awaited hope is wise or hard-hearted (a think question)._

_Odysseus smiles, then. He knows her._  
**Odysseus**: Leave your mother be, Telemachus. She’ll test me. Soon she’ll know me better.  

**Choices**

- **Sit down on the step, out of the way.**
    - You sit on the step. This part is theirs, and you’re only here to see it.
- **Look at Penelope.**
    - She is looking at him the way she looked at her loom all those nights: row by row, checking every stitch.
- **Hold your Nubbin still.**
    - You hold your Nubbin still. It badly wants to go to one of them, and can’t decide which.

#### `a14-20-hall-done`

_He goes to bathe._  
_When he comes back Athena has made him taller and stronger, with hair curling like hyacinth petals, and he sits down across from her again._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile with a flower paints a picture  
> _His hair curls “like hyacinth petals”. A hyacinth is a spring flower with small, tightly curled petals. What picture does the simile give you?_  
> - ✅ Soft, tight curls, dark and glossy. → Yes. You can almost see the curls. A simile lets a writer say a lot in a few words by comparing one thing to something you already know.
> - Straight, flat hair. → Hyacinth petals curl, so the simile points to the opposite: tight, soft curls.
> - Hair that is very short. → The simile is about the shape, not the length. Hyacinth petals curl, so the hair has curls.
> _For grown-ups: Pictured a simile (hair like hyacinth petals) and what it says about the hair._


#### `a14-20-bed`

**Odysseus**: Strange woman. The gods made you harder than anyone. Nurse, make me up a bed out here. I’ll sleep alone.  
**Penelope**: I’m not proud, and I’m not cold. I know very well what you looked like when you sailed.  
**Penelope**: Eurycleia, move the great bed out of our room, the one he built himself. Make it up for him out here.  
_Odysseus goes white. He stands up._  
**Odysseus**: Who moved my bed? Nobody could. Nobody living could shift it, however young and strong, unless a god helped him.  
**Odysseus**: I built it. An olive tree grew in the courtyard, tall and thick and green, and I built our room round it, stone by stone.  
**Odysseus**: I roofed it and hung the doors. Then I cut away the branches, trimmed the trunk, and made it the bedpost. I bored the holes myself.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): roots anchor a tree, so a bedpost made from a living trunk can’t be moved  
> _Odysseus built the bed from a living olive trunk, still rooted in the ground. Why is a tree with roots so hard to move?_  
> - ✅ Its roots anchor it deep in the ground. → Yes. Roots spread out and grip the soil, which holds a tree in place in strong winds. A bed built from a rooted trunk is part of the house itself.
> - Because the trunk is made of iron. → Wood isn’t iron. It is the roots under the ground that hold a living tree fast.
> - Because nobody has tried to move it. → The point is that nobody could. A rooted tree is held by its roots.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that roots anchor a tree, which is why a bed built round a living trunk cannot be moved._

**Odysseus**: That was our secret. Has someone cut the trunk? Tell me. Is my bed still there?  
_Her knees give way. She runs to him, and puts her arms round his neck, and kisses him._  
**Penelope**: Don’t be angry with me. So many men have come with stories. I had to be sure it was you.  
_He holds her and weeps. She is to him what the land is to a swimmer who has been a long time in the sea._  
_Athena holds back the dawn at the edge of the world, and keeps the horses of the morning in their stable, so the night goes on._  
**Odysseus**: Penelope. It’s me. It’s Odysseus.  
_It is the first time he has said his own name aloud since the giant’s island, and you hear it._  
_It sounds different, said quietly, at home._  

#### `a14-20-bed-done`

_You go quietly out of the hall with your Nubbin, and leave them by the fire._  
_There is a lot to tell, and the night is as long as Athena has made it._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the olive tree was sacred to Athena, and Athens is named for her  
> _In the old Greek story of how Athens got its name, Athena won the city by giving it the first olive tree, which brought food, oil and wood._  
> _The city of Athens is named for her, and olives are still a big part of Greek life today._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the old story of Athena and the olive tree, and that Athens is named for her._


#### `a14-20-orchard`

_Morning. Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus and you walk out to old Laertes’s farm in the hills, among the vines._  
_Laertes is alone in the orchard, digging round a young tree. His tunic is patched and dirty, with leather gaiters against the thorns._  
_Odysseus stands under a tall pear tree and watches him, and can’t speak for a while._  
**Odysseus**: Old man, you know your work. Every plant here is cared for: fig and vine and olive and pear. Only you aren’t cared for.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): how to look after older people  
> _Odysseus sees that every plant in the orchard is cared for, but old Laertes is not. How can we help look after older people we know?_  
> - ✅ Visit, listen, help with jobs, and show we care. → Yes. Time and company matter as much as help. Even a short visit and a good listen can brighten someone’s day.
> - Leave them alone. They don’t need anyone. → Most people, young or old, need company and care. Laertes shows how lonely it can get when nobody visits.
> - Only family should help. → Family often does, but neighbours and friends can help too. Anyone who cares can make a difference.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ways to care for older people: visiting, listening, helping._

**Laertes**: Who are you? Have you come from far off? I had a son once. I suppose he’s dead.  
_Odysseus begins to tell him a story, a clever one, and stops halfway. He can’t do it, not to this old man._  
**Odysseus**: Father, it’s me. I’m the one you’ve been grieving for. I’ve come home, in the twentieth year.  
**Laertes**: If you’re my son, give me a sign. A real one.  
**Odysseus**: The scar, from the boar on Parnassus. And the trees. When I was little I followed you round this orchard asking the name of every tree.  
**Odysseus**: You gave me thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees and forty figs, and fifty rows of vines, each ripening at its own time.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add three numbers to find a total  
> _Laertes’s gift to his son was thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees and forty fig trees. How many trees is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 63 trees → Yes. 13 + 10 = 23, and 23 + 40 = 63.
> - 53 trees → Close. 13 + 10 = 23, but 23 + 40 is 63, not 53.
> - 36 trees → Add each number: 13 + 10 = 23, then 23 + 40 = 63.
> _For grown-ups: Added 13 + 10 + 40 to find 63 trees._

_Laertes’s knees give way. He puts his arms round his son’s neck, and Odysseus catches him as he falls._  

**Choices**

- **Count the pear trees.**
    - You count them: thirteen, still. Some of them are very old now, and still bearing.
- **Fetch the old man a stool.**
    - You fetch a stool from the hut. Laertes sits, and holds on to his son’s hand, and won’t let go of it.
- **Let your Nubbin carry his gloves.**
    - Your Nubbin carries Laertes’s gardening gloves for him, one at a time, and lays them very carefully on the wall.

#### `a14-20-orchard-done`

**Laertes**: Father Zeus, the gods are still on Olympus after all, if those men have had what they deserved.  
_Then the families of the suitors come up the road from the town, angry, with spears, wanting payment for their shame._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): ways to settle a quarrel between two groups peacefully  
> _Two angry groups face each other with spears. What are some ways to settle a quarrel peacefully?_  
> - ✅ Stop, listen, and let a fair go-between help them agree. → Yes. Putting down weapons, hearing both sides, and having a fair person help are the beginnings of peace.
> - Fight until one side wins. → That might end a quarrel for a while, but the losers stay angry and the fight can start again. Peace needs both sides to agree.
> - Ignore it and hope it goes away. → Quarrels left alone usually get worse. Someone has to start the talking.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that peace needs stopping, listening and a fair go-between._

_Before anyone can lift a spear, old Mentor steps between the two sides. When he speaks, it isn’t Mentor’s voice at all._  
**Athena**: Men of Ithaca, stop. No more of this. Make peace, and let it hold.  
_Out of a clear sky comes thunder. The spears go down, and the families stand in the road, and then, one by one, go home._  
_Athena, still in Mentor’s shape, makes peace between the house and the town, and both sides swear to keep it._  
**Penelope**: Take my loom, guest. The big one upstairs. I won’t need a loom that works backwards any more.  
_Telemachus brings a cutting from the olive in the bedroom wall, wrapped in wet cloth._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): a cutting needs moisture to grow roots and become a new tree  
> _Telemachus wraps an olive cutting in wet cloth so that it can grow into a new tree. Why keep the cutting wet?_  
> - ✅ Roots need moisture to start growing. → Yes. A cutting has no roots yet, so it needs damp to grow them. Once it has roots, it can take water from the soil and grow into a tree like its parent.
> - So that it floats. → A cutting isn’t going on a boat. Moisture lets the cut end sprout roots.
> - To keep it clean. → Cleanliness isn’t the reason. Without moisture the cut stem would dry out, and roots couldn’t grow.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a cutting needs moisture to grow roots and become a new plant._

**Odysseus**: Plant it by your water. Build something round it, if you like. That’s what they’re for.  
_The sea goes blue again under your fingers, and the island goes small, and you are home, with the atlas on your knee._  
_In one hand there is an olive cutting in wet cloth. Your Nubbin is holding the corner of a very large loom._  
_A long road home, and a house that waited. Odysseus could have stayed safe on Calypso’s shore, and chose to be well instead._  

## A15-1. The Grey Prairie

- `a15-01-s1`: Step into the grey page and find the farmhouse. · _Touch the page, then walk across the prairie to the only house on it._
- `a15-01-s2`: Help Uncle Henry and Aunt Em make ready for the storm. · _Watch the sky to the north, then help at the square door in the floor._
- `a15-01-s3`: Ride out the cyclone, then step out of the page where the house comes down. · _Keep hold of your Nubbin. When the edge of the page curls, step through._

#### `a15-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page that is almost all grey: flat land to the edges of the paper, and one small house._  
_Someone painted the house once, long ago. Years of sun and rain have worn every scrap of colour away._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, ask): weathering: sun, wind and rain wear things away  
> _The paint on the house has worn off. What slowly wore it away?_  
> - ✅ Sun, wind and rain, over many years → Yes. Slow wearing away is called weathering. It wears down rock the same way, only far more slowly.
> - One big snowstorm → Snow can help, but this took years. Sun, wind and rain, bit by bit, is weathering.
> - Toto → Toto is good at many things, but not that one. It was the weather, over many years.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sun, wind and rain slowly wear materials away (weathering)._

_The grey goes soft under your fingers. Then it is dry grass, and you and your Nubbin are standing in it._  
_There is no tree, no hill, no fence. The sky comes all the way down to the ground on every side._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4-ESS2-2, ask): what a prairie looks like; where Kansas is  
> _Kansas is in the middle of the United States, on the Great Plains. What would you see for miles around?_  
> - ✅ A flat sea of grass → Yes. Wide, flat grassland is called prairie. In 1900 the farms out here were far apart.
> - Snowy mountains → The Rocky Mountains are far to the west. Kansas itself is flat grassland, called prairie.
> - A rainforest → A rainforest is hot and wet and full of trees. Kansas is flat, dry grassland, called prairie.
> _For grown-ups: Read the land: Kansas is on the flat grassland of the Great Plains, called prairie._

_A small black dog races up and barks at your Nubbin, as if he has waited all day for something new._  
**Dorothy**: Toto! Come back!  
**Dorothy**: Oh. Hello.  
**Dorothy**: I didn’t know anybody lived out this way.  
**Dorothy**: I’m Dorothy, and that’s Toto. He’s the only thing round here that isn’t grey, and he knows it.  
_Your Nubbin and Toto sniff noses. Toto decides it is all right, and sneezes._  

**Choices**

- **Tell her your name.**
    - **Dorothy**: That’s a nice name. It sounds like it comes from somewhere with trees.
- **Ask why everything is grey.**
    - **Dorothy**: The sun, mostly, and the wind. Aunt Em came out here young and pretty, Uncle Henry says.
    - **Dorothy**: It took the shine off her.
- **Let your Nubbin play with Toto.**
    - Your Nubbin and Toto race twice round you and tumble in the dust. It is the first noise the prairie has heard all day.

**Dorothy**: Come up to the house. Aunt Em will want to look at you.  
**Dorothy**: She watches the sky like a sailor watching the sea. She is always waiting for the weather to turn.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): similes  
> _Dorothy says Aunt Em watches the sky like a sailor watching the sea. What is being compared, and why?_  
> - ✅ Aunt Em and a sailor; both watch for weather that could turn dangerous → Exactly. A comparison using “like” or “as” is called a simile. This one tells you Aunt Em is wary.
> - The sky and the sea; both are blue → Good eye, but look who is doing the watching. Aunt Em is compared to a sailor.
> - Dorothy and Toto → Not quite. The sentence compares how Aunt Em watches with how a sailor watches.
> _For grown-ups: Read a simile and said what it compares and what it tells us about a character._

_The house is a long way off across the grass. It is the only thing to walk towards._  

#### `a15-01-storm`

_The house is one room: a stove, a table, a cupboard, two beds and a square door in the floor._  
_Uncle Henry stands on the step, looking at the sky. It has gone a darker grey than usual._  
**Uncle Henry**: Storm’s coming, Em. A big one.  
**Uncle Henry**: I’m going to see to the animals.  
_From the north comes a low wail. The long grass bows flat, all the way to the edge of the world._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, ask): tornadoes come when warm damp air meets cold dry air, mostly in spring  
> **Uncle Henry**: Storms like this build when warm, damp air from the south meets cold, dry air from the north. When does that happen most in Kansas?  
> - ✅ In spring and early summer → That’s the one. Spring and early summer bring most of the tornadoes. Baum’s book calls them cyclones.
> - In the middle of winter → Winter has its own storms, but the big spinning ones come mostly in spring and early summer.
> - Only in autumn → Autumn can have them, but spring and early summer are the busiest time.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that tornadoes (Baum’s “cyclones”) form where warm damp air meets cold dry air, mostly in spring._

**Aunt Em**: Dorothy! The cellar!  
**Aunt Em**: Now, child!  
_Aunt Em flings open the trap door and climbs down the ladder into the small dark hole beneath._  
_Toto jumps out of Dorothy’s arms and hides under the bed. She goes down on her knees after him._  
**Dorothy**: Toto! Come out!  
**Dorothy**: Oh, you bad dog, come out this minute!  

**Choices**

- **Hold the trap door open for her.**
    - You kneel and hold the trap door. Aunt Em is calling from below, and the whole house has begun to shake.
- **Reach under the bed for Toto.**
    - You get a hand on Toto’s collar and pass him, wriggling, to Dorothy. The floor is already shaking.
- **Grab your Nubbin first.**
    - Your Nubbin is in your arms before you know you have reached for it. It is trembling, and so is the floor.

#### `a15-01-storm-done`

_The wind gives a great shriek. The house shakes so hard that Dorothy sits down on the floor._  
_Then the house turns round twice, quite slowly, and lifts off the ground like a balloon._  
_Far below, the cellar stays dark and still, and Aunt Em is safe in it._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): where to shelter in a tornado  
> _Aunt Em knew where to go. Where is the safest place in a tornado?_  
> - ✅ Underground, or in a room with no windows on the lowest floor → Quite right. Glass breaks, and wind throws things about. Low and windowless is best, and go early.
> - Next to a window, to watch it come → Never. Windows shatter. Go to the lowest room with no windows, and stay away from glass.
> - In a parked car → A car can be tossed about. A cellar, or a low inside room with no windows, is far safer.
> _For grown-ups: Learned where to shelter in a tornado: underground, or a low room with no windows._


#### `a15-01-cyclone`

_The house is carried up into the very middle of the cyclone, where it is strangely quiet. It rocks along like a cradle._  
_Toto runs about barking. Then he goes too near the open trap door and falls in._  
_The wind holds him up. Dorothy lies flat, reaches down, and pulls him back by one ear._  
**Dorothy**: There. That is quite enough adventure for one dog.  
_Hours go by. Dorothy shuts the trap door and lies down on her bed, with Toto beside her._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): multiplying a speed by a time to find a distance  
> _Suppose the house flies at 60 kilometres an hour for 3 hours. How far does it travel?_  
> - ✅ 180 km → Yes. 60 + 60 + 60 = 180, or 3 × 60 = 180. That is a long way to travel in a house, and nobody even steered.
> - 63 km → That adds 60 and 3, but speed and time are multiplied. Three hours of 60 km each is 3 × 60 = 180 km.
> - 120 km → That is only two hours, and there are three: 60 + 60 + 60 = 180 km.
> _For grown-ups: Found a distance from a speed and a time: 3 × 60 = 180 km._

**Dorothy**: If the house is going to fall, I would rather be asleep for it.  
_You stay awake with your Nubbin in your lap. Somebody ought to._

**Choices**

    - You step through. Behind you the house drops the last few feet, with a bump that makes the whole page jump.
- **Take a last look at Dorothy, asleep.**
    - She is fast asleep, with one arm over Toto. You step through the gap, and the house comes down behind you.

_Behind you the grey farmhouse sits in the middle of it all, a little crooked, as if it had sat down suddenly._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): feeling two things at once  
> _Your Nubbin is thrilled and nervous at the same time. Can a person feel two feelings at once?_  
> - Yes, they mix together → That’s a fair answer. Feelings often arrive in a pair, like excitement and nerves before something new.
> - No, only one at a time → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes one feeling is so big it hides the other. Notice what the quiet one says.
> - I am not sure → That’s a fair answer, and an honest one. Next time something new happens, check: is there more than one feeling in there?
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether two feelings can happen together, using a new place as an example._

> **Lesson** (art, RL.4.3, notice): contrast: a dull colour makes a bright one glow  
> _The artist William Wallace Denslow drew the pictures for the first edition of this book, in 1900._  
> _Artists often put a dull colour next to a bright one so the bright one seems to glow._  
> _That is why green looks so rich after all that grey._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that contrast between a dull and a bright colour makes the bright one stand out._

### Glossary

- **prairie**: A wide, flat stretch of grassland with very few trees.
- **cyclone**: Baum’s word for a tornado: a spinning funnel of wind that comes down from a storm cloud.
- **cellar**: A small room under a house, below the ground.

#### `a15-02-council`

_Three men and a woman come up, no taller than Dorothy. They wear blue, and round pointed hats with little bells that tinkle._  
_The woman is very old, in a white gown sprinkled with stars. She bows low to Dorothy._  
**The Witch of the North**: Welcome to the land of the Munchkins, my dear. This is the East, and they thank you for setting them free.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions  
> _The old woman says this is the East. If you stand facing north, which hand points east?_  
> - ✅ Your right hand → Yes. Facing north, east is on your right and west is on your left. “Never Eat Soggy Waffles” goes clockwise: north, east, south, west.
> - Your left hand → That one is west. Facing north, east is on your right.
> - Straight ahead → Straight ahead is north. East is a quarter turn to your right.
> _For grown-ups: Used a compass: facing north, east is on your right._

**Dorothy**: I think you have muddled me up with somebody else. I haven’t done anything.  
**The Witch of the North**: Your house did, which comes to the same. Look there, under the corner.  
**Dorothy**: Oh. Oh, the poor thing.  
**Dorothy**: It came down right on top of her.  
**The Witch of the North**: She was the Wicked Witch of the East. She kept these people working for her night and day.  
**A Munchkin**: Night and day! For years!  
**A Munchkin**: And now we are free!  
_When you look again, the feet are gone. Only the silver shoes are left, lying in the grass._  
**The Witch of the North**: The shoes are yours now. They hold some magic, though nobody ever learned what.  

**Choices**

    - **Dorothy**: They fit exactly, as if they had been waiting for me.
- **Tell her to be careful with them.**
    - **The Witch of the North**: Wise. A charm is like a dog: best to know what it will do before you take it for a walk.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff the shoes.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs, sneezes, and sits on the shoes, as if somebody ought to keep them warm.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): asking for help  
> _Dorothy asked strangers for help. Is asking for help a sign of weakness or of strength?_  
> - Strength: it takes courage → That’s a fair answer. It often takes more courage to ask than to struggle on alone.
> - Weakness: you should manage alone → That’s a fair answer, and many people feel it. Yet even the strongest people ask. Dorothy could not cross a desert alone.
> - It depends what you ask → That’s a fair answer. Choosing who to ask, and when, is a skill too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether asking for help shows strength or weakness._

**The Witch of the North**: Keep to the road of yellow brick and you cannot go wrong. I cannot come with you, but I can give you my kiss.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why a character acts as she does  
> _Why does the Witch of the North kiss Dorothy on the forehead?_  
> - ✅ To protect her on the road → Yes. She cannot go along, so she gives Dorothy protection. A character’s motive is the reason behind what she does.
> - To say a polite goodbye → A kiss is a kind goodbye, but listen to what she says next. The mark is meant to protect.
> - Because she is bored → Not bored at all. She is worried for Dorothy and wants her safe.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character’s motive from what she says._

_She kisses Dorothy on the forehead. Where her lips touch there is a round, shining mark._

- **Look closely at the mark.**
    - It shines faintly, like a coin at the bottom of a well. Dorothy cannot see it, but everyone else can.
- **Hold your Nubbin up to say goodbye.**
    - The Witch of the North taps your Nubbin once on the nose. It goes cross-eyed with pride, and stays that way some time.

_You notice that the smallest bells ring the highest notes, and a bigger bell on a fence post gives a deeper one._  

> **Lesson** (music, 4-PS3-2, ask): pitch: small things make higher sounds  
> _Which makes the higher note: a tiny hat bell or a big bell on a fence post?_  
> - ✅ The tiny hat bell → Yes. Smaller things vibrate faster, and faster vibrations make a higher pitch. Big bells are slower and deeper.
> - The big bell → The other way round. The big bell vibrates slowly, so its note is deep. The tiny bell is high.
> - They sound the same → Listen again. Small and big make different notes. Small is higher, big is lower.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that smaller bells vibrate faster and sound higher._


#### `a15-02-boq`

_By evening you have walked a fair way along the road of yellow brick. Dorothy has changed into her clean blue-and-white checked frock._  
_You come to a big house where a rich Munchkin called Boq is giving a feast. Everyone for miles seems to be there._  
**Boq**: Welcome, Sorceress! And the Sorceress’s friend!  
**Boq**: And the Sorceress’s friend’s… whatever that is.  
**Dorothy**: I am not a Sorceress. I am Dorothy.  
**Boq**: Only witches and sorceresses wear white, and your frock has white in it. Now: the tables!  
**Boq**: Five of them, and every plate must be blue.  
_You carry dishes. Each table gets four blue plates, and each plate gets a little iced cake._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: 5 × 4  
> _Five tables, with four blue plates at each. How many plates do you carry?_  
> - ✅ 20 → Yes. Five groups of four is 5 × 4 = 20. You could also count in fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20.
> - 9 → That adds 5 and 4. Five tables of four plates is 5 × 4, which is 20.
> - 16 → That is four tables of four. There are five tables, so 5 × 4 = 20.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups: 5 tables of 4 plates make 20._

**Boq**: And where shall the Sorceress’s friend’s whatever-it-is sit?  

**Choices**

- **Next to Toto, at the end.**
    - Your Nubbin and Toto share the end of the bench, and a blue cake, and nobody minds at all.
- **Next to Dorothy, of course.**
    - **Boq**: Of course! A place of honour!
    - **Boq**: Fetch the tall stool!
- **Under the table, where the crumbs land.**
    - **Boq**: Ah, a practical creature. My grandmother was the same.

#### `a15-02-boq-done`

_Three Munchkins strike up on fiddles and everyone else dances. Dorothy laughs, for the first time since the cyclone._  
_The plates are a deep, dark blue. The cups are a pale, sky blue._  
_You wonder how you would paint both with only one pot of blue._  

> **Lesson** (art, L.3.4, ask): tints and shades  
> _You have one pot of blue paint. How do you make the pale blue of the cups?_  
> - ✅ Add white → Yes. Adding white makes a tint, a paler colour. Adding black makes a shade, a darker one.
> - Add black → Black makes it darker, like the plates. For pale blue, add white.
> - Add more blue → More blue makes it stronger, not paler. To lighten a colour, add white.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that adding white makes a paler tint and adding black a darker shade._


#### `a15-02-complete`

_Boq gives Dorothy his best bed, with blue sheets. She falls asleep at once, with Toto curled at her feet._  
_You sit up a while with Boq on his front step. The yellow road runs off into the dark, glowing faintly._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): welcoming a stranger  
> _Boq welcomed a girl, a dog and a creature nobody could name. What makes a stranger feel welcome?_  
> - ✅ Someone says hello and finds them a seat → Just so. A kind word and a place at the table cost very little, and mean a great deal.
> - Asking a lot of questions about them → Questions can be friendly, but too many can feel like a test. A hello and a seat come first.
> - Leaving them alone until they speak → Some quiet is fine. But a first hello makes the first step much easier.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes a newcomer feel welcome._

**Boq**: It is a long way to the City of Emeralds. Many days.  
**Boq**: Mind the wild parts.  
**Boq**: But she has the Witch’s kiss, and the silver shoes. And she has you, which I suppose is something.  
_Your Nubbin falls asleep beside the silver shoes, one paw on each, as if they might walk off without it._  

### Glossary

- **Munchkin**: One of the small people of the eastern land of Oz, who wear blue.
- **feast**: A big meal with lots of people and lots of good food.

## A15-3. The Scarecrow

- `a15-03-s1`: Help lift the Scarecrow down from his pole. · _Climb the fence into the cornfield and hold the pole steady while Dorothy lifts._
- `a15-03-s2`: Help the Scarecrow find his feet. · _Walk beside him on the yellow bricks and catch him when he tips._
- `a15-03-s3`: Sit by the road and listen while Dorothy tells him about Kansas. · _Sit with them on the bank while Dorothy eats her bread._

#### `a15-03-pole`

_In the morning the road runs past a big field of ripe corn._  
_High on a pole in the middle, keeping the birds off, there is a Scarecrow._  
_His head is a little sack stuffed with straw, with a face painted on it. He wears an old pointed blue hat._  
_As you look at him, he winks: slowly, with his left eye._  
**Dorothy**: Did you see that? I must have dreamed it.  
**Dorothy**: Scarecrows in Kansas never wink.  
**The Scarecrow**: Good morning. How do you do?  
**The Scarecrow**: Not very well myself, if you want the truth. It is dreadfully dull, up a pole all day.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): materials and their properties  
> _The Scarecrow is stuffed with straw. Why is straw a good filling for him, and not iron?_  
> - ✅ Straw is light and soft, so it is easy to carry and cannot hurt anyone → Precisely. Light and soft. I am much easier to lift than a lump of iron, and I never bruise anyone I fall on.
> - Straw is stronger than iron → Hardly. Iron is much stronger. It is also far too heavy and hard for a person like me.
> - Straw is shinier → I am sorry to say that I am not shiny at all. The point of straw is that it is light and soft.
> _For grown-ups: Compared materials (straw, iron) by their properties and chose by what each is for._

**The Scarecrow**: There is a pole up the back of my coat, you see. If you could lift me off it, I would be ever so grateful.  
_Dorothy reaches up with both arms. Someone must hold the pole steady, or it will go over with him on it._  

**Choices**

- **Hold the pole steady.**
    - You hold the pole. Dorothy lifts him off, and the pole jumps in your hands as if it is glad too.
- **Stand underneath, ready to catch him.**
    - Dorothy lifts him off. He tips, and lands on you, which is like being hit by a large, polite pillow.

#### `a15-03-pole-done`

**The Scarecrow**: Thank you. Thank you both.  
**The Scarecrow**: I feel ever so much more like a person down here.  
_He stretches, yawns, and falls flat on his face. Then he gets up, and falls over sideways._  
_You notice that he stands with his feet together, and wobbles like a skittle._  

> **Lesson** (health, 3-PS2-1, ask): balance: a wide base is steadier  
> _How could the Scarecrow stand more steadily?_  
> - ✅ With his feet wide apart → Yes. A wide base is steadier, because the middle of your weight stays over your feet. Try it yourself.
> - With his feet together → That is how he is wobbling. A narrow base tips easily. Feet apart is steadier.
> - On one foot → One foot is the hardest of all. A wide stance on two feet is steadiest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that standing with feet apart gives a steadier base._


#### `a15-03-feet`

_The Scarecrow has never walked before. His legs go wherever they like, and they do not consult each other first._  
**The Scarecrow**: I was only made the day before yesterday. Before that I was nothing at all, which is restful, but not interesting.  
**Dorothy**: I am going to the City of Emeralds, to ask the great Oz to send me back to Kansas.  
**The Scarecrow**: Does he have brains to spare, do you suppose? Straw legs I do not mind.  
**The Scarecrow**: But a straw head is another matter. People call you a fool.  
**Dorothy**: I do not know. But come anyway.  
**Dorothy**: If he has none, you will have lost nothing but the walk.  
_He takes six steps, and steps into a hole in the road and goes full length on the bricks. He is not hurt in the least._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication word problem  
> _Say the Scarecrow manages 6 steps before each tumble, and he tumbles 4 times before noon. How many steps has he taken?_  
> - ✅ 24 → Yes. Four groups of six: 4 × 6 = 24. He is learning fast, and falling faster.
> - 10 → That adds 6 and 4. Four tumbles with six steps in each is 4 × 6 = 24.
> - 18 → That is three groups of six. He has tumbled four times, so 4 × 6 = 24.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a multiplication word problem: 4 groups of 6 steps is 24._


**Choices**

- **Offer him your arm.**
    - **The Scarecrow**: An arm! The very thing.
    - **The Scarecrow**: I shall try very hard not to take it home with me.
- **Walk ahead and call out the holes.**
    - “Hole,” you call, and he steps round it; “hole,” and he steps round; “brick,” and he falls over the brick.
- **Let your Nubbin lead him.**
    - Your Nubbin walks in front, very slowly. The Scarecrow copies every step, and falls over only twice.

#### `a15-03-feet-done`

_By noon he can walk a straight line. By afternoon he can very nearly walk a curved one._  
_His legs, which once did not consult each other, now seem at least to be on speaking terms._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification  
> _The narrator says the Scarecrow’s legs “do not consult each other”. What is the author doing?_  
> - ✅ Giving legs a human habit, to be funny → Yes. This is personification: treating a thing as if it were a person. Here it makes his clumsiness funny.
> - Telling us legs can really talk → Not really. The author is joking. Legs cannot consult anyone, but a person could.
> - Comparing legs with sticks, using “like” → There is no “like” or “as” here. That would be a simile. This gives legs a human habit.
> _For grown-ups: Spotted personification: a thing given a human habit for humour._

_You find yourself walking in step with him, left, right, left, right, all the way along the yellow bricks._  

#### `a15-03-kansas`

_You sit down on the bank, and Dorothy shares out her bread. The Scarecrow does not eat, but he likes being passed things._  
**The Scarecrow**: Tell me about your country. Kansas, was it?  
**Dorothy**: It is all grey. The ground and the house and the sky.  
**Dorothy**: Even Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, nearly.  
**The Scarecrow**: But here there is green, and birds, and corn. Why would anyone go back to all that grey?  
**Dorothy**: Even if a home is plain and dreary, it is where your own people are. You would rather be there than anywhere, however beautiful.  
**Dorothy**: That is what makes it home.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what makes a place home  
> _Dorothy would choose her grey farm over a beautiful land. What makes a place feel like home?_  
> - The people who live there → That’s a fair answer. Home is who is waiting, more than where.
> - The things in it, like my own bed → That’s a fair answer. Familiar things are comforting. They keep us company when people are away.
> - It needn’t be one place at all → That’s a fair answer, and a surprising one. Perhaps home can travel, in a person or a song.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what makes a place feel like home._

**The Scarecrow**: I see. So it is not the paint that makes a home.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _Which sentence states the theme of this scene?_  
> - ✅ A home is made by the people we love, not by how it looks → Exactly. A theme is the big idea under a story, and here it is about what makes a home.
> - Grey farms are dull → That is a detail, not the big idea. The scene says that plain places can still be home.
> - Scarecrows do not eat → True, but it is a small detail. The theme is bigger: what makes a home.
> _For grown-ups: Found the theme of a short scene._


**Choices**

- **Tell him what you miss about your own home.**
    - **The Scarecrow**: There you are, then. Everybody with brains has a place somewhere that they would rather be.
- **Ask him where his home is.**
    - **The Scarecrow**: A pole in a cornfield. I do not miss it at all.
    - **The Scarecrow**: Perhaps that is how you can tell it was not home.
- **Watch your Nubbin, asleep in Dorothy’s lap.**
    - Your Nubbin is asleep in Dorothy’s lap, and Toto in yours. Nobody has asked them about home.
    - They seem to have found it anyway.

#### `a15-03-kansas-done`

_The road goes on, and the fields begin to give way to trees. The Scarecrow walks between you, nearly straight._  
_Behind you the corn stands tall and gold in the sun, row after row._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): what plants need to grow  
> _The corn grew tall in the fields. What does corn, like any plant, need to grow?_  
> - ✅ Sunlight, water and soil → Yes. Plants make their food from sunlight and water, and roots hold them in soil that gives them minerals.
> - Only soil → Soil matters, but without light and water the corn would not grow. Plants need all three.
> - Only water → Water is vital, but plants also need light to make food, and soil to hold their roots.
> _For grown-ups: Named what plants need: sunlight, water and soil._

_Dorothy hums as she walks. Toto trots at her heel, and your Nubbin trots at yours._  

#### `a15-03-complete`

**The Scarecrow**: Shall I tell you a secret? I am afraid of exactly one thing.  
**Dorothy**: Crows?  
**The Scarecrow**: No. Crows are all bluster.  
**The Scarecrow**: Matches. A lighted match.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): fire needs fuel, heat and air  
> _A fire needs three things to burn: fuel, heat and air. What is the Scarecrow, as far as a fire is concerned?_  
> - ✅ Fuel: straw burns easily → Yes. Straw is dry and burns fast, which is why he is right to be careful. Matches are for grown-ups: if you find some, do not touch, tell an adult.
> - Air → There is plenty of air everywhere, but the Scarecrow is made of dry straw. That makes him fuel.
> - Heat → Heat comes from the flame. The Scarecrow is made of dry straw, and dry straw is fuel.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fire needs fuel, heat and air, and why matches are for grown-ups._

_You quietly move your matches to the bottom of your bag, under everything._  
_That night he stands in a corner, since he never gets tired._  
_He watches over you all till morning, and says it is the most useful he has ever felt._  

### Glossary

- **ripe**: Fully grown and ready to be picked and eaten.
- **bluster**: Loud, empty noise that sounds fierce but means nothing.

## A15-4. The Tin Woodman

- `a15-04-s1`: Follow the groaning sound into the forest. · _Leave the road where the trees are thickest, and listen._
- `a15-04-s2`: Find the oil-can in the Woodman’s cottage. · _Look along the shelf for the can with the long thin spout._
- `a15-04-s3`: Oil the Woodman’s joints, in the right order. · _Start with whatever lets him speak, then whatever is tiredest._

#### `a15-04-groan`

_In the morning Dorothy goes into the trees to look for water. Not far off, somebody groans._  
**Dorothy**: What was that?  
_In a clearing stands a man made all of tin, with his axe raised over his head as if he had stopped in the middle of a stroke._  
_A tree beside him is half chopped through, and has been for some time._  
**The Tin Woodman**: Mm. Mm-hm.  
**The Tin Woodman**: I have been groaning for a year or more. You are the first to come and see why.  
_He speaks through his teeth, because his jaw will not open. His voice comes out like a gate that wants oiling._  
**The Tin Woodman**: Oil, please. I rusted solid in a rainstorm.  
**The Tin Woodman**: There is a can of it on the shelf in my cottage, just through the trees.  
**The Tin Woodman**: Strictly speaking, tin hardly rusts. It is my iron hinges that seized.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): rust: iron meets water and air  
> _The Woodman’s iron hinges rusted in the rain. What two things must iron meet before it rusts?_  
> - ✅ Water and air → Just so. Iron, water and the oxygen in the air make rust, that flaky red-brown crust. Oil keeps the water off.
> - Sunlight and sand → Sand and sunlight do not rust anything. It takes water and the air together. Rain is the worst.
> - Cold and dark → Cold and dark alone do not do it. It takes water and air. That is why a dry iron gate lasts longer.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that iron rusts when it meets water and air, and that oil keeps the water off._


**Choices**

- **Say you will fetch it.**
    - **The Tin Woodman**: Thank you. Mind the step.
    - **The Tin Woodman**: I made it before I was tin, and it has never been level.
- **Ask how it happened.**
    - **The Tin Woodman**: A rainstorm. I was chopping, and it rained, and I forgot to shelter.
    - **The Tin Woodman**: That is all. It is always all.

#### `a15-04-groan-done`

_The cottage is just through the trees. You go, with your Nubbin at your heels._  
_Behind you the Woodman does not move, because he cannot. His eyes follow you all the way into the trees._  
**Dorothy**: He waited a whole year, and nobody even stopped.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): helping when someone is in trouble  
> _When you notice that someone seems to be stuck or in trouble, what is the best first thing to do?_  
> - ✅ Stop and ask what is wrong → Yes. Stopping is the hard part, and often the only part that matters.
> - Assume someone else will help → That is easy to do. People in crowds often wait for someone else, so nobody acts. Be the one who asks.
> - Walk on, it is not your business → A year of walking on is how he ended up stuck. A question costs a minute.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what to do when someone seems to be in trouble: stop and ask._


#### `a15-04-cottage`

_The cottage is small and very tidy. Everything has been put away by somebody with all the time in the world._  
_There is a bed nobody sleeps in, a table nobody eats at, and a shelf of tins, each with a little dust on top._  
_On the shelf stand three oil-cans: a big square one, a small round one, and a middle one with a long thin spout._  
_A label says the big square can holds one litre. The small round can holds a quarter of a litre._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: how many quarters make a whole  
> _The big can holds 1 litre. The small round can holds 1/4 of a litre._  
> _How many small cans fill the big one?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. Four quarters make one whole: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.
> - 3 → Three quarters is not quite a whole litre. It takes four: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.
> - 2 → Two quarters make a half. It takes four quarters to make a whole.
> _For grown-ups: Used unit fractions: four quarters make one whole._

_Behind the door a picture is pinned up: a Munchkin girl, drawn in pencil, smiling at someone outside the frame._  
_Under it someone has written a name, crossed it out, and written it again._  

**Choices**

- **Take the one with the long spout.**
    - The long spout will reach right into the joints. You tuck the can under your arm, and it sloshes, comfortably full.
- **Take the big square one, to be sure.**
    - The big one is empty, and the one with the spout is full. You take that one instead, and feel you have learned something.
- **Look at the picture a little longer.**
    - She has a kind, untidy face. Somebody drew it very carefully, a long time ago.
    - You take the can with the long spout, and go.

#### `a15-04-cottage-done`

_You run back through the trees. The Woodman has not moved, but his eyes are glad to see you._  
_You keep thinking of the girl in the pencil picture: a kind, untidy face, drawn very carefully._  
_Whoever drew it took trouble over her eyes._  

> **Lesson** (art, 1.G.A.3, ask): proportion in a drawn face  
> _Artists who draw faces place the eyes with care. Where do the eyes sit on a real head?_  
> - ✅ About halfway down → Yes. Most people draw them too high. The eyes sit about halfway between the top of the head and the chin.
> - Near the top → That is the usual mistake! Look in a mirror: the eyes are about halfway down.
> - Near the chin → Too low. Check in a mirror: the eyes are about halfway down the head.
> _For grown-ups: Learned a drawing rule: the eyes sit about halfway down the head._


#### `a15-04-oil`

**Dorothy**: Where shall we start?  
**The Tin Woodman**: Mm. Mmm-m.  
**The Scarecrow**: I think he says “neck”. Though I may only think so because I have no brains.  
_The neck is rusted so badly that Dorothy has to work the head from side to side while you drip in oil._  
_At last it turns, with a long, slow creak. The Woodman moves his head carefully, as if it might come off._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): sound words that show what we hear  
> _The head turns with a long, slow creak. What kind of word is “creak”?_  
> - ✅ A word that sounds like the noise it names → Yes. Words like creak, drip and clank copy a sound. They help a reader hear the page.
> - A word for a colour → Not a colour. It is a word that imitates a sound, like drip and clank.
> - A word for a person → A creak is a noise. The word sounds like the noise it names.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed sound words that imitate the noise they name._

**The Tin Woodman**: Thank you. Now my arms, please.  
**The Tin Woodman**: I have held this axe up for a year, and I should like to put it down.  
_You oil the arms. They creak, then give._  
_He lowers the axe and leans it against the tree with a great sigh._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): friction: oil makes surfaces slide  
> _The arms creaked, then gave. Why does oil help a stiff joint move?_  
> - ✅ It makes the surfaces slippery, so they rub less → Yes. Rubbing between surfaces is called friction. Oil in the gap lowers it, so the joint swings freely.
> - It makes the metal softer → The metal stays the same. The oil sits between the surfaces and lets them slide, which lowers friction.
> - It makes the joint heavier → Oil weighs almost nothing. What it does is lower the friction, so the surfaces slide.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that oil lowers friction between rubbing surfaces._

**The Tin Woodman**: And now, if you would, my legs.  

**Choices**

- **Do his legs.**
    - You oil his legs, one joint at a time, until he can walk. He takes three steps, then three more, for the pleasure of it.
- **Give his jaw another drop first.**
    - **The Tin Woodman**: Ah. Yes.
    - **The Tin Woodman**: Much better. I had not liked to ask.
    - Then you do his legs, and he takes three steps for the pleasure of it.
- **Oil everything you can find, twice.**
    - You oil him from top to toe, twice. He shines like a new kettle.
    - **The Tin Woodman**: I may slip over. But I shall slip over very smoothly.

#### `a15-04-oil-done`

**The Tin Woodman**: Another year and I would have been a statue. I am more obliged to you than I can say.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words  
> _The Woodman says he is “more obliged to you than I can say”. What does obliged mean here?_  
> - ✅ Very thankful → Yes. Here it means grateful. The word can also mean forced to, as in “you are obliged to wear a seat belt”.
> - Forced to → That is its other meaning. Here nobody is forcing him. He is saying he is very thankful.
> - Angry → He is anything but angry. In this sentence, obliged means very thankful.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out which meaning of obliged fits the sentence._

_He bows, a little stiffly, and for the first time in a year something in the clearing is moving._  
_Dorothy helps him pick up his axe, and he tucks it carefully under one arm._  

#### `a15-04-complete`

**The Tin Woodman**: May I ask why you are in the great forest?  
**Dorothy**: We are going to the City of Emeralds, to see the great Oz. I want to go home, and the Scarecrow wants some brains.  
**The Tin Woodman**: This Oz. Might he have a heart he could spare?  
_He taps his chest. It rings hollow, like an empty pail._  
**The Tin Woodman**: I was a man once, and I loved a Munchkin girl. Then my axe was enchanted, and I lost myself one piece at a time.  
**The Tin Woodman**: The tinsmith made me new pieces, but he never made a heart. And without one I forgot how to love her.  
**The Scarecrow**: I shall still ask for brains. A heart is no use to somebody who cannot think what to do with it.  
**The Tin Woodman**: A clever man can be miserable. I would rather be happy, and a heart is how.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what matters most for a good life  
> _The Scarecrow wants brains and the Woodman wants a heart. Which matters more for a good life: being clever, or being kind?_  
> - Being clever → That’s a fair answer. A clever person can solve a great many problems, including other people’s.
> - Being kind → That’s a fair answer. A kind person is welcome everywhere, even when they are not the cleverest.
> - You need both → That’s a fair answer, and probably the wisest one. It is why the pair of us walk together.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether cleverness or kindness matters more for a good life._

_Dorothy puts the oil-can into your hands. From now on, it seems, it is yours to carry._  

### Glossary

- **rust**: The red-brown crust that forms on iron when it meets water and air.
- **obliged**: Very thankful to someone. It can also mean forced to do something.

## A15-5. The Cowardly Lion

- `a15-05-s1`: Walk on through the deep forest. · _Stay together on the yellow bricks. The woods are darker here._
- `a15-05-s2`: Let your Nubbin decide about the Lion, in its own time. · _Sit down on the roadside and wait. Do not pull your Nubbin forward._

#### `a15-05-roar`

_The road runs into thick woods. It is dim under the trees, and now and then something growls a long way off._  
_Your Nubbin walks so close to your boots that you keep treading on it._  
_Then comes a terrible roar, and out of the trees bounds a great Lion._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, ask): animals in groups: lions and their prides  
> _Real lions live in family groups called prides, and a roar can carry about eight kilometres. Why would a lion roar so loudly?_  
> - ✅ To call to its pride and warn rivals to keep away → Yes. A roar says “here I am” to family and “stay out” to strangers. Living in a pride helps lions hunt and guard their young.
> - To scare earthworms → Earthworms are not listening. A roar carries far, so a lion can reach its pride and warn off rivals.
> - Only because it is hungry → Hunger is not the reason. A roar is for calling the pride together and warning rivals away.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that lions live in prides and roar to call their family and warn rivals._

_One blow of his paw spins the Scarecrow to the side of the road. His claws strike the Woodman, and only scratch the tin._  
_Little Toto runs at the Lion, barking. The Lion opens his great mouth._  
_Dorothy rushes forward and smacks the Lion right on the nose._  
**Dorothy**: Leave him alone! You great bully, picking on a little dog.  
**Dorothy**: Shame on you!  
**The Cowardly Lion**: I did not bite him.  
_The Lion rubs his nose where Dorothy hit it. His eyes are filling up._  

**Choices**

- **Stand still. Your Nubbin is behind your boots.**

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step word problem  
> _Leaving out your Nubbin: four walkers have two legs each, and two walkers have four legs each. How many legs are on the road?_  
> - ✅ 16 → Yes. Four walkers on two legs is 4 × 2 = 8. Two walkers on four legs is 2 × 4 = 8. Then 8 + 8 = 16.
> - 12 → Close. Do the two groups separately: 4 × 2 = 8 and 2 × 4 = 8. Then 8 + 8 = 16.
> - 14 → Check each group: 4 × 2 = 8 legs, and 2 × 4 = 8 legs. Together that is 16.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step word problem: 4 × 2 and 2 × 4 make 16 legs._

#### `a15-06-ditch`

_The road comes to a ditch, right across it, wide and very deep. At the bottom are big jagged rocks._

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): measurement word problem in metres  
> _The ditch is 4 m across and the Lion can leap 5 m. By how many metres could he clear it?_  
> - ✅ 1 metre → Yes. 5 − 4 = 1. Not much spare for a nervous lion, with a rider on his back.
> - 9 metres → That adds them. To see what is left over, subtract: 5 − 4 = 1 metre.
> - 2 metres → Check the sum: 5 take away 4 leaves 1 metre.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted lengths in metres to find a safety margin._

**The Scarecrow**: Then you are our bridge! One at a time, on your back.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): slow breathing calms a racing heart  
> _When we are scared, our hearts beat faster. What helps them slow down again?_  
> - ✅ Slow, deep breaths → Yes. Breathing in slowly and out more slowly tells your body the danger has passed. Try it: in for four, out for six.
> - Running about → Running makes your heart beat faster still. Sit, and breathe slowly.
> - Holding your breath → Holding your breath makes the body more tense. Slow breaths are better.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that slow breathing helps a racing heart settle after a fright._

_Your Nubbin climbs out of your coat and sits beside him, panting too, to keep him company._

**The Cowardly Lion**: Those are the Kalidahs. They live in this part of the forest.  
**The Cowardly Lion**: Great beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers, and long, long claws. I am more afraid of them than of anything.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): describing a character or setting in depth  
> _Which sentence paints the clearer picture of a Kalidah?_  
> - ✅ Its great bear body shook the bracken, and its tiger eyes shone green in the dark. → Yes. Strong details (a body, a sound, a colour) let a reader see it. “Scary” only tells.
> - It was a very scary animal. → It is true, but it only tells us how to feel. Details such as shaking bracken and shining eyes let us see it.
> - It was an animal in the forest. → That is correct, but nearly empty. Good description uses sights and sounds.
> _For grown-ups: Chose the description that uses concrete details instead of just telling._

_You walk at the back. Every time a twig snaps, your Nubbin checks behind you, and then behind itself._

**The Scarecrow**: A bridge! That is just the sort of thing I shall think of myself, once I have brains.

#### `a15-06-watch-done`

_The Woodman has cut a deep notch on the side of the trunk that faces the ditch. Now he chops from the other side._  
_The tree begins to creak. Behind you, in the dark wood, something else begins to move._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): forces: which way a cut tree falls  
> _The notch is on the ditch side. Which way will the tree fall?_  
> - ✅ Towards the notch, across the ditch → Yes. Gravity pulls the tree down, and the cut leaves it weakest on the notch side, so it tips that way. Woodcutters plan every fall.
> - Away from the notch → It is the other way. The notch removes wood on that side, so the trunk gives way there first.
> - Straight up → Nothing falls up. Gravity pulls it down, towards the weakened side.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about how a cut weakens one side of a tree and gravity makes it fall that way._

_Everyone goes quiet and takes hold of the rope._

> _The Lion is shaking, and he stands in front of his friends anyway. Is he brave if he is scared the whole time?_

> - No: brave means not feeling fear → That’s a fair answer, and a common idea. Yet then nobody who felt fear could ever be called brave, which seems a pity.
> - Both can be true → That’s a fair answer. A person can shake and still stand. I should know.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a person can be brave and frightened at the same time._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step word problem  
> _The ditch is 8 m wide and the tree is 12 m long, lying straight across with equal ends on each bank._  
> _How much rests on each bank?_  
> - ✅ 2 m → Yes. 12 − 8 = 4 m is left over, and shared between two banks that is 2 m each.
> - 4 m → That is the total left over, but there are two banks. 4 ÷ 2 = 2 m on each.
> - 8 m → That is the width of the ditch. The part on the banks is 12 − 8 = 4 m, or 2 m on each.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step measurement problem: 12 − 8 = 4, shared over two banks, is 2 m each._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4-ESS2-2, ask): rivers: source and mouth  
> _Every river has a source, where it starts, and a mouth, where it ends at the sea or a bigger river. Which is usually higher up?_  
> - ✅ The source → Yes. Rivers run downhill, so they start high, in hills or mountains, and end low, at the sea.
> - The mouth → The mouth is where the river finishes, and it is the low end. Water flows downhill, from the high source.
> - They are at the same height → Then the water would not flow! A river runs because its source is higher than its mouth.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rivers flow from a high source to a low mouth._

#### `a15-07-raft`

_By morning the Woodman has cut enough logs. He pegs them together, and you tie every join twice, to be sure._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): floating: wood is less dense than water  
> _Why does a raft made of logs float?_  
> - ✅ Wood is lighter than the same amount of water → Yes. The scientist’s word is less dense. A log weighs less than the water it pushes aside, so the water holds it up.
> - Because logs are flat → Shape helps a raft stay steady, but a flat stone sinks. Wood floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water.
> - Because water likes wood → Water has no likes! Wood floats because it is less dense: lighter than the same amount of water.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wood floats because it is less dense than water._

**The Tin Woodman**: I do not know any knots. I was a woodman.  
**The Tin Woodman**: Woodmen only know how to make things fall down.  
_Your Nubbin holds the rope ends in its mouth and hands them to you one at a time, very solemnly._  
_The Scarecrow cuts poles to push the raft along. He cuts one for himself, very long, and is proud of it._  
**The Cowardly Lion**: I shall sit in the middle and keep very still. It is what I am best at.  
**Dorothy**: Where did you learn your knots?  

**Choices**

    - **Dorothy**: Mine are Aunt Em’s. She ties the bread-cloth so tight you need a knife to get in.
- **From a book with pictures in it.**
    - **The Scarecrow**: A book! Brains come in books, I have heard.
    - **The Scarecrow**: Perhaps I could stuff one in.
- **Your Nubbin taught you. It chews them.**
    - Your Nubbin, hearing this, chews the next knot. You tie it again.

#### `a15-07-raft-done`

_The raft has seven logs, side by side, pegged and tied. It floats, and everyone climbs aboard._  
_It sinks a little under the Lion, and comes up again._  
_You count the joins between the logs. Each one is tied twice._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step problem: joins and knots  
> _Seven logs lie side by side, and every join between neighbours is tied twice. How many knots is that?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Seven logs have 6 joins between them, and each is tied twice: 6 × 2 = 12 knots.
> - 14 → That would be 7 joins. But the last log has no neighbour on its far side: 6 joins, and 6 × 2 = 12 knots.
> - 7 → That counts only the logs. There are 6 joins, and each is tied twice, so 6 × 2 = 12.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem: 7 logs have 6 joins, tied twice each, so 12 knots._


#### `a15-07-current`

_At first the raft goes well. Then, in the middle, the current takes it and carries it downstream, away from the yellow road._  
**The Scarecrow**: We are going the wrong way! This river runs west, to the Wicked Witch’s country!  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): rivers: where the current is strongest  
> _The raft went wrong in the middle of the river. Where is a river’s current usually strongest?_  
> - ✅ In the middle → Yes. Banks and the river bed rub against the water and slow it down, so the fastest water is out in the middle.
> - Right beside the bank → The bank slows the water down by rubbing against it. The fastest water is out in the middle.
> - It is the same everywhere → Not quite. Water near the banks is slowed down. The middle runs fastest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a river’s current is usually strongest in the middle._

> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people do frightening things to help someone else._

#### `a15-08-poppies`

_The road leads you through meadows of flowers, yellow and white and blue. Then, ahead, a great field of scarlet poppies._  
_Bees hum from flower to flower. The smell is very strong and very sweet._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, ask): pollination  
> _A bee visits a poppy to collect pollen. What does the bee also do, without meaning to?_  
> - ✅ Carries pollen to the next flower, helping it make seeds → Yes. That is pollination. Pollen from one flower must reach another of the same kind before seeds can form.
> - Eats the flower’s roots → Bees do not eat roots. As they travel from flower to flower, pollen sticks to them and helps flowers make seeds.
> - Makes the flower grow taller → The bee does not make it taller. By carrying pollen to the next flower, it helps seeds to form.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bees carry pollen between flowers, helping them make seeds._

_You feel it too: a heaviness in your arms and legs. Real poppies cannot do this; it is only the story’s magic._

_The Lion is lying asleep among the poppies, a long way back. He very nearly made it._

_Your Nubbin yawns, and you wonder how much sleep a person really needs._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): how much sleep children need  
> _About how many hours of sleep does a child of 7 to 10 need each night?_  
> - ✅ 9 to 12 hours → Yes. Sleep is when your body grows and your brain sorts out what you learned. Most children aged 7 to 10 need 9 to 12 hours.
> - 5 to 6 hours → That is far too little for a child. Children aged 7 to 10 need about 9 to 12 hours.
> - 14 to 16 hours → That is closer to what a very small baby needs. At 7 to 10, 9 to 12 hours is right.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that children aged 7 to 10 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep._


#### `a15-08-wildcat`

_You lay Dorothy on the grass by the river, where the fresh breeze can wake her._  
_A low growl, and a great yellow wildcat comes bounding through the grass, chasing something small and grey._  
_It is a little field mouse, running for her life. The wildcat is gaining on her with every bound._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, ask): food chains: producers  
> _Seeds feed the mouse, and the mouse feeds the wildcat. Which part of this chain makes its own food from sunlight?_  
> - ✅ The plant the seeds come from → Yes. Plants are the producers: they make food from sunlight, water and air. Everything else in a food chain depends on them.
> - The mouse → The mouse eats seeds, so it is a consumer. The plant that grew them makes its own food from sunlight.
> - The wildcat → The wildcat eats other animals, so it is a consumer. Plants make their own food from sunlight.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plants are the producers at the start of a food chain._

_The Woodman, though he has no heart, knows it is wrong for the big one to catch the small one._  
_He charges, shouting, with his axe held high._  
_The wildcat takes one look at a bellowing man of tin, and bolts for the trees._  
**The Queen of the Field Mice**: Oh, thank you! Thank you!  
**The Queen of the Field Mice**: I thought that was the end of me.  
**The Tin Woodman**: Please do not mention it. I have no heart, you see, so I try to help anyone who needs a friend.  
**The Tin Woodman**: Even a mouse.  
**The Queen of the Field Mice**: A mouse? I am the Queen.  
**The Queen of the Field Mice**: The Queen of every Field Mouse there is!  
_Out of the grass come mice, dozens of mice, then hundreds, all running and squeaking to their Queen._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): is anyone too small to matter?  
> _The Woodman helped a mouse, and now mice will help a lion. Is anyone ever too small to matter?_  
> - No: small helpers can do big things → That’s a fair answer. This afternoon rather proves it.
> - Yes: some jobs need real size → That’s a fair answer. Some jobs do. But you can often split a big job into small pieces, as the mice will show.
> - It depends on the job → That’s a fair answer, and a careful one. Match the helper to the task.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether small helpers can matter in a big job._


#### `a15-08-strings`

**The Scarecrow**: Woodman, make us a cart with wheels. Your Majesty, tell your people to bring a long piece of string each.  
_The Woodman chops and pegs. In an hour he has made a low cart, with wheels cut from a tree trunk._  
_The mice arrive with their strings, and the first of them line up in rows of eight, twelve rows in all._  
**The Scarecrow**: Now: one string round each mouse, very loose. Round the middle, not the neck.  
**The Scarecrow**: They must be comfortable.  
_So you tie: loop, knot, next mouse; loop, knot, next mouse. Your Nubbin hands you the strings._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication in arrays  
> _The first mice stand in 12 rows of 8. How many strings have you tied for them?_  
> - ✅ 96 → Yes. 12 rows of 8 is 12 × 8 = 96. You can check: 10 × 8 = 80, and 2 × 8 = 16, and 80 + 16 = 96.
> - 20 → That adds 12 and 8. Twelve rows of eight mice is 12 × 8 = 96.
> - 86 → Close, but not quite. Try 10 × 8 = 80, then 2 × 8 = 16. Together that is 96.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied an array: 12 rows of 8 mice make 96._

**The Queen of the Field Mice**: Mind the little one at the end. She is very young and very proud of being asked.

    - You get to four hundred and twelve, then a mouse moves and you have to start again. You decide “a great many” will do.
- **Tie the little one’s string last, with a bow.**
    - **The Queen of the Field Mice**: A bow! She will be impossible now.
    - **The Queen of the Field Mice**: Thank you.

_The Scarecrow and the Woodman go into the poppies, without breathing, and roll the sleeping Lion on to the cart._  
_Then the Queen gives the word, and the mice pull, thousands together, and the heavy cart begins to move._  
_They pull in time, with a tiny chant, one squeak for each step. It is an old way to share out a heavy job._  

> **Lesson** (music, RL.2.4, ask): a steady beat helps people work together  
> _Sailors and workers have long sung work songs while hauling ropes. Why does a steady beat help them?_  
> - ✅ Everyone pulls at the same moment → Yes. A steady beat keeps a crowd in step, so all the pulls land together. That is what rhythm is for.
> - It makes the rope lighter → The rope weighs the same! The beat helps everyone pull together at the same moment.
> - It scares the rope → Ropes are not scared! The beat simply keeps everyone pulling in time.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a steady beat helps a group pull together in time._

> _The Queen promises help whenever Dorothy calls. Why do communities work better when members help each other?_  
> - ✅ Together they can do things nobody could do alone → Just so. A mouse cannot pull a lion, and a thousand mice can. That is what a community is.

- `a15-09-s3`: Walk through the streets of the Emerald City. · _Follow the Guardian through the streets to the Palace in the middle._

#### `a15-09-gate`

_The fences by the road are painted green now, and so are the houses. Even the light seems a little green._  
_Ahead there is a green glow in the sky. Then a great high wall, bright green, and a gate studded with emeralds._  

> **Lesson** (art, 2-PS1-1, ask): mixing colours  
> _The Munchkins wear blue and the Winkies wear yellow, and the City is green. Which two paints mix to make green?_  
> - ✅ Blue and yellow → Yes. Blue and yellow make green. Red and yellow make orange, and red and blue make purple.
> - Red and yellow → Those make orange. For green you need blue and yellow.
> - Red and blue → Those make purple. For green you need blue and yellow.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that blue and yellow paint mix to make green._

_Dorothy pushes the button by the gate, and a silvery tinkle sounds inside. The gate swings slowly open._  
_Before you stands a little man in green from head to foot, and even his skin is faintly green._  
**The Guardian of the Gates**: And what brings you to the Emerald City?  
**Dorothy**: Please, we should like to see the Great Oz.  
**The Guardian of the Gates**: To see Oz? Nobody has asked that in years.  
**The Guardian of the Gates**: A foolish errand might make him very angry.

- **Say you have all come a very long way.**
    - **The Guardian of the Gates**: Everybody has, to get here. It is a long way from everywhere.
    - **The Guardian of the Gates**: That is rather the point of it.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): vocabulary in context  
> _The Guardian calls the visit an errand. What does errand mean?_  
> - ✅ A short trip to do a job → Yes. You run an errand to post a letter or buy bread. Calling a long trek an errand is a little joke.
> - A kind of fruit → Not a fruit! An errand is a short trip to do a job.
> - A long holiday → Quite the opposite. An errand is a short trip to do a job, so calling this journey one is a joke.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of errand from context._


#### `a15-09-spectacles`

**Dorothy**: Why spectacles?  
**The Guardian of the Gates**: Because the City is so bright and glorious that it would blind you without them. Everyone wears them, even the people who live here.  
**The Guardian of the Gates**: They are locked on. Oz ordered it so when the City was first built, and I have the only key.  
_He opens a big box of spectacles of every size and shape, and every one has green glass in it._  
_He fits a pair on each of your friends, and a little pair on Toto._  
_Two gold bands go round the back of each head and lock together._  
_For your Nubbin he hunts a long time, and finds a very small pair with round lenses. Then yours._  
_The gold bands click shut behind your ears._  
_Everything is green: the walls, the floor, your own hands. Your Nubbin looks up at you, green, through its little green lenses._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): how coloured filters change what we see  
> _Green glass lets green light through and holds back most other colours. Through it, how would a red apple look?_  
> - ✅ Dark, almost black → Yes. A red apple sends back mostly red light, and green glass blocks red, so little reaches your eye. White things would look green.
> - Bright red → Not through green glass. It blocks red light, so the apple would look dark.
> - Blue → Green glass does not turn red into blue. It blocks the red, so the apple looks dark.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that coloured glass lets its own colour through and blocks others, so colours change._


**Choices**

- **Ask why they have to be locked.**
    - **The Guardian of the Gates**: Because Oz said so. That is the best sort of reason.
    - **The Guardian of the Gates**: It saves everybody a great deal of thinking.
- **Check that your Nubbin is all right.**
    - Your Nubbin turns its head left, then right, then looks at you for a long time, as if to make sure you are still you.

_The others look at one another through green glass, and nobody asks why._  
_It is easier, somehow, not to._  
_You think of the Guardian’s answer: “Because Oz said so.” It sounded like a reason, and it was not one._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): asking why; thinking for yourself  
> _Nobody asked why the spectacles had to be locked. When is it good to ask “why”?_  
> _Is it ever risky never to ask?_  
> - Always ask when it affects you → That’s a fair answer. If a rule affects you, you have a right to know the reason.
> - Ask, but choose your moment → That’s a fair answer. A good question asked kindly and at the right time is often heard better.
> - Some rules can just be followed → That’s a fair answer. Not every rule needs a speech. But a rule that nobody can explain is worth a second look.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to ask “why”, and the risk of never asking._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step money problem  
> _You buy two glasses of lemonade and one bag of popcorn. How many green pennies do you pay?_  
> - ✅ 11 → Yes. Two lemonades is 2 × 4 = 8 pennies. Add the popcorn at 3 pennies: 8 + 3 = 11.
> - 7 → That adds one lemonade and one popcorn. You bought two lemonades: 2 × 4 = 8, and 8 + 3 = 11.
> - 14 → That is two of each. One bag of popcorn is 3: 8 + 3 = 11.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step money problem: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11 pennies._

#### `a15-10-head`

_In the morning the Soldier comes for Dorothy. She holds on to your sleeve, and he looks at you, and lets you come._  
_The Throne Room is big and round, with a high arched roof, and emeralds set close together on walls, ceiling and floor._  
_In the middle is a big throne of green marble. On it, with no body to hold it up, is an enormous Head._  
**Oz**: You stand before Oz, the Great and Terrible. Speak.  
**Oz**: What do you want of me?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: terrible  
> _Oz calls himself “Great and Terrible”. Today terrible means very bad._  
> _What does he want people to think it means?_  
> - ✅ Awe-inspiring and fearsome → Yes. In the old sense, terrible meant something that fills you with fear and wonder. Oz hopes the old meaning scares people, not the new one.
> - Very bad at his job → That is today’s meaning, and it would be funny, since he is a poor Wizard. But Oz is hoping for the old meaning: fearsome.
> - Silly and harmless → That is the opposite of what he wants. He wants to sound fearsome.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that terrible once meant awe-inspiring and fearsome, and which meaning Oz wants._

**Dorothy**: I am Dorothy. I am nobody very much.  
**Dorothy**: I have come to ask for your help.  
**Oz**: Those silver shoes. How did you come by them?  
**Oz**: And the mark on your forehead?  
**Dorothy**: My house fell on the Witch of the East, and the Witch of the North kissed me. Please, I want to go back to Kansas.  
**Oz**: Then you must do something for me first. Nothing is free here.  
**Oz**: You must earn it.

> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether it is fair to demand someone act against their beliefs._

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): fire safety: stop, drop and roll  
> _If your clothes ever caught fire, what should you do?_  
> - ✅ Stop, drop and roll → Yes. Stop where you are, drop to the ground, and roll to smother the flames. Running only feeds the fire with air. Always tell a grown-up afterwards.
> - Run to find help → Running gives the flames more air. Stop, drop and roll instead.
> - Wave your arms → Waving fans the flames. Stop, drop and roll puts them out.
> _For grown-ups: Learned fire safety: stop, drop and roll._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: the sun sets in the west  
> _The Guardian points towards the setting sun. If you face the setting sun, which way are you facing?_  
> - ✅ West → Yes. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. So with the setting sun in front of you, east is behind you.
> - East → East is where the sun rises, the other way. The setting sun is in the west.
> - South → South is on your left when you face west. The setting sun is in the west.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the setting sun shows west._


### Glossary

- **terrible**: In old stories, something so powerful that it fills you with fear and awe.
- **gauze**: A very thin, see-through cloth.

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication word problem  
> _The Scarecrow covers the five of you with straw, and each needs 3 handfuls. How many handfuls does he pull out?_  
> - ✅ 15 → Yes. Five of you with three handfuls each: 5 × 3 = 15. I am rather thin now, but it was worth it.
> - 8 → That adds 5 and 3. Five of you needing three handfuls each is 5 × 3 = 15.
> - 12 → Close. That is four of you. Count again: Dorothy, Toto, the Lion, you, your Nubbin. Five of you, and 5 × 3 = 15.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a multiplication word problem: 5 × 3 = 15 handfuls._
