> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, ask): animals in groups: bee colonies  
> _How many queens does a honeybee colony have?_  
> - ✅ One → Yes. One queen lays the eggs, and thousands of workers gather food, build the comb and care for the young. They help each other survive.

> - Hundreds → Hundreds of workers, thousands even, but only one queen.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): responsibility when you are made to act  
> _The Monkeys say they have no choice. If someone is made to do something, are they still responsible for it?_  
> - Yes: they still choose how they act → That’s a fair answer. Even when choices are narrow, people may choose how gently to do a hard thing.
> - No: if they have no choice, it is not their fault → That’s a fair answer. Blame usually belongs most to whoever gives the orders. I hope you are right.
> - It depends how much choice they had → That’s a fair answer, and a careful one. “How much choice” is the question a good judge asks.

> _Musicians use Italian words to say how loudly to play. What does piano mean?_  
> - ✅ Soft → Yes. Piano means soft. Its partner forte means loud. The instrument piano got its name because it can play both: it was first called a pianoforte.

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows form when something blocks light  
> _A shadow forms where something blocks the light. Which would make the darker shadow: the bucket, or a clear glass jar?_  
> - ✅ The bucket → Yes. The bucket is opaque: light cannot pass through it. A clear jar lets most light through, so its shadow is faint.
> - The glass jar → Glass is clear, so most light passes through. The opaque bucket blocks it and makes the darker shadow.
> - They make the same shadow → Opaque things block light and clear things let it pass, so their shadows are different.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that opaque things block light and make dark shadows, clear things do not._

#### `a15-12-bar`

_One morning the Witch is in a very good mood. She hums, and does not shout once._  
_In the middle of the kitchen floor she has laid an iron bar, and by her magic made it so nobody can see it._

_But your Nubbin stops and sniffs at a place on the floor where there is nothing, and will not walk over it._  
_Dorothy comes in with the pail, humming too, because it seems to be catching._

_Dorothy starts across the floor, and you see your Nubbin’s ears go flat._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how characters respond; clues in a story  
> _Which clue tells you that something unseen lies on the floor?_  
> - ✅ Your Nubbin will not step there, and its ears go flat → Yes. Good readers look for what a character does, not only what is said. The Nubbin’s behaviour is real evidence.
> - The Witch is humming → Her good mood is suspicious, and a fair clue to something being up. But the Nubbin’s behaviour points to the exact spot.
> - Dorothy is carrying a pail → The pail is not a clue about the floor. Look at what the Nubbin does.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s behaviour as a clue to what is happening._


**Choices**

- **Call out to Dorothy to stop.**
    - You call out. Dorothy turns to look at you, steps backwards, and falls over the bar.
- **Kneel and feel the floor where your Nubbin is sniffing.**
    - Your hand finds cold iron where there is nothing to see. Before you can say so, Dorothy walks straight into it.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): first aid for a bruise  
> _Dorothy has bruised her knee. What helps a bruise?_  
> - ✅ Rest it, and put a cool pack wrapped in cloth on it → Yes. Rest and something cool help reduce swelling. Always wrap the cold pack, and tell a grown-up about any bump that really hurts.
> - Run on it as hard as possible → Running would make it worse. Rest the knee and keep it cool.
> - Put something very hot on it straight away → Heat early on can make swelling worse. Cool is better, wrapped in cloth.
> _For grown-ups: Learned first aid for a bruise: rest, a wrapped cool pack, and tell a grown-up._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): dissolving  
> _We say sugar “melts” in hot tea. What really happens to it?_  
> - ✅ It dissolves: it breaks into tiny pieces that spread through the water → Yes. The sugar is still there, just too small to see. Taste the tea and you would know. That is dissolving, which is different from melting.
> - It disappears for ever → Matter does not just vanish. The sugar spreads out in tiny pieces. You can taste it, so it is still there.
> - It turns into water → Sugar does not become water. It dissolves, spreading through the water as tiny pieces.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sugar dissolves in water: it spreads out in tiny pieces and is still there._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): accidents, blame and feeling sorry

> _Whose fault is an accident?_  
> - Yes: feeling sorry is natural → That’s a fair answer. Sorrow does not always need a fault. It can just mean we cared about what happened.
> - It was the Witch’s own fault → That’s a fair answer. The Witch chose to be cruel. Yet notice that Dorothy still feels sad. Both things can be true.
> - It was nobody’s fault → That’s a fair answer. An accident is something nobody planned. What matters is how we act next.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about feeling sorry and blame when something happens by accident._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division as equal sharing  
> _Twelve handfuls of straw are needed, and each Winkie carries three. How many Winkies carry the straw?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, because 4 × 3 = 12. Four Winkies, three handfuls each.
> - 9 → That subtracts 3 from 12. The question is how many threes fit into twelve: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
> - 36 → That multiplies. Here we share twelve between carriers of three: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 12 handfuls into groups of 3 to get 4 carriers._

> **Lesson** (art, 2-PS1-1, ask): the colour wheel: opposite colours  
> _On a colour wheel, which colour sits opposite yellow, so that the two make each other glow?_  
> - ✅ Purple → Yes. Purple (violet) is opposite yellow. Artists call opposites complementary colours, and put them side by side for punch.
> - Orange → Orange sits next to yellow on the wheel, so the two blend rather than clash. The opposite of yellow is purple.
> - Green → Green is next to yellow too, and a mix of blue and yellow. The opposite of yellow is purple.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that purple is opposite yellow on the colour wheel (complementary colours)._

> _The tinsmiths beat the little cap thin from a lump of gold. Gold can be hammered into very thin sheets without breaking._  
> _What is that property called?_  
> - ✅ Malleable → Yes. A malleable metal can be hammered or pressed into shape without cracking. Gold is one of the most malleable metals there is.
> - Brittle → Brittle things snap or shatter when hit, like glass. Gold bends and spreads instead. That is called malleable.
> - Magnetic → Magnetic means attracted to a magnet, which gold is not. Being easy to hammer thin is called malleable.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a malleable metal such as gold can be hammered thin without breaking._

### Glossary

- **tinsmith**: A person who makes and mends things out of tin and other thin metal.
- **malleable**: Able to be hammered or pressed into a new shape without breaking.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: sunrise is east  
> _You set out in the morning, walking towards the rising sun. Which way are you going?_  
> - ✅ East → Yes. The sun rises in the east. With no landmarks, people tend to drift in circles, which is why we met the same bush three times.
> - West → West is where the sun sets. We walked towards where it rises, which is east.
> - North → North is a quarter turn to the left of east. The rising sun is in the east.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the sun rises in the east, and that people without landmarks drift in circles._

**Dorothy**: I know! The Queen of the Field Mice!

**The Queen of the Field Mice**: Friends! What do you need?  
**Dorothy**: We are lost. Which way is the Emerald City?  
**The Queen of the Field Mice**: Miles and miles. But you are wearing the Cap that calls the Winged Monkeys.  
**The Queen of the Field Mice**: Did you not know? They could fly you there before lunch.  
_Dorothy turns the Cap over and hands it to you. You are the one who reads the signs, and this seems to be a sign._

> - The cottage had a good deal of charm. → Here charm means a pleasing, attractive quality. The magic-spell meaning is the one in the Cap sentence.
> - Her charm made everyone smile. → Here charm means a pleasing, winning quality of a person. The Cap sentence is the magic one.
> _For grown-ups: Told two meanings of charm apart in context._

    - He flies on in silence. Every so often you see him look up at the sky, as if it had changed.
- **Say nothing. Listen to the wind.**
    - You say nothing. The King flies on, and the wind takes his story away behind you, over the fields.

**The Scarecrow**: Now that is how to travel. No ditches at all.  
_You look up at the Monkeys, now small as birds. From up there the whole road looked like a map._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-2, ask): maps show the land from above  
> _A map shows the land as if seen from straight above. Why is that view so useful?_  
> - ✅ You can see the whole layout and the distances at once → Yes. From above you see where everything is, and how far apart. That is what a map is for.
> - It makes things look bigger → Things look smaller from above, not bigger. The view lets you see the whole layout at once.
> - It hides the roads → The opposite. From above, roads, rivers and walls all show up clearly.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that maps give a view from above, showing layout and distances._

_He opens his big box and locks the green spectacles on you all again, seven pairs in all. The gold bands click shut behind your ears._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): doubling and equal groups  
> _There are seven pairs of spectacles, and each is held on by two gold bands. How many gold bands is that?_  
> - ✅ 14 → Yes. Seven pairs with two bands each is 7 × 2 = 14. That is double seven.
> - 9 → That adds 7 and 2. Seven pairs, two bands in each pair: 7 × 2 = 14.
> - 12 → Close. Six pairs would be 12. There are seven pairs: 7 × 2 = 14.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups: 7 pairs × 2 bands = 14._

### Glossary

- **charm**: A magic spell or object. It can also mean a pleasing quality.
- **oral history**: The past, kept alive by telling it aloud from one generation to the next.

## A15-14. The Humbug

- `a15-14-s1`: Go into the Throne Room together, all of you. · _Stand together in the middle of the room, and keep your eyes open._
- `a15-14-s2`: Hear the little man out. · _Stand still and let him talk. He is more frightened than you are._
- `a15-14-s3`: Decide whether to keep his secret. · _He is asking you, of all of them. Answer him._

#### `a15-14-voice`

_Oz keeps you waiting four days. On the fifth, the Scarecrow sends word that the Winged Monkeys might be asked their opinion._  
_You are let in at once, all of you together._  
_There is no Head, no Lady, no Beast and no Ball of Fire: only the empty throne, and a hush._  
**Oz**: Oz, the Great and Terrible, is listening. Why have you come?  
_The voice comes from near the top of the great dome. It seems to come from everywhere at once._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound reflects off hard curved walls  
> _Why does a voice in a big round hall seem to come from everywhere at once?_  
> - ✅ Sound bounces off the curved walls and reaches you from many directions → Yes. Sound waves reflect off hard surfaces, and a dome sends them in every direction. A ventriloquist can use that, too.
> - Sound is louder in green rooms → Colour makes no difference to sound. It is the hard curved walls bouncing the sound around.
> - The voice is really in your head → You are hearing it with your ears. The sound bounces off the dome and arrives from every direction.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound bounces off hard curved walls, so a voice can seem to come from everywhere._

**Dorothy**: We have come for what you promised us. The Wicked Witch is gone.  
**Oz**: Is she really gone? Goodness.  
**Oz**: Melted. Well… give me a day.  
**Oz**: I shall need a little time to think it over.  
**The Tin Woodman**: You have had weeks to think!  
**The Scarecrow**: Not one more day. Not one.  
**The Cowardly Lion**: I think… I think I should roar now.  

**Choices**

- **Let go of your Nubbin.**

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): turning point in a story  
> _What changes at this turning point?_  
> - ✅ The friends find out that Oz is only a man, not a great Wizard → Yes. A turning point is where the story swings a new way. Everything after this scene is different.
> - Toto learns to bark → Toto has barked all along. The turning point is that the friends discover who Oz really is.
> - The Lion gets his courage → That comes later, and in a very different way. This moment is where they discover Oz is only a man.
> _For grown-ups: Named the turning point of a scene and what it changes._

**Oz**: Yes. Humbug is quite the right word for it.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): where Omaha is  
> _Omaha is a city in the state of Nebraska, just north of Kansas. If Dorothy walked from Kansas to Omaha, which way would she go?_  
> - ✅ North → Yes. Nebraska lies directly north of Kansas. Omaha stands on the Missouri River, on the border with Iowa.
> - South → South would take her towards Texas. Nebraska is north of Kansas.
> - West → West would take her towards Colorado. Omaha is to the north.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Omaha is in Nebraska, north of Kansas._

**Oz**: Then I went up in balloons at the circus, to draw the crowds. One day the ropes got twisted, and I could not come down.  
**Oz**: I came down out of the clouds, and the people thought I was a Wizard. It was green, so I called it the Emerald City.  
**Oz**: Then I had to make the name come true, so I gave everybody green spectacles, locked on. It was only a small lie, to begin with.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): how a small fib can grow  
> _Oz says a small lie grew until everyone wore locked spectacles. How can a small untruth grow?_  
> - You need more lies to cover the first one → That’s a fair answer, and it is exactly what happened to me. One fib wanted a second to keep it company.
> - People start to rely on it → That’s a fair answer. Once everyone was comfortable, nobody wanted the truth to spoil it, least of all me.
> - It cannot grow: a small lie stays small → That’s a fair answer, and I wish it were true. Sometimes it does stay small. Mine did not.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how one small lie can lead to bigger ones._

> _Which sort of secret should you always tell a trusted grown-up about?_  
> - ✅ One that makes you feel scared, unsafe or uncomfortable → Yes. A surprise party is a happy secret. A secret that frightens you or makes your tummy flip is one to share with a grown-up you trust. So is any secret a grown-up asks you to keep from other grown-ups, like this one.
> - A surprise birthday party → A surprise party is a happy secret, and fun to keep until the day. The ones to tell are those that make you feel scared or unsafe.
> - Where a friend hid a present → That is a harmless secret, and kind to keep. The ones to tell a grown-up are secrets that make you feel scared or unsafe.
> _For grown-ups: Learned to tell happy secrets from secrets that should be shared with a trusted adult._

## A15-15. The Magic Art

- `a15-15-s1`: Help Oz mix the Scarecrow’s brains. · _Measure out the bran, then hand Oz the pins and needles, points away from you._
- `a15-15-s2`: Help Oz make the Woodman’s heart. · _Hold the silk heart steady while Oz stuffs it with sawdust._
- `a15-15-s3`: Pour out the Lion’s courage. · _Hold the green dish while Oz pours from the square green bottle, then pass it to the Lion._

#### `a15-15-brains`

_In the morning the Scarecrow goes in first. Oz asks for an assistant, and looks at you._  
**Oz**: Sit there, if you please. I shall have to take your head off, only for a minute.  
**Oz**: Brains go in at the top.  
**The Scarecrow**: Take it off by all means. I hardly use it.  
_Oz unpins the Scarecrow’s head and takes out the straw. Then he fetches a sack of bran from the back room._  
**Oz**: Now. I need exactly one cup of bran.  
**Oz**: This scoop holds a quarter of a cup. Fill it for me, will you?  
_You fill the quarter-cup scoop three times and tip it in._  
_Then you hand him pins and needles, a pinch at a time, points away from you._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions of a cup  
> _You have tipped in three scoops, and each scoop is 1/4 of a cup._  
> _What fraction of a cup is that, and how many more scoops make a full cup?_  
> - ✅ 3/4 of a cup, and one more scoop → Quite right. Three quarters, and one more quarter makes four quarters, which is one whole cup.
> - 3/3 of a cup, and no more → Not quite. The pieces are quarters, so the bottom number is 4: three scoops is 3/4. It takes one more to make the whole.
> - 1/3 of a cup, and two more scoops → Look at the scoop: it holds a quarter, so there are four in a cup. Three scoops is 3/4, and one more makes a whole.
> _For grown-ups: Used unit fractions: three quarter-cups make 3/4 of a cup, and one more makes a whole._

_He stirs them in with a wooden spoon. One more scoop makes the full cup._  

**Choices**

- **Suggest a few more pins, to be safe.**
    - **Oz**: More pins. Yes.
    - **Oz**: He will be very sharp. Sharp is good in a Scarecrow; it keeps the crows thoughtful.
- **Ask what the spoon is for.**
    - **Oz**: For stirring. And for looking busy.
    - **Oz**: Most of magic is looking busy, my dear.
- **Watch your Nubbin, who is eating the bran.**
    - Your Nubbin eats a mouthful of bran, makes a face, and does not try any more brains.

**The Scarecrow**: I feel wise. Very wise.

_A real human brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms. It does the thinking, remembering and feeling, and runs your body too._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): the brain and what protects it  
> _A real brain is soft. What protects it?_  
> - ✅ The skull → Yes. The skull is a hard case of bone around the brain, and the soft tissue and fluid inside cushion it too. That is why helmets matter.
> - Your hair → Hair keeps your head warm, but it is the skull, the bone, that protects the brain.
> - Your ears → Ears are for hearing. The skull, a hard bone case, protects the brain.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the skull protects the brain, which does our thinking and runs the body._

> Check: `edu:count:pulse:15s`
> _For grown-ups: Found a pulse and counted beats in 15 seconds to estimate a heart rate._

> _When we say someone has a good heart, what do we mean?_

> - That their heart beats well → That would be a doctor’s meaning. As a figure of speech, a good heart means kindness.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _Which sentence best states the theme of what Oz tells the Lion?_  
> - ✅ Courage is going on despite fear, not feeling no fear → Exactly. The theme is the idea beneath the story: the Lion has been brave all along, because he went on while frightened.
> - Lions are always brave → If that were so, this Lion would not be here asking. The idea is that courage is going on despite fear.
> - Green drinks are magic → The drink is only green. The idea Oz gives him is the real gift: courage is going on despite fear.
> _For grown-ups: Stated the theme of a speech: courage is acting despite fear._

> **Lesson** (art, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry  
> _The base of the bottle is a square. How many lines of symmetry does a square have?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. Two run through the middles of opposite sides, and two run corner to corner. Fold a square along any of them and the halves match.
> - 2 → A rectangle that is not a square has two. A square has two more, running corner to corner: four in all.
> - 1 → Try folding a square paper: you can fold it four different ways so that the halves match.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a square has four lines of symmetry._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): real versus pretend help  
> _Your friends feel better, but the brains were bran, the heart was sawdust and the courage was green water._  
> _Does it matter that the magic was not real?_  
> - Yes: they were fooled → That’s a fair answer. Being told something that is not true, even kindly, is a kind of trick. And a trick can break.
> - No: it helped them see what they had → That’s a fair answer. Perhaps the bran only gave them permission to notice what they already could do.
> - Both can be true → That’s a fair answer. A kind trick can help and still be a trick. Oz himself is not sure, and neither is your Nubbin.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether it matters that a comforting gift was not real._

**Oz**: Dorothy will be harder. You cannot fill a girl’s head with bran and tell her she is in Kansas.  

### Glossary

- **bran**: The rough outer layer of grain, which is sifted out when flour is made.
- **solder**: To join pieces of metal using a melted metal that sets hard.

- `a15-16-s1`: Help sew the great green balloon. · _Hold the silk strips straight while Dorothy sews the seams._

#### `a15-16-sew`

_On the third day Oz sends for Dorothy._  
_He has thought of a way, he says: he came here in a balloon, and he will leave in one._  
**Oz**: And I will come too. I have had enough of humbugging.  
**Oz**: A circus would suit me better; at least everyone knows the clown is a clown.  
**Dorothy**: Oh! Shall we really go home?  
**Oz**: We shall make a balloon of silk and fill it with hot air. Hot air I have plenty of.  
**Oz**: It is the silk we need.  
_So for three days you sit with Dorothy and sew strips of green silk together, while Oz cuts them out._  
_The finished balloon will be more than twenty feet long, which is about six metres._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): measurement and division  
> _The balloon is about 6 metres long, and each silk strip is 2 metres long. How many strips laid end to end make 6 m?_  
> - ✅ 3 → Yes. 6 ÷ 2 = 3, because 3 × 2 = 6. Three strips, end to end.
> - 4 → Check it: 4 strips would be 4 × 2 = 8 m. Three strips make 6 m.
> - 12 → That multiplies 6 and 2. Here we ask how many twos fit into six: 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a length in metres into equal strips: 6 ÷ 2 = 3._

_You hold the strips straight while Dorothy sews. Your Nubbin sits in the pile of offcuts like an egg in a green nest._  
**Oz**: Then a coat of glue inside, to keep the air in. And a big clothes-basket to sit in.

    - **Dorothy**: Aunt Em taught me. Small and even, she says.
    - **Dorothy**: Small and even, and do not pull.
- **Test the clothes-basket with your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin climbs in, turns round three times, and goes to sleep. The basket seems to work.
- **Ask Oz if he has ever steered one.**
    - **Oz**: Steered? My dear, nobody steers a balloon.
    - **Oz**: You go where the wind likes. That is how I got here.

_Along its length run the seams, where each strip is stitched to the next._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: seam  
> _In which sentence does seam mean the join between two pieces of cloth?_  
> - ✅ Dorothy checked every seam for gaps in the silk. → Yes. In sewing, a seam is the line where two pieces of cloth are stitched together.
> - A seam of coal ran through the hill. → That is another meaning: a long layer of coal or rock. The silk sentence is about stitching.
> _For grown-ups: Told two meanings of seam apart and chose the sewing one._

_Dorothy runs her hand along them, finds a place where the stitches pull, and sews it again._  

#### `a15-16-launch`

_Word goes round the City that the Great Oz is going up into the clouds. Everybody comes to see._  
_The Woodman has built a fire. Oz holds the bottom of the balloon over it, and the hot air fills it out._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): how a hot-air balloon flies  
> _Why does the balloon fill out and rise when the air inside is heated?_  
> - ✅ Hot air is lighter than the cooler air around it, so the balloon is pushed up → Yes. Heating the air makes it spread out, so a balloonful weighs less than the same amount of cool air outside. The first people to fly this way did so in France, in 1783.
> - The fire pulls the balloon up → Fire does not pull. It heats the air, and hot air is lighter than the cooler air outside, so the balloon floats up.
> - The silk is magic → The silk is only silk. It is the hot air inside, lighter than the cool air outside, that lifts the balloon.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heated air is lighter than cool air, so a hot-air balloon rises._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): a near miss and disappointment  
> _Dorothy missed the balloon by a few steps. How do you feel when you narrowly miss something you wanted?_  
> _What helps?_  
> - Angry at myself → That’s a fair answer. Anger at ourselves is common. It helps to remember that Toto was loose and nobody could have planned for a kitten.
> - Sad, and then ready to try again → That’s a fair answer. Letting yourself be sad first often makes it easier to find a new plan.
> - I want someone to comfort me → That’s a fair answer. Asking for comfort is wise, and a friend beside Dorothy right now would help.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the feelings that follow a near miss and what helps._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): what makes a desert  
> _A desert gets less than about 250 millimetres of rain a year. Which of these places is a desert?_  
> - ✅ A place with 100 mm of rain a year → Yes. Deserts are defined by how little rain they get, not by heat. Parts of Antarctica are deserts too.
> - A place with 900 mm of rain a year → That is plenty of rain, enough for woods and fields. A desert gets under about 250 mm a year.
> - A place with 1,500 mm of rain a year → That is a very wet place, even a rainforest. A desert gets under about 250 mm a year.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a desert is defined as a place with under about 250 mm of rain a year._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): add and subtract word problem  
> _Each owner may call the Monkeys three times, and Dorothy has used two._  
> _How many calls has Dorothy left, and how many has the Cap been used for in all, counting the Witch’s two?_  
> - ✅ 1 left, 4 in all → Yes. 3 − 2 = 1 call left for Dorothy, and 2 + 2 = 4 calls used by the two owners together.
> - 2 left, 5 in all → Check it: Dorothy has used two of her three, so 3 − 2 = 1 is left. The total used is 2 + 2 = 4.
> - 1 left, 5 in all → One left is right. But the Witch used two and Dorothy two, so 2 + 2 = 4 in all.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-part problem: 3 − 2 = 1 call left; 2 + 2 = 4 calls used in total._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): what tree roots do  
> _Real trees cannot grab, but their roots do two important jobs. What are they?_  
> - ✅ Hold the tree in the ground and take in water → Yes. Roots anchor a tree against wind and soak up water and minerals from the soil. Without them a tree could not stand or drink.
> - Make leaves and flowers → Leaves and flowers grow higher up. Roots anchor the tree and take in water and minerals.
> - Catch passing travellers → Not in real life! Roots anchor the tree and take in water and minerals.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the two jobs of roots: anchoring the tree and taking in water._

**The Cowardly Lion**: Only the first row fights, I think. They are guarding the wood.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: ruffled  
> _Ruffled can mean untidy, or upset. Which fits the Scarecrow here?_  
> - ✅ Both: his straw is untidy and he is cross → Yes. Authors love a word that does two jobs. His straw sticks out and his feelings are rumpled.
> - Neither: he is calm → Look at him: straw sticking out and a cross face. He is untidy and upset.
> - Only untidy → Untidy is right, but he has been flung about by trees and is not happy. Upset is part of it too.
> _For grown-ups: Understood that ruffled can mean untidy and upset, and saw it do both jobs._

_Behind you the first row shakes out its branches and settles down, looking very pleased with itself._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a rectangle  
> _One section of the wall is 12 m long and 3 m high. What is its area?_  
> - ✅ 36 square metres → Yes. Area is length × height: 12 × 3 = 36 square metres. That is 36 squares, each one metre by one metre.
> - 15 square metres → That adds 12 and 3. Area multiplies length by height: 12 × 3 = 36.
> - 30 square metres → Close. Try it in steps: 10 × 3 = 30, then 2 × 3 = 6, and together that is 36.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a rectangle by multiplying: 12 × 3 = 36 m²._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): where the word china comes from  
> _In English, fine plates and cups are called china. Why?_  
> - ✅ Porcelain was first made in China, long ago → Yes. Potters in China perfected porcelain, and fine dishes travelled the world under the name of their country.
> - Because they ring like a chime when tapped → Fine china does ring when you tap it, but that is not the reason. The name comes from China, where porcelain was first made.
> - Because they are white as chalk → They are often white, but the name comes from the country, China, where porcelain was first made.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that china dishes are named for China, where porcelain was first made._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): baking clay: changes that cannot be reversed  
> _China is made by baking soft clay in a very hot oven called a kiln, until it goes hard._  
> _Can baked china be turned back into soft clay?_  
> - ✅ No, baking is a change that cannot be undone → Yes. Some changes, like melting ice, can be reversed. Baking clay cannot. Once it has set hard, it stays hard.
> - Yes, just add water → Unbaked clay goes soft again with water, but baked china does not. The change in the oven is permanent.
> - Yes, if you wait long enough → Waiting does not help. The change in the kiln is permanent: baked clay does not go soft again.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that baking clay is a change that cannot be reversed._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe versus well  
> _Is keeping something safe the same as keeping it well? Is it kind to keep what you love safe if it can no longer be itself?_  
> - Safe is not the same as well → That’s a fair answer. A thing can be perfectly safe and still be unhappy, like a bird in a cage with plenty of seed.
> - Safe comes first → That’s a fair answer. Staying alive matters most of all. But notice that the Princess says pretty is all they would be.
> - It depends on the thing and on what it wants → That’s a fair answer. The wisest answer starts by asking what the lamb, and the Nubbin, really want.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether keeping something safe is the same as keeping it well._

> _A plain rectangle that is not a square has how many lines of symmetry?_  
> - ✅ 2 → Yes. One down the middle and one across the middle. A square has four, but a rectangle’s diagonals do not work.
> - 4 → Four is for a square. A rectangle that is longer than it is wide has just two.
> - 1 → Try folding paper: you can fold a rectangle in half two different ways so the halves match.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): spiders have eight legs; insects have six  
> _The Tiger says the spider has eight legs. Which of these animals also has eight legs?_  
> - ✅ Another spider → Yes. All spiders have eight legs and two body parts. Insects, like beetles, have six legs and three body parts, so a spider is not an insect.
> - A beetle → A beetle is an insect, with six legs. Spiders have eight.
> - A mouse → A mouse has four legs. Spiders have eight.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that spiders have eight legs and are not insects._

**The Tiger**: It creeps through the forest and hunts us, one by one. None of us is safe.

- **Pick up your Nubbin.**
    - You pick up your Nubbin. Its heart is going fast, and so is yours.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fair ways to choose a leader  
> _Which way of choosing a leader is the fairest?_  
> - ✅ Everyone gets a vote → Yes. When everyone gets an equal say, the leader answers to the group. That is what voting is for.
> - The biggest animal decides → Size is a poor reason. The biggest animal might be the least kind. A fair choice gives everyone a say.
> - The first one to arrive → Being first is luck, not fairness. A fair way gives everyone an equal say.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about fair ways to choose a leader._

**Dorothy**: He was so frightened of the Kalidahs. He was nearly frightened of a mouse.  
**The Scarecrow**: He drank his courage. I saw it.  
**The Scarecrow**: It was green.  
**The Tin Woodman**: I do not think it was ever in the dish. I think it was in him all along.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): respecting a friend’s wish to face something alone  
> _The Lion asked everyone to stay behind, and went alone._  
> _When is it right to let a friend face something alone, and when should you go too?_  
> - Respect their wish, but wait close by → That’s a fair answer. It is the one we chose: he asked, so we waited, and we stayed close.
> - Go with them anyway → That’s a fair answer. A friend beside you can be a comfort. But some tasks only the one person can do, and they may need to do it alone.
> - It depends how dangerous it is → That’s a fair answer, and a careful one. The bigger the danger, the more you must weigh their wish against their safety.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to respect a friend’s wish to go alone and when to go along._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _The Lion left at 9 o’clock in the evening and came back at 6 the next morning. How long was he away?_  
> - ✅ 9 hours → Yes. From 9 at night to midnight is 3 hours, and midnight to 6 is 6 more, so 9 hours in all.
> - 3 hours → That is only as far as midnight. Add the 6 hours from midnight to 6 in the morning: 3 + 6 = 9.
> - 15 hours → That is too long. Split it at midnight: 3 hours, then 6 more, makes 9.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval across midnight: 9 pm to 6 am is 9 hours._

> - Forests are dark → So they are, but it is only the setting. The theme is about courage.

## A15-19. The Hammer-Heads

- `a15-19-s1`: Climb the rocky hill towards the south. · _Follow the Scarecrow up the rocks, and stop when a voice tells you to._
- `a15-19-s2`: Read the charm with Dorothy for her third and last call. · _Stand by Dorothy and read the words inside the Cap with her._

#### `a15-19-hill`

_Past the forest a steep hill rises, covered from top to bottom with great pieces of rock._  
**The Scarecrow**: Rocks. A great many rocks.  
**The Scarecrow**: Well, up we go.  
_He leads the way. You are halfway up the first rocks when a rough voice calls out._  
**A Hammer-Head**: Stop there! Our hill!  
**A Hammer-Head**: Nobody goes over our hill!  
_From behind a rock comes a very odd man with no arms at all, and a big flat head on a neck that folds up like a concertina._  
**The Scarecrow**: Terribly sorry, but we have to get over. We are on our way south, to the Quadlings.  
_Quick as lightning, the man’s head shoots forward on its stretching neck, and the flat top of it hits the Scarecrow in the middle._  
_The Scarecrow goes tumbling, head over heels, all the way down the hill._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): forces and motion on a slope  
> _The Scarecrow rolled all the way down the hill. Which hill would send a ball rolling faster: a steep one, or a gentle one?_  
> - ✅ A steep one → Yes. Gravity pulls things down, and on a steeper slope more of that pull goes into rolling, so things speed up faster.
> - A gentle one → A gentle slope slows things down, since less of gravity’s pull goes into the roll. The steeper the hill, the faster the ball.
> - They are the same → Try it with a ball and a book propped at two angles. The steeper slope gives a faster roll.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a ball rolls faster down a steeper slope, because gravity pulls it down._

_From behind every rock a hundred more Hammer-Heads pop up, laughing a hard, rough laugh. They are a fairy-tale people, and very proud of their hill._  

**Choices**

- **Run down and pick up the Scarecrow.**
    - You find him at the bottom, upside down in a bush.
    - **The Scarecrow**: I have brains now, and I can tell you I did not see that coming.
- **Duck behind a rock with your Nubbin.**
    - You duck behind a rock. A head on a long neck comes round the side, looks at your Nubbin, and goes back again.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): first aid for a knock to the head or face  
> _The Lion has taken a knock on the nose. What is the right thing to do after a knock on the head or face?_  
> - ✅ Rest, hold a wrapped cool pack on it, and tell a grown-up → Yes. Rest and a cool pack help the swelling, and a grown-up should always know about a knock to the head or face, in case it needs checking.
> - Carry on playing as if nothing happened → Carrying on could make things worse. Rest, a cool pack, and tell a grown-up.
> - Rub it hard → Rubbing can hurt more. A wrapped cool pack, rest, and a grown-up are better.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what to do after a knock to the head or face: rest, a wrapped cool pack, tell a grown-up._


#### `a15-19-call`

**Dorothy**: It is no good fighting people who shoot their heads out. What shall we do?  
**The Tin Woodman**: Call the Winged Monkeys. You have one call left.  
**Dorothy**: It is the last one. After this, the Cap will not do anything for me ever again.  
**The Scarecrow**: Then use it on something worth it. This seems worth it.  
**The Scarecrow**: My middle hurts.  
_Dorothy puts on the Golden Cap and says the words. You read them out with her, very clearly, since it is the last time._  
_You tap the beat of the words as you read them, one-two-three-four, the way a band counts in a tune._  

> **Lesson** (music, RL.2.4, ask): beats in a bar  
> _Music is counted in groups of beats called bars. In 4/4 time, how many beats are in each bar?_  
> - ✅ Four → Yes. The top number says how many beats are in a bar, so 4/4 means four. A waltz is 3/4, so it has three.
> - Three → Three beats is a waltz, written 3/4. In 4/4 there are four beats in each bar.
> - Two → Two beats a bar is a march, often written 2/4. In 4/4 there are four.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that 4/4 time has four beats in each bar._

_The Monkeys come down as fast as ever, the whole band, and line up in front of her._  
**The King of the Winged Monkeys**: Third call. The last.  
**The King of the Winged Monkeys**: What is it to be?  
**Dorothy**: Carry us over the hill to the country of the Quadlings.  
**The King of the Winged Monkeys**: Up you come, then.  

**Choices**

- **Thank the Monkey King.**
    - **The King of the Winged Monkeys**: Thank us? Hm.
    - **The King of the Winged Monkeys**: Nobody does that. The Cap does not say anything about thanks.
- **Watch the Monkey King as he lifts you.**
    - He lifts you as gently as before. His wings beat hard and slow, and he looks, you think, very tired.

#### `a15-19-call-done`

_The Monkeys carry you all over the hill. The Hammer-Heads shoot their heads high in the air, and cannot reach._  
_Your Nubbin looks down at them, and they look up at your Nubbin, and that is the end of the Hammer-Heads._  
_The Monkey King flew all this way for a Cap that never once said thank you. His wings are slow, and his arms hang low._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): thanking someone who is made to help  
> _The Monkeys help only because the Cap makes them. Should we thank someone who is made to help us?_  
> - Yes: thanks always matter → That’s a fair answer. Thanks cost nothing, and mean the most to those who are rarely given them.
> - No: they have no choice → That’s a fair answer. Yet being thanked reminds a person that they are seen as a person, not as a tool.
> - Yes, and also ask what they want → That’s a fair answer, and a wise one. Thanks is a start. Asking is the next step.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether to thank someone who has no choice but to help._

_The Monkeys set you down in the country of the Quadlings, and fly away. The King looks back once from the sky._  
_Everything here is red: the fences, the houses, the bridges, the Quadlings’ clothes._  
_The Quadlings are small and cheerful. They give Dorothy something to eat, and she thanks them._  
**Dorothy**: Please, which way is Glinda’s castle?  
_A Quadling points. Far down the road a castle is shining in the sun._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): the lands of Oz and the compass  
> _The Munchkins live in the east and the Winkies in the west. Where do the red-clad Quadlings live?_  
> - ✅ In the south → Yes. East is blue, west is yellow, south is red, with the Emerald City in the middle. A map of Oz is a colour map and a compass in one.
> - In the north → You have come south from the Emerald City, and here is red. The Quadlings live in the south.
> - In the middle → The middle is the green Emerald City. The Quadlings are in the south.
> _For grown-ups: Matched a colour-coded land to its compass direction: the Quadlings live in the south._


### Glossary

- **Quadling**: One of the small, cheerful people of the southern land of Oz, who wear red.
- **cannon-ball**: A heavy iron ball once fired from a cannon.

## A15-20. Glinda

- `a15-20-s1`: Go before Glinda, the Good Witch of the South. · _Walk up to Glinda’s throne with Dorothy and the others, and listen._
- `a15-20-s2`: Hear how Glinda will spend the Cap’s calls, and say your goodbyes. · _Stand with your friends while Glinda tells each of them where they will go._
- `a15-20-s3`: Say goodbye to Dorothy. · _Stay by Dorothy and Toto until she is ready to go._

#### `a15-20-glinda`

_At the castle gate stand three girls in handsome red uniforms. They lead you all into a great room._  
_Glinda sits on a red throne. She is beautiful and young-looking, with rich red hair, and her eyes are blue and kind._  
**Glinda**: Well, my dear. What is it you need?  
**Dorothy**: I want to go home to Kansas. Aunt Em will be sure I am lost for good by now.  
**Glinda**: There is a way, my dear, and I shall tell you. But I shall want the Golden Cap in return.  
**Dorothy**: Gladly. It is no use to me now.  
**Dorothy**: I have used all three calls.  
**Glinda**: The silver shoes will carry you over the desert. You could have gone home the day you came, if you had only known what they do.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): properties of silver  
> _Real silver is a shiny metal. It carries electricity better than any other metal._  
> _It also tarnishes: left in the air, it slowly goes dark, because it reacts with sulphur gases there. That is why people polish it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that silver is a shiny metal that is the best conductor of electricity and tarnishes in air._

**Dorothy**: The very first day?  
**The Scarecrow**: But then I would never have got my brains! I would have spent my whole life up a pole in a cornfield.  
**The Tin Woodman**: And I would still be standing in that clearing with my axe in the air.  
**The Cowardly Lion**: And I would still be roaring at little dogs, and crying about it afterwards.  
_Dorothy looks down at the silver shoes for a long time. They have been on her feet the whole way._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): the journey versus the destination  
> _Dorothy could have gone home on the first day, but she would have missed her friends and everything she learned._  
> _Is the journey worth more than the arrival?_  
> - Yes: the journey made her who she is → That’s a fair answer. What we become on the road is often worth more than the place we reach.
> - No: home matters most, and it was a long detour → That’s a fair answer. Dorothy herself longs for home above all. A detour can be hard, and lonely too.
> - Both together → That’s a fair answer. She needed to go on the journey to value home, and the friends to enjoy it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a journey can be worth more than its destination._


**Choices**

- **Look at the shoes.**
    - They are dusty from the road and scuffed at the toes. They do not look like much.
- **Ask Dorothy if she minds.**
    - **Dorothy**: No. I am glad I did not know.
    - **Dorothy**: I would have gone straight home, and none of them would have anything.

#### `a15-20-glinda-done`

**Glinda**: Knock the heels together three times and tell them where you want to go. They will take you there in three steps.  
_Three steps, over a desert. You wonder how far each step must be._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division word problem  
> _Suppose the desert is 600 km wide and the shoes cross it in three equal steps. How long is each step?_  
> - ✅ 200 km → Yes. 600 ÷ 3 = 200, because 3 × 200 = 600. A very long stride.
> - 300 km → That would be two steps: 2 × 300 = 600. Three equal steps: 600 ÷ 3 = 200 km.
> - 180 km → Check by multiplying: 3 × 180 = 540, which is short. 3 × 200 = 600, so each step is 200 km.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a distance into three equal steps: 600 ÷ 3 = 200 km._

_Dorothy looks at her heels as if she were meeting them for the first time._  

#### `a15-20-goodbye`

**Glinda**: Now. The Golden Cap, and its three calls.  
**Glinda**: Let me see.  
**Glinda**: Scarecrow: the Monkeys will carry you back to the Emerald City, to rule. The people will be lucky in you.  
**The Scarecrow**: Thank you. I have just thought of eleven new laws.  
**The Scarecrow**: I shall begin with those.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness and rules  
> _The Scarecrow has thought of eleven new laws. What makes a law fair?_  
> - ✅ It applies to everyone, including the ruler → Yes. A law that rulers can ignore is not fair. Fairness means the same rules for everybody.
> - It only applies to people the ruler dislikes → That is the opposite of fair. A fair law is one that applies to everyone alike.
> - It never changes, whatever happens → Good laws can be changed when they turn out to be wrong. What makes them fair is that they apply to everyone alike.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes a law fair: it applies to everyone alike._

**Glinda**: Woodman: they will carry you to the land of the Winkies, who want you for their ruler.  
**The Tin Woodman**: I shall rule them kindly. I have the heart for it now.  
**Glinda**: Lion: they will carry you over the Hammer-Heads to your forest, to be King of the Beasts.  
**The Cowardly Lion**: Thank you. I should not care to meet the Hammer-Heads again, even as a King.  
**Glinda**: And then I shall give the Cap to the King of the Monkeys, so that he and his band are free for ever.  
_Dorothy hugs each of them in turn, and cries, and kisses the Lion on his great nose._  

**Choices**

- **Oil the Woodman’s jaw. He is crying.**
    - The Woodman is crying, of course. You oil his jaw one last time, while the Scarecrow holds his hat, as he did once before.
    - **The Tin Woodman**: Keep the can. I mean it.
    - **The Tin Woodman**: You have been the best oil-can-carrier in all of Oz.
- **Shake the Scarecrow’s hand.**
    - **The Scarecrow**: If you ever need a thought, come to the Emerald City. I have plenty now.
    - **The Scarecrow**: I can spare one.
- **Rest your hand on the Lion’s mane.**
    - **The Cowardly Lion**: Goodbye, Keeper. Goodbye, little one.
    - **The Cowardly Lion**: You sat by me first. I shall not forget it.

#### `a15-20-goodbye-done`

_Glinda’s girls bring you a present: a pair of silver shoes, just your size, shining._  
_You put them on, and knock your heels together three times._  
_Nothing happens at all._  
**Glinda**: They are only shoes, dear. Most shoes are.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): humour: understatement  
> _Why is Glinda’s remark funny?_  
> - ✅ She states the obvious in a calm, dry way → Exactly. Saying something plainly obvious, with a straight face, is called understatement. It is a favourite trick of dry humour.
> - She says something that is not true → Quite the opposite. What she says is perfectly true. That is the joke.
> - She shouts it → She is perfectly calm. The humour is in how plain and dry she is.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised understatement as the source of a dry joke._


#### `a15-20-farewell`

_Dorothy turns to you last. Toto is in her arms, and your Nubbin is sitting on your feet._  
_She looks at you as if she is fixing you in her memory, the way you fix a house you are leaving._  
_Glinda’s girls have gone quiet. Even Toto keeps still._  
**Dorothy**: You came with me all the way from the grey. And I still do not know where you are from.  
**Dorothy**: I shall tell Aunt Em about you. She will not believe it.  
**Dorothy**: She believes only what she can sweep.  
**Dorothy**: Is it grey, where you live?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what is good about an ordinary home  
> _Dorothy asks if your home is grey. What is good about a plain, ordinary home?_  
> - The people who live there → That’s a fair answer. It is what Aunt Em and Uncle Henry taught me, even if I did not know it then.
> - It is the one you know → That’s a fair answer. Knowing every creak and corner is a comfort. It is part of what makes it ours.
> - Nothing: prettier homes are better → That’s a fair answer, and I wondered the same once. After the Emerald City, I am not so sure.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what is good about an ordinary home._


**Choices**

- **Tell her it is green, mostly, with a pond.**
    - **Dorothy**: Then you have your own place to go back to. Everybody ought to have one.
- **Tell her there is a grey one there, and you love her.**
    - **Dorothy**: Aunt Em is grey, and I love her better than anything. So you know already.
- **Let your Nubbin say goodbye to Toto.**
    - Your Nubbin and Toto touch noses, the way they did on the prairie. Toto sneezes, and it means what it meant then.

_Dorothy holds Toto tight and knocks the heels of the silver shoes together three times._  
**Dorothy**: Take me home, please. To Aunt Em.  
_She is gone in three great steps. The silver shoes fall from her feet in the air, and are lost in the desert for good._  
_For a moment the page shows Kansas: a new little farmhouse, grey grass, and Aunt Em running across it with her arms open._  
_Then the Monkeys come for your friends: the Scarecrow north, the Woodman west, the Lion over the hill to his forest._  
_Glinda gives the Golden Cap to the King of the Monkeys. He bows, and the band flies off without a word._  
_The page carries you home the way you came. Its last picture is the china wall, and a lamb by it, waiting to see you off._  
_The page folds shut, softly, and you are back in the Grove with the atlas on your knee._  
_A thin silver ribbon keeps the place, and it was not there this morning._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme  
> _Which sentence best sums up the theme of Dorothy’s whole story?_  
> - ✅ What you are looking for may have been with you all along → Yes. The shoes, the brains, the heart and the courage were there from the beginning. The journey helped each to notice what they already had.
> - Never leave home → Dorothy left home and found friends and herself. The theme is not about staying put, but about what we already have.
> - Shoes are magic → The shoes helped, but only at the end. The theme is about finding what we already have.
> _For grown-ups: Stated the theme of a whole story: what you seek may already be with you._


### Glossary

- **ruler**: A person who leads a country or a people and makes its laws.
- **tarnish**: To lose shine and turn dull or dark, as silver does in the air.

## A16-1. Drawing Number One

- `a16-01-s1`: Step into the desert page and find the stranger under the plane. · _Touch the little planet on the page, then walk towards the plane in the dunes._
- `a16-01-s2`: Look at the pilot’s first drawing, and say what you see. · _Sit by the pilot when he takes out his notebook at noon._

#### `a16-01-desert`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page that is almost empty: one small planet, one chair, and a sunset behind it._  
_You touch the sunset. It turns warm like sand, and then it is sand, and you are standing in it._  
_Dunes in every direction, under a sky so clean it looks scrubbed. Your Nubbin sneezes at the size of it._  
_A few dunes away, a small aeroplane sits nose-down in the sand. A pair of legs sticks out from under the engine._  
**The Pilot**: Unless you’re a mechanic, keep back. If you are one, come quickly.  
_He slides out: a man with oil to his elbows and a face that hasn’t slept._  
**The Pilot**: I’m days from anywhere. You’re the last thing I expected to see.  
**The Pilot**: Where did you come from? No, don’t tell me. I’ve stopped expecting sensible answers out here.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): what a desert is, and that the Sahara is the biggest hot desert  
> **The Pilot**: Welcome to the Sahara, by the way. It’s a desert: a place that gets very little rain.  
> **The Pilot**: Less than 25 centimetres (10 inches) in a whole year. Plenty of sand, not much to drink.  
> **The Pilot**: It’s the biggest hot desert on Earth. You’ll want a hat.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a desert gets very little rain, and that the Sahara is the biggest hot desert._


**Choices**

- **Offer to hold the spanner.**
    - **The Pilot**: Hold it, and don’t hand it over unless I ask. I have a system. It’s mostly muttering.
- **Ask if he’s hurt.**
    - **The Pilot**: Only my pride. And the engine. The engine is worse.
- **Sit down in the shade of the wing.**
    - You sit, and your Nubbin sits. After a moment the man sits too, because it seems rude not to.

#### `a16-01-desert-done`

_He slides back under the engine. Every so often a hand comes out for a tool, then disappears again._  
**The Pilot**: Sixteen litres of water, that’s all I have. I drink two a day, and I’m careful about it.  
**The Pilot**: So that’s eight days for me. But water goes faster when somebody shares it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): dividing a total by a daily amount  
> **The Pilot**: Say one more person shares it and drinks two litres a day too. How long do sixteen litres last then?  
> - ✅ Four days. → Yes. Two people use 2 + 2 = 4 litres a day, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Four days. Sharing makes the water go twice as fast.
> - Six days. → Let’s count it. Two people use 4 litres a day: 4, 8, 12, 16. That’s four days, not six.
> - Eight days. → Eight days is for one person. Two people use twice as much, so the water lasts half as long. Half of eight is four days.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 16 litres by 4 litres a day to find how many days the water lasts._

**The Pilot**: When I get this running, I’ll show you something. Nobody has ever got it right. Not once.  

#### `a16-01-drawing`

_At noon the sun is too hot to work in. The pilot crawls out, wipes his hands, and takes a battered notebook from his jacket._  
**The Pilot**: When I was six, I drew this. I showed it to every grown-up I knew.  
_It is a brown shape like a hill, or a lump, or a hat with a very low crown._  
**The Pilot**: I asked if it frightened them. They all said, “Why would anyone be frightened of a hat?”  
**The Pilot**: I still show it to everyone I meet. It’s a test. Go on. What is it?  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): two people can see the same thing differently  
> _The grown-ups saw a hat, but the boy who drew it saw something else._  
> _Why might they see different things?_  
> - Each person looks with their own ideas. → That’s a fair answer. What we already know and expect changes what we see. Looking slowly, like your Nubbin, can show you more.
> - The grown-ups guessed quickly, and the boy knew what he had drawn. → That’s a fair answer. He knew the answer, and they didn’t stop to look closely.
> - It was not a very clear drawing. → That’s a fair answer. A drawing can be hard to read. But someone who looks carefully, like your Nubbin, can find much more in it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why two people can look at the same picture and see different things._

_Your Nubbin climbs onto your knee to see. It studies the drawing for a long time, with its head on one side._  

**Choices**

- **Say it’s a hat.**
    - **The Pilot**: Of course it is. Everybody says so.
    - But your Nubbin is still looking.
- **Wait for your Nubbin.**
    - You wait, and the pilot waits. Your Nubbin is in no hurry at all.
- **Say it looks like something with something inside it.**
    - **The Pilot**: Go on…

#### `a16-01-drawing-done`

_Your Nubbin puts a paw on the lump and traces it: a long body, a tail, and in the middle a great round bulge._  
_Then it lies flat on its tummy and tries to look as full as possible._  
**The Pilot**: A snake. A snake that has swallowed an elephant whole.  
**The Pilot**: Twenty-odd years, and the first one to see it is… that.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): snakes swallow food whole; a real snake could not swallow an elephant  
> **The Pilot**: No real snake could swallow an elephant, mind you. It would never fit.  
> **The Pilot**: But real snakes do swallow their food whole. Their jaws stretch wide, because they can’t chew.  
> **The Pilot**: And one big meal can keep a snake going for weeks.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that snakes swallow their food whole and can go for weeks after a big meal._


#### `a16-01-complete`

_He turns the page. The same snake is drawn again, opened up like a map, with a very calm elephant inside._  
**The Pilot**: I had to draw the inside for them. Grown-ups always need things explained.  

> **Lesson** (art, L.2.4, notice): a cross-section shows the inside of something  
> **The Pilot**: A drawing that shows the inside of a thing is called a cross-section. It’s as if you’d cut it open.  
> **The Pilot**: Engine makers use them all the time. So do doctors, and so do people who dig wells.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a cross-section is a drawing that shows the inside of something._

**The Pilot**: Then they told me to stop drawing and learn something useful. So I learnt to fly, which is how I got here.  
_He looks at the nose-down plane and laughs, which you didn’t expect._  
**The Pilot**: Stay, if you like. It’s a big desert. There’s room for two strangers. Three, with that one.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): welcoming someone new  
> _The pilot is tired and far from home, but he invites strangers to stay. How can you make someone new feel welcome?_  
> - ✅ Say hello, include them, and ask what they would like to do. → Yes. A friendly hello and a real invitation make a stranger feel they belong.
> - Leave them alone until they speak first. → Some people are shy, so it can feel polite to wait. A small hello from you can make it much easier for them.
> - Tell them all the rules straight away. → Rules can help later. But first, people want to feel they are wanted. A smile and an invitation come first.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to make a newcomer feel welcome._


### Glossary

- **dunes**: Hills of sand made by the wind.
- **cross-section**: A picture or cut that shows what is inside something.

## A16-2. Draw Me a Sheep

- `a16-02-s1`: Spend the night by the plane, and see who comes at sunrise. · _Rest in the shade of the wing until the page’s dawn._
- `a16-02-s2`: Watch the pilot try to draw a sheep that is good enough. · _Stay by the boy while the pilot draws._
- `a16-02-s3`: Decide whether to ask for a muzzle for the sheep. · _Talk to the pilot while the boy is busy with his box._

#### `a16-02-dawn`

_That night you sleep on the sand by the wing. There are so many stars that the dark between them looks crowded._  
_At sunrise a small voice wakes the pilot. It is quite a polite voice, and quite certain._  
**The Prince**: Please. Would you draw a sheep for me?  
_A boy stands in the sand with a long scarf, a serious face, and not a speck of dust on him._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-PS3-1, notice): desert nights are cold because the dry, clear air lets heat escape  
> **The Pilot**: Brr. Chilly, this early. You’d never think the sand was baking yesterday.  
> **The Pilot**: In the Sahara it can be over 40 °C (104 °F) by day and near 10 °C (50 °F) by night.  
> **The Pilot**: Dry, clear air has no clouds to hold the heat in. When the Sun goes, the warmth just leaves.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why deserts can be very hot by day and cold at night._

**The Pilot**: A what?  
**The Prince**: A sheep. Please, if you’re not too busy.  
**The Pilot**: I can’t draw. I only ever learnt the one. Here.  
_He draws the snake with the elephant inside, from the outside, and hands it over with a shrug._  
**The Prince**: No, no. Snakes are dangerous, and elephants take up far too much room. A sheep.  
_The pilot’s mouth falls open. Your Nubbin looks delighted, as if it has found a cousin._  

**Choices**

- **Sit down to watch.**
    - You sit cross-legged in the sand. The boy sits too, opposite, and waits for his sheep as if it were a bus.
- **Say hello to the boy.**
    - **The Prince**: Hello. Can you draw sheep?
    - You say sorry, you can’t draw sheep.
    - **The Prince**: That’s all right. Nobody can, it seems.

#### `a16-02-drawings`

_The pilot draws a sheep. The boy studies it with great care._  
**The Prince**: No. That one is poorly already. Another, please.  
_The second sheep is fluffier. The boy smiles kindly, the way you smile at a mistake._  
**The Prince**: That one has horns. That’s a ram. I asked for a sheep.  
_The third is small and neat, with a tidy face._  
**The Prince**: He looks tired already. Mine has to last a long time.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): being honest and gentle together  
> _The boy told the pilot the truth about every drawing, and he never was rude. How do you tell someone you don’t like their work, kindly?_  
> - ✅ Say what you need, in a friendly way, like “I need one that will last”. → Yes. Being honest and gentle at once is a skill. The pilot gets a clear clue, and nobody feels small.
> - Say you love it, even if you don’t. → That’s kind, but then he wouldn’t get the sheep the boy wanted. Telling the truth gently helps both people.
> - Say it’s awful. → That’s honest, but it hurts, and it doesn’t help him draw a better one. We can be honest without being harsh: say what you need.
> _For grown-ups: Practised giving honest feedback in a kind way._

_The pilot glances at his engine, which is waiting, and at the sun, which is climbing. He scribbles four quick lines._  
**The Pilot**: This is a box. The sheep you want is inside.  
_It is a plain box with three holes in the side. The boy’s whole face lights up._  
**The Prince**: That’s him! That’s exactly him! Will he need a lot of grass?  
**The Pilot**: Why?  
**The Prince**: Where I live, there isn’t much room for grass. Or for anything.  
_He bends close to the holes and whispers, so as not to wake anybody._  
**The Prince**: Shh. He’s already asleep.  

#### `a16-02-drawings-done`

_Your Nubbin climbs onto the lid of the box and sits on it gently, as if it might be somebody’s bed._  
_Neither of you can see the sheep. The boy can, and that seems to be enough for everyone._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, notice): inferring: using clues to work out what the story doesn’t say  
> _The boy sees a sheep because a box with holes and a few words give him clues, and his mind fills in the rest._  
> _Readers do this too, using clues to work out what a story doesn’t say. That is called inferring._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that inferring means using clues to work out what is not said._


#### `a16-02-muzzle`

_The boy lies on his front with one eye to the holes. The pilot has gone back under his engine._  
**The Prince**: Sheep eat bushes, don’t they?  
_From under the plane comes a muffled “Mostly.”_  
**The Prince**: Good. That’s very useful.  
**The Prince**: And flowers? Do they eat flowers?  
_The voice under the plane says sheep eat whatever they find, even flowers with thorns._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, notice): sheep are herbivores; what a muzzle is for  
> **The Pilot**: Sheep are herbivores, which means they eat only plants. Mostly grass, but also leaves, shrubs and flowers.  
> **The Pilot**: A muzzle goes round an animal’s nose and mouth so it can’t nibble things it shouldn’t.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sheep are herbivores and what a muzzle is for._

_The boy goes quiet, the way people do when they have thought of something and put it away for later._  
_You look at the box, with your Nubbin on the lid. A sheep that eats everything might need a muzzle, one day._  

**Choices**

- **Ask the pilot to draw a muzzle for the sheep now, before it’s too late.**
    - **The Pilot**: A muzzle. Fair enough. Pass me the pencil.
    - He draws one on a scrap of paper: a little muzzle, a leather strap to fasten it, and a proper buckle.
    - **The Prince**: Not now. He’s asleep. He’d hate it.
    - **The Pilot**: Then I’ll keep it till you need it. Strap and all.
    - He folds the scrap into the very back of his notebook.
- **Leave it. The sheep’s asleep.**
    - You leave it. The boy has his sheep, the sheep has its box, and nobody is thinking about muzzles yet.

#### `a16-02-muzzle-done`

**The Prince**: At night I can put him in his box. Then nobody ever has to tie him up.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what animals need to be safe and happy  
> _The boy would rather not tie his sheep up at all. What helps an animal live safely and happily?_  
> - A safe place to rest, food and water, and room to move. → That’s a fair answer. Animals need safety and freedom, and people who think about what they want.
> - Keeping it tied up, so it can’t run off. → That’s a fair answer. Tying keeps an animal close, and the boy has thought about that too. But a tied-up animal can’t move or choose, so he wants another way.
> - Food, and someone who loves it. → That’s a fair answer. Food and love matter a great deal. Water, shelter and room to move matter too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what animals need to be safe and happy, including freedom._

**The Pilot**: Where’s that? Where do you live?  
_The boy doesn’t answer. He asks what the plane is instead, and is delighted to hear that it fell out of the sky._  
**The Prince**: You fell out of the sky? So did I, in a way. Which star is yours?  

#### `a16-02-complete`

_The pilot laughs and wipes his forehead with his wrist, leaving a long black streak._  
**The Pilot**: Here. One for you as well. Anyone and anything ought to have a sheep.  
_He draws another box with three holes in it, and gives it to you. Your Nubbin climbs in and peers out of a hole._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: 2 groups of 3  
> _Your box has three holes, and so does the boy’s. How many holes are there in the two boxes together?_  
> - ✅ Six. → Yes: 3 + 3 = 6. Or two groups of three: 2 × 3 = 6.
> - Five. → Close! Count again: 1, 2, 3 on one box, then 4, 5, 6 on the other. That makes six holes.
> - Three. → Three is the holes in one box. There are two boxes, so three twice: 3 + 3 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups to work out 2 × 3._

**The Prince**: Yours is asleep too. You can tell from how quiet it is.  

### Glossary

- **muzzle**: A strap or cover that goes over an animal’s nose and mouth, so it can’t nibble or eat things.

## A16-3. Asteroid B-612

- `a16-03-s1`: Listen to the boy tell where he comes from. · _Sit by the plane after dark, when the boy starts talking._
- `a16-03-s2`: Help with one morning’s weeding on the little planet. · _Pull the baobab shoots while they’re tiny. Leave anything that might be a rose._

#### `a16-03-telling`

_It takes days to get anything out of the boy. He asks questions all the time, and hardly hears yours._  
_But at night, by the cold engine, under the stars, he begins to tell._  
**The Prince**: My planet is hardly bigger than a house. You can walk all round it before your tea gets cold.  
_The pilot murmurs that it must be an asteroid, one of the little ones with only a number for a name._  
**The Pilot**: Call it B-612, then, for now. Every little asteroid needs a number.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): asteroids are small rocky worlds; real ones have numbers and names  
> **The Pilot**: Real asteroids are small, rocky worlds left over from when the planets were made.  
> **The Pilot**: Most circle the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. Each gets a number, and many get a name too, like 4 Vesta.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that asteroids are small rocky worlds and that real ones are numbered._

**The Prince**: Grown-ups love numbers. Tell them about a friend, and they ask how much he weighs.  
**The Prince**: It’s forty-one steps round. My steps are small, about half a metre each.  
_He tells it so well that the sand under you curves. The sky comes down close, and you are standing on a planet the size of a house._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): multiplying by a half-metre step and converting units  
> **The Prince**: Forty-one steps, and every step is 50 centimetres. About how far is it all the way round?  
> - ✅ About 20 metres and 50 centimetres. → Yes. 41 × 50 cm is 2,050 cm, and 100 cm make a metre. So it’s 20 metres and 50 centimetres. A tiny planet, but a long walk for a small boy.
> - 41 metres. → That would be if each step were a whole metre. Each step is half a metre, so the answer is about half of 41: 20 and a half metres.
> - 9 metres. → Let’s check. 40 steps of 50 cm is 2,000 cm, which is 20 metres. One more step makes 20 metres and 50 centimetres.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 41 × 50 cm and changed centimetres into metres._


**Choices**

- **Ask what colour his sunsets are.**
    - **The Prince**: Every colour, one after another. You’ll see those too.
- **Ask how many steps it is round.**
    - **The Prince**: That’s a grown-up question.
    - **The Prince**: Forty-one. Not counting going round the rose.
- **Watch your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin has already set off round the planet. It comes back from the other side almost at once, astonished.

#### `a16-03-weeding`

_It is morning on the little planet. There are three volcanoes, each about knee-high, and two of them are warm._  
**The Prince**: I sweep them out every day. Then they burn slow and steady, and I can heat my breakfast on them.  
**The Prince**: That one’s asleep. I sweep it anyway. You never know with volcanoes.  
_Then he kneels and shows you the soil. Tiny green shoots are coming up everywhere, and they all look much the same._  
**The Prince**: These are baobabs. They grow as big as hills, and if you let them, their roots go right through the planet.  
**The Prince**: These others might be roses. You have to tell them apart while they’re small. And then you mustn’t wait.  
_Your Nubbin grips a shoot in both paws and looks up, waiting to be told._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): dealing with small problems early  
> **The Prince**: A baobab shoot is easy to pull when it’s small, and impossible when it’s a tree. So when should I deal with a small problem?  
> - Early, while it’s small. → That’s a fair answer. Small problems are much easier to fix early, like baobab shoots.
> - Later, when I have more time. → That’s a fair answer. Later feels easier. The boy would say that small problems grow, like baobabs, and get harder to pull.
> - It depends how big the problem is. → That’s a fair answer. Some problems do fade away, and others grow. The hard part is telling which is which. Baobabs look harmless at first.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about dealing with small problems before they grow._


**Choices**

- **Pull it. It has a baobab’s fat stem.**
    - Out it comes, root and all. The boy nods once, like a teacher who has seen a sum done right.
- **Ask him which it is first.**
    - **The Prince**: Baobab. Good. Asking is better than pulling up a rose.
    - Out it comes, root and all.
- **Leave it a day, to be sure.**
    - **The Prince**: No. By tomorrow it’ll be too big to tell you anything but trouble.
    - He pulls it himself, gently and at once.

#### `a16-03-weeding-done`

_By the time the sun is properly up, the planet is clean. You have a heap of baobab shoots, and not one rose in it._  
**The Prince**: I knew a planet where a lazy man left three of them. You can’t see the ground there any more.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): real baobabs live in dry lands and store water in their trunks  
> _Real baobab trees are not nearly so dreadful._  
> _They grow in Africa, Madagascar and Australia, and store water in thick trunks to get through dry months._  
> _Some live for more than a thousand years._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real baobab trees store water in their trunks and can live for over a thousand years._


#### `a16-03-complete`

**The Prince**: Every morning, first thing. If you leave it for later, later turns into trees.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): a metaphor says one thing and means another  
> _The boy says “later turns into trees”. Later can’t really grow leaves, so this is a metaphor._  
> _A metaphor talks about one thing to explain another. Here it means a problem you put off keeps on growing._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a metaphor describes one thing by talking about another._

_The telling fades. The sand comes back under you, and the pilot is lying by the plane with his hands behind his head._  
**The Pilot**: Baobabs. All right. I’ll draw you one, so nobody forgets.  
_He draws a little planet with three enormous trees squeezing it. Your Nubbin gives the drawing a very hard look._  

### Glossary

- **asteroid**: A small rocky world that travels round the Sun.
- **baobab**: A real tree with a very thick trunk, which grows in dry lands.
- **metaphor**: Describing one thing by saying it is another, to help explain it.

## A16-4. The Sunsets

- `a16-04-s1`: Sit with the boy on his planet, and watch the sunsets. · _Sit in the chair beside his. Move when he moves._
- `a16-04-s2`: Stay with him until the last sunset is over. · _Keep sitting. Wait for the stars._

#### `a16-04-chairs`

_Another evening by the plane, and another telling. This time the boy says only one word: sunsets._  
_Then you are on his planet again. He sets out his little chair, one for you, and a flat pebble for your Nubbin._  
**The Prince**: On my planet you don’t have to wait for the sun to set. You just move your chair a few steps, and it sets again.  
_The sun goes down. He gets up, moves his chair a few steps and sits, and the sun goes down again._  
_You move your chair, and your Nubbin rolls its pebble. The sun goes down a third time, pink and then gold._  
**The Prince**: Once I watched it lots and lots of times in one day. I lost count somewhere after forty.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, do): multiplication: equal groups of steps  
> **The Prince**: Four chair-steps for every sunset. Move your chair and count along with me.  
> _Ten sunsets make ten groups of four steps. Count them in fours: 4, 8, 12, and on until you reach forty._  
> Check: `edu:count:chair-steps:40`
> _For grown-ups: Skip-counted in fours to find 10 × 4 = 40._

_He doesn’t say why. He moves his chair again, and sits, and holds his knees._  

**Choices**

- **Ask him why.**
    - **The Prince**: You only want that many when something’s wrong.
    - He doesn’t say what.
- **Say nothing, and move your chair when he does.**
    - You move when he moves. Sunset after sunset, nobody says anything, and nobody has to.
- **Let your Nubbin lean on him.**
    - Your Nubbin leaves its pebble and leans on his ankle. He doesn’t look down, but he moves his foot so it fits better.

#### `a16-04-chairs-done`

_Pink, gold, red, violet. The planet is so small you can feel it turning under the chair legs._  

> **Lesson** (art, RL.1.4, notice): warm and cool colours: touch words borrowed for colour  
> _Warm and cool are words for how things feel to touch. Artists borrow them for colours._  
> _Red, orange, pink and gold are warm colours, and blue and violet are cool. A sunset puts them side by side._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the difference between warm and cool colours, and that the names come from touch._

_After a long time he stops moving his chair, and lets the night come._  

#### `a16-04-dark`

_The stars come out over the little planet one by one, the way lamps come on in a street._  
**The Prince**: There’s a flower. On my planet. That’s why I couldn’t stop watching.  
**The Prince**: I’ll tell you about her. Not tonight.  
_The planet lets go of you. You’re back on the sand, and the pilot is turning a bolt over and over in his fingers._  
**The Pilot**: He cries sometimes, you know. I don’t know what to do about it.  
**The Pilot**: I’ve never known what to do when somebody cries. They don’t teach you that with engines.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): how to help someone who is crying  
> _The pilot doesn’t know what to do when someone is crying. What could he try?_  
> - Sit beside him and listen. → That’s a fair answer. Being close and quiet shows someone they’re not alone.
> - Ask him if he would like company or time alone. → That’s a fair answer, and a thoughtful one. Asking lets him choose.
> - Cheer him up with a joke. → That’s a fair answer. A joke can help. Some people need to feel sad first, so it may help to wait and see.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be a good friend to someone who is crying._


#### `a16-04-complete`

_The boy has fallen asleep against the plane’s wheel, with his scarf over his nose._  
_The pilot puts his jacket over him very carefully, as if he has never done it before. He probably hasn’t._  
**The Pilot**: A flower. All that, for a flower.  
**The Pilot**: Well. I suppose that’s as good a reason as any.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): working out a character’s feelings from clues  
> _Why did the boy watch so many sunsets in one day?_  
> - ✅ He was sad about his flower, and the sunsets comforted him. → Yes. He told us you only want that many when something is wrong, and he said “there’s a flower”. Those are the clues.
> - Because he loved sunsets more than anything. → He may love them. But he said you only want that many when something is wrong. That’s a clue that he was sad.
> - Because he couldn’t work out how to stop the sun. → He moved his own chair, so he was in charge of the sunsets. The better clue is what he said about something being wrong.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the story to work out why a character acted as he did._


## A16-5. The Rose

- `a16-05-s1`: See the new flower on the boy’s planet come out. · _Wait by the strange shoot until it opens at sunrise._
- `a16-05-s2`: Help the boy carry a glass globe to the rose, for her nights. · _Carry the globe round the planet to her, and don’t drop it._
- `a16-05-s3`: Be there on the morning the boy leaves his rose. · _Stay by the rose while he says goodbye._

#### `a16-05-bud`

_This time he tells it as soon as the sun is down, as if he has been saving it up._
