_His planet, long ago: one morning, a shoot nobody has seen before, not a baobab and not a weed. He watches it every day._  
_It grows a bud, an enormous one, and then it takes ages. Inside the green, something is choosing its colours very carefully._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): a flower’s life cycle: seed, shoot, bud, flower, new seeds  
> _A flower has a life cycle. It begins as a seed, grows into a shoot, then a bud, then a flower._  
> _The flower makes new seeds. When they grow, the cycle begins all over again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the life cycle of a flowering plant._

**The Prince**: She wanted to come out perfect. She wasn’t going to be rushed. Not by me. Not by the sun.  
_Then one morning, exactly at sunrise, she opens, and yawns._  
**The Rose**: Oh. I’ve only just woken up. Please excuse me. I must look a sight.  
**The Prince**: You look like nothing I’ve ever seen.  
**The Rose**: Naturally. And I came out at sunrise, which is the proper time.  
**The Rose**: I believe it’s time for breakfast. If somebody would be so kind.  
_He runs for the watering can. Your Nubbin runs too, though nobody asked it to and it has no watering can._  

**Choices**

- **Bow to her.**
    - **The Rose**: Well. At least somebody here has manners.
- **Help him fill the watering can.**
    - You hold the can and he pours. The rose watches you both as if she is marking you out of ten.
- **Look at her thorns.**
    - **The Rose**: Four. Quite enough for anything with claws. Let them come.
    - Your Nubbin takes a step back, to be polite.

#### `a16-05-bud-done`

**The Rose**: There’s a wind on this planet that comes from nowhere. A screen would be the least you could do.  
_She coughs, a small cough and possibly an invented one. He runs for the screen anyway._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a narrator’s word choice tells us about a character  
> _The narrator says her cough is “possibly an invented one”. What does that tell us about the rose?_  
> - ✅ She may be exaggerating, to get attention. → Yes. “Possibly invented” is a clue that she might be pretending a little. And the boy runs for the screen anyway, which tells us about him.
> - She is very ill. → The narrator says “possibly invented”, which hints she may not be as ill as she sounds. We can’t be sure, but look at the exact words.
> - She doesn’t like the boy at all. → She does demand a lot. But nothing here says she dislikes him. The clue is in “possibly invented”: she may be pretending to get what she wants.
> _For grown-ups: Used the narrator’s exact words as a clue to a character’s traits._


#### `a16-05-globe`

_After that she is always wanting something: water, the screen, a better angle to the sun. He brings it all, and gets sadder._  
**The Prince**: I believed every word she said. That was the trouble.  
**The Prince**: She filled the whole planet with her sweet smell every morning, and I only noticed the complaining.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): respecting what someone wants by asking them  
> _The boy guessed what the rose needed, and never asked her. How can you find out what someone really wants?_  
> - ✅ Ask them, and really listen to the answer. → Yes. Asking and listening is a way of showing respect.
> - Decide for them. You know best. → It can feel kind. But if you don’t ask, you may give them something they never wanted. Respect means listening first.
> - Wait until they complain. → Complaints can be clues. But the rose complained all the time and was still never asked. Asking calmly is clearer.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about asking people what they want, and listening, as a way of showing respect._

_He has made a glass globe to keep off the cold at night. It is as clear as water, and nearly as heavy._  
**The Prince**: Help me carry it? It’s the only thing on my planet that can break.  
_You take one side and he takes the other. Your Nubbin walks in front, looking for stones to warn you about._  

**Choices**

- **Go slowly round the volcanoes.**
    - Slowly round the warm ones, slower round the sleeping one. The globe catches the sun the whole way.
- **Ask if she asked for it.**
    - **The Prince**: Not exactly. She said she was cold. I thought a globe was the same as listening.

#### `a16-05-globe-done`

_He puts the globe over her that night. Through the glass she looks like a flower in a story, and very far away._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): properties of glass: transparent, hard, brittle, blocks wind  
> _Glass is transparent, which means light passes through it. That is why the boy can see her, and she can see the stars._  
> _It keeps the wind off. But it is hard and brittle, which means it smashes if it is dropped._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned some properties of glass: transparent, hard and brittle._

**The Rose**: It’s warm. Thank you. It’s very quiet in here.  

#### `a16-05-goodbye`

_Then comes the morning he decides to go. He sweeps the volcanoes, all three, and pulls the last baobab shoots._  
_He waters the rose one last time, and his hands are not quite steady._  
**The Rose**: I was difficult. I know I was. I’m sorry.  
**The Rose**: Go and be happy somewhere. That’s an order, since I’m the one giving them.  
_He reaches for the glass globe, the way he does every evening._  
**The Rose**: No, not that. I’m a flower, not a cake on a plate. I can stand a little cold.  
**The Prince**: But at night. Anything could happen.  
**The Rose**: Then it can happen. I have four thorns. I am not made of glass.  
_He turns to you with the globe in his hands. He looks very young, and very frightened for her._  
**The Prince**: Should I put it on her anyway? Just to be safe?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe is not always the same as well; respecting someone’s choice  
> _Safe and well are not always the same thing._  
> _Before you answer him, think: what might the rose lose under glass, and what might she risk without it?_  
> - Let her choose, even if it’s a risk. → That’s a fair answer. Choosing for yourself is part of being well. The rose has said clearly what she wants.
> - Keep her safe, whatever she says. → That’s a fair answer. Wanting to keep someone safe is a way of loving them. It’s worth asking what being safe costs her.
> - It’s hard. Both things matter. → That’s a fair answer too. It is a hard choice, and the boy is stuck on it as well.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between keeping someone safe and respecting their choice._


**Choices**

- **Leave her free.**
    - **The Prince**: Free. Yes. She’d never forgive me otherwise.
    - He sets the globe down beside her, empty. As he turns away, one petal falls, and he puts it in his pocket without a word.
- **Put the globe on her.**
    - He lifts it over her. She looks at him through the glass, and he can’t do it, and lifts it away again.
    - **The Prince**: She said no. I’ll take it with me, so it isn’t sitting here looking at her.

#### `a16-05-goodbye-done`

**The Rose**: Go on, then. Don’t hang about. You’ve decided.  
_She looks hard at the sun, so he can’t see her face. Nobody is prouder than a rose._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, notice): actions can show feelings that words hide  
> _The rose says “Go on, then,” but she looks hard at the sun. Her words and her actions don’t match._  
> _When that happens in a story, the action often shows the real feeling. Here, she is hiding that she is sad._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that what a character does can show a feeling their words hide._


#### `a16-05-complete`

_He goes with a flock of wild birds passing over, and the little planet drops away under him._  
_Back on the sand, the boy is quiet for a long time. Then he takes a stick and draws four tiny thorns._  

> **Lesson** (art, RL.4.3, notice): a few simple marks can stand for a whole thing  
> _Four little marks in the sand, and we know exactly who he means._  
> _Artists don’t have to draw everything. One small part, drawn well, can stand for the whole._  
> _He chose her thorns, the thing she was proudest of. That shows how well he knows her._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a simple mark or shape can stand for something bigger, and what the choice shows about a character._

**The Prince**: I didn’t know how to look after her. I thought looking after was the same as fussing.  
**The Pilot**: Do you think she’s all right?  
**The Prince**: She has four thorns.  

### Glossary

- **transparent**: Clear, so that light goes through and you can see through it.

## A16-6. The King

- `a16-06-s1`: Visit the first planet on the boy’s travels, and the king who rules it. · _Follow the boy onto the planet covered in robe._
- `a16-06-s2`: Ask the king for a sunset, and wait for it. · _Stay with the king until his almanac says it’s time._

#### `a16-06-king`

_The boy tells his travels in order, one planet a night. The first planet is so small that a king’s robe covers nearly all of it._  
_The robe is purple, trimmed with white fur, and you have to step over it to go anywhere._  
**The King**: Ah! A subject! Two subjects! And a… third, smaller subject. Approach.  
**The Prince**: How does he know who we are? He’s never seen us.  
**The King**: To a king, everybody is a subject. It saves a great deal of introducing.  
_It has been a long night’s telling. Your Nubbin yawns, enormously._  
**The King**: A yawn! At court! That is not done.  
_Your Nubbin yawns again. It can’t help it._  
**The King**: Then I command it. Yawn, small subject. Yawn as much as you like. By royal order.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fair rules treat everyone equally and can be followed  
> _The king only gives orders that people will obey anyway. Which of these would be a fair rule for a place everyone shares?_  
> - ✅ “Everyone takes turns on the swing.” → Yes. A fair rule treats everyone the same, and everyone can follow it.
> - “Only the king may use the swing.” → That rule could be obeyed, but it isn’t fair to everybody else. A fair rule treats people equally.
> - “Nobody may ever breathe.” → Nobody could obey that. A rule nobody can follow is a silly rule. It’s as silly as ordering the sun to do something it was going to do anyway.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what makes a rule fair and possible to follow._


**Choices**

- **Bow to the king.**
    - **The King**: Splendid. I command you to bow. There. Obeyed at once.
- **Yawn as well.**
    - **The King**: Yes, yes. Commanded. All of it. Nobody yawns here without my say-so.
- **Ask if you may sit down.**
    - **The King**: Sit! At once! That was my idea, you understand.
    - There is nowhere to sit that isn’t robe. You sit on the robe.

#### `a16-06-king-done`

**The King**: I rule over everything, you know. But I am reasonable about it. I only give orders that can be obeyed.  
**The King**: If I ordered the sand to stand up and dance, and it didn’t, I should look very silly. So I don’t.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): a word can be used with a joke in it; “reasonable”  
> _“Reasonable” means sensible and fair. The king says he is reasonable._  
> _But look: he only orders what would happen anyway, so nobody ever disobeys him. The author is poking gentle fun._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word “reasonable” and spotted gentle humour in how a character uses it._


#### `a16-06-sunset`

**The Prince**: Please, would you order the sun to set? I’d like a sunset.  
**The King**: Certainly. Certainly. You shall have one. At the proper time.  
_He brings out an enormous almanac, licks his thumb, and turns a great many pages._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-2, notice): almanacs list sunrise and sunset times, which change through the year  
> _An almanac is a book of tables for the year. It lists things like sunrise and sunset times._  
> _Sunset comes at a different time each day, because the Earth is tilted as it travels round the Sun._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sunset times change through the year because the Earth is tilted._

**The King**: This evening. At sunset. That is when I shall command it. And you will see how well I am obeyed.  
_The boy sighs. Your Nubbin sits down to wait, which turns out to be the right thing._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: adding minutes to a clock time  
> **The King**: Today sunset is at 5:48 in the evening. It gets two minutes later each day. What time will it be in five days?  
> - ✅ 5:58 in the evening. → Yes. Five days of two minutes is 10 minutes, and 5:48 plus 10 minutes is 5:58.
> - 5:50 in the evening. → That’s only one day later. Five days is five lots of two: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 minutes. 5:48 plus 10 minutes is 5:58.
> - 6:08 in the evening. → Careful. Ten minutes is the total, not twenty. 5:48 plus 10 minutes is 5:58.
> _For grown-ups: Added a time interval to a clock time to find a later sunset._

**The King**: Meanwhile I shall make you my Minister of Justice. There’s an old rat somewhere under the robe. Judge him.  
**The Prince**: I don’t want to judge anybody. And there’s nobody else here.  
**The King**: Then judge yourself. That is the hardest of all. Do that well, and you are wiser than most kings.  

**Choices**

- **Wait for the sunset with the king.**
    - You wait, and the king fidgets with his robe. The sun goes down exactly when it was always going to.
- **Ask the king to make you a minister too.**
    - **The King**: You are Minister of… of Small Subjects. Your first duty is to wait.
    - So you wait, officially. The sun goes down exactly when it was always going to.

#### `a16-06-sunset-done`

**The King**: Sun! I command you to set!  
_The sun sets. The king looks so pleased that nobody has the heart to say anything._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty and kindness: when to say a hard truth  
> _The sun was going to set anyway. The king is proud and happy._  
> _Would you tell him the truth, or let him enjoy it?_  
> - Tell him the truth, gently. → That’s a fair answer. Honesty matters, and a gentle truth shows respect.
> - Let him enjoy it, this time. → That’s a fair answer. Kindness matters too. It can be hard to tell when a small fib stops being harmless.
> - Ask him a question, so he can work it out. → That’s a clever answer. It lets him think for himself without feeling silly.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to be honest and when to be gentle._


#### `a16-06-complete`

**The Prince**: I think I’ll go now.  
**The King**: Go? But I have only just… Then I make you my ambassador! Go! By order!  
_The boy steps off the edge of the planet with your Nubbin under his arm, and the telling lets you down onto the sand._  
**The Prince**: He was nice, really. He just didn’t have anybody to order about but the sun.  
_Your Nubbin is still yawning. Somewhere, a very small king is taking the credit._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, notice): why we yawn; how much sleep children need  
> _Yawns are catching, and they also show a body is tired._  
> _Children between 6 and 12 need about nine to twelve hours of sleep every night. Sleep is when growing bodies mend and learn._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep._


### Glossary

- **reasonable**: Sensible and fair.
- **almanac**: A yearly book of tables, such as sunrise and sunset times.

## A16-7. The Vain Man and the Drinker

- `a16-07-s1`: Visit the planet of the man who wants to be admired. · _Follow the boy to the next planet and meet the man in the hat._
- `a16-07-s2`: Visit the sad man’s planet, quietly. · _Go gently. Stay by the boy._

#### `a16-07-vain`

_The second planet belongs to a man in a very tall hat. He sees you coming from a long way off, and stands up straight._  
**The Man in the Hat**: Visitors! Admirers! I knew you’d come eventually.  
**The Prince**: That’s a funny hat.  
**The Man in the Hat**: It is for raising. When people clap me, I raise it. Unfortunately, hardly anybody comes this way.  
_The boy claps a few times, to be kind, and off comes the hat. It goes on for five minutes and gets very dull._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): changing minutes to seconds and dividing  
> _Say the boy claps once every two seconds, and the hat comes off each time. How many times does it come off in five minutes?_  
> - ✅ 150 times. → Yes. Five minutes is 5 × 60 = 300 seconds, and 300 ÷ 2 = 150.
> - 10 times. → That’s 5 × 2. First change five minutes into seconds: 5 × 60 = 300. Then split 300 into twos: 150.
> - 300 times. → There are 300 seconds, but the hat only comes off once every two of them. So 300 ÷ 2 = 150.
> _For grown-ups: Changed minutes to seconds, then divided to find how many claps and hat-lifts._

_Now the man looks at you hopefully. He has arranged his feet for bowing._  

**Choices**

- **Clap.**
    - You clap, and off comes the hat with a sweep. You clap again, and off it comes again.
    - **The Man in the Hat**: More! More!
- **Let your Nubbin clap.**
    - Your Nubbin claps its paws together, very seriously. The man bows to it so low his hat falls off.
- **Ask him why he wants clapping.**
    - **The Man in the Hat**: Because I deserve it. Ask anyone on this planet.
    - **The Prince**: There’s only you.
    - **The Man in the Hat**: Exactly. And I think so.

#### `a16-07-vain-done`

**The Prince**: Do people really need clapping that much?  
_Your Nubbin looks at the man, then at the hat, then at you. It has never been so baffled in its life._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): where lasting pride comes from  
> _Praise feels nice, but the man needs it all the time._  
> _What helps a person feel good about themselves for longer?_  
> - Doing something they care about, and being proud of it themselves. → That’s a fair answer. Praise is lovely, but pride in your own work lasts after the clapping stops.
> - Having friends who like them as they are. → That’s a fair answer. Being liked for who you are doesn’t need a hat to lift.
> - Getting more and more clapping. → That’s a fair answer. Clapping feels lovely. But it fades the moment it stops, which is why the man always needs more.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between enjoying praise and needing it._


#### `a16-07-drinker`

_The next planet is very small and very quiet. A man sits there, still and alone, with his hands hanging between his knees._  
_He doesn’t look up when you come. He looks as if he hasn’t looked up for a long time._  
**The Prince**: Are you all right?  
**The Drinker**: No. And I know why. There’s something I do over and over, and it makes me feel worse.  
**The Drinker**: I do it so I won’t have to think about it. Then I feel ashamed of doing it. So I do it again.  
_He says it as if it were a sum he has done many times, and always gets the same answer._  
**The Prince**: Isn’t there a way out of it?  
**The Drinker**: I expect there is. I can’t see it from here.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): feeling stuck in a habit, shame, and asking for help  
> _The man feels stuck in a habit that makes him sadder. What could help someone who feels stuck like that?_  
> - ✅ Telling someone who cares, and asking for help. → Yes. Feeling stuck is nothing to be ashamed of. Telling a person you trust is the first step out, and people who know how can help.
> - Hiding it, so nobody finds out. → Shame makes people want to hide. But hiding keeps the feeling stuck. Telling someone safe is the first step.
> - Telling him it’s his own fault. → That wouldn’t help. He already feels ashamed, and that is part of what traps him. Kindness, and help from people who know how, works better.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about feeling stuck, feeling ashamed, and why asking for help matters._


**Choices**

- **Sit with him a moment.**
    - You sit on the edge of his little planet. He doesn’t say anything, but he doesn’t ask you to go.
- **Leave him quietly.**
    - You step away softly, the way you’d leave a room where someone is sleeping badly.

#### `a16-07-drinker-done`

_The boy goes away very sad. He doesn’t say anything for a long time._  
_Neither does your Nubbin. It holds on to the end of his scarf the whole way._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how characters respond to events  
> _Your Nubbin holds the scarf and says nothing. What does that show?_  
> - ✅ It is sad too, and wants to stay close. → Yes. Holding on and staying quiet shows it feels what the boy feels.
> - It is bored. → Look at what it does: it holds on tight and stays quiet. That sounds like worry or sadness, not boredom.
> - It is hungry. → Nothing here is about food. The clue is that it holds on and stays quiet, which shows it feels the boy’s sadness.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s actions as clues to how it feels._


#### `a16-07-complete`

_Back by the plane, the boy throws pebbles at nothing. Your Nubbin brings them back, one by one._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction within 20  
> _The boy throws nine pebbles, and your Nubbin fetches four back. How many are still out in the sand?_  
> - ✅ Five. → Yes. 9 − 4 = 5.
> - Thirteen. → That adds them together. We want the ones still out there, so take four away from nine: five.
> - Four. → Four is how many came back. Nine take away four leaves five.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a subtraction word problem within 20._

**The Prince**: The man in the hat only wanted clapping. The other one only wanted to stop. Neither of them got it.  
**The Pilot**: Grown-ups.  
**The Prince**: Grown-ups.  
_Your Nubbin looks from one to the other. It doesn’t understand them either, and says so by sitting on the pilot’s foot._  

### Glossary

- **admirers**: People who look at someone with pleasure and praise them.
- **habit**: Something you do again and again, often without choosing to.

## A16-8. The Businessman

- `a16-08-s1`: Visit the businessman who says he owns the stars. · _Follow the boy to the planet with the desk._
- `a16-08-s2`: Hear what the boy says to the businessman. · _Stay by the desk while the boy thinks it through._

#### `a16-08-desk`

_The fourth planet is all desk. Behind the desk is a man adding up, so busy that he doesn’t hear you arrive._  
**The Businessman**: Four hundred and six, four hundred and seven… Don’t interrupt. I’ll lose my place.  
**The Prince**: What are you counting?  
**The Businessman**: The little shiny things that idle people stare at and daydream about. I am not idle. I count them.  
_He means the stars. You can tell, because he will not look up at a single one of them._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): a French word: étoile means star  
> _The book this page comes from was first written in French. In French, a star is une étoile, said “ay-TWAL”._  
> _“Les étoiles” means “the stars”. The businessman has never once looked at les étoiles._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the French word étoile (star)._

**The Businessman**: Several hundred million, and rising. They are all mine.  
**The Prince**: How can anybody own a star?  
**The Businessman**: Nobody else had thought of owning them. So I did. That’s how owning works.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): what owning means, and why we need fair rules about it  
> _Can a person own a star, just by being the first to say so? What do you think “owning” means?_  
> - No. Owning needs a fair rule that everyone agrees on. → That’s a fair answer. Owning usually depends on shared rules, like buying something or being given it. Nobody has agreed a rule for stars.
> - Yes, if he really looks after them. → That’s a fair answer, and the boy will say something close to it. Perhaps owning something means taking care of it.
> - It depends who you ask. → That’s a fair answer. People do disagree about what can be owned. That is exactly why we need fair rules.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what owning means and why fair rules matter._


**Choices**

- **Ask what he does with them.**
    - **The Businessman**: I count them, and count them again. Then I put them in the bank.
- **Ask him to look up, just once.**
    - **The Businessman**: Look up? I haven’t time to look up. I have them to count.
    - He still doesn’t.

#### `a16-08-desk-done`

_He writes the total on a slip of paper, puts it in a drawer, and locks the drawer with a little key._  
**The Businessman**: There. In the bank. Perfectly safe.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplying equal bundles and adding the rest  
> _He counts in bundles of five to go faster._  
> _He has seven bundles and three stars on their own. How many stars is that?_  
> - ✅ 38. → Yes. Seven fives are 35, and 35 + 3 = 38.
> - 10. → That adds 7 and 3. But each bundle holds five stars, so first 7 × 5 = 35.
> - 73. → That puts the digits side by side. Seven bundles of five make 35, and 35 + 3 = 38.
> _For grown-ups: Used 7 × 5 plus 3 to count a total in bundles._


#### `a16-08-useful`

**The Prince**: I own a flower. I water her every day.  
**The Prince**: I own three volcanoes. I sweep them out, even the sleeping one.  
**The Prince**: My volcanoes are better for it. My flower is better for it. Are the stars any better for being in your drawer?  
_The businessman opens his mouth, then shuts it again. Nobody has ever asked him that before._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): finding the theme of a scene  
> _The boy says that what you own should be better for belonging to you. What is the big idea the author is showing?_  
> - ✅ What you own matters most when you take care of it. → Yes. That’s the theme: caring for something is what makes it truly yours.
> - Counting is boring. → The businessman does count a lot, but the story is about more than counting. Look at what the boy does for his flower and volcanoes.
> - Stars belong in a bank. → The businessman thinks so, but the boy’s question shows that locking stars in a drawer helps nobody.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the theme of a scene: that caring is what makes something yours._

_Your Nubbin climbs onto the desk and looks at him, then up at the sky, then at him again, to give him the idea._  
**The Businessman**: I… must get on. Where was I?  
_He doesn’t know. For the first time in years, he has lost count._  

#### `a16-08-complete`

_As you leave, you look back. He is bent over his paper, adding it all up again from the start._  
_Above him every one of his stars is shining, and he hasn’t seen a single one._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): the Sun is a star; stars look tiny because they are far away; we can’t see them by day  
> _The Sun is a star, too. The other stars look like tiny dots only because they are very, very far away._  
> _In the daytime the Sun is so bright that we can’t see the other stars. They are still there._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sun is a star and that stars look tiny because they are far away._

**The Prince**: All those stars, and he’s never once looked up. I think that’s the saddest planet so far.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): noticing what matters when you are busy  
> _The businessman is so busy counting that he never looks up._  
> _What could help a busy person notice what really matters to them?_  
> - ✅ Stopping now and then to look around and ask, “What do I care about?” → Yes. A short pause can show us what we are missing.
> - Counting faster, so the work is finished sooner. → That might finish the counting. But there will always be more to count. Stopping is what lets you notice.
> - Asking a friend to remind them. → That’s a good idea. Friends often see what we miss. It also helps to pause and look for yourself.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about pausing to notice what matters when you are busy._

**The Pilot**: Sadder than the sad man’s?  
**The Prince**: No. The other one knows he’s sad.  

## A16-9. The Lamplighter

- `a16-09-s1`: Visit the smallest planet, where a lamplighter never rests. · _Follow the boy to the planet with one street lamp._
- `a16-09-s2`: Help the lamplighter light his lamp, once. · _When the sky goes violet, lift the taper to the lamp._

#### `a16-09-lamp`

_The fifth planet is the smallest of all. There is just room for one street lamp and one lamplighter._  
_As you land it is dusk, and he lights the lamp. Then it is dawn, and he puts it out, and then it is dusk again._  
**The Lamplighter**: Good evening. Good morning. Good evening.  
**The Prince**: Why do you keep lighting it and putting it out?  
**The Lamplighter**: Those are my orders. Light it at dusk, out at dawn. It was a good job once. I had the whole night to sleep.  
**The Lamplighter**: But the planet turns faster every year, and the orders never changed. Now a whole day goes by in a minute.  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): a day is one spin of a planet; size doesn’t decide how long a day is  
> **The Lamplighter**: A day is how long a planet takes to spin round once. The Earth takes 24 hours. My planet takes one minute.  
> **The Lamplighter**: Size doesn’t decide it. Giant Jupiter spins once in about ten hours, and little Mercury takes about 59 Earth days.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a day is one spin of a planet, and that a planet’s size doesn’t decide the length of its day._

_He mops his forehead with a large handkerchief. Dusk: he lights the lamp._  
**The Lamplighter**: I haven’t sat down in a month. Good morning.  

**Choices**

- **Offer to help with the lamp.**
    - **The Lamplighter**: Would you? Just the once. Dusk is coming. It’s always coming.
- **Ask why he doesn’t just stop.**
    - **The Lamplighter**: Then the lamp would be out when it ought to be lit. Somebody might be looking for it.
    - **The Prince**: Who?
    - **The Lamplighter**: I don’t know. That’s why I keep it lit.

#### `a16-09-lamp-done`

**The Prince**: Your planet’s so tiny, you could just stroll after the sun. You’d never get to dusk at all.  
**The Lamplighter**: I don’t want it to be day for ever. I want a night off.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): rules should change when things change  
> _The lamplighter’s orders never changed, even though his planet did. What should happen to a rule when things change?_  
> - Someone should look at it again, and change it if it no longer makes sense. → That’s a fair answer. A good rule serves the people who follow it. When it stops working, it needs another look.
> - Keep it exactly as it is. Rules are rules. → That’s a fair answer. Keeping to a rule feels safe, and rules do matter. But the lamplighter hasn’t slept in a month. What would you say to him?
> - Ask whoever made the rule to change it. → That’s a fair answer. Asking is a calm way to fix a rule that has stopped working.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why rules sometimes need to change._


#### `a16-09-light`

_He hands you a long taper with a small flame at the end. It smells of beeswax._  
**The Lamplighter**: Dusk is in… now. No. Now. Ready?  
_The sky slides from gold to violet in the time it takes to breathe. The lamp waits, cold, at the top of its post._  
**The Lamplighter**: Up, and in, and… there.  
_You lift the taper, with your Nubbin on your shoulder leaning too. The wick catches, and light spreads over the whole planet._  
**The Lamplighter**: Oh, that’s lovely. I haven’t seen it from the outside in years.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.MD.B.3, do): telling the time in hours and half hours; one dusk a minute  
> **The Lamplighter**: One dusk every minute, remember. Count the lightings with me, one for each minute that passes.  
> _Thirty dusks make half an hour, and sixty make a whole hour. In one of our days he lights it 1,440 times._  
> Check: `edu:count:lamp-lightings:30`
> _For grown-ups: Counted one lamp-lighting per minute to find how many in half an hour and an hour._

_For one whole minute he stands back with his hands in his pockets, and just looks at his lamp._  

#### `a16-09-light-done`

_Then it is dawn, and he must put it out. He does, very gently._  
**The Prince**: Of all of them, he’s the one I’d have stayed with. He looks after something that isn’t himself.  
**The Prince**: Only there isn’t room. It’s him, and the lamp, and that’s the whole planet.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): caring for something beyond yourself shows who you are  
> _The boy says the lamplighter looks after something that isn’t himself. Why might that make someone a good friend?_  
> - ✅ People who care for things outside themselves tend to care about friends too. → Yes. How we look after what matters to us shows what kind of person we are.
> - Because he has a lamp. → The lamp is only the clue. What matters is that he cares about something beyond himself.
> - Because he works hard. → Working hard is good. But the boy points at something else. The lamplighter looks after something, not only himself.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why caring for something beyond yourself is a sign of a good friend._


#### `a16-09-complete`

**The Lamplighter**: Here. Take this. It’s a spare, from before the orders got silly.  
_He gives you a small lamp on a short post, green, with brass at the top. It is the right size for a hill._  
**The Lamplighter**: It lights itself at dusk and goes out at dawn. It doesn’t need anybody.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, notice): how a lamp can switch itself on at dusk: light sensor and stored solar energy  
> _How can a lamp light itself? Some have a light sensor, a part that notices when daylight fades and switches the lamp on._  
> _Many garden lights also store the Sun’s energy in a battery by day, and turn it into light by night._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a lamp can use a light sensor and stored solar energy to light itself._

**The Lamplighter**: Good evening. Good morning. Goodbye.  
_He waves his handkerchief until the telling folds him away._  

### Glossary

- **taper**: A thin candle, used for lighting lamps.

## A16-10. The Geographer

- `a16-10-s1`: Visit the old geographer and his books. · _Follow the boy to the planet ten times bigger than the last._
- `a16-10-s2`: Hear what the geographer says about flowers. · _Stay while the boy describes his planet._

#### `a16-10-books`

_The sixth planet is a good deal bigger. An old gentleman lives on it among books piled higher than his head._  
**The Geographer**: An explorer! At last! Sit down, sit down. Tell me everything.  
**The Prince**: What are all these books?  
**The Geographer**: I am a geographer. I write down where the seas are, and the rivers, the towns, the mountains and the deserts.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 2-ESS2-2, notice): maps and the four compass directions  
> **The Geographer**: A map shows where things are. A compass rose on it shows four main directions: north, south, east and west.  
> **The Geographer**: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Stand with the sunrise on your right, and you are facing north.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the four compass directions and how the Sun’s position helps find them._

**The Prince**: Are there seas on your planet?  
**The Geographer**: Haven’t the least idea. Going and looking is for explorers. I sit here, and they come and tell me.  
**The Geographer**: Then I check what they say. If they claim a mountain, I make them bring me a big stone from it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): the word “evidence”: something real that shows whether a claim is true  
> _A stone from the mountain is evidence: something real you can look at and test, not just a story._  
> _Scientists check what people claim by asking for evidence too._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word “evidence”: something real you can check, as scientists do._


**Choices**

- **Describe the Grove for his book.**
    - You tell him about a pond, and a hill, and a gate that sticks. He writes down the pond and the hill.
    - **The Geographer**: A gate? A gate is not geography. Gates change.
- **Ask him if he’s ever seen a mountain.**
    - **The Geographer**: Seen one? Good heavens, no. I have written down four hundred.

#### `a16-10-books-done`

**The Geographer**: Now, young man. Your planet. Describe it.  
_He opens a fresh page and licks his pencil. The boy stands up a little straighter._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): scale: one centimetre on the map stands for one metre  
> **The Geographer**: Draw it small. One centimetre on my map stands for one metre of planet. Yours is about 20 metres round. How long is the line on my map?  
> - ✅ 20 centimetres. → Yes. Each metre becomes one centimetre, so 20 metres is 20 centimetres.
> - 20 metres. → The real planet is 20 metres round. The map shrinks it. One metre becomes one centimetre, so the line is 20 centimetres.
> - 2 centimetres. → That would be if ten metres made one centimetre. Here every single metre is one centimetre, so the answer is 20.
> _For grown-ups: Used a simple scale (1 cm for 1 m) to work out a length on a map._


#### `a16-10-flower`

**The Prince**: There are three volcanoes. Two awake and one asleep.  
**The Geographer**: Asleep or awake, a volcano is a volcano. I’ll put down three.  
**The Prince**: And I have a flower.  
**The Geographer**: We don’t write down flowers.  
**The Prince**: Why not? She’s the prettiest thing on it!  
**The Geographer**: Because flowers don’t last. Geography is for things that stay, like mountains and seas.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): mountains change too, slowly, through erosion  
> _Is the geographer right that mountains stay? Not quite, because mountains change too, only very slowly._  
> _Wind, rain and ice wear mountains away, bit by bit, over thousands and millions of years. That is called erosion._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mountains change slowly through erosion by wind, rain and ice._

**The Geographer**: A flower is here, and then it isn’t. Not tomorrow, perhaps. But one day. That is what flowers are like.  
_The boy goes very still. For the first time since he left, he thinks of his rose with worry instead of hurt._  
**The Prince**: Four thorns. That’s all she’s got. And I just went.  

#### `a16-10-flower-done`

**The Prince**: Where should I go next? Where’s worth seeing?  
**The Geographer**: Try the Earth. Big. Well thought of. Plenty to write down, I hear.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what to do with a worry about someone far away  
> _The boy felt hurt before, and now he feels worried. What could he do with a worry about someone far away?_  
> - Tell someone, and think about what he can do next. → That’s a fair answer. Sharing a worry makes it lighter, and a next step gives it somewhere to go.
> - Keep busy, and try not to think about it. → That’s a fair answer. Being busy can help for a while. But a worry often comes along with us, so it may help to talk about it too.
> - Go back at once. → That’s a fair answer. Going back would show how much he cares. It’s very far, though, so he may need to think about how.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about sharing a worry and choosing a next step._


#### `a16-10-complete`

_So he goes to Earth, thinking about his flower the whole way._  
_The telling stops. By the plane, the boy is sitting with his chin on his knees, looking at nothing._  
**The Pilot**: Is that when you came here?  
**The Prince**: That’s when I came here.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): a turning point is where a character changes direction  
> _A turning point is the moment in a story when a character changes direction._  
> _Before the geographer, the boy was only travelling. After him, he is worried about his rose, and he heads for Earth._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a turning point is in a story._


### Glossary

- **geographer**: Someone who studies and writes about the land, seas and places of the Earth.
- **evidence**: Facts or objects that show whether something is true.
- **erosion**: The slow wearing away of rock and soil by wind, water or ice.

## A16-11. The Yellow Snake

- `a16-11-s1`: Follow the boy’s first night on Earth, in the empty desert. · _Walk with the boy over the dunes._
- `a16-11-s2`: Hear what the snake says, and remember it. · _Stay by the boy while the snake talks._

#### `a16-11-earth`

_In the telling, the boy lands on Earth, in this same desert, a year ago. Nobody is there, nobody at all._  
**The Prince**: I thought I’d got the wrong planet. The geographer said it was full of people.  
_It is a very big planet, and the desert is a very big part of it. Not a person in sight._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): the Sahara is in Africa  
> _This desert is the Sahara. Which continent is it in?_  
> - ✅ Africa. → Yes. The Sahara covers a huge part of northern Africa. It is the biggest hot desert in the world.
> - Asia. → Asia has big deserts too, such as the Gobi. But the Sahara is in the north of Africa.
> - Australia. → Australia has deserts as well. But the Sahara is in the north of Africa.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sahara is a desert in northern Africa._

_Something moves in the sand by his foot: a ring the colour of moonlight, thin as a finger._  
**The Prince**: Good evening.  
_The ring lifts its head. It is a snake, small and yellow, and it says good evening back._  

**Choices**

- **Stay close beside the boy.**
    - You stand at his shoulder. The snake looks at you, and then away, as if you aren’t the one it came about.
- **Pick up your Nubbin.**
    - You pick up your Nubbin. It doesn’t struggle, but watches the snake over your arm without blinking.

#### `a16-11-riddles`

**The Prince**: Which planet is this?  
**The Snake**: The Earth. The desert part. People don’t stay in deserts.  
**The Prince**: You’re a funny animal. You’re as thin as a finger.  
**The Snake**: I’m more than I look.  
**The Prince**: That’s a riddle.  
**The Snake**: Everything I say is. Riddles keep better.  
**The Snake**: You’re very far from home, and very new. One day you may miss your planet more than you can carry.  
**The Snake**: If that day comes, look for me. I’m the shortest way there is.  
_The boy looks at it for a long time. Then he shakes his head._  
**The Prince**: Not yet. I don’t need you yet.  
_The snake doesn’t mind. It settles back into its ring, as if it had all the time in the world._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): riddles and figurative language; reading what a character’s answer shows  
> _A riddle says one thing and means another. The snake calls itself “the shortest way” home, and the boy answers, “Not yet.”_  
> _What does “not yet” tell us about the boy?_  
> - He still has things he wants to do, and a rose to think about. → That’s a fair answer. “Not yet” means he isn’t ready, and the rose is on his mind.
> - He is polite and calm, even when he is unsure. → That’s a fair answer. He answers gently, and doesn’t sound afraid.
> - He doesn’t quite understand the riddle. → That’s a fair answer. Riddles are hard to read. He may not know what it means, but he knows what his answer is.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a character’s short reply tells us, in a scene with a riddling speaker._


#### `a16-11-complete`

_The telling goes quiet. By the plane, the pilot has stopped working, a spanner in one hand._  
**The Pilot**: I don’t like that snake.  
**The Prince**: It wasn’t unkind. It was just very sure.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what to do when something makes you uneasy  
> _The pilot doesn’t like the snake, and your Nubbin turns its back on the dunes. What can help when something makes you feel uneasy?_  
> - ✅ Say how you feel to someone you trust, and stay near them. → Yes. Naming a feeling makes it smaller, and a friend close by helps.
> - Pretend you feel fine. → Pretending can make the feeling louder inside. Saying it out loud, as the pilot does, helps more.
> - Keep staring at whatever it is. → Sometimes looking helps us understand. But turning away, like your Nubbin, is allowed too. Being near someone who cares helps most.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps when something makes you feel uneasy._

_Your Nubbin wriggles round in your arms so that it can keep its back to the dunes for the rest of the night._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): dunes move as wind pushes sand grains along  
> _Dunes are never quite still. The wind pushes sand grains up the gentle side of a dune, and they tumble down the steep side._  
> _Grain by grain, the whole dune creeps along. That is why nobody leaves tracks for long in the Sahara._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wind moves sand grains, so dunes slowly shift._


## A16-12. The Echo and the Garden

- `a16-12-s1`: Cross the desert with the boy, and meet the one flower in it. · _Walk with the boy until you find the flower._
- `a16-12-s2`: Climb the high mountain with the boy, and see what’s at the top. · _Follow him up to the peak._
- `a16-12-s3`: Sit down next to the boy in the garden of roses, and wait. · _When he lies down in the grass, sit beside him. Don’t say anything._

#### `a16-12-flower`

_The boy crosses the desert in the telling. In all that sand he meets one flower: three petals, and nothing much else._  
**The Prince**: Good morning. Where are the people?  
**The Desert Flower**: People? A few went by, a long time ago. They were in a great hurry.  
**The Desert Flower**: They go past. They’re always looking for something, and they never stop long enough to find it.  
**The Prince**: Which way did they go?  
**The Desert Flower**: That way. Or that way. The wind moves the sand about. Nobody leaves tracks here.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): noticing someone who is alone, and offering time  
> _The flower has hardly ever had anyone stop. What could you do for someone who is on their own?_  
> - Stop, say hello, and spend a little time with them. → That’s a fair answer. Time is a big gift, and staying a while shows you care.
> - Ask if they would like some company. → That’s a fair answer. Asking lets them choose, and some people do want space.
> - Give them a present. → That’s a fair answer. A present is kind. Some people say time is the bigger gift. What do you think?
> _For grown-ups: Thought about noticing someone alone and offering time and company._


**Choices**

- **Give her a little shade.**
    - You stand so your shadow falls across her. Her three petals open a little wider, in surprise.
    - **The Desert Flower**: Oh. Thank you. Nobody’s ever stopped before.
- **Thank her, and go on.**
    - **The Desert Flower**: Goodbye. I’ll remember you. There isn’t much else to remember.

#### `a16-12-echo`

_Then a high mountain, the first he has ever climbed. On his planet the volcanoes only came up to his knee._  
**The Prince**: From up there I’ll see the whole planet, and all the people at once.  
_From the top you see peaks, sharp as needles, all the way round. No people at all._  
**The Prince**: Hello?  
**The Echo**: Hello… hello… hello…  
**The Prince**: Who’s there?  
**The Echo**: …there? …there? …there?  
**The Prince**: I’d like a friend. Is anybody there?  
**The Echo**: …anybody… there… there…  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): an echo is sound bouncing back; sound speed makes the delay  
> _An echo is sound that bounces back. Sound travels in waves, and hard, flat surfaces such as cliffs send them back._  
> _Sound travels about 340 metres every second. If a cliff is 340 metres away, the echo comes back after 2 seconds._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an echo is a sound wave bouncing back, and that sound takes time to travel._

_Your Nubbin sits down very firmly on the peak, and looks at the echo as if it has been rude._  
**The Prince**: This planet doesn’t talk back. It only copies.  

#### `a16-12-roses`

_After a long time walking there is a road, and the road leads to a garden, and the garden is full of roses._  
_Five thousand of them, nodding in rows. Every single one looks exactly like his._  
**The Roses**: Good morning. We are roses.  
**The Prince**: Roses.  
_He stares at them. She told him she was the only one of her kind anywhere._  
**The Prince**: If she saw this, she’d be furious. And then she’d be ever so ill, all of a sudden.  
**The Prince**: I thought she was the only one. I thought that made me somebody.  
**The Prince**: She’s just a rose. And my volcanoes only come up to my knee.  
_He lies down in the grass, puts his face in his arms, and cries._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps when someone is very sad  
> _The boy is crying, and you can’t fix this for him. What is the most helpful thing you can do?_  
> - ✅ Sit beside him and wait. → Yes. Staying close, and not rushing him, tells him he isn’t alone.
> - Tell him not to cry. → That comes from kindness. But crying is how big feelings come out. He needs to feel them, not hide them.
> - Explain why he shouldn’t be upset. → The reasons may all be true. But explaining can make a sad person feel unheard. Sitting close and saying nothing often helps first.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to support a friend who is very sad._


**Choices**

- **Sit down beside him, and wait.**
    - You sit down in the grass beside him and don’t say anything. Your Nubbin lies against his side, warm, and waits too.
- **Tell him she’s still special.**
    - **The Prince**: You don’t know that. You’ve never met her.
    - He’s right. So you sit down beside him instead, and wait, and that turns out to be the thing.

#### `a16-12-roses-done`

_The roses nod on their stalks, and the sun moves. After a long time he stops crying, rolls over, and looks at the sky._  
**The Prince**: Thank you for not saying anything.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division with multiples of 100  
> _There are 5,000 roses growing in rows of 100. How many rows is that?_  
> - ✅ 50 rows. → Yes: 50 × 100 = 5,000, so there are 50 rows. Fifty rows of roses, and not one of them is his.
> - 500 rows. → 500 rows of 100 would be 50,000 roses. That’s ten times too many. 50 × 100 = 5,000, so it’s 50 rows.
> - 5 rows. → Five rows of 100 would only be 500 roses. We need ten times as many: 50 rows.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 5,000 by 100 to find the number of rows._


#### `a16-12-complete`

_Someone is watching from under an apple tree at the edge of the garden. Someone with a tail._  
_The telling holds its breath. So does your Nubbin._  
**The Fox**: Good morning.  
**The Prince**: Good morning. I can’t see you properly. Who are you?  
**The Fox**: A fox. And you’re in a bad way. I can tell from here.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): a French word: renard means fox  
> _The book this page comes from was first written in French. In French, a fox is un renard, said “ruh-NAR”._  
> _So this is the renard of the story, the one who teaches the boy the biggest lesson of all._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the French word renard (fox)._


### Glossary

- **echo**: A sound that bounces off a hard surface and comes back to you.

## A16-13. The Fox

- `a16-13-s1`: Meet the fox under the apple tree, and hear what taming is. · _Walk with the boy to the apple tree. Don’t go too close._
- `a16-13-s2`: Help the boy tame the fox: sit at the same hour, a little closer each time. · _When the tree’s shadow touches the white stone, sit. Say nothing. Each time, a little nearer._
- `a16-13-s3`: Say goodbye to the fox, and hear its secret. · _Go and see the roses once more, then come back to the apple tree._

#### `a16-13-fox`

_The fox sits in the grass under the apple tree, tail wrapped round its feet, and comes no nearer._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): the fennec: a desert fox with big ears for hearing and cooling  
> _The real Sahara has a fox a lot like this one: the fennec, the smallest fox in the world._  
> _Its huge ears hear insects moving under the sand. They also give off heat, which helps it stay cool._  
> _Fennecs dig burrows and hunt mostly at night, when the desert is cooler._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about the fennec fox and how its ears help it survive in the desert._

**The Prince**: Come and play with me. Please. I’ve had a very bad day.  
**The Fox**: Play? I can’t. Nobody has tamed me.  
**The Prince**: Tamed?  
**The Fox**: It’s an old word. It means making ties with someone, slowly, one step at a time.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): words with more than one meaning: “tame”  
> _“Tame” has more than one meaning. It can mean not wild, like a tame rabbit._  
> _Here the fox means making friends slowly, one step at a time. The words around a word show which meaning it has._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a word can have more than one meaning and that nearby words show which._

**The Fox**: Right now you’re one more boy, and I’m one more fox. There are plenty of both.  
**The Fox**: Tame me, and I’ll know your step from every other step. You’ll need me, and I’ll need you.  
**The Prince**: I don’t know how to tame anybody. I don’t think I know how to be tamed, either.  

**Choices**

- **Ask the fox how it’s done.**
    - **The Fox**: Patience. That’s nearly all of it. I’ll show you.
- **Hold out your hand to the fox.**
    - The fox leans back all at once, ears flat.
    - **The Fox**: Too fast. That’s the first thing. Never quick.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff the air.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs, and the fox sniffs back. Neither moves an inch, and it seems to be going rather well.

#### `a16-13-hour`

**The Fox**: You must be very patient. First you sit down a little way off, like that, in the grass.  
**The Fox**: Don’t look straight at me, and don’t talk. Talking gets in the way.  
**The Fox**: And come at the same hour each day: when the apple tree’s shadow touches that white stone.  
**The Prince**: Why the same hour?  
**The Fox**: So I know when you’re coming. Then I can start being happy a whole hour before you get here.  
**The Fox**: The closer it gets, the happier I am. Looking forward is half of it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.MD.B.3, do): time intervals: one hour before a clock time  
> **The Fox**: If the boy comes at four o’clock, at what time do I start being happy? Set the clock hands for me.  
> _One hour before four o’clock is three o’clock. The fox starts feeling happy at three, long before the boy arrives._  
> Check: `edu:read:clock:three`
> _For grown-ups: Found one hour before four o’clock to work out when the fox starts looking forward._

_Days on this page are short: a few minutes from sunrise to stars. You watch the shadow crawl towards the white stone._  
_The shadow touches the stone. The boy sits down a long way off and says nothing, and the fox looks at him sideways._  
_Sunset, stars, sunrise. The shadow crawls, and the boy sits down again, a little nearer._  
_And again, a little nearer. On the fourth day, the fox is waiting at the stone before the shadow gets there._  

#### `a16-13-hour-done`

_The fox lets the boy put a hand on its head. Soon they are sitting together, looking at the same sunset._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): how to befriend a shy animal gently  
> _How do you make friends with a shy animal? Think about what the boy did._  
> - ✅ Sit quietly, stay calm, and go a little nearer each day, letting it choose. → Yes. Slow and calm helps a shy animal feel safe, and lets the animal choose.
> - Pick it up at once, so it gets used to you. → Quick moves frighten a shy animal. The boy sat still, a little way off, and let the fox come to him.
> - Stare straight at it until it comes. → Staring can scare an animal. The boy looked away and said nothing, so the fox felt safe.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about gentle, patient ways to make friends with a shy animal._

_You think of the hill where something small and grey once watched._  

#### `a16-13-secret`

_Then the hour comes for the boy to go. The fox knows before he says it._  
**The Fox**: There. Now I’m going to cry. I knew I would.  
**The Prince**: Then taming you was no good to you at all.  
**The Fox**: It was. Wheat never meant anything to me. Now it’s the colour of your hair.  
**The Fox**: Every time the wind moves through the wheat, I’ll have you.  
**The Fox**: Go and look at the roses once more. Then come back, and I’ll give you a secret as a present.  
_So you go back to the garden with him. He stands in front of the five thousand roses, and isn’t afraid of them any more._  
**The Prince**: You’re lovely. But nobody has sat with you. Nobody has waited for you. She’s mine, because she’s the one I looked after.  
_He comes back to the apple tree. The fox is waiting at the white stone, though it isn’t quite the hour._  
**The Fox**: Here is the secret. It’s very simple.  
**The Fox**: Looking only shows you the surface. To see what someone is really like, you have to get to know them.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: knowing someone is how we see what matters  
> _The fox says looking only shows you the surface. You find out what someone is really like by getting to know them._  
> _What do you think that means?_  
> - You learn what someone is like by spending time with them. → That’s a fair answer. Time shows you things a first look can’t.
> - You can’t tell what someone feels just by how they look. → That’s a fair answer. Faces can hide a lot, and friends learn to notice.
> - Things we care for become special because we care. → That’s a fair answer too, and it is close to what the fox says next.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what the fox means by saying that knowing someone shows more than looking._

**The Prince**: So I have to know her. Not just look at her.  
**The Fox**: The hours you spent on your rose are what make her matter so much to you.  
**The Prince**: All those mornings. The water, and the screen.  
**The Fox**: And once someone has come to trust you, you’re the one who looks after them. Always.  
**The Prince**: My rose. I have to look after my rose.

_The fox goes back into the wheat. You can see where it goes by the way the gold moves._  

> **Lesson** (art, RL.1.4, notice): a colour can hold a memory of a person  
> _Ripe wheat is gold, and the wind makes it ripple like water. The fox says it will remind it of the boy._  
> _Artists know that a colour can hold a memory. Gold, for the fox, now means “my friend”._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that artists use colour to stand for feelings and memories._

**The Prince**: I’ll remember. I have to remember.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, notice): crying helps the body let big feelings out  
> _Crying is one way the body lets big feelings out. Afterwards many people feel calmer, and a little tired._  
> _It is a normal and healthy thing to do, for children and for grown-ups._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that crying is a normal way for the body to let big feelings out._

**The Pilot**: A fox told you all that?

## A16-14. The Switchman and the Merchant

- `a16-14-s1`: Watch the trains go by at the switchman’s box. · _Stand by the switchman while the trains rush past._
- `a16-14-s2`: Meet the merchant and his thirst pills. · _Follow the boy to the man with the tray._

#### `a16-14-trains`

_More of the telling, the night after. A railway in the dark, and a switchman in his box, sorting trains._  
**The Switchman**: Evening. Mind the rails. They’re coming through in bundles tonight.  
_A lit-up express roars past one way, rattling the box. A minute later, another roars past the other way._  
**The Prince**: They’re in a great hurry. What are they looking for?  
**The Switchman**: Couldn’t tell you. I don’t think they could either. Everybody wants to be where they aren’t.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): stopping to ask yourself what you really want  
> _Lots of people rush without knowing what they’re looking for. What could help you work out what you really want?_  
> - Stop for a moment, and ask yourself. → That’s a fair answer. A quiet moment can show you what matters.
> - Look out of the window, like the children. → That’s a fair answer. Looking, wondering and noticing are what the children do.
> - Ask a friend what they think. → That’s a fair answer. A friend can help you see what you want. In the end, only you can say what is right for you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about pausing to work out what you really want._

_A third train thunders by. In every window grown-ups sleep or yawn, but here and there a child has its nose to the glass._  
**The Prince**: The children are looking out. They’re the only ones looking.  
**The Switchman**: Hm. I never noticed that. I don’t look in the windows much.  

**Choices**

- **Wave at the children.**
    - You wave. A small hand waves back from a window, and then the train is gone into the dark.
- **Ask where they’re all going.**
    - **The Switchman**: Somewhere else. Then back again. Same as yesterday.

#### `a16-14-pills`

_Then a merchant with a tray round his neck, selling little pills._  
**The Merchant**: One a week, and you’ll never be thirsty. It saves fifty-three minutes. Experts worked it out.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): adding minutes and converting to hours and minutes  
> _The pills save fifty-three minutes a week. After two weeks, how much time is that, in minutes and then in hours and minutes?_  
> - ✅ 106 minutes, which is 1 hour 46 minutes. → Yes: 53 + 53 = 106 minutes. Sixty of them make an hour, and 46 are left over.
> - 53 minutes. → That’s only one week. Two weeks of 53 minutes means adding: 53 + 53 = 106. 106 minutes is 1 hour and 46 minutes.
> - 100 minutes. → Close. But 53 + 53 = 106, not 100. 106 minutes is 1 hour and 46 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Added two lots of 53 minutes and changed the total into hours and minutes._

**The Prince**: What do you do with the fifty-three minutes?  
**The Merchant**: Use them! Anything at all! Experts say it’s very efficient.  
_The boy thinks about it seriously, the way he thinks about everything._  
**The Prince**: Fifty-three spare minutes? I’d use them to walk to a spring. Slowly, all the way there.  
_The merchant looks at his tray, and at the boy, and doesn’t seem to know what to say._  

**Choices**

- **Ask what he does with his own minutes.**
    - **The Merchant**: Mine? I… I haven’t saved enough yet to spend any.
- **Say you’d walk too.**
    - **The Prince**: You see? Two of us. You should sell walks instead.

**The Pilot**: That’s a lovely story. I mean it. But I’ve just drunk the last of the water.  
**The Pilot**: It’s the eighth day. I ought to be walking to a spring myself, if I knew where there was one.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, notice): people need water every day; they can last weeks without food but only days without water  
> _A person can live for weeks without food, but only a few days without water._  
> _More than half of your body is water, and it needs topping up every day. That is why finding a well matters so much._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the body needs water every day, and can manage only a few days without it._

**The Prince**: I’m thirsty too. Let’s look for a well.  

### Glossary

- **switchman**: A railway worker who moves the switches that send trains onto the right track.
- **merchant**: Someone whose job is to sell things.

## A16-15. The Well

- `a16-15-s1`: Walk through the night with the pilot, looking for a well. · _Keep up with the pilot across the dunes. Don’t stop._
- `a16-15-s2`: Find the well at daybreak, and draw up the water. · _Help the pilot haul the bucket. Steady it on the wall._
- `a16-15-s3`: Share the water. · _Hold the bucket so that everyone can drink._

#### `a16-15-night`

_A well, in all this desert, is a silly idea. You set off anyway, all of you together, as the sun goes down._  
_The stars come out. The sand is cold under your feet, and silver, and goes on for ever._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): finding north with the Pole Star  
> **The Pilot**: Keep the Pole Star in front of us. It stays above the north all night, while the other stars wheel round it.  
> **The Pilot**: If it’s straight ahead, which way are we walking?  
> - ✅ North. → Yes. The Pole Star shows where north is, so walking towards it means walking north.
> - South. → South would be behind us. The Pole Star marks north, so if it is straight ahead, we are walking north.
> - West. → West would be on our left. The Pole Star marks north, so if it is straight ahead, we are walking north.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Pole Star shows north and used it to work out a walking direction._

**The Pilot**: Here. Your little one’s shivering.  
_He unwinds the long scarf from his own neck and winds it round and round your Nubbin, until only its eyes show._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): wool traps air, which keeps body heat in  
> _A knitted wool scarf keeps you warm because it traps tiny pockets of air, and trapped air lets heat escape slowly._  
> _That’s why a long scarf makes a good coat for a cold desert night._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wool keeps us warm by trapping air._

**The Prince**: There’s water somewhere. You can tell. The sand goes quiet over it.  
_After a long time the boy stumbles, and sits, and falls asleep where he sits._  
_The pilot picks him up very carefully, as if he might break, and carries him on through the night._  
**The Pilot**: He weighs nothing. I keep thinking I’ll drop him, and he weighs nothing at all.  

**Choices**

- **Carry the sheep box.**
    - You carry the box with holes. Your Nubbin rides on it in its scarf, keeping an eye on the sheep.
- **Carry the empty water tin.**
    - It is very light, and it rattles. You carry it anyway, so you’ll have something to fill.
- **Walk on the windy side of the pilot.**
    - You walk on the wind’s side. The pilot doesn’t say anything, but he walks a little closer.

#### `a16-15-night-done`

_Dawn comes up grey, then gold. The boy wakes in the pilot’s arms, and points._  
_The cold slides out of the sand. The first sunlight is pale, then yellow, then warm on your face._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, notice): colour words and the feelings they carry  
> _The sky goes grey, then gold. Writers use colour words to show a feeling as well as a colour._  
> _Grey feels quiet and tired, while gold feels warm and hopeful. Can you find other colour words in this story?_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that colour words can show feelings as well as colours._


#### `a16-15-well`

_A well. Not a hole in the sand, like desert wells, but a real one: a stone ring, a rope, a pulley and a bucket._  
**The Pilot**: This doesn’t belong here. It’s a village well. Where’s the village?  
**The Prince**: Shh. Listen.  
_He takes hold of the rope and pulls. The pulley turns and creaks, like an old gate that hasn’t been asked to open for years._  
**The Prince**: It’s complaining. Nobody’s woken it up for ages.  
**The Pilot**: Let me. It’s too heavy for you.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): a pulley changes the direction of a pull, so you can use your weight  
> **The Pilot**: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it. Pull down on one end, and the bucket goes up.  
> **The Pilot**: It doesn’t make the bucket lighter. It changes the direction of the pull, so I can lean my weight on the rope.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a pulley changes the direction of a pull to make lifting easier._

_The pilot hauls the bucket up, hand over hand. You steady it on the stone, with the sun shaking in the water._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, notice): a French word: puits means well  
> _In French, a well is un puits, said “pwee”._  
> _Wells like this one reach down to water hidden far below the sand._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the French word puits (well)._


#### `a16-15-well-done`

_The bucket sits on the wall, full to the brim. The water in it is gold with the sunrise._  
**The Pilot**: It holds twelve litres. There are four of us: the boy, you, your Nubbin and me. We’ll share it equally.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, do): sharing equally: dividing within 100  
> **The Pilot**: Pour it into four equal cups. How much does each cup get?  
> _Twelve litres shared by four is three litres each, because 4 × 3 = 12._  
> Check: `edu:share:water:3`
> _For grown-ups: Shared a total equally by dividing, and checked it with multiplication._


#### `a16-15-water`

**The Prince**: Can I have some? That’s the water I wanted. That one.  
_The pilot lifts the bucket to the boy’s lips. He drinks with his eyes shut, as if it were his birthday._  
**The Prince**: It isn’t just the water. It’s the walk.  
**The Pilot**: Your turn.  
_The bucket is heavy and cold on the outside, and the sun is in it._  
_Your Nubbin stands on tiptoe on the stone, looking in._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): fairness when sharing something everyone needs  
> _There is water for everyone, and everyone is thirsty. Who should drink first, and why?_  
> - The one who needs it most. → That’s a fair answer. Needing something is a good reason to go first.
> - Everyone takes a turn, in order. → That’s a fair answer too. Taking turns treats everybody the same.
> - The one who carried the bucket. → That’s a fair answer. Some people would say the others are just as tired, though.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about different ways to share fairly when everyone has a need._


**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin drink first.**
    - You tip the bucket for your Nubbin. It puts its whole face in, scarf and all, and comes up dripping and happy.
- **Drink.**
    - You drink. Your Nubbin drinks after you, with its nose right in the bucket.
- **Hold the bucket for the pilot.**
    - You hold it while he drinks, both hands round it. He nods at you over the rim, and doesn’t stop for a long time.

#### `a16-15-water-done`

_It tastes of the walk: the cold sand and the stars, the creak of the pulley, and being carried._  
**The Pilot**: That’s the best thing I’ve ever drunk.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): why water tastes so good when you are thirsty  
> _Water tastes best when you’re very thirsty. Your body keeps track of how much water it has._  
> _When it runs low, your brain makes you feel thirsty. Drinking switches that feeling off, and it feels wonderful._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that thirst is the body’s signal that it needs water._

_You all sit with your backs against the warm stone. The boy looks at the pilot sideways._  
**The Prince**: You’ll mend your engine soon. I can tell. Then you can fly home.  
**The Prince**: It’s nearly a year since I came down, just near here. That’s a long time to be away.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): a year in weeks and days  
> _A year is 365 days, and a week is 7 days. How many whole weeks are in a year, and how many days are left over?_  
> - ✅ 52 weeks and 1 day. → Yes. 52 × 7 = 364, and 365 − 364 = 1 day left over.
> - 50 weeks. → 50 weeks is only 350 days, so 15 days are left. That’s two more weeks and a day. So it’s 52 weeks and 1 day.
> - 53 weeks. → 53 × 7 = 371, which is more than 365. 52 × 7 = 364, so it’s 52 weeks and 1 day.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 365 days by 7 to find the number of whole weeks and days left over._

**The Prince**: I’m going home to my rose. It’s a long way.  
_The pilot unwinds the scarf from your Nubbin, looks at it, and winds it back on again._  
**The Pilot**: Keep it. It’s walked further than I have tonight.  
_Going home can mean a place, and it can mean someone you look after. For the boy, it means both._

- **pulley**: A wheel with a rope over it, used to lift things.

## A17-1. The Old House

- `a17-01-s1`: Step into the summer page and find Granny at the bus stop. · _Touch the page, then walk down the country road to the bus stop._
- `a17-01-s2`: Help the Kusakabes unload the lorry at the old house. · _Carry the boxes from the lorry to the step. Take your boots off before you go in._
- `a17-01-s3`: Look at the great tree on the hill with the family. · _Stand in the back garden and look up the hill behind the house._

#### `a17-01-road`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a country road in summer. There is a bus stop, green rice fields, and a tree on a hill._  
_The tree is drawn so big that it runs off the top of the page._  
_The page hums under your hand. It is cicadas, thousands of them, and you are standing in the road._  
_An old woman waits at the bus stop in a straw hat. She looks you and your Nubbin up and down._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): Japan is a chain of islands; rice grows in flooded fields called paddies  
> **Granny**: Look at the rice. We grow it with its feet in water, in flooded fields called paddies.  
> **Granny**: Japan is a long chain of islands, and in summer the paddies are bright green.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Japan is a chain of islands and that rice grows in flooded fields called paddies._

**Granny**: You’ll be stopping with me for the summer. Good.  
**Granny**: The girls will call me obaa-chan, and you may as well.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words from other languages: obaa-chan means granny  
> _Granny says her name for the summer is obaa-chan. It means “granny”, and people use it for any older woman they are fond of._  
> - ✅ It is a loving name for an older woman, whether or not she is your own granny. → Yes. In Japan the word is a mark of affection as well as family.
> - It is a kind of rice. → A good guess, with all those rice fields! But no. Obaa-chan means granny, and it is used for any older woman you love.
> - It is the name of the bus. → Not quite. The bus is only a bus. Obaa-chan means granny, a loving name for an older woman.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that obaa-chan is a Japanese word for granny, used for any older woman you are fond of._

_A boy in a vest sits on the fence, pretending not to look at you. He is looking._  
**Granny**: That’s Kanta, my grandson. Say hello, Kanta.  
**Kanta**: …lo.  
_Down the road comes a small lorry piled with furniture. Two girls ride in the back, waving at everything._  

**Choices**

- **Wave back.**
    - You wave. The smaller girl waves with both arms, so hard she nearly falls out, and the bigger one grabs her dress.
- **Ask Granny who they are.**
    - **Granny**: The new family for the old house. A professor and his two girls.
    - **Granny**: Their mother’s in hospital over the hill.
- **Ask Kanta who they are.**
    - **Kanta**: Dunno.
    - He knows. He watches the lorry to the turning, and goes red when you notice.

#### `a17-01-road-done`

**Granny**: Go on, then. They’ll want hands for all that.  
**Granny**: I’ll have supper on.  
_The lorry is a small, rattling thing with three wheels, one at the front and two at the back._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: 2 groups of 3 make 6  
> _This little lorry has 3 wheels. If two lorries like it came down the road together, how many wheels would that be?_  
> - ✅ 6 wheels: two groups of 3. → Yes. 3 + 3 = 6, which is 2 × 3.
> - 5 wheels. → Let’s check: one lorry has 3 wheels, and a second lorry has 3 more. 3 + 3 = 6. Two groups of 3 make 6.
> - 9 wheels. → 9 would be three lorries. Count in threes: 3, then 6. Two lorries have 6 wheels.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups to find that two lorries with 3 wheels each have 6 wheels._

_Your Nubbin is already trotting after it, in the dust._  
_A cloud of cicadas lifts from the hedge as it passes, and settles again behind it._  

#### `a17-01-unload`

_The old house sits back from the road behind a hedge: a wooden house, a little tall, with a porch at one side._  
_A man in round glasses lifts a chest off the lorry. He hands you the other end as if he’d been expecting you._  
**Mr Kusakabe**: Oh, hello! Are you from next door?  
**Mr Kusakabe**: Wonderful. Mind the step, it bites.  
_At the step everybody slips their shoes off and lines them up. Your Nubbin has no shoes, but it waits anyway._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): taking shoes off at the step keeps floors clean and shows respect  
> _In Japan, shoes come off in the entrance hall, called the genkan, and stay there._  
> _Many floors are for sitting and sleeping on, so keeping them clean is a way of being considerate._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that taking shoes off at the genkan is an everyday custom that keeps floors clean and shows consideration._

**Satsuki**: Mei! The porch post is rotten!  
**Satsuki**: Look, it wobbles!  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, ask): why the porch post is rotten: fungi break down damp wood slowly  
> _The porch post is rotten and wobbly. What most likely made it so?_  
> - ✅ Years of damp, which let fungi slowly break the wood down. → Yes. Rot is slow. A damp post that nobody has mended for years is perfect for fungi.
> - The girls pushing it for a minute. → A push can make a rotten post wobble, but it was already weak. The weakness came slowly, from damp and fungi.
> - It was built wobbly. → Possibly, but a sound post of good wood does not go wobbly on its own. Slow rot from damp and fungi is the usual cause.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wood rots slowly when it stays damp, because fungi break it down._

**Mei**: It’s rotten! It’s going to fall down!  
_They push the post together, shrieking, and run off. Something drops off the porch roof and bounces at your feet: an acorn._  
**Mei**: Acorns! Onee-chan, there are acorns!  
_There are no oaks anywhere near the house. Your Nubbin looks up at the roof, and keeps looking._  

**Choices**

- **Put the acorn in your pocket.**
    - It sits in your pocket all afternoon, small and smooth. Every so often you check it is still there.
- **Give it to Mei.**
    - **Mei**: Thank you! Now I’ve got two.
    - She puts both in her pocket and looks up at the roof, the same way your Nubbin does.
- **Leave it where it fell.**
    - You leave it on the step. When you come back with the next box, it has gone.
