_The Tsar puts on one of the shirts, and then sends for the seamstress. He wants to see who made such things with her two hands._  
**Vasilisa**: Me? At the palace? Like this?  
**The Old Woman**: Like that. Wash your face. It’s a very good face.  
_You walk her there. On the steps she stops and puts her hand in her pocket, and takes it out again, steadier._  
_The Tsar looks at Vasilisa, and goes on looking, and forgets entirely what he meant to say._  
**The Tsar**: You made these? All of them?  
**Vasilisa**: Yes, Majesty. With help.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty and sharing credit  
> _Vasilisa says “With help.” Why is that an honest and generous thing to say?_  
> - ✅ It is true, and it shares the credit → Yes. She could have claimed all the praise, but she tells the truth about the help she had. Honesty and generosity often go together.
> - It makes the shirts look better → The shirts are the same either way. Her words are about telling the truth.
> - It makes the Tsar feel sorry for her → She isn’t asking for pity. She is being truthful about who helped.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about honesty and sharing credit: saying who helped is true and generous._

**The Tsar**: Then I don’t want to let you go. Not today, and I’d like it to be not ever. Would you mind that very much?  
_Vasilisa looks at you, and you look at her. She doesn’t need anybody to tell her what to say._  
**Vasilisa**: I wouldn’t mind it at all.  

**Choices**

- **Cheer, out loud, in a palace.**
    - You cheer. Your Nubbin cheers in its own way, which is to run round the throne room twice.
- **Just squeeze her hand.**
    - You squeeze her hand. She squeezes back so hard it hurts, and laughs.

#### `a18-16-tsar-done`

_They are married within the month. Bells ring, somebody throws grain, and your Nubbin eats a good deal of it._  
_The biggest bell in the tower gives a deep note, and the smallest rings high and bright._  

> **Lesson** (music, 1-PS4-1, ask): bigger bells make lower notes  
> _The biggest bell gives the deepest note. Why?_  
> - ✅ Bigger bells vibrate more slowly, and slower vibrations make lower notes → Yes. A big bell shakes slowly, so its note is deep, and a small bell shakes quickly, so its note is high. Pitch depends on the speed of vibration.
> - Bigger bells are simply louder → Loudness and pitch are different. A big bell can be loud, but its note is lower because it vibrates more slowly.
> - Bigger bells are heavier, so they fall asleep → Bells don’t sleep. A big bell vibrates slowly, which gives a low pitch.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that bigger bells vibrate more slowly and so sound lower._


#### `a18-16-complete`

_In the spring the merchant comes home over the hill, thinner and browner, with a sledge full of far-off things._  
**The Merchant**: Married? My Vasilisa? To whom? To the… oh. Oh, my goodness.  
_She takes him to live with her, and the old woman too, who complains about the palace stairs and is very happy._  
_Your Nubbin carries Baba Yaga’s bag of oats down the palace steps, as proudly as it carried it out of the wood._  
_Last of all, Vasilisa gives your Nubbin a painted doll no bigger than a thumb, in a pouch of its own on a cord._  
_The tale ends the way the old books end it: the little doll stayed in her pocket, always._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): the theme of a story  
> _What is the main idea, or theme, of this tale?_  
> - ✅ Caring for others, and being cared for in return, is a kind of strength → Yes. Vasilisa feeds the doll first, shares, and helps, and help returns to her at every turn. A theme is the big idea the story leaves you with.
> - Wealth always wins in the end → Money isn’t what carries Vasilisa through. What helps is care that she gives and receives.
> - Everyone should stay at home → Vasilisa travels, works and meets danger. Her strength comes from kindness, not from staying put.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the story’s theme: caring for others, and being cared for in return, is a kind of strength._

_The page settles, and you are back in the Grove with the atlas on your knee. Your Nubbin checks its pouch twice: the small painted doll is still there._  

### Glossary

- **Tsar**: The title of a ruler in old East Slavic tales, a little like a king.

## A19-1. This Is Berk

- `a19-01-s1`: Come ashore on Berk and find somewhere to sleep. · _Touch the page, then walk up the jetty to the boy counting barrels._
- `a19-01-s2`: Keep the forge fire hot while the raid goes on outside. · _Pump the bellows in time. The fire wants long, steady pushes._
- `a19-01-s3`: Help Hiccup get his home-made launcher out of the forge. · _Take one end of the launcher and wheel it out of the forge door._

#### `a19-01-arrive`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page drawn in charcoal. You blink, and you and your Nubbin are on a rocking boat in the spray._  
_Ahead, an island of cliffs and wooden houses climbs out of the sea. There are sheep on every ledge that will hold one._  
_On the jetty, a skinny boy in a fur waistcoat is counting barrels, badly, because he keeps looking at the sky._  
**Hiccup**: Welcome to Berk. It’s far to the north, it rains nearly every day, and the wind has never once stopped.  
**Hiccup**: I’m Hiccup. Yes, it’s a real name in my story. No, I didn’t pick it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Berk is invented, but the Vikings were real and settled cold islands  
> _Berk is made up, so you will not find it on a map. But the Vikings were real people._  
> _They sailed from Scandinavia in long, narrow ships, from the late 700s to the 1060s._  
> _Real Norse families settled on cold, windy islands like Shetland, the Faroes and Iceland._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Berk is invented but the Vikings were real, and that Norse families settled on cold islands such as Shetland, the Faroes and Iceland._

_A big man stumps down the jetty with a hammer in one hand and a hook where the other should be._  
**Gobber**: Iron for the forge, at last! And what’s that?  
_Your Nubbin, who has been sick twice over the side, peers up at him._  
**Gobber**: A hatchling, from the south by the look of it. No, don’t tell me. If I don’t know what it is, I don’t have to do anything about it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): working out an unknown word from the words round it  
> _Gobber calls your Nubbin a “hatchling”, and an egg hatches. What do you think a hatchling is?_  
> - ✅ A young creature that has just come out of an egg → Yes. The word hides a clue: hatch, plus -ling, which means a small young one.
> - A little door in a roof → A hatch can be a door, but Gobber is talking about your Nubbin. Think of eggs: a hatchling hatches.
> - A kind of hat → It sounds like it, but look at the clue “from the south” and the egg link. A hatchling has just hatched.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of “hatchling” from its parts and the story._


**Choices**

- **Tell him it’s a Nubbin.**
    - **Gobber**: A Nubbin. Right. Never heard of one, so it can’t be on the list of things to hit.
- **Let your Nubbin wave a wing at him.**
    - Your Nubbin waves one stubby wing. Gobber waves his hook back, gravely, as one professional to another.
- **Say nothing at all.**
    - **Hiccup**: That’s the right answer with Gobber. He likes a mystery he doesn’t have to solve.

#### `a19-01-arrive-done`

**Gobber**: You’ll want work. Everyone on Berk works, or gets eaten. There’s a loft over the forge, and bellows with nobody on them.  
**Hiccup**: Welcome to the forge. Mind the sword rack. And the axe rack. And the ceiling.  
_A forge is a workshop with a very hot fire, where a smith heats iron until it can be hammered into shape._  
_The loft is warm and smells of smoke and hot metal. Your Nubbin makes a nest in a pile of old sacks._  
_Down below, crates of iron bars wait to be unpacked._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply equal groups: 3 × 12  
> _The boat brought 3 crates of iron bars, and each crate holds 12 bars. How many bars is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 36 → Yes! Twelve, and twelve, and twelve: 12 + 12 + 12 = 36. Three groups of twelve.
> - 15 → That is 3 + 12. But there are three whole crates of twelve. Try 12 + 12 + 12.
> - 24 → That is two crates. We have three: 12 + 12 + 12 = 36.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 3 equal groups of 12 to find 36._


#### `a19-01-raid`

_You wake in the dark to horns, shouting, and a red light under the loft door that is not morning._  
_Out in the lane a roof is burning. Something with wings lifts a sheep off a wall, and the sheep looks more surprised than anyone._  
**Gobber**: Keeper! Bellows! Every axe on Berk comes back blunt by midnight, and every one of them wants an edge!  
_You pump, and the fire roars white. Your Nubbin sits on the end of the anvil, flinching at every bang from outside._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): a fire needs air to burn, and burning cannot be undone  
> _The fire roars white when you pump the bellows. What are the bellows giving the fire?_  
> - ✅ Air, which a fire needs in order to burn → Yes! Fire eats air as well as wood. Blow more in, and it burns hotter and whiter. And burnt is burnt. Ash never turns back into wood.
> - More wood → The wood is already in there. The bellows push in air, and that is what the fire is hungry for.
> - Water → Water would put the fire out. Bellows give it air.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fire needs air to burn, which is why a forge uses bellows, and that burning cannot be undone._

**Hiccup**: Sorry I’m late. I was out there, briefly. Everybody told me to come back in here, very firmly.  
**Gobber**: Because out there you’re a danger to yourself and everyone near you. In here you’re only a danger to me.  
**Hiccup**: That’s fair. That’s actually fair.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): how kindness changes the way we hear a hard truth  
> _Gobber told Hiccup a hard truth, and Hiccup said it was fair. Is a hard truth easier to hear when someone says it kindly?_  
> - Yes, kindness helps us listen → That’s a fair answer. When we feel safe, we can take in what is true, rather than defending ourselves.
> - No, the truth is the truth, however it is said → That’s a fair answer. The words matter most, but how they are said can decide whether we are able to hear them.
> - It depends on the person → That’s a fair answer. People do differ, and a good friend learns how each person likes to be told.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a hard truth is easier to hear when it is said kindly._

_Vikings run in with blunt axes and run out with sharp ones. Nobody looks at Hiccup, except to step round him._  

#### `a19-01-raid-done`

_By the end your arms are jelly. Your Nubbin has fallen asleep on the anvil, which nobody else on Berk could do._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, notice): tired muscles need rest, food and water to recover  
> _Your arms feel like jelly because your muscles have used up the energy stored in them._  
> _Rest, water and food let them recover. Each time you work them, they get a little stronger._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why muscles feel tired after hard work and that rest, food and water help them recover._

**Gobber**: Not bad, for the help. Hiccup, stay here. Stay. Here.  
_Hiccup holds up his hands. They are black with soot to the elbow._  
**Hiccup**: I am staying. Look. Staying very hard.  
_Outside the horns stop. The raid is over, and the village begins to count what is missing._  

#### `a19-01-launcher`

_The moment Gobber is out of the door, Hiccup is under his workbench, pulling a sheet off something with wheels._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): wheels roll, so there is less rubbing than dragging  
> _Drag something heavy along the ground and friction rubs against it the whole way._  
> _A wheel rolls instead of rubbing, so the same load is much easier to move._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wheels reduce friction, which makes heavy loads easier to move._

_It is a wooden frame with a crank, and three stones tied together on ropes, packed into its jaws like peas in a pod._  
**Hiccup**: Bola launcher. I made it. The ropes wrap round the wings, the dragon comes down, and I stop being… whatever they call me.  
**You**: What do they call you?  
**Hiccup**: Mostly they don’t. That’s the problem.  
**Hiccup**: It needs to go up on the cliff. It’s heavy, it’s badly balanced, and it will probably go off on the way.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what makes it easier to ask for help  
> _Hiccup needs help carrying something heavy, but he finds it hard to ask. What helps someone ask?_  
> - ✅ Knowing a friend will say yes and not laugh → That’s it. It’s the laughing I’m afraid of, more than the asking.
> - Pretending you need nothing → I’ve tried that. You end up carrying everything alone, and it’s heavier than it looks.
> - Doing it all by yourself → Sometimes that works. Not with a launcher. It has opinions.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes it easier to ask for help: a friend who says yes and does not laugh._

_Your Nubbin, awake now, looks at the launcher, then at the open door, then at you._  

**Choices**

- **Take the back end.**
    - You take the back end. It is heavier than it looks, and it creaks in a way that sounds like a warning.
    - **Hiccup**: Thank you. Nobody ever takes the back end.
- **Gobber said to stay here.**
    - **Hiccup**: Gobber also says the soup is fish. It isn’t always fish.
    - He starts pushing it out on his own. You find you have taken the back end anyway.

#### `a19-01-launcher-done`

_Out into the lane you go, past a burning cart and a Viking chasing his own helmet down the hill._  
_The launcher wobbles at every stone. One wheel squeaks like a mouse being stepped on._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile tells us  
> _“One wheel squeaks like a mouse being stepped on.” What does this comparison tell you about the squeak?_  
> - ✅ That it is thin, high and a little pitiful → Yes. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”, and picks the part that matters: the small, high, pitiful sound.
> - That the wheel is very small → Not quite. The comparison is about the sound, not the size of the wheel.
> - That there is a real mouse under the wheel → Ha, no! A simile says one thing is like another, so the squeak is only like a squashed mouse.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a simile says about a sound._

**Hiccup**: Left! Your left! It likes to go left. It’s got opinions.  
_Your Nubbin rides on top, holding on with both paws, looking at the sky._  
_Behind you, the shouting of the raid is a long way off, and getting longer._  

#### `a19-01-complete`

_You get the launcher up the slope behind the forge, to a lip of rock over the dark sea._  
**Hiccup**: There. Now we wait for the one nobody sees.  
_Hiccup kneels behind the crank. His hands are shaking a little, but he holds them still on purpose._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): slow breathing helps when we are nervous  
> _Nerves are a body alarm: the heart races, the hands shake, the breath goes short._  
> _Slow breaths tell the alarm to quieten. Try in for four counts and out for six, a few times._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nerves are a body alarm and that slow breathing, with a longer breath out, helps it calm._

**Hiccup**: If I hit it, they’ll have to look at me. That’s all I want. One look.  
_Out over the water, very high, something screams like tearing cloth._  
_Hiccup breathes in slowly, and out. Whatever comes next, he is going to meet it with steady hands._  

### Glossary

- **hatchling**: A baby animal that has just come out of its egg.
- **jetty**: A small pier of wood or stone that sticks out into the water, where boats tie up.
- **bellows**: A squeezable bag or pump that blows air onto a fire to make it hotter.
- **anvil**: A heavy block of iron that a smith hammers hot metal on.
- **bola**: A set of weighted ropes thrown to tangle up an animal.
- **crank**: A handle you turn round to make a machine work.

## A19-2. The Night Fury

- `a19-02-s1`: Watch the sky with Hiccup, and see where the shot goes. · _Stay by the launcher on the cliff and keep your eyes on the stars._
- `a19-02-s2`: Get Hiccup down to the village in one piece. · _Run for the torch posts in the square and keep behind them._
- `a19-02-s3`: Stand by Hiccup while he tells his father. · _Stay with Hiccup in the square while Stoick listens, or doesn’t._

#### `a19-02-shot`

_Below, a tower of torches burns, and Vikings throw everything they have at the sky._  
_Then there is that sound again, a high rising whistle, and a tower bursts apart in blue-white fire._  
**Hiccup**: That’s it. That’s the one. It never steals, never shows itself, never misses.  
_You look up and see nothing but stars. Then not stars, where something black has crossed in front of them._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): stars are far-away suns, and the Pole Star stays still in the north  
> _Stars are suns, very far away. We only see them at night because the daytime sky is too bright._  
> _Sailors long ago steered by them. In the north, the Pole Star stays almost still while the other stars wheel around it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stars are distant suns, and that sailors in the north steered by the Pole Star._

**Hiccup**: Come on. Give me something. Anything to aim at.  
_The whistle comes again. Hiccup sees the flash, swings the launcher round, and pulls._  
_The bola spins up into the dark. Far out there is a shriek, and a shape tumbles out of the sky behind the ridge._  
**Hiccup**: I hit it. I hit it! Did anybody see that?  
_Down in the village, nobody did. Your Nubbin did, and so did you._  

**Choices**

- **Tell him you saw it.**
    - **Hiccup**: You saw it. Somebody saw it. Right. Good. I’m not mad.
- **Point to where it fell.**
    - You point at the dark ridge. Hiccup lines up your arm with his eye and learns the spot like a map.
- **Ask if he’s sure.**
    - **Hiccup**: No. Yes. It fell. Things don’t fall like that unless something has gone wrong with them.

#### `a19-02-shot-done`

_Behind you, a wooden stake snaps. Something large has landed on the cliff, and it is not black, and it is very awake._  
_It is long and red, with a crest of spikes down its back, and it breathes out a long, low, rumbling sigh._  
**Hiccup**: Ah. Not the one I was hoping for.  
_The rumble shakes the stones under your feet. Your Nubbin’s ears flatten._  

> **Lesson** (music, 4-PS3-2, ask): faster vibrations make a higher sound  
> _The Night Fury’s whistle was high and thin, and this dragon’s rumble is low. Which sound has the faster vibration?_  
> - ✅ The high whistle → Yes. The faster something vibrates, the higher the note: a whistle wiggles the air very fast, and a rumble slowly.
> - The low rumble → Not quite. A low sound is a slow wobble, and the high whistle is the fast one.
> - They vibrate at the same speed → If they did, they would sound the same. The whistle is higher because it vibrates faster.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that faster vibrations make a higher pitch, comparing a whistle and a rumble._

_The Nightmare breathes in, and the air round its jaws begins to glow._  

#### `a19-02-chase`

_It is a Monstrous Nightmare. It heaves the rest of itself over the lip of the cliff, on fire along its whole back._  
**Hiccup**: Ah. Not that one. Run. Running would be good.  
_You run, all three of you, down the slope, with the heat of it on your neck. Your Nubbin runs through Hiccup’s legs, twice._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, notice): the heart beats faster to feed the muscles when we run  
> _When you run, your heart beats faster. It pumps blood, and blood carries oxygen to your leg muscles._  
> _After you stop, it takes a few minutes for your heart and breathing to slow down again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the heart beats faster during exercise to carry oxygen to the muscles._

**Hiccup**: Left! No, other left! Behind the torch post!  
_You throw yourselves behind a torch post. The fire splits round it, and the wood begins to smoke._  
_Then a man the size of a door steps out and meets the Nightmare with nothing but his shoulder and a roar._  
_The Nightmare thinks about it, and goes. Above it, the last of the raid goes too, with half the village’s sheep._  

#### `a19-02-chase-done`

**Stoick**: Hiccup.  
**Hiccup**: Hi, Dad.  
_Stoick the Vast is the chief of Berk. He is very large, very tired, and covered in soot._  
_Hiccup’s shoulders have gone up round his ears. He is trying to look like a person who has done nothing at all._  
_Neither of them says anything else, which says quite a lot._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading what silence shows about characters  
> _Neither of them says any more, “which says quite a lot”. What can the silence tell us?_  
> - ✅ That both of them feel awkward and worried → Yes. What characters do not say can show their feelings as clearly as what they do say.
> - That they have nothing to say → Look at Hiccup’s shoulders. A person with nothing to say would not look so tense.
> - That they are about to sing → Ha, not on Berk! The silence is full of feelings, not songs.
> _For grown-ups: Read what a silence between two characters shows about how they feel._


#### `a19-02-nobody`

**Hiccup**: I hit a Night Fury. Up on the cliff. It came down past the ridge, you could send someone to…  
**Stoick**: Stop. Every time you step outside, something gets broken. Tonight it was a torch post and the fish store.  
**Stoick**: I’ve a village to feed, and the winter coming, and the dragons have had the sheep.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, notice): scarcity means people must choose how to use limited food and time  
> _Stoick has only so much food, so many sheep and so many hours before winter._  
> _When there is not enough of something to go round, people have to choose. That is what scarcity means._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that scarcity means there is not enough to go round, so people have to choose._

**Hiccup**: I know what I saw.  
_Behind Stoick, a few Vikings are laughing: not loudly, just enough._  
**Stoick**: Gobber, see him home. And who’s this?  
**Gobber**: The new help, Stoick. Good arms. The small one’s some sort of hatchling. Southern. Harmless.  
_Stoick looks at you, then at your Nubbin, and decides he has no room in his head for either of you tonight._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): whether being busy excuses not listening  
> _Stoick has a village to feed and little time. Is that a good reason not to listen to his son?_  
> - Being busy is a reason, but not an excuse → That’s a fair answer. Everyone is busy sometimes, but listening for a minute can cost very little.
> - A leader must put the whole village first → That’s a fair answer. A chief has many people to look after, though his son is one of them.
> - It depends how important what Hiccup says is → That’s a fair answer. It is hard to know what is important until you have listened.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being busy is a good reason not to listen to someone._


**Choices**

- **Say you saw it too.**
    - **Stoick**: Then you were both looking at the dark. It’s easy to see things in the dark.
    - He isn’t unkind about it. He just has no room for it tonight.
- **Say nothing. Stand next to Hiccup.**
    - You say nothing. You stand next to Hiccup, close enough that he can tell.
    - **Hiccup**: Thanks.

#### `a19-02-complete`

_Gobber walks you both back to the forge, and leaves you at the door with a look that means stay put this time._  
**Hiccup**: He thinks I’m a joke. They all do. I’ll find it tomorrow. I’ll find it, and I’ll…  
_He doesn’t finish. He goes up to his corner and draws by candlelight for a long time instead._  
_From the loft you can hear the charcoal scratching. It sounds like someone trying to remember exactly what he saw._  

> **Lesson** (art, 2-PS1-1, notice): drawing helps us notice details, and soft charcoal suits shadows  
> _Artists draw to see. When you draw something slowly, you notice shapes, shadows and tiny details you missed._  
> _Each material suits a job. Soft charcoal makes dark, smudgy shadows, and a hard pencil makes fine lines._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that careful drawing helps us notice details, and that soft charcoal suits shadows._

_Charcoal is made by burning wood with very little air, so it comes out black and light, and draws a soft, smudgy line._  

### Glossary

- **ridge**: A long, narrow strip of high ground along the top of a hill.
- **scarcity**: When there is not enough of something to go round, so people have to choose.

## A19-3. The Fleet Sails

- `a19-03-s1`: Go up to the Great Hall and hear what the chief has decided. · _The Great Hall is at the top of the village. Stand near the back._
- `a19-03-s2`: Help load the fleet before it sails. · _Carry stores from the fish sheds down to the ships on the jetty._
- `a19-03-s3`: Look at what Hiccup has been drawing. · _His notebook is open on the forge bench while he fetches charcoal._

#### `a19-03-hall`

_In the morning the Great Hall smells of smoke and wet wool. Stoick stands at the head of the long table with a map._  
**Stoick**: The nest. Find it, and the raids stop. I’m taking the ships out one more time, before the ice.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 2-ESS2-2, ask): compass directions: the way home is opposite to the way out  
> _The nest is far to the north. If the ships sail north to find it, which way must they sail to come home?_  
> - ✅ South → Yes. South is the opposite of north, so sailing home means heading back the way you came.
> - North → If they keep sailing north, they will go further from home. Home is the opposite way: south.
> - East → East is sideways to north. To come straight back, they sail the opposite direction: south.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions: the way back from a journey north is south._

_Nobody cheers. The last time the ships went out, fewer came back._  
**Stoick**: I want every ship. Gobber stays. Somebody has to train the young ones.  
**Gobber**: And Hiccup?  
_Stoick looks down the table at his son, who is trying to be very small behind a jug._  
**Stoick**: Hiccup trains with the rest. It’s time.  
**Hiccup**: Dad, I really don’t think that…  
**Stoick**: You’ll have an axe. You’ll have Gobber. You’ll learn. That’s the end of it.  

#### `a19-03-hall-done`

**Gobber**: Dragon training, then. Morning, in the arena. Bring the lad.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words with more than one meaning: train  
> _Stoick said somebody must “train the young ones”, and “train” can also mean a vehicle on rails. Which does Stoick mean?_  
> - ✅ To teach and practise → Yes, and Vikings had no railways! Here, “train” means to teach someone and let them practise.
> - A vehicle on rails → That meaning exists, but there were no trains in Viking times. Stoick means to teach and practise.
> _For grown-ups: Used the story to choose the right meaning of the multiple-meaning word “train”._

**Gobber**: Bring the hatchling, too. It can learn what not to be.  
_Gobber winks at your Nubbin, who salutes him with one stubby wing._  
_The arena is a deep stone pit behind the Great Hall, roofed over with iron chains._  
_Hiccup groans, softly, into the jug._  

#### `a19-03-docks`

_All day you carry stores down to the jetty: barrels of salt fish, coils of rope, shields stacked like plates._  
_Four ships are being loaded. Each takes twelve barrels of fish and eight coils of rope._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 4 × 12  
> _Four ships each take 12 barrels of fish. How many barrels is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 48 → Yes! 4 × 12 is ten barrels each (40) and two each (8 more), so 40 + 8 = 48.
> - 16 → That is 4 + 12. We need four groups of twelve: 12 + 12 + 12 + 12.
> - 44 → Close. Try 4 × 10 = 40 and 4 × 2 = 8, then add: 40 + 8.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 groups of 12 to find 48 barrels._

_Your Nubbin carries one oar, end first, with tremendous seriousness. It takes most of the afternoon._  
_Hiccup comes down to the jetty at the last minute. His father is checking a rope that does not need checking._  
**Stoick**: Gobber will teach you. Listen to him.  
**Hiccup**: I will.  
**Stoick**: Good.  
_That seems to be everything. Then Stoick puts one great hand on Hiccup’s head, quickly, as if it might be seen, and goes aboard._  
_The ships go out on the grey tide. Hiccup watches until he cannot tell which sail is which._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): a hollow ship floats because it pushes aside enough water  
> _A big wooden ship floats because it is hollow, so it is full of air and light for its size._  
> _Water pushes up on it. A ship floats as long as it pushes aside water that weighs as much as the ship does._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why a large, hollow ship floats._


**Choices**

- **Wave the ships off.**
    - You wave. Your Nubbin waves its oar, which nearly takes Hiccup’s ear off.
- **Stand with Hiccup until the sails are gone.**
    - You stand with him until there is nothing left to watch but grey water.

#### `a19-03-docks-done`

**Hiccup**: He used to do that when I was little. The hand. I’d forgotten.  
_Hiccup is quiet for a moment, still looking at the water._  
_Stoick is not a man for speeches. He shows he cares with things he does, not things he says._  
**Hiccup**: He never said “be careful”. He just checked the rope.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): seeing care in what people do, not only in what they say  
> _Stoick checked a rope that did not need checking, and gave a quick pat. What might that really be saying?_  
> - ✅ That he cares, even though he finds it hard to say → Yes. Some people show love through small actions, because the words feel too big.
> - That he thinks Hiccup is a nuisance → Look at the pat. People who find us a nuisance do not touch our heads gently.
> - That the rope was loose → The story says it did not need checking. The rope was an excuse to stay a little longer.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s small actions to see how much he cares._

_Your Nubbin leans its whole round weight against Hiccup’s leg, and he rests a hand on its head, without noticing._  

#### `a19-03-notebook`

_That night at the forge, Hiccup leaves his notebook open on the bench while he fetches more charcoal._  
_Every page is a dragon: wings, teeth, fire. Next to each one, in small neat letters, is how to bring it down._  
_Gronckle: hit it under the jaw; Nadder: stay out of its blind spot; Nightmare: don’t._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): a blind spot is a place an animal cannot see  
> _A blind spot is a place an animal cannot see. Horses and rabbits have eyes on the sides of their heads._  
> _They see almost all the way round, but miss a patch straight ahead and straight behind._  
> _Hunters like cats have eyes at the front. They see a smaller area, but judge distance very well._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about animals’ blind spots and how eye position affects what they see._

_The last page has nothing drawn on it at all. Just two words at the top: Night Fury._  
**Hiccup**: Nobody’s ever seen one. So nobody can draw it. So nobody knows how to bring one down.  
**Hiccup**: Which means, if somebody did…  
_The drawings are very good. The eyes are drawn with a kind of care you do not usually give to something you want to hurt._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether you can study something carefully and still want to hurt it  
> _Hiccup draws each dragon with great care, yet writes how to defeat it. Can you study something closely and still want to hurt it?_  
> - Looking closely often makes you care → That’s a fair answer. When we really look at a living thing, it can stop feeling like an enemy.
> - You can study something and still be afraid of it → That’s a fair answer. Fear and curiosity can sit side by side.
> - The drawings and the notes say two different things about Hiccup → That’s a fair answer. A character can pull in two directions at once, and that is what makes him interesting.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether careful study of something can change how we feel about it._


**Choices**

- **Ask why the page is still empty.**
    - **Hiccup**: Because I didn’t see it properly. Just the shape. I want to get it right.
    - He says it like an artist, not a hunter. He doesn’t notice that.
- **Ask what he’ll do if he finds it.**
    - **Hiccup**: Finish it, obviously. Bring it home. Be somebody.
    - He says it fast, the way you say a thing you have practised in the dark.
- **Say his drawings are good.**
    - **Hiccup**: They’re for killing things. They’re not supposed to be good.
    - But he looks at the Gronckle for a moment, as if he might fix the eye.

#### `a19-03-complete`

**Hiccup**: The ridge. Where it fell. I’m going out there tomorrow, before training.  
**Hiccup**: Are you coming? You don’t have to. It’s probably dead. Or very angry.  
_Your Nubbin is already at the door. It doesn’t know where you are going, but it likes going._  
_Training starts at six. The ridge is forty minutes’ walk away, and forty minutes back._  
**Hiccup**: I want twenty minutes there, to look. So: forty, twenty, forty…  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): adding time intervals and counting back from a time  
> _Add up the minutes, then count back from six o’clock. When must Hiccup set off to be at the arena at six?_  
> - ✅ 4:20 → Yes! 40 + 20 + 40 = 100 minutes, which is 1 hour 40 minutes. Six o’clock take away 1 hour 40 is 4:20.
> - 5:20 → That is only 40 minutes before six. We need the whole 100 minutes: 1 hour 40 minutes. That makes 4:20.
> - 4:00 → That is two hours, which is more than we need. 100 minutes is 1 hour 40, so 4:20.
> _For grown-ups: Added time intervals (40 + 20 + 40 = 100 minutes) and counted back from six o’clock to 4:20._


### Glossary

- **arena**: A place with a flat floor surrounded by walls, where contests or shows happen.
- **blind spot**: A place that a person or animal cannot see.

## A19-4. The Bound Dragon

- `a19-04-s1`: Search the woods behind the ridge for whatever fell. · _Follow Hiccup’s map. Look for broken trees._
- `a19-04-s2`: Stay with Hiccup while he faces what he brought down. · _Keep back at the top of the rise and watch._
- `a19-04-s3`: Walk back to the village with Hiccup. · _Take the long way round, through the woods, to the arena._

#### `a19-04-woods`

_The woods behind the ridge are dripping and grey. Hiccup has a map with crosses on, and every cross is crossed out._  
**Hiccup**: Nothing. Nothing. Nothing. Some people lose a knife, or a shoe. I lose a whole dragon.  
_He shoves a branch out of the way and it swings back and hits him. Your Nubbin ducks it neatly._  
_Then you all stop. Ahead, a pine is snapped clean in half, and beyond it the earth is torn up in a long dark furrow._  
**Hiccup**: That’s… that’s it. That’s where it came down.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-2, notice): evidence is what we see; an inference is what we work out from it  
> _A scientist keeps what she sees separate from what she thinks it means._  
> _Hiccup sees a pine snapped and the earth torn up by something big. That is evidence._  
> _He works out that something heavy came down here fast. That is an inference: a good guess, built on the evidence._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the difference between evidence (what you observe) and an inference (what you work out from it)._

_The furrow runs over the crest of a little rise. Something is breathing on the other side of it._  

#### `a19-04-bound`

_At the bottom of the rise lies a dragon, black as wet slate, tangled in Hiccup’s ropes from nose to tail._  
_It is long and lean, the size of a big horse, and it is not moving._  
**Hiccup**: I did it. I actually… I brought down a Night Fury.  
_He takes the knife out of his belt and holds it up in front of him with both hands._  
**Hiccup**: Right. I’m a Viking. This is what Vikings do. This is the whole point of me.  
_The dragon opens one eye. It is green and round, and it looks at him, and then it closes, as if it is too tired to watch._  
_Hiccup stands there a long time. The knife goes up a little, and down a little, and nowhere at all._  
**Hiccup**: I can’t. I did this. I did this to you.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): working out a character’s motive  
> _Hiccup raises the knife and cannot use it. Why do you think he cannot?_  
> - The dragon looks tired and frightened, like him → That’s a fair answer. Seeing our own feelings in someone else can stop us hurting them.
> - He is not a very good Viking → That’s a fair answer. But notice that he is not failing at something he wants: he does not want to do it.
> - He did something he regrets and wants to put it right → That’s a fair answer. Cutting the ropes is a way of mending what he did.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about a character’s motive for not doing what he expected to do._

_He cuts the ropes instead, all of them, fast, before he can change his mind._  
_The dragon is up in a black rush. It pins him against a rock with one foot and roars in his face, then crashes away through the trees._  
_Your Nubbin has bolted behind a stump. It is shaking all over, and its ball has gone dark and small._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): fear is catching, and so is calm  
> _Fear is catching, and so is calm. A frightened creature settles best near someone gentle who is not in a hurry._  
> _There is no wrong way to be frightened. Your Nubbin only needs to know that it is safe._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a frightened creature settles best near someone gentle and calm._


**Choices**

- **Scoop your Nubbin up and run.**
    - You scoop it up and run. It is so frightened that its claws go through your sleeve.
    - At the edge of the trees you stop, out of breath. You are holding it too tight, and it is holding you too tight back.
- **Crouch where you are, and let it come to you.**
    - You crouch down in the wet bracken, and you don’t reach for it. You put one hand flat on the ground, and wait.
    - It takes a long time. Then a small shaking shape comes out from behind the stump and pushes hard against your knee.

#### `a19-04-bound-done`

_Hiccup sits up. He looks at the knife in his hand as if somebody else had been holding it._  
**Hiccup**: I couldn’t. Why couldn’t I?  
_His hands are shaking and his heart is going like a drum. That is his body’s alarm, still ringing after the danger has gone._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): a big fright makes the body shake and the heart pound, and it fades  
> _After a big fright, the body releases a rush of chemicals that get you ready to run or fight._  
> _Shaking and a thumping heart are normal. They fade after a few minutes, once your body knows you are safe._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shaking and a pounding heart after a fright are normal and fade once we feel safe._

_Slowly, minute by minute, it quiets. He breathes out, long and shaky._  
**Hiccup**: I’m all right. I think I’m all right.  

#### `a19-04-walk`

_You walk back to the village together, the long way round, without a lot to say._  
**Hiccup**: Don’t tell Gobber. Or anyone. They’ll want to know why I didn’t, and I don’t…  
_He stops in the path. Your Nubbin stops too, and looks up at him._  
**Hiccup**: I don’t know why I didn’t.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): good secrets and worrying secrets  
> _Hiccup asks you to keep a secret. Which kind of secret should you always tell a trusted adult?_  
> - ✅ One that makes you or someone else feel unsafe or worried → Yes. A secret that worries you is a secret to share with a grown-up you trust, even if you promised.
> - A surprise party for a friend → A surprise party is a happy secret, and fine to keep. It ends in a smile.
> - What you are giving someone for their birthday → That is a happy surprise, and fine to keep. A worrying secret is the kind to tell.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the difference between a happy surprise and a worrying secret, and to tell a trusted adult about the second kind._

_Down in the village, the arena horn is blowing for the first day of training._  
**Hiccup**: Oh, good. Brilliant. My favourite. Let’s go and get set on fire.  

**Choices**

- **Promise you won’t tell.**
    - **Hiccup**: Thanks. Really.
    - It is the first secret anyone on Berk has trusted you with. You carry it carefully all day.
- **Ask him why he didn’t.**
    - **Hiccup**: I don’t know. I’ll tell you when I know. Is that all right?
    - You say it is. It turns out to be a promise, too.

#### `a19-04-complete`

_Hiccup goes ahead to the arena with his shoulders up round his ears._  
_You follow, slower. Your Nubbin walks close beside you, and every few steps it checks that you are still there._  
_Far behind you in the woods, something crashes down through the branches, and goes quiet._  
_Many young animals do the same as your Nubbin. A duckling follows its mother in a line, and a lamb stays near its ewe._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): young animals stay close to a safe grown-up and learn from them  
> _Young animals stay near a parent or a safe grown-up. Close by, they are fed, kept warm and watched over._  
> _They also learn from them: what to eat, where to go, and what to be afraid of._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that young animals stay close to a safe adult, who feeds them, protects them and teaches them._

_Staying close to someone safe is how the young learn what is safe._  

### Glossary

- **furrow**: A long, narrow trench in the ground.
- **inference**: A good guess you work out from the evidence you can see.

## A19-5. Dragon Training

- `a19-05-s1`: Report to the arena for dragon training. · _The arena is the stone pit with the chain roof. Go in by the big gate._
- `a19-05-s2`: Hand out the shields before the Gronckle gets loose. · _Run the shields round to each trainee. There are fewer shields than people._
- `a19-05-s3`: Watch the round play out, and stay ready to help. · _Keep by the wall near the gate, where Gobber can reach._

#### `a19-05-arena`

_The arena is a stone pit with a roof of chains, and doors round the edge with things breathing behind them._  
**Gobber**: Right! Dragon training! Lesson one: everything in here wants to eat you. Lesson two: let it try somebody else.  
_Five young Vikings stand in the middle. A tall girl with a braid and an axe is already in her stance._  
**Astrid**: Astrid. Stay out of my way.  
**Fishlegs**: Fishlegs. Hello! Is that a hatchling? What class is it? It isn’t like any of the classes. Does it breathe anything?  
**Snotlout**: Snotlout. Remember the name. You’ll be telling people you met me.  
**Ruffnut**: I’m Ruffnut. He’s Tuffnut.  
**Tuffnut**: I’m Tuffnut. She’s the other one.  
_Hiccup slips in at the back, late, in a helmet too big for him._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide equal groups: 6 ÷ 2  
> _Five young Vikings stand in the middle, and then Hiccup joins them. If Gobber puts them in pairs, how many pairs is that?_  
> - ✅ 3 → Yes! Six trainees make three pairs: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
> - 2 → Two pairs would be four people. There are six, so count in twos: 2, 4, 6. That is three pairs.
> - 4 → Four pairs would be eight people. Count in twos up to six: 2, 4, 6. Three pairs.
> _For grown-ups: Divided six trainees into pairs and found three pairs (6 ÷ 2 = 3)._

**Snotlout**: Hiccup’s doing training? Then I’m safe. They always go for the slowest one first.  

#### `a19-05-arena-done`

_Your Nubbin goes to the wall and does its fiercest face. A twin pats it on the head._  
**Snotlout**: That’s not fierce. That’s a bun with eyes.  
_Your Nubbin looks at him with enormous dignity._  
**Gobber**: Snotlout, you’ll find fierce isn’t a thing you announce. Now, shields.  
_You can tell a lot about the young Vikings already, just from how they said hello._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): character traits from what people say and do  
> _Snotlout said, “Remember the name,” and teased a Nubbin. Which word fits him best?_  
> - ✅ Boastful → Yes. A boastful person talks about how great they are, and Snotlout’s words show that trait.
> - Shy → A shy person hangs back and speaks quietly. Snotlout does the opposite.
> - Gentle → A gentle person is kind to small creatures. Snotlout teased your Nubbin, so “gentle” does not fit.
> _For grown-ups: Used what a character says and does to choose a word for his trait._


#### `a19-05-shields`

**Gobber**: Behind that door is a Gronckle. Before I open it, every one of you wants a shield.  
**Gobber**: Keeper, hand them out. Quick. I’m opening it in… now, really.  
_The door bangs open. Something round and brown and the size of a cart hurtles out, chewing a rock._  
**Fishlegs**: Gronckle! Heavy, slow to turn, eats stone, spits it back hot! Its wings are too small and nobody knows how it flies!  
_You run from Viking to Viking with shields under both arms. Astrid takes hers without looking; Snotlout tries to take two._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Viking round shields were made of wooden planks with an iron boss  
> _Real Viking shields were round, about 80 centimetres across, and made of wooden planks fixed together._  
> _In the middle was an iron dome called a boss, which protected the hand holding the grip behind it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what real Viking round shields were made of: wooden planks, with an iron boss in the middle._

**Ruffnut**: That one’s mine.  
**Tuffnut**: I touched it first.  
**Ruffnut**: You touched it with your face.  
_The twins tug one shield between them until the Gronckle settles it with a bang, and they both sit down._  
**Gobber**: Ruffnut, Tuffnut, you’re out!  
_There is one shield left in your arms, and two people without one._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what makes a choice fair  
> _One shield, and two people without one. What makes a choice fair?_  
> - Whoever needs it most → That’s a fair answer. Need is a good guide, though it can be hard to tell who needs it most.
> - Whoever has not had a turn yet → That’s a fair answer. Turns are a simple, even-handed rule that everyone can see.
> - Share it and take turns → That’s a fair answer. It treats both people alike, though a shield cannot protect two people at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what makes a choice fair when there is not enough for everyone._


**Choices**

- **Give it to Hiccup.**
    - Hiccup takes it. He holds it like a tray and nearly drops it, but he has it.
    - **Hiccup**: Thanks. If I die, it was a good shield.
- **Give it to Fishlegs.**
    - **Fishlegs**: Oh, thank you! Hiccup, you can stand behind me. I’m very wide.
- **Prop it by the wall, for your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin crouches behind the shield and peeps over the rim. It is the only one in the arena with a proper plan.
    - **Gobber**: Ha! The hatchling has more sense than the lot of you.

#### `a19-05-gronckle`

_One by one the Gronckle knocks them out of the game: Fishlegs, reciting, and Snotlout, showing off to Astrid._  
_Then it is only Astrid and Hiccup. Astrid is very good, and Hiccup is everywhere at once, in the wrong way._  
**Astrid**: Get out of the way!  
**Hiccup**: I’m trying! It keeps being where I go!  
_His shield goes rolling across the sand. The Gronckle backs him into the wall and opens its mouth._  
_Gobber gets his hook into its jaw just in time. The shot hits the wall a hand’s width over Hiccup’s head._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat always moves from something hot to something cooler  
> _Heat always moves from something hot to something cooler. The scorch mark is where the hot rock gave its heat to the wall._  
> _That is also why you never touch something hot. It passes its heat to you._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat moves from hot things to cooler things._

**Gobber**: Remember that, all of you. Every dragon you meet in here is dangerous. Respect it.  
_Hiccup touches the black scorch mark over his head. He is thinking of a dragon that had him pinned, and didn’t._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): making an inference about what a character is thinking  
> _Why does Hiccup think about the dragon that pinned him and did not hurt him?_  
> - ✅ It shows that not every dragon behaves the way Gobber says → Yes. Hiccup is comparing what he was told with what he saw, and they do not match.
> - He is just tired → He may be tired, but the story points to something else: a dragon that did not do what Gobber says every dragon does.
> - He enjoys being pinned → Ha, no! Look at the clue, “had him pinned, and didn’t”: he is thinking about the dragon’s surprising kindness.
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference about why a character is thinking about an earlier event._


#### `a19-05-complete`

**Astrid**: You could have got us hurt. Some of us actually want to be good at this.  
**Hiccup**: Noted. Thank you. Very useful.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): handling a hard moment calmly  
> _Hiccup has just been told off in front of everyone. What is a good way to handle a moment like that?_  
> - ✅ Take a breath, then listen for what is fair in it → Yes. A breath gives you a moment, and listening lets you keep what is true and let go of the sting.
> - Snap back at once → It feels good for a second, but it usually makes the next minute worse. A breath first is better.
> - Pretend it didn’t sting → That is understandable, but a feeling we hide often comes out later. Naming it helps.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about handling a hard moment calmly: breathe, then listen for what is fair._

_When Gobber lets them go, Hiccup doesn’t go home. He goes up into the woods, and doesn’t look back to see if you are coming._  
_Your Nubbin looks at you. You both go._  
_Astrid’s anger has a reason: she has worked hard, and Hiccup’s mess cost her the round._  

### Glossary

- **boastful**: Talking too proudly about how good you are.
- **boss**: The iron dome in the middle of a Viking shield.

## A19-6. The Cove

- `a19-06-s1`: Follow Hiccup along the dragon’s trail. · _Follow the broken branches past the furrow to a crack in the rocks._
- `a19-06-s2`: Sit at the edge of the cove and watch, without crowding it. · _Find a place further back than Hiccup and keep still._

#### `a19-06-trail`

_Hiccup goes back to the furrow, and past it, following a trail of broken branches and scratched bark._  
**Hiccup**: It went this way. It isn’t flying. It’s walking. Why is it walking?  
_The trail ends at a crack between two rocks. Hiccup squeezes through, and so do you._  
_Your Nubbin walks through without touching either side, and looks back at you both as if you were making a fuss._  
_Beyond is a cove: a deep round hollow in the rock, with a lake in the bottom and steep walls all round._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): using context to understand a word: cove  
> _A cove is a small, sheltered place. Which clue in the line tells you this one is sheltered?_  
> - ✅ Steep walls all round it → Yes, walls on every side keep out wind and waves. That is what makes a cove sheltered.
> - A lake in the bottom → A lake tells us there is water, but not that it is sheltered. Look for what surrounds it.
> - The sheep on the cliffs → The sheep are on the cliffs outside, not in the cove. Look for what surrounds the hollow.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the text to work out why a cove is called sheltered._

**Hiccup**: Nothing. Of course. Of course it’s nothing.  
_Something black shoots past the end of the lake, right below you, so fast your eyes can’t follow it._  

#### `a19-06-cove`

_The dragon is trying to fly out. It runs, beats its wings, and climbs the air for a moment._  
_Then it tips sideways and comes down hard on the stones. It tries again, and again, and comes down every time._  
**Hiccup**: Its tail. Look at its tail.  
_There are two fins at the end of its tail, like a fish’s. One is whole; where the other should be, there is a torn stub._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): tails, fins and rudders steer  
> _A fish steers with its fins, a bird with its tail feathers, and a boat with a rudder._  
> _Viking ships were steered with a big oar fixed on the right-hand side at the back. That side was the “steerboard”, which is where our word starboard comes from._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fins, tails and rudders steer, and that starboard comes from the Viking steering oar._

**Hiccup**: The ropes. That was me. It can’t steer.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what to do when your actions have hurt someone  
> _Hiccup hurt the dragon, and he feels terrible. What do you think a person should do when something they did has hurt someone?_  
> - Own up to it and try to put it right → That’s a fair answer. Hiccup is already doing it by drawing and watching.
> - Make sure it never happens again → That’s a fair answer. Learning from a mistake is part of mending it.
> - Give them time and space first → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes the hurt one needs room before they trust us again.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what to do when your actions have hurt someone._

_Hiccup sits down on a flat rock at the edge, gets out his notebook, and starts to draw it. His hand is quick and very careful._  
_You sit further back, where the dragon won’t feel crowded. Your Nubbin settles on your foot._  

**Choices**

- **Watch the dragon.**
    - It gives up on the sky and tries the lake instead, snapping at fish. It misses every one.
- **Watch Hiccup.**
    - He rubs out one line and draws it again, slower. He is getting the eye exactly right.
- **Watch your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin watches the dragon from behind your ankle, one eye at a time.

#### `a19-06-cove-done`

_The dragon looks up, straight at the rock. Hiccup drops his charcoal._  
_It rolls over the edge and down into the cove. Nobody moves to get it._  
_The slope pulls it, because gravity pulls everything downhill when nothing stops it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity pulls things down a slope  
> _Why does the charcoal roll down into the cove?_  
> - ✅ Gravity pulls it downhill → Yes, gravity pulls everything towards the ground. On a slope, nothing stops the charcoal, so it rolls.
> - The dragon pushed it → The dragon did not touch it. A force was acting on it, though: gravity.
> - It wanted to go down → A piece of charcoal has no wants. It is pulled by gravity, which acts on everything.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls things down a slope when nothing stops them._

_Hiccup holds his breath, and so do you. The dragon lowers its head and goes back to the lake._  
_A drip of water runs down the rock wall, slow as a clock._  

#### `a19-06-complete`

_It is nearly dark when you come out of the cove. Hiccup has drawn the dragon nine times._  
**Hiccup**: Here. Have this one. I got the eyes wrong. They’re not angry eyes, and I keep drawing them angry.  
_He tears out a page and gives it to you: a black dragon in charcoal, half a tail fin, and eyes that aren’t angry at all._  
_The eyes are big and round, with the lids wide open and a small bright dot of white in each._  

> **Lesson** (art, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): how drawn eyes show feeling  
> _Which drawing choices make eyes look gentle rather than angry?_  
> - ✅ Big, round, wide-open eyes with a bright highlight → Yes. Round shapes and a spark of light read as soft and alive, while low, slanted brows and narrow eyes read as angry.
> - Narrow eyes with low, slanted brows → Those are the marks that make a face look angry, which is the mistake Hiccup kept making.
> - Tiny dark dots → Dots can look blank or distant. Big round eyes with a highlight look more gentle and alive.
> _For grown-ups: Looked at how shapes and highlights in a drawing change the feeling in an eye._

_Hiccup has stopped looking at a monster and started looking at someone._  

### Glossary

- **cove**: A small, sheltered hollow or bay, with walls or land round most of its edge.
- **gravity**: The pull that makes things fall down towards the ground.

## A19-7. The Knife

- `a19-07-s1`: Carry a basket of fish to the cove. · _The basket is by the forge door. It’s heavy, and it leaks._
- `a19-07-s2`: Wait at the cove while the dragon makes up its mind. · _Stay low by the rocks, and don’t move towards it._
- `a19-07-s3`: See what the dragon does when the fish is gone. · _Keep still and keep watching Hiccup._

#### `a19-07-basket`

_Before dawn, Hiccup is at the forge filling a basket with fish: cod, salmon, a smoked eel, and something nobody can name._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Vikings preserved fish by drying, salting and smoking it  
> _Before fridges, people kept fish by drying, salting or smoking it, so it would last through the winter._  
> _Norse fishers dried cod in the cold wind until it was hard as wood. That dried fish is called stockfish, and it kept for a very long time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Norse people preserved fish by drying, salting and smoking it, including dried cod called stockfish._

**Hiccup**: It can’t catch anything down there. It must be starving. So: breakfast.  
**Gobber**: Where are you going with half my fish?  
**Hiccup**: Training! Extra training. Studying dragons. Their… eating.  
**Gobber**: Hm. Well. Bring the basket back.  
_The basket is heavy and it leaks. You carry it between you up through the wet woods, and your Nubbin follows the drips._  
_At the cove, Hiccup takes a breath, and climbs down into it._  

#### `a19-07-knife`

_Hiccup tips the basket out onto the stones. The smoked eel slides out on top._  
_The dragon comes out of the shadows low and fast, sees the eel, and jerks back hissing, as if it had been stung._  
**Hiccup**: No eel. Right. Noted.  
_Hiccup throws the eel into the lake. The dragon comes a step closer, then stops, looking at the knife on his belt._  
**Hiccup**: Oh. Oh, that.  
_Slowly, with two fingers, he lifts the knife out of his belt. The dragon’s eyes follow it all the way._  
_He throws it into the lake. It goes in with a small plop, and that is all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): many animals read slow, low movements as safe and fast movements as a threat  
> _Many animals judge whether a person is safe by how they move. Slow, low, quiet movements say: no threat here._  
> _Sudden movements and loud noises can look like danger. Keep your distance from wild animals, and ask a grown-up first._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals read slow, calm movements as safe, and to keep a distance from wild animals._

_The dragon sits back on its haunches, and the flaps on its head come up like ears. Then it eats._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): whether putting down a weapon is brave or risky  
> _Hiccup puts his knife down so the dragon can see he means no harm. Is that brave, or risky?_  
> - Brave, because he gave up his only protection → That’s a fair answer. Trust sometimes means going first, with nothing in your hands.
> - Risky, because the dragon might attack → That’s a fair answer. It was a real risk, and Hiccup took it knowing that.
> - Both at once → That’s a fair answer. Courage often feels exactly like taking a risk.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether putting down a weapon to show trust is brave, risky, or both._


**Choices**

- **Put your own hands where it can see them.**
    - You hold your hands open on your knees. The dragon glances at them, once, and goes back to its fish.
- **Look away, at the water.**
    - You look at the water. You hear it eating and nothing else, and that is better than watching.
- **Keep a hand on your Nubbin.**
    - Your hand rests on your Nubbin’s back. It is warm, and calmer than you are.

#### `a19-07-name`

_When the fish is gone, the dragon looks at Hiccup, makes a noise in its throat, and coughs half a fish up onto his knee._  
**Hiccup**: Thank you. That’s… very generous.  
_The dragon waits, looking at him. It clearly expects him to eat it._  
**Hiccup**: You want me to… Right. Yes. Fine.  
_He eats it, raw, and gags, and swallows. Your Nubbin watches with enormous respect._  
_The dragon pulls its lips back in a sort of smile. There isn’t a tooth in it, only pink gums._  
**Hiccup**: No teeth? Where did they go? There were teeth. In the woods. Lots of teeth.  
_A row of white teeth slides out, and the smile becomes rather a lot of smile. Then they fold neatly away again._  
**Hiccup**: They fold away. Toothless. I’m going to call you Toothless.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the suffix -less means without  
> _“Toothless” is “tooth” plus “-less”, which means “without”. Which word means “without fear”?_  
> - ✅ Fearless → Yes: fear plus -less means without fear. Hopeless, careless and homeless all use the same ending.
> - Fearful → Fearful has the ending -ful, which means “full of”. It means full of fear, the opposite of what we want.
> - Fearsome → Fearsome means causing fear in others. The word without fear uses -less.
> _For grown-ups: Used the suffix -less (without) to work out that “fearless” means without fear._


**Choices**

- **Laugh.**
    - You laugh, and Hiccup laughs, and Toothless looks from one of you to the other, deciding whether to be offended.
- **Keep a straight face.**
    - **Hiccup**: You’re very polite. He did just sick on me.
- **Say the name suits him.**
    - **Hiccup**: It does, doesn’t it? A Night Fury called Toothless. Nobody on Berk would believe it.

#### `a19-07-complete`

_Toothless lets you all stay till noon. He doesn’t let anyone touch him, but he doesn’t leave._  
**Hiccup**: Gobber’s going to want his basket back.  
**Hiccup**: Keep it. I’ll tell him a dragon ate it. Which is almost true.  
_You carry the empty basket home. It smells of cod for the rest of its life, and so, for a day, do you._  
_Before it went empty, the basket held 12 cod and 8 salmon. Toothless ate half the cod and 3 of the salmon._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step word problem: half of 12, then add 3  
> _Toothless ate half of the 12 cod, and 3 of the 8 salmon. How many fish did he eat altogether?_  
> - ✅ 9 → Yes! Half of 12 is 6, and 6 + 3 = 9: two steps, first the cod and then the salmon.
> - 15 → You may have added 12 and 3. But he ate only half the cod: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, then 6 + 3 = 9.
> - 11 → Close, but half of 12 is 6, not 8. So 6 + 3 = 9.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step word problem: half of 12 is 6, and 6 + 3 = 9._


### Glossary

- **stockfish**: Cod that has been dried in the cold wind until it is hard, so it keeps for a very long time.
- **suffix**: A small word-part added to the end of a word to change its meaning.

## A19-8. The Hand

- `a19-08-s1`: Watch what Toothless does with the stick. · _Stay at the edge of the sand while Toothless draws._
- `a19-08-s2`: Sit very still while Hiccup and Toothless meet. · _Don’t move. Whatever happens next isn’t yours to hurry._
- `a19-08-s3`: Let Toothless decide about your Nubbin. · _Stay where you are and let Toothless come or not, as he likes._

#### `a19-08-lines`

_By the fourth day, Toothless lets Hiccup sit nearer. By the fifth, he is curious about the charcoal._  
_Hiccup draws Toothless in the sand with a stick. Toothless watches, and then picks up a whole branch in his mouth._  
_He drags it round and round the cove in great looping lines, all over the sand._  
**Hiccup**: Is that… is that me? It’s very… bold.  
_When he has finished, Hiccup is standing in the middle of a huge scribble, with no way out that doesn’t cross a line._  
_He steps on one, and Toothless growls. He lifts his foot, and Toothless purrs._  
_So Hiccup steps carefully over each line, one at a time, all the way out, like a game whose rules nobody has explained._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): learning unwritten rules by watching and trying gently  
> _Nobody told Hiccup the rules of the game. How did he learn them?_  
> - ✅ By watching how Toothless reacted, and trying gently → Yes. When nobody tells us the rules, we watch for signals and test gently, ready to back off.
> - By guessing at random → He did not guess at random. He noticed the growl and the purr, and let them guide each step.
> - By ignoring Toothless → He did the opposite. Every step depended on watching Toothless closely.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about learning unwritten rules by watching for signals and trying gently._


**Choices**

- **Step through the lines after him.**
    - You go carefully over every line. Toothless follows you with his eyes and says nothing, which seems to be a yes.
- **Stay outside the lines.**
    - You stay where you are, outside the drawing. Toothless notices, and seems to think better of you for it.

#### `a19-08-hand`

_Hiccup comes out of the last line and finds Toothless right in front of him, closer than he has ever been._  
_Hiccup lifts his hand, slowly. Toothless pulls back his lips._  
_Hiccup stops. He doesn’t pull his hand back, and he doesn’t push it forward either._  
_Then he closes his eyes, and turns his face away, and holds his hand out in the air between them, open._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): many animals read a direct stare as a challenge  
> _Many animals take a direct stare as a challenge, a way of saying “I am watching you, and I am ready”._  
> _Turning the face away says the opposite: “I’m no threat.” It is a kind of animal manners, and it helps both sides stay calm._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals read a direct stare as a challenge, and that looking away shows calm._

_Nobody moves. A drip falls from the rock wall into the lake._  
_Then Toothless leans in, and pushes his nose into Hiccup’s palm._  
**Hiccup**: …Oh.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): whether waiting is the same as doing nothing  
> _Hiccup does nothing but hold out his hand and wait. Is waiting the same as doing nothing?_  
> - No, waiting can be a way of showing trust → That’s a fair answer. Hiccup’s waiting says: you choose, I won’t force you.
> - Yes, but sometimes doing nothing is exactly right → That’s a fair answer. Holding back can be the hardest and best thing to do.
> - It depends what you are waiting for → That’s a fair answer. Waiting for someone to feel safe is very different from waiting for nothing.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether waiting is the same as doing nothing._


#### `a19-08-near`

_Toothless takes his nose out of Hiccup’s hand and looks past him, at you, and at your Nubbin._  
**Hiccup**: He’s looking at you two. Stay still. Let him decide.  
_Toothless pads across the sand. Your Nubbin doesn’t hide: in the woods you crouched, and it came back to you._  
_Toothless lowers his great head until his nose is level with your Nubbin’s, and sniffs it, long and thorough._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): smell tells animals a lot, and many have a far better sense of smell than ours  
> _Why does Toothless sniff your Nubbin for so long?_  
> - ✅ Smell tells him a great deal about who it is → Yes. Many animals learn who you are and whether you are calm just by smell, and a dog’s nose is far keener than ours.
> - He is getting sleepy → Sleepy animals tend to yawn and settle. This is a careful, curious sniff: smell is how he is learning about your Nubbin.
> - He is counting its whiskers → Ha, no! He is using smell, the sense many animals use to say hello.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals use smell to find out who someone is, and that many have a better sense of smell than people._

_Your Nubbin sniffs back. Then, very carefully, it puts its forehead against his nose._  
**Hiccup**: Look at that. He likes it. He doesn’t like anybody.  

#### `a19-08-complete`

**Hiccup**: Did you see that? He’s nothing like the book says. Nothing.  
_Hiccup sits down hard on the sand, as if his legs have given up for a bit. He is grinning at nothing._  
**Hiccup**: The book’s got one rule for every dragon: run, or finish it. Every page. Every single one.  
**Hiccup**: Nobody ever sat still long enough to find out.  
_The story has a quiet idea in it: you only find out what something is really like by being patient, and looking._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): finding the theme of a story  
> _A theme is a story’s big idea. Which is the best theme for this quest?_  
> - ✅ Patience and careful looking can show you the truth about someone → Yes. A theme is the lesson underneath the events, and this one runs through everything Hiccup does.
> - Dragons are always dangerous → That is what the book says. The story shows it is wrong, so it can’t be the theme.
> - Fishing is hard work → Fishing appears in the story, but it isn’t the big idea underneath it.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of a story: patience and careful looking reveal the truth about someone._


### Glossary

- **theme**: The big idea underneath a story.

## A19-9. The Tail Fin

- `a19-09-s1`: Hold the lamp while Hiccup works at the forge. · _Keep the lamp steady over the bench, and quiet._
- `a19-09-s2`: Watch the first flights, and be ready to fish them out. · _Stand at the edge of the lake in the cove._
- `a19-09-s3`: Help Hiccup make a pedal, so he can steer with his foot. · _Hammer the stirrup flat at the forge anvil._

#### `a19-09-forge`

_That night Gobber snores upstairs like a slow saw. Hiccup lights one lamp and gives it to you to hold._  
**Hiccup**: Hold it there. Lower. Bit left. Perfect. Don’t move. Don’t breathe on it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): a lower light source makes longer shadows  
> _Hiccup says, “Lower.” When the lamp moves lower, what happens to the tools’ shadows on the bench?_  
> - ✅ They get longer → Yes! A low light throws long shadows, which is why shadows stretch out at sunset.
> - They get shorter → The other way round. A high light makes short shadows. A low one stretches them.
> - They disappear → They never disappear while there is light. A low lamp just stretches them out.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a lower light source makes longer shadows._

_On the bench he lays out leather, rods and a sheet of his own drawings: a tail fin made to open and close like a fan._  
_He cuts and stitches and rivets for hours. Then he starts on a second thing, a saddle, with straps for a long body._  
**Hiccup**: He can’t steer with one fin. So somebody has to steer the other one. That somebody is, unfortunately, me.  
_A board creaks overhead. The snoring stops, and Gobber’s voice comes down the stairs, thick with sleep._  
**Gobber**: Who’s there? What are you making at this hour?  
_Hiccup looks at you. You look at the saddle, which is about the size of a large dog._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when keeping something hidden is kind or harmful  
> _Hiccup wants to hide his work to keep Toothless safe. Is it ever kind to hide something, and when does hiding start to hurt?_  
> - When it protects someone from harm → That’s a fair answer. Protecting someone can be a good reason, as long as no one else is put in danger.
> - When you tell someone you trust → That’s a fair answer. A secret shared with a trusted person feels lighter and safer.
> - When it stops being a surprise and becomes a worry → That’s a fair answer. A secret that makes us anxious is one to share.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when keeping something hidden is kind and when it starts to hurt._


**Choices**

- **“It’s a saddle. For my Nubbin.”**
    - **Gobber**: A saddle. For the hatchling. Ha! Mad. Southern folk are all mad.
    - He goes back to bed. Hiccup mouths thank you, then looks at the saddle, and then, thoughtfully, at your Nubbin.
- **“It’s a new kind of shield.”**
    - **Gobber**: Looks like a saddle.
    - **Hiccup**: It’s a saddle-shaped shield. For sitting on. In battle.
    - **Gobber**: Bed. Both of you.
- **Blow out the lamp.**
    - You blow out the lamp. In the dark, Gobber grumbles about rats with hammers and goes back to bed.
    - **Hiccup**: Rats with hammers. I’ll take it.

#### `a19-09-strap`

_At the cove, Toothless sniffs the new fin, then the saddle, then Hiccup, as if Hiccup is the strangest part._  
_It takes all morning to strap it on. Toothless rolls over twice, and sits on the saddle once, on purpose._  
**Hiccup**: Right. When I pull this, the fin opens, and you can turn. I hope. In theory.  
_Hiccup climbs on, and Toothless spreads his wings. You hold your breath, and your Nubbin holds its breath too._  
_Toothless jumps, flaps once, and they rise, and turn, and fly in a perfect curve straight into the lake._  
_They come up spitting. Then they try again, and go into the lake again, slightly to the left._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add three numbers: 4 + 6 + 9  
> _On their next three tries, Toothless and Hiccup stay in the air for 4 seconds, 6 seconds and 9 seconds. How long is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 19 seconds → Yes! 4 + 6 = 10, and 10 + 9 = 19. Each try is longer than the last.
> - 18 seconds → Nearly. Add again: 4 + 6 = 10, and 10 + 9 is 19, not 18.
> - 20 seconds → Close. 4 + 6 = 10, and 10 + 9 is 19. We are one second short of twenty.
> _For grown-ups: Added 4 + 6 + 9 to make 19 seconds._


**Choices**

- **Cheer anyway.**
    - **Hiccup**: Thank you! That was nearly flying!
- **Wade in and help fish him out.**
    - You wade in to your knees and haul on the saddle strap. Toothless climbs out by himself and shakes himself all over you.
- **Keep your Nubbin out of the water.**
    - Your Nubbin very much wants to go in after them. You keep a gentle hand in front of it until it gives up.

#### `a19-09-strap-done`

**Hiccup**: He’s turning before I tell him. I need to know when he wants to turn, not just when I do.  
_Hiccup watches Toothless’s ears, tail and wings, trying to read what each one is saying._  
_A friend who cannot talk still tells you things all day: a flick of the tail, an ear going flat, a shift of weight._  
_Hiccup is learning a language with no words in it._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): reading a friend’s feelings without words  
> _How can we learn what a friend feels when they cannot say it in words?_  
> - ✅ Watch their face, body and sounds carefully → Yes, feelings show in faces, bodies and voices. Paying close attention is how we read them.
> - Wait until they tell us in words → Some friends, like Toothless, never will. Watching closely lets us understand them anyway.
> - Decide what they must feel → Guessing is risky. Watching and checking is kinder and more accurate.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about reading a friend’s feelings from their face, body and sounds._

_Your Nubbin, who speaks it fluently, sits on the saddle and says nothing._  

#### `a19-09-pedal`

_Back at the forge, Hiccup draws a pedal: a stirrup on a rod, so his foot can open the fin while his hands hold on._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): a pedal is a lever that carries a push to where the work is done  
> _A pedal is a kind of lever. You press down with your foot at one end, and a rod carries the movement along._  
> _At the far end, the fin opens. A machine can pass a push from where you are to where the work needs doing._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a pedal is a lever that passes a movement from the foot along a rod to the part that does the work._

**Hiccup**: Hammer that flat. No, flatter. Like the edge of a shovel.  
_You hammer it flat. It takes three goes and a burnt thumb, and your Nubbin brings you a bucket of water without being asked._  
**Hiccup**: Now every position means something. Down one: left. Down two: hard left. I’ll write them on a card.  
_He writes them on a scrap of leather and ties it to the saddle, where he can read it with his eyes streaming._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: hard  
> _Hiccup’s card says “Down two: hard left.” What does “hard” mean here?_  
> - ✅ Turn sharply, with force → Yes. “Hard” has many meanings, and on a steering card it means sharply, with force.
> - Difficult → “Hard” can mean difficult, but on a steering card it means a sharp turn.
> - Solid, like stone → That is another meaning of “hard”, but on a steering card it means a sharp turn.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out from context that “hard left” means a sharp turn, not a difficult or solid one._

_At the cove they go up again. Toothless turns, and Hiccup turns with him, and this time they miss the lake._  
_They go up past the rim, out over the trees and the sea, and you lose them in the light._  

#### `a19-09-pedal-done`

_They come back an hour later, wet through and wind-burnt, wearing the same grin._  
_Hiccup’s hands are red and his hair is flat. Toothless shakes himself like a dog and soaks everything within three metres._  
**Hiccup**: Cold. Brilliant. Cold. Brilliant.  
_Gobber has left a dry cloak and a bowl of hot soup by the forge, and says nothing about where they have been._  

> **Lesson** (health, 4-PS3-2, notice): wet clothes cool us faster than dry ones  
> _Wet clothes make you colder than dry ones, because water carries heat away from your body much faster than air does._  
> _That is why wet and windy is a risky mix, and why dry clothes and something warm to eat help so much._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wet clothes cool us faster than dry ones, and that dry clothes and warm food help._

_Hiccup wraps up and eats. The shaking stops._
