**Hiccup**: We flew. Him and me. Neither of us can do it on our own. That’s the whole design.  
_Toothless shoves his head under Hiccup’s arm until Hiccup falls over. Then he lies on him._  
**Hiccup**: Help. Please. He is very heavy and very pleased with himself.  
_You don’t help, and neither does your Nubbin. It is too good to interrupt._  
_A dragon with half a tail cannot steer, and a boy with no wings cannot fly. Together, they can do both._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): teamwork where each partner does what the other cannot  
> _Hiccup and Toothless each have something the other lacks. What is that kind of partnership called?_  
> - ✅ Teamwork, where each does what the other cannot → Yes. The best teams are not two of the same: each partner brings what the other is missing.
> - Showing off → They are pleased, but showing off is about being looked at. This is about needing each other.
> - A rivalry → A rivalry is a contest. Toothless and Hiccup are working together, not competing.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about teamwork in which each partner makes up for what the other cannot do._


### Glossary

- **stirrup**: A loop that holds a rider’s foot.
- **rivet**: A short metal pin hammered through two pieces to hold them together.

## A19-10. Top of the Class

- `a19-10-s1`: Watch Hiccup in the arena. · _Take your place by the gate with Gobber._
- `a19-10-s2`: Keep Hiccup’s secret while the whole village starts to watch. · _Astrid is waiting behind the arena door. Talk to her._
- `a19-10-s3`: Go down to the jetty to meet the ships. · _The fleet is coming in on the evening tide._

#### `a19-10-grass`

_Next morning in the arena, the Gronckle comes at Hiccup like a cannonball._  
_Hiccup doesn’t run. He opens his hand, and in it is a fistful of a pale grass that grows by the cove._  
_The Gronckle stops dead, sniffs it, and rolls over on its back in the sand like a puppy._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): some real plants change how animals behave, such as catnip and cats  
> _Some real plants do change how animals act. Catnip makes many cats roll, rub and purr, and some go completely silly._  
> _Hiccup has found a plant the Gronckle loves. People who work with animals learn which plants animals like, and which are harmful._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some plants, such as catnip, change how animals behave, and that animal keepers learn which plants are safe._

**Fishlegs**: What did you do? That’s not in the book! Nothing is in the book!  
**Hiccup**: I… read ahead?  
_Astrid’s axe is still up. She is not looking at the Gronckle; she is looking at Hiccup._  
**Snotlout**: Lucky. That was lucky.  

#### `a19-10-grass-done`

**Gobber**: Well! Look at that! Hiccup! Who’d have thought it?  
_Gobber claps, and his hook goes clang against his hammer._  
_Hiccup blinks at the cheering. His mouth is open, but nothing is coming out._  
**Hiccup**: I read ahead.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): what a figurative phrase means in context: read ahead  
> _Hiccup says he “read ahead”, but he has not read a book. What does he really mean?_  
> - ✅ He has found things out in the cove before anyone else → Yes. He uses a school phrase as a joke to hide that he has learned something secret, earlier than everybody.
> - He really did read a whole book in the night → There is no book. The phrase is a joke about getting ahead of the others.
> - He read the last page first → That is one way to read ahead in a book, but Hiccup is using it as a joke about the cove.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of a figurative phrase from the story._

_“Read ahead” is a joke: at school it means looking at the later pages before the rest of the class._  

#### `a19-10-eel`

_Day after day it goes the same way. Every dragon they let out, Hiccup puts down without hurting it at all._  
_A Nadder rears up over Snotlout, all spikes. Hiccup holds up a smoked eel, and it shies away like a horse from a snake._  
_A Gronckle corners Fishlegs. Hiccup scratches it under the chin, in one particular spot, and it drops flat and blissful._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): many animals have favourite spots where gentle scratching calms them  
> _Many animals, like cats, dogs and horses, have a favourite spot where scratching calms them down._  
> _It works best when the animal has chosen to come close. Animal keepers find the spots by watching for signs of enjoyment._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals have favourite spots where gentle scratching calms them, and that keepers find them by watching._

_The village starts coming to watch, and cheering. They have never cheered for Hiccup before, and he doesn’t know where to look._  
**Astrid**: Where does he go, every afternoon?  
_Astrid has caught you by the elbow behind the arena door. Her grip is strong, and she isn’t letting go._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): how a fib affects trust  
> _You could tell Astrid that Hiccup goes fishing. What would a fib like that do to her trust in you?_  
> - ✅ It wears the trust thin, if she works out the truth → Yes. Trust is built slowly and thinned quickly, and a fib gives Astrid, who already suspects, a reason to doubt you.
> - It makes the trust stronger → A fib may protect a secret for a while, but it does not build trust. Honest answers do that.
> - Nothing at all → It does something. Even a small fib teaches the other person that your words may not be reliable.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how even a small fib thins trust._


**Choices**

- **Tell her he goes fishing.**
    - **Astrid**: Fishing. Right. He can’t lift a rod.
    - She lets go. She doesn’t believe you, and she lets you see it.
- **Tell her to ask him herself.**
    - **Astrid**: I did. He said he goes for walks. Nobody goes for walks on Berk.
- **Shrug.**
    - **Astrid**: Fine. I’ll find out.
    - It isn’t a threat, exactly. It is more of a schedule.

#### `a19-10-fleet`

_The ships come home on a grey afternoon. Fewer than went out, and every one of them scorched._  
_Stoick comes up the jetty last. He found no nest; you can see it in the way he walks._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time: 12 × 60  
> _Berk is twelve days’ sail from anywhere, and a longship in light winds might make 60 km a day. How far is that in twelve days?_  
> - ✅ 720 km → Yes! 12 × 60 is 10 × 60 = 600, plus 2 × 60 = 120, and 600 + 120 = 720.
> - 72 km → That is only one tenth of the way. Twelve days is twelve lots of 60 km: 600 + 120 = 720.
> - 612 km → That is 600 + 12. But each of the twelve days adds 60, not 1: 10 × 60 + 2 × 60 = 720.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a distance, speed and time problem: 12 days at 60 km a day is 720 km._

**Gobber**: Stoick! You missed it. Your boy. He’s the best in the arena. The best I’ve ever seen.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Viking-age roofs were often turf over timber

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether praise for something you are hiding feels honest  
> _Hiccup is cheered for being good at something he is hiding. Is it fair to be praised for it, and how might it feel?_

> - It depends who he is hiding it from, and why → That’s a fair answer. Hiding something to protect a friend is not the same as hiding it to look good.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether praise feels honest when it depends on a secret._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): short sentences make a moment feel fast and urgent  
> _Astrid shouts just three words, in two short bursts. Why do short sentences suit a moment of fright?_  
> - ✅ They sound fast and urgent, like a heartbeat → Yes, short sentences speed the reader up. Long, flowing ones slow us down.
> - They use fewer letters, so they are easier to write → Length on the page is not the point. What matters is the quick rhythm the reader hears.
> - They make the scene sound sleepy → The opposite! Short sentences create a quick, urgent rhythm.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that short sentences create a fast, urgent rhythm in a frightening moment._

_She swings the axe up, and Toothless crouches to spring. Hiccup throws himself between them with his arms out._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): helping a frightened person without scaring them more  
> _Astrid is running off, frightened. What helps a frightened person without scaring them more?_  
> - ✅ Stay calm, stay where they can see you, and give them a moment to think → Yes. A frightened person calms best when someone is steady and not chasing them.
> - Block the way and shout → Blocking and shouting can feel like a threat, and make the fear bigger.
> - Chase them as fast as you can → Chasing makes a frightened person run faster. A calm presence works better.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how to help a frightened person: stay calm and visible, and give them a moment to think._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide to measure: 12 ÷ 2  
> _The pine is 12 metres tall, and Stoick is about 2 metres tall. How many Stoicks, laid head to toe up the trunk, would match it?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes! 12 ÷ 2 = 6, because six lots of 2 make 12.
> - 10 → Ten Stoicks would be 20 metres. Six lots of 2 make 12, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
> - 14 → That is 12 + 2. We want to know how many 2s fit into 12: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 12 metres by 2 metres to find 6._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): why a low sun looks golden or red  
> _The low sun looks golden. Why do you think low sunlight looks gold or red?_  
> - ✅ Its light crosses more air, which scatters away the blue and leaves the reds and golds → Yes. A low sun’s light travels through much more air before reaching you, so the blue is scattered away and golds and reds are left.
> - The sun gets hotter at the end of the day → It is actually the same sun. What changes is how much air its light passes through.
> - The sea paints the sky gold → It is a lovely idea, but the sea does not colour the sky. The air does, by scattering the blue light away.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that low sunlight looks golden because it passes through more air, which scatters away the blue._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): fog is a cloud at ground level, made of tiny water droplets  
> _Fog is a cloud that touches the ground or the sea. It is made of billions of tiny water droplets hanging in the air._  
> _Sea fog often forms when warm, damp air drifts over cold water and cools. The droplets are why it feels wet on your face._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fog is a low cloud made of tiny water droplets, often formed when warm damp air cools over cold water._

_The fog opens on a mountain in the sea, steaming at the top. The dragons pour in through a crack in its side, and so do you._

_In the middle is a pit full of mist. One by one, the dragons fly over it and drop what they have carried._  
_Fish, sheep, a whole yak: all of it falls into the mist and is gone._  
**Hiccup**: They’re not eating it. Why aren’t they eating any of it?

_Something rises out of the pit, bigger than the Great Hall: a head like a cliff, with eyes like lamps._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile does to our picture of a creature  
> _The writer says the creature has a head “like a cliff” and eyes “like lamps”. What do these comparisons do?_  
> - ✅ They make it seem enormous and glowing → Yes. A cliff is huge and hard, and lamps are bright in the dark, so together they build a frightening picture without every detail.
> - They tell us its exact size → Similes give a feeling, not a measurement. We know it is huge, but not how huge.
> - They make it sound funny → Not here. The comparisons are meant to make the creature feel vast and frightening.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how similes build a picture of a huge, glowing creature._

_The mist closes over the Gronckle, and there is a sound you will not forget._  
_When the mist clears, the place where it hovered is empty._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): saying a fear out loud makes it smaller  
> _Hiccup and Astrid are both frightened, and they say so. Naming a fear out loud often makes it a little smaller._  
> _It does not make us less brave. Bravery is doing the next thing while you are still afraid._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that naming a fear aloud can make it smaller, and that bravery means acting while afraid._

_The great eyes turn. They have seen Toothless, and Toothless is already moving: out, out, through the crack and into the fog._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): when two people both have a good reason  
> _Astrid wants to warn the village, and Hiccup wants time to protect Toothless. Who is right, or can both be?_  
> - Both: safety and loyalty both matter → That’s a fair answer. The hardest choices are between two things that are both good.
> - Astrid: the village’s safety comes first → That’s a fair answer. Many lives are at stake, and she is thinking of them.
> - Hiccup: a friend in danger needs time → That’s a fair answer. A single life matters too, and a rushed decision cannot be undone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about a dilemma in which two people both have a good reason._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals to the minute  
> _They left at 6:00 and landed at 9:45. How long were they away?_  
> - ✅ 3 hours 45 minutes → Yes! From 6:00 to 9:00 is 3 hours, and from 9:00 to 9:45 is 45 minutes more.
> - 2 hours 45 minutes → Count again: from 6:00 to 9:00 is 3 hours, not 2. Then add the 45 minutes.
> - 4 hours 15 minutes → That is the time from 6:00 to 10:15. A quarter to ten is 9:45, so 3 hours and 45 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Found a time interval: from 6:00 to 9:45 is 3 hours 45 minutes._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): echoes: sound bounces off hard surfaces  
> _The arena is a stone pit, so when the crowd roars, the sound bounces back off the walls. What do we call that?_  
> - ✅ An echo → Yes, sound waves bounce off hard, flat surfaces like stone. Caves, canyons and big stone halls are good at echoes.
> - A shadow → A shadow is made by blocking light. A sound bouncing back is an echo.
> - A rainbow → A rainbow comes from light and water. Sound bouncing off stone is called an echo.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound bounces off hard surfaces, which makes an echo._

> _There are four dragons, and each can carry two riders. How many riders is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes! Four groups of two: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8, so 4 × 2 = 8.
> - 6 → That is 4 + 2. We need four lots of two: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8.
> - 4 → That is the number of dragons. Each carries two riders, so count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 groups of 2 to find 8 riders._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why a character jokes when nervous  
> _Why do you think Snotlout makes a joke here?_  
> - ✅ Joking helps him hide that he is nervous → Yes, people often joke when they are afraid. The words say “I’m fine” while the nerves say otherwise.
> - He is sure he is safe → If he were sure, he would not need to say it out loud. The joke gives him away.
> - He wants to be eaten → Ha! No one wants that, least of all Snotlout.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a character might use a joke to cover nerves._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): choice and consent for animals  
> _Hiccup lets each dragon choose its rider. Why might choice matter, and should an animal always get a say?_

> - Animals cannot say yes or no in words, so people must watch very closely → That’s a fair answer. Looking after an animal means reading its signals, because it cannot ask in words.
> - Sometimes an animal’s safety means we must decide for it → That’s a fair answer. Choice matters, but it is not the only thing, and a caring person weighs both.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why choice matters to animals and how people can respect it._

#### `a19-16-mountain`

_The fleet has found the mountain. Stoick’s Vikings have run the ships up on the grey shore and are hammering at the rock._  
_Toothless is chained on the deck of the lead ship. He has seen you coming long before anyone else._  
_The rock face cracks wide. The Vikings cheer, and then stop cheering._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): water freezing in cracks splits rock  
> _Real rock can crack when water seeps into a tiny crack and freezes. Ice takes up more room than water, so it pushes the crack wider._  
> _Over many winters, solid cliffs split. That slow weathering shapes real coasts._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rock can crack when water freezes in small cracks, because ice takes up more room than water._

_What comes out is the thing from the pit, the size of a hill, with six eyes and a mouth like the mouth of a cave._  
**Gobber**: That’s not a dragon. That’s a mountain with a temper.  
_Its fire goes along the line of ships like a hand along a table. Every one of them catches._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile shows about movement  
> _“Its fire goes along the line of ships like a hand along a table.” What does this simile tell you about how the fire moves?_  
> - ✅ Smoothly and sweeping, touching every ship in turn → Yes. A hand along a table touches everything in one long, easy movement, and the fire does the same.
> - Slowly, one ship at a time → A hand sweeping a table is quick and smooth. The simile shows speed and a sweep.
> - Only at the very end of the line → The hand touches the whole table, not just the end. The simile shows the fire catching every ship.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile shows about how the fire moves along the ships._

**Stoick**: Off the ships! Everyone off! Get to the rocks!

**Hiccup**: Then confuse it! Noise! Twins, gas and spark, on its left side!  
_The riders swing round its head like gulls round a ship. It turns, and roars, and snaps at nothing._  
_Fishlegs sets you down on the beach. Your job is the people still on the ships: one at a time, off the burning decks._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): why leaders go last in an emergency  
> _Stoick wants everyone else off the ships before him. Why do leaders in an emergency often go last?_  
> - ✅ Because their job is to look after everyone else first → Yes. A leader’s duty is to the people who depend on them, and ships’ captains still follow this today.
> - Because they are not important → A leader is very important. That is exactly why leaving last is a sign of duty, not of being unimportant.
> - Because they are the slowest → Not at all. Stoick could leave quickly, but he chooses to see everyone else safe.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about why leaders often leave last in an emergency: duty to those who depend on them._

> - It is reckless when you do not think at all → That’s a fair answer. Hiccup acts fast, but he has thought about Toothless for days.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how a character changes over a story  
> _How has Stoick changed since he turned his back on Hiccup on the jetty?_  
> - ✅ He has gone from silent and stern to saying plainly that he was wrong → Yes, a character’s change shows in what they do and say. Stoick’s short, honest sentence is the biggest change in the story.
> - He has not changed at all → Compare the jetty with the water’s edge: he went into the sea after Hiccup and said sorry. That is a big change.
> - He is angrier than ever → His voice is soft, and he says he is sorry. That is the opposite of anger.
> _For grown-ups: Described how a character changes from the beginning of the story to this scene._

**Hiccup**: Me too, Dad.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what makes an apology real  
> _Stoick says sorry. Which of these is the best kind of apology?_  
> - ✅ “I was wrong. I’m sorry.” → Yes. A real apology names what was wrong and does not add an excuse.
> - “Sorry, but you made me do it.” → The “but” takes the apology back. It puts the blame on the other person.
> - “Sorry if you were upset.” → That treats the upset as the problem, not what was done. A real apology owns the action.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes an apology real: say what was wrong, and add no excuse._

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time: 1,800 ÷ 300  
> _Toothless climbs 300 metres every minute, and the cloud is 1,800 metres up. How many minutes does he need to reach it?_  
> - ✅ 6 minutes → Yes, because 1,800 ÷ 300 is the same as 18 ÷ 3 = 6. He climbs 300 m, six times.
> - 5 minutes → Five climbs of 300 m is only 1,500 m. We need 1,800 m: 18 hundreds ÷ 3 hundreds = 6.
> - 60 minutes → That is ten times too long. 1,800 ÷ 300 = 6, because 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a distance by a speed to find the time: 1,800 m at 300 m a minute is 6 minutes._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): the Doppler effect: a sound’s pitch changes as its source moves  
> _The whistle sounds higher while it rushes towards you, and drops as it passes. That is the Doppler effect._  
> _Sound waves bunch up in front of something moving towards you, making a higher note._  
> _They stretch out behind it, making a lower note. Ambulance sirens do the same._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the pitch of a moving sound changes as it approaches and moves away (the Doppler effect)._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what to do when you cannot help yet  
> _Something terrible may have happened, and you cannot help yet. What can you do?_  
> - Stay safe, stay together, and be ready to help when it is safe → That’s a fair answer. Rushing in can add another person in danger, so being ready and close to others is the strongest thing you can do.
> - Rush in at once → That’s a fair answer. The wish to rush is a loving one, though the fire is too hot, and a second person in danger helps nobody.
> - Look away and pretend it is not happening → That’s a fair answer. It is hard to watch, but staying present, even in fear, lets you be useful the moment you can.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what to do when you cannot help yet: stay safe and together, and be ready._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): show, don’t tell: feelings shown through actions  
> _Stoick says nothing to Toothless, but puts a hand on his head. How does the writer show his feeling?_

> - By having Stoick give a long speech → He gives no speech. That is the point: the writer lets a gesture speak.
> - By telling us he feels nothing → He feels a great deal. The gesture shows it, without a word.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): prosthetic legs and feet let people walk, run and dance, and are nothing to hide  
> _Many people use a made leg, foot, arm or hand. These are called prostheses, and a specialist fits each one to its owner._  
> _With them, people walk, run, climb, swim and dance. Some Paralympic sprinters race on curved running blades._  
> _A prosthesis is a tool, like a good pair of boots. There is nothing to hide about it._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): a spring stores energy and gives it back  
> _Gobber put a spring in Hiccup’s new foot. What does a spring do?_  
> - ✅ It stores energy when it is squashed and gives it back as it springs out → Yes. Squash a spring and it stores energy; let go and it pushes back, and that push helps a step along.
> - It makes things heavier → A spring has no weight to add. Its job is storing and returning energy.
> - It only makes a noise → Springs can creak, but their real job is to store energy and give it back.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a spring stores energy when squashed and returns it as it springs out._

- **Hold out your arm.**
    - You hold out your arm. He takes it, and stands, and finds his balance on his own.
    - **Hiccup**: Thanks. I won’t always need it. But thanks.
- **Say nothing, and wait.**
    - You wait. He tries a step, and another, and then he is grinning.
    - **Hiccup**: Well. Toothless and me. Matching now.

#### `a19-18-wake-done`

_He walks to the door with Toothless pressing against his side: step and clunk, step and clunk._  
**Hiccup**: Come on. I want to see what’s outside.  
_Step and clunk. The two sounds have a rhythm, like a slow drum._  
_Your Nubbin begins to walk in time with it, and then Toothless does too, with his tail._  
_Words like “clunk” sound like what they mean. They are called onomatopoeic words, and writers love them._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.4, ask): onomatopoeia: words that sound like their meaning  
> _Which of these words sounds like what it means?_  
> - ✅ Clunk → Yes, “clunk” sounds like a heavy, short knock. Splash, buzz and sizzle work the same way.
> - Table → “Table” is just a name for a thing. It does not sound like anything a table does.
> - Tomorrow → “Tomorrow” names a time. It does not sound like what it means.
> _For grown-ups: Identified an onomatopoeic word: one that sounds like what it means._

_Hiccup opens the door. There are dragons everywhere._  
_A Nadder on a roof. A Gronckle asleep in the square, with three children asleep on her._  
_A Zippleback is steering a fishing boat into the harbour, badly, one head arguing with the other._  
_Nobody is fighting. Somebody is building a long trough for fish, and somebody else a stable with a very tall door._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Viking-age families kept livestock, and Icelandic horses descend from Norse horses  
> _Viking-age families kept sheep, cows, goats and horses, and built barns, byres and stables for them._  
> _The Icelandic horse, a small, sturdy breed still found today, descends from horses the Norse settlers brought over the sea._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Viking-age families kept livestock and that Icelandic horses descend from horses the Norse settlers brought._

**Stoick**: Well? It’s your doing. All of it. Do you like it?  
**Astrid**: He’s up! Everyone, he’s awake!  
_Astrid punches him on the arm, kisses him on the cheek, quickly, and then punches him again for good measure._  
**Fishlegs**: Hiccup! Hiccup, the Gronckle lets me brush her teeth now!  
_Hiccup looks round at all of it, with his father’s hand on his shoulder and his dragon at his side._  

#### `a19-18-village-done`

_Toothless bounds from one end of the square to the other, greeting everyone. He greets your Nubbin twice._  
_The square is about forty metres across, and he crosses it five times in a minute._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 5 × 40  
> _Toothless crosses a 40-metre square five times. How far does he run?_  
> - ✅ 200 metres → Yes! 5 × 40: 5 × 4 = 20, so 5 × 40 = 200.
> - 45 metres → That is 40 + 5. He crosses the square five times, so we need five lots of 40.
> - 400 metres → Check again: 5 × 4 = 20, so 5 × 40 = 200. That would be ten crossings.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 5 × 40 to find 200 metres._

_Your Nubbin counts. It loses count at three, and starts again._

_Gobber has made Toothless a new tail fin, stiffer than the last, with a Nadder scale stitched to its tip for luck._  
**Hiccup**: New tail. New foot. Let’s see if they get on.  

> **Lesson** (art, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Norse craftspeople decorated useful things with animals and knotwork  
> _Norse craftspeople decorated tools, ships and jewellery with swirling animals and knotwork patterns._  
> _A scale stitched on for luck belongs to the same tradition: making a useful thing beautiful, and a little bit lucky._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Norse craftspeople decorated everyday objects with animal designs and knotwork._

_Hiccup sets his new foot in the pedal. It fits the stirrup as if it was made for it, because it was._  
_Toothless crouches, and springs, and they are up: over the square, over the roofs, over the cliffs and the sea._

_Up there, Hiccup lets go with both hands and spreads his arms wide, and Toothless rolls once, slowly, just for him._

_Late in the afternoon, Hiccup and Toothless land on the cliff top, where you are sitting with your Nubbin._

**Hiccup**: Gobber kept asking what the saddle was for, that night at the forge. I thought: why not one for your Nubbin, too.  
_Some things come back if you wait. Some things you have to wait for twice._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether waiting is always the right thing, and what trust is owed  
> _Toothless came to trust only after a long wait. Is waiting always right, and does a creature owe you trust because you were patient?_  
> - Patience helps, but trust has to be earned and freely given → That’s a fair answer. Nobody can be made to trust, however kind we are: it is a gift, and it comes in the other’s own time.
> - Waiting is right when the other one is frightened → That’s a fair answer. Fear needs time, and rushing it usually makes it worse.
> - Sometimes you have to act, as Hiccup did later → That’s a fair answer. Patience is right for some moments and action for others, and wisdom is knowing which is which.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when waiting is right and whether trust is owed to those who are patient._

_Toothless pads over. He drops a whole fish, a good silver one, at your Nubbin’s feet, and sits back, and waits._  
_Your Nubbin looks at the fish, and at Toothless, and at you. Then it puts both paws on the fish, very proud, and doesn’t eat it._  
_The sea goes still and grey, and smudges under your hand. You are back in the Grove, with a small saddle on your knee and a smell of fish._  

### Glossary

- **prosthesis**: A made limb, such as a leg or foot, that a person wears and uses.
- **onomatopoeic**: Describes a word that sounds like the thing it names, such as “splash”.

## A20-1. The Bright One

- `a20-01-s1`: Step into the grey-and-gold page and find Frigg’s hall. · _Touch the page, then go in at the door where the spindle is turning._
- `a20-01-s2`: Carry Frigg’s cloak up to Breidablik, Baldr’s hall. · _Follow the path up the rise to the pale hall; you will see it long before you reach it._
- `a20-01-s3`: Sit with Baldr while your Nubbin sleeps. · _Take the bench by the long table; there is no hurry in this hall._

#### `a20-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page washed in grey and gold: a bright hall, a hall of mists, and a long white plain._  
_Across the top, in plain letters: a story from the Prose Edda, written down in Iceland about eight hundred years ago._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): where Iceland is: an island in the North Atlantic  
> _Iceland is an island in the North Atlantic, just south of the Arctic Circle. Imagine sailing there from Scotland._  
> _Which direction do you sail?_  
> - ✅ North-west → Yes. Iceland lies north-west of Scotland, across open sea.
> - South-east → That would take you towards France. Iceland is the other way: north-west.
> - Due south → South would take you towards Spain. Iceland lies north-west of Scotland.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions to place Iceland: north-west of Scotland._

_Snorri Sturluson wrote it down. He was a Christian, setting out the old stories of his people’s gods._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): the word vellum, and books made by hand  
> _Books in Snorri’s day were written by hand, on vellum. Vellum is animal skin, usually calfskin, scraped thin and smooth._  
> _A big book could need the skins of many calves. That is one reason books were so precious._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word vellum, and how books were made by hand about 800 years ago._

_His book is one telling, not scripture. These gods are still honoured today, by people whose faith is called Heathenry._  
_The page goes cool and soft under your hand, like linen off the line. Then it is swept boards, and you are standing on them._  
_A long hall, full of the small sound of a spindle. A woman sits by the fire with her work in her lap, and looks up._  
**Frigg**: A guest. Come in out of the draught. This is Fensalir, and I am Frigg.  
**Frigg**: There are more errands in this house than there are hands. Will you run some of them, while you stay?  
**Fulla**: And the small one? Does it carry things?  
_Your Nubbin holds up both arms, to show it will carry anything at all._  

**Choices**

- **Bow, as you would to someone old and kind.**
    - Frigg inclines her head to you, exactly as low as you bowed to her.
    - **Frigg**: Guests and hosts bow the same distance in this house. It saves a great deal of arguing.
- **Say your name, plainly.**
    - **Frigg**: A good name. I’ll remember it.
    - She says it back to you once, and you have the odd feeling it has been written down somewhere.
- **Ask what needs carrying first.**
    - **Fulla**: Oh, I like this one.

#### `a20-01-page-done`

**Frigg**: Then the first errand is the easiest. Take this cloak up the hill to my son. He gives his away to anyone who looks cold.  
**Fulla**: Breidablik. The hall on the rise. You can’t miss it. Nobody ever has.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: 12 shared between 4  
> _Baldr gives his cloak to anyone who looks cold. Suppose Frigg sews 12 cloaks for him to share equally between 4 cold travellers._  
> _How many cloaks does each traveller get?_  
> - ✅ 3 → Yes. 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so each traveller gets three cloaks.
> - 4 → 4 is the number of travellers. Sharing 12 equally between 4 is 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
> - 8 → 8 is 12 − 4. Sharing equally is division: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a sharing (division) problem: 12 ÷ 4 = 3._


#### `a20-01-hall`

_Breidablik stands on a rise above everything. Its roof is so pale it is hard to say where it stops and the sky begins._  
_Fulla said nothing unclean can be in this hall. You wipe your feet twice, and your Nubbin wipes both of its._  
_Inside there is a long table, and a man at it, mending a strap. He looks up._  
_He is so kind and so glad that he seems to shine, and the whole room is lighter for him._  
**Baldr**: You’ve come from my mother. I know her cloak. She thinks I’m always cold.  
**Baldr**: I’m never cold. Put it on the bench, and sit. Everyone who climbs this far ought to sit.  
_The light off him is like sun off snow in the morning: everywhere at once, and easy on the eyes._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): snow reflects most of the light that falls on it  
> _The light off Baldr is described as sun off snow in the morning. Snow looks dazzling in sunshine._  
> _What makes it so bright?_  
> - ✅ It reflects most of the light that falls on it → Yes. Fresh snow bounces back most of the sunlight that lands on it. That is why people wear dark glasses on snowy mountains.
> - It makes its own light → Snow cannot make light. It only bounces back what the Sun sends it.
> - It is hot → Snow is cold. Brightness is about light bouncing back, not about heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that snow reflects most of the sunlight that hits it._

_Your Nubbin sits down in it, and blinks, and slowly tips over sideways._  
**Baldr**: Ah. It does that to the small ones. Leave it be. It will wake when it’s ready.  

#### `a20-01-hall-done`

_Your Nubbin is asleep on the warm boards, in the brightest part of the floor, with one arm over its face._  
**Baldr**: Stay till it wakes. I’d like the company.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being loved and still lonely (a think question)  
> _Baldr is loved by everyone, yet he says he would like the company._  
> _Can someone be well loved and still feel lonely?_  
> - Yes: being near people is not the same as feeling understood → A thoughtful answer. Company and closeness are not always the same thing.
> - No: if everyone loves you, you cannot be lonely → A fair view. But think of Baldr, who is loved by all and still asks you to stay.
> - Maybe: it depends on what that person needs → A careful answer. Different people need different kinds of company.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether being loved always stops loneliness (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-01-sit`

_You sit on the bench. Baldr goes back to his strap, and for a while there is no sound but the needle going through leather._  
**Baldr**: My mother says you’re running her errands. That’s kind. She has more of them than usual this year.  
**Baldr**: Everyone climbs up here in the end with a question. Mostly it’s which of two people is right.  
**Baldr**: I tell them as kindly as I can. It’s the part of the day I like best.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s traits from what he does  
> _Baldr settles quarrels by telling people the answer “as kindly as I can,” and says it is the part of his day he likes best._  
> _What does that tell us about him?_  
> - ✅ He cares more about people than about being proved right → Yes. Settling a quarrel kindly shows he wants people to feel looked after, not beaten.
> - He likes bossing people about → Nothing he does is bossy. He listens, and he tells people as kindly as he can.
> - He is bored by everything → He says it is the part of the day he likes best. He is not bored.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character trait (kindness) from what the character does._

_He looks over at your Nubbin, which is snoring very slightly in the light._  
**Baldr**: Ask me something, then. You’ve climbed as far as anyone.  

**Choices**

- **Ask him why he is so bright.**
    - **Baldr**: I don’t know. I’ve never been anything else. I’d like to see the dark properly one day, just to know.
- **Ask him if he has brothers.**
    - **Baldr**: Hödr. He’s blind, and stronger than any of us, and he laughs at my jokes before I finish them.
    - **Baldr**: You’ll meet him. He’s always just outside where the noise is, listening.
- **Don’t ask anything. Just sit.**
    - So you sit. After a while Baldr puts the strap down and sits too, doing nothing, as if he never gets the chance.
    - **Baldr**: That was a good question.

#### `a20-01-complete`

_Your Nubbin wakes when the light moves across the floor. It gets up and moves after it._  
**Baldr**: It’ll follow me about now. The small ones do. I don’t know what they think they’ll find.  
_He folds his mother’s cloak and lays it on the end of the bench, where he will see it every time he passes._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions by folding  
> _Baldr folds his mother’s cloak in half, then in half again._  
> _When it is folded like that, each folded part is what fraction of the whole cloak?_  
> - ✅ One quarter → Yes. Half of a half is a quarter: 1/4. Four equal parts make the whole cloak.
> - One half → One fold makes halves. He folded again, so each part is half of a half: one quarter.
> - One third → Thirds need three equal parts. Folding in half twice makes four equal parts, so one quarter.
> _For grown-ups: Found a unit fraction by folding: half of a half is one quarter._

**Baldr**: Tell her I’ll wear it. She’ll know I mean it kindly.  
_Going down the hill, your Nubbin stops every few steps to look back at the pale hall._  

### Glossary

- **vellum**: Animal skin, usually calfskin, scraped thin and smooth, which books were once written on.
- **Heathenry**: A modern religion that honours the old Norse gods.
- **reflect**: To bounce light back instead of soaking it up.

## A20-2. Bad Dreams

- `a20-02-s1`: Take lamp oil up to Breidablik, late at night. · _Fulla has the oil jar at Fensalir’s door; carry it up the rise._
- `a20-02-s2`: Walk down with Baldr while he tells the gods his dreams. · _Go with Baldr to the great hall where the gods meet, and stay by the door._
- `a20-02-s3`: Keep the hall going through the long council. · _Keep the fire fed and the cups filled until the gods have decided._

#### `a20-02-oil`

_It is late. Fensalir’s fire is down to red, and Fulla is still up, holding a jar of lamp oil._  
**Fulla**: His lamp’s been burning three nights running. He doesn’t sleep. Take this up to him? Mind the step.  
_Breidablik is never dark, but tonight the lamp is lit as well, as if he wanted more light than his own._  
_Baldr sits at the long table with his hands round a cup that has gone cold._  
**Baldr**: Oh. It’s you. Come in. I’m glad it’s you, and not somebody who’d ask how I am.  
**Baldr**: I’ve been dreaming. The same road every night, going down. And at the bottom of it, somebody saying my name.  
**Baldr**: Not unkindly. Quietly. As if they were setting a place for me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what makes a worry smaller  
> _Baldr is glad it is you, and not somebody who would ask how he is._  
> _Which of these is most likely to make a worry smaller?_  
> - ✅ Telling someone I trust, even a little at a time → Yes. A worry shared is usually lighter. In the morning Baldr will tell the gods, and he will feel it ease.
> - Keeping it to myself → Worries kept alone tend to grow in the dark. Baldr has had three nights of that.
> - Pretending it is not there → That is tempting. But the worry waits. Baldr tried it, and the dream came back.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about telling someone you trust as a way to shrink a worry._

_Your Nubbin climbs onto the bench beside him and sits as close to his light as it can get._  

**Choices**

- **Tell him dreams are only dreams.**
    - **Baldr**: That’s what I keep telling myself. I’m not as good at believing me as I used to be.
- **Say he should tell the others.**
    - **Baldr**: Yes. You’re right. I hate to worry them. But it’s worse, keeping it up here alone.
- **Sit, and wait for him to say more.**
    - You sit, and he doesn’t say more. After a while he puts his hand on your Nubbin’s head, and leaves it there.

#### `a20-02-oil-done`

**Baldr**: In the morning I’ll tell them. All of them. Will you walk down with me?  
_He sleeps a little after that, with the lamp still lit. Your Nubbin sleeps in his light, and you keep watch._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): a lamp changes stored energy into light and heat  
> _Baldr’s lamp has burned three nights running, on oil._  
> _A burning lamp changes the energy stored in its oil into two things we can sense. Which two?_  
> - ✅ Light and heat → Yes. That is why you can warm your hands near a lamp flame.
> - Sound and cold → A lamp flame gives a little warmth, not cold, and almost no sound.
> - Wind and water → Burning makes light and heat. Burning oil does not make wind or water.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a lamp changes stored energy in oil into light and heat._


#### `a20-02-telling`

_In the morning the gods are gathered in their great hall. They stop talking when Baldr comes in, because he never looks like this._  
_He tells them plainly: the road, the going down, his name said quietly at the bottom of it._  
_Odin listens with his one eye on his son and says nothing at all. Thor’s hands close and open on his knees._  
**Thor**: A dream. Dreams are smoke. Show me the thing that means him harm, and I’ll deal with it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphor: dreams are smoke  
> _Thor says, “Dreams are smoke.” That is a metaphor: it says one thing is another, to make a point._  
> _What does Thor mean?_  
> - ✅ Dreams are thin and drift away, so there is nothing solid to fight → Yes. Smoke has no shape to grab. Thor wants something he can hit, so a dream seems like nothing to him.
> - Dreams cause fires → Thor is not saying dreams burn things. He means they are as thin and shapeless as smoke.
> - Dreams smell bad → It is not about smell. A metaphor lets one thing stand for the quality of another: thin, drifting, hard to hold.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor (dreams are smoke)._

**Odin**: Not every harm stands where you can reach it.  
**Frigg**: Then we will go where it stands. Whatever it is.  
_They begin to take counsel together, slowly, the way old friends do when a matter is serious._  
_Fulla finds you a stool by the door. Your Nubbin keeps edging along the floor towards Baldr’s light._  

#### `a20-02-telling-done`

_The talk goes on through the morning and into the dark. You fetch, and carry, and listen._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _Suppose the gods began their council at 8 in the morning, and the fire was burning low by 8 in the evening._  
> _For how many hours did they talk?_  
> - ✅ 12 hours → Yes. From 8 in the morning to 8 in the evening is 12 hours: 4 to noon, then 8 more.
> - 8 hours → 8 is the clock number, not the gap. Count on: 4 hours to noon, then 8 more, which makes 12.
> - 20 hours → Careful: we want the gap between the times, not the sum. Count on from 8 to 8: 12 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval across the day: 8 am to 8 pm is 12 hours._


#### `a20-02-council`

_The hall gets dark and the fire gets low. Nobody has noticed but you._  
**Thor**: We could ward him. Stand round him day and night.  
**Odin**: And he would live in a ring of spears. That is no life for him.  
**Baldr**: I’d rather not, if it’s all the same. I’d miss people.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe is not always the same as well (a think question)  
> _Odin says a life inside a ring of spears is no life. Baldr would rather be among people._  
> _Is being safe the same as being well?_  
> - No: a safe life can still be lonely or small → A thoughtful answer. Safety matters, but so does being able to live. Frigg’s plan tries to keep both.
> - Yes: safety is what matters most → A fair view. Safety matters a great deal. Baldr would ask what it costs him to be that safe.
> - It depends on what the safety costs → A careful answer. A little safety costs little. A ring of spears costs a whole way of life.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether being safe is the same as being well (no single right answer)._

_Frigg has said nothing for a long time. She is turning something over, the way she turns her spindle._  
**Frigg**: Then I will ask. Everything in the world, one by one. I will ask each of them to promise not to harm him.  
**Thor**: Everything? There’s a great deal of everything.  
**Frigg**: Then I had better start early.  

**Choices**

- **Build the fire up again.**
    - You build the fire up. Odin watches you do it, and nods, once, as if that were a kind of counsel too.
- **Fill the cups.**
    - You fill the cups, and Thor takes his with a nod. His hands are steadier for having something to hold.
- **Sit by the door and listen.**
    - You sit by the door and listen. It is the kind of night somebody should remember all of, start to finish.

_By dawn it is settled. The gods go out of the hall into a cold, clear morning._  
**Frigg**: Tomorrow we walk. You, and I, and Fulla. We will ask the whole world.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Frigg says tomorrow they will walk. Say she walks 4 kilometres each hour (about 2½ miles), for 6 hours._  
> _How far does she go?_  
> - ✅ 24 km (about 15 miles) → Yes: 4 km × 6 hours = 24 km. That is a long walk for one day.
> - 10 km → 10 is 4 + 6. Walking 4 km an hour for 6 hours means 6 groups of 4: 24 km.
> - 2 km → Not quite. Each hour adds 4 km, so six hours add 6 × 4 = 24 km.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a distance problem: 4 km an hour for 6 hours is 24 km._

**Baldr**: Mother. You don’t have to.  
**Frigg**: I know.

## A20-3. The Oaths

- `a20-03-s1`: Walk with Frigg while she asks the fire, the water, the iron and the stones. · _Keep a step behind Frigg; she stops at each thing she asks._
- `a20-03-s2`: Carry Frigg’s asking to the beasts and the birds. · _Go out over the meadows and along the wood edge; anything that runs, flies or creeps should be asked._
- `a20-03-s3`: Let your Nubbin make its own promise. · _Bring your Nubbin to Frigg on Fensalir’s step._

#### `a20-03-asking`

_Frigg walks out at first light with no escort, only Fulla and you, and your Nubbin trotting to keep up._  
_She stops at the hearth first, and kneels, and asks the fire. The flames lie down low along the logs, all at once._  
**Frigg**: That is yes. Fire never says much.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the word oath  
> _Frigg is asking everything in the world for an oath: a solemn promise._  
> _Which sentence uses “oath” correctly?_  
> - ✅ The knight swore an oath to protect the village. → Yes. An oath is a very serious promise, often spoken aloud.
> - She ate an oath for breakfast. → An oath is not food. It is a serious promise.
> - The oath rained all morning. → Weather is not an oath. An oath is a solemn promise.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word oath (a solemn promise)._

_At the spring she asks the water, and it goes still as glass. At the smithy she asks the iron, and every blade on the wall rings._  
_She asks every metal by name, and the earth, and the stones. The stones say nothing, which for a stone is a promise._  
_She asks the trees, every kind, a whole wood of them. They bend their tops to her as if a wind went over._  
**Fulla**: She asks the sicknesses herself, at night. They take the longest. They always want to argue.  
**Frigg**: Everything can be asked. It only takes time, and remembering not to leave anything out.  
_West of Valhall you pass an old oak. On one of its branches is a sprig so small and new it has only two leaves._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, notice): mistletoe grows on another tree  
> _That little sprig is mistletoe, and it is a real plant. It grows on the branch of another tree, such as an apple or a poplar._  
> _Its green leaves make food from sunlight, but it sends root-like threads into the host tree to take water. So it is called a partial parasite._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mistletoe is a green plant that grows on another tree’s branches._

_Your Nubbin stops and looks at it. Frigg is already walking on._  

#### `a20-03-asking-done`

**Frigg**: The beasts and the birds now. My feet are older than my asking. Will you carry it for me?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): being a trustworthy messenger  
> _Frigg trusts you to carry her asking exactly as she gave it._  
> _What makes someone a good messenger?_  
> - ✅ Passing the words on exactly, without changing them → Yes. A messenger is trusted because the words arrive just as they were sent.
> - Making the message funnier → A joke might be fun, but it changes the message. A good messenger keeps it as it is.
> - Keeping the best parts for yourself → Then the one who is waiting would not get the whole message. A good messenger passes on all of it.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what makes a messenger trustworthy._


#### `a20-03-beasts`

_You go out over the meadows with Frigg’s asking. It sits in your mouth like a smooth stone, and you say it the way she said it._  
_The hare listens with both ears and thumps the ground, once. The bear lies down flat, which takes some time._  
_A reindeer lowers her antlers until they touch the grass. A fox looks away, then back, then sits._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): how body parts help animals survive: the reindeer  
> _A reindeer has wide hooves and a thick coat. Reindeer live in snowy lands._  
> _How do those two features help a reindeer survive there?_  
> - ✅ Wide hooves spread its weight so it does not sink in snow, and the thick coat keeps in body heat → Yes. Wide hooves work a little like snowshoes, and a thick coat keeps the cold out.
> - Wide hooves help it fly, and the coat helps it swim → Reindeer cannot fly, though they are strong swimmers. Their wide hooves and thick coat are for snow and cold.
> - They do not help at all → Every feature of a survivor usually has a job. These two have a big one in the snow.
> _For grown-ups: Linked an animal’s body parts (hooves, coat) to surviving in snow._

_The birds you ask all together, from the top of a hill. They go up in one great turning cloud and come down again._  
_The ravens come last. They hear you out, and nod, and fly off towards Valhall to tell somebody._  
_Snakes and poisons Frigg asks herself. Some askings, she says, are not for guests._  
**Fulla**: That’s everything with legs and wings. Everything with neither, too. Is that all?  
_Your Nubbin is tugging at your sleeve. Nobody has asked it._  

#### `a20-03-promise`

_Frigg is sitting on Fensalir’s step, tired, with her hands open in her lap. Your Nubbin walks straight up to her._  
_It stands in front of her with its feet together and its arms at its sides, as straight as it can stand._  
**Fulla**: Oh. It wants to be asked.  
**Frigg**: Of course it does. Everything should be. Come here, little one.  
**Frigg**: Will you promise not to harm my son? Not ever, not by anything you do?  
_Your Nubbin thinks about this for a long time, very seriously._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): a promise you make yourself (a think question)  
> _Frigg wants your Nubbin to make its own promise, not to have someone promise for it._  
> _Why might a promise mean more when you make it yourself?_  
> - Yes: only the one who promises can choose to keep it → A clear reason. A promise is a choice, and only the promiser can make it.
> - Not quite: a promise passed on can still be honest → A fair point. A messenger can be faithful. But the one who made the promise still has to keep it.
> - It depends on whether the person really means it → A careful answer. A promise is only as strong as the meaning behind it.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what makes a promise mean something (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Let it put its paw in Frigg’s hand.**
    - It puts its paw in her hand, flat, and holds it there until she closes her fingers round it.
    - **Frigg**: That will hold.
- **Let it bow, the way the hare did.**
    - It bows so low it nearly topples. Then, to be sure, it thumps the step with one foot, like the hare.
    - **Frigg**: Twice promised. I’ll count it twice.
- **Promise for it.**
    - **Frigg**: No. Let it promise for itself. A promise carried by somebody else is only an errand.
    - Your Nubbin nods at her, hard, three times. Frigg nods back three times.

#### `a20-03-complete`

_By evening it is done: fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth and trees, sickness, beasts, birds, poison and snakes._  
**Frigg**: Everything has promised. Everything I could think of.  
_She has been spinning as she walked, a twist of thread for every promise. Now the spindle is full, and she cuts the thread._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): drop spindles: spinning thread by hand  
> _Frigg’s spindle is a drop spindle, one of the oldest tools for making thread. People used them for thousands of years before spinning wheels or machines._  
> _You twist wool or flax into thread by letting the spindle hang and turn. Hand-spinners still use them today._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that drop spindles are very old tools for making thread, still used today._

**Frigg**: Keep the spindle. It has done its work. I’d like it to live somewhere far away, where nothing has ever been afraid.  
_Your Nubbin is already asleep on the step, facing up the hill towards the pale hall._  

### Glossary

- **oath**: A very serious promise, often spoken aloud.
- **parasite**: A living thing that lives on another and takes what it needs from it.

## A20-4. The Game

- `a20-04-s1`: Go with the gods to the Thing-field. · _Follow the crowd out to the gods’ meeting-place and its ring of stones._
- `a20-04-s2`: Join the game, or watch it from the edge. · _Thor will offer you something to throw; you don’t have to take it._
- `a20-04-s3`: Find Hödr outside the ring, and tell him what is happening. · _Walk round the outside of the stones to the tall man standing apart._

#### `a20-04-field`

_The Thing-field is the gods’ meeting-place, a wide green with a ring of standing stones. Today it is full of laughing._  
_Baldr stands in the middle of the ring. The gods stand round him, and they throw things at him._  
_A stone bounces off his shoulder and lands softly in the grass. An arrow turns aside as if it had changed its mind._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity pulls thrown things down  
> _Every stone thrown at Baldr curves down to the grass in the end._  
> _Which force pulls thrown things back towards the ground?_  
> - ✅ Gravity → Yes. Gravity pulls everything towards the ground, and a stone thrown from your hand is no exception.
> - Magnetism → Magnets pull on iron, not on stones. It is gravity that pulls the stone down.
> - Wind → Wind can push a stone sideways. It is gravity that always pulls things down.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls thrown objects down towards the ground._

_Nothing hurts him, because everything has promised. The game is a way of honouring him, and everyone wants a turn._  
**Thor**: Your turn again, brother! Stand still. This one’s heavy.  
**Baldr**: I’m always standing still! It’s the one thing I’m good at today!  
_Thor throws a stone the size of a loaf. It stops a hand’s width from Baldr, seems to think about it, and drops._  
_Everyone laughs, and Baldr laughs most of all, with his head back._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): the Thing: an assembly where people had a say  
> _The Norse word “Thing” meant an assembly, where free people met to settle quarrels and make laws._  
> _Iceland’s Althing began in the year 930, and still meets today. It is one of the oldest parliaments in the world._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a Thing was an assembly, and that Iceland’s Althing began in 930._


#### `a20-04-field-done`

_Your Nubbin has found the edge of Baldr’s light, at the very edge of the ring. It lies down in it like a cat in a sunbeam._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile: like a cat in a sunbeam  
> _Your Nubbin lies down “like a cat in a sunbeam.” That is a simile: it compares two things using “like” or “as.”_  
> _Which of these is also a simile?_  
> - ✅ The hall was as quiet as a mouse. → Yes. “As quiet as a mouse” compares the hall to a mouse using “as.”
> - The hall was a mouse. → That is a metaphor: it says one thing is another. A simile uses “like” or “as.”
> - The hall was very quiet. → That is a plain description. A simile makes a comparison.
> _For grown-ups: Told a simile (uses like or as) from a metaphor and a plain description._


#### `a20-04-turn`

**Thor**: Guest! A guest’s throw is good luck. Here.  
_He holds out a pebble from the field, smooth and grey, small enough for a child to throw._  
**Baldr**: Go on. It only tickles. Everything tickles now. I’ve never laughed so much in my life.  
_Outside the ring, a little apart, a tall man is standing with his hands empty. Baldr waves to him whenever something bounces._  
_The tall man can’t see him wave. But he smiles each time the laughing comes, as if he can._  
**Fulla**: That’s Hödr, Baldr’s brother. He can’t see to throw, so he stands out there.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): fair play and being left outside the game (a think question)  
> _Everyone laughs together, but Hödr stands outside the ring with empty hands._  
> _Is a game still a good game if one person cannot take part? What could make it fairer?_  
> - Change the game so he can play in his own way → A generous idea. A game that has room for everyone is a better game.
> - It is fine: he enjoys listening → He does enjoy the laughing. But notice he stands apart, with nothing in his hands. He might like to be in it.
> - The game is not really kind if he is left out → A strong view. Honouring one brother while another stands apart leaves something missing.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness in a game when one player cannot join (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Throw the pebble, gently, underarm.**
    - Your pebble bumps off Baldr’s knee and rolls back to your feet. He bows to it, deeply, and everyone cheers.
- **Give the pebble back. Watch from the edge.**
    - **Thor**: Fair enough. Somebody ought to keep the score.
    - You go and stand at the edge of the ring, where the laughing is quieter.
- **Let your Nubbin have the throw.**
    - Your Nubbin rolls the pebble along the grass. It stops at Baldr’s feet, and he picks it up and hands it back.
    - **Baldr**: A draw.

#### `a20-04-hodr`

_You walk round the outside of the stones to where Hödr stands. He turns his head before you reach him._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): two ears help us tell where a sound comes from  
> _Hödr turns his head towards you before you reach him. He cannot see, but his hearing is sharp._  
> _Having two ears helps us tell where a sound is coming from. Why?_  
> - ✅ A sound reaches the nearer ear a moment sooner, and a little louder → Yes. Your brain notices that tiny difference between your ears and works out the direction.
> - Each ear hears a different language → Both ears hear the same sounds. The difference is when and how loudly they hear them.
> - One ear is only for show → Both ears do real work. Together they let us tell where a sound is coming from.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that two ears let us tell the direction of a sound._

**Hödr**: You’re the guest. Frigg’s errand-runner. You walk like someone who’s been carrying things.  
**Hödr**: Tell me what they’re doing. I can hear them laughing. I like to know what at.  
_So you tell him: Thor’s loaf of a stone, the arrow that changed its mind, your Nubbin asleep at the edge of the ring._  
**Hödr**: The arrow! I wish I’d seen that.  
**Hödr**: I’d throw something myself, if I could see where he was. But it isn’t a game you play blind.  
_He says it lightly. He has said it to himself a good many times before._  

#### `a20-04-hodr-done`

**Hödr**: Come and tell me the next good one. You tell it better than they do. They just laugh and expect me to know.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: 8 × 3  
> _Hödr asks you to tell him every good moment. Suppose eight gods each take three throws at Baldr._  
> _How many throws are there to describe?_  
> - ✅ 24 → Yes: 8 × 3 = 24 throws. Hödr will be there all evening.
> - 11 → 11 is 8 + 3. Eight gods with three throws each is eight groups of three: 24.
> - 16 → 16 is 8 + 8. Three throws each means 8 × 3 = 24.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a multiplication problem: 8 groups of 3 make 24._


#### `a20-04-complete`

_The game goes on till the light goes. Nobody is hurt; nobody can be._  
_Baldr comes out of the ring with grass in his hair and puts an arm round his brother’s shoulders._  
**Baldr**: Did you hear about the arrow? It went round me like a dog round a puddle.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a joke tells us about a character  
> _Baldr says the arrow went round him “like a dog round a puddle,” and he tells it to his brother first._  
> _What does that tell us about Baldr?_  
> - ✅ He wants Hödr to share the fun, even though Hödr could not see it → Yes. He turns what he saw into a story, so his brother can laugh too.
> - He only wants to show off → He tells it to Hödr, who is the one person who missed it. That looks like kindness, not showing off.
> - He is afraid of the arrow → He is laughing, not afraid. The joke is how he shares the moment.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a character’s joke shows about him (kindness and sharing)._

**Hödr**: I heard everything. The guest told me the rest.  
_Your Nubbin follows them home, walking in Baldr’s light and holding on to Hödr’s bootlace._  

### Glossary

- **assembly**: A meeting where people gather to talk and decide things.
- **simile**: A comparison that uses “like” or “as”.

## A20-5. The Old Woman

- `a20-05-s1`: Fetch water for Fensalir. · _Take the pails down to the spring and carry them back up._
- `a20-05-s2`: Sit by Fensalir’s hearth while Frigg talks with the traveller. · _Wind the wool by the fire, and stay in the room._

#### `a20-05-water`

_Fensalir needs water, and the spring is down the slope. You take two pails, and your Nubbin takes a thimble._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of volume: litres and millilitres  
> _You carry two pails, and your Nubbin carries a thimble. There are 1000 millilitres in a litre._  
> _If a pail holds 8 litres, how many millilitres is that?_  
> - ✅ 8000 millilitres → Yes: 8 × 1000 = 8000. The thimble, by comparison, holds only a few millilitres.
> - 800 millilitres → Check the zeros. Each litre is 1000 millilitres, so 8 litres is 8000.
> - 80 millilitres → That is far too small. 8 litres is 8 × 1000 = 8000 millilitres.
> _For grown-ups: Converted litres to millilitres: 8 litres is 8000 millilitres._

_When you come back up the path, there is an old woman at the door, leaning on a stick._  
_She is wrapped in so many shawls that you can see nothing of her but her hands, which do not look old at all._  
**Fulla**: A traveller. Frigg never turns one away. Bring the water in. She’ll want to give her a cup.  
_The old woman looks at your Nubbin. Your Nubbin looks back, and then it goes and stands behind your legs._  
_It has never done that before, with anyone._  

#### `a20-05-talk`

_Frigg gives the old woman the best seat and a cup of the new water. You sit by the hearth with a skein of wool to wind._  
**The Old Woman**: I came by the Thing-field. Such a noise. What are the gods doing there, lady?  
**Frigg**: Making sport. They throw at my son, and nothing harms him. Everything in the world has promised.  
**The Old Woman**: Everything? Every single thing?  
**Frigg**: Every thing but one.  
**Frigg**: There is one little green sprout, growing on an oak to the west. It was so new that I didn’t ask it.  
_The old woman puts her cup down very carefully, as if it had become important not to spill it._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): trust and caution (a think question)  
> _Frigg welcomes the stranger and answers every question. The old woman puts her cup down very carefully._  
> _Is it good to trust everyone? When should we be careful?_  
> - Trust is good, but we can be careful about what we share → A balanced answer. Kindness and caution can go together.
> - We should trust people until they give us a reason not to → A hopeful view. The trouble is that some reasons only show themselves too late.
> - We should be careful with strangers who ask a lot of questions → A cautious view. Frigg noticed afterwards that the guest asked a lot, but by then it was told.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on when to trust and when to be careful (no single right answer)._

**The Old Woman**: Too young. Yes. Very wise.  

**Choices**

- **Keep winding the wool.**
    - You keep winding, round and round your hands, and you don’t look up. Later you will wish you had.
- **Look up at the old woman.**
    - You look up. Under the shawls, for a moment, someone is smiling, and then it is only shawls.
- **Pick up your Nubbin.**
    - You pick up your Nubbin. It is trembling very slightly all over, like a cup of water on a table someone has bumped.

#### `a20-05-talk-done`

_The old woman thanks Frigg, and gets up, and goes out of the door._  
_You go to the doorway a moment after, and the path runs empty both ways. You didn’t see which way she went._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: opposites  
> _The path runs north and south past Fensalir’s door, and the old woman could have gone either way._  
> _If she walked north, which way would she have to walk to come back?_  
> - ✅ South → Yes. South is the opposite of north. East and west are opposites too.
> - East → East is at a right angle to north. The opposite of north is south.
> - West → West is at a right angle to north. The opposite of north is south.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions: south is the opposite of north._


#### `a20-05-complete`

**Frigg**: An odd guest. Kind enough. She asked a great many questions for someone so tired.  
**Fulla**: I’ll bolt the door tonight.  
**Frigg**: Whatever for? Nothing can hurt him.  
_She goes back to her work. Your Nubbin sits by the door all evening, facing west._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Sun sets in the west  
> _Your Nubbin sits by the door all evening, facing west, towards the little sprout._  
> _In the evening, which direction is the Sun in?_  
> - ✅ The west → Yes. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, because Earth turns towards the east.
> - The east → The Sun rises in the east. In the evening it sets in the west.
> - Straight up → That is where it is at midday. In the evening it is low in the west.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sun sets in the west._


## A20-6. Hödr

- `a20-06-s1`: Go back to the Thing-field for the game. · _Walk out to the ring of stones; Hödr will be standing apart again._
- `a20-06-s2`: Run for the ring. · _There is no reaching it in time. Go anyway._
- `a20-06-s3`: Sit with Hödr. · _Stay beside him outside the ring. Don’t leave him alone in it._

#### `a20-06-field`

_A quiet word before this part: Baldr dies in it. It is told gently, and no hurt is shown._  
_The next day the game is on again. The Thing-field is full of the gods, and the ring is full of laughing._  
_Hödr stands outside the ring where he always stands, with his hands empty._  
_Somebody comes up beside him. You can’t see a face, only a cloak, and a hand holding something green._  
**A Voice**: Why aren’t you throwing? Everyone honours your brother but you.  
**Hödr**: I can’t see where he is. And I’ve nothing to throw.  
**A Voice**: Then here’s something. A little sprig. I’ll guide your arm. Do as the others do.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _A stranger hides their face, and offers to guide Hödr’s arm._  
> _Why might someone hide, and let Hödr do the throwing?_  
> - ✅ They want Hödr to do the harm, so they will not be blamed → Yes. Someone who hides and lets another do the deed hopes not to be blamed. That is a clue this is a trick, not a kindness.
> - They want Hödr to win a prize → There is no prize in the story. The hidden face is the clue: kind people do not hide.
> - They are only being kind → Kindness usually does not hide its face. Notice who is not named.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the text to work out a character’s hidden motive._

_The sprig is put in his hand: two leaves. You know it, and your Nubbin knows it, and starts to run._  
**Hödr**: Thank you. I’d like that. I’d like to be in the game, just once.  

#### `a20-06-fall`

_The hand on Hödr’s arm turns him a little, and lifts it. You are running, and the field is very wide._  
_Hödr throws. The sprig goes through the air with nothing to stop it, because nobody asked it to stop._  
_Baldr falls._  
_He falls the way a tall thing falls when it is not ready: all at once, and then still. There is no wound to see._  
_Baldr is dead. His body has stopped working, and it will not start again._  
_Nobody laughs. The field is so quiet you can hear the grass._  
_The gods try to speak to each other, but they are crying too hard, and nobody can find any words._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): crying together is allowed  
> _When someone dies, sadness can be too big for words. The gods cry so hard that nobody can speak._  
> _Crying together is not weakness. It shows how much someone mattered, and it helps to cry with someone beside you._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that crying together is a normal way to show how much someone mattered._

_The cloak at Hödr’s elbow is gone. Nobody saw it go._  
_Your Nubbin doesn’t go to Baldr. It goes past the ring and the weeping gods, straight to Hödr, and sits down by his feet._  

#### `a20-06-hodr`

**Hödr**: What happened? Why has it gone quiet?  
**Hödr**: Somebody tell me. Why has everybody stopped?  
_Nobody answers him; the gods are weeping, and cannot speak. Your Nubbin leans against his shins._  
**Hödr**: You’re there. The guest. Tell me. You always tell it right.  
_You are the one who has to tell him. There is no way of telling it that is right._  
_So you tell him plainly, and he doesn’t move. Then his hand opens, and lets go of nothing._  
**Hödr**: I only wanted to be in the game.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): who is to blame? (a think question)  
> _Hödr threw the sprig, but he could not see, and someone else guided his arm._  
> _Is Hödr to blame for what happened? Who is?_  
> - Hödr is not to blame: he was tricked → A kind and fair view. He did not know what he was throwing, and he trusted a voice he could not see.
> - Hödr is partly responsible: he threw it → A fair point. But blame depends on what a person knew. Hödr did not know.
> - The one who tricked him is responsible → A clear view. The one who planned it and hid is the one who carries the blame.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on who is responsible when someone is tricked (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Sit down next to him, and stay.**
    - You sit down in the grass beside him. After a long time he sits down too, all at once, as if his legs decided.
- **Take his hand.**
    - You take his hand, the hand that threw. He holds on to yours as if the field were tipping.
- **Tell him somebody guided his arm.**
    - **Hödr**: I know. I felt it. It doesn’t help yet. It might one day. Stay anyway.

#### `a20-06-complete`

_No one may take vengeance on the Thing-field. It is a place of peace, so holy that no hand can be raised there._  
_So the gods stand and weep. Odin weeps hardest, because he understands best how much has been lost._  
_Hödr sits in the grass outside the ring. Nobody comes to him but you, and your Nubbin, which has not moved from his feet._  
**Fulla**: Bring him to Fensalir. Frigg says so. Nobody should sit out here alone tonight.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what helps when someone is grieving  
> _Fulla says nobody should sit out there alone tonight._  
> _What helps most when someone is grieving?_  
> - ✅ Staying with them, even when there is nothing to say → Yes. Being there says what words cannot: you are not alone.
> - Cheering them up quickly → Cheerfulness can feel like being told to stop. Being with them is kinder.
> - Giving them space and never checking in → Some space is fine, but nobody should be left entirely alone with it. Check in.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how to help someone who is grieving: stay with them._


## A20-7. Who Will Ride

- `a20-07-s1`: Be in Fensalir when Frigg speaks to the gods. · _Bring Hödr to Fensalir and stay by the door._
- `a20-07-s2`: Bring Sleipnir from Odin’s stable. · _The stable is behind the great hall; the grey horse is the one with too many legs._
- `a20-07-s3`: Say goodbye to Frigg before the road. · _Find Frigg at Fensalir’s door; Hermódr will wait._

#### `a20-07-asks`

_The gods come to Fensalir in the evening, and nobody sits. Hödr sits, because you brought him a stool._  
_Frigg stands by the cold hearth. She has stopped weeping, which is harder to look at._  
**Frigg**: Which of you will ride the road to Hel for me? Find my son, and offer her a ransom, and have all my thanks.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the word ransom  
> _Frigg wants someone to ride to Hel and offer a ransom for her son._  
> _What is a ransom?_  
> - ✅ A payment made to get someone freed or returned → Yes. A ransom is what you give to win someone back.
> - A kind of horse → Hermódr will take a horse, but a ransom is a payment, not an animal.
> - A letter of thanks → A ransom is not a letter. It is a payment made to get someone back.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word ransom (a payment to win someone back)._

_The hall is very quiet. Nobody has ridden the road to Hel and come back to tell it._  
**Hermódr**: I will.  
_It is Hermódr the Bold, Baldr’s brother, a quick, plain man who has never sat still in his life._  
**Hermódr**: I’ll ride. Tell me the way, and I’ll ride it.  
**Frigg**: Thank you.  

#### `a20-07-asks-done`

**Odin**: Take my horse. Nothing else could make that road.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): horses were how people travelled  
> _Before cars, trains and aeroplanes, a good horse was the fastest way for most people to travel over land._  
> _A horse at a steady pace could carry a rider about 30 to 40 kilometres (20 to 25 miles) in a day. Odin’s horse is faster than any._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that horses were the main way to travel over land before engines._


#### `a20-07-sleipnir`

_Odin’s stable is long and warm and smells of hay. At the end of it stands a grey horse, taller than the door._  
_Sleipnir has eight legs. Your Nubbin counts them twice, then counts its own, and looks thoughtful._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication: legs  
> _Sleipnir has eight legs. An ordinary horse has four._  
> _How many legs do two Sleipnirs have between them?_  
> - ✅ 16 → Yes. 2 × 8 = 16 legs: two groups of eight.
> - 10 → 10 is 8 + 2. Two horses with eight legs each is 2 groups of 8: 16.
> - 12 → 12 is 8 + 4. Two Sleipnirs is 2 groups of 8: 16 legs.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication for equal groups: 2 × 8 = 16._

_He lets you take the halter without fuss. He has carried Odin over worse roads, and knows a serious errand._  
_You lead him out. All eight hooves go down on the cobbles in an order you can’t follow._  
**Hermódr**: Good lad. Good. We’ll go far, you and I.  
**Hermódr**: Guest. You’ve run Frigg’s errands all this while. Will you run this one?  
_He looks at the horse’s broad grey back, and then at you. There is room for two._  

#### `a20-07-door`

_Frigg is at the door when you come back leading Sleipnir. She has bread for each of you, and a cloak._  
**Hermódr**: We’ll go after the ship. I’ll see my brother off first, and ride at first light.  
**Frigg**: Yes. He would want you there.  
_She turns to you, puts the cloak round your shoulders herself, and does up the fastening as if you were small._  
**Frigg**: You don’t have to go so far for my son. You came here as a guest.  
_Your Nubbin is already sitting on Sleipnir’s back, holding his mane in both arms. It has decided._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honest promises: trying versus a guarantee (a think question)  
> _You are about to ride a road that nobody has come back from._  
> _Is “I will try” a more honest promise than “I will bring him home”? Why?_  
> - Because trying is in your own hands, but the result is not → A clear reason. We can promise our effort. We cannot promise how the world will answer.
> - Because trying is easier to promise → Often it is. But trying is not always easy. It is an honest promise, which matters more.
> - Because it is more honest about what could go wrong → Yes, that is part of it. An honest promise names only what we truly control.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on why an honest promise is about trying, not guaranteeing (no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **“We’ll bring him home.”**
    - **Frigg**: Don’t promise me that. Promise me you’ll try. That one, I can hold you to.
- **“We’ll try.”**
    - **Frigg**: Thank you. That’s all I asked of the world. Trying.
- **Say nothing. Take her hand.**
    - You take her hand. She holds it a moment, then puts it on Sleipnir’s halter, and steps back.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how a character responds to an event  
> _For the first time, your Nubbin does not know which way to face._  
> _Why? What has changed for it?_

> - It has forgotten how to turn round → It still knows how to turn. What has gone is the thing it was turning towards.
> - It is playing a game → Nothing in the scene is playful. It is missing the light.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a character reacts to a loss: it has lost the light it faced._
