## A20-8. The Ship

- `a20-08-s1`: Help the gods launch Baldr’s ship. · _Put your shoulder to the hull with the others when Thor calls._
- `a20-08-s2`: Watch for the one who comes from Jötunheim. · _Stand back from the hull and watch the road down from the mountains._
- `a20-08-s3`: Lay something on the ship for Baldr, or stand back. · _Wade out to the ship’s side, where Fulla will take what you bring._

#### `a20-08-shore`

_Baldr’s ship is called Hringhorni. It is the greatest of all ships, and it lies on the shore on rollers, its prow to the sea._  
_The gods have carried Baldr down to it, and laid him on board, and covered him. You see nothing but the cloth._  
**Thor**: Now. All together. Push.  
_Everyone puts a shoulder to the hull. You find a place low down by a roller, and your Nubbin finds a place under your elbow._  
_The ship does not move, not a finger’s width. It is as if the shore will not let him go._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): rollers reduce friction  
> _Baldr’s ship sits on rollers, but it still will not move._  
> _Rollers help move a heavy load. Why are they better than dragging it?_  
> - ✅ Rolling has much less friction than sliding → Yes. Friction is the rubbing that holds things back. Rolling rubs far less than sliding.
> - Rollers make the ship lighter → The ship weighs the same. Rollers only cut the friction.
> - Rollers push the ship by themselves → Rollers do not push. They just let the load roll when something else does.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rollers reduce friction, so heavy loads move more easily._

**Thor**: Again!  
_Again, and nothing. The gods stand back, breathing hard, and look at one another._  
**Odin**: Send to Jötunheim. There is one there who could move it.  

#### `a20-08-giantess`

_She comes down from the mountains riding a wolf, with snakes for reins. Her name is Hyrrokkin._  
_The wolf is grey as old ice. Four of Odin’s strongest warriors hold it when she gets down, and even they can hardly hold it._  
_She walks to the prow of Hringhorni without a word to anyone, puts her hands on it, and pushes. Once._  
_The ship goes down the rollers with a roar. Sparks jump from the rollers, and the whole shore shakes._  
_Thor’s hand goes to his hammer. He is grieving, and grief looks for somewhere to go._  
**Odin**: No. She came to help. Let her be.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): where anger that comes from grief should go (a think question)  
> _Thor’s hand goes to his hammer, and Odin tells him to let her be._  
> _Grief can look for somewhere to go, and sometimes it turns into anger. Where should it go instead?_  
> - Say what it is: “I am angry because I am so sad” → A brave answer. Naming the real feeling can take the sting out of it.
> - Do something useful with it, like helping → A strong answer. Thor can put his strength to work on the ship instead of on a guest.
> - Wait, breathe, and let someone steady you, as Odin does → A wise answer. Odin does not shout. He says one calm sentence, and Thor listens.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what to do with anger that comes from grief (no single right answer)._

_Thor takes his hand away. Hyrrokkin looks at him a long moment, and nods, and goes back the way she came._  

#### `a20-08-pyre`

_Baldr’s wife, Nanna, has stood on the shore all morning. When the ship moves, her heart breaks with grief, and she dies there._  
_They lay her on the ship beside him, gently, under the same cloth._  
_Thor stands at the ship’s side and raises his hammer over them, and hallows them both, so that they go well._  
_Odin lays a gold ring on the cloth. It is called Draupnir, and it is the best thing he owns._  
_The ship rocks a little in the shallows, waiting._  
**Fulla**: Everyone gives something. You don’t have to. But you can.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Viking-age ship burials  
> _Real Viking-age people sometimes buried important people in ships._  
> _The Oseberg ship, in Norway, held two women about 1,200 years ago, with beds, cloth and tools._  
> _Giving gifts to the dead was a way of honouring them. We still bring flowers, light candles and tell stories._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real Viking-age ship burials existed, and that people still honour the dead with gifts and stories._


**Choices**

- **Lay a pebble from the Thing-field.**
    - You lay a grey pebble from the game beside Draupnir. It looks small there, and exactly right.
- **Lay a twist of thread from Frigg’s spindle.**
    - You lay a twist of the thread on the cloth: one of the promises, going with him.
- **Lay nothing. Stand back with Hödr.**
    - You stand back on the stones beside Hödr, who can’t see the ship. You tell him, quietly, where everything is.

#### `a20-08-complete`

_Then they light the pyre and push the ship out. You don’t watch the burning; you watch the light go._  
_Out on the water it is one bright thing, then a small bright thing, then a star sitting low on the sea._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): we see things when light reaches our eyes  
> _The ship becomes one bright thing, then a small bright thing, then a star low on the sea._  
> _You can see a lit ship far out at night. What must happen for you to see it?_  
> - ✅ Light from the ship travels to your eyes → Yes. We see something when light from it reaches our eyes. Our eyes receive light. They do not send it out.
> - Your eyes send light out to the ship → A common idea, but not so. Eyes only receive light. The ship’s light travels to you.
> - The ship must be warm → Warmth is not what we see. We see light, and the ship is giving some off.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we see things when light from them reaches our eyes._

_Your Nubbin stands at the edge of the waves and watches it until it is gone. Then it keeps watching the place._  
**Hermódr**: First light.  
**Hermódr**: Eat something. Sleep if you can. We have a long way to go down.

## A20-9. Nine Nights

- `a20-09-s1`: Ride behind Hermódr down the road to Hel. · _Hold on to Hermódr’s belt; Sleipnir knows the way._
- `a20-09-s2`: Cross the gold-roofed bridge over the river Gjöll. · _Ride up to the bridge and answer the woman who keeps it._

#### `a20-09-dales`

_Sleipnir goes down out of the morning into dales so deep and dark that the light can’t follow._  
_You ride behind Hermódr with your arms round his belt. Your Nubbin rides inside your cloak, with just its eyes out._  
_You ride for nine nights. There is nothing to see: not a star, not your own hand in front of your face._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): days of the week and counting nights  
> _You ride for nine nights. Say you set off on a Monday morning, and Monday night is the first night._  
> _On which day does the ninth night fall?_  
> - ✅ Tuesday → Yes. Nights one to seven are Monday to Sunday, the eighth is Monday again, and the ninth is Tuesday.
> - Sunday → Sunday is night seven. Two more nights: Monday, then Tuesday.
> - Wednesday → Wednesday is night ten. The ninth is a day earlier: Tuesday.
> _For grown-ups: Counted nine nights through the days of the week._

**Hermódr**: Still there, guest?  
**You**: Still here.  
**Hermódr**: Good. Keep saying so. I like to know.  
_All you can hear is eight hooves, and the cold, and Hermódr breathing._  

**Choices**

- **Count the nights aloud.**
    - You count them: one, two. By the sixth, Hermódr is counting with you.
- **Talk about Baldr.**
    - **Hermódr**: Yes. Tell me something he did. Anything. I don’t want to forget the sound of him.
    - You tell him about the strap Baldr was mending, and how he said everyone ought to sit. Hermódr laughs, once.
- **Keep quiet, and hold on.**
    - You say nothing. Every so often Hermódr puts one hand back over yours on his belt, to check.

#### `a20-09-bridge`

_On the ninth night there is light ahead: a bridge over a loud river, roofed all over with gold that shines on its own._  
_The river is Gjöll. A woman stands at the near end of the bridge, tall and plain, with her hands folded._  
**Módgudr**: I am Módgudr, and I keep this bridge. Tell me your name and your kin, and why you ride it living.  
**Hermódr**: Hermódr, Odin’s son. I ride for my brother Baldr. Has he come this way?  
**Módgudr**: Yesterday five troops of the dead rode over this bridge, and it hardly made a sound under them.  
**Módgudr**: Tonight it rings under one horse as if an army were crossing. You aren’t dead. None of you. Not even the small one.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): vibrations make sound  
> _The bridge hardly rang under the dead, but it rings like a bell under your living horse._  
> _In real life, what makes any bell, drum or bridge ring?_  
> - ✅ It vibrates: it shakes back and forth very fast, and that pushes the air → Yes. Sound is vibration. The shaking passes through the air to your ears.
> - It glows → Light and sound are different things. A ringing bell is shaking, not glowing.
> - It gets heavier → A bell weighs the same ringing or not. What changes is that it vibrates.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound is made by vibration._

_Your Nubbin puts its head out of your cloak to check._  
**Módgudr**: Baldr rode over. Yes. The road to Hel lies down, and to the north.  

#### `a20-09-bridge-done`

**Módgudr**: Go gently. Everyone down there was somebody’s.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): treating grief with respect (a think question)  
> _Módgudr says, “Go gently. Everyone down there was somebody’s.”_  
> _What does it mean to treat grief gently? How would you do it?_  
> - Speak softly, and do not rush people → A good start. Gentleness is often about pace and tone.
> - Remember that each person who has died mattered to someone → That is Módgudr’s point. Behind every loss is someone who is missing a person.
> - Say less, and listen more → A wise answer. People who are grieving often need to be heard more than advised.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what it means to be gentle around grief (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-09-complete`

_You ride on, down and to the north. The road grows wider and quieter, as if it were used to people._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification  
> _The writer says the road grows wider and quieter “as if it were used to people.”_  
> _When a writer gives a thing a human habit or feeling, that is personification. What does it do here?_  
> - ✅ It makes the road feel like a place that has welcomed many travellers → Yes. A road “used to people” feels old, patient and well worn. It is a quiet way to say many have passed here.
> - It tells us the road can talk → The road does not speak. It is a figure of speech, giving the road a human habit.
> - It tells us the road is dangerous → The words feel calm, not scary. The road seems to be used to company.
> _For grown-ups: Explained personification: a road “used to people.”_

_Ahead there is a gate, very tall, with no one at it._  
**Hermódr**: Hold on. Both of you. Tighter than that.  
_Your Nubbin wraps itself round your middle, under the cloak, and holds on._  

### Glossary

- **personification**: Giving a thing human feelings or habits, in writing.

## A20-10. Hel’s Hall

- `a20-10-s1`: Hold on while Sleipnir leaps Hel’s gate. · _Hold Hermódr’s belt with both hands, and lean when he leans._
- `a20-10-s2`: Stand with Hermódr in Hel’s hall while he asks for his brother. · _Follow your Nubbin to the high seat and stay at Hermódr’s side._
- `a20-10-s3`: Carry Baldr’s and Nanna’s gifts for home. · _Take what Baldr and Nanna give you, and keep it safe for the road._

#### `a20-10-gate`

_Hermódr gets down and pulls the girth tight. Then he mounts again and turns Sleipnir back from the gate, a long way back._  
**Hermódr**: He’s jumped worse. Not much worse. Lean when I lean.  
_Sleipnir runs at the gate. Eight hooves, and then none._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): motion carries things forward  
> _Hermódr turns Sleipnir back a long way from the gate before they charge it._  
> _Why does a run-up help a horse jump higher and further?_  
> - ✅ Its speed carries it forward, and its legs can push it upward → Yes. A moving body keeps moving, so the run-up gives the jump its forward push.
> - A run-up makes the gate lower → The gate stays as tall as it was. The horse gets more speed.
> - It tires the horse out so it jumps better → Tiring a horse would make the jump worse. The speed is what helps.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a run-up gives a jump forward motion._

_He goes over so high and so clean that he never touches it. Your stomach stays on the far side for a moment._  
_Then you are down, inside, on a floor like cold stone, and it is very quiet._  
_Your Nubbin puts its head out of your cloak. Then it wriggles free, drops to the floor, and runs._  

#### `a20-10-gate-done`

_It has seen a light, not a bright one. But it would know it anywhere._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): recognising someone we love (a think question)  
> _Your Nubbin sees a light that is not bright, and would know it anywhere._  
> _Why can we know someone we love from far away, even when they look dimmer or different?_  
> - Because we know the small things about them, not just how they look → A lovely answer. We learn a person’s walk, voice and ways, and those are hard to hide.
> - Because love gives us a sort of sixth sense → A romantic idea. Whatever it is, the Nubbin knows its friend’s light the way you know a voice.
> - Because the Nubbin has been following that light all along → True. Habit and attention teach us who to look for.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how we recognise people we love (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-10-hall`

_Baldr is sitting in the high seat of the hall. His light is low, like a lamp turned down, but it is his._  
_Your Nubbin is already asleep on the step below him, curled up in what light there is._  
**Baldr**: Brother. And the guest. You came all this way.  
_Hel comes into her hall. She is tall and grave, half her face the colour of a winter dusk, and she does not hurry._  
**Hermódr**: Lady. Everyone above weeps for my brother. Let him ride home with me, and name your price.  
**Hel**: Everyone? People say that. I will see whether he is as loved as they say.  
**Hel**: If everything in the world cries for him, every living thing and every stone, he may go home,  
**Hel**: but if one thing will not weep, he stays with me. That is my price, and it is a fair one.  
**Hermódr**: Everything will. You don’t know him.  
**Hel**: No. But I will.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): is Hel fair or cruel? (a think question)  
> _Hel says she will see whether Baldr is as loved as people say. She sets a price, but she calls it fair._  
> _Is Hel cruel, or fair? What in her words makes you think so?_  
> - Fair: she names her rule openly and keeps to it → A reasonable reading. She does not trick anyone. She says plainly what she will do.
> - Cruel: she sets a price she may know cannot be met → A strong reading. If even one thing refuses, the price fails. That is a hard rule.
> - Neither: she is grave, and is doing her work → A careful reading. She is solemn rather than unkind, and she says, “I will see.”
> _For grown-ups: Weighed evidence in the text about a character’s fairness (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-10-gifts`

_Baldr comes down from the high seat to walk you to the door. Your Nubbin wakes and walks with him, in his light._  
_He takes the ring Draupnir from his arm and puts it in Hermódr’s hand._  
**Baldr**: Give this back to Father, for a remembrance. He’ll want something to turn in his hands.  
_Nanna comes behind him with a folded linen smock, and a gold ring._  
**Nanna**: The linen is for Frigg. The ring is for Fulla. Tell her thank you, for all the times she did my hair.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): linen comes from flax  
> _Nanna gives Frigg a folded linen smock._  
> _Linen is made from the fibres inside the stem of a plant. Which plant?_  
> - ✅ Flax → Yes. Flax stems are soaked, beaten and spun into thread. Linen is cool and strong, which is why it was prized.
> - Cotton → Cotton comes from the soft fluff round the seeds. Linen comes from flax stems.
> - Wool → Wool comes from sheep, not from a plant. Linen comes from flax.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that linen is made from the stems of the flax plant._

**Baldr**: Guest. What did my mother say, when you left?  

**Choices**

- **She asked us to try.**
    - **Baldr**: That’s her. She never asks for more than you can carry.
- **She asked the whole world once. She’ll ask it again.**
    - **Baldr**: She will. She’ll ask until her voice gives out. Tell her I’m warm here. It’s true.
- **She sat on the step, and didn’t say anything.**
    - Baldr is quiet a long while.
    - **Baldr**: Then sit with her, when you get back. She won’t ask that either.

> _Sleipnir takes you back up the road: nine nights, the dark, the gold bridge._

> - 9 → 9 is just one way. You rode nine nights down and nine nights back.
> - 81 → 81 is 9 × 9. The two journeys are added: 9 + 9 = 18.

**Hermódr**: Everything has to weep. Everything.

## A20-11. Everything Weeps

- `a20-11-s1`: Go out with the messengers to ask the whole world to weep. · _Choose a road at Fensalir’s door; every road needs somebody._
- `a20-11-s2`: Carry frosted stones from the shade into the sun. · _Pick up the white-rimed stones on the north side and set them down in the sunlight._
- `a20-11-s3`: Stay with your Nubbin. · _Sit down by your Nubbin in the sun._

#### `a20-11-send`

_Hermódr tells it all in Fensalir: the road, the bridge, the high seat, and Hel’s price._  
_Odin turns Draupnir over and over in his hands. Fulla wears her ring on a cord round her neck._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the word keepsake  
> _Odin turns Draupnir over and over in his hands, and Fulla wears her ring on a cord round her neck. They are keepsakes: things kept to remember a person._  
> _Which of these is a keepsake?_  
> - ✅ A ring that a dear friend gave you → Yes. A keepsake carries a memory of the one who gave it.
> - A bus ticket you found on the pavement → It could be, if it reminds you of a special day, but a found ticket has no person attached. A keepsake is tied to someone.
> - A bill you have to pay → A bill is a duty, not a memory. A keepsake is kept because we love what it reminds us of.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word keepsake (something kept to remember a person)._

**Frigg**: Then we ask again. Everything. Every road. Send out messengers.  
**A Messenger**: There are more roads than messengers, lady.  
**Frigg**: Then take the guest. And the small one. It already knows how to ask.  
_Your Nubbin stands up straight, with its feet together, as it did when it made its own promise._  

**Choices**

- **Take the road to the hills.**
    - **A Messenger**: Stones, then, and old snow. Slow to answer. We’ll go slowly.
- **Take the road to the shore.**
    - **A Messenger**: Salt and shingle. The sea will weep. It always looks as if it might.
- **Take the road through the woods.**
    - **A Messenger**: Trees. They weep easily. It’s the iron under the ground I worry about.

#### `a20-11-stones`

_Everywhere you go, things weep: men and women at their doors, beasts in the fields, the earth itself in dark wet patches._  
_In a hollow on the north side there are stones still white with frost. Nobody has asked them yet._  
**A Messenger**: Carry them out, into the sun. You’ll see.  
_You carry the first one out and set it down where the sun is. The frost on it shines, goes clear, and begins to run._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): melting versus condensation  
> _Frost on a stone runs with water when it comes into the sun. Is this melting or condensation?_  
> - ✅ Melting: ice turning to water as it warms above 0°C (32°F) → Yes. Frost is ice, and warmth turns it back into liquid water.
> - Condensation → Close, but different. Condensation is invisible water vapour in warm air touching something cold and turning into drops, like sweat on a cold glass. The frost here is already ice, so it is melting.
> - Evaporation → Evaporation turns liquid water into invisible vapour. Here the frost turns into liquid drops, not vapour.
> _For grown-ups: Told melting from condensation and evaporation._

_Along the bottom of the page, the story goes on in plain print:_  
_Everybody wept, and every animal, and the ground, and the stones, and the trees, and every kind of metal._  
_You know how frost turns to drops of water when you bring it in from the cold? That is how they wept._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): personification: the weeping stones  
> _The story says stones and trees and metals weep. Stones cannot really cry._  
> _Why might a storyteller say it?_  
> - ✅ It shows, through personification, that the whole world mourned → Yes. Giving stones tears makes the loss feel as big as the world.
> - Because Snorri did not know that stones are not alive → People of Snorri’s time knew what stones were. He chose this picture on purpose.
> - Because stones can really cry → Stones cannot cry. But frost melting on them looks like weeping, which is where the picture comes from.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a storyteller gives stones human feelings (personification)._

_You carry stone after stone into the light, and every one of them weeps._  

#### `a20-11-stones-done`

_The iron in a gate weeps, and the copper on a roof. Even the gold on a ring weeps a little, in the warm._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): metals move heat quickly  
> _The iron in a gate, the copper on a roof and even a gold ring all weep in the warm._  
> _Metal feels colder than wood on a cold day, though both are the same temperature. Why?_  
> - ✅ Metal moves heat out of your hand faster, so your skin senses more cold → Yes. Metals conduct heat quickly, so they steal it from your hand.
> - Metal makes its own cold → Nothing makes cold. Metal just carries heat away from your hand faster.
> - Wood is warmer inside → Both are the same temperature. It is the speed at which heat leaves your hand that differs.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that metals conduct heat quickly, so they feel colder._


#### `a20-11-nubbin`

_You look round for your Nubbin. It is sitting in the sun beside the last stone, very still._  
_Water is running down its face, and it isn’t frost. It wipes at it with both arms, and looks at its arms, astonished._  
_It has never done this before. It looks up at you, as if to ask whether it is doing it wrong._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): feelings that arrive without warning (a think question)  
> _Water runs down your Nubbin’s face and it looks at its arms, astonished. It has never done this before._  
> _Have you ever had a feeling arrive that you did not expect? What did you do with it?_  
> - I let it out: crying or talking helped → A sound choice. Feelings tend to soften when they have somewhere to go.
> - I needed someone to sit beside me → So does your Nubbin. It climbs into your lap, and that helps.
> - I tried to push it away, and it grew → That happens to many people. It helps to know you are allowed to feel it.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on feelings that arrive unexpectedly (no single right answer)._

**A Messenger**: Ah. There’s one more thing weeping than we asked.  
_You sit down beside it. It climbs into your lap and goes on weeping, more easily now that it knows what it is._  
_Somewhere very far down, you think, Baldr’s light might be a little brighter._  

#### `a20-11-complete`

_By evening every road you walked is wet, and the sun is going down red over a weeping world._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): negative numbers and temperature  
> _At dawn the hollow was −4°C (about 25°F). By noon the sun has warmed it by 7 degrees._  
> _What is the temperature at noon? Will the frost still be there?_  
> - ✅ 3°C (about 37°F), so the frost has melted → Yes. −4 + 7 = 3, which is above 0°C, so the frost melts.
> - −11°C → That is −4 − 7. The sun warmed it, so we add: −4 + 7 = 3°C.
> - 11°C → 11 is 4 + 7. Starting below zero, −4 + 7 = 3°C.
> _For grown-ups: Added a temperature rise to a below-zero start: −4 + 7 = 3°C._

**A Messenger**: That’s ours done. Everything we asked, wept. Time to go home.  
_Your Nubbin carries one of the frost-stones home in both arms, and won’t put it down._  
_Whenever the sun touches it, it weeps a little still. It always will._  

### Glossary

- **condensation**: When invisible water vapour touches something cold and turns into tiny drops of water.
- **keepsake**: Something kept to remember a person who gave it or who matters to you.

## A20-12. The Cave

- `a20-12-s1`: Walk home with the messengers. · _Follow the road back towards Fensalir, under the cliff._
- `a20-12-s2`: Ask the giantess in the cave to weep for Baldr. · _Go into the cave mouth with the messengers._

#### `a20-12-road`

_The messengers come home along every road at once, wet to the knees and very quiet._  
**A Messenger**: Nothing said no. Not one thing. Not a stone, not a beetle.  
**A Messenger**: He’ll be home by morning. Think of her face.  
_The road home runs under a cliff. In the cliff there is a cave, and in the mouth of the cave somebody is sitting._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, ask): how lava tubes form  
> _The road runs under a cliff with a cave in it. Iceland has many caves, and some are lava tubes._  
> _A lava tube forms when the outside of a lava flow cools and hardens while hot lava keeps running inside. What is left when the lava drains away?_  
> - ✅ A hollow tunnel → Yes. The hardened shell stays behind, and the empty space is the cave.
> - A solid block of rock → The lava inside drains away, so the space it left is empty.
> - A lake → No water fills it as it forms. What the lava leaves is an empty tunnel.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a lava-tube cave forms._

_A giantess. She has her knees drawn up and her arms round them, and her eyes are perfectly dry._  
**A Messenger**: One more. Just one. Then we’re done.  

#### `a20-12-cave`

**A Messenger**: Mother, everything in the world weeps for Baldr, to bring him home from Hel. Will you weep too?  
**Thökk**: My name is Thökk. And no.  
**Thökk**: I’ll weep for him with dry eyes. That’s all he’ll get from me.  
**Thökk**: He was nothing to me living, and he’s nothing to me now. He can stay where he is.  
_The messengers stand very still. They have asked the whole world, and it said yes; they don’t know what to do with no._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): when someone says no (a think question)  
> _Thökk says no, whatever you ask. The messengers have asked the whole world, and it said yes._  
> _When someone says no, is it right to keep asking? What would you do?_  
> - Ask once more, kindly, in case they change their mind → A hopeful answer. But a second “no” may just be a stronger one.
> - Accept the no, and stay kind → A respectful answer. A no can be heard without being answered with anger.
> - Look for a different way to help → A practical answer. Sometimes a door that is shut means looking for another.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how to respond when someone says no (no single right answer)._

_Your Nubbin looks at you. Its face is still wet from the stones._  

**Choices**

- **Plead with her.**
    - **You**: Please. He was kind to everyone. He was kind to me, and I was a stranger.
    - **You**: Please weep. Just a little. It’s all it would take.
    - **Thökk**: Then it’s a great deal, isn’t it, from me. No.
- **Sit down next to her, and say nothing.**
    - You sit down in the cave mouth beside her, a little apart. You don’t ask her anything.
    - She looks at you sideways, and lets you stay. For a while, neither of you says a word.
    - **Thökk**: …It won’t make me weep, you know.
    - You nod. You know.
- **Walk away.**
    - You turn and walk out of the cave, because you can’t look at her. Behind you the messengers ask again, and again.
    - Her answer is the same each time. You can hear it from the road.

#### `a20-12-cave-done`

**Thökk**: Go home. Tell them Thökk wouldn’t.  
_Whatever you do, she will not weep. The cave stays dry, and so do her eyes._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction: 100 − 1  
> _The messengers asked the whole world, and only Thökk refused._  
> _Suppose they had asked 100 beings, and every one but Thökk wept. How many wept?_  
> - ✅ 99 → Yes: 100 − 1 = 99 wept. And one did not.
> - 100 → That would count Thökk too. She did not weep, so take one away: 99.
> - 1 → 1 is how many refused. The rest wept: 100 − 1 = 99.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted one from 100: 99 wept._

**Frigg**: One. Out of everything.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): one telling: how old stories change  
> _Snorri says people believed the giantess was Loki in another shape. He is passing on what others said, not claiming to know._  
> _Stories like this were told aloud for generations before they were written down, and tellers did not always agree._  
> _That is why this page is one telling, not the only one._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that old stories were passed on by word of mouth, and tellers varied._

## A20-13. The Salmon

- `a20-13-s1`: Climb with the gods to the house with four doors. · _Follow the gods up the mountain path; the house is near the top._
- `a20-13-s2`: Help the gods work out what was burned, and make one like it. · _Look closely at the ash by the hearth, then hold the cord while the gods knot._
- `a20-13-s3`: Hold the net across Franang’s Falls. · _Take the bank end of the net and keep it low as the gods walk it down the river._

#### `a20-13-house`

_The gods know now whose hand was at Hödr’s elbow. It was Loki’s, and he has run._  
_They hunt for him a long time. In the end they find a house high on a mountain, with a door in every wall._  
**Thor**: Four doors. So he could watch every way at once.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Sun rises in the east  
> _The house has a door in each of its four walls, so Loki could watch every way at once._  
> _If the four doors face north, east, south and west, which door faces the rising Sun?_  
> - ✅ The east door → Yes. The Sun rises in the east, so the east door catches the first light.
> - The west door → The Sun sets in the west. The east door faces the sunrise.
> - The north door → The north door faces away from the Sun’s path. The east door faces the sunrise.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions: the Sun rises in the east._

_The house is empty, and the fire is still warm. Beside it lies a little heap of grey ash, in a shape like knots._  
**Odin**: He was making something. And he burned it when he saw us on the path.  
_Below the mountain a waterfall comes down white into a deep pool. Your Nubbin goes to the door to look at it._  

#### `a20-13-ash`

_The wisest of the gods, Kvasir, kneels by the hearth and looks at the ash a long time without touching it._  
_It is the shape of a net, and nobody has ever made a net before. Loki made the first one, and then he burned it._  
**Odin**: Then he is in the water. He knew we would make one too, sooner or later. So we shall.  
_The gods sit down and make a net by the shape of the ash. It is slow work, and your Nubbin keeps getting knotted into it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): arrays: knots in a net  
> _The gods knot a net by the shape of the ash._  
> _Suppose the net has 10 knots across and 6 knots down, like a grid. How many knots do they tie in all?_  
> - ✅ 60 → Yes: 10 across × 6 down = 60 knots. That is why it was slow work.
> - 16 → 16 is 10 + 6. A grid has rows of knots, so we multiply: 10 × 6 = 60.
> - 100 → 100 would be 10 × 10. With 6 rows, it is 10 × 6 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication for a grid: 10 × 6 = 60._

**Thor**: Hold still, small one. You’re not the fish.  
_It is the first time anyone has smiled since the Thing-field. It doesn’t last, but it happens._  

**Choices**

- **Hold the cord steady.**
    - You hold it steady through every knot. Kvasir nods to you once, when it is done.
- **Tie some of the knots yourself.**
    - You tie a row of knots. Thor checks every one and doesn’t undo any of them, which is praise.
- **Untangle your Nubbin first.**
    - You untangle your Nubbin. It sits on the bench and watches the rest with great interest and both arms folded.

#### `a20-13-falls`

_The waterfall is Franang’s Falls. In the pool under it, by day, a salmon lies very still, and it is Loki._  
_Thor wades into the middle of the river with the net. You take one end on the bank, and the gods take the other._  
_You drag it down the river. The salmon slips over the top of the net and is away towards the sea._  
_Again. This time the salmon must choose: the open sea, or a leap back over the net._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): the salmon life cycle  
> _The salmon in Franang’s Falls leaps back over the net instead of swimming out to sea._  
> _Real salmon also leap up waterfalls. Why do they swim upstream?_  
> - ✅ To reach the river where they were born, and lay their eggs → Yes. Salmon are born in rivers, live in the sea, and return to their birth river to lay eggs.
> - To escape from the sea → The sea is their feeding home. They go upstream to breed.
> - For fun → Leaping is hard work. They do it to reach the place where they can lay eggs.
> _For grown-ups: Learned part of the salmon life cycle: they swim upstream to breed._

_It leaps. Thor grabs at it in mid-air, and catches it by the tail._  
_It slides through his hand, and his hand closes, and holds. That, the old book says, is why the salmon tapers at the tail._  

#### `a20-13-falls-done`

_In Thor’s hand the salmon is a man again, soaked and still. He doesn’t struggle, and he doesn’t say anything at all._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): sorry, or only caught? (a think question)  
> _In Thor’s hand the salmon is a man again, soaked and still. He does not struggle, and he does not say anything at all._  
> _Is Loki sorry, or just beaten? How could we tell?_  
> - We can only tell by what he does next → A sound answer. Being sorry shows in what a person does afterwards.
> - Silence could mean either → A fair point. A quiet person may be sorry, or may be planning.
> - Being sorry means putting things right → A strong answer. Saying sorry matters most when it is followed by repair.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on telling real sorrow from being caught (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-13-complete`

_The gods take Loki away with them, down the mountain. Nobody speaks._  
_Your Nubbin stands on the bank looking at the falls. Then it looks at you, as if there is a question it can’t find the shape of._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): figurative language: a question with no shape  
> _Your Nubbin looks at you “as if there is a question it can’t find the shape of.”_  
> _What does that phrase tell us?_  
> - ✅ It has a feeling or question it cannot put into words yet → Yes. Saying a question has a “shape” treats the thought like something you could hold, and it has not found it yet.
> - The question is shaped like a circle → It is figurative language, not a real shape. It says the Nubbin cannot put the thought into words.
> - The Nubbin wants a drawing lesson → It is a picture in words: the question is there, but the right words are not.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a figure of speech about a feeling with no words yet._

**Odin**: Go home to Fensalir, guest. What happens next is ours to do.  
_The page turns anyway, the way pages do. There is one more place to go before the snow._  

## A20-14. The Bowl

- `a20-14-s1`: Follow the stair down under the earth. · _Take the steep stair at the back of the cave, and keep your Nubbin close._
- `a20-14-s2`: Stay with Sigyn by the bowl, as near as you can bear. · _Go nearer to Sigyn and the three stones, or stay where you are._
- `a20-14-s3`: See what happens when the bowl is full. · _Stay still; it won’t take long._

#### `a20-14-cave`

_Under the earth there is a cave, and in the cave three flat stones. Loki is bound across them._  
_The page doesn’t show the binding. It shows only that he cannot move, and that he will not be let go._  
_Above his face a snake hangs from the rock. Its venom gathers, slowly, and drips._  
_A woman kneels beside him, holding a bowl up under the drops. It is Sigyn, his wife._  
_She has been holding it a long time. Her arms are shaking._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): loyalty to someone who did wrong (a think question)  
> _Sigyn kneels beside Loki, holding the bowl, though he did a wrong thing and she could walk away._  
> _Is staying loyal to someone who did wrong a good thing? Why?_  
> - Yes: loyalty means staying when it is hard → A warm answer. Sigyn’s loyalty is the thing the story admires in her.
> - Not always: loyalty should not mean excusing harm → A careful answer. She holds the bowl, but she does not say he was right.
> - It depends on whether staying helps anyone → A practical answer. Her staying does help: for a moment, no drops fall on him.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on loyalty to someone who has done wrong (no single right answer)._

_Your Nubbin stops at the bottom of the stair and holds on to your trouser leg._  

#### `a20-14-bowl`

_You go nearer. Sigyn knows who you are: the guest who ran Frigg’s errands, and begged at the cave._  
_She doesn’t look at you. She looks at the bowl, and at nothing else._  
**Sigyn**: You asked so nicely, in the cave. Everybody heard about it.  
**Sigyn**: I don’t ask anything of you. Don’t ask anything of me.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view: Sigyn’s and yours  
> _Sigyn says, “You asked so nicely, in the cave. Everybody heard about it.”_  
> _She does not look at you._  
> _You pleaded for Baldr. How might Sigyn see it differently from you?_  
> - ✅ She is Loki’s wife, so she may hear your plea as aimed at her family → Yes. Your point of view was Baldr’s. Hers is the wife of the one being punished.
> - She did not hear anything → She says everybody heard. She knows exactly what you asked.
> - She agrees with everything you said → Her tone says otherwise. She would like to be left alone.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two points of view in the same scene._

_The bowl fills, drop by drop. Sigyn keeps her eyes on it, and her arms up._  
_Your Nubbin sits down at the edge of the lamplight and doesn’t come any closer._  

#### `a20-14-shake`

_The bowl is full. Sigyn has to take it away to empty it._  
_While she is gone, the drops fall on him. He shudders, so hard that the whole earth shakes._  
_Far above, people feel the ground move and call it an earthquake. In this story, now you know why._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-2, ask): plate boundaries and earthquakes in Iceland  
> _In the story, the earth shakes when Loki shudders. In real life, Iceland has many earthquakes._  
> _Iceland sits where two huge tectonic plates of Earth’s crust are slowly pulling apart, about 2 centimetres a year. What happens when they slip?_  
> - ✅ The ground shakes: an earthquake → Yes. When the plates slip suddenly, energy is released as shaking.
> - The sea turns to ice → Moving plates make shaking and sometimes volcanoes, not ice.
> - The Sun gets brighter → The Sun has nothing to do with it. This happens deep in the Earth.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that earthquakes happen where tectonic plates slip, as in Iceland._

_Then Sigyn is back with the bowl, and the drops fall into it, and the shaking stops._  
_The old book says he lies like this until the end of things. And she kneels there with him, all that time._  
_Your Nubbin is holding on to you with both arms._  

**Choices**

- **Hold your Nubbin close.**
    - You hold it close. It is shaking too, a little, like the earth, and then it isn’t.
- **Stay a while longer, for Sigyn.**
    - You stay, and Sigyn doesn’t look round. But when you go, she lifts one hand off the bowl, just for a moment.
- **Go back up the stair.**
    - You go up the stair into the cold air. Behind you the earth is quiet again, for now.

#### `a20-14-complete`

_You climb up out of the earth into a grey evening. The wind has changed, and it smells of snow._  
_The page turns under your hand. On the other side it is white from edge to edge._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): Iceland: fire and ice  
> _Iceland is sometimes called the land of fire and ice. Glaciers and active volcanoes lie close together on the same island._  
> _The glaciers are there because it is so far north. The volcanoes are there because hot rock rises in the gap between the plates._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Iceland has glaciers and volcanoes side by side._

_There is no road on this side. There is only the plain._  
_Your Nubbin pulls your cloak round both of you, and you step out onto the snow._  

### Glossary

- **tectonic plates**: The huge slabs of rock that make up Earth’s outer shell.

## A20-15. The Fimbulwinter

- `a20-15-s1`: Cross the long white plain. · _Keep the wind at your back and walk towards the dark line of trees._
- `a20-15-s2`: Find the two who are hiding in the wood. · _Walk in under the trees and look for where the snow is trodden._
- `a20-15-s3`: Keep Líf and Lífthrasir company through the winter. · _Sit in the hollow with them; there is nowhere else you need to be._

#### `a20-15-plain`

_Now comes the great winter. The old book calls it the Fimbulwinter._  
_Snow drives in from every side. The frost bites hard, the wind cuts, and the sun hangs pale and gives no heat._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): Earth’s tilt and short winter days  
> _The sun hangs pale, and the days are short. In real life, northern winters are dark because Earth is tilted._  
> _Around 21 December, the winter solstice, Reykjavík gets only about four hours of daylight. Why are northern winter days so short?_  
> - ✅ In winter the north leans away from the Sun → Yes. Earth’s tilt means the north gets less direct sunlight in winter.
> - The Sun moves further away from Earth in winter → Earth is actually a little closer to the Sun in January. It is the tilt that matters.
> - The Sun gets tired in winter → The Sun shines the same. It is Earth’s tilt that changes how much light reaches the north.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Earth’s tilt makes winter days short in the far north._

_Three winters come one after another, with no summer between them. The seasons simply forget to turn._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): counting missing summers  
> _Three winters come one after another, with no summer between them._  
> _In a normal run of three winters, a summer comes between each pair. How many summers does the Fimbulwinter skip?_  
> - ✅ 2 → Yes. Winter, summer, winter, summer, winter: two summers sit between three winters.
> - 3 → 3 is the number of winters. The summers sit between them, so there are 2.
> - 1 → There is a summer between the first and second winter, and another between the second and third: 2.
> _For grown-ups: Counted the summers that sit between three winters._

_You walk with your head down. Your Nubbin rides inside your cloak, tucked up against your chest._  
_You think of a valley you know, where a winter once would not end, and the small ones went still in the long grass._  
_Ahead, through the white, there is a dark line of trees._  

#### `a20-15-holt`

_The wood is called Hoddmímir’s Holt. Under its trees the snow is thinner, and the wind can’t find you._  
_Two people are sitting in a hollow under the roots of a great tree, wrapped in one blanket: a woman and a man._  
**Líf**: Oh. Someone. I thought there was nobody left who could walk.  
**Lífthrasir**: We’re Líf and Lífthrasir. We hide here. We live on the dew, every morning, off the leaves.  
**Líf**: It isn’t much. But it’s enough, if you don’t want very much.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): contentment: enough, if you do not want much (a think question)  
> _Líf says it is not much, “but it’s enough, if you don’t want very much.”_  
> _Can wanting less ever make us safer or happier? When is it not true?_  
> - Yes: when what we need is small, wanting less is a comfort → A fair answer. Líf and Lífthrasir have learned to be glad of enough.
> - Not always: some needs, like warmth, cannot be wanted away → A careful answer. Wanting less helps, but cold is still cold.
> - It helps for wants, but not for needs → A helpful distinction. A want can shrink. A real need cannot.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on wants and needs when there is little (no single right answer)._

_Your Nubbin climbs out of your cloak and goes straight to them. It sits down between them, under the blanket._  
**Lífthrasir**: It’s warm. Can it stay?  

#### `a20-15-company`

_So you stay in the holt, through the snow. Every morning the four of you lick the dew off the leaves, and it tastes of nothing._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, ask): what dew is  
> _Every morning you lick dew off the leaves. Dew is tiny drops of water on leaves and grass._  
> _Where does the water in dew come from?_  
> - ✅ Water vapour in the air turns into drops on cool surfaces → Yes. That is condensation again, outdoors, overnight.
> - It falls as very light rain → Dew forms on a clear night without rain. It comes from vapour in the air.
> - The leaves make water from nothing → Nothing makes water from nothing. The water was in the air as vapour.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dew is water vapour from the air condensing on cool surfaces._

_Every night you sit close, under one blanket and your cloak, and the winter goes on outside the trees._  
_Your Nubbin shares itself out: a night by Líf, a night by Lífthrasir, a night in your lap._  
**Lífthrasir**: We used to have names for the days. We stopped. There didn’t seem to be any point.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): weekday names from Norse gods  
> _Names for the days are older than they seem._  
> _Four English weekdays are named for gods the early English shared with the Norse._  
> _Tuesday is for Tiw (Týr), Wednesday for Woden (Odin), Thursday for Thor, and Friday for Frige (Frigg)._  
> _So every Thursday you say, without thinking about it, “Thor’s day.”_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that four English weekday names come from the gods the Norse also knew._

_Outside, the third winter starts without the second one having ended._  
**Líf**: Tell us something. Anything that isn’t snow.  

**Choices**

- **Tell them about your valley.**
    - **You**: There’s a pond, and a gate that sticks. You have to lift it and push.
    - **Lífthrasir**: A gate that sticks. That sounds like a good place to live.
- **Tell them about the bright hall on the rise.**
    - You tell them about Breidablik, and the light coming off him, and your Nubbin asleep on the boards.
    - **Líf**: Then there was a light once. Good. I hoped there was.
- **Say nothing. Just sit close.**
    - You sit close and say nothing. After a while Lífthrasir puts his head on your shoulder, and sleeps.

#### `a20-15-company-done`

**Líf**: You stayed. Nobody stays anywhere any more. Everybody’s running somewhere.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: 3 winters × 6 months  
> _Líf says nobody stays anywhere any more; everybody is running somewhere._  
> _Suppose each of the three winters lasted six months. How many months of winter is that in all?_  
> - ✅ 18 months → Yes. 3 × 6 = 18 months of winter, a year and a half.
> - 9 months → 9 is 3 + 6. Three winters of six months each is 3 × 6 = 18.
> - 12 months → 12 would be two winters of six months. Three winters make 3 × 6 = 18.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups: 3 × 6 months is 18 months._


#### `a20-15-complete`

_One morning the dew tastes different: not warmer, just different, as if something far off had changed its mind._  
**Lífthrasir**: Something’s coming. I can feel it in the roots.  
**Líf**: Not here, though. It won’t come here. Will it?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): worry about what is coming (a think question)  
> _Lífthrasir can feel something coming through the roots, and Líf hopes it will not come here._  
> _What helps when we are afraid of something coming that we cannot see or stop?_  
> - Staying close to people, and taking one hour at a time → A steady answer. Fear is lighter shared, and smaller when we look at only the next hour.
> - Finding out what we can, then letting go of the rest → A wise answer. Some things we can learn, and some we can only wait through.
> - Doing something with our hands to keep busy → A practical answer. Busy hands can steady a worried mind, the way Frigg turned her spindle while she thought.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how to cope with fear of something we cannot control (no single right answer)._

_Your Nubbin climbs the tree roots to the edge of the holt, and looks out._  

### Glossary

- **solstice**: One of the two days a year when the Sun is furthest north or south, giving the longest or shortest day.
- **flicker**: To shine unsteadily, brightening and dimming.

## A20-16. The Twilight

- `a20-16-s1`: Look out from the edge of the holt. · _Climb the roots at the wood’s edge, where your Nubbin is._
- `a20-16-s2`: Wait at the holt’s edge until it is over. · _Stay with Líf and Lífthrasir; nothing will reach the trees._

#### `a20-16-edge`

_From the edge of the holt you can see a long way: the white plain, the grey sea beyond it, and the sky._  
_Something is happening at the end of the world. It is very far off, and you see it the way you see weather on the hills._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): simile: weather on the hills  
> _The writer says you see it “the way you see weather on the hills.”_  
> _That is a simile, made with “the way” instead of “like”. What does it help us feel?_  
> - ✅ That it is huge, but distant, and cannot reach the holt → Yes. We watch distant weather and know it is not on top of us.
> - That it is a small rain shower → The comparison is about distance, not size. The event is vast, but far away.
> - That it will soon arrive → A storm on far hills may never come near. The simile lets us watch from safety.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile adds: the event is huge but far away._

_Wolves are running across the sky, after the sun and after the moon. They are small with distance, and fast._  
_A ship is coming over the sea. It is huge and dark, and very slow._  
_There is a figure in its bow. It stands looking ahead at the land, and never turns round._  
_On the far edge of the world there is a line of fire, low down, like a sunset in the wrong place._  
_None of it comes near. The holt is very quiet, and your Nubbin is holding on to a root with both arms._  

#### `a20-16-wait`

_Líf and Lífthrasir come up beside you. They don’t look out; they look at you, to see how bad it is._  
**Líf**: Tell us. Is it coming here?  
_You watch the fire, and the running wolves, and the sky. None of it comes towards the trees._  
**You**: No. Not here.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty with frightened people (a think question)  
> _Líf asks if it is coming here, and you say, “No. Not here.”_  
> _If you had not been sure, would it be kinder to say something comforting, or to be honestly uncertain?_  
> - Say something comforting → A kind instinct. But a comfort that turns out false can break trust later.
> - Be honestly uncertain, and stay with them → A brave answer. It is true, and you are still beside them.
> - Say what you can see, and be clear about what you cannot → A balanced answer. You told them what you saw, which is what you honestly knew.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on being honest with someone who is frightened (no single right answer)._

**Lífthrasir**: Then we’ll wait. We’re good at waiting.  
_The light changes. The noise far off gets less, and less, and is gone._  

**Choices**

- **Hold Líf’s hand.**
    - You hold Líf’s hand. Her fingers are cold, and then they aren’t.
- **Tuck your Nubbin inside your cloak.**
    - You tuck your Nubbin inside your cloak. It puts one eye out, to keep watch with you.
- **Keep watching, so that someone does.**
    - You keep watching. It is a hard thing to see, even far off, and someone should, so that it isn’t only told.

#### `a20-16-complete`

_Then it is quiet. Not the quiet of the snow: a new quiet, like a room after everybody has gone home._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): fresh snow absorbs sound  
> _The writer says the quiet is “not the quiet of the snow.” Fresh snow really does make the world seem hushed._  
> _Why does a fresh fall of snow muffle sound?_  
> - ✅ Its tiny air pockets soak up sound instead of bouncing it back → Yes. Fresh snow is full of trapped air, which swallows sound waves.
> - Snow makes sound travel faster → Snow does not speed sound up. It soaks it up.
> - Cold air cannot carry any sound → Cold air carries sound well. It is the soft snow that muffles it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fresh snow absorbs sound._

_The snow stops. Nobody notices for a while, because it has been snowing for so long._  
**Líf**: Is it over?  
_Your Nubbin sniffs the air, and sneezes. The air smells of salt, and of something green._  

## A20-17. The Green Earth

- `a20-17-s1`: Walk out of the holt into the new land. · _Follow Líf and Lífthrasir out from under the trees._
- `a20-17-s2`: Go to the old ground where the gods’ halls stood. · _Walk across the fields to the plain where grass grows over old stones._
- `a20-17-s3`: Look in the grass for what the gods once played with. · _Search the long grass round the old stones._

#### `a20-17-green`

_The sea goes down. Out of it the land comes up again, wet and new, and green as a first leaf._  
_There are fields on it already. Corn is growing in them, and nobody sowed it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a rectangle  
> _Fields of corn are growing on the new land. Say one field is 40 metres long and 25 metres wide._  
> _What is its area?_  
> - ✅ 1000 square metres → Yes. Area is length × width: 40 × 25 = 1000 square metres.
> - 65 square metres → 65 is 40 + 25. Area is found by multiplying, not adding.
> - 130 square metres → 130 is the distance round the edge (the perimeter). Area is 40 × 25 = 1000.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a rectangle: 40 × 25 = 1000 square metres._

_Líf and Lífthrasir walk out from under the trees, slowly, holding on to each other. Then faster._  
**Líf**: Grass. Feel it. It’s grass.  
**Lífthrasir**: And the sun. Look. It’s warm. It’s warm again.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): plants need water and light  
> _Líf says the sun is warm again. Plants need sunlight and water to grow._  
> _Which part of a plant mainly catches the sunlight?_  
> - ✅ The leaves → Yes. Leaves catch sunlight and use it, with water and air, to make food for the plant.
> - The roots → Roots drink water and hold the plant in place. Leaves catch the light.
> - The seeds → Seeds grow into new plants. The leaves catch sunlight.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that leaves catch the sunlight a plant needs._

_The sun had a daughter before the end, the old book says. Now she rides her mother’s road, just as bright._  
_Your Nubbin runs out into the middle of a field and lies down flat in the sun, arms and legs out._  

#### `a20-17-old-ground`

_Where the gods’ halls stood there is a plain of grass, with old stones showing through it here and there._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): ruins and what they show  
> _Where the gods’ halls stood there is a plain of grass, with old stones showing here and there._  
> _How can archaeologists tell what stood at a place like this long ago?_  
> - ✅ They dig carefully, study stones and tools, and compare with written records → Yes. Stones, post-holes and tools show where walls and floors were, and records help fill the gaps.
> - They ask the grass → Grass cannot answer. It is the ground beneath it that holds the evidence.
> - They cannot ever find out → They find out a great deal by careful digging and by comparing evidence.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how archaeologists work out what once stood on a site._

_People are gathering there: the gods’ sons, who came through the end of things, Vídarr and Váli, Módi and Magni._  
_Módi and Magni have their father’s hammer between them. They carry it gently, like something asleep._  
**Vídarr**: Guest. You came through as well. Sit with us. There’s a great deal to talk about, and all the time in the world.  
_Then two more come walking up out of the ground, by the road that goes down. They come from Hel._  
_Baldr comes, and Hödr with him._  
_Baldr’s light is just as it was. Your Nubbin is up and running before you can stand._  

#### `a20-17-old-ground-done`

_Your Nubbin runs straight into Baldr’s light and falls asleep in it, at once, in the grass._  
_It has been trying to get back there all this time._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): a recurring image: the Nubbin and the light (a think question)  
> _All through this page your Nubbin has been trying to get back to Baldr’s light._  
> _A thing a story keeps returning to is a motif. What do you think this motif says about the story’s message?_  
> - That kindness is something people are drawn to, and will follow → A warm reading. The light is not clever or powerful. It is kind.
> - That we keep looking for the people we have lost → A tender reading. The Nubbin never stops turning towards him.
> - That hope can be small and still not go out → A hopeful reading. The light was low, but it was his.
> _For grown-ups: Offered readings of a repeated image in the story (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-17-pieces`

_The brothers sit down on the grass, and the others sit round them, and they talk about old things._  
**Baldr**: Do you remember the Thing-field? The arrow that went round me?  
**Hödr**: I remember the guest telling it. Better than you did, as well.  
_In the long grass by the old stones, your hand closes on something small and cold. You pull it out._  
_It is a game piece, made of gold. There are more of them in the grass: the pieces the gods played with in the old days._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: sharing 18 between 6  
> _There are more golden game pieces in the long grass._  
> _Suppose you find 18, and share them equally between 6 players. How many pieces does each player get?_  
> - ✅ 3 → Yes. 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so each player gets three pieces.
> - 12 → 12 is 18 − 6. Sharing equally between 6 is division: 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
> - 24 → 24 is 18 + 6. We are sharing out, so we divide: 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a sharing problem: 18 ÷ 6 = 3._

**Vídarr**: They were ours, before. Now they’re anybody’s.  

**Choices**

- **Give the first piece to Baldr.**
    - **Baldr**: Ha. I always lost with this one. Every single time.
- **Give the first piece to Hödr.**
    - Hödr turns it over in his fingers, feeling the shape of it.
    - **Hödr**: A little horse. I know this one. I always wanted to be the horse.
- **Set it on the grass between them.**
    - You set it on the grass between the two brothers. They both reach for it at once, and both laugh.

#### `a20-17-complete`

_The sun goes over the new land. The talk goes on, slow and easy, as if there will always be more of it._  
_Hödr turns his face towards you. You find you are sitting beside him, closer than anyone._  
**Hödr**: You rode down to fetch my brother home, and you begged for him in the cave. I heard about that.  
**Hödr**: Thank you for trying.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): does trying count? (a think question)  
> _Hödr thanks you for trying, though you could not bring Baldr home._  
> _Does trying count when it does not change the ending?_  
> - Yes: trying shows we care, whatever happens → A warm answer. Effort and care are real even when the result is out of our hands.
> - Only a little: the result matters most → A fair view. Results matter. But the people you tried for may value the trying too.
> - It depends on whether the trying was honest → A thoughtful answer. Honest effort counts more than showing off.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether effort counts when it does not change the outcome (no single right answer)._

_Before you go, Baldr puts something in your hand: a sprig with two leaves, from a tree at the edge of the old ground._  
**Baldr**: It was too young to be asked, once. It’s older now. So am I. Keep it for me.  
_Your Nubbin wakes in his light and looks at him for a long moment. Then it gets up and comes back to you, on its own._  
_Líf and Lífthrasir walk out together into the morning, across the fields that nobody sowed._  
_You are back in the Grove, the atlas on your knee. Something clinks in your pocket: a golden game piece, and your Nubbin has brought home a sprig to match._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme of the whole page  
> _The page opened with promises, and ends with a sprig kept for Baldr._  
> _Which theme fits the page best?_  
> - ✅ Love shows in staying with people when things are hard → Yes. Frigg’s asking, Hödr’s company and the sprig all say it.
> - Gods always win in the end → The gods lose Baldr, and the page does not say they win everything.
> - Nothing can ever be mended → The page ends green and hopeful, so that does not fit.
> _For grown-ups: Chose the theme of the whole page._


### Glossary

- **archaeologist**: Someone who learns about the past by carefully digging up and studying what people left behind.
- **motif**: An image or idea a story keeps coming back to.

## A22-1. The Candle’s Story

- `a22-01-s1`: Step into the painted page and hear how the candle began. · _Touch the candle in the window on the atlas page, then sit at the edge of the painted bed._
- `a22-01-s2`: Walk into the valley on the morning of Antonio’s ceremony and meet the family. · _Let the page turn, then climb the hill from the market square to the house with green shutters._

#### `a22-01-story`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a valley ringed by green mountains: white walls, red roofs, tall palms and a candle in one window._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): finding Colombia: its coasts, its mountains and its coffee country  
> _This page is set in a real country: Colombia, in the north-west corner of South America._  
> _It has a coast on the Caribbean Sea to the north and on the Pacific Ocean to the west._  
> _The Andes mountains run up through it in three long ranges, and coffee grows on their slopes._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Colombia is in north-west South America, with two coasts, three Andes ranges and coffee country._

_The page does not come alive at once. It stays painted, and you step into the paint._  
_It is night, years ago. In a bedroom made of brushstrokes, an old woman sits beside a little girl in round glasses._  
**Abuela Alma**: Come in, then. You may as well hear it too. Mirabel has heard it a hundred times, and she still wants it.  
**Mirabel**: Tell the river part!  
**Abuela Alma**: First the beginning. When I was young there was trouble in the land where we lived, and we had to leave our home.  
_The painting changes: a young couple on a road at night, with three babies wrapped against the cold._  
**Abuela Alma**: Pedro carried two of the babies, and I carried one. We walked for days with other families who had to leave too.  
_Far behind them, on a ridge, there is a thin dark line of riders. The painting does not bring them any closer._  
**Abuela Alma**: At a river, the trouble caught up with us. Pedro told me to cross with the babies. He stayed on the bank, so that we could.  
**Abuela Alma**: He did not come. Pedro died there, and I have missed him every day.  
_In the painting, the candle in her hand blazes, and the mountains rise round the river like hands closing round a flame._  
**Abuela Alma**: The candle gave us a home where nobody could take us from each other. A house that loves us. A miracle.  

**Choices**

- **Keep listening.**
    - You keep very still. The little girl has her fist in the blanket, holding on to the part about the river.
- **Ask about Pedro.**
    - **Abuela Alma**: He was kind, and he was brave, and he was not very good at dancing. That is enough for one night.
    - She says it lightly. Her hand on the blanket does not move at all.

#### `a22-01-story-done`

**Abuela Alma**: Every child in this family is given a gift when they are old enough. Tomorrow is yours, Mirabel.  
**Mirabel**: What will it be?  
**Abuela Alma**: Sleep, and see.  
_Mirabel lies awake anyway, with Abuela’s story still in the room._  
_Her grandmother’s family left home with almost nothing but each other. In many places and times, families still have to do that._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): imagining what matters most when a family must leave home  
> _Abuela’s family left home in a hurry, carrying three babies and very little else. If you had to leave quickly, what would matter most to take?_  
> - The people I love → That is the answer many families give. People matter most, and they are the hardest thing to leave behind.
> - Something that reminds me of home → A fair answer. A small thing from home can carry a lot of memory, and many families take one.
> - Something to keep me comfortable → A fair answer too. Comfort matters when everything else is changing, and a blanket can feel like home.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what a family would take if they had to leave home quickly, and how that feels._


#### `a22-01-casita`

_The page turns by itself. The paint goes thin and bright and real: morning, ten years later, and a market full of noise._  
_Up the hill is a house with white walls, green shutters and a red roof. Its shutters open and close by themselves._  
_A young woman in round glasses and an embroidered skirt comes down the steps two at a time, with a list._  
_You know the glasses. The little girl from the painting has grown up, and the house is the one the candle made._  
**Mirabel**: Hi! Hello! You’re the traveller. Abuela said there’d be a traveller. Sorry, are you a traveller?  
_The floor tiles clack in a ripple across the doorway, like a dog thumping its tail._  
**Mirabel**: That’s Casita. Casita, be nice. Guest.  
**Mirabel**: Come and meet everyone: my abuela, my tías and tíos, my primos. You’ll lose track.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): Spanish family words: abuela, tía, primo  
> _In Spanish, abuela means grandmother and tía means aunt. From the way Mirabel lists her family, what do you think primo means?_  
> - ✅ Cousin → Yes. A boy cousin is a primo and a girl cousin is a prima. Antonio and Camilo are Mirabel’s primos, and Dolores is her prima.
> - Uncle → Close, but an uncle is a tío. A cousin is a primo, or a prima for a girl.
> - Baby → Not quite. A baby is a bebé. A cousin is a primo, or a prima for a girl.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the Spanish family word primo (cousin) from context, alongside abuela and tía._

_A shutter swings out and taps you gently on the shoulder._  
**Mirabel**: I’m Mirabel. I don’t have a gift, before anyone tells you. It’s fine. It’s totally fine.  

**Choices**

- **Say you are the traveller.**
    - **Mirabel**: Great. Perfect. You’re in the blue room. The house likes guests. Mostly.
- **Point out that your Nubbin is travelling too.**
    - **Mirabel**: Oh, hello! Look at you. Antonio is going to lose his mind. In a good way.
- **Ask what the list is for.**
    - **Mirabel**: Tonight. Antonio’s gift ceremony. My little cousin. Everything has to be perfect, so it’s a long list.

#### `a22-01-lamp`

_Abuela Alma meets you in the courtyard. She is older than in the painting, straight as a broom, with a black shawl._  
_She looks at the little lamp at your belt, the one from your Long-Grass post. Its glass is dark._  
**Abuela Alma**: Nobody in this house walks about in the dark. Come.  
_She lights it from the candle in the window. The flame is gold and steady, and it isn’t yours, and it is very kind of her._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): a flame can light another wick without being used up  
> _Abuela lights your lamp from her candle. Does her candle’s flame get any smaller?_  
> - ✅ No: one flame can light many wicks → Right. The heat from the first flame warms the new wick until it catches. Each flame then burns its own wax.
> - Yes: it gives away half its flame → It is a nice idea, but flames do not work like that. The first flame passes on heat and stays the same size.
> - It goes out → Not at all. Lighting a second wick takes only a little heat, and the first flame keeps burning.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat from one flame can light another wick, and the first flame is not used up._


#### `a22-01-complete`

_Your room is small and blue, with a window over the valley. The bed turns its own covers down when you look at it._  
_Your Nubbin climbs onto the windowsill and looks across the courtyard at the candle in the window opposite._  
_Downstairs somebody is laughing, somebody is cooking, and three people are arguing about chairs._  
_Each of the three is carrying four chairs, and each wants to put them somewhere different._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: 3 × 4  
> _Three people are each carrying four chairs. How many chairs is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ Twelve → Yes. Three groups of four is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, which we write as 3 × 4 = 12.
> - Seven → That is 3 + 4. We need three groups of four: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, or 3 × 4 = 12.
> - Nine → Try it as three groups of four: 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups to find 3 × 4 = 12._

_Somewhere in the walls there is a small scurry, and then nothing._  

### Glossary

- **abuela**: The Spanish word for grandmother.
- **miracle**: A wonderful event that seems impossible.
- **tía**: The Spanish word for aunt.
- **primo**: The Spanish word for a boy cousin. A girl cousin is a prima.

## A22-2. The Family

- `a22-02-s1`: Go down to the market with Mirabel. · _Follow Mirabel down the hill to the square._
- `a22-02-s2`: Meet the rest of the Madrigals at the house. · _Go back up the hill with Mirabel and talk to the family in the courtyard._
- `a22-02-s3`: Eat in the kitchen with Julieta and Agustín. · _Follow the smell of arepas to the kitchen._

#### `a22-02-market`

_Market morning. The square is full of stalls: oranges, coffee sacks, bolts of bright cloth and somebody’s goat._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): coffee country: how coffee grows in the Andes  
> _The coffee sacks are no accident. This valley is in Colombia’s coffee country, high in the Andes, where the cool mountain air suits coffee bushes._  
> _Coffee beans are really seeds. They grow inside bright red fruits called coffee cherries._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Colombian coffee grows on mountain slopes, and that beans are seeds inside red coffee cherries._

**Mirabel**: Okay. Quick tour. Everyone in my family has a gift, and everyone in town knows exactly what it is.  
_A tall young woman walks past with a donkey over each shoulder._  
**Mirabel**: That’s Luisa, my sister. Super strong. Hi, Luisa!  
**Luisa**: Hi. Can’t stop. The church is crooked again.  
_A woman at a stall has a small grey cloud over her head. It is raining on her onions._  
**Mirabel**: Tía Pepa. Her weather is her mood. Tía, the cloud.  
**Tía Pepa**: What cloud? There is no cloud. I am perfectly calm.  
_The cloud thunders, very quietly. A man in a yellow shirt hurries over and fans it away with his hat._  
**Mirabel**: Tío Félix. He says his gift is Tía Pepa.  
**Tío Félix**: It is a very big gift. I am a lucky man!  

**Choices**

- **Tell Tía Pepa the cloud is fine.**
    - **Tía Pepa**: It is fine, isn’t it?
    - The cloud turns into a small, pleased rainbow.
- **Ask Félix how he copes.**
    - **Tío Félix**: Umbrellas. Many umbrellas. And I tell her she’s beautiful, which is true, so it’s easy.
- **Check on your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin has found the goat, and the goat has found your Nubbin. They are deciding whether to be friends.

#### `a22-02-market-done`

_Mirabel ticks something off her list and nearly walks into a post._  
**Mirabel**: Party shopping done: three bags of oranges at four Shells a bag, and one loaf for five Shells. I paid with a twenty-Shell coin.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): two-step money problem: multiply, add, then subtract from 20  
> _How many Shells of change should Mirabel get back?_  
> - ✅ Three → Yes. Oranges cost 3 × 4 = 12 Shells. With the loaf that is 12 + 5 = 17 Shells. 20 − 17 = 3 Shells of change.
> - Eight → That is 20 − 12, which forgets the loaf. With the loaf, 12 + 5 = 17 and 20 − 17 = 3.
> - Seventeen → Seventeen is what she spent. The change is what is left of 20: 20 − 17 = 3.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step money problem: 3 × 4 = 12, 12 + 5 = 17, 20 − 17 = 3._

**Mirabel**: Next, my cousins. Brace yourself.  

#### `a22-02-cousins`

_In the courtyard a young woman steps out of a cloud of petals: perfect hair, perfect smile, roses at her feet._  
**Mirabel**: My sister Isabela. Flowers. Everyone loves her. I love her!  
**Isabela**: Mirabel. And a guest. How nice.  
_She smiles, and an orchid grows out of the wall beside your head. It is a lovely smile, and it never changes._  
_A girl in a pale dress drifts past, whispering very fast to nobody._  
**Mirabel**: Cousin Dolores. She hears everything. If you sneeze in the market, she knows.  
**Dolores**: You did sneeze in the market. Bless you.  
_A boy turns round, and he is Mirabel, then Félix, then himself again, a lanky teenager, grinning._  
**Camilo**: Camilo. Faces. I can do yours if you stand still.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what makes a person themselves, apart from how they look  
> _Camilo can look exactly like Félix, but he is still Camilo. What really makes a person themselves?_  
> - ✅ What they care about and how they treat people → Yes. A face can be copied, but your kindness, your humour and what you care about are yours alone.
> - Their hair and clothes → Those are part of how we look, and they can change. What stays is what we care about and how we treat people.
> - Their gift → Mirabel has no gift, and she is entirely herself. Who we are is what we care about and how we treat others.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what makes a person themselves: values and kindness, not looks or gifts._


**Choices**

    - Camilo looks at you hard, and then you are looking at yourself, a little taller, with better hair.
    - **Camilo**: I improved you. You’re welcome.
- **Don’t stand still.**
    - **Camilo**: Fair. People hate it. Mostly my sisters. Mostly when I do them.

#### `a22-02-kitchen`

_In the kitchen a woman with a kind, tired face is cooking arepas. A boy with a burnt finger eats one, and the burn is gone._  
**Julieta**: You must be hungry. Everyone who comes up that hill is hungry. Sit.  
_The arepa is hot and buttery, with cheese in the middle. The ache in your legs from the long page just stops._  

> **Lesson** (health, K-LS1-1, notice): what corn and cheese give a growing body  
> _Arepas are eaten all over Colombia. They are made from ground corn, grilled or fried, often with cheese._  
> _Corn gives you energy to run about. Cheese gives protein and calcium, which help muscles and bones grow._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that corn gives energy, and cheese gives protein and calcium for growing muscles and bones._

**Agustín**: Welcome! Welcome. Don’t mind the bee. I’m used to the bee.  
_A gentle man in glasses waves from the doorway. A bee is sitting on his nose._  
**Mirabel**: Mamá and Papá. So that’s everyone. Everyone with a gift, I mean, and me.  
_Across the courtyard there is a tower with a dark door. Everybody manages not to look at it, all at once._  
_Félix starts to say a name. Pepa’s cloud cracks with thunder, and Félix turns it into a cough._  
_Then everybody talks at once, about chairs._  

**Choices**

- **Ask about the tower.**
    - **Mirabel**: Oh! That’s nobody. Nobody’s up there. It’s just a room.
    - She says it in a rush. Julieta puts another arepa on your plate, which is also an answer.
- **Let it go.**
    - You let it go. Mirabel gives you a small grateful look, and the house rattles a single tile, like a sigh.
- **Watch your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin is at the courtyard’s edge, looking up at the tower. A small grey face looks back from a crack, and vanishes.

#### `a22-02-complete`

_By afternoon you know the gifts by heart: healing, weather, strength, flowers, hearing, faces._  
_Mirabel hangs paper lanterns, carries chairs and ties ribbons all day, and nobody once asks her to._  
**Mirabel**: It’s fine. Somebody has to do the stuff that isn’t magic.  
_She says it brightly. Your Nubbin leans against her ankle anyway._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading feelings from actions as well as words  
> _Mirabel says “It’s fine” in a bright voice, and your Nubbin leans against her anyway._  
> _How can you tell how someone really feels when their words say one thing?_  
> - Watch their face and what they do → A good clue. Actions often tell us more than words, and a writer shows feelings that way too.
> - Listen to how they say it → Another good clue. A bright voice that is a little too bright can hide a sore feeling.
> - Ask them kindly → The kindest clue of all. Asking gently, and waiting, gives people room to say what is true.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to read someone’s real feelings from their words, voice and actions._
