> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS3-1, ask): variation: animals of one kind can look different from each other  
> _Kotick is white, and all the other pups are dark. What do we call the small differences between animals of the same kind?_  
> - ✅ Variation. → Yes. Variation is why no two animals of a kind are exactly alike. Sometimes it makes an animal stand out, like Kotick, and sometimes it helps an animal survive.
> - Disguise. → Disguise is when an animal hides on purpose. The word you want is variation: natural differences between members of a kind.
> - A mistake. → Nature does not make mistakes in that sense. Differences between animals of one kind are called variation.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that variation means the natural differences between animals of the same kind, such as a rare white seal pup._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals in months: July to October is 3 months  
> _Kotick was born in July and swims well by October. How many months is that?_  
> - ✅ 3 months. → Yes. July to August is 1, to September is 2, to October is 3. Counting on month by month is a handy way to find a time interval.
> - 4 months. → Counting July itself, you would get 4. But July to October is the gap between them. August, September, October: 3 months have passed.
> - 1 month. → One month after July is only August. Count on: August, September, October. That is 3 months.
> _For grown-ups: Counted on to find a time interval of 3 months from July to October._

> - Hearing. → The beach roars, true, and that is hearing. These words show touch and taste.
> _For grown-ups: Identified sense words, such as sharp, wet and stings, that help a reader feel what a character feels._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): why countries make agreements to protect animals that cross borders  
> _Fur seals swim across the whole North Pacific. Why would countries need to agree together to protect them?_  
> - ✅ The seals cross borders, so one country alone cannot protect them. → Yes. Seals do not stop at borders, so many countries must agree on the same rules. Today people on the islands, including Unangax̂ communities, also help look after the seals and their home.
> - So the seals can sign it too. → Ha. Seals cannot sign. People make the agreement on their behalf. It is needed because the seals swim across many countries’ waters.
> - It does not matter. They can look after themselves. → Seals had a very hard time when hunting went unchecked. Countries agree together because seals cross borders.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that countries make shared agreements to protect animals, such as fur seals, that travel across borders._

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, ask): migration: animals travel far for food and to breed  
> _Real fur seals leave their beaches each autumn and swim thousands of kilometres. Why do they make such a long trip?_  
> - ✅ To find food in the open ocean, then return to breed on the beaches. → Yes. This long seasonal journey is called migration. Many animals do it, from whales to birds, to follow food and find a safe place for their young.
> - Because they are lost. → They are not lost. They know exactly where to go. They migrate to find food and to breed.
> - To get away from the cold. → They are built for the cold, with thick fur and blubber. They migrate to find food, and come back to breed.

- **harvest**: The gathering of a crop, or of animals, for people to use.
- **bachelors**: In the seal story, the young male seals that have no place of their own yet.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): compound words: clam-cracker is two words joined to make a new one  
> _Kotick calls Sea Vitch a “clam-cracker”, and the gulls love it. That is a compound word, two words joined into one._  
> _What does it mean?_  
> - ✅ Someone who cracks clams open. → Yes. Clam plus cracker: a walrus really does eat clams from the sea floor, so the name fits. Compound words, like sunshine or notebook, are made by joining two words and combining their meanings.
> - A cracker made out of clams. → That is a funny picture, and you can see how the words might mean that. But here a cracker is someone who cracks things open, so a clam-cracker cracks clams.
> - A crack in a clam. → Good try: both words are in there. In this name the second word is the one who does the cracking: a walrus cracking clams.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of the compound word clam-cracker from its two parts._

_The gulls on the rocks above hear that, and love it. They have never liked Sea Vitch._  
**Gull**: Clam-cracker! Clam-cracker!  
**Gull**: Sea Vitch is a clam-cracker! Clam-crack-crack!  
**Sea Vitch**: Hrrmph. Ask the Sea Cows, then, and leave me in peace.  
**Sea Vitch**: If they are still alive. Nobody has seen them for years.

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying: 5 years of 12 months is 60 months  
> _Kotick searched for 5 years, and every year has 12 months. How many months did he search?_  
> - ✅ 60 months. → Yes: 5 × 12 = 60. Split it up: 5 × 10 = 50, and 5 × 2 = 10, so 50 + 10 = 60. It is a long time to keep looking for something nobody believes in.
> - 17 months. → That is 5 + 12. But there are 12 months in each of the 5 years. So we multiply: 5 × 12 = 60.
> - 50 months. → That would be 5 × 10. Each year has 12 months, not 10. 5 × 12 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 5 × 12 = 60 to turn years into months, splitting 12 into 10 and 2._

**Kotick**: Men cannot come here. Nobody can, unless they are a seal, and swim under the cliffs.

_The Sea Cows never spoke a single word, and yet they led him all the way here._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what characters do can say more than what they say  
> _The Sea Cows never say anything, but they help Kotick more than anyone. What does that show?_  
> - ✅ What a character does can tell us more than what they say. → Yes. A character’s actions show who they are, and often more truly than their words. Good readers watch what characters do, not only what they say.
> - Silent characters are not important. → The Sea Cows are the most important characters in this whole quest. Their actions tell us what they are like.
> - The Sea Cows are shy. → They may be. But look at what they do: they guide him all the way. Actions can show more than words.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a character’s actions can reveal more about them than their words._


#### `a24-18-home`

_Kotick swims all the way home to Novastoshnah and tells the seals about the hidden beaches._  
_They laugh at him, of course: a white seal, with his head full of stories._  
**Old Seal**: Hidden beaches! Go and lie in the sun, white one, and stop bothering your elders.  
_So Kotick, who has grown big and strong in five years of searching, puts his chest against the biggest bull’s chest._  
_And he shoves, and roars, and shoves again, all along the beach, until every bull who laughed has been pushed into the sea._  
**Sea Catch**: That is my son! That is my son!  
**Sea Catch**: Come on, then, who is next? Who else says there are no beaches?  
_Sea Catch joins in, shoving with his scarred old neck and shouting for joy. Nobody bleeds, but everybody is very wet._  
**Kotick**: I am going to the new beaches! Who is coming with me?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): persuading or pushing: is making people do what you think is best the same as helping them?  
> _Kotick shoves the bulls until they follow. Is making people do what you think is best the same as helping them?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - No. Helping is when people choose for themselves. → That is a fair answer. Kotick’s way is rough, and the seals do choose to follow in the end. Many people think the best way to change a mind is to listen and explain.
> - Yes, if it saves them from harm. → That is a fair answer. Kotick is trying to save the seals from the hunt. But he does it by shoving, which makes it hard to tell whether they follow because they agree or because they are pushed.
> - It depends how much harm is at stake, and whether it is only a shove. → That is a thoughtful answer. A little force to prevent a big harm is different from forcing someone for no good reason. Even then, the best result is when the others choose to go.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between persuading and forcing, and whether pushing people toward what we think is best is helping._


**Choices**

- **Cheer from the top of the beach.**
    - Your Nubbin cheers too, like a kettle: a wolf kettle, or a seal kettle. It does not mind which.
- **Look for Matkah.**
    - **Matkah**: He was always going to do it. I told his father so.
    - **Matkah**: His father did not believe me either.

#### `a24-18-home-done`

_The seals stop laughing. They look at the white seal, and they look at each other._  
_And then, a few at a time, then more, then more again, until the sea is full of heads, they follow him out to sea._  
_Ten, then a hundred, then a thousand, and still more behind them. Each count is ten times the last._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a pattern with a rule: each number is 10 times the last  
> _The seals follow Kotick in groups of 10, then 100, then 1,000. Each number is 10 times the one before._  
> _What comes next?_  
> - ✅ 10,000. → Yes. 1,000 × 10 = 10,000. Find the rule, multiply by 10, and carry on. That is how a pattern grows.
> - 2,000. → That would be adding 1,000, but the rule is to multiply by 10. 1,000 × 10 = 10,000.
> - 1,100. → That adds 100, but the rule is multiplying by 10. 1,000 × 10 = 10,000.
> _For grown-ups: Found the next number in a pattern by working out the rule (multiply by 10)._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): protected places and the rules that keep wild animals safe today  
> _Kotick found a safe beach where nobody hunts. Today some places are set aside by law so that wild animals can live safely._  
> _What are they called?_  
> - ✅ Nature reserves, or wildlife refuges. → Yes. Rules keep hunters and builders out. Pench Tiger Reserve, near Seoni, is one for tigers, and fur seals are protected by law too. Safe places are how many wild animals survive.
> - Zoos only. → Zoos care for some animals, but most wild animals live outdoors. Nature reserves and refuges protect their real homes.
> - There are none. Wild animals look after themselves. → Many places are protected, and they matter a great deal. They are called nature reserves or wildlife refuges.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nature reserves and wildlife refuges are places protected by rules so that wild animals can live safely._

- **kelp**: A large brown seaweed that grows in cold, shallow seas, like a forest under the water.

#### `a25-01-shop`

_Nova’s atlas opens at a page that is mostly a glass door, with a little bell above it._  
_It is raining on the page. Real rain, running off the edge and on to your table._  
_You touch the bell. It rings, and you are standing behind it in a dim antiquarian bookshop, full of old and rare books._  
_Books climb to the ceiling. In an armchair between the towers, an old man in a black suit is reading._  
_Nobody looks at you. Your Nubbin waves at the old man, and he turns a page._  
_The door bangs open. A boy tumbles in, soaked, with a school bag on his back._  
_He is about ten, round, with wet hair in his eyes. He shuts the door and leans on it, panting._  
**Mr Coreander**: Out. I don’t sell to children.  
**Mr Coreander**: They sneeze on books and ask whether there are pictures.  
**Bastian**: I’m not buying anything. There are boys outside.  
**Bastian**: Just until they’ve gone past. Please.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what to do when other children are unkind: go somewhere safe and tell a trusted grown-up  
> _Bastian is hiding from boys who were unkind to him._  
> _What is a good thing to do when that happens to you?_  
> - ✅ Get somewhere safe, and tell a grown-up you trust. → Yes. Being unkind to someone is never their fault. It is never yours, either. A grown-up you trust can help it stop, and you don’t have to carry it alone.
> - Hit them back. → It’s very hard to feel so cross. But hitting tends to make more trouble. Getting safe and telling a trusted grown-up can really make it stop.
> - Keep it a secret. → Lots of people do that, because they feel ashamed. But there is nothing to be ashamed of. Telling a trusted person is the braver thing, and it lets help find you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what to do when other children are unkind: get safe and tell a trusted adult._

**Mr Coreander**: Hm. What’s your name?  
**Bastian**: Bastian Balthazar Bux.  
**Mr Coreander**: That’s a lot of b’s for one name. Sit down, then.  
**Mr Coreander**: Don’t touch anything.  

**Choices**

- **Keep very still behind the bell.**
    - You keep still. The bell, which is right by your ear, decides to keep still too.
- **Take out your notebook and write down the shop’s name.**
    - You copy the letters from the glass, backwards first and then the right way round. Your pencil sounds very loud.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff the nearest pile of books.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs the nearest pile, and sneezes on a book. That proves the old man right about something.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): an ancient symbol: the snake that bites its tail (the ouroboros)  
> _A note in Nova’s small writing has appeared in the margin of the page._  
> _“A snake biting its own tail is one of the oldest signs there is. Artists in ancient Egypt drew it over three thousand years ago.”_  
> _“Later, the ancient Greeks gave it the name we still use: ouroboros. It stands for something that goes round and round.”_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the snake biting its tail is a very old symbol from ancient Egypt, with a Greek name, meaning something that goes round and round._


#### `a25-01-run`

_Bastian looks at the book. Then he looks at the back room, where the old man is shouting at the telephone about an invoice._  
_Then he slips the book under his coat and runs, leaving the door open and the bell still ringing._  
_You hurry after him. Your Nubbin follows, running very fast and very flat, the way it runs in thunderstorms._  
**Bastian**: I’m a thief now. I have never taken anything before in my whole life.  
_He can’t go home, he tells a lamp-post. His father doesn’t shout._  
_He hardly says anything any more._  
_The clock over the school gate says twenty-five past nine. School began at nine, and there is a maths test today._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: from 9:00 to 9:25 is 25 minutes  
> _School began at nine o’clock. The clock over the gate says twenty-five past nine._  
> _How many minutes late is Bastian?_  
> - ✅ 25 minutes → Yes. From 9:00 to 9:25 is 25 minutes. “Twenty-five past” means 25 minutes after the hour.
> - 35 minutes → Let’s count it on the clock. From nine to half past is 30 minutes. Twenty-five past is a bit before half past, so it is 25 minutes.
> - 5 minutes → That is the 5 in “twenty-five”, but it is not the answer. “Twenty-five past nine” means 25 minutes after nine, so he is 25 minutes late.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval on a clock: from 9:00 to 9:25 is 25 minutes._

**Bastian**: Can’t go in there either.  
_He goes in by the back door instead, up the back stairs and past the caretaker’s cupboard, all the way to the top._

_At the top of the stairs there is a door nobody uses. It isn’t locked, because it has never needed to be._  
_Bastian stops with his hand on the cold handle. His heart is going very fast._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): making things right after a mistake: honesty, saying sorry, giving back  
> _Bastian knows he took the book without asking._  
> _If you were him, what would you do next?_  
> - Take it back straight away. → That’s a fair answer. Giving something back quickly keeps a mistake small. Bastian is thinking about it too.
> - Tell the bookseller the truth and say sorry. → That is an honest and a brave answer. A sorry works best when it is said to the person.
> - Read a little first, and decide after. → That’s what Bastian says he will do. Many people feel that way when they are scared. But the longer a mistake waits, the heavier it feels.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to make things right after taking something without asking._


#### `a25-01-attic`

_The school attic is long and low, full of broken desks, rolled-up maps and a heap of old gym mats._  
_Rain drums on the roof slates. It is grey up here, and it smells of dust and chalk._  
_Bastian finds some grey army blankets, wraps himself in two, and sits on the mats like a parcel._  
_He takes out his sandwich and his apple, looks at them, and puts them away again._  
**Bastian**: Just the first page. Then I’ll take it back.  
**Bastian**: Probably.  
_He opens the book. Over his shoulder, unseen, you notice that its words are printed in two colours._  
_The words about the attic are rust-red. As he turns the page, words about a forest begin, and they are green._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): how an author can use two colours to show two places (setting)  
> _In this book, the attic is printed in red and the forest in green. Why would an author do that?_  
> - ✅ So readers always know which world they are in. → Yes. The colour is a clue: red is the attic, green is the faraway land. It takes care, too. On a simple press, each colour needs its own run through the machine.
> - Those were the only two inks the printer had. → A printer can use any colour. Using two was a choice, and it took extra work. The choice does a job: it shows where we are.
> - Just to look pretty. → It does look pretty. But it also tells you which world you are reading about.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why an author might print two settings in two colours._

_Your Nubbin burrows into the blankets and settles against his side, because it is warm there._  
_Bastian doesn’t notice. He has already started reading._  

**Choices**

- **Sit beside him on the mats.**
    - You sit down beside him. He shifts over without looking up, the way people do for someone they can’t see.
- **Sit by the skylight and read your own copy.**
    - Your atlas page shows exactly the same words. You read along.

- `a25-02-s2`: Hear what the messengers have seen, and go with them to look. · _Walk with Ückück to the edge of the wood. You don’t have to go close._

#### `a25-02-fire`

_In the clearing sits a will-o’-the-wisp, a little ball of light, singing to keep its courage up. It isn’t working._  
_A rockchewer comes crunching out of the trees. He is the size of a hill, and he is eating a small piece of it._  
_Then a night-hob arrives riding a bat, and a tiny, no bigger than your thumb, on a snail that has run all the way._  
**Blubb**: Strangers! Friendly ones?  
**Blubb**: Say friendly. I’m Blubb, and I’m very nervous.  
**Pyornkrachzark**: Pyornkrachzark. Sit.  
**Pyornkrachzark**: Pebble?  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): respect for other people’s customs: accepting a gift politely  
> _A rockchewer holds out a pebble. To him, it is a kind and tasty gift._  
> _What is the polite thing to do?_  
> - ✅ Take it kindly and say thank you. → Yes. People have different customs, and a gift is a gift. You don’t have to eat it. Thanking him is how you show respect.
> - Say “Yuck!” → A pebble is a strange snack to us. But to him it is a present, and “yuck” would hurt. Saying thank you shows respect for how other people do things.
> - Walk away. → That might feel safe. But it would also say that his kindness didn’t count. Saying thank you is the respectful way.
> _For grown-ups: Practised respecting a different custom by accepting a gift politely._

**Ückück**: I am Ückück. We are all going the same way, it seems: to the Ivory Tower, with bad news.  
**Gluckuk**: Gluckuk. My snail is the fastest in my whole country.  
**Gluckuk**: Please don’t step on him.  
_Your Nubbin sits down next to the snail, very carefully, and the two of them look at each other for a long time._  

**Choices**

- **Accept the pebble, politely.**
    - You hold it as if you might eat it later. Pyornkrachzark nods, pleased.
    - Good manners matter, whatever size you are.
- **Ask what the bad news is.**
    - **Ückück**: The same as everyone’s, I expect. That is what frightens me.

#### `a25-02-fire-done`

_Each came from a different corner of Fantastica to the same fire, carrying the same news._  
_Pyornkrachzark lays his pebbles on a flat stone, ready to share. There are eighteen._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): sharing equally: 18 ÷ 6 = 3  
> _There are six of you: four messengers, you, and your Nubbin._  
> _Share the eighteen pebbles fairly. How many does each one get?_  
> - ✅ 3 each → Yes. 6 groups of 3 make 18, so 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
> - 4 each → Let’s check. Six friends with 4 each would need 6 × 4 = 24 pebbles. We only have 18. Six lots of 3 is 18.
> - 2 each → Six friends with 2 each is 6 × 2 = 12. That leaves 6 pebbles over. Share those as well, and everyone has 3.
> _For grown-ups: Shared 18 things equally between 6 (18 ÷ 6 = 3)._

> _Here is something odd and true about your own eyes._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): naming a scary thing makes it easier to talk about  
> _Why might giving a frightening thing a name make it feel a little smaller?_  
> - ✅ Once it has a name, we can talk about it together. → Yes. A name gives you something to hold on to, and something to share. The Nothing is still there. But talking about it is a first step.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): noticing how someone else feels, and saying something kind  
> _Ückück feels small, one messenger among hundreds. What could you say to him?_  
> - ✅ Your news matters. You came all this way. → Yes. A kind word that is true can make someone feel seen. Ückück really did fly a long way, and that counts.
> - Don’t worry, you’ll feel better soon. → That is kindly meant. But it can make someone feel that their feeling doesn’t count. It helps more to say what is true about them: you came a long way.
> - You’re right, there are a lot of messengers. → That is true about the numbers. But it would make Ückück feel even smaller. A good friend finds the true thing that helps.
> _For grown-ups: Practised noticing how someone feels and choosing a kind, true thing to say._

**Cairon**: If it reaches her, there is no more Fantastica.

> - It doesn’t help. Two problems would be easier. → It can feel that way! But two separate cures would be twice the work. If the problem is really one, one cure might mend both.
> - It means nothing can be done. → It sounds gloomy, and Cairon feels gloomy. But a problem we understand is a problem we can try to solve.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: the Sun rises in the east  
> _The Grassy Sea lies far to the east._  
> _On a clear morning, which way do you face to look at the Sun rising?_  
> - ✅ East → Yes. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Face the rising Sun, and east is in front of you.
> - West → West is where the Sun sets in the evening. Face the Sun as it rises in the morning, and you are looking east.
> - South → South is at your back when you face north, and the Sun does not rise there. The rising Sun is in the east.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sun rises in the east and used it to find a direction on a map._

> _Say Cairon gallops 100 miles every day._  
> _How far will he have gone after 4 days?_  
> - ✅ 400 miles → Yes. Four lots of 100 is 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 400 miles.
> - 104 miles → That is 100 + 4, but there are four whole days, each of 100 miles. 4 × 100 = 400.
> - 300 miles → That is three days: 3 × 100 = 300. We need one more day. 4 × 100 = 400.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied a daily distance by a number of days (4 × 100 = 400 miles)._

> - 15 people → That is 12 + 3. But each of the twelve tents has its own three people. 12 × 3 = 36.
> - 24 people → That is 12 × 2, which would be two people in each tent. With three in each, 12 × 3 = 36.

## A25-5. The Swamps of Sadness

- `a25-05-s1`: Cross the Swamps of Sadness with Atreyu and Artax. · _Keep walking. When you feel like stopping, walk anyway._
- `a25-05-s2`: Stay with Atreyu while Artax stops. · _Don’t look away. You don’t have to do anything._
- `a25-05-s3`: Sit beside your Nubbin in the reeds until it gets up. · _Sit down next to it and wait. There is no hurry, and nothing to press._

#### `a25-05-swamp`

_The swamp is grey and still. Dead trees stand in it, and the air is cold and smells of nothing much._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): a swamp is a wetland habitat, usually full of life  
> _A real swamp is a wetland: ground soaked with water, with trees growing in it._  
> _Real swamps are full of life: frogs, herons, fish and dragonflies._  
> _This swamp is different. All its colour and life has been taken out._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a swamp is a wetland habitat, and that real swamps are full of life._

_Sadness comes up out of the mud like damp. It gets into your boots first, and then into everything._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): a feeling can pass through us; it is not all of who we are  
> _Atreyu says the sadness is “only the swamp. It isn’t you.”_  
> _What might he mean?_  
> - ✅ A feeling can pass through you, and it is not all of who you are. → Yes. Feelings come and go, like weather. You are still you underneath.
> - He means you should never feel sad. → Feeling sad is allowed. Atreyu isn’t telling anyone not to. He means the sadness is a visitor, and it will not stay.
> - He means the swamp is to blame for everything. → The swamp is making it stronger. But he is mostly saying that a feeling is not the whole of you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how a feeling can pass through us without being all of who we are._

_AURYN glints on his chest. Atreyu feels the sadness too, but it can’t quite get hold of him._  
_Artax is slowing down. Each step is a little shorter than the last one._

**Atreyu**: You can. You have to.  
**Atreyu**: Look, there’s higher ground just there.  
**Artax**: I know. It doesn’t matter.  
**Artax**: Nothing matters. I’m sorry.  
**Artax**: Take the little one off my back.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): strong sadness is felt in the body, and rest and company help  
> _When we are very sad, our bodies feel it too. Arms and legs can feel heavy, and starting anything is hard._  
> _That is normal. It does not mean something is wrong with you._  
> _A rest, a drink of water, a hug and someone to sit with can help a heavy body begin to lighten._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that strong sadness can make the body feel heavy, and that rest and company help._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): grief: it is allowed to be sad, and some things help  
> _It is very sad when a friend dies, and it is all right to feel that._  
> _What do you think can help someone who has lost a friend?_  
> - Crying, if they need to. → That’s a fair answer. Tears are a way of carrying a big feeling, and they help many people.
> - Remembering the friend, and telling stories about them. → That’s a fair answer. Atreyu promised not to forget Artax, and remembering keeps a friend close.
> - Having someone sit nearby. → That’s a fair answer. You don’t always need words. Someone beside you can be enough.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps when a friend has died (a think question), with plain words and comfort._


#### `a25-05-artax-done`

_In the red attic, Bastian is crying, and he doesn’t mind. Nobody can see him, and it was Artax._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how readers feel real feelings for characters in a story  
> _Bastian cries for a horse in a book. Why do stories make us feel so much?_  
> - ✅ A good story makes a character feel real, and we care about them. → Yes. Crying at a story is a sign that you care. Bastian cares about Artax.
> - Because Bastian is being silly. → There is nothing silly about it. Readers have wept at stories for as long as there have been stories. It shows how much we can care.
> - Because Bastian is tired. → He may be tired. But the main reason is that Artax felt real to him, and he loved him.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why we can feel real sadness for a character in a story._


#### `a25-05-reeds`

_A little way on, your Nubbin lies down in the reeds and won’t get up. Its eyes are open, but it isn’t looking at anything._  
**Atreyu**: The swamp got into it. It’s so small.  
_You don’t pick it up and you don’t pull. You sit down in the reeds beside it, close enough that it knows._  
_Atreyu sits down too, on its other side, though he has every reason not to._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): helping someone who is very sad: stay close and wait, without trying to fix it  
> _Your Nubbin is very sad and won’t get up._  
> _What helps most?_  
> - ✅ Sit close beside it, and wait kindly. → Yes. You can’t always fix a sad feeling, but you can stay. Staying close tells someone: you’re not alone.
> - Pull it up quickly. → Wanting to fix it is a loving wish. But pulling can frighten someone who is very sad. Staying close and waiting lets them know you’re there.
> - Tell it to cheer up. → It is kindly meant. But “cheer up” can make someone feel they are doing sadness wrong. Sitting beside them says that all their feelings are welcome.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that staying close and waiting kindly can help someone who is very sad._

_The reeds rustle. A long time goes by, or a short one; in the swamp it is hard to tell._  
_Then your Nubbin sits up, and leans against your arm, and then gets up on its own._

> - Horses are the best friends. → Artax was a very good friend. But the story is mostly about what Atreyu learned from waiting with you.
> _For grown-ups: Found the theme of the swamp quest: staying close can help even when you cannot fix things._

- **wetland**: Land that is covered with water, or soaked with it, for much of the year.

> _The mountain is a giant turtle’s shell. A real turtle or tortoise can’t step out of its shell like a house._  
> _It is part of its skeleton: its ribs and backbone have grown into it._  
> _Turtles and tortoises are among the longest-lived animals. Some giant tortoises live well over a hundred years._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a turtle’s or tortoise’s shell is part of its skeleton, and that some giant tortoises live over a hundred years._

**Morla**: Somebody’s there, old one. Somebody small.

**Morla**: We don’t care, though. Do we?

#### `a25-06-shell-done`

_She talks to herself as “we”, and answers herself too. She has had nobody else to talk to for a very long time._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): loneliness: noticing a lonely person and reaching out kindly  
> _Morla has had nobody to talk to for a very long time. What could you do for a very lonely person?_  
> - ✅ Say hello, and keep them company for a while. → Yes. A little company, and a kind hello, can mean a great deal to someone lonely.
> - Walk past quickly. → That can feel easier when we don’t know what to say. But a lonely person often wants most of all to be noticed. Even a small hello helps.
> - Tell them to stop talking to themselves. → People who are alone a lot often do talk to themselves. It is how they keep company. Kind company works better than a telling-off.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be kind to someone who is very lonely._


#### `a25-06-ask`

**Atreyu**: Morla the Aged One. The Empress is ill.  
**Atreyu**: Do you know what the cure is?  
**Morla**: The Empress. Ill.  
**Morla**: We knew her when she was young. She was young then too.  
**Morla**: She is always young.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): oral history: people who remember long ago can tell us about the past  
> _Morla remembers the Empress from long, long ago._  
> _What can we learn from someone who remembers things from a long time ago? What might be lost if nobody asks?_  
> - How life used to be, and what has changed. → That’s a fair answer. Older people can tell us things no book has, because they were there.
> - Stories and old skills that were never written down. → That’s a fair answer. Many skills and songs are only passed on by being told and shown.
> - Maybe it’s best to ask while we still can. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Memories belong to people, and when a person is gone, so is their way of telling it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what we can learn from people who remember the past (a think question)._

**Morla**: Old one, shall we tell him? What for?  
**Morla**: Everything ends. We’ve been old so long we can’t remember not.  
_She sneezes. A wind goes across the swamp, and your Nubbin falls over and gets up again, offended._  
**Morla**: We’re all there is of us. Being old is the whole of us.  
**Morla**: You wouldn’t understand. You’re a boy.  
**Atreyu**: Then help me anyway. You don’t have to care.  
**Atreyu**: Just tell me.

    - **Morla**: Hm. Quiet ones.
    - **Morla**: We like quiet ones. They don’t ask things.
- **Ask her what it is like, being so old.**
    - **Morla**: Long. Long, old one, isn’t it.
    - **Morla**: Like waiting for a sneeze that doesn’t come.

#### `a25-06-ask-done`

**Morla**: The Southern Oracle. Uyulala.  
**Morla**: She might know. We don’t.  
**Morla**: We don’t mind.  
**Morla**: Ten thousand miles away, south. You’d be old as us before you got there.  
**Morla**: Go and find out yourself.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): a distance and a speed: 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000 days  
> _The Oracle is ten thousand miles away. Say Atreyu walks 10 miles every day._  
> _How many days will the walk take?_  
> - ✅ 1,000 days → Yes. 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000 days. A year has 365 days, so that is nearly three years of walking.
> - 100 days → In 100 days he would walk 100 × 10 = 1,000 miles. That is only a tenth of the way. For 10,000 miles he needs 1,000 days.
> - 10,000 days → That would be one mile each day. He walks 10 miles a day, so he needs ten times fewer days. 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a distance by a daily distance (10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000 days)._


#### `a25-06-complete`

_Morla draws her head back into her cave. She is already asleep, or near enough not to matter._  
**Atreyu**: Ten thousand miles. That is years of walking, and the Empress hasn’t got years.  
**Atreyu**: So I’ll start walking. That’s all I can do, isn’t it.  
_He doesn’t say it like a hero. He says it the way you might tie a bootlace: plainly, and then getting on with it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile: what comparing two things tells us about a character  
> _The story says Atreyu spoke “the way you might tie a bootlace”._  
> _What does that comparison tell us about him?_  
> - ✅ He is plain and determined, with no showing off. → Yes. Tying a bootlace is ordinary and necessary. It is a way of saying “just get on with it”. A comparison like this, using “like” or “as”, is called a simile.
> - He is talking about boots. → Boots are in the comparison, but the story isn’t really about boots. It shows how he speaks: plainly, without fuss. That kind of comparison is a simile.
> - He is angry. → He is worried, but he doesn’t sound angry. A bootlace is tied calmly. The simile shows he is calm and ready to start.
> _For grown-ups: Read a simile closely to learn what it shows about a character’s manner._


### Glossary

- **tortoise**: A slow, land-living reptile with a hard shell on its back.
- **skeleton**: The bones that hold up and protect an animal’s body.
- **oracle**: A person or voice in old stories that is asked for answers and advice.

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): mirror symmetry: a shape with a line of symmetry matches itself on both sides  
> _A mirror line splits a shape into two halves that match._  
> _Which capital letter has a mirror line straight down the middle: A, F or R?_  
> - ✅ A → Yes. Fold a capital A down the middle and the two halves match. It has a line of symmetry.
> - F → Try folding an F down the middle. Its arms stick out on one side only. The capital A is the one that matches.
> - R → An R has its bump on one side only, so the two halves don’t match. The capital A matches on both sides.
> _For grown-ups: Found which capital letter has a line of symmetry (A)._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): staying steady when something scary is happening: breathe and hold on to something safe  
> _When something scary is happening, what can help your body stay steady?_

> - Hold your breath tight. → That can make your heart pound faster. A slow breath out is better. Slow breaths and a safe hold help us feel steadier.
> - Close your eyes and wish it away. → Closing your eyes can feel safe for a moment. But a slow breath and a firm hold help your body more.
> _For grown-ups: Practised a calming skill for scary moments: a slow breath and holding on to something safe._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: from 7 in the evening to 5 in the morning is 10 hours  
> _The sun sets at seven in the evening and rises at five in the morning._  
> _How many hours of night will Falkor fly?_  
> - ✅ 10 hours → Yes. From 7 to midnight is 5 hours, and from midnight to 5 is 5 more. That makes 10 hours.
> - 12 hours → That would be seven in the evening to seven in the morning. We stop at five. 5 hours to midnight plus 5 hours after is 10.
> - 2 hours → That is the difference between 7 and 5 on the clock face. But night runs on past midnight. From 7 in the evening to 5 in the morning is 10 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval across midnight: 7 in the evening to 5 in the morning is 10 hours._

#### `a25-12-dive`

**Falkor**: There! I knew it.

_He folds himself up and dives. The sea goes green and cold all round you for one long breath._  
_When you come up, Falkor has the amulet in his mouth, very gently, like a dog with an egg._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): sinking and floating depend on a material’s properties: gold is dense and sinks  
> _The amulet is made of gold, and it sank. Gold is very heavy for its size._  
> _Which of these would sink in the sea: a cork, a gold ring or a wooden spoon?_  
> - ✅ A gold ring → Yes. Gold is much heavier than the same amount of water, so it sinks. Cork and wood are lighter than water, so they float.
> - A cork → A cork is very light for its size, and it floats on water. The gold ring is the one that sinks.
> - A wooden spoon → Most wood is lighter than water, so a wooden spoon floats. Gold is heavier, so the gold ring sinks.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heavy, dense materials like gold sink, while cork and wood float._

**Falkor**: Mmf. Now for the boy.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): weighing a hopeless story: asking who says so and what the evidence is  
> _Gmork says that when people stop believing anything can be different, the Nothing grows._  
> _How can you tell whether a hopeless story is really true?_  
> - Ask someone I trust what they think. → That’s a fair answer. A trusted friend or grown-up can see what we can’t when we are scared.
> - Look for evidence: has it always been true? → That’s a fair answer. Asking “how do I know?” is a strong habit for sorting true from only scary.
> - Notice who is telling it, and who it helps. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Gmork serves the Nothing, so a hopeless story helps him.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to tell whether a hopeless story is true (a think question)._

**Gmork**: I was sent to find the one hunter who might stop it. Some green boy.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): working out feelings from clues, even when nobody says them  
> _Nobody says how Atreyu feels. We only see his face, the quiet, and his cry._  
> _How can we tell what a character feels?_  
> - ✅ From clues: his face, the silence and his cry. → Yes. Good readers use clues, like faces, actions and sounds, to work out what a character feels.
> - We can’t. Nobody said. → Authors often leave the feeling unsaid and let the clues do the work. Atreyu’s face and his cry are clues.
> - He feels happy. → A cry and a silent face don’t fit with happy. They fit with shock and hurt.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in a scene to work out a character’s feelings._

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): forces: an object moves when one force is bigger than the other  
> _Falkor and you pull one way, and the jaws hold the other way._  
> _When does something start to move?_  
> - ✅ When one pull is bigger than the other. → Yes. If the forces are balanced, nothing moves. When one is bigger, the object moves.
> - When the two pulls are exactly equal. → Equal pulls are balanced, so nothing moves. It is like a tug of war that stays level. To move, one pull has to be bigger.
> - Only when something is very heavy. → Heavy things are harder to move, but weight isn’t the whole story. It moves when one force is bigger than the other.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that balanced forces mean no movement and unbalanced forces make things move._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): names often come from a family story, a place or a hope  
> _When the Empress says your Nubbin’s name, it comes out at once._  
> _Names often carry a family story: a grandparent, a place, a hope. What might a name tell us about the people who chose it?_  
> - That they were thinking of someone they loved. → That’s a fair answer. Many people are named after someone dear to their family.
> - That they hoped something for the child. → That’s a fair answer. A name can hold a wish, like “brave” or “bright”.
> - I’d like to ask my family how mine was chosen. → That’s a good idea. Asking is a way of keeping a family story alive.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how names often carry a family story (a think question)._

> _Atreyu thinks he failed. The Empress says he has done more than anyone._

> - I’m no good at anything. → That is a heavy thing to say to yourself, and it isn’t true. Try talking to yourself the way you would talk to a friend: you tried hard, and that counts.

> - The traveller, about themself. → If the traveller told it, it would say “I bow”. Using “the traveller” shows someone else is telling it.
> - Nobody. It just happens. → Every story has someone telling it. Here, the Old Man writes the story as it happens.

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a repeating pattern: finding the 10th step in a cycle of four  
> _The story goes round and round: shop, attic, forest, tower. Then shop, attic, forest, tower again._  
> _Which place comes at the 10th step?_  
> - ✅ The attic → Yes. The pattern repeats every four. Steps 9 and 10 are the shop, then the attic. Another way: 10 is 2 more than 8, and 8 ends a full cycle at the tower.
> - The shop → The shop is step 9. Count on once more: shop is 1, 5 and 9. Step 10 is the attic.
> - The tower → The tower is step 4 and step 8. Step 12 would be next. Step 10 is the attic.
> _For grown-ups: Found the 10th item in a repeating pattern of four (the attic)._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): courage: being brave means acting even when you are scared  
> _Bastian says he isn’t brave. But he is about to speak anyway._  
> _What does being brave really mean?_  
> - ✅ Doing the right thing even though you are scared. → Yes. Brave people feel afraid too. Bravery is what you do next. Bastian is frightened, and he is about to do something very brave.
> - Not feeling scared at all. → Someone who feels no fear isn’t being brave, because nothing is hard for them. Bravery is acting while you feel the fear.
> - Being the strongest person in the room. → Strength can help. But Bastian isn’t strong in that way, and he is about to be brave. Bravery is doing the right thing while scared.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that being brave means acting even when you feel scared._

_Your Nubbin sits on the gym mat in front of him and looks up at him, waiting, the way it waits for breakfast._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a few German words (Mond, Kind, Buch) and how German joins words together  
> _A note in Nova’s writing: “Mond is German for moon, and Kind is German for child. German often joins words into one long word.”_  
> _Joined, with a little “en” in the middle, they make Mondenkind. What name does that give in English?_  
> - ✅ Moon Child → Yes. Moon Child. Mond sounds a bit like “mohnt”, and Kind a bit like “kint”. The German word for the book Bastian is holding is Buch, with a rough “ch” as at the end of “loch”.
> - Child Moon → Close! German puts the describing word first, like English: a moon child is a child of the moon. So Mondenkind means Moon Child.
> - Moon Kind → “Kind” is a German word. In English, it means “child”. So Mondenkind means Moon Child.
> _For grown-ups: Learned three German words (Mond, Kind, Buch) and how German joins words into one: Mondenkind, Moon Child._

_It glows, very faintly. Your Nubbin holds its paw out flat, as if it knew it mustn’t drop it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): sand is tiny bits of rock worn down grain by grain by wind and water  
> _Real sand is made of tiny pieces of rock, shell and other things, worn down by wind and water._  
> _It happens one grain at a time, over thousands of years. One grain is very small, and a beach has a very great many._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sand is tiny pieces of rock worn down by weathering over a very long time._

_The page goes still. Across the bottom there is a long space and a single line of green._  
_This is where your page ends._  
_A boy has given the Empress her new name, and from one grain of sand a whole land can begin again._  
_You tip your Nubbin’s grain into an empty glass vial from your pocket, and stopper it. It glows in your hand like a tiny moon._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: why a name can be a gift  
> _Bastian gave the Empress a name, and it helped to save her._  
> _Why can a name be a gift?_  
> - ✅ It says “I know who you are, and you matter.” → Yes. To be named is to be known. That is a very big gift to give. It is a gift you can only give by paying attention to someone.
> - Because names cost a lot of money. → Names don’t cost anything. The gift is the care in choosing and saying them. A name says “you matter”.
> - A name isn’t really a gift. → That’s an interesting view. But think about how it feels when someone remembers your name. A name can say “you matter”.
> _For grown-ups: Found the theme that a name can be a gift: it says you are known and you matter._

_You close Nova’s atlas, and the rain on the glass goes quiet._  

### Glossary

- **stub**: A short piece that is left over after most of something has been used up.
- **weathering**: The slow breaking down of rock by wind, water and ice.

## A26-1. The Wall

- `a26-01-s1`: Step into the page and walk the wall of Uruk. · _Touch the sunlit wall on the page, then follow the old brickmaker along the top._
- `a26-01-s2`: Find the copper tablet box at the foot of the wall and read the lapis tablet. · _The box is set into the wall’s foundation, by the stair. The brickmaker will show you._

#### `a26-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page so bright it warms your face. A great brick wall stands in the sun, with date palms and a river._  
_Your Nubbin puts both paws flat on the paper, as if to test whether it is hot. It is, a little._  
_The bricks are warm under your feet, and you are standing on the rampart of a city. Two carts could pass side by side up here._  
_Below, flat roofs run down to a river. An old woman with clay to her elbows sits on a stack of bricks, eating a date._  
**Old Brickmaker**: New, are you? Everyone is new once. Walk the wall with me. It is the best way to meet a city.  
**Old Brickmaker**: This is Uruk. It stood in the land between two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. Today that land is part of Iraq.  
**Old Brickmaker**: The Greeks later called it Mesopotamia, which means “between the rivers”. Rivers meant water, crops and boats.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): Mesopotamia means “between the rivers”; Uruk stood in what is now Iraq  
> _(Find the two rivers on Nova’s map. The Tigris and the Euphrates both run south-east through Iraq to the sea.)_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned where Mesopotamia was: between the Tigris and the Euphrates, in what is now Iraq._


**Choices**

- **Ask her how you tell a good brick.**
    - **Old Brickmaker**: You knock it. A good brick rings, and a bad one says “thud” and lets you down when it rains.
- **Ask who built the wall.**
    - **Old Brickmaker**: The king says he did. The king says a lot of things. Come down and I will show you something better.

#### `a26-01-page-done`

_Your Nubbin knocks on the parapet with one paw, and listens with its head on one side. It seems satisfied._  
**Old Brickmaker**: That is how you test a brick. Some of these were baked in a kiln, a very hot oven, and some only dried in the sun.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound is made of vibrations  
> _A knock makes the brick ring. What is a sound made of?_  
> - ✅ Tiny back-and-forth shakes, called vibrations → Yes. The knock shakes the brick, the brick shakes the air, and your ear feels the shaking as sound.
> - Light → Not quite. Light is something we see. Sound is shaking, passed along through the air.
> - Heat → Not quite. A knock does warm a brick a tiny bit, but the ringing is shaking, called vibration.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound is made of vibrations._

**Old Brickmaker**: Now down the stairs. Mind the third one. It has been mended since my grandmother’s day.  

#### `a26-01-tablet`

_At the foot of the stair, set into the oldest bricks, there is a box of copper, green with years. Its lock is a bronze bolt._  
**Old Brickmaker**: Slide the bolt. Go on. It is meant to be opened. That is the whole point of it.  
_Inside lies a tablet of lapis, deep blue and flecked with gold like a night sky. Little wedge-shaped marks run across it._  
_You cannot read them. Then, the longer you look, you can._  
**Old Brickmaker**: That is cuneiform. Scribes pressed a reed into wet clay, and every press left a wedge. This one was cut into stone, to last.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): cuneiform means wedge-shaped; scribes pressed a reed into wet clay  
> **Old Brickmaker**: The word “cuneiform” comes from the Latin for “wedge”. You can see the corner of the reed in every mark.  
> **Old Brickmaker**: Groups of wedges made signs, some for words and some for sounds. People wrote like this more than four thousand years ago.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cuneiform is wedge-shaped writing, pressed into clay, and what the word means._

**Old Brickmaker**: The tablet begins with our city and its high wall. Then it is all about a king who saw everything, and what it cost him.  
_The wedges begin to move like ants in a line. The air smells of hot dust and river water._  

**Choices**

- **Read on.**
    - You read on. The wedges become words, and the words become a street, and you are standing in it.
- **Let your Nubbin turn the tablet over.**
    - Your Nubbin turns the tablet over with great care. On the back, the story keeps going, and so do you.

#### `a26-01-tablet-done`

_When you look up, the brickmaker has put the tablet back in its box and slid the bolt home._  
**Old Brickmaker**: It stays here. That is what it is for. Anyone can come and open the box and read it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): weighing where a very old thing should be kept  
> _The brickmaker puts the tablet back instead of taking it. What do you think is the right place for something so old?_  
> - Where it was found, so people can come to it → That is a fair answer. It matches what the brickmaker believes: a thing stays part of its place.
> - In a museum, where it is kept safe → That is a fair answer. A safe place matters. The brickmaker thinks a thing matters more where it belongs.
> - Anywhere that lets lots of people see it → That is a fair answer. Sharing matters. The question is how to share without taking from the people it belongs to.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about where a very old and precious thing belongs, and how to share it fairly._

**Old Brickmaker**: Go on, then. I will be on the wall when you are done.  

#### `a26-01-complete`

_The street is full of people, all of them tired. Somewhere above them, a drum is beating, and it does not stop._  
_It beats four times, rests, beats four times, rests, and beats four times again. Then it starts over._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): three equal groups of four  
> _The drum beats in three groups of four. How many beats in all, before it starts over?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Three groups of four: 4, 8, 12.
> - 7 → That is 3 + 4. Three groups of four means 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> - 34 → Careful: three groups of four is 4 + 4 + 4, which is 12.
> _For grown-ups: Used three equal groups of four to make 12._

_Your Nubbin takes hold of your trouser leg. You are in the story now, a stranger in Uruk, and the king is awake._  

### Glossary

- **rampart**: The wide top of a city wall, where people can walk.
- **kiln**: A very hot oven for baking clay until it is hard.
- **cuneiform**: Wedge-shaped writing, pressed into wet clay with a reed.
- **lapis**: A deep blue stone with tiny flecks of gold-coloured mineral.

## A26-2. The King Who Never Rests

- `a26-02-s1`: Watch the king’s games in the great square. · _Follow the drum to the great square, and find a place by the well._
- `a26-02-s2`: Go up to the temple with the people of Uruk. · _At dusk the crowd climbs the temple steps. Go with the woman from the square._

#### `a26-02-games`

_In the great square, young men are running races, and carrying stones, and running races again. Nobody looks as if they want to._  
_In the middle, taller than anyone, stands a man with a curled black beard and arms like roof beams._  
**Gilgamesh**: Again! Faster! Who is tired? Nobody is tired! Uruk does not get tired!  
_That is Gilgamesh, king of Uruk. Two parts of him are god, and one part is man, and you cannot tell which part is talking._  
**Woman of Uruk**: He has been at it since the new moon. Games all day, building all night. Nobody may go home.  
_A boy in the race stumbles and sits down in the dust. He does not get up._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): a tired body needs water and rest  
> _The boy is exhausted. Which is the best help for a very tired body?_  
> - ✅ Water and a proper rest → Yes. Water and rest are what a tired body needs. Children your age need about nine to twelve hours of sleep a night.
> - One more race, to toughen him up → Not quite. Pushing a worn-out body harder only makes it more tired. It needs water and rest.
> - Ignoring it until he feels better → He might, in time. But water and rest help sooner, and they are kind.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a very tired body needs water and rest._


**Choices**

- **Take the boy some water from the well.**
    - You draw a bucket and carry the boy a cup. He drinks it all, and looks at you as if you had brought him the sea.
- **Sit down in the dust beside him.**
    - You sit down beside him. After a moment your Nubbin sits too, and so, quietly, does the boy’s mother.

#### `a26-02-games-done`

_The king sees none of it. He has already started another race._  
**Woman of Uruk**: Thank you. It is the first kind thing anyone has done in this square since the new moon.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): small kindnesses matter to someone who has had none  
> _The woman says it is the first kind thing since the new moon. What does that show about small kindnesses?_  
> - ✅ They can matter a lot to someone who is tired and worried → Yes. A cup of water is small, but to someone who has had nothing kind for weeks, it is a great deal.
> - They only matter if the king sees → Not quite. The king saw nothing, and still the kindness mattered. It mattered to the boy and his mother.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how small kindnesses matter, even when nobody important notices._


#### `a26-02-clay`

_At dusk the people climb the temple steps with lamps. They do not shout, because they are too tired to shout._  
**Woman of Uruk**: Gods of the city, he is too strong for us. Give him someone his own size. Someone to wear him out.  
_The lamps flicker, though there is no wind. And for a moment, high over the temple, you see something no one else seems to._  
_A great woman, made of starlight, washes her hands in the evening sky. She pinches off a little clay and rolls it between her palms._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): clay is soft when wet and hard when dry  
> _Aruru shapes wet clay. Why is clay such a useful material for people who want to build and write?_  
> - ✅ It can be shaped while soft, then it dries hard and keeps its shape → Yes. Soft clay becomes a brick, a pot or a tablet, and when it dries or is baked, it stays that way.
> - It never changes → It does change! Clay is soft when wet and hard when it dries. That change is why it is so useful.
> - It dissolves in water, so it is easy to wash away → Wet clay goes soft and muddy, but dry or baked clay holds firm. That is why bricks last.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that clay can be shaped while wet and hardens when it dries._

_That is the goddess Aruru, who made people in the first place. She drops the clay, gently, far away in the wild._  
_Your Nubbin watches it fall all the way, with its mouth open._  

**Choices**

- **Tell the woman what you saw.**
    - **Woman of Uruk**: Clay? In the wild? Well. I asked for help. I did not say what shape.
- **Keep it to yourself for now.**
    - You keep it to yourself. The woman pats your arm, as if you had prayed hardest of anyone.

#### `a26-02-clay-done`

_Far off, beyond the river and the fields, something new opens its eyes in the long grass._  
_The eyes open slowly, like a door in the morning, and the light comes in._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): recognising a simile  
> _“The eyes open like a door in the morning” is a simile. Which of these is also a simile?_  
> - ✅ “He ran like the wind.” → Yes. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”.
> - “He was the wind.” → That compares too, but without “like” or “as”. That is a metaphor.
> - “He ran very fast.” → That is plain description. A simile needs a comparison with “like” or “as”.
> _For grown-ups: Told a simile from a metaphor and a plain sentence._


#### `a26-02-complete`

_Down in the square, the drum keeps going. Gilgamesh is still awake, still building, still certain nothing can stop him._  
_Your Nubbin has turned to face the wild, where the clay fell. Its ears are up._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): what a fair rule about work and rest would look like  
> _The king never lets his people rest. What would a fair rule about work and rest look like in a city?_  
> - Everyone works, and everyone gets time to rest → That is a fair answer. A rule that gives everyone rest, including the king, is hard to argue with.
> - The king decides, because he is the king → That is a fair answer to think about. But the people of Uruk cried out: when one person decides alone, people can get hurt.
> - The people vote on how long to work → That is a fair answer. Many places today let people have a say in rules that affect them.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what a fair rule for work and rest might be._


## A26-3. The Wild Man

- `a26-03-s1`: Go out to the water hole on the steppe. · _Leave Uruk by the river gate and follow the gazelle tracks to the water._
- `a26-03-s2`: Find out who set the pits and snares, and what happened to them. · _Walk the edge of the steppe and look for filled-in pits and torn snares._

#### `a26-03-herd`

_Three days out from the wall, the fields give way to steppe: dry grass, thorn trees, and a sky that goes on for ever._  
_At the water hole, three gazelles are drinking with their knees bent. Four more come trotting up, and two wander off again._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add and take away within 100  
> _Three gazelles are at the water. Four more arrive, and two leave._  
> _How many gazelles are at the water hole now?_  
> - ✅ 5 → Yes. 3 + 4 = 7, and 7 − 2 = 5.
> - 9 → That is 3 + 4 + 2. Two of them left, so take 2 away: 7 − 2 = 5.
> - 7 → That is the number after the four arrived. Two then left, so 7 − 2 = 5.
> _For grown-ups: Added and took away to find five gazelles._

_In among them, on all fours, drinks a man. He is hairy all over, like a goat, and has never worn a stitch._  
_He grazes with the gazelles and drinks with them, and he looks perfectly happy. This is Enkidu, though he does not know he has a name yet._  
_Your Nubbin trots straight past you, down to the water, and drinks beside the smallest gazelle._  
**Enkidu**: Hhh?  
_Enkidu lifts his dripping face and looks at your Nubbin. Then he goes back to drinking, as if it had always been there._  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin stay with the herd.**
    - You let it stay. It lies down in the cool mud with the gazelles, more content than you have ever seen it.
- **Call your Nubbin back.**
    - You call. Your Nubbin looks at you, and flicks an ear, and stays exactly where it is.

#### `a26-03-herd-done`

_You sit under a thorn tree and watch them. Your Nubbin is in the middle of the herd, nose to nose with a fawn._  
_Enkidu grooms a gazelle’s ear with great care. There is nothing wild about the way he does it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, ask): animals in groups help each other survive  
> _Gazelles stay together in a herd. How does a herd help each gazelle survive?_  
> - ✅ Many eyes and ears notice danger sooner → Yes. When one gazelle spots a threat, the whole herd can run.
> - Herds make the grass grow faster → Not quite. The herd does not grow the grass. What it does is spot danger sooner.
> - Gazelles in a herd never get thirsty → Not quite. Every gazelle still needs water. A herd helps by watching for danger together.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that living in a group helps animals notice danger._


#### `a26-03-pits`

_At the edge of the steppe there are pits dug to catch game. Every one of them has been filled in, with care, by hand._  
_The snares have been torn up and laid in a tidy pile. Somebody has been very busy on the herd’s behalf._  
_A man with a net over his shoulder comes over the rise. He stops dead at the pits, and goes pale._  
**Trapper**: Again! Every pit, every snare. Three days I worked on those.  
**Trapper**: It is a man. A wild man, strong as a star from heaven. He runs with them. He sets them free.  
**Trapper**: I cannot feed my family on empty nets. I am going home to my father. He will know what to do.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): seeing both sides when two people need different things  
> _The trapper needs food for his family. Enkidu is freeing the animals._  
> _Who do you think is in the right?_  
> - The trapper, because his family needs to eat → That is a fair answer. A hungry family is a real problem. Enkidu does not yet understand that.
> - Enkidu, because the animals are his friends → That is a fair answer. He is protecting those he cares about. He does not yet know what the nets are for.
> - Both, and they need to understand each other → That is a fair answer. Neither is wicked. They need what the other cannot see.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about a conflict where each side has a real need._


**Choices**

- **Tell him you are sorry about his work.**
    - **Trapper**: So am I. And I am sorry I am frightened of him. I do not think he means harm. He just does not know about nets.
- **Say the herd seemed happy, at least.**
    - **Trapper**: Happy! The gazelles are happy. I am the one with the empty pot.
    - Then he laughs, once, despite himself.

#### `a26-03-pits-done`

_He runs off towards the river, net flapping. Behind you, at the water, the wild man is filling in another pit._  
_He pats the earth flat with both hands, very gently, as if tucking someone in._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why does Enkidu fill in the pits? Think about what he knows and what he cares about._  
> - ✅ He wants to keep his animal friends safe, though he does not understand why the trapper set them → Yes. His motive is care for his friends. He sees danger to them but does not yet understand the trapper’s side.
> - He wants to annoy the trapper → Not quite. He has never met the trapper. His motive is to keep the herd safe.
> - He likes digging and filling → Look at how gently he pats the earth. His motive is care for his friends.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a character’s motive from what he knows and cares about._


#### `a26-03-complete`

_By evening the trapper is far away on the road to his father, and then on the road to Uruk._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): land near rivers was green; land away from them was dry steppe  
> _(Look at Nova’s map.) The land beside the rivers was green and could be farmed, because the rivers brought water._  
> _Further out, it turned to dry steppe, where herds roamed._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that land beside Mesopotamia’s rivers was fertile, while land further away was dry steppe._

_Your Nubbin is still with the herd. It does not look round when you say its name._  

### Glossary

- **steppe**: A huge, dry grassland with few trees.
- **snare**: A trap made of rope or net, set to catch an animal.

## A26-4. Shamhat

- `a26-04-s1`: Walk Shamhat out to the water hole with the trapper. · _Meet the trapper at Uruk’s river gate and carry Shamhat’s bundle._
- `a26-04-s2`: Sit at the water hole with Shamhat until Enkidu understands her. · _Sit by the water. Do not chase. It takes days._
- `a26-04-s3`: Coax your Nubbin back from the herd. · _The gazelles are skittish now. Go slowly, and let your Nubbin come to you._

#### `a26-04-road`

_The trapper comes back from Uruk with a woman from the city. She walks quickly, and carries her own bundle until you take it._  
**Shamhat**: I am Shamhat. The king sent me. He says the wild man needs someone to talk to. I think he is right, for once.  
**Trapper**: He does not talk. He grunts. He drinks out of the pond on his knees.  
**Shamhat**: So did you, once. Somebody sat with you until you did not.  
_The bundle smells of bread and sweet oil. In it are twelve dates, a flat loaf and a clean robe folded small._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): sharing equally: division  
> _Twelve dates shared equally between three people. How many dates does each person get?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, because 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> - 3 → Check it: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9, which is too few. Each person gets 4, because 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> - 6 → Check it: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18, which is too many. Each person gets 4.
> _For grown-ups: Divided twelve dates equally among three people._

**Shamhat**: I will share the dates between me, the trapper and Enkidu, the same number each. Most people want to tame him. I want to be the first person he understands.  

**Choices**

- **Ask her how she will do it.**
    - **Shamhat**: Patience. I will sit where he can see me, and talk, and not need anything. Then one day he will answer.
- **Tell her your Nubbin ran off with the herd.**
    - **Shamhat**: Then we have the same job, you and I. Let us see who finishes first.

#### `a26-04-sit`

_Shamhat sits on a flat rock by the water hole, and you sit a little way off. The trapper hides in a bush and is no help._  
_The first day, Enkidu watches her from behind a gazelle. The second day, he comes and sniffs her bundle._  
**Shamhat**: That is bread. You do not know bread yet. You will. This is my hand. That is yours.  
_By the fourth day he sits across the rock from her, the way your Nubbin sits across from you on the hill at home._  
_She talks about the city, and the river, and the man who never sleeps. Enkidu listens with his whole face._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): why waiting patiently helps someone feel safe  
> _Shamhat never chases Enkidu. She sits, talks and waits._  
> _Why do you think that works better than chasing?_  
> - He gets to come close when he feels safe → That is a fair answer. When you do not push, the other person can choose to come closer.
> - She shows she wants nothing from him → That is a fair answer. Someone who asks for nothing is easier to trust.
> - It does not always work, but here it did → That is a fair answer. Waiting takes time, and it is not a guarantee. It gave Enkidu room to choose.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why patient waiting can build trust._

**Enkidu**: Hand.  
**Shamhat**: Hand. Yes. And what do you call yourself?  
**Enkidu**: …Enkidu.  

#### `a26-04-sit-done`

_He says it again, louder, as if trying the word for size. Then he laughs, a big surprised human laugh._  
**Shamhat**: There you are. I knew there was someone in there.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what an action shows about a character  
> _Shamhat asks Enkidu what he calls himself, instead of giving him a name. What does that show about her?_  
> - ✅ She respects him and lets him choose his own name → Yes. Her question treats Enkidu as a person with a say in who he is.
> - She does not know his name → She might not. But the way she asks shows respect.
> - She is in a hurry → She has waited days. The question shows patience and respect.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s respect from the way she asks a question._


#### `a26-04-coax`

_Enkidu walks back down to the gazelles, the way he has every evening of his life._  
_They lift their heads, and look at him, and run, every one. They do not know him any more._  
**Enkidu**: Wait! It is me!  
_He tries to run after them, and cannot keep up. His legs are a man’s now._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): animals use their senses to know each other  
> _Why might the gazelles stop recognising Enkidu? He has the same face as yesterday._  
> - ✅ He smells different and moves differently now, and gazelles rely on smell and movement → Yes. Many animals recognise each other mostly by smell. Clothes and oil change how he smells.
> - The gazelles forgot him overnight → Not quite. They did not forget. His smell and his movements changed.
> - Gazelles cannot see faces → They do see. But smell matters a great deal to them, and his smell has changed.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals recognise each other by senses such as smell._

_Your Nubbin has been left behind by the herd, too. It sits alone in the grass, skittish and watching them go._  
**Shamhat**: Go to yours. I will go to mine.  

**Choices**

- **Call its name.**
    - You call its name. It hears you, and thinks about it for a long moment, and then it comes, slowly, then all at once.
- **Sit down in the grass and wait.**
    - You sit down in the grass and wait. The sun goes down a finger’s width.
    - Then there is a weight against your side, warm and a bit muddy, as if it had been there all along.
- **Hold out a date from Shamhat’s bundle.**
    - You hold out a date. Your Nubbin comes for the date, and stays for you, and gets very sticky.

#### `a26-04-coax-done`

_Across the water, Enkidu is sitting with his head in his hands, and Shamhat is sitting beside him, saying nothing._  
_After a while he leans against her shoulder, the way your Nubbin leans against yours._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what helps when we feel sad  
> _Enkidu is sad. Shamhat does not talk him out of it._  
> _What is she doing that helps?_  
> - ✅ Staying close, and letting him be sad → Yes. Sometimes we do not need fixing. We need someone to sit beside us.
> - Telling him to cheer up → That is what some people try. It rarely helps. Staying close helps more.
> - Leaving him alone to get over it → Some quiet is fine. But company, without fuss, helps more.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that staying close without trying to fix a feeling can help._


#### `a26-04-complete`

**Shamhat**: You are not less, you know. You are more. You lost the herd and found the whole world. Come and see it.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s words really mean  
> _Shamhat says, “You lost the herd and found the whole world.” What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ He lost one way of living, but gained a much bigger one → Yes. She is comforting him by showing what his loss opens up.
> - He lost a herd of gazelles and found a map → Not a real map. She means a bigger life: people, cities and friends.
> - She is trying to trick him → Her words are kind, and she stays beside him. She is encouraging, not tricking.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of a comforting line from a character._

## A26-5. Bread and Barley

- `a26-05-s1`: Help the shepherds feed Enkidu his first supper. · _Carry the bread and the jugs from the shepherds’ fire to Enkidu._
- `a26-05-s2`: Keep watch over the flocks with Enkidu at night. · _Take a lamp to the sheepfold and stay up with Enkidu._

#### `a26-05-bread`

_The shepherds’ camp is a ring of tents round a fire, and a lot of sheep with opinions. The shepherds crowd round to look at Enkidu._  
**Shepherd**: He is as tall as the king. Taller. Sit down, friend, sit down. You must be hungry.  
_You set a round loaf in front of him, and a jug of thick barley drink. Enkidu looks at them as if they might bite._  
**Enkidu**: What is this?  
**Shamhat**: That is bread. People eat it. And that is a drink. People drink it. Go on. It is what we do.  
_He sniffs the bread, and licks it. He takes a very small bite, and his eyebrows go up into his hair._  
_Then he eats until he is full, and his face shines like a lamp. And then, to everyone’s surprise, including his own, he sings._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): how grain becomes bread  
> _Enkidu has never seen bread made. Which order is right for how a loaf of bread is made?_  
> - ✅ Barley or wheat grows in a field, the grain is ground into flour, then the dough is mixed and baked → Yes. Plants need water and light to grow grain. People turn the grain into flour, then dough, then bread.
> - Dough is baked, then ground, then planted → That order cannot work. The plant comes first, then the flour, then the dough, then the baked loaf.
> - Bread grows on trees like fruit → Bread does not grow on trees, but its grain grows on plants like barley and wheat.
> _For grown-ups: Put the steps of making bread in order, from plant to loaf._


**Choices**

- **Clap along.**
    - You clap along, and so do the shepherds. Your Nubbin hops in time, mostly.
- **Break your own loaf with your Nubbin.**
    - You break your loaf in two. Enkidu watches, and breaks his, and holds out half to the shepherd beside him.

#### `a26-05-bread-done`

_Afterwards the shepherds trim his hair, and he washes in the stream and rubs oil into his skin. Shamhat gives him clothes._  
**Shepherd**: Look at him. He looks like a bridegroom. Or a king.  
**Enkidu**: Is that good?  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): washing helps keep us healthy  
> _Enkidu washes in the stream for the first time. Why is washing good for our health?_  
> - ✅ It removes dirt and germs that can make us ill → Yes. Washing, especially our hands before eating, helps keep germs out of our bodies.
> - It makes us tire out so we sleep → Not the reason. Washing helps because it removes dirt and germs.
> - It is only for looking smart → It does help us look tidy, but its real job is removing dirt and germs.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that washing removes dirt and germs and helps keep us healthy._

**Shamhat**: That depends on the king.  

#### `a26-05-night`

_That night the shepherds sleep, properly, for the first time in a long while. Enkidu keeps watch, and you keep him company._  
_He sits on the fold wall with a big stick across his knees. He does not need a lamp._  
_He sees in the dark like the herd did._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): body parts help nocturnal animals survive  
> _Owls and many other night hunters are nocturnal, which means active at night. Which body part helps a nocturnal animal most?_  
> - ✅ Large eyes that gather light, and sharp hearing and smell → Yes. Many night animals have big eyes, and great hearing and smell, to find their way in the dark.
> - Bright feathers → Bright colours would give them away. Night animals do better with big eyes and sharp senses.
> - A loud voice → A loud voice would warn their prey. Night hunters rely on sharp eyes, ears and noses.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how body parts help nocturnal animals find their way in the dark._

**Enkidu**: The wolves come from there. The lions from over there. I know them. I used to drink with them.  
_Something moves out in the dark. A low grey shape slides along the edge of the grass, then another._  
_Enkidu stands up on the wall and says something to them, not in words. The shapes stop, then turn and slip away._  
**Enkidu**: They know me too. They know whose side I am on now.  

**Choices**

- **Hold the lamp up anyway.**
    - You hold up the lamp. He looks at it, and at you, and smiles.
    - **Enkidu**: That is for the sheep. So they know someone is here. Good.
- **Sit beside him on the wall.**
    - You sit beside him on the wall. Your Nubbin climbs into the gap between you, and falls asleep at once.

_Every night after that, the shepherds sleep, and no lamb is lost. They start calling him “the watchman”._  
_There are three folds, with twelve sheep in each, and every morning he counts them, out loud, and gets the same number._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication in word problems  
> _There are three folds with twelve sheep in each. How many sheep does Enkidu guard in all?_  
> - ✅ 36 → Yes. Three groups of 12: 12 + 12 + 12 = 36.
> - 15 → That is 12 + 3. Three groups of 12 means 12 + 12 + 12 = 36.
> - 24 → That is two folds. With three folds, it is 12 + 12 + 12 = 36.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied three groups of twelve to find 36._

_Enkidu looks at the steppe, and at the flocks, and at you. Then he nods._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): weighing what might go right and wrong before acting  
> _Enkidu wants to stand up to the king. What might go right, and what might go wrong, if he does?_  
> - It might make the king stop, and the people could rest → That is a fair answer. Standing up to unfairness can change things.
> - The king might get angry and hurt someone → That is a fair answer. A strong person who is challenged can react badly. It is good to think ahead.
> - Talking first would be better than fighting → That is a fair answer. Starting with words keeps more doors open.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the possible good and bad results of standing up to someone powerful._
