## A26-6. Ninsun’s Dreams

- `a26-06-s1`: Carry the cups to Ninsun’s hall in the palace. · _The steward at the palace kitchens needs a cup-bearer. Take the tray to the queen mother’s hall._
- `a26-06-s2`: Stay and hear what Ninsun makes of the dreams. · _Stand by the fountain with the tray while Ninsun talks to her son._

#### `a26-06-cups`

_Back in Uruk, the palace steward is short of hands. He looks at you, and at your Nubbin, and gives you a tray of silver cups._  
_The cups stand in three rows of four. Ninsun’s hall is cool and quiet, with a fountain, and the goddess sits beside it, in no hurry about anything._  
_Gilgamesh is pacing in front of her, and for once he is not shouting. He looks like a boy who has had a bad night._  
**Gilgamesh**: Mother, I dreamed again. A star fell out of the sky and landed beside me, like a rock.  
**Gilgamesh**: I tried to lift it and could not. Me! The city came out to stare. And I loved it. I held it as if it were a person.  
_You hold out the tray. He takes a cup without looking, and drinks, and forgets to give it back._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _The cups are in three rows of four. How many cups were on the tray before Gilgamesh took one?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Three rows of four is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Now there are 11.
> - 7 → That is 3 + 4. Three rows of four is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> - 34 → Careful: three rows of four is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> _For grown-ups: Used three rows of four to find 12._


**Choices**

- **Wait with the tray until he has finished.**
    - You wait. Ninsun catches your eye over his shoulder, and the corner of her mouth goes up.
- **Offer Ninsun a cup too.**
    - **Ninsun**: Thank you. Somebody in this palace remembers the rest of us drink as well.

#### `a26-06-cups-done`

**Ninsun**: Sit down, my son. You are wearing a hole in my floor. Tell me the other dream too.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): figurative language in dialogue  
> _Ninsun says her son is “wearing a hole in my floor”. What does she really mean?_  
> - ✅ He has been pacing up and down for ages → Yes. She exaggerates to be funny. She means he has been walking up and down so much it feels as if he might wear the floor away.
> - There is a real hole in her floor → There is not. It is an exaggeration, a joke. She means he has been pacing a great deal.
> - She wants him to dig a hole → No. It is a joke about how much he has been pacing.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of an exaggeration used as a joke._

_Gilgamesh sits at last, still turning the cup in his hands._  

#### `a26-06-meaning`

**Gilgamesh**: There was an axe, lying in the street. A strange one. People were all round it. I loved that too, and wore it at my side.  
**Ninsun**: The star that fell, the axe in the street. They are the same thing, my son. They are a person.  
**Ninsun**: A friend is coming to you. Strong as a star from heaven. He will stand beside you and save you, again and again.  
**Gilgamesh**: A friend? I have a whole city.  
**Ninsun**: You have a city that is tired of you. That is not the same.  
_Gilgamesh opens his mouth to argue, and shuts it again. He looks out of the window, towards the steppe._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): a crowd is not the same as a friend  
> _Gilgamesh has a whole city around him, but Ninsun says he needs a friend. Is a crowd the same as a friend?_  
> - No. A friend knows you and cares about you → That is a fair answer. Many people can be near you without knowing you.
> - Sometimes, if the crowd is kind → That is a fair answer. A kind crowd is lovely. Ninsun says this one is tired of him, which is different.
> - Yes, because more people is better → That is a fair answer to think about. But Gilgamesh is lonely among thousands. Closeness matters more than numbers.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between being surrounded by people and having a friend._


**Choices**

- **Tell him you think she is right.**
    - **Gilgamesh**: Do you? You have been in my city a week. Hm. You have probably seen more of it than I have.
- **Say nothing, and refill his cup.**
    - You refill his cup. He looks at it, then at you, as if he had just noticed someone was holding the tray.

**You**: Nobody’s. I am new here.  
**Gilgamesh**: Well, stay new. Carry my cups. There are not many people who stand still long enough to hear my dreams.  
_That night, for the first time since the new moon, the drum in the square stops before midnight._  
_The moon over Uruk is only a thin silver curve. A few nights ago it was hidden altogether._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Moon’s cycle takes about a month  
> _The people say the games began at the new moon. About how many days pass from one new moon to the next?_  
> - ✅ About 29 or 30 days → Yes. The Moon takes about 29½ days to go through all its phases, from one new moon to the next. That is where we get the idea of a month.
> - About 7 days → That is about a quarter of the cycle, from new moon to first quarter. The whole cycle takes about 29½ days.
> - A whole year → A year is much longer. From new moon to new moon is about 29½ days.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Moon’s cycle takes about 29 and a half days._


### Glossary

- **steward**: A person who looks after a big household and its servants.

#### `a26-07-gate`

_Enkidu comes up the river road in his borrowed clothes, with Shamhat beside him. People leave their work to stare._  
**Woman of Uruk**: Look at him! He is the king’s size exactly. He is like the king’s own shadow, only hairier.  
**Woman of Uruk**: He was raised on milk from the wild. They say he can wrestle a lion.  
_Enkidu sees you by the gate. His face breaks into a grin._  
**Enkidu**: The water-carrier! With the little one that ran with my gazelles!  
_Your Nubbin, embarrassed, hides behind your leg._  
**Shamhat**: He wants to meet your king. I have told him what to expect. He does not believe me.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): why cities grew beside rivers  
> _The road runs beside the river, and so does the city. Why did cities like Uruk grow up beside rivers?_  
> - ✅ Rivers gave water to drink and to grow crops, and a way to travel and carry goods → Yes. Water for people and fields, plus boats for trade. A river was a road, a well and a farm all at once.
> - Rivers kept cities warm in winter → Not the main reason. Cities grew beside rivers for water, crops and travel.
> - There was nowhere else to build → There was plenty of land. Water, crops and boat travel are what drew people to the rivers.
> _For grown-ups: Learned why early cities grew beside rivers._


**Choices**

- **Warn him the king is very strong.**
    - **Enkidu**: Good. So am I. Somebody should tell him so.
- **Tell him the king is lonely.**
    - **Enkidu**: Lonely?
    - He thinks about that for a long time. He knows the word from the steppe, when the herd ran.

#### `a26-07-gate-done`

_The crowd follows you through the streets, getting bigger, all the way to the great square._  
_Five people follow at the gate. At each corner, the crowd doubles._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a doubling pattern  
> _Five people at the gate, then 10, then 20 at the corners. If the crowd doubles once more, how many people follow?_  
> - ✅ 40 → Yes. The rule is “double”: 5, 10, 20, 40.
> - 30 → That would be adding 10 each time. The rule here is doubling, so 20 doubled is 40.
> - 25 → That would be adding 5 each time. The rule is doubling: 20 doubled is 40.
> _For grown-ups: Continued a doubling pattern: 5, 10, 20, 40._


#### `a26-07-door`

_Gilgamesh comes striding across the square towards a great door. Enkidu steps into the doorway and plants his feet._  
**Gilgamesh**: Out of my way.  
**Enkidu**: No.  
_Gilgamesh stops. Nobody has said that word to him in his whole life, and he does not seem to know what to do with it._  
_Then they grab each other like two bulls and wrestle in the street. The doorposts shake and the wall trembles._  
_They wrestle up the street and down it, and neither will give way, and neither will let go._  
_At last Gilgamesh’s knee touches the ground, and everyone gasps. It has never touched the ground before._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced and unbalanced forces  
> _For a long time, neither friend can move the other. Then Gilgamesh’s knee touches the ground._  
> _What changed?_  
> - ✅ The forces stopped being balanced, and one push became stronger → Yes. Equal pushes in opposite directions cancel out, and nothing moves. When one gets stronger, the balance breaks.
> - The forces disappeared → Forces do not disappear. They stop balancing out. One push became stronger than the other.
> - The ground pushed Gilgamesh over by itself → The ground does push back, but what changed was the balance between the two friends’ pushes.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that balanced forces cancel, and unbalanced forces change motion._


**Choices**

- **Hold your Nubbin back from the fight.**
    - You scoop up your Nubbin before it can join in. It wriggles in your arms, cheering on both sides at once.
- **Pull the woman from the square out of the dust.**
    - You pull her back under an awning. She coughs, and grips your arm, and does not take her eyes off the door.

#### `a26-07-door-done`

_Gilgamesh kneels in the dust, breathing hard, with Enkidu over him. For a moment the whole square holds its breath._  
_Then Gilgamesh starts to laugh, and Enkidu laughs too. He holds out a hand, and the king takes it._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): why a fight can end in friendship  
> _They fought hard, and ended as friends. Why do you think that happened?_  
> - Each had finally met someone who would not give way → That is a fair answer. Gilgamesh had never been refused. Respect can grow from being matched.
> - They had both been lonely → That is a fair answer. Both were alone in their own way, and the fight ended it.
> - It is not usual: fights do not often end like this → That is a fair answer. Usually they do not. Here, both could laugh at themselves, which helps.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a fight ended in friendship, and what is unusual about it._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): what a small detail shows about a character  
> _Enkidu “does not know where to put his hands”. What does that small detail show about how he feels?_  
> - ✅ He is shy and unsure, because he has never been mothered → Yes. A small action can show a big feeling without anyone saying it.
> - He is angry → He is not angry here. Not knowing where to put your hands shows shyness and surprise.
> - He is bored → Not bored. The detail shows he is overwhelmed by a kindness he has never known.
> _For grown-ups: Read a character’s feelings from a small detail of what he does._

#### `a26-08-plan`

_You carry a water jar up to the palace roof. The two friends are lying on their backs, looking at the sky._  
**Gilgamesh**: Enkidu. Only the gods last for ever. A person gets a short life, and then it is over.  
**Gilgamesh**: So let us do something they will remember. The Cedar Forest. Humbaba, who guards it. Let us go.  
_Enkidu sits up so fast he knocks the jar. You catch it._  
**Enkidu**: I know that forest. I ran in its edges, when I was wild. Humbaba is as old as the mountains. When he shouts, the cedars bend.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what lasts: a famous name, or what we do for others  
> _Gilgamesh wants to make a name that lasts longer than he does. What do you think lasts longer: a famous name, or something you did for other people?_  
> - A famous name, because people repeat it → That is a fair answer. Names do travel. Gilgamesh’s did, for over four thousand years.
> - What you did for others, because it changes their lives → That is a fair answer. A kindness can live on in people who never knew your name.
> - Maybe both, but they are not the same thing → That is a fair answer. A name tells people who. A deed tells them what you were like.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a famous name or a kind deed lasts longer._

    - You pour them both a cup. Enkidu holds his without drinking, the way people hold something to stop their hands shaking.

_You pour from the jar, which holds two litres. Each cup holds 250 millilitres._  
**Enkidu**: If you go, I will go. Somebody has to bring you back.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of volume: litres and millilitres  
> _The jar holds 2 litres, which is 2000 millilitres. Each cup holds 250 millilitres._  
> _How many cups can you fill?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes. 250 × 4 = 1000, so a litre fills 4 cups, and two litres fill 8.
> - 4 → That is one litre’s worth. The jar holds two litres, so 4 + 4 = 8 cups.
> - 10 → Check: 10 × 250 = 2500, which is more than 2000. It is 8 cups.
> _For grown-ups: Converted litres to millilitres and divided to find eight cups._

_The elders of Uruk sit on their benches by the gate. They hear Gilgamesh out, and shake their heads, all together._  
**Elder of Uruk**: You are young, Gilgamesh. Your heart runs ahead of you. You do not know what you are talking about.  
**Elder of Uruk**: Let Enkidu go first. He knows the road. And come back to us. We have got used to you.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): listening to people who have experience  
> _The elders say Enkidu should lead, because he knows the road. Why is it wise to listen to someone with experience?_  
> - ✅ They have seen what can go wrong, and can help us avoid it → Yes. Experience is knowledge from having been there. Good leaders listen to it, even when they are bold.
> - Older people are always right → Not always. But those who have walked the road know things we do not. Listening helps us decide.
> - It is never worth it → Listening costs little. Gilgamesh does not quite follow this advice, as we will see.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about why it is wise to listen to someone with experience._

_At sunrise Ninsun climbs her roof in her best robe and crown. She lifts incense to the sun god Shamash._

**Ninsun**: Watch over him. Let the long days go fast for him. And bring him home.  
_The sun climbs a little higher, and is very bright. You decide that is a yes._

_The sun is clear of the horizon now, over the east side of the city._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Sun rises in the east  
> _Ninsun prays to the rising sun. In which direction does the Sun rise?_  
> - ✅ East → Yes. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, because the Earth spins.
> - West → That is where it sets. The Sun rises in the east.
> - North → Not north. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sun rises in the east._

_You pack them the way your Nubbin likes its fruit: the soft things on top, so nothing gets squashed._  
**Gilgamesh**: Bread? I am going to face a monster. I do not need bread.

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: sharing equally  
> _Twenty-four loaves go into six packs, the same number in each. How many loaves in one pack?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. 24 ÷ 6 = 4, because 6 × 4 = 24.
> - 6 → Check: 6 packs of 6 would be 36. It is 4 in each, because 6 × 4 = 24.
> - 18 → That is 24 − 6. Division asks how many in each pack: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 24 loaves equally into six packs._

## A26-9. Dreams on the Mountain

- `a26-09-s1`: Make camp on the mountain and keep the fire. · _Gather brush on the slope, then build the fire in the hollow by the well._
- `a26-09-s2`: Keep the watch through the nights on the road. · _Sit up by the fire while the friends sleep._

#### `a26-09-fire`

_They walk fifty leagues a day, which would take anyone else a month and a half. You and your Nubbin trot to keep up._  
_Each evening Gilgamesh climbs a mountain and pours out flour as a gift, and asks for a dream. Then you make camp._  
_You dig a well, and build the fire, and Enkidu builds a little shelter of brush so the king can sleep out of the wind._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): what a fire needs to burn  
> _You build the fire up. A fire gives out heat and light._  
> _What does it need to keep burning?_  
> - ✅ Fuel such as wood, air, and enough heat → Yes. Take away fuel, air or heat, and a fire goes out. Pile the brush loosely so air can get in.
> - Only wood → Wood is the fuel, but a fire also needs air and heat. Pile it loosely so air flows through.
> - Only water → Water puts fires out! A fire needs fuel, air and heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fire needs fuel, air and heat._

_In the night Gilgamesh sits bolt upright._  
**Gilgamesh**: Enkidu! Was that you? Something woke me, and I am cold all over. I dreamed a mountain fell on me, and pinned me like a fly.  
**Enkidu**: A good dream! A very good dream. The mountain is Humbaba, and he will fall. We will stand on him.  

**Choices**

- **Build the fire up higher.**
    - You pile on more brush. The fire jumps up, and the dark backs off a little, and Gilgamesh lies down again.
- **Put your blanket over the king.**
    - You put your blanket over him, and he does not notice. In the morning he will think he dreamed that too.

#### `a26-09-fire-done`

_Enkidu waits until the king is snoring. Then he looks at you across the fire, and his face is not happy at all._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): noticing feelings hidden behind words  
> _Enkidu told the king it was a good dream, but his face is not happy. What does that tell you?_  
> - ✅ He is hiding how worried he really is → Yes. Faces often tell the truth when words do not. Noticing helps us be a better friend.
> - He is sleepy → He might be. But a worried face looks different from a sleepy one. This one is hiding worry.
> - He is angry with the king → He is not angry. He is protecting the king, and hiding his own fear.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that someone’s face can show feelings that their words hide._


#### `a26-09-watch`

_Every night it is the same. A mountain, a dream, a cold wake in the dark._  
_Gilgamesh dreams of a wild bull, of thunder, of a sky that rains down fire and ash._  
_And every morning Enkidu says, cheerfully, it is a good dream, the best dream yet._  
_On the fifth night, while the king sleeps, Enkidu sits down beside you at the fire. Dusk fell at seven, and dawn will not come until five._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _Dusk falls at 7 in the evening, and dawn comes at 5 in the morning. How long is the night watch?_  
> - ✅ 10 hours → Yes. 7 pm to midnight is 5 hours, and midnight to 5 am is 5 more: 10 hours.
> - 12 hours → That would be 7 pm to 7 am. Dawn is at 5 am, so it is 10 hours.
> - 2 hours → That is the gap between 5 and 7 as numbers. The night runs from 7 pm to 5 am, so 10 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval across midnight: 7 pm to 5 am is 10 hours._

**Enkidu**: They were bad dreams. All of them. You know that.  
**Enkidu**: But you cannot send a man to a fight with a bad dream on him. So I tell him it was good. That is what friends are for.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when a kind lie and honesty pull apart  
> _Enkidu tells the king each dream was good, though he knows it was bad. Was that kind, dishonest, or both?_  
> - Kind, because it gave the king courage → That is a fair answer. Enkidu’s aim is to help his friend face the day. The cost is that the king does not hear the truth.
> - Dishonest, because the king deserves the truth → That is a fair answer. Being told the truth is a form of respect. It might also have let the king choose differently.
> - Both, and it is hard to say which matters more → That is a fair answer. Many honest people have faced this. Honesty and kindness can pull in different directions.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a kind untruth is kind, dishonest or both._


**Choices**

- **Tell him he did the right thing.**
    - **Enkidu**: Did I? I hope so. I am new at friends.
- **Ask him who tells him the dreams are good.**
    - **Enkidu**: Nobody. That is all right. I have you, sitting up with the fire.

#### `a26-09-watch-done`

_He falls asleep sitting up, with his head on his knees. You keep the fire till dawn._  
_In the morning, on the skyline, there is a dark green line, and a smell on the wind like a sawmill: cut wood, and sweet, sticky resin. The Cedar Forest._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): language that appeals to the senses  
> _Which phrase in the last line appeals most to the sense of smell?_  
> - ✅ “a smell on the wind like a sawmill: cut wood, and sweet, sticky resin” → Yes. It names smells directly. Good writers use senses so we feel we are there.
> - “a dark green line” → That appeals to sight, because it describes colour and shape.
> - “on the skyline” → That tells us where, but not how it smells.
> _For grown-ups: Picked out words that appeal to the sense of smell._


#### `a26-09-complete`

_The cedars are taller than the wall of Uruk. Their shade is so cool and deep it looks like water._  
_Brown cones lie scattered in the needles._  
**Gilgamesh**: There. Did I not say? Good dreams, every one.  
_Enkidu says nothing. He puts his hand flat on the first cedar, as if to say sorry to it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): conifers and how they reproduce  
> _Cedars are conifers. Which statement about conifers is true?_  
> - ✅ Many keep their needles all year, and their seeds grow in cones → Yes. Cedar, pine and fir are conifers. Seeds inside cones fall and, if they land well, grow into new trees.
> - They lose all their leaves every autumn → Many deciduous trees do. Most conifers keep their needles, which is why forests of them stay green.
> - They have flowers and fruit like apples → Conifers make seeds in cones, not in fruit. Apples are flowering trees.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cedars are conifers whose seeds grow in cones._


### Glossary

- **resin**: The sticky, sweet-smelling sap of some trees, such as cedars.

## A26-10. Humbaba

- `a26-10-s1`: Follow the friends into the Cedar Forest. · _Keep to Humbaba’s path between the cedars, and stay behind Enkidu._
- `a26-10-s2`: Stand by while Humbaba begs, and decide what you will say. · _Stay close to the friends. Choose what to say when Gilgamesh looks round._
- `a26-10-s3`: Help send the great cedar down the river to Uruk. · _Carry the ropes to the riverbank and help lash the raft._

#### `a26-10-forest`

_Humbaba’s path runs straight into the forest, wide and clean, as if someone swept it every morning. Somebody does._  
_The cedars smell of resin and old shade, and no birds sing here. Your Nubbin walks so close to your heels it treads on them._  
**Gilgamesh**: This one. The tallest we have passed. Let us see if he comes.  
_Gilgamesh lifts his axe and cuts into a cedar. The sound goes off through the forest like a dropped plate._  
_Far away, something roars. It is not loud, exactly._  
_It is everywhere, like weather._  
**Humbaba**: Who has come into my forest? Who has cut my tree?  
_Then he is there between the trees: huge, and ancient, with a face like a coil of wool._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, notice): cedar forests grow on the mountains of Lebanon today  
> _Nobody knows exactly where the Cedar Forest was. Many people think of the mountains of Lebanon, where cedar trees still grow today._  
> _(Find Lebanon on Nova’s map.)_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cedar forests still grow in the mountains of Lebanon, and found it on a map._


**Choices**

- **Stand very still.**
    - You stand very still. His eyes pass over you and your Nubbin and move on: you were never the ones he wanted.
- **Pull your Nubbin behind a cedar.**
    - You pull your Nubbin behind a cedar. The bark is warm, and you feel the tree breathe, or you think you do.

#### `a26-10-forest-done`

**Gilgamesh**: Shamash! Now! You promised my mother!  
_Your heart is going like a drum. Your Nubbin’s fur is standing on end._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): slow breathing calms a frightened body  
> _Your heart is racing and you feel frightened. Which helps your body calm down?_  
> - ✅ A slow breath in, and a longer breath out → Yes. A long breath out tells your body it is safe. Try it now: in for four, out for six.
> - Holding your breath → That makes your heart work harder. Slow breathing, with a long breath out, helps.
> - Breathing as fast as you can → That can make you feel dizzier. A slow breath in and a longer one out helps more.
> _For grown-ups: Practised slow breathing to calm a frightened body._


#### `a26-10-plea`

**Shamash**: I hear.  
_The voice comes out of the sun. Then the winds come: thirteen great winds from every side, roaring through the cedars._  
_They pin Humbaba where he stands, like a hand holding down a leaf. He cannot go forward, and he cannot go back._  
**Humbaba**: Gilgamesh. Let me live. I will be your servant. I will cut the cedars for you myself, as many as you want.  
**Humbaba**: This forest is all I have. The god Enlil gave it to me to keep. I have kept it since before your city had a wall.  
_Gilgamesh lowers his axe a little and looks at Humbaba for a long time. Something in his face is changing._  
**Enkidu**: Do not listen to him, my friend. Finish it. Before the great gods hear and stop you. Make your name.  
_Gilgamesh turns his head, and looks at you. Of everyone in the forest, it is you he looks at._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): mercy, fear and the cost of a hard choice  
> _Humbaba begs for his life. Enkidu says to finish it._  
> _Whatever you say could change what happens. What would you weigh up before you answer?_  
> - That Humbaba is begging, and cannot hurt anyone now → That is a fair answer. Mercy looks hardest at someone who can no longer fight back.
> - That Enkidu knows the forest, and may be right to be afraid → That is a fair answer. Enkidu’s fear is real. It is worth asking if fear is a good guide to a choice.
> - That a choice like this cannot be undone → That is a fair answer. When something cannot be taken back, it deserves the slowest thinking.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about mercy and a hard choice that cannot be undone._


**Choices**

- **Speak for Humbaba: let him go.**
    - **You**: Let him go. He is only doing what he was told. He is keeping his trees, like you keep your wall.
    - Enkidu stares at you, and Gilgamesh’s axe drops lower. For a long breath, nobody moves.
- **Say nothing.**
    - You say nothing; you do not know what is right. You hold on to your Nubbin, and the wind roars, and Gilgamesh looks away.
- **Agree with Enkidu.**
    - **You**: Enkidu is right. He knows this forest. If he says finish it, finish it.
    - Enkidu nods at you, grim. Gilgamesh lifts his axe again.

#### `a26-10-plea-done`

_Whatever anyone says, Gilgamesh has already decided. He steps forward into the wind, and Enkidu goes with him._  
_You turn your face away, into your Nubbin’s fur._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): what causes wind  
> _Thirteen winds roar through the cedars. What causes wind in the real world?_  
> - ✅ The Sun heats the Earth unevenly, and air moves from cooler places to warmer ones → Yes. Warm air rises, cooler air rushes in, and we feel moving air as wind. Heat from the Sun drives it.
> - Trees waving their branches → It is the other way round. Wind makes trees wave. The Sun’s uneven heating makes the wind.
> - The Moon pulling on the air → The Moon pulls on the seas, to make tides. For wind, it is the Sun heating the Earth unevenly.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wind comes from the Sun heating the Earth unevenly._

_The wind drops, all thirteen winds at once. And the Cedar Forest goes quiet, the deep quiet of a held breath let go._  
_Humbaba has died, and it cannot be undone. Whatever you chose, it is all right to feel uneasy._  

#### `a26-10-river`

_Afterwards nobody talks much. The friends cut cedars, and Enkidu cuts the tallest of all, whose top scraped the sky._  
**Enkidu**: We will make a door of it. Seventy-two cubits high. For Enlil’s temple. So he is not angry with us.  
_A cubit is about the length of a forearm, roughly half a metre. You carry ropes and lash logs._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): converting old units to metres  
> _A cubit is about half a metre. The door is 72 cubits high._  
> _About how many metres is that?_  
> - ✅ 36 metres → Yes. Half of 72 is 36. That is as tall as a twelve-storey building.
> - 72 metres → That would be one metre per cubit. A cubit is only half a metre, so halve it: 36.
> - 144 metres → That would be doubling. A cubit is half a metre, so halve 72 to get 36.
> _For grown-ups: Converted 72 cubits to about 36 metres by halving._

_Your Nubbin carries one twig at a time, very solemnly, to the raft. Gilgamesh says nothing at all, and keeps looking back at the forest._  
_At last the raft is lashed, and the friends push it out into the Euphrates. It turns once, slowly, and sets off home._  

**Choices**

- **Keep a cedar cone in your pocket.**
    - You pick up a cedar cone and keep it in your pocket. It smells of the forest the whole way home.
- **Look back at the forest until it is gone.**
    - You look back until the forest is only a dark line, and then not even that. Somebody should.

#### `a26-10-complete`

_The river carries you home through the reeds. Herons stand on one leg and watch the raft go by._  
_Gilgamesh has made his name. He does not look as if it fits him quite as he expected._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: what a story is really about  
> _Gilgamesh has the name he wanted, but it does not fit as he expected. Which theme does that suggest?_  
> - ✅ Getting what you want can feel different from what you imagined → Yes. A theme is an idea a story keeps returning to. Here, it is that winning does not always feel like winning.
> - Names are always more important than people → The story hints at the opposite. Gilgamesh looks uneasy with his new name.
> - Rivers are always safer than forests → That is true of nothing in particular. The theme is about the feeling after getting what you wanted.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: getting what you want can feel different from what you imagined._


### Glossary

- **mercy**: Kindness shown to someone you have the power to hurt.
- **cubit**: An old measure of length, about the length of a forearm.

## A26-11. Ishtar

- `a26-11-s1`: Fetch warm water for the king to wash. · _Heat water in the palace kitchen and carry it to the king’s rooms._
- `a26-11-s2`: Stand by while the goddess Ishtar makes her offer. · _Stay by the door with your Nubbin. Do not get between a goddess and a king._

#### `a26-11-wash`

_Home in Uruk, Gilgamesh asks for warm water. You carry it up, jar after jar, until the king’s rooms are full of steam._  
_He washes the forest out of his long hair and shakes it down his back. He puts on clean clothes and his crown._  
**Gilgamesh**: There. Do I look like a king who has made a name?  
**Enkidu**: You look like a king who has had a bath. That is a start.  
_Gilgamesh throws a wet cloth at him. It is the first time either of them has laughed since the forest._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): condensation: some changes can be reversed  
> _Steam rises from the hot water. If the steam touches a cold window, what happens?_  
> - ✅ It cools and turns back into drops of water → Yes. Heating turns water into steam, and cooling turns steam back into water. That kind of change can be reversed.
> - It turns into stone → No. Steam cools back into drops of water on cold glass.
> - It disappears for ever → The water is still there. It cools into tiny drops of liquid on the window.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cooling turns steam back into water, a change that can be reversed._

_Then the light in the room goes gold and strange, as if the sun had come indoors. Your Nubbin’s fur stands up._  

**Choices**

- **Hand Enkidu a dry cloth.**
    - You hand Enkidu a dry cloth. He holds it like a shield, and peers at the gold light.
- **Put down the jar and stand by the door.**
    - You put the jar down and stand by the door. Whoever is coming, you would like to be near the way out.

#### `a26-11-offer`

_The goddess Ishtar stands in the doorway, bright as the evening star. Her eyes are fixed on Gilgamesh, and nobody else._  
**Ishtar**: Gilgamesh. You are beautiful. Stay with me. Be my king, and I will give you a chariot of lapis and gold.  
**Ishtar**: Kings will kneel to you. Your flocks will double every spring. You will want for nothing.  
_Gilgamesh looks at her for a long moment. Then he shakes his head._  
**Gilgamesh**: Everyone you have loved has come to grief. Why would I be different?  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): weighing what you give up against what you gain  
> _Ishtar offers a golden chariot and much more, but it comes with a price. What is wise to do when someone offers you a great gift?_  
> - ✅ Think about what you would give up as well as what you would gain → Yes. Every choice has a cost: when you choose one thing, you give up another. Gilgamesh looks at the whole price.
> - Take it, because gifts are free → Gifts often come with strings. It is wise to ask what it would cost you.
> - Refuse everything on principle → Not always wise either. The point is to weigh what you gain against what you give up.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that every choice has a cost, and that it helps to weigh what we give up as well as what we gain._

_Ishtar’s face goes very still. The gold light in the room turns the colour of a storm._  
**Ishtar**: You will be sorry, king of Uruk.  

**Choices**

- **Bow low as she passes.**
    - You bow low as she sweeps past. You feel her look at you, briefly, as if at a fly on a wall.
- **Keep your Nubbin out of her way.**
    - You scoop your Nubbin out of her path. The hem of her robe crackles past it like summer lightning.

#### `a26-11-offer-done`

**Enkidu**: That was not clever, brother.  
**Gilgamesh**: No. But it was true.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether a true thing can also be unkind  
> _Gilgamesh said something true that made a goddess furious. Can something be true and still unkind?_  
> - Yes. Truth can still be said gently or harshly → That is a fair answer. How we say a true thing can matter as much as what we say.
> - No. If it is true, it is not unkind → That is a fair answer. Honesty is a kindness of a kind. But Ishtar was hurt, which suggests the way of saying matters too.
> - It depends why you say it → That is a fair answer. A true thing said to help is not the same as one said to hurt.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a true thing can be unkind, and how the way we say it matters._

_High above the city, in a place you can only half see, Ishtar weeps in front of her father Anu, king of the gods._  
_She asks him for the Bull of Heaven. At first he says no, but she will not stop asking._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why does Ishtar ask her father for the Bull of Heaven? Think about how she felt after Gilgamesh’s answer._  
> - ✅ She is hurt and angry, and wants to punish him → Yes. Her motive is wounded pride turned to anger. Knowing why a character acts helps us understand the story.
> - She is bored → Not bored. She wept in front of her father, so she was hurt.
> - She wants to help Uruk → If she did, she would not call a Bull to its streets. Her motive is anger.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a character’s motive from how she felt._

## A26-12. The Bull of Heaven

- `a26-12-s1`: Get the children in the market away from the cracks. · _Lead them up the wall stairs, away from the river side of the market._
- `a26-12-s2`: Watch from the wall as the friends face the Bull together. · _Stay on the wall with the children. Keep them back from the edge._

#### `a26-12-bull`

_It comes down out of the sky on the river side of town: a bull the size of a temple, the colour of thunderclouds._  
_It snorts, and the ground cracks open, and a hundred market stalls tip into the hole. It snorts again, and the river leaps its banks._  
**Woman of Uruk**: The children! Somebody get the children!  
_There are twelve of them, stuck by the fruit stalls. You know the way: up the wall stairs, minding the third one._  
_You can lead two at a time. Your Nubbin runs ahead and stops on every step to look back, so the smallest ones have something to follow._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division in a word problem  
> _There are twelve children, and you lead two at a time. How many trips up the stairs do you need?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes. 12 ÷ 2 = 6, because 2 × 6 = 12.
> - 10 → That is 12 − 2. Division asks how many twos fit into 12: 6.
> - 24 → That is 12 × 2. To split 12 into pairs, divide: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Divided twelve children into pairs to find six trips._


**Choices**

- **Lead the children up the stairs.**
    - You lead them up, two at a time, holding hands in a long chain. Nobody lets go.
- **Carry the smallest one.**
    - You lift the smallest child on to your hip. She grips your collar with both fists and does not cry once.

#### `a26-12-bull-done`

_From the top of the wall you can see it all: the Bull, the cracks, and two small figures running straight at it._  
**Woman of Uruk**: That is the king. And his brother. They are mad. They are both completely mad.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): courage and recklessness  
> _The friends run straight at the Bull. Was that brave, or foolish?_  
> - Brave, because they protected the city → That is a fair answer. They went towards the danger to keep others safe.
> - Foolish, because they could have been hurt → That is a fair answer. Courage and carelessness can look the same from outside. The difference is often whether you thought first.
> - Both, depending on the reason → That is a fair answer. Brave and foolish are not always opposites. It is worth asking what you are risking and why.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between bravery and recklessness._


#### `a26-12-fight`

_Enkidu grabs the Bull by its horns. It throws froth in his face and lashes its great tail, and he holds on._  
**Enkidu**: Now, brother! Together!  
_Gilgamesh comes in from the side, and the dust goes up like a wall of its own, and you cannot see anything at all._  
_The children hold their breath. Your Nubbin covers its eyes, then uncovers one._  
_When the dust settles, the Bull of Heaven lies on its side in the square, quite still, like a hill after a landslide. Nobody has been hurt._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): recognising a simile  
> _“Lies on its side, like a hill after a landslide.” Which words show this is a simile?_  
> - ✅ “like a hill”: it compares using “like” → Yes. A simile compares two different things using “like” or “as”. A bull and a hill have little in common, except being huge and still.
> - “lies on its side” → That just tells us what the Bull does. The comparison starts with “like”.
> - “after a landslide” → That adds a time. The comparison itself is “like a hill”.
> _For grown-ups: Picked out the comparison word that makes a simile._

_Ishtar appears on the wall of Uruk, in a storm of gold. Enkidu glares up at her from the square._  
**Enkidu**: Go home! Leave our city alone! And take your storms with you!  
_Ishtar turns away with her women, and weeps for the Bull. Then she is gone._  

**Choices**

- **Cheer with the children.**
    - You cheer, the children cheer, and somebody bangs a pot. The whole wall shakes with it.
- **Look at the Bull for a while.**
    - You look at the Bull for a while. It came because someone was angry; it never chose to come at all.

_That night the friends ride through the streets of Uruk in a chariot. The people line the way, shouting their names._  
**Gilgamesh**: Whose names do we shout tonight? Whose?  
**Woman of Uruk**: Gilgamesh! And Enkidu!  
_Enkidu waves. He catches sight of you in the crowd, and waves harder, until your Nubbin waves back with both arms._  
_Scribes in the crowd are already pressing the night into clay, so that people far in the future can read about it._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how we learn about the distant past  
> _How do we know about people who lived thousands of years ago, such as the people of Uruk?_  
> - ✅ From the writings, buildings and objects they left behind → Yes. Tablets, bricks, pots and walls are clues. Historians put them together like a puzzle.
> - Because they are still alive → Not so! We learn from what they left behind: tablets, buildings and objects.
> - By guessing → Historians do not just guess. They study tablets and objects as evidence.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we know about the distant past from the writings and objects people left._


## A26-13. The Gods’ Council

- `a26-13-s1`: Sit with Enkidu when he wakes from his dream. · _He has called for you before dawn. Go to his room._
- `a26-13-s2`: Go with Enkidu to the cedar door. · _He wants to see the great door at the temple. Walk him there._

#### `a26-13-dream`

_Before dawn a servant shakes you awake. Enkidu is asking for you, and for the king._  
_He is sitting on the edge of his bed with the blanket round his shoulders. He is very pale._  
**Enkidu**: I dreamed. The great gods sat in council: Anu, and Enlil, and Shamash. They were talking about us.  
**Enkidu**: Because we killed Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, one of us has to die. Enlil said so. And it will not be Gilgamesh. It will be me.  
**Gilgamesh**: No. No. It was a dream. I will tell you it was a good one, the way you did for me.  
_Enkidu tries to smile at that. He does not quite manage it._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what helps after a frightening dream  
> _Enkidu has woken from a frightening dream. Which helps most?_  
> - ✅ Telling someone, and slow breaths until the fear shrinks → Yes. Saying a scary dream out loud makes it smaller, and slow breathing calms the body. Dreams are not predictions.
> - Keeping it secret so nobody worries → Secrets can make fear grow. Telling someone you trust helps.
> - Never going to sleep again → Tiredness makes dreams harder to bear. Telling someone and slow breathing are better.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what helps after a frightening dream: telling someone and slow breathing._


**Choices**

- **Sit down on the bed beside him.**
    - You sit down beside him, and the bed creaks. Your Nubbin climbs up on his other side.
- **Bring him a cup of water.**
    - You bring him water. His hands shake, so you hold the cup with him until he has drunk.

#### `a26-13-dream-done`

_Enkidu turns to look at you. He does not say anything at all._  
_He takes your hand, and holds it, quite hard, while the window goes from black to grey._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): when silence is the kindest thing to give  
> _Enkidu says nothing, and holds your hand. When might silence be the best thing to give a friend?_  
> - When words would not help, but company would → That is a fair answer. Sometimes the most useful thing is to stay.
> - When the person is not ready to talk → That is a fair answer. Silence gives room to decide when to speak.
> - Almost never: words are better → That is a fair answer. Many people do find talking helps. It is worth asking your friend which they want.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when silence and company are the kindest thing to give a friend._


#### `a26-13-door`

_He wants to see the cedar door, so you walk him to the temple, slowly. It stands there, huge and fragrant and new._  
**Enkidu**: Door. If I had known what you would cost me, I would have left you standing in your forest.  
**Enkidu**: And the trapper. If he had left me alone at the water. And Shamhat, who taught me to talk. I curse them all.  
_The sun comes up over the wall. It shines straight into the doorway, and the door’s long shadow stretches across the stones._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows change with the Sun’s height  
> _The rising Sun makes the door’s shadow long. When in the day are shadows shortest?_  
> - ✅ Around midday, when the Sun is highest → Yes. A low Sun, in the morning and evening, throws long shadows. A high Sun at midday makes them short.
> - At sunrise → At sunrise the Sun is low, so shadows are long.
> - At midnight → At midnight there is no sunlight to make a shadow.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shadows are shortest around midday and longest when the Sun is low._

**Shamash**: Enkidu. Why curse Shamhat? She gave you your first bread. She gave you clothes to wear.  
**Shamash**: She gave you Gilgamesh for a friend. And when you die, he will weep for you, and the whole city will.  
_Enkidu stands very still in the sunlight. His face crumples, and then, slowly, it clears._  

**Choices**

- **Tell him she gave him bread, too, the first day.**
    - **Enkidu**: She did. I licked it first. You were there.
- **Stay quiet, and let him think.**
    - You stay quiet. The sun is warm on the three of you: Enkidu, you, and your Nubbin, leaning on his leg.

**Enkidu**: Shamhat. I take it back. I wish you a warm house, and a full table, and friends at your door.  
**Enkidu**: You found me in the grass and brought me home. I bless you.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): remembering the good someone did  
> _Enkidu takes back his curses once he remembers what Shamhat gave him. What does that show?_  
> - ✅ When we are hurting, remembering the good someone did can calm us down → Yes. Pain makes us angry at the wrong people. Remembering kindness helps us find the right words again.
> - He changed his mind because he was told to → Shamash reminded him, but Enkidu chose to take the curses back. That took courage.
> - He did not mean either one → He meant the curses when he said them. Taking them back shows he was strong enough to change.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how remembering kindness can calm anger and lead to taking words back._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals to the minute  
> _Enkidu woke at 5:30 in the morning, and by noon (12:00) he is exhausted. How long has he been awake?_  
> - ✅ 6 hours 30 minutes → Yes. 5:30 to 11:30 is 6 hours, and 11:30 to 12:00 is another half an hour: 6 hours 30 minutes.
> - 7 hours → Check: 5:30 plus 7 hours is 12:30, which is past noon. So it is 6 hours 30 minutes.
> - 5 hours 30 minutes → Close, but 5:30 plus 5 hours 30 is 11:00, and noon is an hour later. It is 6 hours 30 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Found a time interval: 5:30 to 12:00 is 6 hours 30 minutes._

- `a26-14-s1`: Sit with Enkidu while he is ill. · _Take water to his room, and stay._
- `a26-14-s2`: Stay with Enkidu and Gilgamesh on the twelfth day. · _Stay in the room. There is nothing to do but be there._
- `a26-14-s3`: Go with Gilgamesh when he has a statue made of his friend. · _Find the king in the smiths’ quarter, with the gold and the lapis._

#### `a26-14-sickbed`

_Enkidu lies ill for twelve days. Each day he is a little more tired, and a little further away._  
_You fetch water and cool cloths. Mostly you just sit, on the stool by the bed, because he likes someone there._  
_Gilgamesh sits on the other side, and does not sleep. You have never seen him sit still so long._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): how to care for someone who is ill  
> _Enkidu is ill. Which of these helps a poorly friend most?_  
> - ✅ Water, rest, and someone calm sitting nearby → Yes. Good care is often simple: comfort, water, rest and company.
> - Lots of noise and visitors → That would tire him out. A quiet room and a calm person help more.
> - Leaving him completely alone → Rest matters, but so does having someone near. Calm company helps most.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how to care for someone who is ill: comfort, water, rest and calm company._

**Enkidu**: Tell me about where you come from. Is it big, like Uruk?  
**You**: No. It is small. There is a garden, and a pond, and a hill.  
**Enkidu**: A hill. Good. I like hills. You can see what is coming.  
_Your Nubbin lies on the end of the bed, across his feet, to keep them warm. He says it is the best blanket he has ever had._  

**Choices**

- **Tell him about the Grove.**
    - You tell him about the Grove: the Nubbins, the fruit trees, the lanterns. He listens with his eyes shut, smiling.
- **Hum the tune he sang at the shepherds’ fire.**
    - You hum the tune he sang at the shepherds’ fire, and get it a bit wrong. He hums it back right, very quietly.
- **Just hold his hand.**
    - You hold his hand. It is very big, and very warm, and it holds yours back.

#### `a26-14-sickbed-done`

**Enkidu**: Water-carrier. Will you do something for me, after?  
**Enkidu**: Look after the gazelles. Not the city ones. The wild ones, at the water hole. Make sure nobody digs pits there.  
**You**: I will.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-4, ask): protecting a habitat  
> _Pits at the water hole put the gazelles in danger. Which would best protect the gazelles’ habitat?_  
> - ✅ Leaving the water hole and grazing land safe and undisturbed → Yes. A habitat is where an animal finds food, water and shelter. Protecting it protects the animals.
> - Fencing the gazelles away from the water → That would leave them thirsty. Protect the water hole instead.
> - Moving the water hole somewhere else → Animals depend on the water that is there. It is better to protect it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that protecting a habitat, such as a water hole, protects the animals that need it._


#### `a26-14-death`

_On the twelfth day the house is very quiet. Even the street outside seems to walk on tiptoe._  
_Gilgamesh has not left the bedside for days. You keep bringing water, and he keeps not drinking it._  
**Enkidu**: Brother. Do you remember the door? Your knee in the dust?  
**Gilgamesh**: I let you win.  
**Enkidu**: You did not.  
_He laughs, a little, and closes his eyes. Your Nubbin is curled against his hand, and it does not move, and neither do you._  
_Some time in the afternoon his breathing goes slower, and softer. Then it stops, as gently as a door being closed._  
_Enkidu has died. That means his body has stopped working, and it will not start again._  
_It is not like sleep._  
_Gilgamesh draws the cloth over his friend’s face, carefully, like a bride’s veil. He gets up and walks the room like a lioness who has lost her cubs._  
**Gilgamesh**: Enkidu was my friend, my brother. He ran with me through the mountains and the cedar forest, and never once let go.  
**Gilgamesh**: Who will I tell my dreams to now?  
_You do not have an answer. Nobody does._  
_You sit on the floor by the bed, and wait, and the light goes._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what helps when someone dies  
> _Enkidu has died. When we are grieving, what helps?_  
> - ✅ Letting the feeling be, and staying close to people who care → Yes. Grief has no timetable. Crying is allowed, and so is company. Remembering helps too.
> - Pretending we feel nothing → Feelings do not go away when we hide them. They often ease when we share them.
> - Getting over it as quickly as possible → Grief takes as long as it takes. There is no right speed.
> _For grown-ups: Talked plainly about death and what helps when we are grieving._

_Your Nubbin climbs down off the bed, and into Gilgamesh’s lap when at last he sits, and stays there._  
_It does not do anything or make a sound all night. It is the kindest thing anyone does._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): staying close helps when words cannot  
> _The Nubbin does not say or do anything all night, and it is the kindest thing anyone does. Why?_  
> - ✅ It stays, which tells Gilgamesh he is not alone → Yes. Sometimes being there is the whole kindness.
> - It cannot talk, so it has no choice → Perhaps. But it chose to stay close, which is a kind act.
> - Because noise would wake the city → That is a thoughtful guess, but the reason is simpler: it stays close, and he is not alone.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that staying close to someone who is grieving can be the kindest thing._

_Gilgamesh calls every smith and jeweller in Uruk. He wants a statue of his friend, and it must be perfect._  
_They make it of gold and lapis, and polish it until it shines. It has Enkidu’s big hands, and his grin._  
_The whole city weeps for him: the elders, the shepherds, the woman from the square. Even the river seems to._  
**Gilgamesh**: He is not in it. Look at it. It is beautiful, and he is not in it.  
_Gilgamesh stands in front of the statue for a long time. Then he looks at his own hands, as if they belonged to someone else._  
**Gilgamesh**: I am going to die too, like him. One day my body will stop, and that will be the end of me. I cannot bear it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): whether a memorial is the same as the person  
> _Gilgamesh says the statue is beautiful, but Enkidu is not in it. Is a memorial the same as the person?_  
> - No. It helps us remember, but the person has died → That is a fair answer. A memorial points to someone. It is not the same as them.
> - Partly, because the memory is part of the person → That is a fair answer. Some people think that remembering keeps part of someone alive.
> - The stories we tell matter more than the statue → That is a fair answer. Stories are carried by people, and they can change people long after.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a memorial is the same as the person it remembers._

- **Stand next to Gilgamesh.**

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): a word problem with distance, volume and time  
> _You carry six waterskins of two litres each. If the three of you drink three litres a day in all, how many days does the water last?_  
> - ✅ 4 days → Yes. 6 × 2 = 12 litres, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 days.
> - 6 days → That is the number of waterskins. The total is 12 litres, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 days.
> - 2 days → That is the litres per skin. The total is 12 litres, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 days.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied and divided to find how many days the water lasts._

#### `a26-15-road`

_Gilgamesh walks the wilderness in his lion skins. His beard grows ragged and his face grows thin._  
_He does not talk. At night he lies awake and looks at the stars as if they owed him money._  
**Gilgamesh**: I used to be afraid of nothing. Now I am afraid of everything, and most of all of dying.  
_You give him water. He drinks it now, at least, a little, which you count as a good day._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what helps when a fear feels too big  
> _Gilgamesh’s fear is huge, and he has told nobody but you. What helps when a fear feels too big?_  
> - ✅ Naming it to someone, and taking small steps while staying close to others → Yes. A fear said aloud is smaller, and small steps are easier than one giant leap.
> - Walking so far that you outrun it → That is what Gilgamesh is trying, and it is wearing him out. Sharing the fear helps more.
> - Pretending it is not there → That is hard to keep up, and fears often shout louder when ignored. Naming it helps.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about what helps when a fear feels too big._

_At last two mountains rise ahead, so tall they hold up the sky, with a gate between them where the sun goes in and out._  
_Your Nubbin, on the pack, has gone very small and quiet. It puts its paws over its eyes, then uncovers one._  

**Choices**

- **Make him eat some bread.**
    - **Gilgamesh**: You sound like him.
    - But he eats it.
- **Lie down and look at the stars with him.**
    - You lie down beside him and look. After a while, without meaning to, he points out a star Enkidu liked.

_By the gate there are two figures, keeping watch. They are people down to the waist, and scorpions below._  
_A real scorpion has eight legs, two pincers and a curved tail with a sting. It is a cousin of the spider._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): arachnids and their body parts  
> _Scorpions have eight legs and are related to spiders. What group of animals are they?_  
> - ✅ Arachnids → Yes. Arachnids have eight legs, no wings and no antennae. Spiders, scorpions and mites are all arachnids.
> - Insects → Insects have six legs. Scorpions have eight, so they are arachnids.
> - Crustaceans → Crustaceans, such as crabs, mostly live in water. Scorpions are arachnids.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that scorpions are arachnids with eight legs, like spiders._

_The scorpion-man is terrible to look at, with a glare that could bring down a mountain. His wife stands at his side._  
**Scorpion-man**: Look, wife. He is two parts god, this one, and one part man. And who is the small one with the water?  
_His wife looks at you, and at your Nubbin, and tilts her head. You think, from her face, that she rather likes small ones._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): words with older meanings  
> _The scorpion-man is “terrible to look at”. In an old story like this, what does “terrible” mean?_  
> - ✅ So great or strange that it makes you afraid → Yes. Its old meaning was “causing terror”. Today we mostly use it to mean “very bad”.
> - Very untidy → Not untidy. Here it means so frightening that you want to look away.
> - Rather silly → Not silly. In old stories, “terrible” means causing terror.
> _For grown-ups: Learned an older meaning of the word “terrible”._

**Gilgamesh**: I am looking for Uta-Napishtim, who lives for ever. I want to ask him about life, and death.  
**Scorpion-man**: No one has ever gone this way. Twelve double-hours of dark, with no light at all. Nobody comes out the other side.  
**Gilgamesh**: I will go anyway. Nothing in your dark is worse than what I carry. Open the gate.  
**Scorpion-man**: Then go, and come back safe. The gate is open.

_The dark inside the mountain is thicker than any night. You cannot see your hand, or Gilgamesh._  
_You can feel his belt, though, and the rough lion skin, and your Nubbin’s breath on your neck. You hold on._  
**Gilgamesh**: One double-hour. Thick dark. Nothing.  
**Gilgamesh**: Four. Five. Still nothing.  
_He counts aloud, so you know he is there. You count with him, so he knows you are._  
**Gilgamesh**: Nine. I feel the north wind on my face.  
**Gilgamesh**: Eleven. There is light. Look. Look!  
_At the twelfth double-hour you step out into the sun, blinking, into a garden where the trees bear jewels._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): a unit of time and multiplication  
> _A Babylonian double-hour was two of our hours. Twelve of them make how many of our hours?_  
> - ✅ 24 hours, a whole day and night → Yes: 12 × 2 = 24. They walked for a whole day, in the dark.
> - 12 hours → That would be single hours. Each double-hour is two hours, so 12 × 2 = 24.
> - 14 hours → That is 12 + 2. Each of the twelve is two hours, so 12 × 2 = 24.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied twelve double-hours by two to get 24 hours._

_Your Nubbin is shivering, from the cold of the dark. Gilgamesh looks at it for a moment._  
_Then he cuts a strip off the edge of his lion skin with his knife, and wraps it round the Nubbin’s shoulders like a cloak._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): we see things when light reaches our eyes  
> _Inside the mountain you could not see your own hand. Why not?_  
> - ✅ There was no light to bounce off things and reach your eyes → Yes. We see when light bounces off objects into our eyes. With no light, there is nothing to see.
> - Your eyes stopped working → Your eyes were fine. With no light, nothing could be seen.
> - The dark is a solid wall → Dark is simply the lack of light. Nothing blocked your eyes. There was just no light.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we see when light bounces off objects into our eyes._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): why a joke can be a sign of healing  
> _This is Gilgamesh’s first joke since Enkidu died. Why might a joke mean someone is beginning to feel a little better?_  
> - It shows he can feel something besides sadness for a moment → That is a fair answer. Grief rarely leaves all at once. A bit of light is a start.
> - It shows he is not thinking about Enkidu any more → That is a fair answer to think about. But people can laugh and still miss someone terribly.
> - It is a way of thanking the Nubbin for its company → That is a fair answer. A kindness returned can look like a joke.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a first small joke can be a sign that someone is beginning to heal._

- **arachnid**: An animal with eight legs and no wings, such as a spider or scorpion.
- **terrible**: In old stories, so great or strange that it makes you afraid.

#### `a26-16-siduri`

_By the sea at the edge of the world there is a little tavern with a vine over the door. Siduri keeps it._  
_She sees a wild man in lion skins coming up the beach, and bars her door, and climbs up on her roof to look._  
**Siduri**: Who are you, looking like that? Your cheeks are hollow. You look like someone who has walked a very long way.  
**Gilgamesh**: I am Gilgamesh. My friend died. I cannot bear it. I am looking for the man who never dies.  
_Siduri looks at him for a long time. Then she climbs down, and opens the door, and gives you each a stool and a cup._  
**Siduri**: Gilgamesh, when people were first made, dying was made with them. Everyone gets a share of it, even kings.  
**Siduri**: So have your supper while it is hot. Get clean. Sing badly, if you like. And look properly at whoever is next to you.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): the theme of a character’s advice  
> _Siduri says: eat, get clean, sing, and look properly at the people next to you. What is the theme of her advice?_  
> - ✅ Life is short, so enjoy it and treasure the people you have → Yes. A theme is the idea underneath. Siduri’s idea is that a short life is made rich by people.
> - Always do what you are told → She is not ordering him around. She is offering a way to live well.
> - Keep searching, never give up → That is what Gilgamesh believes. Siduri says the opposite: enjoy what you have.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of Siduri’s advice: treasure the people you have in a short life._

_Gilgamesh turns his cup round and round. He is not listening, and he does not want to._  

**Choices**

- **Tell Siduri you were listening.**
    - **Siduri**: I know. You have got the face of someone who listens. It is rarer than you would think, in my trade.
- **Hold your Nubbin’s paw.**
    - You hold your Nubbin’s paw under the table. Siduri sees, and does not say anything, and refills your cup.

#### `a26-16-siduri-done`

_Your Nubbin climbs into your lap and goes to sleep there, warm and heavy. It does not need telling._  
**Gilgamesh**: Where is the boatman? The one who crosses the sea.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): why sleep matters  
> _Your Nubbin falls asleep as soon as it can. Why is sleep so important, especially when we are sad or worn out?_  
> - ✅ Our bodies and brains recover and repair while we sleep → Yes. Sleep helps growing bodies, and helps feelings settle too. Children your age need about nine to twelve hours.
> - It makes time pass faster → It can feel that way, but its real job is repair and rest.
> - It is only for babies → Everyone needs sleep, and children need more than adults.
> _For grown-ups: Learned why sleep matters for bodies, brains and feelings._

**Siduri**: Ur-Shanabi. In the woods, by the shore. Be gentle with him. Be gentle with something, for once.

_Gilgamesh runs ahead into the woods. By the time you catch up, there is a crash, and another, and then a silence._  
_In a clearing, among broken pieces of stone, stands a boatman with a pole, staring at the king._  
**Ur-Shanabi**: Those were the Stone Things. They crewed my boat. They could cross the Waters of Death without touching them.  
**Ur-Shanabi**: And you smashed them. Because you were sad, and they were there.  
_Gilgamesh looks at the pieces as if he has just woken up. His hands are grey with stone dust._  
**Gilgamesh**: I did not think.  
**Ur-Shanabi**: No. People do not, when they are grieving. I have ferried enough of them.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): whether grief excuses harm  
> _Gilgamesh broke the Stone Things because of his grief. Does grief excuse breaking things?_  
> - No, but it helps us understand why it happened → That is a fair answer. An explanation is not an excuse. Both matter.
> - Yes, because he could not help it → That is a fair answer. Grief can overwhelm people. Ur-Shanabi is gentle about it, but the Stone Things are still gone.
> - It depends on whether he tries to make it right → That is a fair answer. What we do after a mistake says a lot about us.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between understanding why harm happened and excusing it._


**Choices**

- **Help gather the pieces into a pile.**

    - **Ur-Shanabi**: There is. It is harder. Everything is harder now. Can you hold an axe, little one?

#### `a26-16-poles`

**Ur-Shanabi**: Cut poles. Long ones, straight, and a great many. Each pole may touch the water once, and then you let it go.  
**Ur-Shanabi**: If your hand touches the Waters of Death, you will not need to find Uta-Napishtim. Understand?  
_So Gilgamesh cuts, and you carry, and Ur-Shanabi trims. You stack the poles in rows of ten, six rows high._  
_Your Nubbin, in its lion cloak, drags a small branch to the pile as its share. Ur-Shanabi trims that too, gravely._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: rows and columns  
> _The poles are stacked in six rows of ten, and each pole is used once. How many times can the boat be pushed along?_  
> - ✅ 60 → Yes. Six rows of ten is 6 × 10 = 60.
> - 16 → That is 6 + 10. Six rows of ten is 6 × 10 = 60.
> - 600 → That is 6 × 100. Six rows of ten is 6 × 10 = 60.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied six rows of ten to find 60._

_The work seems to do Gilgamesh good. By the end of the day he is sweating, and tired, and less wild in the eyes._  
**Gilgamesh**: Enkidu would have been better at this. He could fell a tree with a look.  

**Choices**

- **Ask him to tell you about Enkidu.**
    - He tells you, while he works: the steppe, the door, the forest. He laughs twice, and it surprises him both times.
- **Just keep carrying.**
    - You keep carrying, and he keeps cutting, side by side, in a rhythm. Some work is a kind of talking.

#### `a26-16-complete`

_At dawn you push off. The Waters of Death are black and flat and smell of nothing at all._  
_Gilgamesh punts: each pole touches once, he lets it go, and you hand him the next. One by one, the stack shrinks._  
_When the last pole is gone, he holds his lion skins up for a sail, and the wind takes you the rest of the way._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): a sail changes wind into motion  
> _The lion-skin sail catches the wind and the boat moves. What is the sail doing?_  
> - ✅ Catching moving air, so the wind’s energy becomes the boat’s motion → Yes. A sail is a device that turns the energy of moving air into motion, with no engine and no oars.
> - Making the water move by itself → The water is not moving the boat here. The sail catches the wind.
> - Hiding the boat from the dark → It is not there for hiding. It catches the wind to push the boat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a sail turns the energy of moving air into the motion of a boat._

**Ur-Shanabi**: There. The far shore. Somebody has been waiting a long time for someone to come.  

### Glossary

- **tavern**: A place where travellers can sit, eat and drink.
- **grief**: The deep sadness we feel when someone we love has died.
- **punt**: To push a boat along with a long pole.

#### `a26-17-tale`

_On the far shore an old man sits on a bench by his door, watching you come. He does not look like a god._  
_He looks like a grandfather._  
**Gilgamesh**: I want what you have. I want to be immortal, and never die. My friend died, and I cannot stop thinking about it.  
**Uta-Napishtim**: Do we build houses to stand for ever? Do we make promises to last for ever? No. The river rises and goes down. Nothing stays.  
**Gilgamesh**: But you stayed. Tell me how.  
**Uta-Napishtim**: Then sit. It is a long story, and it is mine.  
_He tells how the god Ea whispered through the reed wall of his house: tear it down, and build a boat._  
_He took on board his family, craftsmen, and every kind of animal._  
_The storm lasted six days and seven nights. Then there was only water, flat and grey, as far as anyone could see._  
_He sent out a dove, and it came back; a swallow, and it came back. Then a raven, which did not._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): how the flood tablet was read again in 1872  
> _(Nova’s atlas adds a note. Uta-Napishtim’s flood story was pressed into clay tablets that lay buried for more than two thousand years.)_  
> _(In 1872 a man named George Smith, working on broken tablets at the British Museum in London, read part of it. Nobody had read those words in all that time.)_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the flood tablet lay buried for thousands of years and was read again in 1872._


**Choices**

- **Ask what happened to the animals.**
    - **Uta-Napishtim**: They walked off down the gangplank and never thanked me, not one. I did not mind. That is animals.
- **Ask his wife if she minds living for ever.**
    - **Uta-Napishtim’s Wife**: Some days. The bread is good, though. And he still tells that story as if I was not there.

#### `a26-17-tale-done`

**Gilgamesh**: Then the gods could do it again. For me.  
**Uta-Napishtim**: Could they? Let us see if you can do something smaller first.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether living for ever would be a good thing  
> _Gilgamesh wants never to die. Would you want to live for ever?_  
> _Why, or why not?_  
> - Yes, there is so much to see and learn → That is a fair answer. Curiosity is a good reason. It is worth asking what happens when everyone you love is gone.
> - No, because things matter more when they do not last → That is a fair answer. Many people feel that a limited time makes each day count.
> - I am not sure, and that is honest → That is a fair answer. It is a very big question, and wise people have disagreed about it for thousands of years.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether living for ever would be a good thing._

**Uta-Napishtim**: Stay awake for six days and seven nights. If you cannot beat sleep, how will you beat death?  
**Gilgamesh**: Easily. I have hardly slept since…  
_He sits down on the sand with his back against the house. Before he has finished yawning, he is fast asleep._  
**Uta-Napishtim’s Wife**: Wake him. Let him go home the way he came.  
**Uta-Napishtim**: He will only say he never slept. Bake him a loaf every day, and put it by his head. Then he will know.  
_So every day she bakes a loaf, and every day you set it by his head, in a row. Your Nubbin guards them, mostly._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction in a word problem  
> _One loaf is baked each day and set in a row. How many days older is the first loaf than the fifth?_  
> - ✅ 4 days → Yes. The fifth is baked four days after the first: 5 − 1 = 4.
> - 5 days → That counts the first loaf’s own day. From loaf 1 to loaf 5 is four steps: 5 − 1 = 4.
> - 1 day → Each step is a day, and there are four steps between loaf 1 and loaf 5.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted to find that the first loaf is four days older than the fifth._


**Choices**

- **Let him sleep. He needs it.**

_On the seventh day Uta-Napishtim touches him, and he wakes. The first loaf by his head is dry as a brick._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): some changes cannot be reversed  
> _The loaves change as they age, and the mould is a kind of fungus. Which change cannot be undone?_  
> - ✅ Baking dough into bread → Yes. Heat changes dough for good. You cannot turn a loaf back into dough, just as you cannot un-bake a cake.
> - Melting butter and letting it set again → That one can be undone: cooling sets melted butter again.
> - Freezing water into ice and letting it melt → That one can be undone too. Melting turns ice back to water.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that baking dough into bread is a change that cannot be reversed._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): telling a simile from a metaphor  
> _“A pale flower like a star” compares two things. Which one is a metaphor, not a simile?_  
> - ✅ “The flower was a star.” → Yes. A metaphor says one thing is another, with no “like” or “as”.
> - “The flower was as pale as a star.” → That one uses “as”, so it is a simile.
> - “The flower looked like a star.” → That one uses “like”, so it is a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Told a metaphor from a simile._

**Gilgamesh**: And then I will eat it, and be young again. And everyone I love can have a share.  
_The plant has four equal leaves. He plans to share it with Ur-Shanabi, the elders, and the people of Uruk, and keep a quarter himself._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions  
> _Gilgamesh keeps a quarter of the plant. If the plant is split into four equal parts, how many parts is that?_  
> - ✅ 1 part, because a quarter is 1/4 → Yes. A quarter is one of four equal parts: 1/4.
> - 2 parts → Two of four is a half, 2/4 or 1/2. A quarter is just one part.
> - 4 parts → Four of four is the whole plant. A quarter is one part.
> _For grown-ups: Used four equal parts to find a quarter, or 1/4._

_Something moves in the grass. A snake, long and quiet, slides out, smells the flower, and takes it in its mouth._

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): a snake sheds its skin as it grows  
> _The snake leaves a shed skin on the bank. Why do snakes shed their skin?_  
> - ✅ Their bodies grow, and the old skin gets too small → Yes. A snake’s skin does not stretch much, so it sheds it as it grows. That is part of its life cycle.
> - They shed it to become young again → That is the legend. In real life they shed the skin because they have grown.
> - They shed it when they are cold → Cold does not make them shed. Growing does.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that snakes shed their skin as they grow._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): coping with a big disappointment  
> _Gilgamesh has lost the plant after so much effort. What helps most with a big disappointment?_  
> - ✅ Letting yourself feel it, with a friend walking beside you → Yes. Disappointment needs room. A friend’s company, without lectures, makes it lighter.
> - Telling yourself you should not mind → That tends to bury the feeling. Letting it be, with someone near, helps more.
> - Going straight back to trying again → Sometimes, later. But first a disappointment deserves a pause.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about coping with a big disappointment: feel it, and keep company._

_People in the marshes of southern Iraq still build houses and boats from reeds today. Reeds are light, hollow and bendy, and they float._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): properties of materials and why they suit a job  
> _Reeds are light, hollow and bendy. Which job are those properties best for?_  
> - ✅ Building a boat that floats and a house that bends with the wind → Yes. Lightness and hollow stems help a boat float, and bendiness helps reed walls move without snapping.
> - Making a hammer → A hammer needs to be heavy and hard. Reeds are light and bendy.
> - Building a stone wall → A stone wall needs hard, heavy material. Reeds suit light, floating things.
> _For grown-ups: Linked the properties of reeds to what they are used for._
