## A26-18. The Wall of Uruk

- `a26-18-s1`: Walk the wall of Uruk with Gilgamesh and Ur-Shanabi. · _Climb the wall stair. Mind the third step._
- `a26-18-s2`: Go down to the foot of the wall, where the story started. · _The old brickmaker is waiting by the copper tablet box._

#### `a26-18-wall`

_You come home across the plain at evening. The wall of Uruk is gold in the low sun, and the river runs beside it._  
_Gilgamesh stops. He looks at the wall for a long while, as if he had never properly seen it._  
**Ur-Shanabi**: So that is your city. It is big.  
**Gilgamesh**: It is. Come up. I will show you.  
_You climb the wall stair together. Your Nubbin knows the way, and waits on the third step for you, which wobbles._  
_On top, the wind is warm. The whole city is laid out below, roofs and orchards and smoke from supper fires._  
**Gilgamesh**: Walk the top of this wall, Ur-Shanabi. Look at how it stands, and at its bricks. See how they were baked hard in the fire.  
**Gilgamesh**: Town, orchards and clay-pits, a square mile of each. And half a square mile for Ishtar’s temple. That is what I made.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a rectangle  
> _One square mile is a square one mile long on every side. How many square miles is an orchard that is 2 miles by 3 miles?_  
> - ✅ 6 square miles → Yes. Area is length times width: 2 × 3 = 6.
> - 5 square miles → That is 2 + 3, which is half the distance round (the perimeter). Area is 2 × 3 = 6.
> - 1 square mile → One square mile is a 1 by 1 square. A 2 by 3 orchard is six of them.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied length and width to find an area of 6 square miles._


**Choices**

- **Knock on a brick.**
    - You knock on a brick, and it rings. Gilgamesh hears it, and for the first time in a long time, he smiles.
- **Look at the city with them.**
    - Somebody is calling children in for supper, and somebody is singing. It all goes on, and on.

#### `a26-18-wall-done`

**Gilgamesh**: I went to the end of the world. And here it is. It was here the whole time.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: what Gilgamesh learns  
> _“I went to the end of the world. And here it is.”_  
> _“It was here the whole time.” What idea is Gilgamesh expressing?_  
> - ✅ What we search for far away can be close to home → Yes. That is a theme found in stories all over the world: the treasure was near all along.
> - The world has no end → That is not what he says. He means the thing he wanted was here at home.
> - Walls are better than rivers → He is looking at his own city, and seeing what it is worth.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: what we seek far away can be close to home._


#### `a26-18-foot`

_At the foot of the wall, by the copper box, the old brickmaker is sitting on her stack of bricks, eating a date._  
**Old Brickmaker**: There you are. Long story, was it? They always are, his.  
_Below the wall, on the patch of rough grass by the river, a gazelle is grazing. It lifts its head, and looks at you, and does not run._  
**Gilgamesh**: He asked you to look after them. You did.  
**Old Brickmaker**: Now then. Every brick in this wall has someone’s hand in it. Want yours in?  
_She lays a fresh clay brick in front of you. You press your hand into it, and your Nubbin, after some thought, presses a paw._  
**Old Brickmaker**: Kiln-fired, this one. Sun-dried bricks crumble in the rain. Kiln-fired, they last for thousands of years.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, ask): weathering: why kiln-fired brick lasts  
> _Sun-dried bricks crumble in the rain, but kiln-fired bricks last for thousands of years. Why?_  
> - ✅ Firing changes the clay for good, so water cannot soften it → Yes. Baking clay in a kiln changes it so it will not turn back to mud. Rain slowly wears sun-dried brick away: that is called weathering.
> - Kiln bricks are painted to keep the rain off → There is no paint. The firing itself changes the clay.
> - Sun-dried bricks are made of different mud → The mud is the same. The difference is the fire in the kiln.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that firing changes clay for good, so kiln-fired bricks resist weathering far longer than sun-dried bricks._


**Choices**

- **Ask her if the tablet is still in the box.**
    - **Old Brickmaker**: It is. Always will be, if people leave it be. That one, nobody takes.
- **Ask if she will put her own mark on it too.**
    - **Old Brickmaker**: Me? No. I am on all the others.

**Old Brickmaker**: Not every tablet stays put. Plenty were taken from their places, in living memory.  
**Old Brickmaker**: Some have come home since. Every one that comes home is a little bit of a city put back.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness about things that belong to a people  
> _Many tablets were taken from the places they belonged, and some have come home. What is a fair way to treat a people’s heritage?_  
> - ✅ Protect it, and return it to where it belongs when we can → Yes. Heritage belongs to the people it comes from, and to the whole world to learn from, but taking it without asking is unfair.
> - Keep it, because it is safer in a faraway museum → Safety matters, but that does not make taking it fair. Many countries and museums now work to return what was taken.
> - Sell it to the highest bidder → Selling a people’s treasures would take them away from the people they belong to. That is why many countries have laws against it.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about treating a people’s heritage fairly: protect it and return it where possible._

**Gilgamesh**: For your own tablets. Put your story in it, whatever it is. And leave it where people can open it.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): Persian is spoken in Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan  
> _The Shahnameh is loved in Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan. One language links all three countries._  
> _Which one?_  
> - ✅ Persian. → Yes. Persian, in a few forms: it is called Farsi in Iran, Dari in Afghanistan and Tajik in Tajikistan.
> - Latin. → Not Latin. The language is Persian, in a few forms: Farsi, Dari and Tajik.
> - Greek. → Not Greek. The language is Persian, in a few forms: Farsi, Dari and Tajik.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Persian, in its different forms, links Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan, where the Shahnameh is loved._

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add to find a date: 980 + 30  
> _Suppose Ferdowsi began his book in the year 980 and worked for thirty years. In what year did he finish?_  
> - ✅ 1010. → Yes. 980 plus 30 is 1010, which matches “around the year 1010”.
> - 1000. → Close. Count on: 980 plus 20 makes 1000, then 10 more makes 1010.
> - 1110. → Check the hundreds. 980 plus 30 is 1010. It is about a thousand years ago.
> _For grown-ups: Added 30 years to a start date to find when the Shahnameh was finished, around 1010._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): Persian word parts: shah (king) and nameh (book)  
> _Shahnameh joins two Persian words: shah, which means king, and nameh, which means book. What does Shahnameh mean?_

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS3-1, ask): albinism: some people are born with very little melanin; it is inherited

> _For grown-ups: Learned plainly that albinism is an inherited trait, not a curse, and that people with it are just like everyone else._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a word with two meanings: gift  
> _The nurse said a baby is “a gift”. A gift can mean a present, or a natural talent, like “a gift for music”._  
> _Which meaning did she use?_  
> - ✅ A present, given to be treasured. → Yes. She meant the baby was given to Sam, and should be treasured.
> - A natural talent. → A gift can mean that, as in “a gift for music”. But here she meant a precious present.
> _For grown-ups: Told two meanings of the word gift apart by reading the sentence._

_The nurse looks at you, and doesn’t say anything at all._  

#### `a27-01-complete`

_Sam stands over the cradle for a long time. The baby looks up at him with dark, steady eyes._  
_Sam doesn’t pick him up. That is the first wrong thing._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness: everyone deserves care whatever they look like  
> _Sam hesitates to hold his son because of the baby’s hair. Which idea about fairness does that go against?_  
> - ✅ Everyone deserves love and care, whatever they look like. → Yes. How someone looks is never a fair reason to love them less.
> - People should be treated by how they look. → No. That is just what is unfair here. A person’s looks are not a reason to treat them worse.
> - It depends on the hair. → It does not. Hair colour tells us nothing about who a person is or how much they deserve care.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about fairness: nobody should be treated worse because of how they look._

**Sam**: Leave me. All of you.  
**Sam**: I need to think.  
_The women go out in a hurry. In the passage, the nurse takes your Nubbin’s paw, as if somebody’s paw ought to be held._  

### Glossary

- **Shahnameh**: A very long Persian poem, the Book of Kings, finished by Ferdowsi around the year 1010.
- **albinism**: A condition people are born with, in which the body makes very little of the colour called melanin.

## A27-2. Shame

- `a27-02-s1`: Be in the hall when Sam gives his order. · _The household gathers in the hall at first light._
- `a27-02-s2`: Follow the servants up the mountain path. · _Keep close behind the old servant. The storm is coming from the north._
- `a27-02-s3`: Stay with the baby at the foot of the high rocks. · _Sit with him in the lee of the big stone._

#### `a27-02-order`

_In the morning the whole household is called to the hall. Sam hasn’t slept, and it shows._  
**Sam**: My enemies will laugh. They will say Sam’s son was born old, and that it means something bad for the land.  
_It doesn’t mean anything. It is a baby with white hair, and he is hungry, and crying in the next room._  
**Sam**: Take the child away. Up to the Alborz, where nobody goes.  
**Sam**: Leave him there.  
_Nobody moves. Then an old servant at the back bows slowly, as if his back hurts._  
**The Nurse**: My lord, he is a gift.  
**Sam**: Go.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when and how to speak up to someone powerful  
> _The nurse speaks up, but Sam does not listen. When is it right to speak up to someone powerful, even if it might not work?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - When someone is going to be hurt. → That is a fair answer. Protecting someone who cannot protect themselves is a very good reason.
> - When I can do it kindly and clearly. → That is a fair answer. A calm voice is more likely to be heard than a shout.
> - Only if I have a friend beside me. → That is a fair answer. Speaking up is easier together, and it can be brave to ask someone to stand with you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when speaking up is right, even when it is hard._


**Choices**

- **Speak up for the baby.**
    - **You**: Please. He is your son.
    - **You**: He hasn’t done anything.
    - **Sam**: You are a guest in this house, and a guest does not tell me what my son is.
    - Your hands are shaking, but you said it, and the nurse heard you say it.
- **Look Sam in the eye, and say nothing.**
    - He looks back at you for a moment. Then he looks at the floor, and keeps looking at it.
- **Go and stand with the nurse.**
    - She doesn’t look at you, but she leans on your shoulder, just a little.

#### `a27-02-order-done`

_Sam goes out. The order stays in the room after him, like smoke._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): simile: an order that lingers like smoke  
> _The narrator says Sam’s order stayed in the room “like smoke”. Why is smoke a good comparison?_  
> - ✅ Smoke lingers and is hard to clear away. → Yes. The order hangs in the air, and everyone can feel it.
> - Smoke is cold. → Smoke is usually warm. The point is that it lingers and is hard to clear.
> - Smoke is loud. → Smoke is quiet. The point is that it lingers, as the order does.
> _For grown-ups: Explained why a simile, an order lingering like smoke, works._

**The Nurse**: Go with them. Please.  
**The Nurse**: Somebody kind should be there.  

#### `a27-02-path`

_Two servants carry the baby out of the city in a basket. You and your Nubbin follow._  
_The road becomes a path, and the path becomes stones. Ahead, the Alborz goes up and up into cloud._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, ask): why clouds and rain gather over mountains  
> _Mountains often bring storms. Wind is pushed up the slope, cools, and its water vapour turns into tiny drops._  
> _What forms?_  
> - ✅ Clouds, and then rain. → Yes. Rising air cools, vapour turns to tiny drops, and clouds form. When the drops grow heavy, they fall as rain.
> - Sand. → No. The vapour in the air turns to tiny drops of water, which make clouds.
> - Snowmen. → Ha. Snow can form up high where it is cold, but the first thing to form is cloud.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that air pushed up a mountain cools, and its water vapour forms clouds and rain._

**Old Servant**: You don’t have to come. It isn’t your shame.  
**You**: It isn’t yours either.  
**Old Servant**: I am the one carrying him. That makes it mine, I think.  
_The wind gets up. The first rain comes sideways, hard and cold, out of the north._  

#### `a27-02-path-done`

_By the time the path runs out, the storm is all round you, and you can’t see the city any more._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add distances: 4 + 3 + 2  
> _The servants walked 4 km on the road, 3 km on the path and 2 km on the stones. How far did they walk in all?_  
> - ✅ 9 km. → Yes. 4 plus 3 is 7, and 7 plus 2 is 9.
> - 7 km. → That is the road and the path. Add the 2 km on the stones as well: 9 km.
> - 12 km. → Check the sum: 4 plus 3 plus 2 is 9, not 12.
> _For grown-ups: Added three distances, 4 km, 3 km and 2 km, to make 9 km._


#### `a27-02-rocks`

_At the foot of the high rocks the servants set the basket down, in the lee of a big stone._  
**Old Servant**: This is as far as anyone has ever been. Nobody climbs above here.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, 4-ESS2-2, ask): the Alborz mountains lie south of the Caspian Sea  
> _The Alborz are real mountains, in northern Iran. They run along the southern shore of which sea?_  
> - ✅ The Caspian Sea. → Yes. The Alborz curve along the south of the Caspian Sea. Their highest peak, Damavand, is about 5,600 metres.
> - The Red Sea. → No. The Red Sea is far to the south-west. The Alborz lie south of the Caspian.
> - The Black Sea. → No. The Black Sea is further west, north of Turkey. The Alborz lie south of the Caspian.
> _For grown-ups: Located the Alborz mountains south of the Caspian Sea in northern Iran._

_The other servant is already walking away. The old one stays a moment longer, holding the edge of the basket._  
**Old Servant**: I have carried him up a mountain. I will carry that the rest of my life.  
_He goes, and you don’t. The rain gets in everywhere, and the baby is crying, thin and furious._  
_Your Nubbin climbs into the basket and curls round his feet, the warmest thing it knows how to do._  

**Choices**

- **Wrap him in your coat.**
    - He stops crying for long enough to get angry about the coat instead.
- **Hum to him.**
    - You hum the only tune you can think of. You can’t hear yourself over the wind, but he can, because he goes quiet.
- **Hold him, and keep your back to the wind.**
    - You pick him up and turn your back to the storm. He fits against your chest like he has always been there.

#### `a27-02-rocks-done`

_Above the storm, something very large goes over._  
_For a moment the rain stops falling on you, as if a roof had been put up._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): words that show what we sense: sound words  
> _Writers use sound words so you can hear a storm. Which of these is a sound word: howl, damp or grey?_  
> - ✅ Howl. → Yes. “The wind howls” lets you hear it. Damp and grey are words for touch and sight.
> - Damp. → Damp is a touch word. Howl is the sound word: you can hear a wind howl.
> - Grey. → Grey is a sight word. Howl is the sound word.
> _For grown-ups: Picked out a sound word from words for sound, touch and sight._


#### `a27-02-complete`

_The shadow goes over again, lower. The wind it makes flattens the grass._  
_You hold on to the baby, and your Nubbin holds on to you. Nobody else in the world knows where the three of you are._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): fear is normal; naming it and staying close helps  
> _You are a long way from home, and you are scared. Which of these helps most?_  
> - ✅ Know that fear is normal, and stay close to someone. → Yes. Fear is a sign we care about being safe. Naming it and staying close helps it shrink.
> - Pretend I’m not scared. → Pretending is understandable, but a feeling we hide often gets bigger. Naming it helps.
> - Run off alone. → Running alone could make things worse. Staying close to someone is safer and calmer.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how fear is normal, and how naming it and staying close helps._

_Then the cloud opens, and something comes down out of it._  

### Glossary

- **lee**: The sheltered side of something big, where the wind and rain do not reach.
- **howl**: A long, loud, wailing sound, like a strong wind or a wolf.

## A27-3. The Simurgh

- `a27-03-s1`: Hold on to the baby when the great bird comes down. · _Don’t let go of the basket._
- `a27-03-s2`: Arrive at the nest on the peak. · _There is nothing to do but be carried._

#### `a27-03-descent`

_She comes down out of the cloud like a ship out of fog: a bird bigger than a house._  
_Her feathers are every colour a sunset has ever been, and her tail goes on behind her for a long time._  
_She lands on the big stone above you, and the stone creaks. She looks down at the basket with one gold eye._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): birds of prey have very sharp eyesight  
> _The Simurgh found a small basket in a storm, from high above. Eagles and hawks hunt mainly by sight._  
> _Which sense do they rely on?_  
> - ✅ Very sharp eyesight. → Yes. Many birds of prey see far more sharply than we do, so they can spot small things from high up.
> - A strong sense of smell. → Most birds of prey do not smell well. They rely on very sharp eyesight.
> - Hearing the baby cry. → Hearing helps a little, but the storm was loud. Birds of prey rely mainly on very sharp eyesight.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that birds of prey rely on very sharp eyesight to spot things from high up._

_Then she reaches down, very fast, and takes the baby up in her talons, blanket, coat and all._  
_She looks at you, and at your Nubbin, still hanging on to the blanket with all four limbs. Then she takes you too._  

**Choices**

- **Shout.**
    - You shout. The wind takes the shout away, and the ground takes itself away after it.
- **Hold on, and keep your eyes open.**
    - Below, the whole mountain falls away, and the storm is a grey floor under your feet.

#### `a27-03-descent-done`

_Up through the cloud, and out into sun. Above the storm, the sky is enormous, and very blue, and very quiet._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): add distances in metres and convert to kilometres  
> _She climbs 800 metres to the top of the cloud, then 1,200 metres more. How far is that in kilometres?_  
> - ✅ 2 km. → Yes. 800 plus 1,200 is 2,000 metres, and 1,000 metres make a kilometre.
> - 20 km. → Check the units: 2,000 metres is 2 kilometres, not 20.
> - 1 km. → That is only part of it. 800 plus 1,200 is 2,000 metres, which is 2 km.
> _For grown-ups: Added 800 m and 1,200 m, then converted 2,000 m to 2 km._


#### `a27-03-nest`

_The nest is on the very top of the Alborz, where the peak touches the stars. No one has ever stood up here._  
_It is built of ebony and sandalwood twined with aloe, and it is the size of a cottage._  
_In it are her chicks: four of them, each bigger than a pony, all beak and fluff and appetite._  
_She sets the baby down in the middle of them. The chicks crowd in, beaks first, to see what she has brought._  
_Your Nubbin drops off the blanket and stands in front of the baby, arms out, as tall as it can make itself._  
_The Simurgh looks down at the small white-haired thing, and at the smaller thing guarding it. She feels compassion, and her heart turns over._  
**The Simurgh**: No. Not him.  
**The Simurgh**: He is your brother.  

> **Lesson** (art, RL.4.3, ask): imagining and describing a creature the way painters of the Shahnameh did  
> _Painters of the Shahnameh had to imagine a bird nobody had seen, with bright colours and a long, swirling tail. How would you paint her?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Huge and gold, with a tail like a river of flame. → That is a fair answer. Gold and fire colours fit a bird who comes out of the sunset.
> - Blue and green, with a tail like a swirl of clouds. → That is a fair answer. Painters often placed her among cloud swirls, as if she belonged to the sky.
> - Every colour at once, with eyes like gold coins. → That is a fair answer. “Every colour” is just how the story describes her.
> _For grown-ups: Imagined and described how to paint the Simurgh, as painters of old Persian books did._


#### `a27-03-nest-done`

_The chicks pull their beaks back. One of them, the smallest, sits down hard and looks confused._  
**The Simurgh**: And these two are your nestmates. We have a large family now.  
**The Simurgh**: Sit up and make room.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps a group welcome a newcomer  
> _The chicks wanted to peck at the stranger. What helps a group welcome a newcomer?_  
> - ✅ Someone speaking up for them, and making room. → Yes. The Simurgh spoke up, and she made room. That is how a group learns to welcome someone.
> - Waiting to see if they are useful. → A newcomer should not have to earn a place. Speaking up and making room is how groups welcome people.
> - Ignoring them. → Ignoring someone makes them feel left out. Speaking up and making room helps.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps a group welcome a newcomer._


#### `a27-03-complete`

_The chicks shuffle round until there is a gap in the middle, warm and dark and smelling of sandalwood._  
_You and your Nubbin and the baby are squeezed into it together. A wing comes down over all of you, like a blanket._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): simile: a wing like a blanket  
> _The narrator says a wing came down “like a blanket”. What does that comparison tell us about the wing?_  
> - ✅ It was warm and covering, and made them feel safe. → Yes. A blanket covers and keeps us warm and safe, and so does her wing.
> - It was heavy and scratchy. → A blanket can be heavy, but here the wing is meant to comfort. The comparison is about warmth and safety.
> - It was a real blanket. → It is a simile: the wing is only compared to a blanket. It is not actually one.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile, a wing like a blanket, tells us about the wing._

**The Simurgh**: Sleep. The storm can’t reach up here.  
**The Simurgh**: Nothing can.  
_The baby is asleep before she finishes. Your Nubbin takes longer, because the chick next to it snores._  

### Glossary

- **talons**: The sharp, curved claws of a bird of prey.
- **compassion**: Kind feeling for someone who is in trouble, with a wish to help.

## A27-4. The Nest

- `a27-04-s1`: Help the Simurgh feed everyone in the nest. · _Share out what she brings: the chicks first, then the baby, then yourself._
- `a27-04-s2`: Keep the baby warm through the cold night. · _Sit with him under the Simurgh’s wing until morning._
- `a27-04-s3`: Stop the chicks sitting on the baby. · _Lift him out of the way whenever a chick backs up to sit down._

#### `a27-04-feed`

_The Simurgh hunts at dawn and comes back with breakfast for a nest the size of a cottage._  
**The Simurgh**: You have hands. I have only a beak.  
**The Simurgh**: Share it out: the big ones first, or they will take it anyway.  
_She has brought twenty-five figs for the chicks. For the baby she brings honey in the comb and warm goat’s milk, which she will not explain._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division with remainder: 25 shared among 4  
> _Twenty-five figs are shared equally among four chicks. How many does each chick get, and how many are left over?_  
> - ✅ 6 each, with 1 left over. → Yes. 4 times 6 is 24, so there is 1 fig left: the small one.
> - 5 each, with 5 left over. → If you gave 5 each, 20 figs are used and 5 are left, but the chicks could still have one more each. 6 each, with 1 left.
> - 7 each. → Check: 4 times 7 is 28, which is more than 25. They get 6 each, with 1 left.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 25 figs among 4 chicks: 6 each with 1 left over._

_The chicks eat like a landslide. Your Nubbin watches with great respect, and then tries to keep up._  
**The Simurgh**: Feed them before you feed yourself. That is the only rule in this nest.  
_When the four chicks have had equal shares, there is one fig left. It is a very small fig._  

**Choices**

- **Eat the fig.**
    - You eat it. It is the best fig you have ever had, and the Simurgh brings you two more without a word.
- **Split it with your Nubbin.**
    - Half each. Your Nubbin eats its half in one go and looks at yours with an expression of pure hope.
- **Give it to the smallest chick.**
    - The smallest chick, who is always last to the figs, takes it very politely and swallows it whole.
    - **The Simurgh**: You learn quickly. Most guests take years.

#### `a27-04-feed-done`

_Your Nubbin is round as an apple and still looking about for more. Living with chicks has given it ideas._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): scarcity means choosing  
> _There was only one fig, and three ways to use it. When there is not enough, what is the cost of choosing to eat it yourself?_  
> - ✅ Someone else does not get it. → Yes. That is what scarcity means: when there is not enough, choosing one thing means giving up another.
> - There is no cost. → There is a cost. If you eat the fig, the chick or your Nubbin goes without it.
> - The fig gets lonely. → Ha. The real cost is that someone else does not get it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that when something is scarce, choosing it for yourself has a cost to someone else._


#### `a27-04-night`

_The nights on the peak are cold enough to crack stone. The stars are so close you could knock one off with a stick._  
_The baby sleeps between you and your Nubbin, under the edge of the great wing, with his white hair tucked into your coat._  
**The Simurgh**: His father left him at the foot of my mountain, on the bare ground. I saw.  
**The Simurgh**: I see everything from up here.  
**The Simurgh**: A man who could not see past the colour of a child’s hair. Well.  
**The Simurgh**: I have no use for his eyes.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): feathers trap warm air and insulate  
> _On nights like this, frost can form on top of her wings but not underneath. Feathers insulate: they trap a layer of air._  
> _What does that air do?_  
> - ✅ It holds in her body’s warmth. → Yes. Air is a poor conductor, so a layer of it stops her body heat from escaping.
> - It makes her colder. → No. A trapped layer of air holds warmth in, which is why a coat of feathers keeps a bird warm.
> - It makes her heavier. → Air is very light. It holds in her body’s warmth.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the air trapped in feathers insulates a bird by holding in its body heat._

_She settles lower over all of you. Her heartbeat is slow and very loud, like a drum heard from the next valley._  
**The Simurgh**: This one is mine now, until somebody deserves him.  

#### `a27-04-night-done`

_In the morning there is frost on the outside of her wings, and none at all underneath._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): simile: a heartbeat like a drum heard from the next valley  
> _Her heartbeat was “like a drum heard from the next valley”. What does that simile tell us about it?_  
> - ✅ It was slow, deep and steady, and it carried far. → Yes. A drum in the distance sounds deep and steady, and it fits a bird so large.
> - It was fast and quiet. → The opposite: a distant drum is slow and deep, and her heartbeat is slow and very loud.
> - She was carrying a drum. → It is a simile: her heart sounds like a drum, but she has no drum.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile about a heartbeat and a drum tells us._


#### `a27-04-sitting`

_The chicks love their new brother. They love him so much that they keep trying to sit on him._  
_It is how they show they like something. It is also how they would flatten it._  
_A chick backs up, wriggling its tail feathers, ready to settle right on top of him._  
_You scoop him up just in time. The chick sits on your Nubbin instead, which is less good for your Nubbin._  
**The Simurgh**: Ha. They sat on each other for a month before they learned.  
**The Simurgh**: He will need minding.  
_So you mind him: all day, every day, lifting him out of the way of affectionate chicks the size of ponies._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): meaning well versus the effect on someone  
> _The chicks meant well, but sitting on someone hurts. Does meaning well make up for hurting someone?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Yes, if it was an accident. → That is a fair answer. Accidents are not the same as unkindness, and kind intentions matter.
> - No, it still hurts, so we should learn. → That is a fair answer. The Simurgh says the chicks must learn, and that is what a caring group does.
> - Both: it matters, but so does learning. → That is a fair answer. Intentions matter, and so do the effects. Kind friends try to notice both.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether good intentions are enough, and how to learn when we hurt someone by accident._


#### `a27-04-sitting-done`

_Your Nubbin is pulled out from under the chick slightly flatter than before. It doesn’t seem to bear a grudge._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply equal groups: 3 times 5 minutes  
> _A chick sat on your Nubbin three times today, for five minutes each time. For how many minutes was your Nubbin sat on?_  
> - ✅ 15 minutes. → Yes. 3 groups of 5 make 15.
> - 8 minutes. → That adds 3 and 5. There are 3 sits of 5 minutes each, so multiply: 15.
> - 35 minutes. → Check the sum: 3 times 5 is 15, not 35.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 3 sits of 5 minutes each to make 15 minutes._


#### `a27-04-complete`

_Weeks go by on the peak, and then months. Nobody comes, and nobody calls him anything but “the little one”._  
**The Simurgh**: His name is his father’s to give. Until then, he is my chick.  
_The baby learns to crawl in a nest of ebony and sandalwood. His first word is a sound like a bird calling._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): babies learn speech by copying the sounds around them  
> _His first word sounded like a bird call. Why would that be?_  
> - ✅ Babies learn sounds by copying what they hear around them. → Yes. A baby who hears birds copies birds. A baby who hears people copies them. That is how everyone learns to speak.
> - He was really a bird. → He was a human baby, but the only voices he heard were birds. That is why he copied them.
> - He was cold. → Cold might make a baby cry, but copying is how babies learn their first words.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that babies learn speech by copying the sounds they hear around them._

_Your Nubbin teaches him how to clap. He teaches your Nubbin how to eat a whole fig without chewing._  

### Glossary

- **insulate**: To stop heat from escaping. Feathers and coats insulate by trapping air.
- **scarcity**: Not having enough of something, so that we have to choose.

## A27-5. The Youth on the Mountain

- `a27-05-s1`: Teach the youth some words for things he has never seen. · _Sit with him at the nest’s edge and talk._
- `a27-05-s2`: Climb down to the high pass and meet the caravan. · _The caravan road crosses the shoulder of the mountain, below the cloud._

#### `a27-05-words`

_The page turns over by itself, slowly, like a leaf in no wind. Years go by in it._  
_You and your Nubbin don’t change; atlas pages are like that. The little one does._  
_He is tall now, taller than you, and strong enough to carry a chick under each arm. His hair is still white as frost._  
_He talks like the Simurgh: grand and slow. He has never seen a person except you._  
**The Youth**: There are words she has but cannot show me. Door.  
**The Youth**: Cup. Market.  
**The Youth**: What is a market?  
**You**: Lots of people, all selling things and shouting.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): English has borrowed Persian words: bazaar, caravan  
> _The word for market in Persian is bazaar, and English borrowed it. Which of these English words also comes from Persian?_  
> - ✅ Caravan. → Yes. Caravan comes from a Persian word for a group of travellers. We will meet one soon.
> - Hamburger. → No. Hamburger comes from the German city of Hamburg. Caravan comes from Persian.
> - Pizza. → No. Pizza comes from Italian. Caravan comes from Persian.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that English borrowed bazaar and caravan from Persian._

**The Youth**: Shouting. Like the chicks at breakfast.  
**The Youth**: I think I would like a market.  
**The Youth**: Teach me one more word. One she doesn’t use.  

**Choices**

- **Teach him “friend”.**
    - **You**: Friend. Someone who isn’t family, but stays anyway.
    - **The Youth**: Friend. Then you are my friend.
    - **The Youth**: And the small one too.
    - In Persian a friend is called dust, which sounds like “doost”. He would have liked that.
- **Teach him “home”.**
    - **You**: Home. The place you come back to.
    - **The Youth**: Then this is home. I have never gone anywhere to come back from.
    - **The Youth**: Perhaps one day.
- **Teach him “sorry”.**
    - **You**: Sorry. What you say when you have done something wrong, and you wish you hadn’t.
    - **The Youth**: Nobody has ever said it to me. Is that good?
    - You don’t know what to say to that, so you say nothing.

#### `a27-05-words-done`

_He practises the word all afternoon: to the chicks, to the wind, and to your Nubbin._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 6 times an hour for 4 hours  
> _He says the word six times every hour, for four hours. How many times does he say it?_

> - 10 times. → That adds 6 and 4. There are 4 groups of 6, so multiply: 24.
> - 64 times. → Check: 4 times 6 is 24, not 64.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 hours by 6 times an hour to make 24._

#### `a27-05-caravan`

_Far below the peak, a road crosses the shoulder of the mountain. Caravans go by on it: camels, bells and dust._  
_The Simurgh sets you down on a ledge above the pass, so you can walk the last of the way like a normal person._  
**A Merchant**: A traveller, up here? Have you seen him?  
**A Merchant**: The young man on the peak, with the white hair?  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): caravans on trade roads carried goods, news and stories  
> _Long ago, caravans crossed Iran along trade routes such as the Silk Road. Besides silk and spices, what else did they carry from town to town?_  
> - ✅ News, stories and ideas. → Yes. Travellers carried stories as well as goods, which is how the tale of the white-haired youth spreads.
> - Nothing else. → They carried more. News and stories travelled with every caravan, and still do in this story.
> - Only camels. → Camels carried the goods, but travellers also carried news, stories and ideas from place to place.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that caravans on trade routes carried news, stories and ideas, as well as goods._

**A Merchant**: We see him every spring, at the top of the world with a bird bigger than a cloud. We tell it in every town.  
**A Merchant**: Some say he’s a spirit. Some say he’s a prince.  
**A Merchant**: My wife says he must be very cold.  
_Your Nubbin, who has had nothing but figs for a very long time, is looking at the merchant’s bread with its whole soul._  

**Choices**

- **“He’s a prince. He just doesn’t know it yet.”**

    - **A Merchant**: I will tell them that in Sistan.
- **“He’s a person. A kind one.”**
    - **A Merchant**: A person. Well, that is less exciting, but my wife will be glad.
- **Smile, and say nothing.**
    - **A Merchant**: Ah, a secret. Secrets travel even faster than news.

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, ask): camels store fat in their humps  
> _The camels in the caravan can walk for days in the heat. What is stored in a camel’s hump?_

> - Water. → A common mistake. The hump stores fat, not water. Camels cope with little water in other ways.
> - Air. → No. The hump stores fat, which the camel can use for energy.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a camel’s hump stores fat, which helps it survive long journeys._

#### `a27-06-return`

_You ride down to Sistan with the next caravan, perched on a bale of cotton, to see how the story lands._  
_The champion’s house is the same, only older. So is the old servant at the door, who stares at you._  
**Old Servant**: You. You haven’t changed a hair.  
**Old Servant**: And I have gone white as…  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): hair turns grey or white with age as pigment cells slow down  
> _The old servant’s hair is white because he is old, while the baby’s was white from birth. Why does hair turn white as people age?_  
> - ✅ The cells that make hair colour slowly make less of it. → Yes. As we age, those cells make less melanin, so hair goes grey and then white. Different cause, same colour.
> - Worry makes it go white overnight. → A popular story, but no. Hair turns white as the cells that colour it slow down, over years.
> - The sun bleaches it. → Sun can lighten hair a little, but greying comes from the colour cells slowing down with age.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that hair turns grey or white with age because its colour-making cells slow down, which is different from being born with pale hair._

_He stops, touches his own white head, and doesn’t finish._  
**Old Servant**: Is it true? What the caravans say?  
**Old Servant**: Is he alive?  
_Your Nubbin answers by holding up one end of the merchant’s loaf. Then it remembers, and holds up its white-crested cap instead._  

**Choices**

- **“He’s alive. He’s taller than you.”**
    - The old man sits down on the doorstep, quite suddenly, and puts his face in his hands.
    - **Old Servant**: Then I can put him down at last.
- **“You can stop carrying him now.”**
    - **Old Servant**: Can I? I don’t know how.
    - **Old Servant**: I will practise.

> - ✅ 36 months. → Yes. 3 groups of 12 make 36.
> - 15 months. → That adds 3 and 12. There are 3 years of 12 months each, so multiply: 36.
> - 312 months. → Check: 3 times 12 is 36, not 312.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 3 years by 12 months to make 36 months._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile compares using as or like  
> _The rider says Sam’s beard is “as white as a poplar”. What do we call a comparison that uses “as” or “like”?_

> - A rhyme. → A rhyme is words that sound alike. A comparison using “as” or “like” is a simile.
> - A riddle. → A riddle is a puzzle. A comparison using “as” or “like” is a simile.
> _For grown-ups: Named a simile, a comparison using as or like, in the rider’s words to Sam._

**The Rider**: A bird is raising your child. Is that what you call being a father?

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): it takes courage to say “I was wrong”  
> _Sam has to face that he was wrong. Why might it take courage to say “I was wrong”?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Because people might think less of us. → That is a fair answer. Fear of what others think holds many of us back, and being honest anyway takes courage.
> - Because we have to face what we did. → That is a fair answer. Looking straight at our own mistake is the hardest part.
> - Because it might not be forgiven. → That is a fair answer. Saying sorry with no promise of forgiveness takes a lot of heart.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why it takes courage to admit being wrong._

> **Lesson** (science, 1-LS1-2, ask): animal parents care for their young: crocodiles carry hatchlings in their mouths  
> _The mobed says even a crocodile looks after its young. How does a mother crocodile carry her hatchlings to the water?_  
> - ✅ Gently, in her mouth. → Yes. Her jaws are enormously strong, yet she carries hatchlings in her mouth without hurting them.
> - On her back. → Not quite. She carries them in her mouth, very gently.
> - She leaves them to find it. → Hatchlings can find water, but the mother often helps, carrying them gently in her mouth.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animal parents care for their young, such as a mother crocodile carrying hatchlings gently in her mouth._

> _“Put the kettle on” is an old British saying. What does it mean, and what is the joke?_

> - Go away. → The opposite: it means get ready to welcome guests.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): fire needs fuel, heat and air; fire safety  
> _The feather is for burning on the day of need, so it must stay dry. What three things does a fire need?_  
> _(Fire is dangerous, so only grown-ups light one.)_

> - Sun, wood and sand. → Wood is a fuel, but sun and sand are not what a fire needs. The three needs are fuel, heat and air.

_She sets you down on the slope above the army, a little way off, and goes back up to the edge of the cloud to watch._  
_Sam is still on his knees at the bottom. He hears the stones move, and looks up._  
_The youth starts walking, and then walking faster. For the last of it, he runs._  
_He stops right in front of his father, out of breath, the feather held to his chest._  
_He has never stood this close to anyone but you._  
**The Youth**: You came back for me.  
_Sam can’t say anything at all. He just nods, again and again, like someone who has forgotten how to stop._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): forgiving quickly or making someone earn it  
> _Zal runs to his father at once. Is it right to forgive quickly, or should someone earn it first?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Forgive quickly, if they are truly sorry. → That is a fair answer. Forgiveness can lift a weight off both people.
> - Take time first, so the sorry is real. → That is a fair answer. Time can show whether the sorry will last.
> - Forgive, but remember what happened. → That is a fair answer. We can forgive and still be careful, and Zal does remember.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about forgiving quickly versus making someone earn forgiveness._


#### `a27-09-descent-done`

_Your Nubbin arrives last, rolling the final bit of the slope, and comes to a stop against Sam’s boot._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity pulls things downhill  
> _Your Nubbin rolls all the way down the slope without anyone pushing it. Which force pulls things downhill?_  
> - ✅ Gravity. → Yes. Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth. On a slope nothing balances that pull, so the Nubbin rolls until something stops it: Sam’s boot.
> - Magnetism. → Magnets pull on some metals, but it is gravity that pulls everything downhill.
> - Wind. → Wind can push things, but the pull that makes things roll downhill is gravity.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls objects down a slope, an unbalanced force._


#### `a27-09-oath`

_Sam stands up. He bows, very low, to the great bird at the edge of the cloud, and thanks her with his whole voice._  
_Then he looks at his son properly: tall and strong and handsome, with white hair, and nothing wrong in him at all._  
**Sam**: I was wrong. I was a coward, and I was wrong, and there is nothing I can say that makes it smaller.  
**Sam**: Open your heart to me if you can. I won’t ask for more than you can give.  
**Sam**: I swear it, before the one who made us both: my heart will never be closed to you again.  
_He gives his son a name: Zal, which means the old one, for the white hair. This time, he says it with pride._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: the same feature can be shame or pride  
> _At first Sam was ashamed of the white hair. Now he gives the name Zal, “the old one”, with pride._  
> _What does this show?_  
> - ✅ The same thing can feel like shame or pride, depending on how people choose to see it. → Yes. Nothing about the hair changed. What changed was how Sam saw it.
> - Names do not matter. → In this story the name matters a lot. It turns the shame into pride.
> - The hair turned black. → It is still white. What changed was how Sam saw it.
> _For grown-ups: Explored a theme: how choosing to see something differently can turn shame into pride._

**Zal**: Zal. I like it.  
**Zal**: It sounds like a door shutting on the right side.

> _The tailor’s belt is 95 centimetres long. A metre is 100 centimetres._

> - 195 cm. → That would be adding. We want the difference: 100 minus 95 is 5.

> **Lesson** (music, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound is made by vibrations, which travel through the air  
> _A drum is loud enough to hear in every village. How does a drum make sound?_  
> - ✅ The drum skin vibrates, and the vibrations travel through the air. → Yes. Hit the skin and it shakes, and the shaking pushes the air, so the sound travels to your ears.
> - The drum glows. → A drum makes no light. Its skin vibrates, and the vibrations travel through the air as sound.
> - The drum talks to the army. → Ha. In a way, but the real answer is vibration: the skin shakes and the air carries the sound.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound comes from vibrations, as when a drum skin shakes._

> **Lesson** (art, 4.OA.C.5, ask): repeating patterns on decorated cloth  
> _A festival banner repeats this pattern: red, gold, gold, red, gold, gold, and so on. What colour is the tenth stripe?_  
> - ✅ Red. → Yes. Red falls on every third stripe: 1st, 4th, 7th, 10th.
> - Gold. → Gold fills the 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 6th and so on. The 10th is red, since red falls on 1, 4, 7, 10.
> - Blue. → Blue is not in the pattern. The 10th stripe is red.
> _For grown-ups: Continued a repeating three-stripe pattern to find the tenth stripe._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): manners show respect, and differ between cultures  
> _Zal’s bow is not the court’s bow, yet it is perfect. Why do cultures have rules of manners?_  
> - ✅ They show respect and help people get along. → Yes. Manners differ from place to place, but they all say “I respect you”.
> - To make life harder. → Manners can feel like that, but they exist to show respect and help people get along.
> - Only kings need manners. → Everyone uses manners. They show respect and help people get along.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why cultures have manners: they show respect and help people get along._

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): we see different stars in different seasons because Earth moves round the Sun  
> _Long ago, people watched the stars to tell the seasons. Why do we see different stars in winter and summer?_  
> - ✅ Earth travels round the Sun, so at night we face a different part of the sky. → Yes. As the year goes round, the night side of Earth faces different stars, which is why stars were used as a calendar.
> - The stars move away and come back. → The stars stay in place. It is Earth that moves round the Sun, so we see different ones through the year.
> - Winter stars are brighter. → It is not brightness. Earth moves round the Sun, so different stars are above us in each season.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that different stars are visible in different seasons because Earth moves round the Sun._

> - 38. → Check: 3 times 8 is 24, not 38.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): a fair judge hears both sides  
> _Two neighbours disagree about a goat and some washing. What makes a judge fair?_

> - Siding with the richer one. → That would be unfair. A fair judge hears both sides first.
> - Deciding quickly to save time. → Speed can be useful, but fairness needs listening to both sides first.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fair judge hears both sides before deciding._

> _Zal asks to be told when he is wrong. Why is it hard for powerful people to hear that, and how can we make it easier?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - By being kind when someone tells us. → That is a fair answer. If we thank the person who is honest, they will do it again.
> - By asking for it, as Zal does. → That is a fair answer. Asking out loud makes it safe for others to speak.
> - By remembering we all make mistakes. → That is a fair answer. When we know we can be wrong, hearing it stings less.

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-2, ask): daylight changes through the year because of Earth’s tilt  
> _As the seasons go round, summer days in Iran are longer than winter days. What causes that?_  
> - ✅ Earth’s tilt, as it travels round the Sun. → Yes. Tilted towards the Sun, a place gets longer days. Tilted away, it gets shorter ones.
> - The Sun gets closer in summer. → A common idea, but no. The cause is Earth’s tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
> - Clouds block the Sun in winter. → Clouds can hide the Sun, but the lengths of the days change because of Earth’s tilt.

- **petition**: A request for help or a decision, brought to someone in charge.

> _Kabul is a real city, beside the Kabul River in a valley among mountains. It is the capital of which country today?_  
> - ✅ Afghanistan. → Yes. Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan, where a form of Persian called Dari is widely spoken.
> - Iran. → Not Iran. Iran’s capital is Tehran. Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan.
> - Tajikistan. → Not Tajikistan. Its capital is Dushanbe. Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan, where a form of Persian is widely spoken._

**Zal**: Ask me anything else. Not that.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): refusing kindly versus accepting  
> _Zal had to say no, and still wanted to be kind. When is refusing someone kindly harder than saying yes?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - When we like them and have to disappoint them. → That is a fair answer. A no hurts more when it goes to someone we care about.
> - When we cannot explain our reasons. → That is a fair answer. Zal cannot say all that is on his mind, so he sends a gift instead.
> - When we are afraid of what others will say. → That is a fair answer. Zal is bound by what his father and the Shah would think.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how hard it is to refuse kindly someone we like._

> _The white cloth is 4 metres long and 2 metres wide, with a gold border all the way round the edge._  
> _How long is the gold border?_  
> - ✅ 12 metres. → Yes. The border is the perimeter: 4 plus 2 plus 4 plus 2 is 12.
> - 8 metres. → That is the area in square metres. The border goes round the edge: 4 plus 2 plus 4 plus 2 is 12.
> - 6 metres. → That is only one length plus one width. Go all the way round: 4 plus 2 plus 4 plus 2 is 12.
> _For grown-ups: Found the perimeter of a 4 m by 2 m rectangle: 12 m._

> - Water. → Not water. A bee carries pollen on its body from flower to flower, which helps flowers make seeds.
> - Perfume. → The scent helps bees find the flowers, but what they carry is pollen.

> _What kind of language is this?_  
> - ✅ A metaphor. → Yes. A metaphor says one thing is another, to show what it is like. Rudaba brings light and warmth, as the sun does.
> - A simile. → Close. A simile says “like” or “as”. A metaphor says Rudaba is a sun, without “like”.
> - A rhyme. → A rhyme is about sounds. Calling Rudaba a sun is a metaphor.
> _For grown-ups: Named a metaphor, calling Rudaba a sun, and explained what it shows._

**Zal’s Page**: Well, our sun can shoot an arrow across a river.  
**Rudaba’s Maid**: Ours doesn’t need to. Birds come to her.  
_This goes on for some time. The page is smiling all the way back across the river._  

**Choices**

- **Join in the boasting.**
    - **You**: He was raised by the biggest bird in the world, and she was proud of him.
    - **Rudaba’s Maid**: That’s cheating. You can’t win a boast with a true thing.
- **Declare it a draw.**
    - **Rudaba’s Maid**: A draw. Very well.
    - **Rudaba’s Maid**: We will call it a draw until they meet. Then we’ll see.

**Zal**: Why are you smiling? What did they say?  
**Zal**: Tell me every word.  
_The page tells him. Zal sends you straight back across with pearls and gold for the maids, so they’ll wait._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): pride in others versus boasting  
> _The page is proud of Zal, and the maids are proud of Rudaba. When is pride kind, and when does it turn into boasting?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Pride is kind when it lifts people up. → That is a fair answer. Pride in a friend’s kindness or effort is lovely.
> - Boasting is when we put others down. → That is a fair answer. The maids and the page are playful, but real boasting can sting.
> - It depends on how the other person feels. → That is a fair answer. Reading how someone feels is the best test.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between kind pride and boasting._


#### `a27-12-maid`

_The maid who is wiser than the rest takes the pearls, and asks to see the hero for herself._  
**Rudaba’s Maid**: A secret three people know isn’t a secret any more. So I may as well be one of the three.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step problem: a secret spreads  
> _Three people know the secret. Each of the three tells 2 more people._  
> _How many people know the secret now?_  
> - ✅ 9. → Yes. 3 people each tell 2 more: 3 times 2 is 6 new people, and 3 plus 6 is 9.
> - 6. → That is only the new people. Add the first three: 3 plus 6 is 9.
> - 5. → That adds 3 and 2. Each of the 3 tells 2, so 6 more hear it: 9 in all.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem: 3 plus 3 times 2 is 9 people who know the secret._

_You bring her across, and she looks at Zal, his bow, his white hair. She nods, as if a box has been ticked._  
**Rudaba’s Maid**: She thinks of nothing but you. She asked a stranger seven questions about you last night.  
**Zal**: Then show me a way to see her. Please.  
**Zal**: I can’t think about anything else.  
**Rudaba’s Maid**: Leave it to us. Wait for word.

_Back in the family’s rooms, the maids tell Rudaba everything. She takes a whole rose apart without noticing, petal by petal._  

> **Lesson** (art, RL.4.2, ask): the rose and the nightingale in Persian art and poetry  
> _Persian poets and painters often showed a rose beside a singing bird, the nightingale. What did the pair stand for?_  
> - ✅ Love and longing. → Yes. The nightingale sings to the rose in a way that stands for love and longing, a theme in Persian poetry.
> - War and fighting. → No. The rose and the nightingale usually stand for love and longing.
> - Winter and snow. → No. The rose and the nightingale are a spring and love picture: love and longing.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the rose and the nightingale often stand for love and longing in Persian art and poetry._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): people can be gentle and strong at once  
> _Zal is gentle and a fine archer too. Can a person be gentle and strong at the same time?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Yes. Strength can be gentle. → That is a fair answer. The strongest people often are careful about how they use it.
> - Sometimes. It depends on the moment. → That is a fair answer. Knowing when to be which is part of wisdom.
> - No. They pull in different directions. → That is a fair answer. They can feel like opposites, but Zal shows they can sit together.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a person can be gentle and strong at once._

- **metaphor**: Saying one thing is another to show what it is like, as in “she is a sun”.

## A27-13. The Rope of Hair

- `a27-13-s1`: Go with Zal to the king’s house at dusk. · _Follow the maid through the dark lanes._
- `a27-13-s2`: Keep watch below while Zal goes up. · _Stand at the corner of the lane. Look out for the night porter._
- `a27-13-s3`: Keep the watch until dawn. · _Stay at your corner. The porter comes round once._

#### `a27-13-dusk`

_At sundown the maid comes to the tents, in a dark cloak, and says only: come now. Everything is ready._  
_Zal goes with her, through the back lanes of Kabul. You and your Nubbin go too, because somebody has to keep watch._  
_Rudaba has hung her rooms with silk and carpets and filled them with flowers. You can smell them from the lane._  
_The house is locked for the night. Rudaba is standing on the roof, in the last of the light, waiting._  
_She is like a cypress with the full moon on it. Zal stops walking._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): simile: like a cypress with the moon on it  
> _Cypress trees are tall, slender and dark green. Rudaba is “like a cypress with the full moon on it”._  
> _What does this simile tell us?_  
> - ✅ She is tall, graceful and lit with silver. → Yes. A tall cypress and moonlight make a picture of grace and calm.
> - She is short and round. → The opposite: cypresses are tall and slender, so the simile says she is tall and graceful.
> - She is hiding in a tree. → She is on a roof, not in a tree. The simile paints how she looks.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile about a cypress and moonlight tells us about Rudaba._

**Rudaba**: Welcome, son of a hero. Heaven bless you for coming.  

#### `a27-13-dusk-done`

**Zal**: Heaven bless you for waiting. Only, you are up there, and I am down here.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtract a height from a rope length  
> _The roof is 5 metres up, and Zal’s rope is 8 metres long. How much rope is left over once it reaches the roof?_  
> - ✅ 3 metres. → Yes. 8 take away 5 is 3.
> - 13 metres. → That adds. We want what is left over: 8 take away 5 is 3.
> - 5 metres. → Check: 8 minus 5 is 3.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 5 m from 8 m to find 3 m of rope left over._


#### `a27-13-roof`

_Rudaba unpins her hair._  
_It is black and very long, and she lets it down over the edge of the roof, all the way to the ground._  
**Rudaba**: Here is a rope that will hold you. Take hold and climb.  
**Rudaba**: It’s right that I should catch you.  
_Zal takes hold of the end. Then he lifts it to his face, and lets it go._  
**Zal**: No.  
**Rudaba**: No?  
**Zal**: Never. It would hurt you, and I could not do that.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): choosing the gentle way even when it is harder  
> _Zal could have climbed Rudaba’s hair, which was offered kindly. He chose his own rope so as not to hurt her._  
> _Is the loving choice always the easy one? There is no one right answer._  
> - No. It may mean doing more work. → That is a fair answer. Zal took the harder way, so Rudaba would be safe.
> - Yes, when we love someone it feels easy. → That is a fair answer. Loving feels natural, but choosing gently still takes thought.
> - It depends on what we are willing to give up. → That is a fair answer. Real care often costs us something.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether choosing the loving, gentle way is always easy._

_He makes a running knot in a rope and throws it up. It catches first time._  
_He goes up it in one bound._  

#### `a27-13-roof-done`

_Up on the roof, Rudaba takes his hand, and they go in together. You take up your post at the corner of the lane._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): compare solutions: hair rope or lasso; friction holds a knot  
> _Zal compared two ways up: Rudaba’s hair, or a running knot on his own rope. A running knot tightens when pulled, thanks to friction._  
> _Which is the better solution, and why?_  
> - ✅ The rope: it holds, and nobody is hurt. → Yes. A rope can be hooked over a post and holds safely. The friction in a knot keeps it tight, and nobody is hurt.
> - Her hair: it is nearer. → It might be nearer, but pulling on hair would hurt. Good engineers compare solutions on safety too.
> - Neither would work. → A rope with a running knot works well, and the story shows it catching first time.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two ways of climbing and chose the safer one, learning that friction holds a knot tight._


#### `a27-13-watch`

_The night is long and warm. From the window above come voices, low, talking, and sometimes laughing._  
_Your Nubbin sits on your feet, which is its idea of keeping watch. It is also asleep._  
_At midnight the night porter comes round with his lamp, checking the locks, humming to himself._  
_He stops at the bottom of the rope, which is hanging down the wall in plain sight._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: 7 pm to 5 am  
> _Zal reached the house at 7 in the evening, and the morning drums beat at 5. How many hours was that?_  
> - ✅ 10 hours. → Yes. 7 pm to midnight is 5 hours, and midnight to 5 am is 5 more: 10 hours.
> - 12 hours. → Count it in two parts: 7 pm to midnight is 5 hours, midnight to 5 am is 5 hours. That is 10.
> - 2 hours. → That takes 7 from 5, which does not work across midnight. Count 5 hours to midnight and 5 more: 10.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the time from 7 pm to 5 am: 10 hours._

_He holds his lamp up to it. He looks up the wall, very slowly, towards the window._  
_Your Nubbin is suddenly wide awake. So are you._  

**Choices**

- **Step out and wish him good evening.**
    - You step out and wish him good evening. He jumps, and wishes you one back, and you talk about the weather.
    - You talk about the weather for a long time. You walk him all the way to the next street.
- **Nudge your Nubbin.**
    - Your Nubbin wakes, sees the lamp, and rolls into the lane after it. The porter follows it for three streets, trying to feed it.
- **Keep very still in the shadow.**
    - You keep very still. The porter looks at the rope, decides it is a vine, and goes on: Kabul has unusual vines.

#### `a27-13-watch-done`

_In the camp the drums begin, the drums that mean morning. The voices upstairs say: not yet, please, not yet._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): coping when a happy time has to end  
> _The voices upstairs wish the night would not end. What helps most when a good time has to finish?_  
> - ✅ Remembering it, and looking forward to the next one. → Yes. Holding on to the memory and making a plan to meet again makes goodbyes lighter.
> - Pretending it never happened. → That would lose the good part. Remembering it and planning the next time helps more.
> - Staying angry at the morning. → Feeling cross is natural, but remembering and planning ahead helps more.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about coping when a happy time ends: remember it, and plan the next one._


#### `a27-13-complete`

_The sun takes no notice of them. It comes up anyway._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): day and night come from Earth’s spin  
> _We say the sun “comes up”. What is really happening?_  
> - ✅ Earth spins, and our side turns towards the Sun. → Yes. Earth spins once a day. When your part turns to face the Sun, we call it sunrise.
> - The Sun travels round the Earth. → It looks that way, but no. Earth is the one that spins, and the Sun stays put.
> - Someone switches the Sun on. → Ha. No one has to: Earth spins, and our side turns to face the Sun.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sunrise happens because Earth spins and our side turns toward the Sun._

**Zal**: We have sworn. Neither of us will marry anyone else.  
**Zal**: Not ever.  
**Zal**: My father will be angry. The Shah will be angrier.  
**Zal**: I don’t care.  
_He coils up the rope and hangs it over your shoulder. You find you are going to keep it._

- **cypress**: A tall, slim, dark green evergreen tree, common in Persian gardens.
- **friction**: The rubbing force between two surfaces that slows things down or holds them in place.

- `a27-14-s3`: Take Sam’s answer to Kabul. · _Zal sends you on to Rudaba with the good news._

#### `a27-14-letter`

_In the morning Zal calls a scribe, and walks up and down the tent while he speaks, and the scribe writes._  
**Zal**: Father. You put me out on a mountain.  
**Zal**: A bird raised me. The sun beat on my head, and I ate what she brought.  
**Zal**: All that time you sat in a good house, in silk. I don’t say it to hurt you.  
**Zal**: I say it because it’s true.  
**Zal**: You swore you would give me anything I asked. I have never asked you for anything.  
**Zal**: This is the one thing.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how to write something hard, honestly and kindly  
> _Zal’s letter says hard things: you left me on a mountain, and now I ask you for one thing._  
> _Which helps most when you write something hard?_  
> - ✅ Say what happened, say how you feel, and then say what you ask. → Yes. Zal does all three, and he says plainly that he is not trying to hurt.
> - Make it as angry as possible. → Anger can be honest, but it often stops the other person listening. Zal says what is true without trying to hurt.
> - Leave out the truth. → A letter without the truth cannot help. Zal says it kindly, and says it anyway.
> _For grown-ups: Learned a way to write a hard letter: say what happened, say how you feel, then say what you ask._

**Zal**: You carry it. You were there at the beginning.  
**Zal**: He should see your face when he reads it.

> _You ride for 6 hours each day, for 4 days. How many hours do you ride in all?_  
> - ✅ 24 hours. → Yes. 4 days of 6 hours make 24.
> - 10 hours. → That adds 4 and 6. There are 4 days of 6 hours each, so multiply: 24.
> - 46 hours. → Check: 4 times 6 is 24, not 46.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 4 days by 6 hours to make 24 hours._

> - He is standing in a river. → Not literally. It is a figure of speech meaning stuck between two hard choices.
> - He is cooking dinner. → Ha. No. It means he is stuck between two hard choices.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the figure of speech caught between fire and water._

> - Not if it would hurt someone badly. → That is a fair answer. Some promises must be reconsidered, and that is a hard choice.

> _Sindokht got the whole story in a quarter of an hour. How many minutes is a quarter of an hour?_  
> - ✅ 15 minutes. → Yes. An hour is 60 minutes, and a quarter of 60 is 15.
> - 30 minutes. → That is half an hour. A quarter is half of that: 15 minutes.
> - 45 minutes. → That is three quarters of an hour. One quarter is 15 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a quarter of an hour is 15 minutes._

> _Pomegranates have grown in Iran for thousands of years. On Yalda, the longest night of the year, families gather with pomegranates and poetry._  
> _Which night is the longest in the northern hemisphere?_  
> - ✅ The winter solstice, around 21 December. → Yes. Yalda marks the winter solstice, when the days begin to grow longer again, so it is a night of hope.
> - The summer solstice, around 21 June. → That is the longest day. The longest night is the winter solstice, around 21 December.

## A27-15. The Riddles

- `a27-15-s1`: Sit in the circle while the mobeds question Zal. · _Watch, listen, and see if you can guess before he answers._
- `a27-15-s2`: Hear the last and hardest riddle. · _Stay in the circle. The oldest mobed asks last._
- `a27-15-s3`: Watch Zal at the trials of arms. · _Stand at the edge of the field below the Shah’s roof._

#### `a27-15-riddles`

_At court the Shah reads Sam’s letter, and is moved by it. But he wants to see what Zal is made of first._  
_The mobeds sit in a circle, with Zal in the middle. You and your Nubbin are allowed to sit at the edge, very quietly._  
**The Mobed**: I have seen twelve tall green trees. Each one has thirty branches.  
**The Mobed**: They never grow more, and never fewer.  
**Zal**: The twelve months of the year. Each one has thirty days.  
**The Mobed**: Two fine horses race for ever, one black, one white as crystal. They never catch each other.  
**Zal**: Night and day. They chase each other round the sky, and neither one wins.  
**The Mobed**: Thirty riders pass the king. Look again: one is missing.  
**The Mobed**: Look again: all thirty are back.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the moon’s cycle is about 29 and a half days; mah means moon and month  
> _In Persian, the word mah means both “moon” and “month”. The Moon goes from full to full in about 29 and a half days._  
> _Why would one word do both jobs?_  
> - ✅ Months were first counted by the Moon’s cycle. → Yes. Long ago, people counted a month from one new moon to the next, and the old word for moon also named the month.
> - The Moon changes colour each month. → It does not change colour. It is its shape that changes, and the cycle of shapes gave people a way to count months.
> - It is a coincidence. → Not a coincidence. Months were first counted by the Moon’s cycle, so the word does both jobs.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Moon’s cycle of about 29 and a half days gave us months, and that Persian mah means both moon and month._


**Choices**

- **Whisper: “The moon.”**
    - **Zal**: The days of the month. The moon thins until one night it is gone, and then it comes back whole.
    - He catches your eye. You were nearly right, and he knows you were thinking it, and he is pleased.
- **Whisper: “The stars.”**
    - **Zal**: The days of the month. The moon thins until one night it is gone, and then it comes back whole.
    - Not the stars, then. You were a long way off, and enjoyed it anyway.
- **Keep quiet, and let him think.**
    - **Zal**: The days of the month. The moon thins until one night it is gone, and then it comes back whole.

_The mobeds look at each other. Three riddles, three answers, and he hasn’t hesitated over any of them._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 12 months of 30 days, plus 5  
> _The old Persian year had twelve months of thirty days, plus five extra days at the end. How many days is that in all?_  
> - ✅ 365. → Yes. 12 times 30 is 360, and 5 more days make 365, the same as our year.
> - 360. → That is only the twelve months. Add the five extra days: 365.
> - 42. → That adds 12 and 30. There are 12 months of 30 days, so multiply: 360, plus 5 is 365.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 12 months by 30 days and added 5 to get 365 days._

> - A farmer. → He is a farmer in the picture, but the riddle stands for something bigger. Zal says it is time.
> - A thief. → Not a thief. Zal says the sickle stands for time, which comes for us all.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a riddle in which a man with a sickle stands for time, a metaphor._

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): practice makes muscles and skills stronger  
> _Zal got strong and skilled by practising every day on the peak. Why does practice make us better?_  
> - ✅ Muscles and skills grow stronger with repeated use. → Yes. Each time we practise, our muscles and our brains adjust a little, so we get better step by step.
> - Practice is boring, so it does not matter. → Practice can feel slow, but it is how every skill is built.
> - Only talent matters. → Talent helps, but practice is what turns it into skill.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that practice builds muscles and skills through repeated use._

> _Zal’s arrow flew 85 metres, and the best champion’s flew 70 metres. How much further did Zal’s arrow go?_

> - 155 metres. → That adds the two. We want the difference: 85 take away 70 is 15.
> - 25 metres. → Check: 85 minus 70 is 15.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): the Persian Royal Road used relay riders to carry messages fast  
> _Long ago, Persian kings built a Royal Road with stations where riders swapped tired horses for fresh ones. Why did that make letters travel faster?_  
> - ✅ A fresh horse could go faster, so the message kept moving. → Yes. Each rider only rode a short stretch on a fresh horse, and the message never had to stop and rest.
> - The horses were magic. → No magic: the speed came from the relay system of fresh horses and riders.
> - The road had no hills. → It had hills too. The speed came from swapping tired horses for fresh ones.
> _For grown-ups: Learned how relay riders and fresh horses on the Persian Royal Road made letters travel faster._

### Glossary

- **riddle**: A puzzle told in words, where you work out the answer from clues.
- **sickle**: A tool with a curved blade for cutting grass or grain.

> **Lesson** (art, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry in a square, as in tiles and carpets  
> _Persian tiles and carpets often use symmetry. How many lines of symmetry does a square tile have?_  
> - ✅ 4. → Yes. You can fold a square in half straight across, straight down, and along each diagonal, and both halves match.
> - 2. → Two are across and down, but there are also the two diagonals: 4 in all.
> - 1. → A square has more than that: straight across, straight down, and two diagonals, so 4.
> _For grown-ups: Found that a square has four lines of symmetry, as in the tiles and carpets of Persian art._

_Sindokht is waiting at the door of the king’s house. Sam bows to her as to an old friend._

**Sindokht**: Hide her? She is our sun.  
**Sindokht**: And what is it worth to you, to see her?  
**Sam**: Anything you like. My horses.  
**Sam**: My throne. Name it.  
_She laughs, and takes him in through the curtains to the family’s rooms._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): big happy feelings can leave us speechless  
> _Sam is so happy he has no words. Has a feeling ever been too big for words for you?_

> - Yes, when I was nervous or sad. → That is a fair answer. Big feelings of any kind can leave us quiet.
> - Not yet, but I can imagine it. → That is a fair answer. Imagining another person’s feelings is a good first step.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on a time when a feeling was too big for words._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiply: 7 days of 40 loaves  
> _The cooks bake 40 loaves every day of the seven-day feast. How many loaves do they bake in all?_  
> - ✅ 280 loaves. → Yes. 7 groups of 40 make 280.
> - 47 loaves. → That adds 7 and 40. There are 7 days of 40 loaves, so multiply: 280.
> - 2,800 loaves. → Check the place value: 7 times 4 is 28, so 7 times 40 is 280.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 7 days by 40 loaves to make 280 loaves._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): down feathers trap air and keep young birds warm  
> _Zal held a twist of soft chick-down. Down is a layer of tiny, fluffy feathers._  
> _Why does down keep a chick warm?_  
> - ✅ It traps air, which holds in body heat. → Yes. Thousands of tiny strands trap air, and trapped air stops heat escaping. That is why people stuff coats with down.
> - It makes its own heat. → Down does not make heat. It traps the air that holds in the chick’s body heat.
> - It soaks up the Sun. → Not quite. Down traps air, which holds in the chick’s own body heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that down keeps young birds warm because it traps air that holds in body heat._

> _In Iran today, many weddings still have a lovely decorated spread called a sofreh, with flowers, candles and sweets._  
> _How do customs like this last for hundreds of years?_  
> - ✅ Families pass them on to the next generation. → Yes. Each generation learns the custom from the one before, and adds a little of its own.
> - They are written on the walls. → Some customs are written down, but most are kept alive by families passing them on.
> - They cannot last. → Many customs last a very long time, because families pass them on.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that customs, such as the wedding spread, last because families pass them on._

### Glossary

- **symmetry**: When one half of a shape is a mirror image of the other half.
- **sofreh**: A cloth spread on the floor for a meal. At weddings in Iran it is decorated with flowers, candles and sweets.

#### `a27-17-labour`

_A year goes by. Rudaba is expecting a baby, and the time has come, and it isn’t going well._  
_The labour is long and hard, and days go by. She can’t rest, by day or by night._  
_Zal sits outside her rooms with his head in his hands. He is the bravest man in Iran, and he can’t do anything._  
**Zal**: I have answered every riddle they ever asked me. I don’t know the answer to this one.  
_Your Nubbin climbs up beside him and leans, warm and heavy, on his arm._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps a frightened person most  
> _Zal is frightened for someone he loves. What helps a frightened person most?_  
> - ✅ Someone staying close, and listening. → Yes. You cannot fix everything, but you can stay. Your Nubbin does just that.
> - Telling them not to worry. → That is kindly meant, but it rarely helps. Staying close and listening helps more.
> - Leaving them alone to think. → Some people want a little quiet, but most want company. Staying close and listening helps most.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that staying close and listening helps a frightened person most._

_Zal lifts his head. He is looking at the box on the shelf, where he keeps the things he brought from the mountain._  
**Zal**: The feather.

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of length: centimetres to metres  
> _The feather is as long as Zal’s arm, about 70 centimetres. How long are two such feathers laid end to end?_  
> - ✅ 140 cm, which is 1 metre 40. → Yes. 70 plus 70 is 140 centimetres, which is 1 metre and 40 centimetres.
> - 14 cm. → Check the place value: 70 plus 70 is 140, not 14.
> - 100 cm. → That is one metre. 70 plus 70 is 140 cm, which is 1 metre 40.
> _For grown-ups: Added two 70 cm lengths to make 140 cm, or 1 m 40 cm._


#### `a27-17-fire`

_Zal goes straight to the brazier in the middle of the hall. He doesn’t stop to think, and he doesn’t need to._  
**Zal**: She said: when you are truly in need. This is the day.  
_He puts the feather on the fire himself, with a steady hand._  
_It doesn’t burn like a feather. It burns slowly, like a candle, with a smell of sandalwood._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): burning is a change that cannot be reversed; melting can  
> _Once the feather has burned, it can never be a feather again. Which change can be reversed: melting ice, or burning wood?_  
> - ✅ Melting ice. → Yes. Melted ice can be frozen again. Burning makes new things, such as ash and smoke, and cannot be undone.
> - Burning wood. → No. Burnt wood cannot become wood again. Melting ice can be refrozen.
> - Both can be reversed. → Only one can. Melted ice can be frozen again, but burnt wood cannot be unburnt.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that burning cannot be reversed, but melting can._

_He came straight down the mountain when his father came back, and he goes straight to the fire now. He has never been one to wait._  
_Outside, all at once, the light goes strange._

_A sound like a great wind fills the air. Every shutter in the house rattles._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): onomatopoeia: words that sound like their meaning  
> _Shutters rattle in the wind. Which of these words sounds like the noise it names?_  
> - ✅ Rattle. → Yes. Rattle sounds like what it means. Words like that are called onomatopoeia.
> - Shutter. → Shutter names the thing, but it does not sound like a noise. Rattle does.
> - House. → House names a thing, but it does not imitate a sound. Rattle does.
> _For grown-ups: Picked out an onomatopoeic word, rattle, which sounds like what it means._
