_The pieces come down on the far side of the clearing, on the ants, the frogs and a very surprised goat._  
_None come your way. Your Nubbin holds out its paws anyway, just in case._  
_They stay empty. It is not sorry it tried._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): trying is worthwhile even without a prize  
> _Your Nubbin tried and got nothing, but it is not sorry it tried. What does that show?_  
> - ✅ Trying can be worth it even if you get no prize. → Yes. Having a go is a good thing in itself. You can feel disappointed and still be glad you tried.
> - It should never try again. → Not at all. It is glad it tried. Trying can be worth it, even without a prize.
> - It did not really want any. → Look at how hard it held out its paws. It wanted some. Trying can be worth it, even without a prize.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how trying is worthwhile even when it does not bring a reward._

_The pot lies in three pieces of the same size. You keep them._  
_It still sparkles a little when it tips._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: one of three equal parts  
> _The pot is in three equal pieces. What fraction of the whole pot is each piece?_  
> - ✅ 1/3 → Yes. One of three equal parts is one third, written 1/3. Three of them together make the whole pot.
> - 1/2 → One half would mean two equal pieces. There are three, so each is one third, 1/3.
> - 3/1 → That would be three whole pots. Each piece is one of three equal parts, 1/3.
> _For grown-ups: Named one of three equal parts as the fraction 1/3._


### Glossary

- **dandelion clock**: The round, fluffy seed head of a dandelion that blows away in the wind.

- `a28-10-s1`: Go with Ananse and Aso to the funeral of Aso’s mother. · _Walk with them to the family house, where the drums are._
- `a28-10-s2`: Keep an eye on Ananse. He is up to something. · _Follow Ananse when he slips round the back of the cooking fires._

#### `a28-10-funeral`

_Aso’s mother has died, old and well loved, and the whole family has come to see her off._  
_The yard is full: drums, cooking, cousins, children underfoot, and everybody talking about her at once._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how communities gather to remember someone who has died  
> _In Ghana, a funeral is often a big gathering of family and friends, with food, music and drumming. Why do communities gather this way?_  
> - ✅ To honour the person’s life and support the family together. → Yes. Being together helps people grieve. The food, music and stories keep the person remembered, and sad feelings are shared.
> - Because they have nothing else to do. → People often travel a long way to come. It matters a great deal to them. They gather to honour the person’s life and support the family.
> - To keep the news secret. → It is the opposite. Everybody is told, and everybody comes. They gather to honour the person’s life and support the family.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that funerals in Ghana are often large gatherings that honour a life and support the family._

**Aso**: She would have hated the fuss. She would have counted every chair.  
**A Cousin**: Kwaku! Will you eat?  
**A Cousin**: There is enough here for the whole village.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Eat? At my mother-in-law’s funeral?  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Never! I shall fast, out of respect, until it is all over.  
_Aso looks at him, and so does everybody who knows him. The cousin shrugs and takes the bowl away._  
**Aso**: He has never fasted for anything in his life.  

**Choices**

- **Tell Aso you’re sorry about her mother.**
    - **Aso**: Thank you. She was a hard woman, and fair.
    - **Aso**: She would have liked you.
- **Help carry chairs for the guests.**
    - You carry chairs. Your Nubbin carries a stool on its head and gets cheered by several aunties.

#### `a28-10-funeral-done`

_By noon the drums have been going for hours, deep and steady, and you can feel them in your chest._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): sound is made by vibration  
> _Why does a drum make a sound when it is hit?_  
> - ✅ The skin vibrates, and the vibration travels through the air to our ears. → Yes. Hit it harder and the skin shakes more, so the sound is louder. That is why you can feel a big drum in your chest.
> - The air inside it is hissing. → The air inside helps the sound grow, but the shaking skin starts it. The skin vibrates, and the vibration travels through the air.
> - The wood is singing. → The wood does vibrate a little, but the main source is the skin. The skin vibrates, and the vibration travels through the air.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a drum makes sound when its skin vibrates, and that the vibration travels through the air._

_Ananse is looking at every pot in the yard the way a dog looks at a gate._  

#### `a28-10-beans`

_Ananse slips round behind the cooking fires, where a pot of beans is bubbling, and looks both ways._  
_He does not see you. Or he does, and thinks you are furniture._  
_He scoops a pawful of beans, hot from the pot, and has nowhere to put them._  
_So he takes off his hat, drops them in, and puts his hat back on._  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Ow. Ow.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Ow ow ow.  
_Just then a cousin comes round the corner, and Ananse stands up very straight, smiling, with steam coming out from under his hat._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): promises and trust: a think question  
> _Ananse swore to fast, then hid beans in his hat. Why do people break promises they made out loud?_  
> _What happens to trust when they do?_  
> - They want something so badly that the promise stops feeling real. → That is a fair answer. Wanting can shout louder than a promise. The question is what you do when it does.
> - They forget that other people were listening. → That is a fair answer. A promise says something to everyone who heard it. Aso heard it too, and she knows him well.
> - Trust gets smaller each time, and takes longer to grow back. → That is a fair answer. Trust is easier to break than to mend. That is why people who keep small promises are trusted with big ones.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people break promises and how a broken promise affects trust._


**Choices**

- **Whisper to Ananse to take the hat off.**
    - **Kwaku Ananse**: Take it off? In front of people?
    - **Kwaku Ananse**: With my dignity?
- **Step in front of him, so the cousin can’t see.**
    - You try. Ananse is short, but the steam is tall.

#### `a28-10-dance`

_The beans are very hot. Ananse begins to shake his head, gently at first, then not gently at all._  
**A Cousin**: Kwaku, what are you doing?  
**Kwaku Ananse**: A dance! A hat-shaking dance.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: It is done in my village at funerals. Very old.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Very respectful.  
_He shakes his head harder, and the hat shakes harder. The first round is two shakes, the second is four, and the third is six._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a number pattern with a rule  
> _Ananse shakes his head 2 times, then 4, then 6. If the pattern keeps going, how many shakes in the fifth round?_  
> - ✅ 10 → Yes. The rule is add 2 each round: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Finding the rule lets you jump ahead without counting every round.
> - 8 → That is the fourth round. 2, 4, 6, 8 are rounds one to four. The fifth round is 10.
> - 12 → That is the sixth round. The rule is add 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. So the fifth round is 10.
> _For grown-ups: Continued a number pattern by finding its rule (add 2 each time)._

_Several small children join in, delighted. You fan him with a plantain leaf, which helps nobody._  
**Aso**: Kwaku. Stop.  

#### `a28-10-dance-done`

_Then the hat comes off on its own, sailing up into the air, and the beans come down all over the yard._  
_Every hair on Ananse’s head has been scorched clean away. There is a short silence, and then a very long laugh._  
_The hot beans heated his hat, and the hat heated his head._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): heat moves from hot to cooler  
> _The hot beans made Ananse’s head hot. In which direction does heat move?_  
> - ✅ From hotter things to cooler things. → Yes. Heat always flows from a hotter thing to a cooler thing. That is why a hot drink cools down in a cold room.
> - From cooler things to hotter things. → Heat does not go that way by itself. It flows from hotter things to cooler things.
> - It stays where it is. → Heat spreads out until things are the same warmth. It flows from hotter things to cooler things.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat flows from hotter things to cooler things._


#### `a28-10-complete`

_Ananse runs into the long grass and hides there, hat in hand, for the rest of the afternoon._  
**Aso**: Serves him right. Mother would have laughed till she cried.  
_The funeral goes on, warmer than before, and somebody tells the story of the beans before the drums have even stopped._  
_And that is why the spider is bald to this day, and keeps to the grass when people look at him._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): a “why” story: the pourquoi tale  
> _This kind of story explains why something is the way it is. Which of these is a “why” story, a pourquoi tale?_  
> - ✅ Why the spider is bald. → Yes. It explains how something came to be the way it is. Many cultures have stories that explain animals, weather and the stars.
> - How to tie a knot. → That is a set of instructions, not a story. A why story explains why something is the way it is.
> - A list of market prices. → That is a list of facts. A why story explains why something is the way it is.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised a pourquoi tale as a story that explains why something is the way it is._


### Glossary

- **fast**: To go without food, often for a reason such as respect or religion.
- **pourquoi tale**: A “why” story that explains how something in nature came to be as it is.

## A28-11. Across the Water

- `a28-11-s1`: Follow the page as it turns, and see where the spider has gone. · _Turn the corner of the page when it lifts by itself._
- `a28-11-s2`: Sit on the step and listen to the elder. · _Take the space the children have made for you._
- `a28-11-s3`: Hear Miss Ivy’s way of telling the gum story. · _Stay on the step until the story is done._

#### `a28-11-yard`

_The page lifts on its own, as if a wind has got under it, and turns._  
_It is night again, but a different night: warmer, louder with frogs, and the air tastes of the sea._  
_A yard in Jamaica, with a breadfruit tree and a lamp on a nail. The house door is open, and a radio is talking quietly inside._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): locating Jamaica  
> _Nova’s atlas says this yard is in Jamaica. Where is Jamaica?_  
> - ✅ An island in the Caribbean Sea, south of Cuba. → Yes. Jamaica is an island, and its capital is Kingston. It has warm weather all year, which fits the frogs and the breadfruit tree.
> - A city in Ghana. → Jamaica is far from Ghana, across the Atlantic Ocean. It is an island in the Caribbean Sea, south of Cuba.
> - A country in northern Europe. → That would be much colder. Jamaica is warm. It is an island in the Caribbean Sea, south of Cuba.
> _For grown-ups: Located Jamaica as an island in the Caribbean Sea, and learned that Kingston is its capital._

_On the front step sits an old woman with a cup of tea, and on the steps below her, a handful of children._  
_It is years later, and a long way across the water. You can tell, the way you can tell in dreams._  
_Your Nubbin, without being asked, goes and sits on the bottom step with the children._  

#### `a28-11-yard-done`

_One of the children budges up to make room for you, too. Nobody asks where you have come from._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): making a stranger welcome  
> _The children make room for you and do not ask questions. What does that tell you about them?_  
> - ✅ They are welcoming. → Yes. Making room is a quiet way of saying, “You belong here.” You can do this too, with someone new at school.
> - They have not noticed you. → One child budged up on purpose. They noticed. They are being welcoming.
> - They are bored. → They are eager for a story. They are being welcoming.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how making room for someone new shows welcome._

_The step is crowded and warm, and you fit._  

#### `a28-11-step`

**A Boy on the Step**: Miss Ivy. Tell an Anancy one.  
**A Boy on the Step**: Please.  
**Miss Ivy**: An Anancy one. Hm.  
**Miss Ivy**: Which one have I not told you yet?  
**A Boy on the Step**: You have told us all of them.  
**Miss Ivy**: Then I will tell one again. That is what they are for.  
_She puts her cup down. Before she starts, she says where he comes from, the way you would say where a cousin lives._  
**Miss Ivy**: Anancy came here with people who were enslaved. They were taken by force from the Gold Coast, where Ghana is today, and brought across the sea.  
**Miss Ivy**: They kept him, because he was small and clever and never stayed caught.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): why stories mattered to people who were enslaved  
> _Storytellers often say that enslaved people held on to Anancy because he was small but outwitted the strong._  
> _Why might that story matter so much to them?_  
> - ✅ It gave hope, and it kept their memories and culture alive. → Yes. Stories are one thing nobody can take away. Keeping them alive kept a people’s memory and courage alive too.
> - It was only for fun. → It was often funny, and that mattered too. But it also gave hope, and kept their memories and culture alive.
> - It was the only story they knew. → They knew a great many stories, songs and sayings. Anancy gave hope, and kept their memories and culture alive.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stories such as Anancy’s gave hope to enslaved people and kept their culture alive._

_The children nod; they know. It is not a secret, and it is not the story: it is where the story stands._  

#### `a28-11-step-done`

**Miss Ivy**: Now. Anancy, and the gum.  
_Out in the dark, the frogs have started up, one answering another across the yard._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): why frogs call at night  
> _Why do frogs call out at night?_  
> - ✅ Males call to attract mates and to warn other males away. → Yes. Calling is how frogs communicate, and each kind has its own song. Frogs hear well, and a female listens for the right song.
> - They are practising for school. → Ha! Frogs do not go to school. The males call to attract mates and warn other males away.
> - They are afraid of the dark. → Many frogs are active at night, and the dark suits them. The males call to attract mates and warn other males away.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that male frogs call at night to attract mates and keep rivals away._


#### `a28-11-gum`

**Miss Ivy**: Anancy was stealing peas from a farmer’s field. Every night, a few more peas, and never a sound.  
**Miss Ivy**: So the farmer made a little man out of wood, and covered him in gum, and stood him in the middle of the peas.  
**Miss Ivy**: And Anancy came along in the dark, and said good evening, and the little man said nothing at all.  
_The children are mouthing the next part along with her. Your Nubbin is mouthing too, without knowing the words._  
**Miss Ivy**: So Anancy slapped him. And stuck.  
**Miss Ivy**: And slapped him with the other hand, and stuck again.  
_In her story it is the spider who gets caught. In yours, he did the catching._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): comparing two versions of a story  
> _Miss Ivy’s version and yours are different. What do the two versions share?_  
> - ✅ A silent sticky figure, and a slap that leaves someone stuck. → Yes. The shape of the tale is the same, even though the details are not. That is how a story can change as it travels and still be itself.
> - The same hero and the same ending. → In one the spider is caught, and in the other he does the catching. What they share is a silent sticky figure and a slap that leaves someone stuck.
> - Nothing at all. → Look closer. A lot is the same. Both have a silent sticky figure and a slap that leaves someone stuck.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two tellings of one tale and named what they have in common._


**Choices**

- **Tell her you heard it the other way round.**
    - **Miss Ivy**: Did you now? Where?
    - **You**: A long way off. The spider made the doll, and a fairy got stuck.
    - **Miss Ivy**: Well. That one is right too.
    - **Miss Ivy**: He gets about, that spider.
- **Just listen to the end.**
    - **Miss Ivy**: And how did he get loose? Same way as always.
    - **Miss Ivy**: He talked.
    - The children cheer.

#### `a28-11-gum-done`

_Your Nubbin looks at its paw, which has been stuck to something all the way through this story, and seems comforted._  
_You count up its sticky moments today: silk three times, sap twice, gum four times, and the web once._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): adding four numbers within 100  
> _Silk 3, sap 2, gum 4, web 1. How many sticky moments altogether?_  
> - ✅ 10 → Yes. 3 + 2 = 5, 5 + 4 = 9, and 9 + 1 = 10.
> - 9 → That leaves out the web. 3 + 2 + 4 = 9, and 9 + 1 = 10.
> - 11 → That is one too many. 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 10.
> _For grown-ups: Added four numbers to find a total._


#### `a28-11-complete`

_The lamp on the nail hums. Somebody inside turns the radio off._  
**Miss Ivy**: There are a hundred ways to tell him. Every one of them is right, as long as he gets away at the end.  
_Two tellings of one story, on two sides of an ocean, and neither one is wrong._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): respecting different tellings: a think question  
> _Two tellings of one story, an ocean apart, and neither is wrong. Can two different versions both be right?_  
> _What would make one version wrong?_  
> - Yes. A story belongs to every teller who keeps it alive. → That is a fair answer. Tellers shape a story to fit their audience. Notice that Miss Ivy does not say yours is wrong.
> - Both can be right, but a version that hurts people would be wrong. → That is a fair answer. A story can be changed, but there are limits. Who gets to decide where those limits are?
> - Only the oldest version can be right. → That is a fair answer, and some people hold it. But tellers have always changed stories a little as they passed them on.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether two different versions of a story can both be right._

_The page lifts again, and you feel it begin to turn back._  

### Glossary

- **breadfruit**: A tropical tree with large, round, starchy fruit that is cooked before eating.
- **enslaved**: Made to work without pay or freedom, and treated as someone else’s property.
- **Gold Coast**: The name the British gave to the part of West Africa that is now Ghana.

## A28-12. Take Some Elsewhere

- `a28-12-s1`: Come back to the courtyard fire. · _Let the page turn back, and find your mat by the fire._
- `a28-12-s2`: Tell the courtyard a story of your own. · _Stand by the stool. You know which story it is._
- `a28-12-s3`: Hear the storyteller’s last story of the night. · _Sit back down on your mat._

#### `a28-12-return`

_The page turns back. It is the courtyard again: the fire lower now, the children sleepier, the moths still at the wall._  
_You are sitting on your mat, as if you never left it. Your Nubbin is beside you, sticky in three places._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): burning is a change that cannot be undone  
> _Most of the logs have burned down to grey ash and glowing embers. Could the ash ever turn back into wood?_  
> - ✅ No. Burning changes wood into ash, smoke and heat, and it cannot be undone. → Yes. Some changes, like melting ice, can be reversed. Burning cannot. The wood is gone for good, which is why the fire needs new logs.
> - Yes, if you let the ash cool down. → Cooling the ash leaves cold ash. It does not bring the wood back. Burning is a change that cannot be undone.
> - Yes, if you pour water on it. → Water puts out the embers, but the ash stays ash. Burning is a change that cannot be undone.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that burning is a change that cannot be reversed, unlike melting or freezing._

**Nana Ama**: Again? You want another?  
**Nana Ama**: It is late.  
**Nana Ama**: Long ago, they say, there was a spider, and… no. No, I have told enough.  
**Nana Ama**: Somebody else tells one now.  
_She turns on the stool and looks straight at you._  
**Nana Ama**: You. The one who has been away.  
**Nana Ama**: Your turn.  
_Your Nubbin climbs up on to the stool beside her, as if it has been invited too._  

#### `a28-12-return-done`

_The children turn round on their mats to look at you. There are twenty-four of them, and every one of them is waiting._  
_Half of them are nearly asleep. The other half are wide awake._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: half of 24  
> _There are 24 children, and half are nearly asleep. How many are wide awake?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Half of 24 is 24 ÷ 2 = 12. There were six mats of four children at the start, and that is still 24.
> - 8 → That is a third of 24, not a half. 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
> - 24 → That is all of them. Half of them are asleep. 24 ÷ 2 = 12 are awake.
> _For grown-ups: Found half of 24 by dividing by 2, and recalled the earlier total of 24 children._

**You**: This one is about a fairy, and a doll covered in gum.  
_You tell them about the odum tree, and the yam, and the thank-you that nobody answered._  
_You tell them how she stuck, both hands, and how the spider ran for rope._  
**You**: And while he was gone, somebody stayed by a root and did not help her. It was not their story to change.  
**You**: So she waited for the rope with her chin up, and she went up to the sky caught. But she went up proud.  
_The courtyard is quiet. A small boy at the front is frowning, which is the best sign there is._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): the theme of a story  
> _What is the theme, the big idea, of the story you told?_  
> - ✅ Being caught does not mean losing your dignity. → Yes. The fairy goes up caught, but proud. A theme is the big idea underneath a story, not just what happens in it.
> - Never eat yam. → The yam is a detail, not the big idea. The theme is that being caught does not mean losing your dignity.
> - Spiders always win. → In your story, the spider only ties the rope. The fairy keeps her chin up. The theme is that being caught does not mean losing your dignity.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of a story as its big idea, not just its events._

**Nana Ama**: Hm. That one is a true one.  
**Nana Ama**: Things get caught. That is how it is.  
**Nana Ama**: I will keep a piece of that. The chin.  

#### `a28-12-tell-done`

_The storyteller tucks a piece of your story away to keep._  
_The children whisper it to each other, changing it a little as they go._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what kind of story you would like to tell: a think question  
> _The storyteller calls a story “a clever one”, “a true one” or “a kind one”. Which kind would you most like to tell, and why?_  
> - A clever one, because I like surprises and tricks. → That is a fair answer. Clever stories keep listeners on their toes. Ananse would approve.
> - A true one, because it helps people understand. → That is a fair answer. A true story can be the hardest to tell. Nana kept a piece of the true one.
> - A kind one, because it makes people feel safe. → That is a fair answer. Kind stories can heal. Many of the best tales are all three at once.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what sort of story they would most like to tell, and why._


#### `a28-12-last`

**Nana Ama**: One more. A short one.  
**Nana Ama**: Mine, this time. I heard it from a spider.  
**Nana Ama**: There was a small round one, who once paid a whole buttercup for a story.  
**Nana Ama**: And the story was one word long, and the word was the spider’s own name.  
_Your Nubbin sits up very straight on the stool._  
**Nana Ama**: And the small round one thought it fair. And do you know?  
**Nana Ama**: It was right.  
**Nana Ama**: Because it was a story about someone. And that is all any of them are.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why characters matter in a story  
> _The storyteller says every story is about someone. Why are characters so important?_  
> - ✅ They give us someone to care about and follow. → Yes. We keep reading to find out what happens to the people in it. Even a one-word story has someone to wonder about.
> - They are the only part that rhymes. → Many stories do not rhyme at all. Characters matter because they give us someone to care about.
> - They are not important. → Try imagining a story with nobody in it. Characters give us someone to care about and follow.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why characters are central to a story._


#### `a28-12-last-done`

_For a moment nobody says anything. Then the children stretch, and yawn, and shuffle closer to the fire._  
_The fire crackles, and a handful of sparks rises into the dark, higher and higher._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): hot air rises  
> _Why do sparks float up from a fire?_  
> - ✅ Hot air is lighter, so it rises and carries the sparks. → Yes. Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it floats upwards. That is why smoke rises too.
> - The sparks are alive. → They are tiny bits of burning wood. Hot air is lighter, so it rises and carries them.
> - The sky pulls them. → The sky does not pull. Hot air pushes up. Hot air is lighter, so it rises and carries the sparks.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that hot air rises, which carries sparks and smoke upwards._


#### `a28-12-complete`

_The old woman stands up from the stool, slowly, because she can. She says the last words, the ones that close the story._  
**Nana Ama**: That is my story.  
**Nana Ama**: If you liked it, or if you did not, take a bit of it with you, and bring a bit back to me.  
**The Children**: Some come back!  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how a living tradition survives  
> _Anansesem are still told in Ghana today, and Anancy stories in Jamaica. Why does a tradition like this survive?_  
> - ✅ Because people keep telling it to each new listener. → Yes. A tradition is a custom handed down from person to person. It lives as long as somebody is willing to tell it and somebody is willing to listen.
> - Because it is locked in a museum. → A museum can preserve an object, but a story needs voices. It survives because people keep telling it to new listeners.
> - Because nobody has ever changed it. → Tellers have always changed it a little, and it has survived. It survives because people keep telling it to new listeners.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a living tradition survives because people keep passing it on to new listeners._

_The fire sinks and the walls thin. The courtyard folds itself up into a page, warm under your hands._  
_You are sitting in the Grove with Nova’s atlas open on your knees, and you have brought some of it away._  
_By the cottage hearth sits a carved box you have never seen before. Its lid is closed, and something inside is humming._  

### Glossary

- **tradition**: A custom or story handed down from one generation to the next.

## A29-1. The First Hunters

- `a29-01-s1`: Step into the old ink scroll, and find out where this page is. · _Touch the scroll at the bottom of the page, not the stage._
- `a29-01-s2`: Walk along the scroll, one generation at a time. · _Follow the road along the scroll. Each painting is a new set of hunters._

#### `a29-01-scroll`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page so bright it hums: a stage, a city at night, and a tiger in a hat grinning from a corner._  
_Under the paint, older, there is a long ink scroll. Mountains, small villages, and a road between them._  
_A card from Nova is tucked into the page. It says to find Korea on the big map before you step in._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): finding a place on a map: Korea is a peninsula, with sea on three sides  
> _On Nova’s big map, Korea hangs down from the north like a thumb into the sea. How many of its sides have water?_  
> - ✅ Three sides. → Yes. Land with water on three sides is called a peninsula, and Korea is one. Seoul, the big city in this story, is the capital of South Korea.
> - Only one side. → Not quite. Look at the map again: sea on the west, the south and the east. Water on three sides makes Korea a peninsula.
> - All four sides. → Good thinking. Land with water on all four sides is an island. Korea is joined to the rest of Asia in the north, so it has water on three sides.
> _For grown-ups: Found Korea on a map and learned that it is a peninsula, with water on three sides._

_You touch the scroll. It is cool, like paper left by a window._  
_Then it is mist, and you are standing in the painting._  
_Everything is ink: the hills, the pines, the roofs, even your sleeve. Your Nubbin is a round grey brushstroke at your feet._  
_Over the far mountains come demons, drawn fast and badly, all teeth. Where they pass, the villagers go pale, as if someone wiped the colour off._  
_A voice in the painting says the demons steal people’s cheer and carry it down to their king._  
_He is a red smudge, the only colour in the scroll. His name is Gwi-Ma._  

**Choices**

- **Look at the people in the villages.**
    - A woman in the nearest village holds a bowl of rice and has forgotten why. You want very much to give her back her colour.
- **Pick up your Nubbin.**
    - You lift your Nubbin, and in your arms it goes back to its own colour, and so does your hand. Good.
    - Keep hold.
- **Look at the red smudge.**
    - You look at it a moment too long, and it seems to look back. You look away first.

#### `a29-01-scroll-done`

_On a hill above the villages, three small figures climb to the top. They wear long skirts and short jackets, in the painter’s soft colours._  
_They turn to face the mountains, and take one big breath together._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): a voice is made by vibrations in the throat  
> _Try it: put your fingers lightly on your throat and hum. What do you feel under your fingers?_  
> - ✅ A buzzing, a tiny shaking. → Yes. Your voice is made by tiny vibrations in your throat, and the shaking makes the air shake too. That moving air is what carries a sound to someone’s ear.
> - Nothing at all. → Try again, a little lower, and press just a bit more firmly. There is a buzzing, a tiny shaking. That is the vibration that makes your voice.
> - Something hot. → It can feel warm, because your hand is warm. But the thing to feel is a buzz. A voice is made of vibrations.
> _For grown-ups: Felt the vibration in the throat when humming, and learned that vibrations make a voice._


#### `a29-01-hunters`

_The three women open their mouths and sing. You hear no words, only something like a held breath let go._  
_Where the sound goes, the ink brightens into a shining line. It runs along the mountain ridge and closes like a stitch._  
_The demons hit the line and stop. They pace along it and cannot cross, and the villagers get their colour back._  
_A label in neat brushwork says the line is called the Honmoon. A voice holds it up, and only voices can keep it up._  
_You walk on, and the scroll walks with you. Three new hunters on the hill, then three more, generation after generation._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): working out the meaning of a new word from its context: generation  
> _The scroll says “generation after generation”. Three hunters, then the next three, and the next._  
> _What is a generation?_  
> - ✅ A group of people born around the same time, followed by the next group. → Yes. Your grandparents, your parents and you are three different generations. The hunters pass the Honmoon down the generations, like a family recipe.
> - One single very old person. → Not quite. A generation is a whole group of people of about the same age. The painting shows many groups, one after another, each taking a turn.
> - Everybody who is alive today. → Close, but a generation is smaller: the people born around the same time. The hunters on the scroll are different generations, because they lived in different times.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a generation is a group born around the same time, using the scroll as a clue._

_Each three hope to sing so well that the line is sealed shut for good. Nobody ever has._  
_The last painting shows three girls on a stage, under lights that are not painted at all._  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin hum along.**
    - Your Nubbin hums, flat and happy. The shining line wobbles very slightly, as if it has been tickled.
- **Listen without a sound.**
    - You listen. It is the kind of music that makes you stand up straighter without deciding to.

#### `a29-01-hunters-done`

_The ink goes from black to bright pink, then electric blue: car horns, rain on hot pavement._  
_You step off the scroll into a city at night._  
_Behind you, a label at the edge of the scroll says the painter used a brush and black ink, on a thick, soft paper called hanji._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Korean ink painting: brush, ink and hanji paper made from mulberry bark  
> _The label goes on: hanji is made from the bark of the paper mulberry tree, by hand, in Korea, for hundreds of years._  
> _Painters used it for scrolls like this one. Good hanji can last a very long time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Korean ink paintings are made on hanji, a paper from mulberry bark, and that people have used it for centuries._

**Bobby**: You! Are you the new runner?  
**Bobby**: You’re the new runner. You’re late.  
**Bobby**: It doesn’t matter. Hold these.  
_He gives you a bag of instant noodles, a box of light sticks, and a lanyard with your face on it, somehow._  
**Bobby**: I’m Bobby. I manage Huntrix, the biggest group in Korea.  
**Bobby**: Tonight is a sold-out show, and I am very calm.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): people sometimes say they are fine when they are not  
> _Bobby says he is very calm, and he has not stopped running about. Why might someone say they are calm when they are not?_  
> - To help themselves feel calm. → That is a fair answer. Saying it can help a little, like a cheer for yourself. But it does not always work, and Bobby is the proof.
> - So other people don’t worry. → That is a kind thought. Many people hide a worry to protect others. Sometimes it works better to say it out loud and ask for help. Remember that.
> - Because they are being funny. → That is a fair answer too. A joke can be a way to let out nerves. Bobby is funny, and he is also tired. Both can be true at once.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people say they are calm or fine when they are not._

_Your Nubbin climbs into the merchandise bag among the T-shirts, and looks out like a passenger on a bus._  
**Bobby**: Don’t touch the girls’ cases. Never touch the girls’ cases.  
**Bobby**: Go, go, go.  

### Glossary

- **peninsula**: A piece of land with sea on three sides.
- **generation**: A group of people born around the same time.
- **hanji**: A soft, strong paper made by hand from the bark of the paper mulberry tree.

## A29-2. Huntrix

- `a29-02-s1`: Get the merchandise to the stalls before the doors open. · _Carry the boxes through the backstage corridor to the arena foyer._
- `a29-02-s2`: Watch the show from the wings, out of everyone’s way. · _Stand by the side curtain, behind the yellow tape._

#### `a29-02-backstage`

_Backstage is a corridor of black curtains, tape and people in headsets, all saying “copy” to nobody. A clock on the wall says 7:21._  
_Three girls are warming up in a doorway. One does scales, one does stretches, and one eats a rice ball very fast._  
**Zoey**: Ooh, new runner! I’m Zoey.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): saying thank you: appreciation helps people feel valued

> - Because Bobby asked her to. → Bobby actually forgets to. That is why Rumi does it herself. Good manners are best when they come from you and not from a reminder.
> - She was bored. → Not bored. She has a big show to do, and she still stopped for you. That shows she wanted you to feel noticed.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why saying thank you matters and how it helps others feel noticed._

> _The deep thump you feel in your chest is the bass. Low, loud sounds make big, slow vibrations that shake the air and you._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that loud, low sounds are big vibrations, and why people protect their ears at concerts._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile compares two things using “like”: hums like a struck glass  
> _The line in the sky “hums like a struck glass”. What does that picture help you hear?_  
> - ✅ A clear, ringing note that fades slowly. → Yes. A struck glass rings softly and then fades. A comparison with “like” or “as” is called a simile. It lets you hear with your imagination.
> - A loud crash. → A crash would be a broken glass. Here the glass is only tapped. The simile gives you a clear, soft ringing sound.
> - A sneeze. → Ha! Not this time. Think of tapping a glass with a spoon. That clear ringing is the sound the sky line makes.
> _For grown-ups: Used a simile to imagine a sound: hums like a struck glass._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): equal sharing with division: 6 demons shared between 3 hunters  
> _There are six demons and three hunters. If they share the demons out evenly, how many does each hunter face?_  
> - ✅ 2 each. → Yes. 6 shared between 3 is 2 each, because 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. Mira would call that a very tidy evening.
> - 3 each. → Check by counting: 3 + 3 + 3 is 9, which is too many for six demons. Try 2 each: 2 + 2 + 2 is 6.
> - 6 each. → If every hunter faced 6, that would be 18 demons. With 6 demons shared between 3 hunters, each gets 2.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 6 by 3 to share demons equally between three hunters._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): fear is normal; courage can come after fear  
> _Your Nubbin dived into a speaker, and Zoey said “Same, honestly.” Can a person be scared and brave in the same evening?_  
> - Yes. Being scared is not the opposite of brave. → That is a fair answer. Brave people often feel scared first, and then carry on anyway. Zoey felt it too, and she still stood in the car park.
> - No. Brave people are never scared. → That is a fair thing to think. A lot of stories make it seem that way. But most brave people say they felt afraid first. The brave part is what they do next.
> - Only if no one is watching. → Interesting. Some people find it easier to be brave when someone is with them. Others find it easier alone. There is no single right way to be scared.

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): a coloured filter lets through only light of its own colour  
> _The stage light has a pink filter, and plain white light goes in. Why does pink light come out?_  
> - ✅ The filter lets pink through and stops the other colours. → Yes. White light has all colours in it, and the pink filter holds back most of the rest. That is how stage crews paint a whole show in colour with one white bulb.
> - The bulb itself is pink. → Take the filter off and you would see plain white light. The filter does the colouring by letting only pink pass through.
> - Pink light is hotter. → A filter doesn’t make light hotter. It only picks which colours get through. The filter picks out the pink and blocks the other colours.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a coloured filter lets through only light of its own colour._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): noticing that someone may be hiding something, and wondering why  
> _It is a hot night and Rumi keeps her sleeves down. Why might a person keep something covered, even when it is uncomfortable?_

> - She might just be cold. → That is a fair thought, and you are right to keep it open. We can’t always know. But the room is hot, so the sleeves might mean something else.
> - She might have been told to. → That is a thoughtful answer. People sometimes hide things because someone they trust told them to. You will find out more about that very soon.
> _For grown-ups: Wondered kindly why someone might keep something covered, and thought of different reasons._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: from 2:15 to 3:00 is 45 minutes  
> _The four of you sat down at 2:15 and Zoey was asleep by 3:00. How long was that?_  
> - ✅ 45 minutes. → Yes. From 2:15 to 2:30 is 15 minutes, and from 2:30 to 3:00 is 30 more. 15 + 30 = 45 minutes, a long time to hold chopsticks.
> - 15 minutes. → Fifteen minutes only gets you to half past two. Keep counting to 3:00: that is 15 + 30 = 45 minutes.
> - One hour. → A whole hour would take you to quarter past three. From 2:15 to 3:00 is 45 minutes, which is a quarter of an hour short of an hour.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval, 45 minutes from 2:15 to 3:00._

**Bobby**: Rumi’s visiting Celine. Go with her and carry the fruit.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a simile: a pear wrapped in a net is like a pear in a jumper  
> _The writer says each pear is wrapped “like a pear in a jumper”. What is the picture meant to show?_  
> - ✅ The pear is wrapped up snug and protected. → Yes. A jumper keeps you cosy, and the net keeps the pear safe from bruises. A good simile gives you a fact and a feeling in one go.
> - The pear is cold. → Jumpers can mean cold, but here the net is for protection. The pear is being kept snug and unbruised.
> - The pear is wearing clothes for a party. → That is a funny picture, and it suits the story’s voice. But the real point is that the net keeps the pear safe, like a jumper keeps you snug.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile shows: a pear in a foam net is wrapped up snug, like a pear in a jumper._

> _A hanok is a traditional Korean house, built of wood, clay and tiles._  
> _Its doors and windows are covered in hanji paper, to let in soft light._  
> _Many hanok have a floor warmed from underneath. The smoke and heat from the kitchen stove run through channels beneath the rooms._  
> _That is called ondol._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): thinking about whether you have to fix yourself before you deserve love  
> _Rumi hopes that when her marks go, she will finally be “right”. What do you think about that?_  
> - Nobody has to be changed before they deserve love. → That is a fair answer, and a kind one. Many people hope to be loved just as they are. Rumi isn’t sure of it yet. Keep watching to see.
> - People should try to fit in, to be safe. → That is a fair thought. Fitting in can feel safer, and Celine thinks so because she is afraid for Rumi. But hiding a part of yourself can also be tiring. Keep that in mind as the story goes on.
> - It depends on who is looking. → That is a thoughtful answer. Some people can see all of us, and some can’t. Finding people who can is a big part of this story.

#### `a29-04-gate-done`

_Celine’s voice drops low. Then the gate opens and Rumi comes out, smiling, with her sleeves pulled down to her knuckles._  
_You heard it all through the doors, because paper is so thin._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound passes through thin paper more easily than through thick walls  
> _You heard Celine and Rumi through the paper doors. Why would a thick stone wall have been quieter?_  
> - ✅ Thin paper shakes easily, so more sound gets through. → Yes. Sound is vibrating air, and the vibration shakes thin paper easily and carries on. A thick wall takes up much more of the shaking, so less sound comes out the other side.
> - Paper makes sound louder. → It does not make it louder, but it lets plenty through. Thin paper shakes easily, so the sound passes on.
> - Stone has no vibrations at all. → Stone can shake a little, but it is heavy and hard to move. That is why a thick wall blocks more sound than a paper door.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound travels through thin paper more easily than through a thick wall._

> _Rumi says it “the way people say they’ll be happy when the weather turns”. What does that tell you about how she feels now?_  
> - ✅ She is waiting for something outside herself to change before she can be happy. → Yes. We can’t make the weather turn, and neither can Rumi make the marks go. Waiting to be happy later can make today feel grey.
> - She is very happy already. → Look at how she says it: “soft”, with a wish in it. People who say “I’ll be happy when…” are not happy yet.
> - She loves the rain. → Maybe, but the simile is not really about rain. It is about waiting for a change that she can’t control.
> _For grown-ups: Read a simile for its meaning: waiting for something to change before being happy._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): a screen changes electrical energy into light

> - Sound. → Sound comes out of the speakers, not the screen. The speakers turn electricity into sound. The screen turns electricity into light.
> - Wind. → No wind needed. A screen runs on electricity. Electrical energy goes in, and light comes out.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a screen is a device that changes electrical energy into light._

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction within 100: 30 take away 18  
> _The Saja Boys were 30th and are now 18th. How many places have they climbed?_  
> - ✅ 12 places. → Yes. 30 − 18 = 12. You can count up from 18 to 20, which is 2, then from 20 to 30, which is 10. 2 + 10 is 12. At a place a minute, that is only twelve minutes.
> - 48 places. → Adding 30 and 18 gives 48. But they are going from 30th down to 18th, so we take away. 30 − 18 = 12 places.
> - 8 places. → Almost! Count up from 18 to 30 on your fingers: two to reach 20, then ten more. That is 12 places.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a subtraction within 100, 30 − 18 = 12 places._

#### `a29-05-crowd-done`

_The song ends, the crowd wakes up a bit, and the shimmer stops. The Honmoon flickers, and holds._  
_You noticed your own foot tapping along earlier, and how hard it was to stop._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): noticing when something is pulling you along, and pausing  
> _A catchy song and a big crowd can sweep us along. How can you tell when you have stopped choosing for yourself?_  
> - I could stop and ask myself why I’m doing it. → That is a fair answer. A pause to ask “do I really want this?” is a strong tool. It works for songs, for crowds, and for plenty of other things.
> - I could check with a friend. → That is a good idea. Mira and Zoey noticed because they talked it over. A friend can see what you can’t see from inside the crowd.
> - I might not be able to tell. → That is an honest answer. It really can be hard to tell from the inside. That is why noticing, like you did with your foot, is a good first step.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to notice being swept along by a crowd or a catchy song, and ways to pause._

#### `a29-06-studio`

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): comparing two groups: 5 boys and 3 hunters  
> _There are five Saja Boys and three hunters. How many more boys than hunters are there?_  
> - ✅ 2 more. → Yes. 5 − 3 = 2, or count on from 3: 4, 5. Two more. Huntrix are used to being outnumbered, and they are good at it.
> - 8 more. → 8 is 5 + 3, all of them put together. To find “how many more”, take away: 5 − 3 = 2.
> - 3 more. → Close. Lay out three hunters and five boys in two rows, and match them up. Three match, and 2 boys are left over.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two groups by subtracting: 5 − 3 = 2 more._

_Rumi’s face goes very still. Then she nods, once, and holds out her hand to you without looking, and you give her the sword._

**Choices**

- **Stay by the door.**
    - You stay by the door. Your Nubbin, in the merch bag, peeks out with one eye.
- **Stay by the gear case instead.**

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): red, green and blue light together make white light  
> _Stage lights mix coloured beams. Where red, green and blue light land on the same spot, they add up to white._  
> _Red and green together make yellow. A lighting crew can paint a stage with only three colours._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that red, green and blue light together make white, and that mixing two makes new colours._


#### `a29-06-fight`

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): teamwork comes from practice and trust  
> _The three hunters move together without checking on each other. What helps a team work like that?_  
> - ✅ Practice, and trust that each one will do their part. → Yes. Trust and practice go together. Each of them knows the others will be there. It works for football teams, bands and washing-up crews, too.
> - Everyone doing something different at random. → Random would be messy and risky. Teams work best with practice and trust, so each knows what the others will do.
> - One person giving every order. → A leader helps, but Huntrix don’t wait for orders in a fast fight. They have practised so much that they trust each other’s moves.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what lets a team work well together: practice and trust._

#### `a29-06-fight-done`

**Zoey**: Did he… did he just let you go? Why would he do that?  
**Rumi**: I don’t know.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues in the text to work out a character’s motive  
> _Rumi doesn’t know why Jinu let her go. What clue did Jinu leave that might help?_  
> - ✅ He pulled her sleeve down over the marks before he left. → Yes. He hid her marks from the others. That is a kind act from a rival, and a puzzling one. Good readers collect clues like this before they decide what a character wants.
> - He laughed while he fought. → That is a clue about his style, but it doesn’t explain why he let her go. The strongest clue is that he covered her marks.
> - He had a black coat. → True, but all five boys have those. The clue to look for is what he did for Rumi: he pulled her sleeve down.
> _For grown-ups: Used a clue in the story to work out why Jinu might have let Rumi go._


#### `a29-06-sleeve`

_In the dressing room, Mira and Zoey are arguing in the shower block about who broke the flower stand._  
_Rumi is at the mirror with her back to the door, catching her breath. She has pushed her sleeve up to cool her arm._  
_The marks go from her wrist almost to her shoulder now. In the mirror light they shimmer, violet and silver._  
_She looks up and sees you in the mirror, holding three bottles of water. She doesn’t move._  
_You are the only one who has seen. Mira and Zoey are still arguing behind the door._  
_Your own jacket is on the chair beside you, where you dropped it to carry the case._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): respecting someone’s privacy while still being kind  
> _You are the only one who has seen Rumi’s marks. There is no single right way to help._  
> _What do you think matters most?_  
> - That she feels safe. → That is a fair answer. Feeling safe is where everything else starts. Think about which of the choices below would help her feel safest.
> - That she is the one to decide what happens next. → That is a fair answer. A private thing belongs to the person who has it. Look for the choice that leaves the decision with Rumi.
> - That she knows she isn’t alone. → That is a fair answer. Knowing someone is on your side can make a big secret lighter. Look for the choice that tells her so.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about privacy and kindness together, with no single right answer, before choosing how to help._


**Choices**

- **Hand her the jacket, and say nothing.**
    - You put down the water and hold out the jacket. She takes it and puts it on, fast, and zips it to the chin.
    - **Rumi**: Thank you.
    - She doesn’t say for what. You don’t ask.
- **“I saw. It’s all right.”**
    - **You**: I saw. It’s all right.
    - She looks at you for a long time in the mirror. Then she pulls her sleeve down, slowly, not fast.
    - **Rumi**: You don’t know what it is.
    - **You**: No. It’s still all right.
- **Look away, and let her decide whether you saw.**
    - You look down at the bottles in your arms, as if they are very interesting, and put them on the counter one by one.
    - When you look up again her sleeve is down, and she is smiling at the mirror, and neither of you says anything.

_Mira likes that answer so much that she doesn’t notice it isn’t one._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how a character responds to a question she wants to avoid  
> _Rumi gives Mira an answer that isn’t really an answer. What is she doing?_  
> - ✅ Using a joke to keep a secret safe. → Yes. A joke is a quick way to change the subject and keep something private. Notice that Mira laughs, and does not ask again.
> - Telling Mira exactly what she thinks. → Not quite. Rumi says only what is easy to say. She is protecting her secret with a joke.
> - Being rude on purpose. → She isn’t being rude. She is laughing along, to be kind and to stay safe. She is using a joke to keep a secret.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how a character uses a joke to avoid a question she doesn’t want to answer._


## A29-7. Derpy and Sussie

- `a29-07-s1`: Find out what is knocking over the bins behind the flats. · _Look in the alley behind the building, after dark._
- `a29-07-s2`: Deliver the note the magpie brought. Don’t read it. · _Rumi is on the roof. Take the note up the fire stairs._

#### `a29-07-alley`

_Something is knocking over the bins behind Huntrix’s building every night, and then looking embarrassed about it._  
_You go down with a torch._  
_In the alley there is a tiger: a big one, blue as a bruise, with a wide silly grin and crossed eyes._  
_On the tiger’s head stands a magpie, black and white, with a long tail and a beady, knowing eye. She looks at you sideways._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): the tiger and the magpie in Korean folk painting (minhwa)  
> _A tiger and a magpie together is a famous picture in old Korean folk painting, called minhwa. In those pictures, what does the magpie bring?_  
> - ✅ Good news. → Yes. In Korean folk belief, a magpie’s call means good news is coming. In minhwa pictures the tiger is often goofy and grinning, which is why Derpy fits right in. Families hung these pictures at New Year, for luck.
> - A storm. → Not quite. The magpie is a cheerful bird in these stories. She brings good news, and the tiger is often a bit silly.
> - A warning of danger. → Not here. The tiger in these pictures is more funny than scary. The magpie brings good news.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that in Korean folk painting the magpie brings good news and the tiger is often a bit silly._

_They are not from here. You can tell by the faint smoky shimmer round their edges._  
_Your Nubbin climbs out of the merch bag before you can stop it, walks up to the tiger and holds out the last of its biscuit._  
_The tiger looks at the biscuit, and at your Nubbin. Then he lies down flat on his belly, very carefully, and purrs like a kettle._  

**Choices**

- **Scratch the tiger behind the ear.**
    - He leans into your hand so hard he falls over sideways. The magpie hops off his head just in time, and gives you a look.
- **Nod politely to the magpie.**
    - The magpie looks at you, decides you will do, and nods back. Her long tail bobs.

#### `a29-07-alley-done`

_Your Nubbin climbs up the tiger’s nose and sits on his head where the magpie was._  
_The tiger goes cross-eyed trying to see it, and purrs louder._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): showing a character trait through actions: how can you tell Derpy is gentle?  
> _Nobody says Derpy is gentle. How can you tell?_  
> - ✅ He lies down carefully and lets a small Nubbin sit on his nose. → Yes. What a character does tells you what a character is like, even if the writer doesn’t say it. A big tiger who moves carefully around something small is being gentle.
> - He is blue. → The colour is fun, but it doesn’t tell you about his nature. Look at what he does: he lies down carefully and lets your Nubbin climb up.
> - He knocks over bins. → That shows he is clumsy and hungry, which is funny. His gentleness shows in how he treats your Nubbin.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a character trait, gentleness, from what a character does._


#### `a29-07-note`

_The magpie hops onto the bin lid and drops a folded note in front of you._  
_On the outside, in a careful old hand, it says “Rumi”._  
_The tiger, Derpy as you will learn, has a name tag round his neck. The magpie’s tag says Sussie, and she is clearly in charge._  
_You know who they belong to. The note smells faintly of old smoke, like the studio did._  
_Sussie pecks the note towards you, then taps the fire stairs with her beak. Up: Rumi is on the roof._  
_It is nine flights up, and each flight has 10 steps. You are absolutely not going to read the note, because it isn’t yours._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: 9 flights of 10 steps  
> _There are nine flights of stairs, with 10 steps in each. How many steps will you climb?_  
> - ✅ 90 steps. → Yes. 9 × 10 = 90. Counting in tens: 10, 20, 30… up to 90. That is a lot of stairs for one small note.
> - 19 steps. → 19 is 9 + 10. Here we want 9 groups of 10, which is multiplication. 9 × 10 = 90.
> - 900 steps. → That would be 90 flights. We only have 9. 9 groups of 10 is 90.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 9 × 10 to count the steps in nine flights of stairs._

_It is folded only once._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): respecting other people’s private things, and what to do when you are tempted  
> _The note isn’t yours, and it’s only folded once. What do you think about reading someone else’s note?_  
> - It’s private, so don’t read it. → That is a fair answer. A folded note is a small “please don’t”. Being trusted with a message is a way of being trusted with a person.
> - It might be important to know what’s in it. → That is a fair worry. Sometimes we want to know in order to help. But we can ask the person later, instead of peeking.
> - A quick look is only human. → That is an honest answer. Almost everyone feels tempted. What counts is what we do next, and whether we are honest about it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about being trusted with a private note, being tempted, and being honest._


**Choices**

- **Read it. Just the first line.**
    - “Your friend with the knives pinned my coat to a wall, my best one. Meet me where the old wall goes up the hill.”
    - You fold it back exactly as it was, feeling awful. You also want to know about the coat.
- **Don’t read it.**
    - You don’t read it. You hold it face down all the way up, at arm’s length, like a hot plate.
    - At the top your Nubbin, who can’t read, unfolds it, looks at it upside down with great interest, and folds it back.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): when you have broken someone’s trust, telling the truth and saying sorry helps  
> _If you have read a note you shouldn’t have, what helps most afterwards?_  
> - ✅ Tell the truth and say sorry. → Yes. Honesty and an apology can mend a small break in trust. Rumi laughed because she had guessed, and because the break was small.
> - Pretend you didn’t. → That is tempting. But a hidden mistake can grow, and Rumi can often tell. Telling the truth and saying sorry is better for both of you.
> - Hope nobody asks. → A lot of people try that. But hoping often feels heavy, and it doesn’t fix anything. Telling the truth and saying sorry is lighter.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the Seoul city wall: more than 600 years old and about 18 kilometres long  
> _This is Seoul’s old city wall. It is more than 600 years old, and it runs for about 18 kilometres over four hills._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that Seoul’s city wall is more than 600 years old and about 18 kilometres long._

_Halfway up, Jinu is sitting on the wall in his black coat, with no hat. Derpy is asleep across his feet._

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time: 18 km at 3 km an hour  
> _The wall is about 18 kilometres long. If you walked along it at 3 kilometres an hour, how many hours would it take?_  
> - ✅ 6 hours. → Yes. 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Every hour you go 3 kilometres: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Six hours. Pack a lunch, and some biscuits for your Nubbin.
> - 15 hours. → 15 is 18 − 3. We want to know how many 3s fit into 18. 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 is six jumps, so 6 hours.
> - 54 hours. → 54 is 18 × 3, but we divide to find a time. 18 ÷ 3 = 6 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 18 km by 3 km an hour to find that the walk takes 6 hours._

**Jinu**: You have voices too. I can tell.

**Jinu**: He finds the thing you’re ashamed of, and he talks to it until it’s all you can hear.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): noticing small actions that suggest a character is telling a kinder version of events  
> _Jinu looked away when he said “to feed them”. What might that tell you about his story?_  
> - Maybe it isn’t the whole truth. → That is a fair answer. People often look away when they are not quite telling it straight. Keep that in your pocket as the story goes on.
> - Maybe it hurts too much to say. → That is a fair answer, and a kind one. Pain can make people turn their faces away. Both can be true at once. A hurt can make a story softer.
> - Maybe he was just tired. → That is a fair thought, and a plain one. Not every glance is a clue. But this is a story, and a look at that moment is likely to matter.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a small action and wondered what it might say about whether a character’s story is complete._

- **Notice it, and keep it.**

- **Decide it doesn’t matter tonight.**

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, ask): a voice is made by vibrating vocal cords; tired cords sound rough, and rest helps  
> _Rumi’s voice is rough because she has been singing for days. What will help her voice most?_  
> - ✅ Rest, and sips of water. → Yes. Her vocal cords are two small folds that vibrate to make sound. When they are tired they sound rough, and they recover with rest. Water helps keep them comfortable.
> - Shouting louder. → Shouting would make the folds more tired. Rest and water are what a tired voice needs.
> - Whispering all night. → Whispering can be tiring for the voice too. Resting quietly, and sipping water, helps most.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the voice comes from vibrating vocal cords, and that rest and water help a tired voice._

> _Rumi feels better because someone else knows about the voices in her head. What can help when a worry won’t go quiet?_

> - Keeping it in and waiting. → Some worries do fade with time. But many get louder when we are alone with them. Telling someone you trust usually makes them smaller.

## A29-9. The Harsh Song

- `a29-09-s1`: Make tea while the three of them work. · _Use the kettle in the studio kitchen. Barley tea is in the tin._

#### `a29-09-studio`

_The rehearsal studio has thick foam on every wall and a keyboard with a coffee ring on it. Mira and Zoey have been here all night._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): foam soaks up sound so it does not bounce back as an echo  
> _Why would a music studio cover its walls in foam?_  
> - ✅ Foam soaks up sound, so it doesn’t bounce back as an echo. → Yes. Hard walls bounce sound back at you, which muddles the music. Soft foam takes the shaking out of the air. That is how a studio can make every note sound clean.
> - To keep the room warm. → Foam can keep warmth in, but that is not why studios use it. It soaks up sound, so there is no echo.
> - To make the room look cosy. → It might do that too. But the real job is for the sound. Foam soaks up echoes, so every note sounds clean.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that soft foam soaks up sound, so a music studio has no echo._

**Zoey**: We’ve got it. The thing that brings them down.  
**Zoey**: A new song, all about them. What they really are.  
**Mira**: We call them out in front of everyone. Every fan who loves those boys hears exactly what they are.  
_Zoey plays it on the keyboard: a hard, bright, stabbing tune, all corners. It is very catchy, and quite cruel._  
_Rumi listens with her arms folded and her sleeves down. She doesn’t say anything for a long time._  
**Mira**: Runner, tea. This is going to be a long one.  

**Choices**

- **Make barley tea.**
    - You make boricha, roasted barley tea, toasty and mild and free of caffeine. The studio starts to smell like a bakery, which helps a bit.
- **Make it very strong.**

#### `a29-09-studio-done`

_By the time the kettle clicks off, the music has stopped and the voices have started._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a word with more than one meaning: voices that sing and voices that argue  
> _Earlier in the story, “voices” meant singing. Here, “the voices have started” means something else._  
> _What?_  
> - ✅ People are talking loudly, and arguing. → Yes. “Voice” can mean the sound you sing with, or the way you speak up. When a word has more than one meaning, the sentence around it tells you which.
> - More singing is starting. → The line just said the music has stopped. So here the voices are people arguing.
> - The kettle is whistling. → The kettle just clicked off, so it isn’t whistling now. The voices belong to the people, and they have started arguing.
> _For grown-ups: Used the sentence around a word to choose between two meanings of voices._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): disagreeing without cruelty; being fair to someone you disagree with  
> _Zoey says it doesn’t matter if the song is cruel. Rumi says it does._  
> _What do you think?_

> - If someone is hurting people, they deserve a harsh answer. → That is a fair answer too, and it comes from caring about the fans. Still, it is worth asking if a harsh song is the same as a fair one.
> - You can stop someone without being cruel. → That is a thoughtful answer. You can be firm about what is wrong and still be kind in how you do it. That might be where Rumi is heading.

**Zoey**: We’re doing the song. At the Idol Awards.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): a vote decides by majority, but a fair group still listens to the person who is outvoted  
> _Two of the three voted for the song, and Rumi voted against._  
> _What does a vote like this do, and what should a fair group still do?_  
> - ✅ Two out of three is the majority, and the group should still listen to Rumi’s reasons. → Yes. A vote is a quick fair way to decide. A fair group also listens to the person who lost the vote. Sometimes that one person is seeing something the others missed.
> - Rumi must be quiet now. → A vote decides what the group does. It doesn’t say the one who lost must be silent. A fair group still listens to her reasons.
> - The vote doesn’t count unless all three agree. → Some groups choose to work that way. But this group chose to go with the majority. Even then, the one who disagrees deserves to be heard.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a majority vote decides, and that a fair group still listens to the person who is outvoted._

### Glossary

- **boricha**: Korean tea made from roasted barley. It has no caffeine.
- **majority**: More than half of the votes.

#### `a29-10-rain`

_It is raining over the city, the warm, steady rain of the summer rainy season, which Koreans call jangma._  
_The lamps along the old wall look as if they are melting._  
**Rumi**: Come with me. If I go alone I’ll talk myself out of it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, ask): seasonal weather patterns: Korea’s rainy season comes each year from late June into July  
> _Jangma comes every year, from late June into July. If you kept a rain chart for five summers, what would you expect to see?_  
> - ✅ Lots of rainy days in the same stretch each year. → Yes. Weather data from many years shows patterns by season. Jangma is one of them. That is how people know when to bring an umbrella, long before the clouds arrive.
> - Rain on a different day each summer, never in a pattern. → Weather does change from day to day. But over several years, a rainy season shows up in the same weeks. Charts show the pattern.
> - No rain at all in summer. → That might be true somewhere else. In Korea, summer has a rainy season. The chart would show many rainy days from late June into July.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that weather data over years shows seasonal patterns, such as Korea’s summer rainy season._

_You hold the umbrella. Your Nubbin sits on your shoulder, in its noodle hat, which the rain drums on like a little roof._  
_Jinu is on the wall already. Derpy is sitting beside him getting soaked, and doesn’t seem to mind._  
**Rumi**: I came to offer you something. A bargain.  
**Jinu**: Hunters don’t bargain with demons.  
**Rumi**: This one does.  

**Choices**

- **Hold the umbrella over Rumi.**

- **Hold it over Derpy.**
    - You hold it over the tiger.

**Rumi**: The Idol Awards. Help us win.

**Jinu**: Why would you do that for me?  
**Rumi**: Because you hid my marks. You didn’t have to.  
_She says it plainly, and her voice doesn’t crack at all._  
_You hear it, and so does she: clear, the way it was on the first night._  
_Jinu hears it too. He looks at her for a long time, and the rain runs off his hair._  
**Jinu**: All right. A deal.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): what makes a bargain fair: both sides give and get, and both agree freely  
> _Rumi and Jinu have made a deal. What makes a bargain fair?_  
> - ✅ Both sides get something, and both agree without being forced. → Yes. A fair bargain gives each side something, and nobody is pushed into it. Here, Jinu helps with the awards, and Rumi helps him stay in the world.
> - Only the stronger side gets something. → That would be a one-sided deal, and one side would lose. A fair bargain gives both sides something.
> - One side must agree, even if it doesn’t want to. → If someone is forced, it isn’t a real bargain. Both sides must agree freely.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fair bargain gives both sides something and that both agree freely._


**Choices**

- **Notice her voice.**

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows are longest when the Sun is low in the sky  
> _Jinu’s shadow stretches far down the hill. In the real world, when are shadows longest?_  
> - ✅ In the early morning and evening, when the Sun is low. → Yes. When the Sun is low, it shines across the ground, and shadows stretch out long. At noon, the Sun is high, and shadows are short. Jinu’s shadow isn’t natural at all.
> - At noon, when the Sun is high. → At noon, shadows are at their shortest, because the light comes down from above. They are longest when the Sun is low.
> - Only at night. → At night there is no Sun, so there are no sunlit shadows. Shadows are longest in the early morning and evening, when the Sun is low.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shadows are longest when the Sun is low, in the morning and evening._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): a small kindness can matter a lot to someone who is struggling

#### `a29-11-backstage`

_Backstage at the Idol Awards is ten times the arena: every band in Korea, every stylist, every runner, in one corridor._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: 3 bags of 4 costumes  
> _Bobby says there are three bags with four costumes in each. How many costumes are you carrying?_  
> - ✅ 12 costumes. → Yes. Three groups of four: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, which is 3 × 4. No wonder you are holding them over your head.
> - 7 costumes. → 7 is 3 + 4. Here we want three equal groups of four. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> - 4 costumes. → Four is how many are in just one bag. There are three bags, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
> _For grown-ups: Found the total of three equal groups of four: 3 × 4 = 12 costumes._

_You carry three garment bags over your head through the crush. Your Nubbin rides on top of the bags like a lookout._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues to infer that something is wrong  
> _Mira and Zoey smile and walk past without a word. What clues tell you something is wrong?_  
> - ✅ They didn’t speak, and their eyes are too bright, and they ignored the Nubbin. → Yes. Three small clues add up. Good readers collect clues before they decide what a scene means. Mira and Zoey would never walk past you without a word.
> - They were smiling. → A smile alone is a good sign. But look at what is missing: they said nothing. The silence, and the too-bright eyes, are the clues.
> - It was a busy corridor. → It was busy, but they walked right past you without a word. That, with the too-bright eyes, is what feels wrong.
> _For grown-ups: Used several small clues to work out that something is wrong with how characters behave._

_On the monitor, Huntrix walk out to a roar, Rumi in the middle._

_The crowd goes very quiet. Then it starts to mutter, and the mutter has a hard edge._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): empathy: what helps a person who has been exposed against their will  
> _Rumi’s private marks are on every screen, and nobody asked her. What would help her most right now?_  
> - Someone who stays kind and doesn’t stare. → That is a fair answer. Kindness that doesn’t pry tells her she is still the same person to you. Staring would make anyone feel more exposed.
> - Someone standing next to her on the stage. → That is a fair answer. Having a friend close can make a hard moment feel smaller. Her friends are not beside her yet, which is part of what hurts.
> - A little time, away from all the screens. → That is a fair answer. Some people need to step away and catch their breath first. Space and then company can be a good order.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps someone who has been exposed against their will, with no single right answer._

_On the monitor, “Mira” turns to the camera and smiles, with too many teeth. It isn’t Mira, and it never was._  

#### `a29-11-monitor-done`

_Above the hall, the Honmoon tears like wet paper. The lights all over the city flicker at once._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): water weakens paper because paper is made of tangled fibres  
> _The Honmoon tears “like wet paper”. Why does wet paper tear so much more easily than dry paper?_  
> - ✅ Water gets between the paper’s fibres and loosens them. → Yes. Paper is made of tiny plant fibres tangled together. Water gets in between them, so they slide apart. That is why a soggy page falls to bits in your hand.
> - Wet paper is heavier. → It is a little heavier, but weight isn’t what makes it tear. The water loosens the fibres that hold it together.
> - Wet paper is colder. → Cold has little to do with it. Water loosens the fibres.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that water weakens paper by getting between its tangled plant fibres._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): words that show strong feelings: furious  
> _The writer says Mira and Zoey are “furious”. Which word means almost the same?_  
> - ✅ Very, very angry. → Yes. Furious is a strong word for anger, a bit like “boiling over”. Writers choose strong feeling words to show you how big a feeling is.
> - A little bit sleepy. → Sleepy would be a quiet feeling. Furious is loud. It means very, very angry.
> - Rather pleased. → Mira and Zoey are tied up, so they are not pleased at all. Furious means very, very angry.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that furious means very angry, and noticed how strong feeling words show a big feeling._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): respect for other people’s private things: ask first  
> _Rumi’s private marks were shown to ten thousand people without her say. What is a fair rule for sharing someone else’s private things?_  
> - ✅ Ask them first. It is their story to share. → Yes. A person’s private thing belongs to them, and asking first is how we show respect. If they say no, that is the end of it.
> - If it’s true, anyone can share it. → Being true isn’t enough. A true thing can still be private. The fair rule is to ask first.
> - Share it if lots of people would like to see. → Many people watching doesn’t make it fair. Rumi never agreed. The fair rule is to ask the person first.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that private things belong to the person who has them, and that we should ask first._

- **stagehand**: A person who works backstage, moving scenery and lights.

_Rumi comes off stage with a stagehand’s jacket round her shoulders. Mira and Zoey are waiting in the loading bay._  
**Mira**: You lied to us. For years.

**Rumi**: I didn’t lie. I just didn’t say.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): is not telling the same as lying? Honesty and trust  
> _Rumi says she didn’t lie, she just didn’t say. Zoey says that’s the same._  
> _What do you think?_  
> - Leaving something out can still break trust. → That is a fair answer. When someone relies on us to be open, leaving out a big thing can hurt as much as a lie. That is how Mira and Zoey feel.
> - Not saying and lying are different. → That is a fair answer. A lie says something false, and silence doesn’t. But silence can still leave someone feeling shut out, which is what Mira said.
> - It depends why you didn’t say. → That is a thoughtful answer. Fear and shame are different from trying to trick someone. Rumi was afraid. Her friends were hurt anyway. Both things are true.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether leaving something out is the same as lying, and how silence can affect trust._

_Mira turns and walks out of the bay. After a moment, Zoey follows her, and doesn’t look back, and then does._  

**Choices**

    - You stay, because somebody should. You don’t know yet that you’re the somebody.
- **Catch Zoey’s eye.**

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a sentence can show mixed feelings: Zoey does not look back, and then does  
> _Zoey “doesn’t look back, and then does”. What does that tell you about how she feels?_  
> - ✅ She is hurt, and she still cares. → Yes. Her feet say “go”, and her heart says “wait”. One short sentence can hold two feelings. That is a writer’s trick for showing, not telling.
> - She doesn’t care at all. → If she didn’t care, she would not look back. She is hurt, and she still cares.
> - She forgot something. → Maybe, but the story is about her feelings for Rumi. She is hurt, and she still cares.
> _For grown-ups: Read a sentence that holds two feelings at once, and worked out what it shows about a character._

> - Pretending it never happened. → That is hiding, not owning. Taking responsibility means saying what you did.

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: from 10:15 to 10:50 is 35 minutes  
> _The set ended at 10:15, and the clock now says 10:50. How long ago was that?_  
> - ✅ 35 minutes. → Yes. From 10:15 to 10:45 is 30 minutes, and 5 more minutes gets you to 10:50. 30 + 5 = 35 minutes. It feels longer, doesn’t it?
> - 25 minutes. → Count on from 10:15: to 10:30 is 15, to 10:45 is 30, to 10:50 is 35. That is 35 minutes, not 25.
> - 45 minutes. → Nearly, but 45 minutes after 10:15 would be 11:00. Count on to 10:50: 35 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval, 35 minutes from 10:15 to 10:50._
