> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): comparing two versions of a story to find a character’s true motive  
> _Jinu told two versions of his story. How is this one different from the one on the wall?_  
> - ✅ Before, he said he left to feed his family. Now he says he left because he wanted the voice. → Yes. The first version made him kinder than he was. The second is the truth, and it is harder to say. Comparing two versions of a story is how readers find what a character really wanted.

#### `a29-13-courtyard`

_The city is empty and humming with a red light. Rumi walks through the old lanes with her arm bare, and you walk behind._  
_Celine is in the courtyard, wide awake, as if she has been waiting since the broadcast._  
**Celine**: Come inside. Quickly.  
**Celine**: We’ll put this right. We’ll cover them, and you’ll sing, and we’ll mend the Honmoon, the way it was.  
**Rumi**: The way it was is how we got here.  
**Celine**: Rumi. Inside.  
**Rumi**: You taught me to hide them. You loved me, I know you did.  
**Rumi**: But only the half of me you could look at.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a metaphor: loving only “half” of someone  
> _Rumi says Celine loved “only the half of me you could look at”. What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ Celine accepted the part of Rumi that was easy for her to see, and not the rest. → Yes. Rumi isn’t saying she is cut in half. It is a metaphor for being loved with a part held back. Words used as a picture, not exactly, are called figurative language. They make a feeling clear.
> - Celine only saw half of Rumi’s body. → Not literally. The “half” stands for part of who Rumi is. She means that Celine accepted only the part she found easy to look at.
> - Celine only came to half of the shows. → Nothing in the story says that. The half is a picture for the part of Rumi that Celine could accept.
> _For grown-ups: Read a metaphor for its meaning: being loved for only the part of you that others find easy to see._

**Rumi**: You never loved me all the way. Not once.  
_Celine opens her mouth, and nothing comes out. Rumi turns and goes out of the gate, and doesn’t run, and doesn’t look back._  

#### `a29-13-courtyard-done`

_The gate swings shut, and Celine stays standing in the middle of the courtyard._  
_You are still on the stone step by the gate, where you sat last time._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): naming several feelings at once: what Celine might feel  
> _Celine is standing alone in her courtyard. What might she be feeling?_  
> - ✅ Several things at once: shock, hurt and worry. → Yes. People often feel more than one thing at once, and it can be hard to name them. Naming them one by one makes a big feeling easier to carry.
> - Only anger. → She may be angry, but feelings often come in a bundle. Hurt and worry are probably in there, too.
> - Nothing at all. → She looks still, but being still isn’t the same as feeling nothing. She is probably feeling several big things at once.
> _For grown-ups: Practised naming several feelings that a person might have at the same moment._

> _The wooden floor Celine sits on is called a maru. It is the open, wooden-floored hall or porch of a hanok._  
> _It stays cool in summer, while the rooms beside it, warmed by ondol, stay snug in winter._  
> _The family sits there to talk, eat, or watch the weather._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the maru is the wooden-floored hall of a hanok, cool in summer, where families sit together._

#### `a29-13-sit-done`

_At last Celine gets up, without a word, and goes inside. You hear a kettle._  
_Soon it begins to whistle, and a thin cloud of steam drifts out under the door._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): heating and cooling: water boils at 100 °C (212 °F), and steam turns back to water when it cools  
> _Water boils at 100 °C (212 °F), and the kettle’s steam drifts out into the cool air. What happens to steam when it cools?_  
> - ✅ It turns back into tiny drops of water. → Yes. Heat changes water into steam, and cooling changes steam back to water. That change can be reversed. A cold spoon held in steam gets wet for the same reason.
> - It turns into ice at once. → Ice needs much colder air than a courtyard in summer. Steam turns back into water drops as it cools.
> - It vanishes forever. → It doesn’t vanish. It becomes tiny drops of water in the air, which you can see as mist. Steam cools and turns back into water.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heating turns water into steam and cooling turns steam back into water._

_That is all she says. You drink the tea, and it’s good tea._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what sitting beside someone can say that words cannot  
> _You didn’t say a word to Celine, and she poured you a second cup of tea. What can sitting beside someone say that words can’t?_  
> - That you are not leaving them alone. → That is a fair answer. Staying says “I am here” more loudly than a speech. Celine didn’t say thank you, but the tea was her way.
> - That you aren’t going to judge them. → That is a fair answer. Sitting quietly can show that you are not there to argue. It gives the other person room to feel what they feel.
> - Maybe nothing, and that is all right. → That is an honest answer. Sometimes we can’t tell what company says. But Celine noticed. She came back with tea.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what quiet company can say to someone who is hurting, with no single right answer._

#### `a29-14-crowd`

_The stadium on the river is full. Tens of thousands of people, standing still, faces lifted, eyes blank._  
_A faint shimmer of cheer rises off all of them, like steam off a lake in the morning, and drifts towards the stage._  
_On the stage the Saja Boys are singing, and behind them the great shadow with fire at its heart is drinking it all in._  
_You push through the crowd with the gear case, and nobody stops you or sees you. Bobby is in the third row, smiling at nothing._  
_Two rows behind him is Zoey, and in the aisle is Mira. Both of them blank, both of them shimmering._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): ordinal numbers and adding on: two rows behind row 3  
> _Bobby is in row 3, and Zoey is two rows behind him. Which row is Zoey in?_  
> - ✅ Row 5. → Yes. Two rows behind row 3 means counting on two: row 4, then row 5. Behind means further from the stage, so the numbers go up.
> - Row 1. → Row 1 is in front of row 3. Behind means further back. Count on two from 3: row 4, row 5.
> - Row 2. → Row 2 is in front of Bobby, not behind him. Count on from row 3: row 4, row 5.
> _For grown-ups: Counted on two rows from row 3 to find row 5, using the word “behind”._

_You keep walking. Your Nubbin holds onto your collar with both paws._  

**Choices**

- **Stop by Bobby.**
    - You touch Bobby’s arm, and he doesn’t notice. You straighten his tie, because he would want it straight, and go on.
- **Keep going.**
    - You keep going. The quickest way to help is to get the case where it’s needed.

#### `a29-14-crowd-done`

_Then, at the back of the stadium, the big doors open, and someone walks in alone._  
_The sound of her footsteps rings round the huge space, and comes back a moment late._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound bounces off big, hard surfaces and comes back as an echo  
> _Her footsteps ring back a moment late, in the huge stadium. What makes that echo?_  
> - ✅ The sound bounces off the far walls and comes back. → Yes. Sound travels in waves, and big hard surfaces bounce them back. The farther the wall, the later the echo returns.
> - The footsteps are made twice. → There is only one step. The second sound is the first one coming back. It has bounced off the far walls.
> - Someone else is following her. → Not here. It is an echo, a sound that bounces back. Big, hard walls send sound back to you.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an echo is sound bouncing off a far wall and coming back late._

_It’s Rumi, with no sleeves at all. Her arms are bare, and her neck, and the marks run all over both, violet and silver._  
_She walks down the middle aisle through the blank crowd, and up onto the stage, past the Saja Boys, to the front._  
_She doesn’t sing the old songs, or the harsh one. She opens her mouth and sings something you have never heard._  
_It has no words you can catch, and it is her own. It is like hearing someone tell the truth about herself, and be fine._  
_Under the music the marks glow brighter, not dimmer, and she doesn’t hide them. She holds her arms out so everyone can see._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): the difference between hiding something and choosing to share it  
> _Rumi stops hiding her marks and sings. What is the difference between hiding something and choosing to share it?_  
> - Sharing is a choice you make for yourself. → That is a fair answer. Rumi chose this. Nobody tore her sleeve this time. Choosing makes it hers again.
> - Hiding takes a lot of energy, and sharing frees it. → That is a fair answer. Rumi has hidden for years, and it has been tiring. Notice how much easier her voice is.
> - You can do both at different times. → That is a thoughtful answer. Some things we share with some people and not with others. The key part is that you are the one who decides.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between hiding something and choosing to share it, with no single right answer._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): an action can show trust: handing over a coat  
> _Rumi hands you her coat without a word and walks on. What does that action show?_  
> - ✅ She trusts you with something that mattered to her. → Yes. A coat she had hidden behind is now in your hands. Trust can be shown without a word. Actions can say more than speeches, and good writers use them.
> - She wanted to get rid of it because it was old. → Not here. Look at what the coat has covered. Handing it to you shows trust.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): when different notes sound together they make harmony, because sound waves add up  
> _Three people can sing three different notes at once and it sounds lovely. What is that called?_  
> - ✅ Harmony. → Yes. Each note is a sound wave. When different notes sound together, the waves add up into a fuller sound. It is why a choir sounds bigger than one voice.
> - Echo. → An echo is one sound coming back. Harmony is different notes together. Three voices, three notes, one sound: harmony.
> - Silence. → Silence is the opposite: no sound at all. When different notes sound together, we call it harmony.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that notes sung together make harmony, because their sound waves add up._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): people can choose differently from how they have always chosen  
> _For four hundred years Jinu left people behind. Now he steps in front of Rumi._  
> _Why do you think he chose differently this time?_  
> - Rumi’s kindness to him changed him. → That is a fair answer. Being treated well can make us braver. Rumi offered him a way out, and nobody had done that in four hundred years.
> - He decided it was time to stop running. → That is a fair answer. Sometimes the choice just becomes clear. He had been running from his own story for a very long time.
> - He knew it was the only way, and he was scared. → That is an honest answer. Brave things are often done by scared people. He stepped forward anyway.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a person might choose differently after years of choosing the same way._

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sunlight is all the colours mixed together; a rainbow shows them apart  
> _The new Honmoon has every colour, like a rainbow. What is sunlight made of?_  
> - ✅ All the colours mixed together. → Yes. Sunlight looks white, but it is all the colours of the rainbow mixed up. Raindrops can split it apart, and then we see red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.
> - Only yellow. → The Sun looks yellow from far away, but there is more in it. Sunlight is all the colours mixed.
> - Only white, with nothing inside. → White looks plain, but it has every colour in it. A rainbow is what you get when raindrops split it apart.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sunlight is all colours mixed together, and that a rainbow shows them separately._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how characters respond to an event they do not fully understand  
> _Somebody starts clapping “not knowing why”, and then everybody does. How do the people feel?_  
> - ✅ Relieved and happy, even though they don’t know what happened. → Yes. They have woken up into something good, and clapping is how they say so. Feelings can spread through a crowd, for good as well as for bad.
> - Angry. → Clapping doesn’t sound angry. They are relieved and happy.
> - Bored. → A bored crowd doesn’t clap. They are relieved and happy.
> _For grown-ups: Read a crowd’s response to work out how people feel when they do not know why._

> _Bobby says there are 60 people and the water comes in packs of 12. How many packs do you need for one bottle each?_  
> - ✅ 5 packs. → Yes. 60 ÷ 12 = 5, because 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 is five packs. Five packs, and one very busy runner.
> - 6 packs. → Count the packs: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. That is five. Six would be 72, which is too many.
> - 12 packs. → 12 is how many are in a pack, not how many packs. 60 ÷ 12 = 5 packs.

- **queue**: A line of people waiting their turn.

## A30-1. The Jewish Town

- `a30-01-s1`: Step into the brown-ink page and find the caretaker’s house. · _Touch the page, then follow the lane to the door with the ring of keys._
- `a30-01-s2`: Carry water from the well, and learn where things are. · _Rivka knows the way. The well is where three lanes meet._
- `a30-01-s3`: Fetch the bread from Hannah’s bakery. · _The bakery is the door with the warm step. Your Nubbin has already found it._

#### `a30-01-page`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page of brown ink: a steep-roofed synagogue, a lane of small houses, a river._  
**Ori**: That is Prague, in the Czech lands. The wavy line is the Vltava, the river that runs through the city.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): reading a river on a map  
> **Ori**: Maps use signs. How is a river like the Vltava usually drawn on a map?  
> - ✅ As a wavy blue line → Yes. Rivers are usually wavy blue lines, and they often join the sea or another river.
> - As a straight red line → Red lines are often roads or borders. A river is wavy, and blue like water.
> - As a black square → Small squares often mean buildings. The river is the long, wavy blue line.
> _For grown-ups: Read a map: a river is drawn as a wavy blue line. Placed Prague, in the Czech lands, beside the Vltava._

**Ori**: This page is a legend. Rabbi Judah Loew was a real teacher, from more than four hundred years ago. The clay man came into stories long after.  
_The paper goes cool and gritty under your hand, like a doorstep. Then it is a doorstep, and you are sitting on it._  
_A narrow lane, wet cobbles, the smell of bread. A man with a ring of keys looks down at you both._  
**Avram**: You’ll be the lodger. Good. I’m Avram. I look after the synagogue, which mostly means I look after its keys.  
_Your Nubbin holds up both arms, to show that it will fit anywhere at all._  

**Choices**

- **Shake his hand.**
    - **Avram**: A good grip. You’ll carry water.
    - He says it as if it were the highest praise he knows.
- **Ask which key is which.**
    - **Avram**: This one is the big door. This one is the cupboard. This one, I have no idea. I’ve had it twenty years.
    - **Avram**: One day a door will turn up for it, and I’ll be ready.
- **Take the basket he’s carrying.**
    - He lets you take it. He looks at you sideways, the way people do when they’ve been helped before they asked.

#### `a30-01-page-done`

**Dvora**: Avram, bring them in, you’re letting the warm out. Water first, lodger. Then you can be a guest.  
**Rivka**: I’ll show you the well! I know the well better than anyone.  
_Inside, your Nubbin is already being a guest at the stove._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what helps a newcomer feel welcome  
> _You are new in a stranger’s house. What do you think helps a newcomer feel welcome?_  
> - Being given a job to do → That’s a fair answer. Dvora gave you water to fetch. A job can make you feel you belong.
> - Being given food and a bed → That’s a fair answer. Being looked after tells you that you are wanted.
> - Being asked your name → That’s a fair answer. Being noticed as a person, not just a guest, matters a great deal.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps a newcomer feel welcome. No single right answer._


#### `a30-01-water`

_Rivka is about nine, and walks backwards the whole way so she can talk to you._  
**Rivka**: That’s the study house. That’s the bathhouse. That’s Hannah’s bakery. Don’t look at it, you’ll want everything.  
_Your Nubbin looks at it._  
**Rivka**: Nobody goes in the attic. It’s where the worn-out books go. You don’t throw away a holy book; you put it to rest.  
_At the well two women are talking low, the way people talk about weather that hasn’t arrived yet._  
**Rivka**: Mama says not to listen at wells. Mama listens at wells all the time.  
_Dvora needs thirty litres of water for the big pot. Your buckets hold six litres each, and you carry two._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step word problem with litres  
> _You carry two full buckets of six litres. Dvora needs thirty litres._  
> _How many more bucketfuls?_  
> - ✅ 3 → Yes. Two buckets is 12 litres, and 30 − 12 = 18. Then 18 ÷ 6 = 3 more bucketfuls.
> - 4 → Let’s check: 12 litres carried, so 18 to go. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 bucketfuls, not 4.
> - 5 → 12 litres carried, 18 to go. Each trip is 6 litres, so 3 trips.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem: 30 − (2 × 6) = 18, then 18 ÷ 6 = 3._

_Your Nubbin carries a cup, spills about half of it, and is very proud of the half._  

#### `a30-01-water-done`

**Dvora**: Good. Now you’re a guest. Rivka, take them to Hannah’s before she shuts, and don’t eat the change.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): the meaning of lodger  
> _Avram called you the lodger. From the way Dvora treats you, what is a lodger?_  
> - ✅ Someone who stays in another family’s house → Yes. A lodger lodges, or stays, in someone else’s home, often paying or helping in return.
> - Someone who sells water → A lodger doesn’t sell anything. To lodge means to stay in someone else’s home.
> - Someone who owns the house → The owner is the householder. A lodger is a guest who stays.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of the word lodger from context._

_Rivka looks as if the thought had never crossed her mind._  

#### `a30-01-bakery`

_Your Nubbin is already sitting on the bakery step, which is warm from the oven inside, with its eyes shut._  
**Hannah**: Is this yours? It’s been there since you came round the corner. It hasn’t moved.  
_Hannah is flour to the elbows. Behind her, plaited loaves stand in rows, shining, waiting for Friday._  
**Hannah**: Those are for the Sabbath. Nobody touches those. This, on the other hand, is a crust I burnt.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): some changes cannot be undone  
> _Hannah’s soft dough goes into the hot oven and comes out as bread. Can baked bread be turned back into dough?_  
> - ✅ No, the heat changed it for good → Right. Some changes, like baking, can’t be undone. Others, like melting butter, can.
> - Yes, if you add water → Water won’t help. The heat has changed the dough into something new.
> - Yes, if you let it cool → Cooling won’t help either. Bread stays bread.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that baking is a change that cannot be reversed._

_She holds it out. Your Nubbin takes it in both paws as if it were a medal._  
**Rivka**: She burns one every day. On purpose. Everyone knows.  
**Hannah**: Rivka, if you tell everyone, I’ll have to stop.  

#### `a30-01-complete`

_The loft is small and smells of apples. Through its little window you can see across the lane to the study house._  
_There is still a lamp burning there, late, in one window. Someone is reading._  
**Rivka**: That’s the rabbi. He reads all night sometimes. Papa says it’s because he’s wise. Mama says it’s because he forgets.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): seeing that two reasons can both be true  
> _Papa and Mama give different reasons for the rabbi’s late nights. Could both be right?_  
> - ✅ Yes, people often act for more than one reason → Yes. He could be wise and forgetful. Most people are more than one thing.
> - No, only one can be right → It’s tempting to think so. But people are usually more than one thing, so two reasons can both be true.
> _For grown-ups: Practised seeing that two different explanations can both be true._

_Your Nubbin falls asleep with flour on its nose and the last of the crust under its arm._  

### Glossary

- **legend**: A very old story that many people have told, which may have grown over the years.
- **lodger**: A person who stays in someone else’s home.

## A30-2. The Rabbi

- `a30-02-s1`: Go to the study house with Avram and sit at the back. · _The bench by the door. Sit still, and listen._
- `a30-02-s2`: Answer the rabbi’s question, if you can. · _He is looking at the back bench. There is no wrong answer._

#### `a30-02-study`

_The study house is one long room full of books and noise. Students sit in pairs, arguing over a page, both talking at once._  
**Avram**: It’s meant to be loud. A quiet study house is one where nobody’s thinking.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how people studied in the past, compared with today  
> _Students here study in pairs and argue over a page. Why might that be a good way to learn?_  
> - ✅ Your partner spots things you missed → Yes. Two minds catch more than one, and explaining your idea helps you understand it.
> - It keeps the room quiet → The room is anything but quiet! Arguing in pairs is how they test their ideas.
> - There are no books → There are books everywhere. The pairs are for thinking, not for sharing.
> _For grown-ups: Compared learning in pairs in a study house long ago with learning at school today._

**Avram**: Sit at the back. That is Rabbi Judah Loew. People call him the Maharal, from the first letters of “our teacher, the rabbi Loew”.  
_At the front sits an old man with a plain grey beard and ink on his fingers. The room goes quiet for him without being asked._  
**Rabbi Loew**: I’m going to tell you a story from the Talmud. Rava made a man, and sent him to Rabbi Zeira.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Rabbi Zeira spoke to him, and the man did not answer.  
**Rabbi Loew**: So Rabbi Zeira said to him: then go back to your dust.  
_Your Nubbin, on the bench beside you, has gone very still._  

#### `a30-02-study-done`

_The rabbi lets the story sit in the room a while, the way you let bread rest before you cut it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): recognising a simile  
> _That line compares a story with bread. Which of these is a simile, a comparison using “as” or “like”?_  
> - ✅ The room was as quiet as snow → Yes. “As quiet as snow” compares two things using “as”. That is a simile.
> - The room was a snowfield → That compares without “as” or “like”. It is a metaphor, a close cousin of the simile.
> - The room was silent → That says it plainly, without any comparison.
> _For grown-ups: Told a simile from a metaphor and a plain statement._


#### `a30-02-question`

**Rabbi Loew**: Now. What is a person, if not that? Someone tell me.  
**A Student**: Someone who answers, Rabbi.  
**Another Student**: Someone who can be spoken to. Which is not quite the same.  
**Rabbi Loew**: There’s a psalm in the Bible, a kind of prayer, that says: before I was even made, you saw me.  
**Rabbi Loew**: The Hebrew word there is golmi, “my golem”: me, a lump not yet shaped. So every one of us was clay once, and somebody saw it.  
**Rabbi Loew**: What makes the difference?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): what makes a person a person  
> _The rabbi asks what makes a person different from a clay figure. What do you think?_  
> - Having feelings → That’s a fair answer. Something that can be glad or frightened has an inside, not just an outside.
> - Being able to choose → That’s a fair answer. A person can say no, or change their mind. A clay man only waits.
> - Being loved by other people → That’s a fair answer. We become who we are among people who know us.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what makes a person different from a clay figure. No single right answer._

_He is looking past the students, at the back bench. At you._  

**Choices**

- **“Someone who can answer.”**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: The same as the student said, but braver, from the back of the room. Good.
- **“Someone who can ask.”**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Then this is a room full of people, and I have been worrying for nothing.
- **Look at your Nubbin, who can’t say a word.**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Yes. It doesn’t speak. And it answered me just now: it looked up when I said clay.
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Answering is more than words. Remember that. I may need reminding.

#### `a30-02-complete`

_Afterwards, at the door, the rabbi stops beside your Nubbin and looks down at it for a long moment._  
**Rabbi Loew**: I have never seen one of these. Does it do as it’s told?  
**Avram**: Never, Rabbi. Not once. It’s a great comfort to the household.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Good. I’d worry about it otherwise.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s words show about what he values  
> _The rabbi is glad that the Nubbin never does as it’s told. What does that tell us about him?_  
> - ✅ He values minds that think for themselves → Yes. He is glad of a creature with a mind of its own. Remember that when the clay man comes.
> - He dislikes obedient children → It isn’t about dislike. He is glad of a mind of its own.
> - He is joking and means nothing → There is a joke in it, but it also tells us what he cares about.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred what a character values from what he says._

_He goes out into the lane with a book under each arm, and leaves his coat behind on the peg._  

### Glossary

- **simile**: A comparison that uses “like” or “as”, such as “as quiet as snow”.
- **acronym**: A name or word made from the first letters of other words.

## A30-3. Fear

- `a30-03-s1`: Find out why Avram has come home early. · _He is in the courtyard, sitting on the woodpile, which he never does._
- `a30-03-s2`: Get through the night. · _Choose where to be. Nothing will happen to you. It is only a long night._

#### `a30-03-rumour`

_Avram comes home at noon, which he never does, and sits on the woodpile, which he never does either._  
**Avram**: There’s a story going round outside the walls. About us. It isn’t true.  
**Avram**: I won’t tell you what it is. Saying it again is how it travels.  
**Dvora**: It’s been told before. It’s always been a lie. It always finds people who want it.  
_Dvora puts her hand on his shoulder, and leaves it there._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why untrue stories travel  
> _Avram won’t repeat the lie, because repeating is how it travels. Why do you think untrue stories spread so easily?_  
> - People like exciting news → That’s a fair answer. A thrilling story gets passed on before anyone checks it.
> - People are frightened and want someone to blame → That’s a fair answer. Fear looks for a reason, and a lie can offer a false one.
> - Nobody stops to check → That’s a fair answer. A question like “how do we know?” can stop a lie in its tracks.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why untrue stories spread, and how asking “how do we know?” can slow them. No single right answer._

**Avram**: There were men at the gate last night, talking. Only talking. Tonight there may be more of them.  
**Rivka**: Will they come in?  
**Dvora**: The gates are shut at night. And there are a great many of us, and we’re all very good at shouting.  

#### `a30-03-rumour-done`

**Avram**: Bar the shutters at dusk. That’s all. Then we sleep, if we can.  
_There are four shutters on the house, and each one has two bars, one high and one low._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): equal groups: 4 × 2  
> _Four shutters, two bars on each. How many bars does Avram bar in all?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes. Four groups of two is 4 × 2 = 8.
> - 6 → Try it as four twos: 2, 4, 6, 8. Eight bars.
> - 4 → Four is the number of shutters. Each has two bars, so 4 × 2 = 8.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups to multiply: 4 shutters with 2 bars each make 8._


#### `a30-03-night`

_After dark there is lantern light at the far end of the street, beyond the gate. Voices, low, and then louder._  
_You can’t hear the words. You don’t want to._  
_The house goes very quiet. Shmuel gets into his sister’s bed without asking, and she lets him._  
_Across the lane, in the rabbi’s window, the lamp is lit. It stays lit._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): we see a lamp because its light reaches our eyes  
> _The lane is dark, but you can see the lamp across it. How can you see it?_  
> - ✅ Light from the lamp travels to your eyes → Yes. We see a glowing thing when its light reaches our eyes, and in a dark lane there is nothing to hide it.
> - Your eyes send light to the lamp → Eyes don’t send out light. They catch light that arrives from the lamp.
> - The lamp is warm → Warmth isn’t how we see. It is the light that reaches our eyes.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we see a lamp because its light travels to our eyes._

**Shmuel**: Is the rabbi scared?  
**Rivka**: The rabbi is thinking. It looks the same from outside.  

**Choices**

- **Sit on the floor by the children’s bed.**
    - You sit on the floor with your back to the bed. After a while a small hand comes down and holds your collar.
    - Your Nubbin climbs up between them, and Shmuel goes to sleep with his face in its fur.
- **Keep watch at the shutter with Avram.**
    - **Avram**: There’s nothing to see. I know. I look anyway.
    - You look anyway, together, through the crack in the shutter, until the lights at the gate go out one by one.
- **Watch the rabbi’s window.**
    - Once, very late, a shadow crosses the rabbi’s lamp, back and forth, back and forth. Somebody walking, and not sleeping.

#### `a30-03-complete`

_In the morning the men are gone. Nothing happened, this time._  
_Hannah’s oven is lit, and the lane smells of bread._  
_The rabbi passes on his way to the study house, and nods to Avram. He looks as if he has not slept at all._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Good morning. It is a good morning. They all are, until they aren’t.  
**Dvora**: He didn’t sleep. You can always tell. He gets philosophical before breakfast.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): working out a new word from context  
> _Dvora says the rabbi “gets philosophical”. From his words, what does philosophical mean?_  
> - ✅ Asking deep questions about life → Yes. A philosophical person wonders about big things, like good mornings and how long they last.
> - Very hungry → Not hungry. Look at what he said: he is wondering about mornings and time.
> - Very cheerful → He sounds thoughtful, not cheerful. Philosophical means wondering about big questions.
> _For grown-ups: Used context to work out that philosophical means thinking about big questions._


### Glossary

- **philosophical**: Wondering and thinking about big questions, like what is right or what is real.

## A30-4. The Answer

- `a30-04-s1`: Take the rabbi his supper in the study house. · _Dvora has wrapped it in a cloth. He will forget to eat it._
- `a30-04-s2`: Listen to what the rabbi asks of you. · _He is at the study house door with two men._
- `a30-04-s3`: Light the lantern in Avram’s window. · _The lantern hangs by the door. The window is in the loft._

#### `a30-04-ask`

_Dvora sends you across the lane with bread and a bowl of soup under a cloth. The study house is empty but for him._  
_He is not reading. He is sitting with his hand over his eyes, very still._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Put it there, thank you. I’ll eat it. I may even eat it tonight.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Do you know what I asked for, when I prayed this evening? How to keep them safe. Only that.  
**Rabbi Loew**: It’s a very old question. Usually the answer is: be patient, be careful, be kind to your neighbours, and wait.  
**Rabbi Loew**: I have been all four. I’d like a fifth.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what a fifth thing might be  
> _The rabbi has been patient, careful and kind, and has waited. What might the fifth thing be?_  
> - Courage → That’s a fair answer. Courage can mean doing the hard thing, even when you are afraid.
> - A good plan → That’s a fair answer. Kindness and patience are not always enough without a plan.
> - Help from other people → That’s a fair answer. Nobody keeps a whole town safe alone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what else might help keep people safe. No single right answer._

_Your Nubbin climbs up on the bench and pushes the soup an inch closer to him, as a suggestion._  

#### `a30-04-ask-done`

_When you go back for the bowl in the morning, it is empty. He is asleep at the table with his cheek on a book._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, notice): children need nine to twelve hours of sleep  
> **Ori**: Children your age need about nine to twelve hours of sleep every night. Grown-ups need seven or more.  
> **Ori**: A book makes a hard pillow. Sleep is when our bodies and brains do their mending.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that children need about nine to twelve hours of sleep a night._


#### `a30-04-helpers`

_By noon he is awake, and changed. Something has settled in his face, the way dust settles in a still room._  
**Rabbi Loew**: A question I asked in the night was answered in a dream. That is all I’ll say about it.  
_Two men stand with him: Isaac, his son-in-law, broad and quiet, and Jacob, his pupil, thin and quick._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Isaac, Jacob: be ready tonight, after midnight. Wear old clothes. Bring nothing.  
**Isaac**: Nothing, Rabbi?  
**Rabbi Loew**: Nothing. Our hands will do.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): inferring a plan from what a character says  
> _“Bring nothing. Our hands will do.”_  
> _What does the rabbi’s plan seem to be?_  
> - ✅ To make or do something with their own hands → Yes. No tools and no fuss: just their own hands. The line quietly says a lot.
> - To go to sleep → You don’t bring nothing to go to sleep. “Our hands will do” points to work.
> - To run away → They are told to be ready after midnight, with old clothes. That points to a job.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s plan from his words._

_Then he turns to you, and you think he’s going to tell you something. He doesn’t._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Keep a lantern lit in Avram’s window until we come back. And don’t follow us.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Not because you aren’t trusted. Because some things are better done without anyone watching.  

**Choices**

- **“I’ll keep it lit.”**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Thank you. It helps, coming home, to see a light someone kept.
- **Ask where they’re going.**
    - **Jacob**: To the river.
    - Isaac looks at him. Jacob looks at his shoes.
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Well. To the river. You may as well know that much. It’s not a secret where rivers are.
- **Just nod.**
    - The rabbi nods back, once, as if you have agreed to something larger than a lantern.

#### `a30-04-lantern`

_Dvora lights the lantern, and you carry it up to the loft window. The flame stands up straight in the still air._  
_The lantern has a thin window of horn on each side, to keep the wind off the flame._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): a lantern window lets light out and keeps wind off  
> _Why does a lantern have thin windows of horn or glass?_  
> - ✅ They let light out and keep the wind off the flame → Yes. Light passes through the thin window, but moving air can’t get at the flame to blow it out.
> - They make the flame hotter → The window doesn’t add heat. Its job is to protect the flame and let the light through.
> - They stop people seeing the light → They do the opposite. Light shines out through them.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a lantern window lets light through and shields a flame from wind._

**Rivka**: Why is it lit? Who’s it for?  
_You tell her it’s for the rabbi. She takes this very seriously._  
**Rivka**: Then I’ll mind it too. I’m good at minding things. I minded Shmuel for a whole year and he’s still alive.  
_She sits cross-legged beside the lantern, chin in her hands. Your Nubbin sits beside her, and copies her exactly._  

#### `a30-04-complete`

_The lantern was lit at six in the evening. At midnight the study house door opens and shuts softly._  
_Three shapes go down the lane towards the river. Rivka is still awake, and looks at you, and looks at the lantern._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: 6 pm to midnight  
> _The lantern was lit at six in the evening, and it is now midnight. For how many hours has it burned?_  
> - ✅ 6 hours → Yes. From 6 pm to midnight is six hours: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12.
> - 5 hours → Count the hours on a clock: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. That is six.
> - 12 hours → Twelve is the clock number at midnight. From six to twelve is six hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time interval from 6 pm to midnight._

**Rivka**: Go on, then. I’ll mind it. You’re not very good at not following, are you?  

## A30-5. Clay from the River

- `a30-05-s1`: Follow the three of them to the river, at a distance. · _Keep well back. Stop at the willows above the bank._
- `a30-05-s2`: Let your Nubbin help, if they’ll have it. · _Your Nubbin has made up its own mind. Stay on the bank._

#### `a30-05-follow`

_You follow at a distance, through the sleeping lanes, out by the little water gate to the river._  
_The Vltava is wide and black and talking to itself. It flows on north, far away, to join the great river Elbe._  
_You stop in the willows above the bank. Your Nubbin stops too, and holds on to your trouser leg._  
_Below you, on the mud, three men are kneeling. They have their sleeves rolled up._  
_They are digging clay out of the bank with their hands, and laying it out on the ground._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): why towns grow beside rivers  
> _Prague grew up beside the Vltava. What could a town in the 1500s take from a river?_  
> - ✅ Water, fish, clay for building, and a way to travel → Yes. Rivers gave people drink, food, clay and roads of water, so towns grew beside them.
> - Only water for the fountain → Water was important. But look at these three men: they are digging clay, too.
> - Nothing at all → Many places owe their very start to a river: water, food, clay and travel.
> _For grown-ups: Learned why towns grow beside rivers: water, food, building clay and travel._

_You can see their mouths move. You can’t hear a word over the river, and you don’t try to._  

**Choices**

- **Go a little closer.**
    - You go one tree closer, and stop. It feels like walking into a room where someone is praying.
- **Stay where you are.**
    - You stay in the willows. Your Nubbin looks up at you, then back down at the bank, thinking.

#### `a30-05-clay`

_The clay on the ground is taking a shape: a head, shoulders, two long arms. It is as long as a door._  
_The rabbi bends over the head. The other two work at the arms and legs, smoothing, as if they were making bread._  
_The clay is drying in the wind off the water. Isaac keeps going down to the river with cupped hands, and it’s slow._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): wet clay is soft and dry clay is hard  
> _Isaac keeps wetting the clay while the wind dries it. Why does the clay need to stay wet?_  
> - ✅ Dry clay goes hard and can’t be shaped → Yes. Wet clay is soft, and dry clay is hard. They must shape it before it sets.
> - Wet clay is warmer → Wetness isn’t about warmth. It is about whether the clay is soft enough to shape.
> - The river wants its water back → A nice thought, but the real reason is that dry clay turns hard and can’t be shaped.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that clay is soft when wet and hard when dry._

_Your Nubbin lets go of your trouser leg. Before you can stop it, it is down the bank._

_Isaac looks at it, then up at the willows, straight at you. Then he moves over, and makes room._  
_Your Nubbin goes back to the river, and again, and again. You stay where you are, and the night goes on._  

#### `a30-05-clay-done`

_Near dawn Isaac carries your Nubbin back up the bank himself, and sets it down at your feet, muddy to the ears._  
**Isaac**: Go home. He knows you’re here. He knew before I did.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): whether to follow when told not to  
> _The rabbi asked you not to follow, and you did. What do you think about that?_  
> - It was wrong: he asked you not to → That’s a fair answer. A request deserves respect, even when we are curious.
> - It was fine: nothing bad happened, and your Nubbin helped → That’s a fair answer. Though you can’t always know it will turn out well before you go.
> - It depends why he asked → That’s a fair answer. “It’s dangerous” and “it’s private” are very different reasons.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether it is right to follow when asked not to. No single right answer._

> _Rivka was “minding” the lantern. Which sentence uses mind to mean look after?_

> - I changed my mind → Here, mind means the thinking part of you. It is the same word with another meaning.
> - Never mind → Here it means “don’t worry about it”. Rivka’s meaning is to look after.

#### `a30-06-tellings`

_Before sunrise Jacob knocks at the door. The rabbi wants you at the river, and your Nubbin, he says, especially._  
**Rabbi Loew**: You followed. I thought you would. Come and see, then, and don’t say anything for a little while.  
_The clay man lies on the bank under the grey sky. He is plain and smooth and as long as a door._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Some say the word goes in the mouth, some say on the brow. The tellings don’t agree. They rarely do.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): why oral stories change over time  
> _The rabbi says the tellings “rarely agree”. Why do stories change when they are told again and again?_  
> - ✅ People forget bits, add bits, and tell it for their listeners → Yes. Before books were common, every telling was a little different, and so a story grew.
> - Stories stay exactly the same → Not quite. A story passed from mouth to mouth changes a little each time.
> - Only liars change stories → Most changes are not lies. They are forgetting, adding and fitting the story to the listener.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stories passed on by word of mouth change a little with every telling._

**Rabbi Loew**: In some it is a holy Name, written on a slip of paper. We will leave that where it belongs.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Here it will be a plain word on the brow, one that anyone may read: the word for truth. Three letters. Watch which ones.  

**Choices**

- **“Why truth?”**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Because a guard should stand on something true. And because anyone in the lane can read it, even Shmuel.
- **Say nothing, as he asked.**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Good. You were listening. That is most of it.

#### `a30-06-letters`

**Rabbi Loew**: Hebrew is read from the right. So the first letter goes on the right.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Alef, א. It makes no sound of its own. It only holds a vowel, the way a cup holds water.  
**Ori**: Alef. The quiet one goes first.  
_He draws it on the clay brow with one finger. The clay is cold and takes the line cleanly._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Mem, מ, from near the middle of the alef-bet. And tav, ת, the very last letter of all.  
_Three letters in a row, right to left: אמת._  
**Rabbi Loew**: Emet. Truth. The first letter, one from the middle, and the last. The old teachers liked that: truth stands on all of it.  
**Ori**: With its vowel marks, the word is אֱמֶת. Say it: eh-MET. It means truth.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, do): the letters of emet, read from right to left  
> **Ori**: Put the letters in the order the rabbi wrote them: alef on the right, then mem, then tav on the left.  
> Check: `edu:order:letters:alef-mem-tav`
> _For grown-ups: Ordered alef, mem and tav as they are written, right to left, and learned the word emet, truth._

_He gets up, a head taller than Isaac. He stands with his hands open at his sides, and doesn’t speak._  
**Ori**: The alef-bet has twenty-two letters. Alef is number 1, mem is number 13, and tav is number 22.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction: 22 − 13  
> _Tav is the 22nd letter and mem is the 13th. How many letters come after mem?_  
> - ✅ 9 → Yes. 22 − 13 = 9 letters come after mem.
> - 10 → Check it: 22 − 13 = 9. Mem itself is not counted.
> - 8 → Close. 22 − 13 = 9. Count on from 13 to 22 to check.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 13 from 22 to find how many letters follow mem in the alef-bet._

## A30-7. Yossele’s Work

#### `a30-07-chores`

_Yossele lives in the rabbi’s house now, and works wherever he is sent. He fetches water, chops wood and sweeps._  
_He never speaks, and never tires. He never does one thing more than he is told._  
**Avram**: Told to sweep the step, he sweeps the step. Not the step next to it. I find it very restful.  
_Everywhere he goes, your Nubbin goes too, a step behind. When he stops, it stops; when he turns, it turns._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): life in the past and today: getting water  
> _Yossele fetches water every day. In Prague then, where did most families get theirs?_  
> - ✅ From wells, carried home in buckets → Yes. Most homes had no taps, so water was carried, bucket by bucket.
> - From a tap in the kitchen → Taps came much later. Then, someone had to fetch every drop.
> - From the rain only → Rain helped, but families also relied on wells and the river.
> _For grown-ups: Compared how people got water long ago (wells, buckets) with today (taps)._

_He has never once looked down at it. But he has never once stepped on it either._  
**Rivka**: He’s like a big quiet uncle. Without the opinions.  

#### `a30-07-flood`

**Dvora**: Yossele, fill the barrel for me, there’s a dear. I’ll be back before you know it.  
_The barrel holds sixty litres, and Yossele’s bucket holds five._  
_He fills the barrel. Then he fills it again, because nobody has told him to stop._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: 60 ÷ 5  
> _The barrel holds 60 litres and each bucket holds 5. How many bucketfuls fill it exactly?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. 60 ÷ 5 = 12. After the twelfth bucket, the barrel is full.
> - 10 → Check: 10 × 5 = 50, which is not yet 60. You need 12 buckets, since 12 × 5 = 60.
> - 15 → 15 × 5 = 75, which is too much. 12 × 5 = 60, so twelve.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 60 by 5 to find how many bucketfuls fill a barrel._

**Dvora**: Oh, no. No, no, no. Yossele! That’s enough! Enough!

> _Dvora gives you an apron after the flood, “too late, but kindly meant”. What does that show about her?_  
> - ✅ She is kind even when she is upset → Yes. Her kitchen is ruined, and she still thinks of you. That tells us a lot about her.
> - She is angry with you → Look again: she gives you a gift. That is kindness, not anger.
> - She wants you to leave → Look again: she has just handed you a gift. People don’t give aprons to guests they want gone.

> - It depends on the job → That’s a fair answer. Sweeping a step is one thing. Looking after a lane is another.

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): comparing ways to store onions  
> _Dvora hangs the wet onions in a row from the beam, instead of leaving them in a heap._  
> _Why is that a better way to dry them?_  
> - ✅ Air can reach every onion → Yes. Moving air carries the damp away, so the onions dry instead of rotting in a heap.
> - The beam makes them warmer → The beam is just a hook. It is the air all round each onion that does the drying.
> - It looks neater → Neat is nice, but the real reason is the air.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two ways to dry onions, a heap and a hanging row, and chose the one that lets air reach each onion._

## A30-8. The Night Guard

- `a30-08-s1`: Walk the night round with Yossele. · _Every lane, every gate, once. Your Nubbin will try to keep up._
- `a30-08-s2`: Stand with Yossele at the end of the street. · _He knows where to stand. Stand behind him._

#### `a30-08-round`

_At night Yossele walks the lanes of the Jewish Town, end to end, gate to gate. Tonight you walk with him._  
_The round goes once all the way round a block of lanes, fifty metres long and thirty metres wide._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.D.8, ask): perimeter of a rectangle  
> _The round goes once all the way round a block that is 50 m long and 30 m wide. How far is that?_  
> - ✅ 160 m → Yes. 50 + 30 + 50 + 30 = 160 metres, or 2 × (50 + 30).
> - 80 m → That is only two sides, 50 + 30. All four sides make 160 metres.
> - 1,500 m → That is 50 × 30, the area in square metres. Perimeter adds the four sides: 50 + 30 + 50 + 30 = 160 m.
> _For grown-ups: Found the perimeter of a 50 m by 30 m block: 160 metres._

_He goes slowly, and never stops. The houses are dark, and the cobbles are wet, and your footsteps are the only ones._  
_At every gate he puts his hand flat on the wood for a moment, as if to feel whether it is cold._  
_Your Nubbin keeps up for three lanes. On the fourth it sits down in the road, and holds up both arms._  
_Yossele stops. Nobody has told him what to do about this._  
_You lift your Nubbin up and set it on his shoulder, and he walks on._  
_It holds on to his ear, and is asleep in a minute._  

#### `a30-08-street-end`

_At the street’s end there is lantern light again, beyond the gate. Voices, more than last time._  
_Yossele walks to the middle of the street and stands there, in the light, as tall as a door. He does nothing at all._  
_Your Nubbin is still asleep on his shoulder, with one ear in its mouth._  
_The voices stop. For a long moment nobody on the far side moves._  
_Then the lanterns turn, one by one, and go away up the hill, the way lanterns go when people decide they are tired._  
_Yossele stands there till the last one is gone. Then he turns, and goes on with the round._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): whether standing there is protecting  
> _Yossele did nothing but stand there, and the men went home. Does a guard who only stands still protect anyone?_  
> - Yes, being there is enough to keep people safe → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes the sight of someone calm and strong is all it takes.
> - No, a guard must do something → That’s a fair answer. But notice that nobody was hurt, and nobody had to act.
> - It depends on who is watching → That’s a fair answer. A guard only protects if people know he is there.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether simply being present can protect. No single right answer._


**Choices**

- **Stand close behind him.**
    - You stand at his back, close enough to touch. He is warm, like a wall at the end of a sunny day.
- **Hold your Nubbin’s dangling foot.**
    - You reach up and hold your Nubbin’s foot. It curls its toes round your finger in its sleep.

_Word goes round the lanes by breakfast. Nobody says much about it, but everybody says they slept well._  
**Avram**: I slept like a stone. First time in a month. I dreamt about keys.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what helps us sleep when we are worried  
> _Avram hadn’t slept for a month because he was worried. What helps us sleep when we are worried?_  
> - ✅ Telling someone, slow breaths and a calm bedtime → Yes. Sharing the worry and settling the body both help the mind to rest.
> - Staying up and thinking harder → Thinking harder usually keeps us awake. Calm and company work better.
> - Eating a big meal late → A heavy meal at night can make sleep harder. Calm and company work better.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that telling someone, breathing slowly and a calm bedtime help us sleep when worried._

## A30-9. Fridays

- `a30-09-s1`: Find Yossele before the Sabbath comes in. · _Friday afternoon. Everyone is hurrying. Yossele isn’t._

#### `a30-09-friday`

_Friday afternoon. The whole lane is hurrying: floors swept, pots on, children scrubbed whether they like it or not._  
_Hannah’s plaited loaves go past the window in baskets, shining. Everyone is getting ready for the Sabbath._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): the Sabbath as a day of rest  
> _Everyone is hurrying to be ready before sunset. What is the Sabbath for?_  
> - ✅ A day to stop working and rest, together → Yes. It starts at sunset on Friday, and everything is ready beforehand so that everyone, even Yossele, can rest.
> - A day for the longest journeys → Quite the opposite. It is a day to stay and rest, not to rush about.
> - A day for the hardest work → It is the one day when work stops. That is why Friday is so busy.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Sabbath is a day of rest that begins at sunset on Friday._

**Dvora**: The rabbi will want Yossele before sunset. Go and find him, will you? I’ve got four things on the fire.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): one letter can change a word  
> _Rubbing out one letter changed emet into met. Take the first letter off “plane”._  
> _What word is left?_  
> - ✅ lane → Yes. One letter off the front makes a new word. In Hebrew, losing alef changed “truth” into “dead”.
> - plan → That takes the last letter off. Take away the first letter, p, and “lane” is left.
> - pane → That swaps a letter instead. Take the p away and “lane” is left.
> _For grown-ups: Saw that removing one letter can change a word completely, as alef does to emet._

> - 24 hours → Close. 24 hours takes us to 4:30 pm Saturday. One more hour makes 25.
> - 26 hours → Count again: 24 hours, then one more hour to 5:30 pm. That is 25.

### Glossary

- **Sabbath**: The Jewish day of rest, from Friday at sunset to Saturday after dark.

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understanding a simile  
> _The Sabbath comes in “like a tide”. What do the Sabbath and a tide have in common?_  
> - ✅ Both arrive slowly and steadily and can’t be stopped → Yes. A tide creeps in at its own pace, and so does the evening that begins the Sabbath.
> - Both are made of water → The Sabbath isn’t water. The comparison is about the way it arrives.
> - Both are very loud → Tides can be quiet, and the Sabbath comes in softly. It is the slow, steady arrival they share.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile compares: the slow, steady arrival of the Sabbath and a tide._

_Rivka looks down the lane towards the rabbi’s house. Then she grabs your sleeve._  
**Rivka**: He didn’t. Did he? He didn’t lay Yossele down.

> **Lesson** (health, 4-LS1-1, ask): why the heart beats faster when we run  
> _Your heart is thumping after the run. Why does a heart beat faster when you run?_  
> - ✅ Working muscles need more oxygen, so it pumps blood faster → Yes. Your blood carries oxygen to your muscles. When they work hard, the heart pumps faster to keep up.
> - It is trying to stop → Not at all. It speeds up to send more blood to your working muscles.
> - It is tired of beating → A heart never takes a day off. It beats faster because your muscles need more oxygen.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the heart beats faster when we run, to carry more oxygen to working muscles._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): forgiving a mistake made out of gladness  
> _The rabbi forgot because he was busy being glad about a baby. Does that make forgetting easier or harder to forgive?_

> - The same, because the lane still broke → That’s a fair answer. What happened is what happened, whatever the reason.
> - It depends on whether he learns from it → That’s a fair answer. Being sorry and doing better is how we mend a mistake.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.4, ask): refrain and repeated lines  
> _A line or phrase that comes round again and again in a song or poem has a special name. What is it?_  
> - ✅ A refrain → Yes. A refrain returns, like a chorus. Repeating makes a song easy to remember and gives it a steady beat.
> - A riddle → A riddle is a puzzle. A repeated line is a refrain.
> - A review → A review is an opinion about something. A repeated line is a refrain.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a repeated line in a song or poem is a refrain._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): customs of a Sabbath meal  
> _Which of these belong to the Sabbath table in Avram’s house?_  
> - ✅ Lit candles, a white cloth, blessings, and a covered plaited loaf → Yes. These are the signs that the Sabbath has begun, and that the family rests together.
> - A loud party with a band → Not a band. The Sabbath table has blessings and shared bread, and families often sing together.
> - Everyone cooking at once → The cooking is done before sunset. At the table everyone rests.
> _For grown-ups: Named customs of a Sabbath meal: candles, a cloth, blessings and plaited bread._

#### `a30-12-stars`

_Saturday night. Three stars are out over the steep roof, and the Sabbath is over._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): why we see stars only when it is dark  
> _Three stars are out. Why can we see stars at night, but not at noon?_  
> - ✅ They are there all day, but daylight is too bright to see them → Yes. Stars shine all day too. The Sun’s light scattered through the air drowns them out until it is dark.
> - Stars only exist at night → They are always there. Daylight is too bright for us to see them.
> - The Moon pushes them away → The Moon doesn’t move them. It is the brightness of daylight that hides them.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stars are always there, but daylight is too bright for us to see them._

_It fits. Avram looks at it in the lock for a moment, as if it had been waiting twenty years to be useful._  
_You hold the lantern at the foot of the steps. The three of them carry the clay up into the dark._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): treating worn-out holy books with respect  
> _Why do people keep worn-out holy books in a genizah, instead of throwing them in the rubbish?_  
> - ✅ Out of respect for the words they hold → Yes. Words that matter deeply to people are treated with care, even when the pages are worn.
> - Because attics have lots of spare room → Room isn’t the reason. It is about respect for the words.
> - Because books never wear out → They do wear out, which is exactly why there is a place to lay them to rest.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a genizah keeps worn-out holy books respectfully._

#### `a30-13-bench`

_A week later. The rabbi sits on the bench outside the study house in the sun, and moves over to make room._  
**Rabbi Loew**: I have been thinking about my clay man. I think about very little else. My students have noticed.  
**Rabbi Loew**: He was a good guard. He did what he was told, and only that. I wanted that. I asked for it.  
**Rabbi Loew**: But a thing that only obeys has no brakes of its own. All its brakes are in your hands. And hands forget.  
**Rabbi Loew**: I am not the first, you know. In Chełm, they say, a rabbi made one before me, and it grew, and kept growing.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions on a map  
> _Chełm is a town in eastern Poland, east of Prague. If you travelled from Prague to Chełm, which way would you head?_  
> - ✅ East → Yes. Chełm lies to the east of Prague, more than six hundred kilometres away.
> - West → West would take you away from it. Chełm lies to the east of Prague.
> - South → Prague to Chełm is mostly eastward. A compass would point east.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions: Chełm is east of Prague._

**Rabbi Loew**: He was afraid it would fill the world. So he rubbed out the word, very gently, and his clay man lay down and went still for good.  
**Rabbi Loew**: He had more sense than me. He did it before anyone had to run.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): who should hold the brakes  
> _The rabbi says a thing that only obeys has no brakes of its own, so its maker holds them._  
> _Who do you think should hold the brakes?_  
> - The maker, always → That’s a fair answer. But hands forget, as he says.
> - The one who is made, in time → That’s a fair answer. A being with its own brakes can stop itself.
> - Both, together → That’s a fair answer. Two sets of brakes are safer than one.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about who should hold the brakes on something powerful. No single right answer._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a square: 6 × 6  
> _The tile is a square, six centimetres along each side. What is its area?_  
> - ✅ 36 square centimetres → Yes. 6 × 6 = 36 little squares, each one centimetre by one centimetre.
> - 24 square centimetres → That is 4 × 6, the perimeter. Area is 6 × 6 = 36.
> - 12 square centimetres → That is 6 + 6. Area multiplies: 6 × 6 = 36.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a 6 cm square tile: 6 × 6 = 36 square centimetres._

#### `a31-02-court`

_Below the hill is a ballcourt: two long sloping walls, with a strip of beaten earth between them._  
_Two men are playing on it, and they are loud about it. Every point gets a shout, and every miss gets a louder one._  
**Hun Hunahpu**: Mine! That was mine, and you know it.  
**Vucub Hunahpu**: It hit your knee. Knees don’t count. Knees have never counted.

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add and subtract within 100 in a word problem  
> _Hun Hunahpu has scored 7 points and Vucub has scored 5. How many have they scored together?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. 7 + 5 = 12. And Hun is ahead by 2, which he will mention.
> - 11 → Close: count on five from 7, and you get 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. They have 12 together, and Hun leads by 2.
> - 13 → One too many: count on five from 7, and you get 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. The answer is 12.
> _For grown-ups: Added 7 and 5 in a word problem and found the difference._

**Grandmother**: Hun Hunahpu and his brother, Vucub Hunahpu. Good players. Terrible neighbours.
