#### `s29-brock-knock`

_You knock on the little green door. A long way back in the bank, somebody grumbles, and bolts go back: one, two, three, four._  
**Granny Brock**: Daytime. Good. You can come in for ten minutes and get warm. Then I’m busy.  
_Ten minutes turns into an hour by the red fire._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals: minutes in an hour  
> _Ten minutes turned into an hour. How many lots of ten minutes is that?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes. An hour is 60 minutes, and 60 is six tens.
> - 10 → Ten lots of ten would be 100 minutes. An hour is 60: six tens.
> - 4 → Four tens is 40 minutes. An hour is 60, so six tens.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that an hour is six lots of ten minutes._

_She doesn’t say much, and neither do you, and it suits you both._  
**Granny Brock**: Charcoal’s cooling in the yard. Don’t touch it. It looks cold, and it isn’t.  
_When you leave, she says nothing at all, which from Granny Brock is practically a hug._  

#### `s30-wall-s1`

_The frosts have come, and the Grove is white at dawn round the fourth post._  
_You find Moss at the old wall, by Hush’s lantern post, with frost on his back that he hasn’t bothered to shake off._  
**Moss**: Clover’s gold one. Luna told me. Luna tells me things at dawn, when I am too tired to argue.  
**Moss**: You know she sat with the still ones, the ones who had died. You walked here with me, and heard her ask to be kept.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history  
> _Moss remembers Hush and tells her story aloud. Passing history on by telling it is called oral history._  
> _For most of history, that was how families and villages remembered their past._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what oral history is and how stories carry the past._

**Moss**: I never told you what she thought sad was for.  
**Moss**: People thought it made her a sad thing, the sitting. They were wrong about which part was sad.  
**Moss**: Low in the wall. The flat stone, by your foot. Look at it properly. She meant it to be looked at.  

#### `s30-hole-youngest`

_Then your youngest Nubbin comes down the bank: the one Fossil sat with until dark. It climbs into the hole and sits on Dusty’s boot._  
**Dusty**: Oh, not you as well.  
_Dusty laughs, wetly, gets mud in their mouth, and laughs at that too._  
**Dusty**: She trained you both. Didn’t she. The old madam. Sat on a sill for twenty years and trained the lot of you.  
_Fossil never said a word. She taught by doing, and they learned by watching._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): learning from example  
> _We often learn kindness the way these Nubbins did: by seeing it done, and having it done to us._  
> _For grown-ups: Discussed how kindness is learned by example._

_Dusty wipes their eyes again. This time it doesn’t make it worse._  

#### `s30-gone-helped`

_Early autumn. Clover is at your gate before it is light, in her dressing gown and wellies._  
**Clover**: She’s gone. Dimple. Her basket was cold when I got up.  
**Clover**: She’s taken nothing but the cushion off the sill. Fossil’s cushion, toys and all.  
**Clover**: What does she want with it? She’s done nothing but pile rubbish on it for weeks.  
**Clover**: Drizzle’s under the rain butt and won’t budge. The others are in a heap. I didn’t know who else to come to.  
_Dusty is coming up the lane with a spade on one shoulder. One look at Clover, and they put the spade down._  
**Dusty**: She’s going back to where the happy was. I would. I’ve been trying to all summer.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): inference  
> _“Back to where the happy was.” Where do you think Dimple has gone?_  
> - ✅ Somewhere she was happy with Fossil → That’s a good inference. She took Fossil’s cushion, so it’s somewhere Fossil belonged.
> - To a party → A fair guess after Sparks! But she took Fossil’s cushion, so it’s somewhere Fossil belonged.
> _For grown-ups: Made an inference from clues (the cushion, Dusty’s words)._

_The three of you set off down the lane in the half dark._  

#### `s30-trail-s5`

_On the bank of your pond, where you held Fossil up in the shallows, there is a sock, laid out neatly._  
_Under Hazel’s crooked tree, half a wooden peg, just where the wrinkled fruit once fell into Fossil’s lap._  
**Dusty**: She’s doing the walk. Fossil’s walk. Backwards. The water, the tree, the cliff.  

> **Lesson** (maths, ask): reversing a sequence  
> _Fossil’s walk went cliff, tree, water. Dimple walks it backwards. Which place is second for both of them?_  
> - ✅ The tree → Yes. Reverse a list of three, and the middle stays in the middle.
> - The cliff → The cliff was first for Fossil and last for Dimple. The middle one, the tree, stays put.
> _For grown-ups: Reversed a sequence and noticed the middle stays in place._

**Dusty**: I told it at Clover’s table every night for a fortnight. I thought she was asleep under the sill.  
_From the tree the trail runs east along the stream, a pine cone, then a cotton reel, towards the striped cliff._  
_At the foot of the cliff the rock is striped like a cake. Where it meets the ground, there is a hollow, dug down and in._  
**Dusty**: That’s it. The spoon hole. Where I dug her out. Two days, with a spoon.  
_Dimple is down in it, on Fossil’s cushion, scraping at the back of the hollow as if there might be another egg._  
_The hollow is only waist-deep on you, but on a Nubbin the lip is a cliff. She can’t climb out, and she hasn’t tried._  
**Dimple**: …  

#### `s30-hollow-helped`

_Drizzle is at home under the rain butt. So it is you who climbs down, carefully, and sits in the dust at the back of the hollow._  
_Dimple turns, and the smile goes on like a lamp. She bounces at you, and offers you a pebble, a root, a handful of dust._  
_She performs. She runs the streamer race on her own in a space the size of a bath, and does the hat toss without a hat._  
_You don’t clap, and you don’t stop her. Your knees go cold, and then numb._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): staying without fixing  
> _Why might it help not to clap, and not to stop her either?_  
> - ✅ So she doesn’t have to perform, and doesn’t feel told off → Yes. Clapping keeps the show going; stopping her feels like a scolding. Staying lets her stop herself.
> - Because clapping is rude → Not rude. But clapping keeps the show going. Staying quietly lets her stop when she’s ready.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be with a friend without pushing or fixing._

**Clover**: Shall I come down? I should come down. I’m her… I should…  
**Dusty**: Leave them a minute. Look at her. She’s nearly out of tricks.  
_It takes a long time. It takes longer than the party did._  

#### `s30-hollow-youngest`

_Your youngest Nubbin goes over the lip after them, sliding down on its bottom, and sits on Dimple’s other side._  
_Fossil sat with it once, until dark. It seems to remember how._  
**Dusty**: Course it does.  
_Now there is somebody on each side of Dimple, like bookends._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): similes  
> _Bookends hold up the books between them from both sides. The simile shows Dimple held up, one friend each side._  
> _For grown-ups: Explained a simile about support._

_Nobody up at the rim says anything. Clover holds Dusty’s sleeve, and Dusty lets her._  
_Down in the hollow, nobody moves, and nobody hurries anybody._  

#### `s30-hill-helped`

_That afternoon Dimple walks up the hill. Not on anyone’s shoulder: up the path, past the halfway place, on her own feet._  
_You walk beside her, and every few steps she checks you are still there. Dusty walks behind with Fossil’s cushion._  
_At the top is Fossil’s flower, sandstone-coloured, a little bent by the frost. Dimple sits down in front of it._  
_You sit on one side of her. Dusty sits on the other, cross-legged, and sets the cushion in the grass, dent up._  
_Nobody does anything. The wind goes over, and down in the valley somebody is burning leaves._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): grief and remembering  
> _Going to a special place to remember someone is one way people grieve. It doesn’t make the missing stop._  
> _But it gives the missing somewhere to sit, with friends beside you._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about visiting a special place as one way to remember someone who has died._

_Your Nubbin, who has copied Dimple all autumn, comes and sits down too. It copies the sitting perfectly._  

#### `s30-complete-helped`

_On the way home you stop at the old wall. Clover holds the paper flat; you rub over Hush’s stone with a stub of charcoal._  
_The marks come up black and fine under your hand: rings, and lines, and rings with lines through them._  

> **Lesson** (art, do): texture rubbing  
> _(Rub the charcoal over the paper on the stone.)_  
> _A rubbing copies texture: the raised parts catch the charcoal, the scratches stay pale. Try it on a leaf or a coin at home._  
> Check: `edu:rub:texture:hush-stone`
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a rubbing records the texture of a surface._

**Clover**: Dimple ought to have a mark of her own. On her page. A proper one.  
_In the clean corner of the paper, you draw it for her: a ring with a line through it._  
_Clover takes the charcoal and draws one more beside it, small and close: a plain ring, just touching. Yours._  
**Clover**: That’s the both one. That’s her now.  
_That night you write it up: Hush’s stone, and a page for each of your Nubbins, ringed and lined from what you remember._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): reflecting on feelings  
> _If you made a mark for today, which would it be?_  
> - A ring: a joy kept → A good day to keep. Hush would have scratched it carefully.
> - A line: a grief kept → That’s allowed. A line kept is a lantern lit. Someone will find you.
> - Both: a ring with a line through it → Like Dimple. Like most things, Moss would say.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on their own feelings using Hush’s marks (no single right answer)._

_In the morning there is a parcel on your step: a pale-blue rain hat, and Fossil’s cushion, plumped for the first time in years._  
_The note says Fossil would want it sat on, not kept. Sparks has added a blue-and-gold ribbon, dyed twice._  

#### `s30-after-clover`

_Clover’s shed door stands half shut every dusk now. Fidget sees to it herself; she has decided half is the right amount._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.G.A.3, notice): halves  
> _Half shut is also half open: two equal halves make the whole doorway. Fidget’s fudge, in fractions._  
> _For grown-ups: Saw that two halves make a whole._

_On the deep kitchen sill, Dimple and Drizzle sleep in the sun, gold and pale blue, one pressed against the other._  
**Clover**: She still smiles most of the day. I wouldn’t change it. And now when she isn’t, I know where to look.  
**Clover**: I look at the ball now as well as the face. Took me long enough.  
_Fidget trots past with a tea towel, counting. She counts you twice, to be sure._  
**Clover**: She’s settling. Half shut. That’s progress, that is.  

#### `s30-after-dusty`

**Dusty**: I go up and sit with Fossil on Thursdays. Dimple comes. Gets there first, some weeks. Waits for me.  
**Dusty**: We don’t do anything. It’s the best bit of the week. Don’t tell Clover. She’ll bring a flask.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): remembering together  
> _Remembering someone with a friend can make the missing feel lighter. Dusty and Dimple carry it between them._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about sharing memories of someone with a friend._

_Dusty turns a striped pebble over in their fingers, a little piece of the cliff._  
**Dusty**: I still count the bit, you know. Twenty years and a bit. The bit’s getting longer.  
**Dusty**: That’s all right. It’s meant to.  
_They put the pebble back in their pocket, carefully, like a letter._  

#### `s30-after-byte`

**Byte**: I’m keeping the chart. For science. Dimple’s ball, every time I see her.  
**Byte**: Mostly gold. Sometimes blue. Sometimes both, which my scale didn’t cover, so I drew a new column. It’s my favourite column.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.B.3, ask): reading a scaled bar chart  
> **Byte**: This week: gold 12, blue 4, both 6. How many more gold than both?  
> - ✅ 6 → Six. 12 − 6 = 6. Logged.
> - 8 → That’s gold minus blue: 12 − 4. Gold minus both is 12 − 6 = 6.
> - 18 → That’s gold plus both. “How many more” means subtract: 12 − 6 = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two bars on a chart by subtracting (12 − 6 = 6)._

**Byte**: Also she pulled my laces on Tuesday. Both of them. I’ve logged it as a result.  
_He shows you the chart. The “both” column has been drawn in twice, in two colours of pencil._  
**Byte**: Single knots, still. Obviously. For science.  
_He tucks the chart away before you can say anything about it._  

#### `s30-after-sparks`

**Sparks**: I sat still! On the hill! With Dimple! For…  
**Sparks**: Fifty-one seconds. Byte timed it. Nearly a minute. That’s a personal best. That’s a valley record.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): seconds in a minute  
> **Sparks**: A minute is sixty seconds. How many more seconds would I need for a whole minute?  
> - ✅ 9 → Nine! 60 − 51 = 9. Next time. Probably. Maybe.
> - 19 → Count up from 51: 52, 53… 60. That’s nine. 60 − 51 = 9.
> - 49 → That’s too many! Count up from 51 to 60: just nine seconds.
> _For grown-ups: Used 1 minute = 60 seconds to find a difference (60 − 51 = 9)._

**Sparks**: It was really nice. It was horrible. It was really nice.  
_Sparks is bouncing on her toes as she says it, which rather spoils the effect._  
**Sparks**: Next time, a whole minute. I’m training. I sat through a boiled egg yesterday.  
**Sparks**: Dimple didn’t even need a party. She just needed someone to stay. Who knew?  

#### `s31-guising-sat`

_Late in the evening a ghost comes back up the lane on its own, dragging its bag. It stops at the edge of the long grass._  
**Ned**: Hello. I came to see if he’d come yet.  
**Tam**: Not yet. He’s busy being sincere somewhere.  
**Nettie**: What did you get? Did you get toffee? I didn’t want any. I’m only asking.  
_Ned turns his bag upside down. Five rocks come out, one after another, with a sound like somebody walking on a beach._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): multiply and convert grams to kilograms  
> **Ned**: Each rock weighs about 200 grams. I’ve got five. How heavy is my bag?  
> - ✅ 1 kilogram → Yes. 5 × 200 g = 1,000 g, and 1,000 grams is 1 kilogram. A whole bag of sugar, in rocks.
> - 205 grams → That adds 5 and 200. But there are five rocks of 200 g each: 5 × 200 = 1,000 g, which is 1 kilogram.
> - 100 grams → Lighter than one rock! Five rocks of 200 g make 1,000 g. That’s 1 kilogram.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 5 × 200 g and converted 1,000 grams to 1 kilogram._

_One of them has a little paper label tied on with string._  

#### `s31-guising-party`

_Halfway through the party, the guisers come in on a gust of cold air: a witch, three bats, and a ghost made mostly of holes._  
_The bats and the witch tip their bags out on Sparks’s workbench. Toffee apples, nuts, pennies, a whole honey cake._  
_Ned tips his out last. Five rocks come out, one after another, and roll in among the spanners._  
**Sparks**: Oh, Ned.  
_Pixel stops playing the pianola in the middle of a tune, out of respect._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): empathy: helping someone who feels left out  
> _Everyone is looking at Ned’s rocks. What could the others do that would actually help him?_  
> - ✅ Share some treats, without making a fuss about it → Yes. Quiet sharing helps without making Ned feel more singled out.
> - Laugh, so it feels like a joke → Sometimes laughing together helps, but Ned isn’t laughing. Quietly sharing treats is kinder.
> - Pretend not to notice → That avoids embarrassing him, which is thoughtful. Sharing a few treats as well would help even more.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to help a friend who feels left out without embarrassing him._

_One of the rocks has a little paper label tied on with string._  

#### `s31-if-away`

_Nearly midnight. Three lanterns burn steady across the Grove, and the fourth post stands dark over the long grass._  
_Two small shapes sit beside it under a patchwork quilt and a borrowed blanket. The spare blanket stays folded on the sign._  
_Along the far hedge Luna’s lantern moves slowly, as it does every night. Tonight it passes the long grass more often than usual._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): staying safe: grown-ups knowing where you are  
> _Who knows exactly where Tam and Nettie are tonight?_  
> - ✅ Ivy, Mum, Clover and Luna → Right. Ivy told Mum and Clover, Clover’s lamp is lit, and Luna keeps passing. Being alone in the dark isn’t the same as being unwatched.
> - Nobody → Look again: Ivy told Mum and Clover, and Luna’s lantern keeps passing. Lots of people know.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how the grown-ups kept the children safe by knowing where they were._

**Nettie**: Tam. What if he isn’t coming?  
**Tam**: He’s coming. When he comes, I’ll put in a good word for everybody. The Keeper, even. Even though they went.  
**Tam**: If he comes, I’ll ask… If. I said “if”. Out loud. In the patch.  
_He pulls the quilt over his head. Nettie pats it, the way you pat a dog that has been told off._  

#### `s31-midnight-wisp`

_Just after midnight, something thin and grey comes out of the dark under the hedge. One of its ears is torn to a fringe._  
_It goes straight to the sign, takes Tam’s toffee apple off the top, hanky and all, and carries it a little way off._  
_Then it sits down in full view and eats it, very loudly, with its back to them._  
**Tam**: Is that him?  
**Nettie**: That’s a thief.  
_Wisp licks the hanky clean, thanks nobody, and goes back under the hedge._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness, need and taking  
> _Think: the toffee apple was left out for someone hungry. Wisp was hungry. Was it stealing?_  
> - Yes. It wasn’t meant for him. → That’s a fair point. Things can be meant for someone in particular.
> - No. It was left out for a hungry visitor, and he was one. → A generous reading. Tam might even come round to it, one day.
> - It’s complicated. Animals don’t know our rules. → True. Wisp doesn’t know our rules. He only knew he was hungry, and there it was.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness, need, and whether animals can steal._


#### `s31-shape-sable`

_A grey shape rises out of the white grass by the post. It comes slowly, and the frost doesn’t seem to touch it at all._  
_Tam takes one look, says “Oh,” very politely, and faints clean away._  
_It is Sable. The frost can’t do anything more to her than it has already done._  
_She looks at Tam, flat out in his quilt. Then she looks at you, for a long time._  
_Then she sits down beside you, close enough to touch, and faces the dark lane with you._  
_Sable says nothing. Her ears stay up._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): reading body language; trust  
> _Animals can’t tell you how they feel, but their bodies can. Ears up and sitting close means calm and paying attention._  
> _Sable has chosen to sit near you. With a wary animal, that is a big thing. The kindest answer is to stay still._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned to read an animal’s body language and to respond calmly to its trust._

_You don’t say anything either._  

#### `s31-shape-away`

_A shape rises at the edge of the white grass, where the frost hasn’t reached. Round, and goggled, and trailing a scarf._  
_Tam takes one look, says “Oh,” very politely, and faints clean away._  
_You come back down the lane with a lantern before it’s light. Tam is asleep in his quilt, and your Nubbin is asleep on top of him._  
**Nettie**: Your Nubbin came out of the grass in its glasses, and he FAINTED, and I’ve been the only one awake for HOURS.  
**Nettie**: I didn’t get any toffee. I didn’t get ANYTHING. I sat in a field.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): managing big feelings: tiredness makes anger bigger  
> _Nettie is furious, cold and very tired. What would help her most right now?_  
> - ✅ Listen, say sorry you weren’t there, and get her warm → Yes. Tired, cold anger needs listening and a blanket more than arguments.
> - Explain why you went → Explaining can wait. First she needs to be heard, and warmed up.
> - Tell her to calm down → Being told to calm down rarely works. Listening and a blanket help much more.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps someone who is angry, tired and cold._


#### `s31-four-sable`

_At four o’clock exactly, a lantern comes bobbing down the lane, grumbling._  
**Ivy**: Four o’clock. I said four. Look at the state of…  
_She sees Sable. Ivy has an opinion on everything, and she hasn’t got one about this._  
_She hands her lantern to Nettie and lifts Tam, quilt and all. He doesn’t wake._  
_On the way past, she drops a blanket on you without looking._  
**Ivy**: You look frozen. It’s very stupid, sitting out all night. I’m not saying anything nice about it.  
_Sable doesn’t move. She lets Ivy pass within an arm’s length, and only her ears turn._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): animals’ senses: moveable ears  
> _Many animals can swivel their ears to point at a sound, while their head stays still._  
> _It lets them track a footstep without moving. Your ears can’t turn, so you have to turn your whole head._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals can turn their ears to track sounds._

_Ivy goes off up the lane with Tam, and Nettie trots after with the lantern, yawning, very small._  

#### `s31-four-away`

_At four o’clock exactly, a lantern comes bobbing down the lane, grumbling._  
**Ivy**: Four o’clock. I said four. Look at the state of him.  
_She looks at Tam, asleep in his quilt, and doesn’t laugh. She lifts him, quilt and all._  
_She doesn’t look at you. There is a blanket over her arm, and she keeps it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how a character responds to events  
> _Think: Ivy keeps the blanket this time, and doesn’t look at you. Why might that be?_  
> - She’s cross that I went off and didn’t stay. → That fits. Ivy often shows what she thinks by what she does, not what she says.
> - I wasn’t out in the cold all night, so I don’t need it. → A sharp eye. The blanket was for someone frozen, and tonight that isn’t you.
> - She’s cold herself. → Could be. It’s four in the morning. But she doesn’t look at you, either, and that says something too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what Ivy’s actions, not her words, might mean._

**Ivy**: Nettie. Home.  
_Nettie stamps off up the lane after them with the lantern, furious all the way, and very small._  

#### `s31-light-sable`

_Up the lane, a light goes on in the end cottage. Ivy gets Tam up the stairs, takes his boots off, and tucks him in._  
_Sable stays beside you until it is light. Neither of you moves._  
_When the sun reaches the top of the hill, she gets up, shakes the frost off her back, and goes to see about breakfast._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, notice): why frost ends the gourd season  
> _Frost is the end of the year for gourd vines. After a hard frost, their leaves go black and limp._  
> _Squash plants are tender. When the water inside their leaves freezes, sharp ice crystals break the leaves apart._  
> _That’s why growers pick every gourd before the first frost. Hardier plants, like kale, can survive it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why frost kills tender plants like squashes, and why gourds are picked before it comes._

_Tam’s sign is still standing, WELCOME GREAT GOURD, with the R still backwards for luck._  

#### `s31-promise-went`

_When Ned has gone home, Tam turns round on the wall and looks at you, and then looks away._  
**Tam**: I don’t need anybody, you know. To wait. I can do it on my own. I nearly did.  
**Tam**: Nettie doesn’t count. She was asleep for the important bit.  
_He gets down off the wall and goes home, holding his quilt up off the mud._  
_Next morning there is a second sign in the long grass, smaller, beside the first. It is painted on the lid of a biscuit tin._  
_It says: SEAT FOR A KEEPER (IF)._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character says versus what he means  
> _Tam says he doesn’t need anybody. Then he paints a seat for you. What does the “(IF)” tell you?_  
> - ✅ He hopes you’ll come, but he’s scared to count on it → Yes. The sign is an invitation, and the brackets protect him in case you don’t.
> - He doesn’t want you there → Then why paint a seat? The “(IF)” is him being careful with his hopes.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s real feelings from his actions and a small detail._


#### `s31-complete-strays`

_Next morning, Tam is down at the long grass before anyone else is up. By the foot of his sign, someone has left something._  
_A small heap of fruit: six windfall plums, two apples, and a pear with one bite out of it. Someone has left it for the strays._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): total and share equally  
> _Six plums, two apples and a pear. If three strays share all of it equally, how many pieces does each get?_  
> - ✅ 3 each → Yes. 6 + 2 + 1 = 9 pieces, and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 each. The bitten pear counts.
> - 2 each → Count them all first: 6 + 2 + 1 = 9. Then 9 ÷ 3 = 3 each.
> - 9 each → 9 is the whole heap. Shared between three strays, 9 ÷ 3 = 3 each.
> _For grown-ups: Added three groups to make 9, then divided 9 equally by 3._

**Tam**: He got the letter. He couldn’t carry it all the way to the Hollow, so he left it here for us to take.  
_You put it out at the edge of the Grove that evening. By morning it has all gone, and nobody saw who ate it._  
_Sparks won’t take the goggles back. She says they’ve seen action now, and it would be wrong._  
_Your gourd lantern goes on the wall by the gate, where it can be seen from the air._  

#### `s31-complete-busy`

_Next morning, Tam is down at the long grass before anyone else is up. By the foot of his sign, someone has left something._  
_…Or hasn’t. There is nothing at all: just the sign, the frost going off it, and the long grass._  
**Tam**: Nothing. He didn’t come and he didn’t send anything. Because we said he needn’t, if he was busy.  
**Tam**: So he was busy. And he was polite back. That’s proof, that is.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): evidence and reasoning: what counts as proof  
> _Think: Tam says nothing turning up is proof. Is it?_  
> - Not really. Nothing would turn up either way. → A sharp answer. Proof should be something that wouldn’t happen if you were wrong.
> - For Tam, yes. It fits what he asked for. → That’s kind. It does match his letter, even if it can’t prove it.
> - It doesn’t matter. It makes him happy. → Sometimes that is the point. Moss would probably agree with you.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what counts as proof, and when it matters._

_Sparks won’t take the goggles back. She says they’ve seen action now, and it would be wrong._  
_Your gourd lantern goes on the wall by the gate, where it can be seen from the air._  

#### `s31-ambient-tam`

**Tam**: I’m practising sitting. For next year. You have to start early or your knees go.  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): keeping joints warm and moving in the cold  
> _Tam is half right. Muscles and joints feel stiff when they’re cold and still. Moving about now and then keeps them comfortable._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that cold, still muscles stiffen and moving helps._


#### `s31-ambient-ivy`

**Ivy**: I’ve told Tam the Great Gourd isn’t real eleven times. He writes it down each time. I think he’s keeping score.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.D.10, do): tally marks in groups of five  
> _Draw Tam’s tally of eleven: two gates of five (four lines and one across), then one more line._  
> Check: `edu:tally:times:11`
> _For grown-ups: Drew eleven as tally marks in groups of five._


#### `s31-ambient-ned`

**Ned**: I gave my best rock away. Byte says I can start again. He’s bringing me a granite.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): granite and basalt: slow and fast cooling make different crystals  
> _Granite also starts as melted rock, but it cools slowly, deep underground, so its crystals grow big enough to see._  
> _Basalt cools fast, so its crystals stay tiny. Same start, different speed, different rock._  
> _For grown-ups: Compared granite and basalt by how fast they cooled._


#### `s31-ambient-nettie`

**Nettie**: I’m going guising next year. I’ve decided. Unless Tam says.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): making your own decisions  
> _Nettie is learning that she can choose for herself. It’s fine to listen to a friend, and fine to decide differently._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about making your own decisions while still caring about friends._


#### `s31-ambient-lantern`

**Tam**: Did you see? The fourth one lit. By itself. At dawn. Nobody touched it.  
**Tam**: It was him. The Great Gourd. I told you that patch was sincere.  
**Tam**: Ivy says he’s very late. I say he’s very thorough.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): word choice changes meaning  
> _“Late” and “thorough” describe the same wait. One makes it sound like a failure; the other makes it sound careful._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how choosing a word changes how something sounds._


#### `a02-15-which-monk`

_The two Monkeys tumble down out of the sky and land in the road in front of the monk, still fighting._  
_One of them steps back, and the other steps back too, in exactly the same way. Both look at you._  
**Monkey**: On White Tiger Ridge you took his side, not mine. You said you can’t strike on a hunch.  
**Monkey**: On White Tiger Ridge you took his side, not mine. You said you can’t strike on a hunch.  
_Two voices, one sentence. Both faces are looking at you, hopeful and furious, exactly alike._  
**Monkey**: So no hunches now, Cousin’s keeper. Tell them. Which one of us is me?  
_Your Nubbin is holding both their tails, one in each paw, and won’t let go of either._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): a rule you made yourself (a think question)  
> _On the ridge you said you cannot strike on a hunch, and now you cannot tell which Monkey is real. Does that rule still help?_  
> _There is no single right answer. Think about it, then choose._  
> - Yes: it tells me not to guess → That is a fair answer. The rule you chose before protects you now from a confident mistake.
> - It helps, but I still need a way to find out → That is a fair answer. A rule keeps us from harm, and finding the answer needs some other tool.
> _For grown-ups: Your child applied a rule they had chosen to a new problem._


**Choices**

- **Point at the one on the left.**
    - **Monkey**: Ha! You see? The little luggage-carrier knows me.
    - **Monkey**: Ha! You see? The little luggage-carrier knows me.
    - They say it at the same moment, in the same voice, with the same grin. Your pointing finger feels very foolish.
    - **Monkey**: That settles nothing, Cousin’s keeper. I’m sorry I asked.
- **Point at the one on the right.**
    - **Monkey**: There! Somebody with eyes in their head at last.
    - **Monkey**: There! Somebody with eyes in their head at last.
    - Both of them bow to you. Both bows are exactly as deep, and exactly as rude.
    - **Monkey**: That settles nothing, Cousin’s keeper. I’m sorry I asked.
- **Say it plainly: “I can’t tell. I won’t pretend I can.”**
    - Both Monkeys open their mouths, and then neither of them says anything at all.
    - **Monkey**: Good. Everyone else has been guessing, and guessing is how you lose a monk.
    - **Sandy**: Then we stop asking people who can’t know, and go to the one who does.

#### `a02-19-complete-monk`

**Monkey**: Gone. It went when I stopped needing it. Of course it did.  
_He turns to you. His eyes are still little suns, but kinder now, the way the sun is kinder in the evening._  
**Monkey**: On the ridge you took his side. I was so angry. You were right not to just take my word, though.  
**Tang Sanzang**: And he was right about the demon. We were both a little right. That is how it usually goes.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): two people can both be partly right  
> _The monk says, “We were both a little right.” Can two people who disagree both be partly right?_  
> - ✅ Yes: each may see a different part of the truth → Yes. Hearing the other side can show us the part we missed.
> - No: one must be wrong → Sometimes, but not always. Often each sees part of it.
> _For grown-ups: Your child considered that two people can each be partly right._

_Monkey plucks a hair and blows on it. It becomes a thin gold band, just Nubbin-sized._  
**Monkey**: This one does nothing at all. It doesn’t tighten. It doesn’t come off unless you want it to. That’s the best kind.  
**Monkey**: And here. A little cloud. For when your Grove feels too big. Somersault, Cousin, and there you are.  
_Your Nubbin tries the cloud at once, rolls over twice, and lands in your arms. Then the page turns, and you are home._  

> **Lesson** (art, ELOF: Approaches to Learning, do): make a shadow puppet  
> _(Hold your hand between a lamp and a wall. Shape a monkey with your fingers, and make it somersault across the wall.)_  
> Check: `edu:shadow:hand:monkey`
> _For grown-ups: Your child made a shadow puppet with their hands._


#### `a05-09-chamber-done-lullaby`

_Balla plays Sogolon’s lullaby. On this balafon it is huge and slow, like a grinding stone going round under the whole of Sosso._  
_Your Nubbin sways, and the owls close their eyes. Somewhere below, a door bangs, and heavy feet climb the stairs fast._  
_Soumaoro Kanté fills the doorway, tall, in a cloak the colour of iron, his face like thunder. Then he hears the tune._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: My mother hummed that. At night, at the grinding stone, when she thought I was asleep.  

> **Lesson** (music, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): music can bring back memories of people we love  
> _Soumaoro, the fearsome king, is stopped by a lullaby, because it reminds him of his mother._  
> _Music and memory are closely linked: a tune heard long ago can bring back a person, a place and a whole feeling, years later._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that music can bring back memories and feelings of people we love._

**Soumaoro Kanté**: Nobody touches that balafon.  
_Balla doesn’t stop. He plays the tune to its end, then moves into a praise song for Soumaoro._  
_It names the forges, his fathers and the walls of Sosso, and gets every one right._  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Hm.  
**Soumaoro Kanté**: Dankaran Touman sent you as a gift, griot. I think he gave me more than he knew. You stay here, and you play for me.  
_Balla bows. When he straightens, he looks at you once, and you understand: he isn’t free, but he isn’t finished._  

#### `a05-14-complete-lullaby`

_The ring falls quiet. Balla stands before the kings to tell, for the first time, the story of Sundiata._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Before I begin, my apprentice’s round friend will play us in. It learned the tune I’d have chosen myself.  
_Your Nubbin plays Sogolon’s lullaby on Balla’s balafon. Thousands of people go quiet to hear it._  
**Kolonkan**: That’s our mother’s grinding tune. She never knew anyone heard it.  
**Sundiata**: She’d be cross to be the first thing in the story. Then she’d be very pleased.  
**Balla Fasséké**: Eight hundred years from now, my children’s children will still be telling this. And they’ll argue about it.  
**Balla Fasséké**: That’s how you know a story is alive. Nobody argues about a dead one.  
_He puts the little balafon into your arms, and the beaters into your Nubbin’s hands._  
**Balla Fasséké**: Go home, apprentice. Remember us properly.  
_The red earth goes soft under your feet, then smooth, then paper._  
_You are back in the Grove with Nova’s atlas on your knee. From under the cover a tune keeps going, and your Nubbin taps it out, very nearly in time._  

> **Lesson** (music, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the balafon today: the Sosso-Bala is still kept in Niagassola  
> _A very old balafon called the Sosso-Bala is still kept in Niagassola, in Guinea, by Kouyaté families._  
> _Tradition says it is Soumaoro’s own great balafon, the one Balla played in the tower._  
> _UNESCO lists its tradition as heritage worth protecting._  
> _Balafons are still played at weddings, celebrations and ceremonies across West Africa, and the keys are still tuned by ear._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the balafon tradition is alive today, and that the Sosso-Bala is kept in Niagassola, Guinea._

_You think about what you chose to keep, and what a griot would keep for you._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): later Mali: Mansa Musa and the libraries of Timbuktu  
> _Less than a hundred years after Sundiata, Mali’s most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made a celebrated journey to Mecca._  
> _He carried so much gold that people talked about it for generations._  
> _Under later Malian and Songhai rulers, Timbuktu became a centre of learning._  
> _Its libraries still hold hundreds of thousands of handwritten manuscripts: science, law, poetry and history._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that Mansa Musa ruled Mali less than a century later, and that Timbuktu’s libraries hold ancient manuscripts._


#### `a06-margin-hazel`

_In the margin beside the round city, in soft pencil you have never noticed before, there is a note. You know the hand._  
_“Seven voyages, and he still came home to tell it to a porter. Somebody has to stay put and listen. I volunteer. H.”_  
_Underneath, smaller, is a whale drawn in three quick lines, with a tree growing out of its back._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): a margin note is a quiet conversation across time  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: the margin is the empty edge of a page. Readers have always written notes there, and a note can talk to every later reader.  
> **Nova**: Hazel’s note is short and warm and a bit funny, like her. A margin note is how a reader says, “I was here, and I thought about this.”  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a margin note is a reader’s message to later readers._


#### `a06-05-complete-left`

_The carpet and the cushions are back, and the porter is holding his breath._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: I came home rich. I gave a good part to the poor, as you should, and then I sat on the rest and got bored.  
_Your pockets are empty. The porter notices you checking them._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Nothing? You were in a valley of diamonds, and you brought back nothing?  
**Sinbad the Porter**: That’s either very wise or very silly. I’ll think about it tonight.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): think: is leaving something behind wise or silly?  
> _The porter can’t decide whether leaving the diamonds was wise or silly. What do you think? There’s no single right answer._  
> - Wise: some things are better left than owned. → A fair answer. Not everything beautiful needs to be taken home.
> - Silly: the stone could have helped the porter. → A fair answer. A small stone could have meant a lot to a poor friend. It’s a real cost.
> - Neither: it was your choice, and a choice can be both. → A thoughtful answer. Choices often hold a gain and a loss together.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on whether choosing to take nothing was wise or silly, with no right answer._

**Sinbad the Sailor**: Everything I brought out of that valley, I spent. You can’t spend what you left there.  

#### `a06-14-complete-kept`

_Sinbad stays. A season passes in a page: a dry season, then the rains._  
_Three times the herd walks past the master’s gate, slow and huge and calm. Three times they harm nothing, not even his garden._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, do): seasons and the rains  
> _A dry season, then the rains. In many hot lands the year has wet and dry seasons instead of winter and summer. Put the two in order of the story._  
> Check: `edu:order:seasons:rains`
> _For grown-ups: Put a dry season and a rainy season in order, as in many hot lands._

**The Ivory Merchant**: Three times. They could flatten this house in a minute, and they walk round my beans.  
**The Ivory Merchant**: I’m done. No more arrows. No more hunting, not by me, and not by anyone I pay.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): seeing kindness can change a mind  
> _The master changed his mind not because he was argued with, but because he watched the herd and saw gentleness he hadn’t expected._  
> _Changing your mind when you learn something new is a strength, not a weakness. It takes courage to say, “I was wrong.”_  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that observing kindness can change a mind and that changing one’s mind takes courage._

**The Ivory Merchant**: Go home, Sinbad. You’re free. I’ve nothing to give you, and I’m sorry for that.  
**Young Sinbad**: You’re giving me home. That’s plenty.  

#### `a06-15-quay-kept`

_Sinbad comes home late, on the last of the winds, on a ship that carries him for nothing, with only a staff and a borrowed cloak._  
_From Basra he walks the river road to Baghdad, because he can’t pay for a boat. It takes eleven days._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Sinbad walks about 40 kilometres a day. How far does he walk in eleven days?_  
> - ✅ 440 kilometres. → Yes! 40 × 11 = 440 km: about the real distance from Basra to Baghdad by the river road.
> - 51 kilometres. → That adds 40 + 11. Forty kilometres a day for eleven days is 40 × 11 = 440 km.
> - 400 kilometres. → That is 40 × 10. There are eleven days, so it’s 40 × 11 = 440 km.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 40 km × 11 days = 440 km._

**Young Sinbad**: Home. Poor, late, and in one piece. That still counts.  
_At the palace he tells the Caliph that the King of Serendib is reading. The Caliph thanks him, and gives him supper._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): contentment  
> _Sinbad is poor, but calm. That’s contentment: feeling you have enough, whatever you carry._  
> _Contentment isn’t the same as giving up. Sinbad still cares, and still tells the truth. He just no longer needs more to feel at peace._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the meaning of contentment._

**Young Sinbad**: Fair enough. He doesn’t owe me for elephants.  
**Young Sinbad**: Seven times. And I swear it now, in front of you two: there is no eighth.  
_For once, he keeps it. You can tell, because the old man in the long room is sitting so very still._  

**Choices**

- **Say you believe him this time.**
    - **Young Sinbad**: So do I. That’s new.
- **Ask how long it will last.**
    - **Young Sinbad**: Ha! Fair.
    - **Young Sinbad**: This time, for good. I’ve nothing left to go to sea for, and I find I don’t mind.

#### `a06-15-street-kept`

_The carpet turns back into a carpet. The old man is smiling down at his own hands._  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: I came home with nothing that time. It’s the voyage I’m proudest of.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Nothing? After all that?  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Not a coin. I sat on the steps of this house, which was shut up, and I didn’t have the key.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: Then tonight you eat at mine.  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Porter, I have a cook.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: You have a cook. I have lentils, a daughter, and a roof that only leaks a bit. Come on.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): hospitality: sharing what you have  
> _The porter has little, and still shares his supper with the old man. What does his sharing say about him?_  
> - ✅ That generosity doesn’t depend on being rich. → Yes. The porter gives what he has, which is the true meaning of generous. Wealth isn’t needed, just willingness.
> - That he is trying to impress the old man. → Not likely: the old man has a cook. He is doing it because his friend needs a meal, which is simple kindness.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned that generosity does not depend on wealth._

_The porter’s home is one room, swept clean. His daughter gives the old man the best cushion, which is the only cushion._  
**The Porter’s Daughter**: Baba says you were poor once too. Is that true?  
**Sinbad the Sailor**: Once. Only for a season. It was a very good season.  

**Choices**

- **Eat the lentils with them.**
    - **Sinbad the Sailor**: I’ve eaten at the Caliph’s table. These are better. Don’t tell him.
- **Let your Nubbin sit with the daughter.**
    - She feeds it lentils one at a time, and tells it the whale story, wrong, with tremendous confidence.

#### `a06-16-telling-nothing`

_The last evening. The long room is full: the steward, the cook, the porter’s daughter, and the old man, for once a listener._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: I’ve never told a story. I’ve carried a few. Bear with me.  
_He sets nothing on the low table. He looks at the empty place where something could be, and smiles._  
**Sinbad the Porter**: I had nothing, so I listened.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: That’s my first line. A friend went into a valley of diamonds and brought me nothing back. I’ve decided it was a present.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral storytelling: every teller begins by listening  
> **Nova**: Nova’s notes: for most of history, stories were told aloud. A teller learned a tale by listening, then told it in their own way.  
> **Nova**: “I had nothing, so I listened” is how every teller starts. Tales like Sinbad’s travelled for centuries this way, mouth to ear.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stories were passed on aloud by people who first learned them by listening._

**Sinbad the Porter**: My story is short. I’m a porter in Baghdad. I carry paper to the House of Wisdom, and I can’t read, so I listen.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: I listened to a rich man for seven nights, and I found out he was paid for, the same as me. Only in different coins.  

#### `a06-16-telling-done-kept`

**Sinbad the Porter**: And at the end, a herd walked past a gate three times, and nobody shot at them, and nobody ever will.  
**Sinbad the Porter**: The elephants were paid for in a season.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphor in the porter’s last line  
> _“Paid for in a season.” What is the porter saying about what Sinbad’s freedom cost?_  
> - ✅ That it cost time: a patient season of waiting, not a price in coins. → Yes. “Paid for in a season” turns time into a kind of coin. Sinbad’s freedom cost him patience.
> - That someone paid the master a lot of money. → Not literally. A season is a stretch of time, so the “payment” was waiting and patience.
> _For grown-ups: Interpreted a figurative use of “paid for” in a different ending._

_Nobody says anything. Then the old man claps, slowly, and the steward joins in, and then everybody does._  

#### `a7-10-water-promise`

_For a while, nobody says anything. Héctor and Miguel just look at each other, as if they are learning a song by heart._  
**Héctor**: You play like me. I knew it. Tonight on the stage. I knew it, and I didn’t know what it was.  
**Miguel**: She remembers you. Mamá Coco. She still asks for you. She asks if her papá is coming home.  
**Héctor**: She still asks?  
_His hand shines gold at the edges, brighter than ever. He holds it up and looks through it at the water._  
**Héctor**: Not for long, though. She’s fading up there. So I’m fading down here. It’s the same thing.  
_He looks across at you. You say his name, just once, quietly: Héctor._  
**Héctor**: Still got it, eh? The promise. Still in there.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: how remembering keeps people close  
> _Héctor says Coco fading and himself fading are “the same thing”. What do you think the story is saying about remembering? (There is no one right answer.)_  
> - People live on in those who remember them → A thoughtful theme. Many stories say that we continue in the memories we leave.
> - Remembering takes effort, from everyone → A fair theme. A name spoken aloud is something you do, not just something you feel.
> - Being forgotten is a real loss → A fair theme. The story takes that loss seriously, and shows what we can do about it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the theme of remembering in the story._

_The gold at his edges dims, just a little, for just a moment. As if one more person holding on makes a difference._  

#### `a7-12-coco-promise`

_Mamá Coco is in her chair in her room, with the curtains half drawn. She is looking at nothing at all._  
**Miguel**: Mamá Coco? Mamá Coco, it’s me. It’s Miguel.  
_She doesn’t answer, and her eyes don’t move. Miguel’s face crumples._  
**Miguel**: Please. You have to remember your papá. If you forget him, he’ll be gone. Gone for good.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): some very old people forget; patience, touch and music can help  
> _Some people find remembering harder as they grow very old. It isn’t their fault, and they are still the same person inside._  
> _Patience, gentle touch and familiar songs can help. Families often find that music reaches memories words cannot._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that forgetting in old age is not anyone’s fault, and that patience, touch and music can help._

_You promised. So you kneel down by her chair, and take her hand, and say it clearly, so she can hear._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): keeping a promise by saying the name aloud  
> _You kept your promise by saying Héctor’s name aloud. Why does keeping a promise matter, even a small one?_  
> - ✅ It shows people they can trust you → Yes. Each kept promise builds trust, and trust is what lets people lean on one another.
> - It doesn’t matter if no one checks → Promises matter most when no one is checking. They show who we are.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about why keeping promises matters._

**You**: Héctor. Your papá’s name is Héctor. He was on his way home to you.  
_Her fingers tighten on yours. Her lips move, as if trying the shape of a word she hasn’t said in a long time._  
**Mamá Coco**: H… Hé…  

#### `a7-12-song-done-promise`

_Miguel fits the corner back into the old photo. It is mended: a family of three, all their faces showing._  
_Imagine folding the photo in half, and in half again. Coco’s corner would fill exactly one of the equal parts._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions  
> _Folded in half twice, a photo has 4 equal parts. Coco kept 1 of them. What fraction is that?_  
> - ✅ 1/4 → Yes. One part out of four equal parts is one quarter, written 1/4.
> - 1/2 → A half would be 1 out of 2 equal parts. This is 1 out of 4, so 1/4.
> - 4/1 → The top number is the parts you have, and the bottom is how many equal parts: 1/4.
> _For grown-ups: Named a unit fraction: one of four equal parts is 1/4._

_Mamá Coco touches the man’s face in the photo, and then she looks at you, as if she knows you from somewhere._  
**Mamá Coco**: You said his name. Before. You said it first. Thank you.  

#### `a7-12-complete-both`

_The atlas turns its own page, gently. It is a year later, and Día de Muertos again._  
_The Riveras’ ofrenda is bigger than ever. Héctor’s photo is on it now, in the middle, the ribbon still tied round the frame._  
_Mamá Coco’s photo is on it too, beside her papá’s. She died in the spring, in her chair, with her family round her._  
_Tonight she is crossing the marigold bridge, holding her papá’s hand and her mamá’s, coming home to visit._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): when someone dies it is very sad, and remembering together helps  
> _When someone dies, their body stops working and cannot start again. It is very sad, and feeling sad is okay._  
> _Families also find comfort in remembering together: a photo, a story, a favourite song._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked plainly about death, that sadness is okay, and that remembering together helps._

_This year Miguel put Héctor’s photo up himself, and Mamá Imelda’s right beside it, touching at the frames._  
_On the bridge, Héctor walks between his wife and his daughter, and keeps stopping to wave at people. Mamá Imelda lets him._  
_Miguel plays in the courtyard, and the whole street comes in to listen. Abuelita dances, badly, and doesn’t care who sees._  
_You think about the ofrenda, and how it is built from small things: a photo, a flower, a name, a song._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme of the whole page  
> _What is the biggest idea this page of the atlas is trying to share?_  
> - ✅ People live on while we remember them and tell their stories → Yes. That is the heart of it, and it is also the heart of Día de Muertos.
> - Music is dangerous → The page shows the opposite. Music helped Coco remember.
> - Never talk to strangers → The page is about family and remembering, not strangers.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme: people live on while we remember them._

_The page settles under your hand. You are back in the Grove, with a marigold petal still glowing in your pocket._

#### `a08-14-bard-loop`

**Getafix**: Form 0. Application to Find Out Whether You Need This Form. Please attach a completed copy of this form.  
_Every clerk in the building has dutifully attached a completed copy. It unrolls down to your knees, and keeps going._  
_There is a silence. Then the chief laughs so hard he falls off his shield, and the whole village goes with him._  
**Getafix**: It never ends. It cannot be finished. Of course: it is perfect for him.  

> **Lesson** (maths, ask): logic: why a loop never ends  
> _The form says, “Attach a completed copy of this form.” Each copy needs another copy attached. Why can it never be finished?_  
> - ✅ Every copy needs another copy first → Yes. Each form waits for another form, which waits for another, so there is never a first one finished. That is a loop with no way out.
> - The clerks are too slow → Speed is not the problem. Even the fastest clerk would be stuck, because the rule needs a finished copy before it can finish one.
> - The paper runs out → It might, but the real problem is the rule itself, which always sends you back to the start.
> _For grown-ups: Reasoned about why a self-referring rule can never be completed._

_They wind it round Cacofonix and the oak tree seven times, and there is still some left over to tie a bow._  
**Cacofonix**: This is an outrage. I shall write a song about it. In forty-two verses.  
**Obelix**: You cannot. Your arms are inside a form.  

#### `a08-14-bard-boar`

**Getafix**: Proof That You Are Not a Boar. To be signed by a boar. And it has been, by a boar who signs with his knuckle.  
_Obelix goes pink with pride. Every clerk has stamped it, and somebody has added a note: “Boar to be found.”_  
**Vitalstatistix**: Ha! Our referee made it! The silliest form in Gaul!  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): seals, signatures and trust  
> **Getafix**: Long ago, people proved a document was real with a signature or a seal. A seal was a mark pressed into soft wax, often with a ring.  
> **Getafix**: The Romans used seals too. A document was only trusted if the right person had marked it. That is why the form needed the boar’s mark.  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that signatures and wax seals were used to show a document could be trusted._

_The notes run on for pages, each asking politely after the boar. It unrolls to your knees, and keeps going._  
_They wind it round Cacofonix and the oak tree until only his hat shows over the top._  
**Cacofonix**: I am not a boar. I wish to state, for the record, that I am not a boar.  
**Getafix**: It is all right. You have it in writing now.  

#### `a08-14-useful`

**Getafix**: Name. What you need. Signature. One page.  
_Getafix reads it twice, slowly, and then he does not hand it over. He rolls it up and tucks it in his robe._  
**Getafix**: This is far too good for tying up a bard. I shall file this under “Useful”. It is the only thing in that folder.  
**Asterix**: It did not win, though. It was too sensible to win.  
**Getafix**: Sensible things often lose on the day. Then people use them for years.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): when a good idea does not win  
> _Your sensible form did not win, but Getafix is keeping it. How do you feel when a good idea loses on the day?_  
> - A bit disappointed, but proud of it → A fair answer. Both feelings can sit together. Being proud of good work does not depend on winning.
> - Fine, because it will be useful for years → A fair answer. Getafix thinks so too. Some ideas win slowly, by being used again and again.
> - Annoyed: clear and sensible should win → A fair answer. It can feel unfair. Plain, clear writing respects the reader, even when the silly form gets the laughs.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about handling disappointment and taking pride in a good idea that did not win._

_In the end they tie Cacofonix up with an old fishing net, which he says, through the holes, is an insult to his art._  

#### `a09-11-dark-home`

_The lamps go out one by one, to save oil. The kitchen clock says twenty to nine._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): minutes to the hour  
> _“Twenty to nine” means 20 minutes before nine o’clock. What time is that written as? And how long is it until 8:42?_  
> - ✅ 8:40, so 2 minutes until 8:42. → Yes. Twenty to nine is 8:40, and 8:42 is two minutes later.
> - 9:20, so 22 minutes to go. → “To” means before the hour, so twenty to nine is earlier than nine: 8:40. 8:42 is two minutes after that.
> - 8:20, so 22 minutes to go. → “Twenty to nine” means 20 minutes before 9:00, which is 8:40. “Twenty past eight” would be 8:20.
> _For grown-ups: Read “twenty to nine” as 8:40 and found 2 minutes until 8:42._

_Outside, the sky is so red it comes in at the cave mouth and lies on the sand like a carpet._  
_A sound begins, very far off. It is like the whole sky taking in a breath._  
_Sniff is at the very back of the cave, as far back as there is. You go and sit down beside him._  
_For a long time he doesn’t say anything. Then, in the dark, very small, he does._  
**Sniff**: We’re home by then. You said. We’re home by then.  
_He has been carrying it since the mountain, like a button in a pocket. Now he gives it back to you to hold._  
**Sniff**: And we are. We’re home. So that part came true.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): keeping someone’s words, and saying a worry aloud  
> _Sniff kept your words “We’ll be home by then” for days, and now says them back._  
> _Kind words can stay with a person a long time._  
> _And saying a worry out loud, as Sniff does here, is how it begins to ease._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that kind words stay with a friend, and that saying a worry out loud helps it ease._

_You sit there together and wait, and that is the whole of what you can do._  

#### `a09-12-dawn-done-shell`

_You take the pink shell out of your pocket and hold it to your ear._  
_Very faint, very far, there is the sound of the sea in it again. It must have got back first._  
**Moomintroll**: Let me listen! Oh. Oh, it’s home.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): why a shell sounds like the sea  
> _The “sea” in a shell is not the sea at all._  
> _The hollow shell catches the small sounds around you, such as moving air and far-off voices, and makes some of them louder._  
> _That is called resonance. Try it with a mug held to your ear: you will hear almost the same rushing._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the sound in a shell is the resonance of ordinary background noise._


#### `a09-12-dawn-done-garnet`

_You hold out the garnet to Sniff. You were only holding it, after all._  
**Sniff**: No. You keep it. I gave it to you to hold, and you held it all night, and that’s keeping.  
_He looks surprised at himself. Then he looks pleased, which surprises him more._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what generosity gives the giver  
> _Sniff gives away his garnet and is surprised to feel pleased. Why might giving feel good?_  
> - ✅ Caring for a friend feels good, and so does trusting them. → Yes. Generosity usually gives the giver a warm feeling, and Sniff has found that out.
> - He is glad to have less to carry. → That may be a tiny part of it, but the real warmth comes from sharing with a friend.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on why generosity can feel good for the giver._


#### `a10-12-manta-wave`

_The manta turns in the water and rises, and rolls along the side of the canoe, up with each swell and down with it._  
_It isn’t swimming. It is riding the sea: rising when the water rises, sinking when it falls, its wing-tips rolling over._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): swells lift floating things without carrying them  
> _A swell passing under a canoe lifts it up and lets it back down. The wave’s energy travels on, but the canoe stays about where it was._  
> _That is why the manta and your Nubbin can ride the swell together without being carried away._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a swell lifts and lowers a floating object while its energy travels on._

_Your Nubbin stands up very slowly on the deck._  
_Then it goes up on its toes, and down and back, rolling its little arms, the way Gramma taught it, right on the beat of the sea._  
_The manta rises, and your Nubbin rises. They go up the side of the canoe together, the big one in the sea and the small one on deck._  
**Gramma Tala**: There. You didn’t forget. I told you it doesn’t come off.  
_Moana laughs, wet-faced. It is the first time she has laughed since the barrier._  

#### `a10-14-bow-wave`

_The whole village goes up the stream and through the waterfall. One by one, the great canoes come out of the cave into the light._  
_You carry the end of a steering oar and your Nubbin carries Heihei. Pua carries nothing, and supervises._  
_The sails go up, all of them. Moana stands at the steering oar of the first canoe, holding her hand out flat to the horizon._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): what the name Hōkūleʻa means  
> _The canoe Hōkūleʻa is named for the star Arcturus, called “star of gladness” in Hawaiian. Arcturus passes straight overhead in Hawaiʻi._  
> _Its 1976 voyage to Tahiti showed the world that Pacific peoples could navigate by nature alone._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what Hōkūleʻa’s name means and why its 1976 voyage mattered._

_Out past the reef, a blue light comes up under the hulls. The manta, rising and sinking with the swell beside you._  
_Your Nubbin climbs to the very tip of the bow. Then it rises on its toes, and sinks, and rolls its arms: Gramma’s wave step, on the beat._  
_The manta rolls with it. The people on the canoes see, and point, and some of them begin to laugh, and some to cry._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, speed and time  
> _Hawaiʻi to Tahiti is about 4,000 kilometres. If a canoe could sail 100 kilometres every day, how many days would it take?_  
> - ✅ 40 days → Yes, 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40. Hōkūleʻa took about 34 days in 1976, so it sailed a little faster.
> - 4 days → 4 days would need 1,000 km a day. 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40.
> - 400 days → 400 would be 10 km a day. At 100 km a day, 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40.
> _For grown-ups: Divided a voyage distance by a daily distance to find the days taken._

**Chief Tui**: That’s my mother’s step. She did it on the beach every evening. I thought it was just her.  
**Moana**: It’s never just one person. That’s the whole point of it.  

#### `a10-14-complete-word`

_Moana finds you at the bow at sunset, and sits beside you a while._  
**Moana**: You never told me where you came from. Somewhere past the reef, Gramma said.  
**You**: A garden. With a pond in it. I’m a long way from it.  
**Moana**: Then you know the way home. You always know where you started.  
**Moana**: What you said to her, on the path. That you remembered. I think she heard that. I think it helped.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being remembered  
> _Moana says Te Kā heard you say you remembered her. Why can being remembered help someone who feels lost?_  
> - It tells them they still matter to someone → Yes. Being remembered is a way of being held.
> - It reminds them who they were → A deep answer. Names and memories can bring a person back to themselves.
> - It might not help everyone → True. But it often does, and it costs nothing to offer.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why being remembered can comfort someone._

_The page gives a long, slow sigh, like a sail letting go of the wind._  
_You are back in the Grove with Nova’s atlas on your knee. The ground will not hold still; it sways like a deck, and your Nubbin smells of salt._  
_By the pond there is a small voyaging canoe, twin-hulled, with a woven sail no bigger than a tablecloth._  
_Up on the hill, a ring of flat stones has appeared in the grass, each one marked with a house of the rising stars._  
_Along the canoe’s hull runs a line of small carved spirals, one for each thing remembered. Your Nubbin counts them, and loses count._  

#### `a10-14-complete-walk`

_Moana finds you at the bow at sunset, and sits beside you a while._  
**Moana**: You never told me where you came from. Somewhere past the reef, Gramma said.  
**You**: A garden. With a pond in it. I’m a long way from it.  
**Moana**: Then you know the way home. You always know where you started.  
**Moana**: On the path, you didn’t say anything. You just came. That was the bravest thing on the whole sea, after me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): showing up without words  
> _Moana says you said nothing on the path, you just came. Why can simply showing up be one of the bravest and kindest things we do?_  
> - It shows you care without needing credit → Yes. Quiet courage often goes unnoticed, and that is part of its power.
> - It is brave because you cannot hide behind words → A sharp answer. When all you have is yourself, you cannot pretend.
> - It is not enough on its own → Sometimes you must do more. But showing up is often where help starts.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why simply showing up for someone can be brave and kind._

_The page gives a long, slow sigh, like a sail letting go of the wind._  
_You are back in the Grove with Nova’s atlas on your knee. The ground will not hold still; it sways like a deck, and your Nubbin smells of salt._  
_By the pond there is a small voyaging canoe, twin-hulled, with a woven sail no bigger than a tablecloth._  
_Up on the hill, a ring of flat stones has appeared in the grass, each one marked with a house of the rising stars._  
_On the canoe’s bow deck, two pairs of small footprints are painted: yours, and a rounder pair beside them. Your Nubbin stands in its pair._  

#### `a11-11-door-thistle`

_Eeyore goes in, turns round, and comes out again to look at his step._  
_Beside the step, its purple top just showing through the snow, is the thistle your Nubbin gave him. He has planted it._  
**Eeyore**: I didn’t eat it. I thought it ought to have somewhere to live. Everybody should, it turns out.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): plants rest in winter and grow in spring  
> **Christopher Robin**: Eeyore has planted the thistle by his step in the snow. Many plants rest through winter, and grow again when the ground warms.  
> **Christopher Robin**: A thistle needs water and sunlight to grow, and spring brings both. Give it time, and it will be a plant again.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plants rest through winter and need water and light to grow._


#### `a11-11-door-sat`

_Eeyore goes in, turns round, comes out again, and sits down on his new step._  
_Then he shuffles to one side. There is a space left exactly the size of you, and a smaller one beside it._  
**Eeyore**: I kept you a place. In case. Not that you have to. Sit, I mean.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): reading between the lines  
> _Eeyore says you do not have to sit there. But he has kept a space exactly your size, and a smaller one for your Nubbin._  
> _Reading between the lines, he very much hopes you will. Sitting with a gloomy friend is the sort of kindness that gets remembered._  
> _For grown-ups: Read between the lines of what a character says and does._


#### `a11-16-bounced-sat`

_Eeyore stands dripping on the bank. He looks round at everybody, and then, slowly, at you._  
**Eeyore**: You tell them. You’re the one who sits. They’ll believe you.  
_So you tell them, plainly, that Eeyore was bounced. Everyone listens, and Eeyore stands a little taller while you say it._  
_Tigger, arriving, says he only coughed. Everyone looks at Tigger, and Tigger looks at the sky._  
**Tigger**: Well. It was a bouncy sort of cough. Sorry, Eeyore.  
**Eeyore**: Hm. That’s the first sorry I’ve had this year. I shall keep it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): trust grows from kindness  
> _Eeyore asks you to tell the others, because you are the one who sits with him. They will believe you._  
> _Trust is built from small kindnesses over time. People believe those who have been steady and kind to them._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that trust is built from kind actions over time._


#### `a11-17-mist-rabbit`

_At the top of the Forest, in a hollow, Rabbit whispers “Now!”, and you duck behind a bank with him and Pooh and Piglet._  
_Tigger bounces on without noticing. His bounces get further off, and then there are no bounces at all._  
**Rabbit**: There. Now we go home.  
_Rabbit leads you all home. After a while you pass a sand-pit, and after a while longer you pass the same sand-pit again._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): people walk in circles when they cannot see far  
> **Christopher Robin**: Rabbit passes the same sand-pit twice. Experiments show that people who cannot see landmarks, in thick fog or a dark forest, tend to walk in circles.  
> **Christopher Robin**: With no marker to aim at, tiny differences in each step add up. That is why “stop and call out” beats “keep walking”.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people tend to walk in circles when they cannot see landmarks._

**Pooh**: Every time we try to get away from this pit, we find it. So if we tried to find it, we might get away.  
**Rabbit**: Nonsense. I’ll walk away from it and come straight back, and you’ll see.  
_Rabbit walks off into the mist to prove it, and doesn’t come back._  
_Pooh hears his honey calling him from far off, and he and Piglet follow it home. You don’t, because Rabbit is out there on his own._  
_So you go after him, with your Nubbin, into the white. You find him in a hollow, small and damp, listening to every noise._  
**Rabbit**: Is that you? Oh. Good. I wasn’t lost. I was waiting for somebody to come. That’s all.  

#### `a11-17-found-rabbit`

_You sit with Rabbit in the hollow while the mist drips. Rabbit doesn’t say anything, and neither do you._  
_Then, far off, you hear it before Rabbit does: a bounce, and another. Then a voice, calling._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): sitting quietly with a scared friend  
> _You did not need words in the hollow. Sitting quietly beside Rabbit while the mist drips was enough._  
> _A scared person often does not need advice. They need to know they are not alone._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that sitting quietly with a scared friend helps them feel less alone._

**You**: Listen.  
**Tigger**: Rabbit? Keeper? Tiggers are good at finding! I can hear you being quiet!  
**Rabbit**: Tigger. Oh, Tigger. I am glad to see you.  

#### `a11-19-signed-rabbit`

_Rabbit signs next to you, very neatly, and then stays there, and clears his throat._  
**Rabbit**: About the mist. In the hollow. I was grateful for the company. That’s all. It has been noted.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): formal words show discomfort  
> _Rabbit says “It has been noted.” Hardly anybody talks like that unless they are uncomfortable._  
> _Formal words are a way of keeping feelings at arm’s length. Reading between the lines, Rabbit is saying thank you._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that formal words can show someone is uncomfortable with feelings._

_He goes back to his list at once, and doesn’t look up for some time._  

#### `a11-19-scroll-thistle`

_Rabbit rolls up the scroll. Something falls out of it: a thistle, pressed flat, its purple top gone pale._  
**Eeyore**: I put that in. From my step. It’s not much. Well. It is, actually.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how pressing preserves a plant  
> **Christopher Robin**: Eeyore’s thistle is pressed flat and dry. Pressing squeezes out the water, and a dry plant can last for hundreds of years.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Botanists keep pressed plants in a herbarium, a library of dried plants, as a record of what grew where and when.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pressing a plant dries it so it can be kept as a record._

_Everyone walks to Christopher Robin’s house together. At the door, nobody wants to go first._  
_In the end Eeyore goes first, because it is his poem, and everybody else crowds in behind him._  
**Christopher Robin**: What’s this?  
**Eeyore**: It’s a Rissolution. From all of us. You read it. We’ll just… we’ll go.  
_Christopher Robin reads it right to the end, and all the names, and he doesn’t say anything for a moment._  
**Christopher Robin**: Thank you. All of you. Thank you.  

#### `a11-19-scroll-sat`

_Rabbit rolls up the scroll. Eeyore stops him with a hoof, asks for it back, and adds one more line at the bottom._  
**Eeyore**: Somebody sat with me.  
_He doesn’t explain it. He hands it back, and doesn’t look at you, and doesn’t need to._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): kindness is remembered  
> _Eeyore writes one line at the bottom: Somebody sat with me. He does not say who, and he does not need to._  
> _Small kindnesses often matter more than we know. Sitting with someone, with nothing to give, is one of the biggest._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that quiet kindness is remembered._

_Everyone walks to Christopher Robin’s house together. At the door, nobody wants to go first._  
_In the end Eeyore goes first, because it is his poem, and everybody else crowds in behind him._  
**Christopher Robin**: What’s this?  
**Eeyore**: It’s a Rissolution. From all of us. You read it. We’ll just… we’ll go.
