#### `a11-20-complete-thistle`

_Christopher Robin and Pooh go off together, out of the far side of the circle. You don’t follow, because this bit is theirs._  
_Your Nubbin has carried something up the hill: a thistle head from Eeyore’s step. It plants it at the edge of the circle and pats the earth down._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, notice): thistle seeds travel on fluff  
> **Christopher Robin**: A thistle’s seeds each have a fluffy parachute, so the wind carries them far. Goldfinches love to eat them, and spill some, which helps them spread.  
> **Christopher Robin**: That is how thistles end up planted in places nobody chose. This one is planted by choice, at the edge of the ring.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that thistle seeds travel on wind and are spread by birds._

_Whatever comes next for them, there is a ring of trees at the top of the Forest that nobody can count._  
_A boy and his Bear are playing in it. Nobody ever stops them._  
_The page settles under your hand, gently, like a door somebody is careful not to bang._  
_You are back in the Grove, with Nova’s atlas on your knee. There is a stick in your Nubbin’s mouth, and nobody saw where it came from._  
_Down by the Grove stream there is a little wooden bridge that wasn’t there this morning. A thistle is coming up at the far end._  

#### `a11-20-complete-sat`

_Christopher Robin and Pooh go off together, out of the far side of the circle. You don’t follow, because this bit is theirs._  
_Your Nubbin turns round three times in the grass at the edge of the circle, and sits. It leaves a flattened round, like the one by Eeyore’s step._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): signs animals leave: a hare’s form  
> **Christopher Robin**: A flattened round in the grass is a sign that somebody has rested there. A hare’s resting place is even called a form.  
> **Christopher Robin**: Naturalists read signs like these: flattened grass, feathers, tracks and droppings tell them who has been there, and when.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that flattened grass is a sign an animal has rested there._

_Whatever comes next for them, there is a ring of trees at the top of the Forest that nobody can count._  
_A boy and his Bear are playing in it. Nobody ever stops them._  
_The page settles under your hand, gently, like a door somebody is careful not to bang._  
_You are back in the Grove, with Nova’s atlas on your knee. There is a stick in your Nubbin’s mouth, and nobody saw where it came from._  
_Down by the Grove stream there is a little wooden bridge that wasn’t there this morning. One place on its parapet is worn smooth, just right for sitting._  

#### `a11-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the last page of the Forest, where the ring of trees stands on top of the hill._  
_Beside the trees, in soft pencil you have never noticed, there is a note in the margin. You know the hand._  
_“Read this to the little one, the summer they stayed. They asked where Christopher Robin went.”_  
_“Somewhere, I said. Not away.”_  
_And under it, one letter: H._  
_You don’t remember that summer. Or you do, a little: a lap, a voice, a page turning._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): writing keeps people close  
> _Hazel wrote this note long ago, for a child who would read it later. And here it is, reaching you._  
> _We are made partly of being remembered. A note, a drawing or a letter can keep someone close, long after the pencil has stopped._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that a written note can keep someone close._

_Your Nubbin climbs into your lap. You sit with the page open for a long time, and it waits with you._  

#### `a12-01-ember-forgiven`

_Your Nubbin is carrying something: a little lantern, and in it Cinder’s ember, small and red._  
_It burns steady, the colour of a hearth with the door shut. Grandmother holds her hands out to it without thinking._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what a fire needs  
> _A fire needs three things: fuel to burn, air, and heat. The lantern glass lets air in but keeps the wind from blowing the flame about._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fire needs fuel, air and heat._

**Grandmother**: Now that’s a good little fire. Bring it up with you; the eaves get cold.  

#### `a12-01-ember-remembered`

_Your Nubbin is carrying something: a little lantern, and in it Cinder’s ember, small and red._  
_It flickers now and then, as if it’s remembering something. It never goes out._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): why flames flicker  
> _Why does a flame flicker?_  
> - ✅ Moving air pushes it about → Yes. Every draught nudges it. A lantern keeps out the worst.
> - It is tired → Flames don’t get tired! Moving air pushes them about.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that flames flicker when air moves around them._

**Grandmother**: That one’s got a story in it. Bring it up with you; the eaves get cold.  

#### `a12-04-kept`

_As it comes round the square again, the white sledge doesn’t pass you. It stops, right beside you._  
_The driver looks down. Under the white cap is a face of ice, lovely and still, with eyes like two stars._  
**The Snow Queen**: You keep things too.  
_She says nothing about the stone in your pocket. She doesn’t need to._  
_She lifts the edge of her white bearskin and holds it open. Inside it’s soft and white and very quiet._  
_It’s a place where you will never feel the cold again. Never hurt, and never warm, either._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): safe is not the same as well  
> _A place where nothing could ever hurt you, but nothing would ever feel warm or happy either. Would you want it?_  
> - No. I want the warm feelings too → That’s a thoughtful answer. The good feelings and the hard ones come together.
> - Sometimes, on a bad day → That’s honest: on hard days, feeling nothing can sound restful. A hug usually helps more.
> - I’m not sure → It’s a big question. Notice how cold the fur looks, even though it’s soft.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being safe from all feelings is the same as being well._


**Choices**

- **“No.”**
    - **You**: No, thank you.
    - She looks at you a moment longer, without anger. Then she lets the bearskin fall, and drives on.
- **Say nothing. Step back.**
    - You step back, out of reach of the fur. She watches you do it, and she almost smiles.
    - Then she lets the bearskin fall, and drives on.

#### `a12-10-free-night`

_The robber girl comes to you before she goes to Bae. Your Nubbin is in her arms, still half asleep._  
_She holds it out to you. You didn’t ask, and she gives it back anyway._  
**The Robber Girl**: There. I gave it back. Nobody made me.  
**The Robber Girl**: And if I can give one back, I can give two.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): trust and keeping your word  
> _You trusted her for one night, and she kept her side. Why does it matter to her that nobody made her?_  
> - It shows she chose to be fair → That’s a fair answer. Doing the right thing by choice feels different from being forced.
> - She’s proud of herself → Yes, I think she is. Being trusted can help people trust themselves.
> - She wanted you to notice → Maybe! People often want someone to see when they’ve done well.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about trust and choosing to keep your word._

_She goes to Bae and puts her hand flat on his neck, by the copper ring._  
**The Robber Girl**: Bae, I’m untying you. Run home to Lapland and carry this girl to the Snow Queen’s, where her friend is.  
**The Robber Girl**: You heard her story. You were listening; she talks loud enough.  
_Bae leaps for joy. The robber girl lifts Gerda onto his back, ties her on, and gives her a little cushion to sit on._  
**The Robber Girl**: Here are your fur boots. It’ll be cold. I’m keeping the muff; it’s too pretty.  
**The Robber Girl**: But you’re not freezing on my account. Have Mother’s big mittens. They come right up to your elbows.  
**The Robber Girl**: Two loaves and a ham. And don’t cry. I hate it when people cry. Look happy.  
**Bae**: Climb on behind her, lodger. You weigh less than a sack of salt, and I’ve carried worse.  
_The robber girl coaxes the big dogs inside. Then she cuts Bae’s rope with her knife, and opens the door._  
**The Robber Girl**: Run! And look after her!  

**Choices**

- **Wave goodbye to the robber girl.**
    - You wave. She doesn’t wave back, but she watches until you’re out of sight, which is nearly the same.
- **Nod to her, as one equal to another.**
    - You nod. She nods back, once, hard, like somebody shutting a box.

#### `a12-12-ember-forgiven`

_The Finnish woman stops. She’s looking at the little lantern your Nubbin carries, and the ember burning steady in it._  
**The Finnish Woman**: That was a fierce fire once.  
**The Finnish Woman**: It only keeps someone warm now. That’s the right size for a fire.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): metaphor  
> _“The right size for a fire”: she might be talking about more than fire. What else could be fierce once, and warm now?_  
> - A big angry feeling that has calmed → That’s a thoughtful reading. Anger that settles can turn into warmth.
> - A person who has changed → Yes, it could be. People can change from fierce to kind.
> - Just the fire → That works too. Sometimes a fire is just a fire.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about a line that could be a metaphor._

_She bends and warms her hands at it for a moment, as if she were greeting somebody._  

#### `a12-12-ember-remembered`

_The Finnish woman stops. She’s looking at the little lantern your Nubbin carries, and the ember flickering in it._  
**The Finnish Woman**: That was a fierce fire once.  
**The Finnish Woman**: It only keeps someone warm now. That’s the right size for a fire.  
_The ember flickers while she looks at it. It doesn’t go out._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): fire safety  
> _In real life, fire is for grown-ups to handle. Even a small flame can burn, so keep back and let an adult look after it._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about leaving fire and flames to grown-ups._


#### `a12-13-wait-forgiven`

_You unroll the Sámi woman’s reindeer skin and sit on it. Your Nubbin sets its little lantern down between your feet._  
_Cinder’s ember burns steady inside it. It isn’t much of a fire, and it’s exactly enough._  
_The cold comes right up to the edge of its light and stops there, as if it knows better._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from warm to cold  
> _Heat always spreads from warmer things to colder ones. The ember warms the air nearest to it, so the coldest air stays further away._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat moves from warmer things to colder things._

_There’s no wind here. Just the quiet, and the bush, and the red berries._  
_The nearest branch has six bunches of berries, with five berries in each bunch. You count them, twice, and decide not to mind._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Six bunches, five in each. How many berries?_  
> - ✅ 30 → Yes: six fives are thirty.
> - 11 → That’s six plus five. Six groups of five make thirty.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups to find a total._

_You don’t know how long it will be. You know you’ll be here when it’s over._  

**Choices**

- **Count the berries again.**
    - Thirty again, or twenty-nine. Your Nubbin points at one you’ve missed.
- **Hum Gerda’s rose tune, under your breath.**
    - You hum it, not loud. Your Nubbin hums it back a beat behind, the way it did under the rose arch.
- **Just sit.**
    - You just sit, and it turns out you’re good at it. You didn’t use to be.

#### `a12-13-wait-remembered`

_It keeps you both from freezing. That’s all it does now, and it does it all night._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from warm to cold  
> _Heat spreads from warm things to cold ones. Even a small, flickering ember sends out enough warmth to keep the nearest cold away._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat moves from warmer things to colder things._

_There’s no wind here. Just the quiet, and the bush, and the red berries._  
_The nearest branch has six bunches of berries, with five berries in each bunch. You count them, twice, and decide not to mind._  
_You don’t know how long it will be. You know you’ll be here when it’s over._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): patience  
> _What helps you wait, when you don’t know how long it will be?_  
> - Keeping busy, like counting → Good idea. A gently busy mind makes time pass.
> - Having a friend near → Yes. Your Nubbin and the ember are company.
> - Remembering why I’m waiting → A wise answer. Waiting for someone you care about has a point.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about strategies that make waiting easier._


**Choices**

- **Count the berries again.**
    - Thirty again, or twenty-nine. Your Nubbin points at one you’ve missed.
- **Hum Gerda’s rose tune, under your breath.**
    - You hum it, not loud. Your Nubbin hums it back a beat behind, the way it did under the rose arch.
- **Just sit.**
    - You just sit, and it turns out you’re good at it. You didn’t use to be.

#### `a12-14-prayer-kept`

_Gerda folds her hands and says her prayer. Her breath turns to smoke, and the smoke turns to small bright figures._  
_There are more of them with every breath. They break the guards into a hundred pieces, and she walks on, quickly and bravely._  
_Then some of the snowflakes turn, and come running along the ground towards you._  
_They reach the edge of the skin and stop. Then they part, left and right, like servants at a door._  
_In your pocket the stone hums, which it has never done before. It sounds pleased._  
_The road to the palace lies open in front of you, clear and smooth and white. Nothing would stop you._  
_You could walk in. You know exactly how welcome you would be._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): keeping a promise when it’s easy to break  
> _The road is open, and nobody would stop you. Why might you stay on the skin anyway?_  
> - Because this part is Gerda’s → That’s a fair answer. Some journeys belong to one person.
> - Because I said I’d wait → Yes. Keeping your word matters most when breaking it would be easy.
> - Because being welcome there isn’t good → A sharp answer. Being welcome somewhere cold isn’t the same as belonging.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about keeping a promise when breaking it would be easy._


**Choices**

- **Sit back down.**
    - You sit down on the reindeer skin. After a while the snowflakes close the road again, as if disappointed.
    - The stone goes quiet. Your Nubbin climbs back inside your coat.
- **Turn your back on the road.**
    - You turn round and face the way you came. Behind you the snowflakes close up, softly, like a door being shut.
    - The stone goes quiet. Your Nubbin climbs back inside your coat.

#### `a12-17-rider-night`

_The first birds are singing, and the forest has green buds. Out of it comes a fine horse that Gerda knows: it pulled the golden coach._  
_On it rides a girl in a bright red cap. It’s the robber girl._  
**The Robber Girl**: I got bored at home. I’m off to see the world. North first, and somewhere else if north’s no good.  
_Two wood pigeons ride on her saddle, and they aren’t tied. They could go whenever they liked, and they don’t._  
_You look at the pigeons, and then at her._  
**The Robber Girl**: They’re not tied any more.  
**The Robber Girl**: Mostly.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): trust can change people  
> _She used to tie everything, and now the pigeons are free and stay anyway. What do you think changed her?_  
> - Being trusted with the Nubbin → That’s a thoughtful answer. Being trusted can teach someone to trust.
> - Seeing that things stay if they want to → Yes. Your Nubbin came back to you without a rope.
> - She just grew up a bit → That too. People can change as they grow.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how being trusted can change someone._

**The Robber Girl**: So this is him. Hm. I wonder if he was worth running to the end of the world for.  
**Kay**: I wonder that too.  
**Gerda**: How are the prince and princess? And the ravens?  
**The Robber Girl**: The prince and princess have gone abroad. The raven died. He was old.  
_He died: his body stopped working, and it won’t start again. He had a long life, and a good one._  
**The Robber Girl**: His sweetheart wears a black thread round her leg now, to remember him, and tells everybody about him.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): symbols in a story  
> _The black thread is a symbol: a small thing that stands for something big. Hers stands for remembering him._  
> _It’s all right to feel sad that the raven died. Remembering him, as his sweetheart does, is a way of keeping him close._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a symbol is, and talked about how remembering helps when someone dies._


**Choices**

- **Say you’re sorry about the raven.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: Don’t be. He had a good post and all the scraps he wanted. Not many get that.
- **Admire her red cap.**
    - **The Robber Girl**: It’s a good cap. You can’t have it.

#### `a12-18-pocket`

**Grandmother**: Lodger. Why is your hand always on your pocket?  
_You look down, and it is. You hadn’t noticed._  
**Grandmother**: Kay kept his hand on that burning-glass of his, all that last winter. I’d not like to see it again.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): noticing your habits  
> _Sometimes we do things without noticing, like keeping a hand on something. Why might it help to notice?_  
> - So I can choose, not just do it → That’s a wise answer. Noticing a habit gives you the choice back.
> - It doesn’t matter → Some habits don’t. Grandmother thinks this one might.
> - To understand how I feel → Yes. Habits can be clues to what we’re worried about.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about noticing habits and what they can tell us._


**Choices**

- **“Habit.”**
    - **Grandmother**: A habit’s only a thing we’ve stopped noticing. Notice it, then. That’s all I ask.
- **“Something I’m keeping.”**
    - **Grandmother**: Keeping is fine. Just make sure it’s you doing the keeping, and not the other way about.
- **Say nothing. Take your hand out of your pocket.**
    - You take your hand out. It’s cold, and Grandmother holds it in both of hers until it isn’t.

#### `a12-18-complete-night`

_A wood pigeon comes down out of the sky and lands on the roses in the gutter. Nothing is tied to its leg, and it stays._  
_It might be one of the robber girl’s, and it might not. Either way, nobody tied it, and it chose this._  
_Your Nubbin, in its red cap, sits down beside it, and they look out over the rooftops together._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): freedom and friendship  
> _Nobody tied the pigeon, and it stays. What’s the difference between holding on to a friend and a friend choosing to stay?_  
> - A friend who chooses is a real friend → That’s a fair answer. Choosing to stay means something.
> - Holding on is safer → It can feel safer. But the robber girl found that untied things can stay too.
> - Trust is the difference → A wise answer. Trust is what lets the rope go.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about freedom, trust and friendship._

_The page settles under your hand, like a paper cut-out laid flat on a table._  
_You’re back in the Grove, with Nova’s atlas on your knee. When you open it again, a rose petal slides out of the fold and lands on your boot._  
_On the cottage windowsill stands a window box with a rose tree in it that wasn’t there this morning._  
_Another stands on the lantern shed across the way, and between them somebody has laid a plank._  
_You think of the night you trusted someone with your friend. It came back, and so, it seems, did something else._  

#### `a13-01-page-clank`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page in brown ink: a hill town, a long white road, and along the bottom edge, the sea._  
_The words across the top begin the way stories for children do. Once upon a time there was… a king, you think._  
_No. Once upon a time there was a piece of wood._  
_The ink goes wet under your fingers, and then it is rain. You, your Nubbin and Clank are standing in a steep stone lane, getting wetter._  
**Clank**: Announcement: it’s steps. It’s ALL steps. This whole country is made of steps!  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): a ramp is a simple machine (an inclined plane) that trades distance for force  
> _Steps are a problem for Clank’s wheel. Byte’s ramp solves it._  
> _Why is it easier to roll up a long gentle slope than to lift over one tall step?_  
> - ✅ A long slope spreads the lift over a longer distance, so it takes less push at once. → Yes. A ramp is an inclined plane. You travel farther but push less hard. That is the trade every simple machine makes.
> - A ramp makes Clank lighter. → Clank weighs the same on a ramp. It is the push needed at any moment that gets smaller.
> - Ramps are only for show. → Ramps are used everywhere: wheelchair ramps, loading ramps, even the road up a hill. They really work.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a ramp is a simple machine that makes lifting easier by spreading the effort over a longer distance._

_Clank unfolds the ramp Byte made him for the trip: three hinged boards, sanded smooth, with BYTE pencilled on the underneath._  
**Clank**: Unfold, roll, fold up. Byte made me practise forty times. Forty-one. The last one was for luck. Byte doesn’t believe in luck.  
_One door is open, with sawdust on the step and a warm smell of pine._  
_You go in, and Clank comes in after you, down his ramp._  
**Master Cherry**: Come in, come in, shut the weather out. Mind the shavings. And bring your… kettle. Is that a kettle?  
**Clank**: Announcement: I am Clank! I am a guest! Is this a house? I love it!  
_The carpenter’s nose is so round and red and shiny that it looks like a ripe cherry. Everyone calls him Master Cherry._  
**Master Cherry**: I’m making a table leg. Out of this. A firewood log, a nothing log. Nothing special about it at all.  
_He spits on his hands and lifts the axe._  
**A Small Voice**: Don’t hit me too hard!  

#### `a13-05-coat-clank`

_He comes back an hour later with a spelling-book under his arm, in his shirt-sleeves. There is snow on his shoulders._  
**Pinocchio**: Babbo, where’s your coat?  
**Geppetto**: I sold it.  
**Pinocchio**: Why?  
**Geppetto**: It was too warm.  
_Pinocchio understands. He throws his arms round the old man’s neck and kisses him all over his face._  
**Clank**: He sold his coat. For a thing that kicked him on the nose.  
**Clank**: Is that a job? Is that what a job is?  
**You**: No. It isn’t a job.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what love is, if it is not a job  
> _Clank asks whether it was a job. You said no. If it was not a job, what do you think Geppetto’s act was?_  
> - Love: giving without being paid or asked. → That’s a fair answer. A job is something you do for pay, or because you are told. Love is something you do because the other person matters.
> - Duty: a father looks after his son. → That’s a fair answer. Duty is part of it. But few duties ask a person to sell his only coat in the snow.
> - Foolishness: a coat is worth more than a book. → That’s a fair answer. By the price of things it was a bad trade. By love, it was a very good one.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what love is when it is not a job, and why a loving act can look foolish by price._

_Clank’s chimney-light flickers, as if he has put something down somewhere safe, to look at later._  

#### `a13-10-doctors-done-carried`

_The doctors pick up their bags. The Talking-cricket goes last, very slowly, on one stiff leg._  
_At the door he stops, turns round, and nods to you. One small, exact nod, the kind a hundred-year-old cricket doesn’t give to just anybody._  
_Then he goes down the stairs, and doesn’t look back. He doesn’t need to._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, notice): showing a feeling through an action instead of saying it  
> _The cricket does not say thank you. He nods. Writers call this “showing, not telling”: the nod says it for him._  
> _Readers who watch for small actions, like a nod, a glance or a sigh, catch what a character feels without being told._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that writers show feelings through small actions instead of saying them outright._

> _Pinocchio finally says the cricket was right, but asks you not to tell him._  
> _Why is it so hard to say “I was wrong”, even to ourselves?_  
> - We worry it makes us look weak or silly. → That’s a fair answer. Pride gets in the way. People who can say it tend to learn faster, and are trusted more.
> - We feel ashamed when we remember what we did. → That’s a fair answer. Shame is heavy, and a kind friend helps us carry it.
> - It is not hard if the other person is kind about it. → That’s a fair answer. A kind listener makes honesty much easier.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why it is hard to admit being wrong and what helps._

**Pinocchio**: Don’t tell him I said so.  

#### `a13-19-complete-clank`

_The Tunny carries Pinocchio and Geppetto to the shore. Clank, who would sink like a kettle, rides on his back like a figurehead._

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): why a steel kettle sinks but a steel ship floats  
> _A metal kettle sinks, but a huge steel ship floats. What is the difference?_  
> - ✅ A ship’s shape pushes aside a lot of water, so the water pushes back up hard enough. → Yes. A floating thing must displace its own weight in water. A hollow, wide ship does; a small solid kettle does not. That is why Clank rides on the Tunny.
> - Ships are made of lighter metal. → Both are steel. It is the shape that matters, not the metal.
> - Ships have magic engines. → No magic: engines drive them, but they float by shape alone, even with the engine off.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a ship floats because its shape displaces enough water, unlike a small solid kettle._

_He opens his mouth, and shuts it, and opens it again._

_Clank is looking at Pinocchio, his chimney-light very steady. Something inside him clicks, and clicks again._

> - He is joking, and it means nothing. → He is warm, not joking. The picture makes a hard idea easier to hold.
> _For grown-ups: Interpreted a metaphor: Real and love as neighbours._

**Clank**: Moss said Real lives next door to it. I went next door. This is the house.  
**Clank**: Pixel didn’t put it in. Nobody puts it in. Somebody does it to you first, and then it’s there.  
_He doesn’t become anything. He is still a kettle on one wheel, with a ramp that says BYTE underneath, and that is the whole point._  
**Geppetto**: And take my old bench, traveller. The little Nubbin on it never got finished. It’s lovely as it is.  
_The page settles under your hand like a door closed quietly._  
_You are back in the Grove, with sawdust in your hair and pine on your sleeve._  

#### `a13-grove-clank-dusk`

_Dusk in the Grove. The Nubbins come in from the long grass one by one and climb onto Clank, because he is warm._  
_One on his wheel, one on his hood like a hat. He turns his chimney-light down low for them._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): sunsets look red and orange because blue light is scattered away  
> _At dusk the Sun is low, and its light must travel through far more air before it reaches you._  
> _The air scatters away the blue light, and the reds and oranges get through._  
> _That is why the sky glows warm at the end of the day, and why the Grove looks so gentle when Clank turns his light down._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a sunset is red and orange because the air scatters the blue light._

_Pixel stops polishing. She knows which word; she has always known which word._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): forgiveness: how it feels to be let off  
> _Pixel says sorry, and Clank answers “Don’t be.” How do you think Pixel feels afterwards, and why?_

> - Still guilty, because sorry was not enough. → She might feel a little guilt. But Clank’s kindness, and the laugh that follows, suggest the weight has gone.
> - Embarrassed that she was forgiven so easily. → That can happen. In this scene, her laugh shows relief more than embarrassment.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on the relief of being forgiven after saying sorry._

_Pixel laughs, the way people do when they are let off something they didn’t know they were carrying, and puts Clank’s nose back on._  

#### `a13-grove-clank-idle`

**Clank**: Announcement: still just here.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): after running, breathing speeds up and then slows down with rest  
> _Corvin is a little out of breath because he hurried. When you run, what happens to your breathing?_  
> - ✅ It speeds up, then slows down again when you rest. → Yes. Your body needs more air when you run, so you breathe faster. Resting lets it settle.
> - It stops completely. → Breathing never stops. It speeds up when you run, and slows again when you rest.
> - It stays exactly the same. → Running makes your muscles need more air, so you breathe faster. That is how the body keeps up.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that breathing speeds up when we run and slows down again with rest._

**Corvin Vale**: I saw the atlas open on the step. I hope you don’t mind. There’s no gate on a page, so I couldn’t knock.

#### `a14-14-harbour-shout`

_He wakes. A mist lies over everything, and he doesn’t know where he is._  
**Odysseus**: What country is this? They promised me Ithaca, and they’ve put me down on some strange shore and gone.  
_A young shepherd comes down the path: fine-boned, like a king’s son, with a good cloak and a spear in his hand._  
**A Young Shepherd**: You must be a long way from home, stranger, not to know this place. This is Ithaca. Even at Troy they’ve heard of Ithaca.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): nostalgia comes from the Greek nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain)  
> _The Greeks had a word for homecoming: nostos (NOS-toss). Another Greek word, algos, means pain._  
> _Put them together and you get an English word for the ache of missing home or the past._  
> _What is it?_  
> - ✅ nostalgia → Yes. Nostalgia is “homecoming-pain”. The Odyssey is the most famous homecoming story of all.
> - nostril → A nostril is part of your nose. The word from nostos and algos is nostalgia.
> - nautical → Nautical means to do with ships. The word that means the ache of missing home is nostalgia.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that nostalgia comes from the Greek words nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain)._

_Odysseus’s heart leaps. Then, because he is who he is, he tells the shepherd a long, sad lie about being a runaway from Crete._  
_The shepherd smiles, and is a tall woman, grave and beautiful. You have met her before, more than once, in other faces._  
**Athena**: Even here, on your own island, you’d spin me a tale. That carefulness is why I have never been able to leave you.  
**Athena**: I am Athena, daughter of Zeus, who has stood by you in every trouble. Look. Your harbour. Your olive tree. Your mountain.  
_The mist lifts. He knows it all at once, and kneels, and puts his face to the ground._  
**Athena**: Your house is full of men who court your wife and eat your bread. Nobody must know you yet. Not one person.  
_She touches him with her wand. His skin wrinkles, his hair thins, and his fine clothes are rags that stink of smoke._  
_He is an old beggar with a staff and a torn bag on a cord. He looks down at himself, and laughs._  
**The Beggar**: Well. Nobody will know me now.  
**The Beggar**: And you. Not a word this time. Not even a little one.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about the difference between being careful and being honest  
> _Odysseus lies even to a friendly stranger on his own island, because being careful has kept him alive for twenty years._  
> _Is being careful the same as being honest?_  
> - No. You can be careful by staying quiet, without telling a lie. → That’s a fair answer. Keeping something private is different from saying something false, and many people feel that matters.
> - Sometimes a lie is needed to stay safe. → That’s a fair answer. Odysseus has good reasons. It’s still worth asking what each lie costs, and who gets hurt by it.
> - It depends who you are talking to. → That’s a thoughtful answer. We owe the people we trust more of the truth than we owe a stranger, and Athena has been testing him.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being careful is the same as being honest (a think question)._

#### `a14-16-gate-shout`

_Outside the gate lies a heap of dung from the mules and cattle, waiting to be carried out to the fields._  
_On it lies an old dog._  
_He is crawling with ticks, and nobody looks after him now. His master is away, and the maids don’t bother._  
**Eumaeus**: That’s Argos. The master raised him from a pup, and sailed for Troy before he ever got to hunt with him.  
**Eumaeus**: Once, no deer in the deep woods could get away from him. The best nose on the island. Look at him now.  
_The old dog lifts his head. His nose works at the air._  
_He knows. After twenty years, through the rags and the staff and the old man’s face, he knows._  
_His ears go flat against his head, and his tail thumps once in the dirt, then again. He can’t get up._  
_The beggar can’t go to him. If he kneels to this dog in front of the swineherd, the whole town will know by dinner._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about hiding love to stay safe  
> _The beggar loves his dog, but if he kneels to him the whole town will know who he is._  
> _Is it right to hide love in order to stay safe?_  
> - Yes. His plan matters more than one moment. → That’s a fair answer. He is choosing the bigger good, though it costs him something precious.
> - No. Love is more important than any plan. → That’s a fair answer. Some people would say that a loved one waiting twenty years deserves a kind word, whatever the cost.
> - He can show love in small ways that nobody else notices. → That’s a thoughtful answer. A small, secret sign of love can be a way to keep faith with both his plan and his dog.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether hiding love to stay safe is right (a think question)._

_The beggar turns his face away and wipes a tear off quickly, so that Eumaeus won’t see._  
**Eumaeus**: Come on, old man. They’ll have eaten it all.  
_Eumaeus goes in through the gate, and the beggar follows. He doesn’t look back at the heap, because he can’t._

#### `a14-16-sit-corvin`

_You sit down beside the heap, in the sun, where it’s warm._  
_Your Nubbin goes up to the old dog slowly, the way it would go up to Moss._  
_Argos sniffs it. Then he lets his head go down, and your Nubbin lies against his side, where the ribs show._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): dogs have a keen sense of smell and remember people they love  
> _Argos knew his master through the rags._  
> _Dogs have a far keener sense of smell than people, and can remember the scent and voice of someone they love for years._  
> _Real dogs live ten to fifteen years, so twenty is the poem’s way of saying he waited a very long time._  
> _How did Argos know the beggar?_  
> - ✅ By his smell and his voice → Yes. A dog’s nose and ears are very sharp, and a loved scent stays in a dog’s memory. That is why pet dogs are so thrilled when you come home.
> - By his clothes → The beggar’s clothes are rags, which is no clue at all. A dog knows a person by scent and voice.
> - By his staff → Any old man might carry a staff, so it is no clue. A dog is far more likely to know him by the way he smells and sounds.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dogs recognise loved people by scent and voice, and that a dog’s sense of smell is far keener than ours._

_From the hall comes the noise of the suitors, and the lyre._  
_Out here there is only the sun, and the flies, and the three of you._  
_He smells of dust and age. Somebody once brushed this coat every day: you can tell from the way it lies._  
_Corvin comes back out through the gate and sits down on the ground on your other side, in his good coat._  
_He puts a hand on the old dog’s back. His hands were cold for twenty-two years; they are warm now, and Argos leans into the warmth._  
**Corvin Vale**: Twenty years on a heap, waiting. Nobody waited for me like that.  
**Corvin Vale**: No. That isn’t true, is it. Somebody did.  
_Argos’s tail moves once more in the dust, for no one you can see._  
_His eyes are on the gate, where his master went in. He is very tired, and the waiting is done._  

**Choices**

- **Scratch behind his ears.**
    - You scratch behind his ears, where a good dog’s ears always want scratching. His eyes half close.
- **Just sit with him.**
    - You just sit. You don’t need to do anything, and he doesn’t need you to.
- **Tell him, quietly, that his master’s home.**
    - **You**: He’s home. You were right. He came back.
    - Argos sighs: a long sigh, like a dog lying down at the end of a day in the woods.

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-3, ask): swallows nest under roofs and migrate south each winter  
> _Swallows build mud nests under roofs. When summer ends, they fly thousands of kilometres south to warmer lands, and come back in spring._  
> _What is this long yearly journey called?_  
> - ✅ Migration → Yes. Migration lets animals find food and warmth when their home turns cold. Swallows, whales and many butterflies migrate.
> - Hibernation → Hibernation is when an animal sleeps through the winter. Swallows don’t sleep it off; they fly away to warmer places.
> - Evolution → Evolution is slow change over many generations. A swallow’s yearly flight to warmer lands is called migration.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that swallows migrate: they travel long distances each year to find food and warmth._

#### `a14-20-bed-shout`

**Odysseus**: Strange woman. The gods made you harder than anyone. Nurse, make me up a bed out here. I’ll sleep alone.  
**Penelope**: I’m not proud, and I’m not cold. I know very well what you looked like when you sailed.  
**Penelope**: Eurycleia, move the great bed out of our room, the one he built himself. Make it up for him out here.  
_Odysseus goes white. He stands up._  
**Odysseus**: Who moved my bed? Nobody could. Nobody living could shift it, however young and strong, unless a god helped him.  
**Odysseus**: I built it. An olive tree grew in the courtyard, tall and thick and green, and I built our room round it, stone by stone.  
**Odysseus**: I roofed it and hung the doors. Then I cut away the branches, trimmed the trunk, and made it the bedpost. I bored the holes myself.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): roots anchor a tree, so a bedpost made from a living trunk can’t be moved  
> _Odysseus built the bed from a living olive trunk, still rooted in the ground. Why is a tree with roots so hard to move?_  
> - ✅ Its roots anchor it deep in the ground. → Yes. Roots spread out and grip the soil, which holds a tree in place in strong winds. A bed built from a rooted trunk is part of the house itself.
> - Because the trunk is made of iron. → Wood isn’t iron. It is the roots under the ground that hold a living tree fast.
> - Because nobody has tried to move it. → The point is that nobody could. A rooted tree is held by its roots.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that roots anchor a tree, which is why a bed built round a living trunk cannot be moved._

**Odysseus**: That was our secret. Has someone cut the trunk? Tell me. Is my bed still there?  
_Her knees give way. She runs to him, and puts her arms round his neck, and kisses him._  
**Penelope**: Don’t be angry with me. So many men have come with stories. I had to be sure it was you.  
_He holds her and weeps. She is to him what the land is to a swimmer who has been a long time in the sea._  
_Athena holds back the dawn at the edge of the world, and keeps the horses of the morning in their stable, so the night goes on._  
**Odysseus**: A friend once shouted my name with me, at a giant. It cost me ten years.  
**Odysseus**: I’m not sorry about the company.  
_Penelope looks at you over his shoulder. She will want to hear all of it later, every word._

#### `a14-20-complete-silence`

_Before anyone can lift a spear, old Mentor steps between the two sides. When he speaks, it isn’t Mentor’s voice at all._  
**Athena**: Men of Ithaca, stop. No more of this. Make peace, and let it hold.  
_Out of a clear sky comes thunder. The spears go down, and the families stand in the road, and then, one by one, go home._  
_Athena, still in Mentor’s shape, makes peace between the house and the town, and both sides swear to keep it._  
**Penelope**: Take my loom, guest. The big one upstairs. I won’t need a loom that works backwards any more.  
_Telemachus brings a cutting from the olive in the bedroom wall, wrapped in wet cloth._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): a cutting needs moisture to grow roots and become a new tree  
> _Telemachus wraps an olive cutting in wet cloth so that it can grow into a new tree. Why keep the cutting wet?_  
> - ✅ Roots need moisture to start growing. → Yes. A cutting has no roots yet, so it needs damp to grow them. Once it has roots, it can take water from the soil and grow into a tree like its parent.
> - So that it floats. → A cutting isn’t going on a boat. Moisture lets the cut end sprout roots.
> - To keep it clean. → Cleanliness isn’t the reason. Without moisture the cut stem would dry out, and roots couldn’t grow.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a cutting needs moisture to grow roots and become a new plant._

**Odysseus**: Plant it by your water. Build something round it, if you like. That’s what they’re for.  
**Odysseus**: And thank you. For saying nothing, that day on the ship. For not telling me what I already knew.  
_The sea goes blue again under your fingers, and the island goes small, and you are home, with the atlas on your knee._  
_In one hand there is an olive cutting in wet cloth. Your Nubbin is holding the corner of a very large loom._  
_A long road home, and a house that waited. Odysseus could have stayed safe on Calypso’s shore, and chose to be well instead._

> _Corvin once did something wrong, and he is still trying to make it right. Should people get second chances? What would help someone earn trust back?_

> - Only if the people who were hurt agree. → That’s a fair answer. The people who were hurt get a say in whether they can trust again.

#### `a14-close-guest`

_When you close the atlas it is evening in the Grove, and somebody is at the gate._  
_It is Corvin Vale, with his hands on the top bar. He doesn’t try the latch; he knocks on the gatepost, twice, and waits._  
**Corvin Vale**: I saw the light. I won’t stay. I only wanted to see that you’d come back.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): waiting to be invited in shows respect for someone else’s home  
> _Corvin knocks on the gatepost and waits, instead of trying the latch. What does that show about how he treats a home that isn’t his?_  
> - ✅ He respects that he must be invited in. → Yes. Knocking and waiting is a way of saying “this is your place, and I will come in only if you say so”. It is the same spirit as xenia.
> - He doesn’t know how latches work. → He knows perfectly well. He is choosing not to touch it, out of respect.
> - He is trying to sneak in. → Sneaking in wouldn’t involve knocking twice and waiting. Knocking is the opposite of sneaking.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that knocking and waiting shows respect for another person’s home._

_You lift and push, and let him in for a cup of tea. He watches your hands, and you turn them so he can’t quite see._  

#### `a14-close-shut`

_When you close the atlas it is evening in the Grove. You go down to the gate, for no reason you could name._  
_The lane beyond it is empty. Nobody is standing there._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): a setting can give a mood  
> _The writer tells us the lane is empty, and that you stand there listening. What mood does that give the scene?_  
> - ✅ Quiet, waiting, and a little lonely → Yes. Short, plain sentences about an empty lane make the scene feel still. Writers choose details like these to build a mood.
> - Loud and exciting → There is no noise or action here, just an empty lane and someone listening. That makes a quiet mood.
> - Funny → Nothing here is meant to be funny. The empty lane and the listening give a quiet, waiting mood.
> _For grown-ups: Identified how setting details (an empty lane, listening) build a quiet, waiting mood._

_You lift and push, out of habit, and it sticks, as it always does. You stand there a while anyway, listening._  

#### `a14-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the Argos page: the gate, the heap, the old dog in the sun._  
_In the margin, in soft pencil you have never noticed, there is a note. You know the hand._  
_“Argos waited twenty years and still knew him, even in rags.”_  
_“That’s why our gate sticks.”_  
_“So I’d hear. H.”_  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): cause and effect: a note explains why the gate sticks  
> _Hazel’s note says Argos waited, and that is why the gate sticks, “so I’d hear”. What does she mean by that?_  
> - ✅ A sticking gate lets you hear anyone coming, the way Argos waited and listened. → Yes. She links a cause (the gate sticks) to an effect (you hear visitors) and to the old dog who waited. A margin note can say a lot in a few words.
> - Gates are always broken. → The note says the sticking is on purpose: it’s a way of hearing people come.
> - Argos opened the gate himself. → Argos is only in the story on the page. The gate sticks so that the Keeper will always hear who is arriving.
> _For grown-ups: Read a margin note for cause and effect (the gate sticks so you will hear who comes)._

_You sit with the page open. Outside, faintly, the gate creaks in the wind, and doesn’t open._

#### `a15-14-screen-done-reconciled`

**Oz**: I am not a wicked man, my dear. I am only a very poor Wizard.  
**Oz**: There is a difference, though I grant it is a small one.  
**Oz**: And I was frightened of the Witches, all along. That is why the walls are so high.  
_You knew a man like this._  
_He gave the trick back. His hand was blue._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: humbug  
> _Oz is called a humbug. What does the word mean here?_  
> - ✅ A person who pretends to be more than they are → Yes. A humbug is a fraud or pretender. In Britain it is also a striped mint sweet, which is a very different thing.
> - A striped mint sweet → That is a real meaning too, in Britain. But in this story it means someone who pretends to be more than they are.
> - A big, noisy bird → Not a bird. In this story it means a pretender.
> _For grown-ups: Told apart two meanings of humbug and chose the one that fits._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): a near miss and disappointment  
> _Dorothy missed the balloon by a few steps. How do you feel when you narrowly miss something you wanted?_  
> _What helps?_  
> - Angry at myself → That’s a fair answer. Anger at ourselves is common. It helps to remember that Toto was loose and nobody could have planned for a kitten.
> - Sad, and then ready to try again → That’s a fair answer. Letting yourself be sad first often makes it easier to find a new plan.
> - I want someone to comfort me → That’s a fair answer. Asking for comfort is wise, and a friend beside Dorothy right now would help.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the feelings that follow a near miss and what helps._

_Before Dorothy goes, you take the china lamb out of your pocket to show Glinda._  
_It is cold, and stiff, and its legs are set hard._  
_It is only an ornament now: pretty, and still._  
_Your Nubbin touches it with its nose, and nothing happens, and it touches it again._  
**Glinda**: Ah. You meant to keep it safe.  
**Glinda**: The ones who love them best so often do.  
**Glinda**: You heard what the Princess told you. Carry it home, back over its own wall, and it will wake.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): when love holds too tight  
> _You meant to keep the lamb safe, and it went still. How can love sometimes get in the way of what someone needs?_  
> - Love can hold on too tight → That’s a fair answer. Holding tight feels like caring, but a loved thing sometimes needs room.
> - You meant well, and that counts → That’s a fair answer. Meaning well matters. It is also fine to mend a mistake, which is what we are about to do.
> - The lamb needed its field → That’s a fair answer. Often the kindest thing is to let someone go back to where they can be themselves.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how loving something can lead us to hold it too tight._

**Dorothy**: Is it grey, where you live?  

**Choices**

- **Let your Nubbin say goodbye to Toto.**

_Dorothy holds Toto tight and knocks the heels of the silver shoes together three times._  
**Dorothy**: Take me home, please. To Aunt Em.  
_She is gone in three great steps. The silver shoes fall from her feet in the air, and are lost in the desert for good._  
_For a moment the page shows Kansas: a new little farmhouse, grey grass, and Aunt Em running across it with her arms open._  
_Then the Monkeys carry your friends away, and Glinda puts the Golden Cap into the King’s hands. He holds it a long time, looking at you._  
**The King of the Winged Monkeys**: You asked me what we would do, if we were free. I have thought about it all this way.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why a short answer can carry a lot  
> _The Monkey King answers in one word: “Play.” Why is a one-word answer so powerful here?_  
> - ✅ After years of orders, the simplest wish tells you the most → Quite so. A long speech would have been about rules. One word says what he longed for.
> - He ran out of words → Not at all. He had thought about it all the way. The short answer was chosen.
> - He was being rude → Not rude. It was the plain truth, and it came from a free heart.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how a very short answer can carry a character’s deepest wish._

_The page folds shut, softly, and you are back in the Grove with the atlas on your knee._  
_A thin silver ribbon keeps the place, and it was not there this morning._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a choice shows about a character  
> _The Lion chooses to walk with you rather than fly. What does that show about him now?_  
> - ✅ He is steady, and decides for himself → Quite right. The Lion who ran from a little dog now makes his own plans and keeps a promise.
> - He is afraid of heights → He was, once. But he has crossed ditches and a river since. This time he simply prefers to walk with a friend.
> - He is lazy → Walking all that way is hardly lazy. It is a way of keeping you company.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how a character’s choice shows how much he has grown._

#### `a16-01-desert-t45`

_Nova’s atlas falls open at a page that is almost empty: one small planet, one chair, and a sunset behind it._  
_You touch the sunset. It turns warm like sand, and then it is sand, and you are standing in it._  
_Dunes in every direction, under a sky so clean it looks scrubbed. Your Nubbin sneezes at the size of it._  
_Sable has come with you. She stands inside your shadow, as if the sun might not notice her there._  
_A few dunes away, a small aeroplane sits nose-down in the sand. A pair of legs sticks out from under the engine._  
**The Pilot**: Unless you’re a mechanic, keep back. If you are one, come quickly.  
_He slides out: a man with oil to his elbows and a face that hasn’t slept._  
**The Pilot**: I’m days from anywhere. You’re the last thing I expected to see.  
**The Pilot**: Where did you come from? No, don’t tell me. I’ve stopped expecting sensible answers out here.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, notice): what a desert is, and that the Sahara is the biggest hot desert  
> **The Pilot**: Welcome to the Sahara, by the way. It’s a desert: a place that gets very little rain.  
> **The Pilot**: Less than 25 centimetres (10 inches) in a whole year. Plenty of sand, not much to drink.  
> **The Pilot**: It’s the biggest hot desert on Earth. You’ll want a hat.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a desert gets very little rain, and that the Sahara is the biggest hot desert._


**Choices**

- **Offer to hold the spanner.**
    - **The Pilot**: Hold it, and don’t hand it over unless I ask. I have a system. It’s mostly muttering.
- **Ask if he’s hurt.**
    - **The Pilot**: Only my pride. And the engine. The engine is worse.
- **Sit down in the shade of the wing.**
    - You sit, and your Nubbin sits. After a moment the man sits too, because it seems rude not to.

#### `a16-13-fox-t45`

_The fox sits in the grass under the apple tree, tail wrapped round its feet, and comes no nearer._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): the fennec: a desert fox with big ears for hearing and cooling  
> _The real Sahara has a fox a lot like this one: the fennec, the smallest fox in the world._  
> _Its huge ears hear insects moving under the sand. They also give off heat, which helps it stay cool._  
> _Fennecs dig burrows and hunt mostly at night, when the desert is cooler._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about the fennec fox and how its ears help it survive in the desert._

_Sable is with you, in your shadow. The fox’s ears turn towards her, and then politely away._  
**The Prince**: Come and play with me. Please. I’ve had a very bad day.  
**The Fox**: Play? I can’t. Nobody has tamed me.  
**The Prince**: Tamed?  
**The Fox**: It’s an old word. It means making ties with someone, slowly, one step at a time.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): words with more than one meaning: “tame”  
> _“Tame” has more than one meaning. It can mean not wild, like a tame rabbit._  
> _Here the fox means making friends slowly, one step at a time. The words around a word show which meaning it has._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a word can have more than one meaning and that nearby words show which._

**The Fox**: Right now you’re one more boy, and I’m one more fox. There are plenty of both.  
**The Fox**: Tame me, and I’ll know your step from every other step. You’ll need me, and I’ll need you.  
**The Prince**: I don’t know how to tame anybody. I don’t think I know how to be tamed, either.  

**Choices**

- **Ask the fox how it’s done.**
    - **The Fox**: Patience. That’s nearly all of it. I’ll show you.
- **Hold out your hand to the fox.**
    - The fox leans back all at once, ears flat.
    - **The Fox**: Too fast. That’s the first thing. Never quick.
- **Let your Nubbin sniff the air.**
    - Your Nubbin sniffs, and the fox sniffs back. Neither moves an inch, and it seems to be going rather well.

#### `a16-13-hour-t45`

**The Fox**: You must be very patient. First you sit down a little way off, like that, in the grass.  
**The Fox**: Don’t look straight at me, and don’t talk. Talking gets in the way.  
**The Fox**: And come at the same hour each day: when the apple tree’s shadow touches that white stone.  
**The Prince**: Why the same hour?  
**The Fox**: So I know when you’re coming. Then I can start being happy a whole hour before you get here.  
**The Fox**: The closer it gets, the happier I am. Looking forward is half of it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.MD.B.3, do): time intervals: one hour before a clock time  
> **The Fox**: If the boy comes at four o’clock, at what time do I start being happy? Set the clock hands for me.  
> _One hour before four o’clock is three o’clock. The fox starts feeling happy at three, long before the boy arrives._  
> Check: `edu:read:clock:three`
> _For grown-ups: Found one hour before four o’clock to work out when the fox starts looking forward._

_Days on this page are short: a few minutes from sunrise to stars. You watch the shadow crawl towards the white stone._  
_The shadow touches the stone, and the boy sits down a long way off. Behind you, out of your shadow, Sable sits down too._  
**The Fox**: Oh, look. She’s listening. Same hour, for her as well.  
_Sunset, stars, sunrise, and the shadow touches the stone. The boy moves nearer the fox, and Sable moves one step nearer you._  
_And again, one step, her ears up. She doesn’t look straight at you, and you don’t look straight at her._  
_On the fourth day, when the shadow touches the stone, Sable is sitting one step from your hand._  

#### `a16-13-hour-done-t20`

_The fox lets the boy put a hand on its head. Soon they are sitting together, looking at the same sunset._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): how to befriend a shy animal gently  
> _How do you make friends with a shy animal? Think about what the boy did._  
> - ✅ Sit quietly, stay calm, and go a little nearer each day, letting it choose. → Yes. Slow and calm helps a shy animal feel safe, and lets the animal choose.
> - Pick it up at once, so it gets used to you. → Quick moves frighten a shy animal. The boy sat still, a little way off, and let the fox come to him.
> - Stare straight at it until it comes. → Staring can scare an animal. The boy looked away and said nothing, so the fox felt safe.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about gentle, patient ways to make friends with a shy animal._

_You think of the long grass at home, where something small and grey still runs when you come near. Same hour, a little nearer._

> - Stare straight at it until it comes. → Staring can scare an animal. The boy looked away and said nothing, so the fox felt safe.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about gentle, patient ways to make friends with a shy animal._

_Sable has watched it all from your heel without moving. The fox catches her eye, and its tail twitches, as if they agree._  

#### `a16-13-secret-done-glass`

_Then the fox turns its head, and looks at you as well._  
**The Fox**: You’re the one who wanted her under glass. Keeping someone safe isn’t the same as keeping them close.  
**The Fox**: Think about that, both of you.

> **Lesson** (art, RL.1.4, notice): a colour can hold a memory of a person  
> _Ripe wheat is gold, and the wind makes it ripple like water. The fox says it will remind it of the boy._

#### `a17-09-wait-hunt`

_Mei is asleep on Satsuki’s back. The rain drips off the edge of the shelter, steady as a clock._  

> **Lesson** (music, RL.2.4, do): keep a steady beat, four counts at a time

> Check: `edu:clap:beat:rain-four`
> _For grown-ups: Clapped a steady beat in groups of four to match dripping rain._

_Your Nubbin, under the shelter, slowly turns its head to the right._  
_Next to Satsuki, something is standing in the rain. You hear its claws first, on the wet road._  
_You can’t see past Satsuki and her umbrella. You see two feet: grey, enormous, with claws like garden forks._

_You lean, a little, to see round the umbrella. The feet shift away, politely, the way people do at bus stops._  

**Choices**

- **Lean further to see.**
    - You lean further, and the feet move further. Whatever it is, it isn’t ready to be looked at by you, not yet.
- **Stand still and look at the road.**

#### `a17-11-dance-charm`

_Round the bed you all go, slowly: arms up, bend, arms up, bend. Nobody says a word._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a repeating pattern: up, bend, up, bend  
> _The dance goes up, bend, up, bend, and on. What is the 9th move?_  
> - ✅ Up. → Yes. The odd moves, the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th, are all “up”, and the even moves are “bend”.
> - Bend. → Let’s write it out: 1 up, 2 bend, 3 up, 4 bend, 5 up, 6 bend, 7 up, 8 bend, 9 … The 9th is up.
> - Jump. → Jump isn’t in this dance. The pattern is up, bend, and the 9th is up.
> _For grown-ups: Continued a repeating pattern by rule: odd moves up, even moves bend._

_At the edge of the bed your Nubbin stops dancing. It is digging, with both paws, a little hole beside the girls’ rows._  
_It looks up at you, and then at the acorn on its loop of string round your neck: Moss’s acorn charm._  
_You untie the acorn from the string and put it in the hole. Your Nubbin pats the earth down over it, very firmly._  
_A shoot comes up out of the earth, then another. Then all of them together, and one more, darker, from the little hole._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): an acorn grows into an oak, which takes decades to make acorns of its own  
> _You planted Moss’s acorn in the little hole. If it grows into an oak, how long before it makes acorns of its own?_  
> - ✅ Often twenty to fifty years. → Yes. An oak is slow to grow up, but it may live for hundreds of years.
> - About a week. → A seedling can sprout in weeks, but a tree takes much longer. It is often twenty to fifty years before an oak makes acorns.
> - Never, an acorn cannot grow. → An acorn is a seed, and given soil, water and time, it can grow. It is often twenty to fifty years before an oak makes acorns.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an oak takes many years to grow up and make acorns of its own._

_They rise with his arms, twisting round each other, into a tree as tall as the camphor on the hill._  
**Satsuki**: We did it. We did it!  

**Choices**

- **Cheer with Satsuki and Mei.**
    - You cheer. The great spirit looks round at the noise, and grins, a grin as wide as the hedge.
- **Lie down in the grass by your Nubbin and look up.**
    - You lie down by your Nubbin and look up. Somewhere up there, among all the other leaves, are some that are oak.

#### `a17-11-complete-oak`

_You wake on Granny’s floor at sunrise, with your Nubbin asleep on your chest. Your socks have grass on them._  
_Across the hedge, Satsuki and Mei are already out on the veranda, staring at the garden. There is no great tree._  
_But in the seed bed, in rows and in clumps, there are shoots. Little green ones, just up._  
**Satsuki**: It was a dream! But it wasn’t!  
**Mei**: We did it! We did it!  
_Beside the bed, where you planted the acorn, the earth is smooth and bare. There is nothing there at all._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): a seed sends out its root first, underground, before any shoot shows  
> _Where the acorn is planted, the earth is smooth and bare. Is it doing nothing?_  
> _What is happening underground first?_  
> - ✅ It is growing a root first, which goes down before any shoot comes up. → Yes. The root anchors the seed and drinks water. The shoot comes later.
> - Nothing at all. → A lot goes on out of sight. The seed grows a root first, underground, long before a shoot shows.
> - It is growing leaves already, hidden. → Leaves come after the shoot reaches the light. The root grows first, underground.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a seed grows a root underground first, before any shoot shows._

_The string round your neck is empty, and very light. Your Nubbin looks at it, and then up at the hill, as if it knows something._  

#### `a17-14-tunnel-hunt`

_Satsuki runs into the old house garden, straight at the hedge, and goes in at the gap on her hands and knees._  
_You dive in after her. For one moment it is the tunnel, green and gold, with Satsuki’s heels ahead of you._  
_Then the branches close in front of your face. It is a hedge, just a hedge, and you are stuck in it._  
_By the time you back out, scratched, there is no sound from the other side at all._  
_A bicycle bell rings in the lane. Kanta, on a bicycle much too big for him, stops with one foot down._  
**Kanta**: Where’s Satsuki? I saw her run in here.  
**You**: She’s gone to get help. Somewhere I can’t follow.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): asking for help clearly: say what happened and what you need  
> _You tell Kanta where Satsuki went, and he offers his bicycle. What made it easy for him to help?_  
> - ✅ You said what happened, so he knew what to do. → Yes. A clear message lets a helper act at once.
> - You didn’t say anything. → You did say something, and that helped. Saying what happened lets a helper know what to do.
> - He was already planning it. → He may have been, but you made it easy. Saying what happened lets a helper know what to do.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that saying clearly what happened makes it easy for a helper to act._

**Kanta**: Then we look on our own. Get on.  
**Kanta**: My uncle’s bike. He doesn’t know.

- **Get on the back.**
    - You climb on the carrier with Kanta’s schoolbag digging into your knees, and he pushes off.
- **Look at the hedge once more.**
    - You look back at the hedge. You did go looking for the way in, and it remembers.

#### `a17-14-tunnel-hunt-done`

_Kanta pedals hard along the lane, standing up, shouting Mei’s name at every turning._  
_He rides 2 kilometres in 10 minutes, and does not slow._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): distance, time and rate: 2 km in 10 minutes is 6 km in 30 minutes  
> _Kanta rides 2 kilometres in 10 minutes. If he keeps that pace, how far does he go in 30 minutes?_  
> - ✅ 6 kilometres. → Yes. 30 minutes is three lots of 10 minutes, and 3 × 2 = 6 kilometres.
> - 4 kilometres. → 4 km would be 20 minutes’ riding. 30 minutes is three lots of 10, so 3 × 2 = 6 kilometres.
> - 12 kilometres. → 12 km would be 60 minutes’ riding. 30 minutes is three lots of 10, so 3 × 2 = 6 kilometres.
> _For grown-ups: Used a steady rate: 2 km in 10 minutes gives 6 km in 30 minutes._

_Your Nubbin hangs on to your sleeve, ears flat in the wind._  
_Fields, then a pond, then a bridge, go by in a blur._  

#### `a17-14-call-hunt`

_From the hill behind you comes a roar. It rolls out over the whole valley like thunder._  
**Kanta**: What was that? Thunder?  
**Kanta**: There’s no clouds.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): sound travels about 340 metres a second in air, so a distant roar arrives seconds later  
> _Sound travels about 340 metres every second. The roar came from a hill 3,400 metres away._  
> _About how many seconds did it take to reach you?_  
> - ✅ About 10 seconds. → Yes. 3,400 ÷ 340 = 10, the same sum people use to guess how far away thunder is.
> - About 1 second. → In 1 second sound goes only 340 metres. 3,400 ÷ 340 = 10 seconds.
> - No time at all. → Sound takes real time to travel, unlike what it seems. 3,400 ÷ 340 = 10 seconds.
> _For grown-ups: Used speed of sound (about 340 m per second) to work out how long a sound takes to arrive._

_A wind comes over the rice from behind you. The rice bends flat in a long line, as if something huge is running across it._  
_Two yellow lights go over your heads, along the power lines, and away towards the hills. Nobody in the fields looks up._  
**Kanta**: Did you see that? What did you see?  
_Up top, as it goes, there is a sign. You can just read it: MEI._  
**You**: That way. Follow it.  
**You**: Follow the wind.  

**Choices**

- **Point Kanta after the lights.**
    - **Kanta**: That’s the old road. Out by the statues.
    - **Kanta**: Hold on!
    - He stands on the pedals. The bicycle rattles like a tin of nails.
- **Tell Kanta what you saw.**
    - **Kanta**: A bus. Shaped like a cat.
    - **Kanta**: Running on the wires.
    - He doesn’t laugh. He turns the bicycle that way, and pedals.

#### `a17-14-call-hunt-done`

_The wind dies away ahead of you._  
_Kanta keeps pedalling the way it went, and doesn’t ask any more questions._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): inference: why Kanta stops asking questions  
> _Kanta keeps pedalling and stops asking questions. What does that tell us about him?_  
> - ✅ He has decided to trust you, even though it sounds impossible. → Yes. His silence is a kind of belief, and it comes with action.
> - He has lost interest. → A boy who pedals faster has not lost interest. He has decided to trust you, and shows it by riding on.
> - He is angry with you. → His face is set, but he is not angry with you. He has decided to trust you.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s actions and silence to infer that he has decided to trust someone._

_His face is set, as if he has made up his mind about something._  

#### `a17-14-complete-hunt`

_The old road runs out between the fields, white in the dusk. Kanta is breathing like a pump, and doesn’t slow down._  
**Kanta**: If she’s hurt. If she’s fallen in a ditch.  
**You**: She isn’t. My Nubbin’s with her.  
**Kanta**: Your Nubbin’s the size of a rice ball.  
**You**: It’s with her.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a think question: why keep trusting someone when you have doubts?  
> _Kanta doubts that a Nubbin can protect Mei, but he pedals faster anyway. Why do people act on trust when they still have doubts?_  
> _Think about it._  
> - Because doing something is better than doing nothing. → That’s a fair answer. Action can be a way of coping with worry. Kanta’s pedalling is very much that.
> - Because they trust the person, even without proof. → That’s a fair answer. Trust sometimes goes ahead of proof. He has seen enough of you to take a chance.
> - Because they have nothing to lose. → That’s a fair answer. When someone is missing, any chance is worth taking. Kanta’s face shows how much he cares.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people act on trust when they still have doubts._

_Kanta doesn’t answer. He pedals faster._  

#### `a17-15-statues-hunt`

_The bicycle comes round a bend, and there by the verge stands a row of six small stone statues in red bibs._  
_They are Jizo, keeping the road. Someone has put fresh flowers at their feet._  
_Each bib is a square of red cloth, about 30 centimetres across._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): units of length: 6 × 30 cm = 180 cm = 1 m 80 cm  
> _Each bib is about 30 centimetres of cloth. Laid end to end, how long would the six bibs be, in metres and centimetres?_  
> - ✅ 1 metre 80 centimetres. → Yes. 6 × 30 = 180 centimetres, and 100 centimetres make a metre, so 1 m 80 cm.
> - 30 centimetres. → That is only one bib. 6 × 30 = 180 centimetres, which is 1 m 80 cm.
> - 6 metres. → 6 metres would be 600 centimetres. Six bibs make 180. 6 × 30 = 180 centimetres, which is 1 m 80 cm.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication and metres and centimetres: 6 × 30 cm = 1 m 80 cm._

_Beside them, in a whirl of dust and leaves, Satsuki and Mei are holding each other tight. Mei still has her corn._

**Kanta**: Mei! She’s there!  
**Kanta**: She’s all right! Mei!  
_Kanta can see the girls, but not what they are standing next to. You can._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): relief and joy after a scare: Kanta’s feelings as well as the sisters’  
> _Kanta shouts for Mei, and the sisters hold on to each other. What feeling do they all share?_

> - Boredom. → Nobody is bored after a night like this. They share relief, after a long fright.
> - Anger. → Some of them may be a little cross, but mostly it is something gentler. They share relief after a long fright.
> _For grown-ups: Named relief as the feeling shared after a long fright._

_Your Nubbin comes running down the road to you, as fast as its legs go, and throws itself at your shins._

> - They look exactly the same. → They don’t: you know something Kanta does not. You see a bus leap away; Kanta sees two girls vanish in the wind.
> - Neither of you sees anything. → Both of you see the girls go. You see a bus; Kanta sees only a gust of wind.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two points of view on the same moment: what you can see and what Kanta can see._

#### `a17-15-complete-hunt`

_Kanta’s uncle’s bicycle is very old and very fast downhill._  
_You ride on the carrier, holding your Nubbin and Kanta’s shirt._  
_Up the long hill you walk it, and down the other side Kanta lets it fly, and your Nubbin’s ears blow straight back._  
_You push, and grunt, and puff on the way up, then freewheel on the way down without a single pedal._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity and friction: uphill needs a push, downhill gravity helps  
> _Going up the hill takes a hard push. Going down takes none._  
> _What changes between the two?_  
> - ✅ On the way up, gravity pulls against you; on the way down it pulls you along. → Yes. The same force, gravity, works against you uphill and for you downhill. Friction slows you in both.
> - The bicycle gets lighter. → The bicycle weighs the same either way. Gravity pulls against you uphill, and along with you downhill.
> - The wind turns round. → The wind may do something, but it is gravity that matters here. Gravity pulls against you uphill, and along with you downhill.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls against you going uphill and helps you going downhill._

**Kanta**: I’m going to be in so much trouble.

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): a cold spreads through coughs and touch; washing hands helps stop it  
> _Mrs Kusakabe has a cold. How does a cold spread from person to person, and what helps stop it?_  
> - ✅ Through coughs, sneezes and touch; washing hands helps stop it. → Yes. Cold viruses travel on tiny droplets and on hands. Soap and water are real protection.
> - Through looking at someone. → Looking can’t pass a cold on. Coughs, sneezes and touch spread it, and washing hands helps stop it.
> - Through moonlight. → Moonlight is harmless. Coughs, sneezes and touch spread colds, and washing hands helps stop it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that colds spread through coughs, sneezes and touch, and that washing hands helps._

**Mr Kusakabe**: You’d have come, if it were me.

> _Mr Kusakabe says nothing, but he lifts his hand to you. What does that small action show about him?_  
> - ✅ He understands, and is quietly saying thank you. → Yes. A writer can show a character’s feelings through what he does, without saying them.
> - He is waving goodbye for ever. → It is a quieter gesture than that. He understands, and is quietly thanking you.
> - He is cross. → A cross person wouldn’t lift a hand so gently. He understands, and is quietly thanking you.
> _For grown-ups: Read a small gesture as showing a character’s understanding and thanks._


#### `a17-16-corn-hunt-done`

_They grow small and faint, then smaller, then are only one point of yellow, then nothing._

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, ask): a light looks smaller and fainter the further away it is  
> _The yellow lights shrink and fade as they go. Are they really getting smaller and dimmer?_  
> - ✅ No. They only look smaller and fainter because they are further away. → Yes. The lamp is the same; the light reaching your eyes is less, so it looks smaller and dimmer.
> - Yes, someone is turning them off. → A good guess, but it is only the distance. They look smaller and fainter because they are further away.
> - Yes, lights always shrink at night. → Lights are the same size all the time. It is the distance that makes them look smaller and fainter.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that far-away lights only look smaller and fainter because of distance._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): a think question: is it right to keep some wonders to yourself?  
> _Kanta and you go home having seen things nobody will believe. Is it right to keep some wonders to yourselves?_  
> _Think about it._

> - No, sharing makes wonder grow. → That’s a fair answer. Shared joy often doubles. Mei will certainly be telling it, louder each time.
> - It depends who is listening. → That’s a fair answer. The right listener makes all the difference. Granny, with her lamp, looks like a good one.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): life in the 1950s countryside compared with today  
> _Which of these did people in the 1950s countryside use to send news or get water?_  
> - ✅ A telegram, a crank telephone and a hand pump. → Yes. They are all in this story, and none is quaint to the people who used them. They were everyday tools.
> - A smartphone and a video call. → Those came decades later. A telegram, a crank telephone and a hand pump were the tools of the time.
> - Email and a washing machine tap. → Email came much later, and few country houses had running taps. A telegram, a crank telephone and a hand pump were the tools of the time.
> _For grown-ups: Compared the tools of 1950s country life, such as telegrams and hand pumps, with those of today._

_Then the page goes soft under your hand, and it is the Grove, with Nova’s atlas on your knee._

#### `a17-grove-oak`

_You step out of Nova’s atlas into the Grove. Something on the western hill has changed._  
_By the flat stone where Moss sits there is an oak. Not a sapling: a full-grown oak, its crown spread over half the hill._  
_Moss is on his stone underneath it, looking up. He doesn’t look round when you come up the path._

**Moss**: I planted one of those when the valley was young. It took four hundred years.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): a think question: how does teasing show fondness?  
> _Moss says, “You’ve been cheating.” He is teasing._  
> _How can teasing show that someone is fond of you? Think about it._  
> - A gentle tease says “I notice you, and I like you”. → That’s a fair answer. A kind tease is a way of paying attention. Moss pays attention to everything.
> - It only works if both people are laughing. → That’s a fair answer. Teasing has to be gentle, or it stops being kind. Moss’s tone is warm.
> - It can hide big feelings in a small joke. → That’s a fair answer. Moss is moved by the oak, and a joke is a safer way to say so. He looks at it for a very long time.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how gentle teasing can show fondness._


> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, ask): an oak can live for hundreds of years  
> _Moss says his own oak took four hundred years. How long can a healthy oak live?_  
> - ✅ Often several hundred years, and sometimes more than a thousand. → Yes. Oaks are among the longest-lived trees in many lands, which is why they stand for whole histories.
> - About ten years. → Ten years is a young sapling. Oaks often live for several hundred years.
> - Only as long as a person. → A person’s lifetime is much shorter than an oak’s. Oaks often live for several hundred years.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that oaks can live for hundreds of years, sometimes over a thousand._

#### `a17-grove-oak-sleeps`

_You step out of Nova’s atlas into the Grove. On the western hill, by the flat stone where Moss always sat, there is an oak._
