_The shade falls exactly where he used to sit._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): how a setting detail carries feeling: the shade where Moss sat  
> _“The shade falls exactly where he used to sit.” Why might the writer tell us that?_  
> - ✅ It makes the oak seem to keep his place for him, so we think of him. → Yes. One small detail about a place can hold a lot of feeling.
> - To tell us what time of day it is. → Shade can tell the time, but that isn’t why it is here. The oak seems to keep Moss’s place, so we think of him.
> - Because shade is cool. → It is, but the writer means more than that. The oak seems to keep Moss’s place, so we think of him.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a detail of a setting can carry a feeling: the oak keeps Moss’s place._

_The Nubbins have found it already. They are asleep in a heap in its shade, all of them, breathing slowly together._  
_Something drops through the leaves and lands in your hand. An acorn: the oak’s first._  
_You thread it on to the old string, where his used to be. You sit down on the flat stone a while, and remember him._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): grief: what helps when we are sad that someone has died  
> _Moss has died, and it is natural to feel sad. What helps when we are sad that someone has died?_  
> - ✅ Remembering them with other people, and telling their stories. → Yes. Remembering together keeps them close, and sad feelings are allowed to come and go.
> - Pretending it did not happen. → That is a very natural wish, but the sadness tends to wait. Remembering them with other people helps it ease.
> - Being alone and never speaking of it. → Some quiet is good, but being alone with it all the time is hard. Remembering together, and telling their stories, helps.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that remembering someone with others helps when we are sad that they have died._


#### `a17-grove-camphor`

_You step out of Nova’s atlas into the Grove with a pot in your arms._  
_In it is a young camphor tree, as high as your knee._  
_Its leaves are glossy and new, and they smell clean and sharp, like a medicine chest kept in a forest._  
_Your Nubbin, still in its leaf hat, sits down beside the pot with its chin on its knees._  
_It has learned how you wait for a tree. It means to be very good at it._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): looking after something that grows slowly takes patient, regular care  
> _Your Nubbin has learned to wait for a tree. How can we look after something that grows slowly?_  
> - ✅ Care for it a little, regularly, and be patient. → Yes. Small, regular care adds up, and patience is part of the job.
> - Check on it every five minutes and poke it. → Too much poking can hurt a young plant. A little regular care, and patience, works best.
> - Forget about it until it is big. → Then it might not survive to get big. A little regular care, and patience, works best.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that growing something slowly takes small, regular care and patience._

_You find it a place by the window, where the light is good, and wonder what else it will want._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, ask): a potted plant needs light, water, and drainage so roots do not rot  
> _Your young camphor tree is in a pot. Which set of things does it need to grow well?_  
> - ✅ Sunshine, water when the soil is dry, and a pot that drains. → Yes. Roots need air as well as water, so a pot with drainage holes keeps them healthy.
> - Darkness and no water. → A plant needs light and water to grow. Sunshine, water when dry and a pot that drains keep it well.
> - Water all day, every day. → Too much water can rot the roots. Water when the soil is dry, in a pot that drains.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a potted plant needs: light, water when dry, and drainage._

#### `a18-10-chores-doll`

_Vasilisa sleeps on, as she was told to. The doll climbs down off the bench and goes to work._

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: two dolls’ worth of work  
> _Say one doll can finish 12 jobs in a morning. Fed twice, it works like two dolls._  
> _How many jobs does it finish?_  
> - ✅ 24 → Yes. Two dolls’ worth of 12 jobs is 2 × 12 = 24 jobs. Doubling 12 gives 24.
> - 14 → That’s 12 + 2. Twice the work means two groups of 12: 2 × 12 = 24.
> - 6 → That’s 12 ÷ 2, which halves the work. The doll works twice as hard, so double: 24.
> _For grown-ups: Doubled 12 jobs to find 24, using multiplication as equal groups._

_Once, going past with the washing, the doll pats your Nubbin on the head. It doesn’t stop working to do it._  

#### `a18-10-chores-self`

_Vasilisa sleeps on, as she was told to. The doll climbs down off the bench and goes to work._  
_The broom sweeps the yard with nobody holding it. The pots scrub themselves, and the linen goes into the tub grey and comes out white._  
_Your crust is inside you, and your arms work. So you sift your share yourself, the slow way, a handful at a time._  
_A quarter of oats is a great many oats. Your Nubbin is hungry and droopy, and lies on the sack and watches._  
_You manage six scoops an hour, for eight hours._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication: 8 hours × 6 scoops  
> _You manage six scoops an hour for eight hours. How many scoops is that?_  
> - ✅ 48 → Yes. 8 × 6 = 48 scoops. You can do 8 × 5 = 40 and add one more 8 to get 48.
> - 14 → That’s 8 + 6. Six scoops in each of eight hours: 8 × 6 = 48.
> - 42 → That’s 7 × 6. There are eight hours, so 8 × 6 = 48.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 8 × 6 to find 48 scoops sifted by hand._

_The doll does its share, and Vasilisa’s, and keeps the dinner going. Yours it leaves to you._  
_By the time the white light is high, your hands are raw and the chaff is up to your knees._  
_By the time it has gone red and low, you are done. You checked twice._  

#### `a18-11-poppy-self`

_The doll climbs down off the table and walks into the poppy seed, and the seed and the earth start running apart around it._  
_It works Vasilisa’s half, and leaves your half alone._  
_It looks at you once, and you understand that it isn’t unkind. It is only fair._  
_So you pick earth out of poppy seed, speck by speck, with the point of a pin and a great deal of patience._  
_You begin at half past eight in the morning. Your Nubbin, hungry and slow today, sits by your elbow and noses the specks you’ve missed towards you._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals across the day  
> _You began at 8:30 in the morning and finished at 6:15 in the evening. How long did you work?_  
> - ✅ 9 hours 45 minutes → Yes. From 8:30 am to 5:30 pm is 9 hours, and from 5:30 to 6:15 is another 45 minutes: 9 hours 45 minutes.
> - 10 hours 15 minutes → That’s too long. 8:30 to 6:30 pm is exactly 10 hours, and 6:15 is 15 minutes before that: 9 hours 45 minutes.
> - 8 hours 15 minutes → That’s too short. From 8:30 to 5:30 is 9 hours already, then add 45 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Found a longer time interval, 8:30 am to 6:15 pm, by counting on in hours and minutes._

_By a quarter past six your eyes are watering, and it is done._

#### `a18-12-gate-doll`

_At the gate, Baba Yaga stops you with one long finger. She bends and sniffs your pockets, and Vasilisa’s, and frowns._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): the senses: smell  
> _Baba Yaga finds things out with her nose. People traditionally count five senses._  
> _Which is the sense she is using here?_  
> - ✅ Smell → Yes. The five senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Smell works when tiny particles in the air reach special cells in the nose.
> - Hearing → Hearing uses the ears. She is sniffing, which uses the sense of smell.
> - Touch → Touch uses the skin. Sniffing uses the nose, so it is smell.
> _For grown-ups: Named smell as one of the five senses and how it works._

_At the gate, Baba Yaga stops you with one long finger. She takes your hand, turns it over, and looks at the blisters._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): friction causes blisters  
> _Sifting all day has raised blisters on your hands. What force makes skin blister when it rubs against something rough?_  
> - ✅ Friction → Yes. Friction is the force that resists when two surfaces rub. It turns movement into heat and wear, and enough of it raises a blister. Gloves reduce it.
> - Gravity → Gravity pulls things down. The rubbing that raises blisters is friction.
> - Magnetism → Magnetism acts on certain metals. Blisters come from friction, the force of rubbing.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that friction, the force of rubbing, can wear and blister skin._

**Baba Yaga**: Hm. Honest, at least.  
**Baba Yaga**: You worked. I pay for work.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): shivering: muscles make heat  
> _Your Nubbin shivers in the cold. Why does the body shiver?_  
> - ✅ Tiny rapid muscle movements make heat to keep the body warm → Yes. Shivering is the body’s heater: muscles twitch quickly, and the movement releases warmth. It is the body’s automatic answer to cold.
> - To shake the cold off the skin → Cold doesn’t sit on the skin like dust. Shivering makes heat inside the body.
> - Because the muscles are asleep → The muscles are very active when we shiver; they are making heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shivering is the body making heat with quick muscle movements._

> _Your Nubbin stops shivering after eating oats. Why does food help us keep warm and moving?_

> - Food warms us only because it is hot → Even cold food gives energy. The warmth comes from the body using the food as fuel.
> - Food makes the cold go away → Cold stays cold. Food gives the body fuel to make its own heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the body turns food into energy for movement and heat._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): synonyms: miniature, tiny  
> _The second loom is “no bigger than a slipper”. Which word means the same as very small?_  
> - ✅ Miniature → Yes. Miniature, tiny, minute and petite all mean very small. A good writer picks the one that fits best.
> - Enormous → That means the opposite: very big. A loom no bigger than a slipper is miniature.
> - Ordinary → Ordinary means usual. A slipper-sized loom is unusually small: miniature.
> _For grown-ups: Chose a synonym (miniature) for very small, using context._

#### `a18-15-loom-done-self`

_By morning there is a loom in the corner, small and neat, strung with Vasilisa’s thread. Nobody heard it being made._  
_Your Nubbin is awake and helping, handing up the bobbins one at a time. It has kept close to your hands ever since the oats._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how linen was made by hand long ago, step by step  
> _Long ago, families made linen by hand in five steps: bleach, spin, pull, weave and ret (soak the stems so the woody part rots away)._  
> _Which order did they go in?_  
> - ✅ Pull, ret, spin, weave, bleach → Yes. Pull, ret, spin, weave, bleach, and the bleaching comes last, on finished cloth. Today machines do most of it, in the same order.
> - Weave, pull, spin, ret, bleach → Weaving needs thread, which needs spun fibres, which needs retted flax, which needs a pulled plant. Start with pulling.
> - Bleach, spin, pull, weave, ret → Bleaching comes last. The order starts with pulling the plant: pull, ret, spin, weave, bleach.
> _For grown-ups: Put the five steps of making linen by hand long ago in order (pull, ret, spin, weave, bleach), and compared it with today._

> _A frightened animal that is grabbed can feel trapped. Trapped animals may bolt, or bite in panic._

_Then Toothless leans in, and pushes his nose into Hiccup’s palm._  
**Hiccup**: …Oh.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether one mistake teaches enough  
> _You remember grabbing Sable, and this time you slowed your Nubbin gently. Is it enough to learn from a mistake once?_  
> - Yes, if you really change what you do → That’s a fair answer. A mistake taught you something, and you used it.
> - No, we have to keep choosing differently every time → That’s a fair answer. Habits need practice, and the old reflex is always nearby.
> - It depends how big the mistake was → That’s a fair answer. Some lessons stick at once, and others come back round.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether learning from a mistake once is enough._


#### `a19-08-near-ran`

_Toothless takes his nose out of Hiccup’s hand and looks past him, at you, and at your Nubbin._  
**Hiccup**: He’s looking at you two. Stay still. Let him decide.  
_Toothless takes one step across the sand. Your Nubbin is behind your legs before he takes another._  
_In the woods you scooped it up and ran, and it hasn’t forgotten the running. It is holding your trouser leg in both paws._  
_Toothless stops, and his ears go flat. He watches your Nubbin for a long moment, then lies down right where he is._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-3, ask): giving a wary animal space  
> _Toothless lies down instead of coming nearer. What is the kind thing to do when an animal keeps its distance?_  
> - ✅ Give it space and let it come in its own time → Yes, every animal has a distance it needs to feel safe. Letting it choose to come closer keeps it calm.
> - Move closer to show you are friendly → Moving towards a wary animal can feel like a threat, however friendly we feel. Space works better.
> - Chase it so it learns → Chasing frightens animals and teaches them to avoid us. Patience teaches trust.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a wary animal needs space and time to approach in its own way._

**Hiccup**: That’s all right. He’s just saying: not yet. He said that to me for days.

**Hiccup**: One more round, before the light goes. Small passengers only.  
_He looks at your Nubbin. Toothless looks at it too, and walks over, and sniffs it, long and careful._

**Hiccup**: Not yet, then. Sorry. He’s like that. He decides.

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, ask): shadows are longest when the sun is low  
> _The sun is nearly down, and the shadows on the sand have grown very long. Why are shadows longest at sunrise and sunset?_  
> - ✅ The sun is low, so its light arrives at a shallow angle → Yes. A low sun throws long shadows, and a high noon sun throws short ones.
> - The sun is hotter then → The heat does not change the length of a shadow. The angle of the light does.
> - The sea stretches them → The sea does not stretch shadows. A low sun’s shallow angle does.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shadows are longest when the sun is low in the sky._

_Your Nubbin watches from your lap. It watches Toothless the whole way round._

> - It is harder, because you remember how long it took → That’s a fair answer. Memory can make us tired, and it can make us braver.

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): whether trust is owed to those who are patient

> - It depends on how the creature has been treated → That’s a fair answer. A creature that has been hurt may need much longer to trust anyone.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether patience means a creature owes you trust._

#### `a20-01-ember`

_Your Nubbin is carrying its little lantern, as it does everywhere now. Inside it, the red pebble from the high pass glows._  
**Fulla**: A lamp with no flame. It’s warm, though. My hands are warm just being near it.  
**Frigg**: Somebody gave that away who had very little left to give. Keep it close, little one.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why someone might give away almost the last thing they have (a think question)  
> _Frigg says someone gave that away who had very little left to give._  
> _Why might a person give away almost the last thing they have?_  
> - Because they cared more about someone else than about keeping it → A generous answer. Giving can say “you matter more to me than this.”
> - Because they wanted to be rid of it → Possible. But Frigg says they had little left to give, which sounds more like love than clearing out.
> - Because they hoped it would help someone who needed it → A good reason. A small gift from someone with little can mean more than a big gift from someone with plenty.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone might give away a precious thing (no single right answer)._


#### `a20-11-ember`

_Your Nubbin holds its little lantern up close to a stone that is slow to weep. The red pebble inside glows._  
_The frost on that stone runs at once, faster than any of the others, as if it had only been waiting to be asked kindly._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions of time  
> _The other stones took about 30 minutes to run with water. The stone beside the ember took one third of that time._  
> _How many minutes did it take?_  
> - ✅ 10 minutes → Yes. One third of 30 is 30 ÷ 3 = 10 minutes.
> - 3 minutes → 3 is one tenth of 30. A third of 30 is 30 ÷ 3 = 10.
> - 27 minutes → 27 is 30 − 3. A third of 30 means splitting into three equal parts: 10 each.
> _For grown-ups: Found a unit fraction of an amount: one third of 30 minutes is 10._

**A Messenger**: What’s that you carry?  
**You**: Something warm. From a long way off.

#### `a20-14-bowl-walked`

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view from far away  
> _From the foot of the stair you can see the lamp, the three stones and Sigyn with her bowl, but you cannot hear her._  
> _What do you know about Sigyn from here, and what can you only guess?_  
> - ✅ I can see what she is doing, but only guess what she feels → Yes. Seeing an action is not the same as knowing a feeling.
> - I know everything she is thinking → Nobody can know that from a distance. We can only guess.
> - I know nothing at all → You know a good deal: she kneels, she holds the bowl, her arms are tired.
> _For grown-ups: Told what can be seen from a distance from what can only be guessed._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): shades of meaning: steady  
> _The pebble burns “steady all winter long, never hot, always warm.”_  
> _Which word means almost the same as “steady” here?_  
> - ✅ Constant → Yes. Constant means it keeps going, the same, without changing.
> - Wild → Wild means out of control. A steady light stays calm.
> - Flickering → Flickering lights go up and down. Steady lights stay the same.

> _What does flicker mean?_

> - To shine very brightly → A flicker is unsteady, not bright. A flame that flickers may even be low.
> - To go out completely → If it went out, it would not flicker. The pebble keeps trying.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word flicker._

> _You hear a long creak of timbers and slow oars, but mist hides the ship._  
> _How does a writer make us uneasy by letting us hear what we cannot see?_  
> - ✅ Our imagination fills the gap, and is often worse than a picture → Yes. What we cannot see, we make up, and our minds are good at it.
> - Sound is always scarier than sight → Not always. It works here because the mist takes away the picture.
> - It does not make us uneasy at all → For many readers it does. The creak without a ship is a classic way to build suspense.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how hearing without seeing can build suspense._

_On the far edge of the world there is a line of fire, low down, like a sunset in the wrong place._

#### `a22-01-lamp-flicker`

_Abuela Alma meets you in the courtyard. She is older than in the painting, straight as a broom, with a black shawl._  
_She looks at the lamp at your belt, from your Long-Grass post. A thin blue flame is shivering inside it._  
**Abuela Alma**: That flame is too thin to be on its own. Come.  
_She tips the candle to your wick. Now there are two flames in the glass, a gold one and your thin blue one, leaning together._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): heat from one flame lights another wick  
> _Abuela tips her candle to your wick, and a second flame catches. What does her flame pass to your wick?_  
> - ✅ Heat → Yes. Heat from her flame warms your wick until it catches. Energy moves as heat, and her flame stays just as big.
> - Half of its flame → Flames do not split in half. Her flame passes on heat, and stays the same size.
> - Water → Water would put a flame out. Her flame passes on heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat from one flame can light another wick._


#### `a22-01-lamp-lit`

_Abuela Alma meets you in the courtyard. She is older than in the painting, straight as a broom, with a black shawl._  
_She looks at the lamp at your belt, lit from your Long-Grass post. The flame stands up straight and steady._  
**Abuela Alma**: Someone keeps that one well. Good.  
_She doesn’t offer to light it. She nods at it, the way you nod to a neighbour._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): why a flame points upwards  
> _A flame points up because the hot gases it makes are lighter than the cool air around them, so they rise._  
> _In still air a flame stands straight. A draught bends it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a flame points up because hot gases rise, and that a draught bends it._


#### `a22-01-lamp-warm`

_Abuela Alma meets you in the courtyard. She is older than in the painting, straight as a broom, with a black shawl._  
_She looks at the lamp at your belt, lit from your Long-Grass post. Its flame is a deep red-gold, and the glass is warm._  
**Abuela Alma**: That one burns as if somebody is glad of it.  
_She holds her hands to it for a moment, as if it were a hearth, and then remembers herself._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from a hot flame through glass to your hand  
> _Heat moves from the hot flame, through the glass, to anything cooler that touches it. That is why the glass feels warm._  
> _It is also why you never touch a lamp’s glass while it burns._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat moves from a flame through glass to cooler things, and why we must not touch it._


#### `a22-04-lamp-flicker`

_You look down at the lamp at your belt. Both its flames, Abuela’s gold one and your own thin blue one, are shuddering._  
_They shudder with the candle, all three at once, and steady all at once._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-4, ask): fuel, air and heat: what a flame needs  
> _A flame needs fuel, air and heat. Take one away and it goes out._  
> _In a candle, what is the fuel?_  
> - ✅ The wax, drawn up the wick → Yes. Heat melts the wax, the wick draws it up, and the flame burns the wax vapour.
> - The air → Air is one of the three needs, but the fuel is the wax.
> - The glass → The glass only shelters the flame. The fuel is the wax.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a flame needs fuel, air and heat, and that a candle’s fuel is wax._

**Mirabel**: Yours too. You saw. You saw it.  
_She grips your wrist hard, then lets go, because her grandmother is watching._  

#### `a22-04-lamp-lit`

_You look down at the lamp at your belt, lit from your own Long-Grass post. Its flame stands straight; it didn’t move at all._  
_Mirabel sees it too. She stares at it, then at the candle, then at it again._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): still air keeps a flame steady  
> _Your flame stood still while the candle shuddered. What would keep a flame steady?_  
> - ✅ Still air with no draught → Yes. A flame wobbles when air moves, so still air keeps it steady.
> - A strong wind → A wind would make it flicker or go out. Still air keeps it steady.
> - A very noisy room → Noise hardly matters. Moving air is what makes a flame wobble.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a flame stays steady in still air._

**Mirabel**: Yours didn’t. Something is wrong with ours.  
_She grips your wrist hard, then lets go, because her grandmother is watching._  

#### `a22-04-lamp-warm`

_You look down at the lamp at your belt. Its red-gold flame is warm against your hip, and it didn’t move at all._  
_Mirabel sees it too. She stares at it, then at the candle, then at it again._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): metal conducts heat away, so it feels colder than wood  
> _Your lamp’s warmth is on your hip. On a cold day, a wooden spoon and a metal spoon left outside are the same temperature._  
> _Which feels colder to touch?_  
> - ✅ The metal one, because it carries heat away from your hand faster → Yes. Metal conducts heat well, so it pulls warmth from your skin and feels colder, though both are the same temperature.
> - The wooden one → Wood feels warmer because it carries heat away slowly. The metal spoon feels colder.
> - Neither, they feel the same → They are the same temperature, but they do not feel the same. Metal feels colder because it conducts heat away faster.
> _For grown-ups: Sorted materials by a property: metal conducts heat, so it feels colder than wood._

**Mirabel**: Yours didn’t. Something is wrong with ours.  
_She grips your wrist hard, then lets go, because her grandmother is watching._  

#### `a22-08-prep-done-ears`

_As you pass the stairs, Dolores catches your sleeve. You have sat with her most mornings since the landing, and listened to her listening._  
**Dolores**: I heard. In the nursery. Tío Agustín, and the glass. I heard all of it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): sound is a vibration that travels through air and solids to the ear  
> _Sound is a vibration that travels through air, and through solid things like walls, though more quietly._  
> _Your ear catches the vibrations, and a thin skin inside it, the eardrum, shakes in time with them._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sound travels as vibrations through air and solids and shakes the eardrum._

**Dolores**: I hear everything. I can’t not hear it. And I can’t keep things in. They just come out.  
**Dolores**: Please stay by me tonight. Please.  
_The bell rings at the gate. The Guzmáns are here._  

#### `a22-09-ears`

_Everything happens at once. You remember your job: you are the ears, and Dolores is your friend._  
_She is standing at the foot of the stairs with both hands over her mouth, and more is still coming out._  
**Dolores**: And Mariano, and I always, I always...  
_Whatever she is about to say, it isn’t hers to say in front of the whole table._  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-management, ask): calming big feelings  
> _Dolores’s feelings are too big to hold in. What helps most when feelings feel overwhelming?_  
> - ✅ Slow breathing and a calm friend nearby → Yes. Slow breaths calm the body, and a steady friend helps the feeling settle, which is what you are about to do for her.
> - Holding the feelings in tighter → That usually makes them burst out harder. Breathing and a friend help more.
> - Shouting them out in front of everyone → That can feel like a relief but may hurt others. Breathing and a calm friend help more.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that slow breathing and a calm friend help with overwhelming feelings._

_Across the table Mariano is looking at Dolores, not at Isabela, and doesn’t seem to know why._  
_Mirabel sees you get up, and nods once._  

**Choices**

- **Take her outside.**
    - You take Dolores’s hand and walk her out into the courtyard, fast, before the next word.
    - Behind you, the door swings shut, and Casita leans on it.
- **Knock a jug over to cover her.**
    - You knock a jug off the table. In the crash, you get Dolores out into the courtyard.
    - **Dolores**: Thank you. Thank you.

#### `a22-09-hands`

_Everything happens at once. You remember your job: you are the hands, and Luisa needs them._  
_The crack has gone right under the table, and the table is folding in the middle like a book closing._  
_Luisa has one end of it. Her eye is twitching hard, and her hands are shaking._  
**Luisa**: I can’t... I can’t hold it...  
_The other end is dropping, and all of Julieta’s dishes are sliding down it towards Señora Guzmán’s lap._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): sharing a load equally: 80 ÷ 2  
> _The table and its dishes weigh 80 kilograms. You and Luisa each hold one end._  
> _If you share the weight equally, how much does each of you carry?_  
> - ✅ Forty kilograms → Yes. 80 ÷ 2 = 40, because 40 + 40 = 80.
> - Eighty kilograms → Eighty is the whole weight. Shared between two, each carries 80 ÷ 2 = 40.
> - One hundred and sixty kilograms → That doubles instead of sharing. Each carries 80 ÷ 2 = 40 kilograms.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 80 kg between two people to get 40 kg each._

**Mirabel**: Luisa!  

**Choices**

- **Grab the other end.**
    - You get your shoulder under the other end and push. It is heavier than anything has ever been.
    - Between you, you hold it, dishes and all. Luisa looks across at you over the soup.
- **Get the dishes off first.**
    - You and your Nubbin snatch dishes off the slope as fast as you can. With them gone, Luisa can hold it, just.

#### `a22-13-lamp-flicker`

_At your belt, Abuela’s gold flame goes out with the candle. For a moment your lamp is dark._  
_Then you see it: your own thin blue flicker, from the Long-Grass post, still there at the bottom of the wick. It never quite goes out._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): pupils widen in the dark, so tiny lights look bright  
> _In the dark, the black centres of your eyes, the pupils, open wide to let in more light._  
> _That is why a tiny flame looks so bright after dark._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pupils widen in the dark, which makes small lights look bright._

_Then Mirabel is up and running, out of the ruins, and nobody sees which way._  

#### `a22-13-lamp-lit`

_At your belt, your lamp is still burning. Its flame comes from your Long-Grass post, a long way off, and owes this house nothing._  
_It is the only light in the ruins. The family turn towards it one by one, the way people turn towards a fire._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): light travels in straight lines and makes shadows  
> _Light travels in straight lines, so anything standing in its way makes a shadow on the far side._  
> _See how each shadow stretches away from your lamp._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that light travels in straight lines, which is why objects make shadows._

_Mirabel looks at it, and at the dead candle. Then she is up and running, out of the ruins, and nobody sees which way._  

#### `a22-13-lamp-warm`

_At your belt, your lamp is still burning, a deep red-gold. The night should be cold up here among the mountains, and it isn’t._  
_The air round the ruins is oddly warm, like a kitchen after the cooking. Antonio’s jaguar lies down against your feet._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): a flame gives heat as well as light  
> _A flame gives off heat as well as light._  
> _Sit near a fire and your skin soaks up the heat, even when the air around is cool._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that flames give off heat as well as light._

_Mirabel looks at your lamp, and at the dead candle. Then she is up and running, out of the ruins, and nobody sees which way._  

#### `a22-14-pedro-done-kept`

_Abuela turns, and sees you. She looks at your hands, at the way you are holding them, and takes them in hers._  
_Your hands have been cold since the night at the spring. She doesn’t say a word about it; she just keeps them there._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from warmer things to cooler things  
> _Heat always moves from something warmer to something cooler._  
> _When Abuela holds your cold hands, her warmth flows into them until they are nearly the same temperature._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat flows from warmer things to cooler things._

_The butterflies settle on the rock and on your Nubbin’s crown. Then footsteps: a thin man in a green hood, at the top of the bank._  
**Tío Bruno**: Mamá.  
_Abuela lets go of your hands, gently, and goes to him over the stones, and holds him for a long time._  

#### `a22-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the river, and the old woman sitting on a cold rock beside her granddaughter._  
_Beside the river, in faint pencil you have never noticed, there is a note in the margin. You know the hand._  
_“Abuela sat down by the river and stopped being right.”_  
_“Took her long enough. Took me longer.”_  
_And under it, one letter: H._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): why it can take a long time to say “I was wrong”  
> _Hazel writes that Abuela “stopped being right”. Why can it take a long time to say, “I was wrong”?_  
> - Because it feels like losing → A fair answer. Many people feel that way, though admitting a mistake is really how we win something: a fresh start.
> - Because we fear what it says about us → A thoughtful answer. Being wrong does not make us bad, but it can feel that way until we have practised.
> - Because we have been right for so long → A sharp answer. Years of habit are hard to put down, and Hazel says it took her longer still.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why admitting a mistake can take time, and why it is brave._

_Your Nubbin sits down at the edge of the page, beside the painted rock, and stays there a while._  

#### `a22-15-ears`

_Dolores walks through the ruins with her eyes shut. You walk beside her, as you have for days, and tell her where to step._  
**Dolores**: That wall. It’s humming wrong. Something inside it is loose.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): different materials sound different when tapped  
> _Tap a solid wall and a hollow one, and they sound different, because they vibrate in different ways._  
> _Builders really do tap walls and listen for the hollow spots._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that materials sound different when tapped because they vibrate differently._

_The builders take the wall down and set it again. Dolores listens, nods, and moves on._  
**Dolores**: That beam is creaking in its sleep. And that tile is about to fall on Camilo.  
_Camilo moves, and the tile falls where he was. He stares at Dolores, and so does everybody._  
**Dolores**: My gift’s gone, but I can still hear, the ordinary way. I never noticed how much.  

**Choices**

- **Tell her she’s a marvel.**
    - **Dolores**: Nobody ever...
    - She has to stop. Mariano, beside her, hands her a handkerchief.
- **Ask what she hears now.**
    - **Dolores**: Hammers. Everybody laughing. Tío Bruno, telling the rats a story under the stairs. It’s lovely.

#### `a22-15-hands`

_Luisa is standing in the middle of the ruins with a load of bricks, out of habit. Her arms are shaking._  
_You take the bricks off her, as you have every day since the landing, and put them down._  
**Luisa**: I should be lifting the beams. I always do the beams.  
_The beam she is looking at takes six neighbours to move, and they move it. Nobody needed her to._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): comparing solutions: a wheelbarrow carries heavy loads more easily  
> _To move a huge pile of bricks, would a wheelbarrow or a basket be the better solution, and why?_  
> - ✅ A wheelbarrow: the wheel carries the weight, and the long handles act as a lever → Yes. The wheel takes the load, and the lever of the handles multiplies your lifting, so you can move far more with less effort.
> - A basket → A basket is fine for a few bricks, but you carry all the weight yourself. A wheelbarrow does better with heavy loads.
> - Both work equally well → Both carry bricks, but a wheelbarrow carries more with less strain, so it is the better design for this job.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two ways to carry a heavy load and judged the wheelbarrow better._

_Luisa sits down on a pile of roof tiles, in the sun. She looks surprised to find herself there._  
**Luisa**: I’m sitting down. I haven’t sat down in... I don’t know. Years.  

**Choices**

- **Carry for her.**
    - You carry bricks all morning, and Luisa sits and tells you where to put them. She is very bossy about it, and much happier.
- **Sit down next to her for a minute.**
    - You sit down beside her. Your Nubbin climbs onto her boot and falls asleep, as it did once before, and she laughs.

#### `a22-16-stub-flicker`

_Mirabel takes a candle stub from her pocket and lights it from the new flame in the window._  
**Mirabel**: For you. To take home.  
_You hold your lamp out. Your own thin blue flicker leans towards the new flame, and for a moment they burn together._  
**Mirabel**: Yours is a stubborn one. Look after it. It’ll come right.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): when stubbornness is a strength  
> _Mirabel calls your small blue flame stubborn, and she means it as a compliment. When is stubbornness a strength, and when is it not?_  
> - A strength when we keep trying at something good → A fair answer. Not giving up on something worthwhile is stubbornness at its best.
> - Not a strength when we refuse to listen → A fair answer. Stubbornness that shuts out other people can hurt, like Abuela’s grip.
> - Both, depending on what we are being stubborn about → A thoughtful answer. The same trait can help or harm, so it is worth asking what it is for.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when stubbornness is a strength and when it is not._

_Mirabel takes a candle stub from her pocket and lights it from the new flame in the window._

_You hold your lamp up beside it. The two flames, hers and your own, burn side by side, the same height._  
**Mirabel**: Look at that. Two houses.

> _For grown-ups: Heard that kindness can be shared without running out._


#### `a22-16-stub-warm`

_Mirabel takes a candle stub from her pocket and lights it from the new flame in the window._

_You hold your lamp up beside it. Your red-gold flame and her new one burn side by side, and you feel the warmth on your face._

#### `a22-16-photo-ears`

_The photographer from the village sets up his camera in the courtyard, under a black cloth._  
_The whole family crowds onto the stairs, Bruno too, at the front this time, holding Antonio. The rats are not in it, officially._  
**Mirabel**: Wait. Wait! You too. Get in!  
_You end up at the edge, between Mirabel and Dolores. Dolores leans over to whisper._  
**Dolores**: Mariano’s going to ask me. Next week. I heard him practising in the market.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): a figure of speech that is not literal  
> _If you whisper that her secret is safe, Dolores replies, “I heard you think it.” She cannot really hear thoughts._  
> _What is she doing with that sentence?_  
> - ✅ Making a loving joke: she can guess what you are thinking → Yes. It is a figure of speech, and a warm one: she knows you well enough to guess your thoughts.
> - Telling a lie → A lie is meant to fool someone, and nobody is fooled here. It is a joke between friends.
> - Telling the literal truth → Her gift lets her hear sounds, not thoughts. She is joking, and the narration tells us so.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised a joke that is a figure of speech rather than a literal statement._

**A neighbour**: Everybody, very still!

#### `a22-16-photo-hands`

#### `a22-grove-candle`

_Back in the Grove, you walk out to the fourth post by the long grass and hang the painted tin holder from its hook._  
_The candle stub in it won’t stay lit here, and you knew it wouldn’t. Mirabel said some lights have to be waited for._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what keeps hope alive while we wait  
> _Waiting for a light that may not come for a long time takes hope. What helps people keep hoping?_  
> - A promise or a reminder, like the stub → A good answer. A small keepsake can hold a hope steady until the day arrives.
> - Good company while we wait → A good answer. Hope is easier to carry together, as your Nubbin shows.
> - Having something useful to do → A good answer. Busy hands make the waiting go by, and your Grove is full of jobs.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps people keep hoping while they wait._


#### `a22-grove-candle-lit`

_Back in the Grove, you walk out to the fourth post by the long grass and hang the painted tin holder from its hook._  
_The stub catches from the lantern above it at once, as if it had only been waiting to be introduced._  
_Two flames by the long grass now, one from here and one from a valley far away. Your Nubbin sits under them, very pleased._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, notice): a flame burns the vapour of melted wax  
> _Heat from the lantern melts the stub’s wax, and the wick draws it up as vapour that catches fire._

> _For grown-ups: Learned that a candle flame burns the vapour of melted wax drawn up the wick._


#### `a23-10-desert-rafiki`

_It is dark by the time you reach the baobab. Zazu has gone quiet in your arms, which frightens you more than anything._  
_Rafiki is sitting in the fork of the tree. He doesn’t call down; he already knows._  
**Rafiki**: The wind came by a little while ago. It smelled wrong.  
**Rafiki**: Bring him up.  
_He takes Zazu from you, gently, and looks at the wing you bound. He doesn’t undo any of it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): bird bones are light and hollow, so a hurt wing needs rest  
> _A bird’s wing bones are hollow and light, which is what lets it fly. What does that mean for a hurt wing?_  
> - ✅ It breaks easily, so it must be kept still while it heals → Just so. Light bones are marvellous for flying and delicate when hurt. Rest and a firm wrap give a wing the best chance to mend.
> - It can be flapped to get better → Flapping a hurt wing could make the break worse. Light bones need to be held still while they knit.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a bird’s light, hollow wing bones can break easily and heal best when kept still._

**Rafiki**: That is good work. Slow work.  
**Rafiki**: You did not hurry, even then.  
**Zazu**: The king, Rafiki. And the boy.  
**Zazu**: The boy ran…  
**Rafiki**: I know. Hush.  
**Rafiki**: I know.  
_Rafiki lays him on a bed of leaves. Zazu is asleep before he has finished complaining about it._  

**Choices**

- **Tell Rafiki what you saw.**
    - You tell him all of it, as well as you can. He listens without a word, nodding slowly.
- **Sit down beside him and say nothing.**
    - You sit down beside him. After a while he puts his old hand on top of yours.

#### `a23-10-desert-done-rafiki`

_Rafiki climbs up inside the tree in the dark. You hear him find the painted cub on the wall._  
_He believes the cub is lost for good. He stands looking at the painting for a long time._  
_Then he wipes it out with the flat of his hand._  
**Rafiki**: Pole sana, little one. Pole sana.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a Swahili phrase of sympathy  
> _You know that sana means very. Rafiki says “pole sana”._  
> _When do Swahili speakers say it?_  
> - ✅ To show sympathy when someone is hurting or has lost something → Yes. Pole sana means “I am very sorry”. It is what you say when someone is hurt or grieving.
> - To say hello → Hello is a different phrase. Pole sana is said to show sympathy: “I am very sorry”.
> - To say thank you → Thank you is asante. Pole sana is said to show sympathy: “I am very sorry”.
> _For grown-ups: Learned the Swahili phrase pole sana (I am very sorry), said to show sympathy._


#### `a23-10-help-rafiki`

_In the morning you climb to the top of the baobab with Rafiki to look at the rock._  
_A thin dark lion stands at the very top, where the king used to stand. The lionesses are below him, heads down._  
**Rafiki**: Scar.  
_Up the back path of the rock, in a long grey line, come the hyenas: dozens of them, and then more._  
**Zazu**: He’s letting them in. He’s letting them in!  
_Zazu is up, wobbling, with his bound wing held close, peering through the leaves._  
**Rafiki**: Hyenas eat and eat, and never plant anything. It won’t be long now.  
**Zazu**: I have to go back. Someone has to stand by the queen.  
**Rafiki**: Your wing.  
**Zazu**: I’ll walk. Hornbills are excellent at walking.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): brave or foolish: going on when hurt  
> _Zazu insists on going back to stand by the queen, though his wing is hurt. Is that brave, foolish, or both?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Brave: he is putting his friends before himself → That’s a fair answer. Loyalty can ask a lot of us. Many people admire Zazu for it.
> - Foolish: he should let his wing heal → That’s a fair answer. A hurt wing needs rest, and rest is not weakness. You might say he should have asked for help.
> - Both, and that is what makes it hard → That’s a fair answer, and an honest one. Many brave things are a bit foolish, and many foolish things are done for brave reasons.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether Zazu going back with a hurt wing is brave or foolish, with no single right answer._


**Choices**

- **Help Zazu down the tree.**
    - You carry him down and set him on the path. He walks off towards the rock with his chin up, very small.
- **Ask him to stay.**
    - **Zazu**: I can’t. It’s my job.
    - **Zazu**: It has been my job since before you were born. Whatever you are.

#### `a23-10-complete-rafiki`

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplication word problem  
> _Rafiki has four gourds on his shelf, and each holds 3 litres. How much water could you carry if you filled every one?_  
> - ✅ 12 litres → Yes. Four gourds of 3 litres: 4 × 3 = 12 litres.
> - 7 litres → That is 4 + 3. Each of the four gourds holds 3 litres, so 4 × 3 = 12.
> - 34 litres → That puts the digits side by side. Multiply instead: 4 × 3 = 12 litres.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a multiplication word problem: 4 gourds × 3 litres = 12 litres._

#### `a23-11-oasis-rafiki`

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-1, ask): animals move to where their needs are met  
> _When the grass dies and the river turns to mud, the herds leave. How is that like the Great Migration?_  
> - ✅ Herds travel to find fresh grass and water → Yes. Animals move to where food and water are. The Great Migration is a huge version of this, following the rains.
> - Herds leave because they are bored → Herds leave because they must eat and drink. They go where the grass and water are.
> _For grown-ups: Connected herds leaving a drying plain to the Great Migration: animals move to find food and water._

> - He is angry with you → A lifted chin can look proud or cross. Here it fits better with a friend trying to look brave when someone he trusts turns up.

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, ask): scarcity means choosing  
> _There is very little water, and the rock needs it as much as Nala’s journey does. What does scarcity mean?_  
> - ✅ When there is not enough of something for everyone’s needs → Yes. When something is scarce, people have to choose how to use it. Rafiki chooses to share what he has.
> - When there is far too much of something → That is the opposite: a surplus. Scarcity means there is not enough to go round.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that scarcity means there is not enough of something, so people have to choose._

#### `a23-12-hunt-rafiki`

_Two days out in the desert, the gourds are nearly empty. Then the sand turns to scrub, and the scrub to green._

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS4-1, ask): different habitats, different life  
> _Sand, then scrub, then green. What changes as you walk, to make the plants so different?_  
> - ✅ The amount of water → Yes. Water is what a habitat is built on. Where there is a little, scrub grows; where there is a lot, ferns and fruit trees thrive.
> - The colour of the sky → The sky stays the same. What changes is the water in the ground, and that decides which plants can grow.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the amount of water changes the plants that grow, from sand to scrub to green._

> - It means nothing → It means a lot! It is both a joke and the exact truth. The atlas is a book, and it is why you have not aged.

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _You set off at 6:30 in the morning and reach the thorns at noon (12:00). How long did you walk?_  
> - ✅ 5 hours 30 minutes → Yes. 6:30 to 12:00 is 5 hours 30 minutes: 5 hours to 11:30, then 30 minutes to noon.
> - 6 hours 30 minutes → That is an hour too long. From 6:30 to 11:30 is 5 hours, and 30 more minutes reaches noon: 5 hours 30 minutes.
> - 5 hours → Close, but it misses the last half hour. 6:30 to 11:30 is 5 hours, then 30 minutes to noon: 5 hours 30 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Found a time interval: from 6:30 to 12:00 is 5 hours 30 minutes._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): forgiving ourselves when we acted on what we knew  
> _Rafiki feels terrible that he wiped the cub off the wall. What might help him?_  
> - ✅ Remembering that he did it believing the cub was lost → Yes. We can only act on what we know at the time. Being kind to ourselves about that is part of being able to put things right.
> - Pretending it never happened → That does not help for long. It is better to say what happened, forgive ourselves for not knowing, and then mend it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we can forgive ourselves for acting on what we knew, and then put things right._

#### `a23-13-ridge-done-rafiki`

_Out over the desert, the wind is getting up. You can hear it before you feel it._  
_It blows through the branches of the baobab, and they creak._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): wind is moving air, caused by warm air rising  
> _The Sun warms the ground, and the warm air above it rises. What rushes in to take its place?_  
> - ✅ Cooler air, which we feel as wind → Yes. Warm air rises, cooler air flows in to fill the gap, and that moving air is wind.
> - Water → Water stays in rivers and clouds. It is cooler air that rushes in to fill the gap, and we feel that as wind.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wind is moving air: warm air rises and cooler air flows in._

#### `a23-13-complete-rafiki`

_Rafiki takes his stick and his biggest gourd. He doesn’t lock the tree, because he has never locked it._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): role reversal and irony

> - Rafiki is lost → He is not lost: he is amused. The funny part is that the one who was a guest is now the guide.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a role reversal: the guest has become the guide._

#### `a23-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the still pool among the roots, and a grown lion looking down into it._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): mixed feelings when we find something from someone we love  
> _A note from someone you love, found when you were not expecting it, can stir up more than one feeling. What might you feel?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Happy, because it is like hearing their voice → That’s a fair answer. Familiar handwriting can feel like a visit.
> - Sad, because they are not here to talk to → That’s a fair answer. Missing someone is part of loving them.
> - Both at once → That’s a fair answer. Two feelings can sit side by side, and both are allowed.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the mixed feelings a note from a loved one can bring, with no single right answer._

#### `a23-grove-painting`

_You look into the hollow of Hazel’s crooked tree, the way you do sometimes, for no reason. Something is in there that wasn’t before._  
_A little painting on a piece of bark: your Nubbin in yellow ochre, round and pleased, with a line of fruit-red across its brow._  
_Your Nubbin looks at it for a long time. Then it touches its own forehead, where the red mark used to be._  
_Painting someone means you mean to remember them. Somebody, somewhere, means to._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what it means to be remembered  
> _“Painting someone means you mean to remember them.” Why might being remembered matter to a person, or a Nubbin?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - It tells us we mattered to someone → That’s a fair answer. To be remembered is to be told, quietly, that you were seen and valued.
> - It keeps us connected to people we cannot see → That’s a fair answer. Memory is a bridge between people, even across distance or time.
> - It does not matter, only the living matter → That’s a fair answer, and an honest one. Many people think so. But notice how Rafiki’s wall, and this little painting, comfort those who are still here.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why being remembered matters, with no single right answer._


#### `a24-02-council-done-fern`

_The wolves come one by one to look at Mowgli, and then they go down the hill after the bull._  
_From the edge of the page, faint as pencil, comes a voice you know. Fern, remembering._  
**Fern**: That is what Bramble did for the strays.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): why a memory arrives at a certain moment: motive and connection  
> _Fern’s memory comes at just this moment, when Baloo and Bagheera speak up for a cub who is not theirs. Why?_  
> - ✅ Bramble also took in strays, so the two stories match. → Yes. Fern sees the same kindness in two places: someone taking in a creature who needed a home. Authors link two moments like this to show a pattern, and what it means.
> - Fern was only passing by. → Fern is not really passing by. Her voice is a memory coming from the edge of the page. It arrives here because the two stories match.
> - She wants to interrupt the Council. → She speaks softly, as a memory. She is not interrupting. She is connecting this moment with what Bramble did.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out why a memory appears at a certain point in a story: two moments of kindness echo each other._

**Akela**: He is the pack’s now. Take him home, and bring him up properly.

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): owls fly silently because of soft, fringed feathers  
> _The owl flew right over the hut, and you did not hear its wings. What helps owls fly so quietly?_  
> - ✅ Soft, fringed feathers that muffle the sound of the air. → Yes. Owl feathers have soft edges that break up the noise of air flowing past. That lets an owl sneak up on prey, and listen at the same time.
> - They only glide and never flap. → Owls do flap. It is their feathers that make the silence. Soft, fringed edges muffle the sound.
> - Their wings are very small. → Owls have big wings for their size. The soft feathers do the work.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that owls fly silently because the soft, fringed edges of their feathers muffle the sound of the air._

> - 25 litres. → Twenty-five would be five pails. You make four trips. 5 × 4 = 20 litres.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied 5 × 4 = 20 to find how many litres of water four pails hold._

#### `a24-13-hut-done-messua`

_The back door opens without a sound. Messua leans on you, and her husband leans on Mowgli, both stiff from the ropes._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): small words carry meaning: “and you”  
> _Messua says, “My son. And you.”_  
> _What does adding “and you” tell us?_  
> - ✅ She counts you as one of her family now. → Yes. Two small words show how she feels about you, without having to explain. Good readers notice little words like these.
> - She is just being polite. → She might be. But she says it in a moment of real feeling. It suggests she counts you as family.
> - She has forgotten your name. → She does not use your name because she is too moved to remember to. The words tell us you matter to her.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how two small words, “and you”, show how a character feels about someone._

_She says “and you” as if you had always been in the family._  

#### `a24-13-road-messua`

**Mowgli**: Guest, take them to the road. The road to the town, a long day’s walk.  
**Mowgli**: Walk towards the sunrise. I have to go and talk to Hathi.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: if you face east, west is behind you  
> _Mowgli says to walk towards the sunrise. If you face the sunrise, which direction is behind you?_  
> - ✅ West. → Yes. You face east towards the sunrise, so west, where the Sun sets, is behind you. North is on your left and south is on your right.
> - East. → East is in front of you, where the Sun comes up. Behind you is the opposite direction: west.
> - North. → North would be on your left if you face east. Directly behind you is west.
> _For grown-ups: Used the rising Sun to find east, and worked out that west is behind you when you face east._

#### `a24-13-road-done-messua`

_You watch them go: two small shapes on the road, walking away into the grey of dawn._  
_The grass is wet with dew, though no rain has fallen, and your boots are soaked._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-ESS2-1, ask): dew forms when the night air cools and water vapour turns into drops  
> _The grass is wet, but it did not rain. Where did the water come from?_  
> - ✅ Water vapour in the cool night air turned into drops, called dew. → Yes. Air holds invisible water vapour. When the air cools at night, some of it turns into tiny drops on cold surfaces. When the Sun warms the grass, the dew dries and goes back into the air.
> - The grass sweats. → Plants do not sweat like we do, though a plant can release a little water of its own. Most of the wet comes from water vapour in the night air.
> - The Moon dripped it. → The Moon has no water to drip. The wet comes from water vapour in the cooling air.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dew is water vapour from the air that turns into drops when the night air cools._

_She turns once, at the bend, and lifts her hand, and you lift yours. Then you go back to find Mowgli and Hathi._  

#### `a24-15-lamp-mowgli`

_Messua looks at you over Mowgli’s head, polite and puzzled. She does not know you._

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s welcome shows: generosity to a stranger  
> _Messua does not know you, but she feeds you anyway: “you came in with my son, and that is enough.” What does that show about her?_  
> - ✅ She is generous, and welcomes people who matter to someone she loves. → Yes. She does not need to know you to be kind to you. How a character treats a stranger shows what she is like.
> - She is not very careful. → Being generous is not the same as being careless. She welcomes you because you came with her son.
> - She is hiding something. → Nothing suggests that. Her welcome is real, and shows generosity.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how a character’s kindness to a stranger shows her generous nature._

> - Because she has no one else. → She has Mowgli right there. She trusts you because of what you did when things were hard.

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction: 17 − 1 = 16 years  
> _Mowgli was one year old when Bagheera bought him, and he will be seventeen this summer. How many years have passed?_  
> - ✅ 16 years. → Yes: 17 − 1 = 16. Count on from 1 up to 17, and you take 16 steps. That is a lot of seasons with the pack.
> - 18 years. → That is 17 + 1. But we want the gap between two ages. Take 1 away from 17: 16.
> - 17 years. → He is 17 now, but he was already 1 at the start. So the time between is 17 − 1 = 16 years.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted 1 from 17 to find the number of years between two ages (16)._

#### `a24-17-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the seals’ beach, and the white pup in the shelter of his mother’s rock._

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being safe and being well are not the same thing  
> _Hazel wrote, “Safe beach first. Then a well one.”_  
> _Is being safe the same as being well? There is no one right answer._  
> - No. Safe means nothing can hurt you. Well means you can thrive. → That is a fair answer. A hidden beach keeps the seals safe, and a good life is more than hiding. Kotick wanted both for his herd, and Hazel noticed it.
> - Yes. If you are safe, you are well. → That is a fair answer. Safety is very important, and it comes first. But some safe places can still be lonely or dull. A well place has more in it.
> - Safe comes first, then well. → That is a thoughtful answer, and it is just what Hazel wrote. You cannot thrive if you are always in danger, and you cannot be well just by hiding.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether being safe is the same as being well, using Hazel’s margin note about Kotick as a prompt._

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): how stories carry the past  
> _Enkidu asks you to carry a message to people far away. How do spoken stories carry the past from one person to another?_

#### `a26-18-foot-spoke`

_At the foot of the wall, by the copper box, the old brickmaker is sitting on her stack of bricks, eating a date._  
**Old Brickmaker**: There you are. Long story, was it? They always are, his.  
_Below the wall, by the river, there is a cedar sapling no higher than your knee. You know whose seed it was._  
_Gilgamesh kneels down beside it. He touches one of its little needles, very carefully, with a hand that tore on thorns._  
**Gilgamesh**: You told me to let him go. I should have listened to you.  
**Old Brickmaker**: Now then. Every brick in this wall has someone’s hand in it. Want yours in?  
_She lays a fresh clay brick in front of you. You press your hand into it, and your Nubbin, after some thought, presses a paw._  
**Old Brickmaker**: Kiln-fired, this one. Sun-dried bricks crumble in the rain. Kiln-fired, they last for thousands of years.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, ask): weathering: why kiln-fired brick lasts  
> _Sun-dried bricks crumble in the rain, but kiln-fired bricks last for thousands of years. Why?_  
> - ✅ Firing changes the clay for good, so water cannot soften it → Yes. Baking clay in a kiln changes it so it will not turn back to mud. Rain slowly wears sun-dried brick away: that is called weathering.
> - Kiln bricks are painted to keep the rain off → There is no paint. The firing itself changes the clay.
> - Sun-dried bricks are made of different mud → The mud is the same. The difference is the fire in the kiln.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that firing changes clay for good, so kiln-fired bricks resist weathering far longer than sun-dried bricks._

- **Ask if she will put her own mark on it too.**
    - **Old Brickmaker**: Me? No. I am on all the others.

> - The wall, because it will stand for thousands of years → That is a fair answer. Stone and brick outlast people. The wall of Uruk has, nearly.
> - The story, because people keep telling it → That is a fair answer. You are reading it about four thousand years later.
> - What we do for the people who remember us → That is a fair answer. A kindness is carried on by whoever received it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what lasts: walls, stories, and the kindness we leave behind._

_The sun on the bricks gets warmer and yellower, until it is lamplight on a page, and your own table, and the Grove._  
_In your hands there is a brick, still warm from the kiln. Your handprint is in it, and a small round pawprint beside._  

#### `a26-18-complete-moss-spoke`

_Moss has been quiet all the way home. Now he sits up on your shoulder and looks at the wall, brick by brick._  
**Moss**: He went to the end of the world so as not to die, and came home and pointed at a wall.  
**Moss**: That is the right answer. He just took the long way.  
_He looks down at the cedar sapling by the river for a while._  
**Moss**: And somebody let a tree live. That is the other answer.  
**Gilgamesh**: Go home, water-carrier. Walk on your own wall. Look at its bricks.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): how people and things are remembered  
> _Gilgamesh went to the end of the world to avoid dying, and came home to his wall, where you pressed your hand into a brick. What do you think lasts?_  
> - The wall, because it will stand for thousands of years → That is a fair answer. Stone and brick outlast people. The wall of Uruk has, nearly.
> - The story, because people keep telling it → That is a fair answer. You are reading it about four thousand years later.
> - What we do for the people who remember us → That is a fair answer. A kindness is carried on by whoever received it.

_The sun on the bricks gets warmer and yellower, until it is lamplight on a page, and your own table, and the Grove._

#### `a26-grove-brick`

_You carry the brick up the hill to the flat stone where Moss always sits, and lay it in the grass beside it._  
_Your handprint and the pawprint face the sky. Your Nubbin knocks on the brick with one paw, and listens: it rings._  
_You put the cedar box on the cottage shelf. When you open it, the room smells of a forest a very long way off._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): language that appeals to the senses  
> _“The room smells of a forest a very long way off.” Which sense does this sentence appeal to?_  
> - ✅ Smell → Yes. Writers use senses so that we feel we are in the room. This one gives a smell and a sense of distance.
> - Hearing → The ringing brick is about hearing, but this sentence is about smell.
> - Taste → We might taste air, but a smell comes through the nose. This sentence is about smell.
> _For grown-ups: Identified that a sentence appeals to the sense of smell._

#### `a27-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the great nest on the peak, and the four round chicks, and the small white head among them._  
_Beside the nest, in faint pencil you have never noticed, there is a note in the margin. You know the hand._  
_“White hair at birth. I’d have kept him.”_  
_And under it, one letter: H._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): what it means to keep someone, beyond keeping them safe  
> _Hazel wrote that she would have kept him. What does “keeping” someone mean, beyond keeping them safe?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Loving them as they are. → That is a fair answer. Hazel’s note says the hair was never the problem, and love does not ask for changes.
> - Staying, even when it is hard. → That is a fair answer. Keeping someone means being there, which the Simurgh was.
> - Making a place where they belong. → That is a fair answer. The nest is exactly that, for a baby nobody else wanted.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what it means to keep someone beyond keeping them safe, prompted by Hazel’s margin note._

_Your Nubbin puts one paw on the drawing of the baby, very gently, the way it touched his hair in the cradle._  

#### `a27-07-corvin`

_For a moment he makes you think of someone else: a man at a stuck gate, lifting and pushing, who came back._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why people return to put right what they broke  
> _Sam came back to mend what he broke, and so did the man at the stuck gate._  
> _Why do you think people return to put things right? There is no one right answer._  
> - Because they feel guilty. → That is a fair answer. Guilt can be a push towards doing better.
> - Because they still love someone. → That is a fair answer. Love is a strong reason to try again.
> - Because they finally see they were wrong. → That is a fair answer. Seeing clearly can take a very long time, but it is worth it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people come back to put right what they broke._


#### `a27-09-descent-sat`

_The Simurgh carries you both down through the cloud, one in each set of talons, the way she brought you up._  
_She sets you down on the slope above the army, a little way off, and goes back up to the edge of the cloud to watch._  
_Sam is still on his knees at the bottom. He hears the stones move, and looks up._  
_The youth walks down slowly: he stops, and looks, and walks on. He is taking his time, the way you let him._  
_Sam gets up off his knees, and doesn’t climb, and doesn’t call out. He waits, as long as it takes._  
_At the bottom the youth stops in front of his father, the feather held to his chest._  
_He has never stood this close to anyone but you._  
**The Youth**: You waited for me.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): waiting for someone can be a way of respecting them  
> _Sam waits, and does not climb or call out. Why might waiting be a way of respecting someone?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - It lets them choose for themselves. → That is a fair answer. Waiting gives the other person room to make their own choice.
> - It shows we are not in a hurry to be forgiven. → That is a fair answer. Patience can say “I know I must earn this”.
> - It makes the meeting feel safe. → That is a fair answer. When nobody rushes, both people can breathe.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how waiting for someone can be a way of showing respect._

_Sam can’t say anything at all. He just nods, again and again, like someone who has forgotten how to stop._  

#### `a27-09-descent-night`

_In the grey of the morning the Simurgh carries you both down through the cloud, the way she brought you up._  
_She sets you down on the slope above the army, a little way off, and goes back up to the edge of the cloud to watch._  
_Sam is still on his knees at the bottom, where he has been all night, in the cold. He hears the stones move, and looks up._  
_The youth comes down to him, rested, with the smell of the nest still on him._  
_Sam opens his mouth to speak, and nothing comes out but a whisper. He has prayed all night, and his voice is gone._  
_The youth stops in front of him, the feather held to his chest. He has never stood this close to anyone but you._  
**The Youth**: You stayed. All night, on the stones.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): whether actions or words matter more when saying sorry  
> _Sam stayed all night, until his voice was gone, to show he was sorry. Do actions matter more than words when we say sorry?_  
> _There is no one right answer._  
> - Yes. Actions show we mean it. → That is a fair answer. Staying all night says more than any speech.
> - No. Words are needed too. → That is a fair answer. Sam still has to say it, and the youth still has to hear it.
> - Both, together. → That is a fair answer. Words give the sorry a shape, and actions give it weight.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether actions or words matter more when saying sorry._

_Sam can only nod, again and again. It turns out that is all he needs to say._  

#### `a27-14-letter-sat`

_In the morning Zal calls a scribe, and walks up and down the tent while he speaks, and the scribe writes._  
**Zal**: Father. You put me out on a mountain.  
**Zal**: A bird raised me. The sun beat on my head, and I ate what she brought.  
**Zal**: All that time you sat in a good house, in silk. I don’t say it to hurt you.  
**Zal**: I say it because it’s true.  
**Zal**: You swore you would give me anything I asked. I have never asked you for anything.  
**Zal**: This is the one thing.  
**Zal**: I love Rudaba, Mehrab’s daughter. I want to marry her.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): how to write something hard, honestly and kindly  
> _Zal’s letter says hard things, and asks for something. Which helps most when you write something hard?_  
> - ✅ Say what happened, say how you feel, and then say what you ask. → Yes. Zal does all three, and he says plainly that he is not trying to hurt.
> - Make it as angry as possible. → Anger can be honest, but it often stops the other person listening. Zal says what is true without trying to hurt.
> - Leave out the truth. → A letter without the truth cannot help. Zal says it kindly, and says it anyway.
> _For grown-ups: Learned a way to write a hard letter: say what happened, say how you feel, then say what you ask._

**Zal**: I learned to wait on a mountain. I can wait for you.  
_He seals it, and holds it out to you, not to the messenger who is waiting._  
**Zal**: You carry it. You sat with me, that day at the edge.  
**Zal**: He should see your face when he reads it.

#### `a27-17-fire-sat`

_Zal goes to the brazier in the middle of the hall, and stops, and stands there with the feather in his hands._  
**Zal**: She said: when you are truly in need. This is the day.  
_He holds it a long moment. You don’t hurry him; you never have._  
_Then he turns round and holds it out to you._  
**Zal**: You put it on. You sat with me at the edge until I could stand.  
**Zal**: Sit with me now.  
_You take the feather and lay it on the fire, and sit down beside him on the step. He leans on your shoulder._  
_It doesn’t burn like a feather. It burns slowly, like a candle, with a smell of sandalwood._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): burning is a change that cannot be reversed; melting can  
> _Once the feather has burned, it can never be a feather again. Which change can be reversed: melting ice, or burning wood?_  
> - ✅ Melting ice. → Yes. Melted ice can be frozen again. Burning makes new things, such as ash and smoke, and cannot be undone.
> - Burning wood. → No. Burnt wood cannot become wood again. Melting ice can be refrozen.
> - Both can be reversed. → Only one can. Melted ice can be frozen again, but burnt wood cannot be unburnt.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that burning cannot be reversed, but melting can._

_Outside, all at once, the light goes strange._

#### `a27-17-complete-sat`

_Near morning there is a new sound in the house: small, furious and very much alive._  
_The baby is big and strong, with a fist like a walnut. Rudaba laughs, tired out, and holds him up to see._  
**Rudaba**: His name is Rostam. It means delivered: the pain is over, and here he is.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a word with several meanings: delivered  
> _Rostam’s name means “delivered”. A baby is delivered, a letter is delivered, and a person can be delivered from danger._  
> _What do these meanings share?_  
> - ✅ Something is brought safely from one place to another. → Yes. A baby arrives safely, a letter arrives safely, and a person is brought safely out of danger. That is what the name means.
> - They all mean “sent away”. → Not quite. In each case something is brought safely to where it needs to be.
> - They all mean “lost”. → The opposite: in each case something is brought safely where it needs to be.
> _For grown-ups: Linked the different meanings of delivered, such as a baby, a letter and rescue, to the idea of being brought safely._

_Before noon a rider sets off for Sam with a doll of the baby sewn in silk, so the grandfather can see his face._  
_Zal comes out into the courtyard with his son in his arms, and sits down on the step beside you, and doesn’t say anything at all._  
_He doesn’t need to. You sit there together, all three of you, and let the morning come._  
_Days later, far away in his camp, Sam opens a parcel and finds a little silk doll with his grandson’s face._  
_The last thing you see on the page is Sam, the great champion, holding the doll in both hands and weeping for joy._  
_One feather has drifted down onto the step: grey and gold, long as your arm. The Simurgh doesn’t take it back._  
_You are back in the Grove, the atlas on your knee._  
_The feather has come too, and your Nubbin, fed once already, is asking for second breakfast._

**The Simurgh**: You were right to give him the night.
