#### `a27-close-sable-bonded`

_You shut the atlas, and put the feather in a glass on the cottage mantel, where the light can get at it._  
_When you look back, Sable is curled up asleep on the mantel shelf, right underneath it. You didn’t see her get up there._  
_The tip of the feather moves a little in her breathing. She doesn’t wake, and you don’t wake her._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): trust shows in where someone chooses to rest  
> _Sable chose to sleep right under the feather, in your cottage. What does it tell us about trust when a shy animal sleeps near you?_  
> - ✅ That she feels safe near you. → Yes. A shy animal rests only where it feels safe, so her sleep is a sign of trust you earned.
> - That she is bored. → Possibly, but a shy animal sleeping deeply near you is mostly a sign of trust.
> - That nothing is happening. → A lot is happening. She feels safe enough to sleep, and that is trust.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a shy animal sleeping nearby shows it feels safe and trusts you._


#### `a27-close-sable-wary`

_You shut the atlas. The feather has slipped out of your hand somewhere, and you can’t find it._  
_Then you do: on the ground at the edge of the long grass. Sable is lying in the grass a little way off, watching it._  
_She doesn’t touch it, and she doesn’t go. When you pick it up, her eyes follow it all the way to the mantel._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): trust grows slowly; caution and curiosity can sit together  
> _Sable watches, but stays near. What does it tell us when someone is wary and curious at the same time?_  
> - ✅ That trust is growing, slowly. → Yes. Staying nearby while watching carefully is a first step. Patience and kindness help it grow.
> - That she dislikes you. → Not necessarily. If she disliked you she would leave, but she stays, watching.
> - That she is about to bite. → Unlikely. A wary animal that stays near is usually curious and deciding whether to trust.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an animal that is wary but stays nearby may be starting to trust._


#### `a28-margin-hazel`

_In the margin beside the courtyard, in soft pencil you have never noticed before, there is a note. You know the hand._  
_“Nova says here they tell you it isn’t true before they start. Best manners I ever heard of.”_  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): mixed feelings: a think question  
> _Finding a note in the handwriting of someone you love can bring more than one feeling. What might you feel?_  
> - Warmth, because it feels as if they are near. → That is a fair answer. A note can carry someone’s voice. Hazel’s humour is right there in the margin.
> - Sadness, because they are not here to say it. → That is a fair answer. Missing someone is a way of loving them. It is all right to feel it.
> - Both at once. → That is a fair answer. Feelings often come in pairs. Naming both can help you understand yourself.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the mixed feelings that come from finding a note from someone loved, using Hazel’s margin note._

_Underneath, smaller, is a spider drawn in four quick lines, wearing a hat._  

#### `a28-02-road-wisp`

_At the foot of the thread your bag shifts._  
_A grey head comes out of it, torn ear first, and looks at the forest with deep suspicion._  
_It is Wisp, who would not be left at home. Nor would he leave the egg stone, and it is in his paws now._  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Hello. What is that?  
**Wisp**: …mine.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Of course it is yours. Lovely thing.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Smooth. I would give you a story for it.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Not now, obviously. Once I own them, which will be very soon.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: A story, for the stone. Fair?  
_Wisp hisses, long and low. Then he puts out one paw to shake, and keeps the stone tight in the other._  
_Ananse shakes it with one leg, and keeps three crossed behind his back._  
**Wisp**: deal. …mine still.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Of course. Everything in its time.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Kwaku is my name, by the way, a Wednesday name. Every Akan child has one.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): Akan day names  
> _Kwaku is a Wednesday name. Which day gives a boy the name Kofi?_  
> - ✅ Friday. → Yes. Kofi is for Friday. Monday boys are Kwadwo, and Sunday boys are Kwesi.
> - Monday. → Monday boys are Kwadwo. Kofi is for Friday.
> - Sunday. → Sunday boys are Kwesi. Kofi is for Friday.
> _For grown-ups: Matched the day name Kofi to Friday, building on the Wednesday name Kwaku._

_Your Nubbin, meanwhile, has sat down in a puddle of sap and stuck. Nobody is surprised._  

**Choices**

- **Tell Wisp he doesn’t have to.**
    - **Wisp**: Hsss. Deal.
    - He has decided. You can see it in his ears.
- **Let them shake on it.**
    - You let it be. A thief and a spider deserve each other, and they both look delighted.

#### `a28-08-debt-wisp`

_Ananse sits by the empty box. Wisp climbs out of your bag and sits directly in front of him, staring._  
**Wisp**: story. owed.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Ah. Yes.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: The debt. A spider always pays.  
_He looks at the empty box, and round his doorstep. Then he picks up a small stoppered gourd and holds it out._  
**Kwaku Ananse**: A story. In a gourd.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: Very rare. Do not open it till you are home.  
_Wisp opens it at once. Out comes one hornet, the last of the swarm, very annoyed, and stings him on the nose._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): a “sting in the tail”: multiple-meaning words  
> _An ending that surprises you is sometimes called a “sting in the tail”. What do you think that phrase means?_  
> - ✅ A surprise at the end. → Yes. The word “sting” is doing double duty. Here the hornet really does sting, and the ending really does surprise.
> - A scorpion character. → A scorpion does have a sting in its tail, but this is a figure of speech. It means a surprise at the end.
> - A very long ending. → A sting is sharp and quick, not long. It means a surprise at the end.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of the phrase “sting in the tail” as a surprise ending._

_Your Nubbin, nose still lumpy, watches this with deep and private satisfaction._  
_Wisp sneezes. Then he reaches into the bag behind him and puts something on the step: Fern’s old left glove._  
**Wisp**: warm. was warm.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: A glove! One glove.  
**Kwaku Ananse**: I have eight hands. This is… thank you.  
_Ananse puts the glove on one foot. Wisp puts the gourd in your bag next to the stone._  
_Each of them is quite sure he has won. You decide not to tell either of them._  

**Choices**

- **Check Wisp’s nose.**
    - He lets you look, for once: a small bump. Your Nubbin pats it, gently, as one veteran to another.
- **Ask Ananse where the story is, then.**
    - **Kwaku Ananse**: It is in the gourd. It was the hornet.
    - **Kwaku Ananse**: A short story with a sting in it. All the best ones have.

#### `a28-09-scatter-done-freed`

_The pieces come down on the far side of the clearing, on the ants, the frogs and a very surprised goat._  
_Then something small and quick darts out of the trees: Mmoatia, home from the sky and nobody’s prisoner._  
_She catches one bright piece in her free hand, the hand you gave back, before it can touch the ground._  
**Mmoatia**: Here. A hand for a hand.  
_She drops it into your Nubbin’s paws and is gone again before anyone can thank her. Your Nubbin holds it very still._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): kindness comes back  
> _Mmoatia says, “A hand for a hand.” Why did she help your Nubbin?_  
> - ✅ Because you helped her earlier, and kindness often comes back. → Yes. She is returning a favour. Small kindnesses can be remembered a long time.
> - She was just showing off. → She did it quietly, and left before being thanked. She was returning your kindness.
> - She wanted something in return. → She asks for nothing. She is giving, not trading. She was returning your kindness.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how kindness is remembered and returned._


#### `a28-09-scatter-done-sat`

_Somebody sits down next to you under the tree. It is Mmoatia, home from the sky, and she says nothing at all._  
_The wisdom comes down on the clearing like warm rain, and on the two of you, and on your Nubbin between you._  
_None of you move to catch any. You sit, and get rained on, together._  
_When it stops, she leans, very slightly, against your arm. Then she is gone._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): quiet company  
> _Why can sitting quietly beside someone be a kind thing to do?_  
> - ✅ It shows you are there without needing to fix anything. → Yes. Sometimes company is the kindest help. Mmoatia remembers who sat with her under the odum tree.
> - It means you do not care. → The opposite. Staying close shows you care. It shows you are there without needing to fix anything.
> - It stops them from talking. → A quiet friend leaves room for talking when you are ready. It shows you are there without needing to fix anything.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how quiet company can be a kind way to help._


#### `a28-10-dance-done-freed`

_Behind Ananse, half hidden in the crowd, a small figure is laughing into her free hand. It is Mmoatia._  
_She reaches up with that hand and tips his hat clean off._  
_The beans come down all over the yard. Every hair on Ananse’s head has been scorched clean away._  
**Mmoatia**: A spider caught me once. Fair is fair.  
_There is a short silence, and then a very long laugh, and hers is the loudest._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): heat moves from hot to cooler  
> _The hot beans made Ananse’s head hot. In which direction does heat move?_  
> - ✅ From hotter things to cooler things. → Yes. Heat always flows from a hotter thing to a cooler thing. That is why a hot drink cools down in a cold room.
> - From cooler things to hotter things. → Heat does not go that way by itself. It flows from hotter things to cooler things.
> - It stays where it is. → Heat spreads out until things are the same warmth. It flows from hotter things to cooler things.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat flows from hotter things to cooler things._

_The hot beans heated his hat, and the hat heated his head._  

#### `a28-10-dance-done-sat`

_Then the hat comes off on its own, sailing up into the air, and the beans come down all over the yard._  
_Every hair on Ananse’s head has been scorched clean away. There is a short silence, and then a very long laugh._  
_Later, when he is hiding in the long grass, someone small sits down beside him. It is Mmoatia._  
_She says nothing. She lays a cool, wet leaf on his poor bald head, and stays a while._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): heat moves into a cooler thing  
> _Why does a cool, wet leaf make Ananse’s hot head feel better?_  
> - ✅ Heat moves from his hot head into the cool leaf. → Yes. Heat flows from the hotter thing to the cooler thing. The wet leaf also cools as the water dries, which takes away more heat.
> - The leaf makes cold and puts it in his head. → There is no “cold” that moves. Only heat moves. Heat leaves his head and goes into the cool leaf.
> - Leaves are magic. → A lovely idea, but the real reason is just as clever. Heat leaves his head and goes into the cool leaf.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a cool object cools a hot one because heat moves from the hotter to the cooler._

_Ananse, for once in his life, says nothing either._  

#### `a28-12-tell-freed`

**You**: This one is about a fairy, and a doll covered in gum.  
_You tell them about the odum tree, and the yam, and the thank-you that nobody answered._  
_You tell them how she stuck, both hands, and how the spider ran for rope._  
**You**: And while he was gone, somebody worked one of her hands loose. Only one.  
**You**: The other had to stay.  
**You**: So she went up to the sky caught, but with a hand of her own. And she used it, later.  
**You**: Mostly on hats.  
_The children laugh, and one of them claps with one hand on his knee._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): the theme of a story  
> _What is the theme, the big idea, of the story you told?_  
> - ✅ A small act of help can matter, even when it cannot undo everything. → Yes. One hand free did not undo the capture, but it mattered. A theme is the big idea underneath a story, not just what happens in it.
> - Never trust a fairy. → The fairy is the one who was caught, not the trickster. The theme is that a small act of help can matter.
> - Hats are important. → The hats are a joke, not the big idea. The theme is that a small act of help can matter.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: a small act of help can matter even when it cannot undo everything._

**Nana Ama**: Ha! That one is a clever one.  
**Nana Ama**: One hand free, and the story still holds. I will keep a piece of that.  
**Nana Ama**: The hand.  

#### `a28-12-tell-sat`

**You**: This one is about a fairy, and a doll covered in gum.  
_You tell them about the odum tree, and the yam, and the thank-you that nobody answered._  
_You tell them how she stuck, both hands, and how the spider ran for rope._  
**You**: And while he was gone, somebody sat down next to her. They did not say anything.  
**You**: They just waited with her.  
**You**: She was still caught when the rope came. But she was not on her own.  
_The courtyard is very quiet. A girl at the back leans against her brother, and he lets her._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): the theme of a story  
> _What is the theme, the big idea, of the story you told?_  
> - ✅ Sometimes being there matters more than fixing things. → Yes. Nothing got fixed, but the fairy was not alone. A theme is the big idea underneath a story, not just what happens in it.
> - Never be late with rope. → Rope is part of the plot, not the big idea. The theme is that being there can matter more than fixing.
> - Fairies are always sad. → Mmoatia is sharp and proud, not always sad. The theme is that being there can matter more than fixing.
> _For grown-ups: Identified a theme: being present for someone can matter more than fixing their problem._

**Nana Ama**: Mm. That one is a kind one.  
**Nana Ama**: Nothing got fixed in it, and it is better anyway. I will keep a piece of that.  
**Nana Ama**: The sitting.  

#### `a28-12-last-wisp`

**Nana Ama**: One more. A short one.  
**Nana Ama**: Mine, this time. Nobody asked for it, so listen properly.  
_Wisp has come out of your bag. He sits at the edge of the firelight with the egg stone in his paws._  
**Nana Ama**: There was a grey thief with a torn ear, who wanted every warm thing in the world.  
**Nana Ama**: And he kept a stone that had gone cold. He kept it long after it was any use to anyone.  
**Nana Ama**: He traded with a spider once, and both of them were cheated, and both of them went home pleased.  
**Nana Ama**: But the spider threw something in for nothing, and never knew. The best thing in the whole bargain.  
_Wisp’s ears have come up. He has stopped looking at the fire, and is looking at her._  
**Nana Ama**: A story. Not the one in the gourd.  
**Nana Ama**: This one. The one about him.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): how it feels to hear a story about yourself: a think question  
> _The storyteller tells a story about Wisp, and Wisp is listening. How is hearing a story about yourself different from hearing one about a stranger?_  
> - You listen more closely, because you want to know how you are seen. → That is a fair answer. A story about you carries a kind of mirror. Wisp’s ears come up, and he stops watching the fire.
> - It can feel uncomfortable, and also like being understood. → That is a fair answer. Being seen kindly can be both. Notice that the storyteller tells it gently.
> - It makes the story feel more real. → That is a fair answer. The point of view changes, and so does how much it matters. Wisp listens to the very end.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how hearing a story about yourself differs from hearing a story about someone else._

_Wisp listens to the very end, without moving. Then he gets up, carefully, the way you get up holding something full._  

#### `a28-12-last-driven`

**Nana Ama**: One more. A short one.  
**Nana Ama**: Mine. But I do not know the end, so you will have to help me.  
**Nana Ama**: There was a grey one who was sent away from a garden. A thief, they said, and they were right.  
**Nana Ama**: And still, some evenings, he comes down the lane, and looks at the gate, and does not try it.  
_The children have gone very quiet. Your Nubbin is looking at you._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): open endings: a think question  
> _The storyteller leaves the ending open and asks you to finish it. Why might she do that?_  
> - So the listener can imagine a hopeful ending. → That is a fair answer. An open ending can be a kind of invitation. Saying an ending aloud can make it more likely.
> - Because some true stories are not finished yet. → That is a fair answer. Life does not always tie things up. The storyteller says so herself.
> - Because she forgot how it ends. → That is a fair answer, but she says she does not know, not that she forgot. An unfinished story is still a story.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a storyteller might leave a story’s ending open._

**Nana Ama**: How does it end?  

**Choices**

- **Say, “I don’t know.”**
    - **Nana Ama**: No. Neither do I.
    - **Nana Ama**: That is a good answer. Most true stories end that way, for a long while.
    - **Nana Ama**: Keep it open, then. Somebody will finish it.
- **Say, “He comes back.”**
    - **Nana Ama**: Does he? Good.
    - **Nana Ama**: Then that is how I will tell it.
    - **Nana Ama**: Saying it is half of it. The rest is somebody opening the gate.

#### `a29-01-margin-hazel`

_When you next look at Nova’s atlas, there is a pencil note under the ink scroll, low in the margin. You know the hand._  
_“Never been. Nova says it’s all singing.”_  
_“I’d hum.”_  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a short note can show a person’s character: Hazel’s joke  
> _Hazel’s note is only nine words long. What does it show about her?_  
> - ✅ She would love to go, and she makes a joke so it doesn’t feel too big. → Yes. “I’d hum” is funny, and it is also a wish to join in, said in a small, brave way. Short words can carry a lot, if you read for the character behind them.
> - She dislikes singing. → Then she would not say she would hum. The joke shows she wants to join in.
> - She has been there many times. → The note says “Never been”. It shows she would love to go.
> _For grown-ups: Read a short note for what it shows about Hazel’s character: a wish to join in, said as a joke._


#### `a29-01-sable-hid`

_Something brushes your ankle in the ink: Sable has come with you. She is a grey smudge in the grey mist, keeping very low._  
_She doesn’t come to your hand. She finds the deepest shadow on the scroll and goes into it, and watches you from there._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): a frightened friend needs space and time; staying near without crowding  
> _Sable is frightened, so she hides in the shadow. What helps a frightened friend?_  
> - ✅ Staying nearby, going slowly, and not crowding her. → Yes. Giving space, staying close and being patient is how you earn a scared friend’s trust. Sable chose the shadow. Leaving her there is a kind of respect.
> - Pulling her out into the light. → That would probably frighten her more. Staying nearby and going slowly works better.
> - Ignoring her completely. → She would think you had forgotten her. Staying near and going slowly is best.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a frightened friend needs space, patience and a calm presence nearby._


#### `a29-01-sable-heel`

_Sable has come with you. She walks at your heel through the ink, grey on grey, and her ears are up._  
_She looks at the demons on the far mountains for a long moment. Then she looks at you, and stays where she is._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): trust grows when someone stays near and does not push  
> _Sable looked at the demons, looked at you, and stayed. What does that show about how she feels about you?_  
> - ✅ She trusts you enough to stay close, even when something scary is near. → Yes. Trust shows when someone stays close in a scary moment. You earned that by being patient with her.
> - She doesn’t care about anything. → She looked at the demons and then at you, which says she cares. She trusts you enough to stay.
> - She is waiting for the demons to leave. → She may be, but she looked at you and chose to stay. That shows trust.
> _For grown-ups: Saw how staying close in a scary moment can show trust._


#### `a29-02-stage-hid`

_In a gap under the stage, between two cases of cables, a pair of eyes catches the light._  
_Sable has found the darkest place in the arena._  
_Every time the bass drops she flattens a little. She doesn’t leave._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): loud places can be too much; it is all right to find somewhere quiet  
> _Sable flattens under the stage when the bass drops. Is it all right to find somewhere quieter when a place is too loud?_  
> - ✅ Yes. Everyone has a different amount of noise they can take. → Yes. Looking after yourself, by finding somewhere calm, is a skill. Sable is still at the show. She has just found a way to stay.
> - No. You should always stay in the middle. → Staying in the middle is hard when it is too much. Finding a calmer corner is fine, and it can let you stay longer.
> - Only if somebody lets you. → You can look after yourself without waiting for permission. Sable chose her own spot.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that loud places can be too much, and that finding a quiet spot is a way of looking after yourself._


#### `a29-03-pans-hid`

_When you get back, the kitchen has an extra guest. Sable is behind the stack of noodle pans by the cooker, only her ears showing._  
_Rumi sees her, and doesn’t say anything, and puts a few plain noodles on a saucer by the pans, and leaves them there._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, ask): animals need food that suits them: plain, not spicy  
> _Rumi puts plain noodles on a saucer for Sable, not spicy ones. Why?_  
> - ✅ Animals need food that suits them, and spicy food can upset a pet’s tummy. → Yes. Animals need the right food to stay well, and what suits people doesn’t always suit pets. Rumi chose plain and left it quietly, a kind and careful thing.
> - Spicy food is too expensive. → Cost isn’t the reason here. Spicy food can upset a pet’s tummy, so plain is safer.
> - Sable likes plain things better, always. → We can’t know that, and animals vary. Plain is safer for her tummy.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals need food that suits them, and that plain food is safer for pets than spicy food._


#### `a29-11-store-hid`

_Under the folded tables, at the back of the store room, something grey moves. Sable has been in here all along, hiding from the noise._  
_She watches the tape come off Mira’s wrists. When you go, she comes after you, one shadow at a time._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, ask): many night animals have a reflective layer in the eye, so eyes shine in the dark  
> _In dark places, Sable’s eyes seem to glint. Why do many animals’ eyes shine in the dark?_  
> - ✅ A shiny layer at the back of the eye bounces light back. → Yes. Many night animals have a mirror-like layer in the eye, which helps them see in dim light. That layer sends some light back out, so their eyes seem to glow.
> - Their eyes make their own light. → Eyes don’t make light. They reflect it. The shiny layer inside bounces light back.
> - They are wet and cold. → Wetness isn’t why. It is the shiny layer inside the eye. It bounces light back.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals have a mirror-like layer in the eye that helps them see in the dark._


#### `a29-16-street-hid`

_Sable has found the shade at the foot of the wall, under Sussie. The magpie looks down at her, and hops down, and sits beside her._  
_The two of them watch the queue together from the shade, one grey, one black and white, very still._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): there are many ways of joining in: a quiet way is fine  
> _Sable and Sussie watch from the shade, not from the middle. Can that be a way of joining in?_  
> - ✅ Yes. People join in at their own pace. → Yes. Being there, quietly, still counts. Everyone has their own way and their own speed. Sussie sat beside her, which is a lovely way to say “welcome”.
> - No. If you are not in the middle, you are not joining in. → The middle is only one place to be. Watching from the shade is a way of being there too.
> - Only if you speak to everyone. → Not at all. Some people join in without a word. Sable and Sussie are a good example.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that joining in can be quiet, and that people do it at their own pace._


#### `a29-14-crowd-heel`

_Sable is at your heel the whole way through the crowd. All those blank faces, all that noise, and she doesn’t go under anything._  
_Her ears are up. She walks right beside you, close enough to touch, and keeps walking._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): being brave is easier with a friend beside you  
> _Sable walks through the scary crowd without hiding. What helps her be brave?_  
> - ✅ Having someone she trusts right beside her. → Yes. Many brave things feel smaller when a friend is next to you. Trust is a kind of courage you can share.
> - Not being scared at all. → She may well be scared. Her ears are up, which means she is alert. Being brave is walking on, with someone beside you.
> - The crowd being quiet. → The crowd is blank, which is eerie in its own way. It is her friend beside her that helps.
> _For grown-ups: Saw that being brave can be easier with a trusted friend close by._


#### `a29-16-street-heel`

_Sable walks out into the middle of the pavement, in the full sun, and lies down there, grey and in plain view._  
_The fans in the queue step round her, carefully, the way you step round a cat in a doorway. She stays exactly where she is._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): respecting an animal’s space: step round, do not grab  
> _The fans step carefully round Sable. What does that show?_  
> - ✅ Respect: giving an animal space when it hasn’t asked to be touched. → Yes. Animals have feelings and their own say. Giving them space is a way of being fair. If they want to be petted, they will let you know.
> - The fans are afraid of her. → They aren’t afraid. They are being careful and kind. They give her space.
> - They don’t notice her. → They clearly notice. They step round her carefully. It shows respect.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that giving an animal space, and waiting for it to come to you, shows respect._


#### `a29-grove-luna-heel`

_Luna looks at Sable, who is lying in the middle of the path in the sun, and then at you._  
**Luna**: She went somewhere loud and bright, and didn’t hide? Well.  
**Luna**: Don’t make a fuss of it. She’ll know.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): understatement: Luna’s dry words hide how proud she is  
> _Luna says “Well. Don’t make a fuss of it.”_  
> _What is she really saying?_  
> - ✅ That she is proud, said in a dry way. → Yes. Some people hide big feelings under small, dry words. Luna is one of them. Readers learn to hear what is under what is said.
> - That she is cross with Sable. → If she were cross, she would not say Sable will know. She is proud, quietly.
> - That she doesn’t care. → She watched closely and spoke to you about it. That shows she cares, dryly.
> _For grown-ups: Heard the feeling hidden under Luna’s dry words: quiet pride in Sable._


#### `a29-grove-luna-hid`

_Luna looks at Sable, who is under the bench, and then at you._  
**Luna**: She went somewhere loud and bright, and came home. Hiding still counts as going.  
**Luna**: Don’t make a fuss of it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): understatement: Luna’s dry words hide how proud she is  
> _Luna says “Hiding still counts as going.” What does she mean?_  
> - ✅ That Sable was brave to go, even though she hid. → Yes. Luna is saying that going was the brave part, even if hiding came with it. A dry line can hold a kind thought.
> - That hiding is silly. → She says it counts, which means it matters. She is praising Sable.
> - That Sable shouldn’t have gone. → She says Sable “came home”, which is good news to Luna. She thinks going was brave.
> _For grown-ups: Heard the kind thought under Luna’s dry line: going counts, even if you hide._


#### `a29-12-find-saw`

_The car park under the awards hall smells of exhaust and spilt fizzy drink. The noise upstairs has gone thin and strange._  
_You are sitting on the gear case, because nobody told you where else to sit. Your Nubbin is in the merchandise bag, very quiet._  
_Rumi comes down the ramp fast, looking along the rows of cars. When she sees you, she stops looking._  
_She sits down on the case beside you. She came to you first, before Mira, before Zoey, before Celine._  
**Rumi**: You saw. In the dressing room.  
**Rumi**: And you said it was all right.  
**Rumi**: Was it true? Or were you only being nice?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): comfort only works if it is true  
> _Rumi asks whether “it’s all right” was true, or only nice. Why does it matter that comfort is honest?_  
> - ✅ Because comfort only works if the person can believe it. → Yes. Honest comfort can be trusted, and trusted comfort can be leaned on. You said it was true, and it was, so it held.
> - It doesn’t matter, as long as it is nice. → Nice can feel good for a minute. But if it isn’t true, it can crumble later. Honest kindness lasts.
> - Because lying is always wrong. → Honesty matters, yes, and so does kindness. The best comfort has both. That is what you gave Rumi.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why honest comfort matters, and how true kindness can be trusted._

**You**: It was true. It still is.  
_She lets her breath go, all of it, like someone putting down a heavy bag._  
**Rumi**: Everyone saw tonight. You saw first.  
**Rumi**: That helps. I don’t know why, but it helps.  

#### `a29-12-find-away`

_The car park under the awards hall smells of exhaust and spilt fizzy drink. The noise upstairs has gone thin and strange._  
_You are sitting on the gear case, because nobody told you where else to sit. Your Nubbin is in the merchandise bag, very quiet._  
_Rumi comes down the ramp and stops in front of you. Her arm is bare, and she doesn’t cover it._  
**Rumi**: In the dressing room. That night.  
**Rumi**: You looked away. Did you see?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): different people need different kinds of kindness; you can ask  
> _You looked away that night to be kind, and Rumi still isn’t sure what you saw._  
> _How can you find out what kind of kindness someone needs?_  
> - ✅ Ask them, and listen to the answer. → Yes. People need different things, and the quickest way to know is to ask. Looking away was kind, and asking would have been kind too.
> - Guess, and hope for the best. → Guessing can work, but it can also leave someone unsure. Asking is more certain. Ask, and listen.
> - Do what you would like done to you. → That is a good start. But other people may need something different. Asking tells you what they need.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people need different kinds of kindness, and that asking is a good way to find out._


**Choices**

- **“Yes. I saw.”**
    - **You**: Yes. I saw.
    - **Rumi**: And you let me think you hadn’t.
    - She doesn’t sound angry. She sounds as if she is working something out.
    - **Rumi**: That was kind. I think.
    - **Rumi**: I don’t know any more which kind of kind I need.
- **Say nothing.**
    - You don’t say anything. You don’t look away this time, either.
    - **Rumi**: Right. Yes.
    - **Rumi**: You did.
    - She sits down on the end of the case, not quite next to you, and looks at her own arm.

#### `a29-14-song-done-saw`

_Halfway through, with the marks blazing on her arms, Rumi looks round the stadium once, and finds you at the side of the stage._  
_Only for a moment. Then she looks back out at the crowd, and sings louder._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): a single look can carry a message  
> _Rumi looks for you once, only for a moment, and then sings louder. What does that single look tell you?_  
> - ✅ That she remembers who said it was all right. → Yes. One look can say “thank you” and “I’m ready” at once. Then she looks away, because she doesn’t need to check any more.
> - That she is lost. → She found you at once, so she isn’t lost. The look says she remembers.
> - That she forgot the words. → She sings louder straight after, so she hasn’t forgotten anything. The look says she remembers who helped her.
> _For grown-ups: Read a single look as a message: remembering who said it was all right._

_Mira, halfway down the aisle, blinks, and so does Zoey, two rows behind. They look at each other._  
_Then they are running for the stage, and you are running after them with the gear case banging your knees._  

#### `a29-14-song-done-away`

_Rumi doesn’t look for anyone, not Mira, not Zoey, not you. She sings straight out, at all of them._  
_She doesn’t need to look for anyone. That is the whole point._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): not looking for anyone shows she no longer needs permission  
> _Rumi doesn’t look for anyone, and the story says that is “the whole point”. What does it mean?_  
> - ✅ She no longer needs anyone’s permission to be herself. → Yes. She isn’t checking whether it is safe. She has decided. That is quiet courage, shown by what she doesn’t do.
> - She is angry at everyone. → There is no anger in how she sings. She doesn’t need to look for permission.
> - She can’t see anyone. → She can see. She just doesn’t need to look. She no longer needs permission.
> _For grown-ups: Read what a character does not do, looking for nobody, as a sign of confidence._

_Mira, halfway down the aisle, blinks, and so does Zoey, two rows behind. They look at each other._  
_Then they are running for the stage, and you are running after them with the gear case banging your knees._  

#### `a29-16-complete-saw`

_The fans thin out at last. Bobby counts phones, counts girls, and counts you, and seems happy with all the numbers._  
**Bobby**: Runner. Good work.  
**Bobby**: Strange work, but good. If you ever want a job that’s only a job, call me.  
**Zoey**: Group photo! Huntrix and staff!  
**Zoey**: Bobby, hold the phone up higher. Higher.  
**Zoey**: Like a tall person.  
_You go to step out of the way. Rumi catches you by the sleeve and pulls you into the middle, between her and Mira._  
**Rumi**: You were the first one to say it was all right. You’re in the photo.  
_In the photo, her arm is round your shoulders, marks and all. Your Nubbin is a blur in the front, waving._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): everyone has something they think they should hide; a friend who says it is all right  
> _Almost everyone has something they think they should hide. What helps a person stop hiding?_  
> - Hearing, from someone, that it is all right. → That is a fair answer. You were the first to say it, and Rumi remembered. Kind words, said early, can last a long time.
> - Being brave a little at a time. → That is a fair answer. Rumi took years, then one night, then one sunny street. Small steps count.
> - Meeting others who share it. → That is a fair answer. Finding that you are not the only one makes hiding feel less needed. Rumi’s fans came to look at her arm and smiled.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps people stop hiding what they fear others will judge, with no single right answer._

_Sussie drops a folded leaf into your hand from the wall, and then hops onto your shoulder and stays there._  
_Zoey hands you a flat parcel tied with string. Inside is a small folding screen, from Celine: a silly tiger and a bright magpie._  
_The street goes flat, and bright, and smells of paint._  
_You are in the Grove, with a magpie on your shoulder and a thread of light round your wrist._  

#### `a29-16-complete-away`

_The fans thin out at last. Bobby counts phones, counts girls, and counts you, and seems happy with all the numbers._  
**Bobby**: Runner. Good work.  
**Bobby**: Strange work, but good. If you ever want a job that’s only a job, call me.  
_You pick up the empty boxes and go across the street to the van. When you turn round, Rumi is looking for you over the crowd._  
_She lifts her bare arm and waves, once, a big wave, from right across the street._  
_You wave back, and neither of you comes any closer. That’s enough._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): everyone has something they think they should hide; a friendship does not have to be close to be real  
> _Almost everyone has something they think they should hide. What helps a person stop hiding?_  
> - Someone who gives them space to decide. → That is a fair answer. You looked away, and let Rumi choose. That was a gift. Space can be a kind of care.
> - Being brave a little at a time. → That is a fair answer. Rumi took years, then one night, then one sunny street. Small steps count.
> - Meeting others who share it. → That is a fair answer. Finding that you are not the only one makes hiding feel less needed. Rumi’s fans came to look at her arm and smiled.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what helps people stop hiding what they fear others will judge, with no single right answer._

_Sussie drops a folded leaf into your hand from the wall, and then hops onto your shoulder and stays there._  
_Zoey hands you a flat parcel tied with string. Inside is a small folding screen, from Celine: a silly tiger and a bright magpie._  
_The street goes flat, and bright, and smells of paint._  
_You are in the Grove, with a magpie on your shoulder and a thread of light round your wrist._  

#### `a30-01-ember`

_Your Nubbin is carrying its little lantern, with the red pebble glowing in it. Dvora bends to look._  
**Dvora**: A coal that needs no fire. Well. Don’t put it near my curtains, whatever it is.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): light and heat are energy moving away from a glowing thing  
> **Ori**: Anything that glows gives out light, and often heat too. Both are energy moving away from whatever makes them.  
> **Ori**: Hold your hand near a lamp and you can feel it. Dvora is right to keep the curtains away.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a glowing object gives out light and heat, which are energy moving away from it._

_Your Nubbin holds the lantern a little closer to itself, the way you hold something lent._  

#### `a30-09-order-safe`

_Yossele is standing in the caretaker’s doorway with one arm across it, like a bar on a gate._  
_Behind his arm Shmuel and Mirele are bouncing, trying to get out to the lane. He doesn’t move._  
**Shmuel**: He won’t let us out! We only want to see the bread!  
_Gently, completely, he keeps them in. Every time one of them ducks under, he lifts them back with one hand._  
**Dvora**: He’s started doing that. Every door, all afternoon. They’re safe, I suppose. They’re very safe.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe is not the same as well  
> _Yossele keeps the children safe by keeping them in. What else do children need to be well?_  
> - ✅ Play, fresh air and friends → Yes. Safe matters, but a child shut in all day isn’t well. Play and company matter too.
> - Nothing, safe is enough → Safe is very important. But a well child can also run, play and choose.
> - More bars on the door → More bars make it safer, but they don’t make anyone happier.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between being safe and being well._


#### `a30-09-order-help`

_Yossele is sweeping the caretaker’s step. It is very clean, as if it has been swept a great many times._  
_Every neighbour who passes says “Yossele, would you…” and he would. He has a basket, two buckets and a broom._  
**Rivka**: Old Mrs Weiss asked him to carry her chair in, and he carried her in too. She was sitting in it.  
_Behind him, in a neat row, are six chairs nobody asked to be moved. He has started helping before he’s asked._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division: 6 ÷ 2  
> _Yossele carries two chairs at a time, and there are six. How many trips does he make?_  
> - ✅ 3 → Yes. 6 ÷ 2 = 3 trips, with two chairs each time.
> - 4 → Check it: 4 trips of two would be 8 chairs. 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
> - 2 → 2 trips of two is only 4 chairs. He needs 3 trips for 6.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 6 chairs into groups of 2 to find 3 trips._


#### `a30-09-order-sit`

_Yossele is sitting on the caretaker’s step, as long as the step. Three children are sitting with him._  
_Shmuel is on one knee and Mirele on the other, and Rivka is leaning on his arm, telling him a long story._  
_Your Nubbin is asleep in his lap, on its back, with its paws in the air._  
**Mirele**: He doesn’t talk. But he listens properly. Not like Papa.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): what makes a good listener  
> _Mirele says Yossele “listens properly”. What makes someone a good listener?_  
> - ✅ They stay still, look at you and don’t interrupt → Yes. A good listener gives you their whole attention and lets you finish.
> - They talk louder than you → That isn’t listening. A good listener lets you speak.
> - They think about something else → Then they are not listening at all. Good listeners pay attention.
> _For grown-ups: Named what makes a good listener._

_Yossele doesn’t move. He has been sitting like this since noon, very still, so nobody falls._  

#### `a30-10-grow-safe`

_Yossele is going down the lane, door to door, shutting each one with his hand flat on it. Then the next._  
_Every time he moves he is a little taller. The cobbles crack under his feet._  
_He drags Hannah’s cart across the end of the lane, and the gate behind it, and holds them there. Nobody in, nobody out._  
_People call from behind their shutters, and he doesn’t hear them. He is keeping everyone safe, and he is getting bigger._  
**Rivka**: He’s shut the whole lane in! Mama’s behind one of those doors, and the rabbi doesn’t know!  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness: everyone should be free to come and go  
> _Yossele has shut everyone in. Why is that unfair, even though he means well?_  
> - ✅ Everyone should be free to open their own door → Yes. Fairness means people can come and go from their own homes. Good intentions don’t change that.
> - It is fair, because he is strong → Being strong doesn’t make a rule fair. Fair rules are ones people can live with.
> - It isn’t unfair, it is only noisy → The noise is the sound of people who cannot get out. That is the unfairness.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about fairness and freedom: shutting people in is not fair, even with kind intentions._


#### `a30-10-grow-help`

_Yossele is doing everything at once. Sweeping the lane, fetching water, chopping wood, faster and faster._  
_Every time he moves he is a little taller. The broom snaps in his hands; he picks up another, and that snaps too._  
_The woodpile goes to splinters and the water barrel splits. Hannah’s oven door comes off its hinges._  
_Nobody has asked him. He is helping, and helping, and helping, and he is getting bigger._  
**Dvora**: My pots! He’s scrubbing my pots! He’s scrubbing them into pieces!  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication: 4 × 3  
> _Say Yossele scrubs four pots, and each one breaks into three pieces. How many pieces are there?_  
> - ✅ 12 → Yes. Four groups of three is 4 × 3 = 12 pieces. That is a lot of mending.
> - 7 → That adds 4 + 3. Four pots with three pieces each is 4 × 3 = 12.
> - 9 → Close, but three threes is 9 and there are four pots. 4 × 3 = 12.
> _For grown-ups: Used equal groups: 4 pots with 3 pieces each make 12 pieces._


#### `a30-10-grow-sit`

_In the rabbi’s courtyard Yossele is sitting on the step, with your Nubbin in his lap. He is restless._  
_He grows a little as you watch, then a little more. The step cracks under him._  
_He stands up. Very carefully, before anything else, he lifts your Nubbin and sets it down on the step, on its feet._  
_Then he goes. Barrels roll, the fence goes over, the woodpile spills across the cobbles, and he is getting bigger._  
**Rivka**: He put it down first. Did you see? He put it down first.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): noticing care for someone smaller  
> _Yossele is wild and strong, and still he puts your Nubbin down gently first. What does that show?_  
> - ✅ He cares about someone smaller than him → Yes. Even in the middle of the trouble, he is careful with the one who is little.
> - He doesn’t want to carry it → If he didn’t care, he would simply drop it. He set it down on its feet.
> - It was an accident → Nothing about it looks accidental. It was done carefully, and first.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that gentle, careful behaviour shows care for someone smaller._


#### `a30-10-ember`

_In your Nubbin’s little lantern the red pebble flares up, bright and hot, as Yossele grows._  
_Your Nubbin holds the lantern away from itself with both arms, and looks at you. It knows that light._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): light and heat are both forms of energy  
> _The pebble flares and the lantern grows warm. What are the light and the warmth?_  
> - ✅ Two ways energy moves away from the pebble → Yes. The pebble sends out energy as light you can see and heat you can feel.
> - Two different pebbles → It is one pebble, giving out two kinds of energy: light and heat.
> - Nothing, it is only for show → A flare is energy leaving the pebble as light and heat.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that light and heat are both ways energy moves away from a glowing thing._


#### `a30-10-ember-settle`

_In the little lantern the red pebble dims, slowly, back to its own small glow. It settles, like someone sitting down._  
_Your Nubbin holds it close again._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): a dimmer glow gives out less energy  
> _The pebble has settled back to a small glow. What has changed?_  
> - ✅ It gives out less light and less heat → Yes. A dimmer glow sends out less energy as light and heat.
> - It gives out more light → The opposite. A smaller glow sends out less.
> - It has stopped being a pebble → It is still the same pebble. It is only glowing more softly.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that a dimmer glow gives out less light and heat._


#### `a30-margin-hazel`

_Nova’s atlas lies open at the steep roof of the synagogue, and the little window high in its gable._  
_Beside the window, in faint pencil you have never noticed, there is a note in the margin. You know the hand._  
_“Clay, a word, and a man who forgot one Friday. I’d have forgotten every Friday.”_  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): being honest about our own faults  
> _Hazel says she would have forgotten every Friday. What does that show about her?_  
> - ✅ She can be honest about her own faults, and laugh → Yes. Admitting what we are bad at, kindly, is a sign of a settled heart.
> - She is boasting → Boasting would be saying she is brilliant. She is owning up to a weakness.
> - She doesn’t care about the story → The note shows she read it closely, and saw herself in it.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that admitting our own faults with humour is a sign of self-awareness._

_Your Nubbin puts one paw on the drawing of the attic window, and leaves it there._  

#### `a30-13-order-safe`

**Rabbi Loew**: You told him to keep everyone safe. And he did. On that last night he kept the whole lane in.  
**Rabbi Loew**: A guard who keeps everyone in isn’t a guard any more. He’s a wall.  
**Rabbi Loew**: And a wall, however kind, is not a home. A home has a door that opens.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understanding a metaphor  
> _“A wall is not a home” is a metaphor. What does the rabbi mean?_  
> - ✅ Safety without freedom isn’t a home → Yes. A home is safe and open. A wall is only safe.
> - Walls are made of bricks, homes of wood → He isn’t talking about building materials. The words stand for something else.
> - Homes should have no walls → Homes need walls for shelter. His point is that walls alone aren’t a home.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor: a wall without a door stands for safety without freedom._

**Rabbi Loew**: It was a good order. It was the order I gave him myself, in my heart. That’s why I know.  

#### `a30-13-order-help`

**Rabbi Loew**: You told him to help where he was asked. And at the end he helped where nobody asked at all.  
_He laughs a little, sadly, and shakes his head._  
**Rabbi Loew**: He was a very good servant. That was the trouble.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Help with no one asking for it isn’t help. It’s weather. Dvora’s pots would agree with me.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understanding a metaphor  
> _“It isn’t help, it’s weather.” What is the rabbi comparing?_  
> - ✅ Unwanted help to weather that just happens to you → Yes. You can’t ask the weather to stop. Help nobody asked for just lands on you.
> - Help to the rain, because both are wet → It isn’t about being wet. It is about something you didn’t choose.
> - Dvora to the weather → Dvora is only the one whose pots are broken. The comparison is help and weather.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor: help nobody asked for is like weather, something that simply happens to you._


#### `a30-13-order-sit`

**Rabbi Loew**: You told him to sit with the little ones. I’ve been thinking about that most of all.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Everything in him, I put there. The clay, the word, the work. Even the order was put there, by you.  
**Rabbi Loew**: But at the end, wild as he was, he put your little one down on the step before he went.  
**Rabbi Loew**: Nobody told him to do that. I didn’t put that there. It is the only thing in him I didn’t.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): finding the theme  
> _What is the rabbi’s big idea here, the theme?_  
> - ✅ The best thing in a person may be what nobody put there → Yes. Kindness he chose for himself was the part no one made.
> - Clay is stronger than people → The story isn’t about strength. It is about what the clay man did that nobody told him to do.
> - Orders should always be kept → The rabbi says the opposite: the best thing came from outside any order.
> _For grown-ups: Found a theme: the best thing in a person may be what nobody put there._

_Your Nubbin, at your feet, is looking at the attic window._  

#### `a30-13-kept`

_The rabbi looks at your pocket, where the stone is. You hadn’t thought it showed._  
**Rabbi Loew**: You carry something. Heavy, for its size. What is it?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): private things and secrets that worry us  
> _It is fine to keep some things private. If a secret worries you, what should you do?_  
> - ✅ Tell a grown-up I trust → Yes. Private is fine, but a worry that grows is best shared with someone we trust.
> - Keep it forever, whatever happens → Private things can stay private. A worrying secret is different: it should be shared.
> - Tell everyone I meet → That isn’t wise either. Choose one person you trust.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about the difference between a private matter and a secret that worries us._


**Choices**

- **Tell him about the stone.**
    - You tell him, and it hums one word, safe, while you talk. He listens to the end, and doesn’t interrupt.
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Some things are made to protect. And then they have to be put somewhere high.
    - **Rabbi Loew**: There’s no shame in carrying them up the steps. I did.
- **Keep it to yourself.**
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Then keep it. You’re allowed.
    - **Rabbi Loew**: Only, some things are made to protect, and then have to be put somewhere high. There’s no shame in carrying them up the steps.

#### `a30-13-tile-paw`

_Beside the three letters there is a tiny pawprint, pressed into the corner of the tile._  
**Rivka**: Your Nubbin did that. I was holding it out to show it, and it put its paw on. I didn’t smooth it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-1, ask): prints in soft mud and clay become fossils  
> _A print pressed into soft clay stays when the clay dries. Footprints in mud can turn to rock over a very long time._  
> _What do such fossils tell us?_  
> - ✅ How animals lived and moved long ago → Yes. A fossil footprint is a record of an animal that walked there, long before us.
> - How much the animal weighed to the gram → Prints can hint at size, but not exact weight. They show how animals moved.
> - Nothing, they are only marks → They tell scientists a great deal about how animals lived.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fossil footprints in rock tell us how animals lived long ago._


#### `a30-13-complete-help`

_Rivka walks you to the end of the lane, where the page begins to go thin and brown at the edges._  
_Behind you the steep roof of the synagogue stands against the evening, and high in its gable, the attic window._  
_On the sill outside the attic window, high up where nobody can reach, a broom leans against the wall._  
_Nobody knows how it got there. Nobody has tried to fetch it down._  
_Your Nubbin looks up at the window for a long time. Then it takes your hand, which it doesn’t often do._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): safe is not the same as well  
> _A broom left leaning on a sill: help that has been put down. What does being well need, as well as being helped?_  
> - ✅ Choice, and someone who listens → Yes. Help works best when it is asked for, and when it listens.
> - More helpers, faster → More and faster helpers is what went wrong. Help needs to be asked for.
> - Nobody to help at all → Help is good. It simply needs to be wanted, and to stop in time.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on what helps well: help that is asked for, and that listens._

_You are back in the Grove, the atlas on your knee._  
_Your pocket is heavier by one clay tile, still cool, as if nobody has told it where it is._  

#### `a30-13-complete-sit`

_Rivka walks you to the end of the lane, where the page begins to go thin and brown at the edges._  
_Behind you the steep roof of the synagogue stands against the evening, and high in its gable, the attic window._  
_On the sill of the attic window, high up where nobody can reach, there is a small clay bird. A child’s._  
_Rivka looks up at it, and then at you, and doesn’t say anything. She only had enough clay for one, she said._  
_Your Nubbin looks up at the window for a long time. Then it takes your hand, which it doesn’t often do._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what a small, kind thing can mean  
> _A little clay bird on the sill: made to sit, and to do nothing. What might it mean?_  
> - ✅ Being with someone can matter more than doing for them → Yes. Sitting with someone, without a job to do, is a kind of care.
> - That clay birds can fly → It doesn’t fly. That is its point: it is about being there, not doing.
> - That Rivka ran out of clay → She did, in a way, but the bird stands for something more: being with someone.
> _For grown-ups: Reflected on how being with someone can matter as much as doing for them._

_You are back in the Grove, the atlas on your knee._  
_Your pocket is heavier by one clay tile, still cool, as if nobody has told it where it is._  

#### `a30-grove-tile-cinder`

_You set the clay tile on the cottage hearth, beside Hazel’s old clay tablets, the ones about the Heartstone._  
_Moss comes in from the step, and stops beside it. He looks at the three letters for a long time._  
**Moss**: She’d have liked him. That’s the trouble with her.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what two characters have in common  
> _Moss says “she” would have liked Yossele. What do Cinder and Yossele have in common?_  
> - ✅ Both were protectors who grew too strong to be safe → Yes. Both loved the ones they guarded, and both grew too strong for it to stay safe.
> - Both are made of clay → Only Yossele is clay. What they share is how they protected.
> - Both live in the Grove → Yossele never did. What they share is what they were for.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two characters by what they have in common._

_He goes back out to his flat stone. Your Nubbin puts its night-round lantern down beside the tile, and leaves it there._  

#### `a30-grove-tile`

_You set the clay tile on the cottage hearth, beside Hazel’s old clay tablets, the ones about the Heartstone._  
_Moss comes in from the step, and stops beside it. You tell him what the letters say, and what one letter less says._  
**Moss**: Truth, and then one letter less. That’s how close it always is.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): which letter turns emet into met  
> _You told Moss “what one letter less says”. Which letter do you take away to turn emet into met?_  
> - ✅ Alef → Yes. Take away the silent alef, the first letter, and “truth” becomes “dead”.
> - Mem → Take mem away and only alef and tav are left. It is alef that goes, leaving mem and tav.
> - Tav → Tav is the last letter, and it stays. It is the first letter, alef, that goes.
> _For grown-ups: Remembered that taking away alef turns emet (truth) into met (dead)._

_He goes back out to his flat stone. Your Nubbin sits by the hearth and looks at the tile until it gets dark._  

#### `a30-grove-tile-quiet`

_You set the clay tile on the cottage hearth, beside Hazel’s old clay tablets, the ones about the Heartstone._  
_There is nobody in the cottage to tell what the letters say. You say it anyway, out loud: truth, and then one letter less._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): which Hebrew word means truth  
> _You said two words aloud: emet and met. Which of them means truth?_  
> - ✅ Emet → Yes. Emet is truth. Met is what is left when the first letter goes.
> - Met → Met means dead. Emet, the longer word, means truth.
> _For grown-ups: Recalled that emet means truth and met means dead._

_Your Nubbin sits by the hearth and looks at the tile until it gets dark._  

#### `a31-01-ribbons`

_The girl’s eyes go to your Nubbin’s ribbons: gold and silver, stitched together down the middle in green._  
**Granddaughter**: Why’s it got two colours?  
_She counts the colours anyway, thread and all, under her breath: gold, silver, green, and round again._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a repeating colour pattern: find the 7th  
> _The girl’s colours go gold, silver, green, gold, silver, green, and on. What colour is the 7th?_  
> - ✅ Gold → Yes. The pattern repeats every three: 1 gold, 2 silver, 3 green, 4 gold, 5 silver, 6 green, 7 gold.
> - Silver → Let’s count: 1 gold, 2 silver, 3 green, 4 gold, 5 silver, 6 green, 7 gold. The 7th is gold.
> - Green → Green comes 3rd and 6th. Count on: the 7th starts the pattern again with gold.
> _For grown-ups: Found the 7th item in a repeating three-colour pattern._

_Before you can answer, her grandmother hands her a tortilla, and the question goes in with it._  

#### `a31-11-road-stay`

_The house is very quiet with the twins gone. Xmucane sweeps the floor round the two ears of corn, carefully, not too close._  
**Xmucane**: Don’t stand on them. Don’t breathe on them. I know. I’m being silly.  
_Xquic grinds corn at the stone. You fetch water from the river twice, then a third time, because it’s something to do._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): how corn becomes tortillas, then and now  
> **Xquic**: We soak the dry corn in water with lime, a white powder made from stone, not the fruit. It softens the corn and makes it better for you.  
> **Xquic**: Then it is ground into dough. I use a flat stone, as my mother did. In some houses today, a small mill does that job.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how corn is soaked and ground into tortilla dough, by stone in the past and sometimes by mill today._

_Your Nubbin sits by the corn and looks at it. The corn looks back, being corn._  
**Xmucane**: They’ll be at the crossroads by now. Their father took the black road. I told him not to.  
**Xquic**: Did he listen?  
**Xmucane**: Of course not. He was my son.  

**Choices**

- **Take over the sweeping.**
    - **Xmucane**: Hm. You hold the broom the way he did. All wrong.
- **Sit by the corn with your Nubbin.**
    - You sit down. Nobody tells you to, and nobody tells you not to.

#### `a31-11-lords-stay`

_In the evening the falcon lands on the doorpost, out of breath, which falcons hate._  
**Falcon**: Message. From below. From me, really. I went to look.  
**Falcon**: They sent a mosquito ahead. It bit every lord on the bench, and the real ones yelled each other’s names.  
**Falcon**: So the boys said good day to every one of them, by name. And good day to the wooden ones, for manners.  
**Xmucane**: And the bench? The hot one?  
**Falcon**: Didn’t sit on it. Said they’d been sitting all the way down.  
_Xmucane laughs once, out loud. Then she puts her hand over her mouth, as if she’s been caught._  
**Xmucane**: Their father sat on it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): feeling two feelings at once  
> _Xmucane laughs, then goes quiet with sorrow. Can a person feel funny and sad in the same minute?_  
> - ✅ Yes. Feelings can mix, and that is normal. → Yes: gladness and grief can sit side by side. Xmucane laughs because she is proud, and goes quiet because she misses her son.
> - No. It is one feeling at a time. → It can feel that way, but real feelings mix all the time. Xmucane is proud of the twins and sad about her son at once.
> - Only grown-ups feel that. → Children feel mixed feelings too, like being excited and nervous before a first day somewhere new.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people can feel two feelings at the same time, and that it is normal._


**Choices**

- **Give the falcon some water.**
    - **Falcon**: Thank you. Nobody ever gives the messenger water.
- **Look at the corn.**
    - Green. Both ears, green to the tips.

#### `a31-12-dark-stay`

_That night Xmucane can’t sleep. She sits up by the corn, and you sit with her, and Xquic sleeps against the wall._  
**Xmucane**: They’ll have been given the Dark House tonight. Their father had to keep a torch lit all night. He couldn’t.  
_The fire is low. Your Nubbin curls up in its warm patch and watches the corn with one eye._  
_Before dawn Xmucane puts another log on the coals and sits straight again._  
**Xmucane**: My mother did that when anyone was away. So I do.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): how company helps when you cannot fix a problem  
> _You cannot fix Xmucane’s worry. How does sitting up beside her still help?_  
> - ✅ She does not have to face the night alone. → Yes. Company does not solve the problem, but it makes the waiting bearable.
> - It does not help. Only solving the problem helps. → Some problems cannot be solved yet. Being there is what helps then.
> - It helps you more than her. → Perhaps a little, but Xmucane notices you there all night. Sitting together helps both of you.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that being there for someone helps even when you cannot fix their problem._

_The corn stays green. All night, both ears, green._  

**Choices**

- **Stay awake with her.**
    - You stay awake. When your head nods, she pokes you, kindly, and you sit up again.
- **Let your Nubbin sleep on your feet.**
    - It sleeps on your feet, and you don’t move them for hours. Xmucane notices, says nothing, and approves.

#### `a31-12-dark-done-stay`

**Xmucane**: Still green.  
_She says it every morning after that. By the third morning you are saying it with her._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.4, ask): repeated lines make a refrain  
> _Xmucane says “Still green” every morning, and then you join in. What does a repeated line like that do?_  
> - ✅ It gives the family something steady to hold on to. → Yes: a repeated line is called a refrain. It turns worry into a small, shared habit.
> - It makes the story longer. → It does add words, but its real job is feeling. A refrain gives a worried household a steady rhythm.
> - It is only there to be funny. → There is a gentle smile in it, but mostly it is comfort. By day three even you are saying it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a refrain, a line that repeats, can give comfort and rhythm._


#### `a31-12-houses-stay`

_The days are long. You do the things a house needs: water from the river, wood from the hill, weeds from round the one corn plant._  
**Xmucane**: Hoe that row. No, that row. The boys always did the wrong row.  
**Xquic**: Xibalba’s houses are not as bad as they sound. They’re worse. But my boys are cleverer than their father.  
_Every time you come in from outside, the first thing you do is look at the corn. So does everyone._  
_One ear has six leaves, and the other has seven._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): add within 100 in a word problem  
> _One ear has 6 leaves and the other has 7. How many leaves are there in all, and how many more does the second ear have?_  
> - ✅ 13 in all, and 1 more → Yes. 6 + 7 = 13, and 7 - 6 = 1.
> - 12 in all, and 1 more → Check the adding: 6 + 7 = 13. The difference is right: 7 - 6 = 1.
> - 13 in all, and 2 more → The total is right, but the difference is 7 - 6 = 1.
> _For grown-ups: Added 6 and 7, and found how many more one group has than the other._

**Xmucane**: Still green.  

**Choices**

- **Hoe the wrong row, carefully.**
    - **Xmucane**: …That one’s fine too, I suppose.
- **Count the leaves on the corn.**
    - Six on one ear, seven on the other. The next day you count again: still six and seven.

#### `a31-13-bats-stay`

_In the night you wake, though nobody made a sound. Xmucane is already sitting up, very straight, looking at the corn._  
_One ear has drooped. Its leaves hang down, as if it’s tired, or worse._  
**Xmucane**: No. No, no.  
_She doesn’t touch it, and she doesn’t cry. She looks at it, and you look at it, and the fire ticks._  
_Your Nubbin climbs into your lap without being asked, and holds on to your sleeve._  
**Xmucane**: Sit with me. Don’t say anything. There isn’t anything.  
_So you don’t. You sit together with the corn and breathe slowly, and nobody speaks for a long time._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): calming a big worry  
> _Xmucane has a very big worry in the night. What helps most when a worry is too big to fix?_  
> - ✅ Slow breaths, and someone sitting beside you. → Yes. Slow breathing calms the body, and company calms the heart.
> - Doing something loud to forget it. → A loud distraction can help for a moment. The worry waits, though, and slow breaths do more.
> - Going over every bad thing that could happen. → That tends to make a worry bigger. Slow breaths and a friend help it shrink.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that slow breathing and good company help with a worry that is too big to fix._

_Then, near dawn, the drooping ear lifts. Slowly, leaf by leaf, as if it’s waking up._  
**Xmucane**: Oh.  

**Choices**

- **Put your hand on her arm.**
    - She puts her own hand over yours and leaves it there.
- **Say nothing at all.**
    - You say nothing. It turns out to be the right thing.

#### `a31-13-rat-coati`

_Behind the coati trots a rat, chest out. It went and fetched her specially._  
_It catches your eye and nods once. Lunch, it seems to say, was remembered._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Why did the rat bring the coati to help?_  
> - ✅ Because you shared your lunch with it, and it remembered. → Yes: its motive is gratitude. A small kindness came back at the moment it was needed.
> - Because it wanted a squash. → The rat’s nod is about the lunch. Its motive is thanks.
> - Because the twins ordered it to. → Nobody orders it. It chooses to help the friend who shared with it.
> _For grown-ups: Linked a character’s action to its motive: gratitude for a shared lunch._


#### `a31-13-rat-court`

_Right behind the rabbit goes the rat, who rode all the way down on your Nubbin’s head. It runs between the lords’ legs, squeaking._  
**Rat**: Slow! Call that running? I’ve seen faster cheese!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.3, ask): describing a character in depth  
> _The rat shouts insults at the lords while running between their legs. Which word describes it best?_  
> - ✅ Cheeky → Yes: it is brave, quick and rude in the friendliest way. That is cheek.
> - Shy → A shy rat would stay hidden. This one runs between the lords’ feet and mocks them.
> - Gloomy → The rat is having a wonderful time. Its words are all fun and mischief.
> _For grown-ups: Chose an exact word to describe a character’s personality._

_The lords chase it twice as far. That’s twice as long for Xbalanque._

**Xquic**: Everything?  
**Falcon**: Everything. Both of them are fine. They burst a squash on the lords. You should have seen their faces.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how characters respond to events  
> _Xmucane makes far too many tortillas, very fast. What does that show about how she feels?_  
> - ✅ She is so relieved she cannot sit still. → Yes: her hands need a job. Relief and joy can come out as busyness.
> - She is angry at the falcon. → She gives the falcon the very first tortilla. That is thanks, not anger.
> - She is bored. → A bored person is slow. She is quick, and she makes far too many: that is relief.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s feeling from what she does._

#### `a31-13-rat-coati-told`

**Falcon**: And a rat went and fetched the coati. Said somebody had shared their lunch with it once, and it doesn’t forget.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): coatis: a real animal and its body parts  
> **Grandmother**: A coati is a real animal, a cousin of the raccoon, and it lives in the forests of Central America.  
> **Grandmother**: It has a long, ringed tail for balance, and a long, bendy nose for sniffing out insects and fruit.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that coatis have a long ringed tail for balance and a long nose for finding food._


#### `a31-13-rat-court-told`

**Falcon**: Oh, and a rat. It went down in Hunahpu’s pocket and ran rings round the lords. Kept shouting about cheese.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): animals’ senses: whiskers  
> **Grandmother**: A rat’s whiskers are very sensitive. They brush against walls and corners and tell the rat what is nearby, even in the dark.  
> **Grandmother**: Rats also have an excellent sense of smell, which is why the lords’ legs were not hard to find.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a rat’s whiskers and nose are sensitive senses for finding its way._


#### `a31-14-oven-stay`

_The next day, the corn begins to dry. Not droop: dry, from the tips down, brown and papery._  
**Xmucane**: No.  
_By evening both ears are dry all over, and they rattle when the door opens. Xquic shuts it very gently, so they won’t._  
_Xmucane weeps, and doesn’t hide it. She sits on her stool by the dry corn with her hands in her lap, and weeps._  
_You don’t know what to do. So you pull your stool up beside hers, and stay._  
_Your Nubbin goes and sits right beside the dry corn, close, as if it is keeping it company._  
**Xquic**: They said: if it does both, we’re being clever.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): supporting a friend who is crying  
> _Xmucane is crying and you do not know what to do. What helps most?_  
> - ✅ Staying close and not hurrying her. → Yes: staying close says “I am here”. You do not need the right words.
> - Telling her it will be fine. → Hopeful words are kind, but you cannot promise. Sitting beside her is more honest.
> - Leaving her alone to cry in private. → Some people want that, and it is fine to ask. But staying close is often what helps most.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that staying close and not rushing helps a friend who is crying._

**Xmucane**: I know what they said.  

**Choices**

- **Stay beside her.**
    - You stay. The fire goes down, and you build it up again, and you stay.
- **Sit with Xquic instead.**
